questions.question: Which three properties should you be able to read off every PyTorch tensor?
options: .shape, .grad and .stride
.size, .rank and .names
.shape, .dtype and .device
.dtype, .layout and .requires_grad
questions.explanation: Every tensor carries a shape (how many numbers and how they are arranged), a dtype (what kind of number each element is) and a device (whether its memory is in CPU RAM or on a GPU). These three answer 'how big, what kind of number, and where'. Stride and requires_grad exist too, but they are not the three core properties you check on every tensor.

questions.question: According to the PyTorch foundations material, what are the three categories that account for roughly ninety percent of bugs when training a language model?
options: Bad learning-rate schedules, mislabelled training data, and poor weight initialisation
Memory leaks in the data loader, race conditions, and off-by-one errors
Overfitting, underfitting, and vanishing or exploding gradients in deep stacks
Shape mismatches, dtype surprises, and tensors on the wrong device
questions.explanation: The claim is that most training bugs are shape mismatches, dtype surprises, or a tensor sitting on the wrong device — exactly the three properties every tensor has. That is why fluency with .shape, .dtype and .device is taught first. Learning-rate or data problems are real, but they are not the framing given for why tensor properties matter.

questions.question: In a neural network, which of the following values are represented as tensors?
options: Only the weights; inputs are plain Python lists
Inputs, weights, activations, gradients and the loss
Only inputs and outputs; weights are stored separately
Only gradients; everything else is a NumPy array
questions.explanation: A neural network is nothing but tensors flowing through operations: weights, inputs, activations, gradients and the loss are all tensors. Even the scalar loss is a rank-0 tensor so it can carry the graph for backpropagation. No part of the model is held as plain lists or NumPy arrays.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a tensor is a typed, n-dimensional array
questions.question: In PyTorch, what does the word 'tensor' mean?
options: An n-dimensional array of numbers all of one type
A physics object that transforms under rotations
A matrix that is always square and invertible
A Python list that may hold mixed element types
questions.explanation: Although the word is borrowed from physics, in PyTorch a tensor means exactly an n-dimensional array: a rectangular grid of numbers, all the same type, with a fixed number of axes. There is nothing more mystical about it. It need not be square, and unlike a Python list it cannot mix element types.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a tensor is a typed, n-dimensional array
questions.question: What is the 'rank' of a tensor, and which attribute reports it in PyTorch?
options: The number of axes, reported by .ndim
The total element count, reported by .numel()
The matrix rank (independent rows), reported by .rank
The length of the first axis, reported by .shape[0]
questions.explanation: Rank is the number of axes (dimensions) a tensor has, which PyTorch reports as .ndim. A scalar has rank 0, a vector rank 1, a matrix rank 2. This is not the linear-algebra matrix rank, and it is not the element count, which is .numel().

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a tensor is a typed, n-dimensional array
questions.question: Which tensor rank corresponds to a single number such as 3.0 with no axes?
options: Rank 1, a vector
Rank 2, a matrix
Rank 0, a scalar
Rank 1, a length-1 vector
questions.explanation: A scalar is rank 0: one number and no axes, shape (). A vector like [1, 2, 3] is rank 1 with one axis, and a matrix is rank 2. A length-1 vector, shape (1,), is still rank 1 because it has one axis.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a tensor is a typed, n-dimensional array
questions.question: A tensor holds 2 rows and 3 columns of numbers. What is its rank?
options: 6, because it holds six numbers
2, because it has two axes
3, because the longest axis has length 3
1, because it is a single object
questions.explanation: Rank counts axes, not elements. A 2-by-3 grid has two axes (rows and columns), so it is rank 2 — a matrix. Six is its element count (numel), and 3 is just the length of its second axis.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a tensor is a typed, n-dimensional array
questions.question: Why do neural network libraries use tensors instead of nested Python lists?
options: Tensors can hold any mix of Python objects in one container, which makes them more flexible than lists
Nested Python lists cannot represent more than two dimensions, so higher-rank data needs a tensor type
Tensors store each element as a separately boxed object behind a pointer, which makes random indexing faster
Tensors store one numeric type in one contiguous block and run ops as compiled or GPU-parallel code
questions.explanation: A tensor stores its numbers in one flat, contiguous block of memory of a single type, and every operation runs as tight compiled code — or as thousands of parallel arithmetic units on a GPU. A Python list of lists can hold anything and is stored as scattered pointers, which is slow. The tensor is the disciplined, fast version; it is the list, not the tensor, that is flexible and pointer-based.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a tensor is a typed, n-dimensional array
questions.question: How does a nested Python list of numbers differ physically in memory from a tensor of the same numbers?
options: The list is one flat buffer; the tensor is scattered pointers to objects
Both are flat typed buffers; only the API differs
Both are scattered pointers; the tensor just caches them on the GPU
The list is scattered pointers to objects; the tensor is one flat typed buffer
questions.explanation: A Python list of lists holds pointers to separately allocated Python objects scattered across memory and can hold anything. A tensor puts all its elements, one numeric type, into a single contiguous block. That layout is what lets compiled and GPU kernels process it quickly.

questions.question: What does torch.tensor([[1., 2., 3.], [4., 5., 6.]]) create?
options: A 2x3 float tensor whose shape is taken from how the data is nested
A 1-D tensor of length 6, because torch.tensor flattens nested lists before storing them
A 3x2 float tensor, because torch.tensor reads the nested lists column by column
An uninitialised 2x3 tensor whose values are random until you overwrite them
questions.explanation: torch.tensor takes the actual data, and the shape comes from how the data is nested: two inner lists of three numbers give shape (2, 3). Because the literals have decimal points, the dtype is float32. It does not flatten the data and does not reorder axes.

questions.question: What is the key difference between how torch.tensor and torch.zeros are called?
options: torch.tensor takes the shape; torch.zeros takes a list of zero values
torch.tensor takes the actual data; torch.zeros takes only the shape
Both take the data, but torch.zeros then overwrites every element with zeros
Both take the shape, but torch.tensor fills it with random values
questions.explanation: torch.tensor([...]) is given the actual numbers and infers the shape from the nesting. torch.zeros(2, 3), torch.ones and torch.randn are given the shape, usually as separate positional arguments. Mixing these up — passing data to zeros or a shape to tensor — is a common newcomer trip-up.

questions.question: Which call is the conventional way you will see a 2x3 tensor of zeros created in PyTorch code?
options: torch.zeros((2, 3), (0, 0))
torch.tensor(2, 3, fill=0)
torch.zeros(2, 3)
torch.zeros[2][3]
questions.explanation: torch.zeros takes the shape as separate positional arguments, so torch.zeros(2, 3) is a 2x3 grid of 0.0. torch.zeros([2, 3]) also works, but the positional form is what you will read everywhere. The other forms are not valid PyTorch constructors.

questions.question: What does torch.arange(6) return?
options: tensor([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), an integer range like Python's range()
tensor([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]), a range that includes the endpoint like linspace
A 6x6 identity matrix of floats, the same as calling torch.eye(6)
Six random integers drawn uniformly from the half-open range 0 to 6
questions.explanation: torch.arange works like Python's range() but returns a tensor: arange(6) gives the integers 0 through 5, excluding 6. Because they are integers, its dtype is int64. It is not inclusive of the endpoint and does not produce a matrix or random values.

questions.question: From what distribution does torch.randn draw each element?
options: Independently and uniformly between 0 and 1, like torch.rand
From a normal with mean 0 and variance equal to the number of elements in the tensor
Uniformly between -1 and 1, then normalised to unit length
Independently from the standard normal: mean 0, standard deviation 1
questions.explanation: torch.randn draws every element independently from the standard normal (Gaussian) distribution, a bell curve centred at 0 with standard deviation 1. That is why its values can be negative and occasionally exceed 2 in magnitude. Uniform samples on [0, 1) come from torch.rand, not randn.

questions.question: What two main uses does torch.randn have in ML code examples?
options: Computing gradients numerically and clipping them during backprop
Shuffling datasets and splitting them into batches
Initialising weights and fabricating fake data for demos
Encoding tokens into integer IDs and decoding model outputs into text
questions.explanation: randn appears in almost every code example because it is how weights get initialised with random values and how fake input data is produced for demonstrations and tests. It does not compute gradients or shuffle datasets; those are separate mechanisms.

questions.question: What does calling torch.manual_seed(0) before torch.randn(2, 3) achieve?
options: It makes every value generated afterwards exactly zero until the seed is changed
It fixes the random number generator so the same values come out every run
It forces randn to return consecutive integers starting from the seed value 0
It seeds only the GPU generator, leaving CPU results different on every run
questions.explanation: manual_seed fixes the state of the random number generator, so the 'random' values are identical every run — with seed 0, randn(2, 3) always gives the same six numbers (starting 1.5410, -0.2934, ...). That reproducibility is essential for examples and unit tests. It does not make values zero or integer.

questions.question: What does a tensor's .shape represent?
options: A tuple giving the length of each axis, outermost first
A tuple giving the byte offset of each axis in memory
The total number of elements in the tensor, as one integer
The number of axes the tensor has, as a single integer
questions.explanation: .shape is a torch.Size tuple with the length of each axis, outermost first; for a 2x3 matrix it is torch.Size([2, 3]). The byte-step information is the stride, the element count is numel(), and the number of axes is ndim.

questions.question: For a tensor with shape torch.Size([2, 3]), what do .ndim and .numel() return?
options: .ndim is 6 and .numel() is 2
.ndim is 3 and .numel() is 5
.ndim is 2 and .numel() is 5
.ndim is 2 and .numel() is 6
questions.explanation: .ndim is the number of axes, which is the length of the shape tuple: 2. .numel() is the total element count, the product of the shape entries: 2 x 3 = 6. A common slip is adding the entries (5) instead of multiplying them.

questions.question: How is a tensor's total element count related to its shape?
options: It is the sum of all the shape entries
It is the largest shape entry
It is the product of all the shape entries
It is the first shape entry times the number of axes
questions.explanation: numel() equals the product of the shape entries — for shape (2, 3) that is 6, for (4, 8) it is 32. This product is also what you multiply by bytes-per-element to get memory size. Summing the entries gives a meaningless number.

questions.question: What is described as the usual first step of almost every PyTorch debugging session?
options: Lowering the learning rate and rerunning the failing step
Printing .shape and checking it matches what you expected
Restarting the Python kernel to clear any stale CUDA state
Converting every tensor to float64 to rule out precision
questions.explanation: Because so many bugs are shape mismatches, almost every debugging session starts with printing .shape of the relevant tensors and checking each matches expectations. Changing hyperparameters or dtypes before you know the shapes are right is premature.

questions.section: Indexing and what an index gives back
questions.question: For a 2x3 tensor a, what does a[0] return?
options: The first row, a tensor of shape (3,)
The first column, a tensor of shape (2,)
The first element as a Python float
A tensor of shape (1, 3)
questions.explanation: Indexing works like nested arrays, one index per axis. A single index selects along the first axis, so a[0] is the first row, shape (3,) — the indexed axis disappears. It is still a tensor, not a Python number, and it does not keep a length-1 axis.

questions.section: Indexing and what an index gives back
questions.question: For a 2-D float tensor a, what is the type and shape of a[0, 2]?
options: A plain Python float value
A rank-1 tensor with shape (1,)
A NumPy float32 scalar value
A rank-0 tensor with shape ()
questions.explanation: Indexing every axis gives back a rank-0 (scalar) tensor such as tensor(3.), with shape (). It is still a tensor with a dtype and a device. It is not a Python float; to get one you must call .item().

questions.section: Indexing and what an index gives back
questions.question: How do you extract the plain Python number from a scalar tensor like a[0, 2]?
options: Call .numpy()[0] on the scalar tensor
Call .float() on the scalar tensor
Call .item(), e.g. a[0, 2].item()
Call .detach() on the scalar tensor
questions.explanation: .item() pulls the plain Python number out of a single-element tensor, so a[0, 2].item() returns 3.0. .float() just changes dtype and still returns a tensor; .detach() still returns a tensor too. This is also how training loops log the loss value.

questions.section: Indexing and what an index gives back
questions.question: Why does the distinction between a rank-0 tensor and a Python float matter in deep learning?
options: A Python float can carry a gradient; a scalar tensor cannot
A scalar tensor can carry a gradient; a Python float cannot
Python floats are always more precise than tensors
Scalar tensors cannot be used in arithmetic with other tensors
questions.explanation: A rank-0 tensor still has a dtype, a device, and can be part of the autograd graph, so it can carry a gradient — the loss is exactly such a tensor. A Python float has no connection to the graph. Converting to a float with .item() is fine for logging but cuts any gradient path.

questions.section: Indexing and what an index gives back
questions.question: In the (B, T, C) shape convention used for language-model activations, what do B, T and C stand for?
options: Bytes per element, tokens per batch, and context window size
Batch size, time/sequence length, channels/features per token
Batch size, number of tensors in the graph, and output classes
Blocks, threads, and cores of the GPU kernel launch grid
questions.explanation: B is the batch (how many sequences processed at once), T is time or sequence length (tokens per sequence), and C is channels or features (the size of each token's vector). Every activation inside the language model is a rank-3 (B, T, C) tensor. 'Classes' and 'cores' are distractors.

questions.section: Indexing and what an index gives back
questions.question: What habit does the (B, T, C) convention encourage whenever you read a tensor shape?
options: Assuming the last axis is always the batch
Flattening every tensor to 1-D before use
Ignoring shapes until the loss misbehaves
Asking which axis is which
questions.explanation: The advice is: every time you read a shape, ask 'which axis is which?' — that habit is the whole game. Knowing that axis 0 is batch, axis 1 is position and axis 2 is features is what lets you reason about reductions, broadcasts and reshapes. The batch axis is first, not last.

questions.question: What two things does a tensor's dtype decide that matter enormously at scale?
options: Which device the tensor lives on and the order of its axes in memory
Whether the tensor is contiguous and how large its stride is per axis
How many bytes each element takes and how much precision it carries
Whether the tensor requires gradients and how many axes it has
questions.explanation: dtype determines bytes per element (memory) and precision (how many significant digits and what range). Device, shape and contiguity are separate properties. Because models have hundreds of millions of elements, the bytes-per-element choice dominates memory.

questions.question: How many bytes per element do float32, float16, bfloat16, int64 and bool use?
questions.explanation: float32 is 4 bytes, float16 and bfloat16 are both 2 bytes, int64 (long) is 8 bytes, and bool is 1 byte per element in PyTorch. bfloat16 is the same size as float16 — it just spends its 16 bits differently. Bools are not bit-packed.

questions.question: What distinguishes bfloat16 from float16?
options: bfloat16 uses 4 bytes per element while float16 uses 2
bfloat16 has more mantissa bits but a narrower range than float16
bfloat16 is an integer format used for token IDs
bfloat16 keeps float32's exponent range but has fewer mantissa bits
questions.explanation: bfloat16 ('brain float') has the same exponent range as float32, so it will not overflow, but fewer mantissa bits, so its steps are coarser. float16 has a much narrower range and can overflow to infinity or underflow to zero. Both use 2 bytes per element.

questions.question: Which dtype is described as the standard for training large models?
options: float16
bfloat16
float64
float8_e4m3fn
questions.explanation: bfloat16 has become the default training dtype because it halves memory relative to float32 while keeping float32's exponent range, so values do not overflow. float16 halves memory too but its narrow range causes overflow/underflow trouble. float64 doubles memory and is rarely used for training.

questions.question: Which dtype must token IDs and indices use?
options: int64 (long)
float32 (float)
float16 (half)
uint8 (byte)
questions.explanation: Token IDs are indices into the vocabulary, not measurements, so they must stay int64, also called long. int64 is PyTorch's default integer dtype. Converting them to a float type is a common error that breaks embedding lookups.

questions.question: What is the bool dtype typically used for in language models?
options: Storing token IDs compactly in a single byte each
Holding weights in quantised one-bit form
Masks, such as the causal attention mask
Accumulating gradients across micro-batches
questions.explanation: bool tensors hold true/false values and show up as masks — for example the causal mask that prevents a token from attending to future positions. Token IDs use int64, and weights and gradients use floating-point dtypes.

questions.question: What dtype does torch.tensor([1., 2.]) have, and what about torch.tensor([1, 2])?
options: float64 for the first, int32 for the second
float32 for the first, int64 for the second
float32 for both, since the data is numeric
int64 for both, since the values are whole numbers
questions.explanation: With decimal points, torch.tensor infers float32 (PyTorch's default float). Without decimal points it infers int64. This difference is a silent-surprise default: integer tensors cannot carry gradients, so a forgotten decimal point can break training.

questions.question: What are the default dtypes of torch.zeros(...), torch.randn(...) and torch.arange(6)?
options: int64, float32 and int64
float32, float64 and float32
float32, float32 and float32
float32, float32 and int64
questions.explanation: zeros, ones and randn produce float32 unless told otherwise. arange(6) with integer arguments produces int64 because it is a range of integers. Assuming arange gives floats is a classic surprise when you then try to use it in gradient computations.

questions.question: Why is it a problem if a tensor you want to train has an integer dtype?
options: Integer tensors cannot carry gradients
Integer tensors cannot be moved to a GPU
Integer tensors cannot be indexed
Integer tensors use more memory than any float type
questions.explanation: Autograd only works on floating-point (and complex) tensors; integer tensors cannot have gradients. Anything the network does arithmetic and gradients on must be a float dtype. Integer tensors can live on GPUs and be indexed normally.

questions.question: What does h = a.to(torch.float16) do when a is float32?
options: Converts a to half precision in place and returns None
Moves a to the GPU and keeps its dtype
Returns a copy of a in half precision; a itself is unchanged
Returns a view of a that reinterprets its bytes as float16
questions.explanation: x.to(dtype) returns a new tensor with the values converted to that dtype; the original stays float32. It does not modify in place, so you must assign the result. It does not reinterpret raw bytes, and it does not change device unless you pass one.

questions.section: Why dtype decides memory and precision
questions.question: How is a tensor's memory footprint computed?
options: ndim times bytes per element
Sum of the shape entries times 4
numel times bytes per element
numel times ndim
questions.explanation: Memory = numel() x element_size(). A 2x3 float32 tensor is 6 x 4 = 24 bytes; the same in float16 is 12 bytes. ndim and summed shapes play no role. element_size() reports bytes per element directly.

questions.section: Why dtype decides memory and precision
questions.question: Which PyTorch method reports the number of bytes per element of a tensor?
options: .element_size()
.numel()
.nbytes_per_elem()
.storage_offset()
questions.explanation: .element_size() returns bytes per element — 4 for float32, 2 for float16. Multiplying it by .numel() gives the total bytes of data. .numel() is the element count and .stride() describes memory steps, not sizes.

questions.section: Why dtype decides memory and precision
questions.question: Converting a float32 tensor to float16 changes its memory use how?
options: It quarters it, because float16 stores two values per byte
It leaves it unchanged, because only precision changes
It doubles it, because float16 stores extra exponent bits
It halves it, because each element goes from 4 bytes to 2
questions.explanation: float16 uses 2 bytes per element versus float32's 4, so the same numbers take exactly half the memory — 12 bytes instead of 24 for a 2x3 tensor. That factor of two is the entire reason mixed precision exists. The cost is reduced precision and, for float16, a narrower range.

questions.section: Why dtype decides memory and precision
questions.question: Roughly how much memory do the weights of a ~124-million-parameter GPT-2-scale model take in float32?
options: About 124 MB
About 496 MB
About 248 MB
About 992 MB
questions.explanation: 124,000,000 parameters x 4 bytes = about 496 MB just for the weights. In bfloat16 or float16 it would be about 248 MB. Training needs several more copies of this size for gradients and optimizer state, which is why bytes per element decides whether a model fits on a GPU.

questions.section: Why dtype decides memory and precision
questions.question: Why does training need much more memory than just the model's weights?
options: It also holds gradients and optimizer state, each about weight-sized
It must keep a float64 master copy of the whole training dataset in memory
Every forward pass duplicates the weights onto the CPU as a backup
The weights are replicated once per GPU core so each can read them
questions.explanation: Beyond the weights, training keeps a gradient per parameter and, depending on the optimizer, extra per-parameter state — several more copies of the weight-sized footprint. That is why halving bytes per element can be the difference between fitting on a GPU or not. The dataset and CPU copies are not the reason.

questions.section: Why dtype decides memory and precision
questions.question: What precision risk does float16 carry that bfloat16 largely avoids?
options: Values silently become integers once they exceed 1000 in magnitude
It cannot represent negative numbers, so signed activations are clipped to zero
It rounds every value to two decimal places, losing small gradient updates
Values can overflow to infinity or underflow to zero due to its narrow range
questions.explanation: float16 has a much narrower exponent range, so large values overflow to inf and tiny values underflow to zero. bfloat16 keeps float32's exponent range, so it does not overflow, at the cost of coarser steps. Neither format is restricted to positives or fixed decimals.

questions.section: Why dtype decides memory and precision
questions.question: What is the overall takeaway about dtype in large-scale training?
options: dtype only matters for integer data such as token IDs and attention masks
dtype is a memory-versus-precision dial that takes real engineering effort
Always use float64 everywhere, because precision problems outweigh memory cost
dtype choice affects throughput but never the memory a model occupies
questions.explanation: dtype trades memory for precision: fewer bytes per element lets bigger models fit, but costs significant digits and possibly range. Managing that trade-off (mixed precision) is real engineering work. float64 would double memory and is not the answer; dtype directly sets memory.

questions.section: Why dtype decides memory and precision
questions.question: What happens if you convert token IDs to a float tensor and pass them to an embedding lookup?
options: It works but rounds the IDs to the nearest vocabulary entry
It works and also lets gradients flow back into the token IDs themselves
The embedding lookup raises, because it needs a long (int64) tensor
It silently returns zero vectors for every token whose ID is fractional
questions.explanation: Token IDs are indices into the vocabulary and the embedding layer requires a long tensor; handing it floats raises an error. Indices are not measurements, so there is nothing to round or differentiate. Keep token IDs int64.

questions.question: What does a tensor's .device tell you?
options: Which CPU core or thread will execute operations on it
Whether its elements are laid out contiguously in host memory
Which dtypes the underlying hardware natively supports
Whether its memory lives in CPU RAM or on a specific GPU
questions.explanation: .device reports where the tensor's bytes physically live: device(type='cpu') for ordinary RAM or cuda:N for a GPU's memory. It is not about cores, contiguity or dtype support.

questions.question: What is the idiomatic way to choose a device that works whether or not a GPU is present?
options: device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
device = torch.device("gpu"), which maps to any GPU
device = "cuda" always, since PyTorch falls back silently
device = torch.cuda.current_device() or "cpu"
questions.explanation: Picking 'cuda' only if torch.cuda.is_available() and otherwise 'cpu' gives one device variable that works everywhere. PyTorch does not silently fall back from cuda to cpu; asking for cuda without a GPU raises. 'gpu' is not a valid device string.

questions.question: What causes 'RuntimeError: Expected all tensors to be on the same device, but found at least two devices, cuda:0 and cpu!'?
options: A dtype mismatch between a float32 tensor and a float16 tensor in one op
An operation between a tensor in GPU memory and a tensor in CPU memory
Running out of GPU memory, so PyTorch spills one tensor back to the CPU
Calling .backward() twice on the same graph without retain_graph
questions.explanation: Operations between two tensors require them to be on the same device, because their bytes are in physically different memories. Mixing a cuda:0 tensor with a cpu tensor raises this error — the single most common runtime error in real training code. Dtype mismatch and out-of-memory produce different errors.

questions.question: What is the standard defence against device-mismatch errors?
options: Call torch.cuda.synchronize() before each operation so all tensors agree on device
Convert all tensors to NumPy arrays before combining them, then convert back
Pick one device variable at the top and .to(device) the model, inputs and targets
Wrap every operation in torch.no_grad() so no cross-device graph is built
questions.explanation: Define a single device variable once and move everything — model, inputs, targets — to it with .to(device). That also lets the same code run on GPU later by flipping one variable. Synchronising, NumPy conversion or no_grad do not address where tensors live.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of the .to(device) habit even when running on CPU only?
options: The same code later runs on a GPU unchanged by flipping one variable
It makes CPU computation faster by pinning the tensors in page-locked memory
It automatically converts tensors to bfloat16 so they match GPU kernels
It prevents gradients from accumulating between training steps
questions.explanation: Writing x.to(device) everywhere means the code is device-agnostic: when a GPU becomes available you change one variable and nothing else. On CPU it costs nothing because .to returns the same tensor when nothing needs to move. It does not change dtype or affect gradients.

questions.question: Which statement about x.to(...) is correct?
options: It modifies x in place and returns None, like other trailing-underscore methods do
It always allocates a copy, even when the dtype and device already match
It returns a (possibly new) tensor that must be assigned, e.g. x = x.to(device)
It can change the device or the dtype of x, but never both in a single call
questions.explanation: .to is overloaded: x.to(torch.float16) changes dtype, x.to('cuda') changes device, and x.to('cuda', torch.float16) does both. It returns a new tensor when something actually changes, and the same tensor when nothing needs to move. It never modifies in place, so you must assign the result.

questions.question: You call x.to("cuda") on a line by itself without assigning the result. What happens to x?
options: x is moved to the GPU in place, and later ops on x run on CUDA
x is freed on the CPU and must be recreated from the original data
x becomes a unified-memory view shared between the CPU and the GPU
Nothing: x stays on the CPU because .to does not modify in place
questions.explanation: .to returns a new tensor and does not modify the original. Without x = x.to('cuda'), the GPU copy is discarded and x remains a CPU tensor, which will later trigger a device-mismatch error. Forgetting to assign is a classic mistake.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood — contiguous memory and strides
questions.question: How are a tensor's numbers stored in memory?
options: As one separate heap allocation per row, linked together through a row-pointer table
In one flat 1-D array, with shape and stride describing how to read it as a grid
As a tree of pointers with one level per axis, like nested Python lists
In a hash map keyed by each element's index tuple, so lookups are O(1)
questions.explanation: All elements live in one flat 1-D buffer. The shape and a second tuple, the stride, are metadata telling PyTorch how to interpret that buffer as an n-D grid. There are no per-row allocations or pointer trees.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood — contiguous memory and strides
questions.question: What does a tensor's stride tell you?
options: For each axis, how many elements to skip in the flat buffer to move one step along it
For each axis, how many bytes that axis occupies in total across the whole buffer
How many elements each GPU thread processes when a kernel runs over the tensor
The step size between consecutive values, as used by torch.arange's step argument
questions.explanation: The stride says, per axis, 'to move one step along this axis, skip this many elements in the flat array'. For a row-major 2x3 tensor it is (3, 1): jump 3 to go down a row, 1 to go right a column. Stride is measured in elements, not total bytes, and is unrelated to GPU threads.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood — contiguous memory and strides
questions.question: For x = torch.arange(6).view(2, 3), what is x.stride() and what does it mean?
options: (1, 3): moving down a row skips 1 element, moving right a column skips 3
(2, 3): the same as the shape, since a contiguous view mirrors it
(6, 1): the total element count, then the step between neighbours
(3, 1): moving down a row skips 3 elements, moving right a column skips 1
questions.explanation: Stored row by row, moving down one row in [[0,1,2],[3,4,5]] goes from 0 to 3 in the flat buffer (skip 3), and moving right one column goes from 0 to 1 (skip 1). So the stride is (3, 1). (1, 3) is what you get after transposing it.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood — contiguous memory and strides
questions.question: What does it mean for a tensor to be contiguous (row-major / C-contiguous)?
options: All its elements share one value, so it can be stored as a single number
It is stored entirely on a single GPU rather than split across several
Its flat memory order matches reading the grid left-to-right, top-to-bottom
Its shape has no length-1 axes, so no dimension needs to be squeezed out
questions.explanation: A contiguous tensor's flat buffer order matches reading the logical grid row by row, left to right and top to bottom. This is the default layout, and many fast operations assume it. It has nothing to do with values, devices or size-1 axes.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood — contiguous memory and strides
questions.question: Why can PyTorch hand you a differently-shaped view of a tensor without copying the data?
options: Because PyTorch copies data lazily, only when the view is printed or written to disk
Because shape and stride are metadata over a shared buffer, so a new (shape, stride) label suffices
Because views are stored compressed, so the reshaped copy costs almost no extra memory
Because reshaping rewrites the one buffer in place, so the original layout no longer exists
questions.explanation: Since the numbers live in one flat buffer and shape/stride merely describe how to read it, a view is just a new (shape, stride) label pointing at the same memory. No numbers move, so reshaping is nearly free. The flip side is that the view and its parent share storage.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood — contiguous memory and strides
questions.question: What surprising behaviour follows from views sharing a flat buffer with their parent?
options: Views always have a different dtype from the parent
Views cannot be indexed or sliced any further
Mutating the view also changes the parent tensor
Views double the memory used by the parent tensor
questions.explanation: Because a view and its parent are two labels on the same memory, writing through one changes the other — the 'views share storage' surprise. Views use no extra data memory and share the parent's dtype.

questions.question: How many bytes does a float32 tensor of shape (4, 8) occupy, and how many in bfloat16?
options: 32 bytes in float32 and 16 bytes in bfloat16
128 bytes in float32 and 64 bytes in bfloat16
128 bytes in both, since bfloat16 has float32's range
256 bytes in float32 and 128 bytes in bfloat16
questions.explanation: numel = 4 x 8 = 32 elements. At 4 bytes each, float32 takes 128 bytes; at 2 bytes each, bfloat16 takes 64 bytes — exactly half. Having the same exponent range as float32 does not make bfloat16 the same size.

questions.question: You write ids = torch.tensor([5, 17, 42]) for token IDs. What is the dtype, and is it right?
options: float32, which the embedding layer will reject
int32, which must be cast to long first
float32, which is correct because embeddings are floats
int64 (long), which is correct for token IDs
questions.explanation: Integer literals without decimal points give int64 (long), which is exactly right: token IDs are indices into the vocabulary and the embedding lookup needs long. Writing [5., 17., 42.] would have produced float32, which the embedding layer would reject.

questions.question: A forward pass through a language model is described as a chain of which basic tensor operations?
options: Sorting, hashing and string concatenation over token IDs, then a final lookup
Broadcast bias adds, matmuls with weights, reductions, and reshapes/views into heads
Only matrix multiplications with weights; biases, reductions and reshapes are folded into them
File reads, 2-D convolutions over the token grid, and random sampling at every layer
questions.explanation: Adding a bias is a broadcast, multiplying by a weight matrix is @, averaging over a dimension is a reduction, and splitting activations into attention heads is a view. Reading model code means tracking how each of these changes the shape. It is not only matmuls.

questions.question: Which two topics are singled out as causing a large fraction of real PyTorch bugs?
options: Random seeds and file paths
Python indentation and imports
Learning-rate schedules and dropout
Broadcasting and view/copy confusion
questions.explanation: Broadcasting can silently produce the wrong shape, and view/copy confusion leads to unexpected aliasing or mutations not propagating. Both are made explicit for that reason. The other options are not the stated bug sources.

questions.question: What does a + 10 do when a = torch.tensor([1., 2., 3., 4.])?
options: Appends 10 to the end, giving tensor([1., 2., 3., 4., 10.]) of length 5
Adds 10 only to the first element, giving tensor([11., 2., 3., 4.])
Adds 10 to every element, giving tensor([11., 12., 13., 14.])
Raises a RuntimeError, because shapes (4,) and () do not match
questions.explanation: Arithmetic with a scalar applies to every element independently and returns a tensor of the same shape. So a + 10 is [11, 12, 13, 14]. It does not append or raise; a scalar combines with any tensor.

questions.question: In PyTorch, what does the * operator compute between two tensors?
options: Elementwise (Hadamard) multiplication
Matrix multiplication, the same as @
The dot product, returning one scalar
The outer product, giving an (n, n) result
questions.explanation: In PyTorch * is always elementwise — the Hadamard product — pairing up corresponding elements. For a = [1, 2, 3, 4], a * a gives [1, 4, 9, 16]. Matrix multiplication is a different operator, @. People from a math background often expect * to be a matmul.

questions.question: How do * and @ differ in their effect on shape?
options: * follows the inner-dimension matmul rule; @ always keeps the input shape
* never changes the shape; @ follows the inner-dimension matmul rule
Both keep the shape of the left operand and broadcast the right one
Both always reduce to a scalar, summing the products of paired elements
questions.explanation: Elementwise * returns a tensor of the same (broadcast) shape as its inputs. @ follows the rule (n, k) @ (k, p) -> (n, p), so the shape changes. Keeping them straight avoids models that silently compute the wrong thing.

questions.question: What is a reduction in PyTorch?
options: An operation like sum, mean or max that combines many values into fewer
An operation that lowers a tensor's dtype precision, e.g. float32 to bfloat16
An operation that removes duplicate values, like torch.unique on each axis
An operation that moves a tensor onto a smaller device to free GPU memory
questions.explanation: A reduction combines many values into fewer, e.g. sum, mean, max. The key question is always which axis you reduce over, because that decides the output shape. It has nothing to do with dtype or device.

questions.question: What does m.sum() return for m = torch.tensor([[1., 2., 3.], [4., 5., 6.]])?
options: tensor([5., 7., 9.]), the column sums
tensor([6., 15.]), the row sums, one per row
tensor(21.), a scalar summing all elements
A (2, 3) tensor of running sums along each row
questions.explanation: With no dim argument, a reduction collapses everything to a scalar: 1+2+3+4+5+6 = 21. Column sums need dim=0 and row sums need dim=1. Running sums are cumsum, not sum.

questions.question: What is the rule that tells you the output shape of a reduction with dim=k?
options: dim=k keeps only axis k
dim=k sets axis k to length 2
dim=k reverses the order of the axes
dim=k removes axis k from the shape
questions.explanation: A reduction with dim=k collapses only axis k, and that axis disappears from the shape. For m of shape (2, 3), sum(dim=0) gives (3,) and sum(dim=1) gives (2,). Unless keepdim=True, the axis is removed rather than kept.

questions.question: For m of shape (2, 3) equal to [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]], what does m.sum(dim=0) return?
options: tensor([5., 7., 9.]) of shape (3,), one total per column
tensor([6., 15.]) of shape (2,), one total per row
tensor([[5., 7., 9.]]) of shape (1, 3), keeping the summed axis
tensor(21.), a scalar total over all six elements
questions.explanation: sum(dim=0) removes axis 0 (the length-2 axis), summing down the rows: [1+4, 2+5, 3+6] = [5, 7, 9], shape (3,). Row totals [6, 15] come from dim=1. A (1, 3) result would require keepdim=True.

questions.question: For m of shape (2, 3) equal to [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]], what does m.sum(dim=1) return?
options: tensor([5., 7., 9.]) of shape (3,), one total per column
tensor([[6.], [15.]]) of shape (2, 1), keeping the axis
tensor([6., 15.]) of shape (2,), one total per row
tensor([21.]), the grand total as a 1-element tensor
questions.explanation: sum(dim=1) removes axis 1 (the length-3 axis), summing across the columns of each row: [1+2+3, 4+5+6] = [6, 15], shape (2,). The (2, 1) form needs keepdim=True.

questions.section: keepdim: hold the collapsed axis open as length 1
questions.question: What does keepdim=True do in a reduction?
options: Keeps the original values and skips the reduction entirely for that axis
Keeps the result on the same device as the input
Keeps the gradient from flowing through the reduction
Keeps the reduced axis as length 1 instead of removing it
questions.explanation: keepdim=True holds the collapsed axis open with length 1, so the result has the same number of axes as the input. m.mean(dim=1, keepdim=True) on a (2, 3) tensor gives shape (2, 1) instead of (2,). It does not affect the device or gradients.

questions.section: keepdim: hold the collapsed axis open as length 1
questions.question: Why would you use keepdim=True when computing a row mean?
options: So the mean is accumulated in higher precision than the input dtype
So the result broadcasts cleanly back against the original tensor
So the original tensor is overwritten in place with its row means
So the reduction runs as one fused kernel and finishes faster on GPU
questions.explanation: Keeping the axis as length 1 lets you write m - m.mean(dim=1, keepdim=True) and have the (2, 1) mean stretch across the columns. You will do exactly this in softmax and LayerNorm. It has no effect on precision, mutation or speed.

questions.section: keepdim: hold the collapsed axis open as length 1
questions.question: For m = [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]], what is m.mean(dim=1, keepdim=True)?
options: tensor([2., 5.]) with shape (2,)
tensor([[2.], [5.]]) with shape (2, 1)
tensor([[2.5, 3.5, 4.5]]) with shape (1, 3)
tensor([[3.5]]) with shape (1, 1)
questions.explanation: The row means are (1+2+3)/3 = 2 and (4+5+6)/3 = 5. With keepdim=True axis 1 is kept as length 1, giving [[2.], [5.]] of shape (2, 1). Without keepdim it would be shape (2,). Column means would be [2.5, 3.5, 4.5].

questions.question: What is the shape rule for matrix multiplication with @?
questions.explanation: The two inner dimensions must match (both k) and they vanish, because they are summed over; the outer dimensions n and p survive. So (n, k) @ (k, p) gives (n, p). Matching outer dims instead of inner ones is a common mistake.

questions.question: In A @ B, why must the inner dimensions match?
options: They decide the output dtype through type promotion
They must match so that the result matrix comes out square
They are the dimensions summed over in each dot product
They determine which device the matmul kernel runs on
questions.explanation: Entry (i, j) of A @ B is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B, which sums over the shared inner dimension k. If A's columns and B's rows differ in length, the dot product is undefined. The outer dims set the result shape; nothing forces it to be square.

questions.question: What is entry (i, j) of the matrix product A @ B?
options: The product A[i, j] * B[i, j]
The dot product of column i of A with row j of B
The sum of row i of A plus the sum of column j of B
The dot product of row i of A with column j of B
questions.explanation: Each output entry is a dot product: row i of the left matrix times column j of the right, summed. For A = [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]] and B's first column [1,5,9], entry (1,1) is 1+10+27 = 38. A[i,j]*B[i,j] is the elementwise product, not matmul.

questions.question: What shape results from multiplying a (2, 3) matrix by a (3, 4) matrix with @?
questions.explanation: Inner dimensions 3 and 3 match and vanish; the outer dimensions 2 and 4 survive, giving (2, 4). Every Linear layer is such a matmul, which is why matmul is the workhorse of neural networks.

questions.question: How should you read 'RuntimeError: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (2x3 and 4x5)'?
options: The inner dims 3 and 4 do not match in a (2,3) @ (4,5) matmul
The outer dims 2 and 5 do not match, so no (2, 5) result exists
The two tensors are on different devices, one on CPU and one on GPU
One tensor is float32 and the other float16, so mat1 and mat2 differ
questions.explanation: The message reports the two operand shapes; read it as 'I tried (2,3) @ (4,5) and the inner dims 3 and 4 differ'. The fix starts with printing both operands' .shape and lining up the inner two numbers. Outer dims never need to match, and device/dtype problems give different errors.

questions.question: Why is matrix multiplication called the workhorse of neural networks?
options: It is the only operation that supports gradients
It is the only operation GPUs can run
It replaces all elementwise operations
Every Linear layer is a matrix multiplication
questions.explanation: Every nn.Linear layer — including attention projections and MLP layers — is a matmul, so most of a model's compute is matmuls. Many other operations support gradients and run on GPUs; matmul simply dominates the work.

questions.question: What problem does broadcasting solve?
options: Sending the same tensor to multiple GPUs at once during data parallelism
Converting tensors between dtypes automatically when they are mixed
Combining tensors of different shapes without manually copying data
Printing large tensors compactly by eliding repeated rows
questions.explanation: You constantly need to combine tensors of different shapes — adding a length-C bias to a whole batch, subtracting a per-row mean. Broadcasting is the set of rules that lets PyTorch do this without loops or explicit copies. It is unrelated to multi-GPU communication or dtype conversion.

questions.question: What is the broadcasting rule for deciding whether two shapes are compatible?
options: Align shapes from the left; each pair of axis lengths must be equal or one must be 1
The total element counts must be equal, whatever the individual axis lengths
The tensors must have the same number of axes, and then each pair must match
Align shapes from the right; each axis pair must be equal or one of them must be 1
questions.explanation: Line the shapes up from the right. For each axis the lengths are compatible if they are equal or if one is 1, in which case the 1 is stretched. If neither is 1 and they differ, it is an error. Missing leading axes are treated as 1, so the ranks need not match.

questions.question: In broadcasting, what happens to an axis of length 1 paired with an axis of length 4?
options: It is virtually repeated to length 4
It causes an error because the lengths differ
The length-4 axis is truncated to 1
The two lengths are added to give 5
questions.explanation: A length-1 axis is stretched (virtually repeated) to match the other length. Only when neither length is 1 and they differ is it an error. Nothing is truncated or added.

questions.question: What is the result shape of adding a (3, 1) tensor to a (1, 4) tensor?
options: It raises a shape error
questions.explanation: Aligning from the right, axis 1 is 1 vs 4 (the 1 stretches to 4) and axis 0 is 3 vs 1 (the 1 stretches to 3), giving (3, 4). Entry (i, j) is left[i] + right[j]; for [10,20,30] and [1,2,3,4] that gives rows 11..14, 21..24, 31..34.

questions.question: How does broadcasting avoid using extra memory for the stretched axis?
options: It compresses the repeated values with run-length encoding before the operation
It gives the length-1 axis stride 0, so stepping along it never moves in memory
It allocates the expanded tensor in GPU memory, where the extra space is free
It processes the operation one row at a time in a Python loop, reusing one buffer
questions.explanation: No data is actually copied: broadcasting pretends a length-1 axis has stride 0, so every step along it reads the same element. That costs no extra memory, which is why adding a bias to a (B, T, C) activation is cheap. No compression or Python loop is involved.

questions.question: Why can you add a bias of shape (C,) to activations of shape (B, T, C) with just x + bias?
options: PyTorch reshapes the bias to (B, T, C) by copying it into a full-size tensor first
Bias tensors are special-cased by nn.Linear, which adds them after the matmul
The addition only applies to the first batch element, then is repeated per step
Aligned from the right, (C,) matches the last axis and is stretched across B and T
questions.explanation: Aligning from the right, the bias's single axis matches C, and the missing leading axes are treated as 1 and stretch across every batch and position. This happens for free via stride-0, not by copying. It is general broadcasting, not a Linear-only special case.

questions.question: How does broadcasting treat axes that one tensor is missing on the left?
options: Missing leading axes cause an error
Missing axes are filled with zeros
Missing leading axes are treated as length 1
Missing axes are added on the right instead
questions.explanation: When ranks differ, the shorter shape is padded with 1s on the left, then the usual equal-or-1 rule applies. So (3,) behaves like (1, 3) against a (2, 3) tensor. Nothing is filled with zeros.

questions.question: What is the difference between a view and a copy in PyTorch?
options: A view is a read-only snapshot of the data; a copy is a writable duplicate
A view is a new label on the same buffer; a copy allocates a fresh buffer
A view lives on the GPU next to the kernels; a copy lives in CPU memory
A view stores values at lower precision than a copy of the same tensor
questions.explanation: Some operations return a view — a new (shape, stride) label over the same underlying memory — while others allocate fresh memory, a copy. A mutated view changes the original because they are the same memory. Views are writable and share the parent's device and dtype.

questions.question: After t = torch.arange(6); v = t.view(2, 3); v[0, 0] = 99, what is t?
options: tensor([99, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), because v shares storage with t
tensor([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), because view made an independent copy of t
An error, because tensors returned by view are read-only
tensor([99, 99, 99, 99, 99, 99]), because the write is broadcast
questions.explanation: view gives a differently-shaped label on the same data without copying, so writing 99 through v changes t's first element. This aliasing is a feature — it makes reshaping free — but looks like spooky action at a distance if unexpected.

questions.question: How does reshape differ from view?
options: reshape returns a view if it can and silently copies if not; view raises instead
reshape always copies into fresh memory; view never copies and always succeeds
reshape only works on contiguous tensors, while view works on any layout by copying
reshape changes the dtype to fit the new shape; view only changes the shape
questions.explanation: reshape 'always works': it gives a view if the layout allows and otherwise makes a copy, so you no longer know which you got. view 'only works when it can be a genuine view' and raises otherwise — sometimes exactly the guarantee you want. Neither changes dtype.

questions.question: When might you prefer view over reshape?
options: When you want PyTorch to always copy the data into a fresh buffer for safety
When the tensor is non-contiguous and you want it to work regardless
When you need the guarantee that the result shares memory with the original
When you want to change the tensor's dtype at the same time as its shape
questions.explanation: view either returns a genuine view or raises, so it guarantees aliasing. If you rely on mutations propagating to the parent, reshape could silently return a copy and break that. reshape is the choice when you want it to work regardless of layout.

questions.section: permute / transpose: views that reorder axes
questions.question: What do transpose(i, j) and permute(...) return?
options: Copies with the data physically reordered
Contiguous tensors in the new axis order
In-place modified versions of the input
Views with new strides; no data is moved
questions.explanation: transpose swaps two axes and permute reorders all of them; both return views that just produce new strides over the same buffer. Data does not move, which is why the result is typically non-contiguous. They are not in-place.

questions.section: permute / transpose: views that reorder axes
questions.question: For m = torch.arange(6).view(2, 3) with stride (3, 1), what are the shape and stride of m.transpose(0, 1)?
options: Shape (3, 2), stride (2, 1)
Shape (3, 2), stride (1, 3)
Shape (2, 3), stride (1, 3)
Shape (3, 2), stride (3, 1)
questions.explanation: Transposing swaps both the shape entries and the stride entries: shape (2, 3) becomes (3, 2) and stride (3, 1) becomes (1, 3). Stride (2, 1) would be the contiguous layout for a fresh (3, 2) tensor, which a transpose does not produce.

questions.section: permute / transpose: views that reorder axes
questions.question: Why is a transposed tensor typically non-contiguous?
options: Its data has been split across two devices, one half per axis
Its elements were copied into a new, scattered buffer during the transpose
Its dtype changed during the transpose, so the element size no longer fits
Its logical reading order no longer matches the flat order of its buffer
questions.explanation: After transposing [[0,1,2],[3,4,5]], reading the (3,2) result left-to-right, top-to-bottom visits the buffer as 0, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5 — not in flat order. Logical and physical layouts disagree, which is what non-contiguous means. No copy or dtype change occurs.

questions.section: permute / transpose: views that reorder axes
questions.question: Is a non-contiguous tensor an error state?
options: Yes; nearly every operation raises an error until .contiguous() is called
Yes; it means the tensor's underlying memory has been corrupted
No; it is legal for most operations but some, like view, may fail on it
No; and view always works on it too, since only the stride differs
questions.explanation: Non-contiguous tensors are perfectly legal and fine for most operations. They do, however, set up the classic mistake: view may refuse certain shapes because it cannot relabel the buffer without reordering.

questions.question: What is the first rule any .view(...) shape must satisfy?
options: The new shape must have the same number of axes
The product of the new shape must equal numel()
The new shape must keep the first axis unchanged
The new shape must be square
questions.explanation: A view only relabels the same elements, so the new shape's product must equal the element count. For a (2, 3) tensor, (6,), (3, 2) and (3, -1) are fine; (4, 2) is not, because 8 is not 6. The number of axes may change.

questions.question: What does -1 mean in a call like x.view(3, -1)?
options: That axis's length is inferred from numel and the other axes
The last element along that axis is dropped before reshaping
The axis is reversed, like flipping it with torch.flip
The axis is broadcast to whatever length the other operand has
questions.explanation: One axis may be given as -1 and PyTorch infers it so the product equals numel(). For a 6-element tensor, view(3, -1) gives (3, 2). Only one -1 is allowed because the inference must be unique.

questions.question: Which reshapes always work with view, even on a non-contiguous tensor?
options: Splitting one axis into several, or inserting a size-1 axis
Merging any two axes into one, as long as numel is unchanged
Flattening the tensor to 1-D with view(-1)
Swapping the first and last axes of the tensor
questions.explanation: Splitting an axis or inserting a size-1 axis never requires reordering, so they always work. Merging neighbouring axes, including flattening, works only if those axes already sit back-to-back in memory. Swapping axes is a transpose, not a view reshape.

questions.question: On a non-contiguous tensor, when can view merge neighbouring axes i and i+1?
options: Only if size[i] = size[i+1], so the merged axis is square
Only if stride[i] = 1 for the outer axis
Never; merging non-contiguous axes always requires a copy
Only if stride[i] = stride[i+1] x size[i+1]
questions.explanation: Merging axes i and i+1 works when they already sit back-to-back in memory, which is the condition stride[i] = stride[i+1] x size[i+1]. Equal sizes or a unit stride are not the criterion. If the condition fails, view raises.

questions.question: When view cannot produce a requested shape, what are the two remedies?
options: Call .detach() first to drop the graph, then call .view(...) on the result
Move the tensor to the GPU, or cast it to a dtype that view accepts
Call .contiguous().view(...) for an explicit copy, or use .reshape(...)
Call .transpose() again on the result, or call .squeeze() before .view
questions.explanation: .contiguous() copies the data into flat logical order so view then works; .reshape() copies only when the view rules fail. Detach only cuts the autograd graph and does not change memory layout, and device or dtype changes are irrelevant.

questions.question: For mt = torch.arange(6).view(2, 3).transpose(0, 1) (shape (3, 2), stride (1, 3)), which call succeeds?
options: mt.view(6)
mt.view(3, 1, 2)
mt.view(6, 1)
mt.view(-1, 1, 1)
questions.explanation: view(3, 1, 2) only inserts a size-1 axis, which always works. view(6), view(6, 1) and view(-1, 1, 1) all merge axes 0 and 1, which needs stride[0] = stride[1] x size[1], i.e. 1 = 3 x 2 — false, so they raise.

questions.question: x = torch.arange(24).view(2, 3, 4)[:, :, :2] has shape (2, 3, 2) and stride (12, 4, 1). Does x.view(6, 2) work?
options: No, because x is non-contiguous, and view always fails on such tensors
No, because 6 x 2 = 12 does not equal x.numel(), which is 24
Yes, but only because view silently copies the data into a contiguous buffer
Yes, because merging axes 0 and 1 needs 12 = 4 x 3, which holds
questions.explanation: Slicing the last axis broke contiguity between rows, but axes 0 and 1 are still back-to-back: stride[0] = 12 = stride[1] x size[1] = 4 x 3. So they can be merged into 6 and the view succeeds without copying. This shows non-contiguous does not automatically mean view fails; numel is 12 = 6 x 2.

questions.section: The classic mistake: reshape/view after transpose
questions.question: Why does torch.arange(6).view(2, 3).transpose(0, 1).view(6) raise?
options: The element count changes from 6 to 3 after the transpose, so view(6) is invalid
transpose returns a read-only tensor, and view refuses to relabel read-only data
view cannot relabel the non-contiguous buffer as flat without reordering it
view(6) on a transposed tensor is only implemented for CUDA tensors, not CPU
questions.explanation: The transposed tensor reads its buffer as 0, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5, so a flat length-6 view of the existing buffer in that order is impossible without moving data. view refuses rather than copy, raising 'view size is not compatible with input tensor's size and stride'. The count is still 6.

questions.section: The classic mistake: reshape/view after transpose
questions.question: What do mt.reshape(6) and mt.contiguous().view(6) return for mt = torch.arange(6).view(2, 3).transpose(0, 1)?
options: Both return tensor([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
Both return tensor([0, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5])
reshape returns [0,3,1,4,2,5]; contiguous().view returns [0,1,2,3,4,5]
Both raise the same error as view(6)
questions.explanation: Both flatten in the tensor's current logical order, which for the transpose is 0, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5. reshape copies because it must; .contiguous() first copies into that logical order so view works. Neither recovers the original 0..5 order.

questions.section: The classic mistake: reshape/view after transpose
questions.question: What does .contiguous() do?
options: Allocates a fresh buffer with the numbers laid out in the current logical order
Marks the existing buffer as contiguous by rewriting its strides, without moving data
Sorts the tensor's values in ascending order so they are adjacent in memory
Moves the tensor into one GPU memory page so its elements are physically adjacent
questions.explanation: .contiguous() copies the data into a new buffer arranged in the tensor's current logical order, producing a contiguous tensor that view can reshape freely. It does not just flip a flag, sort values, or deal with GPU pages. If the tensor is already contiguous it returns itself.

questions.section: The classic mistake: reshape/view after transpose
questions.question: Why does multi-head attention code use x.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, T, C)?
options: After the transpose the tensor is non-contiguous, so view cannot merge the heads into C without a copy
contiguous() is required so that gradients can flow back through the following view call into the heads
contiguous() moves the tensor onto the GPU first, because view on CPU cannot handle 4-D tensors
view requires contiguous input in order to reverse the head order back to the original token order
questions.explanation: Transposing the head axis back produces a non-contiguous tensor, and collapsing the heads into the channel dimension is a merge view cannot do on that layout. .contiguous() copies into flat order first, so view(B, T, C) works. It is about memory layout, not gradients or devices.

questions.section: The classic mistake: reshape/view after transpose
questions.question: Why should you not blindly replace every .view with .reshape?
options: reshape is always much slower than view, because it copies the whole data on every single call
If you rely on aliasing, reshape may silently copy, so in-place mutations will not propagate
reshape does not support -1 for inferred axes, so every dimension must be spelled out
reshape detaches its result from the autograd graph, so gradients stop at that point
questions.explanation: reshape copies when the view rules fail, so code that mutates the result expecting the original to change would silently stop working. When reshape can view, it costs the same as view; it supports -1 and keeps autograd tracking. The danger is the hidden copy.

questions.section: The classic mistake: reshape/view after transpose
questions.question: If .view(...) raises 'view size is not compatible with input tensor's size and stride', what is the most likely cause?
options: The input has an integer dtype, which view cannot reinterpret into a new shape
The input requires gradients, and view is not allowed on tensors tracked by autograd
The input lives on the CPU, whereas view's stride logic is only implemented on GPU
The input is non-contiguous, almost always from a recent transpose or permute
questions.explanation: That message means the requested shape cannot be expressed over the existing strides — the input is non-contiguous, almost always because it was just transposed or permuted. Dtype, requires_grad and device do not cause it. Fix with .contiguous() first or use .reshape().

questions.question: A model 'runs but learns nothing'. Which operator mix-up is a possible cause?
options: Using + where torch.add was meant to be called
Using @ where torch.matmul was meant to be called
An elementwise * where a matmul @ belonged
Using .sum() where torch.sum() was meant to be used
questions.explanation: * keeps the shape and multiplies element by element, so it can run without error where @ was intended, yet compute something meaningless. The other pairs are just equivalent spellings of the same operation.

questions.question: What should you always ask yourself before choosing dim in a reduction?
options: Which axis is the longest?
Which axis do I want gone?
Which axis is contiguous?
Which axis has the smallest stride?
questions.explanation: dim=0 and dim=1 give different shapes and meanings; the deciding question is which axis should disappear. Length, contiguity and stride do not determine the correct reduction axis.

questions.question: What goes wrong if you forget keepdim=True before broadcasting a reduced tensor back?
options: The shape fails to line up, or worse, lines up wrongly by accident
The reduction itself returns the wrong numerical values for each row
The reduced tensor is silently moved back to the CPU
Gradients stop flowing through the reduction and the parameters freeze
questions.explanation: Without keepdim the reduced axis vanishes, so aligning from the right may fail with an error — or may match a different axis by coincidence and silently compute the wrong thing. The reduced values themselves are correct; it is the alignment that breaks.

questions.question: You need an independent tensor that will not change when you mutate it and will not affect its source. What should you call?
options: .view()
.transpose()
.clone()
.to(device) with the same device
questions.explanation: Mutating a view mutates its parent, so if you need an independent tensor, .clone() copies the data. view and transpose return views that alias the original, and .to on the same device returns the same tensor.

questions.question: For x of shape (B, T, C) = (2, 4, 6), which line subtracts each position's mean over the channels and returns a (2, 4, 6) tensor?
options: x - x.mean(dim=-1)
x - x.mean(dim=0, keepdim=True)
x - x.mean(dim=(0, 1), keepdim=True)
x - x.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
questions.explanation: x.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True) reduces the channel axis to length 1, giving (2, 4, 1), which broadcasts across the 6 channels when subtracted. Without keepdim the mean is (2, 4), which does not align from the right with (2, 4, 6). dim=0 averages over the batch, and dim=(0, 1) averages each channel over batch and positions instead — this is the centring step inside LayerNorm.

questions.question: For x of shape (5, 3), what shapes do x.sum(dim=0), x.sum(dim=1) and x.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True) have?
questions.explanation: dim=0 removes axis 0 leaving (3,); dim=1 removes axis 1 leaving (5,); with keepdim=True axis 1 is kept as length 1, giving (5, 1). Without keepdim the reduced axis is dropped entirely.

questions.question: Which matrix product is legal: (4, 5) @ (4, 5) or (4, 5) @ (5, 2)?
options: Only (4, 5) @ (4, 5), giving shape (4, 5)
Both are legal, giving (4, 5) and (4, 2)
Neither is legal, as both need a transpose
questions.explanation: (4, 5) @ (4, 5) has inner dimensions 5 and 4, which do not match, so it is illegal. (4, 5) @ (5, 2) has matching inner dims 5 and 5, giving (4, 2). Same-shape operands are fine for elementwise * but not generally for @.

questions.question: Do shapes (2, 3) and (3,) broadcast, and what is the result?
options: No; the ranks differ, so PyTorch raises a shape-mismatch error instead
Yes; (3,) is treated as (1, 3) and added to every row, giving (2, 3)
Yes; each row is paired with every element, giving shape (2, 3, 3)
Yes; (3,) is added down each column instead, giving shape (3, 2)
questions.explanation: Aligned from the right, 3 vs 3 match, and the missing leading axis is treated as 1 and stretches to 2. So [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]] + [10,20,30] = [[11,22,33],[14,25,36]], shape (2, 3). Different ranks are fine for broadcasting.

questions.question: After y = x.view(2, 3) and y[0, 0] = 0, x has also changed. How could you have avoided that?
options: Use x.view(2, 3).detach() so that y no longer shares anything with x
Use x.transpose(0, 1).view(2, 3) to get a reordered layout
Use x.view(2, 3).clone() (or x.clone().view(2, 3)) to get independent data
Use x.view(2, 3) inside a torch.no_grad() block so writes stay local
questions.explanation: view shares storage with x, so mutating y writes into x's buffer. .clone() copies the data, making y independent. detach and no_grad only affect autograd tracking, not memory sharing; transpose is another view.

questions.question: What is training a neural network, at its core?
options: Repeatedly computing the loss gradient with respect to the parameters and stepping each downhill
Storing every training example directly in the model's weights so it can be recalled later
Searching over all possible weight values exhaustively and keeping the set with the lowest loss
Running the forward pass repeatedly until the outputs stop changing between successive iterations
questions.explanation: Training is repeatedly computing the gradient of the loss with respect to millions of parameters and moving each one downhill. Doing that by hand is impossible, which is why autograd exists. It is not memorisation or exhaustive search.

questions.question: Which three steps does every training loop in the course rest on?
options: model.eval(), model.save(), then model.load() at the start of each step
loss.backward(), read .grad, then step and zero the gradients
torch.no_grad(), .detach(), then .item() on the loss each step
forward twice, average the two losses, then print the result
questions.explanation: Every training loop, up to GPT-2, rests on calling loss.backward(), reading the resulting .grad, then stepping the parameters and zeroing gradients. no_grad and detach turn autograd off and are not the core training steps.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the derivative tells each number which way to nudge
questions.question: What does the derivative of the loss with respect to a parameter tell you?
options: The exact value the parameter should be set to in order to minimise the loss
How many optimisation steps training will need before that parameter converges
How fast and in which direction the loss changes if you nudge that parameter
The loss value that will be reached at the optimum for that parameter
questions.explanation: A derivative is the rate of change of the loss with respect to one input: if you nudge the parameter a tiny bit, does the loss go up or down, and how fast. It is a local slope, not a target value or a prediction of training length.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the derivative tells each number which way to nudge
questions.question: If the derivative of the loss with respect to a weight is +5, how should you move the weight to reduce the loss?
options: Increase it, because a positive gradient points towards lower loss
Leave it unchanged, because the gradient is non-zero
Set it to 5, the value the gradient is pointing at
Decrease it, because increasing it would increase the loss
questions.explanation: A positive derivative means increasing the weight increases the loss, so to reduce the loss you move the weight the other way — decrease it. Doing that for every parameter at once is gradient descent. Following the gradient's sign would increase the loss.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the derivative tells each number which way to nudge
questions.question: Why is computing derivatives by hand hopeless for a language model?
options: Derivatives of matrix products are not defined for non-square weight matrices
Language models use integer weights, which have no meaningful derivative
The loss is computed through millions of chained operations
The loss is not a differentiable function of the weights in a language model
questions.explanation: A language model computes its loss through millions of chained operations, so working the derivative out by hand is impractical. Autograd solves this mechanically. Matmuls are differentiable and weights are floats.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the derivative tells each number which way to nudge
questions.question: How does autograd compute derivatives?
options: It records each forward operation in a graph, then walks it backwards applying the chain rule
It numerically perturbs each parameter by a tiny step and measures how the loss changes
It symbolically differentiates and simplifies the model's Python source code ahead of time
It looks up precomputed derivative formulas that are registered for each supported architecture
questions.explanation: Autograd watches every operation during the forward pass, builds a record (the graph) of them and how to differentiate each, and then walks it in reverse multiplying local derivatives via the chain rule. It is not finite differences or symbolic algebra, and it is architecture-agnostic.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the derivative tells each number which way to nudge
questions.question: When you call .backward() on a final scalar, where does autograd deposit the derivatives?
options: Into the .grad attribute of the scalar itself
Into the .grad attribute of each leaf tensor
Into a global dictionary of gradients
Into the optimizer's state
questions.explanation: Backward deposits the derivative of the scalar with respect to each leaf tensor into that leaf's .grad. The scalar you call backward on does not receive it, and the optimizer only reads .grad later.

questions.question: How do you opt a tensor into differentiation in PyTorch?
options: Wrap it in a torch.no_grad() block
Call .detach() on it before use
Give it a float64 dtype on creation
Create it with requires_grad=True
questions.explanation: By default tensors are inert and operations on them are not tracked. Setting requires_grad=True opts a tensor in; anything computed from it inherits a link back. no_grad and detach do the opposite, and dtype alone does not enable tracking.

questions.question: In PyTorch's computational graph, what are the nodes and edges?
options: Nodes are tensors; edges are operations that each know their local derivative
Nodes are layers; edges are the learning rates that scale updates between them
Nodes are GPUs; edges are the communication links that carry gradients between them
Nodes are operations; edges are the Python variables that hold intermediate results
questions.explanation: The graph's nodes are tensors and its edges are the operations that produced them, each knowing how to compute its own local derivative. That structure is what lets the backward pass chain local derivatives together.

questions.question: What does it mean that PyTorch's computational graph is dynamic?
options: It is compiled once ahead of time into a fixed graph and then reused every step
It changes the model's weights while executing, so the parameters shift mid-pass
It is rebuilt only when the batch size or sequence length of the input changes
It is built fresh on the fly each forward pass by ordinary Python execution
questions.explanation: The graph is created anew every time the forward computation runs, simply by executing your Python code. There is no separate compile step. Static-graph frameworks build the graph once ahead of time instead.

questions.question: What practical benefit does a dynamic graph give model authors?
options: Models always run faster than with any static graph, because nothing has to be precompiled
Gradients no longer need to be zeroed, because each step's graph is brand new
You can use ordinary if/for/while in a model, and the graph follows the path that ran
The model's weights are saved automatically each time a new graph is recorded
questions.explanation: Because the graph is recorded as the code runs, normal control flow just works and the graph reflects whichever branch or loop count executed. Static-graph frameworks trade this flexibility for other optimisations. It does not remove the need to zero gradients.

questions.question: Why is PyTorch's choice of a dynamic graph credited with its dominance in research?
options: It guarantees the fastest possible training speed on every supported accelerator
It favours flexibility over the ahead-of-time optimisations static graphs allow
It removes the need for GPUs, since dynamic graphs run efficiently on CPUs
It makes saved models much smaller on disk, because no graph is serialised
questions.explanation: PyTorch chose flexibility: models are plain Python with arbitrary control flow. Static-graph frameworks build the graph once to enable other optimisations. That flexibility is a big part of why PyTorch dominates research; it is not about speed guarantees or model size.

questions.section: 3. The simplest example, by hand then by autograd
questions.question: With x = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True) and y = x**2, what is x.grad after y.backward()?
options: tensor(9.)
tensor(3.)
tensor(6.)
tensor(2.)
questions.explanation: dy/dx = 2x, and at x = 3 that is 6, so x.grad is tensor(6.). 9 is the forward value of y, not the gradient. PyTorch knows the local derivative of squaring is 2x and evaluates it at the stored x.

questions.section: 3. The simplest example, by hand then by autograd
questions.question: When you compute y = x**2 on a tensor with requires_grad=True, what happens besides computing the value 9.0?
options: PyTorch immediately computes and stores x.grad
PyTorch records that y came from squaring x
PyTorch converts y to a plain Python float
PyTorch detaches x from the graph for safety
questions.explanation: The forward pass both computes y and records the operation ('square') linking y back to x. The gradient is only computed later when you call backward. y remains a tensor attached to the graph.

questions.section: 3. The simplest example, by hand then by autograd
questions.question: On what kind of tensor do you call .backward() in a training loop?
options: The final scalar, which in real training is the loss
Each parameter tensor individually, one call per weight
The input batch of token IDs fed to the model
The model's output logits of shape (B, T, V)
questions.explanation: Backward starts from a single number — the final scalar. In real training that scalar is the loss. Calling backward on a non-scalar requires extra arguments and is not the normal pattern.

questions.section: 3. The simplest example, by hand then by autograd
questions.question: After y.backward(), which tensor holds the gradient dy/dx?
options: The output y, in y.grad
Both x and y equally
Neither; it is returned by backward()
The leaf x, in x.grad
