$\log\sum_j e^{z_j}$: exponentiate, sum, take the log
questions.explanation: Logsumexp is literally 'exponentiate, sum, log'. It is the log of the softmax normalization denominator. It is close to the max when one logit dominates, but not equal to it in general.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: In words, what does $\log\operatorname{softmax}(z) = z - \operatorname{logsumexp}(z)$ say?
options: Each token's log-probability is the log of its own score, computed independently
Each token's log-probability is its score divided by one number, the row's max
Each token's log-probability depends only on its own logit, not on the rest of the row
Each token's log-probability is its score minus one number shared by the whole row
questions.explanation: The shared term is the log of the normalization denominator; subtracting it normalizes in log space. Because it is shared, the gaps between log-probabilities equal the gaps between logits. The log-probability depends on all logits through that shared term.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: Why can a log-softmax implementation end with `return logits - logsumexp` and never divide?
options: Because dividing would change the result once the logits are shifted
Because division in probability space becomes subtraction in log space
Because the logits are already normalized, so the sum is always 1
Because the division is done later, inside the loss's mean over rows
questions.explanation: Normalizing by the sum is division in probability space, which corresponds to subtracting its log in log space. Logits are not normalized, and the loss does no further division beyond averaging over rows.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: If the formula $\log q_i = z_i - \log\sum_j e^{z_j}$ is mathematically correct, why does the code subtract the max first?
options: For floating point (overflow and $\log 0$), not mathematics; mathematically the shift changes nothing
Because gradients cannot be computed through logsumexp unless the max is subtracted first
Because the max must be removed for the probabilities to sum to 1 after exponentiating
Because the formula is only an approximation without the shift, accurate to about float32 precision
questions.explanation: The max shift is a numerical-stability measure. It provably leaves the result unchanged in exact arithmetic. Without it the formula is still exact on paper and still normalized, but $e^{z}$ may overflow in float32.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: For any constant $c$, what is $\operatorname{softmax}(z - c)$ compared with $\operatorname{softmax}(z)$?
options: Equal only if $c$ is the max logit
Equal only approximately, within float tolerance
Exactly equal
Smaller by a factor $e^{-c}$
questions.explanation: Softmax is exactly invariant to shifting all logits by the same constant: $e^{-c}$ appears on top and in every term of the bottom and cancels. Any $c$ works mathematically; the max is chosen for numerical safety.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: In the proof that $\operatorname{softmax}(z - c) = \operatorname{softmax}(z)$, why can $e^{-c}$ be pulled out of the sum in the denominator?
options: Because $e^{-c}$ is always equal to 1 for any real constant $c$
Because $e^{-c}$ does not depend on the summation index $j$
Because $c$ is always the max logit, so $e^{-c}$ is the largest term
Because $\log$ is linear, so constants pass through the sum
questions.explanation: A factor that is the same in every term of a sum factors out. Then it appears once on top and once on the bottom and cancels since it is positive. It is not equal to 1 in general.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: Which identity is used to rewrite $e^{z_i - c}$ in the shift-invariance proof?
questions.explanation: Exponent of a difference is a product: $e^{z_i - c} = e^{z_i} e^{-c}$. The other forms are incorrect algebra.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: Does subtracting a constant from the logits make softmax more accurate or approximate it?
options: It changes the result to a temperature-scaled softmax, with temperature set by the constant
It approximates softmax to save compute, trading a tiny error for fewer large exponentials
It makes softmax more accurate by removing a bias that large logits introduce into the normalized result
Neither: it changes which numbers pass through `exp`, while leaving the result exactly unchanged
questions.explanation: The shift changes the representation of the computation, not the mathematical result. Temperature scaling divides logits, which does change the distribution; subtracting a constant does not.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: Why is $c = \max_j z_j$ chosen as the shift in a stable softmax?
options: It minimizes the number of exponentials needed, since the max term can be skipped entirely
It makes all shifted logits positive, so every exponential is at least 1 and none underflow
It makes the largest shifted value 0 and all others negative, so every exponential is at most 1
It is the only constant that keeps softmax unchanged; any other shift would alter the probabilities
questions.explanation: Any constant leaves softmax unchanged; the max is the one that makes it safe. After the shift, $z_i - m \le 0$, so $e^{z_i - m} \le 1$, which prevents overflow.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: Without max-subtraction, what happens to a logit of 90 in float32 softmax?
options: $e^{90} \approx 1.2\times 10^{39}$ exceeds float32's max ($\approx 3.4\times 10^{38}$), becomes `inf`, and `inf/inf = nan`
It is silently rounded down to the float32 maximum ($\approx 3.4\times 10^{38}$), so the softmax comes out only slightly wrong
It underflows to 0, since $e^{90}$ is below float32's smallest normal value ($\approx 1.2\times 10^{-38}$)
Nothing goes wrong; float32 handles exponents up to about $e^{1000}$ before it overflows to `inf`
questions.explanation: Float32 overflows to `inf` above about $3.4\times 10^{38}$, and $e^{90}$ exceeds that. A ratio of infinities is `nan`, which ruins training. With the shift, $90 - 90 = 0$ and $e^0 = 1$.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: Apart from preventing overflow, what second guarantee does subtracting the max provide for $\sum_j e^{z_j - m}$?
options: The sum is at least 1 (it contains $e^0 = 1$), so its log is never $-\infty$
The sum equals the vocabulary size $V$, so its log is always $\log V$
The sum is always less than 1, so its log is always negative and finite
The sum is exactly 1, so the log-sum-exp term vanishes from the formula
questions.explanation: The max entry becomes $e^0 = 1$ and the rest are positive, so the sum is $\ge 1$ and its log is $\ge 0$. It equals 1 only when one logit dominates completely; it equals $V$ only for equal logits.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: What is the relationship $\log\sum_j e^{z_j} = m + \log\sum_j e^{z_j - m}$ called in words?
options: The logsumexp of the shifted row is always zero, so the original row's lse equals its max
The logsumexp is the sum of the logs of the exponentials, shifted by the max
The logsumexp of the row equals the max of the row times the number of entries
The logsumexp of the original row equals the max plus the logsumexp of the shifted row
questions.explanation: Factoring $e^m$ out of the sum and splitting the log of the product gives this exact identity. It is not an approximation (logsumexp $\approx$ max) and the shifted logsumexp is $\ge 0$, not necessarily 0.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: After substituting the shifted logsumexp into $\log q_i = z_i - \log\sum_j e^{z_j}$, what happens to $m$?
options: The $+m$ and $-m$ cancel, leaving $\log q_i = z'_i - \log\sum_j e^{z'_j}$
$m$ remains as an additive correction term, $\log q_i = z'_i - \log\sum_j e^{z'_j} + m$
$m$ is added to every log-probability, shifting the whole row up by the max
$m$ multiplies the final result, scaling every log-probability by the max
questions.explanation: With $z_i = z'_i + m$ and $\log\sum e^{z_j} = m + \log\sum e^{z'_j}$, the $m$'s cancel. The shifted formula is the same log-softmax formula applied to $z'$, not a corrected approximation.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: In the from-scratch `log_softmax`, what does `shifted.exp().sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True).log()` compute?
options: The softmax probabilities $e^{z'_j} / \sum_k e^{z'_k}$, shape `(N, V)`
The row max $m = \max_j z_j$ used for the shift, shape `(N, 1)`
$\log\sum_j e^{z'_j}$ (the logsumexp of the shifted row), shape `(N, 1)`
The log-probability of the true token in each row, shape `(N,)`
questions.explanation: It exponentiates the shifted logits, sums each row, and takes the log: the logsumexp of the shifted row, kept as a column by `keepdim=True`. Subtracting it from `shifted` gives log-probabilities.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: Why does the from-scratch `log_softmax` use `keepdim=True` for `m` and `lse`?
options: To reduce memory usage, since keeping the reduced dimension avoids allocating a new `(N, V)` buffer
So they stay `(N, 1)` columns that broadcast row-wise, subtracting each row's own value from every entry in it
To stop gradients from flowing back through the max and the lse, which would otherwise break the whole backward pass
To make the final output a scalar, so that it can be passed directly to the loss's mean over rows
questions.explanation: A `(N, 1)` column broadcasts across the `V` columns, subtracting each row's own statistic. Without it, an `(N,)` vector would broadcast along the last axis, either failing or silently subtracting per column.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: For row $z = [2, 1, 0]$, $\log(e^2 + e^1 + e^0) = 2.4076$ but the shifted lse is $0.4076$. How are they related?
options: They are unrelated; one of the two was computed incorrectly and should be discarded
$2.4076 \approx 2 \times 0.4076 \times 3$: the shifted lse is scaled by the max and $V$
$2.4076 = 2 + 0.4076$: the unshifted logsumexp equals the max plus the shifted logsumexp
$0.4076 = 2.4076 / 2$: the shifted lse is the unshifted one divided by the max
questions.explanation: The shifted route subtracts the max (2) first and then the remaining 0.4076; the unshifted route subtracts 2.4076 at once. Both give log-probabilities $[-0.4076, -1.4076, -2.4076]$.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: Why is computing `log(softmax(z))` worse than computing log-softmax directly?
options: `log(softmax(z))` cannot be differentiated, because autograd has no rule for the composition
`log(softmax(z))` requires knowing the target token before the probabilities are formed
`log(softmax(z))` is mathematically a different function from log-softmax, not just less stable
The intermediate probabilities can underflow to exactly 0, making `log` return $-\infty$
questions.explanation: Mathematically they are identical, but the two-step version materializes $q$, and a tiny $q$ like $e^{-200}$ rounds to 0 in float32. The direct formula only subtracts ordinary-size numbers, returning about $-200$.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: Where else in the LLM stack does the same max-subtraction trick reappear?
options: In the tokenizer's BPE merge-rule scoring
In weight initialization of the embeddings
In the cosine learning-rate warmup schedule
In attention softmax and in FlashAttention
questions.explanation: Attention computes a softmax over scores, so it uses the same max-shift for stability, and FlashAttention relies on running maxes to compute softmax in tiles. Tokenizers, schedules and initialization do not use it.

questions.section: 6.1 Why these four lines compute exactly log-softmax
questions.question: What does each row of `log_softmax` output satisfy?
options: Exponentiating its entries gives probabilities that sum to 1
Its maximum entry is always exactly 0, like the shifted logits
Its entries sum to 1, like the probabilities they came from
Its entries sum to 0, since the shared lse term cancels out
questions.explanation: Log-softmax returns log-probabilities, so $\sum_i e^{\log q_i} = 1$. The log-probabilities themselves sum to a negative number, and the max entry is $-$(shifted logsumexp), which is 0 only if the max token has probability 1.

questions.question: In tracing `log_softmax` on logits with a row `[0, 0, 0]`, what are the shifted logits and the lse?
options: Shifted `[0, 0, 0]`, lse $= \ln 3 \approx 1.0986$
Shifted `[0, 0, 0]`, lse $= \ln 1 = 0$ exactly
Shifted `[0, 0, 0]`, lse $= 3$, one per entry
questions.explanation: The max is 0, so the shift changes nothing. Each exponential is 1, the sum is 3, and its log is $\ln 3$. The log-probabilities are then all $-1.0986$.

questions.question: Why is no value larger than 1 ever produced by `shifted.exp()` in the stable log-softmax?
options: Every shifted logit is $\le 0$, so every exponential is $\le e^0 = 1$
Because the logits are first normalized into $[0, 1]$ before exponentiating
Because the shift divides each logit by the row max, so all are $\le 1$
Because `exp` is clipped at 1 in PyTorch to prevent overflow in softmax
questions.explanation: Subtracting the row max makes all entries non-positive, so the exponentials lie in $(0, 1]$. There is no clipping or division.

questions.section: 6.3 Verify the by-hand loss against PyTorch
questions.question: The by-hand loss $-\ln 0.6439$, `llmre`'s `cross_entropy` and `F.cross_entropy` are compared on logits $(2, 1, 0, -1)$, target 0. What is found?
options: The by-hand value is larger because it skips the shift
All three agree at about 0.4402 nats
The from-scratch code differs because it subtracts the max
PyTorch's value is in bits and differs by $\ln 2$
questions.explanation: All are in nats and all compute the same mathematical quantity; the max shift does not change the result. They agree to the shown precision.

questions.section: 6.3 Verify the by-hand loss against PyTorch
questions.question: What does `F.cross_entropy` do with its inputs by default?
options: Expects probabilities with one-hot targets, takes their log, and returns per-row losses in nats
Fuses log-softmax and the gather on logits with integer targets and returns the mean over the batch in nats
Expects one-hot float targets, applies softmax, and returns the batch perplexity rather than a loss
Applies softmax to the logits, takes the log, and returns the sum over the batch measured in bits
questions.explanation: `F.cross_entropy` takes raw logits and integer class indices, fuses log-softmax with the gather, and by default averages ('mean' reduction). The result is in nats, matching the from-scratch version.

questions.section: 6.3 Verify the by-hand loss against PyTorch
questions.question: What do the unit tests for the from-scratch metrics assert?
options: That cross-entropy is symmetric in logits and targets, and that the perplexity of uniform logits over $V$ equals $\log V$
That perplexity is always an integer, and that the loss matches `F.cross_entropy` only in float64
That the loss is always below $\ln 2$ on a random batch, and that perplexity of one-hot logits equals $V$
Equality with `F.cross_entropy` to `1e-5` on a random batch, and that perplexity of uniform logits over $V$ equals $V$
questions.explanation: The tests check agreement with the framework on random `(8, 10)` logits and the uniform-model property PPL $= V$. The loss is not bounded by $\ln 2$, perplexity is generally non-integer, and logits/targets are different kinds of inputs.

questions.section: 6.3 Verify the by-hand loss against PyTorch
questions.question: What happens if you apply softmax and pass probabilities to `F.cross_entropy`?
options: Softmax is applied twice, giving a wrong, too-flat loss
The loss is identical, because softmax is idempotent
PyTorch detects the probabilities and raises an error
The loss becomes exactly 0, since the inputs sum to 1
questions.explanation: `F.cross_entropy` applies log-softmax internally, so probabilities get softmaxed again. Softmax is not idempotent: probabilities in $[0,1]$ have small gaps, so the second softmax is near-uniform. No error is raised because shapes and dtypes are legal.

questions.section: 6.3 Verify the by-hand loss against PyTorch
questions.question: What form must the target argument to `F.cross_entropy` take for language modeling?
options: A float tensor of probabilities of shape `(N,)`
A `long` tensor of shape `(N, V)`
A `long` tensor of class indices of shape `(N,)`
A float one-hot matrix of shape `(N, V)`
questions.explanation: For standard usage the targets are integer indices into the vocabulary, one per row. One-hot float matrices are not the expected form here.

questions.question: Why is perplexity reported in addition to cross-entropy loss?
options: Cross-entropy in nats is hard to interpret; perplexity exponentiates it into an intuitive scale
Perplexity is what the optimizer actually minimizes; cross-entropy is only logged for reference
Perplexity contains information about the model that the cross-entropy loss does not capture
Perplexity is independent of the model's predictions, so it gives a fixed baseline for the dataset itself
questions.explanation: Perplexity carries the same information as the loss (it is a monotone function of it) but reads as an effective branching factor. Optimizers minimize the loss, not perplexity directly.

questions.question: If a language model's loss were measured in bits instead of nats, how would perplexity be computed?
options: $e^{\mathcal{L}}$
$10^{\mathcal{L}}$
$\log_2 \mathcal{L}$
$2^{\mathcal{L}}$
questions.explanation: Perplexity uses the base that matches the log used for the loss: $e$ for nats, 2 for bits. Both give the same perplexity number for the same model.

questions.question: What does a perplexity of 20 mean for a language model?
options: The model's average loss is 20 nats per token, summed over the whole validation set
The model considers exactly 20 tokens possible and assigns exactly zero probability to the rest
On average the model is as uncertain as choosing uniformly among 20 equally likely tokens
The model is correct on 20% of tokens, measured by argmax accuracy on the validation set
questions.explanation: Perplexity is the effective branching factor: 'as confused as a fair 20-sided die at each step'. It is not accuracy, and the loss would be $\ln 20 \approx 3.0$ nats. The model still assigns probability to all tokens.

questions.question: What are the best and the uniform-guessing values of perplexity for a vocabulary of size $V$?
options: Best is $V$ (the full vocabulary is covered); uniform guessing gives 1
Best is 0 (the loss is zero); uniform guessing gives 1
Best is 1 (always knows the next token); uniform guessing gives $V$
Best is 1 (always knows the next token); uniform gives $\log V$
questions.explanation: A perfect model has loss 0 and perplexity $e^0 = 1$. A uniform model has loss $\ln V$ and perplexity $V$. $\log V$ is the uniform loss, not its perplexity.

questions.question: Is lower or higher perplexity better?
options: Lower is better
Closer to $V/2$ is better
Higher is better
It depends on the vocabulary size
questions.explanation: Lower perplexity means lower loss, i.e., more probability on the correct tokens. The minimum is 1 for a perfect model.

questions.section: 7.1 Worked example: uniform over 4 gives perplexity 4
questions.question: A model outputs uniform logits over $V = 4$ tokens. What are its loss and perplexity, regardless of the true token?
options: Loss 0 nats, perplexity 1, since all logits are equal
Loss 4 nats, perplexity $e^4 \approx 54.6$
Loss $\ln 4 \approx 1.386$ nats, perplexity 4
Loss $\ln 4$ nats, perplexity $\ln 4 \approx 1.386$
questions.explanation: Every token gets $q = 0.25$, so the loss is $-\ln 0.25 = \ln 4$ for any true token and the perplexity is $e^{\ln 4} = 4$, exactly the vocabulary size.

questions.section: 7.1 Worked example: uniform over 4 gives perplexity 4
questions.question: A model achieves loss 0.4402 nats on a 4-token vocabulary, giving perplexity about 1.553. How is this interpreted?
options: The model considers exactly one or two tokens possible and the rest impossible
The model is correct about 55% of the time, measured by top-1 accuracy
The model has narrowed 4 options down to roughly 1.5 effective live choices
The model is worse than uniform guessing, which would give perplexity 1
questions.explanation: Perplexity 1.553 means the model is as uncertain as a uniform choice among about 1.5 tokens, much better than the uniform ceiling of 4. It is not an accuracy, and the other tokens still have nonzero probability.

questions.section: 7.1 Worked example: uniform over 4 gives perplexity 4
questions.question: Why is $V$ described as the perplexity ceiling for a sane model?
options: Because $V$ is the perplexity of a perfect model that always puts all mass on the true token
A uniform model scores exactly $V$, and any model that has learned anything scores below it
Because perplexity is clipped at $V$ in PyTorch so that it never exceeds the vocabulary size
Because perplexity is defined as $V$ minus the loss, so it can only fall below $V$
questions.explanation: Uniform guessing is the 'learned nothing' baseline at perplexity $V$. It marks 'learned nothing about which token comes next'; a perfect model scores 1.

questions.question: Why do papers and leaderboards report perplexity?
options: It carries the same information as the loss but on a scale humans can reason about
It is unaffected by the choice of tokenizer, so models with different vocabularies compare directly
It is the only metric that is differentiable, so it can double as the training objective
It measures generation speed in tokens per second, which leaderboards rank models by
questions.explanation: Perplexity is just the exponentiated loss, interpretable as an effective number of choices. It is not tokenizer-independent and is unrelated to speed.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: cost of the loss at scale
questions.question: For logits of shape `(B, T, V)` with $B = 8$, $T = 1024$, $V = 50257$ in float32, roughly how large is the logits tensor?
options: About 1.6 GB
About 16 GB
About 16 MB
About 160 MB
questions.explanation: $8 \cdot 1024 \cdot 50257 \cdot 4$ bytes $\approx 1.6$ GB. It is often the largest single activation in the forward pass, which is why the vocabulary projection and loss are a memory concern.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: cost of the loss at scale
questions.question: Why is the logits tensor often the largest activation in a language model's forward pass?
options: Because logits are stored in float64 for the loss, doubling their size versus activations
Its size scales with the vocabulary $V$, which is much larger than the model width
Because logits are kept for every layer, not just the last one, for the backward pass
Because the batch is duplicated for the loss computation, once per target token
questions.explanation: The tensor is $B \cdot T \cdot V$, and $V$ (e.g. 50257) dwarfs hidden widths like 768. It is not stored in float64 or per layer.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: cost of the loss at scale
questions.question: Which technique addresses the memory cost of the vocabulary projection and loss?
options: Larger learning rates
Increasing the vocabulary size
Removing the causal mask
Fused cross-entropy kernels
questions.explanation: Fused cross-entropy kernels avoid materializing and repeatedly reading the full logits tensor. Learning rate, masking and larger vocabularies do not reduce this memory.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: cost of the loss at scale
questions.question: What usually dominates the compute of the loss side of a language model?
options: The softmax and log over the logits, $O(B\cdot T\cdot V)$, done in float32
The mean over positions, which needs a reduction across the whole $(B, T)$ grid
Gathering the true-token log-probability, a random-access read for each of $B\cdot T$ rows
The output projection matmul $O(B\cdot T\cdot C\cdot V)$ that produces the logits
questions.explanation: The projection does $2C$ FLOPs per logit, while softmax+loss does a handful per logit with no factor of $C$. Averaging and gathering are negligible.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: cost of the loss at scale
questions.question: What is the gradient of the cross-entropy loss with respect to the logits $z_i$?
options: $-\log q_i$: the per-token loss itself, evaluated at each logit
$q_i(1 - q_i)$: the diagonal of the softmax Jacobian, per logit
$q_i - p_i$: the predicted distribution minus the one-hot target
$p_i - q_i$: the one-hot target minus the predicted distribution $q$
questions.explanation: The elegant closed form is $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial z_i = q_i - p_i$. The sign matters: with $p_i - q_i$ the descent direction would reverse. $q_i(1-q_i)$ is the diagonal of the softmax Jacobian, not the loss gradient.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: cost of the loss at scale
questions.question: With softmax $(0.6439, 0.2369, 0.0871, 0.0321)$ and true token 0, what does gradient descent do to the logits?
options: Lowers the true token's logit (gradient $+0.3561$) and raises the others (gradients $-q_i$)
Raises all four logits equally, since the gradient is the same $-0.25$ for each of them
Leaves the true token's logit unchanged (gradient 0) and lowers only the others (gradients $+q_i$)
Raises the true token's logit (gradient $-0.3561$) and lowers the others (gradients $+q_i$)
questions.explanation: Gradient descent subtracts the gradient. The true token has negative gradient $0.6439 - 1$, so its logit goes up; wrong tokens have positive gradient $q_i$, so their logits go down, in proportion to the probability they wrongly took.

questions.question: In a language model's output layer, what does the weight matrix $W$ of shape `(C, V)` do?
options: It computes attention scores between all pairs of positions, $QK^\top$
It normalizes the logits into probabilities by dividing by their sum
It maps token ids to embeddings of width $V$ by a lookup into its rows
It maps the hidden vector $h$ of width $C$ to $V$ logits via $z = hW$
questions.explanation: Each logit $z_j = \sum_k h_k W_{kj}$ is a dot product of the hidden vector with one column of $W$. Embedding lookup, softmax normalization and attention are separate operations.

questions.question: How many FLOPs does the output projection cost per position, by the $2C$-per-dot-product convention?
options: $2CV$
$CV$
questions.explanation: Each of the $V$ logits is a length-$C$ dot product, about $C$ multiplies and $C$ adds, counted as $2C$ FLOPs. That gives $2CV$ per position and $2BTCV$ for the batch. $5V$ is the rough softmax+loss cost.

questions.question: Roughly how many FLOPs does softmax+loss cost for a `(B, T, V)` logits tensor?
options: About $B\cdot T\cdot V^2$, one pass per vocabulary pair
About $5\cdot B\cdot T\cdot V$, with no factor of $C$
About $2\cdot B\cdot T\cdot C\cdot V$, same as the matmul
About $5\cdot B\cdot T\cdot C$, with no factor of $V$
questions.explanation: Per logit there are a handful of ops (subtract max, exp, add to sum, subtract lse); the exact constant doesn't matter. What matters is that there is no factor of the model width $C$.

questions.question: What is the ratio of output-projection FLOPs to softmax+loss FLOPs?
options: About $2C/5$, so the wider the model, the more the matmul dominates
About $V/C$, so a larger vocabulary makes the matmul dominate
About 1, independent of width, so both cost about the same
About $5/(2C)$, so wider models are increasingly dominated by softmax
questions.explanation: $2BTCV / 5BTV = 2C/5$. For GPT-2 small ($C = 768$) that is about 307. Only at tiny widths like $C = 2$ are the two comparable.

questions.question: What rule of thumb estimates the FLOPs of a whole forward pass of a transformer language model?
options: About $(\text{parameters})^2$, independent of the token count
About $2 \times (\text{parameters}) \times (\text{tokens})$
About $(\text{parameters}) / (\text{tokens})$ per batch
About $V \times (\text{tokens})$, set by the vocabulary
questions.explanation: A forward pass costs roughly $2N$ FLOPs per token for $N$ parameters (REASONABLE INDUSTRY PRACTICE). For GPT-2 small's 124M parameters on 8192 tokens that is about $2\times 10^{12}$.

questions.question: Why is the output projection a large fraction (about 30%) of GPT-2 small's forward-pass FLOPs?
options: Because the output projection is applied once per layer rather than once per pass
Because the vocabulary $V = 50257$ is very large relative to the model width
Because softmax requires a second $C \times V$ matmul to normalize the logits
Because GPT-2 small has no attention layers, so only the MLPs compete
questions.explanation: The projection costs $2BTCV$, and with $V = 50257$ that is a big chunk compared with the rest of a 124M-parameter model. It is applied once at the end, not per layer.

questions.question: If softmax+loss is about 300 times cheaper in FLOPs than the projection, why is it still a performance concern?
options: Because exp is a very expensive instruction that dominates the FLOP count once it is counted properly
It is memory-bound: it reads and writes the huge logits tensor several times with few FLOPs per byte
Because it must be computed in float64 to stay stable, which runs far slower on the GPU
Because it cannot run on the GPU, so the logits must be copied to the CPU every step
questions.explanation: Softmax passes over the $B\cdot T\cdot V$ tensor multiple times (max, exp-and-sum, subtract) doing little arithmetic per number moved. GPUs compute far faster than they move bytes, so runtime is set by memory traffic.

questions.question: What distinguishes a compute-bound operation from a memory-bound one, in the context of the language-model loss?
options: Compute-bound (matmul) does many FLOPs per number loaded; memory-bound (softmax) does few, so bytes moved set runtime
Compute-bound ops (softmax) run on the CPU cores; memory-bound ops (matmul) run on the GPU's memory controllers
Compute-bound ops (matmul) use float32 throughout; memory-bound ops (softmax) use bf16, which halves their bytes
Memory-bound ops (softmax) require more parameters to be stored, so their weights dominate the bytes moved
questions.explanation: A matmul does hundreds of FLOPs per loaded number, so arithmetic throughput limits it. Softmax does a few per number, so memory bandwidth limits it. This distinction drives fused cross-entropy kernels and FlashAttention.

questions.question: What is the key equation of the GPT-2 training objective?
options: Minimize $\mathrm{KL}(\text{uniform} \parallel p)$
Minimize $\sum_i (x_i - \hat{x}_i)^2$ over tokens
Maximize $\sum_i \log p(x_i \mid x_{<i})$
Maximize $\sum_i \log p(x_{<i} \mid x_i)$
questions.explanation: GPT-2 maximizes the sum of log next-token probabilities, exactly the negative of the summed cross-entropy loss. The reversed conditional and squared error are not the objective.

questions.question: Between GPT-2 and later models like GPT-3, LLaMA and DeepSeek, what changes and what stays the same in pretraining?
options: The objective changes to reinforcement learning from the start; scale and data stay similar
Everything stays the same except the tokenizer, which grows to a larger vocabulary
Scale, data and architecture change; the next-token cross-entropy objective stays the same
The objective changes to masked-token prediction like BERT; scale stays the same
questions.explanation: All of these models pretrain on the same next-token cross-entropy loss; progress comes from scale, data and architectural changes, not a new pretraining objective.

questions.question: A validation loss computed with `F.cross_entropy(F.softmax(logits, -1).view(-1, V), targets.view(-1))` looks suspicious. What is the bug?
options: Targets must be one-hot float vectors for `F.cross_entropy`, so the integer `targets.view(-1)` is misread
Softmax should be over dim 0, the batch axis, not dim -1, so it normalizes the wrong axis of the logits
`view` should be `reshape`, since the softmax output is non-contiguous and `view` silently scrambles rows
Softmax is applied before `F.cross_entropy`, which applies log-softmax again, so it is softmaxed twice
questions.explanation: `F.cross_entropy` expects raw logits. Passing probabilities double-softmaxes, squashing toward uniform and distorting the loss. The fix is to pass `logits` directly.

questions.question: Why does double softmax (softmax, then `F.cross_entropy`) push the distribution toward uniform?
options: Because softmax always outputs uniform probabilities when its inputs already sum to exactly 1
Because the exponentials overflow on the second pass, and `inf/inf` is replaced by $1/V$
Because the second softmax divides every entry by $V$ before exponentiating, which flattens the whole row
Probabilities lie in $[0, 1]$, so they differ little, and softmax of nearly equal values is near uniform
questions.explanation: Softmax depends on differences between inputs. After the first softmax all values are in $[0,1]$, so gaps are at most 1, and the second softmax is nearly flat. No overflow is involved.

questions.question: If probabilities are needed for something other than the loss, what is the correct practice with `F.cross_entropy`?
options: Feed probabilities to the loss and raw logits to everything else downstream
Feed the probabilities multiplied by $V$ so they look like logits
Take the log of the probabilities and feed those as logits
Compute probabilities separately, and still feed raw logits to the loss
questions.explanation: Never call softmax before `cross_entropy`. If you need probabilities, compute them on the side; the loss must receive logits so it can apply its stable log-softmax exactly once.

questions.question: Why must logits, not probabilities, be passed to `F.cross_entropy` and `llmre`'s `cross_entropy`?
options: Both apply log-softmax internally (with max-subtraction), so passing probabilities applies softmax twice
Because probabilities have a different shape than logits, `(N,)` instead of `(N, V)`, and fail to broadcast
Because logits are integer-valued scores, and both functions index them directly as class ids
Because probabilities make the loss negative, since their logs are below zero and the sign flips
questions.explanation: The functions handle normalization themselves for stability and to avoid $\log 0$. Probabilities have the same shape as logits; the problem is the repeated softmax, which yields a wrong, too-flat loss.

questions.question: A model has loss 1.386 nats on a 4-token vocabulary. What does that say about the model?
options: Perplexity is 1.386, just above 1, so the model is nearly perfect
Perplexity is 4 = $V$, the uniform ceiling: it has effectively learned nothing
Perplexity is 2, so the model narrows each choice to two tokens
The loss is impossible on a 4-token vocabulary, since it exceeds the 1-nat maximum
questions.explanation: $e^{1.386} = 4.0 = V$, the perplexity of uniform guessing, as uncertain as a fair 4-sided die. Any useful model would score below 4.

questions.question: Why is the per-token gradient on a wrong token's logit, $q_i - 0 = q_i$, always positive?
options: It is not always positive; it turns negative whenever a wrong token's logit exceeds the true token's logit
Because the loss includes a separate positive penalty term for each wrong token, proportional to that token's probability
Because softmax probabilities are positive, so descent lowers each wrong token's logit in proportion to its probability
Because wrong tokens always have larger logits than the true token, so their gradients are positive
questions.explanation: Softmax outputs are strictly positive, so $q_i > 0$ and the gradient on every wrong token's logit is positive. A descent step lowers each wrong logit, more for tokens that took more probability.

questions.question: When does the gradient $q - p$ of the cross-entropy loss become zero?
options: When the loss equals $\log V$, i.e., the model is uniform
When $q = p$, i.e., the model's distribution matches the target
When the true token has the highest logit, i.e., the argmax is right
When all logits are equal, so softmax is exactly uniform
questions.explanation: The gradient vanishes exactly when predictions match the target, at which point training stops pushing. Having the top logit on the true token is not enough unless its probability is 1 (for one-hot targets).

questions.question: In LLM training, what question does the gradient of the loss answer for each parameter?
options: How many training steps remain before the parameter stops changing
What value the parameter should be set to so the loss becomes exactly zero
Which way, and how hard, to nudge that parameter to make the loss smaller
Which training examples the parameter has memorised most strongly
questions.explanation: Training is repeatedly asking which direction and how strongly to nudge each of millions of parameters to reduce the loss, and the gradient answers exactly that. It gives a local direction and rate, not a target value. It says nothing about remaining steps or memorisation.

questions.question: Every optimizer step in gradient-based LLM training is a step in which direction?
options: Along a random direction scaled by the loss value
Along the direction of the largest single parameter
Along the negative gradient of the loss, -∇(loss)
Along the positive gradient of the loss, +∇(loss)
questions.explanation: Gradient descent steps downhill, and downhill is -∇(loss) because the gradient itself points uphill (steepest increase). Stepping along +∇ would increase the loss. Random or parameter-magnitude directions are not what gradient descent uses.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a derivative is a sensitivity
questions.question: Operationally, what does the derivative f'(x) measure?
options: The largest value f can reach anywhere on its domain, found by scanning x
The value of the output f(x) at the current input x, read off the curve
The average of f over a large interval around x, smoothing out noise
The ratio of output change to input change for a tiny nudge of x
questions.explanation: The derivative is a sensitivity: if you increase x by a tiny amount, how much does f(x) move per unit of x, in the limit of a tiny change. It is not the function value itself (a classic confusion). It is local, not an average over a large interval or a global maximum.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a derivative is a sensitivity
questions.question: If f'(x) < 0 at some point, what happens to f when x is increased slightly there?
options: f goes down
f jumps to zero
f stays exactly the same
f goes up
questions.explanation: The sign of the derivative gives direction. A negative derivative means pushing x up pushes f down. A positive derivative would mean f goes up; a zero derivative would mean f is locally flat.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a derivative is a sensitivity
questions.question: What does the magnitude of a derivative, such as f'(x) = 100 versus f'(x) = 0.001, tell you?
options: Whether f is increasing or decreasing at that point
How many inputs the function f takes
How far x is from the minimum of f
How sensitive f is to x at that point
questions.explanation: Magnitude encodes sensitivity: 100 means f reacts violently to small changes in x, 0.001 means f barely notices. Direction (increasing vs decreasing) comes from the sign, not the magnitude. The magnitude does not directly tell you distance to a minimum.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a derivative is a sensitivity
questions.question: To make the loss go down using its derivative with respect to an input, how should the input be stepped?
options: Only when the derivative is exactly zero
Opposite to the sign of the derivative
By an amount equal to the loss value
In the same direction as the sign of the derivative
questions.explanation: We want the loss to decrease, so we read the derivative and step the input against its sign. Stepping with the sign would increase the loss. Applying this move to every parameter at once is gradient descent.

questions.section: 2. Mathematics: the definition and the three rules we actually use
questions.question: In the limit definition f'(x) = lim_{h→0} [f(x+h) − f(x)] / h, what do the numerator and h represent?
options: The output change and the input change, respectively
The input change and the output change, respectively
The average slope and the tangent slope, respectively
The function value and the derivative value, respectively
questions.explanation: f(x+h) − f(x) is how much the output changes, and h is how much the input changed; their ratio is a rate. Taking h → 0 pins down that rate exactly at x rather than over a finite stretch. Swapping them would give the reciprocal, not the derivative.

questions.section: 2. Mathematics: the definition and the three rules we actually use
questions.question: Why does the limit h → 0 appear in the definition of the derivative?
options: It converts the average rate over [x, x+h] into the function's value at x
It guarantees the derivative is always a positive, finite number for any f
It makes the derivative independent of the particular function f being studied
It pins the rate of change down exactly at x rather than over a finite stretch
questions.explanation: With finite h, the ratio is an average rate of change over [x, x+h]. Shrinking h to zero gives the instantaneous rate exactly at x. It does not force positivity, independence from f, or turn the rate into a function value.

questions.section: 2. Mathematics: the definition and the three rules we actually use
questions.question: How is the notation df/dx meant to be read?
options: As 'd times f over d times x', where d is a constant
As the integral of f with respect to x
As 'f divided by x': the function value over the input
As 'df per dx': output change per input change
questions.explanation: df/dx is deliberately fraction-like: it reads as output change per input change. It is not literally f/x, there is no constant d, and it denotes differentiation, not integration.

questions.section: 2. Mathematics: the definition and the three rules we actually use
questions.question: By the power rule, what is the derivative of f(x) = x^n?
options: n·x^n
questions.explanation: The power rule gives d/dx x^n = n·x^(n−1); for example x^2 → 2x. x^(n+1)/(n+1) is the antiderivative (integral), not the derivative. The other options mis-handle the exponent.

questions.section: 2. Mathematics: the definition and the three rules we actually use
questions.question: Why is the derivative of a constant equal to 0?
options: Because constants cancel out whenever they are added to other terms in f
Because the power rule cannot be applied to constants, so they default to 0
Because a constant never changes, so nudging the input moves it by nothing
Because a constant term is itself always equal to zero once x is fixed
questions.explanation: A derivative measures output change per input change; a constant has no output change at all, so its rate is 0. Constants are not themselves zero, and the power rule actually covers them (x^0 gives 0·x^−1 = 0).

questions.section: 2. Mathematics: the definition and the three rules we actually use
questions.question: What does linearity of differentiation state?
options: The derivative of a·f(x) + b·g(x) is f'(x) + g'(x)
The derivative of f(x)·g(x) is f'(x)·g'(x)
The derivative of f(g(x)) is f'(x) + g'(x)
The derivative of a·f(x) + b·g(x) is a·f'(x) + b·g'(x)
questions.explanation: Linearity says constants factor out and sums differentiate term by term. The product of derivatives is not the derivative of a product, and dropping the constants a, b is wrong. Compositions are handled by the chain rule, not linearity.

questions.section: 2. Mathematics: the definition and the three rules we actually use
questions.question: Why is the derivative of f(x) = 3x + 1 the constant 3 for every x?
options: Because the derivative of any polynomial is constant when evaluated at integer inputs
Because 3x + 1 equals 3 near zero, and that value carries over to every other x
Because the +1 term contributes a slope of 3 at every point, while 3x contributes 0
A line has the same slope everywhere: nudging x by h always moves f by 3h
questions.explanation: By linearity and the power rule, 3x differentiates to 3 and the constant 1 to 0, so f'(x) = 3. That makes sense geometrically: a line has constant slope. The +1 contributes nothing, and derivatives are not generally constant.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example: a derivative as a measured slope
questions.question: Checking f(x) = x^2 at x = 3 with a finite step h = 0.001 gives a ratio of 6.001 instead of the exact 6. What is the 0.001 discrepancy?
options: The second derivative of f, which is 2, being scaled by h and added to the first
Floating-point round-off caused by squaring 3.001 in float32 arithmetic
The error from using a finite h instead of an infinitesimal one
A sign that the power rule is only approximately correct
questions.explanation: The finite-step ratio approximates the limit; the leftover 0.001 comes purely from h not being zero (for x^2 the forward-difference error is exactly h). The power rule is exact. It is not mainly floating-point round-off here.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example: a derivative as a measured slope
questions.question: What is the 'wiggle the input, watch the output' finite-difference check used for in practice?
options: Computing the exact derivative with no approximation error, for any function
Sanity-checking a hand-derived gradient, as torch.autograd.gradcheck does
Replacing backpropagation entirely in large-scale training of big models
Choosing the learning rate for an optimizer automatically before training
questions.explanation: Finite differences approximate the derivative numerically, so they are a good independent check of an analytic or autograd gradient; gradcheck works this way internally. They are approximate, not exact, and far too expensive to replace backprop for many parameters.

questions.section: 4. Partial derivatives: one knob at a time
questions.question: What is the rule for computing a partial derivative ∂f/∂x of a multi-input function?
options: Differentiate with respect to every variable in turn and sum all the results
Differentiate with respect to x, then multiply the result by each other variable
Differentiate in x while treating every other variable as a fixed constant
Set every other variable to zero first, and then differentiate the result in x
questions.explanation: A partial derivative differentiates in one variable while holding all others still as constants. Summing derivatives in all variables is not a partial. Setting others to zero is different from holding them constant at their current values.

questions.section: 4. Partial derivatives: one knob at a time
questions.question: What does the curly symbol ∂ (instead of d) signal in ∂f/∂x?
options: There are other variables, and they are being held still
The derivative is taken with respect to a vector, not a scalar
The derivative is only an approximation of the true slope
The function f has no other inputs besides x
questions.explanation: The curly ∂ marks a partial derivative: f has other inputs and they are frozen while differentiating in x. It is not an approximation marker. If f had only x as input, ordinary d would be used.

questions.section: 4. Partial derivatives: one knob at a time
questions.question: For f(x, y) = x^2·y + y^3, what is ∂f/∂x?
options: 2x + y
2xy
questions.explanation: Holding y constant, x^2·y differentiates to 2xy (y rides along as a constant multiplier) and y^3 contains no x, so it is a constant and contributes 0. x^2 + 3y^2 is ∂f/∂y. Adding 3y^2 wrongly differentiates a term that has no x.

questions.section: 4. Partial derivatives: one knob at a time
questions.question: For f(x, y) = x^2·y + y^3, what is ∂f/∂y?
options: 2xy
questions.explanation: Holding x constant, x^2·y differentiates in y to x^2 and y^3 differentiates to 3y^2, giving x^2 + 3y^2. 2xy is the partial in x. Keeping the y in x^2·y forgets to differentiate it.

questions.section: 4. Partial derivatives: one knob at a time
questions.question: What question does each partial derivative of a multi-input function answer?
options: How sensitive f is to all of its inputs changing together at the same time
How sensitive f is to this one input if all the others are frozen
Which input currently has the largest value, and so dominates f at this point
What value f takes when this one input is set to zero and the others are kept
questions.explanation: Each partial isolates one knob: freeze all other inputs and ask how f reacts to that one. Simultaneous change of all inputs is described by the full gradient (directional derivative), not a single partial.

questions.section: 5. The chain rule: differentiating a pipeline
questions.question: Why is the chain rule needed to differentiate a neural network?
options: A network's loss is always a linear function of its weights
A network has no parameters that depend on the input
A network is a composition of layers, each feeding the next
A network is a sum of independent functions of the input
questions.explanation: Neural networks are compositions: the input flows layer after layer. Differentiating a composition requires the chain rule. Sums differentiate by linearity alone, and the loss is generally highly nonlinear in the weights.

questions.section: 5. The chain rule: differentiating a pipeline
questions.question: If z depends on y and y depends on x, what does the chain rule give for dz/dx?
options: dz/dy · dy/dx
dz/dy + dy/dx
dy/dz · dx/dy
dz/dy ÷ dy/dx
questions.explanation: The chain rule multiplies local sensitivities: how much z moves per unit x equals (z per unit y) times (y per unit x). Sensitivities compose by multiplication, not addition or division. The reciprocal form is upside down.

questions.section: 5. The chain rule: differentiating a pipeline
questions.question: If wiggling x moves y twice as fast, and wiggling y moves z five times as fast, how fast does wiggling x move z?
options: Ten times as fast
Two and a half times as fast
Seven times as fast
Five times as fast
questions.explanation: By the chain rule, sensitivities along a pipeline multiply: 2 × 5 = 10. Adding them (7) or dividing them (2.5) is wrong, and ignoring the first stage (5) drops a factor.

questions.section: 5. The chain rule: differentiating a pipeline
questions.question: How does backpropagation get the gradient of the loss with respect to an early parameter?
options: Add the local sensitivities of every layer in the network together, from input to loss
Take the derivative of only the last layer and ignore earlier ones, which cancel
Multiply the local sensitivities along every step of the path to the loss
Perturb the parameter slightly and rerun the forward pass to measure the effect on loss
questions.explanation: Backprop is the chain rule applied systematically from the loss backward: multiply local derivatives along the path (once per edge). Perturbation is finite differences, which is far more expensive. Ignoring earlier layers would give the wrong gradient.

questions.section: Worked numeric example: y = 3x + 1, z = y^2, at x = 2
questions.question: For y = 3x + 1 and z = y^2 at x = 2, what is dz/dx?
questions.explanation: Forward: y = 7, z = 49. Local derivatives: dy/dx = 3, dz/dy = 2y = 14. Chain: 14 × 3 = 42. 49 is the value of z (not its derivative), and 14 is only dz/dy.

questions.section: Worked numeric example: y = 3x + 1, z = y^2, at x = 2
questions.question: To evaluate dz/dy = 2y for z = y^2 during the backward pass, what does an autodiff system need?
options: Only the symbolic expression of y, never its numeric value
The value of y computed and cached during the forward pass
A second forward pass run after the backward pass finishes
The value of z, from which y is recomputed by square root
questions.explanation: dz/dy = 2y depends on the actual value of y (7 at x = 2), which the forward pass produced. That is why autodiff runs forward first and caches intermediate values for backward. No second forward pass is needed, and recovering y from z is not how it is done.

questions.section: 6. Tensor shapes: the gradient is a vector
questions.question: What is the gradient ∇f of a scalar function f(x) of a vector x?
options: The value of f evaluated at each component x_i
The vector stacking all partial derivatives ∂f/∂x_i
The sum of all partial derivatives ∂f/∂x_i
The largest partial derivative among the ∂f/∂x_i
questions.explanation: The gradient is the vector of every partial: [∂f/∂x_1, ..., ∂f/∂x_n]. It keeps each component separately rather than summing them or picking the largest, and it contains derivatives, not function values.

questions.section: 6. Tensor shapes: the gradient is a vector
questions.question: If a weight tensor has shape (768, 768), what is the shape of the gradient of a scalar loss with respect to it?
questions.explanation: The gradient of a scalar always has exactly the same shape as the variable it is taken with respect to. So a (768, 768) weight has a (768, 768) gradient: one partial per entry.

questions.section: 6. Tensor shapes: the gradient is a vector
questions.question: Why is it essential that a parameter and its gradient share shape, dtype and device?
options: It guarantees the loss decreases after every optimizer step
It makes the optimizer's update param -= lr * param.grad type-check
It lets PyTorch skip storing the gradient in memory entirely
It ensures the gradient always has a smaller norm than the parameter
questions.explanation: The update subtracts lr * grad elementwise from the parameter, which only works if they match in shape, dtype and device. Matching shapes do not save memory, bound the norm, or guarantee a loss decrease.

questions.section: 6. Tensor shapes: the gradient is a vector
questions.question: Where does PyTorch store the gradient of a leaf tensor param, and what shape does it have?
options: In param.grad, with param.grad.shape == param.shape
In param.grad_fn, with shape (1,) for every parameter
In loss.grad, with one row per parameter tensor
In param.data, with shape equal to the loss's shape
questions.explanation: PyTorch stores a tensor's gradient in its .grad attribute, and that gradient always has the tensor's shape. .data holds the values, and grad_fn records how a non-leaf tensor was produced, not its gradient.

questions.section: 6. Tensor shapes: the gradient is a vector
questions.question: For f(x, y) = x^2·y + y^3, what is ∇f at (2, 3)?
questions.explanation: ∇f = [2xy, x^2 + 3y^2]. At (2, 3): 2·2·3 = 12 and 4 + 27 = 31. Swapping the order mislabels which partial is which, and 39 is f(2, 3) itself, not a derivative.

questions.section: 6. Tensor shapes: the gradient is a vector
questions.question: What is the key geometric fact about the gradient ∇f?
options: It points in the direction of steepest increase of f, and its length is how steep
It points along a direction in which f stays constant, tracing a level curve
It points in the direction of steepest decrease of f, and its length is how steep
It points straight toward the global minimum of f, from whatever point it is taken
questions.explanation: The gradient points uphill (steepest increase), with its length measuring steepness; so −∇f points steepest downhill. It is a local direction, not a pointer to the global minimum. Directions where f stays constant are perpendicular to the gradient.

questions.section: 6. Tensor shapes: the gradient is a vector
questions.question: Why does gradient descent step against the gradient rather than along it?
options: Because −∇f is the direction of steepest decrease, walking directly downhill
Because the gradient points toward regions of zero loss, which training must leave
Because stepping along the gradient converges too slowly to be practical at scale
Because autograd computes the gradient with the wrong sign, so the minus corrects it
questions.explanation: The gradient points toward steepest increase, so its negative points toward steepest decrease, which is what we want for a loss. Autograd's sign is correct; the minus sign is deliberate in the update rule.

questions.question: In PyTorch, what does marking x = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True) do?
options: It converts x to float64 so that the derivatives computed later are exact
It freezes x so that its value cannot be changed by an optimizer during training
It immediately computes the gradient of x and stores it in x.grad for later
It tells autograd to record operations on x so gradients wrt x can be computed
questions.explanation: requires_grad=True makes autograd record a graph of operations that use x, so a later backward() can fill x.grad. It does not compute anything immediately, change dtype, or freeze the tensor (that is the opposite).

questions.question: After x = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True); y = 3*x + 1; z = y**2; z.backward(), what is x.grad?
questions.explanation: backward() seeds dz/dz = 1 and multiplies local derivatives back along the chain: 1 · 2y · 3 = 1 · 14 · 3 = 42. 49 is z, 7 is y, and 14 is only dz/dy.

questions.question: When z.backward() runs for z = (3x + 1)^2, what value does it seed at the start of the backward pass?
options: dz/dz = z
dz/dz = 0
dz/dz = 2y
dz/dz = 1
questions.explanation: The backward pass starts from the output's sensitivity to itself, which is 1, then multiplies local derivatives back along the graph. Seeding 0 would make every gradient zero, and seeding z or 2y would scale the result wrongly.

questions.question: During the forward pass of z = (3x + 1)^2 with requires_grad on x, what did PyTorch record for the y**2 step?
options: The numeric value of dz/dx = 42, computed eagerly at forward time and stored
That z came from y via y**2 with local derivative 2y, and it stashed y = 7
That z came from x directly, folding the intermediate y into one node for speed
Only the final value z = 49, discarding y to save memory until backward runs
questions.explanation: Autograd records each op and the values its backward needs: for y**2 that is the local derivative 2y and the cached y = 7. It does not compute dz/dx eagerly, and it keeps the intermediate node y rather than collapsing the graph.

questions.question: For v = torch.tensor([2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True) and f = v[0]**2 * v[1] + v[1]**3, what are f.backward()'s results in v.grad and its shape?
questions.explanation: f = 4·3 + 27 = 39, and ∇f = [2xy, x^2 + 3y^2] = [12, 31]. v.grad always has the shape of v, which is (2,). 39 is the function value, and the swapped order mislabels the partials.

questions.question: On what kind of tensor can .backward() be called without passing any argument?
options: Only a matrix with as many rows as parameters
Only a scalar, such as a loss
Any tensor, regardless of its shape
Only a tensor that has requires_grad=False
questions.explanation: Implicit backward requires a scalar output: the gradient of a scalar with respect to an input has the input's shape, which is what an optimizer needs. For a vector output you must reduce to a scalar or pass an explicit vector.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: why gradients, and not the function itself, are the whole game
questions.question: Why is the gradient, rather than the loss function itself, what training works with for a model of 10^9–10^12 parameters?
options: It describes the entire loss surface globally, including the location of all minima
It is the only quantity that can be computed without running a forward pass first
At any point it gives a cheap local linear picture, enough for one good downhill step
It removes the need to evaluate the loss itself at all during the training loop
questions.explanation: No one can reason about a billion-dimensional surface directly, but the gradient gives a flat local picture: each entry says how the loss reacts to that parameter. That is enough for one step, and training is millions of such steps. It is local, not global, and it requires a forward pass.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: why gradients, and not the function itself, are the whole game
questions.question: Roughly how does the cost of the backward pass compare to the forward pass?
options: About the same order, roughly 2x the forward pass, regardless of parameter count
About one hundred times the forward pass for large models, growing with depth
About the square of the number of parameters, since every pair of weights interacts
About one forward pass per parameter, since each needs its own sensitivity
questions.explanation: Reverse-mode autodiff gets the entire gradient for roughly the cost of a forward pass (about 2x in practice), no matter how many parameters there are. One pass per parameter is the cost of finite differences, which is what reverse mode avoids.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: why gradients, and not the function itself, are the whole game
questions.question: What makes training billion-parameter models feasible from a gradient-computation standpoint?
options: Backprop delivers the full gradient for about the price of a forward pass
The loss surface of large models is linear in the parameters
Only a random subset of parameters needs a gradient per step
Each parameter's derivative can be estimated independently by perturbation
questions.explanation: The chain rule organised as backpropagation yields the full gradient at a cost comparable to one forward pass, independent of parameter count. Per-parameter perturbation would need billions of forward passes. Large-model loss surfaces are not linear.

questions.question: For y = x^3 and z = sin(y), what is dz/dx at x = 1?
questions.explanation: Chain rule: dz/dx = cos(y) · 3x^2. At x = 1, y = 1, so dz/dx = 3·cos(1) ≈ 1.6209; PyTorch's x.grad prints 1.6209069. cos(1) alone omits dy/dx = 3, and sin is not its own derivative.

questions.question: For f(x) = x^2, f(3) = 9 and f'(3) = 6. Which pass of a network computes each kind of quantity?
options: The forward pass gives function values like f(3); the backward pass gives derivatives
Both are produced together by the forward pass alone; backward only applies updates
The forward pass gives derivatives like f'(3); the backward pass gives function values
Both are produced together by the backward pass alone, which re-evaluates the function
questions.explanation: A common mistake is confusing a derivative's value with the function's value. The forward pass evaluates the function (9); the backward pass evaluates its derivative (6). They answer different questions.

questions.question: When differentiating x^2·y with respect to x, what is the correct treatment of y?
options: As a constant multiplier, giving 2xy
As a variable that is also differentiated, giving 2x + x^2
As a variable that is differentiated, giving 2xy + x^2
As zero, so the whole term vanishes
questions.explanation: In a partial derivative all other variables are held fixed; y is just a constant multiplier, so x^2·y → 2xy. Differentiating y too is the common mistake of forgetting to hold others fixed. Treating y as zero changes the function's value, not just freezes it.

questions.question: A parameter tensor has shape (512, 256) but its .grad has shape (256, 512). What does this indicate?
options: Normal behaviour for any parameter used in a matrix multiply
A bug: the gradient must always match the parameter's shape
Normal behaviour: gradients are stored transposed in PyTorch
A sign the learning rate is too large for that parameter
questions.explanation: ∇f always has the shape of the variable it is taken with respect to, so a shape mismatch between a parameter and its .grad is always a bug. PyTorch does not store gradients transposed, and the learning rate does not affect shapes.

questions.question: Calling .backward() with no argument on a vector-valued output raises which PyTorch error?
options: Trying to backward through the graph a second time
element 0 of tensors does not require grad and does not have a grad_fn
one of the variables needed for gradient computation has been modified by an inplace operation
grad can be implicitly created only for scalar outputs
questions.explanation: PyTorch can only implicitly seed backward for a scalar; for a vector output it raises 'grad can be implicitly created only for scalar outputs'. Fix it by reducing to a scalar (e.g. a loss) or passing an explicit vector. The other messages are different autograd errors.

questions.question: What is ∇f for f(x, y, z) = xyz, evaluated at (1, 2, 3)?
questions.explanation: ∇f = [yz, xz, xy], each partial holding the other two fixed. At (1, 2, 3): [2·3, 1·3, 1·2] = [6, 3, 2], a length-3 vector matching the 3 inputs. [6, 6, 6] is just f's value repeated.

questions.question: If ∂L/∂w = −4 for some weight w, how should w move to reduce L under gradient descent with learning rate η?
options: Increase w: w ← w − η·(−4) = w + 4η
Decrease w: w ← w − 4η
Set w to −4, the value of its gradient
Leave w unchanged, since a negative gradient means L is minimal
questions.explanation: A negative partial means increasing w decreases L. Gradient descent moves against the gradient, so w goes up by 4η. The magnitude 4 says L is fairly sensitive to w there. A negative gradient does not imply a minimum.

questions.question: Estimating a model's gradient by perturbing each parameter and rerunning the forward pass costs how many forward passes for a million parameters?
options: About two, one forward and one backward
About a million, one per parameter
About one, the same as reverse mode
About a thousand, the square root of the parameter count
questions.explanation: Perturbation measures one parameter's effect per forward pass, so a million parameters need about a million passes. Reverse-mode autodiff avoids this, getting the whole gradient in roughly 2–3 forward-pass costs.

questions.question: Why does reverse-mode autodiff avoid recomputing work for each parameter?
options: It skips parameters whose gradients are small, so most of the network is never visited
It computes each parameter's gradient in parallel, using a separate forward pass for each
Walking back from L, each node's ∂L/∂(node) is computed once and reused upstream
It approximates every gradient at once with a single shared finite-difference step
questions.explanation: Reverse mode runs one forward pass, caches intermediates, then computes at each step how much L changes per unit of that intermediate; all upstream parameters share that number. E.g. for L = (a+b)^2, ∂L/∂(a+b) = 18 is computed once and used for both w_1 and w_2.

questions.question: For L = (a + b)^2 with a = w_1·x, b = w_2·x, x = 3, w_1 = 1, w_2 = 2, what are ∂L/∂w_1 and ∂L/∂w_2?
options: Both are 54
Both are 18
18 and 36
questions.explanation: a + b = 9, so ∂L/∂(a+b) = 18. Both a and b feed a+b with coefficient 1, so ∂L/∂a = ∂L/∂b = 18. Then ∂L/∂w_1 = 18·x = 54 and ∂L/∂w_2 = 18·x = 54. The w values don't appear in ∂a/∂w_1 = x.

questions.question: Why does the full reverse-mode gradient cost only about 2–3 forward passes, independent of parameter count?
options: Because the backward pass runs in lower precision than the forward pass, so each op is cheaper
Because most parameters have zero gradient and are skipped during the backward pass
Each op is visited once going backward, and its backward costs about as much as its forward
Because the gradients of later layers are reused as the gradients of earlier layers unchanged
questions.explanation: Reverse mode visits each op once in reverse, and each op's backward costs about the same as its forward, so total cost scales with the graph size, not parameter count. It does not rely on sparsity or lower precision, and earlier-layer gradients are computed via local derivatives, not copied.

questions.question: In the next step after the scalar chain rule, the chain rule is lifted to vectors and matrices. What object generalises the derivative there?
options: The integral
The Hessian
The Jacobian
The Laplacian
questions.explanation: Moving from scalars to vector-valued functions of vectors, the derivative becomes the Jacobian matrix of all output-input partials; reverse mode applies it via vector-Jacobian products. The Hessian is the matrix of second derivatives, a different object.

questions.question: In reverse-mode autodiff, backpropagation through a network is carried out as what kind of computation?
options: A single large Jacobian matrix built for the whole network and then inverted
A sequence of Jacobian–vector products evaluated from the input forward
A sequence of vector–Jacobian products evaluated right to left through the network
A finite-difference estimate computed separately for each parameter
questions.explanation: Backprop is the chain rule applied to the chain of vector→vector layers, done as successive VJPs from the loss back toward the input, so it never builds or stores a giant Jacobian. Jacobian–vector products are forward mode. Finite differences need one pass per parameter.

questions.question: Understanding vector–Jacobian products explains which two facts about loss.backward()?
options: Why it is cheap enough for billion-parameter models, and why the loss is a scalar
Why it must run on a GPU for large models, and why it requires float64 precision
Why it is exact only for linear models, and why it needs a batch size of one
Why it overwrites .grad on each call, and why it never needs cached activations
questions.explanation: VJPs carry only a vector backward, which makes backprop cheap, and that works because a scalar loss gives a length-1 seed. Backward does not require GPUs or float64, it accumulates rather than overwrites .grad, and it does need cached activations.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: layers are vector→vector, the loss is the one scalar
questions.question: In a typical neural network, which quantity is a single scalar?
options: Only the loss at the very end
Every layer's input activation
Every layer's output activation
Each weight matrix after training
questions.explanation: Layers map vectors to vectors (n activations in, m out); stacking them gives a composition of vector→vector functions. Only the loss at the end is a scalar, because training needs one number to push down.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: layers are vector→vector, the loss is the one scalar
questions.question: For a vector→vector layer, what replaces the single-number derivative of the scalar chain rule?
options: A scalar equal to the determinant of the layer's weights
A single number equal to the average partial derivative
A whole matrix of partial derivatives, the Jacobian
A vector holding only the diagonal partial derivatives
questions.explanation: When a step maps n inputs to m outputs, its derivative is the m×n matrix of all partials, the Jacobian. Averaging or keeping only the diagonal would lose information, and the determinant is unrelated.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: layers are vector→vector, the loss is the one scalar
questions.question: What is the central trick of reverse-mode autodiff with respect to layer Jacobians?
options: Approximating each Jacobian with its diagonal, which is exact for elementwise layers
Materializing every layer's Jacobian and multiplying them all together at the very end
Applying the chain rule through the chain without materializing the Jacobians
Skipping the Jacobians of layers that have no parameters, since they need no gradient
questions.explanation: Reverse mode applies the chain rule using vector–Jacobian products, so the Jacobians never need to exist in memory. It is exact, not a diagonal approximation, and parameter-free layers still need their VJPs for gradients to flow through them.

questions.section: 2. Mathematics: the Jacobian and its shape
questions.question: For f: R^n → R^m, what does the Jacobian entry J_ij represent?
options: ∂x_j/∂f_i, the partial of input j with respect to output i
f_i · x_j, the product of output i and input j
∂f_j/∂x_i, the partial of output j with respect to input i
∂f_i/∂x_j, the partial of output i with respect to input j
questions.explanation: J_ij = ∂f_i/∂x_j: rows index outputs, columns index inputs. Swapping indices transposes the matrix, which is the most common orientation mistake. Inverse partials or products of values are not Jacobian entries.

questions.section: 2. Mathematics: the Jacobian and its shape
questions.question: What is the shape of the Jacobian of f: R^n → R^m?
options: (n, m): inputs by outputs
(n, n): inputs by inputs
(m, n): outputs by inputs
(m, m): outputs by outputs
questions.explanation: The Jacobian is (outputs, inputs) = (m, n). Saying this orientation out loud every time is most of the battle. Square shapes only arise when m = n.

questions.section: 2. Mathematics: the Jacobian and its shape
questions.question: In the Jacobian of f: R^n → R^m, what is row i?
options: The value of output f_i at every input coordinate
The sum of all outputs' partials with respect to input x_i
The gradient of all outputs with respect to the single input x_i
The gradient of the single output f_i with respect to all inputs
questions.explanation: Row i contains ∂f_i/∂x_1, ..., ∂f_i/∂x_n, which is the gradient of output f_i. Column j (not row i) collects all outputs' partials with respect to one input.

questions.section: 2. Mathematics: the Jacobian and its shape
questions.question: Which relation explains why the Jacobian of f: R^n → R^m must have shape (m, n)?
options: J·J^T must be the identity matrix of size n, which forces J to be (m, n)
J must be square so that it can be inverted to map Δf back to Δx
Δf ≈ J·Δx, and (m,n)×(n,1) = (m,1) is the only shape that type-checks
Δx ≈ J·Δf, and (n,m)×(m,1) = (n,1) is the product that must type-check
questions.explanation: The Jacobian linearly maps a small input change to the resulting output change, Δf ≈ JΔx. Δx is (n,1) and Δf is (m,1), so J must be (m,n). It need not be square or invertible.

questions.section: 2. Mathematics: the Jacobian and its shape
questions.question: What is the Jacobian of a scalar-valued function f: R^n → R (m = 1)?
options: A single row: the gradient ∇f laid on its side
An n×n identity matrix, one entry per input pair
A single number equal to the sum of the partials
A single column of all ones, one per input x_i
questions.explanation: With one output the Jacobian is (1, n), a single row of partials, which is exactly the gradient as a row vector. So the gradient is the special case of the Jacobian for scalar-valued functions.

questions.question: For f(a_1, a_2) = [a_1^2, a_1·a_2, a_2^2], what is the Jacobian in terms of a_1, a_2?
questions.explanation: Three outputs, two inputs, so J is (3, 2). Row 1: ∂(a_1^2) = [2a_1, 0]; row 2: ∂(a_1a_2) = [a_2, a_1]; row 3: [0, 2a_2]. The (2, 3) option is the transpose, and the middle-row swap gets ∂(a_1a_2)/∂a_1 = a_2 wrong.

questions.question: In the Jacobian of f(a_1, a_2) = [a_1^2, a_1·a_2, a_2^2], why is the first row's second entry 0?
options: Because a_2 is held at zero when differentiating
Output a_1^2 does not depend on a_2 at all
Because the Jacobian is always lower-triangular
Because a_1 and a_2 are equal at the evaluation point
questions.explanation: a_1^2 ignores a_2, so ∂(a_1^2)/∂a_2 = 0 at every point. Holding a_2 constant is not the same as setting it to zero, and Jacobians are not structurally triangular.

questions.question: How many entries does the Jacobian of f: R^n → R^m have?
options: m·n
max(m, n)
m^2·n
m + n
questions.explanation: The Jacobian has one partial for every (output, input) pair, so m·n entries; e.g. 3×2 = 6. This count grows fast for real layers, which is why reverse mode avoids forming it.

questions.section: 4. The chain rule as a product of Jacobians
questions.question: For a composition x → y → z of vector→vector maps, how is the chain rule written?
options: J_{z/x} = J_{z/y} ⊙ J_{y/x}, an elementwise product of the two Jacobians
J_{z/x} = J_{y/x} · J_{z/y}, since matrix products of Jacobians commute
J_{z/x} = J_{z/y} + J_{y/x}, a sum of the Jacobians of the two stages
J_{z/x} = J_{z/y} · J_{y/x}, a matrix product where order matters
questions.explanation: The scalar product dz/dy·dy/dx becomes a matrix product of Jacobians, with the later stage on the left. Matrix multiplication does not commute, so order matters. Sums and elementwise products are not the chain rule.

questions.section: 4. The chain rule as a product of Jacobians
questions.question: In the Jacobian chain for a deep network ending in a scalar loss, what is the shape of the leftmost factor J_{L/L_k}?
options: (1, d_k), because the loss is one scalar
(d_k, d_k), because layers are square
(d_k, 1), because gradients are column vectors
(d_k, d_0), because it spans the whole network
questions.explanation: The leftmost Jacobian is of the scalar loss with respect to the last layer's d_k outputs, so it has 1 row and d_k columns. That row-vector shape is what makes reverse mode cheap.

questions.section: 5. Why reverse mode computes VJPs, not Jacobians
questions.question: Evaluating the Jacobian-chain product left to right versus right to left gives what result, and at what cost?
options: Different answers, but the same computational cost
Different answers and different costs, so only one order is correct
The identical answer at exactly the same cost
The identical answer by associativity, but wildly different cost
questions.explanation: Matrix multiplication is associative, so either order yields the same gradient. The cost differs hugely: right to left propagates full matrices, while left to right from a scalar loss carries only a row vector.

questions.section: 5. Why reverse mode computes VJPs, not Jacobians
questions.question: When the Jacobian chain is multiplied right to left (starting from the first layer's Jacobian), what is propagated?
options: Only the diagonal entries of each Jacobian, multiplied together elementwise
A single scalar equal to the loss, rescaled at every layer it passes through
Full matrices, effectively building a Jacobian per input
A single row vector of length d_k, the same object reverse mode carries
questions.explanation: Starting from the (d_1, d_0) Jacobian and multiplying onward keeps full matrices as intermediates, which is forward mode's cost profile here. Carrying a row vector is what happens in the left-to-right (reverse) order.

questions.section: 5. Why reverse mode computes VJPs, not Jacobians
questions.question: In reverse mode, what is the shape after multiplying a (1, d_k) row vector by a (d_k, d_{k−1}) Jacobian?
options: (1, d_{k−1}), still a row vector
(d_{k−1}, 1), now a column vector
(d_k, d_{k−1}), a full matrix
(1, d_k), unchanged in shape
questions.explanation: (1, d_k)×(d_k, d_{k−1}) = (1, d_{k−1}). Every step in reverse mode keeps a row vector; you are only ever carrying a vector, never a matrix.

questions.section: 5. Why reverse mode computes VJPs, not Jacobians
