questions.question: Why does .grad accumulate across multiple .backward() calls?
options: Because the optimizer copies its gradients back into .grad after each step
The sweep adds contributions rather than assigning them, by design for fan-in
Because .grad is stored as a Python list that grows by one entry each call
Because PyTorch averages gradients across calls automatically, for stability
questions.explanation: The same += mechanism that sums gradients over multiple paths also sums across backward calls. That is why optimizer.zero_grad() is needed each step, or the new gradient piles onto the last.

questions.question: What happens if you omit optimizer.zero_grad() between training steps?
options: The gradients are reset automatically by the optimizer
PyTorch raises an error at the second backward call
The model's parameters are reset to their initial values
Each step's gradient piles onto the previous step's
questions.explanation: Because backward accumulates into .grad, skipping zero_grad means the optimizer steps on the sum of the current and stale gradients. No error is raised.

questions.question: Why is topological order mandatory in the backward sweep?
options: Because the GPU can only process nodes in the order they were created
Because leaves must be processed before any intermediate node
Because out-of-order processing would force a recompute of the forward pass
A node's gradient is incomplete until every downstream contribution arrives
questions.explanation: If a node applied its VJP before all downstream contributions were summed, it would propagate an incomplete gradient. Reverse topological order prevents that. Leaves are processed last, not first.

questions.question: Beyond the seed/topo-sort/sweep core, what does the rest of PyTorch's autograd mostly add?
options: Efficiency and coverage: hundreds of ops' VJPs, CUDA kernels, in-place tracking
Automatic learning-rate tuning for every parameter, based on gradient statistics
A second forward pass that refines each gradient after the first backward sweep
A different differentiation algorithm based on symbolic algebra over the graph
questions.explanation: The core algorithm is the whole idea; the rest is engineering around it. PyTorch does not use symbolic differentiation or tune learning rates.

questions.question: What does .backward() do to the graph by default, and why?
options: Saves the graph to disk so later steps and debuggers can inspect it
Frees the graph and its saved tensors, since a step needs it only once
Keeps the graph forever so later steps can reuse it without a forward
Doubles the graph so that a second backward can run in parallel
questions.explanation: Freeing the graph during the sweep reclaims activation memory, since a normal training step backpropagates once. retain_graph=True overrides this.

questions.question: When is retain_graph=True needed?
options: Whenever you want to keep the gradients of intermediate tensors after backward
Whenever you need second-order derivatives such as Hessian-vector products
Whenever the model runs on GPU, since CUDA frees graphs asynchronously
When .backward() must run a second time over the same graph
questions.explanation: Without it, the first backward frees the graph and a second raises 'Trying to backward through the graph a second time.' Intermediate gradients need .retain_grad(), and second-order derivatives need create_graph=True.

questions.question: Why shouldn't retain_graph=True be used routinely?
options: It makes gradients numerically inaccurate
It disables gradient accumulation
It keeps activations alive, costing memory
It prevents the optimizer from updating parameters
questions.explanation: Retaining the graph keeps all saved tensors in memory until it is freed. It doesn't change gradient accuracy or optimizer behaviour.

questions.question: What does create_graph=True enable?
options: Keeping every intermediate tensor's .grad after backward, not just the leaves'
Building the full forward graph ahead of time, before any data flows through it
Recording the backward pass itself, so gradients can be differentiated again
Copying the autograd graph to every GPU in a data-parallel training job
questions.explanation: With create_graph=True, the gradients themselves get a grad_fn, allowing Hessian-vector products, some meta-learning and gradient-penalty terms. It's costlier in time and memory because the backward graph is retained and recorded.

questions.question: Which kind of computation is create_graph=True typically used for?
options: Data loading and tokenization pipelines that build tensors on the fly
Hessian-vector products and some meta-learning or penalty terms
Standard next-token pretraining with a cross-entropy loss
Mixed-precision loss scaling, to avoid fp16 gradient underflow
questions.explanation: create_graph makes the backward differentiable, giving access to second-order derivatives. Ordinary pretraining needs neither create_graph nor retain_graph.

questions.section: 5. From scratch: a scalar autodiff engine
questions.question: In the micrograd-style Value engine, what does each operation store besides its forward value?
options: A copy of the entire graph up to that point, so that backward can be started from any node
The finite-difference estimate of its derivative, computed during the forward pass
A _backward closure that adds incoming gradient times the local derivative into its inputs
A full Jacobian matrix of the op with respect to its inputs, built at forward time
questions.explanation: Each op's _backward closure is the hand-written grad_fn: it multiplies out.grad by the local derivative and adds it into each input's .grad. No Jacobian or finite differences are stored.

questions.section: 5. From scratch: a scalar autodiff engine
questions.question: In the Value class, what do self._prev and self._backward represent?
options: _prev holds the gradient history of the node; _backward clears it before each step
_prev holds the previous step's value; _backward reverts the node to that value
_prev holds the trainable parameters; _backward applies the optimizer update
_prev holds the input nodes (edges); _backward is the local VJP, a no-op for leaves
questions.explanation: _prev is a tuple of child (input) nodes, defining the graph's edges. _backward defaults to a no-op lambda for leaves and is replaced by each op with its local VJP.

questions.section: 5. From scratch: a scalar autodiff engine
questions.question: In the Value engine, what does the _backward closure for a + b do?
options: Adds 1.0 * out.grad into both self.grad and other.grad
Adds other.data * out.grad into self.grad only, leaving other
Sets both self.grad and other.grad to out.data, the sum
Adds out.grad into self.grad and subtracts it from other.grad
questions.explanation: d(a+b)/da = d(a+b)/db = 1, so the incoming gradient flows straight through to both inputs, using +=. Subtraction or using data values would be wrong.

questions.section: 5. From scratch: a scalar autodiff engine
questions.question: In the Value engine, what does the _backward closure for a * b add into self.grad?
options: out.grad alone — multiplication passes the incoming gradient straight through
self.data * out.grad — each factor's derivative with respect to itself is itself
out.data * out.grad — the product's value times the incoming gradient
other.data * out.grad — each factor's local derivative is the other factor
questions.explanation: By the product rule, ∂(ab)/∂a = b and ∂(ab)/∂b = a. So self.grad += other.data * out.grad and other.grad += self.data * out.grad.

questions.section: 5. From scratch: a scalar autodiff engine
questions.question: In the Value engine, what local derivative does tanh's _backward use, and what does it save?
options: sinh(x), using the saved input x from forward
1 − t^2, using the saved output t = tanh(x)
t^2, using the saved forward output t
1 − x^2, using the saved input x itself
questions.explanation: d/dx tanh(x) = 1 − tanh(x)^2, so the closure reuses the saved output t: self.grad += (1 − t*t) * out.grad. This is an example of a VJP needing a saved forward value.

questions.section: 5. From scratch: a scalar autodiff engine
questions.question: How does the build function inside Value.backward() produce a topological order?
options: It visits each node's _prev inputs first and appends the node after them
It appends each node first and only then recursively visits its _prev inputs
It uses the order in which nodes were garbage-collected after the forward pass
It sorts nodes by their data values in ascending order, smallest first
questions.explanation: build(v) recurses into every child in v._prev, then appends v, so each node appears after all its inputs. A visited set prevents processing a shared node twice. Appending before visiting would give reverse order.

questions.section: 5. From scratch: a scalar autodiff engine
questions.question: In Value.backward(), what two steps follow building the topological order?
options: Set every node's grad to 1.0, then sum all of them into the root's .grad
Set self.grad = 1.0 (seed), then call v._backward() for v in reversed(topo)
Call v._backward() for every v in topo order, then set self.grad = 1.0
Set self.grad = 0.0, then call v._backward() for every v in forward topo order
questions.explanation: Seeding the root with 1 and sweeping in reverse topological order matches PyTorch's algorithm. Seeding 0 would zero every gradient, and the forward order would process nodes before their downstream contributions arrive.

questions.section: 5. From scratch: a scalar autodiff engine
questions.question: Why does each _backward closure in the Value engine use += rather than = on the inputs' .grad?
options: Because Python closures cannot rebind an outer variable with plain =
So the gradient is automatically averaged across the examples in a batch
So a reused node accumulates gradient over all its paths (fan-in)
So that older gradients decay over time, like momentum in an optimizer
questions.explanation: A node feeding several ops (like a feeding a*b and a+b) gets a contribution from each; the chain rule sums them. = would overwrite all but the last, giving a wrong gradient.

questions.question: When the Value engine and PyTorch (float64) both compute L = tanh(a*b + b)·(a + b) at a = −3, b = 2, how closely do they agree?
options: In the value but not the gradients, which differ in sign
Only after both are rounded to float16
To full double precision, in the value and both gradients
Only to about 3 decimal places, due to tanh approximations
questions.explanation: Both print 0.999329299739067, ∂L/∂a = −1.0020112011051188, ∂L/∂b = −0.9966473983730152. The toy engine does exactly what torch.autograd does on this expression.

questions.question: For L = tanh(n)·s with n = a*b + b and s = a + b, at a = −3, b = 2, what are n, s and L?
In the trace of L = tanh(n)·s backward, what does the final * send into the tanh branch and the s branch?
options: 1 into both branches, since multiplication passes gradients straight through
s = −1 into the tanh branch, and tanh(n) ≈ −0.99933 into the s branch
L ≈ 0.99933 into both branches, scaled by 1/2 so the two halves sum to L
tanh(n) into the tanh branch, and s into the s branch, each its own value
questions.explanation: For a product, each input's local derivative is the other factor, so the tanh output receives s and s receives tanh(n). Passing 1 straight through is the + rule, not *.

questions.question: In L = tanh(a*b + b)·(a + b), why does a's gradient come from two contributions?
options: a feeds both a·b and a + b, so contributions along both paths are added
Because the seed of 1 is split equally between a and b at the root
Because a is a leaf, and leaves always receive exactly two contributions
Because tanh has two derivatives, one for each side of its input
questions.explanation: a appears in both a*b and a+b, so the chain rule sums contributions along both paths; the Value engine's += handles this. The arithmetic lands on −1.00201, matching PyTorch.

questions.question: In the backward trace of L = tanh(n)·s at n = −4, what factor does tanh multiply its incoming gradient by?
questions.explanation: tanh's local derivative is 1 − tanh^2(n) = 1 − 0.99866 ≈ 0.00134. That tiny value shows how a saturated tanh shrinks gradients, which relates to vanishing gradients.

questions.section: 7. This engine lives in the codebase
questions.question: In the course codebase, where does the micrograd Value engine live and where is its parity test?
options: llmre/optim/micrograd.py, tested by tests/test_optim.py
llmre/training/autograd.py, tested by tests/test_training.py
llmre/model/micrograd.py, tested by tests/test_micrograd.py
scripts/micrograd.py, tested by notebooks/micrograd.ipynb
questions.explanation: The Value class ships as llmre/model/micrograd.py and tests/test_micrograd.py checks it against torch, asserting value and gradients match to 1e-6.

questions.section: 7. This engine lives in the codebase
questions.question: What does tests/test_micrograd.py assert about the Value engine?
options: That the Value engine runs faster than PyTorch on the same scalar expression
That the Value engine uses less memory than PyTorch for the saved activations
That the gradients are all positive for the test expression at a = −3, b = 2
That L.data, a.grad and b.grad match PyTorch's float64 results within 1e-6
questions.explanation: The test builds the same expression with Value and torch (float64), then asserts the absolute differences of the value and both gradients are below 1e-6.

questions.section: 7. This engine lives in the codebase
questions.question: What is needed to add an op such as exp or pow to the Value engine?
options: A full Jacobian matrix of the op, stored on the new node at forward time
A new seed value specific to that op, set before the backward sweep starts
One forward line plus its one-line local derivative in a _backward closure
A rewrite of the topological sort so it knows how to visit the new op
questions.explanation: The pattern is uniform: compute the forward value, create the out node with its children, and define _backward with the local derivative. The sort and sweep are op-agnostic.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: how PyTorch differs from our toy
questions.question: How does a PyTorch autograd node differ from a node in the scalar Value engine?
options: Each PyTorch node is a whole tensor, so its backward is a tensor VJP like a matmul
PyTorch nodes have no backward functions; gradients are inferred from the forward
PyTorch nodes store full Jacobians instead of VJPs, since tensors make them cheap
PyTorch nodes are scalars too, exactly like Value, but are executed on the GPU
questions.explanation: PyTorch operates on tensors, so each _backward equivalent is a tensor VJP (e.g. W^T g for a linear layer). The topological sort and reverse sweep are identical in principle.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: how PyTorch differs from our toy
questions.question: In what language does PyTorch's autograd graph walk run, and how are many backward formulas written?
options: In pure Python, with every backward formula derived symbolically at runtime
In a C++ engine, with many hand-written closed-form backward formulas
In CUDA only, with each backward formula found by finite differences
In JavaScript, with the backward formulas loaded from a remote server
questions.explanation: PyTorch's engine is C++ with hundreds of registered backward formulas, many hand-written closed forms like the fused cross_entropy backward. They are not naive compositions or numerical estimates.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: how PyTorch differs from our toy
questions.question: How does PyTorch manage autograd memory compared with the toy Value engine?
options: It frees the graph and saved tensors after the sweep unless retained, and offers checkpointing
It frees only the leaf tensors after each backward call, keeping every intermediate alive
It copies the graph to CPU memory after every backward call, so the GPU is freed
It never frees the graph, relying on the user to delete tensors with del after each step
questions.explanation: PyTorch explicitly frees saved tensors after backward (unless retained) and supports checkpointing to trade compute for memory. The toy relies on Python's garbage collector.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: how PyTorch differs from our toy
questions.question: What does PyTorch do about in-place modifications that would corrupt values a backward step needs?
options: It silently recomputes the corrupted saved value from scratch during backward
It forbids all in-place operations on every tensor that has requires_grad=True
It tracks in-place changes and errors if one corrupts a saved value
It ignores in-place ops entirely, accepting a possibly wrong gradient as the cost
questions.explanation: PyTorch tracks in-place changes (via version counters) and errors when a saved tensor needed by some backward was modified. The toy engine never mutates data, so it avoids the issue.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: how PyTorch differs from our toy
questions.question: Which sentence summarises what loss.backward() does?
options: Build a graph on the backward pass, seed each leaf with 0, sort by tensor size, sweep forward applying each op's Jacobian, overwrite leaves
Symbolically differentiate the loss expression into a closed form, simplify it, then evaluate it at the current parameter values
Build a graph on the forward pass, seed the root with 1, topologically sort, sweep backward with each op's VJP, accumulate into leaves
Perturb each leaf in turn, rerun the forward pass, and store the change in loss divided by the size of the perturbation
questions.explanation: That one sentence captures the mental model shared by the toy engine and PyTorch. The perturbation option describes finite differences; symbolic differentiation is a different technique.

questions.question: What is the correct _backward rule for a relu method on the Value engine?
options: self.grad = (1.0 if self.data > 0 else 0.0) * out.grad
self.grad += (1.0 if self.data > 0 else 0.0) * out.grad
self.grad += (1.0 if out.grad > 0 else 0.0) * self.data
self.grad += max(0.0, self.data) * out.grad
questions.explanation: relu's local derivative is 1 where x > 0 and 0 where x ≤ 0, multiplied by the incoming gradient and accumulated with +=. Using max(0, x) as the derivative confuses value with slope; using = would break fan-in.

questions.question: For x = −2, w = 3 and y = relu(x·w) + x, what are y, x.grad and w.grad?
options: y = −2, x.grad = 1, w.grad = 0
y = −2, x.grad = 4, w.grad = −2
y = 0, x.grad = 0, w.grad = 0
y = −6, x.grad = 3, w.grad = −2
questions.explanation: x·w = −6 ≤ 0, so relu outputs 0 and its branch is dead (local derivative 0). y = 0 + x = −2. Only the +x path contributes, so x.grad = 1; w's only path goes through the dead relu, so w.grad = 0.

questions.question: Why is w.grad exactly 0 for y = relu(x·w) + x at x = −2, w = 3?
options: Because w is a leaf, and leaves always end up with zero gradient after backward
Because w = 3 is positive, and relu passes no gradient for positive inputs
w's only path to y runs through a relu whose input −6 ≤ 0, so it passes 0
Because the +x term exactly cancels w's contribution along the relu path
questions.explanation: A relu with non-positive input passes no gradient. w reaches y only through that dead relu, so its gradient is 0. Leaves normally do receive gradients.

questions.question: Why does y = x**2; y.backward(); z = y*3; z.backward() raise 'Trying to backward through the graph a second time'?
options: Because z was created with requires_grad=False, so it has no grad_fn to walk
Because multiplication by a constant has no registered backward formula
Because y is a leaf tensor, and a leaf cannot be reused after its backward
The first backward freed y's subgraph and its saved tensors, which z needs
questions.explanation: y.backward() freed y's subgraph. z = y * 3 builds a new node on top of it, so z.backward() tries to walk through the freed part. y is not a leaf, and z does require grad since y does.

questions.question: What is the quick one-flag fix for 'Trying to backward through the graph a second time' when reusing y after y.backward()?
options: Call y.retain_grad() before the first backward
Call z.backward(create_graph=True) on the second call
Call y.backward(retain_graph=True) on the first call
Call torch.no_grad() before the second backward
questions.explanation: retain_graph=True keeps the graph and saved tensors alive for a second backward. create_graph is for second-order derivatives; retain_grad keeps an intermediate's .grad, not the graph.

questions.question: What is usually the better fix than retain_graph=True when two backward calls hit a shared graph?
options: Use one scalar loss and one .backward(), or detach y if it shouldn't get gradients
Call zero_grad() between the two backward calls, which rebuilds the freed graph
Always add retain_graph=True to every backward call by default, just to be safe
Convert all tensors to float64 before the second backward so the graph is kept
questions.explanation: Usually you meant one loss and one backward. If the second computation shouldn't send gradients into the first, use y.detach(). retain_graph=True is correct only when you genuinely need two passes over shared structure, and it costs memory. zero_grad does not restore a freed graph.

questions.question: How can you keep the gradient of an intermediate (non-leaf) tensor after .backward()?
options: Set retain_graph=True on the backward call
Call .retain_grad() on it before backward
Set requires_grad=False on it
Call .detach() on it before backward
questions.explanation: Intermediates' gradients are used during the sweep but discarded by default; .retain_grad() keeps them. retain_graph keeps the graph, not intermediate grads. Detaching removes it from the graph entirely.

questions.question: What does a node's local VJP need before it can run correctly in the backward sweep?
options: Its output gradient fully accumulated from every downstream node
Its forward value recomputed from scratch from its inputs
Its input gradient already computed by its children upstream
The loss recomputed with the node removed from the graph
questions.explanation: The output gradient is the sum of contributions from every downstream node, so all of them must be processed first. Reverse topological order guarantees this.

questions.question: If loss.backward() is called on two consecutive steps without zero_grad(), what do the parameter .grad values hold?
options: The sum of both steps' gradients, so the optimizer steps on stale gradients
Zero, because the two steps' gradients cancel each other when added
The average of both steps' gradients, since backward divides by the call count
Only the second step's gradient, since backward overwrites .grad each call
questions.explanation: Gradients accumulate, so each .grad holds the sum. Fix with optimizer.zero_grad() or param.grad = None at the top of each iteration. Gradient accumulation across micro-batches deliberately exploits this.

questions.question: Which technique deliberately exploits the accumulation of .grad across backward calls?
options: Gradient accumulation across micro-batches
Learning-rate warmup over the first steps
Mixed-precision loss scaling with fp16
Activation checkpointing within each layer
questions.explanation: Running backward on several micro-batches before one optimizer step sums their gradients, simulating a larger batch. It is intentional accumulation; checkpointing, loss scaling and warmup are unrelated.

questions.question: Besides optimizer.zero_grad(), what other way is given to clear a parameter's gradient at the top of each iteration?
options: param.data = 0
param.detach_()
param.requires_grad = False
param.grad = None
questions.explanation: Setting param.grad = None clears accumulated gradients. Changing requires_grad stops tracking, detaching removes graph history, and zeroing data destroys the parameter's values.

questions.question: After autograd internals, what does the next module turn gradients into?
options: Attention: computing scaled dot-product scores between queries and keys
Tokenization: building BPE vocabularies by merging frequent byte pairs
Inference: sampling the next token with temperature and top-k filtering
Learning: stepping parameters downhill with SGD, momentum and Adam
questions.explanation: With derivatives, VJPs, the output gradient and autograd internals in hand, the next step is optimization: SGD, momentum and Adam, which use the gradients to update parameters.

questions.question: How do later optimization techniques such as Adam, warmup/cosine schedules and the LLM pretraining loop relate to plain gradient descent, SGD and momentum?
options: They are refinements built on top of the plain update rule, minibatch gradients and momentum
They replace first-order gradient steps with second-order Newton steps that use the full Hessian
They are separate methods that search parameter space without using the gradient of the loss
They target small models only, while LLM pretraining still relies on exact full-batch gradient descent
questions.explanation: Training a language model is running an update rule like theta <- theta - eta*g millions of times. Adam adds per-parameter scaling, schedules vary eta over time, and the pretraining loop just repeats the step. None of these abandon the gradient or switch to second-order methods; they are bookkeeping on top of the basic ideas.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: walking downhill on the loss surface
questions.question: Why is a neural network's loss minimized by iterative small steps rather than by solving directly for the best parameters?
options: Because the loss of a deep network has no usable gradient, so only random search over parameters is possible
Because the loss depends on huge numbers of parameters through a deep nonlinear network, so there is no closed form
Because the loss is linear in the parameters, so any fixed step size eventually reaches the exact minimum
Because solving for the optimum directly would return parameters that overfit the held-out test set by construction
questions.explanation: The loss L(theta) depends on an enormous number of parameters wired through nonlinear layers, so there is no way to solve for the optimum analytically. What is cheap is computing which direction is downhill at the current point, so training takes a small step that way and repeats, often hundreds of thousands of times.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: walking downhill on the loss surface
questions.question: In which direction does the negative gradient, -grad L(theta), point?
options: The direction of steepest increase of the loss
A direction orthogonal to the loss contours that keeps the loss constant
The direction of steepest decrease of the loss
Directly toward the global minimum of the loss
questions.explanation: The gradient grad L points in the direction of steepest increase, so its negative points in the direction of steepest decrease. That is only a local statement: it does not point straight at the global minimum, which is why gradient descent must recompute the gradient after each step.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: walking downhill on the loss surface
questions.question: What is the core question every deep-learning optimizer answers?
options: Which layers of the network should be frozen and which should keep receiving updates during training
How many training examples should be held out for validation so the loss estimate stays unbiased
Which loss function the model should minimize, given the task and the format of the labels
Given the current gradient (and memory of past ones), how the parameters should change
questions.explanation: Every optimizer maps the current gradient, plus possibly state built from past gradients, to a parameter update. Plain gradient descent gives the simplest answer: step straight downhill by a fixed fraction of the gradient. Momentum and Adam differ only in how they use the gradient and their memory.

questions.question: In the gradient-descent update theta <- theta - eta * grad L(theta), what does the arrow '<-' mean?
options: Overwrite theta with the right-hand side; an in-place update repeated every step
theta converges to the right-hand side only in the limit of infinitely many training steps
theta is compared with the right-hand side and the smaller of the two values is kept
The right-hand side is a constraint that theta must satisfy once it reaches the optimum
questions.explanation: The arrow is assignment: the parameter vector is overwritten with theta - eta*grad L, and this is repeated each training step. It is not a limit, comparison, or constraint; it is the concrete in-place mutation an optimizer's step() performs.

questions.question: What is the shape of the gradient grad L(theta) relative to the parameter vector theta?
options: It is a scalar: the value of the loss evaluated at the current parameters theta
It has the same shape as theta, with entry i equal to dL/d theta_i
It is a square matrix of size len(theta) x len(theta) holding all pairwise derivatives
It has the shape of one minibatch of inputs, one derivative per input feature
questions.explanation: The gradient has one entry per parameter: entry i is the partial derivative of the loss with respect to theta_i, i.e. how much the loss rises per unit increase in that parameter. It therefore has exactly the shape of theta. The square matrix of second derivatives would be the Hessian, which gradient descent never forms.

questions.question: In PyTorch, where does the gradient that gradient descent uses come from?
options: It is computed by the optimizer's step() method from the current parameter values alone
It is approximated by finite differences inside torch.optim, one perturbed parameter at a time
loss.backward() computes it and stores it in each parameter's .grad attribute
It is read from the DataLoader along with each batch, precomputed when the dataset is built
questions.explanation: loss.backward() runs backpropagation and fills each leaf parameter's .grad with dL/d(param). The optimizer's step() only reads .grad and applies the update; it does not compute derivatives itself, and no finite differences are involved.

questions.question: What does the learning rate eta set in the gradient-descent update?
options: The number of training examples averaged into the gradient estimate on each step
The direction of the update, chosen independently of the gradient at the current point
The number of optimizer steps taken before training stops and the model is saved
The step size: parameters move a fraction eta along the negative gradient
questions.explanation: eta is a small positive scalar (e.g. 0.1 or 3e-4) that multiplies the negative gradient. It scales how far each step moves but not the direction, which comes from the gradient. Batch size and number of steps are separate hyperparameters.

questions.question: What does 'full-batch' gradient descent mean?
options: The gradient is the average of per-example gradients over the entire training set
The gradient is computed on one randomly chosen example per step and used directly for the update
The model is trained with the largest batch that fits in GPU memory, reshuffled every epoch
Every layer of the network is updated together in a single step instead of one layer at a time
questions.explanation: Full-batch descent uses L(theta) = (1/N) * sum over all N examples of the per-example loss, so its gradient is the average of all N per-example gradients. That is the true gradient of the training loss. Using one example would be stochastic gradient descent, and 'largest batch that fits' is still a minibatch.

questions.question: Which hyperparameter is described as the single most important one in training?
options: The momentum coefficient mu
The learning rate eta
The number of epochs
The random seed for shuffling
questions.explanation: The learning rate controls step size, and getting it wrong either wastes enormous compute (too small) or makes training oscillate or diverge (too large). That outsized effect is why it is called the most important hyperparameter, and why a whole lesson (03.3) is devoted to scheduling it.

questions.question: What happens when the learning rate is too small?
options: The loss diverges to inf
The loss oscillates wildly between two values
Training is correct but crawls, wasting compute
The gradient becomes zero and training stops immediately
questions.explanation: With a tiny eta each step barely moves the parameters. The direction is still right, so the loss decreases, but very slowly, burning compute for little progress. Oscillation and divergence are the symptoms of a learning rate that is too large.

questions.question: What happens when the learning rate is too large?
options: The steps become smaller near the minimum, so training merely slows down without other harm
Each step lands exactly on the minimum, so training converges in one or two iterations
The optimizer automatically lowers eta until the updates become stable again
A step can overshoot the valley and land higher, so loss oscillates or diverges
questions.explanation: A large eta takes a step that jumps across the downhill valley and can end at a higher loss than before. Repeating that makes the loss oscillate or blow up to inf. Plain gradient descent has no mechanism to lower eta by itself; that is the job of a schedule.

questions.question: For gradient descent on f(x) = x^2 with learning rate 0.1, the update is x <- x - 0.1*2x. What single operation does each step perform on x?
options: Multiplies x by 0.8
Subtracts a constant 1 from x
Multiplies x by 0.2
Divides x by 2
questions.explanation: x - 0.1*2x = x - 0.2x = 0.8x, so every step multiplies x by 0.8. From 5 this gives 4.0, 3.2, 2.56. The subtraction is not constant: the step size 0.2x shrinks as x shrinks.

questions.question: Why do gradient-descent steps on f(x) = x^2 get smaller as x approaches the minimum at 0, even with a fixed learning rate?
options: Because the learning rate is automatically decayed each step
Because the gradient 2x itself shrinks as x approaches 0
Because floating-point rounding truncates small updates
Because the loss becomes negative near the minimum
questions.explanation: The step is eta times the gradient, and the gradient 2x goes to zero as x goes to zero. So even with constant eta the steps naturally shrink near the bottom of a smooth loss. This automatic slowdown is a property of gradient descent on smooth functions, not of any schedule.

questions.question: In a manual PyTorch gradient-descent loop, why is the update 'x -= eta * x.grad' wrapped in 'with torch.no_grad():'?
options: To make the update run on the GPU instead of the CPU, where autograd cannot see the tensor
To convert x to a lower precision for the duration of the update so the step runs faster
Because the update is not part of the forward pass, so autograd must not record it
To automatically zero x.grad after the update so the next backward() starts from a clean slate
questions.explanation: The parameter update is not part of the model's computation, so it must not be added to the autograd graph. torch.no_grad() turns off recording for that block. It does not change device or dtype, and it does not clear .grad; that must be done separately.

questions.question: Why must x.grad be reset to None (or zeroed) after each gradient-descent step in PyTorch?
options: Because backward() raises an error whenever .grad already holds a value from the previous step
Because the optimizer reads .grad only when it is None and otherwise skips the parameter entirely
Because a non-None .grad prevents the next forward pass from running until it is cleared
Because backward() adds into .grad, so it would accumulate the sum of all past gradients
questions.explanation: backward() accumulates: it adds the new gradient to whatever is already in .grad. If you never clear it, step k uses the sum of all k gradients so far. That is why every optimizer has a zero_grad() method. backward() does not raise an error on a populated .grad, which is exactly why the bug is silent.

questions.section: 2.4 Why not just use full-batch descent forever?
questions.question: Why is full-batch gradient descent impractical for training a real LLM?
options: One gradient would need a forward and backward pass over billions of tokens per step
The full-batch gradient is biased, so with enough steps it points systematically away from the minimum
Full-batch gradients cannot be computed with backpropagation once the model exceeds a few layers
Full-batch descent requires a learning rate larger than 1, which makes deep networks diverge
questions.explanation: The true gradient averages over the whole dataset, which for an LLM is billions of tokens. You would wait for a pass over all of it before each step, taking only a handful of steps a day. The full-batch gradient is the exact gradient of the training loss, not biased, and backprop computes it fine; it is simply far too expensive.

questions.section: 3.1 The gradient as an average, and a cheap estimate of it
questions.question: In minibatch SGD, how is the gradient estimate g computed?
options: As the gradient of the single example in the batch that currently has the largest loss
As the average of per-example gradients over a random minibatch B
As the sum of all per-example gradients across the full dataset, recomputed every step
As the difference between the current loss and the previous loss, divided by the step size
questions.explanation: g = (1/|B|) * sum over n in B of grad l(theta; x_n). Because the true gradient is an average over all N examples, an average over a random subset estimates it. Using the worst example or the full sum would not be the minibatch estimate.

questions.section: 3.1 The gradient as an average, and a cheap estimate of it
questions.question: Why is the minibatch gradient g described as 'unbiased'?
options: Because it is exactly equal to the true full-dataset gradient on every single step
Because it is computed in float64, so no rounding error can shift its value
Because a random subset's average has the same expected value as the full average
Because each batch contains every class of example in equal proportion by construction
questions.explanation: Unbiased means the expected value of g, over the random choice of batch, equals the true gradient. Any particular batch still deviates from it, which is why g is also noisy. Unbiasedness comes from random sampling, not from precision or stratified class balance.

questions.section: 3.1 The gradient as an average, and a cheap estimate of it
questions.question: Why is the minibatch gradient estimate described as 'noisy'?
options: Because GPUs add small random noise to floating-point results during matrix multiplication
Because the learning rate is randomly perturbed by the optimizer on each step
Because dropout is applied during the backward pass, randomly zeroing gradient entries
Because any particular small sample deviates from the expected (true) gradient
questions.explanation: A finite random sample's average differs from the full-dataset average by some random amount; that deviation is the noise. It is a statistical property of sampling, not hardware noise or a randomized learning rate.

questions.section: 3.1 The gradient as an average, and a cheap estimate of it
questions.question: Where does the randomness in stochastic gradient descent actually live?
options: In which examples end up in each batch, produced by shuffling the data
In the optimizer's update rule, which adds random noise to each step
In a random scaling of the learning rate at each step
In random initialization of the velocity buffer
questions.explanation: The update theta <- theta - eta*g and the SGD class are fully deterministic. The randomness comes from the data pipeline, which randomly permutes example indices each epoch before chopping them into batches. So which examples share a batch, and therefore every g, is random.

questions.section: 3.1 The gradient as an average, and a cheap estimate of it
questions.question: Why is batching alone, with examples always fed in the same fixed order (e.g. sorted by topic or length), not true SGD?
options: Because fixed-order batches cannot be processed in parallel on a GPU without reshuffling first
Because each batch is then a biased sample, so g points toward what that slice wants
Because fixed-order batches make the averaged gradient exactly zero after one full epoch
Because the optimizer then requires a separately tuned learning rate for each fixed batch
questions.explanation: SGD's justification is that each batch is a random sample, so its average gradient is an unbiased estimate of the full gradient. With a fixed sorted order, consecutive batches come from one slice of the data, and g is biased toward that slice. Shuffling before each epoch restores randomness.

questions.section: 3.1 The gradient as an average, and a cheap estimate of it
questions.question: What is an epoch in minibatch training?
options: One optimizer step on one minibatch, followed by zeroing the gradients
The time it takes to compute one forward pass over a single batch of inputs
One full pass over the training data, after which indices are reshuffled
The number of optimizer steps between two consecutive learning-rate changes
questions.explanation: An epoch is one pass in which every example is used once. Before each epoch the example indices are randomly permuted and sliced into consecutive batches, so every example is seen once per epoch but the batch groupings change.

questions.section: 3.1 The gradient as an average, and a cheap estimate of it
questions.question: What does PyTorch's DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=2, shuffle=True) do at the start of each epoch?
options: Sorts the dataset by example length to reduce padding
Samples examples with replacement so some repeat within an epoch
Keeps the same batch groupings as the previous epoch
Draws torch.randperm(N) and slices the permutation into batches
questions.explanation: With shuffle=True the DataLoader draws a fresh random permutation of the N indices each epoch and slices it into consecutive batches of size 2. Every example is used exactly once per epoch, but which examples share a batch is random and changes between epochs.

questions.section: 3.1 The gradient as an average, and a cheap estimate of it
questions.question: How does LLM pretraining apply shuffling for SGD?
options: Documents are shuffled and seen about once, so each batch mixes sources like web, code and books
Documents are grouped by source so each batch contains only one source, such as all code or all books
Documents are sorted by quality score so the cleanest data is seen last, after the noisy web text
Shuffling is skipped because web-scale LLM datasets are already in an effectively random order
questions.explanation: Pretraining does the same thing as DataLoader shuffling at a larger scale: documents are shuffled and typically seen about once, so each batch is a random mix of web pages, code, books and so on. Grouping or sorting by source would bias each batch's gradient.

questions.section: 3.1 The gradient as an average, and a cheap estimate of it
questions.question: What is the strict meaning of 'stochastic' gradient descent versus 'minibatch SGD', and what does 'SGD' usually mean in practice?
options: Stochastic strictly means full-batch, minibatch means one example, and 'SGD' in practice means full-batch
Stochastic strictly means one example, minibatch SGD means many, and 'SGD' usually means minibatch
Stochastic strictly means momentum is used, minibatch means no momentum, and 'SGD' means the momentum one
Both strictly mean a batch of one example, and practitioners reserve 'SGD' for that single-example case
questions.explanation: Strictly, stochastic gradient descent uses a single example per step and minibatch SGD uses many. In practice everyone calls the minibatch version 'SGD'. Momentum is a separate addition and has nothing to do with the name.

questions.question: Why does noisy minibatch SGD beat exact full-batch gradient descent for a fixed compute budget?
options: Because the minibatch gradient is a more accurate estimate of the true gradient than the full average
Because minibatch steps automatically use a larger learning rate than full-batch steps would
Because you can take thousands of approximate steps instead of a few exact ones
Because minibatch SGD needs no backward pass, only forward passes on each small batch
questions.explanation: Each SGD step only roughly points downhill, but it costs |B| examples instead of N. For the same compute you take vastly more steps, and many approximate steps beat a few exact ones by a huge margin. The minibatch gradient is less accurate, not more.

questions.question: What benefit can the noise in SGD gradients provide beyond cheapness?
options: It guarantees convergence to the global minimum of the loss
It removes the need to choose or tune a learning rate at all
It makes the minibatch gradient exactly unbiased on every step
It can help training escape flat regions and poor sharp minima
questions.explanation: A little randomness in the gradient can push the parameters out of flat regions and poor sharp minima that an exact gradient might stay stuck in. It does not guarantee a global minimum, and unbiasedness comes from random sampling, not from the noise itself.

questions.question: How does the variance of the minibatch gradient estimate change with batch size |B|?
options: It falls like 1/|B|
It grows like |B|
It falls like 1/|B|^2
It is independent of batch size
questions.explanation: Averaging over more independent samples reduces the variance of the mean like 1/|B|. Larger batches therefore give less noisy gradients but cost proportionally more per step, making batch size a compute-versus-noise trade-off.

questions.question: What is the trade-off when choosing a larger batch size for SGD?
options: Larger batches give noisier gradients but are cheaper to compute per step
Larger batches give less noisy gradients but cost proportionally more per step
Larger batches change the expected value of the gradient toward the largest examples
Larger batches remove the need for shuffling since every batch covers the data
questions.explanation: A larger batch averages more samples, lowering gradient variance, but each step processes more examples and so costs more. The expected value is unchanged either way (both are unbiased), and shuffling is still needed for randomness.

questions.question: Does anyone compute a full-dataset gradient when training an LLM?
options: Yes, once per epoch, to recalibrate the learning rate against the true gradient
Yes, but only for the final step of training, to polish the converged weights
No; LLMs are trained with cheap random-minibatch estimates
Only when using momentum, to initialize the velocity buffer before the first step
questions.explanation: Every LLM is trained with SGD-style minibatch gradient estimates; nobody computes the full-dataset gradient. The update is the same theta <- theta - eta*g, just with g as an affordable random-minibatch estimate.

questions.question: In the from-scratch SGD optimizer's step() method, what does p.add_(g, alpha=-self.lr) do?
options: Adds the learning rate to every parameter
Returns a new tensor p + lr*g without modifying p
Sets the gradient to -lr * g
Updates p in place to p - lr * g
questions.explanation: Tensor.add_(other, alpha=a) computes p += a*other in place. With alpha = -lr this is p <- p - lr*g, the SGD update. The trailing underscore means in-place, so no new tensor is returned as a separate copy and .grad is not touched.

questions.question: Why does the from-scratch SGD step() skip parameters whose p.grad is None?
options: Because those parameters got no gradient (e.g. unused this pass), so nothing to apply
Because a None gradient means the parameter has already converged and should be frozen from now on
Because None gradients are produced only by bias terms, which plain SGD deliberately leaves untouched
Because skipping them speeds up the next backward pass by pruning those nodes from the graph
questions.explanation: A parameter whose .grad is None did not receive a gradient, for example because it was not used in the loss computation. There is no update to apply, so step() continues to the next parameter. It says nothing about convergence or about biases specifically.

questions.question: Why are the from-scratch optimizer's step() and zero_grad() methods decorated with @torch.no_grad()?
options: To run them on the CPU even when the model and gradients live on the GPU
So that the in-place parameter updates are not recorded by autograd
To make the methods run asynchronously on a separate CUDA stream from the forward pass
So that the gradients they read are promoted to double precision before use
questions.explanation: Optimizer updates mutate leaf parameters, and autograd must not track that arithmetic as part of the graph. The decorator disables gradient recording within those methods, the same reason a manual loop wraps the update in torch.no_grad().

questions.question: How is the from-scratch SGD optimizer verified to be correct?
options: By checking that the training loss reaches exactly zero on a small synthetic dataset
By comparing its final weights to a closed-form least-squares solution and nothing else
By a test that it reproduces torch.optim.SGD step-for-step on small linear regression
By visually inspecting the loss curve and confirming it decreases smoothly over time
questions.explanation: The test test_sgd_plain_matches_torch runs both optimizers on a small linear-regression problem and checks that every step matches. Matching the reference implementation step by step is a stronger check than looking at a loss curve or only the final result.

questions.question: Why is plain SGD slow on a loss surface shaped like a long narrow valley?
options: Because the gradient there is zero almost everywhere, so the updates stall completely
Because the valley floor has higher loss than the walls, so steps are pushed up the sides
Because the minibatch noise is largest in narrow valleys and swamps the true gradient
Because it zig-zags across the steep walls while creeping along the gentle floor
questions.explanation: In a narrow valley the gradient mostly points across the valley (the steep direction), so SGD bounces between the walls while making little progress along the floor toward the minimum. Plain SGD has no memory, so it cannot exploit the consistent along-valley direction.

questions.question: In a long narrow valley, why can't plain SGD simply use a larger learning rate to speed up progress along the gentle direction?
options: Because the steep direction limits eta: too large and it diverges across the valley
Because a larger eta would make the minibatch gradient biased toward the steep walls
Because a larger eta requires a proportionally larger batch size to remain stable at all
Because the gentle direction has no gradient, so no learning rate can move along it
questions.explanation: The steep direction has high curvature and is stable only for small eta. Raising eta to help the gentle direction makes the steep direction overshoot more each step and diverge. So the steep direction sets the speed limit and starves the gentle direction of progress.

questions.question: For plain gradient descent on f(x, y) = 0.5*(x^2 + 20*y^2), what is the stability limit on the learning rate, and which direction sets it?
options: eta < 2, set by the gentle x-direction with curvature 1
eta < 2/20 = 0.1, set by the steep y-direction
eta < 1/20 = 0.05, set by the x-direction's slow progress
eta < 20, set by the y-direction's curvature of 20
questions.explanation: For a quadratic with curvature L along a direction, gradient descent is stable for eta < 2/L. The y-direction has curvature 20, giving eta < 0.1; x has curvature 1, allowing eta < 2. The steepest direction sets the limit for the whole problem.

questions.question: Running plain SGD with eta = 0.095 on f(x, y) = 0.5*(x^2 + 20*y^2), the y-coordinate is multiplied by 1 - 0.095*20 = -0.9 each step. What does this mean for the y-motion?
options: y moves monotonically toward zero from one side, shrinking by 90% on each step
y grows by 90% each step and diverges to infinity after a few dozen iterations
y flips sign every step and shrinks only 10% each time: wasted oscillation
y stays constant at its starting value because the multiplier cancels the gradient
questions.explanation: A negative multiplier means each step jumps to the opposite wall, and |-0.9| = 0.9 means it shrinks by only 10% per step. That is oscillation across the valley that contributes little progress. Meanwhile x is multiplied by 0.905, a tiny move along the floor.

questions.question: In the narrow-valley example f(x, y) = 0.5*(x^2 + 20*y^2), what happens to the y-oscillation if eta is raised above 0.1?
options: The y-multiplier rises above 1, so y drifts slowly away from the valley floor
The oscillation vanishes because y reaches zero exactly in a single step
The x-direction becomes unstable first and diverges before y does anything
The y-multiplier falls below -1, so the bounce grows instead of shrinking
questions.explanation: The y-multiplier is 1 - 20*eta. At eta > 0.1 it is below -1, so each step flips sign and increases |y|, which diverges. The x-direction, with curvature 1, is still far from its own limit of 2, so it is not the first to fail.

questions.question: How does momentum fix the zig-zag behaviour of SGD in a narrow valley?
options: Across the valley gradients alternate and cancel in the running average; along it they add up
It computes the exact Hessian at each step and rescales every direction by its own curvature
It lowers the learning rate in the steep direction only, leaving the gentle direction unchanged
It detects gradients that point across the valley and discards them before applying the update
questions.explanation: Momentum steps along a running average of recent gradients. The oscillating across-valley components alternate sign and cancel, while the consistent along-valley component adds up and builds speed. It does not compute curvature or use per-direction learning rates; that per-parameter scaling is Adam's idea.

questions.section: 4.2 The mathematics: an exponential moving average of gradients
questions.question: What are the two update equations of SGD with momentum (coefficient mu, learning rate eta, gradient g, velocity v)?
options: v <- g - mu*v; theta <- theta + eta*v
v <- mu*v + g; theta <- theta - eta*v
v <- mu*g; theta <- theta - eta*(v + g)
v <- (1 - mu)*v; theta <- theta - eta*g
questions.explanation: Momentum keeps a velocity v of the same shape as theta, updates it with v <- mu*v + g (keep a fraction mu of the old velocity and add the new gradient), then steps theta <- theta - eta*v. Setting mu = 0 makes v = g and recovers plain SGD.

questions.section: 4.2 The mathematics: an exponential moving average of gradients
questions.question: What is the typical value and allowed range of the momentum coefficient mu?
options: Typically 0.1, in the range (1, 2)
Typically 1.0, exactly
Typically 0.9, in the range [0, 1)
Typically 0.5, in the range [-1, 1]
questions.explanation: mu lies in [0, 1) and is typically 0.9, meaning keep 90% of the accumulated velocity and add the new gradient. mu = 1 would never forget old gradients, and values at or above 1 make the velocity grow without bound.

questions.section: 4.2 The mathematics: an exponential moving average of gradients
questions.question: What does setting the momentum coefficient mu = 0 do?
options: It makes the velocity never change after the first step
It makes the update diverge
It doubles the effective learning rate
It recovers plain SGD, since v = g every step
questions.explanation: With mu = 0, v <- 0*v + g = g, so the step theta <- theta - eta*v is exactly plain SGD. The velocity carries no memory. This is why torch.optim.SGD's default momentum=0 gives plain SGD.

questions.section: 4.2 The mathematics: an exponential moving average of gradients
questions.question: How is the momentum velocity initialized on the very first step?
options: So that v = g, since there is no history yet
To a vector of ones with the same shape as the parameter
To the learning rate times g, so the first step is pre-scaled
To a random vector with the same norm as the first gradient g
questions.explanation: On the first step there are no past gradients, so the velocity is set equal to the current gradient, v = g. That is what torch.optim.SGD does, and it is why plain SGD and momentum produce identical first steps.

questions.section: 4.2 The mathematics: an exponential moving average of gradients
questions.question: Unrolling the momentum recursion v <- mu*v + g, how much does a gradient from k steps ago contribute to the current velocity?
options: k * g, so older gradients count linearly more the longer they stay in the buffer
mu^k * g, fading geometrically with age
g / k, fading harmonically so the weights sum to a fixed constant over time
Exactly g, regardless of age, because the velocity is a running sum of gradients
questions.explanation: Each step multiplies all old contributions by mu, so a gradient from k steps ago carries weight mu^k. This makes the velocity an exponential moving average: recent gradients dominate and older ones fade geometrically.

questions.section: 4.2 The mathematics: an exponential moving average of gradients
questions.question: With momentum coefficient mu = 0.9, roughly how often does a past gradient's influence on the velocity halve?
options: Every step, because 0.9 is close to one half
Every 2 steps, since 0.9^2 is about 0.5
Roughly every 7 steps
Roughly every 100 steps, since 1/(1-0.9)^2 = 100
questions.explanation: A gradient from k steps ago is weighted by 0.9^k, and 0.9^7 is about 0.48, so the weight halves roughly every 7 steps. That gives momentum a memory of a few tens of steps.

questions.section: 4.2 The mathematics: an exponential moving average of gradients
questions.question: What two effects does the momentum velocity have on the gradient signal?
options: It amplifies per-step noise while cancelling out any consistent gradient direction
It reverses the gradient direction every other step to damp oscillation across valleys
It normalizes every incoming gradient to unit length before adding it to the buffer
It smooths per-step noise and accumulates any consistent gradient component
questions.explanation: Because the velocity is an exponential moving average, random fluctuations average out while a consistent direction adds up across steps. Consistent directions get acceleration; oscillating ones get damped. It does not normalize gradient magnitudes.

questions.section: 4.2 The mathematics: an exponential moving average of gradients
questions.question: What extra state and hyperparameter does momentum add on top of plain SGD?
options: One velocity buffer v per parameter and one hyperparameter mu
Two parameter-sized buffers per parameter and two separate decay hyperparameters
No extra buffers at all, only one additional scalar hyperparameter for the decay
One scalar per layer plus a separate schedule that varies eta across training
questions.explanation: Momentum stores one extra buffer v, the same size as each parameter, and introduces one hyperparameter, the coefficient mu. Adam (03.2) is the one that stores two buffers per parameter.

questions.question: In the from-scratch momentum update, what does buf.mul_(self.momentum).add_(g) compute?
options: v <- mu*(v + g), written into a freshly allocated tensor each step
v <- mu*v + g, in place: scale the buffer by mu, then add the gradient
v <- v + mu*g, in place: add the momentum-scaled gradient to the buffer
v <- g - mu*v, written into a new tensor that then replaces the old buffer
questions.explanation: mul_ scales the existing buffer by mu in place, then add_ adds g in place, giving v <- mu*v + g. Both trailing-underscore operations modify buf directly, so no new tensor is allocated and the stored velocity is updated.

questions.question: Why does the from-scratch momentum implementation set buf = g.clone() on the first step instead of starting from a zero buffer and blending?
options: Because clone() is faster than allocating a zero buffer and then blending into it
Because a zero buffer would make the very first update diverge on steep losses
Because that is what torch.optim.SGD does, so the result matches it (to ~1e-6)
Because the gradient must be detached from the autograd graph before any blending
questions.explanation: Initializing the velocity to a copy of the first gradient reproduces torch.optim.SGD's behaviour, which is why the test test_sgd_momentum_matches_torch matches to about 1e-6. It encodes the rule that on the first step there is no history, so v = g exactly. The choice is about matching the reference, not about speed, stability, or autograd.

questions.question: Why does the from-scratch momentum code use g.clone() rather than simply storing g as the velocity buffer?
options: clone() casts the gradient to float64 so the velocity accumulates without rounding error
clone() moves the gradient to the CPU so the velocity buffer does not consume GPU memory
clone() detaches the gradient from the autograd graph, which is required inside no_grad
Storing g directly would alias p.grad, so in-place mul_/add_ would corrupt the gradient
questions.explanation: The velocity is modified in place each step. If it were the same tensor as p.grad, scaling the buffer would also overwrite the gradient, and resetting .grad would affect the velocity. clone() makes an independent copy with the same shape, dtype and device.

questions.section: 4.4 Worked example: momentum converges faster on an ill-conditioned quadratic
questions.question: What is the condition number of the quadratic f(x, y) = 0.5*(x^2 + 100*y^2)?
options: 100, the ratio of largest to smallest curvature
1, since the function is convex and has one minimum
10, the square root of the ratio of the curvatures
101, the sum of the curvatures along the two axes
questions.explanation: The curvatures are 1 in x and 100 in y, and the condition number is their ratio, 100. A large condition number means a stretched, ill-conditioned bowl where one direction is much steeper than another.

questions.section: 4.4 Worked example: momentum converges faster on an ill-conditioned quadratic
questions.question: On f(x, y) = 0.5*(x^2 + 100*y^2), why are plain SGD and SGD with momentum both run with eta = 0.0198?
options: Because momentum requires exactly half the plain-SGD learning rate, and 0.0198 is that half
For a fair comparison: same step just below the limit 2/100 = 0.02, so only momentum differs
Because 0.0198 is the optimal learning rate for momentum and plain SGD also converges best there
Because the gentle x-direction becomes unstable above 0.0198 and that limits both optimizers
questions.explanation: The steep y-direction (curvature 100) makes plain gradient descent stable only for eta < 0.02. Using 0.0198 for both optimizers keeps everything else equal, so any speed difference comes from momentum alone.

questions.section: 4.4 Worked example: momentum converges faster on an ill-conditioned quadratic
questions.question: On the ill-conditioned quadratic f(x, y) = 0.5*(x^2 + 100*y^2) with eta = 0.0198, roughly how much faster does SGD with momentum (mu = 0.9) reach loss below 1e-3 than plain SGD?
options: About the same speed, because both are bounded by the same stability limit
About 1.5 times faster, since momentum only helps the gentle direction
About 4.7 times faster (57 versus 269 steps)
About 100 times faster, matching the condition number of the quadratic
questions.explanation: Plain SGD needs 269 steps and momentum needs 57, about 4.7 times faster with the same learning rate. Momentum accumulates the small consistent gradient in the slow x-direction while damping the oscillating y-direction.

questions.section: 4.4 Worked example: momentum converges faster on an ill-conditioned quadratic
questions.question: On f(x, y) = 0.5*(x^2 + 100*y^2), why do plain SGD and SGD with momentum have exactly the same loss after the first step?
options: Because momentum is switched off for the first 10 steps while the buffer warms up
Because both optimizers use a learning rate of zero on the first step by convention
Because the gradient is zero at the chosen starting point, so neither one moves
Because v is initialized to g, so the first momentum step equals the plain step
questions.explanation: With v = g on the first step, the momentum update theta - eta*v is identical to theta - eta*g. Both runs therefore start at the same loss (48.50 in this example), and differences only appear once the velocity carries history.

questions.section: 4.4 Worked example: momentum converges faster on an ill-conditioned quadratic
questions.question: On a log-scale plot of loss versus step for plain SGD on an ill-conditioned quadratic, why does the curve look like a straight line?
options: Because every step multiplies the loss by the same factor, set by the slow direction
Because the loss decreases by the same constant amount on every step of the run
Because the gradient stays constant along the whole trajectory toward the minimum
Because the learning rate is decayed linearly, which appears straight on a log axis
questions.explanation: On a quadratic, each gradient-descent step multiplies each coordinate by a fixed factor; asymptotically the slow x-direction (factor 0.9802 here) dominates, so the loss shrinks by a constant ratio. Constant-ratio decay is a straight line on a log scale. A constant decrement would curve on a log plot.

questions.section: 4.4 Worked example: momentum converges faster on an ill-conditioned quadratic
questions.question: Why is the loss curve of SGD with momentum on an ill-conditioned quadratic wavy rather than smoothly decreasing?
options: Because fresh minibatch noise is added to the quadratic's gradient on every step
Because the velocity carries the point past the valley floor and back before settling
Because the learning rate itself oscillates between two values under the momentum rule
Because momentum resets the velocity buffer to zero every few steps, restarting progress
questions.explanation: Like a ball rolling downhill, the accumulated velocity carries the iterate past the minimum, then back, so the loss rises and falls. Even so, the peaks stay well below the plain-SGD curve. Momentum is not monotone; it is faster on average. The example uses exact gradients, so there is no minibatch noise.

questions.section: 4.4 Worked example: momentum converges faster on an ill-conditioned quadratic
questions.question: Is SGD with momentum guaranteed to decrease the loss at every step?
options: Yes, because the velocity only accumulates downhill gradients and so only moves downhill
Yes, as long as mu is strictly below 1 and eta is below the stability limit
No; it can overshoot and briefly raise the loss, but is faster on average
No; by design it increases the loss on every second step to escape local minima
questions.explanation: Momentum's velocity can carry the parameters past the valley floor, so the loss is not monotone. On the ill-conditioned quadratic its curve is wavy, but it still reaches the target far sooner than plain SGD. The overshoots are a side-effect, not a fixed alternating pattern.

questions.section: 4.4 Worked example: momentum converges faster on an ill-conditioned quadratic
questions.question: What does torch.optim.SGD(params, lr=eta, momentum=0.9) implement, and what does its default momentum value give?
options: Nesterov momentum by default; setting momentum=0 switches the optimizer to Adam
A dampened update v <- 0.9*v + 0.1*g; setting momentum=0 makes the step a no-op
Momentum applied to the loss, not the gradient; momentum=0 gives full-batch descent
v <- mu*v + g, theta <- theta - eta*v; the default momentum=0 gives plain SGD
questions.explanation: With dampening=0 and nesterov=False (the defaults), torch.optim.SGD uses v <- mu*v + g and theta <- theta - eta*v, the same update as the from-scratch class. Its default momentum=0 reduces it to plain SGD.

questions.section: 4.4 Worked example: momentum converges faster on an ill-conditioned quadratic
questions.question: Which torch.optim.SGD settings does the from-scratch momentum class match?
options: dampening=0 and nesterov=False, the common setting in practice
dampening=0.9 and nesterov=True, the PyTorch defaults for momentum
dampening=1 and nesterov=False, so the gradient is fully averaged
Any dampening value, as long as nesterov=True is also enabled
questions.explanation: PyTorch's SGD also offers nesterov=True (a lookahead variant) and a dampening factor. The from-scratch class implements the common case, dampening=0 and nesterov=False, which is what practitioners actually use.

questions.section: 4.4 Worked example: momentum converges faster on an ill-conditioned quadratic
questions.question: What is the nesterov=True option of torch.optim.SGD?
options: A way to decay the learning rate with a cosine schedule
A lookahead variant of momentum
A per-parameter adaptive scaling like RMSProp
A form of gradient clipping
questions.explanation: nesterov=True selects Nesterov momentum, a lookahead variant of the standard momentum update. It is not a schedule, adaptive scaling, or clipping. The from-scratch class does not implement it, matching the common nesterov=False setting.

questions.question: For a parameter tensor p of any shape, what are the shape, dtype and device of p.grad and of the momentum velocity buffer?
options: p.grad matches p, but the velocity is always a flat float64 CPU vector
Both are scalars on the CPU
Both have the same shape, dtype and device as p
p.grad is float16 on the GPU, and the velocity matches p
questions.explanation: There is one gradient number and one velocity number per parameter number, so both tensors have exactly the shape of p, with the same dtype (float32 in normal training) and on the same device. The optimizer never reshapes or moves them.

questions.question: Why can SGD and momentum be applied to any parameter tensor without knowing whether it is a matrix or a vector?
options: Because the optimizer first flattens all parameters into one long vector before updating
Because PyTorch converts every parameter to a 2-D matrix before the optimizer sees it
Because they update only the bias vectors and leave the weight matrices untouched
Because the updates are elementwise: no shape changes, reductions or broadcasts
questions.explanation: The update p.add_(v, alpha=-lr) acts on each element independently. Since nothing is reduced or broadcast and shapes never change, a (768, 768) weight and a (768,) bias are handled identically. No flattening is needed.

questions.question: How much optimizer state beyond parameters and gradients do plain SGD and SGD with momentum store?
options: Plain SGD stores nothing extra; momentum stores one parameter-sized velocity
Both store two parameter-sized tensors: a velocity and a running squared gradient
Plain SGD stores one parameter-sized tensor; momentum stores two of them
Both store only a single scalar per layer, used to rescale that layer's step
questions.explanation: Plain SGD needs no state beyond params and grads. Momentum adds one velocity tensor the size of the parameters, roughly doubling the optimizer's memory beyond params+grads. Adam, in contrast, stores two such buffers.

questions.question: Compared with SGD with momentum, how many parameter-sized optimizer buffers does Adam store?
options: Zero
Two
One
Four
questions.explanation: Momentum stores one parameter-sized buffer (the velocity), while Adam stores two (first and second moment estimates). Optimizer state like this is a major memory cost, and Module 9 is largely about which GPU holds these buffers when the model is split.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what one step() costs
questions.question: What is the compute cost of one optimizer step with momentum for a parameter tensor of P elements?
options: O(P^2), because it forms the outer product of the gradient with itself
O(P^3), because it inverts a P x P curvature matrix on every step
O(P): a few elementwise passes, negligible next to forward/backward
O(1), independent of the number of parameters, since it is one fused kernel
questions.explanation: A momentum step is one scale, one add for the velocity, and one fused multiply-add for the parameters: a handful of elementwise passes, so O(P). That is tiny compared with the forward and backward pass, which for a Transformer is dominated by large matrix multiplies.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what one step() costs
questions.question: What limits the speed of an optimizer step on a GPU?
options: The number of matrix multiplications it performs per parameter tensor
The time it takes to recompute the loss before each parameter update
The magnitude of the learning rate, since larger steps need more passes
Memory bandwidth: it streams parameter, gradient and velocity tensors once
questions.explanation: The optimizer does very little arithmetic per byte: it reads params, grads and the velocity and writes updated values. Its speed is therefore memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound. It performs no large matrix multiplies.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what one step() costs
questions.question: Why do optimizers use in-place operations like mul_, add_ and addcdiv_?
options: Fresh buffers every step on a billion-parameter model would thrash memory; in-place keeps it flat
In-place operations are the only operations that autograd is able to differentiate through
In-place operations automatically zero the gradients as a side effect of the update
In-place operations run in higher precision than out-of-place ones on the same hardware
questions.explanation: Modifying tensors in place avoids allocating new parameter-sized tensors each step. On models with billions of parameters, repeated allocation would churn memory; in-place updates keep the optimizer's footprint constant across training. They are actually done under no_grad, not differentiated.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what one step() costs
questions.question: What does optimizer.step() in any deep-learning framework actually do?
options: It recomputes the forward pass with the new weights to check the loss went down
It performs the elementwise update arithmetic, looped over parameter tensors
It computes the gradients via backpropagation and then writes them into .grad
It selects the next minibatch from the dataset and moves it to the device
questions.explanation: There is no hidden magic: step() loops over the parameter tensors and applies the update rule (plus any state updates like the velocity). Gradients come from backward(), and batches come from the data pipeline, not from step().

questions.question: For gradient descent on f(x) = x^2, the update is x_{t+1} = (1 - 2*eta)*x_t. What condition on the step multiplier r = 1 - 2*eta determines convergence?
questions.explanation: Since r does not depend on x, x_t = r^t * x_0, and r^t goes to zero exactly when |r| < 1. A negative r with |r| < 1 still converges, just by jumping to the other side each step. r = 1 means no movement at all.

questions.question: For gradient descent on f(x) = x^2, which range of learning rates converges?
options: 0 < eta < 2
eta > 1
0 < eta < 1
questions.explanation: Convergence needs |1 - 2*eta| < 1, i.e. -1 < 1 - 2*eta < 1. The right side gives eta > 0 and the left gives eta < 1. eta = 1 is the boundary. The general rule is eta < 2/L with curvature L = 2 for x^2.

questions.question: Running gradient descent on f(x) = x^2 from x = 5 with learning rate eta = 1.0 gives what behaviour?
options: The iterates bounce 5, -5, 5, -5 forever, never approaching the minimum
The iterates reach 0 in exactly one step, since the multiplier is zero
The iterates diverge to infinity, doubling in magnitude on every step
The iterates converge smoothly to 0 from one side, halving each step
questions.explanation: With eta = 1 the multiplier is r = 1 - 2 = -1, so x flips sign each step without shrinking. The step size equals twice the distance to the minimum, overshooting by exactly the same distance, and the loss stays at 25 forever. That is the stability boundary.

questions.question: For gradient descent on f(x) = x^2, which learning rate lands exactly on the minimum in one step?
options: eta = 0.1
eta = 0.5
eta = 0.9
eta = 1.0
questions.explanation: eta = 0.5 gives r = 1 - 2*0.5 = 0, so x_1 = 0 regardless of x_0. Smaller eta slides toward 0 gradually, eta = 0.9 overshoots but converges, and eta = 1.0 oscillates forever.

questions.question: For gradient descent on f(x) = x^2 with eta = 0.9 (multiplier r = -0.8), what do the iterates do?
options: Slide smoothly toward 0 from the same side, shrinking 20% each step
Diverge to plus or minus infinity, growing by 80% on every step
Overshoot to the other side each step but still converge
Stay stuck at the starting value because the multiplier cancels out
questions.explanation: A negative multiplier means each step jumps past the minimum to the other side, and |r| = 0.8 < 1 means each landing is closer: 5, -4, 3.2, -2.56. Overshooting alone is not divergence; divergence needs |r| > 1.

questions.question: For gradient descent on f(x) = x^2 with eta = 1.1, what happens?
options: The iterates converge, but slowly, shrinking by about 10% each step
The iterates reach 0 in exactly two steps by overshooting once
The iterates oscillate with constant amplitude between 5 and -5
They overshoot by more each step and diverge (5, -6, 7.2, -8.64, ...)
questions.explanation: eta = 1.1 gives r = 1 - 2.2 = -1.2. |r| > 1 means each step lands farther from the minimum on the opposite side, so the iterates grow without bound. Constant-amplitude oscillation happens only at exactly eta = 1.

questions.question: For a quadratic f = 0.5*L*x^2 with curvature L, what is the largest stable learning rate for gradient descent?
options: eta < 2/L
eta < L/2
eta < 1/L^2
eta < 2L
questions.explanation: The multiplier is r = 1 - eta*L, and |r| < 1 requires 0 < eta < 2/L. For x^2 (L = 2) this gives eta < 1. Steeper directions (larger L) allow a smaller maximum learning rate.

questions.question: In a multi-dimensional quadratic with different curvatures along different directions, which direction sets the maximum stable learning rate for gradient descent?
options: The flattest direction, since it needs the most progress and so tolerates the largest step
The steepest direction (largest curvature); it sets the limit for every direction
The direction along which parameters were initialized farthest from the minimum
The average curvature across all directions, weighted by how far each is from the minimum
questions.explanation: Each direction needs eta < 2/L_i, and a single learning rate must satisfy all of them, so the binding constraint is the largest curvature. That is why the steep y-direction forced eta < 0.1 for curvature 20 and eta < 0.02 for curvature 100.

questions.question: What does the sign and magnitude of the step multiplier r tell you about a gradient-descent step on a 1-D quadratic?
options: The sign says whether the loss increases after the step; the magnitude says by how much
The sign says whether eta is positive; the magnitude equals the loss after the step
