Negative r jumps past the minimum; |r| < 1, = 1 or > 1 says closer, same or farther
A negative r always means divergence, and any positive r means guaranteed convergence
questions.explanation: A negative multiplier sends x to the opposite side of the minimum. Its absolute value compares the new distance to the old one: below 1 converges, equal to 1 is stuck, above 1 diverges. A negative r alone does not imply divergence, as eta = 0.9 on x^2 shows.

questions.question: A training loop calls loss.backward() and opt.step() every iteration but never opt.zero_grad(). What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; PyTorch clears the gradients automatically as part of every step() call
The forward pass raises an error on the second iteration because .grad is already set
The learning rate is silently set to zero, so the parameters stop moving entirely
backward() accumulates into .grad, so step k uses the sum of all k gradients
questions.explanation: backward() adds the new gradient into .grad. Without zero_grad(), the gradient on step k is the sum of all previous batches' gradients, making the effective step erratic and often far too large, compounded by momentum. Neither step() nor backward() clears .grad automatically.

questions.question: Where should opt.zero_grad() be called in a standard training iteration?
options: At the start of each iteration, before the forward pass and backward()
Between loss.backward() and opt.step(), so the step sees clean gradients
Only once, before the training loop begins, since step() clears it afterward
Only at the end of each epoch, after the last batch has been processed
questions.explanation: Gradients must be cleared before each new backward() so that .grad holds only the current batch's gradient. Calling it between backward() and step() would erase the gradient before it is used, and calling it once or per epoch would still let gradients accumulate across iterations.

questions.question: Why is there a minus sign in the gradient-descent update theta <- theta - eta*grad L?
options: Because the learning rate is defined as a negative number and the sign makes the step positive
Because grad L points toward steepest increase, so we step the opposite way
Because the loss is always negative, so the minus sign turns its gradient back into a descent step
Because backpropagation returns the gradient with its sign flipped, and the minus sign undoes it
questions.explanation: The gradient points uphill, in the direction of steepest increase. Subtracting it turns that into a step downhill, which is what minimizing the loss requires. The learning rate is positive and backprop returns the true gradient.

questions.question: With momentum coefficient mu = 0.9, approximately what fraction of its original weight does a gradient from 10 steps ago still carry in the velocity?
options: About 90%
About 10%
About 35%
Essentially 0%
questions.explanation: Its weight is mu^10 = 0.9^10, about 0.349, so roughly 35%: still non-trivial. This long memory is what lets momentum accumulate consistent directions and average away noise.

questions.question: For a model with P parameters, how much extra memory does SGD with momentum need compared with plain SGD?
options: None; the velocity is stored inside .grad, overwriting the gradient each step
P^2 numbers for the curvature matrix that momentum uses to rescale the steps
Two tensors of P numbers: a velocity buffer and a copy of the previous gradient
One tensor of P numbers: the velocity, same shape/dtype/device as the params
questions.explanation: Momentum adds exactly one parameter-sized buffer, the velocity. Plain SGD needs nothing beyond params and grads. The velocity is a separate tensor; reusing .grad would be overwritten by the next backward pass.

questions.question: On an ill-conditioned quadratic with curvatures 1 and 100, why can't plain SGD be made faster simply by raising its learning rate above 0.02?
options: Because the steep direction (curvature 100) diverges for eta >= 2/100 = 0.02
Because the slow direction (curvature 1) diverges first once eta passes 0.02
Because learning rates above 0.02 make the gradient estimate biased toward the steep axis
Because torch.optim.SGD silently clips learning rates above 0.02 for quadratic losses
questions.explanation: Gradient descent is stable along a direction with curvature L only for eta < 2/L. The steep direction fixes eta < 0.02 for the whole problem, so raising eta to help the slow direction blows up the steep one. Momentum gains speed in the slow direction without raising eta.

questions.question: What limitation of momentum motivates per-parameter adaptive optimizers like RMSProp and Adam?
options: Momentum cannot be combined with minibatch gradients, so it fails once the data no longer fits
One global learning rate for all parameters, though large-gradient ones need smaller steps
Momentum requires computing the full Hessian, which is impossible at billions of parameters
Momentum is only guaranteed to work for convex losses, and transformer losses are non-convex
questions.explanation: Momentum smooths the gradient direction but still scales every parameter by the same eta. Parameters with large gradients and those with tiny gradients would benefit from different effective step sizes. RMSProp adds that per-parameter scaling; Adam combines it with momentum and bias correction, and AdamW fixes weight decay.

questions.question: Which optimizer is the default for essentially every large language model trained today, including GPT, LLaMA and OLMo?
options: AdamW
Plain SGD
SGD with Nesterov momentum
RMSProp without momentum
questions.explanation: AdamW, Adam with decoupled weight decay, is the standard optimizer for modern LLMs. Its adaptive per-parameter scaling lets one learning rate work across parameters with very different gradient magnitudes, and its decoupled decay regularizes every parameter cleanly.

questions.question: What property of AdamW lets a single global learning rate work across an embedding table, an attention projection and a LayerNorm gain?
options: Its use of second-order Hessian information per layer
Its adaptive per-parameter scaling of the step
Its large fixed learning rate shared by all layers
Its use of full-batch gradients instead of minibatches
questions.explanation: These parameter groups have wildly different gradient magnitudes. Adam-family optimizers divide each parameter's step by an estimate of its own recent gradient magnitude, so every parameter moves at a comparable relative pace under one eta. No Hessian is computed.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: one learning rate cannot fit every parameter
questions.question: Why can a single global learning rate not fit every parameter of a real network?
options: Because each layer is trained against a different loss function, so each needs its own rate
Because gradient scales differ hugely, so a rate safe for large ones is tiny for small ones
Because the learning rate must be an integer, which is too coarse to suit every parameter
Because every parameter receives an identical gradient, so one rate would move them in lockstep
questions.explanation: A rare-token embedding row gets tiny, sparse gradients, while a LayerNorm gain gets large, dense ones. An eta small enough for the large-gradient parameters barely moves the small-gradient ones, and an eta large enough for those blows up the others. One number cannot serve both.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: one learning rate cannot fit every parameter
questions.question: Which kind of parameter typically receives tiny, sparse gradients?
options: A LayerNorm gain, updated on every token
An attention output projection matrix
The final output layer's bias vector
An embedding row for a rare token
questions.explanation: An embedding row only receives a gradient when its token appears in the batch, so a rare token's row gets small, infrequent updates. A LayerNorm gain, in contrast, participates in every forward pass and gets large, dense gradients.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: one learning rate cannot fit every parameter
questions.question: What is the core idea behind adaptive optimizers like RMSProp and Adam?
options: Track each parameter's recent gradient magnitude and divide its step by it
Draw a different random learning rate for each parameter on every step of training
Freeze parameters whose gradients are small so the compute goes to the active ones
Clip each parameter's gradient to a fixed maximum so no single update can be too large
questions.explanation: Adaptive optimizers estimate how big each parameter's gradients have been lately and divide the step by that estimate. Large-gradient parameters take proportionally smaller steps, small-gradient ones take larger steps, so all move at a comparable relative pace under one global eta.

questions.question: What is the RMSProp update, with decay rate beta, gradient g, learning rate eta and small constant epsilon?
options: v <- beta*v + g; theta <- theta - eta*v, applied per parameter
v <- beta*v + (1-beta)*g^2; theta <- theta - eta*g/(sqrt(v) + epsilon)
v <- beta*v + (1-beta)*g; theta <- theta - eta*v/(|g| + epsilon)
v <- g^2; theta <- theta - eta*g*sqrt(v + epsilon) for every parameter
questions.explanation: RMSProp keeps an EMA v of the squared gradient and divides the step by its square root. The first option is momentum, which averages g itself rather than g^2. Multiplying by sqrt(v) would amplify large gradients instead of normalizing them.

questions.question: In RMSProp, why is the gradient squared elementwise before being averaged into v?
options: To make the averaging cheaper on GPUs, since squaring fuses with the EMA kernel
To make the update an unbiased estimate of the true full-batch gradient
So v tracks the gradient's magnitude regardless of sign
So that v grows linearly with the step count and acts as a built-in decay schedule
questions.explanation: Squaring each component removes the sign, so positive and negative gradients both contribute to the magnitude estimate rather than cancelling. v is therefore an estimate of the mean squared gradient, the typical size of the gradient.

questions.question: What is the typical value of RMSProp's decay rate beta, and what does it control?
options: 0.1, controlling how quickly the learning rate itself is decayed
0.5, controlling the size of epsilon added to the denominator
1.0, controlling how many examples go into each minibatch
0.99, controlling how far back the squared-gradient memory reaches
questions.explanation: beta is typically 0.99. Like momentum's mu, it sets the effective memory of the exponential moving average: higher beta averages over more past steps.

questions.question: Where does the name 'RMSProp' come from?
options: sqrt(v), the root of the EMA of squared gradients, is roughly the RMS gradient
It stands for 'Random Minibatch Stochastic Propagation', the sampling scheme it relies on
It refers to the root of the mean squared error loss that the optimizer was designed to minimize
It uses the root-mean-square of the parameters themselves to scale each update step
questions.explanation: v estimates the mean squared gradient, so sqrt(v) is roughly the RMS gradient magnitude, which is what the step is divided by. It concerns the gradient, not the parameters or the loss function.

questions.question: What is the purpose of epsilon (e.g. 1e-8) in the RMSProp and Adam denominators?
options: To set the learning rate for parameters with zero gradient
To avoid dividing by zero when v is small
To add regularization toward zero
To bias-correct the moment estimates
questions.explanation: epsilon is a tiny constant added to sqrt(v) so the division stays finite when a parameter's squared-gradient estimate is near zero. It is not a regularizer and has nothing to do with bias correction.

questions.question: In RMSProp, if a parameter's gradients have recently been large, what happens to its step?
options: It is scaled up, because a large sqrt(v) multiplies the gradient
It is unchanged, because RMSProp uses a single global step size
It is scaled down, since g is divided by a large sqrt(v)
It becomes exactly zero until the recent gradients shrink again
questions.explanation: The step is g/(sqrt(v)+epsilon). A history of large gradients makes sqrt(v) large, shrinking the step. Conversely, a history of tiny gradients makes sqrt(v) tiny, scaling the step up.

questions.question: In RMSProp's steady state, where the gradient is roughly constant at g, what is the ratio g/sqrt(v) approximately, and what does the step size then depend on?
options: Approximately g^2; the step then grows quadratically with the gradient magnitude
Approximately 0; the step vanishes once v has fully absorbed the constant gradient
Approximately 1/g; larger gradients then give smaller steps than smaller gradients
About plus or minus 1; the step depends on sign and consistency, not magnitude
questions.explanation: With a constant gradient, v converges to g^2, so sqrt(v) is about |g| and g/sqrt(v) is about +/-1. The step is then roughly eta in the gradient's sign direction, independent of how large the gradient is. That is the per-parameter normalization adaptive methods aim for.

questions.question: What does RMSProp lack on its own that Adam adds back?
options: Momentum's smoothing of the gradient direction
Per-parameter adaptive scaling of each step
A global learning rate that scales every update
Elementwise operations that keep the step O(P)
questions.explanation: RMSProp is the adaptive-scaling half of Adam: it normalizes step magnitudes but steps along the raw gradient direction. Adam adds a momentum-like EMA of the gradient in the numerator to smooth the direction.

questions.question: What are the two exponential moving averages Adam keeps per parameter?
options: The parameter value and its squared value, used to normalize the weights
The first moment m (EMA of g) and second moment v (EMA of g^2)
The loss and its gradient, averaged over the recent minibatches
The gradient and the learning rate, both smoothed per parameter
questions.explanation: Adam updates m <- beta1*m + (1-beta1)*g, the smoothed direction like momentum, and v <- beta2*v + (1-beta2)*g^2, the magnitude estimate like RMSProp. Both are per-parameter tensors.

questions.question: In Adam, how does the first moment m relate to momentum's velocity?
options: It is unrelated; m tracks the squared gradient while v tracks the direction
It is identical to momentum's velocity, an unscaled running sum of past gradients
It is momentum's velocity with the (1 - beta1) factor: an EMA of g
It is momentum's velocity divided by the learning rate so eta can be tuned separately
questions.explanation: m is an EMA of the gradient, the same idea as momentum's velocity, but with g weighted by (1 - beta1) so m is a true average rather than a growing sum. It represents the smoothed update direction.

questions.question: What are Adam's standard decay rates beta1 and beta2, and what do they imply about memory?
options: beta1 = 0.999 and beta2 = 0.9: long direction memory, short magnitude memory
beta1 = beta2 = 0.5: equally short memories for both direction and magnitude
beta1 = 0.1 and beta2 = 0.01: almost no memory, so each step uses the raw gradient
beta1 = 0.9 and beta2 = 0.999: short direction memory, long magnitude memory
questions.explanation: The standard values are beta1 = 0.9 for the gradient EMA and beta2 = 0.999 for the squared-gradient EMA. A higher beta averages over more steps, so the magnitude estimate reaches much further back than the direction estimate.

questions.question: How are Adam's moment estimates m and v initialized?
options: Both to zero
m to zero and v to one
Both to the first gradient
Both to random small values
questions.explanation: Both moments start at zero. Because an EMA starting from zero underestimates the true average until it fills up, this initialization creates the startup bias that bias correction removes.

questions.question: Why are Adam's moment estimates biased toward zero early in training?
options: Because the gradients are always near zero at the start of training
Because they start at zero and the EMA has not had time to fill up
Because epsilon dominates the denominator during the early steps of training
Because the learning rate is exactly zero at step one, so nothing accumulates
questions.explanation: An EMA initialized to zero gives most of its weight to that initial zero for the first steps. After one step, m = (1 - beta1)*g = 0.1*g, only a tenth of the gradient purely because it started from nothing. This is a startup bias, not a property of the gradients.

questions.question: With beta1 = 0.9 and m initialized to zero, what is m after the first Adam step with gradient g?
options: m = g
questions.explanation: m <- 0.9*0 + 0.1*g = 0.1*g. Only a tenth of the gradient appears, purely because the EMA started at zero. Without correction, Adam would take tiny, wrong steps in the first iterations.

questions.question: What are Adam's bias-corrected moments at step t?
options: m_hat = m*(1 - beta1^t), v_hat = v*(1 - beta2^t)
m_hat = m/beta1^t, v_hat = v/beta2^t
m_hat = m - beta1^t, v_hat = v - beta2^t
m_hat = m/(1 - beta1^t), v_hat = v/(1 - beta2^t)
questions.explanation: Dividing by 1 - beta^t undoes the shrinkage from zero initialization. At t = 1 with beta1 = 0.9, 1 - 0.9 = 0.1, so m_hat = 10*m, exactly cancelling the 0.1 factor. Multiplying would make the bias worse.

questions.question: What happens to Adam's bias-correction factors 1/(1 - beta^t) as the step number t grows?
options: They approach 1, since beta^t goes to 0 once the averages warm up
They grow without bound, so late steps must be clipped to stay stable
They approach 0, gradually turning the update off as training goes on
They oscillate between 0.1 and 10 with a period set by the ratio of beta1 to beta2
questions.explanation: Since beta < 1, beta^t shrinks toward zero, so 1 - beta^t approaches 1 and the correction disappears. Correction matters only early, while the EMAs are still filling up.

questions.question: In Adam's bias correction, what value does the step counter t start from?
options: The number of warmup steps
questions.explanation: t starts at 1 for the first step. At t = 1, 1 - beta1^1 = 0.1, which exactly cancels the factor 0.1 in m after its first update. Starting at 0 would divide by 1 - beta^0 = 0.

questions.question: What is the full Adam parameter update?
options: theta <- theta - eta*m/(v + epsilon), using the raw moments
theta <- theta - eta*(m_hat + sqrt(v_hat)) for every parameter
theta <- theta - eta*m_hat/(sqrt(v_hat) + epsilon)
theta <- theta - eta*g*sqrt(v_hat)/(m_hat + epsilon) elementwise
questions.explanation: Adam divides the bias-corrected first moment by the square root of the bias-corrected second moment plus epsilon, and steps by eta times that ratio. The numerator is momentum's smoothed direction, the denominator RMSProp's per-parameter scale.

questions.question: In the Adam update, which component plays the role of momentum and which plays the role of RMSProp?
options: epsilon plays the momentum role and eta plays the RMSProp per-parameter scale
The denominator sqrt(v_hat) is the momentum; the numerator m_hat is the RMSProp scale
Both terms are RMSProp scales; Adam has no momentum component at all
The numerator m_hat is the momentum; the denominator sqrt(v_hat) is the RMSProp scale
questions.explanation: Adam is momentum in the numerator and RMSProp in the denominator, both bias-corrected. m_hat gives the smoothed direction, sqrt(v_hat) normalizes each parameter's step by its RMS gradient magnitude.

questions.section: 3.4 One full Adam step, by hand
questions.question: On Adam's very first step (t = 1), what are m_hat and sqrt(v_hat) in terms of the gradient g?
options: m_hat = g and sqrt(v_hat) = |g| exactly
m_hat = 0.1*g and sqrt(v_hat) = 0.001*|g|
m_hat = g^2 and sqrt(v_hat) = g
m_hat = 0 and sqrt(v_hat) = epsilon
questions.explanation: At t = 1, m = (1-beta1)*g and dividing by (1-beta1) gives m_hat = g. Likewise v = (1-beta2)*g^2 so v_hat = g^2 and sqrt(v_hat) = |g|. Bias correction fully undoes the zero initialization after one step.

questions.section: 3.4 One full Adam step, by hand
questions.question: How far does Adam move each parameter on its very first step, ignoring epsilon?
options: By eta times the gradient, exactly as plain SGD would on its first step
By almost exactly eta along -sign(g), whatever the gradient magnitude
By zero, since both moment estimates start at zero and cancel each other
By eta divided by the gradient magnitude, so small gradients take huge steps
questions.explanation: At t = 1, m_hat/sqrt(v_hat) = g/|g| = sign(g), so the step is eta*sign(g). A gradient of 0.0001 moves a parameter as far as a gradient of 50. This is adaptive normalization at its most extreme.

questions.section: 3.4 One full Adam step, by hand
questions.question: Running torch.optim.Adam for one step on theta = 1.0 with gradient 0.5, lr = 0.1 and standard betas, what does it produce, and how does it compare to the hand calculation?
options: About 0.95, half the hand-computed step because PyTorch omits bias correction
About 0.5, because the first step equals the gradient regardless of the learning rate
About 0.9000000358, matching the hand result 0.900000002 to ~1e-7
Exactly 1.0, because PyTorch skips the first step while the moments initialize
questions.explanation: The hand computation gives theta = 1 - 0.1*0.5/(0.5 + 1e-8), about 0.900000002. torch.optim.Adam prints 0.9000000357627869, which agrees to float32 precision (about 1e-7). The first-step move is eta = 0.1, not proportional to the gradient.

questions.section: 3.4 One full Adam step, by hand
questions.question: Does the Adam algorithm itself contain a learning-rate warmup?
options: Yes, the bias correction ramps the effective step up from zero, acting as a built-in warmup
Yes, epsilon starts large and ramps down over the first steps so early updates stay small
Yes, beta2 gradually increases from 0 to 0.999 over the first few thousand steps
No; warmup is a separate technique that changes the eta passed in
questions.explanation: The whole Adam algorithm is the moments, bias correction and update; there is no warmup inside it. Warmup is applied outside by feeding Adam a small eta that grows over the first few hundred or thousand steps. Bias correction fixes the zero-init bias but makes the first step full size, which is the opposite of warming up.

questions.section: 3.4 One full Adam step, by hand
questions.question: Why can Adam's first few steps be harmful for a large model?
options: Every parameter moves a full eta from a v built on one noisy minibatch, when gradients are noisiest
The moments start at zero, so the model does not move at all for the first several hundred steps
The gradients are clipped to exactly zero during the first steps while the moments initialize
Bias correction makes the first steps far smaller than later ones, wasting the start of training
questions.explanation: At t = 1 each parameter moves by about eta regardless of its gradient size, and the scaling comes from v_hat estimated from a single noisy batch, so it is basically a guess. Combined with random weights and very noisy early gradients, these big same-sized steps can push the model into a bad region or spike the loss.

questions.section: 3.4 One full Adam step, by hand
questions.question: How does learning-rate warmup address Adam's risky first steps?
options: It replaces Adam's update rule with plain SGD for the first steps, then switches over
It starts eta tiny and ramps it up, so v_hat becomes trustworthy before steps grow
It disables bias correction during the first steps so the moment estimates stay small
It increases epsilon for the first steps so the denominator dominates and damps updates
questions.explanation: Warmup keeps Adam's code unchanged and only varies the eta passed in: tiny at first, ramping up over the first few hundred or thousand steps. By the time steps are large, the second-moment estimate is averaged over many batches and reliable.

questions.question: What is weight decay for?
options: To speed up convergence by increasing the effective step size on large parameters
To normalize the gradients across layers so every layer learns at the same rate
To pull every parameter gently toward zero, discouraging large weights that overfit
To reset parameters that stop changing back to their initial values so they can relearn
questions.explanation: Weight decay is a regularizer: every step it shrinks parameters slightly toward zero. Large weights tend to overfit, so discouraging them improves generalization. It is not a step-size or normalization technique.

questions.question: Are classic L2 regularization and decoupled weight decay equivalent when used with Adam?
options: Yes; they produce identical updates for every optimizer, including Adam
Yes, but only when the learning rate is held constant throughout training
No, and they are equivalent only for RMSProp, never for momentum SGD or Adam
No; with Adam they differ, which is why AdamW exists
questions.explanation: With Adam the two implementations diverge because Adam rescales the gradient by sqrt(v_hat). Folding decay into the gradient passes it through that rescaling, while decoupled decay does not. This subtlety cost the field several years and motivated AdamW.

questions.section: 4.2 Classic L2 (weight decay in the gradient)
questions.question: How does classic L2 regularization implement weight decay?
options: It adds (lambda/2)*||theta||^2 to the loss, so lambda*theta joins the gradient
It multiplies the parameters by (1 - lambda) after each optimizer step, outside the gradient
It subtracts lambda from the learning rate each step, so later updates shrink steadily
It divides the gradient by lambda*theta, so large weights receive proportionally smaller updates
questions.explanation: Classic L2 adds a squared-norm penalty to the loss. Its gradient lambda*theta joins the ordinary gradient before the optimizer sees it, and Adam then runs on g'. Multiplying the parameters directly is the decoupled (AdamW) approach.

questions.section: 4.2 Classic L2 (weight decay in the gradient)
questions.question: Why is classic L2 regularization problematic when combined with Adam?
options: Because an L2 penalty has no gradient, so Adam cannot see it at all
Because lambda*theta is divided by sqrt(v_hat), coupling decay to gradient size
Because Adam ignores any extra term that is added to the raw gradient
Because the L2 term makes the loss non-differentiable at theta = 0 for Adam
questions.explanation: Adam divides the whole gradient, including lambda*theta, by sqrt(v_hat), and the decay term also inflates v_hat. Parameters with large gradients get their decay divided down, so the amount of regularization depends on gradient magnitude rather than being uniform.

questions.section: 4.2 Classic L2 (weight decay in the gradient)
questions.question: Under classic L2 regularization with Adam, which parameters end up receiving the least decay?
options: Parameters with the smallest gradients, whose sqrt(v_hat) amplifies the decay term
Parameters closest to zero, since lambda*theta is already tiny for them
Parameters with large gradients (large sqrt(v_hat)), which most need it
All parameters receive exactly the same decay, independent of their gradients
questions.explanation: A large sqrt(v_hat) divides down the decay term along with the gradient. So parameters with large gradients, which are those that most need regularizing, receive the least effective decay. That coupling is a bug, not a feature.

questions.question: What is the AdamW weight-decay update?
options: theta <- theta - eta*(g + lambda*theta)/(sqrt(v_hat) + epsilon), all in one step
theta <- theta + eta*lambda*theta, then the Adam step on g + lambda*theta
theta <- theta/(1 + lambda), skipping the Adam step whenever decay is applied
theta <- theta*(1 - eta*lambda), then the ordinary Adam step on pure g
questions.explanation: AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) applies decay directly to the parameter, outside the Adam machinery, then runs Adam on the unmodified gradient. The first option is classic L2 folded into Adam, which AdamW was designed to replace.

questions.question: In AdamW, what does decoupled weight decay do to each parameter per step?
options: Shrinks every parameter by the same fraction eta*lambda, leaving g and moments alone
Shrinks each parameter by an amount proportional to its current gradient magnitude
Adds lambda*theta to the first moment only, leaving the second moment unchanged
Sets parameters below a threshold exactly to zero, producing a sparse weight matrix
questions.explanation: Decoupled decay multiplies each parameter by (1 - eta*lambda), a uniform fractional shrink. Because it never enters g, m or v, every parameter receives exactly the intended regularization regardless of its gradient size.

questions.question: Who introduced AdamW and in what year?
options: Kingma & Ba, 2015
Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019
Hinton & Tieleman, 2012
Vaswani et al., 2017
questions.explanation: AdamW, Adam with decoupled weight decay, is from Loshchilov & Hutter (2019). Kingma & Ba introduced the original Adam, and Vaswani et al. introduced the Transformer.

questions.question: What is a typical value for AdamW's weight-decay coefficient lambda in LLM training?
questions.explanation: lambda is typically 0.1. With a learning rate eta, each step shrinks parameters by the fraction eta*lambda. 0.999 is beta2 and 1e-8 is epsilon.

questions.question: In AdamW, what are the moment estimates m and v computed from?
options: From g + lambda*theta, as in classic L2
From the parameters theta, not the gradient
From the decay term lambda*theta alone
From the pure gradient g alone
questions.explanation: In AdamW the EMAs are computed from g alone; weight decay never enters them. That is what makes the decay decoupled and keeps Adam's per-parameter normalization from distorting it.

questions.question: For one step from theta = 1.0 with g = 0.5, eta = 0.1, lambda = 0.1 at t = 1, where do AdamW and Adam-with-classic-L2 land?
options: AdamW at about 0.890, classic L2 at about 0.900
Both at about 0.890, since the decay is identical
AdamW at about 0.900, classic L2 at about 0.890
Both at about 0.900, since the decay is negligible
questions.explanation: AdamW first shrinks theta to 0.99, then the Adam step subtracts about 0.1, giving 0.890. Classic L2 runs Adam on g' = 0.6, but at t = 1 the step is eta*0.6/0.6 = 0.1, giving 0.900. The decay vanished in Adam's normalization.

questions.question: In the one-step comparison, why did classic L2 decay have almost no effect on the Adam update?
options: Because lambda was set to zero for the comparison, so no decay was ever added
Because sqrt(v_hat) grew with the numerator and cancelled the added lambda*theta
Because the combined gradient g + lambda*theta was clipped to the same norm as g
Because PyTorch ignores weight decay on the first step while the moments warm up
questions.explanation: Adding lambda*theta raised the gradient from 0.5 to 0.6, but sqrt(v_hat) also became 0.6, so the ratio stayed 1 and the step stayed eta. The decay was swallowed by Adam's normalization. AdamW applies its 1% shrink outside that ratio.

questions.question: What does torch.optim.AdamW(lr=0.1, betas=(0.9, 0.999), eps=1e-8, weight_decay=0.1) give after one step on w = 1.0 with gradient 0.5?
options: About 0.900, identical to Adam without any decay
About 0.99, the decay alone with no Adam step
About 0.890, matching the hand-computed result
About 0.80, double the Adam step because of decay
questions.explanation: PyTorch prints about 0.89000004529953, matching the hand computation 0.890000002: shrink by (1 - 0.1*0.1) to 0.99, then subtract the Adam step of about 0.1.

questions.question: In what order does the from-scratch AdamW (matching torch.optim.AdamW) apply its operations each step?
options: The Adam step first, then weight decay applied to the stored gradient
Bias-correct the stored buffers, then decay, then update the moments
Update the moments from g + lambda*theta, then take the parameter step
Decoupled decay on the parameter first, then the Adam step on pure g
questions.explanation: torch.optim.AdamW shrinks the parameter by (1 - lr*weight_decay) first, then updates m and v from the pure gradient and applies the bias-corrected step. Matching this order is what lets the from-scratch version match PyTorch to 1e-5.

questions.question: How does the from-scratch AdamW apply bias correction?
options: In the step: lr/bias_correction1 and sqrt(v)/sqrt(bias_correction2) + eps; m, v stay raw
By overwriting m and v with their bias-corrected values at the end of every step
By dividing the incoming gradient by bias_correction1 before it is folded into m
By multiplying the learning rate by bias_correction2 and leaving the denominator untouched
questions.explanation: Folding the corrections into step_size and denom gives exactly eta*m_hat/(sqrt(v_hat)+eps) while leaving m and v biased. The stored buffers must stay biased to keep accumulating correctly; overwriting them would compound the correction.

questions.question: Why must Adam's stored buffers m and v stay uncorrected (biased) rather than being overwritten with m_hat and v_hat?
options: Because the corrected values need float64 storage and would double the optimizer memory
Because the EMA must keep accumulating the biased quantity, or corrections compound
Because PyTorch forbids in-place writes to optimizer state between consecutive steps
Because the corrected values are always zero after the first step and carry no information
questions.explanation: The bias-correction formula assumes m and v are the raw zero-initialized EMAs. If the buffer holds m_hat, the next EMA update mixes in a corrected value and the next correction is applied on top, distorting the step. Apply the correction only when computing the step.

questions.question: What does v.addcmul_(g, g, value=c) compute?
options: v = c*g + g, returning a new tensor and leaving v unchanged
v = v*c*g, computed in place with no temporary allocation
v += c*g*g in one fused in-place pass with no temporary
v = sqrt(v) + c*g, writing the result back into v in place
questions.explanation: addcmul_ is a fused in-place multiply-add: it adds value times the elementwise product of its two tensor arguments to v. Called with g, g it adds c*g^2, which is the second-moment update (after scaling v by beta2).

questions.question: What does p.addcdiv_(m, denom, value=-step_size) compute in the from-scratch AdamW?
options: p = m/denom, overwriting the parameter with the ratio
p += step_size*denom/m, in one fused in-place pass
p -= step_size*m*denom, in one fused in-place pass
p -= step_size*m/denom, in one fused in-place pass
questions.explanation: addcdiv_ is a fused in-place divide-add: p += value*(m/denom). With value = -step_size this is the Adam parameter update theta -= (lr/bc1)*m/(sqrt(v)/sqrt(bc2) + eps).

questions.question: In the from-scratch AdamW, how is decoupled weight decay applied to parameter p?
options: p.mul_(1.0 - self.lr * self.weight_decay), without touching g
g.add_(p, alpha=self.weight_decay) before the moments are updated
m.add_(p, alpha=self.weight_decay) after the first moment is updated
p.sub_(self.weight_decay) once per step, before the Adam update
questions.explanation: The parameter is scaled in place by (1 - lr*weight_decay), which is theta <- theta*(1 - eta*lambda). Adding p to g would be classic L2; adding it to m would also couple decay to the Adam machinery.

questions.question: How is the from-scratch AdamW verified against PyTorch?
options: By comparing only the final loss after training to the PyTorch run's final loss
By a test that it matches torch.optim.AdamW to 1e-5 over five toy steps
By checking that every weight decays to exactly zero after enough training steps
By a visual comparison of the two loss curves plotted on the same axes
questions.explanation: The test test_adamw_matches_torch_over_5_steps runs both optimizers on a toy linear-regression problem and checks they agree to 1e-5 at each of five steps. Step-by-step agreement verifies the operation order and bias-correction handling.

questions.section: 6. Tensor shapes, dtype, device, and cost
questions.question: For a parameter tensor p, what are the shapes, dtype and device of AdamW's state m and v, and of the step counter t?
options: m and v are scalars per tensor; t has the same shape as p
m matches p; v is a flat float64 vector on the CPU to save GPU memory
m and v match p's shape, dtype and device; t is one shared int
m and v are per-layer scalars; t is a float32 tensor on the GPU
questions.explanation: AdamW is elementwise: m and v are full parameter-sized tensors matching p. The step counter t is one Python int shared across parameters, and the bias-correction factors computed from it are scalars.

questions.section: 6. Tensor shapes, dtype, device, and cost
questions.question: For a model with P parameters in float32 trained with AdamW, how many bytes are needed for parameters, gradients and optimizer state, before activations?
options: 4P bytes
8P bytes
12P bytes
16P bytes
questions.explanation: Parameters take 4P bytes, gradients 4P, and the two optimizer buffers m and v another 8P, totalling 16P bytes. Activations come on top of that.

questions.section: 6. Tensor shapes, dtype, device, and cost
questions.question: What do ZeRO and FSDP shard across GPUs to address Adam's memory cost?
options: The optimizer state (m and v, 2x the parameters), too large for one device
The learning-rate schedule, so each GPU follows its own warmup and decay
The training dataset only, with every GPU holding a full copy of the model
The loss function's computation graph, split layer by layer across GPUs
questions.explanation: Adam's two parameter-sized buffers are a large, fixed memory cost. ZeRO and FSDP (Module 9) split this optimizer state, along with params and grads, across devices because for large models it cannot fit on one GPU.

questions.section: 6. Tensor shapes, dtype, device, and cost
questions.question: How do the optimizer-state memory costs of plain SGD, momentum-SGD and Adam/AdamW compare?
options: All three store two parameter-sized buffers, so their optimizer memory is equal
Plain SGD stores none, momentum-SGD one, Adam/AdamW two buffers
Plain SGD stores one, momentum-SGD two, and Adam/AdamW four parameter-sized buffers
Adam stores none because it uses the gradient directly, while momentum-SGD stores one
questions.explanation: Plain SGD keeps no state beyond params and grads. Momentum adds a velocity buffer. Adam and AdamW keep both m and v. Adam's adaptivity is paid for in memory.

questions.section: 6. Tensor shapes, dtype, device, and cost
questions.question: What limits the speed of an AdamW optimizer step?
options: Large matrix multiplications over the parameter tensors and their moments
The number of distinct parameter tensors, not their total size
Memory bandwidth: O(P) elementwise work streaming params, grads, m, v
The cost of computing the Hessian diagonal that rescales each step
questions.explanation: An AdamW step is O(P) elementwise arithmetic, negligible compared with forward and backward. It is memory-bandwidth-bound because it reads and writes params, grads, m and v once each with little computation per byte.

questions.question: Ignoring epsilon, why does Adam's first step have magnitude exactly eta for any nonzero gradient g?
options: Because the learning rate is normalized by the global gradient norm before the first step
Because Adam clips the first update to a maximum of eta to protect random initial weights
Because epsilon dominates the denominator at t = 1 and fixes the step size to eta
Because at t = 1 m_hat = g and sqrt(v_hat) = |g|, so the step is eta*sign(g)
questions.explanation: At t = 1, m = (1-beta1)g gives m_hat = g, and v = (1-beta2)g^2 gives v_hat = g^2. The ratio is g/|g| = sign(g), so the step has magnitude eta whatever the gradient's size. No clipping or gradient-norm normalization is involved.

questions.question: Which separate technique, not part of Adam, addresses the problem that Adam's earliest steps are full-size and based on an unreliable second-moment estimate?
options: Learning-rate warmup: start eta small and ramp it up
Gradient checkpointing of the first few transformer layers
Raising beta2 to 0.9999 for the opening steps
Removing bias correction so early steps shrink
questions.explanation: Warmup feeds Adam a small learning rate that rises over the first steps, so the large fixed-size steps only happen once v_hat is a trustworthy average. Adam's rule is unchanged; only eta varies. Gradient checkpointing saves activation memory and is unrelated.

questions.question: Which parameters are usually excluded from weight decay in practice?
options: The attention query, key and value weight matrices
Biases, LayerNorm gains and embeddings
The MLP up- and down-projection weight matrices
The attention and MLP output projection matrices
questions.explanation: Practice is to decay weight matrices but not biases, LayerNorm gains or embeddings. Decaying a 1-D gain toward zero just fights the normalization. Frameworks split parameters into two groups for this.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to apply weight decay to a LayerNorm gain?
options: Because LayerNorm gains receive no gradient, so decay would be the only update
Because decaying the gain makes the loss non-differentiable at zero
Because decaying a 1-D gain toward zero just fights the normalization
Because LayerNorm gains are stored in integer format and cannot shrink
questions.explanation: A LayerNorm gain sets the scale of normalized activations; pulling it toward zero works against the normalization's purpose rather than regularizing meaningful weights. That is why gains, biases and embeddings are typically put in a no-decay parameter group.

questions.question: What does passing weight_decay to torch.optim.Adam (rather than AdamW) give you?
options: Exactly AdamW's decoupled decay, applied to the parameters
No decay at all; torch.optim.Adam ignores that argument
Decay applied only to biases, leaving weight matrices alone
Classic coupled L2, with lambda*theta folded into g
questions.explanation: torch.optim.Adam's weight_decay adds lambda*theta to the gradient, the coupled version whose decay is distorted by Adam's normalization. Only torch.optim.AdamW applies decoupled decay. Calling the former 'AdamW' is a common mistake.

questions.question: What does the denominator sqrt(v_hat) + epsilon accomplish in the Adam update?
options: A per-parameter step size, dividing by its RMS gradient; epsilon avoids division by zero
It applies weight decay to each parameter in proportion to its squared gradient magnitude
It smooths the gradient direction across steps, filling the role that momentum plays in SGD
It bias-corrects the first moment so early updates are not shrunk toward zero
questions.explanation: sqrt(v_hat) estimates each parameter's RMS gradient, so dividing by it scales large-gradient parameters' steps down and small-gradient ones up. Smoothing the direction is the job of m_hat in the numerator. epsilon only guards against tiny denominators.

questions.question: Why is the second-moment underestimate especially damaging if Adam's bias correction is omitted?
options: Because beta2 = 0.999 is so close to 1 that v warms up very slowly
Because v is initialized to one instead of zero, so it starts far too large
Because v is only updated every 1000 steps rather than on every single step
Because v is computed from the parameters rather than the gradient
questions.explanation: With beta2 = 0.999, after t steps v carries only a fraction 1 - 0.999^t of the true mean square, which stays small for hundreds of steps. Without correction, Adam's denominator is badly wrong for many iterations, producing distorted steps.

questions.question: A model has 1e9 parameters trained in float32 with AdamW. How much memory do the AdamW optimizer states alone occupy?
options: 4 GB
8 GB
16 GB
2 GB
questions.explanation: AdamW stores m and v: 2 x 1e9 x 4 bytes = 8e9 bytes = 8 GB. That is on top of 4 GB of parameters and 4 GB of gradients; 16 GB is the total of all three.

questions.question: On the first Adam step, with eta = 3e-4, how far does a parameter with gradient g = 100 move?
options: About 3e-2, proportional to the gradient of 100
About 3, eta times g scaled by the bias correction
About 3e-4, in the -sign(g) direction
Zero, because both moments start at zero
questions.explanation: At t = 1 the ratio m_hat/sqrt(v_hat) = g/|g| = 1, so the step magnitude is eta = 3e-4 regardless of how large the gradient is. Nothing about the first step is proportional to the size of g.

questions.question: Besides AdamW, which three schedule-and-stability techniques are used on essentially every production LLM training run?
options: Dropout on every layer, batch normalization, and early stopping on validation loss
Label smoothing, mixup of training examples, and heavy data augmentation
Gradient checkpointing, mixed precision training, and tensor parallelism
Learning-rate warmup, cosine learning-rate decay, and global-norm clipping
questions.explanation: Real runs ramp eta up over the first few thousand steps (warmup), decay it along a cosine curve, and clip the global gradient norm to survive the occasional huge minibatch gradient. These are the topics of 03.3.

questions.question: Without warmup and gradient clipping, what commonly happens to large-batch Adam training?
options: It trains normally but converges slightly slower overall
It routinely diverges in the first few hundred steps
It overfits the first batch and then stops improving
It runs out of GPU memory as Adam's state fills up
questions.explanation: Warmup and clipping are not optional polish: without them, large-batch Adam runs routinely diverge early, with the loss shooting to inf or nan in the first few hundred steps. That is why they appear on essentially every production LLM run.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the learning rate should change over training
questions.question: Why should the learning rate start near zero at the very beginning of LLM training?
options: Weights are random, v_hat rests on one or two noisy gradients and Adam's first steps are ~eta, so big eta diverges
Because the gradients are exactly zero at initialization, so any nonzero rate only adds noise to the weights
Because a small initial rate makes the model memorize the first batch, which anchors the rest of training
Because the loss is lowest at initialization and a large step would immediately move the model away from it
questions.explanation: At the start, the per-parameter scale estimate is unreliable and Adam moves each parameter by roughly eta regardless of gradient size. A large eta here can throw parameters wildly off. Starting near zero and ramping up, warmup, avoids that.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the learning rate should change over training
questions.question: Why is the learning rate decayed toward zero near the end of training?
options: To speed up the final steps so the run finishes sooner on the same hardware
To make the minibatch gradient unbiased once the model nears convergence
So the optimizer settles into a minimum instead of bouncing around it
To reduce the memory used by Adam's optimizer state at the end of training
questions.explanation: Late in training, large steps keep the parameters bouncing around the minimum. Shrinking eta lets them settle in. Decay does not change memory use or the gradient's bias.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the learning rate should change over training
questions.question: What is the near-universal default learning-rate schedule for LLM pretraining?
options: A constant learning rate held fixed for the whole run
Step decay by 10x at the end of every epoch
Exponential growth of the learning rate over training
Linear warmup followed by cosine decay to a floor
questions.explanation: The standard schedule ramps eta linearly from near zero over the first W steps, then glides it down a half-cosine to a small floor over the rest of training. It covers the start (warmup), middle (peak) and end (decay) phases.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the learning rate should change over training
questions.question: How does the training loop obtain the learning rate from a warmup + cosine schedule?
options: The schedule is a pure function of the step; the loop writes eta(s) into the optimizer
The optimizer adjusts eta automatically from the recent loss values, lowering it when the loss rises
The learning rate is derived from the gradient norm each step, so large gradients get small rates
The schedule is applied once before training starts, baking every step's rate into the optimizer
questions.explanation: The schedule depends only on the step number s, so each iteration the loop computes eta(s) and sets it in the optimizer. It does not react to the loss or gradients, which also makes the whole curve inspectable before training.

questions.question: In the warmup phase (s < W) of the warmup + cosine schedule, what is the learning rate eta(s)?
options: eta_max * s / T
eta_max * (s + 1) / W
eta_min + eta_max * s / W
eta_max * W / (s + 1)
questions.explanation: Warmup is a straight line eta_max*(s+1)/W, rising from eta_max/W at step 0 to eta_max. Using s+1 rather than s makes the first step's rate nonzero and places the peak exactly at s = W.

questions.question: Why does the warmup formula use (s + 1)/W rather than s/W?
options: To make the schedule decrease slightly during warmup before it rises
To make the warmup phase take W + 1 steps instead of W steps
So the first step's rate is nonzero and the peak is exactly at s = W
To make the learning rate exceed eta_max slightly at the end of warmup
questions.explanation: With s/W, step 0 would get a learning rate of exactly zero, wasting the step. Using s+1 gives eta_max/W at step 0, and the linear ramp meets the cosine branch's value eta_max at s = W.

questions.question: In the cosine-decay phase of the schedule, what is the progress variable p?
options: p = s / T, the fraction of total training completed so far
p = W / T, a constant equal to the warmup fraction of the run
p = (T - s) / W, the remaining steps measured in warmup lengths
p = (s - W) / (T - W), from 0 to 1 over the decay phase
questions.explanation: p measures progress through the decay phase only: it is 0 at s = W and 1 at s = T. The cosine factor is computed from p, so the decay spans exactly the steps after warmup.

questions.question: What is the cosine-decay formula for eta(s) with progress p?
options: eta_min + 0.5*(1 + cos(pi*p))*(eta_max - eta_min)
eta_max * cos(pi*p), clipped below at eta_min
eta_min + cos(p)*(eta_max - eta_min), unscaled
eta_max - 0.5*(1 - cos(pi*p))*eta_min
questions.explanation: The factor 0.5*(1 + cos(pi*p)) runs from 1 at p = 0 to 0 at p = 1, scaling the gap between eta_max and eta_min. So the rate glides from eta_max to eta_min. eta_max*cos(pi*p) would turn negative.

questions.question: Why does the factor 0.5*(1 + cos(pi*p)) go from 1 to 0 as p goes from 0 to 1?
options: Because cos(pi*p) grows linearly in p, so the factor shrinks at a constant rate
Because cos(0) = 1 gives 1 at p = 0 and cos(pi) = -1 gives 0 at p = 1
Because cos(pi*p) stays between 0 and 1, so the factor is already normalized
Because the factor is normalized by the total step count T at every step
questions.explanation: At p = 0, 0.5*(1 + 1) = 1; at p = 1, 0.5*(1 + (-1)) = 0. In between it follows a half-cosine. cos(pi*p) ranges from 1 to -1, not 0 to 1, which is why the 1 + and 0.5 are needed.

questions.question: What is the shape of the cosine-decay curve?
options: Fast decay at the start, then flat
A straight line from eta_max to eta_min
Fast decay in the middle, gentle near both ends
Gentle in the middle and fast near both ends
questions.explanation: A half-cosine is flat at both ends (slope zero at p = 0 and p = 1) and steepest at p = 0.5. So the learning rate leaves the peak gently, falls fastest mid-run, and eases into the floor.

questions.question: What does the warmup + cosine schedule do if the training loop runs past the planned total T steps?
options: It restarts warmup from zero and begins a second cycle
It continues the cosine past p = 1, so the rate rises again
It returns eta_max again, as if a new run had started
It holds the learning rate at the floor eta_min
questions.explanation: Past T the schedule clamps to eta_min. It does not restart, reuse the peak, or let the cosine continue (which would rise back up toward eta_max).

questions.question: With W = 100, T = 1000, eta_max = 6e-4 and eta_min = 6e-5, at which step is the midpoint of the cosine-decay phase, and what is the cosine factor there?
options: s = 550, where p = 0.5 and the factor is exactly 0.5
s = 500, halfway through all T steps, where the factor is 0
s = 550, where p = 0.5 and the factor is still 1
s = 1000, where p = 1 and the factor has fallen to 0.5
questions.explanation: The decay phase runs from W = 100 to T = 1000, so its midpoint is (W + T)/2 = 550, where p = 0.5. cos(pi/2) = 0, making the factor 0.5*(1 + 0) = 0.5, so eta is halfway between eta_min and eta_max: 3.3e-4.

questions.question: What is a common choice for the floor eta_min relative to the peak eta_max?
options: Exactly zero, with no floor
One tenth of the peak
Half the peak value
Equal to the peak value
questions.explanation: A floor of eta_max/10 is common; for example eta_max = 6e-4 with eta_min = 6e-5. GPT-3 also decays to 10% of the peak. A floor of zero is possible but the 10% choice is the documented common shape.

questions.question: What is a typical GPT peak learning rate used in the warmup + cosine schedule example?
questions.explanation: 6e-4 is given as a typical GPT peak learning rate. With 100 warmup steps it starts at 6e-6 at step 0 and decays to a floor of 6e-5.

questions.question: In the from-scratch cosine_warmup_lr function, how are the three phases checked?
options: Cosine first, then warmup, then the floor, so decay takes priority over warmup
Only warmup and cosine are checked; past max_steps the cosine keeps going
Floor first, then cosine, then warmup, so late steps short-circuit everything
Warmup if step < W; else min_lr if step >= max_steps; else the cosine
questions.explanation: The function returns max_lr*(step+1)/warmup_steps during warmup, clamps to min_lr at or past max_steps, and otherwise computes progress and the cosine coefficient. At step == max_steps both the clamp and the cosine give min_lr, so the boundaries agree.

questions.question: How does the training loop apply a schedule's learning rate to a torch.optim optimizer?
options: By setting g['lr'] for each g in opt.param_groups before the step
By passing the learning rate as an argument to loss.backward()
By re-creating the optimizer with the new rate on every step
By scaling every gradient by the learning rate before step()
questions.explanation: torch.optim optimizers store their learning rate in each param group, so the loop writes g['lr'] = cosine_warmup_lr(step, ...) for every group. The from-scratch AdamW exposes self.lr, so there it is just opt.lr = .... Re-creating the optimizer would discard its moment state.

questions.question: What does the test test_cosine_warmup_endpoints_and_shape check about the schedule?
options: That the learning rate stays constant once warmup has finished
That the peak is at s = W, the floor at s = T, and warmup rises monotonically
That the learning rate never drops below eta_max during the decay phase
That the cosine phase decays linearly between the peak and the floor
questions.explanation: The test verifies the schedule's key landmarks and shape: eta_max exactly at the end of warmup, eta_min at the horizon T, and a monotonic increase during warmup.

questions.question: How does PyTorch provide warmup + cosine learning-rate schedules?
options: Inside torch.optim.AdamW as a built-in warmup_steps argument read on every step
Via torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_, which rescales the step size alongside the gradient
Via lr_scheduler.LambdaLR (or CosineAnnealingLR plus warmup), stepped each iteration
Through the DataLoader's shuffle option, which reorders batches to mimic a schedule
questions.explanation: A LambdaLR scheduler takes a function of the step; calling scheduler.step() each iteration overwrites the optimizer's lr, exactly as a manual loop does. AdamW itself has no schedule built in.

questions.question: What is an advantage of writing the learning-rate schedule as a plain function of the step?
options: It makes the schedule adapt automatically to the observed loss curve
It removes the need for warmup, since the function starts at the peak
It reduces optimizer memory because no scheduler object is stored
The whole schedule is inspectable: print the curve before training
questions.explanation: Because eta depends only on step, you can evaluate it for every step in advance and inspect the curve before spending any compute. It does not adapt to the loss or change memory use.

questions.question: Which two facts about Adam make warmup necessary at the start of training?
options: Early steps are ~eta in size whatever the gradient, and v_hat is unreliable early
Adam's early gradients are biased, and its learning rate grows automatically each step
Adam stores no optimizer state early on, and its epsilon is too large for small gradients
Adam ignores the learning rate early, and its momentum buffer is exactly zero for W steps
questions.explanation: At t = 1, m_hat/sqrt(v_hat) = sign(g), so every parameter moves by about eta. And v_hat, an EMA with beta2 = 0.999, needs hundreds of steps to become trustworthy. Large steps with an unreliable scale from a random start is a recipe for divergence.

questions.question: Why does Adam's second-moment estimate v_hat take hundreds of steps to become reliable?
options: Because it is updated only every 100 steps, so it needs many updates to settle
Because it is an EMA with beta2 = 0.999, so early it rests on one or two gradients
Because it is initialized to a large value that takes hundreds of steps to decay
Because it is computed from the parameters, which change slowly at the start
questions.explanation: With beta2 = 0.999, the EMA has a long memory and needs many steps to average over a representative set of gradients. In the first handful of steps it reflects just one or two noisy minibatches, so the per-parameter scaling is essentially a guess.

questions.question: How does warmup prevent divergence at the start of Adam training?
options: It disables Adam's second moment during warmup so steps scale with the raw gradient
It clips the gradient to zero for the first W steps while v_hat accumulates
eta starts near zero and grows linearly, so steps stay tiny until v_hat warms up
It increases the batch size gradually so early gradients are less noisy
questions.explanation: By the time eta reaches its peak at step W, v_hat has accumulated enough history to be reliable and the parameters have moved off the pathological initial point. Adam itself runs unchanged throughout.

questions.question: How does the importance of warmup depend on batch size and model size?
options: It matters mainly for small models, which have the noisiest gradients
It matters mainly for small batches, where each gradient is noisiest
It is independent of both, depending only on the optimizer's betas
It matters more the larger the batch size and the model
questions.explanation: The instability that warmup defuses grows with batch size and model size, which is why every large run uses warmup. It is not a small-model or small-batch concern.

questions.question: In production LLM runs, which aspects of warmup are tuned?
options: Only its length and the peak eta_max; warmup is never turned off
Whether to use it at all, decided per run from a short pilot sweep
Only the floor eta_min, since warmup length is fixed by the token budget
Only the batch size used during warmup, ramped up to the full batch
questions.explanation: Warmup is treated as mandatory; what practitioners tune is how long it lasts and how high the peak learning rate goes. Turning warmup off on a large-batch Adam run is a bug, not an experiment.

questions.question: What is the typical symptom of a missing or too-short warmup on a large-batch AdamW run?
options: The loss stays flat for the whole run because the weights barely move
The loss drops briefly, then shoots to inf or nan within a few hundred steps
The loss decreases smoothly for the whole run but plateaus higher than expected
The loss oscillates gently around a fixed value for the entire run
questions.explanation: Without adequate warmup, the run looks fine for a moment, then the large early steps with an unreliable scale push it into divergence and the loss blows up to inf or nan, typically in the first few hundred steps.

questions.question: If an AdamW run's loss decreases briefly then shoots to inf or nan early on, which two fixes should be tried first?
options: Lower weight decay and remove bias correction
Increase the learning rate and the batch size
Add or lengthen warmup, and turn on gradient clipping
Switch off shuffling and use full-batch gradients
questions.explanation: Early blow-ups are the classic signature of missing or too-short warmup, and gradient clipping caps any catastrophic individual step. Raising the learning rate would make it worse.

questions.question: Which paper documents linear warmup plus cosine decay to 10% of the peak, with warmup over roughly the first 375M tokens?
options: The original Transformer paper (Vaswani et al. 2017)
The Adam paper (Kingma & Ba 2015)
The AdamW paper (Loshchilov & Hutter 2019)
The GPT-3 paper (Brown et al. 2020)
questions.explanation: GPT-3 warms the learning rate up over about the first 375M tokens and then cosine-decays it to 10% of the peak, matching the eta_min = eta_max/10 shape. Nearly every open LLM since, including LLaMA and OLMo, uses this schedule.

questions.question: What problem does gradient clipping address, even when warmup is in place?
options: An occasional bad minibatch whose huge gradient undoes thousands of good steps
The bias of the minibatch gradient estimate relative to the full-batch gradient
The memory cost of Adam's optimizer state, which grows with every large gradient
Gradients that stay too small to make progress once the learning rate has decayed
questions.explanation: Batches with a few pathological examples or rare token combinations can produce huge gradients. One such step can wreck the model, causing a loss spike. Clipping caps the gradient size so no single step is catastrophic.

questions.question: What is the gradient-clipping-by-global-norm rule with threshold c?
options: g <- g - c for every component, shifting the whole gradient down by c
g <- g * min(1, c/||g||), with ||g|| the L2 norm over every component
g <- clamp(g, -c, c) for every component, independently of the others
g <- g / ||g||, normalizing the gradient to unit length on every step
questions.explanation: The factor min(1, c/||g||) is 1 when the norm is within the threshold and c/||g|| otherwise, so the whole gradient is scaled down to length c only when it is too long. Clamping each component would change the direction; always normalizing would also enlarge small gradients.

questions.question: In global-norm gradient clipping, what is ||g|| computed over?
options: Each parameter tensor separately, clipping each one on its own
Only the last layer's gradient, since it is the largest in practice
Every gradient component in the model, as one long vector
The current minibatch's per-example loss values, not the gradients
questions.explanation: The global norm treats all the model's gradients as one flattened vector: ||g|| = sqrt(sum_i g_i^2) over every component. One shared scale is then applied everywhere.

questions.question: What is the near-universal default clip threshold c for global-norm gradient clipping?
questions.explanation: c = 1.0 is the near-universal default. If the gradient's global norm exceeds 1.0, it is scaled down to exactly 1.0; otherwise it is left alone.

questions.question: When global-norm clipping triggers, what happens to the gradient's direction?
options: It is preserved; every component is scaled by the same factor
It is rotated toward the steepest component to damp the spike
It is reversed so the bad step is undone on the next update
It is randomized slightly to help training escape the bad batch
questions.explanation: Multiplying every component by the same factor c/||g|| shortens the vector without changing its direction. The update still points the same way downhill, just with a capped size.

questions.question: Why is gradient clipping done with one global scale rather than per-tensor clipping?
options: Per-tensor clipping requires twice the memory, since each tensor's norm needs its own buffer
Scaling each tensor separately would bend the gradient direction
Per-tensor clipping cannot run on GPUs because the norms must be reduced on the CPU
Global clipping is applied to the parameters, while per-tensor clipping is applied to gradients
questions.explanation: If different tensors were scaled by different factors, the combined gradient vector would point in a new direction, corrupting the step rather than just capping it. One shared factor preserves the true direction.

questions.question: In global-norm clipping, what happens if ||g|| is at or below the threshold c?
options: The gradient is scaled up so that its norm becomes exactly c
The gradient is set to zero so that the step is skipped
The factor min(1, c/||g||) is 1, so nothing changes
The gradient is divided by c, shrinking it slightly
questions.explanation: When ||g|| <= c, c/||g|| >= 1, so min(1, c/||g||) = 1 and the gradient is untouched. Clipping only ever shrinks gradients; it never enlarges small ones.

questions.question: A model's entire flattened gradient is [3, 4] and the clip threshold is c = 1.0. What is the clipped gradient?
questions.explanation: The norm is sqrt(9 + 16) = 5 > 1, so every component is scaled by 1/5 = 0.2, giving [0.6, 0.8] with norm exactly 1. The 3:4 ratio, and thus the direction, is preserved. Clamping each component to 1 would give [1, 1], a different direction.

questions.question: With clip threshold c = 1.0, what happens to a gradient [0.1, 0.2]?
options: It is left untouched, since its norm (about 0.22) is below 1
It is scaled up to norm 1 so its length matches the threshold
It is set to zero, since small gradients are treated as noise
It is scaled by 0.2, the ratio of its largest component to c
questions.explanation: Its norm sqrt(0.01 + 0.04) is about 0.22 < 1, so the clip factor is 1 and the gradient is unchanged. Clipping caps large gradients only.

questions.question: How does the from-scratch clip_grad_norm_ compute the global L2 norm?
options: As the sum of absolute values of all gradient components across the model
As the L2 norm of the per-tensor L2 norms, equal to the norm over all components
As the maximum of the per-tensor L2 norms, so the largest tensor sets the scale
As the average of the per-tensor norms, weighted by each tensor's element count
questions.explanation: It stacks the per-tensor norms ||g_j|| and takes their L2 norm: sqrt(sum_j ||g_j||^2) = sqrt(sum_j sum_i g_ji^2), the norm over every component. The maximum or average of per-tensor norms would not equal the global norm.

questions.question: What value does the from-scratch clip_grad_norm_ return, and why?
options: The post-clip norm, so the loop can verify it equals the threshold
The clip coefficient, which the loop uses to adjust the learning rate
The pre-clip norm, which the loop logs to watch for spikes
Nothing; it only modifies the gradients in place and returns None
questions.explanation: It returns the norm before clipping. Logging it reveals sudden jumps in gradient norm, an early warning that training is becoming unstable. The post-clip norm would hide the spikes, since it is capped at c.

questions.question: In the from-scratch clip_grad_norm_, why is clip_coef computed as max_norm / (total_norm + 1e-6)?
options: The 1e-6 makes the coefficient slightly larger than 1 so small gradients are boosted
The 1e-6 sets the minimum gradient norm below which clipping is skipped entirely
The 1e-6 is the default clip threshold used when max_norm is not given
It guards against division by zero and matches PyTorch's own 1e-6
questions.explanation: If all gradients were zero, total_norm would be zero and the division would fail. Adding 1e-6 guards against that, and using the same epsilon as torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_ lets the test match PyTorch to floating-point precision.

questions.question: In the from-scratch clip_grad_norm_, when are the gradients actually modified?
options: Only when clip_coef < 1.0; each gradient is then scaled in place
Every step, by multiplying each gradient by clip_coef unconditionally
Only when clip_coef > 1.0, which means the norm is above the threshold
Only on the first step, when the gradient norm is at its largest
questions.explanation: The check if clip_coef < 1.0 ensures gradients are only ever shrunk. When the norm is below the threshold, clip_coef > 1 and the gradients are left alone; scaling them up would distort small updates.

questions.question: What is PyTorch's built-in equivalent of the from-scratch global-norm gradient clipping?
options: torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR
torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_
torch.clamp applied to each parameter
torch.optim.AdamW's weight_decay argument
questions.explanation: torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_ computes the global norm, rescales gradients in place when it exceeds max_norm, and returns the norm. The test test_clip_grad_norm_matches_torch checks the from-scratch version returns the same norm and gradients.

questions.section: 5. Where these sit in the training loop
questions.question: In a pretraining loop using clipping, a schedule and AdamW, what is the order of operations within one step?
options: clip_grad_norm_, backward(), zero_grad(), set this step's lr, step()
step(), backward(), clip_grad_norm_, set this step's lr, zero_grad()
zero_grad(), forward, backward(), clip_grad_norm_, set lr, step()
set this step's lr, step(), forward, backward(), clip_grad_norm_
questions.explanation: Gradients are cleared, the forward pass computes the loss, backward() fills .grad, clipping caps the gradient, the schedule sets the learning rate, and step() applies the AdamW update. Clipping must come after backward and before step.

questions.section: 5. Where these sit in the training loop
questions.question: Between which two calls do gradient clipping and setting the scheduled learning rate sit in the training loop?
options: Between zero_grad() and the forward pass
Between the forward pass and backward()
After step(), before the next zero_grad()
Between loss.backward() and optimizer.step()
questions.explanation: Clipping needs the gradients that backward() produces and must change them before step() uses them. The learning rate for this step must also be set before step(). Both slot between backward() and step().

questions.question: What does computing the warmup + cosine learning-rate schedule cost?
options: Plain Python float arithmetic on the step: no tensors, negligible cost
An O(P) pass over all parameters to rescale their stored learning rates
A full forward pass to evaluate the loss before the rate is chosen
One GPU kernel launch per parameter tensor to write the new rate
questions.explanation: The schedule is a simple scalar formula of the step number. It touches no tensors and runs once per step, so its cost is negligible.

questions.question: What does global-norm gradient clipping cost per step for a model with P parameters?
options: O(P^2) work for the pairwise norms, plus an extra P-sized buffer for the clipped copy
O(P) for one scalar norm, another O(P) scale only if it triggers; ~no extra memory
No work at all, since PyTorch computes the global norm for free during backward()
O(1) work regardless of P, since the norm is read from a cached running statistic
questions.explanation: Clipping reduces over every gradient component in one streaming pass to get the norm, and if it triggers, scales each gradient in place in another pass. Only a tiny vector of per-tensor norms and one scalar are stored, so the cost is trivial next to the backward pass.

questions.question: During global-norm clipping, where are the per-tensor norms stacked, and do any tensor shapes change?
options: On the CPU, and every gradient is flattened into a single vector first
On the GPU, and gradients are reshaped into one long contiguous vector
Into a tiny vector on the gradients' device; no gradient changes shape
In a separate float64 buffer the size of the parameters, kept on the CPU
questions.explanation: The per-tensor norms form a small vector on the same device as the gradients, and its norm is the global norm. Gradients are never reshaped or flattened; the 'one long vector' view is conceptual.

questions.question: With eta_max = 3e-4, roughly what warmup length W gives a step-0 learning rate of about 1e-6 under eta(0) = eta_max/W?
options: 3 steps
30 steps
3000 steps
300 steps
questions.explanation: Solving eta_max/W = 1e-6 gives W = 3e-4/1e-6 = 300 steps. Real runs often warm up over hundreds to a couple thousand steps so that v_hat has stabilized and the early steps are tiny.

questions.question: A run with correct warmup, cosine decay and AdamW shows the loss suddenly spiking upward every few thousand steps and then slowly recovering. Which technique most directly addresses this?
options: Gradient clipping by global norm
A longer linear warmup phase
Removing weight decay entirely
Switching from AdamW to plain SGD
questions.explanation: Intermittent spikes after warmup come from occasional outlier minibatches producing huge gradients. Clipping the global norm to c = 1.0 caps exactly those rare updates while leaving normal steps untouched. Warmup only affects the start of training.

questions.question: Why is lowering the learning rate a worse fix than gradient clipping for intermittent loss spikes caused by outlier minibatches?
options: Because lowering the learning rate has no effect on the size of updates from large gradients
It slows every step, including the good ones, while clipping acts only when ||g|| > c
Because a lower learning rate makes each spike larger by keeping the model near the bad region
Because the learning rate is fixed by the schedule and cannot be changed during a run
questions.explanation: A lower eta shrinks all steps to defend against the rare bad ones, hurting convergence everywhere. Clipping is targeted: it only rescales the gradient on steps where the norm exceeds the threshold.

questions.question: How can you confirm that intermittent loss spikes are caused by outlier minibatches with unusually large gradients?
options: By checking that the learning rate is at its floor whenever a spike appears
By measuring the optimizer's memory use and seeing it jump on the bad steps
By logging the pre-clip norm from clip_grad_norm_ and seeing it spike
By inspecting the post-clip norm, which rises well above c on the bad steps
questions.explanation: clip_grad_norm_ returns the norm before clipping. If it jumps on exactly the steps where the loss spikes, outlier gradients are the cause. The post-clip norm is capped at c, so it would hide the size of the spike.

questions.question: At the end of warmup (step s = W), what is the learning rate, and which branch of the schedule produces it?
options: eta_max * (W + 1)/W, slightly above the peak, from the warmup branch
eta_min, from the floor branch, because warmup hands over to the floor
eta_max/2, from the cosine branch, at the midpoint of the decay
Exactly eta_max, from the cosine branch with p = 0
questions.explanation: At s = W the condition s < W is false, so the cosine branch runs with p = 0. The factor 0.5*(1 + cos 0) = 1 gives eta_min + (eta_max - eta_min) = eta_max. The last warmup step, s = W - 1, also reaches eta_max, so the branches meet continuously.

questions.question: Why does warmup specifically help Adam more than plain SGD?
options: Adam's early v_hat is unreliable and its first steps are ~eta; SGD has no such estimate
Because plain SGD uses a fixed learning rate that cannot be scheduled by the training loop
Because Adam has no learning rate during its first steps, so warmup has to supply one
Because plain SGD diverges whenever warmup is used, so it cannot benefit from it at all
questions.explanation: Adam's per-parameter scaling relies on v_hat, which is built from one or two noisy gradients early on, and its first steps have fixed size eta. Warmup keeps eta tiny until v_hat matures. Plain SGD steps proportionally to the gradient and has no such estimate, so it is far less sensitive, though warmup can still help it.

questions.question: A gradient has global norm 10 and the clip threshold is c = 2. By what factor is each component scaled, and what is the resulting norm?
options: Factor 0.5, resulting norm 5
Factor 0.2, resulting norm 2
Factor 2, resulting norm 20
Factor 0.8, resulting norm 8
questions.explanation: The factor is c/||g|| = 2/10 = 0.2. Every component is multiplied by 0.2, so the norm becomes 10*0.2 = 2, exactly the threshold, with direction unchanged.

questions.question: Why must gradient clipping run after loss.backward() but before optimizer.step()?
options: Because clipping modifies the loss value that backward() differentiates
Because step() recomputes the gradients and would overwrite the clipped ones
It needs the gradients in .grad, and must cap them before they update params
Because clipping must be applied to the parameters after they are updated
questions.explanation: backward() populates .grad, so clipping cannot happen before it. step() consumes .grad to update the parameters, so clipping after it would be too late. The order is backward(), clip_grad_norm_(), set lr, step().

questions.question: Which topic follows the optimization module, after warmup, cosine decay and gradient clipping?
options: Distributed training with FSDP and sharded optimizer state
Reinforcement learning from human feedback with PPO
Scaling laws for compute-optimal model and data size
Tokenization: bytes, Unicode and BPE from scratch
questions.explanation: With the optimization toolkit complete (update rule and momentum, AdamW, schedule and clipping), the next module turns to how text becomes numbers the model can consume: tokenization, starting with characters, bytes and Unicode, then BPE.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.section: Prerequisites / Why this matters for ML
questions.question: In a language model, what does the size of the vocabulary determine about the model's prediction at each position?
options: The number of choices the softmax next-token distribution is spread over
The maximum number of tokens the model can read in one context window
The number of attention heads used in each Transformer layer
The number of training steps needed before the loss converges
questions.explanation: A language model puts a softmax distribution over a fixed set of next-token choices and is scored by the cross-entropy of the true token. That fixed set is the vocabulary, so its size V is the number of outcomes in the distribution. Context length is a separate quantity (sequence length T), not the vocabulary size.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
