questions.section: Prerequisites / Why this matters for ML
questions.question: Why is the tokenizer described as the first design decision in an LLM pipeline?
options: It is the only component whose parameters are updated by gradient descent during pretraining
It decides the learning-rate schedule and the optimizer settings used for pretraining
It sets how many GPUs the training run can use in parallel, since shards follow token ids
Context length, dataset size, compute and API price are all counted in tokens
questions.explanation: The tokenizer defines what a 'token' is, and context length, training-set size, the cost of a forward pass, and the price of an API call are all measured in tokens. A bad choice either blows up sequence length or cripples the model on unseen text. The tokenizer is not trained by gradient descent and has nothing to do with the optimizer.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.section: Prerequisites / Why this matters for ML
questions.question: What does the vocab_size field of a GPT model configuration (GPTConfig) control in the network?
options: The hidden dimension C of every Transformer block in the stack
The number of Transformer layers stacked between input and output
The size of the input embedding table and of the output layer
The maximum context length block_size the model can attend over
questions.explanation: vocab_size is the number of rows in the input embedding table and the number of logits the output layer produces. It is independent of the hidden size C, depth, and context length. Changing the tokenizer therefore changes the shape of the first and last layers.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.section: 1. The problem: text is not numbers, but the model only eats numbers
questions.question: What basic property must the rule that converts text to integers for a language model have?
options: It must be learned jointly with the model weights during pretraining
It must be fixed and invertible: string to integers and back
It must map each whole string to a single integer hash value
It must be lossy so that rare characters are removed before training
questions.explanation: A neural network only multiplies matrices of numbers, so text must become integers via a fixed, invertible encode/decode rule. 'Invertible' means decode(encode(s)) returns s. The tokenizer is chosen and frozen before training, not learned jointly with the weights, and it produces a list of ids, not one hash.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.section: 1. The problem: text is not numbers, but the model only eats numbers
questions.question: In a language model, what is a vocabulary?
options: A dictionary of English words with their definitions, used to score generated text
A numbered list of the units the model knows; each id indexes into it
The set of all training documents after deduplication, each assigned an integer id
The list of hidden-layer sizes used in each Transformer block, indexed by layer number
questions.explanation: Each token id is an index into the vocabulary, a numbered list of the atomic units (bytes, subwords, words) the model knows. The embedding table has one row per vocabulary entry and the output layer one logit per entry. It is not a human dictionary or a set of documents.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.section: 1. The problem: text is not numbers, but the model only eats numbers
questions.question: If a language model's vocabulary has V entries, how are its input embedding table and final output layer sized?
options: The embedding table has V rows and the output layer produces V logits per position
The embedding table has V columns and the output layer produces one logit per position
The embedding table has sqrt(V) rows and the output layer produces V^2 logits
Both layers are sized by the sequence length T, independent of V
questions.explanation: The input embedding table has one row per vocabulary entry, and the final output layer produces one logit per vocabulary entry, so at every position the model predicts a distribution over exactly V choices. With hidden size C the embedding is V x C. Sequence length T does not set either layer's width.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.section: 1. The problem: text is not numbers, but the model only eats numbers
questions.question: Which two quantities are in tension when choosing the units of a tokenizer?
options: Learning rate and batch size
Number of layers and number of attention heads
Dropout rate and weight decay
Vocabulary size V and sequence length T
questions.explanation: Picking units trades vocabulary size V (width of the embedding and output layers) against sequence length T (how many units a text becomes). Coarser units shrink T but grow V; finer units shrink V but grow T. The other pairs are optimization or architecture hyperparameters unrelated to tokenization.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.section: 1. The problem: text is not numbers, but the model only eats numbers
questions.question: Why does sequence length T matter so much for the cost of a Transformer?
options: The embedding table has T rows, so its memory grows linearly with T
The output layer produces T logits, so its cost grows like T^3
Attention compares every position with every other: cost ~ T^2
The number of parameters in each layer grows linearly with T
questions.explanation: Self-attention compares every position with every other position, so compute and memory grow with T^2. That is why sequence length is the most expensive knob in a Transformer. The embedding table and parameter count depend on V and C, not on T.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.section: 1. The problem: text is not numbers, but the model only eats numbers
questions.question: How do word, character, and byte units relate to the vocabulary-size versus sequence-length trade-off?
options: All three keep both V and T small, so the choice between them is arbitrary
Words minimize both V and T, while characters and bytes maximize both
Each pushes one of V or T to an extreme, and subword tokenization balances them
Bytes give the shortest sequences and words give the smallest vocabulary
questions.explanation: Words give short sequences but a huge vocabulary; characters and bytes give a tiny vocabulary but long sequences. Each extreme sacrifices one quantity. Subword tokenization (BPE) is the balance between them. Bytes give the longest sequences, not the shortest.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.section: 1. The problem: text is not numbers, but the model only eats numbers
questions.question: When is a tokenizer chosen relative to model training?
options: It is re-learned at the start of every epoch
It is chosen and frozen before training begins
It is chosen after training by inspecting the learned embeddings
It is updated by backpropagation together with the embedding table
questions.explanation: A tokenizer is a fixed string-to-list-of-int codec chosen and frozen before training. Its vocabulary size becomes the model's input/output width, so changing it later would change the shape of those layers. It is not trained by backpropagation.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: What is the appeal of using whole words as tokens?
options: Sequences stay short and each token is meaningful
The vocabulary is small and bounded for every language
Every possible input string is guaranteed to have an id
Related word forms automatically share embeddings
questions.explanation: Splitting on spaces and giving each word an id keeps sequences short ('the cat sat' is three tokens) and each token carries meaning. But word vocabularies are huge and unbounded, have an out-of-vocabulary problem, and give unrelated ids to related forms, so the other options are exactly what words fail at.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: What is the out-of-vocabulary (OOV) problem of a word-level tokenizer?
options: Words that appear too often overflow the numeric range of the embedding table
The tokenizer cannot handle any word longer than the model's context window
Common words get split into too many pieces at inference time, inflating T
A word missing from the fixed vocabulary, like a new name or typo, has no id
questions.explanation: A word vocabulary is fixed at training time, so a word never seen — a new product name, a typo, a rare surname — has no id. The model cannot represent it. Frequency, word length, and over-splitting are not the OOV issue.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: What happens when a word-level tokenizer uses a catch-all <unk> token for unseen words?
options: Each unseen word gets a fresh id appended to the end of the vocabulary at inference time
The unseen word is spelled out character by character automatically by the tokenizer
The model is forced to stop generating as soon as an <unk> appears in its context
Every unseen word maps to one id, so they cannot be told apart or reproduced
questions.explanation: With <unk>, all unseen words map to one id, so the model literally cannot tell them apart or reproduce them in output. For a model that must generate fluent text and handle arbitrary user input, discarding every novel word is fatal. <unk> does not add ids or fall back to characters.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: Why does the <unk> token break a tokenizer's round-trip property?
options: encode(decode(ids)) produces a longer list than the original ids
The <unk> id is larger than the vocabulary size and overflows
decode(encode(s)) no longer equals s whenever s contains an unseen word
Decoding becomes nondeterministic and returns different strings each time
questions.explanation: Once an unseen word becomes <unk>, its original spelling is lost, so decoding returns '<unk>' instead of the original word and decode(encode(s)) != s. A tokenizer that cannot reproduce its input is unusable for generation, which is why the course insists on exact round-tripping.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: Why would a word vocabulary covering most English need to be enormous?
options: Each English word needs several ids, one per possible capitalization and font
Word forms number in the hundreds of thousands, and with code and URLs are unbounded
The vocabulary must include every distinct sentence seen in the training corpus
Word tokenizers must store a separate id for each position in the context window
questions.explanation: There are hundreds of thousands of English word forms, and adding other languages, code, URLs and numbers makes the set effectively unbounded. Covering even most English requires a vocabulary in the hundreds of thousands, which makes the embedding and output layers gigantic.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: With hidden size C and vocabulary size V, how many parameters does the input embedding matrix alone have?
options: V x C
V + C
V^2 x C
questions.explanation: The embedding matrix has one row of length C for each of the V vocabulary entries, so it holds V x C parameters. At V = 500,000 and C = 768 that is about 3.8 x 10^8 parameters just for lookups. It does not scale as V^2 or C^2.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: Besides raw size, why are most rows of a huge word-level embedding table wasted capacity?
options: Most rows are rare words seen a few times, so they get too little gradient
Rows for common words are frozen after the first epoch and stop learning entirely
Rows beyond the first 65,536 cannot be indexed by PyTorch's int16 embedding lookup
Each row is shared between many words, so their gradients cancel each other out
questions.explanation: In a gigantic word vocabulary, most entries are rare words that appear a handful of times. Their embedding rows receive very few gradient updates and stay under-trained, so they are sparse, wasted parameters. Nothing freezes common rows, and indexing is not limited to 65,536.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: What is the 'no morphology' problem of word-level vocabularies?
options: Words with the same spelling but different meanings get merged into one id and one embedding
The tokenizer cannot represent words that contain capital letters without a separate case id
Plural and singular forms are mapped to the same id, so the model loses grammatical number
run, runs, running, runner get unrelated ids, so the shared stem is invisible
questions.explanation: Words are built from reusable parts, but a word vocabulary gives run, runs, running and runner four unrelated integers with four independent embeddings, so the model cannot see the shared stem (same for nation/national/nationalize). A good tokenizer lets the model reuse the piece 'run' across forms.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: What does switching from word units to character units fix?
options: Sequences become shorter and attention becomes cheaper per document
Each token becomes more meaningful, so the model needs fewer layers
A tiny vocabulary, no OOV for those characters, and shared letters
The embedding table grows much larger, giving the model more capacity
questions.explanation: With characters the vocabulary is roughly 100 symbols for English, every word is a sequence of known characters (no OOV for them), and 'run'/'running' share letters. Characters fix everything words got wrong. The price is much longer sequences, so attention becomes more expensive, not cheaper.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: What is the main price of using individual characters as tokens?
options: The vocabulary grows to hundreds of thousands of entries, one per character variant
Much longer sequences: 1,000 words become roughly 6,000 tokens
Unseen words must all be mapped to a single unknown id, as with word tokenizers
The round-trip decode(encode(s)) = s no longer holds for accented characters
questions.explanation: A 1,000-word passage is about 6,000 characters, so character tokenization makes the model process a length-6,000 sequence for content a word tokenizer covers in 1,000 tokens. The vocabulary is tiny and there is no OOV, so the other options describe word-level problems, not character-level ones.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: If character tokenization makes a text six times longer than word tokenization, roughly how much does attention compute and memory grow?
options: About 6 times, because attention cost scales linearly with T
About 36 times, because attention cost scales like T^2
About 216 times, because attention cost scales like T^3
It does not change, because attention cost depends only on V
questions.explanation: Each attention layer compares every position with every other, so work grows like T^2. Six times the length gives roughly 6^2 = 36 times the attention compute and memory for the same text. That is why sequence length is the single most expensive knob in a Transformer.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: Besides attention cost, what capacity is wasted when a model uses character units?
options: Effort learning to spell, re-deriving that t-h-e spells 'the'
Storing a separate embedding for every word it has ever seen in training
Its output layer must predict whole sentences at once instead of single units
It can no longer use positional information once sequences exceed the context
questions.explanation: With character units, a large share of the model's effort goes into reassembling common words from letters — structure a coarser unit would provide for free. Compute spent learning to spell is compute not spent on meaning. Storing per-word embeddings is the word-level problem.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: Why is a 'character' an imprecise unit for a universal tokenizer?
options: Characters cannot be converted to integers in most programming languages without a lookup table
Every character occupies exactly four bytes in memory, wasting space for plain ASCII text
Characters are defined only for the Latin alphabet, so other scripts have no character unit
Accents, emoji modifiers and combining marks make 'one character' ambiguous
questions.explanation: Across the world's scripts, accents, emoji modifiers and combining marks make it ambiguous what counts as one character. A tokenizer needs a unit that is precise and universal, which is what bytes provide. Characters do have integer code points, and UTF-8 uses one to four bytes per character, not always four.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: Which combination of properties is the subword compromise trying to achieve?
options: The longest possible sequences with the smallest possible vocabulary
One token per word with an unbounded vocabulary
Short-ish sequences, a bounded vocabulary, and no out-of-vocabulary inputs
One token per character with an <unk> fallback for rare symbols
questions.explanation: Words give short sequences but an unbounded, sparse vocabulary with an OOV cliff; characters give a tiny vocabulary with no OOV but explosive T^2 cost. The goal is short-ish sequences and a bounded vocabulary and no OOV simultaneously — the subword compromise.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: What is a Unicode code point?
options: A byte value between 0 and 255, the range defined by ASCII
The position of a character within a particular string
An integer id assigned to each character in every script
A token id produced by a byte-level BPE tokenizer for a character
questions.explanation: Every character in every script — Latin, Chinese, Arabic, emoji — has a Unicode code point, an integer identifier. For example A is U+0041 (65) and 😀 is U+1F600 (128,512). Code points can be far larger than 255, so they are not bytes, and they are independent of any tokenizer.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: Why not use Unicode code points directly as a model's vocabulary?
options: Code points change between operating systems, so the ids would be unstable across machines
~150,000 assigned code points (room for 1M+) bring back the huge vocabulary
Code points cannot represent emoji or non-Latin scripts, so many inputs would be lost
Code points are floating-point values and cannot be used to index an embedding table
questions.explanation: Unicode has about 150,000 assigned code points and room for over a million. Using them as the vocabulary would recreate the huge, sparse embedding-table problem of word vocabularies. Code points are stable integers that cover all scripts including emoji.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: What does UTF-8 do?
options: It maps each Unicode code point to one to four bytes
It maps each word to a unique 32-bit integer id
It compresses text by merging frequent byte pairs
It maps each code point to exactly two bytes, always
questions.explanation: UTF-8 is the standard encoding that turns each code point into one to four bytes, where a byte is an integer in 0..255. ASCII characters take one byte; other characters take two, three, or four. Merging frequent pairs is BPE, not UTF-8.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: How are ASCII characters represented in UTF-8?
options: As two bytes, a marker byte followed by the code point
As four bytes padded with zeros
As a variable number of bytes depending on their frequency
As a single byte equal to their code point
questions.explanation: ASCII characters (the common English set, code points 0–127) are encoded as a single byte whose value equals the code point; for example A (U+0041) is the byte 65. Only non-ASCII characters expand to two, three, or four bytes. Byte length never depends on frequency.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: Why is a byte-level alphabet guaranteed to have no out-of-vocabulary symbols?
options: The tokenizer adds a new byte value whenever it meets an unseen character in the input
Rare characters are replaced with the closest ASCII equivalent before tokenizing
UTF-8 supports only the characters seen during tokenizer training, so none are unseen
Any string in any language is a sequence over the 256 byte values
questions.explanation: Because UTF-8 represents any string in any language as bytes, every input is a sequence from a fixed alphabet of exactly 256 symbols. There is no such thing as an out-of-vocabulary byte. Nothing is added or substituted at encoding time.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: In UTF-8, how many bytes encode the character é (U+00E9), and what are they?
options: One byte, [233]
Three bytes, [228, 184, 150]
Two bytes, [195, 169]
questions.explanation: é is not ASCII, so UTF-8 encodes it as two bytes, 195 and 169. Its code point value 233 never appears, because UTF-8 does not store non-ASCII code points directly; it uses a multi-byte pattern. [228, 184, 150] is 世 and [240, 159, 152, 128] is 😀.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: Why doesn't the byte 233 appear in the UTF-8 encoding of é, even though its code point is U+00E9 = 233?
options: UTF-8 subtracts 38 from every code point above 127 so it fits into fewer bits
Only code points 0–127 are a raw byte; 128 and above use a multi-byte pattern
Byte 233 is reserved in UTF-8 as a special end-of-text marker and cannot appear
Python reverses the byte order of non-ASCII characters when it encodes a string
questions.explanation: Only ASCII code points (0–127) are stored as their own single byte. Any code point of 128 or above, including U+00E9, is encoded with a multi-byte pattern where the leading byte signals the length and continuation bytes carry the rest. So é becomes 195, 169 rather than 233.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: How many UTF-8 bytes do the characters 世 (U+4E16) and 😀 (U+1F600) take?
options: 世 takes three bytes and 😀 takes four bytes
Both take one byte each, like ASCII characters
世 takes two bytes and 😀 takes three bytes
Both take four bytes each, the UTF-8 maximum
questions.explanation: UTF-8 uses more bytes for larger code points: 世 (U+4E16) becomes three bytes [228, 184, 150], and the emoji 😀 (U+1F600) becomes four bytes [240, 159, 152, 128]. Only ASCII characters fit in one byte.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: In Python, how do you get the UTF-8 bytes of a string and turn them back into the string?
options: s.encode("utf-8") gives the bytes; b.decode("utf-8") inverts it exactly
ord(s) produces the bytes of the whole string and chr(b) inverts it exactly
bytes(s) produces the UTF-8 bytes directly and str(b) inverts it exactly
s.split() produces the bytes and "".join(b) inverts it exactly
questions.explanation: str.encode("utf-8") returns a bytes object holding the UTF-8 bytes, and bytes.decode("utf-8") turns it back into exactly the original string. ord gives a single character's code point, not its UTF-8 bytes. Wrapping the bytes in list(...) gives the integer values.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: How many UTF-8 bytes does the string "café" occupy, and why?
options: Four: UTF-8 stores one byte per character, accents included
Eight: UTF-8 uses two bytes for every character in the string
Six: one byte per character plus a two-byte terminator
Five: c, a, f are one byte each and é is two bytes
questions.explanation: "café" is four characters but five bytes, [99, 97, 102, 195, 169]: the ASCII letters c, a, f take one byte each and é takes the two bytes 195, 169. This length inflation is the one downside of bytes, which BPE claws back.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: What Python type and dtype do the integers from list("café".encode("utf-8")) have?
options: A torch.long tensor on the CPU, one entry per byte
A torch.uint8 tensor on the current default device
Plain Python ints in 0..255; no tensor, dtype or device
A NumPy array of dtype uint16, one entry per character
questions.explanation: encode returns a Python bytes object, and list(...) of it gives ordinary Python ints in 0..255. There are no tensors, dtypes or devices at this stage. Token ids only become a torch.long tensor later, when the data loader hands batches to the model.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: What two properties make raw bytes a good base alphabet for a tokenizer?
options: Sequences are shorter than word-level ones and every token is meaningful
The vocabulary is exactly 256 symbols and nothing is ever out of vocabulary
Bytes align with word boundaries and preserve morphology
Bytes are learned from data, so they adapt to each language
questions.explanation: Byte units give a tiny, bounded vocabulary of exactly 256 and no OOV, because every string is by definition a sequence of bytes. As a result decode(encode(s)) = s for every string. Bytes do not shorten sequences or align with words, and they are fixed, not learned.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: Why are raw bytes alone not a satisfactory tokenizer?
options: Some strings cannot be represented as bytes and must fall back to an <unk> token
Sequences are long, even a bit longer than the character count
The vocabulary of 256 is too large for the embedding table of a small model
Decoding bytes back into text is lossy for non-English scripts such as Chinese
questions.explanation: Byte tokenization has the same drawback as characters: long sequences, slightly longer than the character count because non-ASCII characters take several bytes. Representation, round-trip, and vocabulary size are all fine. So bytes serve as the floor on which larger units are learned.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: What role do bytes play in byte-level BPE?
options: They are the base alphabet that can spell anything; larger units build on top
They are a fallback used only when the corpus contains emoji or rare scripts
They are discarded once training finishes, leaving only the merged tokens behind
They are used only for decoding, while encoding works on whole words instead
questions.explanation: Bytes are the perfect floor: a base alphabet that can spell anything with no OOV. Byte-level BPE keeps all 256 bytes in the vocabulary and learns larger, more efficient units on top of them. Bytes are never discarded, which is what keeps the no-OOV guarantee.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: How does Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) build its vocabulary?
options: Starting from all words, it repeatedly splits the rarest word into two halves
It assigns ids to the most frequent whole words and maps the rest to <unk>
It trains a small neural network to predict word boundaries and uses its outputs
From the 256 bytes, it repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair
questions.explanation: BPE starts from the 256 bytes and learns merges: it repeatedly finds the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols in a training corpus and fuses it into a new symbol. Running this a few thousand times produces a vocabulary in the sweet spot. It does not split words top-down or use <unk>.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: In a trained BPE vocabulary, what happens to very common words such as 'the', 'and', ' of'?
options: They are removed from the vocabulary as stop words before the merges are learned
They are always split into individual bytes to save vocabulary space for rarer words
Their bytes are merged early into one token, so frequent text is short
They are all mapped to the same id to reduce the vocabulary size
questions.explanation: Common words occur constantly, so the pairs inside them are among the most frequent and get merged early into one unit. Frequent text therefore becomes short. Note ' of' includes its leading space, since spaces are ordinary bytes.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: How does a BPE tokenizer handle a rare word like 'tokenization'?
options: It maps the whole word to a single <unk> id reserved for rare words
It adds the word as a new vocabulary entry at encoding time
It splits it into known pieces such as 'token' + 'ization'
It drops the word from the input entirely and encodes the rest
questions.explanation: Rare words split into a few subword pieces, like 'token' + 'ization', reusing pieces the model already knows. Related forms share stems — the morphology sharing word vocabularies lacked. BPE never uses <unk> and does not grow the vocabulary at encoding time.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: Why can a byte-level BPE tokenizer never have an out-of-vocabulary input?
options: Its merges are trained on every possible string in every language, so all inputs are covered
Its vocabulary keeps all 256 bytes, so anything unmerged falls back to bytes
It maps unseen inputs to the nearest learned token by edit distance before encoding
It refuses to encode strings containing characters it has not seen, so none reach the model
questions.explanation: Because the BPE vocabulary keeps all 256 bytes as its foundation, any string the merges do not cover — a never-seen emoji, a random hash — is representable as its raw bytes. The exact round-trip survives. No nearest-neighbour substitution is involved.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: In BPE, what does adding one more merge do to vocabulary size V and sequence length T?
options: It grows V by one and shrinks T for text that uses that merge
It shrinks V by one and grows T for all text, since a pair is removed
It grows V by one and leaves T unchanged for every input text
It doubles V and halves T for every input, whatever its content
questions.explanation: Each merge adds one new symbol to the vocabulary (V + 1) and fuses a pair into one token wherever it occurs, shortening sequences that contain that pair. This is how BPE deliberately controls the V-vs-T trade-off.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: What is the downside of training a BPE tokenizer with very many merges (a large V)?
options: Sequences become as long as raw byte sequences, losing the benefit of merging
The tokenizer loses the ability to round-trip arbitrary strings exactly
Common words are split into more pieces than before, lengthening sequences
A big embedding table with many rare, under-trained rows
questions.explanation: Many merges make frequent words single tokens and sequences short, but the vocabulary becomes large: a big embedding table and many rare tokens whose rows get little gradient signal. That is the word-vocabulary problem returning. Round-tripping still holds thanks to the byte fallback.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: What happens with very few BPE merges (a small V)?
options: The tokenizer is close to word-level: short sequences but a huge vocabulary
The tokenizer can no longer encode non-ASCII text
The embedding table becomes larger than the output layer
The tokenizer is close to byte-level: a short vocabulary but long sequences
questions.explanation: With few merges, almost all text stays as raw bytes, so the vocabulary is small but sequences are long, like a byte-level tokenizer. Non-ASCII text still encodes as bytes, and the embedding and output layers both have V rows.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: What vocabulary size does GPT-2 use, and where do modern models mostly sit?
options: GPT-2 uses 256; the field mostly sits between about 1k and 4k
GPT-2 uses 500,000; the field mostly sits above one million
GPT-2 uses 50,257; the field mostly sits at about 32k to 128k
GPT-2 uses 32,000; the field mostly sits between about 4k and 16k
questions.explanation: GPT-2's vocabulary has V = 50,257 entries, and real models mostly pick between about 32k and 128k. GPTConfig.vocab_size defaults to 50257 because it matches the GPT-2 tokenizer. 256 is just the byte base, and 500,000 would be a word-level-sized table.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: How many characters and how many UTF-8 bytes is the string "世"?
options: One character and one byte, since it is a single code point
One character (code point U+4E16) but three UTF-8 bytes
Three characters and three bytes, one per UTF-8 byte
One character and two bytes, like any non-ASCII character
questions.explanation: "世" is a single character with a single code point, U+4E16, but UTF-8 encodes it as three bytes. Confusing characters, code points and bytes is a common mistake. Byte-level tokenizers count in bytes, so their lengths follow the byte count.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: In Python, what are len("café") and len("café".encode("utf-8"))?
options: 4 and 5
4 and 4
5 and 5
5 and 4
questions.explanation: len on the str counts characters, giving 4. len on the encoded bytes counts UTF-8 bytes, giving 5, because é takes two bytes. Byte-level tokenizers' sequence lengths are driven by the byte count, not the character count.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: Why is it a mistake to estimate a subword model's cost by counting words?
options: A token is only roughly a word for common English; code, numbers and other languages take several
Subword tokenizers produce exactly two tokens per word, so word counts are off by a constant factor
Token counts are always smaller than word counts, so a word-based estimate is consistently too high
Cost depends only on the number of characters, so neither words nor tokens predict it
questions.explanation: For a subword tokenizer, one token per word is only roughly true for common English. Rare words, code, non-English text and numbers can each become several tokens. Since everything is billed and computed in tokens, count tokens, never words.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: Why can ' the' (with a leading space) and 'the' (at the start of a line) be different tokens in byte-level BPE?
options: The tokenizer lowercases words differently depending on their position in the line
Tokens at the start of a line get a special positional prefix id added to them
BPE assigns a new id to every repeated occurrence of a word to avoid collisions
The space is an ordinary byte of the data, so the byte sequences differ
questions.explanation: Byte-level BPE treats the space as just another byte, so ' the' and 'the' are different byte sequences and can be learned as different tokens. Forgetting the leading space is a common mistake. No lowercasing or positional prefixes are involved.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: Why does a pure word-level vocabulary force a choice between an <unk> token and an impractically large table?
options: Word embeddings cannot be learned for words shorter than three letters, so many need <unk>
The softmax over words becomes numerically unstable above a few thousand entries
Possible words are unbounded, so a fixed table must omit rare ones or balloon
Words must be sorted alphabetically, which requires reserving ids for words not yet seen
questions.explanation: New names, typos, code and other languages make the word set effectively unbounded. A fixed table must either omit rare words, collapsing them to <unk> (losing information and exact reconstruction), or include them, growing to hundreds of thousands of mostly under-trained rows. Neither gives faithful round-tripping with a manageable table.

questions.chapter_name: Characters, bytes, Unicode, the vocab problem
questions.question: You increase a BPE vocabulary from 8k to 64k merges. Which pair correctly names one improvement and one cost?
options: Better: a smaller embedding table and output layer; worse: longer sequences per document
Better: shorter sequences; worse: wider embedding/output layers, rarer rows
Better: exact round-tripping becomes possible; worse: unseen emoji now become <unk>
Better: faster tokenizer training; worse: common words are split into more pieces
questions.explanation: More merges turn more frequent words and pieces into single tokens, so the same text takes fewer positions and attention is cheaper. But V grows, so the embedding table and output layer cost more parameters and memory, and the extra tokens are rarer, receiving less gradient signal. Round-tripping holds at any vocabulary size.

questions.section: Prerequisites / Why this matters for ML
questions.question: Which tokenizer family is the byte-level BPE built from scratch in llmre.tokenizer.bpe?
options: The tokenizer family that sits in front of GPT-2 and most models since
A word-level tokenizer with an <unk> fallback, as used by early RNN language models
A character-level tokenizer that maps each Unicode code point to one fixed id
A learned neural tokenizer trained jointly with the language model
questions.explanation: The byte-level BPE built in llmre.tokenizer.bpe is the actual tokenizer family in front of GPT-2 and most models since. It is reused for every training run in the course. It is neither word-level nor character-level, and it is not trained by gradient descent.

questions.section: Prerequisites / Why this matters for ML
questions.question: Which production facts does understanding byte-level BPE help explain?
options: Why GPUs need FP16 for training, why batch size must be a power of two, and why dropout helps
Why attention uses softmax, why LayerNorm comes first, and why residuals exist
Why models hallucinate, why RLHF is needed, and why temperature changes outputs
Why a token is ~3/4 of a word, why leading spaces matter, and why numbers tokenize oddly
questions.explanation: Byte-level BPE explains concrete tokenization facts: a token averages roughly three-quarters of an English word, leading spaces become part of tokens, and numbers split into odd digit chunks. The other options are about numerics, architecture, or alignment, not tokenization.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: build a vocabulary by fusing what co-occurs
questions.question: What single greedy step does BPE repeat while training?
options: Find the rarest symbol in the corpus and split it back into its two constituent bytes
Find the longest repeated substring in the corpus and assign it a brand-new vocabulary id
Find the most frequent adjacent pair in the whole corpus and glue it into one new symbol
Find the most frequent whole word in the corpus and add it to the vocabulary as one token
questions.explanation: BPE's core idea is greedy: find the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols in the whole corpus, glue it into a single new symbol, add it to the vocabulary, and repeat. It works only with pairs, not longest substrings, and never splits or removes symbols.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: build a vocabulary by fusing what co-occurs
questions.question: In BPE, what is a merge?
options: Combining two separately trained tokenizers into one shared vocabulary with remapped ids
One glue operation that fuses an adjacent pair of symbols into a new vocabulary symbol
Joining two adjacent training documents into one sequence with an end-of-text separator
Averaging the embedding vectors of two adjacent tokens into a single shared vector
questions.explanation: Each glue operation in BPE — fusing an adjacent pair like e + s into a new symbol 'es' — is called a merge. Merges are recorded in order and replayed during encoding. They have nothing to do with combining tokenizers, documents, or embeddings.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: build a vocabulary by fusing what co-occurs
questions.question: How can BPE produce multi-character units like 'est ' if each merge only fuses two symbols?
options: Each merge fuses as many adjacent symbols as the longest common substring shared across words
Merged symbols can be merged again later: e+s → es, then es+t → est, then est+space → 'est '
A final pass after training concatenates all tokens that fall inside the same whitespace word
The tokenizer is seeded with a dictionary of common English suffixes before any merges run
questions.explanation: A merged symbol is a first-class symbol that later merges can consume. So a first merge might create 'es', a later one 'est', and a later one 'est ' with a trailing space. Long units grow out of pairs without ever handling more than two symbols at once.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: build a vocabulary by fusing what co-occurs
questions.question: After a few thousand BPE merges, what kinds of symbols make up the vocabulary?
options: Whole common words, frequent prefixes and suffixes, and the raw bytes as a fallback for rare text
Only whole words from the training corpus, with every rare or unseen word mapped to <unk>
Only the 256 single bytes, since the learned merges are discarded once training has finished
Fixed-length chunks of exactly four bytes each, chosen by how often they recur in the corpus
questions.explanation: The surviving symbols are the byte-chunks that recur in the language: common whole words, frequent prefixes and suffixes, and — a fallback that never disappears — the raw bytes for anything rare. There is no <unk>, and merges are kept, not discarded.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: build a vocabulary by fusing what co-occurs
questions.question: Where does the name Byte-Pair Encoding come from?
options: It encodes each input byte as a pair of hexadecimal digits so the vocabulary stays printable
It pairs each input byte with its position in the sequence to form a positional token id
It splits every byte into a pair of four-bit nibbles and assigns each possible nibble pair its own code
A compression scheme that repeatedly encodes the most frequent adjacent byte pair as one new symbol
questions.explanation: The name literally describes the algorithm: repeatedly encode the most frequent pair of adjacent symbols (originally bytes) as one. It started as a data-compression scheme; using it to build tokenizer vocabularies is the twist that made it central to LLMs.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: build a vocabulary by fusing what co-occurs
questions.question: What are the four steps of the BPE training loop?
options: Split on spaces, count words, keep the top V words as the vocabulary, and map every other word to <unk>
Encode to bytes, sort the bytes by frequency, drop the rarest bytes, and renumber the remaining ones
Count adjacent pairs, pick the most frequent, mint a new id and record it, rewrite the corpus fused
Count characters, pick the rarest one, split it into two bytes, and retrain the vocabulary from scratch
questions.explanation: BPE training loops over: (1) count every adjacent symbol pair, (2) pick the most frequent, (3) mint a new symbol id and record the merge, (4) rewrite the corpus with that pair fused. It stops when the vocabulary reaches the target size. Encoding later replays the recorded merges.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: build a vocabulary by fusing what co-occurs
questions.question: When does BPE training stop?
options: When every word in the corpus has been reduced to exactly one token, so no word can shrink further
When the encoded corpus has been compressed below 50% of its raw UTF-8 byte length
When the vocabulary reaches the target size (or, in the course code, when no pair repeats)
After exactly one full left-to-right pass over the corpus, merging each pair once
questions.explanation: BPE stops when the vocabulary reaches the target size, i.e. after vocab_size − 256 merges. The course's train() also stops early if the most frequent pair occurs fewer than 2 times, since merging a non-repeating pair saves nothing. There is no compression-ratio or one-pass rule.

questions.section: 2. The setup: a tiny corpus and its byte view
questions.question: For an all-ASCII training corpus, what is the initial symbol sequence BPE starts from?
options: The whitespace-separated words of the corpus, each assigned one integer id
The characters themselves, one byte each, equal to their code points
Overlapping pairs of adjacent characters, each pair treated as one symbol
Multi-byte UTF-8 sequences of two to four bytes for every single character
questions.explanation: When every character is ASCII, each character is a single UTF-8 byte equal to its code point (e is 101, s is 115, space is 32). So the starting symbols are just the characters. On non-ASCII text the same algorithm runs, but the starting symbols include multi-byte sequences.

questions.section: 2. The setup: a tiny corpus and its byte view
questions.question: Does BPE training work differently on non-ASCII text such as 'é'?
options: No — the same algorithm runs, but the starting symbols are multi-byte, as é → [195, 169]
Yes — non-ASCII characters are first mapped to an <unk> token before any merges are counted
Yes — non-ASCII characters skip BPE entirely and are added to the vocabulary as single tokens
Yes — non-ASCII text must first be transliterated to ASCII so every character is one byte
questions.explanation: The algorithm is identical; it simply starts from the UTF-8 bytes, which for non-ASCII characters are multi-byte (é is [195, 169]). BPE may later merge those bytes into one token if the pair is frequent. There is no <unk> or transliteration step.

questions.section: 3. The training algorithm, worked by hand
questions.question: When counting adjacent pairs for BPE on the word 'newest', which pairs does it contribute?
options: n, ne, new, newe, newes
n, e, w, e, s, t
ne, we, st
ne, ew, we, es, st
questions.explanation: BPE counts every adjacent pair of symbols. 'newest' is n e w e s t, so its overlapping adjacent pairs are ne, ew, we, es, st — five pairs from six symbols. Triples are not counted, and pairs overlap rather than being disjoint.

questions.section: 3. The training algorithm, worked by hand
questions.question: In BPE training, when two pairs are tied for most frequent, how does the worked example break the tie?
options: Randomly, by sampling one of the tied pairs using a fixed random seed for reproducibility
By choosing the tied pair whose combined byte values are larger, e.g. 's t' over 'e s'
By merging both tied pairs in the same training step, since each would save the same number of symbols
Deterministically: the pair that appears first when scanning the corpus left to right wins
questions.explanation: In the worked corpus, 'e s' and 's t' both occur 5 times. The tie is broken deterministically by the pair that appears first scanning left to right; in 'newest' e s comes before s t, so e s wins. Only one pair is merged per step.

questions.section: 3. The training algorithm, worked by hand
questions.question: What new id does the first BPE merge receive, and why?
options: 0, because merges are numbered from the start of the vocabulary
1, because id 0 is reserved for padding
256, because ids 0–255 are already the raw byte values
50257, because it follows the GPT-2 vocabulary
questions.explanation: The base vocabulary is the 256 byte values 0..255, so the first learned merge gets id 256, the next 257, and so on. In the worked example the first merge is recorded as (101, 115) → 256, the byte ids of e and s.

questions.section: 3. The training algorithm, worked by hand
questions.question: How much does a BPE merge shorten the corpus sequence?
options: By exactly one symbol regardless of how often the pair occurs
By one symbol for each occurrence of the pair that gets fused
By half, because every adjacent pair in the sequence is fused at once
By the length of the new merged token measured in bytes
questions.explanation: Each fusion replaces two symbols with one, removing one symbol per occurrence. In the worked example e s occurs 5 times, so the 34-symbol corpus becomes 29. The saving depends on the pair's count, not on token length.

questions.section: 3. The training algorithm, worked by hand
questions.question: After the first BPE merge creates 'es' (id 256), how are pairs counted for the next merge?
options: Pairs are recounted in the rewritten sequence, where 'es' is a single symbol
The original byte-level pair counts from round one are reused unchanged for every merge
Only pairs that do not involve the new symbol are counted, to avoid double counting
Pairs are counted in a freshly re-encoded copy of the raw text
questions.explanation: After a merge, the corpus is rewritten with the pair fused, and the next round counts pairs in that rewritten sequence. That lets the new symbol participate: in the example, (es, t) = (256, 116) now occurs 5 times and becomes merge 1.

questions.section: 3. The training algorithm, worked by hand
questions.question: Why is 'merges compound' described as the crucial move in BPE?
options: A merged symbol is first-class, so later merges can consume it and grow long units from pairs
Each merge doubles the size of the vocabulary, so a few dozen merges already cover the language
Merges are applied simultaneously during encoding, so their individual length savings multiply
Each merge also merges the embeddings of its two children, compounding what the model knows
questions.explanation: Because merged symbols can be used by later merges, BPE builds long units (like 'est' from 'es' + 't') while only ever handling two symbols at a time. Each merge adds exactly one vocabulary entry, and embeddings are not involved in tokenizer training.

questions.section: 3. The training algorithm, worked by hand
questions.question: In the worked BPE example, merge 2 fuses 'est' with a following space into 'est '. What does this show about byte-level BPE?
options: Spaces are always stripped before training, so this merge reflects a bug in the worked example
Spaces can only appear inside special tokens, so this merge marks a reserved end-of-word token
Spaces are merged only at the very end of the corpus, where padding bytes accumulate
Spaces are ordinary bytes, so tokens routinely include a leading or trailing space
questions.explanation: Because spaces are just bytes (32), BPE can and does merge them into tokens. That is why a real GPT-2 vocabulary has ' the' (with its space) as a single common token distinct from 'the'. Spaces are not stripped or treated specially.

questions.section: 3. The training algorithm, worked by hand
questions.question: Why does the order of a BPE merge table matter?
options: The order only matters for display and debugging; any permutation produces identical encodings
Merges must be applied in reverse learned order, longest tokens first, so encoding is maximally greedy
Encoding must replay merges in learned order, since a later merge can use a symbol an earlier one made
The order determines each token id's dtype, so reordering changes the size of the output tensor
questions.explanation: The merge table is ordered, e.g. (101,115)→256, (256,116)→257, (257,32)→258. Merge 1 can only fire after merge 0 has produced symbol 256. Shuffle the order and you get a different or broken tokenizer.

questions.section: 3. The training algorithm, worked by hand
questions.question: After three BPE merges on top of the byte alphabet, how many entries does the vocabulary have?
options: 3 — only the merged symbols are kept
259 — the 256 bytes plus 3 merged symbols
256 — merges replace existing bytes
512 — each merge adds a pair of entries to the table
questions.explanation: Each merge adds exactly one entry, and the 256 byte entries are kept as the fallback. So three merges give 256 + 3 = 259 entries; in the example the last three are 'es', 'est', and 'est '.

questions.section: 3. The training algorithm, worked by hand
questions.question: Is the vocabulary that BPE produces the optimal set of subwords for a corpus?
options: Yes — BPE provably finds the minimum-length encoding of the corpus for the chosen vocabulary size
No — BPE greedily fuses the most frequent pair each step and never reconsiders, so it is only good enough
Yes — BPE searches over all possible merge orders with dynamic programming and keeps the shortest result
No — BPE picks pairs at random each step, so the vocabulary and its quality vary on every run
questions.explanation: BPE is greedy, not optimal: at each step it fuses the single most frequent pair and never reconsiders. There is no claim the units are the theoretically best subwords, only that this cheap, deterministic procedure works well in practice. It is not random either.

questions.section: 3. The training algorithm, worked by hand
questions.question: What happens if two BPE implementations break ties between equally frequent pairs differently?
options: They produce different but equally valid tokenizers
One of them will fail to round-trip some strings
They always converge to the same vocabulary after enough merges
The one with more merges will be strictly better
questions.explanation: Tie-breaking is a free choice in greedy BPE, so different tie-breaks or corpora give different vocabularies. Both are valid tokenizers that round-trip correctly via the byte fallback, but they encode text differently. This is why the exact merge list must ship with a model.

questions.section: 4. Encoding: replay the merges in order
questions.question: When encoding a new string with a trained BPE tokenizer, which present pair is fused first?
options: The present pair that occurs most frequently in the input string being encoded right now
The leftmost pair in the input string, regardless of its position in the merge table
The present pair whose fusion produces the longest resulting token in bytes
The present pair whose merge was learned earliest in training (smallest merge id)
questions.explanation: Encoding converts the string to bytes and repeatedly fuses, among the present pairs that are in the merge table, the one with the smallest merge id. It stops when no present pair is mergeable. Frequency in the input is irrelevant at encoding time; that is a common bug.

questions.section: 4. Encoding: replay the merges in order
questions.question: Why must BPE encoding apply merges in 'earliest learned first' order?
options: Earlier merges always produce longer tokens, so applying them first gives the best compression ratio
Later merges are learned from fewer examples, so they are unreliable and are skipped when they conflict
A later merge may use a symbol an earlier merge creates, so learned order reproduces training's symbols
It lets encoding run in constant time per token, because each merge is checked only once per string
questions.explanation: Merge 1 (es, t) needed the 'es' symbol from merge 0. Replaying merges in learned order reproduces exactly the symbols training built. Earliest-first has nothing to do with token length or speed.

questions.section: 4. Encoding: replay the merges in order
questions.question: With a BPE tokenizer whose merges are (e,s)→256, (es,t)→257, (est,space)→258, how is the standalone word 'newest' encoded?
options: [258] — a single token for the whole word
questions.explanation: The bytes are n e w e s t. Merge (e,s)→256 fires, then (es,t)→257, giving [110, 101, 119, 257]. The merge (est, space)→258 does not fire because standalone 'newest' has no trailing space. The rarer prefix 'new' stays as three bytes.

questions.section: 4. Encoding: replay the merges in order
questions.question: Why might the same word get different BPE tokens in different contexts?
options: The tokenizer quietly re-trains its merge table on each new input string that it encodes
Which merges fire depends on the surrounding bytes, such as whether a space follows
BPE encoding is randomized at inference time to act as a form of data augmentation
Tokens depend on the absolute position of the word inside the model's context window
questions.explanation: BPE operates on byte sequences, so neighbouring bytes matter. For example, 'newest' followed by a space could use the 'est ' merge, while standalone 'newest' cannot. Encoding is deterministic and position-independent; it never retrains.

questions.section: 4. Encoding: replay the merges in order
questions.question: Encoded with a three-merge BPE tokenizer trained on 'newest newest widest widest lowest', what do 'newest', 'widest' and 'lowest' share?
options: All three end in the single suffix token 257 ('est')
All three are encoded as exactly one whole-word token each
All three begin with the same merged prefix token 256
Nothing — each one is encoded as its raw UTF-8 bytes
questions.explanation: Each of these words ends with the merged suffix 'est' (id 257), so they share that token exactly. This is the morphology sharing that word vocabularies lacked. The prefixes (new, wid, low) stay as raw bytes because no merges cover them.

questions.section: 5. Decoding: expand ids back to bytes
questions.question: How does a BPE tokenizer decode a list of ids back into a string?
options: Replay the learned merges in reverse order to split every merged token back into its bytes
Run the encoder repeatedly on candidate strings until its output ids match the input ids
Look up each id in a stored dictionary of English words and join them with spaces
Look up each id's stored byte string, concatenate them, and UTF-8-decode the result
questions.explanation: Each id maps to a fixed byte string (256 → b"es", 257 → b"est", 110 → b"n"). Decoding looks up every id, concatenates the bytes, and UTF-8-decodes. It needs no merge logic at all.

questions.section: 5. Decoding: expand ids back to bytes
questions.question: Why does BPE decoding exactly invert encoding for any string?
options: Decoding keeps a cache of every string the encoder has ever seen and looks the id list up in it
Encoding is lossy, but decoding repairs the dropped bytes using a small language model
Both functions share the same random seed, so the sampled splits always line up exactly
Encoding only emits ids whose byte expansions concatenate back to the original UTF-8 stream
questions.explanation: Every id the encoder emits stands for a contiguous chunk of the original bytes, so concatenating the chunks reproduces the exact byte stream, which decodes back to the original string. Even an unseen emoji survives because it stays as raw bytes.

questions.section: 5. Decoding: expand ids back to bytes
questions.question: Which state does each direction of a BPE tokenizer need?
options: Decode needs the ordered merge list; encode needs only the vocabulary
Both need the full training corpus at inference time to recount pair frequencies
Decode needs only the id→bytes vocabulary; encode needs the ordered merge list
Neither needs stored state; both are computed directly from UTF-8 encoding rules
questions.explanation: Decoding is a context-free lookup of each id's bytes, so the vocabulary suffices. Encoding must choose which pairs to fuse in which sequence, and those choices depend on training order, so it needs the ordered merges. Together they compose to the identity.

questions.section: 5. Decoding: expand ids back to bytes
questions.question: Why does BPE decoding not need the merge order, while encoding does?
options: Decoding processes the ids right to left, which automatically reverses the merge order the encoder applied
Each id expands to fixed bytes regardless of neighbours, while encoding must choose what to fuse and when
Decoding only ever sees byte ids 0–255, because merged ids are expanded before they are stored
The merge order is embedded in the high bits of every token id, so decode can read it back out
questions.explanation: Decoding has no choices to make: each id's byte expansion is fixed, so concatenation reconstructs the bytes. Encoding must decide which pairs to fuse and in which order, and a later merge may need an earlier one's symbol, so it requires the ordered merge list.

questions.question: In the BPE helper get_stats(ids), what does zip(ids, ids[1:]) yield?
options: Exactly the adjacent pairs, e.g. [1,2,3] gives (1,2) then (2,3)
Every pair of elements in the list, e.g. [1,2,3] gives (1,2), (1,3), (2,3)
Non-overlapping pairs, e.g. [1,2,3,4] gives (1,2) then (3,4)
Each element paired with its index, e.g. (0,1), (1,2), (2,3)
questions.explanation: zip(ids, ids[1:]) walks the sequence one step out of phase with itself, so it yields each element with its successor: the overlapping adjacent pairs. get_stats then counts how often each pair appears in a dict mapping (a, b) to count.

questions.question: What does the BPE helper merge(ids, pair, new_id) do when it finds the pair at position i?
options: Appends new_id to the output and advances i by 2 to skip both symbols
Appends both original symbols followed by new_id, then advances i by 1
Replaces only the first symbol with new_id and advances i by 1 to keep scanning
Stops scanning and returns the list with that single occurrence fused
questions.explanation: merge scans left to right; when ids[i], ids[i+1] equal the pair it emits new_id and skips past both (i += 2), otherwise it copies ids[i] and advances by 1. It fuses every non-overlapping occurrence, not just the first.

questions.question: In the from-scratch BPE train(), how many merge iterations are attempted for a target vocab_size?
options: vocab_size, one iteration for each entry in the final vocabulary
256, one iteration per possible byte value in the base alphabet
log2(vocab_size), since each merge round doubles the current vocabulary
vocab_size − 256, one iteration per merge on top of the byte alphabet
questions.explanation: train() loops for i in range(vocab_size - 256), because the 256 bytes already exist and each iteration adds one merge with id 256 + i. It may break early if no pair repeats.

questions.question: In the from-scratch BPE train(), why does the loop break if stats[pair] < 2?
options: Pairs seen fewer than twice make merge() index past the end of the id list and raise an IndexError
Python dicts keyed by tuples cannot reliably store pairs whose count is exactly one
If even the most frequent pair occurs once, nothing repeats, so further merges would not compress
It guarantees the final vocabulary size is always a power of two, which GPUs handle best
questions.explanation: The most frequent pair is chosen with max(stats, key=stats.get). If its count is below 2, no pair repeats, so merging would only add useless vocabulary entries without shortening the corpus. The loop stops early.

questions.question: In the from-scratch BPE train(), how is the byte string for a new merged id computed?
options: self.vocab[new_id] = bytes([new_id]), storing the new id itself encoded as a single byte
self.vocab[new_id] = self.vocab[pair[0]] + self.vocab[pair[1]], concatenating the children's bytes
self.vocab[new_id] is left empty during training and filled in lazily the first time decode sees it
self.vocab[new_id] = the most common corpus word containing the pair, stored as UTF-8 bytes
questions.explanation: Each new id stores the concatenation of its two children's byte strings, so every id — byte or merged — always knows the exact bytes it stands for. That is what makes decode a pure lookup.

questions.question: In the from-scratch BPE encode(), what does min(stats, key=lambda p: self.merges.get(p, float("inf"))) select?
options: The present pair with the lowest occurrence count in the input, so that rare pairs fuse first
The present pair with the smallest merge id (learned earliest); unlearned pairs rank last
The present pair with the smallest byte values, which keeps ASCII letters merging first
The present pair that appears first in the input string, scanning from left to right
questions.explanation: For a learned pair the key is its merge id, its rank: smaller id means learned earlier and applied first. Unlearned pairs get float("inf"), larger than any real id. So min picks the earliest-learned present pair and never prefers an unlearned one.

questions.question: Why does the BPE encode() key use float("inf") as the default in self.merges.get(p, float("inf"))?
options: Unlearned pairs need a key above every real merge id; otherwise .get returns None and min crashes
It marks the end of the input, so the while loop knows when there is nothing left to encode
It converts every merge id to a float so the ranks can be averaged across present pairs
It forces unlearned pairs to sort first, so encoding tries novel pairs before the learned ones do
questions.explanation: min needs a comparable number for every present pair. A never-learned pair has no merge id, so the default float("inf") ranks it after all learned pairs. Without a default, .get would return None and comparing None with an int raises an error.

questions.question: In the from-scratch BPE encode(), when does min() return an unlearned pair, and what happens then?
options: Whenever an unlearned pair is more frequent than every learned one; it is then merged into a new id
Never; min filters unlearned pairs out of stats before comparing, so it cannot return one
On the first iteration only; the loop then restarts from raw bytes using the learned pairs
Only when every present pair is unlearned; then 'if pair not in self.merges' breaks the loop
questions.explanation: Because unlearned pairs have key infinity, min only returns one when all present pairs are unlearned. Then 'if pair not in self.merges: break' stops encoding, since no further merge can apply.

questions.question: With merges = {(104, 105): 256} (only h+i learned), what does the from-scratch BPE encode("hi!") return?
options: [104, 105, 33] — three raw bytes
[256] — one token for the whole string
[256, 33] — two tokens
[104, 256] — two tokens
questions.explanation: 'hi!' is [104, 105, 33]. Round 1: (104,105) has key 256 and (105,33) has key inf, so min picks (104,105) and merges it, giving [256, 33]. Round 2: the only pair (256,33) is unlearned, so the loop breaks. The result is two tokens.

questions.question: What types does the from-scratch BPE tokenizer produce from encode()?
options: A torch.long tensor already moved to the GPU, ready to feed into the embedding layer
A NumPy uint8 array holding one raw byte per entry, to keep memory small
A plain Python list[int]; only the data loader turns ids into a torch.long tensor
A torch.float32 tensor of ids normalized to [0, 1] by dividing by vocab_size
questions.explanation: The tokenizer works with plain Python ints and bytes — no tensors, dtype, or device. encode returns a list[int]. Converting lists of ids into a torch.long tensor happens later in the data loader.

questions.question: Why is the from-scratch BPE training loop too slow for gigabytes of text?
options: It uses floating-point arithmetic for every pair count, which is slow in pure Python
It does O(n) work per merge because it re-scans the whole sequence each time
It must run on a GPU but the code only supports CPU
It stores the whole corpus as a tensor, which cannot exceed 2 GB on a single device
questions.explanation: Each merge re-counts all pairs and rewrites the whole sequence, so training costs O(n) per merge — fine for tiny corpora, far too slow at scale. Production tokenizers run the same algorithm with a Rust core and incremental pair counts.

questions.question: How do production tokenizers like tiktoken or HuggingFace tokenizers differ from the from-scratch BPE?
options: Same algorithm, built for speed: Rust core, incremental pair counts, and a regex pre-split
They replace merges with a small neural network that scores candidate splits for every word
They use large word-level vocabularies with an <unk> token instead of a byte fallback
They skip the byte alphabet and start merging from Unicode code points to save memory
questions.explanation: tiktoken and HuggingFace tokenizers run the identical byte-level BPE algorithm with a Rust core, incremental pair counts, and the regex split. Same math, engineered for throughput. The course implements the mechanism first, then reaches for the fast library.

questions.section: 7. Token count shrinks as merges grow
questions.question: With zero BPE merges (vocabulary of 256), how long is the encoding of a corpus?
options: Exactly its word count, since each word starts as one symbol
Exactly its character count, regardless of encoding
Zero, because no tokens exist before the first merge
Exactly its raw byte count — it is a byte-level tokenizer
questions.explanation: With no merges, every byte is its own token, so a 34-byte corpus encodes to 34 tokens. This is exactly the byte-level tokenizer. For non-ASCII text the byte count exceeds the character count.

questions.section: 7. Token count shrinks as merges grow
questions.question: Why do real BPE vocabularies stop in the tens of thousands instead of chasing ever-shorter sequences?
options: Tokenizer ids are stored as uint16, so vocabularies can never represent ids above 65,535
After roughly 50,000 merges, BPE starts making sequences longer again because merged tokens begin to overlap
Merges beyond about 32k break the decode(encode(s)) == s round-trip guarantee on rare text
On real text the length curve flattens — later merges save less — while each extra row costs parameters
questions.explanation: Early merges capture very frequent pairs and remove many symbols; later merges target progressively rarer pairs and save fewer tokens. Past a point, extra rows cost embedding parameters and gradient sparsity for little length savings. Round-tripping never breaks, and id width is not the limit.

questions.section: 7. Token count shrinks as merges grow
questions.question: Moving to a BPE tokenizer with more merges buys what, at what cost?
options: A smaller embedding table, at the cost of longer sequences
Exact round-tripping, at the cost of slower decoding
Shorter sequences, at the cost of a wider embedding table
Fewer special tokens, at the cost of more <unk> tokens
questions.explanation: More merges means a larger V and shorter encodings — the concrete face of the V-vs-T trade-off. The cost is a wider embedding table and output layer. Round-tripping holds at any size, and BPE has no <unk>.

questions.section: 8. GPT-2's byte-level BPE and the regex pre-split
questions.question: What refinement does GPT-2 add to plain byte-level BPE?
options: It lowercases and Unicode-normalizes all text before counting any pairs, to shrink the vocabulary
It first splits text with a regular expression into chunks and only allows merges within a chunk
It removes all spaces before training and has the decoder re-insert them between words
It merges triples of adjacent bytes instead of pairs, so units grow three times as fast
questions.explanation: Before counting pairs, GPT-2 splits text with a regex into chunks — roughly runs of letters, numbers, and punctuation, with leading spaces attached to the following word. BPE merges are only allowed within a chunk, never across boundaries. It still merges pairs and preserves case and spaces.

questions.section: 8. GPT-2's byte-level BPE and the regex pre-split
questions.question: In GPT-2's regex pre-tokenization, where do leading spaces go?
options: They are attached to the following word, so ' the' and ' dog' are chunks
They are attached to the preceding word, so 'the ' and 'dog ' are the chunks
They become separate one-byte chunks that are never merged with anything
They are deleted by the regex and re-inserted by the decoder between words
questions.explanation: GPT-2's regex attaches a leading space to the following word. That is why it tends to tokenize a leading-space-plus-word as one clean token like ' the' or ' dog'. Spaces are kept as bytes, not deleted.

questions.section: 8. GPT-2's byte-level BPE and the regex pre-split
questions.question: Why does GPT-2 forbid BPE merges across regex chunk boundaries?
options: To stop greedy merges straddling a word and punctuation (like 'dog.') and fusing numbers with words
To let the tokenizer train in parallel, one worker per chunk, without locking the shared pair counts
To guarantee every word in the corpus becomes exactly one token once training has finished
To cap the vocabulary at 256 entries per chunk type, keeping the embedding table small
questions.explanation: Without the split, greedy BPE could learn units like 'dog.' or 'the "' that mix a word with its neighbour's punctuation, or fuse numbers with words. Restricting merges to chunks keeps tokens clean. It does not guarantee one token per word.

questions.section: 8. GPT-2's byte-level BPE and the regex pre-split
questions.question: What consequence of GPT-2's regex pre-split affects how numbers tokenize?
options: Every number becomes exactly one token regardless of how many digits it has
Numbers are spelled out as English words before tokenization begins
Numbers are replaced by a single <num> special token and the digits are dropped
Long numbers break into digit-chunks rather than fusing with surrounding words
questions.explanation: The regex separates runs of numbers from letters and punctuation, and merges stay within chunks, so long numbers break into digit-chunks. This is one reason numbers tokenize oddly. Numbers are not converted or replaced with a special token.

questions.section: 8. GPT-2's byte-level BPE and the regex pre-split
questions.question: Which facts about GPT-2's tokenizer are publicly documented?
options: Its exact training corpus, plus the token count of every document in it
The exact merge lists of all the newer GPT-4-class proprietary models
The regex pre-split, the byte-level BPE design, and the vocabulary size of 50,257
The tokenizer's private held-out test set together with its benchmark compression scores
questions.explanation: The GPT-2 regex, byte-level BPE design, and vocabulary size 50,257 are publicly documented in the GPT-2 paper and OpenAI's released code. The precise merge lists of proprietary newer models are generally not documented.

questions.section: 8. GPT-2's byte-level BPE and the regex pre-split
questions.question: What is safe to say about the tokenizer of a proprietary GPT-4-class model?
options: It uses exactly the GPT-2 vocabulary of 50,257 tokens, unchanged since 2019 for backward compatibility
Same byte-level-BPE-with-regex-presplit family, but its exact merge list is generally undocumented
It is a word-level tokenizer with a very large vocabulary and an <unk> fallback for rare words
Its full merge list is published alongside the model weights, so anyone can reproduce it exactly
questions.explanation: Following the honesty rule, you should not assume a specific vocabulary for GPT-4-class models — their precise merge lists are generally not documented. What is safe to say is they use the same byte-level BPE with regex pre-split family.

questions.section: 8. GPT-2's byte-level BPE and the regex pre-split
questions.question: Which paper introduced byte-level BPE with a regex pre-tokenization split, and why did it go byte-level?
options: BERT (Devlin et al., 2018), so masked language modeling could predict any byte, including rare ones
GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019), to guarantee no out-of-vocabulary inputs while keeping the vocabulary modest
Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017), to shorten sequences and cut the quadratic attention cost
GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020), so in-context learning prompts could contain arbitrary Unicode text
questions.explanation: Byte-level BPE with a regex pre-split is introduced in the GPT-2 paper by Radford et al., 2019. Its section 2.2 explains that going byte-level guarantees no out-of-vocabulary inputs while keeping the vocabulary modest.

questions.section: 9. A unit test that pins the behavior down
questions.question: What does the BPE test test_roundtrip_unicode_emoji_and_accents check?
options: decode(encode(s)) == s for emoji, accents, and unseen scripts, plus the empty and one-char strings
That every emoji is mapped to one dedicated <emoji> special token instead of being kept as raw bytes
That the tokenizer raises a ValueError when asked to encode any character never seen in training
That every accented character in the French-ish corpus becomes exactly one merged token
questions.explanation: The test trains on a small French-ish corpus and asserts exact round-trip on strings including 😀, 🚀, 日本語, accents, "" and "a". This holds thanks to the byte fallback — unseen characters stay as bytes.

questions.section: 9. A unit test that pins the behavior down
questions.question: What does the BPE test test_training_creates_merges_and_compresses assert?
options: Training learns exactly 20 merges and the encoded corpus is at most half its raw byte length
Every distinct word in the training corpus becomes a single token after training finishes
The final vocabulary size equals the number of distinct words found in the training corpus
Training learns at least one merge and the encoded corpus is shorter than its raw byte count
questions.explanation: It checks len(tok.merges) > 0 (training actually learned merges) and len(tok.encode(corpus)) < raw byte length (it shortened the corpus). It does not require an exact merge count or one token per word.

questions.section: 9. A unit test that pins the behavior down
questions.question: What invariant does test_vocab_size_is_256_plus_num_merges assert for the BPE tokenizer?
options: tok.vocab_size == len(tok.merges)
tok.vocab_size == 2 * len(tok.merges)
tok.vocab_size == 256 + len(tok.merges)
tok.vocab_size == 256 * len(tok.merges)
questions.explanation: The vocabulary is the 256 base bytes plus one entry per learned merge, so vocab_size must equal 256 + number of merges. The other formulas ignore the base bytes or assume merges add more than one entry each.

questions.question: To save and load a trained BPE tokenizer, what is the minimal state you must persist?
options: Only the id→bytes vocabulary; the ordered merges can always be recomputed from it on load
The full training corpus, so the tokenizer can be retrained deterministically each time it is loaded
Only the ordered merge list; the vocab is rebuilt by replaying merges over the 256 base bytes
Both the vocab and a frequency count for every pair, so encode can rank pairs by count
questions.explanation: decode needs vocab and encode needs merges, but vocab is derivable: replay the merges in order, concatenating child bytes, exactly as train does. So the ordered merge list is the entire learned state. This is essentially the format of GPT-2's released merges.txt.

questions.question: When loading a BPE tokenizer saved as one 'a b' line per merge, how is each merge's new id determined?
