options: new_id is stored explicitly as a third column on each 'a b' line
new_id = 256 + line number, because merges were written in learned order
new_id = a + b, the sum of the two child ids, which is always unique
new_id is chosen at random on load and recorded in a separate id-map file
questions.explanation: The save routine writes merges sorted by their id, one pair per line, so the i-th line's merge has id 256 + i. On load, vocab is reset to the 256 bytes and each merge's bytes are rebuilt as vocab[a] + vocab[b].

questions.question: Which released GPT-2 file uses essentially the 'one ordered merge per line' format?
options: merges.txt
vocab.json
config.json
pytorch_model.bin
questions.explanation: Persisting just the ordered merge list, one pair per line, is essentially the format of GPT-2's released merges.txt. The vocabulary is a derived cache that can be rebuilt from it.

questions.question: A buggy BPE encode() picks the pair with max(stats, key=stats.get), copied from train(). What is wrong?
options: It should use min(stats, key=stats.get) instead, so the rarest pair in the input is fused first
max cannot be applied to a dict keyed by tuples, so it raises a TypeError at runtime
It merges the chosen pair twice per step, producing duplicate ids in the output list
It picks pairs by frequency in the input instead of by how early training learned them
questions.explanation: In train, picking the most frequent pair is how a merge gets learned. In encode the merges are fixed, and the correct question is which present pair has the smallest merge id. The fix is pair = min(stats, key=lambda p: self.merges.get(p, float("inf"))).

questions.question: When several keys tie in Python's max(stats, key=stats.get), which one does max return?
options: The last one it encounters
A random one among the tied keys
The one with the largest key value
The first one it encounters
questions.explanation: max returns the first maximal element it sees when keys tie. In the buggy BPE encode on 'newest', all five pair counts are 1, so max returns the first pair (110, 101), 'n e'.

questions.question: Why does the buggy max-frequency BPE encode() return raw bytes for 'newest' even though (e, s) was learned?
options: merge() silently fails on pairs that appear only once, so every fusion in 'newest' is a no-op
The learned pair (e, s) is skipped because encode only ever fuses pairs at the start or the end of a word
max returns the unlearned pair (n, e), so the 'if pair not in self.merges: break' guard fires at once
get_stats only counts pairs made of two consonants, so the vowel-containing (e, s) is never seen
questions.explanation: All pairs tie at count 1, so max returns (110, 101) = n e, which was never learned. The guard breaks on the first round, so the learned pair (e, s) in the same sequence is never reached and nothing is merged — 6 tokens instead of 4.

questions.question: Why is the 'if pair not in self.merges: break' guard correct in the proper BPE encode() but harmful in the max-frequency version?
options: The guard is harmful in both versions; a correct encoder must keep scanning past unlearned pairs until the whole string ends
With the merge-id key min prefers learned pairs, so break means none apply; with max it fires when the top pair is unlearned
In the proper version the guard is never reached, because min only ever returns pairs from the merge table
With max, the guard raises a KeyError instead of breaking, because self.merges is indexed before the check
questions.explanation: In the correct loop, min with the merge-id key always picks a learned pair if one exists, so breaking means no merge applies. In the buggy loop, the most frequent pair in new text (like 'z z' or 'n e') is often unlearned, so it breaks early while learned pairs remain.

questions.question: Why is 'the BPE vocabulary' of a corpus not unique, and what does that imply for shipping a model?
options: Greedy tie-breaking is a free choice, so implementations learn different merges; the exact list must ship
BPE is randomized on every run, so each user must retrain the tokenizer and fine-tune the model to match
The vocabulary depends on the GPU type used in training, so models ship one tokenizer per supported device family
Vocabularies are unique for a given corpus, so only the corpus name and vocabulary size need to ship
questions.explanation: Two tokenizers trained on the same corpus with different tie-breaks are both valid but encode text into different id sequences. A model's embeddings are tied to specific ids, so you must ship the exact merge list with it.

questions.question: With the three-merge tokenizer (e,s)→256, (es,t)→257, (est,space)→258, what is the encoding of 'widest'?
options: [257] — a single token
questions.explanation: widest is w i d e s t. Merge 0 fuses e s → es, merge 1 fuses es t → est. There is no trailing space, so merge 2 does not fire. Result: 4 tokens, sharing suffix token 257 with newest and lowest.

questions.question: On real text, why do later BPE merges shorten sequences less than early merges?
options: Later merges produce longer tokens that the encoder must split again whenever they happen to cross a regex chunk boundary
Later merges are only applied near the end of each document, where the remaining byte pairs are concentrated
Early merges are applied twice during encoding, once on the raw bytes and once on the merged sequence
Early merges fuse the most frequent pairs and fire across the corpus; later ones fuse rarer pairs and fire less
questions.explanation: Early merges fuse very common pairs and remove many symbols; later merges fuse progressively rarer pairs that occur on less text. Sequence length falls fast then flattens, so beyond the tens of thousands extra rows cost parameters and gradient sparsity for little gain.

questions.section: Prerequisites / Why this matters for ML
questions.question: Why is a pretraining data loader considered one of the most invisible sources of training bugs?
options: If the (x, y) shift is off or documents bleed together, the model silently learns the wrong objective
It is the only component that runs custom CUDA kernels, so any indexing error crashes the entire GPU process
It rebuilds the model architecture every epoch, so a bad batch silently changes the layer count
It owns the learning-rate schedule, so a wrong batch count makes the optimizer diverge mid-run
questions.explanation: The data loader is called every training step. If the target shift is wrong or documents bleed into each other, nothing crashes — the model just learns the wrong objective and you chase a mysteriously bad loss for days.

questions.section: Prerequisites / Why this matters for ML
questions.question: In next-token pretraining, how are the input x and target y of a batch related?
options: y is an independent random window drawn from elsewhere in the stream
y is x reversed in time, so the model learns to predict in both directions
y is the document label of x, one class id per window
They are the same slice of the token stream, shifted by one position
questions.explanation: The input x and target y are the same slice of the stream shifted by one position, so y[t] is the token that follows x[t]. That shift is the entire supervision signal for pretraining. Random or reversed targets would teach nothing useful.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: from a pile of documents to training windows
questions.question: What three jobs turn a pile of tokenized documents into pretraining batches?
options: Sort documents by length, pad each one to the longest with zeros, and shuffle the padded rows every epoch
Remove stop words, lowercase all text, and deduplicate repeated sentences before tokenizing
Mark document boundaries, pack all ids into one stream, cut fixed-length windows with a one-step shift
Split documents into sentences, label each sentence by topic, and batch together sentences with one label
questions.explanation: Three jobs stand between raw documents and the model: mark boundaries (so documents do not run into each other), pack (concatenate all ids into one long 1-D array), and cut windows of length block_size paired with the same window shifted one step.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: from a pile of documents to training windows
questions.question: Why must pretraining mark the boundary between documents?
options: Otherwise the tokenizer cannot decode the stream back into separate documents
Otherwise the model learns to run one article straight into an unrelated one
Otherwise the concatenated stream overflows the model's fixed context window
Otherwise the embedding table ends up with too few rows for the merged documents
questions.explanation: Without a boundary, concatenated documents look like one continuous text, so the model learns spurious continuations from one article into the next. Marking boundaries gives it an explicit 'document over' signal. The tokenizer and context window are unaffected.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: from a pile of documents to training windows
questions.question: What is the advantage of packing documents into one long 1-D stream of ids?
options: Each document keeps its own fixed-length row, simplifying masking
No padding and no wasted space — every token is training signal
Short documents are automatically discarded
The model sees each document only once per epoch in order
questions.explanation: Packing concatenates every document's ids into one stream, so there is no padding and every token contributes to the loss. Padding-based batching would waste compute on pad tokens.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: from a pile of documents to training windows
questions.question: In the pretraining data pipeline, what is block_size?
options: The model's fixed context length T, the length of each training window
The number of separate documents packed into each training batch of windows
The number of raw bytes stored for each token id in the stream
The size of the tokenizer's vocabulary, including special tokens
questions.explanation: block_size (written T) is the model's fixed context length. The packed stream is sliced into T-length windows, each paired with the same window shifted one step right. The batch size and vocabulary size are separate quantities.

questions.question: What is a special token?
options: A byte value that UTF-8 never produces, so it can safely mark boundaries inside the raw stream
The learned merge that occurs more often than any other, promoted to a fixed reserved id after training
A token that the loss function always masks out, so the model never learns to predict it
A reserved vocabulary id that does not stand for any byte or subword and carries structural meaning
questions.explanation: A special token is an id in the vocabulary with structural, not lexical, meaning — it does not stand for any byte or subword. The most fundamental pretraining example is <|endoftext|>, the document separator.

questions.question: What is <|endoftext|> in GPT-2-style pretraining?
options: A marker placed at the start of every sentence so the model knows a new clause begins
The padding token used to fill short documents up to block_size before batching
The end-of-text separator placed between documents to signal 'this document is over'
The token that replaces out-of-vocabulary words the byte-level tokenizer cannot encode
questions.explanation: <|endoftext|> is GPT-2's name for the end-of-text separator. It is placed between documents so the model sees an explicit end-of-document signal. Byte-level BPE has no OOV, so it is not an unknown-word token, and packing uses no padding.

questions.question: If 'The cat sat.' and 'Quantum error correction…' are concatenated without a separator, what does the model learn?
options: Nothing harmful, because the tokenizer inserts a document boundary automatically
To ignore the second document entirely, since its topic is unrelated to the first one shown
To predict 'Quantum' as the natural continuation of 'The cat sat.' — a nonsense dependency
To translate the first document into the second, treating the two as a parallel sentence pair
questions.explanation: Without a separator, the training target after 'The cat sat.' is 'Quantum', so the model is trained to predict a nonsense cross-document continuation and wastes capacity on it. The tokenizer inserts nothing automatically.

questions.question: Because the causal mask still lets attention look back across an <|endoftext|> boundary, what does the model learn about that token?
options: That tokens before <|endoftext|> must be copied verbatim after it
That <|endoftext|> means 'reset — a new document starts now'
That <|endoftext|> should never be predicted, only consumed as input
That attention must be fully blocked across every document boundary
questions.explanation: Attention can still see across the boundary, so the model learns <|endoftext|> as a reset signal: what follows is a fresh, independent document. This is exactly what lets a trained model stop generating at the end of a sample.

questions.question: Why does including <|endoftext|> in training let a model stop generating?
options: The model learns to emit the end-of-text token where documents end, giving an explicit stop signal
Generation always stops automatically once exactly block_size new tokens have been sampled
The token resets the model's weights to their initial values, which cleanly ends the current generated sample
The decoder deletes every token generated after the first repeated phrase it detects
questions.explanation: Having seen <|endoftext|> at every document end, the model learns to predict it when a sample is complete. Emitting it is the explicit 'document over' signal that ends generation. It does not touch weights.

questions.question: Which additional special tokens do chat models add beyond <|endoftext|>?
options: One token per supported language
Separate tokens for each digit 0–9
A token for every punctuation mark
Role markers and turn boundaries
questions.explanation: Chat models add more special tokens such as role markers and turn boundaries to structure conversations; the course builds those in Module 14. Digits and punctuation are ordinary byte/subword tokens.

questions.question: If a BPE tokenizer has V ordinary tokens, how is the <|endoftext|> id typically added?
options: Reuse id 0, replacing the null byte, so the vocabulary size and both tables stay at exactly V rows each
Map it onto the most frequent merged token, so it inherits an already well-trained embedding
Store it outside the vocabulary as a string flag, so it has no embedding row or output logit
Reserve one more id, e.g. V itself, so the embedding table and output head each get an extra row
questions.explanation: You reserve one extra id (say V) for <|endoftext|>, so the model's embedding table and output head both have one more row for it. It is a real vocabulary id with its own embedding, not a reused byte or an out-of-vocabulary marker.

questions.section: 3. Packing: one corpus, one id stream
questions.question: What does pack_documents(list_of_id_lists, eot_id) do?
options: Pads every document to the same length with eot_id and stacks them into a 2-D tensor
Inserts eot_id only between the first and the last document, leaving the middle ones joined directly
Concatenates every document's ids into one stream with eot_id appended after each document
Replaces the most frequent id in each document with eot_id to mark where it ends
questions.explanation: pack_documents extends a list with each document's ids and appends eot_id after every document, then returns the stream as a 1-D torch.long tensor. It does not pad; eot_id follows every document, including the last.

questions.section: 3. Packing: one corpus, one id stream
questions.question: What is pack_documents([[10, 11, 12], [20, 21]], eot_id=0)?
questions.explanation: Each document is followed by eot_id 0, so the result is [10, 11, 12, 0, 20, 21, 0], a 1-D tensor of length 3 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 7. The two zeros are the boundaries. The separator goes after each document, not before.

questions.section: 3. Packing: one corpus, one id stream
questions.question: Why do token-id tensors use dtype torch.long?
options: Token ids index the embedding table, and PyTorch's embedding lookup requires an integer index type
long is the fastest dtype for matrix multiplication on GPUs, so the lookups can run directly on tensor cores
Token ids can be negative after packing, which requires a signed 64-bit floating-point type
long uses less memory per element than uint8, which matters for multi-gigabyte corpora
questions.explanation: Ids index the embedding table, and PyTorch's embedding lookup (and cross-entropy target) require an integer index type; long (64-bit) is the dtype every id tensor uses in the course. Float ids would be meaningless as indices.

questions.section: 3. Packing: one corpus, one id stream
questions.question: How are very large pretraining corpora stored in practice?
options: Ids are streamed to a memory-mapped uint16 file on disk and opened with np.memmap for training
The whole corpus is held as one Python list of ints in RAM and sliced into windows each step
Each document is stored as a separate float32 tensor kept resident on the GPU throughout training
Ids are stored as JSON text files and re-parsed into tensors at the start of every training step
questions.explanation: Real corpora are too large for a Python list. Documents are streamed through the tokenizer and ids written to a memory-mapped uint16 file, then np.memmap lets the OS page in only the windows you touch. The packing logic is identical.

questions.section: 3. Packing: one corpus, one id stream
questions.question: Why is uint16 enough to store token ids for a GPT-2-sized vocabulary on disk?
options: Token ids are always below 256
uint16 stores floats with enough precision for ids
The embedding table is limited to 16 columns
A vocabulary under 65,536 entries fits in 16 bits
questions.explanation: uint16 holds integers 0..65,535, so any vocabulary under 65,536 (like GPT-2's 50,257) fits, halving storage versus 32-bit. Ids go above 255 once merges exist, so 8 bits would not suffice.

questions.section: 3. Packing: one corpus, one id stream
questions.question: What does np.memmap give a pretraining data loader?
options: Automatic placement of the whole dataset in GPU memory before the first training step
Built-in shuffling of documents at every epoch, so get_batch can read windows in order
The OS pages in only the windows actually touched, so the full corpus never has to fit in RAM
Compression of the stored ids to 4 bits each, shrinking the corpus file on disk roughly fourfold
questions.explanation: A memory-mapped file is accessed like an array, but the OS loads only the disk pages for the windows read. With memmap the main cost of a batch is the pages faulted in. It does not move data to GPU, shuffle, or compress.

questions.question: For a pretraining window x, how is the target window y defined?
options: y[t] = x[t-1] — x slid one step to the right
y[t] = x[t+1] — x slid one step to the left
y[t] = x[t] — the same window
y[t] = x[T-1-t] — the window reversed
questions.explanation: At every position t the model must predict the token that actually comes next, so y[t] = x[t+1]. Using y = x would train the model to predict tokens it can already see.

questions.question: How many next-token prediction problems does one length-T training window supply?
options: 1 — only the final position of each window is supervised by the loss term
T — position 0 predicts token 1, position 1 predicts token 2, and so on
T^2 — every pair of positions forms a separate prediction problem
T/2 — only even positions get a target, so windows never overlap
questions.explanation: Each of the T positions has a target, so one window gives T prediction problems at once. The causal mask ensures position t uses only tokens at positions ≤ t, so this is not cheating.

questions.question: What guarantees that position t in a training window cannot peek at its own target?
options: The causal mask, which lets position t use only tokens at positions ≤ t
The <|endoftext|> token, which hides every future token from attention
Random sampling of window start positions, so targets are never adjacent
The torch.long dtype of the id tensor, which blocks reading ahead
questions.explanation: The causal attention mask blocks position t from attending to later positions, so it cannot see token t+1, its target. Without it, supervising all T positions at once would be trivial cheating.

questions.question: How many consecutive tokens from the stream are needed to build one (x, y) training example of length T?
options: T — x and y are exactly the same T tokens of the stream
2T — x and y are two disjoint consecutive windows of T tokens each
T − 1 — the last token of each window is dropped from both
T + 1 — the first T are x and the last T, offset by one, are y
questions.explanation: x is data[i : i+T] and y is data[i+1 : i+1+T], so together they span T + 1 consecutive tokens. Forgetting the extra token is the root of off-by-one errors.

questions.question: In get_batch, why is high = data.numel() - block_size?
options: It reserves the final block_size tokens of the stream as a held-out validation set that training never sees
It makes the largest start exactly N - block_size, so the very last window of the stream is sampled twice as often
randint's high is exclusive, so the largest start is N - block_size - 1, where x and shifted y still fit
It ensures every sampled start index is a multiple of block_size, so windows never overlap one another
questions.explanation: The target slice data[i+1 : i+1+block_size] reads up to index i + block_size, so we need i ≤ N − block_size − 1. Since randint's high is exclusive, high = N − block_size makes the max draw exactly that. Off by one wastes the last window or indexes past the end.

questions.question: What does data.numel() return for the 1-D packed token stream?
options: The number of documents packed into the stream
The number of distinct token ids that appear in it
The number of elements, i.e. the stream's length N
The size of the stream in bytes, i.e. 8 bytes per id
questions.explanation: numel() returns the total number of elements in a tensor; for a 1-D id stream that is just its length N. It does not count documents, distinct ids, or bytes.

questions.question: What does ix = torch.randint(low=0, high=high, size=(batch_size,)) produce in get_batch?
options: A (batch_size, block_size) tensor of random token ids drawn from the vocabulary
A 1-D int64 tensor of shape (batch_size,) with uniform random start positions in [0, high)
A single random integer that is used as the start position for every row of the batch
A float tensor of probabilities over start positions, later sampled from with torch.multinomial
questions.explanation: torch.randint returns int64 values uniformly from [0, high), here batch_size of them, one start per row. Sampling indices, not data, is nearly free and lets get_batch slice views from the one big tensor.

questions.question: Why does get_batch draw random window starts rather than sweeping through the stream in order?
options: Random starts make successive batches near-independent, so consecutive gradients are not highly correlated
Sequential sweeps would need the entire stream resident in GPU memory, which exceeds capacity at scale
Random starts guarantee that every token is seen exactly once per epoch, unlike sequential sweeps
torch.stack only accepts slices taken in random order, so a sequential sweep raises an error
questions.explanation: Marching through the stream in order gives consecutive batches from adjacent text, so gradients are highly correlated and training less stable. Random starts make batches near-independent. They do not guarantee exactly-once coverage.

questions.question: Why does get_batch sample start indices instead of shuffling the data itself?
options: Shuffling the stream in place would silently convert it from torch.long to a float dtype
Index tensors can be sent to the GPU, but the packed data tensor itself is pinned to the CPU
Shuffling would remove the <|endoftext|> separators, since they are sorted to the end of the stream
A handful of integers is almost free and lets it slice views from the one big tensor without copying
questions.explanation: Drawing batch_size integers is trivially cheap, and slicing data[i : i+block_size] gives views into the existing tensor. Shuffling a giant array would be expensive and would also destroy the contiguous order windows depend on.

questions.question: In get_batch, what shape does torch.stack produce from batch_size slices each of shape (block_size,)?
options: (batch_size * block_size,), concatenated end to end
(block_size, batch_size), along a new trailing axis
(batch_size, block_size, 1), with an extra singleton axis
(batch_size, block_size), along a new leading axis
questions.explanation: torch.stack joins tensors along a new dimension 0, giving (batch_size, block_size). torch.cat would instead concatenate the windows end to end into one 1-D tensor, which is why stack is used.

questions.question: In get_batch, how do the slices and the stacked batch differ in memory?
options: Both the slices and the stacked batch are views into data, so no memory is allocated per batch
The slices are copies of data, while torch.stack returns a view that stitches those copies together
The slices are views into data, while torch.stack allocates a new contiguous tensor independent of it
Both are fresh copies, so each call temporarily doubles memory compared with the stream itself
questions.explanation: Basic slicing data[i : i+block_size] returns a view sharing storage with data. torch.stack allocates a new tensor, so the batch is contiguous and independent of the stream.

questions.question: Why must get_batch reuse the same ix for building y as for x?
options: Reusing ix halves the random-number generation cost, but drawing a fresh ix for y would work equally well
So y[b, t] = data[i+1+t] = x[b, t+1]; fresh random starts would make targets unrelated to inputs
torch.randint can only be called once per batch, since a second call resets the global generator state
Drawing a new ix for y would change its dtype from torch.long to int32, breaking cross-entropy
questions.explanation: x[b] and y[b] come from the same start i, so y[b, t] = data[i+1+t] and x[b, t] = data[i+t], giving y[b, t] == x[b, t+1]. If y used different random starts, the targets would have nothing to do with the inputs and the model would learn nothing.

questions.question: Why does get_batch do its indexing on the CPU and call .to(device) only at the end?
options: Integer bookkeeping is cheap on CPU, and moving only finished batches avoids forcing the stream onto the GPU
GPUs cannot index tensors with integer index tensors, so every slice has to be computed on the CPU first
torch.stack is not implemented for CUDA tensors, so the batch must be stacked on the CPU before transfer
Calling .to(device) before slicing would silently change the dtype of the stream from long to float32
questions.explanation: The slicing and stacking are cheap integer work on CPU; only the two finished (B, T) batches are transferred to the compute device. Threading device through as an argument avoids putting the entire data stream on the GPU up front. If device is 'cpu', .to('cpu') is effectively a no-op.

questions.question: Which two guard clauses does the real get_batch in llmre.data.loader add, and why?
options: That data is 1-D and that data.numel() > block_size, because both failures are otherwise silent or opaque
That data is float32 and that batch_size is even, because odd batches break the stacking logic
That the device is CUDA and that block_size is a power of two, because randint needs an aligned range
That every document ends with eot_id and that ids are sorted, because packing assumes sorted input
questions.explanation: A 2-D data tensor would make the slices mean the wrong thing silently, and a stream no longer than block_size gives high ≤ 0, which torch.randint rejects with an opaque error. Failing early with a clear message is cheaper than debugging symptoms.

questions.question: What vectorized alternative to the Python loop builds a get_batch batch in one indexing op?
options: x = data.view(batch_size, block_size) and y = x.roll(1) over the time dimension
x = data[ix] and y = data[ix + 1], gathering one token per row of the batch
x = torch.cat([data[ix]] * block_size) and y = x + 1, broadcast over every position
idx = ix[:, None] + torch.arange(block_size), then x = data[idx] and y = data[idx + 1]
questions.explanation: Broadcasting ix[:, None] + arange(block_size) gives a (batch_size, block_size) index matrix; gathering data[idx] and data[idx + 1] yields x and y in one fused op, faster on GPU since it launches one kernel instead of batch_size slice-and-stack steps.

questions.question: With data = torch.arange(12), block_size = 4, if a row of x is [4, 5, 6, 7], what is the matching row of y?
questions.explanation: y is x shifted one token: from start i = 4, x = data[4:8] = [4, 5, 6, 7] and y = data[5:9] = [5, 6, 7, 8]. Position 0 sees 4 and predicts 5; position 1 sees 4, 5 and predicts 6.

questions.question: What one-line sanity check confirms a pretraining data loader's targets are correctly shifted?
options: torch.equal(x, y) returns True for the whole batch
torch.equal(x[:, 1:], y[:, :-1]) returns True
torch.equal(x[:, :-1], y[:, 1:]) returns True
x.sum() == y.sum() for every row of the batch
questions.explanation: If y is x shifted left by one, then every target except the last equals the next input: y[:, :-1] == x[:, 1:]. Run this boolean whenever you touch a data loader. torch.equal(x, y) being True would indicate the unshifted bug.

questions.question: What symptom indicates the classic data-loader off-by-one y = data[i : i + block_size]?
options: Training loss stays exactly constant from the first step, as if the gradients were all zero
Training loss plummets to near zero within a few steps while the model learns nothing useful
The loss becomes NaN immediately on the first backward pass because the targets overflow
The model quickly collapses to predicting only <|endoftext|> at every single position
questions.explanation: Without the +1, y equals x, so the model is trained to predict a token it can already see — trivial to fit. A suspiciously low training loss in the first few steps almost always means the targets are not shifted.

questions.question: What are the shape and dtype of the packed token stream in the pretraining pipeline?
options: (N,), torch.long — the whole corpus with documents joined by eot_id
(B, T), torch.long — one fixed-length row per original document
(N, C), torch.float32 — every token already looked up in the embedding
(N,), torch.float16 — ids normalized to [0, 1] by the vocabulary size
questions.explanation: The packed stream is a 1-D long tensor of length N containing every document's ids separated by eot_id. Batches cut from it are (B, T). Embeddings (B, T, C) come later in the model.

questions.question: What are the shape and dtype of a pretraining batch x and its target y?
options: x is (B, T) long and y is (B,) long
x is (B, T, C) float32 and y is (B, T) long
Both (T, B) with dtype torch.float32
Both (B, T) with dtype torch.long
questions.explanation: x holds B input windows of length T = block_size, and y holds the same windows shifted one token left, so both are (B, T) long. y supplies one target per position, not one per window.

questions.question: Where do x and y go after get_batch returns them?
options: x goes to the cross-entropy loss as the target, and y is looked up in the embedding table
Both are embedded to (B, T, C) and concatenated along the channel axis before the first layer
x enters the embedding table, (B, T) → (B, T, C); y is the target for the cross-entropy loss
x is decoded back into text for logging, and y is discarded once the batch has been validated
questions.explanation: The input ids x are looked up in the embedding table to become (B, T, C) activations, and y is passed as the integer target to cross-entropy. y is never embedded.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: why random windows, and the cost
questions.question: What is the cost of one get_batch call, and how does it compare to training?
options: O(N) per call because it scans the whole stream to find document boundaries before sampling starts
O(N log N) per call because it sorts the stream by token id before drawing the window start positions
O(B · T) memory copies, negligible next to the forward/backward pass, so re-sampling each step is fine
O(B · T^2) per call because it computes causal attention over each window before returning it
questions.explanation: get_batch draws B random integers and gathers B windows of length T, so its cost is O(B · T) copies — negligible next to the model's forward and backward pass. With a memmap, the only real cost is the disk pages the OS faults in.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: why random windows, and the cost
questions.question: What mild side benefit comes from sampling window starts uniformly over the stream?
options: Every document is guaranteed to appear in exactly one batch per epoch, so coverage is perfectly even
A token is seen in many different context alignments, with window boundaries in different places
Rare tokens are automatically oversampled relative to common ones, which balances the vocabulary
The model never sees an <|endoftext|> token at a window boundary, so documents are never split
questions.explanation: Because starts are uniform, a given token lands at different positions with different preceding context across an epoch, and window boundaries fall in different places. That is a mild, free form of data augmentation. It does not guarantee coverage or rebalance tokens.

questions.question: For data = torch.arange(100), what are the shapes and dtype of x and y from get_batch(data, block_size=8, batch_size=16)?
options: Both (16, 8) with dtype torch.long
Both (8, 16) with dtype torch.long
x is (16, 8) and y is (16, 9), dtype torch.long
Both (16, 8) with dtype torch.float32
questions.explanation: get_batch returns batch_size windows of length block_size for both x and y, so (16, 8). torch.arange of integers is int64 and slicing preserves it, so the dtype is torch.long.

questions.question: For data = torch.arange(100) and block_size = 8, what is the largest start index get_batch can sample?
options: 92, since high = 100 − 8 = 92 is inclusive for torch.randint
99, the last valid index of the stream, since y can wrap around
88, the last multiple of block_size that fits before the end of the stream
91, since high = 92 is exclusive and y = data[92:100] ends at the last token
questions.explanation: high = numel − block_size = 92 is the exclusive upper bound for torch.randint, so the max start is 91. Then x = data[91:99] and y = data[92:100], ending at index 99. A start of 92 would need index 100, which does not exist.

questions.question: Is <|endoftext|> just a string marker, or a real part of the model?
options: It is a text marker that the tokenizer strips out before training, so no id is ever stored
It is a hard-coded rule in the sampler that halts generation, not an entry in the vocabulary
It is a byte sequence that BPE splits into ordinary tokens like any other piece of text
It is a real vocabulary id with its own embedding that the model can predict and emit
questions.explanation: The separator is a reserved vocabulary id with its own embedding row and output logit. The model learns to predict it at document ends, which provides the 'document over' signal used to stop generation.

questions.question: Given x[0] = [4, 5, 6, 7] and correctly shifted targets, what does position 2 see and predict?
options: It sees 4, 5, 6, 7 and is trained to predict 8, the next token after the window
It sees only 6, its own position, and is trained to predict 7
It sees 4, 5, 6 (the causal mask blocks 7) and is trained to predict 7
It sees 4, 5 (the mask blocks its own token) and is trained to predict 6
questions.explanation: y[0] = [5, 6, 7, 8], so the target at position 2 is y[0][2] = 7. The causal mask lets position 2 attend only to positions 0–2 (tokens 4, 5, 6), so it cannot see 7, its answer.

questions.question: A model reaches a training loss near 0 within 10 steps on real text. What is the single most likely bug?
options: The learning rate is far too low, so the optimizer barely moves the weights
The targets are not shifted — y equals x (or is shifted the wrong way)
The tokenizer vocabulary is too small, so every token becomes easy to guess
The batch size is too large, so each gradient step averages away the noise
questions.explanation: Real text cannot be predicted near-perfectly in 10 steps. The likely cause is y equal to x, so the model 'predicts' a token it can already see. Check torch.equal(x[:, 1:], y[:, :-1]).

questions.question: Why would float32 token ids be wrong in PyTorch?
options: Embedding lookup and the cross-entropy target both need integer (long) indices, so floats are a type error
float32 cannot represent integers above 65,535 exactly, so ids from large vocabularies get corrupted
float32 ids would make training noticeably slower on GPUs but would still give exactly correct results
float32 ids are automatically rounded during lookup, which causes off-by-one errors near large ids
questions.explanation: Token ids are integer indices into the embedding table. nn.Embedding and cross-entropy's target argument both require an integer index type, so passing floats is both meaningless and a type error.

questions.question: In a GPT-style language model, what does every layer after the embedding layer actually see as its input?
options: The original text characters of the prompt, re-read at each layer
Vectors produced by the embedding layer, never the raw text or ids
The integer token ids, rescaled to [0, 1] by dividing by vocab_size
One-hot vectors of length vocab_size, one per position in the batch
questions.explanation: Embeddings are the model's entire interface to language: after the lookup, every downstream layer operates only on real-valued vectors of shape (B, T, C). The integer ids and the text are gone. One-hot vectors are never materialized — the lookup is the efficient form of one-hot times a matrix.

questions.question: What role do positional embeddings play in a GPT-style transformer?
options: They compress the vocabulary so the token table needs far fewer rows for rare words
They normalize every token vector to unit length so attention scores stay in a fixed range
They turn a permutation-blind bag of vectors into a representation of an ordered sequence
They replace the token embedding entirely for every position after the first one in a sequence
questions.explanation: Attention by itself treats its input as a set, so without position information word order is invisible. Positional embeddings add a per-position signal so the same token at different positions yields different vectors. They do not replace or normalize the token embedding; they are added to it.

questions.question: Why is it misleading to treat token id 3797 as 'bigger' than token id 464?
options: Because ids are sorted by corpus frequency, so a larger id means a rarer token
Because ids are hashed by the tokenizer and change on every training run
Because larger ids always refer to subword fragments rather than whole words
Because token ids are names (indices into the vocabulary), not quantities
questions.explanation: A token id is just an index into the vocabulary; its numeric value carries no meaning. 3797 is not 'more' than 464 in any useful sense. That is why ids must be converted into learned vectors before a network, which computes with quantities, can use them.

questions.question: What is a token embedding, in the simplest terms?
options: A lookup table with one learned row (a vector of C numbers) per vocabulary entry
A fixed hash function mapping each id to a random but unchanging vector of C numbers
A small neural network that predicts a C-vector from the decimal digits of the id
A frequency count of each token in the training corpus, normalized to sum to one
questions.explanation: An embedding is a lookup table: token id i selects row i, a vector of C numbers. Those rows start random and are trained by gradient descent with the rest of the model. It is not a fixed hash and not computed from the id's digits — it is a learned parameter matrix.

questions.question: After training, how are the embedding rows for 'cat', 'dog' and 'parliament' expected to relate?
options: All three are mutually orthogonal, since embedding tables are kept orthonormal in training
'cat' and 'dog' sit near each other while 'cat' and 'parliament' sit far apart
They are identical vectors, since meaning is only added later by the attention layers
'cat' and 'parliament' are closest because their ids happen to be adjacent in the vocab
questions.explanation: Because the rows are trained by gradient descent, tokens used in similar ways end up with similar vectors, so 'cat' and 'dog' end up close and 'cat' and 'parliament' far apart. Nothing forces embeddings to be orthogonal, and id adjacency is irrelevant to meaning.

questions.question: How are the values in a token embedding table initialized and updated?
options: They are copied from a pretrained word2vec model and kept frozen during training
They are set to one-hot vectors at initialization and never change afterwards
They start random and are trained by gradient descent along with the rest of the model
They are computed once from character n-gram counts when the tokenizer itself is trained
questions.explanation: The embedding rows start as random numbers and are learned jointly with every other parameter by gradient descent. That is why the table ends up encoding meaning: similar usage yields similar gradients and similar rows. They are not frozen or derived from counts.

questions.question: What are the shape and meaning of the token embedding table `wte` in GPT?
options: (n_embd, vocab_size); column i is the vector for token i
(block_size, n_embd); row t is the vector for position t
(vocab_size, vocab_size); a learned token-to-token similarity matrix
(vocab_size, n_embd); row i is the vector for token id i
questions.explanation: `wte` has shape (vocab_size, n_embd): one row per vocabulary entry, each of width C = n_embd. Looking up id i means 'take row i'. The (block_size, n_embd) shape describes the positional table `wpe`, not `wte`.

questions.section: 2. Why raw ids cannot feed a network
questions.question: Why would feeding raw token ids directly into a linear layer Wx be a problem regarding magnitude?
options: The layer would treat the arbitrary id value as a magnitude, so large ids give huge activations
The linear layer cannot accept integer inputs at all, so the forward pass raises a dtype error first
Large ids would overflow float16 and small ids underflow to zero, so the inputs lose precision
The linear layer would round every id to the nearest power of two, merging unrelated tokens
questions.explanation: A linear layer multiplies its input by weights, so id 50000 would yield an activation 100x larger than id 500 purely because of an arbitrary id assignment. The numeric value of an id encodes no useful structure, so this magnitude is meaningless noise. The issue is semantic, not a dtype error.

questions.section: 2. Why raw ids cannot feed a network
questions.question: Why can a single scalar token id not express that two tokens play similar roles?
options: Because scalars cannot be differentiated by autograd, so similar tokens never get gradients
Adjacent ids can be unrelated words, and one number cannot encode similarity geometrically
Because ids are assigned as unique primes, so no two ids share any arithmetic relationship
Because measuring similarity between tokens requires complex numbers rather than real ones
questions.explanation: Ids 464 and 465 might be 'the' and 'zebra' — adjacent numbers, unrelated meanings. A single scalar cannot express similarity, but a C-dimensional vector can, because similarity becomes geometric closeness. Scalars are perfectly differentiable; the problem is representational.

questions.section: 2. Why raw ids cannot feed a network
questions.question: Why is one number per token too little capacity, compared to a C = 768 vector?
options: Because a single number cannot be stored precisely in float32, so nearby token ids collide in memory
Because GPU tensor cores require vector inputs of length at least 768 before they will run matrix multiplies
Word usage has many facets (syntax, topic, sentiment, formality); a vector gives each its own directions
Because 768 is the number of characters needed to spell out the longest token in the vocabulary
questions.explanation: Word usage has many facets — syntax, topic, sentiment, formality, and more. A single scalar cannot hold all of them, while a 768-dimensional vector can devote different directions to different facets. The limitation is capacity, not hardware or precision.

questions.section: 2. Why raw ids cannot feed a network
questions.question: If onehot(i) is a length-V row vector and W has shape (V, C), what is onehot(i) W?
options: The sum of all rows of W
Column i of W
A V-by-C matrix with only row i non-zero
Exactly row i of W, a C-vector
questions.explanation: A one-hot row vector with a 1 at position i selects row i when multiplied by W: onehot(i) W = W_i. That is why an embedding lookup is mathematically a one-hot times a weight matrix. It yields a C-vector, not a column or a matrix.

questions.section: 2. Why raw ids cannot feed a network
questions.question: How does an embedding lookup relate to multiplying a one-hot vector by a weight matrix?
options: It computes the same result without materializing the V-long one-hot or multiplying by zeros
It is an approximation of the one-hot product that is only exact for small vocabularies of a few thousand
It is unrelated; embedding tables use hashing into buckets rather than matrix algebra
It performs the full one-hot by matrix multiply, but in a fused kernel on the GPU
questions.explanation: Indexing row i gives exactly onehot(i) W, so the lookup is the efficient form of that multiplication: it skips building the huge one-hot and doing the wasteful multiply-by-zeros. The result is exact, not an approximation, and no full multiply happens at runtime.

questions.question: In GPT-2 small, what are typical values of V (vocab_size) and C (n_embd) for the token embedding table W_te in R^(V x C)?
questions.explanation: GPT-2 uses a vocabulary of 50257 tokens and an embedding width of 768 for the small model, so W_te is 50257 x 768. The value 1024 is GPT-2's block_size (max context length), which sizes the positional table, not the token table.

questions.question: Given token ids idx of shape (B, T), what does the lookup tok[b, t, :] = W_te[idx[b, t]] produce?
options: A tensor of shape (B, C) — the C-vectors of each sequence averaged over its T positions
A tensor of shape (T, C) that is shared across every sequence in the batch
A tensor of shape (B, T, C) where each scalar id is replaced by its C-vector row
A tensor of shape (B, T, V) holding a probability for every vocabulary entry
questions.explanation: Each scalar id at position (b, t) is replaced by the whole C-vector in that id's row, so the shape grows by one trailing axis: (B, T) becomes (B, T, C). It does not pool over positions, and (B, T, V) is the shape of the output logits, not the embedding.

questions.question: What dtype must the token-id tensor idx have when fed to the embedding lookup?
options: float32, to match the dtype of the table
bfloat16, to halve the memory of the index
bool, as a mask selecting vocabulary rows
int64 (long), since it is used for indexing
questions.explanation: idx holds integer row indices, dtype int64/long. Indexing an embedding with floats raises an error because a fractional row number makes no sense. The output, however, has the table's dtype (float32).

questions.question: What is the (B, T, C) tensor that every later GPT layer operates on commonly called?
options: The residual stream
The attention mask
The logit buffer
The key-value cache tensor
questions.explanation: After the embedding lookup, all later layers read and write the (B, T, C) tensor known as the residual stream. The integers are gone from this point on. The KV cache, attention mask and logits are other objects with different shapes and roles.

questions.section: 5. The order problem: attention is permutation-blind
questions.question: What happens to attention's outputs if you shuffle the positions of its input vectors (with no positional information)?
options: The outputs become random noise, since the attention weights get scrambled too
The outputs are shuffled the same way but the computed values are the same
The outputs are unchanged and stay in the original, unshuffled order
Attention raises an error because its input positions must be sorted
questions.explanation: Attention treats its input as a set: permuting the inputs permutes the outputs identically without changing their values (permutation equivariance). It has no built-in notion that position 1 precedes position 2. This is why position must be injected explicitly.

questions.section: 5. The order problem: attention is permutation-blind
questions.question: Without positional information, why would 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' be a problem for attention?
options: Attention would assign the two sentences to different vocabularies based on word order
Attention would crash on repeated tokens, since keys must be unique
They would produce the same bag of vectors, so the model could not tell them apart
The tokenizer would merge each whole sentence into a single shared token
questions.explanation: Both sentences contain the same tokens, so without position they form the same set of vectors and permutation-blind attention sees no difference. Since order is meaning in language, this is fatal. Positional information must be injected into the vectors before attention sees them.

questions.section: 5. The order problem: attention is permutation-blind
questions.question: When must position information be injected in a GPT-2-style model?
options: Only in the final output layer, just before the softmax over the vocabulary
Only during inference, since training batches already arrive in order
Inside the loss function, as a penalty term on out-of-order predictions
Into the input vectors themselves, before attention ever sees them
questions.explanation: Because attention is order-blind, each position's vector must already carry 'which token and where' when it enters the first block. GPT-2 does this by adding a positional embedding to the token embedding at the input. Adding it only at the output or only at inference would leave attention order-blind.

questions.question: What is GPT-2's positional embedding table `wpe`?
options: A second learned table of shape (block_size, n_embd), indexed by position
A fixed table of sine and cosine values computed directly from the position index
A learned table of shape (vocab_size, n_embd), indexed by token id
A single learned scalar per position that scales the token embedding
questions.explanation: GPT-2 keeps a second learned table W_pe in R^(T_max x C), with T_max = block_size (e.g. 1024). Row t is a learned vector for 'what it means to be at position t'. Sinusoidal encodings are the original Transformer's fixed alternative, not GPT-2's.

questions.question: How are the token and positional embeddings combined in GPT-2?
options: They are concatenated along the channel axis, giving width 2C
They are added elementwise: h[b,t] = W_te[idx[b,t]] + W_pe[t]
They are multiplied elementwise, so position gates each channel
The positional vector replaces the token vector at even positions
questions.explanation: GPT-2 simply adds the positional vector to the token vector at each position. Both are C-vectors, so the sum stays width C and the tensor stays (B, T, C). Concatenation would double the width; multiplication is not used.

questions.question: Why does the positional term W_pe[t] broadcast across the batch?
options: Because the batch size is always 1 during pretraining, so there is nothing to broadcast over
Because PyTorch duplicates the positional table B times in memory before the addition
Position t gets the same vector in every sequence — the table has no batch dependence
Because each sequence in the batch uses its own block_size, so positions must be shared
questions.explanation: The positional table depends only on position, not on which sequence it is, so position t receives the same W_pe[t] in every sequence. A (T, C) positional tensor therefore broadcasts against the (B, T, C) token tensor. Broadcasting does not copy the data B times.

questions.section: Why not just feed the real position number?
questions.question: Why is adding the raw position number t (e.g. t = 1023) to the token embedding a bad idea?
options: Because t is an integer tensor, and PyTorch cannot add integers to float32 embeddings at all
Because adding a scalar to every channel makes the forward pass several times slower
Because positions must be negative and centred on zero for the attention softmax to work correctly
Its magnitude swamps the small (~±1) token-embedding entries, drowning token identity late on
questions.explanation: Token-embedding entries are around ±1, while the raw position near the end of a GPT-2 context is about 1023. Adding it turns [-0.70, 0.80, 0.90] into roughly [1022, 1024, 1024], so the token identity becomes a rounding error. Early positions barely change while late ones drown everything.

questions.section: Why not just feed the real position number?
questions.question: What can a linear layer compute from a single raw position scalar t, and why is that insufficient?
options: Only things proportional to t, while the model needs categorical facts like 'am I first?'
Only the parity of t (odd or even), which collapses most positions into two classes
Nothing at all, because scalar inputs cannot pass through a linear layer's weight matrix in PyTorch
Only exponentials of t, which overflow float32 once t passes a few hundred positions
questions.explanation: A single number lets a linear layer compute quantities proportional to t. But useful positional facts — 'am I first?', 'is this the token right after the previous one?', 'am I near the sentence start?' — are categorical and not straight-line functions of t. A per-position C-vector can encode all of them in different directions.

questions.section: Why not just feed the real position number?
questions.question: Why do neighbouring raw positions such as 500 and 501 make a poor positional signal?
options: Because the model treats neighbouring positions as the same token id once they are embedded
They differ by only ~0.2%, so mixed into many channels 'the token right before me' is hard to see
Because odd positions are ignored by attention, so position 501 never contributes a signal
Because float32 cannot represent 501 exactly, so it rounds to the same value as position 500
questions.explanation: Positions 500 and 501 differ by about 0.2%; once mixed into 768 channels by a weight matrix that difference is tiny relative to everything else. Yet 'the token right before me' is the single most useful positional relation in language. Float32 represents both integers exactly — the problem is relative scale.

questions.section: Why not just feed the real position number?
questions.question: Why does normalizing the position as t / T not rescue the raw-position approach?
options: Because dividing by the sequence length is not differentiable, so no gradient reaches the input
Because dividing t by T makes every position equal to exactly 1 once the whole sequence is full
The same value then means different places at different lengths (0.5 is 5 of 10 or 500 of 1000)
Because t / T always exceeds the token embedding's magnitude, swamping the token identity
questions.explanation: Dividing by the length fixes the size problem but changes the meaning: 0.5 is position 5 in a 10-token sequence and position 500 in a 1000-token sequence. The same input value no longer denotes the same place. Division is differentiable and the values stay in [0, 1], so those are not the issue.

questions.section: Why not just feed the real position number?
questions.question: How does the sinusoidal positional encoding handle the raw-position problem differently from GPT-2's learned `wpe`?
options: It ignores position entirely and relies on the causal mask alone to recover word order
It learns a separate vector for each position from scratch, exactly like a learned lookup table
It adds the raw integer t to every channel but clips the result to a maximum value of 1
It maps the real number t through C sines and cosines of different frequencies, kept in [-1, 1]
questions.explanation: Sinusoidal encoding does use the actual number t, but maps it through sines and cosines at many frequencies across C channels. Each value stays in [-1, 1] and nearby positions remain distinguishable. Learning a separate vector per position is what `wpe` does instead.

questions.section: Why not just feed the real position number?
questions.question: In what sense is the learned positional table `wpe` the same trick as the token embedding table?
options: Each position is a category with its own learned C-vector; indexing is 'one-hot times a matrix'
Both tables share the same rows, so position t and token id t always use exactly one learned vector
Both tables are computed from the characters of the token, so no rows are learned for either
Both tables are frozen right after initialization, so neither is updated by gradient descent
questions.explanation: Just as for token ids, each position is treated as a category and given its own learned C-vector, and indexing the table is equivalent to multiplying a one-hot by the matrix. Rows have the same scale as token vectors and can differ as much as training needs. The two tables are separate parameters, both trained.

questions.question: Why does GPT-2 add the positional embedding to the token embedding rather than concatenate them?
options: Concatenation is not supported by autograd, so gradients could not flow back into either table
Adding keeps the width at C; concatenating would double it and widen every downstream matrix
Adding makes the positional signal fade after the first layer, which acts as a useful regularizer
Concatenation would make the model permutation-invariant again, undoing the positional signal
questions.explanation: Adding keeps the residual width at C, whereas concatenation would double it and widen every downstream matrix. Because both tables are learned jointly, the model can carve out separate directions for positional and token information. Concatenation is fully differentiable; the reason is cost.

questions.question: If token and positional vectors are added into the same C-dimensional space, how can the model still use both?
options: It cannot; the positional signal is lost in the sum and only the token identity survives the add
A fixed projection matrix separates the two signals again at the start of every transformer block
Both tables are learned jointly, so the model carves out separate directions for position and token
The positional vectors are constrained to be orthogonal to all token vectors by construction
questions.explanation: Both tables are trained together, so the model can learn to use certain directions in the C-dimensional space for positional signal and others for token identity. Nothing forces exact orthogonality and there is no fixed separating projection — the separability is learned.

questions.question: Why is GPT-2's positional scheme called 'absolute'?
options: Because positions are measured in absolute bytes of raw text rather than in tokens
Because the encoding takes the absolute values of sines to keep every entry positive
Because it encodes the absolute distance between every pair of tokens in the sequence
Because each position 0, 1, 2, ... gets its own free vector, learned from scratch
questions.explanation: It is absolute because it answers 'where am I' with a per-position vector: position 0 has one vector, position 1 another, each learned independently. Relative schemes like RoPE instead make attention depend on the distance between positions.

questions.section: The real limit: a row is only as good as its training
questions.question: In a GPT-2-style model whose `wpe` has block_size rows, what position vectors exist at inference?
options: Only positions 0 to block_size − 1; there is no vector for position block_size or beyond
Any position at all, because extra rows are generated on demand from the trained ones
Positions up to 2 × block_size, since rows are mirrored around the final trained index
Only even positions have rows; odd positions are interpolated from their two trained neighbours
questions.explanation: `wpe` has exactly block_size rows, so there is no vector for position block_size or beyond. Unlike a formula-based encoding, a learned table cannot generate new rows on demand.

questions.section: The real limit: a row is only as good as its training
questions.question: If you build `wpe` with 8192 rows but only train on 1024-token sequences, what happens to rows 1024 to 8191?
options: They are learned by interpolation from the neighbouring trained rows
They never receive a gradient and stay at their random initialization
They are automatically copied from rows 0–1023 when the model is loaded
They are pruned away at the end of training to save parameter memory
questions.explanation: Row t of `wpe` only gets a gradient when some training sequence has a token at position t. With 1024-token training sequences, rows 1024 onward never get updated and stay random, so at inference position 5000 gets noise. The usable context is the longest sequence length you trained on, not the table size.

questions.section: The real limit: a row is only as good as its training
questions.question: Why do people often train on shorter sequences than the positional table could support?
options: Because longer sequences overflow the tokenizer's maximum input length
Because the embedding table grows quadratically with sequence length
Because attention cost grows as T squared, so long-sequence training is expensive
Because positional embeddings only work for lengths that are powers of two
questions.explanation: Attention's cost grows quadratically with sequence length, so training on long sequences is expensive. That is why a model may be trained at 1024 tokens even if more rows exist. The positional table itself only grows linearly with length.

questions.section: The real limit: a row is only as good as its training
questions.question: Why can you not cheaply extend a trained GPT-2 from 1024 to 4096 tokens by adding rows to `wpe`?
options: Because PyTorch does not allow resizing an nn.Embedding once the model has been trained and saved
Because the token table would also need to quadruple in size to keep the two tables aligned row by row
Because the new rows would collide with the ids reserved for special tokens such as <|endoftext|>
The new rows are untrained and nothing learned for rows 0–1023 transfers, so long training is needed
questions.explanation: You can add 3072 rows, but they are untrained, and knowledge in the existing rows does not transfer to them. The fix is substantial training at the new length, costing close to a real training run. Resizing is mechanically possible; it is the learning that is expensive.

questions.section: The real limit: a row is only as good as its training
questions.question: Why is a RoPE model much cheaper to extend to longer contexts than a learned `wpe` model?
options: RoPE has nothing per-position to learn: one formula covers every position, so rescale it and fine-tune briefly
RoPE models never degrade beyond their trained length, so any context size works without further training
RoPE stores a much larger positional table from the start, so the extra rows are already trained at pretraining
RoPE removes attention's quadratic cost, so training directly at the longer length becomes cheap enough
questions.explanation: RoPE computes each position's rotation from a formula, so position 5000 uses the same rule as position 5. Methods like position interpolation and YaRN rescale the formula so long positions map onto angles the model saw, and a short fine-tune suffices — how real models go from 4K–8K pretraining to 128K. RoPE still degrades if used naively far beyond its trained length.

questions.section: The real limit: a row is only as good as its training
questions.question: What happens to a RoPE model used naively far beyond its training length, without any adjustment?
options: It works perfectly, since the rotation formula is defined for every position
It also degrades, because it meets rotation angles it never saw in training
It raises an IndexError at the first unseen position, just as a learned table would
It automatically switches to sinusoidal encoding beyond its limit
questions.explanation: Neither scheme runs past its trained length for free. A RoPE model used naively far beyond that length meets unseen rotation angles and degrades. The difference from `wpe` is that fixing it is cheap — rescale the formula and fine-tune briefly — rather than training new rows from scratch.

questions.section: The real limit: a row is only as good as its training
questions.question: Why is learning the relation 'the token right before me' inefficient with a learned absolute `wpe` table?
options: Because `wpe` cannot represent adjacent positions at all, since neighbouring rows are tied together
Because the relation has to be encoded in the token table instead, which has no positional rows
It must learn it separately for each pair of rows: (W_pe[10], W_pe[11]), (W_pe[500], W_pe[501]), …
Because attention ignores the positional table after the first layer, so the relation is lost early
questions.explanation: With absolute rows, the relative fact 'one step back' must be learned again for every adjacent pair of positions. RoPE makes the attention score depend directly on the distance i − j, so the relation is learned once and holds everywhere.

questions.section: The real limit: a row is only as good as its training
questions.question: Overall, how does extending context differ between learned absolute positions and RoPE?
options: Learned positions can be extended freely by appending rows, while RoPE models cannot be extended at all
Both can be extended with no additional training, since the trained weights generalize to new positions
Both require identical full retraining from scratch, because the attention weights depend on the length
A difference of degree: both need training, but RoPE needs a short fine-tune and a table needs new rows trained
questions.explanation: Neither lets a trained model exceed its limit on demand. But a RoPE extension only rescales a formula and keeps everything learned about relative distance, so a short fine-tune works, while a learned table needs new rows trained from scratch at the new length. That cost gap is why modern models switched.

questions.question: After adding positional embeddings, what happens if the same token id appears at two different positions?
options: It produces two different input vectors h, so the model can tell the occurrences apart
It produces identical vectors, since the token id is the same at both positions
The second occurrence is dropped as a duplicate before reaching the first block
The two vectors are averaged together into one shared representation of the token
questions.explanation: h = token embedding + position embedding, and the position embeddings differ between positions, so the same token at two positions yields two different h vectors. That is how order information enters the vectors. Nothing is deduplicated or averaged.

questions.question: What is the tensor h = tok + pos used for in GPT-2?
options: It is the final output that is fed to the softmax
It is the input to the first transformer block
It is the target used to compute the loss
It is cached as the key tensor for later attention
questions.explanation: h, the sum of token and positional embeddings, is the position-aware input to the first transformer block. The softmax operates on logits at the end of the model, and keys are computed later inside attention from the block's inputs.

questions.question: What does PyTorch's `nn.Embedding(V, C)` hold and return?
options: It holds a (C, V) matrix and returns the dense matrix product of that matrix with the input ids
It holds a hash table and returns a fresh random vector for each id on every forward call
Its .weight is a (V, C) matrix, and calling it with integer indices returns the selected rows
It holds V scalar weights and returns their sum over the ids in each input sequence
questions.explanation: `nn.Embedding(V, C)` is exactly the lookup table: its .weight is a (V, C) matrix, and calling it with integer indices gathers the corresponding rows. The same class with (T_max, C) serves as the positional table.

questions.question: In the from-scratch GPT input layer, what does `wpe(torch.arange(T))` produce?
options: A (B, T, C) tensor holding one positional block for each sequence
A (T,) tensor of the position indices 0 to T−1, unchanged
A (V, C) copy of the token embedding table's weight matrix
A (T, C) tensor of positional vectors for positions 0 to T−1
questions.explanation: `torch.arange(T)` builds the position indices [0, 1, ..., T−1], and `wpe(...)` gathers their rows into a (T, C) tensor. It has no batch axis; it broadcasts across the batch when added to the (B, T, C) token tensor.

questions.question: In `h = tok + pos` with tok of shape (B, T, C) and pos of shape (T, C), what does broadcasting do?
options: It reuses the same positional vectors for every sequence in the batch
It raises a shape error, because the two tensors have different ranks
It sums pos over T first, then adds that one vector to every position
It adds pos only to the first sequence in the batch and zero to the rest
questions.explanation: Broadcasting aligns trailing dimensions, treating pos as (1, T, C) and applying it to every sequence in the batch. The same positional vectors are reused for all B sequences. Differing ranks are fine under broadcasting rules when trailing dims match.

questions.question: What does `nn.Embedding` actually do at runtime when you call it on token ids?
options: A full one-hot by weight-matrix multiply executed as one dense GEMM on the GPU
An indexed gather that reads the selected rows directly from the (V, C) weight buffer
A softmax over the vocabulary followed by a weighted sum of all the table's rows
A sparse matrix multiply between a CSR-format one-hot and the weight matrix
questions.explanation: `nn.Embedding` is an indexed gather, not a matrix multiply: it reads the selected rows directly from the weight buffer. The one-hot multiply is short-circuited into a memory read. That makes embedding a token O(C) work rather than O(V·C).

questions.question: What is the computational cost of embedding one token with `nn.Embedding(V, C)`?
options: O(V · C), the cost of a one-hot multiply
O(V), one comparison per vocabulary entry
O(C), reading one row of C floats
O(C squared), due to a projection
questions.explanation: Because the lookup is a direct row read, embedding a token costs O(C) — just copying C floats. The O(V·C) cost would apply only to an explicit one-hot multiply, which is never performed.

questions.section: 9. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — the full accounting
questions.question: Which statement about dtypes in the GPT embedding layer is correct?
options: idx is float32 to match the table, and the output tok is int64
Both idx and the output tok are int64, since lookups copy indices
Both idx and the output are bfloat16 by default in a GPT model
idx is int64, while wte.weight, tok, pos and h are float32
questions.explanation: Token ids are integers (int64) because they are row indices; the tables and all gathered or summed vectors are float32 by default. The output takes the table's dtype, not the index dtype.

questions.section: 9. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — the full accounting
questions.question: Why does indexing an embedding table with a float tensor raise an error?
options: Because you cannot use a fractional row number as an index
Because float tensors always live on the CPU, not the GPU
Because embeddings only accept bool masks over the vocabulary
Because float inputs would first require a softmax over rows
questions.explanation: Embedding lookup selects rows by index, and a row number must be an integer; a fractional index makes no sense. So idx must be an int64/long tensor. Device placement is a separate concern.

questions.section: 9. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — the full accounting
questions.question: On a GPU model, what goes wrong if you write `pos = self.wpe(torch.arange(T))` without a device argument?
options: The positions are silently reversed on the GPU, so the last token in the sequence gets row 0 of wpe
torch.arange creates a CPU tensor, so the lookup or the add fails with a device mismatch
The whole positional table is silently copied back to the CPU on every forward step
Nothing goes wrong; PyTorch automatically moves the new tensor onto the model's GPU
questions.explanation: `torch.arange(T)` defaults to the CPU, while the model and idx are on the GPU, so you get a device-mismatch error. The fix is `torch.arange(T, device=idx.device)`. PyTorch does not silently move tensors across devices for you.

questions.section: 9. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — the full accounting
questions.question: What happens if a token id in idx is greater than or equal to vocab_size?
options: The id silently wraps around modulo vocab_size, so it reads the embedding of an unrelated token
The embedding returns an all-zero vector for that id, and training continues without any warning
It indexes past the table's end: an IndexError on CPU, often a corrupted-memory crash on CUDA
The table automatically grows to fit the new id, initializing the added row with random values
questions.explanation: An out-of-range id indexes past the end of `wte`. On CPU you get a clear IndexError; on CUDA the error often surfaces later as a memory-corruption crash far from the real cause. A common source is a special token the vocab wasn't sized for, so asserting idx.max() < vocab_size helps debugging.

questions.section: 9. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — the full accounting
questions.question: Which simple debugging assertion helps catch out-of-range token ids before they hit the embedding table?
options: assert idx.dtype == torch.float32
assert idx.min() > 0
assert idx.shape[1] == vocab_size
assert idx.max() < vocab_size
questions.explanation: Asserting idx.max() < vocab_size catches ids (e.g. forgotten special tokens) that would index past the end of `wte`. idx must be int64, not float32, and id 0 is a valid id, so idx.min() > 0 would be wrong.

questions.section: 10. Under the hood: memory, parameters, and gradients
questions.question: Approximately how many parameters does GPT-2 small's token embedding table `wte` contain?
options: About 38.6 million (50257 × 768)
About 0.79 million (1024 × 768)
About 124 million (the full model)
About 3.9 million (50257 × 77)
questions.explanation: `wte` is 50257 × 768 ≈ 38.6M parameters. The positional table `wpe` is 1024 × 768 ≈ 0.79M. 124M is the whole GPT-2 small model.

questions.section: 10. Under the hood: memory, parameters, and gradients
questions.question: Roughly what fraction of GPT-2 small's 124M parameters is the token embedding table?
options: About 3%
About 31%
About 65%
About 90%
questions.explanation: 38.6M / 124M ≈ 31%, so the token table is a large fraction of GPT-2 small. Embeddings are not a footnote in parameter count, which is one motivation for weight tying.

questions.section: 10. Under the hood: memory, parameters, and gradients
questions.question: How does GPT-2 avoid paying twice for its 38.6M-parameter token embedding?
options: It quantizes the embedding table to 4-bit integers once pretraining has finished
It shares the table across layers, reusing it as attention keys
It ties the `wte` matrix to the output projection, reusing it at both ends
It drops rare tokens from the vocabulary to shrink the number of table rows
questions.explanation: GPT-2 ties `wte` to the output (unembedding) projection, so the same matrix maps ids to vectors at the input and vectors to logits at the output. This reuses the 38.6M parameters rather than paying for a separate output matrix.

questions.section: 10. Under the hood: memory, parameters, and gradients
questions.question: In the backward pass of an embedding lookup, which rows of `wte.weight` receive gradient?
options: All rows equally, each scaled by 1/V of the total
Only row 0, the padding row, which absorbs all gradient
Rows chosen at random each step, as a form of regularization
Only the rows for ids that actually appear in the batch
questions.explanation: The lookup gathers only the rows for ids present in the batch, so the backward pass writes gradients into only those rows (via a scatter-add). A token absent from the batch gets zero gradient that step and its embedding does not move.

questions.section: 10. Under the hood: memory, parameters, and gradients
questions.question: Why do rare tokens' embeddings tend to be noisier than common tokens' embeddings?
options: They are updated only on the rare steps they appear, so they get far fewer gradient updates
Because rare tokens are given a smaller learning rate by design to avoid overfitting to them
Because rare tokens are initialized with larger variance so they stand out from common ones
Because the optimizer skips low-frequency tokens entirely until they have appeared enough times
questions.explanation: A token's row only gets gradient when that token appears in a batch, so a token seen five times gets far fewer updates than one seen five million times. Its embedding therefore learns slowly and stays noisy. No special learning rate or initialization is involved.

questions.section: 10. Under the hood: memory, parameters, and gradients
questions.question: How does autograd accumulate gradients into an embedding table after a lookup?
options: It multiplies the incoming gradient by a dense one-hot matrix of shape (B·T, V)
It performs a scatter-add of incoming gradients into wte.weight at the used row indices
It averages the incoming gradients and spreads them evenly over the whole vocabulary
It recomputes the forward pass once for every vocabulary row to get exact gradients
questions.explanation: The backward of a gather is a scatter-add: incoming gradients for each (b, t) position are added into the row of wte.weight corresponding to that position's id. Repeated ids accumulate their gradients in the same row. No dense one-hot is formed.

questions.section: 10. Under the hood: memory, parameters, and gradients
questions.question: What is the main cost of the embedding layer: compute or memory?
options: Compute, because the lookup is a large (B·T, V) by (V, C) matrix multiply
Neither; embedding tables are free in both compute and memory terms
Memory: the big tables cost far more than the B·T row reads and B·T·C additions
Compute, because adding positional vectors is quadratic in the length T
