questions.explanation: The forward lookup is B·T row reads of C floats and the positional add is B·T·C additions — negligible compared to the block's matrix multiplies. But the tables themselves are large (38.6M parameters for wte), so the layer's cost is mostly memory.

questions.section: 11. A brief contrast: sinusoidal and what comes later
questions.question: How did the original Transformer paper encode position, compared with GPT-2?
options: With learned per-position vectors identical to GPT-2's, trained jointly with the rest of the model
With RoPE rotations applied to the queries and keys inside every attention layer of the model
With no position encoding at all, relying on the decoder's causal mask to supply word order
With fixed sinusoidal encodings, sin(t / 10000^(2j/C)) and cos, computed rather than learned
questions.explanation: The original Transformer used fixed sinusoidal encodings: deterministic sine and cosine functions of position t and channel j. GPT-2 instead learns a vector for each position. RoPE came later.

questions.section: 11. A brief contrast: sinusoidal and what comes later
questions.question: What is an advantage of sinusoidal positional encoding over GPT-2's learned table?
options: It is defined for any position, even beyond training, and nearby positions are smoothly related
It always gives better perplexity than a learned table at every model size and context length
It has more trainable parameters than a learned table, which makes it strictly more flexible
It makes attention cost linear in sequence length, since the encodings are computed on the fly
questions.explanation: Because sinusoidal encoding is a formula, it produces a vector for any position, including ones never seen in training, and nearby positions have smoothly related values. It has zero trainable parameters, so flexibility is the learned table's advantage, not sinusoidal's.

questions.section: 11. A brief contrast: sinusoidal and what comes later
questions.question: What is the advantage of GPT-2's learned absolute positional embeddings over sinusoidal ones?
options: They work for positions beyond the training length, since learned rows extrapolate
Flexibility: the model can shape each position vector however training finds useful
They require no memory at all, because rows are computed on the fly when needed
They encode relative distance directly inside the attention scores at every layer
questions.explanation: A learned table lets training shape each position vector freely. Sinusoidal encodings are the ones defined for any position. Encoding relative distance in the attention score is what RoPE does.

questions.section: 11. A brief contrast: sinusoidal and what comes later
questions.question: What do sinusoidal and learned absolute positional encodings have in common?
options: Both rotate the query and key vectors inside attention by an angle proportional to position
Both are learned from data by gradient descent, so neither has a closed-form definition
Both are absolute: they add a per-position vector to the token embedding to answer 'where am I'
Both make attention scores depend only on the distance between tokens, not their positions
questions.explanation: Both schemes are absolute: each position has its own vector, added to the token embedding at the input. One is computed, the other learned. Rotating Q and K so scores depend on distance is RoPE, a relative scheme.

questions.section: 11. A brief contrast: sinusoidal and what comes later
questions.question: How does RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) encode position?
options: By adding a learned vector to the input token embedding once, before the first transformer block
By appending the integer position index as an extra channel to every token's embedding vector
By masking out all future positions so each token can only attend to the tokens before it
By rotating queries and keys inside attention so the score depends only on the distance between positions
questions.explanation: RoPE rotates Q and K by position-dependent angles inside attention, so their dot product depends on the relative distance between positions rather than absolute indices. It is applied at every layer, not once at the input like `wpe`.

questions.section: 11. A brief contrast: sinusoidal and what comes later
questions.question: Where is GPT-2's `wpe` applied, compared with RoPE?
options: `wpe` is a learned lookup added once at the input; RoPE rotates Q and K at every layer
Both are added once to the token embeddings at the input, before the first block runs
`wpe` is re-added at every transformer layer, while RoPE is applied only at the input
Both are applied only to the output logits, after the final layer norm of the model
questions.explanation: `wpe` is added to the token embeddings once, before the first block. RoPE instead rotates the queries and keys inside every attention layer. This is the key contrast to remember when reading the RoPE paper (Su et al., 2021).

questions.question: For a model with wte of shape (50257, 768), what is the shape and dtype of tok = wte(idx) when idx has shape (4, 128)?
options: (4, 128), int64, same as idx
(4, 768), float32, pooled
questions.explanation: The lookup keeps the (B, T) = (4, 128) axes and appends a trailing channel axis of length 768, giving (4, 128, 768). The dtype is the table's float32, even though idx is int64. A (128, 768) tensor is the positional lookup, which broadcasts over the batch.

questions.question: A learner writes `self.wpe = nn.Embedding(cfg.n_head, cfg.n_embd)` in a GPT input layer. What goes wrong?
options: The token embeddings silently become position-dependent, because the two tables now share their rows
Nothing; in GPT-2 n_head equals block_size, so the table has exactly the right number of rows anyway
Once T exceeds n_head (e.g. 12), torch.arange(T) indexes past wpe: IndexError on CPU or a CUDA crash
The model becomes permutation-invariant again, since 12 rows cannot distinguish any token positions
questions.explanation: The positional table must have one row per position slot, so it should be nn.Embedding(cfg.block_size, cfg.n_embd). Sizing it by n_head (e.g. 12) means any sequence longer than 12 tokens indexes out of range. In GPT-2, n_head = 12 while block_size = 1024.

questions.question: Why does adding wpe[t] solve the problem that attention is permutation-invariant?
options: It sorts the tokens into position order before attention runs, so the set becomes an ordered list
It makes attention ignore repeated tokens, so each distinct word is only attended to a single time
It removes the softmax from attention, so the scores become linear and keep track of token order
It gives each position a distinct signature, so one token at different positions gets different vectors
questions.explanation: Attention treats an unordered set of vectors, so order must be in the vectors themselves. Adding wpe[t] makes each position's vector distinct, so the model can use word order. It does not change attention's mechanics.

questions.question: In GPT-2, what is the shape of wpe.weight and what does it depend on?
options: (block_size, n_embd): one row per position slot up to the maximum context length
(vocab_size, n_embd): one row per token, shared with the token embedding table
(n_head, n_embd): one row per attention head, broadcast over the positions
(B, T): one learned scalar per token position in the current training batch
questions.explanation: wpe.weight is (T_max, C) = (block_size, n_embd), one learned row per position slot. Its size depends on maximum context length, not on vocab size, number of heads, or the batch.

questions.question: Why is attention described as the operation that makes a transformer a transformer?
options: It is the only layer in the model with trainable parameters, so all learning happens inside attention
It is how each token pulls in information from other tokens; every GPT layer is attention plus an MLP
It converts the integer token ids into the dense vectors that the rest of the network operates on
It computes the final next-token probabilities, turning the last hidden state into a distribution over ids
questions.explanation: Attention is the mechanism by which each position gathers information from other positions. Every GPT layer is attention plus a small MLP, so once you understand attention the rest is assembly. Converting ids to vectors is the embedding's job, and probabilities come from the output head.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a soft, learned dictionary lookup
questions.question: Before attention, what does each position's C-vector in a GPT know about?
options: The entire sequence
Only the previous token
Only its own token (and position)
The average of all tokens in the batch
questions.explanation: Coming out of the embedding layer, each position's vector only encodes its own token plus its position. To predict the next word it needs information from other positions — e.g. the subject a verb agrees with or the noun a pronoun refers to — and attention is how it gathers that.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a soft, learned dictionary lookup
questions.question: Which of these is an example of information a position needs from other positions, motivating attention?
options: The vocabulary size
The learning rate schedule
The dtype of the embedding table
The noun a pronoun refers to
questions.explanation: Predicting the next token requires context: the subject a verb agrees with, the noun a pronoun refers to, the opening bracket a closing one must match. Those live at other positions, so attention gathers them. Vocab size, dtype and learning rate are not per-sequence contextual information.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a soft, learned dictionary lookup
questions.question: Why is attention described as a 'soft' dictionary lookup?
options: Each query is compared to every key and gets a blend of all values, weighted by how well each key matched
It looks up the single key that exactly equals the query and returns that one value, like a hash map
It stores keys as floating-point vectors instead of strings, so lookups tolerate small rounding errors
Its keys are kept sorted, so a binary search over them returns the nearest value in logarithmic time
questions.explanation: A normal dictionary returns exactly one value for one exact key. Attention instead does a fuzzy, weighted lookup: the query is matched against every key and the output is a weighted blend of all values. The 'soft' refers to this weighting, not to the data type.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a soft, learned dictionary lookup
questions.question: In attention, what is the role of the query vector q?
options: What a position hands over if another one attends to it
What the current position is looking for — its question
What a position advertises to all of the other positions
The position's integer index within the sequence
questions.explanation: The query is 'what I am looking for' — the current position's question. The key is 'what I offer' (an advertisement), and the value is 'what I hand over' if attended to.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a soft, learned dictionary lookup
questions.question: In attention, what is the role of the key vector k?
options: What a position hands over (its content) if another position attends to it
The normalizing constant of the softmax, shared by every query in the same row
What a position offers — an advertisement that queries are compared against
The final output of the head, after the weighted blend of values
questions.explanation: Each position publishes a key, 'what I offer'. Queries are dotted against keys to decide how much to attend to each position. The value, not the key, is what actually gets blended into the output.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a soft, learned dictionary lookup
questions.question: In attention, what is the role of the value vector v?
options: The question that this position asks of all the others
The raw score between two positions, computed before the softmax
The causal mask entry for that position in its own row
What a position hands over (its content) when attended to
questions.explanation: The value is 'what I hand over': once the query-key matches produce weights, the output is a weighted blend of the values. Keys decide how much to listen; values decide what is received.

questions.section: 2. Q, K, V are three learned linear projections
questions.question: How are the queries, keys and values computed from the input x of shape (B, T, C) in single-head attention?
options: By three learned linear maps Q = x W_Q, K = x W_K, V = x W_V, each weight (C, d_h)
By splitting x into three equal chunks along the time axis T and using one chunk for each
By applying softmax to x three times with different temperatures, one for each of Q, K and V
Q, K and V are all set equal to x itself, so no extra parameters are needed in the head
questions.explanation: Q, K and V come from three separate learned linear projections, each weight matrix of shape (C, d_h) in the single-head case. They are not chunks of the sequence and are not copies of x. Each result has shape (B, T, d_h).

questions.section: 2. Q, K, V are three learned linear projections
questions.question: In single-head attention with input x of shape (B, T, C) and W_Q of shape (C, d_h), what is the shape of Q?
options: (B, C, d_h)
(B, T, d_h)
(B, T, T)
(B, T, C, d_h)
questions.explanation: Multiplying (B, T, C) by (C, d_h) contracts the C axis and gives (B, T, d_h): one d_h-vector per position. (B, T, T) is the shape of the score matrix, which comes later.

questions.section: 2. Q, K, V are three learned linear projections
questions.question: Why does attention learn three separate projections W_Q, W_K, W_V instead of one?
options: To triple the number of attention heads without increasing the model's residual width C
To make the model permutation-invariant, so word order no longer affects the attention output
So one token can ask for one thing (query), advertise another (key) and contribute a third (value)
Because the softmax function requires three separate input tensors to compute a valid distribution
questions.explanation: Separate projections let one token play three different roles: what it seeks, what it advertises, and what it hands over. Nothing forces q, k and v to be equal or related except training. It is unrelated to the number of heads.

questions.section: 2. Q, K, V are three learned linear projections
questions.question: Are a token's query, key and value vectors required to be related in any way?
options: Yes — the key must equal the query so that each token can attend to itself
Yes — the value must be the average of the query and the key for each token
Yes — the three vectors must be mutually orthogonal to avoid redundancy
No — nothing forces them to be equal or related except through training
questions.explanation: The three projections are independent learned matrices, so q, k and v can be completely different vectors for the same token. In a worked example, the same input row became query [2, 0], key [1, 1] and value [1, 0]. Only training shapes any relationship.

questions.section: 2. Q, K, V are three learned linear projections
questions.question: In the formula Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_h) + M) V, what does each part do?
options: Q K^T gives raw scores, sqrt(d_h) scales them, M masks the future, softmax makes row weights, V is averaged
Q K^T is the causal mask, M is the output buffer, and multiplying by V normalizes the scores to sum to one
sqrt(d_h) is the number of heads, M is the learning rate, and softmax picks the single best-matching key
softmax is applied to V first, and the result is multiplied by Q K^T and rescaled by sqrt(d_h) at the end
questions.explanation: The formula reads left to right as: raw query-key scores, scaled by 1/sqrt(d_h), causal mask added, softmax per row to turn scores into weights, then a weighted average of values. M is the mask, not the output, and softmax acts on scores, not on V.

questions.section: 2. Q, K, V are three learned linear projections
questions.question: In real GPT code, how is the Q/K/V projection typically implemented?
options: As three softmax layers
As a single nn.Linear
As an nn.Embedding lookup
As a convolution over T
questions.explanation: In practice the projection is a single nn.Linear (in the CausalSelfAttention module it produces Q, K and V together). It is a learned linear map, not an embedding lookup or softmax.

questions.section: 3. The setup for the worked example
questions.question: When computing Q = x W_Q by hand, what is an easy way to read row i of Q?
options: As column i of W_Q, read off directly from the weight matrix W_Q
As the diagonal of x times W_Q, one entry for each of the input rows
As a mix of W_Q's rows, with the entries of x_i as the mixing amounts
As the sum of all entries of x, repeated across every column
questions.explanation: Row i of x W_Q equals the sum over c of x_ic times row c of W_Q. So row i of Q is a weighted mix of W_Q's rows, with x_i's entries as the weights. This is equivalent to the dot-product-per-entry definition Q_ij = sum_c x_ic (W_Q)_cj.

questions.section: 3. The setup for the worked example
questions.question: In a hand-worked attention example, the input row x_1 = [1, 1, 0] became query [2, 0], key [1, 1] and value [1, 0]. What does this illustrate?
options: That the three projection matrices are identical, since all three outputs came from one row
That attention ignores the input row and only uses the learned weights to build its vectors
That keys are always all-ones vectors, while queries and values vary from token to token
That the same input row produces three different vectors via the three learned projections
questions.explanation: One input vector passed through W_Q, W_K and W_V gives three distinct vectors — the 'ask one thing, advertise another, hand over a third' idea made concrete. It shows the projections are different, not identical.

questions.section: 4. Step one — scores are dot products
questions.question: In attention, how is the score s_ij between query i and key j computed?
options: As the dot product q_i · k_j = sum over m of q_im k_jm
As the Euclidean distance between q_i and k_j, negated
As the product of the norms of q_i and k_j alone
As the cosine of the angle between the values v_i and v_j
questions.explanation: The score is the dot product of query i and key j, summed over the d_h dimensions. It is large and positive when the vectors point the same way, near zero when unrelated, and negative when opposed. Values do not enter the score.

questions.section: 4. Step one — scores are dot products
questions.question: What does a large positive dot product between a query and a key indicate in attention?
options: The two positions are far apart in the sequence, so the key is stale
The query and key point in a similar direction — a strong match
The key belongs to a future position and should therefore be masked
The value vector for that key is zero, so the score has no effect
questions.explanation: A dot product is large and positive when vectors point the same way, near zero when unrelated, and negative when opposed. So a large score means the query matches that key well and that position will get more attention weight.

questions.section: 4. Step one — scores are dot products
questions.question: Why does computing S = Q K^T produce all query-key dot products at once?
options: Because the transpose sums K over its rows, collapsing all of the keys into one long vector
Because K^T has shape (T, d_h), the same as Q, so the product is taken elementwise
Transposing K makes its rows (keys) columns, so entry (i, j) of the product is q_i · k_j
Because Q and K are always square (T, T) matrices, so any product covers all pairs
questions.explanation: K has keys as rows; K^T has them as columns. Multiplying Q (T, d_h) by K^T (d_h, T) gives a (T, T) matrix whose (i, j) entry is row i of Q dotted with column j of K^T, i.e. q_i · k_j. Q and K are generally not square.

questions.section: 4. Step one — scores are dot products
questions.question: For a single sequence with Q and K of shape (T, d_h), what is the shape of the score matrix S = Q K^T?
options: (T, d_h)
(d_h, d_h)
(d_h, T)
(T, T)
questions.explanation: (T, d_h) times (d_h, T) gives (T, T): one score for every (query position, key position) pair. The head dimension d_h is summed away by the dot product.

questions.question: In scaled dot-product attention, what are the raw scores divided by before the softmax?
options: sqrt(d_h), the square root of the head dimension
d_h, the head dimension itself, without a root
T, the current sequence length of the batch
sqrt(T), the square root of the sequence length
questions.explanation: The scores are divided by sqrt(d_h). With d_h = 2 the scale is about 0.7071; with d_h = 64 it is 1/8. It does not depend on sequence length.

questions.question: Why do raw attention scores tend to grow as the head dimension d_h grows?
options: Because the softmax amplifies them, multiplying every score by d_h before it is normalized
A dot product over d_h dimensions sums d_h products, so its magnitude tends to grow with d_h
Because the causal mask adds d_h to every allowed score, inflating the larger heads more
Because the value vectors are multiplied in before the scores, adding d_h extra factors
questions.explanation: A dot product sums d_h terms, so with more dimensions the sum tends to be larger in magnitude. Real models use d_h = 64, making unscaled scores large. Softmax and the mask come after the score computation.

questions.question: What goes wrong when softmax is applied to large-magnitude scores?
options: It returns negative weights for the smaller scores, so the output subtracts some of the values
It produces weights that sum to more than 1, so the output grows larger with every layer
It saturates: nearly all weight goes to the top score (near one-hot) and the gradient goes flat
It becomes approximately linear in its inputs and loses the nonlinearity attention relies on
questions.explanation: Large inputs push softmax into saturation: a near-one-hot distribution that acts as a hard pick instead of a soft blend, with a nearly flat gradient that stalls learning. Softmax weights stay non-negative and sum to 1 regardless.

questions.question: If the entries of q and k are independent with unit variance, what is the variance of q · k, and how does scaling fix it?
options: Variance 1; scaling is unnecessary
Variance d_h squared; dividing by d_h restores unit variance
Variance sqrt(d_h); dividing by d_h restores unit variance
Variance d_h; dividing by sqrt(d_h) restores unit variance
questions.explanation: Summing d_h independent unit-variance products gives variance d_h. Dividing by sqrt(d_h) divides the variance by d_h, restoring unit variance and keeping softmax in its sensitive regime regardless of head size.

questions.section: 6. Step three — the causal mask: no peeking at the future
questions.question: Why must GPT forbid position i from attending to positions after i during training?
options: It is trained to predict the next token, and seeing future tokens is cheating that fails at generation
Because future positions have no positional embeddings yet, so their keys are undefined during training
Because attending to future positions doubles the memory cost of the score matrix at every layer
Because softmax cannot handle more than i entries in row i without overflowing in float32 arithmetic
questions.explanation: GPT predicts the next token, so at position i it may use only positions 1..i. Attending to later positions would let it read the answer, making training a cheat that does not work at generation time, when the future is unavailable.

questions.section: 6. Step three — the causal mask: no peeking at the future
questions.question: How does the causal mask M enforce 'no peeking at the future' in attention?
options: By setting every future value vector in V to zero, so future positions contribute nothing to the output
By adding −infinity to every future score (j > i) before softmax, leaving entries j ≤ i unchanged
By multiplying every future score by 0.5 before softmax, so the future is down-weighted but still visible
By removing the future tokens from the input sequence entirely before Q, K and V are ever computed
questions.explanation: M has 0 on and below the diagonal and −infinity above it, and is added to the scaled scores before softmax. Allowed entries (j ≤ i) are untouched while future entries become −infinity. The input sequence itself is not modified.

questions.section: 6. Step three — the causal mask: no peeking at the future
questions.question: Why is the causal mask filled with −infinity rather than 0?
options: Because a score of 0 would make the softmax undefined, dividing by zero in the normalizer
Because −infinity makes training faster by letting the kernel skip the masked entries
exp(−infinity) = 0, so a masked score gets exactly zero weight and the rest still sum to 1
Because the mask is multiplied with the scores, not added, so 0 would erase the allowed entries
questions.explanation: Adding 0 would leave a score unchanged, so it would not mask anything. Adding −infinity makes exp(score) exactly 0, switching the future position off entirely; the remaining weights still sum to 1. The mask is added, not multiplied.

questions.section: 6. Step three — the causal mask: no peeking at the future
questions.question: What is the structure of the causal mask M for T = 3?
options: All zeros, so every position can attend everywhere
−infinity on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere
0 above the diagonal and −infinity on and below it
0 on and below the diagonal, −infinity above it
questions.explanation: Row i may attend to columns j ≤ i, so those entries are 0 and the upper-right (j > i) entries are −infinity. Putting −infinity on the diagonal would stop a position from attending to itself, which causal attention allows.

questions.section: 7. Step four — softmax turns each row into weights
questions.question: What does softmax do to each row of masked, scaled attention scores?
options: It turns the row into non-negative weights that sum to 1 — how much to attend to each position
It sorts the row in descending order so the best-matching key always comes first in the output
It sets the maximum entry of the row to exactly 1 and every other entry to exactly 0, a hard argmax
It divides every entry of the row by the row's length, giving equal weight to all positions
questions.explanation: softmax(r)_j = exp(r_j) / sum_k exp(r_k), giving non-negative weights summing to 1. It is a smooth weighting, not a hard argmax (that only happens when it saturates).

questions.section: 7. Step four — softmax turns each row into weights
questions.question: Why is softmax applied independently to each row of the attention score matrix?
options: Because each column is one key distributing its attention over the queries
Because each row is one query distributing its attention over the keys
Because each row must sum to zero for the output to stay centred
Because a softmax over the whole matrix at once is mathematically undefined
questions.explanation: Row i holds query i's scores against every key, so normalizing across that row gives how query i distributes its attention. Normalizing columns would instead mix different queries.

questions.section: 7. Step four — softmax turns each row into weights
questions.question: In causal attention, what weight does the first position (row 1) always get?
options: Uniform weights spread evenly over all T positions in the sequence
Zero weight everywhere, since the first row is fully masked out
All weight (1.0) on itself, since it is the only unmasked entry
Weight 0.5 on itself and 0.5 on the next position in the sequence
questions.explanation: Row 1 can only see position 1 — every other entry is masked to −infinity. Softmax over a single live entry gives it weight 1, so the first position's output is just its own value vector.

questions.section: 7. Step four — softmax turns each row into weights
questions.question: If two unmasked scaled scores in an attention row are exactly equal and all others are masked, what weights does softmax give?
options: The first gets 1, the second 0
Both get 1
Weights depend on the sequence length
0.5 and 0.5 — a tie
questions.explanation: Softmax of two equal values gives equal weights, and because they must sum to 1 each gets 0.5. Masked entries contribute exp(−infinity) = 0. This is what happens when a query dots equally with two allowed keys.

questions.section: 7. Step four — softmax turns each row into weights
questions.question: What two sanity checks hold for a correct causal attention weight matrix A?
options: Every row sums to 1, and the matrix is lower-triangular (future entries exactly zero)
Every column sums to 1, and the matrix is symmetric because scores are dot products
The diagonal is all zeros, since no token attends to itself, and every row sums to T
The matrix equals the identity, since each token attends only to itself under the mask
questions.explanation: Each row is a probability distribution, so it sums to 1, and the causal mask makes everything above the diagonal exactly zero, giving a lower-triangular matrix. Columns do not in general sum to 1 and the matrix is not symmetric.

questions.section: 8. Step five — output is a weighted average of values
questions.question: How is the attention output for query i computed from the weights and values?
options: As the elementwise maximum of the allowed value vectors
As the weighted sum of value vectors, sum_j A_ij v_j
As the dot product of the query q_i with its own value v_i
As the softmax of the value vectors, taken over the keys
questions.explanation: Each query's output is the weighted average of the value vectors, using that row's attention weights. Stacking all queries, this is the matmul O = A V. Values are blended, not maximized or softmaxed.

questions.section: 8. Step five — output is a weighted average of values
questions.question: For a single sequence with A of shape (T, T) and V of shape (T, d_h), what is the shape of O = A V?
options: (T, T)
(d_h, d_h)
(T, d_h)
(d_h, T)
questions.explanation: (T, T) times (T, d_h) gives (T, d_h): one d_h-dimensional output per query position, the same shape as V.

questions.section: 8. Step five — output is a weighted average of values
questions.question: What is the order of operations in scaled dot-product attention?
options: mask (+M) → scores (Q K^T) → softmax per row → scale (/sqrt(d_h)) → output (A @ V)
softmax per row → scores (Q K^T) → scale (/sqrt(d_h)) → mask (+M) → output (A V)
scale (/sqrt(d_h)) → output (A V) → scores (Q K^T) → mask (+M) → softmax per row
scores (Q K^T) → scale (/sqrt(d_h)) → mask (+M) → softmax per row → output (A V)
questions.explanation: The pipeline is scores, then scale, then add the mask, then softmax each row, then multiply by V. The mask must come before softmax so masked entries get exactly zero weight.

questions.section: 9. From scratch in PyTorch — and matching the fused kernel
questions.question: Why does attention code write `Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1)` rather than `Q @ K.T`?
options: Swapping only the last two axes stays correct when there are leading batch/head axes
Because .T is not differentiable, so autograd would drop the gradient flowing into K
Because transpose(-2, -1) also applies the 1/sqrt(d_h) scale as part of the operation
Because .T would silently apply the causal mask, zeroing the upper triangle of the scores
questions.explanation: transpose(-2, -1) swaps only the last two axes, so the same line works for (T, d_h), (B, T, d_h) or (B, nh, T, d_h). It is purely a shape choice — it does not scale or mask.

questions.section: 9. From scratch in PyTorch — and matching the fused kernel
questions.question: What does `scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, float('-inf'))` do when mask = torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T))?
options: It zeroes out the lower-triangular scores, leaving only the future positions with their values
It writes −infinity into the future (upper-triangular) positions where the tril mask is 0
It multiplies all the scores elementwise by the mask, so future positions become exactly zero
It replaces every score in the matrix with −infinity, so the softmax output becomes uniform
questions.explanation: torch.tril(ones) is 1 on and below the diagonal and 0 above it. masked_fill writes −infinity wherever the mask is 0 — the future positions — leaving the allowed scores unchanged. A later softmax then gives those positions zero weight.

questions.section: 9. From scratch in PyTorch — and matching the fused kernel
questions.question: In attention code, why is softmax called with dim=-1 on the (T, T) score matrix?
options: dim=-1 normalizes down each column, over all the queries for that key
dim=-1 normalizes the whole (T, T) matrix so that all entries sum to 1
dim=-1 normalizes along each row, so each query's weights over keys sum to 1
dim=-1 is simply required by PyTorch whenever softmax gets a 2-D tensor
questions.explanation: The last axis indexes keys, so dim=-1 normalizes across keys within each query's row. That makes each query's attention a distribution summing to 1. dim=-2 would normalize over queries, which is wrong.

questions.section: 9. From scratch in PyTorch — and matching the fused kernel
questions.question: What does `F.scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, is_causal=True)` compute relative to a hand-written scale/mask/softmax/matmul?
options: A faster approximation of attention that differs noticeably from the hand-written version on long inputs
Non-causal attention that silently ignores the mask unless an explicit attn_mask tensor is also passed
Only the (T, T) attention weights, leaving the final multiplication by V to be done by the caller
The same math with different bookkeeping — it matches the from-scratch result to float tolerance
questions.explanation: PyTorch's fused kernel with is_causal=True computes identical causal scaled dot-product attention; torch.allclose with the from-scratch output returns True. The difference is implementation efficiency, not the math.

questions.section: 9. From scratch in PyTorch — and matching the fused kernel
questions.question: Why is `Q[None, None]` used when passing a (T, d_h) tensor to F.scaled_dot_product_attention?
options: To add leading batch and head axes, giving shape (1, 1, T, d_h)
To detach Q from the autograd graph before the fused call
To cast Q to float16, which the fused kernel requires
To transpose Q so its last two axes are swapped for the call
questions.explanation: Indexing with None inserts new axes of length 1, giving (1, 1, T, d_h) — a batch of 1 with 1 head — matching the (B, nh, T, d_h) layout the fused function expects. It does not change dtype or gradients.

questions.section: 10. Tensor shapes: where the T x T comes from
questions.question: In multi-head attention with n_h heads, what is the shape of the attention weight tensor A?
options: (B, T, n_h, d_h)
(B, n_h, T, T)
(B, T, T, n_h)
(n_h, T, d_h)
questions.explanation: Each head has its own Q, K, V and therefore its own T x T grid, and the head axis goes right after the batch axis: (B, n_h, T, T). Q, K, V and O are (B, n_h, T, d_h).

questions.section: 10. Tensor shapes: where the T x T comes from
questions.question: For B = 2, n_h = 3, T = 4, how many separate T x T attention weight grids are there?
questions.explanation: There is one T x T grid per sequence per head: 2 × 3 = 6 grids of 4 × 4, i.e. 96 numbers in an A tensor of shape (2, 3, 4, 4).

questions.section: 10. Tensor shapes: where the T x T comes from
questions.question: Why do `transpose(-2, -1)` and `softmax(dim=-1)` work unchanged when a head axis is added to attention tensors?
options: Because the heads are processed one at a time in a Python loop, so each call sees only 2-D tensors
Because the head axis is always placed last, so transpose and softmax never touch the (T, T) grid
Because PyTorch silently ignores any extra axes beyond the first two when a tensor has rank four
The head axis is just another leading batch-like axis; attention only acts on the last two axes
questions.explanation: With shapes (B, n_h, T, d_h), the head axis is a leading batch-like axis. The math inside each (T, T) grid is exactly the single-head math, and negative-index axis operations address only the last two dimensions.

questions.section: 10. Tensor shapes: where the T x T comes from
questions.question: Why does it matter that attention's output has the same per-position width convention as its input?
options: It lets attention slot into a stack of layers and preserves the residual-stream structure
It halves the activation memory, since the output can overwrite the input buffer fully in place
It makes attention permutation-invariant, so token order no longer changes the output
It removes the need for a causal mask, since output positions already line up with inputs
questions.explanation: Because the output keeps the shape convention, attention can feed the next sub-layer and block, and its output can be added back to the residual stream. A layer changing the per-position width would break that structure.

questions.section: 10. Tensor shapes: where the T x T comes from
questions.question: What dtype and device does the attention output have?
options: Always float64 on the CPU, for numerical stability in the softmax
Whatever x is (float32, or bfloat16 in mixed precision), on x's device
Always int64 on the GPU, since the weights are computed from token ids
Always float16, on whichever device currently has the most free memory
questions.explanation: Attention is computed from x via matmuls and softmax, so its output follows x's dtype — float32, or bfloat16 under mixed precision — and stays on x's device.

questions.section: 11. Under the hood: the T x T matrix is the bottleneck
questions.question: How does the size of the attention score and weight matrices grow with sequence length T?
options: Linearly, as T, one row per position
Logarithmically, as log T, via tiling
Quadratically, as T squared
It does not depend on T at all, only d_h
questions.explanation: S and A are (B, n_h, T, T), so their size grows with T squared. At T = 1024 that is about a million entries per sequence per head; at T = 8192 it is about 67 million. This quadratic scaling is attention's defining cost.

questions.section: 11. Under the hood: the T x T matrix is the bottleneck
questions.question: Why can materializing the attention weight matrix be infeasible at long context, e.g. T = 8192, B = 8, n_h = 12 in float32?
options: Because float32 cannot represent weights below about 1e-8, so long rows underflow to all zeros
Because softmax overflows at long context once a row has more than 4096 finite entries in it
Because the causal mask stops being triangular once T exceeds the model's block_size setting
The weights alone take about 8·12·8192²·4 bytes ≈ 26 GB — more than most GPUs, for one layer
questions.explanation: The tensor has 8 × 12 × 8192² entries at 4 bytes each, about 26 GB for a single layer's attention weights. This dominates activation memory at long context. It is a memory-size problem, not a numerical one.

questions.section: 11. Under the hood: the T x T matrix is the bottleneck
questions.question: What is the compute cost of forming the attention scores S, and how does it scale with T?
options: O(B · n_h · T² · d_h) multiply-adds, growing as T²
O(B · T · d_h), growing linearly with T
O(B · n_h · d_h²), independent of T entirely
O(B · n_h · T³), cubic in T because of softmax
questions.explanation: Each of the B · n_h · T² scores is a d_h-length dot product, so forming S costs O(B · n_h · T² · d_h). The A V product costs the same order. Both grow quadratically with T.

questions.section: 11. Under the hood: the T x T matrix is the bottleneck
questions.question: How does FlashAttention compute attention without materializing the T x T weight matrix?
options: By approximating the softmax with a linear kernel function, so the T x T matrix is never needed at all
It streams over the scores in tiles, keeping a running max and sum and accumulating A V on the fly
By skipping the 1/sqrt(d_h) scaling step, which removes the need to store the full score matrix in memory
By dropping half of the keys at random in each tile, which halves the memory needed for the weights
questions.explanation: FlashAttention tiles the computation, maintains a running max and sum for the softmax, and accumulates the weighted sum of values incrementally, so A is never stored. The result is the same weighted average; only memory traffic changes. It is exact, not an approximation.

questions.section: 11. Under the hood: the T x T matrix is the bottleneck
questions.question: What is the one-line thesis of the FlashAttention paper (Dao et al., 2022)?
options: Attention is bottlenecked by FLOPs, so a lower-precision kernel doing fewer multiplies is the main win
Attention should be replaced by long convolutions, which reach the same quality at linear cost in T
Attention is bottlenecked by memory reads/writes of the T x T matrix, so avoid materializing it
Attention needs no softmax at long context, since the weights become nearly uniform past a few thousand
questions.explanation: FlashAttention argues the bottleneck is memory traffic for the T x T matrix, not the arithmetic. Avoiding materializing it — not reducing multiplies — is what speeds attention up.

questions.section: 11. Under the hood: the T x T matrix is the bottleneck
questions.question: During backpropagation through causal attention, what gradient reaches masked (−infinity) entries?
options: A large gradient that pushes the masked scores back toward zero
The same gradient as the diagonal entries, scaled by the row length
A gradient equal to the learning rate, applied as a constant offset
Zero gradient, so no signal flows to forbidden positions
questions.explanation: Masked entries have exactly zero softmax weight, and their gradient through softmax is zero, so no signal flows to future positions. Autograd's backward rules for @, softmax and masked_fill respect the causal structure in the backward pass too.

questions.question: With B = 4, T = 512 and a single head with d_h = 768, what is the shape of the score matrix S?
options: (4, 512, 512), about one million entries
(4, 512, 768), one score per channel
(4, 768, 768), one score per channel pair
(512, 512, 768), shared across the batch
questions.explanation: S has one score per (query, key) pair per sequence: (B, T, T) = (4, 512, 512) = 1,048,576 entries. d_h does not appear in S's shape — it was summed away by the dot product. It controls the cost of each score, not the size of S.

questions.question: How does the head dimension d_h affect the attention score matrix S?
options: It sets the number of columns of S, one column per channel of the head
It controls the cost of forming each score but not the size of S
It sets the number of rows of S, one per head dimension
It has no effect on either the cost or the size of S
questions.explanation: Each score is a dot product over d_h dimensions, so d_h determines the cost per score. But d_h is summed away, so S's shape is (B, T, T) regardless of d_h.

questions.question: What is the typical symptom of forgetting to divide attention scores by sqrt(d_h) at realistic head sizes like d_h = 64?
options: Attention weights become nearly uniform across all positions, so every token averages its context
The causal mask stops working, so future tokens leak into the attention output during training
Attention weights collapse to near one-hot almost immediately and training stalls or diverges
The output shape changes from (B, T, d_h) to (B, T, T), breaking the next layer's matmul
questions.explanation: Without the scale, scores are large and softmax saturates, producing near-one-hot weights and tiny gradients. Training stalls or diverges. Uniform weights would come from scores that are too small, the opposite problem.

questions.question: Why is it wrong to apply the causal mask by zeroing future weights after softmax?
options: Because zeroing weights after softmax is much slower than adding −infinity before it on a GPU
Because zeroing after softmax changes the output shape from (T, d_h) to a (T, T) weight matrix
Because zeroing after softmax makes the model attend to the future even more than before
The surviving weights then sum to less than 1, breaking the weighted-average interpretation
questions.explanation: Softmax already distributed weight over future positions; zeroing them afterward leaves the remaining weights summing to less than 1. Adding −infinity before softmax excludes those positions from both numerator and normalizer, so the surviving weights still sum to 1.

questions.question: What goes wrong if attention uses F.softmax(scores, dim=-2) instead of dim=-1?
options: It normalizes down columns over queries instead of across keys, so queries no longer distribute attention
It produces exactly the same result, because attention score matrices are always symmetric in i and j
It raises a dimension error, because softmax over dim=-2 is not defined for 2-D score tensors in PyTorch
It applies the causal mask a second time, so the lower triangle is also zeroed and every row is empty
questions.explanation: dim=-2 normalizes along columns, i.e. over queries for each key. Each query must distribute its own attention over keys, which is a row-wise normalization, dim=-1. Scores are not symmetric in general, so the results differ.

questions.question: For B = 8 sequences, n_h = 12 heads and T = 1024, what is the shape of the attention-weight tensor?
options: (8, 1024, 12, 64), heads after the time axis
(8, 12, 1024, 1024), over 100 million entries
(8, 12, 1024, 64), one row per query position
(12, 1024, 1024), shared by all 8 sequences
questions.explanation: The weights are (B, n_h, T, T) = (8, 12, 1024, 1024), about 100 million entries. Because it grows as T squared, it dominates activation memory at long context. (8, 12, 1024, 64) would be the shape of Q, K, V or O with d_h = 64.

questions.question: In causal attention, a query's two allowed keys give equal scaled scores. Why does it get weights [0.5, 0.5, 0] over three positions?
options: Because the third position has a zero value vector, so softmax gives it no weight at all
Because softmax always splits weight evenly across whichever positions are not masked out
The third position is masked to −infinity, and softmax of two equal values is [0.5, 0.5]
Because the 1/sqrt(d_h) scale factor halves every weight before the mask is applied
questions.explanation: The third (future) position is masked, so it gets exactly zero weight. The two live scores are equal, and softmax of two equal values splits the weight evenly. Softmax only splits evenly when the scores are equal.

questions.question: Why does understanding multi-head attention's split-and-merge matter for later architecture variants like GQA, MQA and MLA?
options: Because those variants drop the softmax and use linear attention instead
Because those variants change exactly the head structure of attention
Because those variants only change how positions are encoded in Q and K
Because those variants replace LayerNorm with RMSNorm inside each block
questions.explanation: GQA, MQA and MLA all modify how heads are structured (e.g. how keys and values are shared across heads). Knowing the split-and-merge lets you read any GPT attention module, reason about its memory, and modify it.

questions.question: Why is a single attention head limiting for language modelling?
options: Because a single head cannot apply a causal mask over a full context, so it leaks future tokens unless the sequence is split into blocks
Because a single head's softmax saturates once d_k exceeds 64, so its weights become one-hot and its gradients vanish in training
Because a token relates to different positions for different reasons at once, and one set of Q, K, V forces a single compromise blend
Because a single head can only attend to a fixed window of nearby positions, so long-range links such as coreference are lost
questions.explanation: A token may simultaneously need its subject (agreement), its antecedent (coreference) and the previous token (position). One attention gives one blended view, forcing a compromise. Multiple heads let different heads specialize in different relationships.

questions.question: How do the heads in multi-head attention interact before their outputs are combined?
options: They share one set of Q, K, V weights and differ only in which positions each one is allowed to see
Each head reads the softmax scores of the other heads and renormalizes so the heads attend to disjoint positions
They run sequentially, each head refining the previous head's output before passing it to the next one
They are fully independent: no shared weights and no access to each other's scores until the end
questions.explanation: Each head is an independent attention on its own channel slice: no shared weights, no shared scores. Their outputs are only combined at the end, by concatenation and the output projection W_O. They run in parallel, not sequentially.

questions.question: Which summary of multi-head attention is correct?
options: Split C into n_h slices of size C/n_h, attend in each, concatenate back to width C, then mix with a learned W_O
Run one attention n_h times on the full width C with different seeds, average the n_h outputs, then apply W_O
Duplicate the input n_h times along the channel axis, run attention once on width n_h·C, then project back to C
Split the T positions into n_h chunks of length T/n_h, attend within each chunk, then concatenate chunks back to T
questions.explanation: Multi-head attention partitions the channels into n_h slices of size d_h = C/n_h, runs the same scaled dot-product attention independently in each, concatenates back to C, and applies W_O. It splits channels, not positions, and does not average full-width copies.

questions.question: In GPT-2 small with C = 768 and n_h = 12, what is the per-head dimension d_h?
questions.explanation: d_h = C / n_h = 768 / 12 = 64. Each head operates on its own contiguous block of 64 channels.

questions.question: In multi-head attention, how are Q, K, V first produced before splitting into heads?
options: As n_h separate (C, d_h) projections, each called in a Python loop over heads
By slicing x along T into n_h chunks and projecting each chunk with its own W
Each of shape (B, T, C), the full width, using a single linear projection
By computing one head's Q of width d_h and repeating it n_h times along C
questions.explanation: The projection produces full-width (B, T, C) Q, K and V, and only then is the channel axis reshaped into (n_h, d_h). This is the same math as having n_h separate (C, d_h) projections, but done in one big matmul.

questions.question: What reshape sequence turns a (B, T, C) query tensor into per-head form?
options: transpose(1, 2) to (B, C, T), then view to (B, n_h, d_h, T)
view directly to (B, n_h, T, d_h), with no transpose needed at all
view to (B, T, d_h, n_h), then transpose(2, 3) to (B, T, n_h, d_h)
view to (B, T, n_h, d_h), then transpose(1, 2) to (B, n_h, T, d_h)
questions.explanation: First view re-groups the C channels as (n_h, d_h), giving (B, T, n_h, d_h); then transpose(1, 2) swaps T and n_h to give (B, n_h, T, d_h). A direct view to (B, n_h, T, d_h) would scramble data because memory is laid out with T before the channels.

questions.question: What does the `view(B, T, n_h, d_h)` step in multi-head attention do to the underlying memory?
options: Nothing is moved — it only reinterprets how the existing contiguous memory is indexed
It copies the data into a new buffer laid out as (B, T, n_h, d_h) for speed
It physically reorders the channels so each head's slice is stored contiguously in a new buffer
It allocates n_h new tensors of shape (B, T, d_h) and fills each with one slice
questions.explanation: A view re-groups the C channels into n_h groups of d_h without moving any data; it just changes the indexing of the same contiguous buffer. The later transpose also does not move data but makes the tensor non-contiguous.

questions.question: After splitting Q into shape (B, n_h, T, d_h), what do the last two axes represent and how many such matrices are there?
options: (n_h, d_h) matrices, one per (sequence, position), so B·T of them
(T, d_h) matrices, one per (sequence, head), so B·n_h of them
(T, T) matrices, one per sequence, so B of them shared by all heads
(d_h, T) matrices, one per head, so n_h of them shared by the batch
questions.explanation: After transpose(1, 2), the last two axes are (T, d_h), exactly the per-head query matrix. There are B·n_h of them, one for each sequence and head. Batched matmul treats the leading (B, n_h) axes as batch axes.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example: splitting one vector into heads
questions.question: With C = 4, n_h = 2 and query vector q = [10, 20, 30, 40], how does the view split it into heads?
options: head 0 = [10, 30], head 1 = [20, 40] (interleaved)
head 0 = [10, 20], head 1 = [30, 40] (contiguous halves)
questions.explanation: The view splits the channels into contiguous blocks of d_h: head 0 gets channels 0:2, head 1 gets channels 2:4. Channels are not interleaved or duplicated.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example: splitting one vector into heads
questions.question: In multi-head attention, which channels of the query does head 0 see when C = 4 and n_h = 2?
options: All four channels, but with its own Q, K and V weights
Channels 1 and 3, the odd-indexed ones, interleaved with head 1
Only channel 0, since each head gets one channel per head index
Only channels 0 and 1; it never sees channels 2 and 3
questions.explanation: Head 0 owns the first d_h = 2 channels and runs its own attention using only that slice. It never sees channels 2 and 3, which belong to head 1.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example: splitting one vector into heads
questions.question: Why do all n_h heads compute at once without a Python loop over heads?
options: Because the head slices sit on a separate axis, so attention runs as one batched matmul
Because PyTorch automatically parallelizes Python for-loops over heads on the GPU
Because only one head is actually computed and the other heads are copies of it
Because the heads share one attention score matrix, so softmax runs only once per layer
questions.explanation: Putting heads on their own axis makes them a batch dimension for @, so all heads compute in a single batched matmul. PyTorch does not auto-parallelize Python loops, and heads have independent scores.

questions.section: 4. Attention per head, in one batched matmul
questions.question: How does PyTorch's `@` operator handle tensors of shape (B, n_h, T, d_h) and (B, n_h, d_h, T)?
options: It multiplies over the first two axes and broadcasts the rest, giving (B, n_h)
It treats all leading axes as batch axes and returns (B, n_h, T, T)
It flattens everything to 2-D first, giving one (B·n_h·T, T) score matrix
It raises an error, because @ only accepts 2-D or 3-D input tensors
questions.explanation: Batched matmul treats all leading axes as batch axes and multiplies the last two: (T, d_h) times (d_h, T) gives (T, T). The result is (B, n_h, T, T) — one score matrix per head per sequence.

questions.section: 4. Attention per head, in one batched matmul
questions.question: How is a single (T, T) causal mask applied to multi-head scores of shape (B, n_h, T, T)?
options: It must be expanded explicitly with repeat to (B, n_h, T, T) before it can be added
It is applied to head 0 only, and the other heads inherit the mask through W_O
It broadcasts over the leading (B, n_h) axes, so one triangular matrix masks every head
It is transposed for odd-numbered heads so half the heads look forward in time
questions.explanation: Broadcasting aligns the mask's (T, T) with the last two axes, so the same triangular mask applies to every head and every sequence. No explicit copy is needed.

questions.section: 4. Attention per head, in one batched matmul
questions.question: What is the shape of the per-head attention outputs A v in multi-head attention?
options: (B, n_h, T, T, d_h)
(B, n_h, T, T)
(B, T, n_h, d_h)
(B, n_h, T, d_h)
questions.explanation: (B, n_h, T, T) weights times (B, n_h, T, d_h) values gives (B, n_h, T, d_h): each head's own attended output. Merging heads later brings it back to (B, T, C).

questions.section: 4. Attention per head, in one batched matmul
questions.question: In multi-head attention, which scale factor is applied to each head's scores?
options: 1/sqrt(d_h), with d_h the per-head dimension
1/sqrt(C), with C the full model width
1/n_h, averaging the heads' scores
No scale; each head's d_h is small enough to skip it
questions.explanation: Each head is a standard scaled dot-product attention over d_h dimensions, so its scores are divided by sqrt(d_h) (e.g. sqrt(64) = 8 in GPT-2). The dot products are over d_h channels, not C.

questions.question: How are the per-head outputs merged back into a (B, T, C) tensor?
options: By averaging over the head axis, then repeating the result n_h times along C
By transpose(1, 2) then view to (B, T, C), concatenating the heads end to end
By summing over the head axis, then projecting d_h back up to C with W_O
By taking the maximum over the head axis, then tiling it back to width C
questions.explanation: Reversing the split, transpose(1, 2) moves the head axis back next to d_h, and view merges (n_h, d_h) into C. This concatenates each position's n_h head outputs end to end. It is neither an average nor a sum.

questions.question: With C = 4 and n_h = 2, if head 0 outputs [a0, a1] and head 1 outputs [b0, b1] at a position, what is the merged vector?
questions.explanation: The merge is concatenation in head order, the exact inverse of the split: head 0's d_h channels first, then head 1's. So the merged vector is [a0, a1, b0, b1].

questions.question: What is the formula for the multi-head attention output after merging?
options: MultiHead = mean over heads of head_i, with no learned projection
MultiHead = softmax(Concat(head_1, ..., head_n_h)) W_O, then normalized
MultiHead = Concat(head_1, ..., head_n_h) W_Q, with W_Q of shape (C, C)
MultiHead = Concat(head_1, ..., head_n_h) W_O, with W_O of shape (C, C)
questions.explanation: The concatenated head outputs are multiplied by a learned output projection W_O of shape (C, C). W_Q is the query projection, used at the start. There is no extra softmax at the end.

questions.question: Why does multi-head attention need the output projection W_O?
options: Because concatenation leaves each head in its own channel slice; W_O mixes across heads into all C channels
Because the concatenated vector has width n_h·C, so W_O must project it back down to width C before the residual
Because W_O applies the causal mask after attention, zeroing contributions from future positions
Because W_O rescales each head's output to unit norm so no single head dominates the residual stream
questions.explanation: Concatenation leaves each head's output in its own d_h-wide slice with nothing combining them. W_O maps every head's slice onto all C output channels, blending the independent results. The width is already C after concatenation; W_O is for mixing, not resizing.

questions.question: What is the total number of weights in a multi-head attention layer's four projection matrices (ignoring biases)?
options: 3C², for W_Q, W_K, W_V
4C², for W_Q, W_K, W_V and W_O, each (C, C)
4C²·n_h, since each head has its own four matrices
C², since the split shares one matrix
questions.explanation: W_Q, W_K and W_V are each (C, C) — the split carves each into n_h slices of (C, d_h) — plus one extra (C, C) W_O: 4C² in total. The split and merge are pure reshapes with no parameters, and heads do not multiply the parameter count.

questions.question: Why is the output projection W_O mathematically redundant with a single attention head?
options: Because a single head has no value projection
Because single-head attention already includes a softmax over channels
Because A(x W_V) W_O = A x (W_V W_O), so W_O can be folded into W_V
Because W_O equals the identity in single-head models
questions.explanation: With one head, the output is A x W_V W_O, and the product W_V W_O is just another matrix, so W_O adds no expressive power. With several heads it cannot be folded, because each head writes only its own slice and W_O is the only thing mapping every slice onto all C outputs.

questions.question: Why can W_O not be folded into W_V when there are multiple heads?
options: Because W_V is frozen in multi-head attention, so any learned mixing must live in W_O
Because W_O is applied before attention, so it acts on x rather than on the head outputs
Because a softmax across heads sits between W_V and W_O, making the composition nonlinear
Because each head writes only its own d_h slice, and only W_O maps every slice onto all C outputs
questions.explanation: Each head's value projection only produces its own d_h channels, so no per-head W_V can write to other heads' channels. W_O is the single place where all head outputs get combined across the full width, so it cannot be absorbed into the per-head value projections.

questions.question: Why does real single-head transformer code usually still include an output projection?
options: For a uniform layer shape, even though it is mathematically redundant there
Because without it the gradients reaching W_V would be exactly zero in training
Because the causal mask is applied inside it, so removing it would leak the future
Because it doubles the usable context length by projecting into a wider space
questions.explanation: In practice code keeps the output projection for a uniform layer structure, even though with one head it could be folded into W_V. It has no effect on masking or gradients being non-zero.

questions.question: After `y.transpose(1, 2)` in the multi-head merge, why must `.contiguous()` be called before `.view(B, T, C)`?
options: Because transpose casts the tensor to float32, and view must restore the original dtype first
Because transpose makes it non-contiguous and view needs contiguous memory, else it raises an error
Because otherwise view would silently interleave the heads in the wrong order without raising any error
Because .contiguous() applies the output projection W_O before the heads are merged
questions.explanation: Transposing changes the strides so the axes no longer match the memory layout. view requires contiguous memory, so without .contiguous() PyTorch raises an error about the view being incompatible with the stride layout. .contiguous() copies data into the matching layout.

questions.section: 6. From scratch in PyTorch — the CausalSelfAttention module
questions.question: In the CausalSelfAttention module, what does `self.c_attn = nn.Linear(C, 3 * C)` compute?
options: Three separate attention heads, each of full width C, in one layer
The output projection W_O, applied to the concatenated head outputs
Q, K and V stacked in one fused matmul, (B, T, C) → (B, T, 3C)
The causal mask, as a learned (C, 3C) matrix of additive biases
questions.explanation: c_attn is a fused linear whose weight stacks W_Q, W_K and W_V into one (C, 3C) matrix. Its output is split into the three (B, T, C) tensors with .split(n_embd, dim=2). The output projection is c_proj.

questions.section: 6. From scratch in PyTorch — the CausalSelfAttention module
questions.question: Why does CausalSelfAttention use one fused Linear of width 3C instead of three separate Linears of width C?
options: Because three separate Linears would compute different math, since their biases interact
Because a fused Linear has a third of the parameters, as Q, K and V share one weight matrix
Because three separate Linear outputs cannot be reshaped into heads without an extra copy of x first
Because it is the same math, but one larger matmul runs more efficiently on a GPU than three
questions.explanation: Stacking W_Q, W_K, W_V into one (C, 3C) matrix computes exactly the same result with the same parameter count, but a single larger matmul uses the GPU more efficiently than three small ones.

questions.section: 6. From scratch in PyTorch — the CausalSelfAttention module
questions.question: In CausalSelfAttention, what does `q, k, v = self.c_attn(x).split(self.n_embd, dim=2)` do?
options: Carves the 3C-wide output into three (B, T, C) tensors along the channel axis
Splits the sequence into three time chunks of length T/3 along the time axis
Splits the batch into three groups of B/3 sequences for Q, K and V separately
Splits each channel into three heads of width C/3 along the channel axis
questions.explanation: .split(n_embd, dim=2) cuts the last (channel) axis of the (B, T, 3C) output into three pieces of width C: q, k and v. It does not touch the time or batch axes.

questions.section: 6. From scratch in PyTorch — the CausalSelfAttention module
questions.question: Why is the causal mask in CausalSelfAttention registered with `register_buffer` rather than as an nn.Parameter?
options: Because buffers are excluded from state_dict, so the mask is never saved in checkpoints
Because it carries no gradient but should still move with .to(device) and be part of the module
Because nn.Parameter cannot hold −infinity values, so the mask would turn into NaN
Because buffers are rebuilt from scratch on every forward pass, so the mask always matches the current T
questions.explanation: A buffer is module state that is not trained (no gradient) but moves with the module across devices. The mask is built once in __init__ and sliced to the current T in each forward. It is not recomputed every forward.

questions.section: 6. From scratch in PyTorch — the CausalSelfAttention module
questions.question: How is the causal mask stored in CausalSelfAttention and used in forward for a sequence of length T?
options: As a (T, T) boolean computed fresh in every forward pass with torch.tril and then inverted
As a (B, n_h, T, T) tensor of zeros and ones that is multiplied into the attention weights
As (1, 1, block_size, block_size), 0 on/below the diagonal and −infinity above, sliced to the current T
As a learned (block_size, block_size) parameter initialized lower-triangular and trained with the model
questions.explanation: The mask is built with torch.triu(torch.full(..., -inf), diagonal=1), reshaped to (1, 1, block_size, block_size), and sliced to the current T. The leading 1s broadcast over batch and heads.

questions.section: 6. From scratch in PyTorch — the CausalSelfAttention module
questions.question: What does `torch.triu(torch.full((N, N), float('-inf')), diagonal=1)` produce?
options: −infinity in every entry, including the main diagonal
−infinity on and below the diagonal, 0 strictly above it
An identity matrix with −infinity on the main diagonal only
0 on and below the diagonal, −infinity strictly above it
questions.explanation: triu with diagonal=1 keeps the entries strictly above the main diagonal and zeroes the rest, so the result has −infinity above the diagonal and 0 on and below — exactly an additive causal mask.

questions.section: 6. From scratch in PyTorch — the CausalSelfAttention module
questions.question: What does the test `test_causality_future_does_not_leak_into_past` check for CausalSelfAttention?
options: It perturbs the token at one position and asserts outputs at all earlier positions are unchanged
It checks that the output shape is (B, T, C) across several batch sizes and sequence lengths
It checks that each row of attention weights sums to 1 and that masked entries are exactly zero
It checks that the module produces identical outputs on CPU and on GPU for one batch
questions.explanation: The test verifies causality empirically: changing a later token must not affect any earlier position's output. A separate test checks that forward maps (B, T, C) to (B, T, C).

questions.question: For B = 8, T = 1024, C = 768, what is the shape of the output of `c_attn` in GPT-2 small's attention?
questions.explanation: c_attn maps C to 3C, so the output is (8, 1024, 3·768) = (8, 1024, 2304). After splitting it becomes three (8, 1024, 768) tensors and after the head split (8, 12, 1024, 64).

questions.question: For B = 8, T = 1024, C = 768, n_h = 12, what are the shapes of the attention input and the final output of CausalSelfAttention?
options: (8, 1024, 768) in, (8, 12, 1024, 64) out, since heads stay separate
(8, 1024, 768) in, (8, 1024, 2304) out, holding Q, K and V stacked
Both (8, 1024, 768): attention preserves the residual stream's shape
(8, 12, 1024, 1024) in, (8, 1024, 768) out, after the score matmul
questions.explanation: The input and output are both (8, 1024, 768). Attention is a shape-preserving map on the residual stream, which is what allows the residual add and stacking.

questions.question: Do the heads in multi-head attention add width to each position's representation?
options: Yes, the total width becomes n_h · C, one full copy of C per head
Yes, each head appends d_h channels, so the width grows to C + n_h · d_h
Yes, but only inside attention; W_O then projects n_h · C back down to C
No — n_h · d_h = C, so the heads partition C rather than add width
questions.explanation: With n_h · d_h = 12 · 64 = 768 = C, the heads partition the same C channels. Splitting into heads just re-slices the same numbers onto a new axis.

questions.question: How does multi-head attention's Q/K/V compute compare with a single-head attention of width C?
options: It is the same — splitting into heads only re-slices the same numbers
It is n_h times larger, since each head has its own full C to C projection
It is n_h times smaller, since each head projects only to d_h channels
It grows quadratically in n_h, because every head pair interacts in W_O
questions.explanation: Q, K and V are still one C to C projection each, so the projection compute is identical. Splitting into heads is essentially free, a reshape. What multiple heads buy is representational: independent relationship subspaces.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: why the head axis goes next to the batch axis
questions.question: Why must the head axis be placed right after the batch axis, giving (B, n_h, T, d_h)?
options: So the causal mask can be stored as an nn.Parameter of shape (n_h, T, T)
So the last two axes are (T, d_h) and @ runs B·n_h matmuls in one batched call
So the softmax normalizes across heads, making each position's head weights sum to 1
So that the later merge can call view without needing .contiguous() first
questions.explanation: Batched @ treats all axes before the last two as batch axes. Placing n_h after B makes the last two axes (T, d_h), so q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) becomes B·n_h independent (T, d_h) x (d_h, T) matmuls launched together. The layout is the parallelism.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: why the head axis goes next to the batch axis
questions.question: What would go wrong if the head axis were left in the (B, T, n_h, d_h) layout when computing q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)?
options: Nothing; batched matmul ignores axis order, so the result would be identical
It would compute attention across the batch axis, mixing tokens from different sequences
The last two axes would be (n_h, d_h), so the matmul would mix heads, not positions
It would raise an error, because the −infinity mask cannot be added to it
questions.explanation: With (B, T, n_h, d_h), the last two axes are (n_h, d_h), so the matmul would compare heads with each other at each position instead of positions with each other within a head. The result would be meaningless.

questions.section: 8. Under the hood: why the head axis goes next to the batch axis
questions.question: How does the memory cost of multi-head attention's score/weight tensors scale?
options: Linear in T and independent of n_h, since the heads share one score matrix
Quadratic in n_h and linear in T, since every head pair forms a score matrix
Independent of both T and n_h, since only d_h-wide tensors are ever stored
Quadratic in T and linear in n_h, since there is one T x T matrix per head
questions.explanation: The tensors are (B, n_h, T, T): quadratic in T and linear in n_h. More heads mean more T x T matrices, though each is formed over a smaller d_h and so is cheaper to compute. FlashAttention addresses this bottleneck identically for multi-head.

questions.question: A model has C = 512. What is d_h with n_h = 8, and why does n_h = 7 fail?
options: d_h = 64; 512/7 is not an integer, so view(B, T, 7, d_h) is impossible
d_h = 8; n_h = 7 fails because the head count must be an even number
d_h = 64; n_h = 7 also works, with the last head zero-padded to width 73
d_h = 4096; n_h = 7 fails because a prime head count cannot be batched
questions.explanation: d_h = 512/8 = 64. With 7 heads, 512/7 ≈ 73.14 is not an integer, so there is no d_h with 7·d_h = 512 and the view is impossible. The assert n_embd % n_head == 0 catches this. Parity or primality is not the issue — divisibility is.

questions.question: Which assertion in CausalSelfAttention's __init__ guards against an invalid head count?
options: assert cfg.n_head % 2 == 0
assert cfg.n_embd % cfg.n_head == 0
assert cfg.block_size % cfg.n_head == 0
assert cfg.n_head <= 12
questions.explanation: n_head must divide n_embd evenly so each head gets an integer d_h. The assert n_embd % n_head == 0 enforces exactly that. Head count need not be even or relate to block_size.

questions.question: What is a valid alternative to `.contiguous().view(...)` when merging attention heads after a transpose?
options: .flatten(0), which merges the batch and head axes
.detach().view(...), which drops the old strides
.reshape(...), which copies when needed
.squeeze(...), which removes the transposed axis
questions.explanation: reshape works on non-contiguous tensors by copying when necessary, so it can replace .contiguous().view(...). detach does not change contiguity, and flatten(0) or squeeze would produce wrong shapes.

questions.question: Why must the head split be applied to the channel axis (dim 2 of (B, T, C)) and not the time axis?
options: Because the time axis is always of length 1 during training
Because splitting time would multiply the parameter count by n_h
Because view can only regroup the last axis of a tensor in PyTorch
Because splitting time would scramble positions across heads
questions.explanation: Heads are channel subspaces: each head sees every position but only its d_h channels. Splitting the time axis would distribute different positions to different heads, scrambling the sequence.

questions.question: Which causal mask shape would misalign against 4-D multi-head scores of shape (B, n_h, T, T)?
options: (B, T, T), missing the head axis
(1, 1, T, T), with singleton batch and head axes
(T, T), a plain lower-triangular matrix
(1, 1, block_size, block_size) sliced to T
questions.explanation: (1, 1, T, T) and (T, T) both broadcast correctly over (B, n_h). A (B, T, T) mask aligns its B against n_h under broadcasting rules and so misaligns against the 4-D scores.

questions.question: With C = 768, n_h = 12 and a batch (B, T) = (4, 256), what is the shape of the per-head query tensor?
questions.explanation: d_h = 768/12 = 64, and after the split and transpose q has shape (B, n_h, T, d_h) = (4, 12, 256, 64). (4, 256, 12, 64) is the intermediate shape before transpose(1, 2), and (4, 12, 256, 256) is the score shape.

questions.question: At the highest level, what is a GPT model composed of?
options: An embedding, a stack of identical blocks, a final norm, and an output head
A single very wide attention layer followed by a softmax over the vocabulary
An encoder stack that reads the prompt, followed by a decoder stack that writes
A recurrent cell applied T times, with attention over its hidden states
questions.explanation: A GPT is literally token + positional embeddings, n_layer identical transformer blocks, a final LayerNorm, and a language-model head. Once you can build one block you have built the whole model up to bookkeeping. It is decoder-only, not encoder-decoder.

questions.question: Why is the pre-norm + residual structure of a transformer block described as 'the load-bearing wall'?
options: Because it halves the parameter count, so 100-layer models fit in GPU memory
Because it is the reason very deep (e.g. 100-layer) transformers train at all
Because it replaces attention in the deeper layers, so only early blocks attend
Because it makes the model permutation-invariant, so no positional encoding is needed
questions.explanation: Pre-norm with residual connections keeps a clean gradient path through the depth of the network, which is what makes very deep transformers trainable. It does not change parameter count meaningfully and is complementary to attention.

questions.question: What are the two steps of a pre-norm GPT transformer block's forward pass?
options: x = attn(x) + mlp(x), with both sub-layers computed in parallel
x = ln_1(attn(x)); then x = ln_2(mlp(x)), with no residual add
x = x + attn(ln_1(x)); then x = x + mlp(ln_2(x))
x = mlp(attn(ln(x))), with a single residual add around both
questions.explanation: A block first does x = x + attn(ln_1(x)) (communication between positions) and then x = x + mlp(ln_2(x)) (per-position computation). Each sub-layer is preceded by a LayerNorm and wrapped in a residual add.

questions.question: In a transformer block, where does information move between different positions?
options: Only in the MLP's hidden layer
In both the LayerNorm and the MLP
In the residual add between blocks
Only in attention
questions.explanation: Attention is the only place information moves between positions. The MLP transforms each position individually, and LayerNorm normalizes each position on its own. The residual add is elementwise per position.

questions.question: What is the 'computational rhythm' of a transformer, alternating across its sub-layers?
options: Mix across positions (attention), then think per position (MLP)
Normalize across the batch, then normalize across the sequence (LayerNorm)
Expand the sequence to 4T positions, then compress it back to T (MLP)
Compute the logits first, then compute the embeddings from them (head)
questions.explanation: Each block alternates communication (attention mixes information between positions) and computation (the MLP transforms each position independently). Stacking blocks repeats this rhythm.

questions.question: Why can transformer blocks be stacked one after another?
options: Because each block halves the sequence length, so the stack ends at T = 1 token
Because each block takes a (B, T, C) activation and returns the same shape
Because each block has its own vocabulary and passes token ids to the next
Because each block outputs (B, T, V) logits that the next block re-embeds
questions.explanation: A block maps (B, T, C) to (B, T, C), so the output of one block is a valid input to the next. Blocks do not change the sequence length or produce logits — that is the job of the final head.

questions.question: How does the position-wise MLP in a transformer block treat different positions?
options: It mixes all positions together like attention does, but without a causal mask
It uses a different weight matrix for each position up to block_size
It transforms each position independently, with the same weights everywhere
It only processes the last position, since only that one predicts a token
