questions.explanation: The MLP applies the same two linear layers and nonlinearity to every position independently. Weights are shared across positions, and no information moves between positions in the MLP.

questions.question: What is the formula for the transformer MLP?
options: MLP(x) = phi(W_1 x) ⊙ phi(W_2 x), with both W_1 and W_2 mapping C to 4C
MLP(x) = W_1 x + W_2 x + b, with W_1 and W_2 both (C, C) and no nonlinearity
MLP(x) = softmax(W_1 x) W_2, with W_1: C to 4C and W_2: 4C back to C
MLP(x) = W_2 phi(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2, with W_1: C to 4C and W_2: 4C to C
questions.explanation: The MLP is two linear layers with a nonlinearity phi (GELU) between them: W_1 in R^(4C x C) expands to 4C, then W_2 in R^(C x 4C) projects back to C. There is no softmax.

questions.question: Why does GPT-2's MLP expand the hidden width to 4C?
options: It is the standard capacity/compute trade-off; the hidden layer holds per-token capacity
Because GPT-2 uses 4 attention heads, and the MLP needs one C-wide slot per head
Because GELU's tanh approximation requires a hidden width that is a multiple of 4
Because a 4C hidden layer makes the MLP mathematically equivalent to a second attention layer
questions.explanation: The hidden layer holds the block's per-token capacity, and 4x expansion is the conventional trade-off between capacity and compute used by GPT-2 and most descendants. It is unrelated to the number of heads or GELU's requirements.

questions.question: What would happen to the transformer MLP if the nonlinearity phi were removed?
options: It would turn into a softmax layer, since W_2 would then normalize the 4C outputs
W_2 W_1 would collapse into one linear map, so the second layer would add nothing
It would become permutation-invariant over channels and lose all positional signal
It would double its parameter count, since the biases would have to absorb phi's role
questions.explanation: Without phi, W_2 (W_1 x) equals (W_2 W_1) x, a single linear map, so having two layers gains nothing representationally. The nonlinearity is what lets the MLP represent nonlinear functions of its input.

questions.question: What is the GELU nonlinearity used in GPT-2's MLP?
options: phi(z) = max(0, z), the rectified linear unit applied per element
phi(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(−z)), the logistic sigmoid of the input
phi(z) = z · Phi(z), where Phi is the standard-normal CDF
phi(z) = tanh(z), squashing every input into the range (−1, 1)
questions.explanation: GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit) is phi(z) = z Phi(z), with Phi the standard normal CDF. It is a smooth relative of ReLU. max(0, z) is ReLU and 1/(1+exp(−z)) is the sigmoid.

questions.question: How does GELU treat large positive and negative inputs?
options: It zeroes large positive inputs and passes large negative inputs through almost unchanged
It passes both large positive and large negative inputs through essentially unchanged
It clips both large positive and large negative inputs smoothly to the range ±1
It passes large positives almost unchanged and squashes negatives smoothly toward zero
questions.explanation: GELU behaves like a smooth ReLU: large positive inputs pass through almost unchanged and negative inputs are smoothly squashed toward zero. It does not clip to ±1 like tanh.

questions.question: Approximately what is GELU(1.0), and how does it compare to ReLU(1.0)?
options: About 0.8413 — most of the input, while ReLU would keep all of it (1.0)
Exactly 1.0 — for positive inputs GELU and ReLU agree exactly (1.0)
About 0.5 — half the input, since Phi(1) is 0.5, while ReLU gives 1.0
About 1.1587 — slightly more than the input itself, while ReLU gives 1.0
questions.explanation: GELU(1.0) = 1.0 × Phi(1.0) ≈ 0.8413, since Phi(1) ≈ 0.8413. ReLU would return exactly 1.0. GELU keeps most of the input while being smooth.

questions.question: What are the tensor shapes through a GPT MLP for input (B, T, C)?
options: (B, T, C) → (B, 4T, C) → GELU (B, 4T, C) → (B, T, C)
(B, T, C) → (B, T, 4C) → GELU (B, T, 4C) → (B, T, C)
(B, T, C) → (B, 4, T, C) → GELU (B, 4, T, C) → (B, T, C)
(B, T, C) → (B, T, C/4) → GELU (B, T, C/4) → (B, T, C)
questions.explanation: The first linear expands the channel axis to 4C, GELU keeps the shape, and the second linear projects back to C. Batch and time axes are unchanged; the MLP acts on the last axis only.

questions.question: Which axis do the MLP's linear layers act on, for an input of shape (B, T, C)?
options: The batch axis B, mixing the same position across different sequences
The batch axis B, mixing the same position across the different sequences in a batch
The last (channel) axis only, with the same weights for every (B, T) position
All three axes jointly, after flattening (B, T, C) into one long vector
questions.explanation: nn.Linear multiplies along the last axis, so the MLP transforms each position's C-vector independently, with the same weights for every (b, t). It does not mix across batch or time.

questions.question: How large is the MLP's hidden activation relative to the block input, and why does it matter?
options: The same size as the input, so it adds nothing extra to activation memory
Half the size of the input, which is how the MLP saves activation memory
Twice the size of the input, which matters only for the MLP's FLOP count
4× the size of the input — relevant when accounting for activation memory
questions.explanation: The hidden activation is (B, T, 4C), four times the input's size. That makes it significant when accounting for activation memory during training.

questions.question: In the course's MLP module, what are the layers in order?
options: c_fc (C → 4C), GELU, c_proj (4C → C), dropout
c_proj (C → 4C), dropout, c_fc (4C → C), GELU
GELU, c_fc (C → C), c_proj (C → C)
c_attn (C → 3C), GELU, c_proj (3C → C), dropout
questions.explanation: MLP.forward applies c_fc (expand C to 4C), then GELU, then c_proj (project 4C back to C), then dropout. c_attn is the attention's fused QKV projection, not part of the MLP.

questions.question: What does a residual (skip) connection compute in a transformer block?
options: y = f(x), replacing the input with the sub-layer's output each block
y = x + f(x), keeping the input and adding the sub-layer's output
y = x · f(x), gating the input elementwise by the sub-layer's output
y = f(x) − x, so the sub-layer's output is measured relative to x
questions.explanation: A block computes x + sublayer(x) rather than replacing x. The input passes through unchanged along the identity path, and the sub-layer contributes an additive update. That single + is what lets dozens of blocks be stacked.

questions.question: With a residual connection y = x + f(x), what does the sub-layer f have to learn?
options: To reproduce the input x exactly, plus a small correction
To output the next token's logits directly at every block
Only what to change — an additive update on top of x
To normalize x to zero mean and unit variance per position
questions.explanation: Because x reaches the output unchanged via the identity path, f does not need to reproduce x; it only learns the update to add. If f(x) = 0, the block simply passes its input through.

questions.question: Why is a freshly initialized residual block whose sub-layer outputs are small a safe starting point for a deep stack?
options: Because the gradients through a small sub-layer are exactly zero, freezing the block
Because it forces all blocks to learn identical weights, so depth adds no instability
Because small sub-layer outputs make the training loss exactly zero at initialization
Because y ≈ x, so the block starts close to 'do nothing' and preserves its input
questions.explanation: If f(x) is near zero, y = x + f(x) ≈ x, so each block starts near the identity. A deep stack of near-identity blocks passes signals through cleanly, which is a safe initial state. Gradients are not zero and the loss is not zero.

questions.question: For a residual block y = x + f(x) with upstream gradient g = dL/dy, what is dL/dx?
options: g (I + df/dx) — an identity contribution plus a learned contribution
g · df/dx only — the identity branch carries no gradient at all
g / (1 + df/dx) — the skip divides the learned contribution back out
g − g df/dx — the skip subtracts the learned branch's contribution
questions.explanation: By the chain rule, dL/dx = g (I + df/dx): the identity branch passes g back unchanged and the learned branch adds g df/dx. Without the skip, only the g df/dx term would remain.

questions.question: In a scalar residual toy y = x + 0.2x with upstream gradient g = 1, what are the two gradient contributions to dL/dx?
options: 0.2 from the identity branch and 1 from the learned branch, total 1.2
1 from the identity branch and 0.2 from the learned branch, total 1.2
1 from each branch, since both branches see the same input, total 2
0.2 from each branch, since the skip copies the learned factor, total 0.4
questions.explanation: The identity branch passes g · 1 = 1 unchanged, and the learned branch contributes g · f'(x) = 0.2, giving 1.2 in total. The identity contribution is the one that bypasses any learned factor.

questions.question: Without residual connections, why do gradients in a deep stack of N layers tend to vanish or explode?
options: Because softmax saturates in every layer, so its Jacobian is zero throughout a deep stack
Because LayerNorm divides by a variance that reaches zero after enough layers
Because the gradient is a product of N factors g df/dx, which tends to shrink or blow up
Because the effective learning rate is multiplied by N, once per stacked layer
questions.explanation: With y = f(x), the only gradient path multiplies each layer's Jacobian, so N layers give a product of N factors. Such products tend to shrink (vanishing) or grow (exploding). The residual adds a path that bypasses learned factors.

questions.question: What does a residual connection add to the backward pass that helps deep networks train?
options: A learned per-layer scale on the gradient, tuned to keep its norm near 1
A gradient clipping step that caps the norm before it reaches early layers
A second, per-layer loss function that gives each block its own signal
A path where the upstream gradient reaches x without any learned factor
questions.explanation: The identity branch carries the upstream gradient straight to x, so every layer gets a direct, well-scaled signal from the loss. It is not a clipping step or extra loss.

questions.question: Does a residual connection guarantee that gradients never vanish?
options: No — the learned part can cancel it (f'(x) = −1 gives 0), and (I + df/dx) still multiplies across layers
Yes — the identity term keeps the total gradient at least 1 at every layer, whatever f'(x) is
Yes — residuals force every sub-layer Jacobian to equal the identity, so gradients are preserved exactly at every layer
No — residuals make gradients vanish faster, since the identity term halves the signal per layer
questions.explanation: The total is g (1 + f'(x)); with f'(x) = −0.5 it is 0.5 and with f'(x) = −1 it is 0. Across many layers the factors (I + df/dx) still multiply, so gradients can still grow or shrink. Residuals make training much easier, but normalization, initialization and LR schedules do the rest.

questions.question: Besides residual connections, what other techniques help keep deep transformer training stable?
options: Removing the MLP and attention from the deepest half of the blocks
Normalization, careful initialization, and learning-rate schedules
Training with a single very large batch only, never with a small one
Training each layer separately and freezing it before the next one
questions.explanation: Residuals make deep networks easier to train but do not alone guarantee healthy gradients. Normalization (LayerNorm), careful initialization and learning-rate schedules do the remaining work.

questions.question: In a real GPT sub-layer, how does the Jacobian df/dx differ from the scalar toy f(x) = 0.2x?
options: It is always exactly 0.2, whatever the input and the size of the model
It is always zero, since real sub-layers are initialized with zero weights
It is an input-dependent matrix on (B, T, C), but still identity plus learned
It is a scalar equal to the learning rate, applied uniformly to every channel of x
questions.explanation: A real sub-layer (attention or MLP) acts on (B, T, C) tensors, so its Jacobian is a matrix that depends on the input. The scalar 0.2 is only a teaching example. The structure of the gradient — identity plus learned contribution, summed — is identical.

questions.question: Why is LayerNorm used in deep transformers?
options: To shuffle the order of channels so each block sees its features in a fresh arrangement
To compute the attention weights, since the softmax is applied to the normalized x
To reduce the vocabulary size by normalizing the logits before the output projection
Because activation scales drift across layers; LayerNorm re-centers and re-scales them
questions.explanation: As activations flow through many layers, some feature vectors grow and others shrink, destabilizing optimization. LayerNorm re-centers each position's vector to zero mean and unit variance, then applies a learned scale and shift.

questions.question: What is the LayerNorm formula?
options: LN(x) = (x − mu) / sqrt(sigma² + eps) ⊙ gamma + beta, stats over the C channels
LN(x) = x / max(|x|) ⊙ gamma + beta, scaling each position by its largest channel
LN(x) = (x − mu_batch) / sqrt(sigma²_batch + eps), with stats over the batch
LN(x) = softmax(x) ⊙ gamma + beta, so each position's channels sum to one
questions.explanation: LayerNorm subtracts the per-position mean over channels, divides by sqrt(variance + eps), then applies the learned per-channel scale gamma and shift beta. Statistics over the batch would be BatchNorm.

questions.question: Why does LayerNorm include a learned per-channel scale gamma and shift beta?
options: To rescale the output so its channels always sum to 1
So the network can undo the normalization if it needs to
To store the running mean and variance across training batches
To mask future positions before the attention softmax
questions.explanation: After normalizing to zero mean and unit variance, gamma and beta let the network re-scale and re-shift each channel, even undoing the normalization if useful. LayerNorm keeps no running statistics.

questions.question: Over which axis does LayerNorm compute its mean and variance for a (B, T, C) activation?
options: Over the batch axis B, separately per channel
Over the time axis T, separately per channel
Over the last (channel) axis C only
Over all three axes jointly, once per batch
questions.explanation: LayerNorm reduces over the last (channel) axis only, per position and per sequence. Reducing over the batch is what BatchNorm does; LayerNorm's choice makes it independent of batch size and sequence length.

questions.question: Why is LayerNorm preferred over BatchNorm for language models?
options: Because BatchNorm has no learnable scale or shift, so it cannot undo the normalization afterwards
Because LayerNorm runs faster on CPUs, which is where most language-model inference happens today in practice
Because BatchNorm cannot normalize bfloat16 activations, which modern language models train in
Because channel statistics don't depend on the batch, which matters for varied lengths and batch size 1
questions.explanation: LayerNorm's statistics come from each position's own channels, so they do not depend on the batch. That works for variable-length sequences and batch size 1, unlike BatchNorm whose statistics depend on the batch.

questions.question: What is the role of epsilon (default 1e-5) in LayerNorm?
options: It prevents division by zero when the variance is very small
It is the learning rate used for the gamma and beta updates
It is the dropout probability applied after the normalization
It sets the target variance that the output is normalized to
questions.explanation: epsilon is added to the variance inside the square root so the denominator never becomes zero. It is not a learning rate, dropout rate, or target variance.

questions.question: Which variance does torch.nn.LayerNorm use?
options: The unbiased sample variance, dividing by C − 1
The biased (population) variance, dividing by C
The variance across the batch, per channel, like BatchNorm
The median absolute deviation, for robustness to outliers
questions.explanation: LayerNorm uses the biased population variance, dividing by C. Using the unbiased variance (C − 1) gives subtly wrong values that do not match torch.nn.LayerNorm.

questions.section: Every token gets its own μ and σ
questions.question: For one sequence of 100 tokens with C = 768, how many means and variances does LayerNorm compute?
options: One mean and one variance for the whole input
768 means and 768 variances, one per channel
100 means and 100 variances, one per token
76,800 means and variances, one per element
questions.explanation: LayerNorm computes a separate mean and variance for each token's C-dimensional vector, so 100 tokens give 100 means and 100 variances, each of shape (1, 100, 1). Per-channel statistics would be a different normalization.

questions.section: Every token gets its own μ and σ
questions.question: With a batch of 8 sequences of 100 tokens each, how many (mu, sigma²) pairs does LayerNorm compute?
options: 8, one per sequence
100, one per position
768, one per channel
questions.explanation: Each token is normalized with its own statistics, so there are 8 × 100 = 800 separate (mu, sigma²) pairs. Tokens never share statistics.

questions.section: Every token gets its own μ and σ
questions.question: In LayerNorm, which quantities are shared across tokens?
options: Only the learned gamma and beta, each of shape (C,)
The mean and variance, averaged over the whole batch
The mean only; each token keeps its own variance
Nothing at all; gamma and beta are per token too
questions.explanation: Each token gets its own mean and variance, so one token cannot affect another's normalization. Only gamma and beta (shape (C,), 768 numbers each in GPT-2 small) are shared: the same scale and shift applied to every token after its own normalization.

questions.section: Every token gets its own μ and σ
questions.question: Can one token's large values change how another token in the same batch is normalized by LayerNorm?
options: Yes, because the mean and variance are computed over the whole batch
No — each token is normalized with its own statistics, never shared
Yes, because gamma and beta are recomputed from each batch's statistics
Only if the tokens are adjacent, since the stats use a sliding window
questions.explanation: LayerNorm statistics are computed per token over its own channels, so a token with large values (e.g. [0, 10, 0, 10]) has no effect on another token's normalization. gamma and beta are learned parameters, not recomputed per batch.

questions.question: What does LayerNorm with gamma = 1 and beta = 0 produce for x = [2, 4, 4, 6]?
options: [0, 0.5, 0.5, 1], scaled to the range 0 to 1
[-2, 0, 0, 2], centered by subtracting the mean
[-1, 0, 0, 1], divided by the max absolute value
questions.explanation: The mean is 4 and the biased variance is 8/4 = 2, so sigma ≈ 1.4142. (x − 4)/1.4142 gives about [-1.4142, 0, 0, 1.4142]. [-2, 0, 0, 2] is only the centered vector before dividing by sigma.

questions.question: In a from-scratch LayerNorm, why is `keepdim=True` used when computing the mean and variance?
options: To make the variance unbiased by keeping the C − 1 correction
To keep gradients from flowing back through the mean and variance
To store the statistics in a buffer that persists across forward calls
To keep the reduced axis as length 1 so it broadcasts against x
questions.explanation: keepdim=True leaves the channel axis as size 1, giving shape (..., 1), which broadcasts against x of shape (..., C) for the subtraction and division. It has nothing to do with bias correction or gradients.

questions.question: In the from-scratch LayerNorm, how are gamma and beta initialized?
options: gamma = ones(C), beta = zeros(C)
gamma = zeros(C), beta = ones(C)
Both random normal
gamma = ones(C), beta = ones(C) too
questions.explanation: self.weight (gamma) starts as ones and self.bias (beta) as zeros, so at initialization LayerNorm is a pure normalization with no extra scale or shift. Training then adjusts them.

questions.question: Which are the two most common LayerNorm bugs?
options: Computing in float32 instead of bfloat16 and forgetting to apply dropout afterwards
Reducing over the wrong axis (e.g. the batch) and using unbiased variance (C − 1)
Using an epsilon below 1e-8 and forgetting to add the learned bias beta at the end
Applying it before attention and after the MLP, instead of after both sub-layers
questions.explanation: Reducing over the wrong axis or using unbiased=True gives subtly wrong values that still 'look normalized'. Always normalize over the last (channel) axis with the biased variance.

questions.section: 5. Pre-norm vs post-norm, and the block
questions.question: What is the difference between pre-norm and post-norm transformer blocks?
options: Pre-norm normalizes the logits before the head; post-norm normalizes the embeddings
Pre-norm uses BatchNorm over the batch; post-norm uses LayerNorm over the channel axis
Pre-norm normalizes before the sublayer; post-norm normalizes after the residual add
Pre-norm blocks have no residual connection at all; post-norm blocks do have one
questions.explanation: In pre-norm the LayerNorm is applied to the sublayer's input (x + f(LN(x))); in post-norm it is applied after the residual add (LN(x + f(x))). Both use LayerNorm and both have residuals.

questions.section: 5. Pre-norm vs post-norm, and the block
questions.question: Which normalization placement did the original 2017 Transformer use, and which do modern LLMs (GPT-2 onward) use?
options: Both use pre-norm throughout
Original: pre-norm; modern LLMs: post-norm
Both use post-norm throughout
Original: post-norm; modern: pre-norm
questions.explanation: The original Transformer used post-norm, while GPT-2 onward use pre-norm.

questions.section: 5. Pre-norm vs post-norm, and the block
questions.question: Why do modern LLMs prefer pre-norm over post-norm?
options: It keeps the residual path free of normalization, so deep stacks train stably without delicate warmup
It removes one LayerNorm per block, cutting the parameter count enough to fit deeper stacks in memory
It removes the need for causal attention masking, since normalized inputs can no longer attend to the future
It makes LayerNorm unnecessary at inference, so the norm layers can be folded away into the weights
questions.explanation: In pre-norm the raw x flows down the residual path untouched, so the identity gradient path has no normalization in it. That makes deep stacks train more stably without delicate warmup. It does not remove LayerNorm or reduce parameters meaningfully.

questions.section: 5. Pre-norm vs post-norm, and the block
questions.question: In a pre-norm Block's forward `x = x + self.attn(self.ln_1(x))`, what does LayerNorm act on?
options: The residual stream itself, so x stays normalized in place for every later block
A copy fed into the sublayer, while the raw x continues down the residual path
Only the attention output, which is normalized before being added back to x
The attention weights, normalizing each row of the score matrix after softmax
questions.explanation: ln_1 is applied to the input of attention only; the original x is what gets added to attention's output. So the residual stream is never normalized in place — that is the point of pre-norm.

questions.section: 5. Pre-norm vs post-norm, and the block
questions.question: Why is the course's `Block` module stackable?
options: Because it contains its own embedding layer for token ids
Because it outputs logits of shape (B, T, V) for the next one
Because its output shape equals its input shape, (B, T, C)
Because it halves T each time, so the stack always terminates
questions.explanation: Block maps (B, T, C) to (B, T, C), so blocks can be chained n_layer times. Logits are produced only by the final head after the last block.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: parameter and compute cost of one block
questions.question: Approximately how many parameters does one transformer block with width C have, and where do they come from?
options: About 4C², all from attention, since the MLP's weights are tied to QKV
About 8C², all from the MLP, since attention has no learned parameters
About C², mostly from the two LayerNorms' gamma and beta, each (C, C)
About 12C²: 4C² from attention (QKV plus output) and 8C² from the MLP
questions.explanation: Attention contributes C·3C + C·C = 4C² and the MLP contributes C·4C + 4C·C = 8C², giving about 12C². The two LayerNorms add only about 4C, which is negligible.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: parameter and compute cost of one block
questions.question: For GPT-2 small (C = 768, 12 blocks), approximately how many parameters are in the transformer blocks?
options: About 85M (≈ 7.1M per block × 12), the bulk of the ~124M
About 7.1M in total, since the 12 blocks share their weights
About 124M — every GPT-2 parameter sits inside the blocks
About 38.6M, with the rest of the ~124M in the embeddings
questions.explanation: 12 × 768² ≈ 7.1M per block, times 12 blocks ≈ 85M. That is the bulk of GPT-2 small's ~124M parameters; the rest is mostly embeddings (38.6M is the token embedding table).

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: parameter and compute cost of one block
questions.question: In a transformer block, which part's compute usually dominates, and when does that change?
options: Attention always dominates, since its score matrix is formed at every sequence length
The MLP's 8C² FLOPs per token, until T is long enough for attention's T² term
LayerNorm dominates at short sequences, since its reductions are memory-bound
The residual add dominates at long sequences, since it touches every activation
questions.explanation: Per token, the MLP's 8C² FLOPs usually outweigh attention's work. As sequences grow, attention's T² score-matrix term eventually takes over — the crossover that motivates FlashAttention. LayerNorm and residual adds are negligible.

questions.question: In a 12-layer model, a bug writes `x = self.attn(self.ln_1(x))` (dropping the residual `x +`). Why does training diverge or learn nothing?
options: Because LayerNorm becomes undefined once its input is no longer the residual stream
Because the causal mask is attached to the residual path, so dropping it leaks the future
Because each layer multiplies the gradient by its Jacobian; 12 factors vanish or explode
Because the output shape changes to (B, T, 3C), which breaks the next block's input
questions.explanation: Without the identity term, dL/dx = dL/dy · df/dx at every layer, so 12 such factors multiply. If their singular values are below 1 the gradient vanishes in early layers; above 1 it explodes into NaNs. The shape is unchanged, which is why the bug is not caught by shape checks.

questions.question: Why might a 1-layer model with the residual add accidentally dropped still appear to train?
options: Because a 1-layer model adds the residual automatically inside nn.Module's forward hook
Because a single layer has no Jacobian, so the backward pass skips straight to the loss
Because LayerNorm rescales the output to unit variance, fully compensating for the residual
Because one Jacobian factor barely compounds, so the bug hides until the model goes deep
questions.explanation: With a single layer there is only one multiplicative factor in the gradient, so the compounding that kills deep stacks doesn't happen. That is exactly why this bug hides until you go deep.

questions.question: What is the shape of the MLP's hidden activation for input of shape (4, 128, 768)?
questions.explanation: The first linear expands the last axis from C = 768 to 4C = 3072; batch and time are unchanged, giving (4, 128, 3072).

questions.question: For LayerNorm on x = [1, 1, 1, 5] with gamma = 1 and beta = 0, what are mu and the biased sigma²?
options: mu = 2, sigma² = 4
mu = 2, sigma² = 3
mu = 2, sigma² = 2
mu = 8, sigma² = 12
questions.explanation: mu = 8/4 = 2, and the biased variance is (1 + 1 + 1 + 9)/4 = 3, so sigma ≈ 1.732 and the largest normalized entry is (5 − 2)/1.732 ≈ 1.732. sigma² = 4 would be the unbiased variance (12/3).

questions.question: In a pre-norm transformer block, does the normalization sit on the residual highway?
options: Yes — x is normalized in place before being added back onto the residual stream
Yes — a LayerNorm is applied to the residual stream right after every residual add
No — the norm is applied only to the copy fed into the sublayer; raw x flows on
No — pre-norm blocks contain no normalization at all, only the final LayerNorm
questions.explanation: In pre-norm, ln_1(x) feeds attention while the raw x is what the residual adds to. The norm is off the highway, keeping the gradient path clean. Normalizing after every residual add would be post-norm.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: In a from-scratch GPT-2, which four named components does the full model consist of, besides the dropout after the embeddings?
options: The embedding tables wte and wpe, n_layer blocks, a final LayerNorm ln_f, and lm_head
A tokenizer, an encoder stack over the prompt, a decoder stack, and a softmax output layer
The embedding table wte, a single wide attention layer, an MLP, and a learned softmax head
The embedding tables wte and wpe, a convolutional stem, a pooling layer, and lm_head
questions.explanation: GPT-2 is the token and position embeddings (wte, wpe), n_layer identical pre-norm blocks, a final LayerNorm ln_f, and a linear head lm_head that maps to vocabulary logits. There is no encoder/decoder split and no convolution; softmax is applied inside the loss or the sampler, not as a learned layer.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: In GPT-2's forward(idx, targets), what are the shapes of the input token ids and the output logits?
options: idx is (B, T, C) floats and logits are (B, T, V) floats
idx is (B, T) integers and logits are (B, V), one per row
idx is (T,) integers and logits are (T, C)
idx is (B, T) integers and logits are (B, T, V)
questions.explanation: The input is a batch of B sequences of T token ids, an integer tensor of shape (B, T). The model produces a score for every vocabulary token at every position, so logits are (B, T, V). Producing only (B, V) would mean predicting a single next token per sequence, which is what generation slices out afterward, not what forward returns.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: What does weight tying mean in GPT-2?
options: The query, key and value projections in each block share one (C, C) weight matrix
All transformer blocks in the stack reuse one set of block weights, n_layer times over
The token-embedding table wte and the LM head lm_head share one weight tensor
The position embedding wpe is initialized as a copy of the first block_size rows of wte
questions.explanation: Weight tying makes wte.weight and lm_head.weight the same Parameter object, both of shape (V, C). It does not share weights between Q/K/V or across blocks (that would be a different idea, cross-layer sharing), and it is aliasing rather than a one-time copy.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Why is the assembled GPT-2 class described as the point where 'no more machinery is hiding'?
options: Because GPT-2 adds a large hidden memory module on top of the stack that stores past contexts
Because a GPT is just an embedding, a stack of identical blocks, a norm, and a linear head
Because the class wraps the HF Transformers implementation, so nothing else needs explaining
Because all remaining computation is delegated to a pretrained tokenizer and its merges
questions.explanation: Once the Module 5 block exists, the whole GPT is that block stacked plus thin translation layers at each end: embeddings in, final norm and linear head out. Every later model in the course is this class or a small variation of it, so it is a concrete object you can instantiate, count and call.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a GPT is four things in a row
questions.question: What does a single pre-norm Block do to the residual stream x?
options: x = LayerNorm(x + attn(x)), then x = LayerNorm(x + MLP(x))
x = x + attn(LayerNorm(x)), then x = x + MLP(LayerNorm(x))
x = attn(LayerNorm(x)), then x = MLP(LayerNorm(x)) with no residual adds
x = x + LayerNorm(attn(x) + MLP(x)) computed in a single step
questions.explanation: In a pre-norm block each sub-layer reads a normalized copy of the stream and its output is added back: normalize, attend, add back; normalize, MLP, add back. Placing the LayerNorm after the addition is the post-norm design of the original Transformer, not GPT-2's pre-norm block.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a GPT is four things in a row
questions.question: In the GPT-2 front end, how are the token embedding and position embedding combined before entering the block stack?
options: They are added element-wise and then passed through dropout
They are concatenated along the channel axis to width 2C
They are multiplied element-wise and then layer-normalized
Only the token embedding is used; positions are added inside attention
questions.explanation: x = wte(idx) + wpe(positions), followed by dropout, is the input to the stack. Concatenation would change the width to 2C and break the (B, T, C) invariant; GPT-2 uses learned absolute positions added at the input, not positions injected inside attention.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a GPT is four things in a row
questions.question: In a GPT training step, how are the next-token targets related to the inputs?
options: Targets are identical to the inputs, so the model learns to reproduce each token in place
Targets are the inputs shifted right by one, so each position's target is the previous token
Targets are random tokens drawn from the vocabulary, used as negative samples for each position
Targets are the inputs shifted left by one, so each position's target is the following token
questions.explanation: The language-modeling objective is next-token prediction: targets[b, t] is the token that follows position t. Building them by shifting the input sequence left by one achieves that. Using identical targets would make the task trivial copying, a classic data leak.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a GPT is four things in a row
questions.question: Inside the GPT-2 block pseudocode, which non-linearity sits between the two linear layers of the MLP?
options: ReLU
Softmax
GELU
Tanh
questions.explanation: The MLP is Linear2(GELU(Linear1(LayerNorm(x)))). GPT-2 uses GELU, a smooth relative of ReLU. Softmax appears in attention and in the loss, not in the MLP.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a GPT is four things in a row
questions.question: In the GPT training pseudocode, which part does Module 6 build, as opposed to the Module 7 training loop?
options: Only the optimizer step, gradient clipping and the learning-rate schedule for each batch
Only the tokenizer and the data loader that produces shuffled (B, T) batches of ids
Everything between clearing gradients and the cross-entropy loss: the forward pass
The evaluation and model-saving steps that run after the training loop has finished
questions.explanation: The outer loop (batching, backprop, clipping, weight and learning-rate updates) is Module 7. Module 6 builds the model itself: embeddings, blocks, final norm, head and loss, i.e. what runs between ClearGradients() and CrossEntropy.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a GPT is four things in a row
questions.question: In the GPT training pseudocode, which steps follow Backpropagate(loss) within each training batch?
options: Clear gradients, re-embed the inputs, recompute the logits
Clip gradients, update the weights, update the learning rate
Save the model, evaluate, then tokenize new training text
Apply dropout, run the final LayerNorm, project to the vocabulary
questions.explanation: After the backward pass, each iteration clips gradients, applies the optimizer update, and advances the learning-rate schedule. Clearing gradients happens at the start of the iteration; evaluation and saving happen after the loop.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a GPT is four things in a row
questions.question: Where in GPT-2 does essentially all of the 'thinking' happen, and what do the two ends do?
options: In the stack of blocks; the ends only translate ids to vectors and vectors to scores
In the embedding tables; the blocks only smooth the embeddings toward the output head
In the final LayerNorm; the blocks and embeddings just prepare its normalized input
In the LM head; the blocks only compress the input into a small code for it to decode
questions.explanation: The front end turns integer ids into C-dimensional vectors, and the back end turns the final vectors into a score per vocabulary token. All context mixing and computation happens in the repeated blocks; the ends are pure translation.

questions.section: 2. The front end: two embedding tables — Intuition and math
questions.question: Why does GPT-2 look up a learned vector for each token id instead of feeding the integer id directly into the network?
options: Integers cannot be stored in GPU memory, so ids must be converted to floats first
Embedding lookups are faster than any arithmetic performed on raw integer inputs
Feeding integers directly would make the model invariant to the order of the tokens
Integer ids carry no useful geometry: token 5 is not 'half of' token 10
questions.explanation: Token ids are arbitrary indices into the vocabulary; their numeric values and differences mean nothing. A learned embedding table gives each token a vector whose geometry training can shape. GPUs handle integers fine; the issue is meaning, not storage.

questions.section: 2. The front end: two embedding tables — Intuition and math
questions.question: In GPT-2, what are the shapes of the token-embedding table wte and the position-embedding table wpe?
options: wte is (C, V) and wpe is (C, block_size), transposed
wte is (V, C) and wpe is (V, block_size)
wte is (block_size, C) and wpe is (V, C)
wte is (V, C) and wpe is (block_size, C)
questions.explanation: Row i of wte is the C-dimensional vector for token id i, so wte has V rows. Row t of wpe is the vector for position t, and there are block_size positions. Both have width C so the two lookups can be added.

questions.section: 2. The front end: two embedding tables — Intuition and math
questions.question: What does the input to GPT-2's transformer stack at batch b, position t equal?
options: E_tok[idx[b, t]] * E_pos[t]: the token vector scaled element-wise by the position vector
E_tok[idx[b, t]] only; the position is supplied later by the causal mask
E_tok[idx[b, t]] + E_pos[t]: which token, plus which position
E_pos[idx[b, t]] + E_tok[t]: the position table indexed by token id
questions.explanation: x[b, t] = wte[idx[b, t]] + wpe[t]: a per-position sum of 'what token is here' and 'where here is'. The causal mask restricts which positions attend to which, but it does not tell the model where a token sits.

questions.section: 2. The front end: two embedding tables — Intuition and math
questions.question: Which property of self-attention makes positional embeddings necessary?
options: Attention is non-differentiable with respect to the order of its input tokens
Attention is permutation-invariant: it treats its inputs as an unordered set
Attention only sees the last token, so earlier positions need explicit labels
Attention has quadratic cost in T, which positional embeddings help to reduce
questions.explanation: Without position information, attention computes the same result for any reordering of tokens, so it could not tell 'the dog bit the man' from 'the man bit the dog'. Adding a position-dependent vector breaks that symmetry. Positional embeddings do not change attention's cost.

questions.section: 2. The front end: two embedding tables — Intuition and math
questions.question: What kind of positional encoding does GPT-2 use?
options: Learned absolute position embeddings: wpe is a table trained like any other weight
Fixed sinusoidal encodings computed from sine and cosine formulas, with no training
Rotary position embeddings that rotate the queries and keys by a position angle
Relative position biases added to the attention scores, one learned bias per offset
questions.explanation: GPT-2's wpe is just another nn.Embedding of shape (block_size, C), learned by gradient descent. Rotary embeddings (RoPE) replace it later in the course (Module 12); sinusoidal encodings were the original Transformer's choice.

questions.section: 2. The front end: two embedding tables — Intuition and math
questions.question: After the embedding step in GPT-2, what does everything downstream of the embeddings see about the input tokens?
options: Only the summed embedding vectors; the integer ids are never seen again
Both the vectors and the raw integer ids, which attention uses as keys
Only the integer ids, re-embedded at the start of every block
Only the position vectors, since the token vectors are dropped after block 1
questions.explanation: Once wte[idx] + wpe[positions] is formed, the blocks, ln_f and lm_head operate purely on those (B, T, C) vectors. The ids are not passed further; each block works on the residual stream it receives.

questions.section: 2. The front end: two embedding tables — Tensor shapes
questions.question: In GPT-2's front end, what is the positions tensor fed to wpe, and what is its dtype?
options: arange(V) = 0 .. V-1, of dtype float32, shape (V,)
The token ids idx themselves, of dtype int64, shape (B, T)
arange(block_size) always, of dtype float32, shape (block_size,)
arange(T) = 0, 1, ..., T-1, of dtype int64, shape (T,)
questions.explanation: Positions are just the indices 0 to T-1 for the current sequence length, an int64 vector of length T used as lookup indices into wpe. They do not depend on the token ids, and only the first T rows of wpe are used, not all block_size.

questions.section: 2. The front end: two embedding tables — Tensor shapes
questions.question: In GPT-2, tok_emb has shape (B, T, C) and pos_emb has shape (T, C). What happens when they are added?
options: PyTorch raises a shape-mismatch error unless pos_emb is explicitly repeated B times
pos_emb broadcasts over the channel axis, giving each channel a different position
pos_emb broadcasts over the batch axis, so every sequence gets the same position vectors
The sum has shape (B, T, 2C), because the two embeddings' channels are stacked
questions.explanation: Broadcasting aligns trailing dimensions: (T, C) matches the last two axes of (B, T, C) and is stretched across B. That is exactly correct, because position t means the same thing in every sequence of the batch.

questions.section: 2. The front end: two embedding tables — Tensor shapes
questions.question: What are the shape and dtype of wte(idx) in GPT-2 when idx is (B, T) int64?
options: (B, T) floating point: one scalar weight per token
(B, T, C) floating point: one C-vector per token
(B, C) floating point: one vector per sequence
(B, T, V) int64: one-hot vectors over the vocabulary
questions.explanation: An embedding lookup replaces each integer id with its row from the (V, C) table, adding a trailing axis of size C. The output is a float tensor; the lookup never materializes one-hot (V-wide) vectors.

questions.section: 3. The back end: final norm and the LM head
questions.question: After the last transformer block of GPT-2, what shape is x, and what must the back end produce from it?
options: x is (B, C) after pooling; the back end must produce one token id per sequence
x is (B, T, C); the back end must produce a length-V logit vector per position
x is (B, T, V) already; the back end only needs to apply a softmax over V
x is (B, T, C); the back end must produce a single scalar loss for each sequence
questions.explanation: The stack preserves (B, T, C): one refined vector per position. To predict the next token, each position needs a score for every vocabulary entry, so the back end (ln_f then lm_head) maps C to V, giving (B, T, V) logits.

questions.section: 3. The back end: final norm and the LM head
questions.question: Why does GPT-2 need the final LayerNorm ln_f before the LM head?
options: With pre-norm blocks nothing normalizes the residual stream itself, so ln_f does it once
Because the LM head has no weights of its own and relies on ln_f's gamma and beta to project
Because the last block's MLP has no LayerNorm of its own, unlike all of the earlier blocks
Because cross-entropy requires inputs already normalized to sum to 1 across the vocabulary
questions.explanation: In pre-norm blocks each LayerNorm sits on the branch feeding a sub-layer, never on the stream. So the stream leaving the final block has never been normalized; ln_f normalizes it once. Every block (including the last) has its two LayerNorms; and cross-entropy takes raw logits, not normalized probabilities.

questions.section: 3. The back end: final norm and the LM head
questions.question: What is GPT-2's lm_head layer?
options: A two-layer MLP from C to 4C to V with a GELU between the two layers
A linear map from C to V with a bias, followed by a learned softmax layer
A linear map from V to C that compresses the vocabulary distribution to C
A linear map from C to V with no bias, whose weight has shape (V, C)
questions.explanation: lm_head is a single nn.Linear(C, V, bias=False). Its weight is (V, C), so x @ W^T maps each C-vector to V scores. Having no bias is what lets it be exactly tied to the (V, C) embedding table.

questions.section: 3. The back end: final norm and the LM head
questions.question: How should row i of GPT-2's LM-head weight W_lm be interpreted?
options: As the probability that token i appears anywhere in the training corpus, learned as a prior
As the position embedding for position i, reused by the head to locate the next token
As a detector for token i: its dot product with x_t scores token i coming next
As the attention weights that token i assigns to every other token in the context
questions.explanation: logits[t, i] = x_t . W_lm[i], so each row acts as a template for one vocabulary token; a larger dot product means the model favors that token next. It is not a corpus frequency, a position vector, or an attention pattern.

questions.section: 3. The back end: final norm and the LM head
questions.question: What are GPT-2's logits fed into during training?
options: A sigmoid and binary cross-entropy for each vocabulary token
A mean-squared-error loss against the target embeddings
Softmax and cross-entropy against the next-token targets
An argmax that is compared to the target for a 0/1 accuracy loss
questions.explanation: The (B, T, V) logits are exactly the raw scores that softmax turns into a next-token distribution, scored by cross-entropy against the true next token. Argmax accuracy is not differentiable, and next-token prediction is multi-class, not independent binary classification.

questions.section: 4. Weight tying: wte and lm_head are the same tensor
questions.question: In PyTorch, which single line implements GPT-2's weight tying?
options: self.transformer.wte.weight.data.copy_(self.lm_head.weight.data)
self.transformer.wte.weight = self.lm_head.weight
self.lm_head.weight = self.transformer.wpe.weight
self.lm_head.weight.requires_grad = False
questions.explanation: Assigning the Parameter object makes both attributes point to one tensor, sharing memory and gradient. copy_ would only copy values once, after which the two would drift apart; tying to wpe has the wrong shape; freezing the head is unrelated.

questions.section: 4. Weight tying: wte and lm_head are the same tensor
questions.question: What happens to the gradients of wte and lm_head once they are tied in GPT-2?
options: They share one gradient: the embedding and head contributions accumulate in one tensor
Each keeps its own gradient, and the two are averaged together before the optimizer step
Only the head receives a gradient; the embedding is effectively frozen once they are tied
Only the embedding receives a gradient; the head is effectively frozen once they are tied
questions.explanation: Because both names refer to one Parameter, autograd adds the gradient from the input lookup and from the output projection into that single .grad. Nothing is averaged or frozen; one tensor is updated by both roles.

questions.section: 4. Weight tying: wte and lm_head are the same tensor
questions.question: Why is tying GPT-2's wte and lm_head possible from a shape point of view?
options: Both weights have shape (C, C), so they are square and interchangeable
The embedding is (V, C) and the head is (C, V), which are transposes stored identically
The head is padded to match the embedding's shape before tying
Both weights have shape (V, C), so one tensor can serve both
questions.explanation: nn.Embedding(V, C).weight is (V, C), and nn.Linear(C, V).weight is also (V, C), because Linear stores weights as (out_features, in_features). So the same tensor fits both without reshaping or padding.

questions.section: 4. Weight tying — Why this is natural
questions.question: Why is weight tying a natural choice for a language model?
options: Because the head must never learn anything beyond what the embedding table already learned
Because tying makes the model invariant to any permutation of the vocabulary's token ids
Because the embedding of a token should equal the average of the logits it produces
Both are organized around 'the vector for token i', so one dictionary can serve both
questions.explanation: The embedding maps id i to row i; the head scores token i by dotting with row i. Using the same row for both directions makes the input and output maps transposes of one learned dictionary. Tying does not freeze the head or create any vocabulary-order invariance.

questions.question: In GPT-2 small, roughly how many parameters does weight tying save?
options: About 0.8M (one 1024 x 768 table), under one percent of the model
About 7M (one transformer block), under a tenth of the model
About 38.6M (one 50257 x 768 table), about a third
About 85M (all transformer blocks), more than half of the model
questions.explanation: The token table is 50257 x 768 = 38.6M parameters. Untied, wte and lm_head would each pay for it; tied, it is paid once, saving about 40M of a 124M model. 0.8M is the size of wpe, and 85M is the whole block stack.

questions.question: Besides saving parameters, what quality benefit is attributed to weight tying in language models?
options: It removes the need for positional embeddings by encoding token order inside the head
It improves perplexity, partly because rare tokens' output vectors also train as inputs
It makes the model's logits exactly calibrated probabilities, with no softmax required
It guarantees that the model never predicts the same token twice in a row when sampling
questions.explanation: Press and Wolf (2016) found tying improves language-model perplexity, and GPT-2 uses it. Keeping input and output representations consistent means a token's vector is trained by both roles, which particularly helps rarer tokens. It has nothing to do with position encoding or repetition.

questions.question: Which paper is credited with showing that tying input and output embeddings improves language-model perplexity?
options: Press and Wolf (2016)
Holtzman et al. (2020)
Vaswani et al. (2017)
Kaplan et al. (2020)
questions.explanation: Press and Wolf 2016 introduced and evaluated output-embedding tying, and GPT-2 adopted it. Holtzman et al. 2020 is the nucleus-sampling paper; Vaswani et al. 2017 is the original Transformer; Kaplan et al. 2020 is about scaling laws.

questions.question: Is weight tying in GPT-2 an aliasing of one tensor or a copy of values?
options: Aliasing: two attributes point to one tensor, so reassigning either breaks the link
A copy: values are copied once at construction, and the two are then trained independently
A copy: values are re-copied from wte into lm_head after every single optimizer step
Aliasing that PyTorch automatically restores whenever either of the weights is reassigned
questions.explanation: Tying is a Python assignment making both names refer to one Parameter. If you later assign a fresh tensor or module to either, they silently become separate tables. PyTorch does not re-tie for you, so you must redo the tie yourself.

questions.question: After reloading or resetting one of GPT-2's tied weights, what must you do, and what symptom reveals that you forgot?
options: Nothing, since the tie survives any reassignment; there is no visible symptom at all
Call model.eval() to restore the tie; forgetting shows up as dropout staying on
Re-run the initializer; forgetting shows up as a NaN loss on the very first step
Redo the tie afterward; forgetting shows up as about 38.6M extra parameters
questions.explanation: Assigning a fresh tensor to lm_head.weight breaks the alias, so you end up training two separate (V, C) tables. The tell is that the parameter count grows by one table's worth (about 38.6M for GPT-2 small). The fix is to re-execute the tie line.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass, end to end
questions.question: In the GPT-2 forward pass, what does the assertion at the top check?
options: That the batch size B does not exceed block_size
That every token id is smaller than the embedding width C
That the sequence length T does not exceed block_size
That targets were provided whenever the model is in training mode
questions.explanation: assert T <= self.cfg.block_size guards the position embedding: wpe has only block_size rows, so a longer sequence would index past the table. The vocabulary bound is V, not C, and targets are optional.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass, end to end
questions.question: In the GPT-2 forward pass, what does the method return when targets is None?
options: Only the sampled next token
The logits and a loss of None
The logits and a loss of zero
The pre-head hidden states and None
questions.explanation: forward always computes logits of shape (B, T, V); the loss is only computed when targets is given, otherwise it stays None. Sampling is a separate generate method, and the return value is the projected logits, not pre-head hidden states.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass, end to end
questions.question: In the from-scratch GPT-2 class, which Module 5 components are imported rather than re-implemented?
options: Embedding and Linear
Block and LayerNorm
Dropout and cross_entropy
GPTConfig and ModuleDict
questions.explanation: The GPT class imports the pre-norm Block and the LayerNorm built in Module 5 from llmre.model.block. Embedding, Linear, Dropout, ModuleDict and cross_entropy come from PyTorch itself, and GPTConfig is the config dataclass.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass, end to end
questions.question: In GPT-2's forward pass, which modules are applied, in order, from token ids to logits?
options: wte and wpe lookups, add, dropout, each block in h, ln_f, lm_head
wte lookup, each block in h, wpe lookup, ln_f, dropout, lm_head
wte and wpe lookups, add, ln_f, each block in h, dropout, lm_head
dropout, wte lookup, each block in h, lm_head, ln_f
questions.explanation: Embeddings are looked up and summed, dropout is applied to the sum, the blocks run in sequence, the final LayerNorm normalizes the stream, and lm_head projects to the vocabulary. Applying ln_f before the blocks or after the head would put the normalization in the wrong place.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass, end to end
questions.question: In the GPT-2 forward pass, why is the input token sequence's shape preserved throughout the block loop 'for block in self.transformer.h: x = block(x)'?
options: Each block reduces T by one, and padding restores the original length
Each block widens C, and ln_f later projects it back to the original width
Each block outputs (B, V), and the loop re-embeds the result before the next block
Each block maps (B, T, C) to (B, T, C), so blocks can be stacked any number of times
questions.explanation: A block reads and writes the residual stream at the same shape. That invariance is exactly why blocks are stackable: the output of one is valid input to the next. Only the two ends change the last axis.

questions.question: Why does the GPT-2 class group its sub-modules under self.transformer as an nn.ModuleDict?
options: It makes the forward pass faster by fusing all of the registered sub-modules into one kernel
It is required by PyTorch for any module that contains more than one layer of parameters
It names every weight like transformer.h.3.attn.c_proj.weight, matching OpenAI's checkpoints
It hides the sub-modules from model.parameters() so the embeddings are not trained
questions.explanation: Module attribute names become state_dict keys. With this exact layout the keys match the official GPT-2 checkpoints, so the pretrained weights can be loaded directly. ModuleDict does not fuse kernels, is not mandatory, and its contents are registered as trainable parameters.

questions.question: In the from-scratch GPT-2, why are the transformer blocks stored in an nn.ModuleList called h?
options: A plain Python list would work identically, so using ModuleList here is purely cosmetic
ModuleList automatically shares one set of weights among all the blocks it contains
It registers each block and names them h.0, h.1, ... to match the checkpoint layout
ModuleList runs the blocks in parallel on separate streams instead of sequentially
questions.explanation: nn.ModuleList registers each Block so its parameters are tracked, saved and moved with the model, and names them by index (transformer.h.3...), matching OpenAI's naming. A plain list would hide the blocks from parameters() and state_dict. It neither shares weights nor parallelizes.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass — The loss: flatten, then cross-entropy
questions.question: In GPT-2's loss computation, what does targets[b, t] contain?
options: The token at position t in sequence b itself
The token that should follow position t in sequence b
The probability that position t in sequence b ends a sentence
The position index t, used to look up wpe
questions.explanation: Targets are the next-token labels built by shifting the input left by one, so targets[b, t] is the token that comes after position t. Using the current token would be copying, not prediction.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass — The loss: flatten, then cross-entropy
questions.question: Why does GPT-2 flatten logits with logits.view(-1, logits.size(-1)) before F.cross_entropy?
options: Cross-entropy expects (N, V) logits and (N,) targets, so B*T rows become independent classifications
Cross-entropy only accepts a single sequence at a time, so each batch element is otherwise processed alone
Flattening sums the logits over the time axis so that the loss is computed once per sequence
Flattening removes the vocabulary axis so that the loss is computed as one scalar per position
questions.explanation: F.cross_entropy takes a 2-D (N, classes) input and a 1-D (N,) target. Reshaping (B, T, V) to (B*T, V) and targets to (B*T,) turns every position of every sequence into one V-way classification. Nothing is summed over time and the vocabulary axis is kept.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass — The loss: flatten, then cross-entropy
questions.question: What loss does GPT-2 compute from its flattened logits and targets?
options: The sum over positions of the squared difference between the logits and the one-hot targets
The maximum over positions of -log softmax(logits[b,t])[targets[b,t]], the worst position
The mean over positions of the softmax probability assigned to each target token
The mean over positions of -log softmax(logits[b,t])[targets[b,t]]
questions.explanation: L = (1/BT) sum over b,t of -log softmax(logits_{b,t})[target_{b,t}]. It is the average negative log-likelihood of the true next tokens, the same objective as in 01.4. Averaging probabilities or taking a max would not be the cross-entropy objective.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass — The loss: flatten, then cross-entropy
questions.question: What does passing ignore_index=-1 to F.cross_entropy do in GPT-2's loss?
options: Positions whose target is -1 are treated as predicting the last vocabulary token, V - 1
The final position of every sequence is ignored, since it has no next token to predict
Tokens with id -1 in the inputs are skipped during the embedding lookup and the loss
Positions whose target is -1 (e.g. padding) add no loss and send no gradient
questions.explanation: ignore_index marks target values to exclude. Setting padded targets to -1 removes them from the average and from the backward pass. It acts on target values, not on positions by index or on input ids.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass — Numerical example: B = 2, T = 2, V = 3
questions.question: With ignore_index in cross-entropy, what does the 1/(BT) normalization actually divide by?
options: Always the full B*T, so ignored positions count as zero loss in the average
The batch size B only, giving a per-sequence summed loss
The number of non-ignored positions, not the total B*T
The vocabulary size V, giving a per-class average
questions.explanation: Ignored rows are excluded from both the numerator and the count. With 4 rows and one ignored, the mean is over 3 rows. Dividing by the full B*T would dilute the loss with zeros for padding.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass — Numerical example: B = 2, T = 2, V = 3
questions.question: For a single row of logits z with correct token y, what is the cross-entropy loss written in log-sum-exp form?
options: z_y - log(sum_j exp(z_j))
log(sum_j exp(z_j)) - z_y
log(sum_j exp(z_j - z_y))^2
exp(z_y) / sum_j exp(z_j)
questions.explanation: -log softmax(z)[y] = -(z_y - log sum_j e^{z_j}) = log sum_j e^{z_j} - z_y. The reversed sign would give the log-probability (non-positive), and exp(z_y)/sum is the probability itself, not the loss.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass — Numerical example: B = 2, T = 2, V = 3
questions.question: If a row of logits has all entries equal over a V-token vocabulary, what is its cross-entropy loss?
options: log V, because the prediction is uniform with probability 1/V each
0, because equal logits mean the model is perfectly calibrated over V
1/V, because each token receives the same probability of exactly 1/V
V, because each of the V tokens contributes a loss of exactly 1 each
questions.explanation: Equal logits give softmax probability 1/V for every token, so -log(1/V) = log V. For V = 3 that is about 1.0986. This 'uniform guess' value is what an untrained model scores.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass — Numerical example: B = 2, T = 2, V = 3
questions.question: What loss should you expect at step 0 from an untrained GPT-2 with V = 50257?
options: About ln(50257), roughly 10.82
About 0, since the weights are near zero
About 1.0986, the same as any vocabulary
About 50257, one unit per token
questions.explanation: An untrained model predicts roughly uniformly, so the loss is about log V. For GPT-2's vocabulary that is ln 50257, about 10.82. ln 3 = 1.0986 is only the value for a 3-token vocabulary.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass — Numerical example: B = 2, T = 2, V = 3
questions.question: In GPT-2's loss with ignore_index, what happens to a padding position whose logits strongly favor some token?
options: Its loss is computed normally but scaled down by half before averaging
It is penalized for confidently predicting a token where padding should be
Its logits are reused as the target distribution for the previous position
Nothing: it adds no loss and sends no gradient, whatever its logits are
questions.explanation: An ignored position is excluded entirely: no loss term, no contribution to the averaging denominator, and zero gradient into its logits. What it happens to predict is irrelevant.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass — Numerical example: B = 2, T = 2, V = 3
questions.question: In GPT-2's loss, after flattening logits of shape (B, T, V), how should each row be thought of?
options: As one step of a recurrence whose loss depends on the previous row's prediction
As a regression target that is compared against the next token's embedding vector
As an independent V-way classification: which token comes next at this position
As a binary decision about whether the sequence continues past this position or ends
questions.explanation: Every (b, t) position becomes its own row with one correct class out of V. The rows are scored independently and averaged, which is why all positions can be trained in parallel.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass — Numerical example: B = 2, T = 2, V = 3
questions.question: Why does logits.view(-1, logits.size(-1)) not copy data when collapsing (B, T, V) to (B*T, V)?
options: view moves the tensor to a new buffer but PyTorch frees the old one immediately
view only reinterprets the strides of the existing contiguous memory
view stores only the last time step, discarding the rest
view converts the tensor to half precision so it fits in place
questions.explanation: For a contiguous tensor, merging the leading axes is just a different indexing of the same memory, so view returns a new tensor header with different shape and strides. No data is moved, dropped, or recast.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass — Numerical example: B = 2, T = 2, V = 3
questions.question: How does F.cross_entropy compute log-softmax in a numerically stable way?
options: It clips the logits to the range [-1, 1] before exponentiating them, so exp stays small
It subtracts the row maximum before exponentiating, so exp never overflows
It computes the softmax in float64 and then takes the logarithm of the probabilities
It adds a small epsilon inside the logarithm of the softmax output to avoid log(0)
questions.explanation: log_softmax uses the max-subtraction (log-sum-exp) trick: z - max(z) has a maximum of 0, so exp never overflows, and the log is computed directly. It then gathers the target entry of each row, the negative-log-likelihood step. Clipping or epsilons would change the result.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass — Numerical example: B = 2, T = 2, V = 3
questions.question: After computing log-softmax, what step does F.cross_entropy perform to get the per-row loss?
options: It gathers the log-probability at each row's target index and negates it
It sums the log-probabilities over all V classes in each row and negates the sum
It takes the argmax of each row and compares it to the target for a 0/1 loss
It multiplies the log-probabilities by the logits and averages them over each row
questions.explanation: Cross-entropy = log_softmax followed by negative log-likelihood: pick out the entry for the correct class in each row and negate it. Summing over all classes or using argmax would not be the cross-entropy loss.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass — Full shape trace
questions.question: In GPT-2 small, which dimensions does the shape trace use for the embedding width C and vocabulary V?
questions.explanation: GPT-2 small has n_embd = 768 and a 50257-token BPE vocabulary. 1024 is its block_size (context length), not its width.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass — Full shape trace
questions.question: In a GPT-2 shape trace, which steps change the last axis of the tensor?
options: Every block widens the last axis by C, and ln_f then shrinks it back to C
Only the attention layers, which map the last axis from C to T for scores
Only the two ends: wte maps an id to C, and lm_head maps C to V
Only ln_f, which maps the last axis from C to V just before the LM head
questions.explanation: Inside the stack every tensor stays (B, T, C). The embedding turns ids into C-vectors and the head turns C-vectors into V scores; LayerNorm preserves shape.

questions.section: 5. The forward pass — Full shape trace
questions.question: For idx of shape (4, 128) and V = 50257, what shape do GPT-2's logits have, and what shape just before F.cross_entropy?
options: (4, 50257), flattened to (4, 50257) with targets (4,)
(4, 128, 768), flattened to (512, 768) with targets (512,)
(4, 128, 50257), flattened to (512, 50257) with targets (512,)
(4, 128, 50257), flattened to (4, 6433024) with targets (4, 128)
questions.explanation: Logits are (B, T, V) = (4, 128, 50257). Flattening batch and time gives 4 x 128 = 512 rows of 50257 scores, and the targets flatten to 512 labels. 768 would be the hidden width before the head.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood — The logits tensor is huge
questions.question: In GPT-2 small, by roughly what factor is the logits tensor larger than one activation inside the block stack?
options: About 2x, since the head doubles the width
About 65x, since V / C = 50257 / 768
About 12x, one per transformer layer
About 1000x, since V is close to T squared
questions.explanation: Activations are (B, T, C) while logits are (B, T, V). The ratio is V/C = 50257/768, about 65. So a single tensor at the end of the model dwarfs any one activation inside it.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood — The logits tensor is huge
questions.question: For B = 2, T = 1024 in fp32 with GPT-2 small dimensions, roughly how large is the logits tensor in memory?
options: About 412 MB
About 6.3 MB
About 41 MB
About 4.1 GB
questions.explanation: 2 x 1024 x 50257 is about 103M floats; at 4 bytes each that is about 412 MB. 6.3 MB is the size of a (2, 1024, 768) activation inside the stack.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood — The logits tensor is huge
questions.question: During GPT-2 training, why is the vocabulary-sized logits memory paid more than once?
options: Because each transformer block keeps its own copy of the logits to use during its backward
Because the optimizer stores two Adam momentum buffers for the logits tensor at every step
Because the logits are recomputed once per vocabulary token during the backward pass
Forward keeps logits and log-softmax for backward, which adds a same-sized logit gradient
questions.explanation: The forward pass holds the logits and the log-softmax that cross-entropy saves for backward, and the backward pass produces dLoss/dlogits, again (B, T, V). Logits are activations, not parameters, so the optimizer has no state for them.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood — The logits tensor is huge
questions.question: How does long-context training reduce the memory cost of GPT's final projection and cross-entropy?
options: By shrinking the vocabulary to a few hundred tokens for the long-context training phase only
By skipping the final LayerNorm so that the head can run in place on the residual stream
By computing the loss only on the first position of each sequence instead of all T positions
By fusing them and computing the loss in chunks of positions, never forming all of (B, T, V)
questions.explanation: The (B, T, V) logits scale with both B and T, so long sequences make them huge. Fusing the head with the loss and processing positions in chunks keeps only a slice in memory at a time. Dropping positions or the vocabulary would change the objective.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood — The logits tensor is huge
questions.question: In GPT-2 training, what happens to the logits-related memory if you double the sequence length T?
options: It stays the same, because the logits tensor depends only on the sizes V and C
It quadruples, because the logits tensor scales with T squared like attention scores
It doubles, because the logits, log-softmax and logit gradient are all linear in T
It halves, because longer sequences are processed in fewer batches per optimizer step
questions.explanation: Each of these tensors is (B, T, V), so its size is linear in T. Attention scores are what scale with T squared; the logits do not.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood — arange is on-device
questions.question: In GPT-2's forward pass, why must the positions be built with torch.arange(T, device=idx.device)?
options: So the positions are float32 rather than int64, which nn.Embedding lookups require
So the positions are created on the model's device instead of the CPU default
So the positions are sorted in descending order, as the causal mask expects them
So the positions are cached on the module between calls and never recomputed
questions.explanation: torch.arange defaults to the CPU. If the model and idx are on a GPU, indexing wpe with a CPU tensor fails. Passing device=idx.device creates the indices where the data already lives. The dtype is long, and positions are ascending.

questions.question: You tie GPT-2's weights, load a checkpoint, then run model.lm_head = nn.Linear(cfg.n_embd, cfg.vocab_size, bias=False). What goes wrong?
options: The new Linear has its own fresh weight: the tie breaks, the head is random, and ~40M parameters are added
Nothing goes wrong; PyTorch re-establishes the tie automatically whenever lm_head is replaced on the model
The loaded embedding weights in wte are overwritten in place with the new head's random initial weights
The model raises an error at construction, because a tied lm_head must be created with a bias term
questions.explanation: Creating a new nn.Linear allocates a separate weight, so wte and lm_head no longer share a tensor. The head starts from random init instead of the loaded weights, the two tables drift apart, and the parameter count rises by one table (about 38.6M). The fix is to re-run self.transformer.wte.weight = self.lm_head.weight afterwards.

questions.question: With weight tying, how many parameters do GPT-2's token embedding (V, C) and LM head (V, C) contribute together?
options: V * C, counted once, because they are the same tensor
2 * V * C, because each of the two keeps its own copy
V * C + V, because the head adds a bias
V + C, because tying stores only one row and one column
questions.explanation: Tied weights are one Parameter, so their V * C entries count once: about 38.6M for GPT-2 small, not 77M. lm_head has no bias, so there is no extra V term.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Why is 'the loss at step 0 is near ln(V)' the first sanity check of an LLM training run?
options: If step 0 is far from ln(V), the model or data pipeline is broken before any training
Because ln(V) is the target loss the model must reach before training is allowed to stop
Because the optimizer needs the step-0 loss to set its initial learning rate and warmup length
Because ln(V) measures how many tokens the model has already memorized at initialization
questions.explanation: An untrained model predicts nearly uniformly, giving loss about ln V. A very different value at step 0 signals exploding logits or a data leak immediately, which is the cheapest smoke test available. It is a starting point, not a training target.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Why is knowing a model's parameter count 'cold' useful to an ML engineer?
options: It determines the vocabulary size the tokenizer must be trained to use
It fixes the peak learning rate the optimizer must use for the run
It determines the number of attention heads each block is required to have
It lets you predict memory, FLOPs and cost without running anything
questions.explanation: Parameter count drives weight, gradient and optimizer-state memory and the FLOPs per token, so you can estimate hardware and cost on paper. It does not by itself fix the vocabulary, learning rate, or head count.

questions.section: 1. Initialization: why the starting weights matter
questions.question: What is the goal of a weight initialization scheme for a deep network like GPT-2?
options: That the untrained network already outputs the most frequent token at every position
That every weight starts at exactly zero, so training begins from a perfectly neutral point
That a fresh network passes a roughly unit-scale signal through every layer, at any depth
That all activations equal exactly 1 at every layer, so LayerNorm has nothing left to do
questions.explanation: Too-large weights make activations and gradients explode through depth; too-small makes the signal vanish. A good init keeps the scale roughly constant. All-zero weights would make units identical and break learning.

questions.section: 1. Initialization: why the starting weights matter
questions.question: How does GPT-2 initialize every nn.Linear and nn.Embedding weight and every bias?
options: Weights uniform in [-1, 1]; biases all set to 1 so units start active
Weights from a normal distribution with mean 0 and std 0.02; biases to 0
Weights from a normal with std 1/sqrt(C); biases from the same normal
Weights set to the identity matrix; biases set to the constant 0.02
questions.explanation: GPT-2's scheme is N(0, 0.02^2) for every linear and embedding weight and zeros for every bias. 1/sqrt(C) is the more 'principled' alternative it does not use.

questions.section: 1. Initialization: why the starting weights matter
questions.question: What does self.apply(self._init_weights) do in a PyTorch nn.Module?
options: Calls _init_weights only on the top-level module, not on any of its children
Recursively visits every sub-module and calls _init_weights on each
Applies _init_weights to the gradients after every backward pass during training
Registers _init_weights as a forward hook that runs on each call
questions.explanation: Module.apply walks the module tree and runs the function on every sub-module (and the module itself), so one rule reaches all 100+ weight tensors. It runs once when called; it is not a hook or a gradient transform.

questions.section: 1. Initialization: why the starting weights matter
questions.question: In GPT-2's _init_weights, how are nn.Linear and nn.Embedding modules treated differently?
options: Both get N(0, 0.02^2) weights; only Linear may have a bias, which is zeroed
Linear weights are zeroed, while Embedding weights get N(0, 0.02^2) and no bias
Embedding weights are zeroed, while Linear weights get N(0, 0.02^2) and zero bias
Both get N(0, 1) weights, and both have their biases initialized to the constant 0.02
questions.explanation: Both kinds of weight use std 0.02. The only difference is that a Linear may have a bias, which is set to zero when it exists; an Embedding has no bias.

questions.section: 1. Initialization: why the starting weights matter
questions.question: Why does GPT-2 use std 0.02 for its weights rather than the more principled 1/sqrt(C) (about 0.036 for C = 768)?
options: 0.02 is exactly 1/sqrt(C) for C = 768, so the two choices give the very same initialization
1/sqrt(C) would cause a division by zero for the embeddings, whose width is not defined
0.02 is derived from the vocabulary size as 1/ln(V), which is the principled choice for LMs
0.02 is what GPT-2 shipped: small enough to keep early activations calm, and it trained well
questions.explanation: 1/sqrt(768) is about 0.036, not 0.02. GPT-2's 0.02 is an empirical choice that keeps early activations small and trains well; the course reproduces it rather than re-deriving it.

questions.question: In GPT-2's residual stream, each block does x = x + sublayer(ln(x)). If each of L additions adds independent variance v, what is Var(x_L) roughly?
