A tuple (logits, loss): the per-position vocabulary scores and the scalar loss
The logits, the loss, and a copy of the parameters after one update
questions.explanation: The assembled GPT's forward takes token ids and optional targets and returns (logits, loss). The training loop ignores the logits and keeps the scalar loss to call backward() on. Gradients are not produced by forward; they come later from loss.backward(), and parameters only change in optimizer.step().

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Which sequence lists the core operations of one canonical GPT training step in the order the course's loop runs them?
options: get_batch, backward, model(x, y), zero_grad, clip, step, set lr
zero_grad, get_batch, step, model(x, y), backward, clip, set lr
set lr, get_batch, model(x, y), zero_grad, backward, clip, step
get_batch, model(x, y), step, backward, clip, zero_grad, set lr
questions.explanation: The loop computes the learning rate for the step, draws a batch, runs the forward pass to get the loss, clears old gradients, backpropagates, clips the gradient norm, then lets the optimizer update the parameters. Backward must follow the forward that built the graph, and clipping must sit between backward and step. Any order that steps before backward or clips after step trains wrongly.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: When a small GPT is trained to overfit a short repeated token sequence as a sanity check, what loss curve indicates the training code works?
options: Loss starts near ln(vocab_size) and falls toward zero
Loss starts near zero and rises toward ln(vocab_size)
Loss starts near 1/vocab_size and stays flat throughout
Loss starts near vocab_size and halves at every step
questions.explanation: An untrained model predicts roughly uniformly, so its first loss is about ln(V). A working training setup can memorize a tiny repeated pattern, so the loss should drop toward zero. A curve that does not fall from ln(V) toward zero on such a trivial dataset signals a bug.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: How do data work, scale, parallelism, fine-tuning and RLHF relate to the canonical next-token training loop?
options: They are variations on, or wrappers around, that same short loop
Each one replaces the loop with an entirely different algorithm
They avoid backpropagation and update weights by other means
They only apply to inference and never touch the training loop
questions.explanation: The canonical loop is pretraining, and nearly everything else in the field is built on or around it: more data, bigger models, more workers, different data (fine-tuning) or different losses (RLHF). None of these throw away the get-batch, forward, backward, step structure. That is why owning this loop demystifies training a language model.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the same six steps, forever
questions.question: In a neural-network training step, what is the 'loss'?
options: A per-parameter tensor giving how far each weight should move this step
The learning rate the schedule assigns to this step, read before backward
A single number measuring how wrong the predictions were versus the targets
The fraction of target tokens the model predicted exactly right in the batch
questions.explanation: The forward pass runs the model on the inputs and compares its predictions with the answers, collapsing the result into one scalar: the loss. Per-parameter change information is the gradient, which backward() computes from that scalar. Accuracy is a different metric; training minimizes the loss.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the same six steps, forever
questions.question: What does loss.backward() put into each parameter's .grad?
options: The parameter's new value, computed ahead of the optimizer's update
The parameter's value from the previous step, saved for momentum
How the loss would change if that parameter were nudged slightly
A random perturbation the optimizer uses to explore the loss surface
questions.explanation: backward() runs backpropagation through the graph built by the forward pass and fills every parameter's .grad with the derivative of the loss with respect to that parameter. It does not change the parameters; the optimizer does that in step(). The gradient says which direction is downhill for each weight.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the same six steps, forever
questions.question: Why does the training loop clip gradients before the optimizer step?
options: So that the gradients are cleared to zero before the next backward pass runs
So that a single freak batch with a huge gradient cannot blow up the weights
So that the learning rate follows the warmup schedule during the first steps
So that the loss is normalized by batch size and sequence length before step
questions.explanation: Clipping rescales the gradient if its norm is too large, acting as a guard-rail against occasional outlier batches. Clearing gradients is zero_grad's job, and the learning rate comes from the schedule. Without clipping, one bad batch can produce an update large enough to wreck the model.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the same six steps, forever
questions.question: In the 'step' part of the training loop, what happens?
options: The model generates text from the current weights so the loss can be measured on fresh samples
The gradients are averaged over the last few steps and stored so the next backward can reuse them
The optimizer moves each parameter slightly downhill, and the schedule sets the next learning rate
The batch is shifted left by one token to build the next batch's targets, and the data pointer advances
questions.explanation: The optimizer (AdamW here) reads the gradients and updates each parameter in the direction that reduces the loss, by an amount controlled by the learning rate from the schedule. The loop then repeats thousands to millions of times. Gradients are not stored across steps; they are cleared each step.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the same six steps, forever
questions.question: For language-model pretraining, what is the target y for an input sequence x?
options: A human-written label describing the topic or genre of the whole sequence
The same sequence in reverse order, so the model learns bidirectional context
The same sequence shifted by one position, so each target is the next token
A copy of x in which a random 15% of the tokens are replaced by a mask token
questions.explanation: In next-token prediction the answer at every position is simply the following token, so y is x shifted by one. No human labels are needed. Masked-token objectives belong to other model families, not the GPT loop.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the same six steps, forever
questions.question: Why is the data for language-model pretraining described as 'free', and why does that matter?
options: Public text datasets are licensed at no cost, so data budgets never constrain how large a run can be
Text is its own supervision, since targets are just the next tokens; that is what lets LMs scale
The model generates its own training text as it learns, so no external corpus is needed after step 0
Only a few hand-labelled examples are needed because the model generalizes from them to the rest
questions.explanation: Since the target is the next token of the same text, every piece of raw text supplies its own labels. That removes the human-labelling bottleneck and lets training use enormous corpora, which is the root of why language models scale. It does not mean the model invents its own data.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the same six steps, forever
questions.question: In the canonical loop as the code runs it, when is the step's learning rate computed and written into the optimizer?
options: After optimizer.step(), so the new value takes effect on the following step
Only once before training starts, then held constant for the entire run
Inside loss.backward(), alongside the gradient computation for each layer
At the start of the step, before the forward pass and the optimizer step
questions.explanation: The loop begins each iteration with lr = schedule(step) and writes it into the optimizer, so the update at step k uses the learning rate for step k. Setting it after step() causes an off-by-one where every step uses the previous step's rate. The rate changes every step under the cosine-warmup schedule.

questions.question: In the pretraining loss L(theta) = (1/(B T)) * sum over b and t of -log p(y_{b,t} | x_{b,1..t}), what does the 1/(B T) factor do?
options: It makes the loss the mean cross-entropy over all B times T token positions
It converts natural logs to base-2 logs so the loss is reported in bits per token
It scales the loss by the learning rate before backpropagation begins
It normalizes the softmax so each position's probabilities sum to one
questions.explanation: There are B sequences of T positions, each contributing one negative log-probability of the true next token. Dividing the sum by B*T gives the average per-token cross-entropy. The softmax handles normalization of probabilities; the learning rate is applied by the optimizer, not the loss.

questions.question: In the next-token loss, the model's prediction for target y_{b,t} = x_{b,t+1} is conditioned on which tokens?
options: The tokens x_{b,1} through x_{b,t}, the prefix up to and including position t
All tokens of sequence b, including those after position t, read in both directions
Only the single token x_{b,t} at the current position, with no earlier context
The tokens at position t from every sequence in the batch, pooled across b
questions.explanation: A causal language model predicts token t+1 from the prefix x_1..x_t only. Seeing future tokens would leak the answer. Sequences in a batch are independent; one sequence never conditions on another.

questions.question: In the pretraining loss, what is p_theta(.)?
options: The fraction of the training corpus in which each vocabulary token appears at least once
The per-parameter learning rate that AdamW assigns from its second-moment estimate
A fixed uniform distribution over the vocabulary, used as the baseline at initialization
The softmax over the model's logits, giving a probability for each vocabulary token
questions.explanation: The model outputs logits, one score per vocabulary token per position, and a softmax turns them into a probability distribution. The loss takes minus the log of the probability assigned to the true next token. Token frequencies and learning rates are unrelated to this definition.

questions.question: In the update theta <- theta - eta_step * AdamW(grad L), where does eta_step come from in the course's loop?
options: From the pre-clip gradient norm that clip_grad_norm_ returns on that step
From the cosine-warmup schedule, computed as cosine_warmup_lr(step, ...)
From AdamW's second-moment buffer v, kept separately for each parameter
From the step-0 loss divided by ln(vocab_size), fixed for the whole run
questions.explanation: Each symbol maps to code you built: the loss is model.forward, the gradient is loss.backward, the update rule is AdamW.step, and eta_step is cosine_warmup_lr(step, ...). The schedule warms up then decays the learning rate as a function of the step number. The gradient norm is only used for clipping.

questions.section: The one number to anchor on: the untrained loss
questions.question: Why should a freshly initialized language model report a loss of about ln(V) at step 0, where V is the vocabulary size?
options: Random weights give a roughly uniform prediction, assigning about 1/V to the correct token
Random weights always predict the most frequent token with probability one at every position
The loss function adds ln(V) as a regularization penalty that is removed after warmup ends
The optimizer has not stepped yet, so the loss is undefined and is reported as ln(V) by default
questions.explanation: With random weights the output distribution over the V tokens is close to uniform, so the true token gets probability about 1/V. The cross-entropy is then -log(1/V) = log V. It is a consequence of near-uniform predictions, not an added penalty.

questions.section: The one number to anchor on: the untrained loss
questions.question: Your step-0 loss is wildly different from ln(vocab_size). What should you conclude and do?
options: The learning rate is too low; raise it and the loss will move toward ln(V) within a few steps
Something is broken, e.g. bad init, wrong vocab size or a label bug; stop and fix it first
Nothing; the step-0 loss is essentially random and carries no diagnostic information at all
The model is already partly trained from the init; reduce the number of planned training steps
questions.explanation: A random-init model should sit near ln(V). A large departure points to a bug like a broken initialization, a mismatched vocabulary size or misaligned labels. The learning rate cannot affect the step-0 loss because no update has happened yet.

questions.section: The one number to anchor on: the untrained loss
questions.question: For GPT-2, with a vocabulary of V = 50257 tokens, roughly what step-0 loss should an untrained model report?
options: About 50257, the vocabulary size itself
About 3.0, the loss of a well-trained run
About 10.82, which is ln(50257)
About 0.00002, which is 1/50257
questions.explanation: The step-0 loss is ln(V); ln(50257) is about 10.82. A good GPT-2-small run trains down to about 3.0. 1/V is the per-token probability, not the loss, which is its negative log.

questions.section: The one number to anchor on: the untrained loss
questions.question: Why is checking the step-0 loss against ln(V) recommended on every training run?
options: It is required to calibrate the peak value of the learning-rate schedule before warmup starts
It determines how many warmup steps the schedule needs, since higher ln(V) needs longer warmup
It is the cheapest reliable bug-catcher: one line, run before any GPU-hours are wasted
It is the only way to measure the model's final accuracy without running a separate eval set
questions.explanation: The expected value is known in advance, so comparing the first loss to ln(V) catches init, vocabulary and label bugs immediately and for free. It does not set any hyperparameters. Skipping it can mean discovering the bug only after an expensive run.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example: the loop by hand for one step
questions.question: A fresh model with V = 16 reports a step-0 loss of 2.8103, slightly above ln(16) = 2.7726. Why the small excess?
options: The optimizer has already taken one step before the loss is reported
Gradient clipping added a small penalty to the loss
The random initialization's predictions are not perfectly uniform
The vocabulary size was off by one token
questions.explanation: ln(V) assumes an exactly uniform prediction; a real random init is only approximately uniform, so the loss lands slightly above ln(V). The loss is computed before any update. A small excess like this is healthy; a wild difference would indicate a bug.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example: the loop by hand for one step
questions.question: A small GPT trained on a short 16-token pattern repeated many times drives its loss to nearly zero. What does this show?
options: The model has learned general language from the pattern and is ready to be deployed on new text
The loss function is broken, because a correctly computed cross-entropy can never approach zero
The model has memorized the pattern, which is exactly what this overfit sanity check should show
The learning rate is far too high and training has diverged, which collapses the loss toward zero
questions.explanation: On a trivially repetitive dataset the next token is fully predictable, so a working setup memorizes it and the loss approaches zero. That is the intended outcome of overfitting a tiny dataset. It says nothing about general language ability, and divergence would show the loss rising, not falling.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example: the loop by hand for one step
questions.question: What is the second-cheapest training bug-catcher after the step-0 loss check?
options: Running the full-scale job for one day and inspecting the final loss against the published value
Checking the model can overfit a few examples; if it cannot, the training code is broken
Comparing the model's parameter count with the published model card before launching the run
Checking that validation loss is already lower than training loss at step 0, before any updates
questions.explanation: A correct training setup can always memorize a tiny dataset. If the loss will not go near zero on a handful of examples, something in the model or loop is wrong, and there is no point launching a big run. Running the full job first wastes compute on a known-broken pipeline.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example: the loop by hand for one step
questions.question: While overfitting a tiny repeated sequence, the loss briefly bumps up at a few steps after reaching near zero. What explains the bumps, and what settles them?
options: The data loader occasionally repeats a batch; switching to a fresh random seed settles it
The optimizer briefly overshoots near zero loss; the cosine decay of the learning rate settles it
The gradients overflow in float32 near zero loss; switching the model to float64 settles it
The model forgets the pattern between steps as capacity runs out; adding more layers settles it
questions.explanation: Near a minimum, a step size that was fine earlier can overshoot, producing small loss bumps. As the cosine schedule lowers the learning rate, steps shrink and the bumps fade. These bumps are normal optimizer dynamics, not overflow or capacity problems.

questions.section: 4. Tensor shapes: what flows through one step
questions.question: In one training step with batch size B and context length T, what are the shape and dtype of the input x returned by get_batch?
options: (B, T), int64 token ids
(B, T, V), float32 scores
(B, T, C), float32 embeddings
(T, B), float16 token ids
questions.explanation: The data loader returns integer token ids arranged as B sequences of T tokens, shape (B, T), dtype int64. Embedding to width C happens inside the model, and (B, T, V) is the shape of the logits the model outputs.

questions.section: 4. Tensor shapes: what flows through one step
questions.question: What is the shape and dtype of the logits that model(x, y) returns for a (B, T) batch with vocabulary V?
options: (B, V), float32: one score per vocabulary token per sequence
(B, T), int64: the predicted token id at each position
(V,), float32: one score per vocabulary token for the whole batch
(B, T, V), float32: one score per vocabulary token per position
questions.explanation: The model produces a full distribution's worth of scores at every position of every sequence, giving (B, T, V) floats. The argmax of those scores would be (B, T) ids, but the model returns the raw scores. Every position gets its own prediction, so the sequence and position dimensions are kept.

questions.section: 4. Tensor shapes: what flows through one step
questions.question: What is the shape of the loss tensor returned by the training forward pass?
options: Shape (B,), one mean loss per sequence in the batch
A scalar with shape (), the mean cross-entropy
Shape (B, T), one loss per token position
Shape (V,), one loss per vocabulary token
questions.explanation: The forward pass averages the per-token cross-entropies into a single scalar of shape (). backward() is called on that scalar. Per-sequence or per-token losses exist internally but are reduced by the mean.

questions.section: 4. Tensor shapes: what flows through one step
questions.question: After loss.backward(), how does each parameter's .grad tensor relate to the parameter itself?
options: It is always a scalar holding the parameter's total gradient
It has identical shape, dtype and device to the parameter
It has the same shape but is always stored on the CPU
It has the shape of the logits, (B, T, V), for every parameter
questions.explanation: Backprop writes a gradient tensor into every leaf parameter, matching it element for element: same shape, same dtype, same device. That lets the optimizer read .grad and update the parameter in place. Gradients stay on the parameter's device.

questions.section: 4. Tensor shapes: what flows through one step
questions.question: What changes in the model between one training step and the next?
options: The number of layers grows as the loss decreases
The vocabulary size shrinks to the tokens seen so far
The parameter shapes are resized to match the next batch
Only the values of the parameters; no tensor shapes change
questions.explanation: The optimizer writes updated values into the existing parameters in place. Architecture, vocabulary and all parameter shapes are fixed throughout the run. Batches of the same (B, T) flow through the same fixed shapes every step.

questions.section: 4. Tensor shapes: what flows through one step
questions.question: In the training batch, how is the target tensor y related to the input tensor x?
options: y is x with a random 15% of its tokens replaced by a special mask token
y is x reversed along the time dimension, so y[:, t] is x[:, T-1-t]
y is x shifted left by one position, so y[:, t] is the token after x[:, t]
y is identical to x, and the model learns to copy x[:, t] to position t
questions.explanation: For next-token prediction, y at position t is the token at position t+1 in the original stream, i.e. x shifted left by one. In get_batch this is y = stream[i+1 : i+1+T] versus x = stream[i : i+T]. Copying x itself would be trivial and teach nothing about prediction.

questions.section: 5. From-scratch PyTorch: a fully runnable overfit
questions.question: In a from-scratch get_batch, random start indices are drawn with torch.randint(0, stream.numel() - T - 1, (b,)). Why subtract T + 1 rather than just T?
options: Because the last token of every stream is reserved for an end-of-text marker that is never sampled
Because torch.randint includes its upper bound, so one extra must be subtracted to stay in range
Because each batch must skip one token so that it does not overlap with the previous batch
Because the target window y extends one token past x, and it must still fit inside the stream
questions.explanation: x takes stream[i : i+T] and y takes stream[i+1 : i+1+T], so the last index y touches is i+T. The start index must leave room for that extra token. Without the extra -1, a start near the end would produce a short or out-of-range target window.

questions.section: 5. From-scratch PyTorch: a fully runnable overfit
questions.question: In the course's train() function, what happens first when cfg.seed is not None?
options: The model's weights are re-initialized from zero so every seeded run starts identically
The learning rate for the first step is set to cfg.seed and then handed to the schedule
torch.manual_seed(cfg.seed) is called so the run's random choices are reproducible
A checkpoint named after the seed is loaded from disk so the run resumes where it stopped
questions.explanation: Seeding PyTorch's RNG makes initialization-dependent choices, batch sampling and dropout reproducible across runs. The seed has nothing to do with the learning rate or checkpoints. Reproducibility is covered in depth in 07.3.

questions.section: 5. From-scratch PyTorch: a fully runnable overfit
questions.question: The course's train() builds the optimizer from [p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad]. What does that filter do?
options: It hands the optimizer only trainable parameters, skipping frozen ones
It removes parameters whose gradients were zero on the last step
It keeps only the embedding parameters, which are updated most
It drops parameters that are stored on the CPU rather than GPU
questions.explanation: requires_grad marks a tensor as trainable; frozen parameters have it set to False and receive no gradient. Passing only trainable parameters keeps the optimizer from allocating state for, or touching, tensors that should not change. It is a static property, not based on last step's gradient values.

questions.section: 5. From-scratch PyTorch: a fully runnable overfit
questions.question: In the cosine-warmup learning-rate schedule used by the training loop, what is the purpose of the warmup phase?
options: To hold the learning rate at its peak for the final steps of training
To lower the learning rate gradually so late steps fine-tune
To set the learning rate to zero until the loss reaches ln(V)
To ramp the learning rate up so the first, noisiest steps do not lurch
questions.explanation: Early in training the gradients are noisy and the optimizer state is cold, so large steps can destabilize the model. Warmup starts small and ramps up to the peak. Gently lowering the rate for late steps is the cosine decay phase, not warmup.

questions.section: 5. From-scratch PyTorch: a fully runnable overfit
questions.question: In the cosine-warmup learning-rate schedule, what is the purpose of the cosine decay phase?
options: To ease the learning rate down so late steps fine-tune
To ramp the learning rate up so the first steps do not lurch
To make the learning rate oscillate and escape local minima
To keep the learning rate constant once warmup finishes
questions.explanation: After warmup the cosine curve smoothly lowers the learning rate toward a floor (min_lr), so later updates are smaller and refine rather than disrupt what has been learned. Ramping up is the warmup phase. A cosine decay is monotonic, not an oscillating restart schedule.

questions.section: 5. From-scratch PyTorch: a fully runnable overfit
questions.question: Why must the training loop call optimizer.zero_grad() every optimizer step?
options: Because backward() raises an error if a parameter's .grad already holds a value from before
Because zero_grad() also resets AdamW's moment buffers m and v, which must restart each step
Because backward() adds into .grad; without clearing, this step's gradient adds onto last step's
Because the current learning rate is stored inside .grad and must be reset before the next step
questions.explanation: PyTorch's backward adds into existing .grad tensors rather than overwriting them. If you do not clear them, gradients from earlier steps pile up into the current update, which is wrong. zero_grad does not touch the optimizer's moment state, and backward does not error on a non-empty .grad.

questions.section: 5. From-scratch PyTorch: a fully runnable overfit
questions.question: The fact that backward() adds into .grad rather than overwriting it is exploited for which technique?
options: Gradient clipping by global norm
Gradient accumulation across micro-batches
Cosine-warmup learning-rate scheduling
Weight tying between embedding and head
questions.explanation: Because gradients accumulate, you can run several micro-batch backward passes and let their gradients sum before one optimizer step, emulating a larger batch. That is gradient accumulation (07.2). The same behavior that makes forgetting zero_grad a bug becomes a feature when done deliberately.

questions.section: 5. From-scratch PyTorch: a fully runnable overfit
questions.question: In the course loop, the line _, loss = model(x, y) discards the first return value. What is discarded and why?
options: The gradients, because the optimizer recomputes them itself inside optimizer.step()
The targets, because they were already consumed when get_batch built the batch
The logits, because the training step only needs the scalar loss for backward
The learning rate, because it is set separately from the schedule at the step start
questions.explanation: model(x, y) returns (logits, loss). Training only needs the scalar loss to backpropagate, so the logits are ignored. Gradients are not returned by forward at all; they come from loss.backward().

questions.section: 5. From-scratch PyTorch: a fully runnable overfit
questions.question: What does clip_grad_norm_(params, grad_clip) do in the course's training loop?
options: Sets every gradient element larger than grad_clip to exactly grad_clip, returning how many were clipped
Zeroes the gradients of any parameter whose own norm exceeds grad_clip, returning the remaining norm
Divides the learning rate by the gradient norm whenever that norm exceeds grad_clip for the step
Rescales the whole gradient so its global L2 norm is at most grad_clip, returning the pre-clip norm
questions.explanation: Global-norm clipping computes the L2 norm across all parameters' gradients and, if it exceeds the threshold, scales every gradient by the same factor. That preserves the direction while capping the size. It returns the norm measured before clipping, which is useful for logging. Element-wise clamping is a different method.

questions.section: 5. From-scratch PyTorch: a fully runnable overfit
questions.question: What does AdamW's optimizer.step() do in the course training loop?
options: Reads each .grad, updates the moment estimates, and nudges every parameter
Runs the forward pass again and computes a fresh loss on the same batch
Clears every .grad and resets the moment estimates to zero for the next step
Computes the gradients by backpropagating from the loss through every layer
questions.explanation: step() consumes the gradients that backward produced, updates AdamW's running first and second moment estimates, and applies the update to each parameter. Forward and backward happen before step, and clearing gradients is zero_grad's job. The moment estimates persist across steps.

questions.section: 5. From-scratch PyTorch: a fully runnable overfit
questions.question: Why are ordering bugs in the training loop (for example clipping after optimizer.step()) described as the worst kind of bug?
options: PyTorch raises an exception whose traceback is very hard to read
The model still trains, just wrongly, so the failure is silent
The program crashes immediately and loses all unsaved progress
The loss becomes NaN at step 0 and the run cannot be recovered
questions.explanation: zero_grad must come before backward (or right after step), and clip must come after backward but before step. If you get the order wrong the code still runs and the loss may still fall, so nothing alerts you. Bugs that crash are easy; silent ones corrupt results unnoticed.

questions.question: In the training loop, why must clip_grad_norm_ run after backward() but before optimizer.step()?
options: Clipping must see the updated parameters, which only exist once optimizer.step() has run
Clipping resets the gradients to zero, so it must run before the next backward refills them
Clipping changes the loss value itself, so it has to run before backward reads that loss
Gradients exist only after backward, and step consumes them, so clipping must sit between
questions.explanation: Clipping rescales .grad tensors, which backward computes. The optimizer reads .grad inside step(), so if clipping runs after step it clips nothing that matters. The sandwich is backward, clip, step. Clipping touches gradients, not parameters or the loss.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what each step actually costs
questions.question: Why does the forward pass hold onto the activations of every layer?
options: Because the optimizer reads them to update its moment buffers
Because the next batch reuses them as a cache to save compute
Because the backward pass needs them to compute gradients
Because they are written to the checkpoint at every step
questions.explanation: Backprop computes each layer's gradients from that layer's saved inputs/activations, so they must be kept until backward runs. This is why activation memory grows with batch size. The optimizer uses gradients, not activations, and batches do not share activations.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what each step actually costs
questions.question: For a GPT-2 batch of shape (B, T), which single tensor is typically the largest, and why?
options: The token-id input, shape (B, T), because it is stored as int64
The scalar loss, because it accumulates every token's error
The logits, shape (B, T, V), because V = 50257 dwarfs the hidden width
The position embedding table, because it covers the whole context
questions.explanation: The logits carry one score per vocabulary token at every position. With V = 50257, far larger than the model width, this tensor dwarfs the activations inside the transformer stack. Token ids are small integer tensors and the loss is a single number.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what each step actually costs
questions.question: What usually limits how large a training batch fits in GPU memory?
options: Parameter memory, since the weights are copied once per example in the batch
Activation memory, which grows with the batch, rather than parameter memory
The token-id tensors, which are stored as int64 and dominate memory per example
The learning-rate schedule, which keeps a separate value stored for each example
questions.explanation: Parameters are a fixed size regardless of batch, but the activations saved for backward scale with B and T, with the (B, T, V) logits a big contributor. So activations, not weights, usually cap the batch. Token ids are tiny by comparison.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what each step actually costs
questions.question: Roughly how does the arithmetic of the backward pass compare with the forward pass, and what rule does that lead to?
options: Backward is about half of forward, because it reuses cached activations, giving the 3N FLOPs per token rule
Backward equals forward exactly, because it runs the same layers in reverse, giving the 4N FLOPs per token rule
Backward is negligible next to forward, because it only multiplies by the loss, giving the 2N FLOPs per token rule
Backward is about twice forward, since it computes gradients for both activations and weights: the 6N rule
questions.explanation: Backward computes gradients with respect to both the layer inputs and the weights, roughly doubling the forward's work. With forward at about 2N FLOPs per token for N parameters, forward plus backward is about 6N. This rule is used for throughput and MFU accounting in 07.4.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what each step actually costs
questions.question: AdamW's optimizer.step() touches every parameter three times. What does that imply about memory?
options: Adam's optimizer state is one third of the model's size, shared across the passes
Adam's optimizer state, the m and v buffers, is twice the size of the model
Adam keeps three copies of the gradient, so gradient memory triples per step
Adam needs no extra memory, because it updates every parameter fully in place
questions.explanation: For each parameter AdamW reads and writes the parameter itself plus two moment buffers, m and v, each the same size as the parameter. So the optimizer state alone is 2x the model size, a fact that shapes memory planning for every large run.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what each step actually costs
questions.question: Why is calling loss.item() every step a concern on a GPU?
options: It detaches the loss from the autograd graph, so backward() no longer works
It converts the model's parameters to float64 on the host, doubling memory
It resets the accumulated gradients to zero, silently undoing the backward pass
It forces a GPU-to-CPU sync to read the scalar back to Python, stalling the GPU
questions.explanation: item() copies a scalar from the device to Python, which forces the CPU to wait for all queued GPU work to finish. Doing that every step throttles throughput. For study it is fine; real runs log it every N steps. It does not affect gradients or parameter dtypes.

questions.question: A training loop calls loss.backward() twice on the same batch without zero_grad() in between. What ends up in each .grad?
options: Twice the true gradient, 2 times grad L, because backward adds into .grad
The true gradient, because the second backward overwrites the first
Zero, because the two backward calls cancel each other out
The square of the true gradient, because the calls multiply
questions.explanation: backward() accumulates: each call adds its gradient into .grad. Two calls on the same batch therefore leave 2 times the gradient. There is no overwriting or cancellation; that additive behavior is exactly why zero_grad is needed.

questions.question: If the gradient fed to AdamW is accidentally doubled, why does the parameter step not simply double?
options: AdamW clips every gradient to unit norm before updating, so a doubled gradient is clipped back
AdamW ignores the gradient's magnitude entirely and steps using only the sign of each element
AdamW halves its learning rate whenever the gradient norm grows, cancelling out the doubling
AdamW is partly scale-invariant: it divides by sqrt(v), and v scales with the gradient squared
questions.explanation: Adam's update is roughly m / sqrt(v); if gradients double, m doubles and sqrt(v) roughly doubles, so the ratio is largely unchanged. The run is still subtly wrong because the moment dynamics and bias correction are computed from mis-scaled gradients. AdamW is not sign-based and does not automatically adjust its learning rate.

questions.question: Why does a training run with a doubled-gradient bug still show a plausible falling loss curve?
options: The gradient direction is unchanged, so the steps are still mostly downhill
The optimizer automatically detects the doubling and divides it back out each step
The loss is computed before backward runs, so a gradient bug cannot affect it
Gradient clipping always rescales the doubled gradient back to the exact correct one
questions.explanation: Both backward calls point the same way, so the update direction is still downhill and the loss keeps falling. Only the scale and dynamics are off. That plausibility is why this bug class is dangerous: nothing obviously breaks.

questions.question: What is the correct pattern for backward() and zero_grad() calls in a loop that may accumulate gradients?
options: One zero_grad() per accumulation micro-step, and backward() exactly once after all the micro-steps finish
Two backward() calls per accumulation micro-step, and zero_grad() immediately after every single backward
One backward() per optimizer step on the summed loss, and zero_grad() only once at the very start of training
One backward() per accumulation micro-step, and one zero_grad() per optimizer step, before the micro-steps
questions.explanation: Each micro-batch contributes its gradient via one backward call, and gradients should accumulate across those micro-steps. Clearing once before the accumulation loop, per optimizer step, gives the right sum. Zeroing inside the micro-loop discards earlier micro-batches; never zeroing mixes steps.

questions.question: What symptom typically appears when a training loop forgets zero_grad() entirely?
options: A loss that stays exactly at ln(V), because the accumulated gradients cancel and no update happens
A loss that drops to zero in the very first step and then stays there for the rest of the run
No visible symptom at all, because the optimizer clears the gradients itself inside step()
NaNs or a loss that explodes after a few steps, as gradients from every past step pile up
questions.explanation: Without zeroing, each step's .grad holds the sum of all previous gradients, so the effective update grows and the loss diverges or thrashes, often to NaN. Updates still happen, so the loss does not freeze at ln(V). The optimizer's step does not clear gradients.

questions.question: What goes wrong if a training loop sets the learning rate after optimizer.step() instead of before?
options: The learning rate is ignored entirely and AdamW falls back to its default value of 1e-3 for every step
Step k uses step k-1's LR: warmup is off by one and the first step runs at the peak or floor LR
The gradients get scaled by the new learning rate twice, so each update is effectively squared
The schedule runs backwards, decaying the learning rate during warmup and raising it afterwards
questions.explanation: If the rate is assigned after stepping, each update uses the value meant for the previous step, and the very first update uses whatever the optimizer was constructed with (the peak or floor), not the warmup start. Set the learning rate before step() so step k uses the rate for step k.

questions.question: A fresh model with a 1000-token vocabulary reports a first loss of 6.9. Is that expected?
options: No, because a fresh model should report a loss near 1/1000 = 0.001
Yes, because ln(1000) is about 6.91, the uniform-prediction baseline
No, because 6.9 is far above the loss of a well-trained small model
No, because a fresh model should report a loss near the vocab size, 1000
questions.explanation: A random-init model predicts roughly uniformly, so the step-0 loss is about ln(V). ln(1000) = 6.9078, so 6.9 is exactly the healthy signal. 1/V is a probability, not a loss, and an untrained model is not supposed to match the much lower loss of a trained one.

questions.question: A model cannot drive the loss near zero on a tiny repeated dataset. What should you NOT do next?
options: Inspect the label alignment between x and y in get_batch
Check the step-0 loss against ln(vocab_size) on a fresh model
Launch a large, expensive run to see whether it works at scale
Re-read the order of zero_grad, backward, clip and step in the loop
questions.explanation: Failure to overfit a handful of examples means the code or model is broken. Scaling up only multiplies whatever bug exists and burns compute. Debugging labels, the step-0 loss and loop order are exactly the right next steps.

questions.question: In a loop with grad_accum_steps = G, why does the backward call use (loss / G).backward()?
options: So that summing the G micro-batch gradients equals one full-batch gradient
So that the logged loss comes out G times larger and is easier to read in logs
So that the learning rate is automatically multiplied by G inside AdamW
So that only the last micro-batch's gradient ends up contributing to .grad
questions.explanation: Gradients accumulate across the G backward calls. Dividing each micro-batch loss by G makes the accumulated sum equal the gradient of the full-batch mean loss. The logging uses loss.item() / G for the same reason. With G = 1 both reduce to the plain loss.

questions.question: What hardware does the tiny 26k-parameter overfit example need?
options: One modern data-center GPU for about an hour, roughly one GPU-hour
Any laptop CPU, about 1 to 2 seconds for 200 steps, with zero GPU-hours
Eight GPUs in data parallel for a few minutes, about half a GPU-hour
A GPU with at least 24 GB of memory to hold the logits, for ten minutes
questions.explanation: The tiny model has about 26k parameters and uses a few MB of memory, so 200 steps take a second or two on any CPU. No GPU is needed. The heavy hardware numbers apply to real pretraining, not this sanity check.

questions.question: For GPT-2 small (124M parameters), what loss trajectory should a good pretraining run show?
options: From about 3.0 at step 0 down to about 0.0
From about 10.82 at step 0 down to about 3.0
From about 2.77 at step 0 down to about 1.0
From about 50257 at step 0 down to about 10.82
questions.explanation: GPT-2's vocabulary of 50257 gives a step-0 loss of ln(50257) = 10.82. A good run of GPT-2 small reaches about 3.0. Real language is not memorizable like a toy pattern, so the loss does not approach zero.

questions.question: Between a tiny CPU overfit run and a frontier pretraining run on thousands of GPUs, what changes in the training loop?
options: The frontier run replaces backward() with a different, cheaper gradient algorithm
The frontier run skips gradient clipping, because its far larger batches never spike
The frontier run computes the loss only on every hundredth token to save compute
The loop is identical; only the model size, token count and number of workers change
questions.explanation: The same get-batch, forward, backward, clip, step loop trains both. Scaling up changes how big the model is, how many tokens it sees and how many workers run it in parallel. The algorithmic core is unchanged.

questions.question: Why do real pretraining runs need gradient accumulation on top of the basic training loop?
options: They need to avoid computing gradients for most parameters, so only a subset updates per step
They need to update the weights several times per batch so each batch is used more fully
They need an effective batch of hundreds of thousands of tokens per step, more than fits in memory
They need to store every past gradient on disk so later analysis can replay the run exactly
questions.explanation: Large runs want huge batches per optimizer step for stable, low-noise gradients, but one device cannot hold the activations for that many tokens. Gradient accumulation sums gradients over several small micro-batches before one step. It neither skips parameters nor stores old gradients.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: With micro-batch size b, gradient-accumulation steps G and data-parallel workers W, what is the global batch size in sequences?
options: b * G / W
b + G + W
b * W / G
b * G * W
questions.explanation: Each worker processes b sequences per micro-step, repeats that G times before stepping, and W workers do so in parallel, so B_global = b * G * W sequences per optimizer step. G and W both multiply the batch; neither divides it.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: How many tokens does one optimizer step learn from, in terms of b, G, W and sequence length T?
options: b * G * W / T
b * G * W * V
(b + G) * W * T
b * G * W * T
questions.explanation: Tokens per step = B_global * T = b * G * W * T, because each of the B_global sequences has T tokens. b * G * W * V wrongly uses the vocabulary size V in place of the sequence length T. The course's tokens_per_step(b, G, W, T) computes exactly this product.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Why does gradient accumulation exist?
options: To get the gradient of a large effective batch that does not fit in memory
To reduce the total arithmetic needed per optimizer step on very large models
To let each micro-batch use its own learning rate within the same optimizer step
To remove the need for gradient clipping once batches grow beyond a few thousand
questions.explanation: The batch size that gives good learning dynamics is often too large to fit in one device's memory. Accumulation runs it in pieces and sums their gradients. It does not reduce total compute and does not change how learning rates or clipping work.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: How is gradient accumulation implemented correctly when every micro-batch has the same number of tokens?
options: Scale each micro-batch loss by 1/G before calling backward
Multiply each micro-batch loss by G before calling backward
Call optimizer.step() after every micro-batch
Call zero_grad() after every micro-batch
questions.explanation: Dividing each micro-batch loss by G makes the summed gradients equal the gradient of the full-batch mean. Multiplying by G or forgetting the scale inflates the gradient. Stepping or zeroing after each micro-batch defeats accumulation.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: What does gradient accumulation decouple in a large-model training configuration?
options: The forward pass from the backward pass, so they can run on different devices
The batch size the learning math wants from the batch size memory allows
The learning-rate schedule from the total number of optimizer steps in the run
The model's parameters from its optimizer state, so they can live on separate GPUs
questions.explanation: Large models train on global batches of hundreds of thousands to millions of tokens, but each device fits far less. Accumulation lets the effective batch be chosen for learning dynamics while each micro-batch is sized for memory. A training config is largely a choice of b, G and W.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the batch you want vs. the batch that fits
questions.question: Why is a larger batch per gradient step generally beneficial for training?
options: It gives a less noisy gradient estimate, allowing larger, more confident steps
It reduces the number of parameters that must be updated on each optimizer step
It makes each forward pass cheaper per token, because the work is shared across examples
It guarantees the model cannot overfit, since every step averages over many examples
questions.explanation: Averaging the gradient over more examples reduces its variance, so the step direction is more reliable and larger steps become safe. This is part of why large-scale training uses millions of tokens per step. It does not shrink the model or make forward passes cheaper.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the batch you want vs. the batch that fits
questions.question: Why can a batch of a million tokens not simply be run in one forward and backward pass on a single GPU?
options: The optimizer can only process one sequence per step, so the batch must be split up
The loss function cannot average over more than a few thousand tokens at once
The learning rate would have to be driven to zero to stay stable on such a batch
The activations saved for backward would be far too large for the GPU's memory
questions.explanation: Activation memory scales with batch size and sequence length, so a million-token batch would need enormous memory just for saved activations. The loss and optimizer have no such limit. That memory wall is what accumulation works around.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the batch you want vs. the batch that fits
questions.question: During gradient accumulation, what does the optimizer see when it finally steps?
options: A list of G separate gradients, which it averages internally before updating
One big accumulated gradient, with no knowledge that the batch arrived in pieces
Only the gradient of the most recent micro-batch, since earlier ones are overwritten
The individual losses of each micro-batch, which it re-differentiates at step time
questions.explanation: The micro-batch gradients are summed in place in .grad, so the optimizer reads a single tensor per parameter, identical to what a full batch would produce. It never knows how many pieces there were. The latest micro-batch alone would only result from zeroing inside the loop, a bug.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the batch you want vs. the batch that fits
questions.question: In gradient accumulation, what is the effective batch size chosen for, and what is the micro-batch size chosen for?
options: Effective batch for learning dynamics; micro-batch for memory
Effective batch for memory; micro-batch for learning dynamics
Effective batch for disk space; micro-batch for throughput
Both are chosen purely for memory and must be equal
questions.explanation: The optimizer sees the effective (global) batch, so it is set to give good gradient quality and learning behavior. The micro-batch is what one forward/backward must hold, so it is set by memory. Accumulation lets the two differ.

questions.question: In batch-size vocabulary, what is the micro-batch size b?
options: The total number of sequences per optimizer step across all workers
The number of tokens in each sequence
The number of micro-batches summed before an optimizer step
The number of sequences in one forward/backward on one worker
questions.explanation: b is what a single worker processes in one forward/backward pass, set by that device's memory. The total per step is B_global, the tokens per sequence is T, and the number of micro-batches summed is G.

questions.question: In batch-size vocabulary, what is G?
options: The number of GPUs that each hold a model copy in data parallelism
The global batch size, counted in sequences across all workers
The number of tokens in each micro-batch on a single worker
Micro-batches whose gradients are summed per optimizer step
questions.explanation: G is the gradient-accumulation step count. Each worker runs G micro-batches and accumulates their gradients before stepping. The number of devices is W, and the global batch is b * G * W.

questions.question: In batch-size vocabulary, what does T denote?
options: The sequence length or block size, in tokens per sequence
The total number of optimizer steps planned for the run
The total number of tokens processed per optimizer step
The softmax temperature used when sampling from the logits
questions.explanation: T is the context length: how many tokens each sequence contains. Multiplying B_global by T gives tokens per step. It is unrelated to the number of training steps or sampling temperature.

questions.section: What a "data-parallel worker" is (first look — built in Module 9)
questions.question: In data-parallel training, what is a 'worker'?
options: One layer of the model assigned to its own GPU
One thread that loads data while the GPU computes
One process driving one device, typically one per GPU
One micro-batch within an accumulation loop
questions.explanation: A worker is a process that runs the training loop on one device. With data parallelism you launch W of them, commonly one per GPU, such as W = 8 on an 8-GPU machine. Splitting layers across GPUs is a different strategy (model/pipeline parallelism).

questions.section: What a "data-parallel worker" is (first look — built in Module 9)
questions.question: In data-parallel training, what does each worker hold?
options: A distinct slice of the model's layers, passed along in turn
A full, identical copy of the model and the optimizer state
Only the optimizer state, with the model stored on a server
A smaller distilled copy of the model that it trains locally
questions.explanation: Every data-parallel worker has the complete model and optimizer state, identical across workers. What differs is the data each one reads. Splitting the model itself is a different form of parallelism covered later.

questions.section: What a "data-parallel worker" is (first look — built in Module 9)
questions.question: In data-parallel training, what data does each worker process?
options: A different slice of the training data from every other worker
Exactly the same batch as every other worker, for redundancy
Only the validation data, while one main worker trains
A random subset of tokens from each sequence in a shared batch
questions.explanation: Each worker reads different sequences, so W workers together cover W times as much data per step. Processing the same batch everywhere would waste the extra devices. The averaged gradient then reflects all workers' data.

questions.section: What a "data-parallel worker" is (first look — built in Module 9)
questions.question: What does the all-reduce operation do in data-parallel training?
options: One main worker gathers all W gradients, averages them, and keeps the result to itself
Every worker sends its freshly updated weights to every other worker after stepping
Every worker discards its gradient except the largest one, which all workers then use
Every worker contributes its gradient and every worker receives the average of all W
questions.explanation: All-reduce is a collective communication: each worker supplies a gradient tensor and each receives the same averaged result. Then every worker applies that identical gradient. Weights are never exchanged; only gradients are averaged.

questions.section: What a "data-parallel worker" is (first look — built in Module 9)
questions.question: Why do data-parallel workers stay identical after each optimizer step without ever sending their weights to each other?
options: A main worker broadcasts the new weights after every step
They start identical and each applies the same averaged gradient
Each worker re-reads the latest checkpoint from disk after stepping
They use the same random seed, which forces identical weights
questions.explanation: Identical starting weights plus an identical update (the all-reduced average gradient) give identical new weights, so no weight transfer is needed. A shared seed alone would not keep them identical if they applied different gradients. No checkpoint reload is involved.

questions.section: What a "data-parallel worker" is (first look — built in Module 9)
questions.question: With W = 2 workers, b = 4 and G = 2, what is each worker's gradient after the all-reduce equivalent to?
options: The gradient one device would get from a single batch of 16 sequences
The gradient one device would get from a single batch of 8 sequences
The gradient one device would get from a single batch of 4 sequences
The sum of 16 separate one-sequence gradients, with no averaging applied
questions.explanation: Each worker processes 4 * 2 = 8 sequences and the two together process 16. Averaging their gradients yields exactly the mean gradient over all 16, as if one device had processed a batch of 16. It is an average, not an unscaled sum.

questions.section: What a "data-parallel worker" is (first look — built in Module 9)
questions.question: Both gradient accumulation (G) and data parallelism (W) multiply the global batch. How do they differ in what they spend?
options: G buys a bigger batch with more devices in parallel; W buys it with more time on one device
G buys a bigger batch with more time on one device; W buys it with more devices in parallel
G cuts activation memory per device; W cuts the total arithmetic needed per step
G rescales the learning rate per micro-batch; W changes the sequence length per worker
questions.explanation: Accumulation runs extra micro-batches sequentially on the same device, costing time. Data parallelism runs them simultaneously on more devices. Both enlarge the batch the optimizer sees by the same multiplicative rule.

questions.question: Why is tokens per optimizer step the key number for reading a training config and for scaling laws?
options: It is the number of parameters that get updated in each step
It is how much text the model learns from between weight updates
It is the number of steps needed to reach the target validation loss
It is the amount of GPU memory each worker needs for activations
questions.explanation: Tokens per step, b * G * W * T, measures the data in each update, which is what scaling laws and batch-size choices reason about. It is not a parameter count, a step count or a memory figure.

questions.question: Why does the full-batch mean loss equal the average of the G micro-batch mean losses?
options: Because the cross-entropy loss is always convex
Because every micro-batch contains the same number of tokens
Because the optimizer averages the losses automatically
Because the micro-batches are drawn with the same random seed
questions.explanation: A mean over all tokens equals the average of per-chunk means only when each chunk has the same token count, so every token gets equal weight. Convexity and the optimizer play no role. This equal-count condition is what breaks with padding or ragged tails.

questions.question: Why can the full-batch gradient be computed as the sum of gradients of L_g / G over micro-batches?
options: Because the gradient of each micro-batch is always smaller in norm than its loss value
Because backward() divides every accumulated gradient by G automatically at the end
Because AdamW normalizes away any scaling of the gradient, so the 1/G factor is cosmetic
Because the gradient is linear: the gradient of an average is the average of gradients
questions.explanation: The gradient of a sum is the sum of gradients, so the gradient of (1/G) * sum L_g equals sum of grad(L_g / G). That is why calling (loss_g / G).backward() and letting .grad accumulate yields the full-batch gradient. backward does not divide by G for you.

questions.question: What happens if gradient accumulation forgets the 1/G scaling of each micro-batch loss?
options: The gradient is G times too small, like secretly dividing the learning rate by G
Only the first micro-batch contributes, because later backward calls are ignored
Nothing, because AdamW renormalizes any gradient scale exactly before each update
The gradient is G times too large, like secretly multiplying the learning rate by G
questions.explanation: Summing G unscaled micro-batch gradients gives G times the mean gradient. In effect the learning rate is multiplied by G, which usually destabilizes training. AdamW is only partly scale-invariant, so this is not harmless.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example: two micro-batches, worked by hand
questions.question: Is the equality between the full-batch mean loss and the 1/G-weighted sum of equal-size micro-batch mean losses exact or approximate?
options: Approximate: it holds only on average over many randomly drawn batches
Approximate: it holds only when G is large enough for the micro-batch noise to average out
Exact: it is an identity; a test on a tiny GPT matches gradients to about 1e-5
Exact only for G = 1, and approximate for any larger G due to rounding
questions.explanation: When every micro-batch has the same token count, the identity holds exactly for any G. The course's test_grad_accumulation_matches_full_batch confirms the gradients agree to 1e-5 on a real GPT, differences being floating-point noise. It is not a statistical approximation.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example: two micro-batches, worked by hand
questions.question: What condition must hold for the plain 1/G averaging of micro-batch losses to be exact?
options: Every micro-batch holds the same number of real target tokens
Every micro-batch is drawn from the same source document
The micro-batch size b is a power of two, such as 8 or 16
The learning rate is held constant throughout the accumulation loop
questions.explanation: The identity weights each micro-batch equally, which is correct only if they all contain the same number of real targets. Pretraining get_batch returns full (b, T) windows, so it is exact there. Document source, power-of-two sizes and learning rate are irrelevant.

questions.section: When micro-batches have different token counts
questions.question: What is a 'ragged tail' in the context of gradient accumulation?
options: A sequence that is longer than the context length T and gets cut at the end
A last micro-batch of an epoch that is shorter than b because the dataset ran out
A gradient whose norm sits far above the clipping threshold on the final step
A worker that finishes its micro-batches later than the others and stalls the all-reduce
questions.explanation: When iterating a fixed dataset in order, the final micro-batch of an epoch can contain fewer sequences, such as 3 instead of 8. That breaks the equal-token-count assumption behind plain 1/G averaging. It is unrelated to sequence length limits or slow workers.

questions.section: When micro-batches have different token counts
questions.question: In fine-tuning with padded sequences, why can two micro-batches of identical shape break plain 1/G averaging?
options: Padded positions get double weight in the cross-entropy, inflating the shorter batch
The padding token has a larger embedding norm than real tokens, skewing the gradient
Ignored positions get target -1 and add no loss, so real-token counts can differ greatly
Micro-batches containing any padding are skipped by the optimizer, so the step silently loses data
questions.explanation: Padding and often prompt tokens are given target -1, which GPT.forward passes as ignore_index=-1, so they add no loss. Two (b, T) batches can then hold very different numbers of real targets, and averaging their means weights tokens unequally. Padding positions get zero weight, not double.

questions.section: When micro-batches have different token counts
questions.question: Micro-batch 1 has 3 real tokens and micro-batch 2 has 1 real token. Why does plain 1/G averaging of their mean losses give the wrong full-batch loss?
options: The three tokens in micro-batch 1 are each counted twice, inflating its share of the loss
The mean of micro-batch 2 is undefined because a mean needs at least two tokens to compute
Its single token gets the same total weight as all three in micro-batch 1: it counts 3x as much
The plain average always gives exactly half of the true loss when G = 2 micro-batches
questions.explanation: Averaging two micro-batch means gives each micro-batch weight 1/2 regardless of size. The lone token in micro-batch 2 then carries as much weight as the three tokens of micro-batch 1 combined, distorting the per-token mean. The error depends on the counts; it is not a fixed factor.

questions.section: When micro-batches have different token counts
questions.question: When micro-batches have different numbers of real target tokens, what is the correct way to accumulate the loss?
options: Compute each micro-batch loss as a mean and backpropagate it divided by G, as for equal sizes
Compute each micro-batch loss as a mean and multiply it by its own token count, with no division
Drop the micro-batch with fewer tokens and double the other's loss to keep the scale
Compute each loss as a sum S_g over its tokens and backpropagate S_g / N, N the total real tokens
questions.explanation: Summing per-token losses and dividing by the total real-token count N across all micro-batches gives each token equal weight, matching the true full-batch mean. Plain mean/G is the special case when counts are equal. Dropping and doubling would distort the result.

questions.section: When micro-batches have different token counts
questions.question: When does the token-weighted recipe, backpropagating S_g / N, reduce to the plain recipe L_g / G?
options: When every micro-batch has the same number n of real tokens, so N = G * n
When G equals 1 but the token counts differ between steps of the run
When the loss uses reduction='mean' instead of 'sum' inside each micro-batch
When the micro-batch size b equals the sequence length T on every worker
questions.explanation: If each N_g = n, then N = G * n and S_g / N = (S_g / n) / G = L_g / G. So the plain recipe is a special case of the general one. The other conditions do not make the two equal in general.

questions.section: When micro-batches have different token counts
questions.question: In token-weighted gradient accumulation, why are all G micro-batches fetched before the first backward call?
options: The optimizer requires all G batches resident in memory to compute its moment estimates
Fetching them together makes the data loader deterministic across restarts
The total real-token count N must be known before any S_g / N can be backpropagated
The forward pass needs all G batches at once to compute attention across them
questions.explanation: Each micro-batch's loss is divided by N, the total real tokens across all G micro-batches, so N has to be counted first. The optimizer and attention do not need the batches together. Fetching early is purely for computing the normalizer.

questions.section: When micro-batches have different token counts
questions.question: In the token-weighted accumulation code, how is the number of real target tokens N computed?
options: Multiplying b by T by G
Counting nonzero entries of the logits
Summing the loss values of every micro-batch
Summing (y != -1) over all G target tensors
questions.explanation: Ignored positions have target -1, so counting entries where y != -1 across all fetched batches gives the real-token total. b * T * G counts padding too. Logits and losses are not token counts.

questions.section: When micro-batches have different token counts
questions.question: In token-weighted accumulation, which cross-entropy reduction is used for each micro-batch loss, and why?
options: reduction='mean', so each micro-batch is averaged over its tokens before weighting
reduction='none', so each token's loss is backpropagated separately through the model
reduction='sum', so the micro-batch contributes S_g, the sum over its real tokens
reduction='max', so only the hardest token in each micro-batch drives the gradient
questions.explanation: The recipe needs S_g, the sum of per-token losses over real tokens (with ignore_index=-1 skipping padding), which is then divided by the global N. A mean would reintroduce per-micro-batch normalization, the source of the bug.

questions.section: When micro-batches have different token counts
questions.question: What is the memory cost of fetching all G micro-batches up front in token-weighted accumulation?
options: All G micro-batches' activations must be held at once, multiplying peak activation memory by G
The model weights must be copied G times, one copy for each fetched micro-batch
All G (b, T) int64 token-id tensors sit in memory, which is tiny next to activations
The optimizer state grows by a factor of G, since each micro-batch needs moments
questions.explanation: Only the integer token ids for all G batches are kept, which are small. Activations are still created for one micro-batch at a time during its forward/backward. Model and optimizer state are unaffected.

questions.section: When micro-batches have different token counts
questions.question: In pretraining, what simple alternative handles the ragged-tail problem in gradient accumulation?
options: Duplicate the short batch's sequences until it reaches full size b
Drop the short last batch, as DataLoader(..., drop_last=True) does
Raise the learning rate on the short batch in proportion to its size
Skip gradient clipping on the short batch so its update is not shrunk
questions.explanation: Dropping the final incomplete batch is standard in pretraining: losing one batch among millions does not matter, and every remaining micro-batch is full. Duplicating examples would overweight them. Learning-rate or clipping tweaks do not fix the token-weighting error.

questions.section: When micro-batches have different token counts
questions.question: Why is token-weighted accumulation required in fine-tuning rather than just dropping problematic batches?
options: Fine-tuning datasets are too small to iterate more than once, so no batch can be lost
Fine-tuning always uses G = 1, so plain gradient accumulation is impossible there
Fine-tuning disables ignore_index, so padded positions cannot be masked from the loss
Padding varies in every batch, so it cannot be dropped the way a single ragged tail can
questions.explanation: In fine-tuning nearly every batch has a different count of real tokens because of padding and masked prompts, so there is no single short batch to drop. The token-weighted sum / N recipe is needed. Fine-tuning does use ignore_index and can use accumulation.

questions.section: When micro-batches have different token counts
questions.question: With W > 1 data-parallel workers and token-weighted accumulation, what must N be?
options: The real-token count summed across all workers, via one extra all-reduce of a single number
Each worker's own local token count, so no communication is needed for the normalizer
The token count of worker 0, broadcast to the others so every worker divides alike
The local token count multiplied by W, assuming every worker sees the same padding
questions.explanation: To weight every token equally globally, the normalizer must be the total over all workers. That needs one cheap all-reduce of a scalar. Using local counts would weight workers' tokens unequally when their counts differ, and multiplying by W assumes equal counts.

questions.section: 4. Tensor shapes: nothing new, just repeated
questions.question: What new tensors does gradient accumulation add to a training step?
options: None; only each parameter's .grad persists and gets added to G times
A separate gradient buffer per micro-batch, costing G times the model size
A saved copy of the activations for every micro-batch until the step
A second set of optimizer moments for each of the G micro-batches
questions.explanation: Each micro-step is an ordinary forward/backward. The only thing carried across micro-steps is .grad, which is the same shape as each parameter and accumulates in place until step() reads it and zero_grad() clears it.

questions.section: 4. Tensor shapes: nothing new, just repeated
questions.question: With gradient accumulation, what sets peak activation memory?
options: The global batch B_global, regardless of the choice of b
The micro-batch size b, not the global batch B_global
The number of data-parallel workers W in the run
The number of accumulation steps G before each update
questions.explanation: Only one micro-batch's activations exist at a time, so peak activation memory depends on b (and T). You pay for a batch of b in memory but learn from b * G * W. That is the whole payoff of accumulation.

questions.section: 5. From-scratch PyTorch: the accumulation inner loop
questions.question: In a gradient-accumulation loop, where is optimizer.zero_grad() called?
options: Inside the micro-step loop, before each micro-batch backward
Inside the micro-step loop, after each micro-batch backward
Once per optimizer step, outside and before the G micro-step loop
Only once at the very start of training
questions.explanation: The G micro-batch gradients must accumulate, so they are cleared only once per optimizer step, before the micro-loop starts. Zeroing inside the loop keeps only the last micro-batch. Never zeroing between steps mixes gradients across steps.

questions.section: 5. From-scratch PyTorch: the accumulation inner loop
questions.question: In a gradient-accumulation loop, why are clipping and optimizer.step() run once, after all G micro-batches?
options: So clipping sees the true full-batch gradient norm and one update covers all G
So clipping can act on each micro-batch's gradient separately before summing
So the learning rate can be re-adjusted between micro-batches by the cosine schedule
So the optimizer can skip micro-batches whose losses come out unusually large
questions.explanation: After G micro-steps .grad holds the full-batch gradient, so clipping its norm matches what clipping would do without accumulation, and a single step applies the update. Clipping each micro-batch would clip a different quantity.

questions.section: 5. From-scratch PyTorch: the accumulation inner loop
questions.question: In a gradient-accumulation loop, why is the logged step loss accumulated as loss.item() / G?
options: So the reported loss is on the same scale as a single full-batch mean loss
So the logged value comes out G times larger than the true loss and stands out
So the gradient of each micro-batch is scaled correctly for backward()
So the GPU never needs to synchronize with the CPU when the loss is logged
questions.explanation: Summing loss.item() / G over G equal micro-batches gives the full-batch mean, matching what one large batch would report. The gradient scaling is handled separately by (loss / G).backward(). item() still synchronizes with the device.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: accumulation is compute-for-memory
questions.question: What does gradient accumulation trade?
options: Accuracy for speed: it approximates the full-batch gradient with fewer FLOPs
Wall-clock time for memory: the arithmetic is the same, just done sequentially
Memory for time: it holds more activations in memory so the step finishes faster
Disk space for compute: it caches intermediate gradients on disk between steps
questions.explanation: The GPU does the same total arithmetic as processing the whole batch at once; it just does it in G sequential pieces, so it takes about as long as that larger batch would. What you save is peak activation memory, which scales with b instead of b * G. The gradient is exact, not approximate.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: accumulation is compute-for-memory
questions.question: Why is LayerNorm unaffected by how a batch is split into micro-batches?
options: It normalizes each token over its feature dimension, independently of other examples
It normalizes over the batch dimension, and accumulation preserves the batch statistics
It has no learnable parameters, so the gradients never depend on how the batch is split
It is only applied at evaluation time, so training-time batch splits never reach it
questions.explanation: LayerNorm computes its mean and variance per token across features, so no statistic depends on which other examples share the batch. That makes it invariant to micro-batch slicing. It does have learnable scale and shift and is active during training.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: accumulation is compute-for-memory
questions.question: Why would BatchNorm break the exactness of gradient accumulation?
options: Its statistics span the batch dimension, so G micro-batches of b differ from one batch of b*G
It has too many parameters to fit in the accumulated gradient buffer, so it is dropped
It normalizes each token independently, so it ignores which batch the token arrived in
It requires the learning rate to be rescaled by the batch size whenever G changes
questions.explanation: BatchNorm's mean and variance are taken over the examples in the batch, so a small micro-batch gives different normalization than the full batch, and the result depends on how you slice. That breaks the equivalence accumulation relies on. Per-token normalization describes LayerNorm.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: accumulation is compute-for-memory
questions.question: Why do transformers use LayerNorm or RMSNorm rather than BatchNorm?
options: They are the only normalizations that support float16 and bfloat16 mixed-precision training
They are invariant to how the batch is sliced, so accumulation and data parallelism stay exact
They let the model skip the backward pass through normalization layers, saving compute
They reduce the vocabulary size needed for the output layer by normalizing the logits
questions.explanation: Per-token normalization does not depend on other examples in the batch, so splitting the batch across micro-steps or workers gives exactly the same result. This is one of several reasons transformers avoid BatchNorm. Dtype support and vocabulary size are unrelated.

questions.question: Given a target tokens-per-step, sequence length T, workers W and maximum micro-batch b, how do you find the accumulation steps G?
options: Divide the token target by T to get B_global in sequences, then G = B_global / (b * W)
Divide the token target by b to get sequences per worker, then G = result / (T * W)
Multiply the token target by T to get B_global in tokens, then G = result / (b * W)
Divide the token target by W to get each worker's share in tokens, then G = result / b
questions.explanation: First convert tokens to sequences: B_global = tokens / T. Then solve B_global = b * G * W for G. For example 491,520 tokens with T = 1024 gives 480 sequences, and with b = 6 and W = 8, G = 480 / 48 = 10.

questions.question: If a target tokens-per-step does not divide evenly by b * W * T, what is the practical choice?
options: Round G to the nearest integer and accept slightly different tokens per step
Change the vocabulary size until the token target divides evenly by b * W * T
Abandon gradient accumulation entirely and run with G = 1 on every worker
Use a fractional G by running one partial micro-batch at the end of each step
