questions.question: For GPT-2 small at B = 8, T = 1024 in fp32, how does the logits tensor compare with the fixed params + grads + Adam state (≈1.99 GB)?
options: At ≈25 MB, it is negligible next to the fixed training state
At ≈16 GB, it is about eight times the fixed training state
At ≈1.65 GB, it alone is nearly as large as all the fixed state
It is exactly equal, because both scale with vocabulary size V
questions.explanation: Logits have B·T·V ≈ 4.1×10⁸ elements, about 1.65 GB in fp32, roughly 83% of the 1.99 GB fixed state, and that is one tensor. 25 MB is the size of one (B, T, C) activation. This is why a 124M model does not train at 8×1024 on a small GPU without help.

questions.section: The full memory picture: GPT-2 small, fp32, B = 8, T = 1024
questions.question: In a naive GPT-2 implementation, about how many (B, T, C)-sized tensors does each transformer block save for backward, and which parts are largest?
options: About 3; only the Q, K and V projections are saved for the backward pass
About 16; the attention probabilities account for 12 of them at width C
About 1; only the residual stream entering each block is saved for backward
About 16; the MLP hidden state before and after GELU are 4 each, at width 4C
questions.explanation: Per block: LayerNorm-1 input and output (2), Q, K, V (3), attention output before W_O (1), LayerNorm-2 input and output (2), MLP hidden before GELU (4) and after GELU (4), totaling 16. The attention probabilities are a separate T×T-per-head tensor counted on their own line.

questions.section: The full memory picture: GPT-2 small, fp32, B = 8, T = 1024
questions.question: In naive attention, why is the attention-probability tensor (B·H·T² per layer) a separate, large activation, and what removes it?
options: It is the KV cache, which grows with T²; it is removed by using smaller micro-batches
It is the materialized T×T softmax per head; FlashAttention-style kernels never store it
It is the gradient of W_O, which is per-position; it is removed by gradient clipping
It is a copy of the logits reshaped per head; it is removed by tying the embeddings
questions.explanation: A naive implementation stores the full T×T probability matrix per head for backward. For GPT-2 small at B = 8, T = 1024 that is about 4.8 GB over 12 layers, 36% of the total. FlashAttention-style kernels recompute it in tiles and never store it.

questions.section: The full memory picture: GPT-2 small, fp32, B = 8, T = 1024
questions.question: In a GPT-2 small memory tally (B = 8, T = 1024), the attention-probability line equals the 16-tensor per-layer line. Why?
options: Because attention probabilities are always 16 tensors of size (B, T, C)
Because FlashAttention stores both in the same buffer
By coincidence: H·T = 12·1024 happens to equal 16·C = 16·768
Because both scale with T² by design
questions.explanation: Attention probabilities are B·H·T² floats per layer and the 16 tensors are 16·B·T·C. They match only because H·T = 12,288 = 16·768. Change T and the two diverge, since one scales with T² and the other with T.

questions.section: The full memory picture: GPT-2 small, fp32, B = 8, T = 1024
questions.question: In a GPT-2 small fp32 memory tally (B = 8, T = 1024), how do the activation lines scale when you change B or T?
options: All scale with B; attention probabilities scale with T² and the rest with T
All activation lines scale with T², and none of them depend on B at all
Only the logits scale with B; the rest are fixed by the model width C
All activation lines are fixed; only the Adam state grows as T increases
questions.explanation: The four activation lines (about 85% of the total) are proportional to B. Attention probabilities grow with T², the others linearly with T. Halving B to 4 cuts the total to about 7.7 GB; doubling T to 2048 raises it to about 34.4 GB. Params, grads and Adam state stay at 1.99 GB.

questions.section: The full memory picture: GPT-2 small, fp32, B = 8, T = 1024
questions.question: Activation-memory estimates are approximate. What is the recommended way to get the exact peak figure in PyTorch on a GPU?
options: Read it from model.num_params() multiplied by the bytes per element
Measure it with torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() during a short run
Compute 16P from the parameter count and add the size of the logits tensor
Check the size of the saved checkpoint file on disk after one step
questions.explanation: What is saved depends on the implementation's fusion choices, so estimates can be off. torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() reports the actual peak. 16P covers only the fixed state, and checkpoint size reflects params (and maybe optimizer state), not activations.

questions.section: The full memory picture: GPT-2 small, fp32, B = 8, T = 1024
questions.question: How does mixed precision reduce training memory?
options: It removes the Adam second-moment buffer, since bf16 gradients need no variance estimate
It shrinks the vocabulary to fit bf16 token ids, which halves the logits tensor size
It shares one gradient buffer between neighbouring layers, since bf16 values are small
It stores activations, often plus a weight copy, at 2 bytes in bf16/fp16, about halving them
questions.explanation: Mixed precision stores activations, and often a working copy of the weights, in 2-byte formats instead of 4-byte fp32. That roughly halves activation and parameter-copy memory. It does not remove the 4P fixed state, which is addressed by sharding.

questions.section: The full memory picture: GPT-2 small, fp32, B = 8, T = 1024
questions.question: What trade does activation checkpointing make?
options: It saves activations to disk during forward so that the next epoch can reuse them directly
It skips the backward pass for half the layers, trading gradient accuracy for lower memory
It stores only the gradients and discards the parameters, rebuilding them from the optimizer
It drops most activations in forward and recomputes them in backward: more FLOPs, far less memory
questions.explanation: Checkpointing keeps a few activations and recomputes the rest during backward, so memory falls a lot while compute rises. It is not disk saving, and it still computes full gradients.

questions.section: The full memory picture: GPT-2 small, fp32, B = 8, T = 1024
questions.question: Which technique attacks the fixed 4P (params + grads + Adam state) cost rather than activations?
options: Activation checkpointing, which recomputes the saved tensors during backward
FlashAttention, which avoids storing the T×T attention-probability matrix
Optimizer-state sharding such as ZeRO/FSDP, splitting that state across GPUs
Gradient accumulation, which runs smaller micro-batches before each step
questions.explanation: Mixed precision, checkpointing, FlashAttention and gradient accumulation all target activations. The 4P fixed state does not depend on batch, so it is reduced by sharding params, grads and optimizer state across data-parallel GPUs, as in ZeRO and FSDP.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: why these estimates are trustworthy
questions.question: Why is the 6N FLOP estimate trusted despite dropping attention scores, softmax, LayerNorm and embedding lookups?
options: For standard shapes at moderate context, the omitted terms are ~10% or less of the total
Those omitted terms are exactly zero on modern GPUs, which fuse them into the matmuls
The factor 6 already includes a built-in safety margin that covers all of those terms
Those terms only appear during evaluation, so the training-time count never includes them
questions.explanation: For large models at ordinary context, weight matmuls dominate and the omitted terms are about 10% or less. The exception is small models with large vocabularies such as GPT-2 small, where the omitted LM head alone is about 29%. The 6 is exactly 2+2+2, not a padded margin.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: why these estimates are trustworthy
questions.question: In which situations should you switch from the 6N estimate to a fuller FLOP count?
options: Any model trained in bf16 rather than full fp32 precision
Very long context, very small models, or MoE routing
Any run that uses more than one GPU or more than one node
Any model with tied input embeddings and output head
questions.explanation: 6N stops being accurate when the omitted terms stop being small: at very long context the attention scores grow, in very small models the LM head and overheads loom large, and with MoE routing not all parameters are active per token. Precision, GPU count and weight tying do not by themselves break the estimate.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: why these estimates are trustworthy
questions.question: What is the main practical value of the 6N estimate?
options: It gives an exact FLOP count, accurate to 0.1%, for any transformer at any context length
It predicts the final validation loss of the run from the parameter count and token count
It needs only the model config, so it budgets GPU-hours and model size before any code exists
It measures the actual runtime of each kernel, so slow layers can be found before profiling
questions.explanation: The point is not perfect accuracy but a number you can compute from the config alone, right to within about 10% at ordinary context. That is enough to budget GPU-hours and choose a model size. It does not predict loss or measure kernels.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: why these estimates are trustworthy
questions.question: Why is activation memory usually measured with a short profiling run, while parameter and optimizer memory are predicted precisely in capacity planning?
options: The first three are exact (P × dtype size), while activations depend on fusion and what is saved
Activations are random and change from step to step by a large factor, so only a run can show them
Optimizer state is stored on the CPU and is never measured, so it can only be predicted
Parameter memory depends on the training data, so it is fixed only after the first batch
questions.explanation: Params, grads and optimizer state are P × dtype size, so they are exact. Activation memory depends on which tensors the implementation keeps and how it fuses operations, so it is estimated and then confirmed by profiling. That asymmetry shapes capacity planning.

questions.question: Given a training run's total FLOPs and a cluster's effective (MFU-adjusted) FLOP/s, how do you estimate wall-clock training time?
options: Multiply total FLOPs by the effective FLOP/s
Divide total FLOPs by the effective FLOP/s
Divide the effective FLOP/s by total FLOPs
Divide total FLOPs by the peak FLOP/s, ignoring MFU
questions.explanation: Time = work ÷ rate. With total FLOPs ≈ 6ND and an effective rate of MFU × peak, time ≈ 6ND ÷ (MFU × peak). Using the peak rate instead of the effective rate assumes 100% MFU and badly underestimates time.

questions.question: Why does a 1.3B-parameter model not train on a single 16 GB GPU in plain fp32 with AdamW, even before activations?
options: Its weights alone (≈ 1.3 GB) leave too little room on the GPU for the tokenizer and data loader
Its gradients are stored per token rather than per parameter, and so exceed 16 GB at any batch
Its 6N FLOPs per token exceed the GPU's peak FLOP/s, so the step cannot be scheduled on it
Its fixed state, 16P bytes ≈ 20.8 GB, already exceeds 16 GB, needing sharding or mixed precision
questions.explanation: Params + grads + Adam state in fp32 are 16 bytes per parameter: 16 × 1.3×10⁹ ≈ 20.8 GB. That alone exceeds 16 GB, before any activation. Billion-parameter training therefore relies on sharding or mixed precision. FLOPs per token affect speed, not fit.

questions.question: What is the approximate compute-optimal ratio of training tokens to parameters (Chinchilla-style)?
options: About 1 token per parameter (D ≈ N)
About 20 tokens per parameter (D ≈ 20N)
About 200 tokens per parameter (D ≈ 200N)
About 0.2 tokens per parameter (D ≈ N/5)
questions.explanation: The Chinchilla compute-optimal ballpark is D ≈ 20N, covered in the scaling-laws module. So a 1.3B model on 26B tokens is roughly in that regime. Training far beyond 20N is possible and sometimes desirable, but 20N is the compute-optimal reference point.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes FLOPs from FLOP/s?
options: FLOPs and FLOP/s are the same quantity; the /s is notation for the per-second peak only
FLOPs is a rate; FLOP/s is a count accumulated over one second, so 6ND is a rate
FLOPs is a count of work, FLOP/s a rate: 6ND is a count, peak a rate, MFU a ratio of rates
6ND is a rate of work, peak FLOP/s is a count, and MFU is a count divided by a rate
questions.explanation: FLOPs counts operations (work), FLOP/s is operations per second (speed). 6N and 6ND are counts, a GPU's peak is a rate, and MFU divides one rate by another, so it has no unit. Confusing the two leads to nonsensical time or utilization estimates.

questions.question: A capacity plan uses 2N instead of 6N FLOPs per token. What is the consequence?
options: Compute, time and cost are underestimated threefold, since the backward pass is forgotten
Compute is overestimated threefold, because 2N already double-counts the forward pass
Compute is underestimated by only about 10%, roughly the share of attention and elementwise work
Only memory is underestimated, not compute, because FLOPs do not depend on backward
questions.explanation: 2N is the forward pass only; backward adds about 4N, so the true cost is 6N. Using 2N underestimates FLOPs, wall-clock time and cost by a factor of 3.

questions.question: A team budgets GPU memory for weights and gradients only, then the run fails with an out-of-memory error at the first optimizer step. What did they forget?
options: The logits tensor computed on the validation set each step
The tokenizer's vocabulary table, which is loaded on the GPU
The learning-rate scheduler's state, one value per parameter
Adam's m and v buffers, which double the parameter memory
questions.explanation: AdamW keeps two buffers per parameter, as much memory as weights and grads combined. Budgeting only for weights + grads underestimates the fixed state by half. In PyTorch these buffers are created lazily in the first step(), so the failure shows up exactly there.

questions.question: When reporting or comparing MFU across runs, what must you always state?
options: The random seed and the data order, since MFU varies between otherwise identical runs
The dtype and the exact peak FLOP/s used (e.g., dense vs sparse, fp16 vs fp32)
The number of layers and attention heads, since MFU depends on model shape
The tokenizer and vocabulary size, since they set the tokens counted per step
questions.explanation: MFU depends entirely on its denominator, and the same GPU has very different peaks by dtype and by dense vs sparse. Without stating which peak, two MFUs cannot be compared.

questions.question: A single-GPU run reports 8% MFU. Which is a plausible cause?
options: The micro-batch is too small, or time is lost to data loading and host-device copies
The model has too few FLOPs per token to ever exceed the GPU's peak FLOP/s
The learning rate is too low for the model size, so each step does less work
The optimizer is AdamW instead of SGD, and AdamW's FLOPs are excluded from MFU
questions.explanation: Low MFU means the arithmetic units sit idle part of each step. Plausible causes include a tiny micro-batch that under-uses the GPU between kernel launches, time lost to data loading, host-device transfers or communication, or a small model and short context where non-matmul work is a larger share. Learning rate and optimizer choice do not change FLOP/s.

questions.question: Why does activation memory, unlike parameters, gradients and optimizer state, depend on batch size and context length?
options: Activations store one value per parameter for every example, which grows with the batch size
Activations are copies of the gradients made once per token, so they scale with B × T × P
Activations hold the optimizer's moments for each batch element and each position in it
They are per-example, per-position intermediates, so their size scales with B × T (and V for logits)
questions.explanation: Params, grads and optimizer state describe the model: one number (or two) per parameter. Activations are forward-pass results, with one set per example per position, so they grow with B × T, and the logits additionally with V. That is why batch and context are the knobs for activation memory.

questions.question: Which parts of FLOP, MFU and memory accounting can be done on a CPU-only machine?
options: None of them; even the 6N FLOP estimate requires a GPU profiler to count the launched kernels
Only the memory estimate; FLOP counting needs CUDA to enumerate every matmul kernel
All estimates are pure arithmetic; only measuring real MFU and tokens/sec needs the accelerator
Only tokens/sec can be measured on CPU; MFU and memory estimates need a TPU or GPU
questions.explanation: The 6N, MFU and memory-bucket formulas are pure Python arithmetic that run instantly on any machine. Measuring actual tokens/sec and MFU requires running on the accelerator you are profiling, e.g. an A100 at about 312 TFLOP/s bf16 for GPT-2-small-scale experiments.

questions.question: Why are FLOP counts alone not enough to predict how long a GPU kernel will take?
options: A kernel with few FLOPs can still be slow if it moves a lot of data across the memory hierarchy
FLOP counts ignore the time spent in the Python interpreter, which usually dominates GPU runtime
FLOP counts are only defined for matrix multiplies, so elementwise kernels have no FLOP count
GPUs execute FLOPs at a rate that varies randomly, so counts never correlate with runtime
questions.explanation: Runtime depends on both arithmetic and data movement. A kernel that does very little arithmetic but drags a large tensor through HBM is limited by bandwidth, not by its FLOP count. This is why the memory hierarchy is needed alongside FLOP accounting to reason about performance.

questions.question: What single governing fact about GPUs underlies most performance decisions for LLM kernels?
options: Arithmetic is expensive and moving data is cheap, so most LLM kernels are compute-bound
Kernel launches are free, so splitting work into many tiny kernels is always faster
Host RAM is faster than HBM, so tensors should be kept on the CPU whenever possible
Arithmetic is cheap and moving data is expensive, so most LLM kernels are memory-bound
questions.explanation: A GPU can perform far more arithmetic per second than its memory can deliver bytes. As a result, most kernels outside the large matmuls spend their time waiting on data rather than computing. Recognizing this is what makes the roofline, fusion and FlashAttention make sense.

questions.question: According to the GPU-performance view of training, how does FlashAttention achieve its speedup?
options: It approximates softmax with a cheaper polynomial, cutting the FLOPs per score
It skips attention for most token pairs, using a fixed block-sparse pattern
It avoids moving large intermediates through HBM, without reducing the math
It runs attention on the CPU while the GPU handles the projection matmuls
questions.explanation: FlashAttention does essentially the same arithmetic as standard attention (slightly more, in fact). Its win comes from not writing and re-reading the large score matrices to and from HBM. Understanding where data lives explains why that is faster even though the math is not reduced.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a GPU is a very wide, very shallow factory
questions.question: How does a typical CPU's design differ from a GPU's?
options: A CPU has thousands of simple lanes; a GPU has a few powerful out-of-order cores with big caches
A CPU has a few powerful out-of-order cores and big caches; a GPU has thousands of simple lanes
A CPU and a GPU share the same core design, but the GPU runs every core at a higher clock
A CPU has no caches, while a GPU relies on large branch predictors and out-of-order execution
questions.explanation: A CPU is tuned to finish one complicated, branchy instruction stream as fast as possible, with 8–64 sophisticated cores. A GPU bets on raw parallel width: thousands of simple lanes executing the same operation across many data elements. The clock-speed answer is wrong because the difference is architectural, not frequency.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a GPU is a very wide, very shallow factory
questions.question: What kind of workload is a CPU's design (deep out-of-order cores, branch prediction) best suited for?
options: Large dense matrix multiplications with no data dependency between output elements
Branchy, pointer-chasing code such as operating systems, web servers and compilers
Applying an activation function independently to every element of a huge tensor
Adding two vectors of a million floats element by element with no branches at all
questions.explanation: Branch prediction and out-of-order execution help when the instruction stream is irregular and dependent, as in OS kernels, servers and compilers. Dense, uniform, branch-free work like matmuls and elementwise ops is the GPU's territory, because thousands of lanes can do it in parallel.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a GPU is a very wide, very shallow factory
questions.question: Why does deep learning run 10–100x faster on GPUs than on CPUs?
options: It is mostly identical operations on many independent elements, run across thousands of lanes
Deep learning code is full of branches, which GPU branch predictors handle better than CPUs
GPUs have larger per-core caches than CPUs, so each individual operation finishes sooner
GPUs execute Python bytecode directly, avoiding the interpreter overhead that CPUs suffer
questions.explanation: Matmuls, vector adds and elementwise activations have no branching and no dependency between elements, so the same instruction can be applied across thousands of lanes at once. That data-parallel structure maps directly onto GPU hardware. GPUs are not better at branches; branchy code is actually expensive on them.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a GPU is a very wide, very shallow factory
questions.question: What is usually the real performance question on a GPU?
options: Whether there are enough arithmetic units to perform the required FLOPs
Whether the CPU clock speed is high enough to run the kernels
Whether the kernel's code has been compiled with optimization flags
Whether data can be delivered to the compute units fast enough
questions.explanation: GPU arithmetic units can consume numbers much faster than memory can supply them. So the bottleneck is rarely raw compute; it is almost always feeding data to the lanes. This is the theme of the whole GPU-performance module.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: a GPU is a very wide, very shallow factory
questions.question: Because a GPU trades single-thread cleverness for raw parallel width, which resource becomes scarce?
options: Arithmetic throughput
Instruction decoding
Data movement
Branch prediction capacity
questions.explanation: With thousands of lanes, arithmetic is abundant and cheap. The scarce resource is moving data to those lanes, so most GPU optimization is about not moving data you do not have to. Arithmetic throughput is the abundant resource, not the scarce one.

questions.section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
questions.question: In NVIDIA's CUDA execution model, what is a thread?
options: A group of 32 lanes that execute the same instruction in lockstep on different data
The physical processor that holds a register file, shared memory and Tensor Cores
The smallest unit of work: one lane running the kernel, usually on one element
A group of warps guaranteed to run on the same SM and share its on-chip memory
questions.explanation: A thread is the finest unit: one lane running the kernel on (usually) one element, and a launch can create millions of them. A group of 32 lockstep threads is a warp, a group of warps on one SM is a thread block, and the physical processor is the SM.

questions.section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
questions.question: How many threads make up a warp on NVIDIA GPUs?
questions.explanation: Threads execute in lockstep groups of 32 called warps. 1024 is the maximum size of a thread block, not a warp. The warp is the real unit of scheduling: the hardware issues one instruction per warp.

questions.section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
questions.question: What does SIMT (single instruction, multiple threads) mean for the threads of a warp?
options: All threads in the warp execute the same instruction at the same time, each on its own data
Each thread in the warp runs a different instruction stream independently
Only one thread in the warp runs at a time while the others wait
The threads of a warp share a single register so they always compute the same value
questions.explanation: In SIMT, the 32 threads of a warp are issued one instruction together, and each applies it to its own data element. The hardware issues instructions per warp, not per thread. Threads are not independent instruction streams, which is why divergence costs performance.

questions.section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
questions.question: What is the real unit of scheduling on an NVIDIA GPU?
options: The individual thread: each thread is scheduled independently
The whole kernel: the GPU schedules one kernel instruction at a time across all SMs
The SM: one instruction is issued per SM for all its threads
The warp: the hardware issues one instruction per warp
questions.explanation: Although threads are the smallest unit of work, the hardware issues instructions to whole warps of 32 threads. That is why warp-level behaviour (lockstep execution, divergence, latency hiding by switching warps) matters for performance.

questions.section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
questions.question: What property distinguishes a thread block (CTA) from an arbitrary set of threads?
options: Its threads are guaranteed to be spread across different SMs for load balancing
Its threads each get a private region of HBM that no other block is allowed to read
It always contains exactly 32 threads that execute the same instruction in lockstep
Its warps share one SM, so they can use shared memory and sync at a barrier
questions.explanation: A thread block is a group of warps (up to 1024 threads) placed together on one SM. That placement lets them share a fast scratchpad (shared memory) and synchronize with a barrier. Exactly 32 lockstep threads describes a warp, not a block.

questions.section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
questions.question: What is the maximum number of threads in a single CUDA thread block?
questions.explanation: A thread block can hold up to 1024 threads, organized as warps of 32. 32 is the warp size and 108 is the number of SMs on an A100.

questions.section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
questions.question: Which capability of thread blocks does FlashAttention exploit?
options: A block can write directly into another GPU's HBM without going through NVLink
A block can load a tile into shared memory once and have all its threads reuse it
A block can skip computing scores whose values its threads predict to be small
A block can be spread over several SMs at once to get access to more registers
questions.explanation: Threads in a block share on-chip shared memory and can synchronize. FlashAttention uses this to stage tiles of Q, K and V in shared memory once and reuse them across many computations, instead of repeatedly reading from HBM. A block is never split across SMs.

questions.section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
questions.question: How many streaming multiprocessors (SMs) do an A100 and an H100 have, respectively?
options: 32 and 64
questions.explanation: An A100 has 108 SMs and an H100 has 132. The numbers 80 and 141 are HBM capacities in GB, and 1024 is the maximum thread-block size.

questions.section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
questions.question: What are Tensor Cores?
options: Dedicated matrix-multiply-accumulate units in each SM that do most transformer FLOPs
A separate chip next to the GPU that stores tensors between consecutive kernel launches
The portion of HBM reserved for model weights so they are never evicted during training
Software threads PyTorch uses to schedule tensor operations from the CPU onto the GPU
questions.explanation: Each SM contains, along with its register file, shared memory and warp schedulers, a set of arithmetic units including Tensor Cores. These are specialized matrix-multiply-accumulate units, and they perform most of the FLOPs in transformer training. They are hardware compute units, not memory.

questions.section: 2. The execution hierarchy: threads, warps, blocks, SMs
questions.question: In GPU terminology, what is a kernel?
options: A single SM together with its private register file and its shared memory
The operating-system driver that copies tensors from host RAM into the HBM
A group of 32 threads that execute the same instruction in lockstep on an SM
One function launched across a whole grid of threads, blocks and SMs
questions.explanation: A kernel is one GPU function, launched over a grid of many thread blocks that the GPU distributes across its SMs. The hierarchy is thread, warp, thread block, SM, GPU. A group of 32 lockstep threads is a warp.

questions.question: Why do GPUs want many warps in flight (high occupancy)?
options: Because each additional resident warp raises the clock speed of the SM it runs on
Because warps share registers, so more warps means more registers for every thread
So a warp stalled on memory can be swapped for a ready one, keeping units busy
Because a kernel can only start once every SM is filled with exactly one warp of work
questions.explanation: Many warps are about latency hiding, not per-warp speed. When a warp waits on a slow memory read, the SM switches instantly to another ready warp so the units never sit idle. More warps actually means fewer registers per thread, since the register file is shared.

questions.question: Why can a training run with a tiny batch or very short sequence show low MFU even though the kernels are correct?
options: Tiny batches force every operation to run in fp64, which is much slower on Tensor Cores
Too few warps exist to hide memory latency, so arithmetic units idle during stalls
Short sequences make attention compute-bound, which leaves the Tensor Cores starved
The GPU disables its Tensor Cores whenever the batch size falls below 32 sequences
questions.explanation: With too little parallel work, the scheduler has no other ready warp to switch to when one stalls on memory. The arithmetic units then idle, and model FLOPs utilization drops. This is one concrete cause of very low MFU numbers on small workloads.

questions.question: What happens when the threads of one warp take different sides of an if statement?
options: Each thread runs only its own path in parallel with the others, at no extra cost
The warp runs both paths in turn, masking inactive threads, which wastes throughput
The GPU moves the diverging threads to a different SM so each path runs separately
The kernel aborts with a launch error, because divergent branches are not allowed
questions.explanation: Because a warp issues one instruction for all 32 threads, divergent threads cannot run their paths simultaneously. The warp runs both paths in turn and masks out threads not on the current path. Data-parallel numeric code avoids this, which is part of why deep learning suits GPUs.

questions.section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
questions.question: What trade-off defines the levels of the GPU memory hierarchy?
options: Size against speed: small memories are fast and near the units, large ones slow and far
Precision against range: each lower level stores numbers in a lower-precision format
Cost against reliability: the larger, cheaper levels lose or corrupt data more often
Read speed against write speed: each level is fast for one but slow for the other
questions.explanation: The hierarchy trades capacity for speed. Each level down is roughly 10x bigger and several times slower. Registers are tiny and instant; host RAM is huge and slowest.

questions.section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
questions.question: Which ordering of GPU memory levels runs from fastest/smallest to slowest/largest?
options: Shared memory/SRAM, registers, HBM, L2 cache, host RAM
Registers, L2 cache, shared memory/SRAM, host RAM, HBM
HBM, L2 cache, shared memory/SRAM, registers, host RAM
Registers, shared memory/SRAM, L2 cache, HBM, host RAM
questions.explanation: The order is registers (per-thread, instant), shared memory/SRAM (per-SM scratchpad), L2 (one cache for the whole GPU), HBM (the large off-chip 'GPU memory') and host RAM (CPU memory across PCIe). Each step down is bigger and slower.

questions.section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
questions.question: Why does each GPU thread get only a few dozen registers?
options: Registers are stored in HBM, which limits how many each thread can address
Each thread is allowed exactly one register for every warp it belongs to
An SM's ~256 KB register file is split across all of its live threads
Registers are pooled across all SMs, so each thread gets a slice of the whole GPU
questions.explanation: Registers are per-thread private storage physically inside the SM, with effectively zero-cycle access. But the whole SM has a register file of roughly 256 KB, divided among all live threads, so each thread has only a few dozen registers. Registers are on-chip, not in HBM.

questions.section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
questions.question: Roughly how much shared memory (SRAM) is available per SM on an A100 and an H100?
options: About 40 MB on A100 and about 50 MB on H100
About 80 GB on A100 and about 141 GB on H100
Up to about 164 KB on A100 and about 228 KB on H100
About 256 bytes on A100 and about 512 bytes on H100
questions.explanation: Shared memory is a small configurable scratchpad per SM: up to ~164 KB on A100 and ~228 KB on H100. The 40–50 MB figures are the L2 cache for the whole GPU, and 80–141 GB are HBM capacities.

questions.section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
questions.question: Why is the aggregate bandwidth of on-chip shared memory enormous even though each SM's scratchpad is small?
options: Shared memory is one cache spanning all SMs, connected by a single 1 PB/s bus
Each SM gets a few hundred GB/s and there are 100+ SMs, so tens of TB/s in total
Shared memory is backed by HBM, so it simply inherits HBM's multi-TB/s bandwidth
Shared memory compresses tiles on the fly, so each access moves far fewer bytes
questions.explanation: Shared memory is per-SM and on-chip, with a few hundred GB/s per SM. Multiplied across ~100+ SMs, aggregate on-chip bandwidth reaches tens of TB/s, far above HBM's ~2–3 TB/s. That is why staging data in SRAM pays off.

questions.section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
questions.question: Which memory level does FlashAttention use to stage tiles of Q, K and V so it can do lots of arithmetic without going back to HBM?
options: Shared memory / SRAM
The GPU-wide L2 cache
Pinned host RAM
HBM, the off-chip DRAM
questions.explanation: FlashAttention lives in shared memory: it loads tiles of Q, K and V into the per-SM SRAM and does many operations on them there. The point is to avoid HBM traffic, so HBM is the level it minimizes, not the one it stages in.

questions.section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
questions.question: What is the L2 cache on an A100/H100-class GPU?
options: A private per-thread store of a few dozen values with effectively instant access
A per-SM scratchpad of up to ~228 KB that each thread block manages explicitly
The off-chip DRAM stack of 40–80 GB holding weights, gradients and activations
One ~40–50 MB cache shared by all SMs that caches recent HBM data automatically
questions.explanation: L2 is one cache for the whole GPU (~40 MB A100, ~50 MB H100). It caches recent HBM accesses automatically and sits between SRAM and HBM in speed. The explicitly managed per-SM scratchpad is shared memory, and the off-chip DRAM is HBM.

questions.section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
questions.question: When someone says 'an 80 GB A100', which memory level are they referring to?
options: The L2 cache shared by all SMs on the die
The total shared memory of all SMs combined
The host RAM the GPU reaches over PCIe
HBM, the off-chip DRAM stacked by the die
questions.explanation: The quoted 'GPU memory' is HBM (High-Bandwidth Memory), off-chip DRAM stacked beside the die. It is where weights, gradients, optimizer state and activations live. L2 and shared memory are tiny by comparison.

questions.section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
questions.question: Roughly what HBM bandwidth do the A100 and H100 provide?
options: About 32–64 GB/s on both, set by the PCIe link
About 312 TB/s on A100 and 990 TB/s on H100
About 1.5–2 TB/s on A100 and 3.3 TB/s on H100
About tens of TB/s on both, like on-chip SRAM
questions.explanation: HBM bandwidth is ~1.5–2 TB/s on A100 and ~3.3 TB/s on H100. 32–64 GB/s is PCIe to host RAM, and tens of TB/s is aggregate on-chip SRAM bandwidth. 312 is the A100's bf16 TFLOP/s figure, not a bandwidth.

questions.section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
questions.question: Where do a model's weights, gradients, optimizer state and activations actually live during GPU training?
options: In the L2 cache
In HBM
In registers
In shared memory
questions.explanation: These large tensors live in HBM, the big off-chip GPU memory. Every time a kernel reads a tensor 'from GPU memory', it reads from HBM. Registers, shared memory and L2 are far too small to hold them.

questions.section: 3. The memory hierarchy: the central object of this module
questions.question: Why should tensors be moved from host to device (or between GPUs) rarely?
options: PCIe/NVLink is about 10x slower than HBM, so every crossing is a bottleneck
Each transfer permanently reduces the HBM capacity available to the program
Host-to-device copies silently upcast the tensor's dtype to fp64 on arrival
The GPU must flush and reset its L2 cache and all SMs after every transfer
questions.explanation: Host RAM is reached over PCIe (~32–64 GB/s) or NVLink, an order of magnitude slower than HBM. Calling .to('cuda') or moving data between GPUs crosses this slow link, so the practice is to move data to the GPU once and keep it there.

questions.section: Representative numbers (approximate — orders of magnitude, not spec sheets)
questions.question: Relative to HBM bandwidth, roughly how fast is host RAM accessed over PCIe?
options: About 0.02–0.03x of HBM
About 2–5x faster than HBM
About 10–20x faster than HBM
About the same speed as HBM
questions.explanation: PCIe gives ~32–64 GB/s against HBM's ~1.5–3.3 TB/s, about 0.02–0.03x. The 2–5x figure is L2 and 10–20x is shared memory, both faster than HBM.

questions.section: Representative numbers (approximate — orders of magnitude, not spec sheets)
questions.question: Why should the GPU memory sizes and bandwidths quoted for A100/H100 be treated as orders of magnitude rather than exact specs?
options: Bandwidth figures drift every time the GPU is rebooted, so no value is stable for long
Vendors publish no official figures, so every quoted number is a community estimate
The effective values depend on the Python and PyTorch versions used to run the model
They vary by SKU (40 vs 80 GB, SXM vs PCIe) and by peak vs sustained quoting
questions.explanation: The numbers are ballpark, publicly documented figures. Real values differ between variants such as 40 GB vs 80 GB A100 or SXM vs PCIe, and between peak and sustained quotes. They are meant for reasoning, not for spec-sheet precision.

questions.section: Representative numbers (approximate — orders of magnitude, not spec sheets)
questions.question: Which two A100 numbers should be held side by side to understand GPU performance?
options: About 108 SMs and about 32 threads per warp
About 40 MB of L2 and 256 KB of registers per SM
About 2 TB/s HBM and about 312 TFLOP/s bf16
About 80 GB of HBM and about 64 GB/s of PCIe
questions.explanation: Comparing ~312 TFLOP/s of bf16 compute with ~2 TB/s of HBM bandwidth reveals how many FLOPs the chip can do per byte read. That ratio is what decides whether a kernel is memory-bound or compute-bound.

questions.section: 4. The central fact: arithmetic is cheap, data movement is expensive
questions.question: Roughly how many FLOPs can an A100 perform in the time it reads one byte from HBM?
options: About 1
About 150
About 15
About 1500
questions.explanation: Dividing ~312x10^12 FLOP/s by ~2x10^12 bytes/s gives about 156 FLOPs per byte. A kernel needs at least that many FLOPs per byte of HBM traffic to keep the arithmetic units busy.

questions.section: 4. The central fact: arithmetic is cheap, data movement is expensive
questions.question: A kernel reads a byte from HBM and does only one or two FLOPs with it before needing the next byte. On an A100, what happens?
options: The kernel is compute-bound, because each FLOP has to wait for the FLOP before it
The arithmetic units idle ~99% of the time waiting on data: it is memory-bound
The kernel runs at peak FLOP/s, because it does so little work for each byte read
The kernel automatically keeps its data in registers, so HBM is never read again
questions.explanation: The A100 can do ~150 FLOPs per HBM byte. Doing only 1–2 FLOPs per byte leaves the units waiting almost all the time, so runtime is set by how fast HBM delivers bytes. That is the definition of a memory-bound (bandwidth-bound) kernel.

questions.section: 4. The central fact: arithmetic is cheap, data movement is expensive
questions.question: What makes a kernel compute-bound?
options: It does hundreds of FLOPs per byte loaded, like a large matmul reusing each value
It reads very large tensors from HBM and does one FLOP per element it loads
It launches thousands of tiny kernels in a row, each saturating the Tensor Cores
It moves data between the CPU and GPU every step, keeping the PCIe link busy
questions.explanation: A compute-bound kernel has enough arithmetic per byte that the arithmetic units stay saturated and memory is not the bottleneck. Large matmuls achieve this by reusing each loaded value across a whole row or column of outputs. Elementwise ops over big tensors are the classic memory-bound case.

questions.section: 4. The central fact: arithmetic is cheap, data movement is expensive
questions.question: Which of these transformer operations is typically memory-bound on a GPU?
options: The QKV projection matmul
The MLP up-projection matmul
The attention output projection matmul
LayerNorm
questions.explanation: Elementwise and reduction operations such as activations, LayerNorm, dropout, bias add, softmax and the attention score matrix are memory-bound. The large weight matmuls (QKV, output projection, MLP layers) reuse each loaded value many times and are compute-bound.

questions.section: Why LLM kernels are so often memory-bound
questions.question: Why are the big weight matmuls in a transformer (QKV, output projection, MLP) considered 'good' from a performance standpoint?
options: They are memory-bound, which makes them the easiest ops to speed up with fusion
They do almost no FLOPs, so they finish instantly compared with elementwise ops
They are compute-bound: each loaded number is reused, keeping Tensor Cores busy
They run on the CPU in parallel, freeing the GPU for the attention computation
questions.explanation: These matmuls are the 6N FLOPs of training and genuinely compute-bound. Each loaded value participates in many multiply-adds, so the Tensor Cores stay saturated. The inefficiency lies in the elementwise and reduction ops around them.

questions.section: Why LLM kernels are so often memory-bound
questions.question: Why can the many small elementwise and reduction ops between transformer matmuls eat a large share of wall-clock time despite having few FLOPs?
options: Each one is dispatched to the CPU instead of the GPU, adding a PCIe round trip
Each one recomputes the whole forward pass from scratch to get its inputs back
Each reads a big activation from HBM and writes it back, a bandwidth-bound trip
Each one forces the GPU into fp64 precision, which runs at a fraction of peak
questions.explanation: Ops like bias add, GELU, dropout, LayerNorm, residual add and softmax do tiny arithmetic per element but read and write whole activation tensors in HBM. Their arithmetic intensity is near the floor, so their runtime is set by bandwidth, and summed together they cost a lot.

questions.section: Why LLM kernels are so often memory-bound
questions.question: Which attention-related cost is singled out as a crucial memory-bound part of the transformer forward pass?
options: Loading the Q, K and V weight matrices, which are kept in fp32
The softmax and the reading/writing of the T x T score matrix
The positional embedding lookup repeated at every layer
The token embedding matmul over the whole vocabulary
questions.explanation: Among the memory-bound tail, the attention softmax and the T x T score matrix traffic stand out, since that matrix grows quadratically with sequence length. FlashAttention is designed specifically to stop touching HBM for it.

questions.section: Why LLM kernels are so often memory-bound
questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches the next GPU-performance tools to the memory-bound problem?
options: Roofline/fusion: measure and cut round trips; profiler/mixed precision: find kernels, halve bytes; FlashAttention: skip HBM
Roofline/fusion: halve bytes and add FLOPs; profiler/mixed precision: fuse kernels; FlashAttention: raise score precision
Roofline/mixed precision: find hot kernels; fusion: halve bytes per element; FlashAttention: move scores to host RAM
Profiler/fusion: change dtypes; roofline: avoid HBM entirely; FlashAttention: time kernels and approximate the softmax
questions.explanation: The roofline quantifies memory-bound versus compute-bound and fusion cuts HBM round trips. The profiler finds the offending kernels and mixed precision halves the bytes moved. FlashAttention rebuilds attention so the score matrix never goes to HBM.

questions.section: 5. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — where a tensor physically lives
questions.question: What does a PyTorch tensor's device attribute tell you physically on a GPU system?
options: How many bytes each element occupies, such as 4 for fp32
How many elements the tensor holds across all its dimensions
Which SM will execute the next operation on the tensor
Which memory holds the bytes: host RAM, or GPU N's HBM
questions.explanation: device says where the bytes are stored: 'cpu' means host RAM and 'cuda:0' means the HBM of GPU 0. Bytes per element is the dtype, and element count comes from the shape.

questions.section: 5. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — where a tensor physically lives
questions.question: What physically happens when you call x.to('cuda') on a CPU tensor?
options: The tensor is marked as GPU-ready but stays in host RAM until first use, at no cost
The tensor is moved into the L2 cache of every SM
The tensor's dtype is converted to bf16 for the GPU
The tensor's bytes are copied across the PCIe bus into the GPU's HBM
questions.explanation: x.to('cuda') performs a real copy across the slow PCIe link into HBM. Because that transfer is slow, data should be moved to the GPU once and kept there. It does not change the dtype.

questions.section: 5. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — where a tensor physically lives
questions.question: How does a tensor's dtype affect GPU performance?
options: It only affects numerical accuracy and has no effect on the bytes each op must move
It decides which SM the tensor is stored on, and so which SM runs ops that use it
It sets bytes per element, so it fixes both HBM storage and bytes moved per op
It sets the number of elements in the tensor, and so how many threads are launched
questions.explanation: dtype fixes the element size: fp32 is 4 bytes and bf16/fp16 are 2 bytes. That size multiplies both storage and the bandwidth cost of every op reading or writing the tensor, so halving it halves both — the core performance argument for mixed precision.

questions.section: 5. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — where a tensor physically lives
questions.question: How is the total byte size of a PyTorch tensor computed?
options: numel() divided by element_size()
numel() times element_size()
The product of the shape dimensions only, ignoring dtype
element_size() times the number of dimensions
questions.explanation: The total bytes are the number of elements (from the shape) times bytes per element (from the dtype). The shape alone gives element count but not bytes.

questions.section: 5. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — where a tensor physically lives
questions.question: Why did the GPT-2-small logits tensor of shape (8, 1024, 50257) in fp32 dominate the activation memory bucket?
options: It is about 1.65 GB, written to HBM by the final matmul and read back by the loss
It is kept in host RAM and must cross the PCIe bus twice in every training step
It is stored in fp64 by default, which doubles its size relative to the hidden states
It is recomputed from scratch in every layer, so its traffic is multiplied by n_layer
questions.explanation: 8 x 1024 x 50257 x 4 bytes is about 1.65 GB. That much data is written to HBM and read back by the loss, so its size directly sets its HBM cost and memory footprint. Its large vocabulary dimension is what makes it so big.

questions.section: 5. Tensor shapes, dtype, device — where a tensor physically lives
questions.question: What does F.gelu(x) do on the GPU for an activation x of shape (B, T, 4C) in HBM?
options: A kernel reads every element of x from HBM, does a few FLOPs each, and writes y back
GELU runs entirely inside the L2 cache, so x and y never need to touch HBM at all
PyTorch sends x to the CPU, applies GELU there with SIMD, and copies the result back
GELU runs on the Tensor Cores as a matrix multiply against a precomputed lookup table
questions.explanation: The GELU kernel reads x from HBM, computes a handful of FLOPs per element in registers, and writes y back. Bytes moved are a full read plus a full write, with tiny arithmetic, making it a textbook memory-bound kernel and a prime fusion candidate.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what happens when you call one PyTorch op on the GPU
questions.question: When PyTorch runs c = a + b on CUDA tensors, what is the first thing that happens?
options: The GPU immediately starts reading a and b from HBM without the CPU being involved
PyTorch copies a and b back to host RAM so it can check their shapes and dtypes
The SMs JIT-compile a new kernel from the Python source of the expression a + b
PyTorch's C++ dispatcher selects the CUDA kernel for that op and dtype
questions.explanation: The Python call goes into PyTorch's C++ dispatcher, which picks the right kernel (here elementwise add for fp16 on CUDA). Then PyTorch launches that kernel, which the GPU schedules across its SMs.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what happens when you call one PyTorch op on the GPU
questions.question: Why is launching thousands of tiny GPU kernels slow?
options: Each launch reloads the model weights from host RAM before the kernel can start
Each launch forces the GPU to clear and re-zero the HBM regions it will write
Each launch has a fixed overhead of a few microseconds, however little work it does
Each launch can only use a single SM, so thousands of kernels serialize on one SM
questions.explanation: Every kernel launch costs a few microseconds of fixed overhead. With thousands of tiny kernels this overhead adds up, which is one reason fusing ops into fewer kernels helps.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what happens when you call one PyTorch op on the GPU
questions.question: In c = a + b for fp16 tensors of shape (4096, 4096), what is the approximate arithmetic intensity and what does it imply?
options: About 170 FLOPs/byte, above the ~150 ridge, so the kernel is compute-bound
About 0.17 FLOPs/byte, far below the ~150 ridge, so the kernel is memory-bound
About 1.7 FLOPs/byte, just at the ridge for fp16, so the kernel is balanced
About 150 FLOPs/byte, right at the ridge, so it runs near peak FLOP/s
questions.explanation: The add does one FLOP per element (~1.7x10^7 FLOPs) while moving two reads and one write of 2-byte elements (~100 MB). That gives ~0.17 FLOPs/byte, hopelessly below the ~150 ridge, so runtime is set by HBM bandwidth.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what happens when you call one PyTorch op on the GPU
questions.question: For an elementwise add that moves about 100 MB on an A100, what sets its runtime?
options: Peak FLOP/s: about 1.7x10^7 FLOPs / 312 TFLOP/s, well under a microsecond
HBM bandwidth: about 100 MB / 2 TB/s ≈ 50 µs, with the math hidden behind it
Kernel launch overhead alone, since one launch dwarfs any data the add moves
PCIe bandwidth: about 100 MB / 64 GB/s, since the inputs come from host RAM
questions.explanation: Because the kernel is memory-bound, its runtime is essentially bytes moved divided by HBM bandwidth, about 50 microseconds. The arithmetic is essentially free and overlaps with the memory traffic. PCIe is not involved since the tensors are already in HBM.

questions.question: Why does a GPU want thousands of threads in flight even though it can physically execute only a limited number at once?
options: Extra warps hide memory latency: the scheduler runs others while some wait on HBM
More resident threads raise the clock speed of each SM through dynamic boosting
Each extra thread brings its own share of HBM bandwidth, so total bandwidth grows
The GPU driver rejects any kernel launched with fewer than a thousand threads
questions.explanation: The extra threads are latency hiding, not raw throughput. When a warp stalls on a slow HBM read, the SM switches to another ready warp. With too few warps, the units idle during every stall and utilization collapses.

questions.question: A GELU over a (B, T, 4C) activation does few FLOPs per element. What is the fix for its cost, as previewed for the roofline/fusion discussion?
options: Rewrite GELU with a cheaper approximation so it does fewer FLOPs per element
Run GELU on the CPU in parallel so the GPU is free for the next matmul
Assign more SMs to the GELU kernel so its arithmetic finishes sooner
Fuse GELU with the bias add and dropout so intermediates stay on chip
questions.explanation: GELU is memory-bound: its cost is the HBM round trip of a big tensor, not its arithmetic. Fusing it with bias add and dropout means one HBM read and one write instead of three round trips. Reducing FLOPs would barely help since arithmetic is not the bottleneck.

questions.question: Why is the roofline model useful before attempting a GPU optimization?
options: It shows whether a kernel is bandwidth- or compute-bound, so whether a fix can help
It guarantees a 2x speedup for any kernel it is applied to, once the ridge is known
It replaces the need to ever profile a training run, since it predicts exact timings
It automatically rewrites memory-bound kernels so that they run on the Tensor Cores
questions.explanation: The roofline is a back-of-envelope diagnosis. If a kernel is memory-bound, more FLOP/s does nothing and you must move fewer bytes; if compute-bound, the reverse. Getting this right separates optimizations that double throughput from ones that change nothing.

questions.question: If a kernel is memory-bound, what effect does buying a GPU with more peak FLOP/s (or using lower-precision matmul arithmetic) have on it?
options: It speeds up proportionally to the increase in peak FLOP/s
It makes the kernel compute-bound automatically, since the roof moves up
It slows the kernel down because of higher clock overhead
Essentially none; you must move fewer bytes to speed it up
questions.explanation: A memory-bound kernel is limited by how fast bytes arrive, not by arithmetic. Raising the compute ceiling does not lift the bandwidth ceiling it is pinned under. Only reducing bytes moved (fusion, smaller dtypes, better reuse) helps.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: two ways a kernel can be slow
questions.question: What are the two fundamentally different reasons a GPU kernel can be slow?
options: It uses too many registers per thread, or it launches too few threads per warp, starving the SM
It runs in fp32 instead of bf16, or it runs in fp16 and overflows its accumulators
Too much arithmetic for the units (compute-bound), or data too slow from HBM (memory-bound)
It has too many Python lines per step, or it uses too few concurrent CUDA streams
questions.explanation: Either the arithmetic units are the limit even with instant data (a huge matmul, compute-bound), or the arithmetic is trivial and HBM bandwidth is the limit (an elementwise add, memory-bound). Which regime you are in decides which optimizations can help.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: two ways a kernel can be slow
questions.question: Which kernel is the canonical example of being limited by having too much arithmetic?
options: An elementwise add of two tensors
A huge matrix multiply
A dropout mask applied per element
A bias add broadcast over a batch
questions.explanation: A large matmul does so many FLOPs per byte that even with instant data, the arithmetic units' FLOP/s rate is the ceiling. Elementwise ops like add, dropout and bias add are memory-bound.

questions.question: How is the arithmetic intensity (AI) of a kernel defined?
options: Total bytes moved to/from HBM divided by the total FLOPs the kernel does
Total FLOPs the kernel does divided by total bytes it moves to/from HBM
Peak FLOP/s of the GPU divided by its HBM bandwidth in bytes per second
Number of threads launched divided by the number of SMs that run them
questions.explanation: AI = FLOPs / bytes moved to or from HBM, measured in FLOPs per byte. It answers how much useful arithmetic each expensive byte buys. Peak FLOP/s divided by bandwidth is the ridge point, a property of the hardware, not of the kernel.

questions.question: What does a high arithmetic intensity indicate about a kernel?
options: Each expensive byte moved is spread over many cheap FLOPs, so it tends to be compute-bound
The kernel moves many bytes for every FLOP it does, so it starves waiting for data
The kernel will always run slower than a low-AI kernel, since it does more arithmetic
The kernel must be running in fp64, since only double precision reaches high arithmetic intensity
questions.explanation: High AI means lots of arithmetic per byte, which keeps the units busy: compute-bound. Low AI means each byte is barely used before the next is needed, so the units starve: memory-bound.

questions.question: In computing arithmetic intensity, which data movement counts in the 'bytes moved' denominator?
options: All reads and writes at every level of the hierarchy, including register traffic
Only the traffic between host RAM and the GPU across the PCIe or NVLink link
Only HBM traffic; data kept in registers or SRAM does not count
Only the writes back to HBM, since the reads are absorbed by the L2 cache
questions.explanation: The denominator is traffic to the slow memory level, HBM. Data staying in registers or SRAM is not counted. That is exactly why fusion and FlashAttention raise AI: they keep data on-chip so it never adds to the byte count.

questions.question: Is arithmetic intensity a property of the hardware or of the algorithm?
options: Of the hardware; it is fixed by the GPU model's FLOP/s and bandwidth alone
Of the driver version; it changes as CUDA updates alter the kernel launch path
Of the algorithm; it can be computed on paper before launching a kernel
Of the batch size only, independent of which operation the kernel performs
questions.explanation: AI depends on how many FLOPs the computation does and how many bytes it must move, which is a property of the algorithm. The hardware sets the ridge point it is compared against. You can compute AI before running anything.

questions.section: 3. Worked example A: elementwise add (very low AI → memory-bound)
questions.question: For c = a + b with fp32 vectors of length n, what are the FLOPs and HBM bytes moved?
options: 2n FLOPs and 8n bytes (a multiply and an add per element; read a and b)
n FLOPs and 8n bytes (read a and read b; the write of c is not counted)
n FLOPs and 12n bytes (read a, read b, write c at 4 bytes each)
n^2 FLOPs and 12n bytes (every element of a meets every element of b)
questions.explanation: One add per element gives n FLOPs. Reading a and b and writing c, each 4n bytes in fp32, totals 12n bytes. So AI = 1/12 ≈ 0.083 FLOPs/byte.

questions.section: 3. Worked example A: elementwise add (very low AI → memory-bound)
questions.question: Why does the arithmetic intensity of an elementwise add not depend on the vector length n?
options: Because GPUs process all vectors in fixed-size chunks of 32, one per warp
FLOPs and bytes both scale linearly with n, so n cancels in the ratio
Because vectors longer than a few MB are automatically cached in the L2
Because the FLOP count is constant regardless of n, while bytes stay fixed
questions.explanation: FLOPs = n and bytes = 12n, so AI = n/12n = 1/12. The intensity is fixed by the computation's structure — one FLOP per 12 bytes — not its size. Making the vector bigger does not help.

questions.section: 3. Worked example A: elementwise add (very low AI → memory-bound)
questions.question: Roughly what fraction of A100 peak FLOP/s can an fp32 elementwise add achieve?
options: About 0.06%
About 50%
About 6%
About 100%
questions.explanation: AI ≈ 0.083 against a ridge of ~150 means roughly 0.083/150 ≈ 0.06% of peak. The kernel is almost purely bandwidth-limited, so its runtime is bytes moved divided by HBM bandwidth.

questions.section: 3. Worked example A: elementwise add (very low AI → memory-bound)
questions.question: Which transformer operations have arithmetic intensity in the same tiny neighbourhood as an elementwise add?
options: The QKV projection and MLP matmuls, which read large weight matrices
Only the vocabulary head matmul, because its output has V columns
The embedding lookup and the AdamW optimizer step, but no op in the forward pass
Bias add, GELU, dropout, residual add, and LayerNorm's scale-and-shift
questions.explanation: All these elementwise ops do roughly one FLOP or a few per element while making a full HBM round trip, giving AI around 0.1 FLOPs/byte. Individually cheap in FLOPs, together they are a real cost. The weight matmuls are the high-AI exception.

questions.section: 4. Worked example B: a large matmul (high AI → compute-bound)
questions.question: How many FLOPs does a matmul of an (n x k) matrix by a (k x n) matrix take?
options: n^2k
2nk
2n^2k
questions.explanation: Each of the n^2 output elements is a length-k dot product: k multiplies and k adds, i.e. 2k FLOPs. Total 2n^2k, which for square matrices (k = n) is 2n^3.

questions.section: 4. Worked example B: a large matmul (high AI → compute-bound)
questions.question: In the ideal case, what is the arithmetic intensity of a square fp32 matmul C = AB with all matrices n x n?
options: 1/12 FLOPs/byte
n^2/6 FLOPs/byte
n/6 FLOPs/byte
6/n FLOPs/byte
questions.explanation: FLOPs = 2n^3; bytes = read A, read B, write C = 3n^2 x 4 = 12n^2. AI = 2n^3/12n^2 = n/6. For n = 1024 that is ~171 FLOPs/byte.

questions.section: 4. Worked example B: a large matmul (high AI → compute-bound)
questions.question: Why does the arithmetic intensity of a square matmul grow with its size n?
options: Larger matrices are stored in lower precision
FLOPs grow as n^3 while the data grows only as n^2
Larger matrices fit better in registers
Both FLOPs and data grow as n^2, but caches improve with size
questions.explanation: The FLOP count is 2n^3 but only 3n^2 elements are moved, so their ratio is proportional to n. Bigger matmuls therefore reuse each byte over more FLOPs and have higher intensity.

questions.section: 4. Worked example B: a large matmul (high AI → compute-bound)
questions.question: A 1024 x 1024 fp32 matmul has AI of about 171 FLOPs/byte. On an A100, what is it, and which change would speed it up?
options: Compute-bound; faster or lower-precision arithmetic would help, faster HBM would not
Memory-bound; faster HBM would help, while faster or lower-precision arithmetic would not
Memory-bound; fusing it with neighbouring elementwise ops would cut its bytes
Compute-bound; moving its operands to host RAM would free up HBM bandwidth
questions.explanation: 171 is above the A100 ridge of ~150, so the matmul sits on the flat compute ceiling. Its limit is FLOP/s, so lower-precision Tensor Cores or faster arithmetic help. Faster HBM addresses a limit it is not hitting.

questions.section: 4. Worked example B: a large matmul (high AI → compute-bound)
questions.question: What fundamental asymmetry makes deep learning fast on GPUs?
options: Matmul, the dominant cost, has AI that rises with size, so it is compute-bound
Elementwise ops have rising arithmetic intensity, while matmuls stay fixed at 1/12
Matmuls move no bytes at all once weights are cached, so their cost is purely FLOPs
GPUs have more bandwidth than compute, so every kernel ends up compute-bound
questions.explanation: Large matmuls naturally achieve high AI, putting the dominant workload on the good side of the roofline. The performance problem is the elementwise and reduction work around the matmuls, which stays at fixed low AI.

questions.section: 4. Worked example B: a large matmul (high AI → compute-bound)
questions.question: What is it that buys arithmetic intensity?
options: Tensor size: bigger tensors always have higher intensity
Fewer kernel launches, each covering more of the model
Using fp32 instead of fp16, so each byte carries more
Reuse: using each loaded value in many computations
questions.explanation: Matmuls reuse each loaded value across a whole row or column of outputs; elementwise ops use each value once. Reuse — not tensor size — is what raises FLOPs per byte. A huge elementwise add still has AI ≈ 1/12.

questions.question: What is the roofline model's formula for attainable FLOP/s?
options: max(P_max, B x AI), with P_max peak FLOP/s and B HBM bandwidth
P_max x B / AI, with P_max the peak FLOP/s and B the HBM bandwidth
min(P_max, B x AI), with P_max peak FLOP/s and B HBM bandwidth
B / (P_max x AI), with P_max peak FLOP/s and B HBM bandwidth
questions.explanation: Performance is capped by the lower of two ceilings: peak compute P_max, and bandwidth times intensity B x AI. You can only feed B bytes/s and each byte yields AI FLOPs, so B x AI is the bandwidth-limited rate.

questions.question: On a roofline plot, what does the compute ceiling look like?
options: A slanted line rising with arithmetic intensity until it meets the ridge
A flat line at peak FLOP/s that no kernel exceeds at any intensity
A vertical line at the ridge point, separating the two kernel regimes
A curve that falls as intensity increases past the hardware's ridge point
questions.explanation: The compute ceiling P_max is horizontal: no matter how high your AI, you cannot beat peak arithmetic rate. The slanted line is the bandwidth ceiling B x AI.

questions.question: On a roofline plot, why does the bandwidth ceiling rise with arithmetic intensity?
options: Higher-intensity kernels are served from faster memory levels such as L2 and SRAM
You feed only B bytes/s and each byte yields AI FLOPs, so FLOP/s is B times AI
Higher intensity raises the GPU's boost clock, so more FLOPs complete per second
Effective bandwidth increases when fewer bytes are moved, so the line slopes up
questions.explanation: The bandwidth ceiling is B x AI. At fixed bandwidth, getting more FLOPs out of each byte means more FLOP/s, so the line slopes upward until it hits peak compute.

questions.question: On what axes is the roofline usually plotted?
options: Arithmetic intensity on x and attainable FLOP/s on y, both log scale
Wall-clock time on x and memory usage on y, both on a linear scale
Batch size on x and training loss on y, with loss on a log scale
Bytes moved on x and the number of active SMs on y, both on a log scale
questions.explanation: With AI on the x-axis and attainable FLOP/s on the y-axis (log-log), the two ceilings form a rising diagonal meeting a flat cap. A kernel sits under the roofline at its own AI.

questions.question: Where is the ridge point of the roofline?
options: At AI = B / P_max, where the compute ceiling meets the bandwidth ceiling
At AI = 1 FLOP/byte on every GPU, since one FLOP needs at least one byte
At the AI of the largest matmul in the model, which sets that GPU's limit
At AI = P_max / B, where the bandwidth ceiling meets the compute ceiling
questions.explanation: The lines cross where B x AI = P_max, so AI_ridge = P_max / B. It is a hardware property: peak FLOP/s divided by bandwidth.

questions.question: What is the A100's ridge point using its 2039 GB/s HBM bandwidth and 312 TFLOP/s bf16 peak?
options: About 9.6 FLOPs/byte
About 683 FLOPs/byte
About 153 FLOPs/byte
About 0.083 FLOPs/byte
questions.explanation: 312x10^12 / 2039x10^9 ≈ 153. Using the rounded 2 TB/s gives ~156. The 9.6 figure is the ridge for plain fp32 compute (19.5 TFLOP/s).

questions.question: A kernel's AI is below the ridge point. Which optimizations can make it faster?
options: Only buying a GPU with higher peak FLOP/s, since it is under the compute roof
Only reducing the number of FLOPs it performs, for example with approximations
Moving fewer bytes: fusion, lower precision, better reuse, or higher AI
Only switching to faster Tensor Cores or lower-precision matmul arithmetic
questions.explanation: Below the ridge the kernel is on the slanted bandwidth line and memory-bound. Only fewer bytes or higher AI moves it up. Extra peak FLOP/s or fewer FLOPs does not lift the bandwidth limit.

questions.question: A kernel's AI is above the ridge point. Which optimizations can make it faster?
options: Buying a GPU with more HBM bandwidth at the same peak FLOP/s
Doing fewer FLOPs or using faster/lower-precision arithmetic
Fusing it with neighbouring elementwise ops to save HBM bytes
Moving its inputs to pinned host memory to free HBM traffic
questions.explanation: Above the ridge the kernel sits on the flat compute ceiling. Its limit is arithmetic, so fewer FLOPs or faster arithmetic helps. More bandwidth or fewer bytes addresses a limit it is not hitting.

questions.section: Placing our two examples on the roofline
questions.question: What is the attainable FLOP/s of an elementwise add (AI ≈ 0.083) on an A100?
options: About 1.7x10^11 FLOP/s, roughly 0.05% of the 312 TFLOP/s peak
About 312 TFLOP/s, the full peak, since adds are the cheapest op
About 150 TFLOP/s, half of peak, set by the warp issue rate
About 1.7x10^14 FLOP/s, about half of the bf16 Tensor Core peak
questions.explanation: B x AI = 2x10^12 x 0.083 ≈ 1.7x10^11 FLOP/s. The arithmetic is almost entirely idle; the GPU is acting as a bandwidth machine for this kernel.

questions.section: Placing our two examples on the roofline
questions.question: How does a square matmul's position on the A100 roofline change as n grows from 64 to 1024 to 4096?
options: Its AI stays at 1/12 regardless of n, so it never leaves the memory-bound slope
Its AI falls as n grows, so it slides down the slope into memory-bound territory
It sits on the flat roof at every n, because matmuls are compute-bound by their very nature
Its AI rises (~10.7, 171, 683): it climbs the slope, crosses the ridge, then levels off
questions.explanation: AI = n/6 gives ~10.7 at n=64 (memory-bound), ~171 at 1024 and ~683 at 4096 (both compute-bound). Once past the ridge, extra intensity does not raise attainable FLOP/s, since the compute cap is flat.

questions.section: Placing our two examples on the roofline
questions.question: Why can the same kernel become more memory-bound when moved from an A100 to an H100?
options: The H100 has less HBM bandwidth than the A100, so every kernel slows down
The H100 lacks Tensor Cores for fp32 work, so the kernel falls back to the slower CUDA cores
The H100 counts register traffic as HBM traffic, lowering the measured AI
The H100's peak FLOP/s grew faster than its bandwidth, so its ridge moved right
questions.explanation: The ridge is P_max / B. On the H100, peak compute increased more than bandwidth, so the ridge sits at higher AI. A kernel at fixed AI that was near the ridge on A100 can fall to the memory-bound side on H100.

questions.section: Placing our two examples on the roofline
questions.question: On the A100 roofline, where does LayerNorm sit, given an AI of about 2 FLOPs/byte?
options: On the flat compute ceiling, since normalization is reduction-heavy
Exactly at the ridge point, where both ceilings limit it equally
On the memory-bound slope, far left of the ~153 ridge
Above the compute ceiling, because its FLOPs run in registers
questions.explanation: AI ≈ 2 is far below ~153, so LayerNorm is deep in memory-bound territory, alongside elementwise ops. Its position does not improve with tensor size, because its AI is fixed by the computation.

questions.section: 6. Kernel fusion: raise AI by not writing intermediates to HBM
questions.question: What is the most important practical way to make a memory-bound elementwise chain faster?
options: Rewriting each op with a cheaper approximation so it uses fewer FLOPs
Kernel fusion, so intermediates are not written to and read back from HBM
Running each op in fp64, so that every byte moved carries more useful arithmetic
Splitting each op into more, smaller kernels so more SMs work in parallel
questions.explanation: The roofline says memory-bound kernels need fewer bytes moved. Fusion achieves that by performing the chain in one kernel with intermediates kept in registers. Fewer FLOPs would not help a bandwidth-limited kernel.

questions.section: 6. Kernel fusion: raise AI by not writing intermediates to HBM
questions.question: Unfused, what HBM traffic do bias add, GELU and dropout generate for an fp16 activation tensor of M elements?
options: About 12M bytes: each of the three ops reads and writes 2M bytes
About 4M bytes: one read and one write of 2M bytes for the chain
About 6M bytes: each op reads its 2M-byte input but writes in place
About 36M bytes: each op reads all three tensors and writes three
questions.explanation: Each op reads its input (2M bytes) and writes its output (2M bytes), 4M bytes per op, and three ops give ~12M bytes, for only a few FLOPs per element.

questions.section: 6. Kernel fusion: raise AI by not writing intermediates to HBM
questions.question: When bias add, GELU and dropout are fused into one kernel, where do the intermediates h and g live?
options: In registers on the SM; they never leave the chip
In HBM, but written in a compressed fp8 format to save traffic
In pinned host RAM, reached over the PCIe link
In the L2 cache, evicted to HBM after the kernel
questions.explanation: The fused kernel reads z once, does bias, GELU and dropout in registers, and writes y once. The intermediate tensors h and g never reach HBM, cutting traffic to about 4M bytes.

questions.section: 6. Kernel fusion: raise AI by not writing intermediates to HBM
questions.question: By how much does fusing bias add, GELU and dropout change HBM traffic and arithmetic intensity?
options: Traffic halves and arithmetic intensity halves, since FLOPs drop with bytes
Traffic stays the same but FLOPs drop by a third, since bias is folded in
Traffic triples and intensity falls to a third, because tiles are re-read
Traffic falls to one third and arithmetic intensity triples, same FLOPs
questions.explanation: Fused traffic is 4M bytes versus 12M unfused, a third, while FLOPs are unchanged. AI = FLOPs/bytes therefore triples, sliding the kernel up its bandwidth line toward the ridge.

questions.section: 6. Kernel fusion: raise AI by not writing intermediates to HBM
questions.question: Besides reducing HBM traffic, what other saving does fusing three elementwise kernels into one give?
options: It removes the need for an optimizer step on the fused parameters
It lets the fused kernel run on the CPU while the GPU does matmuls
It removes two of the three kernel launches and their fixed cost
It halves the number of FLOPs, since bias and GELU share a multiply
questions.explanation: Each kernel launch has a few microseconds of fixed overhead. Fusing three kernels into one removes two launches. The FLOPs remain the same.

questions.section: 6. Kernel fusion: raise AI by not writing intermediates to HBM
questions.question: Why can kernel fusion not speed up an already compute-bound matmul?
options: Because fusion always increases FLOPs by recomputing the fused intermediates twice
It is limited by the arithmetic ceiling, so cutting HBM traffic does not help
Because a matmul cannot be placed inside a fused kernel with other operations
Because fusion only lowers launch overhead, which a single matmul barely has
questions.explanation: Fusion lowers bytes moved, which helps kernels under the bandwidth ceiling. A compute-bound matmul sits on the flat compute cap, so reducing its HBM traffic changes nothing. Fusion is the lever for the memory-bound tail.

questions.section: 6. Kernel fusion: raise AI by not writing intermediates to HBM
questions.question: What does torch.compile with TorchInductor actually do to a run of pointwise ops?
options: Converts them to fp64 kernels for accuracy and then dispatches each one separately
Fuses them into one generated kernel (often Triton): one HBM read and one write
Offloads them to the CPU so the GPU can focus entirely on the large matmuls
Removes them from the graph entirely by folding them into the adjacent matmul weights
questions.explanation: TorchInductor generates one fused kernel for a run of elementwise ops, often through Triton. Its effect is the byte-count reduction of fusion. Knowing that predicts when compile will help: a memory-bound tail a lot, a compute-bound kernel little.

questions.section: 6. Kernel fusion: raise AI by not writing intermediates to HBM
questions.question: In a roofline explorer, as more elementwise ops are added to a chain, how do the unfused and fused dots move?
options: The unfused dot stays put; the fused dot slides right, since its bytes stay fixed
Both dots slide left by the same amount, because each added op brings more bytes with it
The unfused dot slides right while the fused dot stays put at one read and write
Both dots move up onto the compute ceiling once the chain has enough FLOPs in it
questions.explanation: Unfused, every added op is another full round trip, so FLOPs and bytes grow together and AI stays constant. Fused, FLOPs grow but bytes stay fixed, so AI rises and the dot moves right.

questions.section: 7.1 The chain we want to fuse
questions.question: Standard attention for one head is a chain of which three kernels?
options: Bias add, GELU and dropout, applied to the attention scores
LayerNorm, the QK matmul, and a residual add of the values
The Q projection, the K projection and the V projection
