S = QK^T/sqrt(d) (matmul), P = softmax(S), O = PV (matmul)
questions.explanation: Standard attention computes the scores S with a matmul, applies row-wise softmax to get P, and multiplies by V to get O. S and P are written to and read from HBM between kernels.

questions.section: 7.1 The chain we want to fuse
questions.question: For one attention head, what sizes are Q, K, V, O and the intermediates S and P?
options: All six are T x d, including S and P
Q, K, V, O are T x T; S and P are T x d
Q, K, V, O are T x d; S and P are T x T
All six are d x d, including S and P
questions.explanation: Inputs and output are T x d, but the scores and probabilities are T x T. That quadratic size is what makes attention's intermediates so expensive.

questions.section: 7.1 The chain we want to fuse
questions.question: For one head with T = 4096, d = 64 and fp16, roughly how large is the score matrix S?
options: About 0.5 MB
About 2 MB
About 33.5 MB
About 34 GB
questions.explanation: 4096^2 x 2 bytes ≈ 33.5 MB, compared with ~0.5 MB for each of Q, K, V, O. 34 GB is the size of a T x T matrix at T = 131,072.

questions.section: 7.1 The chain we want to fuse
questions.question: For standard attention with T = 4096 and d = 64, what are its approximate arithmetic intensity and roofline regime on an A100?
options: About 124 FLOPs/byte; compute-bound near peak on the flat roof
About 32 FLOPs/byte; memory-bound, at most about 21% of peak
About 0.083 FLOPs/byte; memory-bound, at about 0.05% of peak
About 683 FLOPs/byte; compute-bound, well past the ~153 ridge
questions.explanation: About 4.3 GFLOP over ~136 MB of traffic gives AI ≈ 32, left of the ~153 ridge. The bandwidth ceiling caps it near 21% of peak.

questions.section: 7.1 The chain we want to fuse
questions.question: In standard attention with T = 4096 and d = 64, what fraction of HBM bytes are the S and P intermediates?
options: About 98%
About 2%
About 50%
About 25%
questions.explanation: Writing and reading S and P is ~134 MB of the ~136 MB total; the inputs and outputs are only ~2 MB. Those intermediates are not needed once the output is computed, which is exactly what fusion targets.

questions.section: 7.2 Why section 6's fusion does not work as-is
questions.question: Why can softmax not be fused the same simple way as GELU?
options: Softmax needs fp64 exponentials, which cannot be computed in registers on the SM
Softmax has almost no FLOPs, so there is nothing to gain by fusing it at all
Each softmax output needs the max and sum over a whole row of T scores
Softmax must run on the CPU, because the exp function is not available in CUDA
questions.explanation: gelu(h_i) depends only on h_i, so chunks can be processed independently. P_ij = exp(S_ij - m_i) / sum_k exp(S_ik - m_i) needs the row max m_i and the row sum over all T scores before producing any output.

questions.section: 7.2 Why section 6's fusion does not work as-is
questions.question: Why does a block of 128 query rows of the score matrix not fit on chip for T = 4096?
options: It is only 16 KB, but shared memory cannot hold floating-point values at all
It fits in SRAM, but registers are too slow to read it at the needed rate
It is kept in host RAM by the driver and cannot be moved onto the SM
In fp32 it is 2 MB, versus ~164 KB of SRAM per SM, and it grows with T
questions.explanation: 128 rows x 4096 columns x 4 bytes is 2 MB, about 12x the ~164 KB of SRAM per SM, and it grows linearly with T. Unlike GELU's intermediates, attention's intermediates do not fit on chip.

questions.section: 7.2 Why section 6's fusion does not work as-is
questions.question: Why is processing attention one query row at a time a bad way to make it fit on chip?
options: One row of 4096 fp32 scores is 16 MB, which is too large to fit in an SM's SRAM
It requires approximating the softmax, since a row's max is not known in advance
Each row re-reads all of K and V from HBM: ~4 GB at T = 4096, ~30x worse
It increases the number of FLOPs by a factor of T, since each row redoes QK^T
questions.explanation: One row of 4096 scores is 16 KB and fits, but every one of 4096 rows would read all of K and V (~1 MB) again, ~4 GB total. Tiny tiles destroy data reuse, and reuse is what buys arithmetic intensity.

questions.question: How does FlashAttention tile attention so the work fits in SRAM?
options: It cuts the vocabulary into tiles and processes each tile in a separate kernel
It keeps blocks of B_q query rows in SRAM and streams K, V tiles past each block
It splits each head's d dimensions across several GPUs so each fits in SRAM
It keeps the whole T x T score matrix in the L2 cache so that HBM is never touched
questions.explanation: Each kernel instance owns a Q block (say 128 rows) held in SRAM and streams K and V tiles of B_k rows past it. A 128 x 128 fp32 score tile is 64 KB and fits on chip.

questions.question: In FlashAttention's tiling, why does each K, V tile get high data reuse?
options: Each K, V tile is used by all B_q query rows of the block: matmul-like reuse
Each K, V tile is loaded only once for the whole model and kept on chip
Each K, V tile stays in registers across all layers of the forward pass
Each K, V tile is shared across all heads, since heads use the same keys
questions.explanation: With 128 query rows in SRAM, every K, V tile streamed in participates in 128 rows of computation. That keeps arithmetic intensity high, unlike the one-row-at-a-time approach.

questions.question: What state does online softmax keep for each query row?
options: A running max m, a running sum l, and a running output accumulator
The full row of T scores, kept in SRAM until the row is complete
Only the final probabilities, written to HBM after each K, V tile
A random sample of the scores used to estimate the row's maximum
questions.explanation: Online softmax tracks a running maximum, running sum of exponentials and an output accumulator per row. This removes the need to see the whole row of scores at once.

questions.question: When online softmax encounters a tile with a larger max than seen before, what does it do?
options: Discards all previous tiles and restarts the row from the first tile
Ignores the new tile's max and keeps using the old one for stability
Approximates the new values by clamping them to the old maximum
Rescales what it has accumulated so far by exp(m_old - m_new)
questions.explanation: Previous exponentials were computed relative to the old max. Multiplying the accumulators by exp(m_old - m_new) re-expresses them relative to the new max, keeping the result exact.

questions.question: Is the result of online softmax an approximation of the true softmax?
options: Yes; it drops scores far below the running max to save SRAM space
Yes; it uses a low-rank approximation of the score matrix per tile
No; after dividing by the running sum, it is exactly the full softmax
Yes; it estimates the row sum from the tiles seen so far and stops early
questions.explanation: Online softmax rescales its accumulators exactly whenever the max changes and divides by the running sum at the end. The output equals full-row softmax, not an approximation.

questions.question: How does FlashAttention's backward pass avoid storing the T x T probability matrix P?
options: It approximates the gradients with a low-rank sketch, so P is never needed
It recomputes score tiles from Q, K and saved m, l, trading FLOPs for bytes
It stores P in pinned host RAM between forward and backward, off the GPU
It skips the backward pass for attention entirely and only updates the MLP weights
questions.explanation: Backward recomputes score tiles from Q, K and the saved per-row statistics. This trades extra FLOPs, which are cheap, for not storing and re-reading T x T bytes, which are expensive — a roofline decision.

questions.question: For T = 4096, d = 64 and B_q = 128, how many times does FlashAttention stream K and V?
options: Once per query row, 4096 times
T / B_q = 32 times
T = 4096 times, once per key
d = 64 times, once per dim
questions.explanation: Each of the 4096/128 = 32 query blocks streams K and V once, about 33.6 MB in total. That plus Q and O gives ~35 MB of traffic.

questions.question: What is FlashAttention's approximate HBM traffic and arithmetic intensity for T = 4096, d = 64, B_q = 128?
options: About 35 MB and about 124 FLOPs/byte, versus 136 MB and 32 for standard
About 136 MB and about 32 FLOPs/byte, the same as standard attention
About 4 GB and about 1 FLOP/byte, because K and V are re-read for every row
About 2 MB and about 2000 FLOPs/byte, since only Q, K, V, O are moved
questions.explanation: Reading Q, writing O (~1 MB) plus 32 passes of K and V (~33.6 MB) gives ~35 MB for the same 4.3 GFLOP. AI ≈ 124, lifting it from ~21% to ~81% of peak.

questions.question: What is the bigger win of FlashAttention, beyond reduced HBM traffic?
options: FLOPs drop from O(T^2) to O(T), since only the needed tiles are computed
Attention no longer needs the K and V matrices after the first query block
Training no longer needs a backward pass through the attention layers
Memory held drops from O(T^2) to O(T), since the T x T matrix never exists
questions.explanation: Because S and P are never materialized, attention memory is O(T). At T = 131,072 a single fp16 T x T matrix would be ~34 GB per head per layer, so without this long context does not fit.

questions.question: In FlashAttention, what still grows like T^2, and what drops to O(T)?
options: The memory held still grows like T^2; the K, V traffic drops to O(T)
Both the K, V traffic and the memory held drop to O(T) with tiling
K, V re-read traffic still grows like T^2; the memory held drops to O(T)
Neither changes with T; only the FLOPs drop, from O(T^2) to O(T)
questions.explanation: K and V are re-read T/B_q times, so traffic is still quadratic, but scaled by d/B_q, about 4x below standard attention's S/P traffic here. What becomes linear is the memory held.

questions.question: As T grows, how do the arithmetic intensities of standard attention and FlashAttention behave?
options: Both rise linearly with T, since longer rows give more reuse per byte
Standard attention's AI rises with T while FlashAttention's falls with T
Both barely move (about d/2 and B_q), while the standard T x T matrix grows
Both fall toward zero, since K and V traffic grows faster than the FLOPs
questions.explanation: Standard attention's AI stays around d/2 and FlashAttention's around B_q regardless of T. The dramatic change with T is the size of the standard version's score matrix, from megabytes to tens of gigabytes.

questions.question: Which summary correctly describes FlashAttention?
options: A sparse approximation of attention that skips scores below a learned threshold
Fusion of the whole attention chain with tiling, online softmax and recompute
A compiler pass that fuses only the elementwise ops around the attention matmuls
A way to run attention in fp64 for accuracy while keeping fp16 memory traffic
questions.explanation: Fusion is the goal: never write S or P to HBM. Tiling makes intermediates fit in SRAM with high reuse, online softmax computes softmax tile by tile exactly, and backward recomputes instead of storing P.

questions.question: A LayerNorm over M fp16 elements reads M elements, writes M elements and does about 8 FLOPs per element. What is its arithmetic intensity?
options: 2 FLOPs/byte
8 FLOPs/byte
0.5 FLOPs/byte
16 FLOPs/byte
questions.explanation: Bytes = 2M read + 2M write = 4M; FLOPs = 8M. AI = 8M/4M = 2 FLOPs/byte, far below the A100 ridge, so it is memory-bound.

questions.question: What dominates a LayerNorm's cost on an A100, and what helps?
options: Its ~8 FLOPs per element; reducing its arithmetic helps most
Its kernel launch; running it on the CPU removes that cost
Its weight matrix; quantizing the gain and bias weights helps
Two HBM passes over the tensor; fusing with its neighbour helps
questions.explanation: With AI ≈ 2, LayerNorm is memory-bound. Its cost is streaming the tensor in and out of HBM. Fusing its output into the next kernel avoids writing and re-reading the normalized tensor; faster arithmetic would change nothing.

questions.question: Why does rewriting a softmax or LayerNorm kernel to use fewer arithmetic operations barely change its runtime?
options: It is compute-bound, so its runtime is set by FLOP/s, which fewer ops cannot raise
The arithmetic for these ops is performed on the CPU, so the GPU timing is unaffected
Its FLOPs run on Tensor Cores, which finish them in a negligible fraction of the time
It is memory-bound, so its runtime is set by bytes moved, not by its FLOPs
questions.explanation: Softmax and LayerNorm sit far left of the ridge. Their runtime is bandwidth-bound, so reducing arithmetic does not help. Always diagnose with arithmetic intensity before optimizing.

questions.question: Why would counting register and SRAM traffic in the AI denominator be a mistake?
options: Register traffic is always far larger than HBM traffic, so AI would collapse
SRAM traffic is measured in FLOPs rather than bytes, so the units would mix
Fusion would look useless, since it just moves traffic from HBM to on-chip memory
It would make every kernel appear compute-bound, hiding all memory bottlenecks
questions.explanation: AI is FLOPs per byte moved to and from the slow level. Fusion keeps intermediates in registers and SRAM; counting that traffic would erase its measured benefit. Only HBM traffic belongs in the denominator.

questions.question: Your bottleneck kernel is memory-bound. Why may buying a GPU with more peak FLOP/s but similar bandwidth give little gain?
options: Newer GPUs always ship with less bandwidth than older ones, so it gets slower
The kernel is under the bandwidth ceiling, which more peak FLOP/s does not raise
Peak FLOP/s figures only apply to fp64, so bf16 kernels never see the increase
More FLOP/s makes each kernel launch slower, offsetting any gain in arithmetic
questions.explanation: A memory-bound kernel needs more bandwidth or fewer bytes. Raising the compute ceiling leaves it where it is. State which ceiling you are under before buying hardware.

questions.question: Why can small matmuls (tiny batch, small hidden size) be memory-bound?
options: Matmul AI grows like n/6, so it is small when the dimensions are small
Small matmuls skip the Tensor Cores and so do almost no FLOPs at all
Small matmuls are always kept in host RAM and must cross PCIe each call
Small matmuls need a T x T intermediate that dominates their HBM traffic
questions.explanation: Compute-bound is not automatic for matmuls; it depends on size. With AI ≈ n/6, a matmul of n = 64 has AI ≈ 10.7, well below the ridge, so it is memory-bound.

questions.question: A kernel on an A100 (ridge ≈ 150) has AI = 4 FLOPs/byte and runs at 3% of peak FLOP/s. What should you conclude?
options: Expected: the roofline caps it near 2.6% of peak, so cut the bytes it moves
A bug: a kernel doing so few FLOPs per byte should run at peak FLOP/s
It is compute-bound at AI = 4 and needs faster or lower-precision Tensor Cores
It is limited by PCIe bandwidth, so its inputs should be moved to host memory
questions.explanation: B x AI = 2x10^12 x 4 = 8x10^12 FLOP/s ≈ 2.6% of 312 TFLOP/s, so ~3% is essentially at the bandwidth ceiling. Fuse with neighbours, use a smaller dtype, or reuse data on chip; optimizing its arithmetic is pointless.

questions.question: A colleague says 'FlashAttention is just torch.compile fusing the attention ops.' What is missing from that claim?
options: Nothing; torch.compile emits exactly FlashAttention's tiled kernel for any attention code it sees
FlashAttention is not fusion at all; it cuts FLOPs by skipping low-scoring blocks of keys
FlashAttention runs only on the CPU, while torch.compile generates fused GPU kernels
Plain fusion can't handle softmax's row dependency or SRAM size; it needs tiling and online softmax
questions.explanation: The goal is fusion: never send S or P to HBM. But elementwise fusion cannot do it, because softmax needs a full row of T scores and a block of those rows does not fit in SRAM. Tiling plus online softmax make it possible, exactly.

questions.question: Why is mixed precision described as the single highest-leverage change for LLM training performance?
options: It halves memory-bound traffic and activation memory, and unlocks 16-bit Tensor Cores
It removes the need for a full backward pass, since 16-bit gradients come from the forward
It halves the number of FLOPs in every matmul, since each multiply is on 16-bit values
It eliminates kernel launch overhead, because 16-bit kernels are fused automatically
questions.explanation: Switching most training to 16-bit halves the traffic of every memory-bound kernel, roughly halves the activation memory bucket, and lets Tensor Cores run at their fast 16-bit rate. The FLOP count of a matmul stays the same; it just runs on faster hardware.

questions.question: Which numeric format is nearly every modern LLM trained in?
options: Pure fp16 with no fp32 master copies
Pure fp64 for stability at scale
int8 throughout, with fp32 scales
bf16 mixed precision
questions.explanation: Modern LLM pretraining overwhelmingly uses bf16 mixed precision: bf16 for the throughput-critical work with fp32 master weights and accumulation. fp16 needs loss scaling and pure low precision loses updates.

questions.question: Why profile before optimizing a transformer training step?
options: Profiling automatically fuses the slowest kernels, so it must come before any manual changes
The roofline cannot be applied to transformers, so only a profile can say anything useful
A step runs thousands of kernels; the roofline says what fix fits, not which kernels matter
Profiling converts the model to bf16, which is required before other optimizations apply
questions.explanation: The roofline diagnoses the kind of fix but cannot tell you where time is actually spent. A profiler records each kernel's duration and CPU/GPU overlap for a real step, so you attack only the top of the list.

questions.question: What does torch.profiler record?
options: Only the total wall-clock time of the training loop, as a single summary number
Every operator and CUDA kernel with timestamps, as a sorted table or a timeline
Only the GPU memory capacity and the peak allocation reached during the profiled region
Only Python function call counts, grouped by the module that made each call
questions.explanation: torch.profiler wraps a code region and records every operator and kernel with timestamps. key_averages().table() prints a sorted summary and export_chrome_trace writes a trace for a timeline viewer.

questions.question: In torch.profiler, what does record_shapes=True add?
options: Python source line attribution for each op, so time maps back to code
Tensor shapes for each op, so you can tell which matmul a row refers to
Memory allocation tracking per op, attributing bytes to each operator
Automatic padding of each op's shapes to powers of two for faster kernels
questions.explanation: record_shapes keeps input shapes, distinguishing, for example, the MLP matmul from the vocab head. Python line attribution is with_stack=True, and allocation tracking is profile_memory=True.

questions.question: In torch.profiler, what does profile_memory=True do?
options: Tracks allocations, feeding the accounting of params, grads, optimizer state and activations
Prints the GPU's total HBM capacity and the memory the driver reserves for itself at startup
Disables the caching allocator so every free returns memory to the driver
Forces all tensors into fp16 so that the profile shows the run's minimum memory footprint
questions.explanation: profile_memory=True records allocations so you can attribute memory to operations, connecting the profile to the memory buckets of training.

questions.question: What does setting with_stack=True in torch.profiler enable?
options: Recording the input tensor shapes of every op
Tracking memory allocations made by each op
Profiling every GPU in the node at the same time
Attributing time to Python source lines
questions.explanation: with_stack=True records Python stack information so time can be attributed to source lines (and adds python_function events in the trace). It has extra overhead, so it is off by default.

questions.question: Why does a profiling snippet run a few steps rather than one?
options: Because the profiler cannot record a single step and needs at least two
To make the trace file smaller by averaging steps into one summary row
So the schedule warms up and the profiled steps are representative
Because the first step always runs on the CPU before moving to the GPU
questions.explanation: Running several steps lets the work settle into a steady pattern (for example, cuBLAS kernel selection happens in warm-up). Profiling only one cold step would mislead.

questions.question: What is the purpose of with record_function('train_step') inside a profiled loop?
options: It speeds up the step by fusing all kernels launched inside the span
It forces every op inside the span to run in fp16 under autocast
It creates a named span in the trace and table marking the step's work
It disables autograd for the span so the step can be timed cleanly
questions.explanation: record_function adds a labelled region visible in both the table and the timeline, and on the GPU row as a gpu_user_annotation. It is a label for analysis, not an optimization.

questions.question: In the profiler table, why does the same time appear twice, once on an aten:: row and once on a cryptically named row?
options: The profiler measures every kernel twice and reports both runs for accuracy
aten:: rows are PyTorch operators; the rows under them are the GPU kernels launched
One row is the forward time of the op and the other is its backward time
One row is the fp32 time of the op and the other is its time under fp16 autocast, side by side
questions.explanation: An aten:: operator like aten::mm launches a GPU kernel such as volta_sgemm_128x64_nt. The operator's CUDA time is the time of its kernel, so the same time shows on both rows; summing both would double-count.

questions.question: In a profile of a transformer training step, which operator is the forward of every nn.Linear, and which is the backward?
options: aten::addmm is the forward; aten::mm is the backward
aten::mm is the forward; aten::addmm is the backward
aten::bmm is the forward; aten::gelu is the backward
aten::linear for both
questions.explanation: nn.Linear's forward with bias is aten::addmm. Backward needs two matmuls per Linear (gradient w.r.t. input and w.r.t. weight), recorded as aten::mm, which is why mm has twice addmm's call count.

questions.question: In a 5-step profile of a model with 17 Linear layers, why does aten::addmm show 85 calls and aten::mm 170?
options: Each Linear runs 17 times per step, and backward doubles that count
aten::mm counts both the forward and backward of each Linear twice per step
The profiler counts each mm call twice, once on the CPU and once on the GPU
17 Linears x 5 steps = 85 forwards; backward does two matmuls each, so 170
questions.explanation: Forward: one addmm per Linear per step, 17 x 5 = 85. Backward: input gradient and weight gradient, two mm per Linear, 170.

questions.question: In a healthy transformer profile, what does it mean that the sgemm kernels make up about two thirds of GPU time?
options: The model is starving for data from the loader
The memory-bound tail dominates the step time
The profiler is double-counting the gemm rows
Compute-bound matmuls lead, the healthy picture
questions.explanation: Having large matmuls dominate means the GPU spends most of its time on compute-bound work. GELU, dropout and LayerNorm form the smaller memory-bound tail fusion would remove.

questions.question: Why must both ProfilerActivity.CPU and ProfilerActivity.CUDA be enabled when profiling?
options: CUDA activity cannot be recorded unless CPU activity is also recorded in the same run
CPU activity records the memory allocations, while CUDA activity records the shapes
The CPU launches kernels and the GPU runs them, so both timelines must line up
The profiler crashes when only one activity is enabled, so both are always required
questions.explanation: Work happens on two devices: Python and the dispatcher on the CPU queue kernels, the GPU executes them. Seeing both lets you detect gaps where the GPU waits for the CPU.

questions.question: Why does torch.cuda.synchronize() matter when timing GPU code manually?
options: It clears cached GPU memory so each timed region starts from the same state
CUDA is asynchronous, so without it a timer measures only kernel launches
It converts tensors to fp32 so the timed kernels run at a consistent precision
It forces the profiler to use fewer threads, so it does not distort the timing
questions.explanation: loss.backward() queues kernels and returns immediately. A wall-clock timer without synchronize stops before the GPU finishes, measuring launches only. The profiler uses CUDA events, but manual timing must synchronize or the numbers are fiction.

questions.section: 2.1 Run it yourself on a Colab T4
questions.question: What hardware does the self-contained profiling experiment target, and can it run on CPU?
options: A free Colab T4 GPU; it cannot run on CPU, since the point is to see GPU kernels
An 8x H100 node; it also runs on CPU in a few hours with a smaller model config
Any CPU; a GPU is optional and only shortens the runtime of the experiment
A TPU v4; it falls back to the CPU when no TPU is attached to the session
questions.explanation: The experiment uses a free Colab T4 (16 GB), runs in about a minute with under 2 GB of GPU memory, and requires a GPU since it profiles GPU kernels.

questions.section: 2.1 Run it yourself on a Colab T4
questions.question: In the 'starving GPU' experiment with batch 1 x 16 tokens, why is the GPU busy only a fraction of the wall time?
options: Every kernel is tiny, so the GPU finishes each before the CPU launches the next
The model is too large for the T4's 16 GB, so weights are paged in from host RAM
fp32 matmuls are disabled at small batch sizes, so cuBLAS falls back to slow loops
The profiler blocks the GPU after every kernel to read its hardware counters
questions.explanation: With tiny kernels, the GPU's work per kernel is shorter than the CPU's launch time, so the GPU sits idle between launches. This is the CPU-GPU gap.

questions.section: 2.1 Run it yourself on a Colab T4
questions.question: Why is fp16 (rather than bf16) used for the mixed-precision experiment on a Colab T4?
options: bf16 is slower than fp32 on every GPU, so it would hide the speedup
fp16 needs no GradScaler, which keeps the experiment's code simpler
bf16 cannot be used with autocast, which only supports fp16 on CUDA
The T4 has fp16 Tensor Cores but no bf16 hardware support
questions.explanation: The T4 (Turing) supports fp16 Tensor Cores but not bf16. bf16 requires Ampere or newer; on older GPUs, fp16 plus GradScaler is the fallback.

questions.section: 2.1 Run it yourself on a Colab T4
questions.question: Why does the profiling script run a few warm-up steps before profiling?
options: To download and cache the model weights and the tokenizer before the timed steps begin
To compile the Python model code into CUDA kernels on the first steps
cuBLAS picks kernels in the first steps, so warm-up makes the profile representative
To fill the GPU's HBM with zeros so that later allocations are not slowed by page faults
questions.explanation: Early steps include one-time costs such as cuBLAS selecting kernels. Running warm-up and synchronizing ensures the profile shows steady-state behaviour.

questions.section: 2.1 Run it yourself on a Colab T4
questions.question: When building a per-kernel breakdown from prof.key_averages(), why does the script drop rows starting with aten::, autograd:: or train_step?
options: Those rows are CPU-only bookkeeping and record no GPU time at all
Those rows repeat the time of the kernels they launched and would double-count
Those rows are always zero once the profiler has finished warm-up steps
Those rows describe memory allocations only, not any kernel execution time on the GPU
questions.explanation: Operator, autograd and annotation rows aggregate time already counted on their child kernel rows. Keeping only real kernels avoids double counting when summing GPU time.

questions.section: 2.1 Run it yourself on a Colab T4
questions.question: In the healthy T4 experiment, why are there exactly three gemm kernels each with 17 calls per step?
options: There are three attention heads per layer, each with its own matmul per Linear
Each of the 17 Linears does one forward and two backward matmuls, each a different layout
Each Linear is run three times in the forward pass because activation checkpointing is on
Three GPUs were used with data parallelism, and each one reports its own gemm kernel
questions.explanation: 17 Linears (4 per block x 4 blocks plus the head) each launch a forward gemm and two backward gemms (input grad, weight grad), giving three kernel variants with 17 calls each.

questions.section: 2.1 Run it yourself on a Colab T4
questions.question: In the starving experiment (8.3 ms wall, 1.7 ms GPU work per step), why would making kernels faster change nothing?
options: The GPU idles ~80% of the time waiting on launches, so the fix is fewer, bigger kernels
Because the kernels already run at peak FLOP/s, so there is no headroom left for any gain
Because the GPU is memory-bound on the PCIe link, which faster kernels cannot change
Because the profiler hides the true kernel time, so the measured gap is an artifact
questions.explanation: The bottleneck is CPU launch rate, not kernel speed. Bigger batches, fusion, torch.compile or CUDA graphs cut the number of launches and close the gaps.

questions.section: 2.1 Run it yourself on a Colab T4
questions.question: What do the digits in a kernel name like turing_fp16_s1688gemm indicate?
options: The number of SMs the kernel runs on, 1688
The cuBLAS kernel version number, 16.8.8
The output tile size, 16 x 88 elements per block
The Tensor-Core instruction shape, 16x8x8
questions.explanation: In fp16_s1688gemm, '1688' is the 16x8x8 Tensor-Core instruction shape. Its appearance signals the matmuls moved from fp32 CUDA cores to fp16 Tensor Cores.

questions.section: 2.1 Run it yourself on a Colab T4
questions.question: In the T4 mixed-precision experiment, why does the non-matmul share of GPU time rise from 27% to 44%?
options: The elementwise kernels became slower in fp16, since they must upcast every element
fp16 adds extra cast kernels to every layer, and those conversions dominate the step
The matmuls got much faster, so the unchanged memory-bound tail is a bigger share
The profiler misattributes fp16 matmul time to elementwise kernels on Turing GPUs
questions.explanation: The gemm kernels dropped from ~78 ms to ~20 ms per step. The memory-bound tail shrank less, so its share grew. After speeding up the compute-bound part, the memory-bound tail is the next target.

questions.section: 2.1 Run it yourself on a Colab T4
questions.question: What speedup did fp16 autocast give in the clean T4 timing of the small transformer?
options: About 1.1x
About 16x
About 2.7x
About 0.5x (it slowed down)
questions.explanation: Clean timing showed fp32 at ~121 ms/step and fp16 autocast at ~45 ms/step, a ~2.7x speedup, from both Tensor-Core matmuls and halved bytes.

questions.question: How is the 'GPU busy' percentage of a profiled run computed?
options: Number of kernels launched divided by the number of SMs available on the GPU
Sum of all GPU kernel durations divided by the profiled wall-clock time
Peak FLOP/s divided by the achieved FLOP/s over the profiled steps
It is read directly from the trace viewer's colour of the GPU row
questions.explanation: GPU busy = total kernel time / wall time. The numerator sums self_device_time_total over real kernel rows; the denominator is perf_counter around the steps with a synchronize at the end.

questions.question: Why is it legitimate to add kernel durations to get GPU busy time when all kernels run on one CUDA stream?
options: Kernels on one stream run one after another and never overlap, so the sum is busy time
Because kernels on one stream always run for the same duration, so sums are exact
Because the profiler automatically subtracts any overlap between kernels on the same GPU
Because a single stream uses only one SM, so no two kernels can share the hardware
questions.explanation: On one stream, kernels are serialized, so their summed durations are exactly the busy time. With multiple streams (e.g. overlapping communication), kernels overlap and the sum can exceed 100%; then measure per stream.

questions.question: In a chrome trace JSON, which event categories correspond to GPU work?
options: cpu_op and cuda_runtime, which mark the launch calls
user_annotation and python_function from the CPU
ac2g only, the arrows from each launch to its kernel
kernel, gpu_memcpy and gpu_memset
questions.explanation: GPU work events have cat 'kernel', 'gpu_memcpy' or 'gpu_memset'. cpu_op and cuda_runtime are CPU-side; ac2g are the CPU-to-GPU flow arrows.

questions.question: Why does a busy percentage computed from trace.json (first kernel start to last kernel end) come out slightly higher than the script's wall-time version?
options: The trace double-counts each kernel once on the CPU row and once on the GPU row
The trace uses milliseconds instead of microseconds, which inflates the computed busy ratio
The trace includes CPU ops such as cudaLaunchKernel in the GPU busy sum
The trace span omits the launch time before the first kernel that wall time includes
questions.explanation: The span starts at the first kernel, so it omits the launch time before it. The script's wall time includes that, so its denominator is bigger and its percentage smaller.

questions.question: In a trace, a large GPU idle gap immediately after a Memcpy DtoH almost always indicates what?
options: The data loader blocked the step while the next batch was prepared
A kernel was fused incorrectly and had to be relaunched by the runtime
A .item(), .cpu() or print(loss) forced a host synchronization
The GPU ran out of HBM and spilled activations to host memory
questions.explanation: Device-to-host copies come from pulling values to the CPU, which forces a sync and stalls the queue. A large hole at the start of every step instead usually points to the data loader.

questions.question: In a trace, a big GPU idle hole at the start of every training step usually means what?
options: A loss.item() call is forcing a sync
The data loader is blocking the step
The optimizer is running on the CPU
The matmuls are memory-bound
questions.explanation: Idle time at the start of each step suggests the GPU waits for the next batch. Holes after a DtoH memcpy point to a host sync like .item().

questions.section: How to tell matmul from attention from everything else
questions.question: In a GPU kernel name, what does 'gemm' indicate?
options: A General Matrix Multiply (C = AB), i.e. a matmul kernel
A gradient memory kernel that zeroes .grad before backward
A generic elementwise kernel generated by the JIT compiler
A GPU memory copy between HBM and the L2 cache of an SM
questions.explanation: gemm is the BLAS name for general matrix multiply. Names like volta_sgemm_128x64_nt, ampere_bf16_s16816gemm and cutlass_..._gemm are all matmuls.

questions.section: How to tell matmul from attention from everything else
questions.question: What does a kernel name containing 'gemv' usually indicate?
options: A matrix-vector multiply, typical of batch-1 inference decode
A fused attention kernel with the softmax folded into the GEMM
An optimizer update applied to many parameter vectors at once
A LayerNorm reduction computing the mean and variance per row
questions.explanation: gemv is matrix times vector, which appears when the batch is 1, as in inference decoding.

questions.section: How to tell matmul from attention from everything else
questions.question: In kernel names such as fmha_cutlassF_... and fmha_cutlassB_..., what do F and B mean?
options: Float32 and bfloat16 variants of the same attention kernel
First and best kernel variants chosen by the autotuner
Fill and broadcast phases of the attention mask setup
Forward and backward of a fused attention kernel
questions.explanation: fmha kernels are fused multi-head attention (scores, softmax and weighted sum in one kernel). F denotes forward and B backward.

questions.section: How to tell matmul from attention from everything else
questions.question: In a vectorized_elementwise_kernel name, how do you tell which elementwise op it is?
options: The thread count in the name, which is unique to each elementwise op
The prefix volta_ or ampere_, which encodes the op for that generation
The functor in angle brackets, e.g. GeluCUDAKernelImpl or MulFunctor
It cannot be determined from the name; only the shapes reveal the op
questions.explanation: The template argument names the operation: GeluCUDAKernelImpl is GELU, MulFunctor a multiply, FillFunctor a fill (zeroing, e.g. from zero_grad).

questions.section: How to tell matmul from attention from everything else
questions.question: Which kernel name indicates the optimizer, such as a foreach AdamW update?
options: fmha_cutlassF
multi_tensor_apply
cunn_SoftMaxForward
vectorized_layer_norm_kernel
questions.explanation: multi_tensor_apply kernels update many parameters per launch, which is how foreach optimizers like AdamW are implemented.

questions.section: How to tell matmul from attention from everything else
questions.question: What is cunn_SoftMaxForward typically in a language-model training profile?
options: The QK^T attention-score matmul, the largest kernel in the step
The log-softmax inside cross-entropy, part of the memory-bound tail
The optimizer step that normalizes each parameter's update
A host-to-device copy of the next batch's token IDs
questions.explanation: cunn_SoftMaxForward is the softmax kernel, commonly the log-softmax inside cross-entropy. Softmax, layer_norm, reduce_kernel and fused_dropout are the memory-bound tail.

questions.section: How to tell matmul from attention from everything else
questions.question: In a cuBLAS kernel name like volta_sgemm_128x64_nt running on a T4, what does the 'volta_' prefix mean?
options: The GPU generation the kernel was written for, reused on Turing for fp32
The GPU generation currently running the kernel, here reported as Volta
That the kernel uses Volta-style Tensor Cores for its multiply-accumulates
That the kernel is a voltage-control routine run alongside each matmul
questions.explanation: The prefix names the architecture the kernel was written for, not the one you have. cuBLAS reuses Volta fp32 kernels on the Turing T4 because Turing added nothing new for fp32.

questions.section: How to tell matmul from attention from everything else
questions.question: What does the 's' in 'sgemm' mean?
options: Sparse matrix, using 2:4 structured sparsity
Shared memory only, with no HBM reads at all
Streamed across all SMs in a single wave
Single precision (fp32), on ordinary CUDA cores
questions.explanation: sgemm is single-precision gemm on CUDA cores. h means half (fp16); names like fp16_s1688gemm or bf16_s16816gemm are Tensor-Core kernels.

questions.section: How to tell matmul from attention from everything else
questions.question: In volta_sgemm_128x64_nt, what does '128x64' describe?
options: The sizes of the two input matrices, 128 and 64 rows
The number of SMs and warps the kernel launches with
The output tile that each thread block computes
The Tensor-Core instruction shape used for each step
questions.explanation: 128x64 is the output tile per thread block, the tiling idea from the GPU hierarchy. The Tensor-Core shape appears as digits like 1688 in fp16 kernel names.

questions.section: How to tell matmul from attention from everything else
questions.question: What do the suffixes nt, nn and tn in gemm kernel names indicate?
options: The number of threads and the number of tiles in each thread block
Whether the kernel belongs to the forward pass or the backward pass
Whether the first and second operands are read normal or transposed
Whether the result and the accumulator are stored as fp16 or fp32
questions.explanation: Each letter refers to an operand being normal or transposed. One nn.Linear produces three layouts: forward Y = XW^T, and in backward dL/dX = (dL/dY)W and dL/dW = (dL/dY)^T X.

questions.section: How to tell matmul from attention from everything else
questions.question: If attention is computed by hand (q @ k.transpose, softmax, @ v), what do you see in the profile instead of an fmha kernel?
options: A single flash_fwd_kernel, since SDPA is called under the hood anyway
Batched gemm kernels launched by aten::bmm, plus a softmax kernel
Only elementwise kernels, because the matmuls are folded into them
A Memcpy kernel per head, as q, k and v are copied into one buffer
questions.explanation: Unfused attention runs as batched matmuls (names with batched or strided, from aten::bmm) and a softmax kernel. The names say 'matmul'; you recognise it as attention only from the launching op and shapes.

questions.section: How to tell matmul from attention from everything else
questions.question: How can you find out which CPU operator launched a cryptically named GPU kernel in the profiler table?
options: Look at the parent aten:: operator, such as aten::addmm, aten::mm or aten::bmm
Check the kernel's tile size, which maps one-to-one to the operator that launched it
Count the kernel's calls and match the count to the number of layers in the model
It is impossible without reading the CUDA source of every kernel in the library
questions.explanation: Every kernel has a parent CPU op with a readable name. addmm is a forward Linear, mm a backward Linear, bmm a batched matmul, and _efficient_attention_forward or _scaled_dot_product_flash_attention fused attention.

questions.section: How to tell matmul from attention from everything else
questions.question: How can you see which specific matmul a profiler row refers to, by its shapes?
options: Use with_stack=True and sort by CPU time to see each matmul's call site
Use profile_memory=True, since allocation sizes reveal each operand's shape
Export to trace.json and count the rows per kernel to match the layers
Use record_shapes=True and key_averages(group_by_input_shape=True)
questions.explanation: Grouping by input shape (with shapes recorded) splits rows per shape. A shape like [16,256,512] x [2048,512] identifies the first MLP layer of a d=512 model, and [4096,8000] the vocab head.

questions.section: How to tell matmul from attention from everything else
questions.question: In a trace viewer, how do you trace a GPU kernel back to the CPU call that queued it?
options: Read the kernel's tile dimensions and match them to the op's tensor shapes
Look at the kernel's start time and pick the CPU op that ran just before it
Follow the flow arrow (correlation ID) from the kernel to its cudaLaunchKernel
Check the GPU's stream number, which equals the thread ID of the CPU caller
questions.explanation: Clicking a kernel shows a correlation ID; an arrow (flow event) connects it to the cudaLaunchKernel on the CPU row, which sits inside the aten:: op that wanted it.

questions.section: What you see in the trace viewer
questions.question: In a PyTorch trace, why does the CPU main thread show one long backward block doing nothing but waiting?
options: The backward pass runs entirely on the GPU, so the CPU has nothing to launch
The main thread is blocked by the data loader prefetching the next batch
backward() hands the graph to autograd's engine thread, which launches the ops
The profiler pauses CPU recording during backward to keep its overhead low
questions.explanation: The autograd engine runs backward on a separate C++ worker thread (one per GPU). All the ...Backward0 ops and backward kernel launches appear on that thread; the main thread just waits.

questions.section: What you see in the trace viewer
questions.question: Why is there typically only one GPU row in a simple training trace?
options: The GPU has only one SM visible to the profiler at a time
All kernels were queued on the default CUDA stream
The profiler merges all CUDA streams into a single row
Only forward kernels are shown on the GPU row by default
questions.explanation: The GPU row is labelled with a stream number; with everything on one default stream there is a single row, which is also why summing durations gives busy time.

questions.section: What you see in the trace viewer
questions.question: What is a train_step bar of category gpu_user_annotation on the GPU row of a trace?
options: The record_function span mirrored onto the GPU as a label, not GPU work itself
A real GPU kernel that runs the whole training step as one fused launch
A host-to-device memory copy of the batch, labelled with the step name
An error marker the profiler inserts whenever a step exceeds its expected time budget
questions.explanation: record_function spans are mirrored on the GPU as gpu_user_annotation bars. They are labels, not work; naming spans data, forward, backward, optim makes the GPU row a readable map.

questions.section: What you see in the trace viewer
questions.question: When clicking a block in a trace viewer, what is Self Time?
options: Wall Duration minus the time covered by blocks nested inside it
The time the block spent on the CPU only, excluding GPU work
The time from the start of the trace to the start of the block
The time from the block's end until the next kernel starts
questions.explanation: Self Time excludes nested children. A kernel has no children, so its Self Time equals its Wall Duration. A large Self Time on an annotation means much of its window has no nested kernel: idle GPU or kernels on another row.

questions.section: What you see in the trace viewer
questions.question: In a trace viewer, what does an External id on a clicked block let you do?
options: Identify which SM ran the kernel and how many warps it used
Set the kernel's stream priority for the next profiled step
Export only that block and its children to a separate trace
Jump to the matching CPU-side event that has the same id
questions.explanation: External id links GPU-side blocks to the CPU event with the same id; search for it to find the corresponding op.

questions.section: What you see in the trace viewer
questions.question: What does the trace event category 'ac2g' represent?
options: Accumulated GPU gradients, written once per backward pass
A CUDA caching-allocator event for a device-side allocation
The arrows linking an async CPU launch to its GPU kernel
An annotation that appears on the CPU timeline only
questions.explanation: ac2g stands for async CPU to GPU: the flow link from a launch to the kernel it produced.

questions.section: What you see in the trace viewer
questions.question: Why is 'the GPU row looks solid when zoomed out' not enough to declare a trace healthy?
options: The viewer hides all gaps by design, so even long stalls never show up as white space
Gaps of a few microseconds are sub-pixel at that zoom, so compute the busy percentage
A solid colour on the GPU row means the GPU is thermally throttling during the step
Zooming out shows only CPU events, so the GPU row is not actually being displayed
questions.explanation: A 4-microsecond gap is invisible zoomed out. 'No gaps' only means 'no big gaps', so compute the busy fraction and zoom in to see individual kernels.

questions.section: What you see in the trace viewer
questions.question: In a healthy trace, how do the launch-to-kernel arrows slant, and what does it mean?
options: They are vertical, because each kernel starts the instant it is launched
They lean right, because the CPU runs ahead and queues work for the GPU
They lean left, because kernels are scheduled before their launch calls
There are no arrows at all in a healthy trace, only in a starving one
questions.explanation: When the CPU runs ahead, kernels execute well after launch, so arrows slant right. In a starving trace they are nearly vertical: each kernel runs as soon as launched and the GPU then waits.

questions.section: What you see in the trace viewer
questions.question: Why is Perfetto recommended over chrome://tracing for viewing trace.json?
options: chrome://tracing is deprecated and slow on big traces; Perfetto stays fast at hundreds of MB
Perfetto is the only viewer that can open JSON traces; chrome://tracing needs a protobuf file
chrome://tracing cannot show GPU rows, so kernel timing is only visible in Perfetto
Perfetto automatically closes the GPU gaps it finds and writes a corrected trace file
questions.explanation: Perfetto opens the same trace file, scales to very large traces and supports drag-selecting a region to compute busy fraction.

questions.section: 3. Reading the trace: hot kernels and CPU↔GPU gaps
questions.question: In a profiler table, what does it suggest if elementwise, LayerNorm, softmax or copy kernels are near the top?
options: Healthy compute-bound behaviour, as these kernels feed the matmuls
The model is too small for the GPU, so the batch should be lowered
The GPU's Tensor Cores are broken and work fell back to CUDA cores
A memory-bound tail that fusion or torch.compile should collapse
questions.explanation: In a healthy step the big matmuls lead. If low-intensity kernels dominate, the step is wasting time on HBM round trips that fusion can eliminate.

questions.section: 3. Reading the trace: hot kernels and CPU↔GPU gaps
questions.question: What is a CPU-GPU gap in a profiler timeline?
options: A period where the CPU is idle while the GPU is busy computing queued kernels
The time spent copying the model weights from host RAM to HBM at startup
White space on the GPU track: the GPU has drained its queue and waits on the CPU
A gap between two GPUs in a cluster while they wait for an all-reduce to finish
questions.explanation: A gap means the GPU has no queued work, waiting on launch, a forced sync (.item(), .cpu()), or the data loader. MFU is lost to no kernels rather than slow ones.

questions.section: 3. Reading the trace: hot kernels and CPU↔GPU gaps
questions.question: A training loop calls print(loss) or loss.item() every step and the trace shows GPU gaps. What is the fix?
options: Increase the learning rate so fewer steps, and so fewer syncs, are needed
Use more HBM so the logged values can stay resident on the device
Log less often: accumulate on device and call .item() only occasionally
Switch the model to fp64 so the loss can be printed without a sync
questions.explanation: Each .item() or print forces a host sync that drains the GPU queue. Logging every N steps keeps the GPU fed.

questions.section: 3. Reading the trace: hot kernels and CPU↔GPU gaps
questions.question: Which fix addresses GPU gaps caused by a Python-heavy loop that cannot launch kernels fast enough?
options: Add more data-loader workers and prefetch batches with pinned memory
Fuse ops or use torch.compile to launch fewer, bigger kernels
Use a lower learning rate so each step needs fewer launches
Disable the profiler, since its hooks cause the launch delay
questions.explanation: If launches are the bottleneck, reducing their number with fusion or compilation closes the gaps. More data-loader workers addresses a different cause.

questions.section: 3. Reading the trace: hot kernels and CPU↔GPU gaps
questions.question: Which fixes address GPU gaps caused by a data loader blocking the step?
options: More num_workers, prefetching and pinned memory
torch.compile and fusion to cut kernel launches
Using bf16 instead of fp32 for the input batches
Calling torch.cuda.synchronize() more often
questions.explanation: A blocking loader is solved by parallel loading, prefetching and pinned memory for faster host-to-device copies.

questions.question: Why does storing tensors in a 16-bit format instead of fp32 move fewer bytes?
options: 16-bit formats are compressed automatically on write
16-bit tensors live in registers instead of HBM
16-bit tensors are never written back to HBM
fp32 uses 4 bytes per number; 16-bit formats use 2
questions.explanation: Halving the dtype halves every tensor's storage and traffic, which helps memory-bound kernels, activation memory, and Tensor-Core throughput.

questions.section: Two different mechanisms: fewer bytes vs a higher ceiling
questions.question: In the runtime model t ≈ max(FLOPs/P_max, bytes/B), what does halving bytes do?
options: Shrinks the first term, which helps only compute-bound kernels
Shrinks both terms equally, so every kernel speeds up by 2x
Raises P_max, since 16-bit data feeds the Tensor Cores faster
Shrinks the second term, which helps only memory-bound kernels
questions.explanation: Halving bytes reduces bytes/B. That matters only if it is the larger term, i.e. for memory-bound kernels.

questions.section: Two different mechanisms: fewer bytes vs a higher ceiling
questions.question: In the runtime model t ≈ max(FLOPs/P_max, bytes/B), what does switching to the 16-bit Tensor-Core path do?
options: Lowers B and shrinks the second term, helping memory-bound kernels
Halves the FLOP count, shrinking the first term for every kernel
Raises P_max and shrinks the first term, helping compute-bound kernels
Has no effect on either term, since only storage dtype matters
questions.explanation: The 16-bit Tensor-Core path increases peak FLOP/s, reducing FLOPs/P_max. This only matters if compute is the binding limit.

questions.section: Two different mechanisms: fewer bytes vs a higher ceiling
questions.question: On an A100, what are P_max for plain fp32 and for bf16 Tensor Cores?
options: 312 TFLOP/s for both fp32 and bf16
19.5 TFLOP/s for fp32, 312 TFLOP/s for bf16
2 TB/s for fp32 and 3.3 TB/s for bf16
9.6 TFLOP/s for fp32, 153 TFLOP/s for bf16
questions.explanation: Plain fp32 on CUDA cores peaks at 19.5 TFLOP/s; bf16 Tensor Cores at 312. The 9.6 and 153 values are the corresponding ridge points in FLOPs/byte.

questions.section: Two different mechanisms: fewer bytes vs a higher ceiling
questions.question: For an n = 4096 matmul on an A100 in fp32, what happens if you only halve the bytes (16-bit storage, fp32 arithmetic)?
options: Zero speedup: the ~7 ms compute term dwarfs the memory term
About a 2x speedup, since halving the bytes halves the runtime
About a 16x speedup, since 16-bit data feeds the Tensor Cores
It becomes memory-bound, so the runtime roughly doubles instead
questions.explanation: Compute takes ~7.05 ms and memory ~0.1 ms. Halving memory to ~0.05 ms leaves the max at 7.05 ms. You shrank a term that was not the bottleneck.

questions.section: Two different mechanisms: fewer bytes vs a higher ceiling
questions.question: For an n = 4096 matmul on an A100, roughly what speedup comes from moving fp32 arithmetic to bf16 Tensor Cores?
options: About 16x, all from the higher compute ceiling
About 2x, all from halving the bytes moved
None, since the matmul is already memory-bound
About 1.5x, limited by the fp32 accumulation inside each tile
questions.explanation: Compute drops from ~7.05 ms to ~0.44 ms (19.5 to 312 TFLOP/s) while memory stays small, so runtime ≈ 0.44 ms, ~16x faster.

questions.section: Two different mechanisms: fewer bytes vs a higher ceiling
questions.question: For a memory-bound elementwise add of 10^8 elements on an A100, what does switching from fp32 to bf16 storage do?
options: Gives about a 16x speedup, since the add now runs on Tensor Cores
Has no effect, since the add's runtime is set by its FLOP count
Doubles the runtime, because bf16 adds need extra rounding steps
Roughly halves runtime (~0.59 to ~0.29 ms), all from halved bytes
questions.explanation: The memory term dominates; halving bytes from 12 to 6 per element halves it. Elementwise ops do not run on Tensor Cores, so faster arithmetic does nothing.

questions.section: Two different mechanisms: fewer bytes vs a higher ceiling
questions.question: Why does a faster arithmetic unit not help an elementwise add?
options: Elementwise adds are compute-bound, so they already run at the arithmetic peak
Elementwise adds are executed on the CPU, so GPU arithmetic speed is irrelevant
Its compute term is tiny, and there is no matmul for Tensor Cores to speed up
Tensor Cores make elementwise ops slower, because they must pad to 16x16 tiles
questions.explanation: The add's compute term is microseconds versus a memory term of hundreds of microseconds. There is no matmul for Tensor Cores to accelerate.

questions.section: Two different mechanisms: fewer bytes vs a higher ceiling
questions.question: On the roofline, what does halving the bytes do to a kernel's position, and which kernels benefit?
options: It halves AI, moving the dot left; compute-bound kernels may turn memory-bound
It doubles AI: memory-bound dots climb the slope, compute-bound ones gain nothing
It raises the flat roof, so every kernel gains the same 2x speedup from the change
It moves all kernels to the ridge, balancing compute and bandwidth for each one
questions.explanation: Halving bytes doubles FLOPs/byte. An elementwise add (0.083 to 0.167) climbs the bandwidth line; an n=4096 matmul (683 to 1365) slides along the flat cap, no higher.

questions.section: Two different mechanisms: fewer bytes vs a higher ceiling
questions.question: What does the bf16 Tensor-Core path do to the roofline picture?
options: It steepens the bandwidth line, so memory-bound dots rise with the same AI
It raises the roof (19.5 to 312 TFLOP/s), lifting only compute-bound dots
It moves memory-bound dots to the right, since 16-bit halves their bytes
It lowers the ridge point, so more kernels end up on the compute-bound side
questions.explanation: The Tensor-Core path increases P_max, raising the horizontal ceiling. Memory-bound kernels under the slanted line do not benefit.

questions.section: Two different mechanisms: fewer bytes vs a higher ceiling
questions.question: Why does the A100 ridge point depend on dtype?
options: The ridge is P_max/B, and P_max is ~19.5 TFLOP/s in fp32 vs ~312 in bf16
Because HBM bandwidth doubles in bf16, which moves the ridge to the left
Because the ridge is defined per tensor, from the bytes per element of its dtype
It does not depend on dtype; only the kernels' own AI values shift
questions.explanation: With P_max of 19.5 TFLOP/s for fp32 the ridge is ~9.6; with 312 TFLOP/s for bf16 it is ~153. Changing dtype changes which side of the ridge a kernel sits on.

questions.section: Two different mechanisms: fewer bytes vs a higher ceiling
questions.question: Why is an n = 256 matmul compute-bound in fp32 but memory-bound in bf16 on an A100?
options: bf16 increases its FLOP count, because each product must be rounded twice
fp32 matmuls are never memory-bound, while every bf16 matmul is memory-bound
bf16 halves the effective HBM bandwidth, pushing the kernel under the slope
Its AI (~43 fp32, ~85 bf16) is above the fp32 ridge (9.6), below bf16's (153)
questions.explanation: In bf16, Tensor Cores collapse the compute term so much that bytes become the limit, and the halved bytes keep that limit at 0.19 µs instead of 0.39 µs. Such a kernel needs both wins.

questions.section: Two different mechanisms: fewer bytes vs a higher ceiling
questions.question: Why are many small, skinny matmuls (small heads, small inference batches) bandwidth-limited in bf16?
options: Small matmuls cannot use bf16, so they fall back to slow fp32 CUDA cores
Small matmuls are dispatched to the CPU, so PCIe bandwidth becomes the limit
bf16 Tensor Cores raise the ridge to ~153, and small matmuls' AI is below it
Small matmuls are always compute-bound, so bandwidth only limits large ones
questions.explanation: Once the compute term is collapsed by Tensor Cores, small matmuls with modest AI are limited by the bytes they move.

questions.section: Two different mechanisms: fewer bytes vs a higher ceiling
questions.question: Before predicting what mixed precision will buy a particular kernel, what should you do?
options: Assume a 2x speedup for every kernel, since all bytes are halved
Check only its FLOP count, since Tensor Cores speed up all FLOPs
Place it on the roofline: left of the ridge bytes, right of it FLOP/s
Check only its memory footprint, since activations halve in 16-bit
questions.explanation: Halved bytes help memory-bound kernels; Tensor Cores help compute-bound ones. Which applies depends on the kernel's position relative to the ridge.

questions.section: Two different mechanisms: fewer bytes vs a higher ceiling
questions.question: What is mixed precision, as opposed to making everything 16-bit?
options: Alternating between fp16 and bf16 every step so neither format's errors accumulate
Running error-tolerant matmul ops in 16-bit while sensitive parts stay in fp32
Using fp32 for the forward pass and fp16 for the backward pass, where errors matter less
Storing the weights in int8 and the activations in fp16, with fp32 only for the loss
questions.explanation: Some ops lose too much accuracy in 16-bit. Mixed precision keeps them in fp32 while fast, tolerant ops run in 16-bit; torch.autocast automates the per-op choice.

questions.section: 5. The four formats: dynamic range vs precision
questions.question: In a floating-point format, what do the exponent bits and mantissa bits respectively determine?
options: Exponent sets the dynamic range; mantissa sets the precision
Exponent sets the precision; mantissa sets the dynamic range
Both set the range; precision comes from the sign bit alone
Exponent sets the sign and scale; mantissa sets the range
questions.explanation: More exponent bits allow larger and smaller magnitudes; more mantissa bits give more significant digits within a magnitude.

questions.section: 5. The four formats: dynamic range vs precision
questions.question: What is the bit split of fp32?
options: 1 sign, 5 exponent, 10 mantissa
1 sign, 8 exponent, 7 mantissa
1 sign, 11 exponent, 52 mantissa
1 sign, 8 exponent, 23 mantissa
questions.explanation: fp32 uses 8 exponent and 23 mantissa bits, giving range up to ~3.4x10^38 and eps ~1.2x10^-7. 5/10 is fp16, 8/7 is bf16, 11/52 is fp64.

questions.section: 5. The four formats: dynamic range vs precision
questions.question: What is tf32?
options: A 19-bit storage format that halves weight memory compared with fp32
A 16-bit storage format with fp32's 8 exponent bits and a 7-bit mantissa
A synonym for fp16 used in NVIDIA's Tensor-Core documentation
A Tensor-Core mode: 8 exponent bits, 10-bit mantissa; storage stays fp32
questions.explanation: tf32 is not a storage format: tensors stay fp32 in memory, and only the matmul rounds internally to a 10-bit mantissa. It gives a big matmul speedup almost free and is controlled by torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32.

questions.section: 5. The four formats: dynamic range vs precision
questions.question: What is the bit split of fp16?
options: 1 sign, 8 exponent, 7 mantissa
1 sign, 8 exponent, 23 mantissa
1 sign, 5 exponent, 10 mantissa
1 sign, 6 exponent, 9 mantissa
questions.explanation: fp16 has 5 exponent and 10 mantissa bits: finer precision than bf16 but a narrow range, max 65504.

questions.section: 5. The four formats: dynamic range vs precision
questions.question: What is the bit split of bf16?
options: 1 sign, 5 exponent, 10 mantissa
1 sign, 8 exponent, 7 mantissa
1 sign, 7 exponent, 8 mantissa
1 sign, 8 exponent, 10 mantissa
questions.explanation: bf16 keeps fp32's 8 exponent bits and has 7 mantissa bits, so it has fp32's range but coarser precision. 8/10 describes tf32's compute mode.

questions.section: 5. The four formats: dynamic range vs precision
questions.question: What is the largest finite value representable in fp16?
questions.explanation: fp16's max is 65504; anything larger overflows to inf. fp32 and bf16 go up to about 3.4x10^38.

questions.section: 5. The four formats: dynamic range vs precision
questions.question: What is fp16's smallest normal value, below which values start underflowing?
options: About 6.1x10^-5
About 7.8x10^-3
About 9.8x10^-4
questions.explanation: fp16's smallest normal is ~6.1x10^-5. fp32 and bf16 share ~1.18x10^-38. 7.8x10^-3 and 9.8x10^-4 are the eps values of bf16 and fp16.

questions.section: 5. The four formats: dynamic range vs precision
questions.question: What is the relative precision (eps) of bf16, and roughly how many significant decimal digits does that give?
options: About 1.2x10^-7, roughly 7 digits
About 9.8x10^-4, roughly 4 digits
About 6.1x10^-5, roughly 5 digits
About 7.8x10^-3, roughly 3 digits
questions.explanation: bf16's 7 mantissa bits give eps ≈ 7.81x10^-3, about 3 significant decimal digits. fp32's eps is ~1.2x10^-7 and fp16's ~9.8x10^-4.

questions.section: 5. The four formats: dynamic range vs precision
questions.question: How can you verify the max, smallest normal and eps of a PyTorch dtype?
options: With torch.iinfo(dtype), reading .max, .min and .bits
With tensor.element_size() and the dtype's bit width
With torch.finfo(dtype), reading .max, .tiny and .eps
With torch.cuda.get_device_properties() for the GPU
questions.explanation: torch.finfo gives floating-point properties: max, tiny (smallest normal) and eps. iinfo is for integer types.

questions.section: 5. The four formats: dynamic range vs precision
questions.question: How do fp16 and bf16 differ, given that both are 16 bits?
options: fp16 has more exponent bits (wider range); bf16 has more mantissa bits (finer precision)
fp16 has more mantissa (finer, narrow range); bf16 more exponent (fp32's range)
They have identical bit splits, but run on different Tensor-Core hardware paths
bf16 has more total bits than fp16, using the extra ones for its wider exponent
questions.explanation: fp16 spends 5 bits on exponent and 10 on mantissa; bf16 spends 8 and 7. For training, range matters more than the last bits of precision, so bf16 won.

questions.section: 5. The four formats: dynamic range vs precision
questions.question: Outside what magnitude range do fp16 values overflow to inf or underflow to zero?
options: Roughly 10^-38 to 3.4x10^38
Roughly 6x10^-5 to 6.5x10^4
Roughly 10^-4 to 10^4 overall
Roughly 10^-7 to 10^7
questions.explanation: fp16 covers about [6x10^-5, 6.5x10^4] in magnitude for normal numbers. bf16 and fp32 cover about [10^-38, 3.4x10^38].

questions.section: 6. Why bf16 is preferred for training (and needs no loss scaling)
questions.question: Why does bf16's fp32-equal exponent matter for training?
options: Activations and gradients span huge ranges and spike, and bf16 keeps them representable
It makes bf16 matmuls run twice as fast as fp16 matmuls on the same Tensor Cores
It gives bf16 more significant digits than fp16, so rounding error is smaller
It removes the need for fp32 master weights, since bf16 updates are never rounded away
questions.explanation: With the same range as fp32, a gradient of 10^-10 or an activation of 10^5 stays representable. The cost is only ~3 significant digits, tolerated because master weights and accumulation stay fp32.

questions.section: What the fp32 master weights do — and do not — buy you
questions.question: What do fp32 master weights do in bf16 mixed-precision training?
options: They make the gradients exactly equal to the gradients of a full-fp32 run
They make the forward and backward passes run in fp32 instead of bf16 under autocast
They double the speed of the optimizer, since fp32 updates fuse better
They keep small updates from rounding away; they don't restore lost precision
questions.explanation: Gradients from a bf16 forward/backward stay approximate. The fp32 master copy accumulates small updates that would vanish in bf16, so learning continues. It stops further loss, it does not restore lost precision.

questions.section: What the fp32 master weights do — and do not — buy you
questions.question: Near 1.0, what is the spacing between adjacent bf16 values?
questions.explanation: bf16 has 7 mantissa bits, so near 1.0 consecutive values differ by 2^-7. The next value above 1.0 is 1.0078125; anything below the midpoint 1.00390625 rounds back to 1.0.

questions.section: What the fp32 master weights do — and do not — buy you
questions.question: If a weight of 1.0 is stored directly in bf16 and you add 0.001 each step, what happens?
options: It reaches about 1.004 after 4 steps, as in fp32
It overflows to inf once enough updates pile up
It never changes; each update rounds back to 1.0
It jumps to 1.0078125 on the very first step
questions.explanation: 1.001 is below the rounding midpoint 1.00390625, so it rounds back to 1.0 every time. Stored in bf16 alone, small updates are lost forever.

questions.section: What the fp32 master weights do — and do not — buy you
questions.question: With an fp32 master weight starting at 1.0 and +0.001 updates, when does the bf16 copy used for compute first change?
options: At step 1, when the master first becomes 1.001 and the copy rounds up
At step 4, when the master (~1.004) crosses the midpoint to 1.0078125
Never, since every update is below the rounding midpoint of 1.0
At step 8, when the master reaches 1.008 and passes 1.0078125
questions.explanation: The fp32 master accumulates 1.001, 1.002, 1.003, 1.004. At 1.004 it exceeds 1.00390625, so the bf16 copy rounds to 1.0078125. Small updates are kept, not made exact.

questions.section: What the fp32 master weights do — and do not — buy you
questions.question: What does fp32 accumulation inside a bf16 matmul accomplish?
options: An fp32 accumulator avoids new rounding error at each add; input rounding stays
It converts the bf16 inputs back to their exact original fp32 values before use
It doubles the matmul's FLOPs, because every product is computed twice for the fp32 sum
It removes the need for Tensor Cores, since fp32 adds run on CUDA cores
questions.explanation: Accumulating in fp32 prevents error from compounding during the sum. Rounding already in the bf16 inputs remains.

questions.section: What the fp32 master weights do — and do not — buy you
questions.question: Does bf16 mixed-precision training produce the same numbers as full fp32 training?
options: Yes, exactly, because fp32 master weights reproduce every fp32 step
Yes, as long as dynamic loss scaling is used alongside autocast
No, and it diverges after a few thousand steps without loss scaling
No; losses differ slightly, but it learns about as well as fp32
questions.explanation: Mixed precision does not reproduce fp32 results. It keeps errors small so learning is essentially as good.

questions.section: 6. Why bf16 is preferred for training (and needs no loss scaling)
questions.question: What happens to many gradients when training in fp16 without loss scaling?
options: They overflow to inf every step, because fp16's max is only 65504
They are automatically promoted to fp32 by autograd, so nothing is lost
They are rounded to the nearest power of two, adding a small bias
They fall below fp16's ~6.1x10^-5 normal and underflow to zero
questions.explanation: Gradients are often tiny. In fp16 they underflow to zero, silently erasing updates. Loss scaling moves them into the representable range.

questions.section: 6. Why bf16 is preferred for training (and needs no loss scaling)
questions.question: How does loss scaling with GradScaler work?
options: Divide the loss by s before backward to prevent overflow, then multiply gradients by s
Clip every gradient to fp16's max of 65504 before backward, then rescale by s
Multiply the loss by s so gradients rise into fp16's range, then unscale in fp32
Cast the loss to bf16 before backward, then cast gradients back to fp16 for the step
questions.explanation: Scaling the loss scales every gradient by s, lifting small values above fp16's underflow threshold. Unscaling in fp32 restores the true magnitude for the update.

questions.section: 6. Why bf16 is preferred for training (and needs no loss scaling)
questions.question: What does GradScaler do when it detects inf or nan gradients?
options: Raises the scale factor s and retries the same step
Skips that optimizer step and lowers the scale factor s
Stops training with an error naming the bad parameter
Replaces the inf values with zeros and continues the step
questions.explanation: An inf/nan means the scaled gradients overflowed fp16's top. The scaler skips the step and reduces s, adjusting dynamically over training.

questions.section: 6. Why bf16 is preferred for training (and needs no loss scaling)
questions.question: What is the decisive reason modern LLM pretraining uses bf16 rather than fp16?
options: bf16 removes the loss-scaling failure mode; both run at the same speed
bf16 runs twice as fast as fp16 on Tensor Cores, halving the step time
bf16 has higher precision than fp16, so gradients are more accurate
bf16 uses fewer bytes per value than fp16, so activations are smaller
questions.explanation: Speed is the same; both are 2 bytes. bf16's range covers where gradients live, so nothing underflows and no scaler is needed, eliminating a class of bugs.

questions.section: 6. Why bf16 is preferred for training (and needs no loss scaling)
questions.question: What hardware is required for bf16 training, and what is the fallback on older GPUs?
options: Ampere/A100 or newer; older GPUs fall back to fp16 with GradScaler
Any GPU since Pascal; no fallback is needed for bf16 training
Only Hopper/H100; older GPUs fall back to fp64 for stability
Volta or newer; older GPUs fall back to int8 with per-tensor scales
questions.explanation: bf16 needs Ampere-class hardware or newer. Older GPUs such as the T4 or V100 use fp16 with loss scaling.

questions.section: 7. torch.autocast: how mixed precision is actually used
questions.question: What does wrapping the forward pass in torch.autocast do?
options: Casts every tensor and weight permanently to 16-bit for the rest of training
Runs the whole forward in fp64 and casts results down to fp32 at the end
Converts the model to int8 for the forward pass, with fp32 scales per tensor
Picks a dtype per op: matmuls in 16-bit, sensitive ops like softmax in fp32
questions.explanation: autocast applies a per-op policy: matmul-shaped, error-tolerant ops in 16-bit, fragile ops in fp32. Weights stay stored in fp32 and are cast on the fly.

questions.section: 7. torch.autocast: how mixed precision is actually used
questions.question: Under torch.autocast, in what dtype are the model's weights stored?
options: bf16 permanently, converted when autocast is entered
fp16 permanently, with an fp32 copy only in the optimizer
fp32, as the master copy, cast to 16-bit on the fly
int8 with per-channel scales, dequantized for each op
questions.explanation: The weights remain fp32 in memory so the optimizer updates a precise copy. The 16-bit versions used by matmuls are transient.

questions.section: 7. torch.autocast: how mixed precision is actually used
questions.question: Which ops does autocast keep in fp32?
options: Linear layers and matmuls, where long sums accumulate error
Fragile ones: softmax, layernorm's reduction, log/exp, the loss
Convolutions and attention, since their inputs span wide ranges
All ops in the backward pass, since gradients are very small
questions.explanation: Linear, matmul, conv and attention run in 16-bit for speed and halved bytes. Fragile ops stay in fp32 so precision is preserved where it matters.

questions.section: 7. torch.autocast: how mixed precision is actually used
questions.question: What extra code does the fp16 autocast training loop need compared with the bf16 loop?
options: A call to model.half() before training, so all weights become fp16
Three scaler calls: scale(loss).backward(), step(optimizer), update()
A second optimizer that keeps the fp16 copies of the parameters in sync
Nothing; the fp16 and bf16 autocast loops are identical line for line
questions.explanation: Apart from the dtype, the only difference is the three GradScaler calls. That is the entire practical cost of fp16's narrow range.

questions.section: 7. torch.autocast: how mixed precision is actually used
questions.question: In the fp16 training loop, what does scaler.step(optimizer) do?
options: Unscales the gradients and skips the step if inf or nan is seen
Scales the loss up by s before backward so gradients do not underflow
Adjusts the scale factor for the next step based on recent overflows
Zeroes the gradients after the optimizer has applied the update
questions.explanation: scaler.step unscales gradients and calls the optimizer only if they are finite. scaler.scale scales the loss and scaler.update adjusts the factor.

questions.section: 7. torch.autocast: how mixed precision is actually used
questions.question: In the bf16 autocast training loop, why is no GradScaler needed?
options: bf16 gradients are computed in fp64 under autocast
Autocast disables the scaled backward for bf16 dtypes
bf16 gradients are clipped to a safe range automatically
bf16's range is fine for gradients, so none underflow
questions.explanation: With fp32-equal exponent range, bf16 gradients remain representable, so there is nothing to scale.

questions.section: 8. Numerical example: fp16 overflows where bf16 does not
questions.question: What happens when you compute 300 x 300 in fp16 versus bf16?
options: Both give 90000 exactly, well within their range
fp16 gives 90000; bf16 overflows to inf here
fp16 overflows to inf; bf16 gives 90112
Both overflow to inf, since 90000 > 65504
questions.explanation: 90000 exceeds fp16's max of 65504, so it overflows. bf16's range easily covers it; coarse precision rounds it to 90112.

questions.section: 8. Numerical example: fp16 overflows where bf16 does not
questions.question: What does storing 70000.0 as fp16 and as bf16 give?
options: fp16 gives 70000; bf16 gives inf
Both give 70000
fp16 gives inf; bf16 gives 70144
fp16 gives 65504; bf16 gives 70000
questions.explanation: fp16 cannot store values above 65504, so 70000 becomes inf. bf16 stores it as 70144, showing its ~3-digit precision but no overflow.

questions.section: 8. Numerical example: fp16 overflows where bf16 does not
questions.question: Why can the fp16-overflow versus bf16 demonstration run on a CPU?
options: CPUs have Tensor Cores that emulate fp16 and bf16 math
It is purely about number formats, not GPU hardware
PyTorch emulates a full GPU on the CPU for these dtypes
bf16 is only supported on CPU, so the demo must run there
questions.explanation: Overflow is a property of the format's range, so the same behaviour shows wherever the dtype is supported.

questions.section: 8. Numerical example: fp16 overflows where bf16 does not
questions.question: Which intermediate values in training can exceed fp16's range?
options: Large activations, pre-softmax attention scores, squared terms in a variance
Only the token ids, which exceed 65504 whenever the vocabulary is large enough
Only the learning rate and its warmup schedule early in training
Only the bias vectors, which grow without bound when weight decay is turned off
questions.explanation: Such values appear routinely. fp16 would produce inf/nan requiring loss scaling, while bf16 handles them.

questions.question: A profile shows 55% of CUDA time in matmuls and 30% in elementwise, layer_norm and softmax kernels. What should you try for the 30%?
options: Rewrite the matmuls to use fewer FLOPs per token in the step
Switch the matmuls to fp64 so the tail has less to correct
Split the tail into more kernel launches so more SMs are used
Fuse it, e.g. with torch.compile, to cut HBM round trips
