questions.explanation: Elementwise, LayerNorm and softmax are the memory-bound tail. Fusing them reduces HBM traffic; the compute-bound matmuls are left alone (apart from the bf16 speedup).

questions.question: Why does calling loss.item() every step create gaps in the GPU timeline?
options: It doubles the size of the loss tensor by copying it into fp64 on the GPU
It runs the backward pass again to recompute the loss value for printing
It moves the model weights to host RAM so the scalar can be read safely
It copies a scalar to the CPU, forcing a sync that drains the GPU queue
questions.explanation: The host sync stops the CPU running ahead. Logging every N steps or accumulating on-device removes it from the hot path.

questions.question: When switching a run from fp32 to bf16 autocast, which cost center benefits most in relative terms, and why?
options: Only the matmuls benefit, through Tensor Cores; the memory-bound tail is unaffected
Neither benefits in speed; only activation memory use changes with the dtype
The memory-bound tail, as halving the dtype halves its traffic; matmuls also gain
The data loader benefits most, since bf16 batches cross PCIe in half the time
questions.explanation: The memory-bound kernels gain from halved bytes; matmuls gain from the faster 16-bit Tensor-Core path; activation memory roughly halves.

questions.question: What is the consequence of using fp16 without a GradScaler?
options: The program crashes on the first step with an overflow error from autocast
Small gradients silently underflow to zero and the model fails to learn
Training becomes faster with no downside, since scaling only adds overhead
The model automatically switches to bf16 once underflow is detected
questions.explanation: Underflow is silent: updates vanish and the loss curve just looks bad. Either scale the loss or use bf16.

questions.question: Why should you not expect bf16 training to match fp32 loss curves to many digits?
options: bf16 has ~3 significant digits, and master weights only stop further loss
bf16 overflows on every step, so some updates are skipped by the optimizer
bf16 disables fused AdamW, so the optimizer follows a different update rule
bf16 uses a different loss function, computed with a bf16 log-softmax
questions.explanation: Small run-to-run differences are normal. Master weights and fp32 accumulation keep training progressing, not identical.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to assume mixed precision speeds up a compute-bound matmul by halving bytes?
options: Its win is the 16-bit Tensor-Core path; halving an n=4096 matmul's bytes gives 0%
Matmuls do not move any bytes once their weights are cached in the GPU's L2 cache
Halving bytes makes matmuls slower, since 16-bit tiles need extra conversion
Mixed precision does not affect matmuls at all; it only changes the tail
questions.explanation: Different mechanisms apply to different kernels. The tail gains from bytes, the matmuls from the higher ceiling (16x for the n=4096 case).

questions.question: You autocast to bf16 but the model's weights are still fp32 in memory. Is that a bug?
options: Yes; autocast should have converted the weights to bf16 permanently on entry
Yes; it means autocast is disabled and every op still runs in fp32
Yes; it doubles the FLOPs, since each op casts and recomputes its weights
No; fp32 weights are the master copy, cast to bf16 on the fly
questions.explanation: This is how mixed precision works. The master copy keeps small updates from being rounded away, while the 16-bit path provides throughput.

questions.question: What was the main obstacle that capped the context length of transformer models before FlashAttention?
options: The O(T^2) memory of materializing the T×T attention score matrix
The O(T^3) FLOP cost of multiplying the query and key matrices
The limited number of positions in learned positional embeddings
The quadratic number of parameters in the attention projections
questions.explanation: Standard attention stores a T×T score/probability matrix per head per layer, so its memory grows quadratically with sequence length T. That quadratic memory was the wall on context length. The QK^T matmul costs O(T^2 d), not O(T^3), and the projection weights do not depend on T at all.

questions.question: How does the output of FlashAttention compare with the output of standard softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d))V attention?
options: It is a sparse approximation that drops low-scoring keys
It is a low-rank approximation with a small bounded error
It is the exact same output, up to floating-point rounding
It matches only when the sequence length is a multiple of the block size
questions.explanation: FlashAttention changes how the computation is scheduled through memory, not the mathematics. Tiling plus the online-softmax recurrence reproduces full-row softmax exactly, so the only differences are rounding at the ~1e-6 level in fp32. It is not a sparse or low-rank approximation like some efficient-attention methods.

questions.question: How much memory does FlashAttention need for the attention activations as a function of sequence length T?
options: O(1), because every tile is discarded immediately after use
O(T log T), because tiles are merged in a tree reduction
O(T^2), the same as standard attention but with a smaller constant
O(T), because only per-row statistics and small tiles are kept
questions.explanation: FlashAttention never stores the T×T matrix; it keeps the output and a few running numbers per query row, which is linear in T. Standard attention is O(T^2). It is not O(1) because the output O itself and the per-row statistics scale with T.

questions.question: Why is FlashAttention described as a natural capstone of a module on GPU architecture, the roofline and kernel fusion?
options: It applies the SRAM/HBM hierarchy, the roofline and fusion to the operation that most needed them
It replaces the separate SRAM and HBM levels with a single unified memory pool managed by the kernel
It is the first algorithm that makes attention compute-bound by deliberately adding more FLOPs per byte
It is the only kernel that runs both matmuls and the softmax on tensor cores rather than CUDA cores
questions.explanation: FlashAttention is essentially the memory hierarchy (fast small SRAM vs slow large HBM), the roofline (attention is bandwidth-bound) and fusion (do everything in one kernel to avoid HBM round trips) applied to attention. It does not change the hardware, and its point is fewer bytes moved, not more FLOPs.

questions.question: Roughly what change in model context lengths is FlashAttention credited with enabling?
options: From about 128k tokens to tens of millions of tokens
From about 1–2k tokens to 128k tokens and beyond
From about 128 tokens to roughly 512 tokens
From about 512 tokens to roughly 2k tokens
questions.explanation: By removing the quadratic memory of the score matrix, FlashAttention is credited with letting models move from 1–2k contexts to 128k+ contexts. It is now standard in every serious training and inference stack.

questions.section: 1. The problem: standard attention is memory-bound
questions.question: For single-head attention with Q, K, V of shape (T, d), what are the shapes of the score matrix S = QK^T/sqrt(d), the probability matrix P = softmax(S), and the output O = PV?
options: S is (d, d), P is (d, d), O is (T, d)
S is (T, T), P is (T, T), O is (T, d)
S is (T, T), P is (T, d), O is (T, d)
S is (T, d), P is (T, d), O is (T, T)
questions.explanation: QK^T contracts over the d dimension, giving one score per (query, key) pair, so S is T×T; softmax is applied row-wise and keeps that shape. Multiplying the T×T P by the T×d V gives a T×d output. The d×d option would be K^T Q, which is not attention.

questions.section: 1. The problem: standard attention is memory-bound
questions.question: In a naive (unfused) attention implementation, where do the intermediate matrices S and P live between steps?
options: In on-chip SRAM, kept resident so they never touch main memory
In CPU RAM, copied over PCIe to the host and back between steps
In HBM (GPU main memory), written and read back between steps
In registers only, because each element is consumed exactly once
questions.explanation: The naive implementation runs separate kernels: compute S and write it to HBM, read S back to apply softmax and write P to HBM, then read P back to multiply by V. Each T×T intermediate therefore makes round trips through slow HBM. They are far too large to fit in SRAM or registers at long T.

questions.section: 1. The problem: standard attention is memory-bound
questions.question: Which sequence describes the HBM traffic of naive attention?
options: Write P; read P and write S; read S and write O
Read Q once; stream K and V; write O once
Read S once; write O once; never store P
Write S; read S and write P; read P and write O
questions.explanation: Naive attention computes S = QK^T/sqrt(d) and writes it to HBM, reads it back to apply softmax and writes P, then reads P back and multiplies by V to write O. The option 'read Q once, stream K and V, write O once' describes FlashAttention's traffic, not the naive pattern.

questions.section: 1. The problem: standard attention is memory-bound
questions.question: For T = 8192 in fp16, approximately how large is one T×T attention matrix for a single head?
options: About 1.1 GB
About 8 MB
About 134 MB
About 16 MB
questions.explanation: One T×T matrix has 8192^2 ≈ 67 million elements; at 2 bytes each in fp16 that is about 134 MB. Naive attention reads and writes such matrices several times per head per layer, so the traffic and memory add up quickly.

questions.section: 1. The problem: standard attention is memory-bound
questions.question: Why is the softmax step of standard attention considered memory-bound?
options: It must synchronize all SMs after every element is processed
It performs a large matrix multiplication that saturates the tensor cores
It reads a huge matrix, does only a few FLOPs per element, and writes it back
It requires a division that is much slower than multiplication on GPUs
questions.explanation: Softmax is a low-arithmetic-intensity reduction: per element it does a max, a subtraction, an exp and a division, but it must move every element in and out of HBM. Its runtime is therefore set by bandwidth, not FLOPs. It contains no large matmul.

questions.section: 1. The problem: standard attention is memory-bound
questions.question: Where does standard long-sequence attention sit on the roofline plot?
options: Exactly at the ridge point between the two regimes
Far right, on the flat compute-limited ceiling
Above the compute ceiling, due to tensor-core boosts
Far left, on the bandwidth-limited slope
questions.explanation: Because naive attention is dominated by shuttling the T×T matrix through HBM, its arithmetic intensity is low and it sits on the bandwidth slope at the left of the roofline. Nothing can sit above the compute ceiling; that is the hardware maximum.

questions.section: 1. The problem: standard attention is memory-bound
questions.question: Besides bandwidth, why does the O(T^2) score matrix make long context run out of GPU memory during training?
options: It must be stored in fp64 for numerical stability
It is a parameter that must be stored with its optimizer state
It is an activation that must be kept for the backward pass
It is copied to every GPU in the data-parallel group
questions.explanation: In training, the score/probability matrix is an activation that autograd saves for the backward pass, so it stays in memory per head per layer. That quadratic activation memory is what overflows the GPU at long context. It is not a parameter and is not stored in fp64.

questions.section: 1. The problem: standard attention is memory-bound
questions.question: Switching attention from fp32 to bf16 halves the bytes of the score matrix. Why does that not solve the long-context memory problem?
options: It helps only by a constant factor and leaves the O(T^2) scaling unchanged
It makes the softmax unstable so the matrix must be recomputed in fp32
It increases the number of elements in the matrix to compensate
It only affects the weights, not the activations of attention
questions.explanation: Halving the dtype halves every byte count, but the matrix still has T^2 elements, so doubling T still quadruples memory. To break the quadratic wall you must avoid writing the full matrix at all, which is what FlashAttention does.

questions.section: 1. The problem: standard attention is memory-bound
questions.question: According to the analysis of standard attention, what is the real bottleneck at long sequence length?
options: Scaling every score by 1/sqrt(d) before the softmax step
Loading the Q, K and V projection weights from HBM each step
Materializing the T×T score/probability matrix in HBM
Running the two matrix multiplications QK^T and PV on tensor cores
questions.explanation: The matmuls are compute-efficient; the problem is writing and reading the T×T intermediates through HBM, which costs O(T^2) memory and bandwidth and feeds a memory-bound softmax. The scaling is a trivial elementwise op and the weights are tiny by comparison.

questions.section: 2. The idea: tile into SRAM, never store the full matrix
questions.question: What property of the attention output makes it possible to compute O = PV without ever holding the whole matrix P?
options: The matrix P is symmetric, so only its upper triangle has to be computed and kept in SRAM
The rows of P are identical across queries, so one row can be computed once and reused for all
The matrix P is always low-rank, so it can be factorized exactly into two thin T×r matrices
Each output row O_i = Σ_j P_ij V_j is a sum over keys that can be accumulated incrementally
questions.explanation: The output row for query i is a weighted sum over keys, and a sum can be built up block by block. FlashAttention brings one block of keys/values into SRAM, folds its contribution into a running output and discards it. P is generally neither low-rank, symmetric, nor constant across rows.

questions.section: 2. The idea: tile into SRAM, never store the full matrix
questions.question: In FlashAttention, what is the largest score object that exists in memory at any moment?
options: One full T × T matrix, held in HBM
One small B_q × B_k tile, held in SRAM
One T × B_k strip, held in HBM
One B_q × T strip, held in L2 cache
questions.explanation: For each query block FlashAttention loops over key blocks and computes only the B_q × B_k tile of scores, in on-chip SRAM. The full T×T matrix, or even a full row strip, never exists. That is what drops memory from O(T^2) to O(T).

questions.section: 2. The idea: tile into SRAM, never store the full matrix
questions.question: How are the block sizes in FlashAttention chosen?
options: So that every block contains exactly one row maximum
So that the number of blocks equals the number of attention heads
So that the block size divides the vocabulary size evenly
So the Q, K and V tiles fit in the SM's shared memory (SRAM)
questions.explanation: Tiles are sized to fit into each SM's fast shared memory, so all arithmetic on a tile happens on-chip. Block size has no effect on correctness, only on memory traffic and throughput. It is unrelated to the number of heads or vocabulary.

questions.section: 2. The idea: tile into SRAM, never store the full matrix
questions.question: In FlashAttention, what is the HBM traffic for Q, K, V and O?
options: Q, K and V are each read once, and the full T×T score matrix is written once to HBM
Q is re-read once per key block, while K, V and O are each read or written exactly once
All four tensors are read and written once per tile, so traffic grows with the tile count
Q is read once, O is written once, and K and V are streamed once per query block
questions.explanation: Each query block is loaded once, the key/value blocks are streamed through SRAM once per query block, and the normalized output block is written once. The T×T score matrix is never written or read, which is the whole saving.

questions.section: 2. The idea: tile into SRAM, never store the full matrix
questions.question: For T = 4096, d = 64 and 128-row query blocks, roughly how does FlashAttention change the HBM traffic of one attention head?
options: From about 35 MB to about 136 MB
From about 136 MB to about 1 MB
From about 136 MB to about 35 MB
From about 1.1 GB to about 136 MB
questions.explanation: The worked numbers quoted for this configuration drop traffic from roughly 136 MB to roughly 35 MB, a large constant-factor reduction, while the memory held drops from O(T^2) to O(T). The traffic does not fall to near zero, because K and V are still streamed once per query block.

questions.section: 2. The idea: tile into SRAM, never store the full matrix
questions.question: What is the main subtlety that tiling attention into key blocks introduces?
options: Softmax normalizes over the whole row of keys, but only one block of keys is seen at a time
The 1/sqrt(d) scale must be recomputed per block because each block has its own head dimension
Key blocks must be processed in descending order of their scores so the max always arrives first
Matrix multiplication is not associative, so per-block partial products cannot be combined exactly
questions.explanation: Softmax needs the row maximum and the sum of exponentials over all keys, yet tiling shows only one key block at a time. The online-softmax recurrence solves this by maintaining running statistics and correcting them as new blocks arrive. Block order does not matter for the final result.

questions.section: 3. Online softmax: running max m and running denominator ℓ
questions.question: Which two whole-row quantities does a numerically stable softmax need?
options: The row mean and the row variance of the scores
The row sum of the scores and the row product
The row maximum and the sum of exponentials
The row minimum and the row maximum of the scores
questions.explanation: Stable softmax subtracts the row max before exponentiating and divides by the sum of exponentials (the denominator). Online softmax computes both incrementally. Mean and variance are what normalization layers use, not softmax.

questions.section: 3. Online softmax: running max m and running denominator ℓ
questions.question: Why is the maximum score subtracted before exponentiating in softmax?
options: To make all softmax probabilities sum to exactly one
To remove the need for the 1/sqrt(d) scaling
To prevent exp of a large score from overflowing
To make the softmax output sparse
questions.explanation: exp of a large positive score overflows floating point; subtracting the max makes every exponent ≤ 0, so every exp is ≤ 1. Mathematically the max cancels between numerator and denominator, so it does not change the probabilities; they sum to one with or without it.

questions.section: 3. Online softmax: running max m and running denominator ℓ
questions.question: Which three running quantities does online softmax keep per query row?
options: Running max m, running minimum, and running already-normalized output
Running max m, running denominator ℓ, and running unnormalized output o
Running mean, running variance, and running normalized output vector
Running sum of raw scores, running sum of value vectors, and key count
questions.explanation: Online softmax maintains m (the max of scores seen so far), ℓ = Σ exp(score − m) and o = Σ exp(score − m)·v. The answer at the end is o/ℓ. Keeping a normalized output would require knowing the final denominator in advance.

questions.section: 3. Online softmax: running max m and running denominator ℓ
questions.question: What are the initial values of the running max m, running denominator ℓ, and running output o in online softmax?
questions.explanation: Starting m at −∞ means any first block's max becomes the running max, and with α = exp(m − m_new) = 0 the empty initial sums ℓ = 0 and o = 0 contribute nothing. Starting ℓ at 1 would add a phantom term to the denominator.

questions.section: 3. Online softmax: running max m and running denominator ℓ
questions.question: In online softmax, what is the running denominator ℓ?
options: The exponential of the running maximum score, exp(m)
The sum of exp(score − m) over all scores seen so far
The sum of the raw scores seen so far, before any exp
The number of keys processed so far across all blocks
questions.explanation: ℓ accumulates exp(score − m) over the processed keys, referenced to the current running max m. At the end it equals the full-row softmax denominator (relative to the true max). It is neither a count nor a sum of raw scores.

questions.section: 3. Online softmax: running max m and running denominator ℓ
questions.question: In online softmax, what is the running output o?
options: The softmax-normalized weighted average of the value vectors seen so far
The plain unweighted sum of all value vectors seen so far, divided at the end
The value vector of the single key with the largest score seen so far
The unnormalized sum of exp(score − m) times each value vector seen so far
questions.explanation: o = Σ exp(score − m)·v is the numerator of the softmax-weighted average, not yet divided by the denominator. Normalization happens once, at the end, as o/ℓ. Storing it already normalized would require knowing the final denominator in advance.

questions.section: 3. Online softmax: running max m and running denominator ℓ
questions.question: When a new block of scores arrives in online softmax, how is the new running maximum computed?
options: m_new = m + m_blk, adding the new block's max to the running max
m_new = (m + m_blk)/2, the average of the running and block maxima
m_new = m_blk, always replacing the old running max with the block's max
m_new = max(m, m_blk), where m_blk is the max score within the new block
questions.explanation: The running max is the max over all scores seen so far, so it is the larger of the old running max and the new block's max. Always replacing it with m_blk would lose the old maximum whenever a later block has smaller scores.

questions.section: 3. Online softmax: running max m and running denominator ℓ
questions.question: In online softmax, what does the correction factor α = exp(m − m_new) do?
options: It rescales the new block's exponentials so that they are expressed relative to the old running max
It normalizes the final output so that the attention weights across all keys sum to one
It rescales the old ℓ and o, computed against the old max, so they are relative to the new max
It scales the raw scores by 1/sqrt(d) before exponentiation to keep the softmax stable
questions.explanation: ℓ and o were accumulated with exponents referenced to the old max m. Multiplying them by exp(m − m_new) re-references them to m_new, so they can be added to the new block's terms, which are computed against m_new. The final normalization is o/ℓ, a separate step.

questions.section: 3. Online softmax: running max m and running denominator ℓ
questions.question: What values can the online-softmax correction factor α = exp(m − m_new) take?
options: α ≥ 1 always, and α = 1 on the very first block because nothing is rescaled
α can be any positive number, depending on block size and the score scale
α ≤ 1 always, and α = 0 on the very first block because m starts at −∞
α is always exactly 1, except on blocks where every key is masked out
questions.explanation: Because m_new = max(m, m_blk) ≥ m, the exponent m − m_new is ≤ 0, so α ≤ 1. On the first block m = −∞, so α = exp(−∞) = 0, which wipes out the empty initial state. α = 1 occurs whenever the max does not change.

questions.section: 3. Online softmax: running max m and running denominator ℓ
questions.question: In online softmax, against which maximum are the new block's scores exponentiated?
options: Against zero, with no max subtraction
Against the new running max m_new
Against the old running max m
Against the block's own max m_blk only
questions.explanation: The new block's terms are p_t = exp(s_t − m_new), the same reference as the rescaled old sums α·ℓ and α·o, so all terms share one scale before being added. Using m_blk alone would leave old and new terms on different scales whenever m_blk < m.

questions.section: 3. Online softmax: running max m and running denominator ℓ
questions.question: What is the online-softmax update for the running denominator ℓ when a new block with exponentials p_t arrives?
options: ℓ ← α·ℓ + Σ_t p_t
ℓ ← ℓ + α·Σ_t p_t
ℓ ← ℓ·Σ_t p_t
ℓ ← α·(ℓ + Σ_t p_t)
questions.explanation: The old denominator is rescaled to the new max by α, then the new block's terms (already computed against m_new) are added. Applying α to the new terms or to the sum of both would put them on the wrong scale. The output o is updated the same way with p_t·v_t.

questions.section: 3. Online softmax: running max m and running denominator ℓ
questions.question: After all key blocks have been processed by online softmax, how is the attention output for a query row obtained?
options: Divide the accumulated output by the accumulated denominator: o/ℓ
Apply a fresh softmax over the entries of the accumulated output o
Multiply the accumulated output by the final running max: o·m
Use o directly, since each block already normalized its contribution
questions.explanation: o is the softmax numerator Σ exp(s − m)·v and ℓ is the denominator Σ exp(s − m), so o/ℓ is exactly the softmax-weighted average of the values. o by itself is unnormalized.

questions.section: 3. Online softmax: running max m and running denominator ℓ
questions.question: How much state per query row does online softmax need, independent of sequence length?
options: O(log T): one partial sum per level of a reduction tree
O(T): one stored exponential per key, kept for the final divide
O(1): a max, a denominator and an output vector of size d
O(T^2): the full score row for every query-key pair
questions.explanation: Per query row, online softmax keeps only m, ℓ and the d-dimensional o, regardless of how many keys there are. This O(1)-per-row state (constant in T) is why the full score matrix never needs to be stored.

questions.section: 3. Online softmax: running max m and running denominator ℓ
questions.question: Why does online softmax give a result identical to computing softmax over the whole row at once?
options: It approximates the denominator per block, and the errors average out to zero over many blocks
It processes keys in sorted order of their scores, so the row maximum is always seen in the very first block
It recomputes the whole row from scratch whenever a new block raises the running maximum score
The correction factor lets the max change midstream and retroactively fixes the accumulated sums
questions.explanation: Whenever a later block contains a larger score, α rescales the stored ℓ and o to the new reference max, so the running state is always equivalent to having exponentiated all seen scores against the current max. No sorting, recomputation or approximation is required.

questions.question: In a one-query online-softmax example with scores [1, 2, 3, 0] and values [10, 20, 30, 40] processed in two blocks of two, the provisional output after block 1 is about 17.31 and the final output is about 26.21. Why does it change so much?
options: The provisional value is computed in lower precision than the final value
Block 2 holds the highest-scoring key, which carries most of the softmax weight
Block 2 is processed with a larger correction factor than block 1
The final value includes the 1/sqrt(d) scaling, which the provisional value omits
questions.explanation: After block 1 only scores [1, 2] with values [10, 20] are known, so the weighted average sits near 17. Block 2 contains score 3 with value 30, which gets weight ≈ 0.64 in the full softmax; folding it in (after rescaling the old sums by α) pulls the output to 26.21. The provisional output is only correct over the keys seen so far.

questions.question: In online softmax, if the running max is 2 after the first block and the second block contains a score of 3, what is the correction factor α applied to the old sums?
options: 1, because the correction only applies on the first block
questions.explanation: α = exp(m_old − m_new) = exp(2 − 3) = e^{-1}. It shrinks the old ℓ and o because they were referenced to a smaller max; it is always ≤ 1. e^{+1} would push them in the wrong direction.

questions.question: After online softmax has processed every key block of a row, how does the final running denominator ℓ compare with the full-row softmax denominator Σ exp(s − max s)?
options: ℓ is larger by a factor of the number of blocks
They are equal
They differ unless the max appears in the first block
ℓ is smaller by the product of all correction factors
questions.explanation: By the end, m equals the true row max and ℓ = Σ exp(s − m) over all keys, which is exactly the full-row denominator. This holds regardless of which block held the maximum, because α corrected any earlier blocks.

questions.section: 4.1 Why it is exact — the proof, checked on the same numbers
questions.question: What is the invariant that proves online softmax is exact?
options: After any number of blocks, m, ℓ and o are the max, Σ exp(s − m) and Σ exp(s − m)·v over the scores seen so far
After any number of blocks, the correction factor α equals one, so the running sums never need rescaling
After any number of blocks, o/ℓ already equals the final attention output computed over every key in the full row
After any number of blocks, ℓ equals the full-row softmax denominator taken over all keys, seen or not
questions.explanation: The invariant says the running state is exactly what you would compute directly over the seen subset, referenced to that subset's max. It does not claim ℓ or o/ℓ are final before all keys are seen; those hold only after the last block, when 'seen' is every key.

questions.section: 4.1 Why it is exact — the proof, checked on the same numbers
questions.question: In the proof that online softmax is exact, why does the base case (first block) work?
options: m starts at −∞, so α = 0 and the update reduces to sums over the first block relative to its max
m starts at 0, so α = 1 and the first block's exponentials are added to the empty state unchanged
The first block always contains the row maximum, so no correction is ever needed for that block
ℓ starts at 1, which exactly cancels the normalization of the first block's exponentials
questions.explanation: With m = −∞, α = exp(−∞) = 0 wipes the empty initial state, leaving ℓ = Σ_blk exp(s − m_new) and o = Σ_blk exp(s − m_new)·v, which is the invariant for the first block. The first block need not contain the global max.

questions.section: 4.1 Why it is exact — the proof, checked on the same numbers
questions.question: In the inductive step of the online-softmax proof, what identity shows that α·ℓ is the old sum re-referenced to the new max?
options: exp(m − m_new)·Σ exp(s) = Σ exp(s − m), because the max ends up subtracted twice inside
exp(m − m_new) + Σ exp(s − m) = Σ exp(s − m_new), because exponentials of differences add
exp(m_new − m)·Σ exp(s − m) = Σ exp(s + m_new), because the exponents add term by term
exp(m − m_new)·Σ exp(s − m) = Σ exp(s − m_new), because the m cancels inside the exponent
questions.explanation: Multiplying each term exp(s − m) by exp(m − m_new) gives exp(s − m + m − m_new) = exp(s − m_new). So rescaling by α is exactly the same as having exponentiated the old scores against m_new from the start. The same argument, multiplied by v, works for o.

questions.section: 4.1 Why it is exact — the proof, checked on the same numbers
questions.question: Why does the choice of reference maximum not affect the final online-softmax result o/ℓ?
options: The reference maximum is subtracted only from the values, not the scores
The reference maximum is added back after normalization
The reference maximum is always zero after scaling by 1/sqrt(d)
The factor exp(−m) appears in both numerator and denominator and cancels
questions.explanation: o/ℓ = Σ exp(s − m)·v / Σ exp(s − m) = exp(−m)Σ exp(s)·v / (exp(−m)Σ exp(s)), and exp(−m) cancels, leaving the ordinary softmax-weighted average. Any reference max gives the same answer mathematically.

questions.section: 4.1 Why it is exact — the proof, checked on the same numbers
questions.question: If the reference max cancels out of o/ℓ mathematically, why does online softmax keep track of it at all?
options: To compute the 1/sqrt(d) scaling factor
To keep every exponential ≤ 1 so nothing overflows
To decide which key blocks can be skipped
To make the final output sum to one across value dimensions
questions.explanation: The max exists only for numerical safety: subtracting it keeps every exponent ≤ 0 and every exp ≤ 1, so large scores never overflow. Mathematically it cancels; numerically it is essential.

questions.section: 4.1 Why it is exact — the proof, checked on the same numbers
questions.question: In online softmax, rescaling the old running denominator by α = exp(m_old − m_new) is equivalent to what?
options: Having exponentiated the old scores against the new max m_new from the start
Discarding the old scores entirely and keeping only the new block's exponentials
Having exponentiated the old scores against zero instead of against any running max
Averaging the old and new denominators with equal weight before adding the new block
questions.explanation: Checking numerically, α·ℓ equals Σ exp(s_old − m_new) computed directly; for example 0.3679 × 1.3679 = 0.5032 = e^{1−3} + e^{2−3}. Rescaling is literally the same as re-referencing the old terms to the new max. Nothing is discarded.

questions.section: 4.2 A full FlashAttention pass by hand: two queries, d = 2
questions.question: When FlashAttention processes a tile with several query rows, how does the online-softmax recurrence apply?
options: It runs on every query row of the tile independently, each with its own m, ℓ and o
It runs once for the whole tile, sharing a single max across all query rows
It runs only on the query row with the largest score in the tile
It runs once per value dimension, sharing ℓ across query rows
questions.explanation: Softmax is row-wise, so each query row has its own running max, denominator and output vector. Sharing one max across rows would still be mathematically valid but is not what the algorithm does, and different rows have their maxima in different blocks.

questions.section: 4.2 A full FlashAttention pass by hand: two queries, d = 2
questions.question: In flash_attention_reference, the correction factor corr has shape (B, nh, Bq, 1). How is it applied to the running output acc of shape (B, nh, Bq, hd)?
options: It is broadcast across hd, multiplying every column of each query row's output
It multiplies only the first column of each query row's output, leaving the rest unchanged
It is applied only to the running denominator l, never to the running output acc
It is summed over Bq and then applied as one scalar to every entry of the whole tile
questions.explanation: α is one correction per query row, and that row's entire output vector was accumulated relative to the old max, so every one of its hd entries must be rescaled. The trailing size-1 dimension broadcasts across hd. Both l and acc are multiplied by corr.

questions.section: 4.2 A full FlashAttention pass by hand: two queries, d = 2
questions.question: In online softmax, if a query row's maximum score appears in the first key block and no later block exceeds it, what is the correction factor on the later blocks?
options: α = 0, because the max was already found
α equals the number of remaining blocks
α = e^{-1}, the default correction per block
α = 1, because the running max never changes
questions.explanation: α = exp(m_old − m_new); if m_new = m_old then α = exp(0) = 1 and the old sums need no rescaling. α = 0 occurs only on the first block, when m_old = −∞.

questions.section: 4.2 A full FlashAttention pass by hand: two queries, d = 2
questions.question: For a FlashAttention tile with 2 query rows and head dimension d = 2, what are the shapes of the running max m, running denominator ℓ and running output o?
questions.explanation: m and ℓ are one scalar per query row, so (B_q, 1) = (2, 1); o holds one d-dimensional output per row, (B_q, d) = (2, 2). Nothing in the state has a key dimension; that is why the full score matrix is never needed.

questions.section: 4.2 A full FlashAttention pass by hand: two queries, d = 2
questions.question: In FlashAttention, once a key/value block has been folded into the running state for a query block, when must it be read again for that query block?
options: Once per value dimension of the output, since each column is accumulated separately
Every time a later block raises the running max, to re-exponentiate its scores
Once more at the end, to compute the final denominator used to normalize o
Never; its contribution is already in m, ℓ and o, so the tile is discarded
questions.explanation: Thanks to the correction factor, a later increase in the max is handled by rescaling the stored sums, not by revisiting earlier keys. So each key block is read once per query block and then discarded.

questions.question: What happens if online softmax accumulates ℓ and o across blocks without the correction factor α?
options: Only rows whose max is in the first block get the wrong output; all other rows stay correct
Rows whose max grows in a later block get the wrong output, pulled toward earlier blocks' values
Every row's output becomes NaN, because the unrescaled exponentials overflow in fp32 after a few blocks
All rows still get a correct output, but the denominator is off by a constant factor per block
questions.explanation: Without α, earlier blocks were exponentiated against a smaller max, so their weights are too large relative to later blocks (by e^{Δmax}), and the output is biased toward early values. Rows whose max is in the first block have α = 1 anyway and remain correct.

questions.question: Why is a missing online-softmax correction factor a dangerous, silent bug?
options: It still passes any test where the first block holds the row maximum
It only fails in fp16, where exp overflows, and never shows up in fp32
It only fails when the block size is one, a size no test would ever use
It always raises an exception, which the autograd engine catches and suppresses
questions.explanation: When the first block holds the row max, the max never changes and α would be 1 anyway, so omitting it has no effect. Tests that happen to have that structure pass while real data, where the max can appear anywhere, gets wrong outputs.

questions.question: Without the online-softmax correction, if block 1's scores were exponentiated against a max of 2 and block 2's against a max of 3, how are block 1's weights distorted relative to block 2's?
options: They are e^1 ≈ 2.7 times too large
They are unchanged; only the denominator is wrong
They are 2/3 of their correct size
They are e^1 ≈ 2.7 times too small
questions.explanation: Block 1's terms exp(s − 2) are e^{3−2} = e times larger than they would be against the common max 3. Without α to shrink them, they get about 2.7× too much relative weight, pulling the output toward block 1's values.

questions.question: flash_attention_reference assumes self-attention with equal query and key lengths. How do you run it on 2 queries against 4 keys?
options: Repeat Q twice to 4 rows and average the two output halves
Transpose Q so that its length dimension matches that of K
Pad Q to 4 rows and read only the first 2 output rows
Truncate K and V to their first 2 rows so they match Q
questions.explanation: Because the function requires T_q = T_k, the extra query rows are padding; each query row's output depends only on its own query and all keys, so the first two rows are unaffected by the padding rows. Truncating K and V would change the attention itself.

questions.question: flash_attention_reference applies the 1/sqrt(d) scale itself. If your Q has already been divided by sqrt(d), how do you avoid double scaling?
options: Square the attention output afterwards to undo the extra scaling
Set block_size equal to d so that the internal scale becomes one
Pre-multiply Q by sqrt(d) so the internal scale cancels it
Divide K by sqrt(d) as well, so the two scalings cancel out
questions.explanation: The internal scale multiplies scores by 1/sqrt(d); multiplying Q by sqrt(d) beforehand cancels that, leaving the intended pre-scaled scores. Dividing K too would scale twice more, and block size has no effect on scaling.

questions.question: When flash_attention_reference is compared with naive attention and F.scaled_dot_product_attention in fp32, the maximum difference is about 4×10^-6. What does that difference reflect?
options: An approximation error inherent to tiled attention
Floating-point rounding, not an algorithmic difference
The error from skipping the 1/sqrt(d) scale
The error from padding the query matrix
questions.explanation: Different operation orders round differently in fp32, producing differences at the 1e-6 level. Mathematically the three methods are identical; FlashAttention is exact, not an approximation.

questions.question: What happens to the output of flash_attention_reference if block_size is changed from 2 to 1 or 4?
options: It becomes slightly less accurate with smaller blocks
Nothing; tiling never changes the answer
It becomes slightly less accurate with larger blocks
It changes because the correction factor depends on block size
questions.explanation: The online-softmax recurrence is exact for any partition of the keys into blocks, so block size only changes the schedule of computation, not the result (beyond rounding). The correction factors differ along the way but the final o/ℓ is the same.

questions.question: What do the tests in code/tests/test_flash.py assert about flash_attention_reference?
options: It uses strictly less than O(T) memory on every input size and stays under a fixed byte budget per call
It matches softmax(QK^T/√d)V and F.scaled_dot_product_attention to 1e-4, causal and non-causal, for any block size
It is at least twice as fast as naive attention on CPU for every sequence length, block size and dtype tested
It matches naive attention to 1e-4, but only for non-causal inputs whose lengths are powers of two
questions.explanation: The tests check exactness against both a plain implementation and PyTorch's SDPA, in both causal and non-causal modes, and that the result does not depend on block size. They do not test speed, since the reference is slower on CPU.

questions.question: Why is flash_attention_reference deliberately not a fused kernel?
options: Fusing the block ops would change the numerical result of attention in fp32
Each block op is an ordinary PyTorch call so it runs on CPU and proves the numerics
Fused kernels cannot express the online-softmax recurrence across key blocks
PyTorch forbids Python loops inside custom autograd functions, so it cannot be fused
questions.explanation: The reference exists to demonstrate the algorithm's correctness on any machine. Writing it with ordinary PyTorch ops in Python loops makes it slow but transparent; the same recurrence runs inside a fused GPU kernel in production without changing the result.

questions.question: In flash_attention_reference, what is the shape of the score tile s computed inside the inner loop?
options: (B, nh, T, Bk), all queries against one key block
(B, nh, Bq, Bk), one tile of query block by key block
(B, nh, T, T), the full score matrix
(B, nh, Bq, hd), the size of the output block
questions.explanation: s = q_blk @ k_blk^T × scale is a B_q × B_k tile per batch and head. It is the only score object that ever exists and is never T×T. The output block is (Bq, hd), a different tensor.

questions.question: How does flash_attention_reference handle causal masking efficiently?
options: It reverses the key order so that future keys are processed last and simply ignored
It masks only within diagonal tiles and breaks out of key blocks that are entirely in the future
It builds one full T×T lower-triangular mask up front and then applies a slice of it to every tile
It runs non-causal attention over all keys and then zeroes the upper triangle of the output
questions.explanation: For each query block, any key block starting after the block's last query is entirely future and is skipped with break, so causal attention does roughly half the work. Inside a diagonal tile it masks future keys to −∞. Building a full T×T mask would reintroduce O(T^2) memory.

questions.question: In flash_attention_reference, when is the running output acc divided by the running denominator l?
options: Only when the running max changes, so that acc is renormalized to it
Before the first key block, to initialize the output to a valid average
After every key block, so that acc always holds a normalized average
Once, after all key blocks for that query block have been processed
questions.explanation: acc is the unnormalized numerator; normalizing once at the end (out = acc / l) is both cheaper and exact. Normalizing after every block would require un-normalizing again when new keys arrive.

questions.question: How does the CPU reference flash_attention_reference relate to a real GPU FlashAttention kernel?
options: The two Python loops become the kernel's internal loops, with tiles held in SRAM
The GPU kernel removes the inner loop by processing every key of the row at once
The GPU kernel materializes the full score matrix, but in fp16 instead of fp32
The GPU kernel uses a different, approximate recurrence that trades accuracy for speed
questions.explanation: The reference and the GPU kernel run the same recurrence; on a GPU the loops over query and key blocks run inside one kernel with tiles in shared memory, which is what yields the speed and memory win. Processing all keys at once would require the full row.

questions.question: In flash_attention_reference, what does the tensor corr = exp(m − m_new) represent?
options: The causal mask applied to keys that lie in the future of each query
The softmax probabilities of the current tile, before multiplying by V
The online-softmax correction factor α, which is 0 on the first block
The 1/sqrt(d) scaling factor of the scores, applied before exponentiation
questions.explanation: corr is α, one value per query row, used to rescale l and acc before adding the current tile. On the first block m = −∞, so exp(−∞) = 0. The tile's probabilities are p = exp(s − m_new).

questions.section: 6. An illustrative Triton kernel (will not run here)
questions.question: What is Triton?
options: A distributed-training framework for splitting large models across many GPUs
A CUDA library that ships pre-built attention kernels and nothing else
A Python-like language for writing GPU kernels that compile to fast code
A PyTorch profiler that records per-kernel timings and memory on the GPU
questions.explanation: Triton lets you write GPU kernels in Python-like syntax, compiled to efficient code; many production attention and fusion kernels are written in it, and TorchInductor (torch.compile's backend) emits Triton. It is not a profiler or a distributed framework.

questions.section: 6. An illustrative Triton kernel (will not run here)
questions.question: Which PyTorch compiler component emits Triton kernels?
options: Autograd engine
TorchScript JIT
DataLoader
TorchInductor
questions.explanation: TorchInductor, the backend of torch.compile, generates Triton code for fused GPU kernels. Autograd computes gradients and DataLoader feeds data; neither generates kernels.

questions.section: 6. An illustrative Triton kernel (will not run here)
questions.question: In a Triton FlashAttention forward kernel, what do tl.load and tl.store represent?
options: Synchronization barriers between thread blocks
Transfers between CPU RAM and GPU memory
Reads and writes of the Python-level attention module's parameters
Explicit transfers between HBM and on-chip SRAM
questions.explanation: In Triton, tl.load moves a block from global memory (HBM) into on-chip memory and tl.store writes results back. Making these explicit is how the kernel guarantees tiles stay on-chip and the T×T matrix never goes to HBM.

questions.section: 6. An illustrative Triton kernel (will not run here)
questions.question: In a Triton FlashAttention forward kernel, what does each kernel instance identified by tl.program_id(0) own?
options: One query block, which it loads once and loops over all key/value blocks for
One key/value block, which it loads once and broadcasts to every query block
One attention head over the whole sequence, computed without any tiling
One element of the output matrix, computed as a full dot product over all keys
questions.explanation: Each program loads its query block once, keeps running m, ℓ and acc on-chip, streams K/V blocks through, and writes its output block once. Parallelism comes from many programs working on different query blocks.

questions.section: 6. An illustrative Triton kernel (will not run here)
questions.question: Why does the fused Triton FlashAttention kernel deliver the real speed and memory win, while the CPU reference does not?
options: The Triton kernel uses fewer FLOPs because it approximates the softmax with a cheap polynomial
Everything is one kernel, so tiles really stay on-chip and the T×T matrix is never written to HBM
Triton uses a more accurate exponential than PyTorch, so fewer blocks need to be recomputed later
The Triton kernel skips the correction factor on most blocks, saving one exp per row per block
questions.explanation: The win comes from the IO pattern: within one fused kernel, scores and probabilities live only in SRAM, and HBM sees just Q, K, V reads and the O write. The recurrence and FLOPs are the same as the reference; it is neither approximate nor less work.

questions.question: Some Triton FlashAttention kernels use tl.exp2 with scores pre-multiplied by log2(e). Does this change the attention weights?
options: No; but it requires recomputing the denominator in base e at the end
No; 2^(x·log2 e) = e^x, so the weights are identical
Yes; it introduces a constant bias that the output must correct
Yes; base-2 exponentials give sharper attention distributions
questions.explanation: Since 2^(x·log2 e) equals e^x exactly, using exp2 with rescaled scores yields the same weights; it is chosen because exp2 maps well to hardware. No correction at the end is needed.

questions.question: What extra per-row quantity does a FlashAttention forward kernel typically save for the backward pass?
options: The full T×T score matrix S, stored in fp16
The per-row log-sum-exp L of the scores
The full T×T probability matrix P, in bf16
The value matrix V transposed, for dV
questions.explanation: Saving one log-sum-exp per query row lets the backward pass recompute the probabilities tile by tile without storing P, keeping memory O(T). Saving P or S would reintroduce the O(T^2) memory FlashAttention eliminates.

questions.question: What does F.scaled_dot_product_attention use on capable GPUs?
options: A CPU fallback that runs the Python reference
A sparse approximation that drops low-scoring keys
A FlashAttention backend, as a fused kernel
A naive three-kernel implementation that materializes P
questions.explanation: PyTorch's SDPA dispatches to a fused FlashAttention backend on capable GPUs, giving the IO-aware speed and memory benefits. It computes exact attention, which is why the course's tests compare against it.

questions.question: On a CPU-only machine, what is the main job of the attention benchmark script that compares naive attention, SDPA and flash_attention_reference?
options: Memory: it measures the SRAM usage of each path and reports peak bytes per kernel
Profiling: it identifies which CUDA kernels dominate runtime for each of the three paths
Correctness: it asserts all three agree to 1e-3 and reports the naive score-tensor size
Speed: it demonstrates that the flash reference is the fastest path even without a GPU
questions.explanation: Without a GPU there is no SRAM/HBM gap to exploit, so CPU timings cannot show the win. The script's value on CPU is checking that the three implementations agree and showing how large the T×T tensor is that naive attention allocates and flash never does.

questions.question: Why is the flash_attention_reference path slower than naive attention on a CPU?
options: It always computes in fp64, which is much slower than fp32 arithmetic on CPUs
It computes attention approximately and must iterate several times to converge
Its block loop runs in Python and the CPU has no SRAM/HBM distinction to exploit
It performs many fewer FLOPs, and CPUs run small, sparse workloads inefficiently
questions.explanation: The reference loops over blocks in Python, adding interpreter overhead, and the benefit of tiling depends on a fast-on-chip vs slow-off-chip gap that does not exist in the same way on CPU. The speedup is a GPU HBM-traffic effect, so CPU timings should not be read as a speedup.

questions.question: What GPU results are representatively expected from FlashAttention (or the SDPA flash backend) at long context, e.g. T = 4k–16k?
options: About 100× faster than naive attention, with constant memory independent of sequence length
About the same speed as naive attention, but with half the attention memory at every length
About 2× slower than naive attention because of recomputation, but with linear memory
About 2–4× faster than naive attention, with linear instead of quadratic attention memory
questions.explanation: Representative figures from the FlashAttention paper and common reports are ~2–4× speedups and, more importantly, O(T) instead of O(T^2) memory for attention activations. That memory difference often decides between out-of-memory and fitting a long context.

questions.question: What hardware is recommended to actually observe the FlashAttention speed and memory win?
options: A TPU pod running the pure-Python reference implementation under XLA compilation
An A100/H100-class GPU with bf16 and a FlashAttention-capable PyTorch build
Any multi-core CPU with at least 32 GB of RAM and AVX-512 vector units
A consumer GPU running the kernel in fp64 for maximum numerical accuracy
questions.explanation: The win is an HBM-traffic effect on GPUs, so an A100/H100-class GPU with bf16 and a PyTorch build that has a FlashAttention backend is recommended. The correctness check, however, runs on any CPU.

questions.question: What is the central argument of the FlashAttention paper (Dao et al. 2022)?
options: Attention is bottlenecked by parameter count; sharing K and V projections across all heads removes the redundancy
Attention is bottlenecked by HBM reads/writes; tiling plus online softmax gives exact attention with far fewer accesses
Attention is bottlenecked by FLOPs; a low-rank approximation of the score matrix removes most of them with small error
Attention is bottlenecked by softmax's numerical instability; computing scores in fp64 fixes it at modest cost
questions.explanation: The paper's title stresses IO-awareness: attention's cost is dominated by memory traffic, not arithmetic, and an IO-aware algorithm computes exact attention with O(T) memory. Sharing K/V across heads is a different technique (multi-/grouped-query attention).

questions.question: What do FlashAttention-2 and FlashAttention-3 change relative to the original FlashAttention?
options: They refine tiling and work partitioning for newer GPUs; the core algorithm is the same
They remove online softmax entirely and store the full score matrix in fp8 instead
They move part of the attention computation from the GPU to the CPU to save HBM
They replace exact attention with an approximate low-rank method for very long contexts
questions.explanation: The follow-ups improve how work is split across threads and SMs and tune tiling for newer hardware. The underlying tiled online-softmax algorithm, and exactness, are unchanged.

questions.question: If the four keys of an online-softmax example are processed in reverse block order (the block containing the max first), is the final attention output the same?
options: Only if the block size is one, so that each key is its own block
Yes; online softmax is exact regardless of the order blocks arrive
No; reversing the order changes the denominator and therefore the weights
No; the output is only exact when the max arrives in the last block
questions.explanation: Online softmax computes the exact softmax for any order and any partition of keys; only the intermediate running values differ. The final o/ℓ is the same number.

questions.question: If an online-softmax pass processes first the block that contains the row's global maximum, what is the correction factor α on the subsequent blocks?
options: α > 1, because later blocks have smaller scores and the old sums must grow
α = 0, because the max has already been found and the old sums are reset
α < 1, because each later block shrinks the old sums by a constant factor
α = 1, because the running max is already the true max and never changes
questions.explanation: Once m equals the global max, every later m_new = max(m, m_blk) = m, so α = exp(0) = 1 and no rescaling is needed. The first block still has α = 0 because m starts at −∞.

questions.question: What do block-size and block-order invariance tell you about how to choose FlashAttention's block_size on a GPU?
options: Choose it as large as possible, because larger blocks give more accurate results
Choose it as small as possible, because smaller blocks reduce rounding error
Choose it equal to the sequence length so the correction factor is never needed
Choose it to fit tiles in SRAM and maximize throughput; it has no effect on correctness
questions.explanation: Because the result is invariant to block size and order, block size is purely a performance knob: it should make the Q, K, V tiles fit in SRAM and keep the SM busy. Block size equal to T would mean materializing the full row, defeating the purpose.

questions.question: Is FlashAttention an approximation to softmax attention?
options: No; it is exact up to floating-point rounding and changes memory traffic, not math
Yes; it approximates the softmax denominator with a running estimate per block
Only in causal mode, where whole future blocks are skipped instead of computed
Yes; it drops attention scores below a small fixed threshold to save memory and FLOPs
questions.explanation: FlashAttention is exact attention; the running denominator is not an estimate but an exact sum corrected by α. In causal mode, skipped blocks are exactly the ones that would be masked to zero weight anyway, so skipping them is also exact.

questions.question: How does FlashAttention's FLOP count compare with naive attention's?
options: It is reduced by half in general, because only about half of the score tiles are ever computed
It is reduced from O(T^2 d) to O(T d), because the score matrix is never formed
It is identical, with zero extra operations of any kind beyond the naive version
It is not reduced and is slightly higher, due to recomputed exponentials and rescaling
questions.explanation: FlashAttention's win is fewer HBM bytes and O(T) memory, not fewer FLOPs; the rescaling and recomputation add a little arithmetic. Confusing FLOPs saved with bytes saved is a common mistake. Causal skipping saves work in causal mode, but that is not a general halving of the algorithm.

questions.question: Why is materializing the causal mask as a full T×T tensor a mistake in a FlashAttention-style implementation?
options: It reintroduces the O(T^2) memory the algorithm was designed to avoid
It produces numerically incorrect attention weights in fp16 and bf16
It forces all key blocks to be processed in reverse order of position
It prevents the correction factor α from being computed for masked rows
questions.explanation: A full T×T mask is just as large as the score matrix FlashAttention avoids. The correct approach applies the mask per tile from row/column indices and skips fully-future blocks, never building the whole mask.

questions.question: FlashAttention performs slightly more arithmetic than naive attention, yet runs faster on a GPU. Why?
options: The extra arithmetic lets the GPU skip one of the two large matrix multiplications entirely
GPUs execute recomputed exponentials faster than cached ones, thanks to the special function units
Attention is memory-bound, so cutting HBM traffic from O(T^2) to O(T) outweighs the extra FLOPs
The extra FLOPs are offloaded to the CPU and run in parallel with the GPU's matmuls
questions.explanation: At long context attention's runtime is set by HBM bandwidth, not FLOP count. Trading a little extra arithmetic for a large reduction in bytes moved wins, exactly as the roofline predicts for a kernel on the bandwidth slope.

questions.question: What is the through-line of GPU-performance reasoning that carries into distributed training across many GPUs?
options: Larger batch sizes always remove the data-movement bottleneck
Lower precision always makes a kernel compute-bound
Memory is cheap and arithmetic is expensive
Arithmetic is cheap and moving data is expensive
questions.explanation: From the memory hierarchy through the roofline, fusion, mixed precision and FlashAttention, the recurring lesson is that FLOPs are plentiful while data movement limits speed. In distributed training the same problem scales up to moving data between GPUs.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: How does a fused linear cross-entropy relate to the plain lm_head followed by F.cross_entropy?
options: It replaces cross-entropy with a cheaper surrogate loss
It computes the same loss but only for the last position of each sequence
It computes exactly the same loss without holding the full logits tensor
It computes an approximate loss that converges to the same optimum
questions.explanation: Fused linear cross-entropy is an exact reimplementation: the lm_head + F.cross_entropy loss remains the definition, and fused versions reproduce that number (up to rounding order) while never materializing all logits. The plain version is still the right code for small models.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: Which earlier technique does fused linear cross-entropy reuse to avoid the full logits tensor?
options: Low-rank factorization of the LM-head weight into two thin matrices, so V×C is never formed
Top-k sampling of the vocabulary during training, keeping only the k largest logits per position
Gradient checkpointing of every transformer block, discarding activations and recomputing them
The online-softmax recurrence from FlashAttention (running max, running sum, correction)
questions.explanation: The softmax denominator over the vocabulary can be accumulated tile by tile with a running max and running sum, corrected by α when the max rises, exactly as FlashAttention does over keys. This is exact, unlike low-rank or top-k approximations.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: What is the gradient of the cross-entropy loss of one position with respect to its logits z?
options: log softmax(z) − onehot(y)
onehot(y) − softmax(z)
softmax(z) · onehot(y)
softmax(z) − onehot(y)
questions.explanation: Differentiating lse(z) − z_y gives softmax(z) for the logsumexp term and −1 at the target index, so the gradient is softmax(z) − onehot(y). Its sign matters: the negative of this is the gradient of log p_y.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: Why are the logits often the single largest activation in modern LLM training?
options: The logits are duplicated once per attention head before the loss
The logits are stored in fp64 to keep the softmax numerically stable
The logits must be kept for every layer, not just the final layer
Vocabularies of 128k–262k tokens make the (B, T, V) tensor enormous
questions.explanation: The logits tensor has one entry per position per vocabulary token, so with V in the hundreds of thousands it can exceed all per-layer activations of a small model. It exists only once, at the output head, and is normally fp32 for the loss, not fp64.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: Which training frameworks are listed as integrating Liger Kernel's fused linear cross-entropy?
options: Hugging Face Trainer, TRL, Axolotl and LLaMA-Factory
Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed, JAX/Flax and Keras 3
vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, ONNX Runtime and llama.cpp
PyTorch Lightning, fairseq, MosaicML Composer and JAX
questions.explanation: Liger Kernel's fused linear cross-entropy is integrated into the Hugging Face Trainer, TRL, Axolotl and LLaMA-Factory, among others. vLLM and TensorRT-LLM are inference engines, which need full logits for sampling.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: What did TRL v1.15.0 (October 2026) change regarding the LM head?
options: It made the LM head run on CPU to save GPU memory
It made full fp32 logits the default for all trainers
It removed the LM head and used embedding similarity instead
It made a fused LM head the default in six trainers
questions.explanation: TRL v1.15.0 added a fused LM head that projects hidden states in tiles and reduces directly to per-token log-probs and entropy, and turned it on by default across its SFT, DPO, KTO, GRPO, RLOO and Distillation trainers.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: What is needed to get the real speed and memory benefit of fused cross-entropy, as opposed to verifying the algorithm?
options: A pure-PyTorch implementation running on a many-core CPU with plenty of RAM
A larger batch size, so that each row chunk is bigger and its overhead is better amortized
Running the naive loss in bf16 instead of fp32 to halve the size of the logits tensor
A GPU kernel such as Liger Kernel, Cut Cross-Entropy or TRL's fused LM head
questions.explanation: A pure-PyTorch from-scratch implementation proves the algorithm and runs on CPU, but the speed and memory win comes from GPU kernels that keep tiles on-chip and avoid HBM round trips. Using bf16 for the naive path only halves the size and loses precision.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 1. Intuition: you need two numbers per row, not V
questions.question: How is the cross-entropy loss of a single position expressed in terms of its logits z and target y?
options: softmax(z)_y − 1
logsumexp(z) − z_y
z_y − logsumexp(z)
log(z_y) − Σ_j z_j
questions.explanation: Cross-entropy is −log softmax(z)_y = −(z_y − logsumexp(z)) = logsumexp(z) − z_y: the log of the softmax denominator minus the target logit. The reverse sign is the log-probability, which is negative.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 1. Intuition: you need two numbers per row, not V
questions.question: How many numbers per position are actually needed to compute the cross-entropy loss?
options: Two: one log-normalizer and one target logit
C: one per hidden dimension of the final state
One: just the target logit, with no normalizer
V: one logit per vocabulary entry, all stored
questions.explanation: The loss is lse(z) − z_y, which needs only the log-normalizer and the target logit. The naive code nonetheless builds and stores all V logits per position, which is what fused methods avoid.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 1. Intuition: you need two numbers per row, not V
questions.question: For N = 32,768 tokens and a vocabulary of V = 151,936 in fp32, roughly how large is the full logits tensor?
options: About 19.9 GB
About 131 KB
About 622 MB
About 2.5 GB
questions.explanation: 32,768 × 151,936 × 4 bytes ≈ 19.9 GB. 622 MB is the size of a 1,024-row chunk, and 131 KB is the size of one (N,) fp32 statistic, which is what vocabulary tiling keeps.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 1. Intuition: you need two numbers per row, not V
questions.question: Besides building all V logits per position, what extra memory does the naive cross-entropy path keep for backward?
options: Nothing; backward recomputes everything from the hidden states
A same-size (N, V) tensor of saved softmax or gradient
A copy of the full transformer activations in fp64
An (N, N) attention matrix for the LM head
questions.explanation: The naive path writes the logits, reads them back for logsumexp, and keeps an (N, V)-sized tensor (softmax or gradient) for the backward pass, doubling the problem. Recomputing in backward is what the vocabulary-tiled method does.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 1. Intuition: you need two numbers per row, not V
questions.question: How is the target logit z_y computed without building all V logits?
options: As the logsumexp of the full logit row minus the per-position loss value
As the average of all logits in the row, which tracks the target logit on average
As a single dot product h · w_y between the hidden state and the target's weight row
As the maximum over all logits in the row, found with a running max over the vocabulary tiles
questions.explanation: z_y = h · w_y needs only the target token's row of the LM-head weight, so it costs O(C) per position instead of O(CV). The max of the row is the stabilizer for logsumexp, not the target logit.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 1. Intuition: you need two numbers per row, not V
questions.question: What does the row-chunked approach to fused cross-entropy (Liger Kernel) do?
options: Computes the loss on a random subset of positions per step and rescales it to the full batch
Stores logits for all positions but in 8-bit precision, dequantizing them for the backward pass
Builds full (n, V) logits for n positions at a time, computes loss and gradients, then discards them
Walks across the vocabulary B_v columns at a time keeping only a running max and sum for all positions
questions.explanation: Chunking the rows means each chunk has complete logits for its positions, which is enough for an exact loss and exact gradients for those rows. Memory is one chunk. Walking the vocabulary with running statistics is the vocabulary-tiled (Cut Cross-Entropy) approach.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 1. Intuition: you need two numbers per row, not V
questions.question: What does the vocabulary-tiled approach to fused cross-entropy (Cut Cross-Entropy) do?
options: Stores logits for all positions in pinned CPU memory and streams them back to the GPU tile by tile during backward
For all positions, walks the vocabulary B_v columns at a time with running statistics; recomputes tiles in backward
Prunes the vocabulary to the most frequent tokens before the LM head, so the logits are much narrower
Builds full logits for a chunk of positions at a time and computes that chunk's gradients in the forward pass
questions.explanation: Tiling the columns keeps only O(N) per-row statistics (running max and sum) in forward, then recomputes each tile in backward. That is Cut Cross-Entropy. Computing gradients in the forward pass per row chunk is the Liger approach.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 1. Intuition: you need two numbers per row, not V
questions.question: How does a production fused cross-entropy GPU kernel typically tile the (N, V) logits matrix?
options: Not at all; it streams the full matrix through L2 cache
Only along the position axis, with full rows in HBM
Only along the vocabulary axis, with full columns in HBM
Along both axes, so each tile lives in on-chip SRAM
questions.explanation: A real kernel tiles both N and V so each tile fits in SRAM; a pure row-chunk or column-tile scheme is the simplified algorithm. Keeping tiles on-chip is what avoids HBM round trips.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: What is the shape and layout of the LM-head weight W in the cross-entropy formulation z_ij = h_i · w_j?
options: (V, V), mapping each vocabulary token to every other token
(V, C), with row w_j for token j, the nn.Linear(C, V) layout
(C, V), with column w_j for token j, the transpose of nn.Linear
(N, V), one row of weights per position in the flattened batch
questions.explanation: nn.Linear(C, V) stores its weight as (out_features, in_features) = (V, C), so each row w_j is token j's output vector. With weight tying this same matrix is the token embedding. (N, V) is the logits shape, not the weight.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: With weight tying in a GPT-style model, what else is the LM-head weight W?
options: The attention output projection
The token embedding matrix
The final layer-norm weight
The positional embedding matrix
questions.explanation: Weight tying shares one (V, C) matrix between the input token embedding (wte) and the output LM head. That sharing has consequences for gradients: both uses must contribute to the same parameter's gradient.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In a batch with ignored target positions, what is the cross-entropy loss divided by?
options: The vocabulary size V, so the loss is a per-class average
The total number of positions in the batch, including ignored ones
The number of valid positions in each chunk, applied chunk by chunk
The global number of valid (non-ignored) positions in the batch
questions.explanation: The loss is (1/|V_valid|) Σ_{i valid} (lse_i − z_{i y_i}), using the global valid count. A chunked implementation must use the same global denominator in every chunk; dividing per chunk gives a mean of means, which is wrong.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In fused cross-entropy, what is lse_i?
options: The plain sum Σ_j z_ij of position i's logits over the vocabulary
log Σ_j exp(z_ij), the log-normalizer of position i's logits
The largest logit at position i, max_j z_ij, used as the stabilizer
The logit of the target token at position i, h_i · w_{y_i}
questions.explanation: lse_i = log Σ_{j=1}^V exp(z_ij) is the log of the softmax denominator. The loss per position is lse_i minus the target logit. The max is used only to compute lse stably.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 2.2 The gradient with respect to the logits
questions.question: What is the derivative of lse_i = log Σ_j exp(z_ij) with respect to the logit z_ij?
options: The indicator 1[j = y_i]: 1 at the target and 0 elsewhere
1 for every j, because the log of a sum is linear in each z
The softmax probability p_ij = exp(z_ij − lse_i)
exp(z_ij), the unnormalized exponential of that logit
questions.explanation: ∂/∂z_ij log Σ exp(z) = exp(z_ij)/Σ exp(z) = p_ij. The indicator 1 at j = y_i comes from the −z_{i y_i} term, not from lse.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 2.2 The gradient with respect to the logits
questions.question: What is the gradient g_ij of the batch cross-entropy loss with respect to logit z_ij, including masking?
options: (1[i valid]/|V_valid|)·(p_ij − 1[j = y_i])
(1[i valid]/|V_valid|)·(1[j = y_i] − p_ij)
p_ij − 1[j = y_i], with no masking or scaling
(1/N)·(p_ij − 1[j = y_i]), counting ignored positions
questions.explanation: Each valid row contributes p_ij − onehot, scaled by the global mean factor 1/|V_valid|; ignored rows contribute zero. Dividing by N would wrongly count ignored positions, and flipping the sign gives the gradient of log-prob.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 2.2 The gradient with respect to the logits
questions.question: Given z = H W^T with H of shape (N, C) and W of shape (V, C), what is the gradient of the loss with respect to H?
options: G^T H, of shape (V, C)
G W, of shape (N, C)
H G^T, of shape (N, N)
W G, of shape (C, N)
questions.explanation: Backprop through z = H W^T gives ∂L/∂H = G W, with G the (N, V) logit gradient; the shape matches H. G^T H is the gradient with respect to W.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 2.2 The gradient with respect to the logits
questions.question: Given z = H W^T with H of shape (N, C) and W of shape (V, C), what is the gradient of the loss with respect to W?
options: H^T G, of shape (C, V)
G^T H, of shape (V, C)
W^T G, of shape (C, N)
G W, of shape (N, C)
questions.explanation: ∂L/∂W = G^T H, a (V, C) matrix matching W. It is a sum over rows i of outer products g_i h_i^T, which is why chunks can each add their contribution. H^T G has the transposed shape (C, V).

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 2.2 The gradient with respect to the logits
questions.question: Why are row chunks of the logits matrix self-contained for computing cross-entropy gradients?
options: Each row's gradient depends on all other rows through the softmax, so chunks are only approximately independent
Row chunks share no parameters at all, so their gradients are independent and need no accumulation
Row i of G needs only row i's logits and lse_i, so a chunk's gradients can be computed immediately
Each chunk uses its own private copy of the LM-head weight, which is averaged after backward
questions.explanation: Softmax is row-wise, so g_i depends only on row i's logits and its normalizer (plus the global valid count). Once a chunk's logits exist, its rows of G, its rows of ∂L/∂H, and its contribution to ∂L/∂W can all be computed. The chunks do share W, which is why ∂W contributions are added.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 2.2 The gradient with respect to the logits
questions.question: How does a row chunk contribute to the gradient of the LM-head weight ∂L/∂W in chunked cross-entropy?
options: It contributes nothing; with tied weights W's gradient comes only from the embedding lookup
It overwrites ∂L/∂W with G_chunk^T H_chunk, so the last chunk's value is the gradient
It adds G_chunk^T H_chunk, an additive contribution accumulated over chunks
It contributes only after all chunks' logits are concatenated into one (N, V) tensor
questions.explanation: ∂L/∂W = G^T H is a sum over rows, so each chunk's G_chunk^T H_chunk is added to a running total. Overwriting would keep only the last chunk's gradient, a common bug.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 2.2 The gradient with respect to the logits
questions.question: Why can the vocabulary-tiled backward compute gradients without storing any logits?
options: For a vocabulary tile, g_ij needs only that tile's logits and the saved scalar lse_i, so tiles are recomputed
The gradient for each tile can be read back from the optimizer's saved first-moment state for the weight W
