The gradient is identical across vocabulary tiles, so computing one tile and broadcasting it to the rest suffices
The gradient does not depend on the logits at all, only on the targets and the global valid count
questions.explanation: g_ij = (exp(z_ij − lse_i) − 1[j = y_i])/|V_valid|. Saving lse_i from forward is enough; backward recomputes z for each tile from h_i and w_j and discards it. That is the recomputation trade.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In online logsumexp over vocabulary tiles, how is the running sum ℓ updated when tile k arrives?
options: ℓ^(k) = ℓ^(k−1)·exp(m^(k) − m^(k−1)) + Σ_{j in tile} exp(z_j − m^(k−1))
ℓ^(k) = ℓ^(k−1) + Σ_{j in tile} exp(z_j), with no max subtracted at all
ℓ^(k) = ℓ^(k−1)·exp(m^(k−1) − m^(k)) + Σ_{j in tile} exp(z_j − m^(k))
ℓ^(k) = max(ℓ^(k−1), Σ_{j in tile} exp(z_j − m^(k)))
questions.explanation: The old sum is rescaled by α = exp(m_old − m_new) ≤ 1 to the new max, and the tile's terms are exponentiated against the new max. Summing raw exp(z) would overflow; the reversed exponent would grow rather than shrink the old sum.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: After processing all vocabulary tiles with online logsumexp, how is the log-normalizer lse obtained from the running max m and running sum ℓ?
options: lse = ℓ − m
lse = log m + ℓ
lse = m · ℓ
lse = m + log ℓ
questions.explanation: ℓ = Σ exp(z − m), so log Σ exp(z) = log(exp(m)·ℓ) = m + log ℓ. Adding m back undoes the max subtraction used for stability.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In online logsumexp over vocabulary tiles, what are the initial values of the running max and running sum?
questions.explanation: With m = −∞ the first tile's max becomes the running max, and α = exp(−∞) = 0 multiplies the empty ℓ = 0, so nothing spurious is carried forward. Starting ℓ at 1 would add a phantom term to the denominator.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: Why do RL and distillation trainers need per-token log-probabilities log p_{i y_i} rather than just a loss?
options: For computing a per-token learning-rate schedule during the update
For selecting which transformer layers to freeze in each step
For building the causal attention mask over generated tokens
For importance ratios, KL penalties and distillation divergences
questions.explanation: RL objectives such as PPO/GRPO use importance ratios between policy log-probs, KL penalties against a reference model, and distillation divergences, all of which need per-token log-probs. These trainers score tokens rather than just training on a mean loss.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In GRPO-style trainers, what is per-token entropy H_i used for?
options: As the learning rate for each token
As the main policy-gradient reward
As a monitoring signal and an optional bonus
As the denominator of the advantage normalization
questions.explanation: Entropy indicates how spread out the policy's distribution is, making it a useful monitoring signal (for example, to spot collapse), and some trainers add it as an optional bonus. It is not the reward itself.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: How is the per-token log-probability log p_{i y_i} computed from the log-normalizer?
options: lse_i − z_{i y_i}
log(z_{i y_i}) − log(lse_i)
z_{i y_i} / lse_i
z_{i y_i} − lse_i
questions.explanation: log p_y = log(exp(z_y)/Σ exp(z)) = z_y − lse. The opposite sign, lse − z_y, is the cross-entropy loss.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: How can the per-token entropy H_i = −Σ_j p_ij log p_ij be computed online from running statistics?
options: H_i = s_i − lse_i, where s_i = Σ_j exp(z_ij) is the raw running sum
H_i = m_i − log ℓ_i, using only the running max and running sum
H_i = lse_i − s_i/ℓ_i, where s_i = Σ_j exp(z_ij − m_i)·z_ij
H_i = lse_i + s_i·ℓ_i, where s_i = Σ_j z_ij is the plain logit sum
questions.explanation: Substituting log p = z − lse gives H = lse − Σ_j p_j z_j, and Σ p z = s/ℓ with s the running exp-weighted sum of logits. So the entropy needs one extra running sum s besides m and ℓ.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In online entropy computation over vocabulary tiles, how is the extra running sum s = Σ exp(z − m)·z updated when the running max rises?
options: It is divided by α = exp(m_old − m_new) instead of multiplied, so the old terms grow to match
It is multiplied by the same correction α = exp(m_old − m_new) as ℓ, then the tile's terms are added
It is reset to zero and recomputed from the new tile only, since older terms are now negligible
It is left unchanged, because the logits z inside s do not depend on the running max
questions.explanation: s has the same exp(z − m) weights as ℓ, so re-referencing it to a new max requires the same α. Leaving it unchanged would mix terms referenced to different maxima.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: How many running numbers per row are needed to compute both the log-prob and the entropy without the (N, V) logits tensor?
options: V: one stored probability per vocabulary entry, kept for backward
Two: the running sum ℓ and the target logit, nothing else needed
Three: m, ℓ and s (plus the target logit by a dot product)
One: the running max m, from which both lse and entropy follow
questions.explanation: m and ℓ give lse = m + log ℓ, which with the target logit gives the log-prob; s gives Σ p z, and H = lse − s/ℓ. Three per-row numbers suffice.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: When computing cross-entropy with vocabulary tiles, why does the target logit need no tile at all?
options: It is a single dot product h · w_y that can be computed directly
It is recovered afterwards from the loss as lse minus the loss value
It is always exactly zero after the running max has been subtracted
It is always the largest logit, so it simply equals the running max m
questions.explanation: z_y = h · w_y only needs the target's weight row, so it can be computed independently of the vocabulary loop. The target logit is not necessarily the largest logit.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In the vocabulary-tiled backward of fused cross-entropy, what does each vocabulary tile need to produce its rows of ∂L/∂W?
options: The full softmax matrix stored during the forward pass, read back tile by tile
The upstream gradient of the next transformer layer's attention output
Only its own logits (recomputed) and the scalar log-normalizer lse per position
The recomputed logits of every other tile, to renormalize this tile's softmax
questions.explanation: g for tile J is exp(z_J − lse) − onehot restricted to J, which needs only that tile's recomputed logits and lse. Then grad_w[J] = g^T h. No other tile or stored softmax is required.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In what unit is entropy expressed when computed with natural logarithms, as in H = lse − Σ p z?
options: Nats
Bytes
Decibels
Bits
questions.explanation: Using natural log (base e), as logsumexp does, yields entropy in nats. Bits would correspond to log base 2.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: What dtype and ignore convention are used for targets in fused cross-entropy?
options: int8, with 0 marking ignored positions to save memory on the targets
float32, with NaN marking ignored positions so they drop out of sums
bool, with False marking ignored positions and True marking valid ones
int64, with −100 (or −1 in the course GPT) marking ignored positions
questions.explanation: Targets are int64 token ids; −100 is PyTorch's default ignore_index and the course GPT uses −1. Ignored rows contribute neither loss nor gradient and are excluded from the valid count.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In fused cross-entropy, what is the shape and dtype of the per-row state lse, m, l and s?
options: (N, C), bf16
(N, V), fp32
questions.explanation: These are one scalar per position, so (N,), and they are kept in fp32 for precision. They are the only per-row state the vocabulary-tiled method keeps.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In fused cross-entropy, what are the sizes of grad_h and grad_w?
options: (C, N) and (C, V), the transposes of the input shapes
(N, V) and (V, C), since grad_h is built from logits
(N, C) and (V, C), the same as the inputs, never (N, V)
(N, V) and (V, V), one entry per logit and per token pair
questions.explanation: grad_h matches h and grad_w matches the LM-head weight. The point of fused methods is that no (N, V) tensor is materialized, even for gradients.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: Why should fused cross-entropy accumulate in fp32 even when the hidden states and LM-head weight are bf16?
options: Summing exp terms over ~150k vocabulary entries and G^T H over thousands of rows loses precision in bf16
bf16 cannot represent negative logits, so the max-subtracted exponents underflow to exactly zero in every tile
bf16 matmuls are not supported by tensor cores for the tall, skinny LM-head shape used in the loss
fp32 accumulation makes the kernel execute fewer FLOPs, because each exp needs fewer correction steps
questions.explanation: bf16 has few mantissa bits, so long sums lose digits; the logsumexp over a huge vocabulary and the weight gradient summed over many rows are exactly such long sums. bf16 represents negative numbers fine; the issue is precision, not range or support.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In the vocabulary-tiled path of fused cross-entropy, what is the shape of one vocabulary tile of logits?
options: (N, B_v), all positions by one block of vocabulary columns
(B_v, C), one block of LM-head weight rows for B_v tokens
(n, V), one chunk of positions against the whole vocabulary
(N, V), the whole logits matrix, built once and then sliced
questions.explanation: A vocabulary tile covers all N positions and B_v columns; a GPU kernel would additionally tile N. (n, V) is a row chunk in the row-chunked scheme.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In the row-chunked fused cross-entropy implemented as a custom torch.autograd.Function, what does the forward pass save for backward?
options: The softmax probabilities of each chunk, in bf16 to save space
Only the scalar loss, from which backward rederives the gradients
Only grad_h and grad_w, already computed during forward
The full (N, V) logits tensor, so backward can recompute softmax
questions.explanation: The forward loop computes the loss and the gradients chunk by chunk and saves only the gradients (which are the size of the inputs). Saving logits or softmax would defeat the memory saving.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In row-chunked fused cross-entropy, what does the backward pass do?
options: It multiplies the saved gradients by the upstream scalar grad_out
It recomputes the loss from the saved logits to verify that it matches
It does nothing; the gradients were already written directly into .grad
It recomputes every chunk's logits and softmax, then forms G^T H again
questions.explanation: Because gradients were computed in forward, backward only scales them by grad_out. This works because the loss is the last operation, so any later transformation is a scalar multiplication captured by grad_out.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: Why does computing cross-entropy gradients during the forward pass cost nothing extra?
options: The optimizer recomputes the gradients regardless
Backward would need the same softmax anyway
The forward pass already runs on idle tensor cores
Gradients are free because they are always zero for most rows
questions.explanation: The gradient is softmax − onehot; computing the softmax for the loss and immediately forming the gradient avoids storing it. The work simply moves from backward into forward.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In row-chunked fused cross-entropy, what does the line g *= (v / n_valid)[:, None] accomplish?
options: It converts the gradient to bf16 before it is accumulated into grad_w
It zeroes ignored rows and applies the global mean over valid positions
It scales the gradient by the learning rate so the optimizer step is correct
It normalizes each row's softmax probabilities so that they sum to one
questions.explanation: v is a 0/1 validity mask and n_valid is the global count of valid positions, so multiplying applies both the mask and the global-mean scaling of the loss. This is what avoids the per-chunk-mean bug.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In row-chunked fused cross-entropy, how is the LM-head weight gradient grad_w handled across chunks?
options: grad_w is set to zero because the weight is tied
grad_w = g^T @ hc, overwritten by each chunk
grad_w += g^T @ hc, accumulated over chunks
grad_w is computed once after all chunks from stored logits
questions.explanation: ∂L/∂W is a sum over all rows, so each chunk adds its g^T h contribution. Overwriting would keep only the last chunk; storing logits would defeat the purpose.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: What does the forward pass of the vocabulary-tiled fused cross-entropy keep for backward?
options: grad_h and grad_w, precomputed during the forward pass
Only the per-row log-normalizer lse (plus inputs)
The full softmax matrix, stored compactly in bf16
Every vocabulary tile of logits, kept in HBM for reuse
questions.explanation: The vocabulary-tiled forward runs the online logsumexp and saves lse; backward recomputes each tile. Precomputing grad_h and grad_w is the row-chunked method.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: What trade does the vocabulary-tiled backward make, analogous to FlashAttention?
options: Fewer optimizer steps per epoch in exchange for proportionally larger batches
Storing logits in pinned CPU memory instead of GPU HBM, at the cost of PCIe transfers
One extra matmul to recompute logit tiles instead of storing a huge intermediate
Lower-precision fp8 arithmetic in the tiles instead of exact gradients in fp32
questions.explanation: Backward recomputes z for each tile, forms exp(z − lse) − onehot, and accumulates grad_h and grad_w, never storing logits. Recomputing is cheap compute; storing is scarce memory and bandwidth. This is the FlashAttention bargain.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: What does fused_logprobs_and_entropy(h, weight, targets, block_v, temperature) return, and is it differentiable?
options: Per-token (logprobs, entropy), computed under torch.no_grad()
The full (N, V) log-softmax tensor, differentiable via autograd
Per-token logits for the target token only, differentiable end to end
A scalar mean loss over valid positions with full autograd support
questions.explanation: It runs the online loop with the extra running sum s and returns per-token log-probs and entropy for scoring, under no_grad. Making it differentiable for the log-prob output is left as a follow-up exercise.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: When naive, row-chunked and vocabulary-tiled cross-entropy are run on random data with N = 2048, C = 256 and V = 32,000, the loss is about 10.686. Why is it close to log 32000 ≈ 10.37?
options: The random targets always happen to be the most likely token at each position
The fused methods approximate the loss by log V instead of computing it exactly
Random small weights give a near-uniform distribution over the vocabulary
The loss is clipped from above to the log of the vocabulary size for stability
questions.explanation: With random small LM-head weights the logits are nearly equal, so softmax is close to uniform and cross-entropy is close to log V; random weight noise adds a little. All three methods print the same value because they are exact.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: For N = 2048 and V = 32,000 in fp32, how does the largest intermediate change from naive logits to a 256-row chunk or a 4096-wide vocabulary tile?
options: From about 262 MB to about 33 MB
From about 33 MB to about 262 MB
From about 262 MB to about 131 KB
From about 19.9 GB to about 622 MB
questions.explanation: 2048 × 32,000 × 4 ≈ 262 MB for the full logits; 256 × 32,000 × 4 and 2048 × 4096 × 4 are each about 33 MB. The 19.9 GB and 622 MB figures are for the much larger Qwen-size configuration.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: On a CPU, what is the point of comparing naive, row-chunked and vocabulary-tiled cross-entropy?
options: Measuring the SRAM usage of each method with the CPU profiler and cache counters
Showing that the fused methods reach a lower loss than the naive path on the same data
Demonstrating that the fused methods are roughly 10× faster than naive even on CPU
Which tensors exist (memory), not speed; timings are similar and vary by machine
questions.explanation: All three give the same loss and gradient norm; on CPU timings are of the same order and their order varies. The demonstration is about which intermediates are allocated. Speed benefits require GPU kernels.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 6. What production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: What does Liger Kernel's LigerFusedLinearCrossEntropyLoss implement?
options: A Triton row-chunked scheme with the gradient computed in the forward pass
A CPU kernel that streams logits to disk and reads them back for backward
A CUDA vocabulary-tiled scheme with recomputation of logit tiles in backward
An approximate sampled softmax over a random subset of the vocabulary each step
questions.explanation: Liger (LinkedIn) chunks over positions and computes gradients in forward, in Triton. Vocabulary tiling with recomputation is Cut Cross-Entropy's approach.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 6. What production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: What memory and throughput results are reported for Liger Kernel (authors' measurements)?
options: Higher peak memory from extra buffers, but roughly 2× training throughput across all of its kernels
About 10% memory reduction for fused-linear kernels, with no measurable throughput change overall
Up to 99% memory reduction and 5× throughput for every kernel, including RMSNorm, RoPE and SwiGLU
Up to 80% memory reduction for fused-linear kernels; about 60% less memory and 20% more throughput overall
questions.explanation: The README reports up to 80% memory reduction for the fused-linear kernels, and the paper reports about 60% lower memory and 20% higher throughput for its kernel set against Hugging Face baselines. These are publicly documented authors' measurements.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 6. What production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: How does Cut Cross-Entropy (Apple; Wijmans et al., ICLR 2025) compute the loss?
options: It computes only the target logit and a blockwise logsumexp in SRAM, never writing logits to global memory
It quantizes the logits to 4 bits before storing them in HBM, then dequantizes them again in the backward pass
It chunks positions and stores each chunk's full logits in HBM, computing gradients in the forward pass
It samples a subset of the vocabulary per step and estimates the softmax denominator from that sample
questions.explanation: CCE implements the vocabulary-tiled scheme as an SRAM-resident kernel: target logit via indexed dot product plus blockwise logsumexp. It is exact, not a sampled approximation. It also skips gradient entries too small to matter at the working precision.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 6. What production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: What extra optimization does Cut Cross-Entropy apply in its backward pass?
options: It drops the onehot target term for the most frequent tokens in the batch
It stores the full softmax in fp8 so the backward pass avoids recomputation
It averages gradients across vocabulary tiles instead of summing them
It skips gradient entries too small to matter at the working precision
questions.explanation: Most softmax probabilities over a large vocabulary are tiny, so their gradient contributions vanish at bf16/fp16 precision; CCE skips them. It does not store the softmax, which is the point of recomputation.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 6. What production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: For Gemma 2 2B, what loss-computation memory reduction does the Cut Cross-Entropy paper report?
options: From about 24 GB to about 12 GB
From about 24 GB to about 1 MB
From about 80 GB to about 24 GB
From about 1 GB to about 1 MB
questions.explanation: The paper reports loss-computation memory falling from about 24 GB to about 1 MB, and classifier-head training memory from 28 GB to 1 GB, without slowing training or hurting convergence (authors' measurements).

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 6. What production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: Which TRL v1.15.0 trainers got the fused LM head by default?
options: Only SFT and DPO, the two offline trainers
PPO, ORPO and reward modeling, but no others
Only GRPO, for its RL log-prob scoring pass
SFT, DPO, KTO, GRPO, RLOO and Distillation
questions.explanation: TRL v1.15.0 added the fused LM head to six trainers — SFT, DPO, KTO, GRPO, RLOO and Distillation — and turned it on by default. It reduces directly to per-token log-probs and entropy.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 6. What production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: What improvements did TRL v1.15.0 report for its fused LM head on gemma-3-1b (262k vocabulary, one 79 GiB GPU, bf16, batch 1)?
options: About 10% higher throughput for every trainer, with no change in peak memory or maximum sequence length
Max trainable sequence length up 100× across all trainers and about 99% lower peak memory at 8,192 tokens
Max trainable sequence length unchanged, but roughly 2× faster training steps for DPO, KTO, GRPO and RLOO
Max sequence length up 4.0–6.9× for DPO, KTO, GRPO and RLOO scoring; 52–82% lower peak memory at 8,192 tokens
questions.explanation: The notes report 5.8× (DPO), 6.9× (KTO), 4.0× (GRPO scoring) and 4.3× (RLOO scoring) longer max sequence length versus v1.14.2, and peak memory drops of 52–82% at 8,192 tokens. These are maintainer measurements.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 6. What production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: In TRL v1.15.0, what happened to SFT's existing default chunked_nll loss?
options: It was removed in favor of the naive lm_head loss path
It was already memory-efficient and was left unchanged
It was replaced by Liger's fused kernel as the new default
It was renamed and rewritten to run about 2× faster
questions.explanation: SFT already used a memory-efficient chunked_nll loss by default, so its behavior did not change. The big gains were in preference and RL trainers.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 6. What production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: Which conditions did the TRL v1.15.0 release notes say were not measured for the fused LM head?
options: The DPO and KTO trainers on long sequences
bf16 precision and a batch size of exactly 1
Multi-GPU training and real generation
Single-GPU training on purely synthetic data
questions.explanation: The notes explicitly say multi-GPU and real generation were not measured; their numbers come from one 79 GiB GPU in bf16 at batch size 1. Reading what was not measured is part of interpreting such claims.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: What are the FLOPs of the LM-head matmul in forward and backward, regardless of the cross-entropy scheme?
options: 4NCV in forward and 2NCV in backward
2NCV in forward and 2NCV in backward
2NCV in forward and 4NCV in backward
NCV in forward and NCV in backward
questions.explanation: Forward is one (N, C) × (C, V) matmul, 2NCV FLOPs. Backward has two matmuls of the same size, for ∂H and ∂W, so 4NCV. Fused schemes do not change this baseline.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: How many extra FLOPs does the row-chunked (Liger) cross-entropy scheme add?
options: +2NCV, to recompute logits in backward
+NV, to recompute the softmax
None; backward work is moved into forward
+4NCV, to recompute both gradients
questions.explanation: The row-chunked scheme computes gradients during forward from the same chunk logits, so no extra matmul is needed. Recomputing logits (+2NCV) is the vocabulary-tiled scheme's cost.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: How many extra FLOPs does the vocabulary-tiled (Cut Cross-Entropy) scheme add?
options: None, because tiles are cached in SRAM
+4NCV, to recompute both gradient matmuls
+NC, for the target-logit dot products only
+2NCV, to recompute the logit tiles in backward
questions.explanation: Backward must recompute z = h W^T for each tile, one extra forward-sized matmul of 2NCV FLOPs. In exchange it keeps only O(N) statistics instead of (N, V) logits.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: For V = 151,936 in fp32, how large is a 1,024-row chunk of logits, and how does it compare with full logits for N = 32,768?
options: About 131 KB, a 150,000× reduction from about 19.9 GB
About 622 MB, a 32× reduction from about 19.9 GB
About 6.2 GB, a 3× reduction from about 19.9 GB
About 62 MB, a 320× reduction from about 19.9 GB
questions.explanation: 1,024 × 151,936 × 4 ≈ 622 MB, and 32,768/1,024 = 32, so a 32× reduction. 131 KB is the size of one (N,) fp32 statistic for vocabulary tiling.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: Why are fused cross-entropy kernels usually faster, not just smaller, than the naive path on a GPU?
options: Softmax and logsumexp are memory-bound, so avoiding the round trip of NV floats through HBM saves time
They skip the backward matmuls entirely, since the gradients are derived analytically from the loss
They use integer arithmetic for the softmax, which runs faster than floating point on the GPU's tensor cores
They perform far fewer matmul FLOPs than the naive path, because only the target logit is ever formed
questions.explanation: At a few FLOPs per element the softmax/logsumexp is limited by bytes moved; keeping logits on-chip removes those HBM round trips. The matmul FLOPs are the same or slightly higher.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: Why must the row-chunked cross-entropy scheme know that the loss is final?
options: It deletes the hidden states after forward, so they are gone before backward can use them
It requires the optimizer step to run inside forward, right after the gradients are computed
It cannot compute the scalar loss value itself until the backward pass has fully finished
It computes ∂W in forward, so any later change to the loss must be folded into the kernel
questions.explanation: Gradients are computed during forward assuming the loss is the last op; a later scalar multiply is handled by grad_out, but anything else applied to the logits or loss (a second loss term, a weight) must be implemented inside the kernel.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: Why do logit soft-capping, z-loss, label smoothing and temperature have to be implemented explicitly inside a fused cross-entropy kernel?
options: They change the logit gradient g_ij, and the logits are never available outside the kernel
They only apply at inference time, so the training kernel must emulate them for consistency
They require the full vocabulary to be sorted by logit, which only the kernel can do on-chip
They are incompatible with fp32 accumulation, so the kernel must switch them to bf16 internally
questions.explanation: Each of these transforms the logits or the loss, which changes g_ij. Since fused kernels never expose the logits, a trainer cannot apply them afterwards; the kernel must implement them.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: Why does TRL's fused LM head force Liger's fused_linear_cross_entropy off?
options: Both try to own the same LM-head computation
Liger's kernel does not support bf16 inputs
TRL's fused head only works on CPU, not GPU
Liger's kernel is numerically incorrect at long T
questions.explanation: Both kernels take over the hidden-states-to-loss computation through the LM head, so only one can be active. The release notes state this explicitly.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 7. Side by side, and when to keep the original
questions.question: Which cross-entropy scheme makes the full logits available?
options: All three make the full (N, V) logits available after the forward pass
Naive: yes; row-chunked: per chunk only; vocabulary-tiled: never
None of the three ever forms logits, even for a single chunk or tile
Naive: never; row-chunked: yes; vocabulary-tiled: per tile only
questions.explanation: The naive path builds the entire (N, V) logits; the row-chunked path has full logits for one chunk at a time; the vocabulary-tiled path keeps only per-row statistics and never has a full logit row.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 7. Side by side, and when to keep the original
questions.question: Which cross-entropy schemes need a custom backward?
options: Row-chunked and vocabulary-tiled; the naive path uses ordinary autograd
None of them; all three use ordinary autograd on the scalar loss value
Only the naive path, because it is the one that stores the full logits tensor
Only the row-chunked path; the vocabulary-tiled path uses plain autograd instead
questions.explanation: The naive path is lm_head + F.cross_entropy under autograd. Row-chunked computes gradients in forward and vocabulary-tiled recomputes tiles in backward, both via a custom autograd.Function.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 7. Side by side, and when to keep the original
questions.question: When should you keep the naive lm_head + F.cross_entropy instead of a fused cross-entropy?
options: When you need logits: generation, logging the full distribution, storing teacher top-k logits, or a small model
Whenever the sequence length exceeds 8k tokens, because fused kernels lose precision on long rows of positions
Whenever the vocabulary exceeds 100k tokens, because the fused vocabulary tiles no longer fit in on-chip SRAM
Whenever training uses bf16 weights, because fused kernels require fp32 hidden states and fp32 LM-head parameters
questions.explanation: Sampling (top-k, top-p), logging distributions, and saving teacher top-k logits for offline distillation all need logits, and small models have cheap logits. Large vocabularies and long contexts are exactly when fused methods help most. The naive path is also the reference for tests.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: 7. Side by side, and when to keep the original
questions.question: When is each fused cross-entropy scheme a good choice?
options: Both are only appropriate for small vocabularies, where the extra kernel overhead is negligible
Row-chunked only for generation-time scoring; vocabulary-tiled only for debugging the naive path
Row-chunked as a simple robust default; vocabulary-tiled for the largest V and N with minimal memory
Row-chunked for the largest V and N with minimal memory; vocabulary-tiled for small, short-context models
questions.explanation: Row chunking is simple and robust; vocabulary tiling minimizes memory to O(N) statistics at the cost of recomputation, which pays off at the largest vocabularies and token counts.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: Exercise: add z-loss to the vocabulary-tiled path
questions.question: What is PaLM's auxiliary z-loss, and what is it for?
options: λ·H_i per valid row, an entropy bonus that encourages exploration
λ·z_{i y_i}^2 per valid row, to keep the target logit itself near zero
λ·lse_i^2 per valid row (λ ≈ 1e-4), to keep the log-normalizer near zero
λ·||W||^2 summed over the LM-head weight, an L2 penalty on its rows
questions.explanation: z-loss penalizes the squared log-normalizer, encouraging lse to stay near zero for numerical stability. It is not weight decay or an entropy bonus.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: Exercise: add z-loss to the vocabulary-tiled path
questions.question: Adding z-loss λ·lse_i^2 to cross-entropy changes the logit gradient how?
options: The whole gradient g_ij is multiplied by λ·lse_i^2; nothing else changes
The factor multiplying p_ij becomes (1 + 2λ·lse_i); the onehot term is unchanged
A constant 2λ is added to every g_ij, independent of the probabilities
The onehot term is multiplied by (1 + 2λ·lse_i); the p_ij term is unchanged
questions.explanation: ∂(λ lse_i^2)/∂z_ij = 2λ lse_i·p_ij, so g_ij becomes (1 + 2λ lse_i)p_ij − 1[j = y_i], scaled as before. lse is already saved in forward, so the (N,) factor is computed once outside the tile loop.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: A chunked loss computes F.cross_entropy(..., ignore_index=-100) per chunk (mean per chunk), sums chunks and divides by the number of chunks. Why is it wrong on SFT batches with masked prompts?
options: It is a mean of means, which over-weights tokens in chunks with few valid tokens
It double-counts the ignored tokens in every chunk's denominator and numerator
It computes a gradient of the wrong sign for any chunk that contains masked rows
It divides by the vocabulary size instead of the number of valid tokens in the batch
questions.explanation: Each chunk is averaged over its own valid count, then chunks get equal weight, so tokens in sparsely valid chunks count more. This equals the global mean only when every chunk has the same number of valid tokens.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In a chunked cross-entropy that averages per chunk with ignore_index, what happens to a chunk whose targets are all prompt tokens set to −100?
options: It returns zero and is harmless
It returns NaN (0/0) and poisons the total loss
It raises an exception before the forward pass
It returns the log of the vocabulary size
questions.explanation: With no valid tokens, the per-chunk mean is 0/0 = NaN, and adding NaN to the running loss makes the whole loss NaN. Summing per-row losses and dividing once by the global valid count avoids this.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: What is the correct fix for a chunked cross-entropy over masked SFT batches?
options: Average per chunk, then multiply by the number of chunks and divide by N
Drop any chunk that contains masked tokens, so all chunks are fully valid
Sum per-row losses with reduction='sum' and divide once by the global valid count
Use a smaller chunk size so each chunk has one token and the means coincide
questions.explanation: Summing per-row losses and dividing by the global count reproduces the true mean over valid tokens. This is the same 'normalize by what?' question as Dr. GRPO's length normalization and gradient accumulation.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: Which weight-tying mistake can arise with a hand-written fused cross-entropy?
options: Tying makes the LM-head gradient always zero, because the embedding lookup absorbs all of it
Tying requires the logits to be stored in fp64, which a hand-written fused kernel cannot provide
Writing .grad by hand can overwrite the embedding's gradient instead of adding the LM-head one
Tying doubles the effective vocabulary size, so every fused vocabulary tile must be twice as wide
questions.explanation: With tied embeddings, the shared weight receives gradient from both the embedding lookup and the LM head, and they must be summed. Returning grad_w from a custom autograd.Function lets autograd add it; writing .grad manually can silently clobber the embedding's contribution.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: Why does the fused cross-entropy test multiply the loss by 2.5 before calling backward?
options: To catch implementations that ignore the upstream gradient grad_out
To simulate a learning-rate warmup factor applied to the loss
To check that the gradients are invariant to scaling the loss
To make the loss large enough that fp32 rounding cannot hide errors
questions.explanation: If the loss is scaled (loss scaling, gradient accumulation by loss/k), precomputed gradients must be multiplied by grad_out. A test with 2.5·loss catches backward functions that return the unscaled saved gradients.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: What happens if a trainer applies temperature or soft-capping to logits when using a fused cross-entropy kernel that does not implement them?
options: The modifier is applied only in the backward pass, so loss and gradients disagree
It either errors out or silently skips the modifier, because the logits no longer exist
The modifier is applied twice, once by the trainer and once again inside the kernel
The kernel automatically detects the modifier from the trainer config and applies it itself
questions.explanation: Fused kernels never expose the logits, so a modifier meant to act on them has nothing to operate on; the trainer may raise an error or quietly skip it. Modifiers must be implemented inside the kernel.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: What to read / what to skip
questions.question: When reading the Cut Cross-Entropy paper, which parts deserve focus and which can be skimmed?
options: Read the indexed-matmul plus blockwise-logsumexp method and the memory table; skim gradient filtering and vocabulary sorting
Read the gradient filtering and vocabulary sorting sections closely; skim the indexed-matmul method and the memory table
Read only the related-work section and the abstract closely; skim the rest, since the method mirrors Liger's chunking
Read the RMSNorm, RoPE and SwiGLU kernel benchmarks closely; skim the blockwise-logsumexp loss method and the memory table
questions.explanation: The core idea is computing the loss as an indexed matmul (target logit) plus a blockwise logsumexp, and the memory table shows the impact. Gradient filtering and vocabulary sorting are kernel-writer details.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.section: What to read / what to skip
questions.question: When reading the Liger Kernel paper, what is recommended to skip?
options: The fused linear cross-entropy section and its chunking scheme
The per-kernel benchmarks for RMSNorm, RoPE and SwiGLU
The description of chunking with the gradient computed in forward
The memory reduction results for the fused-linear kernels
questions.explanation: For this topic, the fused linear cross-entropy section (chunking, gradient in forward) is what matters; the other kernels' benchmarks are not needed.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: What is the gradient of the per-token log-probability log p_{i y_i} with respect to the logits z_ij?
options: p_ij − 1[j = y_i], exactly the same as the cross-entropy gradient
−(p_ij − 1[j = y_i]), the negative of the cross-entropy gradient
p_ij, the softmax probability, with no target term at all
1[j = y_i], the onehot target, since lse does not depend on z
questions.explanation: log p_y = z_y − lse, whose gradient is 1[j = y] − p_j = −(p_j − onehot). A GRPO loss multiplies this by an upstream per-token gradient.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: In discussions of how closed labs compute the LM-head loss, which claim falls under inference rather than public documentation?
options: That Liger lists the Hugging Face Trainer and TRL among its integrations
That Cut Cross-Entropy and Liger report their own memory savings
That a given closed lab uses one specific fused cross-entropy scheme
That TRL v1.15.0 enables a fused LM head by default in six trainers
questions.explanation: The CCE and Liger results, Liger's integrations and TRL v1.15.0's defaults are all publicly documented. Which scheme a closed lab uses is inference, since labs rarely say and the schemes produce the same numbers.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: Which practices around LM-head loss computation are classified as reasonable industry practice?
options: Using sampled-softmax approximations of the loss for all large-vocabulary pretraining runs
Disabling weight tying whenever a fused kernel is used, so the LM head has its own gradient
Storing all logits in fp64 for exact bitwise reproducibility across different GPU types
fp32 accumulation inside fused kernels and never materializing logits at long context or large V
questions.explanation: Accumulating in fp32 and avoiding full logits in large-vocabulary or long-context training are reasonable industry practice. The other options are not supported practices.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: Why can the row-chunked scheme compute ∂L/∂W during the forward pass?
options: ∂W does not depend on the hidden states at all, only on the targets and the global valid count
The forward pass stores the full logits anyway, so a separate backward pass is simply unnecessary
The LM-head weight is frozen during training, so its gradient can be precomputed once up front
g_ij depends only on that row's logits and the global valid count, and ∂W = G^T H sums over rows
questions.explanation: Once a chunk's logits exist, its G rows are known and its contribution G_chunk^T H_chunk can be added to ∂W immediately. The only assumption is that the loss is final apart from a scalar, which grad_out handles.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: The vocabulary-tiled backward recomputes every logit tile. Why is that a good trade?
options: Recomputation is free, because GPUs cache recent matmul results in L2 and return them on reuse
The recompute is one compute-bound 2NCV matmul; storing logits costs NV floats and HBM round trips
Storing logits is impossible in fp32 on any current GPU, so recomputation is the only option left
Recomputation produces more accurate gradients than stored logits, because rounding errors cancel
questions.explanation: A compute-bound matmul runs fast on tensor cores, whereas storing logits uses scarce memory and makes the memory-bound softmax shuttle bytes. Trading cheap FLOPs for scarce bytes is the roofline argument and FlashAttention's choice.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: What is the cost of computing all target logits z_{i y_i} directly, compared with computing all logits?
options: O(CV) instead of O(NCV)
O(NV) instead of O(NCV)
O(N) instead of O(NC)
O(NC) instead of O(NCV)
questions.explanation: Gathering row y_i of W and taking one C-dimensional dot product per position costs O(NC), a factor of V less than building every logit.

questions.chapter_name: Fused linear cross-entropy: the loss without the logits
questions.question: What common pattern do FlashAttention and fused cross-entropy share?
options: Store the big intermediate in pinned CPU memory and stream it back to the GPU when needed
Never materialize the big intermediate, trading a little recomputation for far fewer bytes
Approximate the big intermediate with a low-rank factorization whose error is provably bounded
Compute the big intermediate in fp8 and store it, halving the bytes relative to bf16
questions.explanation: FlashAttention avoids the T×T scores and fused cross-entropy avoids the N×V logits; both use online-softmax statistics and recomputation instead of storing the intermediate. The same trade reappears when scaling to many GPUs.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: In data parallelism with W workers, what does each worker hold and process during a training step?
options: A 1/W slice of the model's layers and the full global batch
A 1/W slice of each weight matrix and a 1/W shard of the batch
A complete copy of the model and the full global batch, processed redundantly
A complete copy of the model and a 1/W shard of the global batch
questions.explanation: Data parallelism replicates the full model on every worker and splits each global batch into W shards, one per worker. The workers then average their per-shard gradients with an all-reduce. Splitting layers or weight matrices across workers is model (pipeline or tensor) parallelism, not data parallelism.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: In data parallelism, why do all W workers apply the identical optimizer update each step?
options: Because each worker's shard happens to produce the same local gradient
Because worker 0 computes the update and broadcasts new weights to the others
Because the optimizer state is shared in one memory location across GPUs
Because an all-reduce gives every worker the same averaged gradient before the step
questions.explanation: Each worker computes a different local gradient from its own shard, but the all-reduce replaces every local gradient with the common average. Since every worker starts with identical weights and applies the identical averaged gradient, they stay identical. No weight broadcast is needed after the step.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: How many communication steps does ring all-reduce take for W workers, and how much of the tensor does each link carry per step?
options: 2(W-1) steps, each carrying 1/W of the tensor
W steps, each carrying the full tensor
W-1 steps, each carrying 2/W of the tensor
log2(W) steps, each carrying half the tensor
questions.explanation: Ring all-reduce runs a reduce-scatter phase of W-1 steps followed by an all-gather phase of W-1 steps, for 2(W-1) steps total. On every step each link carries exactly one chunk, which is 1/W of the tensor. That keeps per-worker traffic near 2 tensors' worth regardless of W.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Why is data parallelism described as the foundation for the rest of a distributed-training toolkit (ZeRO, FSDP, tensor/pipeline parallelism)?
options: Because those strategies replace the training loop entirely and only reuse its data loader
Because those strategies require the model to be replicated unchanged on every worker
Because those strategies are all built on top of the same collective-communication operations
Because those strategies only work when the global batch fits on one GPU
questions.explanation: Data parallelism introduces the collective (all-reduce, and its parts reduce-scatter and all-gather) that coordinates devices. ZeRO, FSDP and tensor/pipeline parallelism are all built on top of these collectives. ZeRO and FSDP in particular specifically stop replicating the full model state, so they do not require unchanged replication.

questions.question: A NumPy example simulates data parallelism with a Python loop that plays all W workers in one process. What does such a simulation demonstrate?
options: The wall-clock speedup to expect when the same job runs on W real GPUs
The network bandwidth an all-reduce of the gradients would consume on NVLink
The arithmetic of gradient averaging and all-reduce, not a multi-GPU speedup
How much gradient computation and communication overlap on real multi-GPU hardware
questions.explanation: A single-process loop executes each simulated worker in turn, so it reproduces the numbers the collective produces but cannot run anything in parallel. It therefore says nothing about speedup, bandwidth, or overlap. Those require real multi-GPU hardware.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: clone the model, split the batch, agree on the update
questions.question: What is the correct order of the four things data parallelism does every training step?
options: Shard the batch, all-reduce the inputs, compute local gradients, replicate the update
Replicate the model, compute the full-batch gradient, shard it, all-reduce the weights
Replicate the model, shard the batch, compute local gradients, all-reduce the gradients
Shard the model, replicate the batch, all-reduce activations, compute gradients
questions.explanation: Every worker holds an identical replica, the global batch is cut into W shards, each worker runs forward and backward on its shard to get a local gradient, and an all-reduce averages those gradients across workers. Then each worker runs the identical optimizer step. The all-reduce operates on gradients, not inputs, activations, or weights.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: clone the model, split the batch, agree on the update
questions.question: With a global batch of B examples split across W data-parallel workers, how many examples does each worker's local gradient come from?
options: B/W examples
B examples
W examples
B times W examples
questions.explanation: The global batch of B examples is cut into W equal shards, so each worker processes B/W examples and computes its local gradient from them. The all-reduce then combines the W local gradients into one gradient that reflects all B examples.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: clone the model, split the batch, agree on the update
questions.question: What does an all-reduce do?
options: Combines one tensor from every worker and returns the combined result to all of them
Sends one worker's tensor, unchanged, to every other worker in the group
Combines one tensor from every worker and leaves the combined result only on worker 0
Splits one tensor into equal pieces and gives each worker a different piece of it
questions.explanation: An all-reduce takes an equally shaped tensor from every worker, combines them element-wise (for data parallelism, by averaging), and leaves the same combined result on every worker. Sending one tensor unchanged to everyone is a broadcast; leaving the result on one worker is a reduce; giving each worker a different piece is a scatter.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: clone the model, split the batch, agree on the update
questions.question: Why do data-parallel workers remain bit-for-bit identical across training steps?
options: They periodically compare weights and roll back any worker that drifted
They start identical and every step applies the same averaged update
They all process the same shard of data each step
They share one set of weights stored on worker 0
questions.explanation: Workers begin with identical weights and, after the all-reduce, each applies exactly the same averaged gradient with the same optimizer. Identical inputs to identical updates give identical outputs, so the replicas never diverge. They process different data, which is why their local gradients differ before averaging.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: clone the model, split the batch, agree on the update
questions.question: Relative to a single-GPU training loop, what is the one new operation that data parallelism introduces?
options: An all-reduce of the gradients
A second backward pass per step
A new optimizer that accepts W gradients
A broadcast of the loss value after each step
questions.explanation: Data parallelism runs the same loop on W workers, each on different data. The only new step is the all-reduce that averages gradients across workers. The optimizer is unchanged, and the loss value is not what is synchronized.

questions.section: 2. The correctness fact: averaging shard gradients == the full-batch gradient
questions.question: Is data-parallel training with gradient averaging an approximation of full-batch training or an exact equivalent?
options: An approximation whose error shrinks as the number of workers W grows
Exactly equal to the full-batch gradient, for a mean loss and equal shards
An approximation whose error shrinks as the global batch size B grows larger
Exactly equal, but only when W is a power of two so the shards stay balanced
questions.explanation: For a mean loss and equal-size shards, the average of per-shard mean-loss gradients equals the full-batch mean-loss gradient exactly, as an algebraic identity. Only floating-point reduction order can cause tiny numerical differences. There is no approximation error that depends on W or batch size.

questions.section: 2. The correctness fact: averaging shard gradients == the full-batch gradient
questions.question: A worker computes the gradient of the mean loss over its shard of B/W examples. Why does its local gradient carry a factor of W/B in front of the sum of per-example gradients?
options: Because the gradient is pre-scaled by W so that it cancels the later averaging over workers
Because the shard mean divides by the shard size B/W, which equals multiplying by W/B
Because the learning rate is divided by B on each worker before the gradient is formed
Because each example is counted W times in total across all of the workers' shards
questions.explanation: A mean over a shard of B/W examples divides the sum by B/W, which is the same as multiplying by W/B. When the W local gradients are then averaged (multiplied by 1/W), the W cancels and leaves 1/B times the sum over all examples, which is the full-batch gradient.

questions.section: 2. The correctness fact: averaging shard gradients == the full-batch gradient
questions.question: In the proof that averaged shard gradients equal the full-batch gradient, why does the double sum over workers and over each worker's indices collapse into one sum over all B examples?
options: Because the shards overlap, so each example is counted once on average
Because gradients of different examples are orthogonal
Because the shards partition the batch: every example is in exactly one shard
Because the per-example losses are all equal at initialization
questions.explanation: The shards are disjoint and together cover the whole batch, so summing over workers and then over each worker's examples visits every example exactly once. That makes the double sum identical to a single sum over all B examples. Overlapping shards would double-count examples and break the identity.

questions.section: 2. The correctness fact: averaging shard gradients == the full-batch gradient
questions.question: Which two conditions does the exact equality 'average of per-shard gradients = full-batch gradient' require?
options: A sum loss and an even number of workers
Identical shards and a sum loss
A convex loss and a learning rate below 1
A mean loss and equal-size shards
questions.explanation: The proof relies on each worker's loss being a mean over its shard and on all shards having the same size, so that a plain average over workers gives the global mean. With a sum loss or unequal shards, a plain average no longer reproduces the full-batch mean-loss gradient. Convexity and the learning rate play no role.

questions.section: 2. The correctness fact: averaging shard gradients == the full-batch gradient
questions.question: If data-parallel shards have unequal sizes, how should per-worker mean-loss gradients be combined to recover the full-batch mean-loss gradient?
options: A size-weighted average, weighting each worker by its share of the examples
A plain sum over workers, since each shard mean is already normalized
A plain average over workers, exactly as with equal-size shards
Keep only the gradient from the largest shard and broadcast it to all workers
questions.explanation: With unequal shards, each worker's mean already divides by its own size, so a plain average over-weights examples in small shards. Weighting each worker's gradient by its share of the examples restores the global mean. A plain sum would scale the gradient by roughly W.

questions.section: 2. The correctness fact: averaging shard gradients == the full-batch gradient
questions.question: Why does the data-parallel all-reduce use an average rather than a sum of the per-worker gradients?
options: Because the averaged gradient has lower variance than the sum, which is what stabilizes training
Because averaging per-shard mean-loss gradients reproduces the full-batch mean-loss gradient
Because NCCL only supports averaging collectives, not sums, for floating-point tensors
Because summing W fp32 gradient tensors would overflow the fp32 range for large W
questions.explanation: Each worker's gradient is from a mean loss over its shard. Averaging W such gradients gives exactly the full-batch mean-loss gradient, while summing them gives a gradient W times larger. Collective libraries support sums; averaging is a sum followed by division by W.

questions.question: For the mean-squared-error loss (1/n) sum_i (x_i . theta - y_i)^2 used in a linear-regression check of data parallelism, what is the closed-form gradient with respect to theta?
options: (1/n) X^T (X theta - y)
2 X^T (X theta - y)
(2/n) X^T (X theta - y)
(2/n) (X theta - y)^T X theta
questions.explanation: Differentiating (1/n) times the sum of squared residuals gives 2/n times X transposed times the residual vector (X theta - y). The factor 1/n comes from the mean, and the factor 2 from differentiating the square. Dropping the 1/n would give the gradient of a sum loss instead.

questions.question: A NumPy check of data parallelism finds the maximum absolute difference between the full-batch gradient and the average of four shard gradients is about 2.2e-16. What does this show?
options: The two gradients differ by a small approximation error that grows with the number of workers W
The shard gradients were computed in fp16, so they lost precision relative to the full batch
The two gradients are equal up to floating-point noise, i.e. exactly equal mathematically
The averaged gradient is slightly biased toward the first shard, which is reduced first
questions.explanation: A difference around 2.2e-16 is at the level of double-precision machine epsilon, which is pure floating-point rounding. It confirms the algebraic identity: the averaged shard gradient equals the full-batch gradient. It is not an approximation error that depends on the number of workers.

questions.question: Training uses a per-token mean loss on variable-length sequences with padding, so data-parallel workers have different numbers of valid tokens. What is wrong with a plain average of worker gradients?
options: Nothing: per-token mean losses always make a plain average over workers exact
It double-counts the padding tokens, so padding gradients must be summed instead of averaged
It is subtly wrong; each worker's gradient must be weighted by its share of the valid tokens
It is only wrong if W is odd, since an even split always balances the valid tokens
questions.explanation: A plain average assumes each worker contributes equally to the global mean. When valid-token counts differ, the global token-mean gradient is sum(n_w * g_w) / sum(n_w), so each worker must be weighted by its token count. Ignoring this silently changes how much each token contributes.

questions.question: What symptom does getting the data-parallel gradient normalization wrong (for example, using a sum loss with a plain average) typically produce?
options: An immediate crash in the all-reduce with a tensor shape mismatch error
An effective learning rate that depends on the number of workers W
Workers whose weights slowly diverge from each other over many steps
A deadlock in the all-reduce once the gradient values grow too large
questions.explanation: If the gradient is scaled by a factor that depends on W, the step size the optimizer actually takes scales with W too, so changing the worker count silently changes the effective learning rate. This is a classic silent scaling bug: no error is raised, and the replicas still stay identical because they all use the same wrong gradient.

questions.question: What property must the element-wise combine operation of an all-reduce have, so that partial results can be combined in any grouping?
options: It must be idempotent
It must be associative
It must be invertible
It must be linear in the learning rate
questions.explanation: An all-reduce combines tensors from many workers in some order and grouping chosen by the algorithm, so the operation must be associative (sum, max, and so on). For data parallelism the op is a sum, followed by division by W to get the mean. Idempotence or invertibility are not required.

questions.question: Which of these is a family of collective communication operations that coordinate many devices at once?
options: all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, broadcast
forward, backward, optimizer.step, zero_grad
fork, join, mutex, semaphore, condition variable, barrier
map, filter, sort, shuffle, partition, group-by
questions.explanation: Collective communication operations involve all participating devices together: all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, and broadcast are the standard members. Ring all-reduce itself is built from a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather. The other options are training-loop steps or generic programming primitives.

questions.question: In a naive all-reduce where every worker sends its tensor to worker 0, which sums and sends the result back, what is the problem?
options: The result is numerically different from a true sum because of the reduction order at worker 0
Workers other than worker 0 never receive the summed result, so they cannot step
Worker 0's link carries W-1 tensors in and W-1 out, a bottleneck that worsens as W grows
It only works when W is a power of two, so arbitrary GPU counts cannot use it
questions.explanation: The naive scheme is correct but funnels all traffic through worker 0: it receives W-1 tensors and sends W-1 back. With gradients of hundreds of megabytes and hundreds of workers, that single link becomes a fatal bottleneck. Ring all-reduce avoids routing everything through one node.

questions.question: In ring all-reduce, which workers does worker w send to?
options: Every other worker, in parallel
Only worker 0
Worker w+1 in reduce-scatter and worker w-1 in all-gather, plus worker 0
Only worker w+1, wrapping around at the end
questions.explanation: Ring all-reduce arranges workers in a logical ring: worker w sends only to its right neighbour w+1, with the last worker wrapping to worker 0. No node handles all the traffic. Every link carries the same small amount per step.

questions.question: Before ring all-reduce starts exchanging data, how does each worker divide its tensor?
options: Into 2 halves
Into W-1 chunks
Into W chunks
Into one chunk per layer
questions.explanation: Each worker splits its tensor into W chunks (near-equal when the length does not divide evenly). Each step of the ring moves one chunk per link. After the reduce-scatter phase, each worker owns one fully summed chunk.

questions.question: What is the state at the end of the reduce-scatter phase of ring all-reduce (after W-1 steps)?
options: Every worker already holds the full summed tensor, all W chunks
Each worker holds the fully summed value of one distinct chunk
Worker 0 holds the full sum and the other workers hold nothing
Each worker still holds its original tensor, with nothing summed yet
questions.explanation: During reduce-scatter, each worker repeatedly sends one chunk to its right neighbour and adds the chunk it receives into its own buffer. After W-1 steps each worker has the complete sum for exactly one distinct chunk: the sum is 'scattered' across workers. The all-gather phase then spreads those finished chunks to everyone.

questions.question: What happens during the all-gather phase of ring all-reduce?
options: Each worker adds the chunks it receives into its own buffer to finish the partial sums
The finished chunks are passed around the ring until every worker has all W of them
Worker 0 broadcasts the full summed result to all the other workers in one step
Each worker discards all chunks except its own finished chunk and divides by W
questions.explanation: After reduce-scatter, each worker owns one finished chunk. The all-gather phase circulates these finished chunks around the ring for W-1 steps until every worker holds all W finished chunks. It copies results rather than adding them.

questions.question: Over a whole ring all-reduce, roughly how much data does each worker send, as W grows large?
options: About W tensors' worth, one per other worker
About log2(W) tensors' worth, as in a tree
About 1/W of a tensor, its own chunk only
About 2 tensors' worth, independent of W
questions.explanation: Each worker sends one chunk (1/W of the tensor) per step over 2(W-1) steps, which totals 2(W-1)/W, approaching 2 tensors' worth regardless of W. This is why ring all-reduce is called bandwidth-optimal. The naive scheme instead piles 2(W-1) tensors onto one link.

questions.question: Why is ring all-reduce called bandwidth-optimal?
options: Because per-worker data stays about 2 tensors regardless of W, and no single link is a bottleneck
Because it finishes in a constant number of communication steps, regardless of how large W gets
Because it compresses the gradients to a lower precision before sending them around the whole ring
Because it only sends the nonzero entries of the gradient, which cuts the bytes on every link
questions.explanation: Each link carries only 1/W of the tensor per step, and the total each worker moves stays near 2 tensors' worth however many workers there are. No link carries more than its share. Its number of rounds, 2(W-1), still grows with W, so latency is not constant.

questions.section: Worked example: three workers, by hand
questions.question: In ring all-reduce with three workers holding [1,2,3], [4,5,6] and [7,8,9], what does each worker hold at the end of the full all-reduce with op='mean'?
questions.explanation: The element-wise sum is [12, 15, 18]; dividing by W = 3 gives the mean [4, 5, 6], which every worker ends up holding. [12, 15, 18] is the op='sum' result. [6, 15, 24] would be per-worker sums, which is not what an all-reduce computes.

questions.section: Worked example: three workers, by hand
questions.question: In the second reduce-scatter step of a ring all-reduce, which chunk does worker i send onward?
options: Its own original chunk i again, unchanged from the start
A random chunk chosen by the ring scheduler each step
The chunk it just updated in the previous step, (i-1) mod W
Chunk 0 always, which every worker forwards first in each step
questions.explanation: On each reduce-scatter step a worker forwards the chunk it just accumulated into, which for step 1 is chunk (i-1) mod W. That keeps partial sums moving around the ring and growing by one contribution per hop. After W-1 hops each chunk has collected all W contributions on one worker.

questions.section: Worked example: three workers, by hand
questions.question: In a three-worker ring all-reduce of [1,2,3], [4,5,6], [7,8,9], after reduce-scatter which finished chunk does each worker own?
options: Worker 0 owns chunk 0 (12), worker 1 owns chunk 1 (15), worker 2 owns chunk 2 (18)
Worker 0 owns all three chunks; workers 1 and 2 own none
Worker 0 owns chunk 1 (15), worker 1 owns chunk 2 (18), worker 2 owns chunk 0 (12)
Worker 0 owns chunk 2 (18), worker 1 owns chunk 0 (12), worker 2 owns chunk 1 (15)
questions.explanation: Tracing the ring, worker 0 finishes chunk 1 (2+13 = 15), worker 1 finishes chunk 2 (6+12 = 18), and worker 2 finishes chunk 0 (7+5 = 12). Together they are the true sum [12, 15, 18], scattered one per worker. All-gather then distributes them so everyone holds the full result.

questions.question: In a simulated ring all-reduce, each round first copies every worker's outgoing chunk into a 'sent' list before any worker adds. Why?
options: So no worker reads a neighbour's already-updated value mid-step, mirroring simultaneous sends
To save memory by reusing the same send buffers across all rounds instead of allocating new ones
To convert the chunks to fp16 before sending, halving the bytes that travel around the ring
So that the whole reduce-scatter phase can be skipped when there is only one worker, W = 1
questions.explanation: On real hardware all workers send at the same moment from the state they had at the start of the step. In a sequential loop, updating worker i before worker i+1 reads from it would leak updated values into the same round. Snapshotting the outgoing chunks first reproduces the simultaneous semantics.

questions.question: In a ring all-reduce implementation, why does the reduce-scatter phase add received chunks while the all-gather phase overwrites with them?
options: Reduce-scatter combines partial sums; all-gather only copies already finished results around
Adding is faster during the first phase and overwriting is faster during the second phase
All-gather must undo the additions made during reduce-scatter, so that each chunk is counted only once
Overwriting during all-gather is what converts the accumulated sum into the final mean
questions.explanation: During reduce-scatter each chunk accumulates contributions from all workers, so received data must be added. During all-gather the chunks are already fully summed, so a worker just copies the finished chunk into place. Adding during all-gather would double-count and give wrong results. The mean comes from a separate division by W.

questions.question: Why does a ring all-reduce implementation compute W near-equal chunk bounds rather than assuming the tensor length divides by W?
options: So it works for tensor lengths that do not divide evenly by the number of workers
Because NCCL requires chunks of different sizes for each worker position in the ring
So that the last worker receives an empty chunk and can skip communication
Because the first chunk must be twice as large to hold the running partial sums
questions.explanation: Real gradient tensors rarely have a length that is an exact multiple of W. Near-equal chunk bounds let the algorithm split any length into W pieces whose sizes differ by at most one element. The accompanying tests specifically cover lengths that do not divide evenly.

questions.question: Why is a ring all-reduce implementation tested against np.sum and np.mean for worker counts 1 to 8 and uneven tensor lengths?
options: Because ring all-reduce is only approximate and needs a tolerance check against exact sums
Because ring all-reduce only works for even W, and the odd counts must be shown to fail
Because NumPy uses a different reduction order for each worker count, so results must be compared
Because the reduce-scatter/all-gather index arithmetic is fiddly and easy to get off by one
questions.explanation: The schedule of which chunk each worker sends on each step is easy to get subtly wrong by one position. Comparing the ring's output to a direct sum or mean across many worker counts and awkward lengths catches such off-by-one errors. If you re-derive the schedule, the test protects you.

questions.section: 5. Tying it back to the training loop: data_parallel_grads
questions.question: In data-parallel training, what does the ring all-reduce combine?
options: Gradients, before the optimizer changes the weights
Model predictions from different workers
Training examples from different workers
Updated weights, after each worker's optimizer step
questions.explanation: Data parallelism all-reduces the .grad tensors produced by backward, before optimizer.step() runs. It does not move examples, predictions, or updated weights. Averaging weights after independent local updates would be a different (and here incorrect) algorithm.

questions.section: Follow one optimizer step, with actual numbers
questions.question: Three data-parallel workers start with the same parameters and compute different local gradients. After all-reduce and SGD, why do they hold the same new parameters without exchanging weights?
options: Because SGD is invariant to the gradient value, so any gradient gives the same step
Because each worker's local gradient was already equal to the global average beforehand
Because worker 0 sends its updated weights to all the other workers after each step
Because all workers apply the same averaged gradient to the same starting weights
questions.explanation: The all-reduce replaces each worker's local gradient with the common average, and every worker starts from identical parameters. Applying theta_new = theta_old - lr * g_avg on each worker therefore gives identical results. No weight broadcast is needed after the step.

questions.section: Follow one optimizer step, with actual numbers
questions.question: If data-parallel workers use Adam instead of SGD, what additional condition is needed for their weights to stay identical?
options: Nothing; Adam is stateless
Each worker must use a different learning rate
A separate all-reduce of the updated weights after every step
Matching optimizer state and settings on every worker
questions.explanation: Adam keeps per-parameter moment buffers and hyperparameters. Identical averaged gradients only yield identical updates if every worker also has the same moment state and settings. Starting from the same state and applying the same gradients keeps that state identical too.

questions.section: Follow one optimizer step, with actual numbers
questions.question: Which action in a data-parallel training step actually changes the model's parameters?
options: loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
The gradient all-reduce
optimizer.zero_grad()
questions.explanation: backward() computes gradients into .grad, and the all-reduce makes those gradients agree across workers, but neither touches the parameters. Only optimizer.step() reads .grad and updates the parameters. zero_grad() only resets gradients.

questions.question: In a manual data-parallel training step, where should the gradient all-reduce be inserted?
options: Before the forward pass, so every worker starts the step from synchronized gradients
After local backward and before gradient clipping and optimizer.step()
After optimizer.step() and before the next forward, so the new weights get averaged
Between gradient clipping and optimizer.step(), so each local gradient is clipped first
questions.explanation: Local backward first fills each parameter's .grad, then the all-reduce averages them, then clipping and the optimizer act on the averaged gradient. Synchronizing after the step is too late because the workers would already have diverged. Clipping before averaging gives a different result because clipping is nonlinear.

questions.question: A manual data-parallel loop calls dist.all_reduce(parameter.grad, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM) and then parameter.grad.div_(world_size). What is the purpose of the division?
options: To normalize by the number of parameters
To reduce the learning rate for stability
To undo the in-place modification made by all_reduce
To convert the sum into the mean gradient
questions.explanation: The SUM all-reduce leaves the sum of all workers' gradients in .grad. Dividing in place by world_size turns that sum into the mean, which is the gradient equal to the full-batch mean-loss gradient. Without it the gradient would be W times too large.

questions.question: How does torch.distributed.all_reduce deliver its result?
options: It returns a new result tensor and leaves the input tensor unchanged on every process
It writes the result only into rank 0's tensor, leaving the others with their local values
It modifies the supplied tensor in place on every participating process
It stores the result in a separate pinned buffer on the CPU that each process must read
questions.explanation: all_reduce overwrites the tensor you pass on each process. For example, worker 0's .grad [1, 2, 3] becomes the sum [12, 15, 18] after a three-worker SUM all-reduce, and dividing by 3 gives [4, 5, 6]. The optimizer then reads that updated .grad.

questions.question: Does data-parallel training require a special optimizer that understands multiple workers?
options: Yes; it needs a special optimizer that accepts all W gradients
No; the ordinary optimizer reads the already averaged .grad
Yes; it needs an optimizer that broadcasts updated weights
Only if the model has more than one layer of parameters
questions.explanation: After the all-reduce, each parameter's .grad already holds the averaged gradient. The ordinary optimizer just reads .grad and updates its local copy as usual. Synchronization happens entirely in the gradient step.

questions.question: A manual data-parallel loop iterates 'for parameter in model.parameters(): dist.all_reduce(parameter.grad, ...)'. What does each iteration of that loop correspond to?
options: One worker process in the data-parallel group of W
One micro-batch of the gradient accumulation window
One training example from this worker's shard of data
One parameter tensor, such as a layer's weight or bias
