questions.explanation: The loop walks over parameter tensors, not workers; every worker runs the same loop. A linear layer has a weight tensor and a bias tensor, so it causes two collective calls. The other workers participate by making matching calls in the same order.

questions.question: Across processes participating in manual gradient all-reduces, what must agree for the collectives to work correctly?
options: Their random seeds for dropout and data shuffling
Tensor shapes, types, and the order of collective calls
Their local loss values at the end of each step
Their data shards, which must contain the same examples
questions.explanation: Collectives pair up tensors across processes by call order, so every process must issue the same sequence of calls with matching shapes and dtypes (weights with weights, biases with biases). Losses, dropout masks, and data shards are expected to differ across workers.

questions.question: What goes wrong if each data-parallel worker calls optimizer.step() on its local gradient and the gradients are averaged afterward?
options: The workers have already made different updates, so their weights diverge
Nothing; the order of stepping and averaging does not matter at all for plain SGD
The all-reduce fails because .grad was already cleared by the step
The learning rate ends up applied twice to the same averaged gradient
questions.explanation: If each worker steps on its own local gradient, the replicas apply different updates and their weights no longer match. Averaging gradients afterward cannot undo that. The all-reduce must come before the step so everyone uses the same gradient.

questions.question: In data-parallel training, why should gradient clipping be applied after averaging rather than to each local gradient?
options: Because clipping is nonlinear, so clipping local gradients first generally gives a different result
Because clipping before averaging is mathematically identical but needs W separate norm computations
Because local gradients are always below the clip threshold, so clipping them would do nothing
Because the all-reduce itself clips the gradients, so only the averaged result needs checking
questions.explanation: Clipping rescales a gradient based on its norm, which is nonlinear: the average of clipped gradients is not the clipped average. To clip the gradient the optimizer actually uses, average first and then clip. The all-reduce does not clip anything.

questions.question: A helper data_parallel_grads(grad_fn, params, batch, world_size) splits the batch, computes a gradient per shard, and ring-all-reduces them with op='mean'. What does it return?
options: Updated parameters after one SGD step on the batch
The mean loss over the batch, averaged across shards
A list of W per-shard gradients, one for each worker
One averaged gradient; it does not update params
questions.explanation: The helper only produces the gradient: it splits the batch into world_size equal shards, calls grad_fn on each, and averages them with a ring all-reduce. Updating parameters is a separate step, for example theta = theta - lr * grad. Keeping gradient computation and the update separate mirrors the real training loop.

questions.question: In data_parallel_grads(grad_fn, params, batch, world_size), what must grad_fn(params, shard) compute?
options: The gradient of the sum loss over the whole batch at the given parameters
The updated parameters after one optimizer step taken on that shard
The gradient of the mean loss on that shard at the given parameters
The scalar loss value on the shard, which the helper then differentiates
questions.explanation: grad_fn must return the gradient of the mean loss over its shard at the current parameters. Averaging those mean-loss gradients over equal shards gives the full-batch mean-loss gradient. A sum-loss gradient would make the result scale with shard size.

questions.question: A single-process simulation of data parallelism returns just one copy of the averaged gradient. What does it reproduce, and what does it not?
options: It reproduces the parallel execution but not the arithmetic
It reproduces both the arithmetic and the parallel speedup
It reproduces the arithmetic, not the parallel execution
It reproduces neither; it is only a placeholder
questions.explanation: One Python process computes each shard's gradient in turn and the ring helper returns one copy because all simulated workers' buffers agree. That reproduces the numbers exactly. On real GPUs each process keeps its own copy of the averaged gradient and updates its own model concurrently.

questions.section: What “one process per GPU” actually means
questions.question: What does 'torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=4 train.py' start on a machine with four GPUs?
options: One Python process that loops over the four GPUs, running each shard in turn
Four threads sharing one model and one optimizer inside a single Python process
Four Python processes running the same file, each with its own model, optimizer and GPU
One process per layer of the model, each pinned to one of the four GPUs in a pipeline
questions.explanation: torchrun launches four separate Python processes, each running train.py with its own model replica, optimizer, Python variables, and assigned GPU. Each process is one worker. There is no single process looping over the GPUs.

questions.section: What “one process per GPU” actually means
questions.question: In PyTorch distributed training, what do world_size, rank, and local_rank mean?
options: world_size = total processes; rank = this process's ID in the whole group; local_rank = its GPU index on its machine
world_size = GPUs per machine; rank = index of this machine in the job; local_rank = index of the layer this process owns
world_size = number of machines; rank = this process's GPU index; local_rank = index of the thread inside the process
world_size = global batch size; rank = index of the current micro-batch; local_rank = index of this worker's data shard
questions.explanation: world_size is the total number of processes in the job, rank uniquely identifies a process across the whole job, and local_rank is the GPU index of that process on its own machine. On one four-GPU machine rank and local_rank coincide (0 to 3).

questions.section: What “one process per GPU” actually means
questions.question: In a multi-machine data-parallel job, how do global ranks and local ranks behave?
options: Both restart at zero on each machine, so ranks repeat across machines
Global ranks are unique across the job; local ranks start at zero on each machine
Global ranks start at zero on each machine; local ranks are unique across the job
Both are unique across the job, so local rank always equals global rank
questions.explanation: The global rank is a unique ID for every process in the whole job, while the local rank indexes GPUs on one machine, so it restarts at zero on every machine. A process uses local_rank to pick its GPU and rank to identify itself in collectives.

questions.section: What “one process per GPU” actually means
questions.question: On a four-GPU data-parallel job with a global batch of 32, how is backward executed?
options: One process runs backward four times in a loop, once for each GPU's 8-example shard
Four processes each run one local backward on 8 examples concurrently and join the collectives
One process runs backward on all 32 examples and then broadcasts the gradients to the other GPUs
Each of the four processes runs backward on all 32 examples redundantly and keeps its own result
questions.explanation: Each of the four processes handles its own 8-example shard and performs one local backward, at the same time as the others, then participates in the gradient collectives. No process loops over the other GPUs' backward calls.

questions.question: With micro-batch size b, A accumulation steps per optimizer update, and W data-parallel workers, how many examples does one optimizer update cover?
options: b times A
b times A divided by W
b times (A + W)
b times A times W
questions.explanation: Each worker processes A micro-batches of b examples before the update, and W workers contribute, so the global batch is b * A * W. For b = 2, A = 4, W = 3, that is 24 examples per update. Changing any of the three factors changes the global batch.

questions.question: When combining gradient accumulation over A equal micro-batches with data parallelism over W workers, how is the overall averaging achieved for mean losses?
options: Divide each micro-batch loss by A·W before backward and then use a plain sum all-reduce instead
No division is needed at all; gradient accumulation averages the micro-batches automatically
Divide the learning rate by A and the gradient by W, so the two factors are applied separately
Divide each micro-batch loss by A before backward; the worker average supplies the 1/W factor
questions.explanation: Backward adds into .grad, so dividing each micro-batch's mean loss by A makes the accumulated gradient an average over the accumulation window. The data-parallel all-reduce then averages across workers, contributing the separate 1/W. Without the 1/A, the accumulated gradient would be A times too large.

questions.question: What is the distinction between gradient accumulation and data parallelism?
options: Accumulation combines work across workers; data parallelism combines work over time on each single worker
Both combine work across workers, but accumulation uses a sum while data parallelism uses a mean
Accumulation combines work over time on each worker; data parallelism combines work across workers
Accumulation changes the model's effective depth; data parallelism changes the optimizer's state
questions.explanation: Gradient accumulation adds several micro-batches' gradients on one worker over successive backward passes. Data parallelism averages gradients computed concurrently on different workers. In both, optimizer.step() runs only once the intended combined gradient is ready.

questions.question: What is NCCL?
options: A file format for sharded checkpoints written by each GPU in a distributed job
A PyTorch module that shards the input batch across GPUs and chooses which data each one sees
A compiler that fuses CUDA kernels across GPUs to reduce launch overhead
NVIDIA's Collective Communications Library, which runs collectives across NVIDIA GPUs
questions.explanation: NCCL (pronounced 'nickel') is NVIDIA's library of GPU collective communication operations such as all-reduce and all-gather. PyTorch distributed uses it as the backend that actually moves and combines tensors between GPUs. It does not choose data or shard batches.

questions.question: In data-parallel training, which component is responsible for executing the collectives across NVIDIA GPUs over the available connections?
options: The training loop
The NCCL backend
PyTorch distributed / DDP
The optimizer
questions.explanation: The training loop chooses data, computes the loss, requests backward, and runs the optimizer. PyTorch distributed and DDP coordinate processes and request gradient collectives. The NCCL backend executes those collectives across the GPUs using whatever links exist.

questions.question: What does NCCL know about the training it supports?
options: It knows the loss value and adjusts the learning rate when gradients grow too large
It knows the model architecture and reorders layers to overlap their communication
It knows which examples each worker processed and reweights the workers' gradients by their counts
It knows tensors and collective operations, but nothing about examples, losses or learning rates
questions.explanation: NCCL just combines corresponding entries of tensors as requested by a collective. The interpretation of the result as 'training on a larger batch' comes from the mean-loss definition and the averaging proof. NCCL itself has no notion of examples, losses, or learning rates.

questions.question: Is the ring algorithm a requirement of the all-reduce operation used by NCCL?
options: No; ring is one implementation, and NCCL can pick other algorithms and transports with the same result
Yes; all-reduce is defined as the ring schedule, so any other algorithm would give a different result
Yes, but only across nodes; within one node NCCL must use NVLink broadcasts instead of an all-reduce
No; NCCL always uses a naive gather to rank 0 followed by a broadcast, and the ring is only a teaching aid
questions.explanation: All-reduce is defined by its result, not its schedule. Ring is one implementation; NCCL can select other algorithms and transports depending on NVLink, PCIe, or network connections. The mathematical result is the same, apart from tiny floating-point differences caused by different reduction orders. NCCL does not always gather to rank 0.

questions.question: A DDP script is run on a machine without CUDA. What backend does it use and what should you expect?
options: NCCL on the CPU, with the same speedup as on GPUs
Gloo on the CPU: correct results with no speedup
It cannot run at all without CUDA
MPI only, with approximate gradients
questions.explanation: Without CUDA, the same DDP code can fall back to the Gloo backend on the CPU. It performs the same gradient averaging, so results are correct, but it is not faster. NCCL is specific to NVIDIA GPUs.

questions.question: Which statement about GPU collective communication in data-parallel training is accurate?
options: It requires NVLink between GPUs and is always free, because copy engines handle all of it
It is GPU work scheduled on CUDA streams that may overlap computation; NVLink is not required
It runs only on the host CPU and never uses any GPU resources such as SMs or memory bandwidth
It can be measured precisely, including overlap and speedup, by a single-process CPU simulation
questions.explanation: Collectives are GPU work scheduled on CUDA streams and may overlap computation, but they are not guaranteed to be a free transfer handled only by copy engines. NVLink improves bandwidth but is not required. A CPU simulation cannot measure this overlap or predict speedup.

questions.section: 7. PyTorch DDP: overlapping the all-reduce with backward
questions.question: What is PyTorch's DistributedDataParallel (DDP)?
options: A data loader that shards each batch across the GPUs in the job automatically
An optimizer that averages parameter updates across the GPUs
A wrapper around the model that arranges gradient synchronization during backward
A launcher that starts one Python process per GPU and sets each process's rank
questions.explanation: DDP wraps a model and hooks into backward so that gradients are synchronized (averaged across ranks) as they become ready. It is not an optimizer, a data loader, or a launcher; torchrun launches processes and DistributedSampler chooses data.

questions.section: What changes in the training step?
questions.question: After wrapping a model with DistributedDataParallel, should you also add a manual loop that all-reduces each parameter's .grad and divides by world_size?
options: Yes; DDP only sums gradients across ranks, so the manual division by world_size is still needed
Only when using plain SGD, since adaptive optimizers like Adam normalize the gradient scale anyway
Yes; otherwise the optimizer on each rank would still see only its own local gradients
No; default DDP already averages gradients, and an extra all-reduce plus division would be wrong
questions.explanation: Default DDP already averages gradients during backward. Adding the manual all-reduce loop would synchronize twice, and the extra division by W would shrink the gradient incorrectly. The manual loop only explains what DDP does.

questions.section: What changes in the training step?
questions.question: Which of these does DDP not do for you?
options: Average gradients across ranks during backward
Synchronize the starting model across ranks
Shard the input batch or call the optimizer
Group gradients into buckets for communication
questions.explanation: DDP averages gradients, broadcasts the initial model state, and buckets gradients for overlapped communication. It does not decide which examples each rank sees (that is the data pipeline, e.g. DistributedSampler) and it does not call optimizer.step(). You still write those parts of the loop.

questions.section: Why communication can begin before backward finishes
questions.question: Why can DDP begin communicating gradients before backward has finished?
options: Because DDP skips the gradients of early layers, which change slowly, and only sends later ones
Because DDP computes all of the gradients during the forward pass and caches them for the backward pass
Because the optimizer step can safely run on each layer before the rest of backward completes
Because backward produces later layers' gradients first, and those can be reduced while it continues
questions.explanation: Backward runs in reverse order, so an output layer's gradients exist before an input layer's. Communicating the output layer's gradients does not require waiting for the rest. DDP launches the reduction for a ready bucket while backward continues on other layers.

questions.section: Why communication can begin before backward finishes
questions.question: In DDP, what is a gradient bucket?
options: Exactly one layer's gradients, sent as soon as that layer's backward pass is done
A copy of the optimizer state for one parameter, kept in sync across ranks
A buffer holding the loss values from all ranks, reduced together once per step
A group of parameter gradients reduced together when ready; it need not be one layer
questions.explanation: DDP groups parameter gradients into buckets and launches one reduction per bucket when all its gradients are ready. A bucket can hold several parameter tensors and does not have to align with a layer. Bucketing enables overlap and amortizes launch overhead.

questions.section: Why communication can begin before backward finishes
questions.question: Three layers each take 4 ms of backward and each bucket takes 3 ms to communicate. With DDP-style overlap the step takes 15 ms rather than 21 ms. What does the remaining 3 ms beyond the 12 ms of computation represent?
options: Optimizer step time, which runs after backward and cannot overlap anything
Exposed communication: the last bucket's reduction cannot overlap any remaining backward
Launch overhead of the first bucket's collective, paid before any overlap starts
Time spent in the forward pass, which DDP counts as part of the training step
questions.explanation: The first bucket's gradients become ready only after backward has computed them, and the last bucket (the input layer's) becomes ready when backward finishes, leaving nothing to overlap with. Its 3 ms of communication is still exposed. Overlap hides 6 ms here, not all 9 ms.

questions.section: Why communication can begin before backward finishes
questions.question: What trade-off governs DDP bucket size?
options: Bucket size only affects correctness, not speed, since every gradient is reduced exactly once
Larger buckets use less memory for communication buffers, but they are slower to compute during backward
Smaller buckets always win, because they start earlier and launch overhead is negligible
Larger buckets cut launch overhead but become ready later; smaller ones start earlier but need more calls
questions.explanation: Bucketing avoids paying collective-launch overhead for every tiny parameter tensor, so larger buckets mean fewer calls. But a larger bucket waits for more gradients, so its communication starts later. Real performance depends on both the computation and the interconnect.

questions.section: Why communication can begin before backward finishes
questions.question: What does DDP's communication/computation overlap achieve?
options: It makes the all-reduce disappear entirely, since all communication hides under backward
It starts reducing ready gradients while others are computed; leftover communication still finishes before step
It lets the optimizer run on partially reduced gradients, then corrects them after the next step
It removes the need for any collective after backward, because gradients are exchanged during forward
questions.explanation: Overlap hides some communication under remaining backward computation, but it does not eliminate communication. Any communication still in flight at the end of backward must finish before the optimizer can use those gradients. It also cannot guarantee proportional speedup from more workers.

questions.section: A complete, small DDP training script
questions.question: In a DDP training script, what ensures that all ranks start from the same model weights, even if they initialized differently?
options: torch.manual_seed must be identical on every rank, otherwise training fails to start
The optimizer copies the weights from rank 0 to every other rank when it takes its first step
DDP synchronizes the starting model across ranks by default when the model is wrapped
DistributedSampler broadcasts rank 0's model weights when the first batch is drawn
questions.explanation: When a model is wrapped in DistributedDataParallel, DDP synchronizes the initial model state across ranks by default. Setting a seed is still good practice but is not what guarantees identical starting weights. The optimizer and sampler do not move model weights.

questions.section: A complete, small DDP training script
questions.question: What is the role of DistributedSampler in a DDP training script?
options: It averages gradients across ranks after each backward
It launches one process per GPU and assigns each a rank
It chooses which dataset indices each rank processes
It shards the model's parameters across the GPUs
questions.explanation: Every rank refers to the same logical dataset, and DistributedSampler selects a different subset of indices for each rank, so workers see different examples. DDP itself does not split data; the sampler does. Gradient averaging is DDP's job and launching is torchrun's.

questions.section: A complete, small DDP training script
questions.question: Why does a DDP training loop call sampler.set_epoch(epoch) at the start of each epoch?
options: To reset the learning-rate schedule at the start of each new training epoch
To produce a new shuffle each epoch that is coordinated across ranks
To change which GPU each rank uses, balancing load across epochs
To clear the DDP gradient buckets so the new epoch starts fresh
questions.explanation: DistributedSampler shuffles using a seed combined with the epoch. Calling set_epoch changes that shuffle every epoch while keeping all ranks consistent, so their shards still partition the data. Without it, every epoch would repeat the same ordering.

questions.section: A complete, small DDP training script
questions.question: A DDP script sums each rank's batch losses into loss_sum and then calls dist.all_reduce(loss_sum) before rank 0 logs it. Why is that all-reduce needed?
options: Because DDP synchronizes gradients, not the Python loss variable, so a global loss must be aggregated
Because the optimizer needs the global loss value on every rank to compute its next parameter update
Because DDP requires one extra collective per epoch to keep the ranks' model replicas in sync
Because without it the gradients would not be averaged across the ranks during backward
questions.explanation: DDP only synchronizes gradients; each rank's loss value stays local. To report a global mean loss you must aggregate it yourself, which this separate all-reduce does. It plays no role in gradient synchronization or the optimizer step.

questions.section: A complete, small DDP training script
questions.question: In a DDP script, why set drop_last=True on both DistributedSampler and the DataLoader?
options: To keep shard and batch sizes regular: the sampler drops examples to split evenly, the loader drops partial batches
To make the shuffle deterministic across ranks, so that every rank draws exactly the same sequence of batches each epoch
To skip the first batch of each epoch, which DDP uses for warmup and bucket construction on every rank
To prevent DDP from synchronizing the last batch of the epoch, which would otherwise deadlock the job
questions.explanation: With drop_last on the sampler, examples that do not divide evenly among ranks are discarded rather than padded; without it the sampler can pad with repeated indices. With drop_last on the loader, incomplete final local batches are discarded. Together they keep every rank's batches the same size, which the equal-shard averaging assumes.

questions.section: A complete, small DDP training script
questions.question: A DDP script uses a local batch of 8 per rank and is launched with four ranks. How many examples contribute to each optimizer step?
options: 8 examples
16 examples
32 examples
128 examples
questions.explanation: Each of four ranks processes a local batch of 8, and DDP averages their gradients into one update, so 8 * 4 = 32 examples contribute per optimizer step. Adding ranks while keeping the local batch fixed increases the global batch.

questions.section: A complete, small DDP training script
questions.question: A DDP script checks whether LOCAL_RANK is in the environment and raises an error if not. What does that check enforce?
options: That the script was launched by torchrun or an equivalent launcher, not plain 'python train.py'
That the machine has at least one CUDA GPU visible, since DDP cannot run on a CPU-only machine otherwise
That only rank 0 runs the training loop while the other ranks just serve gradients
That the dataset was downloaded to local disk on every machine before training starts
questions.explanation: torchrun sets LOCAL_RANK (and RANK, WORLD_SIZE, etc.) for every process it launches. If it is missing, the script was probably started directly with python and has no process group to join. The error message tells the user to launch with torchrun.

questions.section: A complete, small DDP training script
questions.question: In a DDP script on a CUDA machine, why does each process call torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank) and check local_rank < torch.cuda.device_count()?
options: So that NCCL falls back to running its collectives on the CPU
So that all processes share GPU 0 and the other GPUs stay free
So that each local process uses its own distinct GPU
So that the model's layers are sharded across GPUs by local rank
questions.explanation: Each process should own one GPU on its machine, selected by its local rank. The check fails fast if more local processes were launched than there are GPUs. With NCCL, one process per GPU is the standard arrangement.

questions.section: A complete, small DDP training script
questions.question: In a DDP script, what do dist.init_process_group and dist.destroy_process_group do?
options: They create the model replicas on each rank and delete them all at the end of training
They start the CUDA kernels on each GPU and stop them when training ends
They load the latest checkpoint on start-up and save a final checkpoint on exit
They connect the processes into a communication group and clean it up at the end
questions.explanation: init_process_group connects the launched processes with the chosen backend (NCCL or Gloo) so collectives can run. destroy_process_group, placed in a finally block, releases those resources at the end even after errors. Launching processes is torchrun's job.

questions.section: A complete, small DDP training script
questions.question: In a DDP script's main(), exceptions are logged with the rank and then re-raised. Why re-raise instead of swallowing the error?
options: So that the other ranks continue training without this one
So the launcher can report the failure
So that DDP retries the step automatically
So that the process group is not destroyed
questions.explanation: Logging with the rank identifies where the failure happened, and re-raising lets the launcher see the process failed and report it. Swallowing the error would hide the failure and could leave peers waiting in collectives. The finally block still destroys the process group.

questions.section: A complete, small DDP training script
questions.question: In a DDP run, which component is responsible for each job: launching processes, connecting them, choosing each rank's data, synchronizing model and gradients, updating the local replica?
options: DDP; torchrun; the optimizer; DistributedSampler; NCCL
torchrun; init_process_group; DistributedSampler; DDP; the optimizer
init_process_group; DDP; torchrun; the optimizer; DistributedSampler
The optimizer; DistributedSampler; DDP; torchrun; init_process_group
questions.explanation: torchrun launches the processes, init_process_group connects them, DistributedSampler chooses each rank's indices, DDP synchronizes the model and gradients, and the optimizer updates the local replica. Keeping these roles separate helps locate bugs.

questions.section: A complete, small DDP training script
questions.question: On Windows, torchrun may fail with a libuv error in CPU builds. How can a DDP script still be launched with four ranks?
options: Set WORLD_SIZE, MASTER_ADDR, MASTER_PORT, RANK and LOCAL_RANK yourself and start four processes
Run 'python train.py' once and let DDP spawn the other three ranks automatically from inside its wrapper
Install the NCCL backend for Windows and rerun torchrun with the same arguments
Use a single process with world_size=4, so that one process plays all four ranks
questions.explanation: torchrun just sets environment variables and starts processes. You can do the same manually: set WORLD_SIZE, MASTER_ADDR and MASTER_PORT, and for each of four processes set RANK and LOCAL_RANK, then start them. The script then runs with Gloo on the CPU.

questions.section: A complete, small DDP training script
questions.question: When launching a Gloo DDP job on the CPU, each process prints a 'client socket has failed to connect' warning before training proceeds normally. What does it mean?
options: One rank crashed and the others are training alone
The process group failed and gradients are not being averaged
It is harmless: Gloo probing the machine's hostname
MASTER_PORT is wrong and must be changed
questions.explanation: This warning comes from Gloo probing the hostname before falling back to a working address. It is harmless, and rank 0 then prints the falling epoch losses. Real failures would stop training or hang.

questions.section: When accumulation or conditional branches enter the picture
questions.question: When using DDP with gradient accumulation over A micro-batches, how should model.no_sync() be used?
options: Around backward only, for the last micro-batch, so that the final gradient is not synchronized
Around both forward and backward for the first A-1 micro-batches; synchronize normally on the last
Around optimizer.step() only, so that the step does not trigger an extra all-reduce of the weights
Around every micro-batch including the last, followed by one manual all-reduce of .grad after the window
questions.explanation: no_sync() suppresses the all-reduce for the micro-batches inside it, so gradients just accumulate locally. Wrapping forward and backward for the first A-1 micro-batches and synchronizing on the last means one all-reduce per optimizer step. If every micro-batch were inside no_sync, gradients would never be averaged.

questions.question: What does a backward pass inside DDP's model.no_sync() context do?
options: It skips computing gradients entirely, so .grad is left unchanged
It skips the all-reduce and just adds the gradient into this rank's .grad
It all-reduces gradients as usual but skips the next optimizer step for the window
It averages gradients only within the local machine, not across nodes
questions.explanation: Inside no_sync(), backward still computes gradients and accumulates them into .grad as usual, but DDP does not launch the all-reduce. The first backward outside the block all-reduces .grad, which already holds the sum of the earlier micro-batches, so one exchange averages the whole window.

questions.question: Why must the forward pass, not just the backward pass, be inside DDP's no_sync() block?
options: Because forward allocates the gradient buffers that no_sync() later frees, so both must be inside
Because DDP's forward prepares the reducer and, inside no_sync(), marks it 'do not communicate'
Because forward performs an all-reduce of activations, which no_sync() must also suppress
Because no_sync() only takes effect on code that creates new tensors, which backward does not
questions.explanation: DDP's forward sets up the reducer that launches all-reduce hooks during backward. The 'skip communication' decision is recorded at forward time inside no_sync(). If only backward is wrapped, the reducer was prepared normally and DDP still synchronizes.

questions.question: With W ranks, A micro-batches per window, each micro-batch loss divided by A, and one all-reduce at the end, what gradient does every rank hold?
options: The sum over all W*A micro-batch gradients, with no averaging applied
The mean over all W*A micro-batch gradients: (1/(W A)) sum_w sum_a g_{w,a}
The mean over the A micro-batches on rank 0 only, which is then broadcast to all ranks
The mean over the W ranks of only the last micro-batch in the window
questions.explanation: Each rank's accumulated gradient is G_w = sum_a g_{w,a}/A, and the final all-reduce averages over ranks, giving (1/W) sum_w G_w = (1/(W A)) sum over all micro-batch gradients. For equal-size micro-batches that is exactly what one big batch would give.

questions.question: If you forget model.no_sync() when accumulating gradients with DDP, what happens?
options: The result is wrong, because the gradients get averaged across ranks A times too many times
Training deadlocks after the first micro-batch, because the ranks wait on mismatched collectives
The result is still correct, but you pay A full-gradient all-reduces per optimizer step instead of one
The gradients are summed across ranks rather than averaged, so they end up W times too large
questions.explanation: Averaging is linear, so averaging each micro-batch's gradient and then adding gives the same final gradient as one average at the end. What changes is cost: every micro-batch triggers a full all-reduce. For a 1B-parameter model with fp32 gradients that is about 4 GB per micro-batch, so A = 8 moves 8 times more data.

questions.question: How much extra memory does DDP's no_sync() cost during gradient accumulation?
options: One extra gradient copy per micro-batch, held until the final synchronizing backward
A communication buffer the size of the activations, allocated once per accumulation window
One extra full copy of the model's parameters, used to store the unsynchronized gradients
None; accumulation happens in the existing .grad tensors, with shape, dtype and device unchanged
questions.explanation: no_sync() does not create tensors; backward just keeps adding into the .grad tensors that already exist. Each .grad keeps its parameter's shape, dtype, and device. Skipping communication saves bandwidth without adding memory.

questions.question: In a DDP accumulation loop, sync_ctx = contextlib.nullcontext() if is_last_in_window else model.no_sync(). What is contextlib.nullcontext() for?
options: It disables gradient computation for that micro-batch, like torch.no_grad()
It is a do-nothing with-block, so the same code synchronizes normally on the last micro-batch
It forces an all-reduce of the loss value on the last micro-batch of each window
It frees the gradient buffers after the optimizer step so the next window starts clean
questions.explanation: nullcontext() is a do-nothing context manager. Choosing between it and no_sync() lets one 'with sync_ctx:' block handle both cases: skip communication on intermediate micro-batches, and synchronize normally on the last one.

questions.question: In a DDP accumulation loop that synchronizes when (i + 1) % A == 0, why do all ranks reach the synchronizing micro-batch at the same i?
options: Because no_sync() aligns the ranks' loop counters before every micro-batch
Because DDP automatically pauses fast ranks until the slow ones catch up
Because DistributedSampler gives every rank the same number of batches
Because the optimizer broadcasts its step index to every rank after each update
questions.explanation: Collectives must be called in matching order on all ranks. DistributedSampler (with drop_last) gives every rank the same number of batches, so the same index i is the end of a window everywhere and all ranks join the same all-reduce together.

questions.question: In a DDP accumulation loop, what happens if len(loader) is not a multiple of A?
options: The leftovers accumulate into .grad without a step; drop them or make the epoch's last batch end a window
DDP raises an error at the end of the epoch, because the ranks' collective counts no longer match
The leftover micro-batches are automatically averaged into the next epoch's first step, with correct scaling
The optimizer steps on each leftover micro-batch individually, using its unaveraged local gradient
questions.explanation: The loop only steps when (i + 1) % A == 0, so trailing micro-batches add into .grad but are never used. With zero_grad placement, they could also leak into the next window. Either drop them or make the last batch of the epoch also end a window.

questions.question: How can you verify that DDP's no_sync() reduces the number of all-reduces during gradient accumulation?
options: Count the optimizer steps per epoch with and without no_sync() and compare the two totals
Compare the loss values and final gradients with and without no_sync() on the same batches
Register a counting comm hook via model.register_comm_hook that increments a counter, then all-reduces
Check torch.cuda.memory_allocated() after each micro-batch, since every all-reduce allocates a buffer
questions.explanation: A communication hook runs whenever DDP reduces a bucket. A counting hook that also performs the all-reduce shows one call per A micro-batches with no_sync() and one per micro-batch without it, for a single-bucket model. The losses and final gradients are the same either way, so they cannot reveal the difference.

questions.question: What can happen in DDP training if one rank skips a backward pass, crashes, or runs out of batches early?
options: DDP silently averages over the remaining ranks
The other ranks automatically continue with W-1 workers
Its peers can be left waiting in a collective
Nothing; collectives are independent per rank
questions.explanation: Collectives require every rank to participate in a compatible sequence. If one rank never issues the matching call, the others block waiting for it, so the job hangs or times out. Investigate the first error across all ranks before retrying.

questions.question: When might a DDP model need find_unused_parameters=True?
options: When the model has branches so some parameters may not receive gradients in a step
Whenever ranks have mismatched training loops or issue different sequences of collectives
Whenever gradient accumulation with no_sync() is used across micro-batches
Whenever the model is larger than 1B parameters and needs many gradient buckets
questions.explanation: Models with conditional branches may leave some parameters unused in a step, and DDP must be told to expect that. The flag is specific to unused parameters; it is not a general fix for ranks with mismatched loops or collective sequences.

questions.question: A single GPU trains with micro-batch 8 and 4 accumulation steps. Moving to 4 GPUs with DDP, both settings are kept. How many examples contribute to each optimizer step before and after?
options: 32 before, 32 after
32 before, 8 after
8 before, 32 after
32 before, 128 after
questions.explanation: Examples per update are micro_batch * accumulation * world_size: 8 * 4 * 1 = 32 before and 8 * 4 * 4 = 128 after. DDP's averaging normalizes the gradient, but it does not cancel the extra examples processed by additional workers.

questions.question: Moving from 1 to 4 GPUs with micro-batch 8, how can you keep the original global batch of 32 examples per optimizer step?
options: Disable DDP's gradient averaging
Multiply the learning rate by 4
Set micro-batch to 32
Set gradient accumulation to 1
questions.explanation: With 4 workers and micro-batch 8, accumulation 1 gives 8 * 1 * 4 = 32. When the worker count grows, one of the other factors must shrink to keep the product constant. Changing the learning rate does not change the number of examples per update.

questions.question: A 4-GPU run processes 128 examples per update while a 1-GPU run processes 32. For equal example exposure, which comparison is fair?
options: 250 updates of the 4-GPU run versus 1,000 of the 1-GPU run
1,000 updates of each run
4,000 updates of the 4-GPU run versus 1,000 of the 1-GPU run
1,000 updates of the 4-GPU run versus 250 of the 1-GPU run
questions.explanation: 1,000 updates at 32 examples is 32,000 examples, and 250 updates at 128 examples is also 32,000. Comparing equal step counts would give the larger-batch run four times the data. For language models, also count valid training tokens.

questions.question: When a change in the number of GPUs changes the global batch size, what should you do about the learning rate?
options: Always multiply it by the GPU count, since the gradient noise falls by exactly that factor
Re-evaluate the learning rate, warmup and schedule; there is no universal multiply-by-GPU rule
Always keep it unchanged, because gradient averaging already makes the step size independent of W
Always divide it by the GPU count, because the averaged gradient is W times larger than before
questions.explanation: A changed global batch can change optimization behavior, so the learning rate, warmup, and schedule should be re-evaluated. There is no universally correct rule like multiplying the learning rate by the GPU count, and a larger batch does not automatically make convergence worse. First decide whether to preserve the original setup or tune a new one.

questions.question: What is wrong with 'all-reduce updates the weights on every worker' as a description of data parallelism?
options: All-reduce combines gradients; the optimizer then updates each local copy of the weights
Nothing; all-reduce averages the weights directly, so that description is exactly right as stated
All-reduce combines activations from the forward pass, not the weights or the gradients
All-reduce only runs on rank 0, which then sends the updated weights to the others
questions.explanation: Confusing gradients with weights is a common mistake. The all-reduce averages gradients; each worker's optimizer then updates its own local replica of the weights using that averaged gradient. No weights are communicated in standard data parallelism.

questions.question: A user wraps the model with DDP and, after loss.backward(), additionally divides every .grad by world_size, believing this is needed to average. What is the effect?
options: The gradients are correct, because default DDP only sums and never divides by W
The gradients are W times too small, because DDP had already averaged them
The gradients become W times too large, because the division is applied before averaging
DDP detects the manual division and skips its own averaging, so the result is unchanged
questions.explanation: Default DDP already averages gradients during backward, so an extra division by W shrinks the gradient by a factor of W. That silently reduces the effective learning rate. The manual all-reduce-and-divide loop explains DDP's job; it is not extra code to add after DDP backward.

questions.question: Why can adding data-parallel workers accidentally change your training setup?
options: Because DDP changes the model architecture by adding synchronization layers to each block
Because more workers reduce the number of trainable parameters stored on each replica
Because DDP automatically lowers the learning rate in proportion to the number of data-parallel workers
Because keeping the local micro-batch and accumulation count fixed increases examples per update
questions.explanation: The global batch is micro_batch * accumulation * world_size, so adding workers with the other two factors fixed increases examples per update. Recalculate all three factors together whenever the worker count changes.

questions.question: Does wrapping a model with DDP make each rank see different training examples?
options: Yes; DDP splits each batch among the ranks automatically when the model is wrapped
No, and having different examples on each rank would break DDP's gradient averaging
Yes, but only on the first epoch; afterwards every rank reverts to the full dataset
No; the input pipeline (e.g. DistributedSampler) must give the workers different samples
questions.explanation: DDP does not choose examples. If every rank loads the same data, they all compute the same gradient and the extra GPUs are wasted. Configure the input pipeline so each worker contributes different samples.

questions.question: With local mean-loss gradients g_w and valid-token counts n_w per data-parallel worker, what is the global token-mean gradient?
options: sum(g_w) / W
sum(n_w * g_w) / W
sum(n_w * g_w) / (W * sum(n_w))
sum(n_w * g_w) / sum(n_w)
questions.explanation: Each g_w is already a mean over n_w tokens, so n_w * g_w recovers the sum over that worker's tokens. Summing those and dividing by the total token count gives the global per-token mean. The default equal worker average sum(g_w)/W only matches when all n_w are equal.

questions.question: What should you do when training with a sum loss under data parallelism?
options: Nothing; averaging the local sums across workers is always equivalent to the global sum
Multiply the learning rate by the global batch size to undo the averaging across workers
Switch the all-reduce to a max, so the largest local sum is used as the global gradient
Decide whether the intended objective is a global sum or a global mean, then scale consistently
questions.explanation: Averaging local sums equals neither the global sum nor the global mean without the appropriate factor. Decide which objective you want and apply the matching scaling. Otherwise the effective learning rate silently depends on W or the batch size.

questions.question: When using mixed-precision gradient scaling together with gradient clipping in data-parallel training, what is the correct order?
options: Clip, then average, then unscale
Average, then unscale, then clip
Unscale, then clip each local gradient, then average
Clip, then unscale, then average
questions.explanation: Clip the gradient the optimizer will actually use: average first, and with a gradient scaler, unscale before clipping so the threshold applies to true gradient magnitudes. Clipping local or still-scaled gradients clips the wrong quantity.

questions.question: Which of these breaks synchronization between data-parallel replicas, even if their gradients match?
options: Different dropout masks on each rank during the forward pass
Different local loss values on each rank at the end of each step
Different optimizer settings or restored optimizer states on each rank
Different training examples on each rank, as drawn by DistributedSampler
questions.explanation: Matching gradients only yield matching updates if optimizer settings, optimizer state, and update counts also match. Different local losses, dropout masks, and data are expected in data parallelism and do not by themselves break synchronization.

questions.question: What happens if data-parallel workers sum their gradients instead of averaging them (equal shards, local mean losses)?
options: The gradient is W times larger than the global mean-loss gradient
Nothing changes, because the optimizer normalizes the gradient's scale
The gradient is W times smaller than the global mean-loss gradient
The workers' weights diverge, because each applies a different update
questions.explanation: For equal shards with mean losses, the average reproduces the global mean-loss gradient, so the sum is W times larger. The replicas still agree, but the effective step size scales with W. Even when averaging, different floating-point reduction orders can cause tiny differences from single-device results.

questions.question: In ring all-reduce of an S-byte tensor across W workers with equal chunks, how many bytes does each worker send?
questions.explanation: Each worker sends W-1 chunks of S/W bytes in each of two phases, for 2(W-1)S/W bytes, and receives the same amount. Each direction approaches 2S as W grows, so sent plus received approaches 4S.

questions.question: Ring all-reduce keeps per-worker bandwidth roughly constant as W grows. Does that make its latency constant too?
options: Yes, the ring finishes in constant time
Yes, because chunks get smaller
No; the ring still has 2(W-1) rounds
No; latency grows as W squared
questions.explanation: Bandwidth accounting shows each worker moves about 2S bytes regardless of W, but the algorithm still runs 2(W-1) sequential rounds. Per-round latency costs therefore grow linearly with W. Bandwidth-optimal does not mean latency-constant.

questions.question: After a normal synchronized DDP backward, what is ready on every rank, and what remains local?
options: Averaged gradients are ready; the scalar loss stays local unless explicitly aggregated
Updated weights are ready on every rank; the gradients themselves remain local
The global mean loss is ready on every rank; the gradients themselves remain local to each rank
Averaged activations are ready on every rank; the gradients and loss remain local
questions.explanation: DDP arranges gradient communication during backward, so every rank ends with averaged gradients ready for the optimizer, which still runs on every rank. Forward and backward used local data, so each rank's loss value is local. Aggregate it explicitly to report a global loss.

questions.question: What can DDP's overlap of communication with backward not guarantee?
options: That some communication runs while backward is still computing other layers' gradients
That the optimizer step sees fully synchronized gradients on every rank
That the final gradients on every rank are correctly averaged across ranks
That all communication is hidden or that adding workers gives a proportional speedup
questions.explanation: Overlap can reduce the time spent waiting after gradient computation, but it cannot guarantee that all communication is hidden, that communication costs no GPU resources, or that more workers scale linearly. Correct averaged gradients are guaranteed regardless of overlap.

questions.question: How does ordinary DDP's per-worker memory for model state change as you add workers?
options: It is divided by W, since each worker holds only 1/W of the model state
It shrinks only for the optimizer state, which ordinary DDP shards evenly across the workers
It doubles with each added worker, because of extra communication buffers
It does not shrink; every worker keeps a full model, gradients and optimizer state
questions.explanation: Ordinary DDP replicates the full model, gradient tensors, and optimizer state on every worker, plus communication buffers. Adding workers adds throughput, not per-worker capacity. Sharding model state is what ZeRO and FSDP add.

questions.question: A memory estimate of 16P bytes for model state is quoted for training. When does it apply?
options: To every optimizer and precision setup, since all training state always scales as 16 bytes per parameter
Only to SGD without momentum in fp32, where weights, gradients and buffers add up to exactly 16 bytes per parameter
To one Adam accounting (4 bytes each for params and grads, 8 for moments, or the mixed-precision equivalent)
Only to inference with a KV cache, where weights and cached keys and values total 16 bytes
questions.explanation: 16P comes from a specific accounting of Adam training: parameters, gradients, and two moment buffers. Other optimizers, precisions, or master-weight choices give different constants. Treat 16P as a model of that setup, not a universal law.

questions.question: For a fixed amount of training work, what happens to total GPU-hours when scaling from 1 to W GPUs with data parallelism?
options: Total GPU-hours always rise by a factor of W, because every GPU repeats the same work in full
Total GPU-hours always fall by a factor of W, because the work is split evenly across the GPUs
Total GPU-hours always stay exactly constant, because communication is fully hidden by overlap
Ideally GPU-hours stay constant, but communication, data loading and small local batches can raise them
questions.explanation: Ideal scaling runs W GPUs for 1/W of the time, keeping GPU-hours constant. Real overheads reduce scaling efficiency, so GPU-hours can increase. Measure throughput and time to the desired training quality rather than assuming linear speedup.

questions.question: When is plain DDP the right tool, and what problem does it not solve?
options: When you need to split each matmul across GPUs; it does not handle data loading or sampling
When the model is too large for one GPU's memory; it does not make training any faster
When the model fits on one GPU and you want several GPUs on the data; it does not fix a model-state memory limit
When the batch does not fit on one GPU; it does not average gradients, so a manual all-reduce is needed
questions.explanation: DDP distributes examples while replicating the full model state, so it helps when the model already fits on one GPU. If model state exceeds one GPU's memory, replication does not help; ZeRO and FSDP partition optimizer state, gradients, and/or parameters to share the memory burden.

questions.question: What do ZeRO and FSDP change compared with ordinary DDP?
options: They partition optimizer state, gradients and/or parameters across workers instead of replicating them
They replace gradient averaging with periodic weight averaging, so that workers synchronize only every few steps
They split each individual matmul across GPUs so that no single device holds a full weight matrix
They remove the need for collectives by giving each worker an independent copy that never syncs
questions.explanation: ZeRO and FSDP keep the data-parallel structure but change what each worker stores: depending on stage, they shard optimizer state, gradients, and parameters across workers. That lets workers share the memory burden as well as the computation. Splitting individual matmuls is tensor parallelism.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: In plain data parallelism, which parts of a training step's memory are replicated on every worker?
options: Parameters, gradients and optimizer state: all of the model-sized memory
Only the parameters; gradients and optimizer state are split across the workers
Only the optimizer state; each worker keeps a private slice of the weights
Nothing; data parallelism shards all model state evenly across the workers
questions.explanation: Plain data parallelism gives every worker a full copy of the parameters, the (all-reduced) gradients, and the optimizer state. The workers differ only in which data they process. That redundancy is exactly what ZeRO removes.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Which bucket does each ZeRO stage add to the set being sharded across data-parallel workers?
options: Stage 1: parameters; stage 2: gradients; stage 3: optimizer state
Stage 1: gradients; stage 2: optimizer state; stage 3: activations
Stage 1: optimizer state; stage 2: gradients; stage 3: parameters
Stage 1: activations; stage 2: parameters; stage 3: gradients
questions.explanation: ZeRO-1 shards the optimizer state, ZeRO-2 additionally shards the gradients, and ZeRO-3 additionally shards the parameters. Each stage keeps the previous stage's sharding. Activations are not part of ZeRO's three model-sized buckets.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: How does PyTorch FSDP realize ZeRO stage 3?
options: It keeps all parameters on rank 0 and streams each layer's weights to the other ranks on demand
It offloads all parameters to CPU memory and copies each layer back to the GPU right before use
It permanently splits each matmul's weight columns across devices and all-reduces the outputs
It all-gathers each layer's parameters just in time for forward/backward, then frees them
questions.explanation: FSDP stores only a 1/W shard of each unit's parameters on every worker. Right before a unit runs, it all-gathers the full parameters, computes, and frees the gathered copy. That trades extra communication for a large memory saving.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Why can a billion-parameter model fail to train on a single GPU no matter how small the batch is made?
options: Because the ~16P bytes of params, grads and Adam state are fixed and do not depend on batch
Because activation memory is dominated by the attention cache, which does not shrink with batch
Because the learning rate must scale with parameter count, which forces a minimum effective batch
Because GPU matmul kernels need a batch of at least 1024 before tensor cores can be scheduled
questions.explanation: Parameters, gradients, and Adam's two moment buffers cost about 16 bytes per parameter regardless of batch size. Shrinking the batch only reduces activation memory. For large P that fixed cost alone exceeds one GPU, which is why ZeRO/FSDP shard it.

questions.question: Why can a ZeRO/FSDP lesson be largely verified on a single CPU?
options: Because ZeRO runs identically on one device, so a single CPU reproduces every stage's behaviour
Because ZeRO's communication cost is zero, so a single process measures everything that matters
Because FSDP has a CPU mode that faithfully reproduces multi-GPU timing and memory for every rank
The per-stage memory arithmetic is exact and computable directly; only sharded execution needs GPUs
questions.explanation: Much of ZeRO is accounting: how many bytes per worker each stage keeps. That arithmetic is exact and checkable with a few lines of Python. The actual all-gather/free behaviour and its communication overhead require a real sharded multi-GPU job.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: data parallelism wastes memory W times over
questions.question: In fp32 training with Adam, how many bytes per parameter go to the parameter, its gradient, and the optimizer state?
options: 2 + 2 + 4 = 8 bytes
questions.explanation: Each fp32 parameter takes 4 bytes, its gradient another 4, and Adam's two moment buffers m and v take 4 bytes each, for 8. That totals 16 bytes per parameter, or 16P bytes, before any activations.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: data parallelism wastes memory W times over
questions.question: Using 16 bytes per parameter for fp32 params, grads and Adam state, roughly how much model-state memory does a 7.5B-parameter model need?
options: 7.5 GB
30 GB
1.2 TB
120 GB
questions.explanation: 16 * 7.5e9 = 1.2e11 bytes, which is 120 GB. That exceeds any single current GPU, such as an 80 GB A100, before activations are counted.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: data parallelism wastes memory W times over
questions.question: In plain data parallelism on 64 GPUs, how many of the 64 copies of the 16P bytes of model state are redundant?
options: None
questions.explanation: All 64 workers hold identical parameters, gradients (after all-reduce), and optimizer state. Only one copy is needed in principle, so 63 are pure redundancy. ZeRO's name, Zero Redundancy Optimizer, comes from eliminating that.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: data parallelism wastes memory W times over
questions.question: What is the central idea of ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer)?
options: Compress gradients to low-bit integers before the all-reduce so communication shrinks about W-fold
Split the replicated model state into W disjoint shards, one per worker, gathering full tensors only when needed
Run the optimizer step on rank 0 only and broadcast the result, so other workers hold no optimizer state
Store all model state in fp8 so each replica's 16P bytes drop to about 4P bytes on every single worker
questions.explanation: Instead of replicating everything, ZeRO splits the model-state bytes into W disjoint shards, gives one to each worker, and rebuilds full tensors only for the brief moment they are needed. The math and result of training are the same as plain data parallelism.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: data parallelism wastes memory W times over
questions.question: Why is ZeRO described as a spectrum rather than a single technique?
options: Because each stage only works for a certain range of model sizes, so you pick it by parameter count
Because each stage shards more state, trading progressively more communication for less memory
Because accuracy degrades as you shard more, so each stage trades a bit of model quality for memory
Because each stage pairs with a different optimizer: SGD for stage 1, Adam for 2, Adafactor for 3
questions.explanation: Reconstructing sharded tensors costs communication. Each successive stage shards another bucket, saving more memory but adding more communication. The training result is unchanged at every stage.

questions.section: 2. The memory a step holds, in bytes
questions.question: Why is activation memory not part of ZeRO's sharding?
options: They scale with batch and context length, not with P, and are handled separately (e.g. checkpointing)
Activations are always smaller than gradients, so sharding them would save too little to be worth it
Activations are automatically shared across workers by the gradient all-reduce, so are never replicated
Activations are always kept in CPU memory during training, so they never compete for GPU memory
questions.explanation: ZeRO targets the three model-sized buckets: parameters, gradients, and optimizer state. Activations are a fourth bucket that grows with batch size times context length. Techniques like activation checkpointing and mixed precision address them.

questions.section: 2. The memory a step holds, in bytes
questions.question: How does the per-worker model-state memory of plain data parallelism change as the number of workers W grows?
options: It falls as 16P/W, since every added worker takes a share of the state
It falls to 8P once W exceeds 8, because gradients get split automatically
It grows as 16P times W, because each worker buffers everyone's gradients
It stays at 16P per worker whether W is 1 or 1000
questions.explanation: Plain data parallelism replicates all 16P bytes on every worker, so per-worker memory is independent of W. ZeRO's purpose is to make that per-worker number fall as W grows.

questions.section: 2. The memory a step holds, in bytes
questions.question: In the common mixed-precision accounting used by the ZeRO paper, how do the bytes per parameter break down?
options: bf16 params 2 + fp32 grads 4 + fp32 m and v 8 = 14 bytes total
fp16 params 2 + fp16 grads 2 + fp16 master, m and v 6 = 10 bytes
fp32 params 4 + fp16 grads 2 + fp32 master, m and v 12 = 18 bytes
fp16 params 2 + fp16 grads 2 + fp32 master, m, v 12 = 16 bytes
questions.explanation: Mixed-precision Adam keeps fp16 parameters (2 bytes) and gradients (2 bytes), plus an fp32 optimizer state of a master weight copy, m, and v (4 bytes each, 12 total). That also totals 16P bytes. The sharding structure is the same as in the pure-fp32 breakdown.

questions.section: 2. The memory a step holds, in bytes
questions.question: Does switching from pure-fp32 accounting to mixed-precision accounting change how ZeRO stages shard memory?
options: Yes; mixed precision already halves gradient memory, so stage 2 has nothing left to shard
No; the constants change, but each stage still divides one more bucket by W
Yes; fp16 parameters cannot be sharded, so stage 3 is unavailable under mixed precision
No; the per-bucket constants and totals stay identical to the fp32 accounting in every case
questions.explanation: Mixed precision changes which bucket holds how many bytes per parameter, but ZeRO's structure is the same: stage 1 shards the optimizer state, stage 2 also the gradients, stage 3 also the parameters. Per-bucket constants differ (for example 2/2/12 versus 4/4/8).

questions.question: Why is the optimizer state the natural first bucket for ZeRO to shard?
options: It is only ever read on rank 0, which applies the update and then broadcasts the new weights
It is the smallest of the three buckets, so sharding it is cheap and needs no extra collective
It is recomputed from the gradients every forward pass, so no worker needs to keep it resident
It is only touched inside optimizer.step(); between steps it just sits there
questions.explanation: The Adam moment buffers are read and written only during the optimizer step. So each worker can store only the slice it is responsible for updating. It is also the largest fp32 bucket (8P), so sharding it saves the most.

questions.question: In ZeRO stage 1, what happens during the optimizer step?
options: Each worker updates only the slice it holds optimizer state for, then an all-gather shares the new params
Every worker updates all parameters with its local state, then an all-reduce averages the new weights
Rank 0 updates all parameters using the full optimizer state and broadcasts them to every other worker
Each worker skips parameters it does not own, so each replica's other slices stay one step stale
questions.explanation: Worker w owns m and v for its 1/W slice of the parameters and updates only that slice. An all-gather then shares the updated slices so every worker again has the full weights for the next forward pass.

questions.question: In ZeRO stage 1, does each worker run forward and backward on only its slice of the parameters?
options: No; forward and backward are unchanged from plain DP, with full weights and full averaged gradient
Yes; each worker runs forward and backward on its slice only and computes just that slice's gradients
Yes; each worker computes on its own slice and the partial activations are combined by an all-to-all
No; only rank 0 runs the forward pass, and the other workers run backward on its stored activations
questions.explanation: In ZeRO-1, 'owns a slice' only refers to who performs the optimizer update and stores m and v. Every worker still holds full weights, runs the whole model on its micro-batch, and receives the full averaged gradient. Only the duplicated optimizer work and state are removed.

questions.question: What is the per-worker memory of ZeRO stage 1 in the fp32 accounting (P parameters, W workers)?
options: 8P + 8P/W
16P/W
questions.explanation: ZeRO-1 keeps full parameters (4P) and full gradients (4P) but shards the 8P optimizer state, giving 8P + 8P/W bytes per worker. 4P + 12P/W is ZeRO-2 and 16P/W is ZeRO-3.

questions.question: With P = 4 parameters and W = 2 workers under ZeRO-1, worker 0 updates theta_0 and theta_1 and worker 1 updates theta_2 and theta_3. What does each worker hold after the all-gather?
options: All 4 new values, exactly what plain data parallelism would give
Only its own two updated values; the other two stay at the previous step's values
All 4 values, but the two from worker 1 are one optimizer step behind worker 0's
An element-wise average of the two workers' full parameter vectors after the update
questions.explanation: Both workers compute all 4 gradients, each updates its two parameters, and the all-gather assembles all 4 updated values on both workers. The result is identical to plain data parallelism; ZeRO-1 only removed the duplicated optimizer work and state.

questions.question: Why can ZeRO stage 2 shard the gradients once stage 1 is in place?
options: Because gradients are recomputed from scratch during the optimizer step, so none need be stored
Worker w only updates its own parameter slice, so it only needs that slice's gradients
Because gradients are no longer averaged across workers once the optimizer state is sharded
Because gradients are stored alongside the activations, which each worker already keeps locally
questions.explanation: Under ZeRO-1, each worker updates only its slice of parameters, so the other (W-1)/W of the averaged gradient is never used locally. ZeRO-2 therefore avoids storing it.

questions.question: Which collective does ZeRO stage 2 use for gradients instead of an all-reduce, and why?
options: All-gather, so every worker receives every other worker's full gradient before averaging locally
Broadcast, so rank 0's gradient is copied to every worker and no averaging is needed at all
Reduce-scatter: it averages gradients and leaves each worker only its 1/W slice
All-to-all, which routes each raw gradient slice to its owner without averaging the values
questions.explanation: An all-reduce leaves the full averaged gradient on every worker. Reduce-scatter performs the same averaging but leaves each worker with only its own shard, which is all it needs. This is what makes gradient sharding possible.

questions.question: What is the per-worker memory of ZeRO stage 2 in the fp32 accounting?
options: 8P + 8P/W
16P/W
questions.explanation: ZeRO-2 keeps the full parameters (4P) and shards both the gradients (4P/W) and the optimizer state (8P/W): 4P + 12P/W bytes. ZeRO-1 is 8P + 8P/W and ZeRO-3 is 16P/W.

questions.question: In ZeRO stage 3, how does a worker run a layer whose parameters it only stores 1/W of?
options: It all-gathers the layer's full parameters just before it runs, computes, then frees the copy
It computes on its local shard and all-reduces the partial outputs, like a tensor-parallel matmul
It sends its input activations to the worker that owns the layer and waits for the output to return
It skips the layer in forward and runs it only in backward, once all the gradient shards have arrived
questions.explanation: A forward pass needs a layer's full weights. ZeRO-3 all-gathers them from all workers immediately before the layer runs and discards the non-owned part right after, keeping only its own slice. The same all-gather-then-free happens again in backward.

questions.question: What is the per-worker memory of ZeRO stage 3 in the fp32 accounting?
options: 16P/W
8P + 8P/W
questions.explanation: ZeRO-3 shards all three buckets: 4P/W + 4P/W + 8P/W = 16P/W bytes per worker. It is the only stage whose per-worker model-state memory keeps shrinking as W grows.

questions.question: As the number of workers W grows very large, what floor does per-worker model-state memory approach for each ZeRO stage?
options: ZeRO-1: 8P; ZeRO-2: 4P; ZeRO-3: approaching zero
ZeRO-1: 4P; ZeRO-2: 8P; ZeRO-3: a floor of 4P per worker
All three stages approach zero as W grows without bound
ZeRO-1: 16P; ZeRO-2: 8P; ZeRO-3: a floor of 4P
questions.explanation: ZeRO-1 keeps full parameters and gradients (8P), and ZeRO-2 keeps full parameters (4P), so they plateau at those floors. ZeRO-3 shards everything, so 16P/W keeps falling toward zero. That is why only ZeRO-3 scales model size with W.

questions.question: Which ordering of per-worker model-state memory is correct for W greater than 1?
options: plain DP < ZeRO-1 < ZeRO-2 < ZeRO-3
ZeRO-1 < ZeRO-2 < ZeRO-3 < plain DP
ZeRO-3 < ZeRO-2 < ZeRO-1 < plain DP
ZeRO-2 < ZeRO-3 < ZeRO-1 < plain DP
questions.explanation: Each stage shards one more bucket: plain DP is 16P, ZeRO-1 8P + 8P/W, ZeRO-2 4P + 12P/W, and ZeRO-3 16P/W. More sharding means less memory per worker, at the cost of more communication.

questions.question: For P = 7.5B on W = 64 workers in fp32, why does ZeRO-1 nearly halve per-worker memory compared with plain data parallelism?
options: Because the 8P optimizer state is the biggest bucket and it is now sharded
Because ZeRO-1 stores the parameters in fp16, halving the 4P weight bucket on every worker
Because the gradients are discarded right after backward instead of being kept for the step
Because the activations are offloaded to CPU memory, freeing roughly half of the GPU
questions.explanation: Plain DP needs 16P = 120 GB. ZeRO-1 shards the 8P optimizer state to 8P/64, leaving 8P + 8P/64, about 60.9 GB. The biggest bucket accounts for half the total, so sharding it almost halves the memory.

questions.question: A 7.5B-parameter model in fp32 needs 120 GB per worker with plain data parallelism. On 64 workers, which is the first ZeRO stage that fits on an 80 GB GPU (model state only)?
options: ZeRO-3, at about 1.9 GB
ZeRO-2, at about 31.4 GB
ZeRO-1, at about 60.9 GB
None of the stages fit
questions.explanation: ZeRO-1 gives 8P + 8P/64, about 60.9 GB, which fits in 80 GB. ZeRO-2 (about 31.4 GB) and ZeRO-3 (about 1.88 GB) leave even more room for activations, at higher communication cost.

questions.question: Why does ZeRO-3 reduce per-worker memory for a 7.5B model on 64 workers all the way to about 1.88 GB, and what does it cost?
options: It compresses the optimizer state to 8 bits; the cost is a measurable drop in final accuracy
It offloads parameters to NVMe disk; the cost is much slower checkpoint save and restore times
Nothing model-sized stays fully resident; the cost is all-gathering every layer's weights each pass
It drops the gradients after each step; the cost is needing a larger learning rate to converge
questions.explanation: ZeRO-3 shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer state, so each worker holds 16P/64 = 0.25 bytes per parameter. Since no worker permanently holds the full weights, each layer's weights must be all-gathered in both forward and backward. That makes it the most communication-heavy stage.

questions.question: Why do ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 plateau in per-worker memory on very large W, while ZeRO-3 keeps falling?
options: ZeRO-3 discards the optimizer state entirely and recomputes it from the gradients each step
ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 spend more on communication, and their comm buffers grow linearly with W
ZeRO-3 stores everything in mixed precision, while ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 remain in pure fp32
ZeRO-1/2 keep a full-model bucket resident (8P or 4P); ZeRO-3 shards every bucket
questions.explanation: ZeRO-1 keeps full parameters and gradients (8P), ZeRO-2 keeps full parameters (4P); those terms do not shrink with W. ZeRO-3 has no unsharded term, so its 16P/W keeps falling. The trade is that ZeRO-3 has the highest communication cost.

questions.section: 5. FSDP: PyTorch's stage-3, and the all-gather/free dance
questions.question: What is FSDP, and what does 'fully sharded' mean?
options: A DeepSpeed feature that shards only the optimizer state, leaving parameters and gradients replicated
PyTorch's native ZeRO-3: params, grads and optimizer state all sharded, ~1/W of the model per worker
A Megatron mode that splits each matmul across GPUs so every layer's compute is fully partitioned
A PyTorch data loader that fully shards the dataset so each worker reads a disjoint subset of files
questions.explanation: FSDP (Fully Sharded Data Parallel) is PyTorch's implementation of ZeRO stage 3. 'Fully sharded' means all three model-state buckets are sharded. Each worker permanently stores only its 1/W shard.

questions.section: 5. FSDP: PyTorch's stage-3, and the all-gather/free dance
questions.question: In FSDP, what is a 'wrapping unit'?
options: A pipeline stage placed on its own GPU, passing activations to the next stage
A single parameter tensor, sharded and gathered independently of all others
A micro-batch of training examples whose gradients are accumulated as one
A group of layers whose parameters FSDP all-gathers and frees together
questions.explanation: FSDP groups layers into wrapping units and performs just-in-time reconstruction unit by unit: all-gather the unit's parameters, compute, free. The size of the units determines the transient memory spike from materializing full parameters.

questions.section: 5. FSDP: PyTorch's stage-3, and the all-gather/free dance
questions.question: What is the correct sequence FSDP follows for each wrapping unit during a training step?
options: Compute forward on the local shard, all-reduce the partial outputs, then all-gather the gradients
All-gather params, forward, free; in backward all-gather, compute, free, then reduce-scatter grads
Broadcast parameters from rank 0, compute forward and backward, then all-reduce the full gradients
All-gather every parameter once at the start of training and keep them; reduce-scatter grads each step
questions.explanation: Before a unit's forward, FSDP all-gathers its full parameters, computes, and frees the non-owned part. In backward it repeats the all-gather, computes gradients, frees, and combines gradients with a reduce-scatter so each worker keeps only its gradient shard.

questions.section: 5. FSDP: PyTorch's stage-3, and the all-gather/free dance
questions.question: Why is FSDP's per-worker memory approximately 16P/W plus a transient term, and what is that transient term?
options: The transient term is a full unsharded copy of the optimizer state, gathered for each optimizer step
Only one or a few prefetched units are materialized at once, so the extra is the largest unit's params
The transient term is a full copy of the whole model's gradients, held until the reduce-scatter ends
There is no transient term: memory is exactly 16P/W because gathers write into the shard in place
questions.explanation: FSDP materializes full weights only for the unit currently running (plus any prefetched). So on top of the 16P/W shards, memory includes the transient full parameters of the largest unit, never the whole model.

questions.section: 5. FSDP: PyTorch's stage-3, and the all-gather/free dance
questions.question: In FSDP, what does the all_gather collective do with each worker's shard of a layer's weight?
options: Concatenates the shards so every worker briefly holds the identical full tensor
Sums the shards element-wise so every worker holds a tensor of the shard's original size
Keeps only rank 0's shard and copies it to every worker, overwriting their local shards
Averages the shards element-wise, the same reduction used for gradients in plain DDP
questions.explanation: All-gather collects each worker's shard and concatenates them into the full tensor on every worker. Unlike an all-reduce, it does not add values. The full tensor is used for the unit's computation and then dropped.

questions.section: 5. FSDP: PyTorch's stage-3, and the all-gather/free dance
questions.question: How does FSDP's communication per step compare with plain DDP's?
options: FSDP communicates only during the optimizer step, when it gathers the updated parameter shards
FSDP communicates less than DDP, because each worker sends only its 1/W shard of the gradients
Both communicate exactly the same amount, since each exchanges the full gradient once per step
FSDP all-gathers each unit's params twice per step (forward, backward); DDP moves gradients once
questions.explanation: FSDP must reconstruct each unit's parameters before forward and again before backward, plus reduce-scatter gradients. DDP only all-reduces gradients once per step. FSDP trades this extra traffic for much lower memory.

questions.section: 5. FSDP: PyTorch's stage-3, and the all-gather/free dance
questions.question: How does FSDP hide the cost of its extra all-gathers?
options: By skipping the all-gather in backward and reusing the weights kept resident from the forward pass
By compressing the gathered parameters to int8 so each all-gather moves a quarter of the bytes
