By prefetching: it starts all-gathering unit k+1's parameters while unit k computes
By running the optimizer during forward, so the gathers overlap with the parameter update
questions.explanation: Prefetching overlaps communication with computation, just as DDP overlaps the gradient all-reduce with backward. When tuned well, FSDP keeps throughput close to DDP while using a fraction of the memory.

questions.section: 5. FSDP: PyTorch's stage-3, and the all-gather/free dance
questions.question: When does ZeRO-3/FSDP stop being efficient?
options: On a slow interconnect, where per-layer all-gather traffic no longer hides under compute
When the model has more than 32 layers, since each extra wrapping unit adds a fixed sync cost
When training with Adam instead of SGD, since Adam's two moments double the gathered traffic
When the global batch is larger than the number of workers, so shards no longer divide evenly
questions.explanation: ZeRO-3/FSDP rely on overlapping their per-layer all-gathers with compute. They are most efficient with fast links like NVLink within a node or high-bandwidth fabric across nodes. On slow links, communication is exposed and throughput drops.

questions.section: 5. FSDP: PyTorch's stage-3, and the all-gather/free dance
questions.question: What is a common practical recipe for combining FSDP with plain data parallelism?
options: FSDP only on rank 0, which holds the master weights, with plain data parallelism on all others
Plain data parallelism within each node, and FSDP sharding across the slower inter-node links
FSDP within a fast-linked group of GPUs, plain data parallelism across groups
Alternate FSDP and DDP on every other step so the communication cost averages out over time
questions.explanation: FSDP's heavy all-gather traffic belongs on the fastest links, so it is used within a fast group (such as one node). Across groups, where links are slower, plain data parallelism needs only one gradient all-reduce per step. This hybrid maps communication cost to the hardware topology.

questions.section: 6. Which stage should you reach for?
questions.question: When is plain DDP the right choice instead of a ZeRO stage?
options: When model and optimizer state fit comfortably on one GPU and you only want speed
When the model does not fit on one GPU, since DDP spreads its replicas across all the workers
When the interconnect is very fast, since DDP is the only mode that can saturate NVLink
When you need the largest possible batch per GPU, since DDP leaves the most free memory
questions.explanation: If model state fits on one GPU, sharding adds communication without a needed memory benefit. Plain DDP gives the speedup with the least communication. Climb the ZeRO ladder only when memory forces you.

questions.section: 6. Which stage should you reach for?
questions.question: Why is ZeRO-1 often enough when you are just over the memory limit?
options: It shards the biggest bucket (8P optimizer state) for little extra traffic: one param all-gather
It shards the activations, which are usually the largest bucket once the batch size is non-trivial
It removes the gradient all-reduce entirely, so it actually communicates less than plain DDP does
It halves the parameter count by sharing weights across layers, shrinking every bucket at once
questions.explanation: The optimizer state is the largest fp32 bucket, so sharding it frees the most memory. The only extra communication is the all-gather of updated parameters after the step. That makes it the best memory saved per unit of extra communication.

questions.section: 6. Which stage should you reach for?
questions.question: When should you reach for ZeRO-3 or FSDP?
options: When the model easily fits on one GPU, since ZeRO-3 then adds the least overhead of any stage
Always, because ZeRO-3 has the lowest communication volume of all the stages, including DDP
When it won't fit even with grads and optimizer state sharded, or to maximize batch/model per GPU
Only when training without an optimizer, because ZeRO-3 cannot shard Adam's moment buffers
questions.explanation: ZeRO-3/FSDP give the lowest memory but the highest communication, due to per-layer all-gathers. They are the right rung when lower stages cannot fit the model, or when you need maximum memory headroom for batch or model size.

questions.section: 6. Which stage should you reach for?
questions.question: What rule of thumb governs how far up the ZeRO ladder to climb?
options: Always use the highest stage available, since higher stages save memory at no extra traffic cost
Climb only as far as the memory wall forces you, since each rung adds communication
Use the ZeRO stage equal to the number of nodes, so each node owns exactly one sharded bucket
Use stage 2 whenever the model exceeds 1B parameters, and stage 3 whenever it exceeds 10B
questions.explanation: Each stage trades more communication for less memory. Stage 1 buys the most memory per unit of extra communication; stage 3 buys the most memory overall but pays with per-layer all-gathers. So use the lowest stage that fits.

questions.question: Which paper introduced ZeRO's three stages and their per-stage memory formulas?
options: GPipe: Efficient Training of Giant Neural Networks using Pipeline Parallelism
Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism (Shoeybi et al., 2019)
ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models (Rajbhandari et al., 2019)
Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017)
questions.explanation: The ZeRO paper by Rajbhandari et al. (2019) introduced the 'zero redundancy' framing and the three stages, whose per-stage memory formulas are its central result. Megatron-LM is the companion foundational paper on tensor parallelism.

questions.question: In which widely used software do the ZeRO paper's ideas ship today?
options: vLLM and NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM inference servers
Hugging Face Tokenizers and SentencePiece
Microsoft DeepSpeed (ZeRO) and PyTorch FSDP
NumPy, SciPy and the JAX array libraries
questions.explanation: DeepSpeed implements ZeRO stages 1 to 3, and PyTorch FSDP implements ZeRO-3-style full sharding. Both are configured on top of a DDP-style training loop.

questions.question: A 3B-parameter model is trained on 8 GPUs with 40 GB each, using fp32 accounting and ignoring activations. Does plain data parallelism fit?
options: Yes, at 6 GB per worker
No, it needs 48 GB per worker
Yes, at 27 GB per worker
No, it needs 96 GB per worker
questions.explanation: Plain DP needs 16P = 16 * 3e9 = 48e9 bytes = 48 GB per worker, regardless of the number of workers. That exceeds 40 GB, so it does not fit.

questions.question: A 3B-parameter model on 8 GPUs (fp32, ignoring activations): what is the per-worker memory under ZeRO-1, and does it fit in 40 GB?
options: 24 GB, fits
48 GB, does not fit
6 GB, fits
27 GB, fits
questions.explanation: ZeRO-1 is 8P + 8P/W = 24e9 + 3e9 = 27 GB per worker. That fits in 40 GB with about 13 GB left for activations.

questions.question: A 3B-parameter model on 8 GPUs (fp32, ignoring activations): what is the per-worker memory under ZeRO-3?
options: 6 GB
27 GB
48 GB
3 GB
questions.explanation: ZeRO-3 is 16P/W = 48e9 / 8 = 6 GB per worker. It fits easily, leaving about 34 GB for activations and a larger batch, at the cost of per-layer all-gathers.

questions.question: If both ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-3 fit a model on the available GPUs, which should you normally choose, and why?
options: ZeRO-3, because ZeRO-1 does not actually shard anything and only reorganizes the optimizer step
ZeRO-3, because sharding all state always gives higher throughput than sharding only one bucket
ZeRO-1, the cheapest stage that fits; go to ZeRO-3 only for more activation headroom or batch
Plain DP, because ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-3 both change the numerical result of each training step
questions.explanation: ZeRO-1 adds almost no communication, while ZeRO-3 requires per-layer all-gathers. Since both fit, ZeRO-1 is cheaper. Only climb further if the extra memory headroom is needed.

questions.question: What does plain data parallelism do for the memory wall?
options: It shards the activations, so each worker holds only its micro-batch's share
It divides model-state memory by W, since each worker sees only 1/W of the data
It halves the optimizer state, because the averaged gradients are stored only once
Nothing: it saves time, but every worker still holds the full 16P bytes
questions.explanation: Data parallelism only adds throughput. Every worker still holds full parameters, gradients, and optimizer state, so per-worker memory is unchanged. That is the entire reason ZeRO exists.

questions.question: Why can a model still run out of memory after enabling ZeRO-3?
options: ZeRO shards only model-sized buckets; activations (batch x context) are untouched and often the limit
Because ZeRO-3 re-replicates the optimizer state on every worker during the optimizer step
Because ZeRO-3 doubles gradient memory by keeping both full and sharded copies until the step
Because ZeRO-3 is incompatible with Adam and silently falls back to unsharded plain DDP
questions.explanation: ZeRO handles parameters, gradients, and optimizer state, but activations scale with batch and context length and are not sharded by it. Pair ZeRO with activation checkpointing and mixed precision to address them.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to assume ZeRO-3 is always the best stage?
options: It gives less memory saving than ZeRO-1, because gathered parameters are never freed afterwards
Its per-layer all-gathers are the heaviest traffic of any stage; on slow links a lower stage wins
It changes the training result, because sharded optimizer updates are applied in a different order
It cannot be combined with mixed precision, so it forces fp32 and doubles the parameter memory
questions.explanation: ZeRO-3 saves the most memory but communicates the most. If a lower stage already fits, the extra traffic is pure overhead, and on slow links it can dominate step time. Climb only as far as memory forces you.

questions.question: What is the difference between how plain DDP and ZeRO-2/3 combine gradients?
options: Both all-gather the gradients, then each worker averages the full set locally before the step
DDP reduce-scatters to each worker's shard; ZeRO-2/3 all-reduce so every worker has the full average
DDP all-reduces (full averaged gradient everywhere); ZeRO-2/3 reduce-scatter (each keeps its shard)
DDP sums the gradients across workers; ZeRO-2/3 take the element-wise maximum to bound the update
questions.explanation: An all-reduce leaves the full averaged gradient on every worker, which DDP needs because every worker updates all parameters. A reduce-scatter leaves each worker with only its averaged shard, which is all a ZeRO-2/3 worker needs. That difference makes gradient sharding possible.

questions.question: Why does adding more GPUs with plain data parallelism not help a model that is too big for one GPU?
options: Data parallelism requires the model to be split by layers first, which the big model cannot do
Data parallelism is limited to 8 GPUs per job, so it cannot add enough memory for a large model
Data parallelism shards only activations, and activations are not what makes the model too big
It replicates all 16P bytes on every GPU, adding throughput but not per-worker capacity
questions.explanation: Each worker in plain data parallelism holds the complete model, gradients, and optimizer state. A model that does not fit on one GPU therefore does not fit on any of them. Sharding the bytes across workers, as ZeRO/FSDP do, is required.

questions.question: For P = 7.5B and W = 64 in fp32, ZeRO-1 needs about 60.9 GB per worker but ZeRO-3 only about 1.88 GB. Where do the extra savings come from?
options: ZeRO-3 also removes the activations from GPU memory by recomputing them during backward
ZeRO-3 compresses the already-sharded optimizer state further, from 8P/W down to about 1P/W
ZeRO-3 also shards the 4P parameters and 4P gradients that ZeRO-1 keeps on every worker
ZeRO-3 stores all model state in fp16 while ZeRO-1 keeps it in fp32, halving every bucket
questions.explanation: ZeRO-1 still keeps 8P = 60 GB of full parameters and gradients and shards only the optimizer state to about 0.9 GB. ZeRO-3 shards all three buckets, so they all become 1/64 of their size: 16P/64 = 1.88 GB.

questions.question: Roughly how does per-step throughput of ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-3/FSDP compare with DDP when communication overlaps well?
options: Both are about twice as fast as DDP, because sharding halves the bytes each GPU must process
ZeRO-1 matches DDP; ZeRO-3/FSDP is a few % to ~20% slower, much worse on a weak interconnect
ZeRO-1 is about 50% slower than DDP, while ZeRO-3/FSDP matches DDP thanks to prefetching
Both are always more than 2x slower than DDP, regardless of interconnect or overlap quality
questions.explanation: ZeRO-1 adds only a parameter all-gather after the step, so it is close to DDP. ZeRO-3/FSDP's per-layer all-gathers cost a few percent to about 20% per step when well overlapped. On a slow interconnect the gap grows much larger.

questions.question: What hardware does real ZeRO/FSDP training need to run efficiently?
options: A single GPU with very large memory, since ZeRO gains nothing from adding more devices
W GPUs on a fast interconnect (NVLink/InfiniBand) so the all-gather traffic hides under compute
Any cluster of CPUs on standard Ethernet, since the sharded traffic per step is negligible
GPUs with no interconnect at all, since ZeRO avoids inter-device communication entirely
questions.explanation: ZeRO/FSDP add communication to save memory. They need W GPUs with fast links, such as NVLink within a node or InfiniBand across nodes, so that communication overlaps with computation rather than stalling it.

questions.question: How do DeepSpeed and PyTorch FSDP relate to a DDP-style training loop?
options: FSDP requires rewriting the model as a pipeline of stages, and DeepSpeed requires a custom trainer
Both replace the training loop with a new API that has no explicit optimizer or backward call
DeepSpeed works only for inference, while FSDP is a drop-in replacement for the PyTorch optimizer
Both are configuration on a DDP-style loop: DeepSpeed offers ZeRO 1-3, FSDP offers full sharding
questions.explanation: The training loop of forward, backward, and step stays the same. DeepSpeed and FSDP are configured on top of it to choose a sharding strategy. DeepSpeed offers ZeRO stages 1 to 3; FSDP offers ZeRO-3-style full sharding.

questions.question: What limitation of ZeRO/FSDP motivates model parallelism (tensor, pipeline, expert)?
options: After gathering, each worker still runs each layer's full compute, which fails when one layer is too big
ZeRO/FSDP cannot shard the optimizer state, so it must be split across devices by layer instead
ZeRO/FSDP do not support more than 8 GPUs, so larger clusters need tensor or pipeline splits
ZeRO/FSDP change the model's output slightly, so exact-result training needs model parallelism
questions.explanation: ZeRO/FSDP shard memory across data-parallel workers but every worker still computes every layer in full. When a single layer's weights, compute, or activations are too large for one device, the math itself must be split: within matmuls (tensor parallelism), across layers (pipeline), or across experts (expert parallelism).

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: What is '3D parallelism' in frontier-model training?
options: Running three independent training runs on separate clusters and averaging their weights
Splitting a model's layers across exactly three GPUs, one third of the depth on each device
Combining data, tensor and pipeline parallelism at the same time
Sharding parameters, gradients and optimizer state at once, as in ZeRO stage 3
questions.explanation: 3D parallelism combines data parallelism (split the data), tensor parallelism (split within layers), and pipeline parallelism (split across layers). Expert parallelism is added on top for Mixture-of-Experts models. Sharding all three model-state buckets is ZeRO-3, a different idea.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Why is it useful to know what each parallelism axis splits and what it costs in communication?
options: It determines the model's final accuracy, since each axis changes the loss curve
It lets you read a large-model training report and plan a training layout
It replaces scaling laws, since the layout alone fixes the optimal model size
It lets you pick a layout that avoids inter-device communication entirely
questions.explanation: Frontier runs use several parallelism axes at once, each with its own communication pattern and cost. Knowing them lets you interpret the configuration in a training report and map axes to hardware when planning one. Parallelism does not change what the model learns.

questions.question: A tensor-parallel example is simulated in one process by computing each device's partial result with NumPy and summing them. What does it reproduce, and what does it not?
options: It reproduces the all-reduce's numbers, not the real gain of fitting or speeding up a big layer
It reproduces the real multi-GPU speedup, but not the exact numbers that an all-reduce would produce
It reproduces both the all-reduce's numbers and the per-device memory savings of the split
It reproduces neither the numbers nor the memory savings, since NumPy has no collectives
questions.explanation: Summing per-device partials in one process gives exactly the output an all-reduce would produce. But the point of real tensor parallelism, fitting a layer that does not fit on one device and computing it faster, can only be shown on real multi-device hardware.

questions.section: 1. When data parallelism and ZeRO run out
questions.question: What assumption do data parallelism and ZeRO/FSDP share that breaks for the largest models?
options: That the full training dataset fits in each node's CPU memory for shuffling
That a single device can, at least momentarily, hold and compute one full layer
That all GPUs sit on one machine and share a single NVLink switch fabric
That the optimizer is plain SGD, so no per-parameter state ever needs to be stored
questions.explanation: Data parallelism replicates the model, and ZeRO/FSDP gather each layer's full weights before computing it. Both assume one device can hold and compute one layer. When a layer's weights or activations are too large, the model itself must be split across devices.

questions.section: 1. When data parallelism and ZeRO run out
questions.question: Which description matches tensor parallelism?
options: Splitting one operation such as a matmul so each device holds part of the weight and output
Assigning a contiguous block of layers to each device and passing activations to the next one
Placing different MoE experts on different devices and routing tokens to their owners
Giving each device a different shard of the training data and averaging the gradients
questions.explanation: Tensor parallelism splits within a layer, across the width of a matmul. Assigning layer ranges is pipeline parallelism, placing experts is expert parallelism, and sharding the data is data parallelism.

questions.section: 1. When data parallelism and ZeRO run out
questions.question: Which description matches pipeline parallelism?
options: Each device holds a column slice of every weight matrix and all-reduces outputs
Each device holds a contiguous range of layers and passes activations to the next
Each device holds a subset of the MoE experts and receives tokens via all-to-all
Each device holds a slice of the token positions and exchanges keys and values for attention
questions.explanation: Pipeline parallelism splits the layer stack (depth) across devices. Each stage computes its layers and sends activations forward, while backward flows in reverse. Slicing every weight matrix is tensor parallelism and slicing token positions is sequence parallelism.

questions.section: 1. When data parallelism and ZeRO run out
questions.question: Which description matches expert parallelism?
options: Each device computes a column block of every matmul and all-reduces the outputs
Each device holds a contiguous range of layers and forwards its activations to the next device
In an MoE, experts live on different devices and tokens are routed to their expert's device
Each device processes a different data shard and the gradients are all-reduced
questions.explanation: Expert parallelism is specific to MoE models. Experts are distributed across devices, and tokens are sent to the device hosting the expert the router selected. It composes with the other parallelism axes.

questions.section: 1. When data parallelism and ZeRO run out
questions.question: How do data parallelism and ZeRO relate to tensor, pipeline and expert parallelism?
options: They compose on top of all three
They are alternatives that cannot be combined with them
They replace tensor parallelism at large scale
They only work with pipeline parallelism
questions.explanation: Data parallelism and ZeRO split the data and the memory, while tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism split the model itself. Real runs use them together: model-parallel groups form replicas, and data parallelism or ZeRO runs across replicas.

questions.section: 2. Tensor parallelism: split the matmul (Megatron style)
questions.question: What is the key design goal of the Megatron-LM tensor-parallel split for a Transformer MLP?
options: Removing the nonlinearity between the two matmuls so they fuse into one
Making every device hold the full weight matrices to avoid gathering them
Splitting the two matmuls so they need only one communication between them
Communicating the 4C-wide hidden activations after every matmul in the block
questions.explanation: Megatron chooses how to split the MLP's two weight matrices so that the pair needs only one collective (an all-reduce at the end) per pass. The wide hidden activations never have to be communicated.

questions.section: The column-then-row trick for an MLP
questions.question: In a Transformer MLP Y = ReLU(X A) B, what are A and B?
options: A is the attention score matrix; B is the value projection applied to it
A is the C to 4C up projection; B is the 4C to C down projection
A is the 4C to C down projection; B is the C to 4C up projection
A and B are both C by C matrices, so the hidden width stays at C
questions.explanation: The MLP widens the representation from C to 4C with A, applies an element-wise nonlinearity, and projects back from 4C to C with B. GPT-2 uses GELU rather than ReLU, but the tensor-parallel splitting is identical.

questions.section: The column-then-row trick for an MLP
questions.question: In Megatron's column-parallel split of the MLP's first matmul, why can each device apply the nonlinearity without communication?
options: Because ReLU is linear on its domain, so applying it before or after the sum gives an identical result
Each device computes its own slice of the hidden activations, and the nonlinearity is element-wise
Because each device holds the full 4C-wide hidden activations after an implicit all-gather
Because the nonlinearity is deferred until after the all-reduce that follows the second matmul
questions.explanation: Splitting A by columns means device d computes X A_d, a slice of the hidden activations. An element-wise function like ReLU or GELU needs only each element itself, so it can be applied to the slice locally. That is why the column split is placed before the nonlinearity.

questions.section: The column-then-row trick for an MLP
questions.question: In Megatron's MLP split, how is the second matmul B partitioned, and what does each device produce?
options: Row-parallel: B is split by rows matching the hidden slices; each device gives a full-shape partial
Column-parallel: B is split by columns, so each device produces a disjoint slice of the output columns
Replicated: every device holds all of B and produces the full, correct output without communication
Split by batch: each device holds all of B and produces the outputs for a different subset of tokens
questions.explanation: B is split by rows so device d multiplies its hidden slice by B_d. The result has the full C-wide output shape but contains only that device's contribution. The full output is the sum of these partials.

questions.section: The column-then-row trick for an MLP
questions.question: How does Megatron's tensor-parallel MLP obtain the complete output Y on every device?
options: An all-reduce sums the partial outputs: Y = sum over d of ReLU(X A_d) B_d
An all-gather concatenates each device's output columns into the full width-C Y
Rank 0 gathers every partial, computes Y alone, and broadcasts it to the others
Each device already holds the full Y after the row-parallel matmul, with no communication
questions.explanation: Each device's row-parallel result is a partial contribution to Y. One all-reduce with sum adds them, leaving the full Y on every device. Concatenating would be wrong because the partials overlap in shape rather than covering disjoint columns.

questions.section: The column-then-row trick for an MLP
questions.question: Why is Megatron's column-then-row MLP split bandwidth-thrifty?
options: It avoids all communication in the backward pass, since gradients are computed fully locally per shard
It compresses the weight shards to int8 before sending them, cutting each transfer by four
It communicates only the gradients of the nonlinearity, which are tiny compared with activations
The 4C-wide hidden activations are never sent; only the C-wide output is all-reduced once a pass
questions.explanation: Each device keeps its own hidden slice through the nonlinearity, so the wide intermediate never crosses the network. Only the narrower final output is all-reduced, once in forward and once in backward.

questions.question: A two-device tensor-parallel MLP gives device partial outputs [5, 2] and [5, 9], and the single-device output is [10, 11]. What does this demonstrate?
options: Tensor parallelism introduces a small approximation error that is tolerable in practice for training
Summing the row-parallel partials with an all-reduce exactly reconstructs the single-device output
The partials must be concatenated, not summed, to recover the true single-device output
Each device already computed the full output; the two copies differ only by rounding noise
questions.explanation: The element-wise sum [5+5, 2+9] = [10, 11] matches ReLU(XA)B computed on one device. Tensor parallelism is exact: each device held only half of A and half of B and computed on a hidden slice half as wide.

questions.question: In a two-device tensor-parallel MLP with C = 2 (hidden width 4), what does each device hold and compute?
options: Half of A's columns and half of B's rows, computing on a hidden slice of width 2
All of A and half of B's rows, computing on the full hidden width 4 before splitting
Half of A's rows and half of B's columns, computing on half of the input features
All of A and all of B, computing the full MLP on half of the tokens in the batch
questions.explanation: Device 0 takes columns 1 to 2 of A and rows 1 to 2 of B; device 1 takes columns 3 to 4 and rows 3 to 4. Each computes on a hidden slice of width 2 instead of 4. That is how a matmul too big for one device is split and reassembled with one all-reduce.

questions.question: In a tensor-parallel split of an MLP whose first matmul is A, which slices of A and B must a device hold together?
options: The columns of A and the rows of B that correspond to the same hidden units
Any columns of A and any rows of B, since the all-reduce fixes any mismatch
The rows of A and the columns of B that correspond to the same hidden units
All of A, plus only the rows of B that correspond to its assigned hidden units
questions.explanation: Device d's hidden slice is X A_d for some block of hidden units; its partial output multiplies that slice by the rows of B for the same hidden units. Mismatched slices would multiply the wrong hidden activations by the wrong weights.

questions.section: 2. Tensor parallelism: split the matmul (Megatron style)
questions.question: How is multi-head attention tensor-parallelized in Megatron style?
options: Each device computes all heads on a subset of the key dimensions and concatenates the scores
Each device gets a subset of tokens and all heads, exchanging keys and values with the other devices
Each device runs a subset of heads in full; the output projection is row-parallel, one all-reduce
Attention is replicated on every device and only the MLP block is split column-then-row
questions.explanation: Heads are independent, so splitting by heads is natural: each device computes its heads' QKV projections and attention locally. The output projection is split by rows, and one all-reduce sums the partials. That mirrors the MLP's column-then-row pattern.

questions.section: 2. Tensor parallelism: split the matmul (Megatron style)
questions.question: Why is tensor parallelism normally confined to GPUs within one node over NVLink?
options: Because it only supports up to two GPUs, and nodes typically hold exactly that many
Because NVLink hardware is required to execute a split matmul's partial products
It all-reduces in every layer's forward and backward, making it communication-heavy
Because it communicates only once per step, so cross-node latency would simply be wasted
questions.explanation: Tensor parallelism needs an all-reduce in every layer's forward and backward pass. That traffic is affordable only on the fastest links, typically NVLink within a node. Pipeline and data parallelism, which communicate less often, are used across nodes.

questions.section: 3. Pipeline parallelism: split the layer stack
questions.question: With 4 pipeline stages and 32 layers split evenly, which layers does stage 1 hold?
options: Layers 0 to 7
Layers 8 to 15
Layers 1, 5, 9, ...
Layers 16 to 23
questions.explanation: Pipeline parallelism gives each stage a contiguous range of layers. With 32 layers and 4 stages, stage 0 holds 0 to 7, stage 1 holds 8 to 15, and so on. Forward flows stage 0 to stage 3 and backward flows in reverse.

questions.section: 3. Pipeline parallelism: split the layer stack
questions.question: What memory problem does pipeline parallelism solve?
options: It shards activations along the sequence dimension, so long contexts fit on each device
Each device holds only its slice of the model's depth, so a far deeper model fits
It eliminates the optimizer state, since each stage updates its layers with plain SGD
It shrinks each weight matrix by splitting its columns across the pipeline stages
questions.explanation: By assigning different layers to different devices, each device needs only its layers' parameters and their computation. A model too deep for one device can thus be spread across several. Individual layers are still held whole, unlike tensor parallelism.

questions.question: In naive pipeline parallelism with one batch pushed through, what is the 'pipeline bubble'?
options: Extra memory held by in-flight activations waiting for their backward pass
Idle time while stages wait on others, e.g. stages 1-3 idle while stage 0 computes
A numerical error introduced when activations are cast to pass between devices
The time every stage spends waiting on the optimizer step at the end of each full batch
questions.explanation: When one batch flows through, each stage is busy only while that batch is on it, so most devices are idle most of the time. That wasted time is the bubble. It is the fill and drain time at the ends of the pipe.

questions.question: How does pipeline parallelism reduce the bubble?
options: Add more pipeline stages, so each stage's share of the compute and of the idle time shrinks
Split the batch into m micro-batches fed in a staggered stream so all stages stay busy
Run the optimizer step during the forward pass so that idle stages update their layers
All-reduce the activations between stages so every stage can start at the same time
questions.explanation: Once stage 0 passes micro-batch 1 on, it starts micro-batch 2, and so on, like an assembly line. After a short fill, all stages are busy. Only fill and drain at the ends remain as bubble, which more micro-batches amortize.

questions.question: What is the pipeline bubble fraction for S stages and m micro-batches?
questions.explanation: Filling the pipe takes S-1 slots before the last stage starts, and draining takes another S-1, spread over a schedule of m + S - 1 slots. The bubble fraction is (S-1)/(m+S-1). Increasing m amortizes the fixed fill/drain over more useful work.

questions.question: Why does increasing the number of micro-batches m shrink the pipeline bubble fraction?
options: The S-1 fill/drain overhead is fixed, so more micro-batches spread it over more work
Smaller micro-batches compute proportionally faster than full batches on each stage
With enough micro-batches the pipe never has to drain, so the overhead disappears
Each micro-batch is assigned its own stage, so more of them occupy more stages at once
questions.explanation: The fill and drain overhead depends on the number of stages, not on m. Adding micro-batches adds useful slots in the denominator m + S - 1 while the numerator S-1 stays fixed.

questions.question: With 4 pipeline stages and only 1 micro-batch, what fraction of the hardware time is wasted in the bubble?
questions.explanation: Bubble = (S-1)/(m+S-1) = 3/4 = 0.75 with m = 1. With 8 micro-batches it falls to about 27%, and with 32 to under 9%.

questions.question: Why do more sophisticated pipeline schedules such as GPipe and the interleaved 1F1B of Megatron/DeepSpeed exist?
options: To remove the need for a separate backward pass by fusing it into forward
To avoid micro-batches entirely by pipelining individual layers instead
To shrink the bubble and the activation memory further
To allow tensor parallelism to run efficiently across slow inter-node links
questions.explanation: Plain staggered micro-batching still leaves a bubble and keeps many micro-batches' activations alive. Schedules like GPipe and interleaved one-forward-one-backward (1F1B) reorder work to reduce idle time and how much activation memory is held at once.

questions.question: What rule of thumb relates micro-batches m to pipeline stages S?
options: Use m much larger than S, for example m at least 4S
Use m equal to S, so each stage holds exactly one micro-batch
Use m less than S, so that activation memory stays small
Use m = S - 1, which exactly cancels the fill/drain overhead
questions.explanation: Because the bubble is (S-1)/(m+S-1), m near S wastes a large fraction of the hardware. Using m much larger than S, such as m at least 4S, keeps the bubble small.

questions.question: Why does using many pipeline micro-batches increase activation memory?
options: Each in-flight micro-batch keeps its activations alive until its backward pass
Each micro-batch stores its own full copy of the stage's parameters and gradients
Micro-batch activations are kept in fp64 to avoid error accumulating across stages
Each micro-batch's activations are replicated on every stage of the pipeline
questions.explanation: A micro-batch's forward activations must be retained until its backward pass uses them. The more micro-batches are in flight at once, the more activation memory is held. Schedules like GPipe and 1F1B largely differ in how they manage this.

questions.question: Why does load-balancing layers across pipeline stages matter?
options: Unbalanced stages increase the number of gradient all-reduces each step needs
Unbalanced stages produce wrong gradients, because the slow stage lags a step behind
A stage stalls if its input isn't ready, so an uneven split idles fast stages on slow ones
Load balancing lets each stage drop redundant layers, reducing the model's total parameter count
questions.explanation: A pipeline runs at the pace of its slowest stage. If one stage has more compute, the others wait for it. Assigning layers so each stage has equal compute keeps all stages busy.

questions.section: 4. Sequence / context parallelism and expert parallelism
questions.question: What does sequence (context) parallelism split, and what does it target?
options: The batch dimension B; it targets optimizer state, which grows with the global batch size
The sequence length T; it targets memory growing with T, like attention scores and LayerNorm
The hidden width C; it targets the weight matrices, which are too wide for a single device
The experts; it targets MoE routing tables, which grow with the number of tokens per batch
questions.explanation: Sequence parallelism gives each device a slice of the token positions. It shards the activations that grow with sequence length, which tensor parallelism leaves whole. This is what makes very long context lengths trainable.

questions.section: 4. Sequence / context parallelism and expert parallelism
questions.question: Why does sequence parallelism require communication inside attention?
options: Because experts are placed on different devices and every token must visit all of them
Because LayerNorm needs a global mean over the batch, which spans every device's tokens
Because the optimizer state is split by sequence and must be gathered for each step
Each position's query must still see all keys, which may live on other devices
questions.explanation: Attention mixes information across positions: every query attends over all keys. If token positions are split across devices, each device needs keys and values from the others, so communication across the sequence dimension is required. Sequence parallelism composes with tensor parallelism.

questions.section: 4. Sequence / context parallelism and expert parallelism
questions.question: In an MoE layer, what does the router do?
options: Sends each token to every expert and averages their outputs by learned weights
Sends each token to only one or a few of many expert MLPs
Chooses which GPU runs each token's attention computation for the current layer
Selects which Transformer layers each token skips to save compute at inference
questions.explanation: An MoE layer replaces one MLP with many expert MLPs plus a router. The router picks one or a few experts per token, so each token uses only a small part of the layer's parameters.

questions.section: 4. Sequence / context parallelism and expert parallelism
questions.question: Which collective does expert parallelism use to move tokens to their experts and back?
options: All-gather
All-reduce
All-to-all
Broadcast
questions.explanation: In expert parallelism, every device may have tokens for experts on every other device. An all-to-all lets each device send each of its tokens to the device holding its chosen expert and receive the results back.

questions.section: 4. Sequence / context parallelism and expert parallelism
questions.question: Why can an MoE have a huge total parameter count while each device stores and computes only a small part?
options: MoE parameters are stored in int4, so even a huge expert count fits on each device
Each token uses only a couple of experts, and experts are distributed across devices
Experts share all their weights and differ only in a small per-expert bias vector
Only the router has trainable parameters; the experts are frozen random projections
questions.explanation: Total parameters scale with the number of experts, but each token's forward pass touches only the few experts it was routed to. With experts spread across devices, per-device storage and per-token compute stay small.

questions.question: What is the universal performance trick for every parallelism axis' communication?
options: Route all communication through a single designated GPU per node
Compress every communicated tensor to fp8 before it leaves the device
Run all communication only at the end of the step, after backward finishes
Overlap communication with computation so the network cost hides under compute
questions.explanation: Every axis adds communication. Starting the next matmul or all-gather while the current collective is still in flight hides network time under compute, as with DDP and FSDP. A well-tuned run is bottlenecked by arithmetic, not idle waiting.

questions.question: In a typical 3D-parallel layout, how are the axes mapped to the hardware topology?
options: Tensor within a node, pipeline across a few nodes, data parallelism/ZeRO across the rest
Data parallelism within a node, tensor parallelism across nodes, pipeline across racks
Pipeline within a node, tensor parallelism across all nodes, data parallelism per GPU
All axes on the slowest inter-node links, to leave NVLink bandwidth free for compute
questions.explanation: Tensor parallelism's per-layer all-reduces go on the fastest links (NVLink within a node). Pipeline parallelism sends only activations, so it can cross slower links between a few nodes. Data parallelism or ZeRO, with one gradient all-reduce per step, spans the remaining groups.

questions.question: Which framework is the reference implementation of tensor and sequence parallelism?
options: PyTorch FSDP (Meta AI)
DeepSpeed (Microsoft)
Megatron-LM (NVIDIA)
vLLM (UC Berkeley)
questions.explanation: Megatron-LM implements the column-then-row tensor split, sequence parallelism, and interleaved pipeline schedules. Reach for it when you need to split the model's math across devices.

questions.question: Which framework is home to ZeRO and offers memory features such as ZeRO-Offload?
options: PyTorch FSDP (Meta AI)
Megatron-LM (NVIDIA)
DeepSpeed (Microsoft)
NVIDIA NCCL library
questions.explanation: DeepSpeed provides the ZeRO stages and pipeline parallelism, along with optimizer and memory features like ZeRO-Offload. It is the choice for memory-efficient data parallelism with easy ZeRO stages.

questions.question: What does PyTorch FSDP primarily provide among large-scale training frameworks?
options: Native ZeRO-3-style fully sharded data parallelism with little code, gaining TP support
The reference implementation of sequence and tensor parallelism for Transformer blocks
Pipeline schedules such as interleaved 1F1B, with automatic layer-to-stage balancing
All-to-all expert routing and load-balancing losses for Mixture-of-Experts training
questions.explanation: FSDP is PyTorch's native way to shard a model's parameters, gradients, and optimizer state across data-parallel workers. It increasingly supports tensor parallelism too.

questions.question: In practice, what does an ML engineer usually do with large-scale parallelism frameworks?
options: Avoid parallelism frameworks and scale everything with plain DDP and larger batches
Re-implement the NCCL collectives for each project to match the cluster's topology
Write a custom pipeline schedule and tensor split by hand for every new model
Configure the axes and reason about their memory and communication cost
questions.explanation: Correct production versions of topology-aware collectives, overlapped communication, interleaved pipelines, and all-to-all routing are large systems efforts, which is why Megatron, DeepSpeed, and FSDP exist. Building toy versions makes config options like tensor_parallel_size, pipeline_parallel_size, zero_stage, and num_micro_batches understandable.

questions.question: Which paper introduced the column-then-row tensor-parallel split for the MLP and multi-head attention?
options: Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism (Shoeybi et al., 2019)
ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models (Rajbhandari et al., 2019)
GPipe: Efficient Training of Giant Neural Networks using Pipeline Parallelism (Huang et al., 2019)
Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity (Fedus et al., 2021)
questions.explanation: Megatron-LM (Shoeybi et al., 2019) introduced the column-then-row tensor-parallel split and showed it scaling to billions of parameters. With ZeRO it is one of the two foundational large-model systems papers.

questions.question: With 32 GPUs, tensor parallelism degree 4, and 4 pipeline stages, how many data-parallel replicas can you run?
questions.explanation: One replica uses tensor size times pipeline size = 4 * 4 = 16 GPUs. 32 / 16 = 2 data-parallel replicas, giving the 3D layout tensor(4) * pipeline(4) * data(2) = 32.

questions.question: In a 3D-parallel layout of tensor(4) x pipeline(4) x data(2), what communication happens each step?
options: Only one all-reduce of gradients across all 32 GPUs, as in plain data parallelism
The 2 replicas all-reduce grads; inside each, TP all-reduces per layer, PP passes activations
Only activations are passed between stages; no all-reduce of any kind occurs during the step
Each GPU broadcasts its weight shard to all 31 others before every forward and backward pass
questions.explanation: Data parallelism across the two replicas needs a gradient all-reduce. Inside a replica, tensor parallelism all-reduces partial outputs on every layer, and pipeline parallelism sends activations forward and gradients backward between stages.

questions.question: With 4 pipeline stages, what is the minimum number of micro-batches to keep the bubble below 10%?
questions.explanation: 3/(m+3) < 0.10 requires m + 3 > 30, so m > 27 and the minimum integer is 28. At m = 28 the bubble is 3/31, about 9.7%.

questions.question: What is the key difference between tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism?
options: Tensor splits across layers and passes activations; pipeline splits within a layer
Tensor splits within a layer, all-reducing per layer; pipeline splits layers, passing activations
Tensor splits the data batch across devices; pipeline splits the optimizer state across stages
They are two names for the same technique, differing only in which framework implements it
questions.explanation: Tensor parallelism divides a matmul's width across devices and needs per-layer all-reduces. Pipeline parallelism assigns layer ranges to devices and sends activations between them. They solve different fit problems and are usually combined.

questions.question: What happens if tensor parallelism is run across slow inter-node links?
options: It automatically falls back to pipeline parallelism across the slow links
It becomes more accurate, because the slower all-reduce uses higher precision
Its per-layer all-reduces dominate and throughput collapses
Nothing much; tensor parallelism communicates only once per optimizer step
questions.explanation: Tensor parallelism all-reduces on every layer's forward and backward. On slow links that traffic cannot hide under compute, so throughput collapses. Keep it on the fastest interconnect, within a node.

questions.question: What is wrong with running a pipeline with a number of micro-batches close to the number of stages?
options: The stages deadlock waiting on each other's backward passes
The gradients become incorrect because micro-batches overlap
The model no longer fits in memory once the stages fill up
The bubble wastes a large fraction of the hardware
questions.explanation: With m near S, (S-1)/(m+S-1) is large: for example S = 8, m = 8 gives about 47% wasted. Use m much larger than S.

questions.question: A pipeline has 8 stages. What bubble fractions do 8 and 64 micro-batches give?
options: About 88% and about 50%
About 12% and about 1%
About 47% and about 10%
About 47% and about 1%
questions.explanation: (S-1)/(m+S-1) with S = 8: m = 8 gives 7/15, about 0.467; m = 64 gives 7/71, about 0.099. More micro-batches amortize the fixed 7-slot fill and drain.

questions.question: In the Megatron MLP split, why is the first matmul column-parallel and the second row-parallel, rather than the reverse?
options: Column-first keeps the element-wise nonlinearity local; row-second gives partials one all-reduce sums
Because row-parallel matmuls run faster on GPUs, so the larger 4C-wide matmul should use them
Because the reverse order would need each device to hold twice as much weight memory overall
Because the reverse order changes the model's output, since ReLU does not commute with the split
questions.explanation: If the first matmul were row-split, each device would get a partial pre-activation that must be summed before the nonlinearity, forcing a communication of the wide hidden layer. Column-then-row avoids that, needing only one all-reduce of the C-wide output.

questions.question: What hardware does real tensor parallelism typically need, and what degree is common?
options: CPU clusters with many cores; degree equal to the number of cores per socket
GPUs across many nodes over standard Ethernet; a degree of 64 or more is typical
A single GPU with tensor cores, which split each matmul internally across units
GPUs on the fastest link (NVLink within a node); degree 2 to 8 is typical
questions.explanation: Because it all-reduces on every layer's forward and backward, tensor parallelism needs the fastest interconnect, typically NVLink within one node. Degrees of 2 to 8 within a node are typical.

questions.question: Why can pipeline parallelism span nodes over slower links?
options: It compresses activations to 1 bit before sending them across the node boundary
It does not communicate at all, since each stage owns its layers and its own data
Only activations cross stage boundaries, lighter than TP's per-layer all-reduces
It replicates every stage on every node, so traffic stays within each node's NVLink
questions.explanation: Pipeline stages exchange only the activations (and their gradients) at stage boundaries, which is much less frequent than per-layer all-reduces. That makes pipeline parallelism tolerant of slower inter-node links, though it still needs many micro-batches.

questions.question: Does model parallelism reduce the total compute needed to train a model?
options: No; it roughly doubles total compute, because every layer is recomputed across devices
Yes; splitting the matmuls halves the FLOPs per token compared with a single device
Yes; it divides the total compute by the number of GPUs used in the parallel layout
No; it makes a too-big model trainable and spreads the work, but total compute stays ~6ND
questions.explanation: Training compute is about 6 times parameters times tokens regardless of how the work is split. Model parallelism spreads that compute and memory across devices so the model can be trained at all; it does not reduce the total.

questions.question: After data parallelism, ZeRO/FSDP and tensor/pipeline/expert parallelism, what question do scaling laws address?
options: How to overlap each axis's communication with computation on a given cluster
How to split the matmuls across GPUs so that each one fits in device memory
How big to make the model and how much data to use for a given compute budget
How to route tokens to experts so the load stays balanced across devices
questions.explanation: Parallelism is about how to train a given model fast. Scaling laws step back to ask how to choose model size and token count so that a compute budget yields the best model.

questions.question: Before launching a training run, which three back-of-the-envelope numbers can be computed from a GPT model config plus a token budget?
options: The number of GPUs needed, the achieved MFU, and the final validation perplexity
The final loss, the peak learning rate, and the critical batch size for the run
The tokenizer vocabulary, the context length, and the dropout rate to train with
The parameter count N, the training compute C ≈ 6ND, and the memory footprint
questions.explanation: From a config alone you can compute a closed-form parameter count N, the training compute C ≈ 6ND for D tokens, and the memory footprint (params + grads + optimizer state + activations). Loss and perplexity are outcomes of training that must be measured or predicted with scaling laws, not read off the config.

questions.question: Why does estimating N, D, C, wall-clock and memory before a run matter so much in practice?
options: Because the optimizer's learning rate is computed directly from the run's total FLOP count
Because these estimates determine the final loss exactly, removing the need to train at all
Because PyTorch refuses to launch a training run unless these numbers are declared up front
Mistakes show up as OOM at step 0, or as learning weeks in that the run takes far too long
questions.explanation: Every real run starts as a spreadsheet: a lab estimates size, data, compute, time and memory before spending GPU money. Getting them wrong means either an out-of-memory failure immediately or learning mid-run that it will take far longer than budgeted. The estimates do not determine loss or hyperparameters automatically.

questions.question: How do FLOP and parameter counting relate to scaling laws such as Kaplan and Chinchilla?
options: Counting formulas measure the final loss, while scaling laws measure memory per GPU
Scaling laws replace the need to count parameters or FLOPs, since they fit the loss directly
Scaling laws say how to choose N and D; the counting formulas are the arithmetic they use
They are unrelated: scaling laws only concern the shape of the learning-rate schedule
questions.explanation: Scaling laws are the theory of how to split a budget between model size N and data D, and they are expressed in terms of N, D and C = 6ND. Without the counting arithmetic you cannot even state the allocation problem.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: three numbers from a config
questions.question: In planning a training run, what does the parameter count N primarily determine?
options: Model quality (capacity) and memory
Only the number of training tokens
Only the wall-clock time, independent of tokens
The tokenizer's vocabulary size
questions.explanation: N sets how much capacity the model has, which drives quality, and it directly determines parameter, gradient and optimizer memory. Wall-clock depends on C = 6ND, which also involves the token count D.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: three numbers from a config
questions.question: In the compute estimate C ≈ 6ND, what does the estimate set for a training run?
options: Whether the model fits in GPU memory, once divided by the bytes per parameter
The irreducible loss of the data, once divided by the number of training tokens
The wall-clock time and dollar cost, once divided by an achieved throughput
The vocabulary size of the tokenizer, once divided by the embedding width C
questions.explanation: C ≈ 6ND is the total arithmetic of training; dividing by an achieved FLOP/s rate turns it into time, which turns into dollars. Whether the model fits is a memory question governed by the 16P floor plus activations.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: three numbers from a config
questions.question: Which of the following determines whether a model fits on a GPU at all?
options: Memory: params + gradients + optimizer state + activations
The achieved FLOP/s rate the GPU sustains during the run
The total training compute 6ND alone, divided by the batch
The number of training tokens D alone, divided by the context
questions.explanation: Fitting is a memory question: the model's parameters, their gradients, the optimizer's state, and saved activations must all fit. Compute and token count determine how long the run takes, not whether a step can execute.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: three numbers from a config
questions.question: How does the treatment of the 6N rule and the memory buckets differ between a running-loop view and a planning view?
options: In planning, the 6N rule is replaced by a cheaper 2N rule, since no backward pass has been run yet
In planning, memory is ignored entirely and only the compute budget 6ND is estimated up front
In planning, all three come from just a config and a token budget, before anything is allocated
In planning, the numbers are measured by profiling a short real run first and then extrapolated
questions.explanation: Earlier the 6N rule and four memory buckets were seen inside one running loop; the planning view lifts them so that from a config and token budget alone you compute N, C and memory to within a few percent by hand, with no tensors allocated.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: three numbers from a config
questions.question: In the formulas N ≈ VC + 12·n_layer·C² and C ≈ 6ND, what is the source of potential confusion with the letter C?
options: C is the context length in the parameter formula and the number of GPUs in the compute formula
C means the same thing in both formulas: the number of channels in each transformer block
C is the embedding width (n_embd) in the parameter formula but total FLOPs in the compute one
C is the cost in dollars in the compute formula and the cache size in the parameter formula
questions.explanation: By convention model-shape code uses C for channels per token (e.g. 768), while scaling-law papers use C for total compute in FLOPs (e.g. 8.67×10^17). Magnitude disambiguates: widths are hundreds to thousands, compute budgets are 10^17 and up.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: three numbers from a config
questions.question: You see the value C = 1024 in a scaling discussion. Which interpretation is most plausible, and why?
options: An embedding width, because compute budgets are 10^17 FLOPs and up
A context length, because C stands for context
A number of GPUs, because C stands for cluster size
A training compute budget in FLOPs, because C always denotes compute
questions.explanation: Width values are a few hundred to a few thousand, whereas realistic training compute budgets are around 10^17 FLOPs or more. A value like 1024 is therefore an embedding width (n_embd), not a compute budget.

questions.question: In a GPT, how many parameters does the token embedding table wte contain, for vocabulary size V and width C?
options: 4·V·C — four projections (Q, K, V, O) per vocabulary token
C² — one C×C matrix shared by every vocabulary entry
V·C — one C-vector per vocabulary entry
T_max·C — one C-vector for each position in the context
questions.explanation: The token embedding is a V×C lookup table with one C-dimensional vector per vocabulary entry, so it holds V·C parameters. T_max·C is the positional embedding.

questions.question: How many parameters does the learned positional embedding wpe have in a GPT with maximum context T_max and width C?
options: T_max·C
T_max²·C
12·C²
V·T_max
questions.explanation: wpe is a T_max×C table with one C-vector per position, giving T_max·C parameters. V·T_max mixes the vocabulary size with the context length and matches no table in the model; T_max²·C would scale like an attention-mask-sized object, not a per-position parameter table.

questions.question: Ignoring biases, how many weights do the attention projections of one transformer block hold, for width C?
options: 8C² — two C→4C matrices, one for keys and one for values
4C² — W_Q, W_K, W_V and the output W_O, each C×C
C² — a single C×C projection shared by Q, K and V together
3C² — only W_Q, W_K and W_V; the output projection is free
questions.explanation: Attention has four C×C matrices: query, key, value, and the output projection W_O, giving 4C². Forgetting W_O gives the tempting but wrong 3C²; 8C² is the MLP.

questions.question: Ignoring biases, how many weights does the MLP of one GPT block hold, for width C?
options: 16C² — a C→4C Linear counted four times
4C² — two C×C Linears with a GELU between
2C² — one C→2C Linear followed by a gate
8C² — a C→4C Linear plus a 4C→C Linear
questions.explanation: The MLP expands to 4C and projects back: C×4C plus 4C×C, i.e. 4C² + 4C² = 8C². This is twice the attention projections' 4C².

questions.question: Why are the biases (~9C per block) and LayerNorm parameters (4C per block) dropped from the closed-form parameter count?
options: They are not trainable, so they are not parameters
They are shared across all layers, so they count only once
They are recomputed every forward pass rather than stored
They grow linearly in C and are tiny next to the 12C² terms
questions.explanation: Biases and LayerNorm gains/biases are trainable parameters, but they scale as C while the matrices scale as C². For realistic widths the linear terms are a negligible fraction (about 0.1% in GPT-2 small).

questions.question: With a tied output head, how many new parameters does lm_head add to a GPT?
options: V·C — one full vocabulary projection, separate from wte
C² — a square projection applied right before the softmax
Zero — it reuses the same tensor as the token embedding wte
T_max·C — one output projection for each position in the context
questions.explanation: Weight tying makes lm_head the same tensor as wte, so it contributes no additional parameters. An untied head would add another V·C.

questions.question: What is the closed-form approximate total parameter count of a GPT with vocab V, width C, max context T_max and L layers?
options: N ≈ V·C + T_max·C + 12·L·C²
N ≈ 12·L·C² + 4·V·C + T_max
N ≈ V·C + T_max·C + 12·L·C
N ≈ 6·L·C² + V·T_max + V·C
questions.explanation: Summing the dominant terms gives token embedding V·C, positional embedding T_max·C, and 12C² per block over L blocks. The tied head adds nothing, and linear-in-C terms are dropped.

questions.question: Why does the scaling literature call 12·L·C² the non-embedding parameter count and use it as N?
options: Because the embedding table is stored on the CPU, not on the GPU
Because those weights do the matmul work, while embeddings are lookups
Because 12·L·C² is always larger than the total parameter count
Because the embedding parameters are frozen and never updated in training
questions.explanation: The block weights participate in matrix multiplies on every token, so they dominate FLOPs. Embedding tables are indexed lookups with negligible arithmetic, so scaling-law N excludes them. In the course code this is non_embedding_params(cfg) in llmre.training.metrics.

questions.question: Per transformer layer, how do the closed-form weights split between attention and MLP?
options: Attention 8C², MLP 4C², total 12C²
Attention 3C², MLP 9C², total 12C²
Attention 6C², MLP 6C², total 12C²
Attention 4C², MLP 8C², total 12C²
questions.explanation: Four C×C attention projections give 4C²; the MLP's C→4C and 4C→C Linears give 8C². So the MLP holds two thirds of each block's weights.

questions.question: For GPT-2 small (V=50257, C=768, T_max=1024, L=12), how close is the closed-form estimate V·C + T_max·C + 12·L·C² to the exact count of 124,439,808?
options: Exactly equal, because the closed form includes every single bias and LayerNorm term
Within about 0.1%; the missing ~121k parameters are biases and LayerNorm gains
Off by about 38.6M, because the tied output head is not counted in the formula
Off by about 30%, because the closed form leaves out the MLP weights entirely
questions.explanation: The closed form gives about 124.3M versus 124.4M exact, within 0.1%. The difference is precisely the dropped linear-in-C terms (biases, LayerNorms). Two integers and a multiply predict size to three significant figures.

questions.question: In GPT-2 small, roughly what fraction of the ~124M total parameters are in the token embedding table?
options: About 90% (≈112M of ≈124M)
About 68% (≈85M of ≈124M)
About 1% (≈1M of ≈124M)
questions.explanation: V·C = 50257·768 ≈ 38.6M, about a third of the 124M total. The non-embedding 12LC² ≈ 85M is the other big piece, and wpe is only ~0.8M. This is why total and non-embedding N differ substantially for small models.

questions.question: How does the closed-form non-embedding count 12·L·C² for GPT-2 small compare with its true non-embedding count?
options: 84.9M vs 124.4M — the closed form misses the MLP
They differ by a factor of 12 because L is counted twice
84.9M vs 38.6M — the closed form double-counts attention
84.9M vs 85.06M — within about 0.15%
questions.explanation: 12·12·768² = 84,934,656 compares with the true 85,056,000, within 0.15%; the difference again is biases and LayerNorm parameters inside the blocks.

questions.section: Callout: exact count from the model
questions.question: In PyTorch, why does sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) count a tied wte/lm_head tensor only once?
options: model.parameters() de-duplicates shared tensors, yielding each Parameter once
Tied tensors are registered as buffers rather than parameters, so they are skipped
PyTorch stores the tied head in half precision, which halves its reported count
numel() returns zero for any tensor that is a view of another module's tensor
questions.explanation: parameters() yields each unique Parameter object once, so a tensor registered under two module attributes is counted a single time. That is why weight tying saves V·C ≈ 38.6M parameters in GPT-2 small versus an untied head.

questions.section: Callout: exact count from the model
questions.question: When should you use the closed-form parameter formula versus model.num_params()?
options: Closed form after training; num_params() only before the model has been built
Closed form to plan before the model exists; num_params() for exact truth once built
Always the closed form, because num_params() double-counts the tied wte/lm_head weights
Always num_params(), because the closed form is typically off by tens of percent
questions.explanation: The closed form needs only config integers and is accurate to ~0.1%, ideal for planning. Once the model is instantiated, num_params() gives the exact count including small terms, with tied weights counted once.

questions.question: Why does one forward+backward pass cost about 6N FLOPs per token?
options: 6 layers of computation per token, each costing N FLOPs over the weights
3N forward and 3N backward, since the backward pass mirrors the forward
2N forward (2 FLOPs per weight) plus 4N backward (two matmuls per weight)
N forward, N backward, and 4N more for AdamW's optimizer step on each weight
questions.explanation: Forward does one multiply-add per weight per token, counted as 2 FLOPs, so 2N. Backward needs two matmuls per weight — gradient with respect to the input and with respect to the weight — so about 4N. Total 6N.

questions.question: Why is the backward pass about twice the cost of the forward pass in the 6N rule?
options: It must also update the optimizer's two moment buffers m and v for every weight
It computes gradients w.r.t. both the layer's input and its weight: two matmuls
It runs in fp32 while the forward pass runs in bf16, halving tensor-core throughput
It must redo the whole forward pass from scratch before computing any gradient
questions.explanation: Each weight matrix participates in two backward matmuls: one propagates the gradient to the input (for earlier layers), the other produces the weight gradient. Each is about as costly as the forward matmul, giving 4N versus 2N.

questions.question: What does the total-training-compute formula C ≈ 6ND compute, given N parameters and D training tokens?
options: The number of optimizer steps, given N parameters and D tokens per step
The memory needed in bytes to hold D tokens' activations for N parameters
The total FLOPs of training: 6N per token times D tokens processed
The FLOP/s rate the GPU must sustain to process D tokens in one second
questions.explanation: 6N FLOPs per token for forward plus backward, multiplied by the D tokens the run processes, gives total training work in FLOPs. It is a count of work, not a rate.

questions.question: In C ≈ 6ND as used in scaling laws, which N is used?
options: The number of attention heads times width
The total parameter count including embeddings
The number of layers
The non-embedding parameter count
questions.explanation: The scaling convention uses non-embedding N, because embedding lookups contribute negligible FLOPs; it is the block matmuls that perform the 6N work per token.

questions.question: Which FLOPs does the 6ND estimate deliberately omit, and when is that safe?
options: The backward pass FLOPs, which are small for short contexts
The MLP FLOPs, which are small while the vocabulary is large
The optimizer FLOPs, which dominate only for models under 1M parameters
The attention-score FLOPs (~6·L·T per token), which are small while T ≪ 12C
questions.explanation: 6ND counts weight matmuls only. The QK^T and attention-times-V work grows with context length T and is small relative to the weight matmuls while T is much less than 12C. At very long contexts the attention term must be added back.

questions.question: What does training_flops(N, D) in llmre.evaluation.scaling return?
options: 6.0 * N * D divided by the GPU's peak FLOP/s
16 * N bytes plus activations
questions.explanation: The function is literally return 6.0 * N * D: total training FLOPs. 2ND would be forward-only (inference) work, and dividing by FLOP/s would give time, not compute.

questions.question: Why is C ≈ 6ND described as a measure of work rather than speed?
options: It is measured in FLOP/s, so it already includes the speed of the hardware
It is a FLOP count; time requires dividing by an achieved FLOP/s rate
It depends on the GPU type, so it really measures how fast the hardware is
It changes with the run's MFU, so it encodes how efficient the pipeline is
questions.explanation: 6ND counts operations and is hardware-independent. Converting it to wall-clock requires an achieved FLOP/s rate, which depends on hardware and on how efficiently the pipeline runs (MFU).

questions.question: Training N = 85M non-embedding parameters on D = 1.7B tokens is described as Chinchilla-ish. Why?
options: It uses 1.7 tokens per parameter like GPT-3
It uses exactly 6 tokens per parameter, matching 6ND
It is about 20 tokens per parameter
It uses one token per parameter
questions.explanation: 1.7×10^9 / 8.5×10^7 = 20 tokens per parameter, the Chinchilla compute-optimal ratio justified later in the module.

questions.question: When converting training FLOPs to GPU-hours on an A100, which number is publicly documented and which is an assumption?
options: The 32% MFU is published by NVIDIA for every model; the 312 TFLOP/s peak is an assumption
The ~312 TFLOP/s bf16 dense peak is a spec-sheet figure; the MFU (e.g. 32%) is assumed
Both the peak and the MFU are measured constants that hold for every model and pipeline
Neither is known in advance; it is the FLOP count itself that is the modelling assumption
questions.explanation: NVIDIA advertises ~312 TFLOP/s (3.12×10^14) bf16 dense peak. The fraction actually achieved (MFU) depends on model size, context length and pipeline tuning, so a figure like 32% is a stated assumption, not a vendor or measured number.

questions.question: How do you convert a training compute C in FLOPs into wall-clock time?
options: t = 6ND / batch size, then divide by 3600 for hours
t = C / (6 × peak FLOP/s), then divide by 3600 for hours
t = C / achieved FLOP/s, then divide by 3600 for hours
t = C × peak FLOP/s, then divide by 3600 for hours
questions.explanation: Time is work divided by rate: t = C / achieved FLOP/s, in seconds. The achieved rate (peak × MFU), not the peak, should be used; dividing by 6 again would double-count the 6 already in C.

questions.question: The same 8.67×10^17-FLOP run takes ~2.4 GPU-hours at 1.0×10^14 FLOP/s but ~12 at 2×10^13 FLOP/s. What lesson does this illustrate?
options: GPU-hours are independent of MFU, so the gap must come from a miscount of FLOPs
The FLOP count is objective; the time depends on an achieved-throughput assumption
The 6ND rule is wrong by a factor of five for poorly tuned input pipelines
Poorly tuned pipelines perform fewer FLOPs in total, so they should finish faster
questions.explanation: The arithmetic is identical in both cases; only the achieved FLOP/s differs (32% vs 6.4% MFU), giving a 5× difference in time. Always state the throughput assumption, because time is not determined by the FLOP count alone.

questions.section: 4. Memory: the four buckets, in one number
questions.question: In fp32, how many bytes per parameter do parameters, gradients and AdamW state require in total?
options: 16 bytes: 4 params + 4 grads + 8 for Adam's m and v
12 bytes: 4 weights + 4 gradients + 4 for one Adam buffer
4 bytes: just the weights; grads and state are transient
8 bytes: 4 weights + 4 gradients, with Adam state on CPU
questions.explanation: Each fp32 value is 4 bytes. Weights 4, gradients 4, and AdamW's two moment buffers m and v 4 each (8 total), summing to 16 bytes per parameter before any activations.

questions.section: 4. Memory: the four buckets, in one number
questions.question: Why does AdamW's optimizer state cost 8P bytes in fp32?
options: It keeps a full copy of the gradient history over the last 8 steps, per parameter
It stores a master copy of the weights in fp64, which takes 8 bytes per parameter
Two buffers per parameter, first moment m and second moment v, at 4 bytes each
It keeps one buffer m per parameter that needs 8 bytes because its values are squared
questions.explanation: AdamW tracks a running mean of gradients (m) and of squared gradients (v), one value each per parameter. Two fp32 buffers equal 8 bytes per parameter, twice the weights themselves.

questions.section: 4. Memory: the four buckets, in one number
questions.question: What do activations scale with, as opposed to the other three memory buckets?
options: The optimizer choice, e.g. Adam versus SGD
Batch size × context length, not the parameter count P
Only the parameter count P, like the other three
The number of training tokens D seen so far in the run
questions.explanation: Activations are intermediate forward tensors saved for backward, so their size grows with how many tokens are in flight (batch × context). Params, grads and optimizer state are fixed by P and independent of batch size.

questions.section: 4. Memory: the four buckets, in one number
questions.question: Which memory bucket do gradient accumulation, activation checkpointing and mixed precision primarily attack?
options: Optimizer state, the largest fixed bucket under AdamW
Parameters, by deleting unused weights after each step
Gradients, by skipping part of the backward pass entirely
Activations, the bucket that scales with batch and context
questions.explanation: The 16P fixed floor does not change with batch size; activations do. Gradient accumulation shrinks the micro-batch, checkpointing recomputes instead of saving, and mixed precision halves bytes per activation. (Sharding attacks optimizer state.)

questions.question: For GPT-2 small at batch 8 and context 1024, why does the logits tensor alone matter for memory?
options: B·T·V ≈ 4.1×10^8 floats ≈ 1.65 GB in fp32, rivaling the ~2 GB fixed cost
It is tiny (a few MB), because logits are only computed for the final token
It replaces the need to store gradients, so it frees memory rather than using it
It is stored in int8 by default, so its footprint is negligible next to the weights
questions.explanation: Logits have shape (B, T, V) = 8×1024×50257 ≈ 4.12×10^8 values, about 1.65 GB in fp32 — nearly as large as the ~1.99 GB of params+grads+Adam. A single activation tensor can rival the entire fixed floor, which motivates mixed precision and checkpointing.

questions.question: What is the fp32 fixed memory floor (params + grads + Adam) for GPT-2 small with P ≈ 124.4M parameters?
options: About 124 MB
About 8 GB
About 0.5 GB
About 2 GB
questions.explanation: 16 bytes × 1.244×10^8 ≈ 1.99×10^9 bytes ≈ 2 GB, paid before any activation. 0.5 GB would be weights only (4P).

questions.section: 5. Under the hood: why the estimates are trustworthy
questions.question: Why is the 6ND compute estimate trustworthy for a standard transformer at moderate context?
options: Weight matmuls dominate; the dropped attention scores, softmax and LayerNorm are a few %
Because GPUs only execute matmuls and skip elementwise operations such as softmax entirely
Because 6ND is recalibrated by profiling every new model architecture before training
Because the attention-score FLOPs exactly cancel out the dropped embedding-lookup FLOPs
questions.explanation: The omitted operations are small relative to the dense weight matmuls in standard shapes. When that stops being true — very long context, tiny models, MoE routing — you switch to a fuller count.

questions.section: 5. Under the hood: why the estimates are trustworthy
questions.question: In which situations should you abandon the bare 6ND estimate for a fuller FLOP count?
options: Very long context, tiny models, or MoE routing
Whenever training uses AdamW instead of SGD
Any model larger than 1B parameters
Whenever the vocabulary exceeds 50k tokens
questions.explanation: 6ND assumes weight matmuls dominate. With very long context, attention-score FLOPs grow; in tiny models, non-matmul ops are a bigger share; in MoE, only some parameters are active per token. Those cases need a fuller accounting.

questions.section: 5. Under the hood: why the estimates are trustworthy
questions.question: Why can capacity planning predict parameter/optimizer memory to the byte but must profile activation memory?
options: Parameter memory varies with the batch size, while activations are fixed per model
Optimizer memory must be profiled, while activations are exact from the config alone
Activations are random from step to step, so they cannot be predicted in any way
The other buckets are exact (P × dtype size); activations depend on what is saved
questions.explanation: Params, grads and optimizer state are just P times known byte sizes. Activation memory depends on implementation choices about which intermediates are saved for backward, so it is measured with a short run.

questions.section: 5. Under the hood: why the estimates are trustworthy
questions.question: Why does the whole scaling-laws module rest on C = 6ND?
options: It gives the final loss of any model directly from its N and D
It removes the need for any experiments when planning a new run
It makes planning analytic: given C, how to split it between N and D
It sets the peak learning rate as a closed-form function of N
questions.explanation: Writing compute in terms of N and D turns 'bigger model or more data?' into a constrained optimisation. You cannot ask that question until C is expressed as a function of N and D, which is what Kaplan and Chinchilla then answer.

questions.question: In llmre, what does model_flops_per_token(cfg) return for GPT-2 small?
options: 6 × the non-embedding parameter count, ≈ 5.1×10^8
The total training FLOPs for the full 1.7B-token budget
The number of parameters each token touches, ≈ 8.5×10^7
2 × the total parameter count, ≈ 2.5×10^8 FLOPs per token
questions.explanation: model_flops_per_token returns 6·N_nonemb = 6 × 84,934,656 = 509,607,936 FLOPs per token, the forward+backward cost. Multiplying by D gives training_flops.

questions.question: Since training_flops is a one-line function, where does its value lie?
options: In calling it before launch, with the right non-embedding N and an honest D
In automatically detecting the achieved MFU of the GPU it is run on
In profiling the actual run and reporting the measured FLOPs per step
In its fused GPU kernel, which is faster than computing 6ND by hand
questions.explanation: The function is deliberately trivial; the discipline of estimating compute up front, with the correct N convention and a realistic token count, is what prevents nasty surprises.

questions.question: If both the non-embedding parameter count N and the token budget D grow 10×, how does training compute C = 6ND change?
options: It grows 20×
It grows about 3.2×
