questions.explanation: PII is data that identifies a real individual — for example names tied to addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, government IDs and credit-card numbers. Pipelines detect and redact or drop it.

questions.question: Why is PII in a pretraining corpus specifically a problem for a language model?
options: PII raises the symbol ratio of a document, so it breaks the quality filters downstream
A model can memorize and regurgitate training text verbatim, leaking PII and creating liability
PII tokens such as emails cannot be encoded by BPE, so they corrupt the packed stream
PII makes the training loss diverge, because each identifier is a unique and unpredictable token
questions.explanation: LMs can memorize training text and reproduce it verbatim at generation time. So PII in the corpus can leak private information to users, which is both a privacy harm and in many jurisdictions a legal liability.

questions.question: What do pipelines typically do with detected PII in pretraining data?
options: Detect and redact or drop it — replace emails/phones with placeholders, or drop dense documents
Encrypt it in place so the model learns only the encrypted versions of each identifier
Move it into a separate held-out evaluation set used to measure memorization later
Upsample it so the model learns to recognize PII and can refuse to repeat it when asked at inference
questions.explanation: The standard approaches are redaction (replacing detected emails, phone numbers, etc. with placeholders) or dropping documents that are dense with personal data. Both aim to prevent the model from memorizing and regurgitating it.

questions.question: Why does a data-engineering course deliberately NOT build a real PII detector (e.g. a toy email regex)?
options: Because PII is never present in Common Crawl, since sites with personal data block crawlers
Because building PII detection is legally prohibited without a licence in most of the jurisdictions
Because PII is already removed automatically by language identification and quality filters
A toy detector gives false safety; real PII detection is high-stakes, and half-working is worse
questions.explanation: A toy regex would catch some emails but miss many forms of PII, giving false confidence. Missing something like a Social Security number is a serious failure, so you should use a vetted tool in any real pipeline.

questions.question: What is the causal chain that makes PII in training data harmful?
options: Tokenization → packing → loss divergence
Duplication → contamination → benchmark inflation
Memorization → regurgitation → privacy/legal harm
Filtering → upsampling → overfitting
questions.explanation: The model memorizes training text, can regurgitate it verbatim, and that output leaks personal information, causing privacy and legal harm. That chain is why the PII stage exists.

questions.section: 8. Where this hands off to Module 4
questions.question: How does the output of the data-cleaning funnel (extraction, langid, quality, dedup, decontamination) relate to Module 4's packing pipeline?
options: It replaces Module 4's tokenizer, since clean text no longer needs BPE
It is exactly the 'pile of documents' Module 4 assumed as its input
It is fed directly to the model as raw bytes, skipping tokenization
It is used only for evaluation sets, while training uses the raw crawl
questions.explanation: Everything in the cleaning funnel runs before the tokenizer. Its output — clean, right-language, quality-passing, decontaminated text — is the document pile that Module 4 encodes with BPE, packs and samples with get_batch.

questions.section: 8. Where this hands off to Module 4
questions.question: In the full hand-off from raw crawl to model, which comes immediately after `quality_filter`?
options: Deduplication
BPE encoding
Language identification
get_batch
questions.explanation: The order is raw WARC → extract → langid → quality_filter → dedup → decontam → documents → BPE encode → pack_documents → get_batch → model. Dedup comes right after quality filtering.

questions.section: 8. Where this hands off to Module 4
questions.question: Why does every gate in the data funnel improve training at fixed compute?
options: It reduces the number of parameters the model needs to reach a given loss
It increases the learning rate the optimizer can use without diverging
It makes the packed token stream cleaner, and at fixed compute cleaner tokens buy lower loss
It eliminates the need for a held-out validation set during pretraining
questions.explanation: Only surviving documents are tokenized and packed. Each gate removes junk, so the compute you spend goes to better tokens, which yields lower loss at the same budget.

questions.question: A ~500-word document that is one comma-separated list of distinct city names ('Paris, London, Tokyo, …') is run through `quality_filter` with default thresholds. Which gate does it most likely fail?
options: Word count — 500 words exceeds the maximum allowed for one document
Mean word length — city names push the average well above 10 characters
Symbol ratio — one comma per ~6 letters gives ~0.14, above the 0.10 ceiling
Repetition ratio — a list repeats the same words, pushing it above 0.40
questions.explanation: Word count (~500) is in range, mean word length (~5–7) is in range, and repetition is low because the cities are mostly distinct. But one comma per word, with ~6 letters per word, gives a symbol ratio near 1/7 ≈ 0.14, above 0.10. List spam looks fine on every metric except punctuation density.

questions.question: Which dedicated rule do real Gopher filters add to catch list-style documents?
options: A minimum-perplexity rule, computed by scoring each document with GPT-2
A 'fraction of lines ending in a bullet/list marker' rule
A maximum number of distinct URLs or hyperlinks per document rule
A rule rejecting any document that contains more than one comma
questions.explanation: Beyond the simple symbol ratio, real Gopher filters include a rule on the fraction of lines ending in (or marked by) bullets or list markers, which directly targets list-style spam.

questions.question: What is wrong with trusting a corpus simply because it loaded cleanly via `load_dataset`?
options: Tidy text means someone else filtered it, and their choices are now yours, sight unseen
Clean-loading corpora are always contaminated with benchmark test sets, by construction
Clean-loading corpora are always tokenized with the wrong tokenizer for your model
Clean-loading corpora always consist of duplicate documents copied from other sets
questions.explanation: A tidy corpus reflects someone else's filtering decisions — what they kept, dropped and how. Those decisions now shape your model, even though you never examined them.

questions.question: Why is using Common Crawl WET files blindly, without re-extracting, a common mistake?
options: WET files contain only raw HTML, so they must be tokenized differently from plain text
WET files are encrypted and unreadable without a separate commercial licence key
WET files skip all non-English pages, so multilingual corpora cannot be built from them
Generic tag-stripping keeps boilerplate; the corpora that win re-extract from WARC
questions.explanation: WET's generic extraction leaves menus, footers and related-article blocks in the text. Winning corpora run a purpose-built extractor on the raw HTML in WARC instead.

questions.question: Why is tuning quality-filter thresholds without inspecting rejected documents dangerous?
options: It always makes the filter too lenient, so junk floods the training stream without anyone noticing
It makes the filter slower to run, since the thresholds must be recomputed on every pass over data
A rule that quietly deletes all your code or dialogue can hurt a capability unseen in aggregates
It causes the tokenizer to fail on rejected documents that later re-enter the corpus
questions.explanation: Aggregate statistics such as 'percent kept' can look reasonable while a rule silently removes an entire category of useful text. Only by inspecting rejects do you catch that.

questions.question: Why should you not roll your own PII or toxicity detector for a real pretraining pipeline?
options: Because they are far too slow to run on CPU at the scale of billions of documents
These are high-stakes systems that are easy to get subtly, dangerously wrong; use vetted tools
Because they require labeled benchmark data that cannot be obtained outside large labs
Because homemade detectors always over-filter code, deleting most of the programming data in the crawl
questions.explanation: PII and toxicity detection are specialized and high-stakes; a homemade version can miss serious cases while appearing to work. Vetted tools are the right choice.

questions.question: Which paper documents a frontier-model Common Crawl pipeline using a learned quality classifier plus fuzzy deduplication, and is a canonical reference for what the data funnel looks like at scale?
options: GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020)
Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., 2022)
Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017)
BERT (Devlin et al., 2018)
questions.explanation: GPT-3's data section describes filtering Common Crawl with a learned quality classifier toward high-quality reference text and applying fuzzy deduplication. Llama 3 and OLMo 2 are later references for modern data-quality and annealing details.

questions.question: A document scores mean word length 6.0, symbol ratio 0.03, repetition ratio 0.05, and has 12 words. With default `quality_filter` thresholds, is it kept?
options: Yes — three of the four signals are fine, which is a majority
Yes — word count is only a soft signal
No — its symbol ratio is above the ceiling
No — 12 is below min_words = 20, and every gate must pass
questions.explanation: The mean word length, symbol ratio and repetition ratio are all within thresholds, but the word count of 12 fails min_words=20. Because quality_filter requires all gates to pass, it is dropped. Short snippets are usually nav stubs or titles.

questions.question: After quality filtering, what major problem still remains in clean, right-language web documents that the next stage addresses?
options: Every document is still in raw HTML, so it must be re-extracted from WARC before tokenizing
Documents are still in many languages, since language ID only flags them for later manual review
Massive duplication — articles mirrored across sites and paragraphs templated onto many pages
Documents still lack an end-of-text separator, so they cannot be packed into windows
questions.explanation: Even quality-passing documents contain huge amounts of duplication from mirrors and templates. Duplicated data wastes compute and worsens memorization, which is why exact and fuzzy (MinHash) deduplication follow.

questions.question: Which basic property of a hash function does exact document deduplication rely on?
options: A hash maps similar inputs to similar outputs
A hash maps data to a fixed-size integer, and equal inputs give equal hashes
A hash is reversible, so the document can be recovered from it
A hash always produces a unique output for every distinct input with no collisions possible
questions.explanation: Exact dedup relies on hashing being deterministic: equal inputs produce equal fixed-size fingerprints. Hashes are not similarity-preserving (that is why fuzzy dedup needs MinHash) and are not reversible.

questions.question: Why is every serious pretraining corpus deduplicated?
options: Duplicates waste compute, worsen memorization, and inflate evaluation via contamination
Duplicates bloat the tokenizer vocabulary, since repeated text spawns many redundant merges
Duplicates make the training loss go NaN, because identical batches produce exploding gradients
Duplicates are illegal to train on under copyright law, while a single copy is fair use
questions.explanation: The web is enormously redundant. Training on duplicates spends compute relearning the same tokens, makes the model memorize and potentially regurgitate repeated text, and can leak benchmark items into training. Dedup addresses all three.

questions.question: What is the standard way to perform near-duplicate deduplication at web scale?
options: Exact SHA-1 hashing of whole documents
Training a classifier to predict duplicates
Sorting all documents alphabetically and comparing neighbors
MinHash + LSH (locality-sensitive hashing)
questions.explanation: MinHash estimates Jaccard similarity from small signatures, and LSH banding finds candidate pairs without comparing all pairs. Together they are the standard near-duplicate method in large corpora. Exact hashing only catches byte-identical copies.

questions.question: If the same 2,000-word article appears 500 times in a crawl and you train on all copies, what is the 'wasted compute' harm?
options: The GPU runs out of memory, because each duplicate is cached separately in the activations
The optimizer's learning rate is effectively multiplied by 500 for that article's tokens
You spend 500× the FLOPs on one article instead of 500 different ones
The tokenizer must be retrained for each copy, since each one shifts the merge statistics
questions.explanation: At a fixed compute budget, every duplicated token displaces a token of new information. 500 copies means 500× the compute on one article that could have gone to 500 different ones.

questions.question: Why does duplicated training text worsen memorization in a language model?
options: Duplicates are stored in a special cache inside the model that bypasses its normal weight updates
Text seen many times gets memorized rather than generalized, so it can be reproduced verbatim
Duplicates increase the vocabulary size, so rare words get their own memorized embeddings
Duplicates disable dropout for the repeated tokens, so the model overfits them exactly
questions.explanation: Repeated exposure pushes the model to store the exact text instead of generalizing. Heavily duplicated passages can then be regurgitated verbatim — a privacy and copyright hazard and a sign capacity went to storage instead of learning.

questions.question: How can duplication in training data cause evaluation contamination?
options: If a duplicated document overlaps a benchmark item, the model has effectively seen the test
Duplicates cause the evaluation harness to count each correct answer twice, doubling scores
Duplicates change the benchmark's answer key, since repeated items are re-labelled on load
Duplicates lower the validation loss but have no effect at all on downstream benchmark scores
questions.explanation: If text overlapping a benchmark appears (often many times) in training, the model can answer from memory rather than reasoning. That inflates benchmark scores, which is the contamination problem.

questions.question: What does exact deduplication remove?
options: Documents that share at least one full sentence, found by hashing each sentence separately
Documents with Jaccard similarity above 0.8, found by comparing MinHash signatures
Documents on the same topic, found by clustering their embeddings and keeping one per cluster
Byte-for-byte identical documents, found by hashing each one and dropping repeated hashes
questions.explanation: Exact dedup hashes each document and drops any document whose hash was already seen. It only removes byte-identical copies; near-identical documents need fuzzy dedup.

questions.question: What does fuzzy (near-duplicate) deduplication remove that exact hashing misses?
options: Documents in different languages that say the same thing, e.g. an article and its translation
Documents that are byte-for-byte identical, which exact hashing cannot detect reliably
Nearly identical documents — e.g. the same article with a changed date or an added footer
Documents that contain PII, since names and emails differ slightly between copies
questions.explanation: Fuzzy dedup targets near-duplicates: the same content with small changes such as a different date or extra footer. Exact hashing misses these because one different byte gives a completely different hash.

questions.question: Why does exact hashing miss near-duplicate documents?
options: Hashes are too short to represent long documents faithfully
One different byte gives a completely different hash
Hash collisions make near-duplicates look unique
Exact hashing ignores whitespace
questions.explanation: Hash functions scramble their input so that any small change — even one byte — produces an unrelated output. Two nearly identical documents therefore get unrelated fingerprints and both survive exact dedup.

questions.question: Why is exact dedup implemented by comparing 64-bit hashes rather than full document strings?
options: Comparing fixed-size hashes is far cheaper than comparing strings, and set lookup is O(1)
Full strings cannot be compared for equality in Python once they exceed a few megabytes in size
Hashes preserve similarity, so near-duplicates map to nearby values and are also caught
Hashes compress each document losslessly, so it can be decoded later if it is needed
questions.explanation: A fixed-size fingerprint makes each comparison cheap, and storing seen fingerprints in a hash set gives average O(1) membership tests. That makes exact dedup a single linear pass.

questions.question: In an exact-dedup function that iterates over documents, hashes each, and keeps a `seen` set, which occurrence of a repeated document is kept?
options: The last occurrence
A random occurrence
None of them — all copies are removed
The first occurrence
questions.explanation: The loop appends a document only if its hash is not in seen, then adds the hash. So the first copy is kept and later copies are dropped.

questions.question: Why should a real deduplication pipeline use a stable content hash (e.g. `hashlib.sha1` or `blake2b`) instead of Python's built-in `hash()`?
options: Python's built-in `hash()` is too slow for large documents, since it walks every byte twice
Python's built-in `hash()` only works on integers and tuples, not on str or bytes objects
Python's built-in `hash()` is salted per process, so values differ between runs and shards
Python's built-in `hash()` produces 1024-bit outputs, far too large to store for every document
questions.explanation: For strings and bytes, Python's built-in hash is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). Values computed in one run or worker do not match another, so they cannot be saved or compared across shards. A stable hash like sha1 or blake2b of the bytes gives the same value everywhere.

questions.question: What kind of changes cause exact hash-based dedup to see two documents as different, even though a human sees the same article?
options: A different font or stylesheet in the rendered page, which changes how the text looks
Tiny edits like a changed timestamp, a visitor counter, or a 'Share on X' line
Being served from a different country, so the page arrives through a different CDN
Being crawled in a different month, even when the stored bytes are exactly identical
questions.explanation: Any byte change — a timestamp, a counter, a share line — changes the hash completely. The web is full of such small variations, which is why a similarity measure tolerant of small edits is needed.

questions.section: 3. Fuzzy dedup: documents as sets of shingles
questions.question: What is a k-shingle (k-gram) in near-duplicate detection?
options: A window of k consecutive units — here, k consecutive words joined by spaces
A random sample of k words drawn from the document, with their order discarded
The k most frequent words in the document, ranked by their raw counts
The first k characters of the document, used as a cheap fingerprint of it
questions.explanation: A k-shingle is a sliding window of k consecutive words. Sliding it across the document one word at a time produces the document's shingle set.

questions.section: 3. Fuzzy dedup: documents as sets of shingles
questions.question: What is the 3-shingle set of 'the quick brown fox jumps'?
options: {'the quick brown', 'quick brown fox', 'brown fox jumps', 'fox jumps'}
{'the quick brown fox', 'quick brown fox jumps'}
{'the quick', 'quick brown', 'brown fox', 'fox jumps'}
{'the quick brown', 'quick brown fox', 'brown fox jumps'}
questions.explanation: Sliding a 3-word window across 5 words yields 5 − 3 + 1 = 3 shingles: 'the quick brown', 'quick brown fox', 'brown fox jumps'. The 2-word windows would be 2-shingles.

questions.section: 3. Fuzzy dedup: documents as sets of shingles
questions.question: Why does a small edit to a document change only a few of its k-shingles?
options: Because shingles are hashed with a similarity-preserving hash, so nearby edits map to nearby values
Because shingles skip all words shorter than k letters, so most small edits are ignored
Only the few shingles whose window spans the edited position change; the rest stay the same
Because the shingle set is sorted alphabetically, so an edit only moves a single entry
questions.explanation: Each shingle covers k consecutive words. A local edit only affects the shingles whose window includes the edited word, so two near-identical documents still share most shingles.

questions.section: 3. Fuzzy dedup: documents as sets of shingles
questions.question: When a document is converted to a set of shingles, what information is collapsed away?
options: Vocabulary and spelling
Order and repetition
Word boundaries
All content information
questions.explanation: Representing a document as a set discards the order of shingles and how many times each appears. What remains is which k-word runs the document contains, which is what near-duplicate comparison uses.

questions.section: 3. Fuzzy dedup: documents as sets of shingles
questions.question: Why is near-duplicate detection done on sets of shingles rather than the raw word sequence?
options: It measures how much content two documents share, not order, so reordered pages still overlap
Because sets are faster to tokenize with BPE than sequences, which matters at web scale
Because raw word sequences cannot be hashed, while sets of shingles can be hashed and compared directly
Because sets preserve the exact order of paragraphs, which sequences of words lose
questions.explanation: Near-duplicate detection asks how much content is shared. Reordering paragraphs barely changes the shingle set, so set overlap correctly flags such pages as duplicates.

questions.section: 3. Fuzzy dedup: documents as sets of shingles
questions.question: What is the effect of using a larger k for word shingles in near-duplicate detection?
options: More unrelated documents are flagged as duplicates, since long shingles match each other more often
Shingle sets become smaller than the vocabulary, so every document looks almost identical
Order information is fully restored, so the set becomes equivalent to the raw sequence
Accidental overlap between unrelated documents becomes very unlikely, as long runs rarely coincide
questions.explanation: Short runs like 2 words are shared by chance among unrelated texts; long runs like 8 words almost never are. Larger k therefore reduces spurious overlap between unrelated documents.

questions.section: 3. Fuzzy dedup: documents as sets of shingles
questions.question: What are typical shingle sizes k (in words) for web near-duplicate detection?
options: 1–2 words
50–100 words
5–10 words
Exactly one sentence
questions.explanation: Typical values are 5–10 words: long enough that accidental shared runs are rare, short enough that small edits leave most shingles intact.

questions.section: 4. Jaccard similarity: the quantity we want
questions.question: What is the Jaccard similarity $J(A, B)$ of two sets A and B?
options: $|A \cap B| / |A|$ — the size of the intersection over the size of A alone
$|A \cap B| / |A \cup B|$ — the size of the intersection over the union
$|A \cup B| / |A \cap B|$ — the size of the union over the intersection
$|A| \cdot |B| / |A \cup B|$ — the product of the sizes over the union
questions.explanation: Jaccard is intersection over union. It equals 1 for identical sets and 0 for disjoint sets. Normalizing only by |A| would make it directional rather than symmetric.

questions.section: 4. Jaccard similarity: the quantity we want
questions.question: What does Jaccard similarity J = 1 mean for two shingle sets?
options: The sets are identical — every shingle is shared
The sets are disjoint — no shingle is shared at all
Exactly one shingle is shared between the two sets
One set is twice the size of the other, by count
questions.explanation: J = 1 when intersection equals union, i.e. the sets are identical. J = 0 means disjoint; values in between are the fraction of all distinct shingles that both contain.

questions.section: 4. Jaccard similarity: the quantity we want
questions.question: What does a Jaccard similarity strictly between 0 and 1 represent for two shingle sets?
options: The fraction of document A's words that also appear anywhere in document B's vocabulary
The probability that the two documents are written in the same language
The number of shared shingles divided by k, the shingle length in words
The fraction of all distinct shingles (across both) that both documents contain
questions.explanation: Since J = |A∩B| / |A∪B|, it is exactly the share of the union that lies in the intersection: the fraction of all distinct shingles present in both documents.

questions.section: 4. Jaccard similarity: the quantity we want
questions.question: Around what Jaccard threshold does a dedup pass commonly declare two documents near-duplicates?
options: About 0.1
About 0.3
About 0.8
Exactly 1.0
questions.explanation: A common near-duplicate threshold is around J ≥ 0.8. Exactly 1.0 would only catch identical shingle sets, and low thresholds would delete merely related documents.

questions.section: 4. Jaccard similarity: the quantity we want
questions.question: What kind of computation is Jaccard similarity of shingle sets in a dedup pipeline?
options: GPU matrix multiplication on float16 embeddings of each shingle
CPU set arithmetic on set counts — nothing is a tensor
A forward pass of a small transformer over both shingle sets
Gradient computation on token ids from the two documents
questions.explanation: Every symbol in the Jaccard formula is a set size. Computing it is plain CPU set intersection and union, not tensor math.

questions.section: 5. The problem: exact Jaccard is too expensive at scale
questions.question: Why is computing exact Jaccard similarity for every pair of documents infeasible at web scale?
options: Each pair requires intersecting large shingle sets, and there are ~$10^{18}$ pairs for $n = 10^9$
Jaccard can only be computed on a GPU, and no cluster has enough memory to hold every shingle set
Jaccard requires training a small model for each pair, which costs minutes per comparison
Jaccard is undefined for sets larger than 1,000 elements, which most web documents exceed
questions.explanation: Two costs explode: storing and intersecting big shingle sets per pair, and the number of pairs, which grows quadratically. With a billion documents that is about 10^18 comparisons — utterly infeasible.

questions.section: 5. The problem: exact Jaccard is too expensive at scale
questions.question: Which cost of exact pairwise Jaccard does MinHash attack, and which does LSH banding attack?
options: MinHash attacks the number of pairs (bucketing similar documents); LSH banding attacks the per-pair cost
Both attack only the per-pair cost: MinHash shrinks the sets and banding shrinks them further
Both attack only the number of pairs: MinHash skips dissimilar pairs and banding skips the rest
MinHash attacks the per-pair cost (small signatures); LSH banding attacks the number of pairs
questions.explanation: MinHash replaces full shingle sets with small signatures so each comparison is cheap. LSH banding avoids comparing most pairs at all by bucketing likely-similar documents. Together they make near-duplicate detection tractable.

questions.section: 6. MinHash: estimating Jaccard from a tiny signature
questions.question: In MinHash, given a random permutation π of the shingle universe, how is minhash(A) defined?
options: The element of A with the largest rank under π: $\arg\max_{x \in A} \pi(x)$, i.e. the last
The number of elements of A whose rank under π falls below |A|
The element of A with the smallest rank under π: $\arg\min_{x \in A} \pi(x)$
The average rank of A's elements under π, rounded down to an integer
questions.explanation: A random permutation assigns every shingle a rank. The MinHash of a set is its member with the smallest rank. Max-based variants exist in principle, but the defined quantity here is the argmin.

questions.section: 6. MinHash: estimating Jaccard from a tiny signature
questions.question: What is the key identity that MinHash rests on?
options: For a random permutation, P(minhash(A) = minhash(B)) = |A ∩ B|
For a random permutation, P(minhash(A) = minhash(B)) = J(A, B)
For a random permutation, minhash(A) = minhash(B) only when A = B
For a random permutation, P(minhash(A) = minhash(B)) = 1 − J(A, B)
questions.explanation: The probability that two sets share their MinHash under a random permutation equals exactly their Jaccard similarity. That makes each permutation a Bernoulli trial succeeding with probability J.

questions.section: 6. MinHash: estimating Jaccard from a tiny signature
questions.question: Why does P(minhash(A) = minhash(B)) equal the Jaccard similarity J(A, B) under a random permutation?
options: The smallest-ranked element of A ∪ B is uniform over the union, and they match iff it lies in A ∩ B
Because the permutation always ranks shared elements first, so the match rate tracks their overlap size
Because each set's MinHash is drawn uniformly from that set, independently of the other set
Because the permutation is applied separately to A and to B, so the two minima are independent
questions.explanation: Under a random permutation, the overall minimum of the union is uniformly distributed over the union. Both sets have that element as their MinHash exactly when it is in both sets. So the match probability is |A∩B| / |A∪B| = J.

questions.section: 6. MinHash: estimating Jaccard from a tiny signature
questions.question: How is a MinHash signature of a set built?
options: As the sorted list of all the set's shingles, truncated to keep only the first m entries
As a single hash of the concatenated shingles, repeated m times for redundancy
As the m most frequent shingles in the document, stored as their hash values
As the length-m vector of the set's MinHashes under m independent permutations
questions.explanation: Apply m independent random permutations (or hash functions) and record the MinHash under each. The resulting length-m vector is the signature, replacing a set of thousands of shingles.

questions.section: 6. MinHash: estimating Jaccard from a tiny signature
questions.question: How is Jaccard similarity estimated from two MinHash signatures of length m?
options: The cosine similarity of the two signature vectors, treating each slot's hash value as a coordinate
The Euclidean distance between the two signatures divided by m, then subtracted from one to get a similarity
$\hat{J} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i} \mathbb{1}[\text{sig}_A[i] = \text{sig}_B[i]]$ — the fraction of equal slots
The fraction of slots where sig_A[i] < sig_B[i], doubled to correct for symmetry
questions.explanation: Each slot matches with probability J, so the fraction of equal slots estimates J. Cosine or Euclidean distance on hash values has no meaningful relation to J.

questions.section: 6. MinHash: estimating Jaccard from a tiny signature
questions.question: Is the MinHash estimator $\hat J$ (fraction of matching signature slots) biased or unbiased for J?
options: Biased upward by a factor of m, so it must be divided by m
Unbiased — each slot matches with probability exactly J
Biased downward because hash collisions are ignored
Unbiased only when J = 0.5, and biased toward 0.5 otherwise
questions.explanation: Since each slot is an independent trial that matches with probability J, the expected fraction of matches is J. The estimator is unbiased; more slots just reduce its variance.

questions.section: 6. MinHash: estimating Jaccard from a tiny signature
questions.question: How does the standard deviation of the MinHash Jaccard estimate scale with the signature length m?
options: It shrinks like $1/\sqrt{m}$
It shrinks like $1/m^2$, quadratically
It grows like $\sqrt{m}$
It does not depend on m at all
questions.explanation: The estimate is an average of m Bernoulli(J) trials, so its standard deviation is sqrt(J(1−J)/m), shrinking like 1/sqrt(m). More permutations give a tighter estimate.

questions.section: 6. MinHash: estimating Jaccard from a tiny signature
questions.question: After MinHashing, what does comparing two documents cost?
options: Intersecting their full shingle sets
One forward pass of a classifier
O(n^2) comparisons over the corpus
m integer comparisons
questions.explanation: A signature of a few hundred integers replaces a set of thousands of shingles, so comparing two documents is just m equality checks.

questions.section: 7. Tiny MinHash example, worked entirely by hand
questions.question: For A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5, 6}, what is the true Jaccard similarity?
options: 1/2 (intersection {3,4} of size 2 over |A| = 4)
2/3 (the 4 elements outside the intersection over the union of 6)
1/3 (intersection {3,4} of size 2 over union of size 6)
1/4 (intersection {3,4} of size 2 over |A| + |B| = 8)
questions.explanation: A ∩ B = {3, 4} has size 2 and A ∪ B = {1,…,6} has size 6, so J = 2/6 = 1/3. A tempting mistake is to divide by |A| = 4, giving 1/2.

questions.section: 7. Tiny MinHash example, worked entirely by hand
questions.question: For A = {1,2,3,4} and B = {3,4,5,6}, under which condition on a random permutation do minhash(A) and minhash(B) match?
options: When element 1 is ranked first, since 1 is the smallest element of A
When the smallest-ranked element of the union is 3 or 4, in the intersection
When the permutation is the identity ordering, so each element's rank equals its value
When elements 5 and 6 are ranked last, so they cannot be B's MinHash
questions.explanation: A match happens exactly when the minimum-ranked element of A ∪ B is in both sets, i.e. is 3 or 4. If element 1 is first, minhash(A) = 1 but B's MinHash is something else.

questions.section: 7. Tiny MinHash example, worked entirely by hand
questions.question: Why might a MinHash estimate with only six permutations land exactly on the true Jaccard, and what happens as the number of permutations grows?
options: With few permutations it is partly luck, since the estimate has variance; with many it concentrates
Six permutations always give the exact answer for any sets; more permutations just confirm the same value
The estimate is exact for small m but becomes biased as the number of permutations grows
It is exact only when J = 1/3; with more permutations the estimate drifts steadily toward 0.5
questions.explanation: Six trials is a very noisy sample, so hitting 1/3 exactly is partly luck. As m grows the estimate concentrates — 100,000 random permutations give about 0.3336 for the same sets.

questions.section: 8. From permutations to hash functions (what the code does)
questions.question: Why does real MinHash use hash functions instead of literally shuffling the universe of all shingles?
options: Shuffling with a standard PRNG is not random enough for the MinHash identity to hold
Hash functions give the exact Jaccard similarity instead of a noisy estimate, removing variance
Shuffling would reveal each document's content to the workers that hold the permutation
The universe of possible shingles is astronomically large, so a hash simulates a permutation
questions.explanation: You cannot materialize a permutation over every possible shingle. A hash function assigns each shingle a pseudo-random value, and the smallest hash value plays the role of the smallest rank.

questions.section: 8. From permutations to hash functions (what the code does)
questions.question: What form of universal hash function is used to simulate permutations in MinHash?
options: $h(x) = x^2 \bmod 2$, so that each shingle maps to one of two buckets
$h(x) = \lfloor x / p \rfloor$ with p prime and no random coefficients
$h(x) = (a \cdot x + b) \bmod p$ with large prime p and random a, b
$h(x) = a \cdot x$ with a fixed to 1, so every shingle keeps its rank
questions.explanation: A universal hash (a·x + b) mod p with large prime p and random a, b maps each shingle's base hash to a pseudo-random value. Different (a_i, b_i) pairs give the m independent hash functions.

questions.section: 8. From permutations to hash functions (what the code does)
questions.question: In MinHash with universal hashes, how are the m independent 'permutations' obtained?
options: By using m different prime moduli, chosen at random on each call
By using m different random $(a_i, b_i)$ coefficient pairs
By shuffling the document's words m times before shingling
By using m different shingle sizes k, one per hash function
questions.explanation: Each (a_i, b_i) pair defines one hash function. Drawing m such pairs gives m independent functions, standing in for m random permutations.

questions.section: 8. From permutations to hash functions (what the code does)
questions.question: In the `MinHasher.signature` implementation, what is the shape and dtype of the `hashed` array, and what does `min(axis=1)` do?
options: Shape (m, |s|), uint64 on CPU; min over axis 1 reduces each hash function's row to its MinHash
Shape (|s|, m), float32 on the GPU; min over axis 1 picks the smallest shingle per hash function
Shape (m,), int64 on the CPU; min over axis 1 collapses the vector into a single scalar MinHash
Shape (m, m), uint8 on the CPU; min over axis 1 picks the diagonal entry of each hash function
questions.explanation: Broadcasting (m,1) coefficients against (1,|s|) base hashes gives an (m, |s|) uint64 array: row i is hash function i applied to every shingle. Taking the min along axis 1 yields one MinHash per function, a length-m signature returned as a list of ints.

questions.section: 8. From permutations to hash functions (what the code does)
questions.question: Why does the course's `MinHasher` use `_stable_hash` based on `blake2b` for shingles, and take a `seed` for its coefficients?
options: So signatures are as short as possible, since blake2b digests compress well
So that two different documents can never collide in any signature slot
So that the hash coefficients change on each run, giving better randomness overall
So signatures are reproducible across runs and processes, unlike salted `hash()`
questions.explanation: Python's built-in hash is salted per process, so it would give different signatures in different runs. Using blake2b for base hashes and a fixed seed for the a, b coefficients makes signatures identical across runs and workers.

questions.section: 8. From permutations to hash functions (what the code does)
questions.question: What does `estimate_jaccard(sig_a, sig_b)` compute?
options: The size of the intersection of the two signatures as sets, divided by their union
The mean absolute difference between the two signatures, normalised by the largest value in either
The number of positions where the two signatures are equal, divided by the signature length
The maximum of the two signatures' minimum values, scaled into the range 0 to 1
questions.explanation: estimate_jaccard counts equal slots with zip and divides by len(sig_a). That fraction of equal slots is the unbiased MinHash estimate of Jaccard.

questions.section: 9. It works on real text — and m controls accuracy
questions.question: When estimating Jaccard with MinHash at increasing signature sizes m (16, 64, 256, 1024), how does the error behave?
options: It decreases strictly monotonically at every step, halving each time m quadruples
It trends down roughly as $1/\sqrt{m}$, though not monotonically since the estimate is random
It stays roughly constant regardless of m, since the estimator is already unbiased
It increases with m, because longer signatures produce more accidental collisions between slots
questions.explanation: At m = 16 the estimate is noisy; by 64–1024 it hugs the true value. Errors trend down like 1/sqrt(m) but can bounce around (e.g. 256 slightly worse than 64) because each estimate is random.

questions.section: 9. It works on real text — and m controls accuracy
questions.question: What is the accuracy/cost trade-off controlled by the MinHash signature length m?
options: Bigger signatures cost more storage and comparison but estimate J more precisely
Bigger signatures are both cheaper and more precise, since they compress better
Bigger signatures cost more but are less precise, because more slots add noise
Signature length has no effect on cost, since each comparison is a single hash-table lookup
questions.explanation: Storage and comparison cost grow linearly with m, while estimation error shrinks like 1/sqrt(m). You choose m to meet the precision your dedup threshold needs.

questions.section: 9. It works on real text — and m controls accuracy
questions.question: What does the course's dedup unit test assert about `estimate_jaccard`?
options: That `estimate_jaccard` returns exactly the true Jaccard for any m and any pair of sets
That `estimate_jaccard` is always strictly below the true Jaccard, for every seed and every m tested
That `estimate_jaccard` runs faster than exact `jaccard` for any m on large shingle sets
With m ≥ 128 and a fixed seed, it lands within ~0.1 of the true `jaccard` for overlapping sets
questions.explanation: The test checks that with at least 128 hash functions and a fixed seed, the MinHash estimate is within about 0.1 of the exact Jaccard. It allows for randomness rather than demanding exactness.

questions.section: 10. LSH banding: avoiding the O(n^2) comparison
questions.question: What problem does LSH banding solve in near-duplicate detection?
options: It makes each pairwise comparison cheaper than checking m integers, by hashing whole signatures
It computes the exact Jaccard similarity instead of an estimate, using the band structure
It avoids comparing all $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs by only comparing likely-similar documents
It removes byte-identical copies before MinHash runs, so the signatures are all distinct
questions.explanation: MinHash made each comparison cheap, but there are still too many pairs. LSH banding generates candidate pairs that are likely similar, so most pairs are never compared at all.

questions.section: 10. LSH banding: avoiding the O(n^2) comparison
questions.question: In LSH banding of MinHash signatures, how is a length-m signature divided?
options: Into r bands of b rows each, with m = b + r slots
Into b bands of r rows each, with m = b · r
Into m bands of one row each
Into two halves compared separately
questions.explanation: Each signature is split into b bands, each containing r consecutive MinHash values, so m = b·r. Each band is then hashed into a bucket.

questions.section: 10. LSH banding: avoiding the O(n^2) comparison
questions.question: In LSH banding, when do two documents become a candidate pair?
options: When they land in the same bucket for at least one band — sharing all r values of that band
When they land in the same bucket for every one of the b bands, i.e. across the whole signature
When at least one of their m MinHash values is equal, in any position of the signature
When their signatures have the same sum, which is cheap to compare across all documents
questions.explanation: A candidate pair needs to match on all r rows of at least one band. Requiring all bands would be too strict; requiring one single slot would flag far too many pairs.

questions.section: 10. LSH banding: avoiding the O(n^2) comparison
questions.question: What is the probability that a pair of documents with Jaccard J becomes an LSH candidate pair with b bands of r rows?
options: $1 - J^{r \cdot b}$
questions.explanation: A band matches entirely with probability J^r; it fails with probability 1 − J^r; all b bands fail with probability (1 − J^r)^b. So at least one band matches with probability 1 − (1 − J^r)^b.

questions.section: 10. LSH banding: avoiding the O(n^2) comparison
questions.question: What is the shape of the LSH candidate probability $1 - (1 - J^r)^b$ as a function of J, and roughly where is its threshold?
options: Linear in J, with no threshold: doubling J doubles the chance of becoming a candidate
Bell-shaped, peaking at J = 0.5 and falling off for both very similar and very dissimilar pairs
S-shaped: near 0 below a threshold and near 1 above it, with the threshold near $(1/b)^{1/r}$
Decreasing in J, so dissimilar pairs are the most likely to become candidate pairs
questions.explanation: The curve is an S: pairs with low J almost never become candidates and pairs with high J almost always do. The steep transition sits near (1/b)^(1/r), which b and r tune.

questions.section: 10. LSH banding: avoiding the O(n^2) comparison
questions.question: What do the LSH banding parameters b and r tune?
options: The length of each shingle in words, which sets how strict the overlap test is
Where the S-curve cutoff sits — how similar documents must be before you compare them
The size of the stable hash in bits, which sets how often two different shingles collide
The number of documents per shard, which sets how many workers the job can use
questions.explanation: Choosing b and r moves the threshold near (1/b)^(1/r). More rows per band make matching a band harder (higher threshold); more bands make it easier (lower threshold).

questions.section: 10. LSH banding: avoiding the O(n^2) comparison
questions.question: With MinHash plus LSH banding, roughly how does total dedup work scale with the number of documents n?
options: Roughly linear in n, instead of quadratic
Quadratic in n, but with a smaller constant
Cubic in n, since bands multiply the pairs
Constant, independent of n once tuned
questions.explanation: Only candidate pairs from shared buckets are compared, and their number is small for a well-tuned banding. So the total work is roughly linear in n instead of O(n^2).

questions.section: 10. LSH banding: avoiding the O(n^2) comparison
questions.question: What is the full near-duplicate deduplication pipeline in order?
options: MinHash each document → shingle the signature → compare all pairs exactly → LSH band the survivors
LSH band the raw text → shingle each band → MinHash the shingles → compare all pairs exactly
Exact hash each document → shingle → train a duplicate classifier → drop documents it flags as duplicates
Shingle → MinHash signature → LSH band into candidate pairs → compare only candidates, drop above threshold
questions.explanation: Shingling captures content, MinHash makes each comparison O(m), and banding makes the number of comparisons about O(n). Only candidate pairs are compared and those above the threshold are dropped.

questions.section: 10. LSH banding: avoiding the O(n^2) comparison
questions.question: Why does LSH banding work — why do similar documents tend to share a band while dissimilar ones do not?
options: Because banding sorts documents by length first, so documents of similar length end up sharing buckets
Because bands are computed only from the first shingle, which near-duplicates usually share
Similar documents agree on most slots, so likely on all r rows of some band; dissimilar ones rarely do
Because dissimilar documents are removed before banding by an exact-hash pass over the whole corpus
questions.explanation: High-J pairs match most slots, making a full-band match likely somewhere among b bands. Low-J pairs rarely match r slots in a row, so they almost never share a bucket.

questions.question: Two documents have shingle sets of size 100 each and share 60 shingles. What is their exact Jaccard similarity?
questions.explanation: The union is not 200: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| = 100 + 100 − 60 = 140. So J = 60/140 = 3/7 ≈ 0.43. Dividing by 100 or 200 is the common mistake.

questions.question: Two documents with Jaccard similarity J are MinHashed with m hash functions. How many signature slots do you expect to match?
options: m · J
m / J
J / m
questions.explanation: Each slot independently matches with probability J, so the expected number of matching slots is m·J. For J ≈ 0.43 and m = 200, about 86 slots.

questions.question: Why is the near-duplicate Jaccard threshold a deliberate choice rather than something to set low?
options: Set it too low and exact duplicates survive the pass
Set it too low and the MinHash estimate becomes biased upward
Set it too low and the signatures must become longer
Set it too low and you delete merely-related documents
questions.explanation: A low threshold flags documents that share a lot of content but are not truly duplicates, deleting useful related text. The threshold encodes how similar is 'the same document'.

questions.question: A MinHash signature implemented as `[min(hash((i, x)) for x in s) for i in range(self.m)]` flags different duplicate pairs every time a sharded pipeline runs. What is the bug?
options: The min should be a max: MinHash only matches J when the largest hash in each row is kept
The tuple (i, x) cannot be hashed consistently, since tuples of str are unhashable in Python
Built-in `hash()` is salted per process for str/bytes, so workers compute different signatures
The signature length m is too small, so random estimate noise changes the flagged pairs each run
questions.explanation: Built-in hash is randomized per process via PYTHONHASHSEED for str and bytes. Within one process signatures are consistent, so local tests pass, but different workers get different values. Fix it with a stable hash such as hashlib.blake2b of the encoded shingle.

questions.question: Why does a MinHash bug caused by Python's salted built-in `hash()` only show up across processes, not in a single local test?
options: Because the bug only affects documents too large for RAM, which local tests never use
Within one process the hash values are self-consistent; only another process has a new salt
Because the salt changes every time hash() is called, which the local test happens to mask
Because multiprocessing disables hash randomization in the parent process but not in workers
questions.explanation: The salt is fixed for the life of a process, so all hashes within it are consistent and a local test passes. A different worker has a different salt, so the same shingle hashes differently and collisions across shards disagree.

questions.question: What makes hashing reproducible in a sharded MinHash dedup job?
options: A stable content hash (e.g. `hashlib.blake2b` of the shingle) plus a fixed coefficient seed
Calling Python's built-in `hash()` twice per shingle and averaging the two results to cancel the salt
Setting a different random seed per worker, so each shard's coefficients are independent
Sorting the shingles before hashing them with built-in `hash()`, so order cannot matter
questions.explanation: Reproducibility needs both a process-independent base hash (blake2b or sha1 of the bytes) and the same a, b coefficients everywhere, which a fixed seed guarantees. Reproducible hashing is not optional when work is sharded.

questions.question: Which deduplication method did GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) apply to its Common Crawl data?
options: Only exact deduplication with SHA-1
No deduplication at all
Semantic deduplication with sentence embeddings
Fuzzy deduplication with MinHash-LSH
questions.explanation: GPT-3 applied fuzzy MinHash-LSH dedup to Common Crawl, and the technique is standard in major open corpora since (C4, RefinedWeb, Dolma, FineWeb).

questions.question: Which paper makes the empirical case that deduplicating training data improves language models and reduces memorization?
options: "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" (Kaplan et al., 2020)
"Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models" (Hoffmann et al., 2022)
"Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better" (Lee et al., 2021)
"Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017)
questions.explanation: Lee et al. (2021) show directly that dedup improves models and reduces memorization. Kaplan and Hoffmann are scaling-law papers; Vaswani introduced the transformer.

questions.question: Why can exact hashing not catch the same article republished with a changed publication date, while fuzzy dedup can?
options: Exact hashing ignores dates and numbers, so the two articles hash identically anyway
The changed bytes give a completely different hash, but the shingle sets still overlap almost entirely
Fuzzy dedup strips all dates and timestamps before hashing, so the copies become identical
Exact hashing only works on documents under 1,000 words, and news articles are usually longer than that
questions.explanation: Any byte change produces an unrelated hash, so exact dedup sees two distinct documents. Only the few shingles spanning the date differ, so Jaccard of the shingle sets stays near 1 and fuzzy dedup flags them.

questions.question: For A = {1,2,3,4} and B = {3,4,5,6}, under the permutation ordering 5, 6, 1, 3, 2, 4 (first listed has rank 0), what are minhash(A) and minhash(B)?
options: minhash(A) = 1 and minhash(B) = 5 — no match
minhash(A) = 5 and minhash(B) = 5 — match
minhash(A) = 3 and minhash(B) = 3 — match
minhash(A) = 1 and minhash(B) = 3 — so no match
questions.explanation: Ranks are 5→0, 6→1, 1→2, 3→3, 2→4, 4→5. A's smallest-ranked member is 1 (rank 2); B's is 5 (rank 0). They differ, so this permutation gives no match. 5 is not in A, so A cannot have MinHash 5.

questions.question: You double the MinHash signature length m from 128 to 256. What happens to accuracy and cost?
options: The standard deviation halves, since error scales like 1/m, while storage and comparison cost stay the same
The standard deviation shrinks by about 0.71, but storage and comparison cost both quadruple
Accuracy is unchanged because the estimator is unbiased, but storage and cost double
The standard deviation shrinks by $1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.71$, while storage and comparison double
questions.explanation: Error scales like 1/sqrt(m), so doubling m multiplies it by 1/sqrt(2) ≈ 0.71. Storage and comparison are linear in m, so they double. It is a direct accuracy-vs-cost trade.

questions.question: After deduplication removes redundancy within the training corpus, what subtler leak remains that the next stage targets?
options: Duplicate tokens within a single document, which repeat the same phrases many times over
Documents in the wrong language that slipped through the language-ID threshold
Text from an evaluation benchmark sneaking into training, silently inflating scores
HTML boilerplate inside documents that the extractor failed to strip completely
questions.explanation: Dedup handles within-corpus redundancy, but benchmark text can still be present in training. Detecting that requires an n-gram contamination check, followed by mixing and curriculum decisions.

questions.question: How does an n-gram used for benchmark contamination checks relate to a k-shingle used in deduplication?
options: An n-gram is a random sample of n words, while a shingle is consecutive
They are the same idea: a window of n (or k) consecutive words
An n-gram is a character window, while a shingle is a sentence
An n-gram is a hash, while a shingle is the original text
questions.explanation: A word n-gram and a word k-shingle are the same object — a sliding window of consecutive words. Contamination detection reuses the representation from near-duplicate detection, but with a different, directional measure.

questions.question: How does data-side contamination handling relate to eval-side contamination handling?
options: Data-side removes leakage before training; eval-side detects afterwards that a model was likely contaminated
They are unrelated phenomena with different causes, so each side needs its own detector and its own threshold
Data-side handles toxicity and PII in the corpus, while eval-side handles contamination of the benchmark scores
Data-side deletes leaked benchmarks from the eval suite, while eval-side deletes the matching training documents
questions.explanation: Contamination can be fought before training by removing overlapping training documents (data side) or after training by detecting likely contamination during evaluation (eval side). Both target the same leakage.

questions.question: Why can two models with identical architecture and compute differ enormously in quality?
options: Because of floating-point nondeterminism on GPUs
Because one used a larger batch size for evaluation
Because of differences in the tokenizer's special tokens only
Purely because of what data they saw and in what proportion
questions.explanation: Data choices — contamination, mixture proportions and ordering — are among the highest-leverage decisions in pretraining, and they are invisible in the model code. Same architecture and FLOPs can still yield very different models.

questions.question: Why is benchmark contamination described as making a mediocre model look great on paper?
options: Contamination makes training faster, so the model reaches a lower loss on the same compute budget
Contamination increases the effective parameter count, since memorized items occupy extra capacity
Test-set text in training lets the model score by remembering rather than reasoning, inflating benchmarks
Contamination makes the evaluation harness select easier questions, which lowers the benchmark's difficulty
questions.explanation: If benchmark questions or answers were in training, the model can recall them, so the score reflects memorization rather than capability. This is a real, recurring scandal on LLM leaderboards.

questions.question: Among contamination, mixing and curriculum, what does each primarily affect?
options: Contamination affects training speed; mixing affects tokenizer size; curriculum affects the model's width and depth
Contamination affects trust in eval scores; mixing decides which capabilities appear; curriculum adds quality
All three only affect the learning rate schedule, which in turn sets every downstream capability
Contamination affects memory usage; mixing affects the batch size; curriculum affects the sequence length
questions.explanation: Contamination inflates evaluation, mixing determines what capabilities the model gets, and curriculum (ordering, annealing) extracts more quality from the same data. All are high-leverage and invisible in the model definition.

questions.question: What is benchmark contamination (leakage)?
options: Test data leaking into the training data, inflating evaluation
Training data leaking into the model's output at inference time
The benchmark's answer key containing errors or ambiguous labels
A model forgetting earlier training data as later data arrives
questions.explanation: Contamination is when benchmark items (questions or answers) are present in the training corpus. The model then scores well by remembering rather than reasoning.

questions.question: Why does benchmark contamination happen so constantly in LLM pretraining?
options: Because benchmark authors deliberately leak test sets onto the web to promote their benchmark's adoption
Because tokenizers copy benchmark text into the vocabulary, so every model sees it during tokenization itself
Because evaluation harnesses train briefly on the test set by default before reporting their scores
Benchmarks are built from the public web, and the training data is the public web, so test items get crawled
questions.explanation: Benchmarks are drawn from or discussed on the web, and web crawls scoop up quiz sites, solutions and forum answers. Unless you actively remove them, you are very likely training on some of your own test set.

questions.question: What does a decontamination pass do?
options: After training, removes the benchmark questions that the model answered correctly from the reported set
Before training, removes near-duplicate documents within the corpus using MinHash over k-shingles
Before training, scans the corpus for overlap with every reported benchmark and removes matching documents
After training, re-weights the benchmark scores by item difficulty to cancel out any likely memorization effect
questions.explanation: Decontamination runs before training: it checks the corpus against every benchmark you will report and deletes the overlapping training documents. Without it you cannot trust your own eval numbers, and neither can anyone else.

questions.question: What is the consequence of skipping a decontamination pass before reporting benchmark results?
options: The model will fail to converge, because leaked items cause loss spikes
You cannot trust your own eval numbers, and neither can anyone else
The benchmark becomes unusable for every other lab that evaluates on it
The tokenizer will overfit to benchmark text and inflate its vocabulary
questions.explanation: Without decontamination, any benchmark score might reflect memorization of leaked items. The numbers lose their meaning both for you and for readers.

questions.question: How does the standard n-gram contamination detector decide whether a benchmark item leaked into a training document?
options: It measures what fraction of the benchmark item's word n-grams also appear in the training document
It computes symmetric Jaccard similarity between the two n-gram sets and flags any pairs above 0.8
It checks whether the two texts share the same MinHash signature across all of the hash bands
It compares the perplexity of the benchmark item under the model with that of a held-out paraphrase
questions.explanation: Each text becomes a set of word n-grams. The detector measures the fraction of the test item's n-grams present in the training document; a high fraction means the benchmark text is in training.

questions.question: Why is the n-gram contamination measure directional (asymmetric) rather than symmetric Jaccard?
options: Because symmetric Jaccard cannot be computed when the two n-gram sets have very different sizes
Because directional measures are cheaper to compute on GPUs than unions over large n-gram sets
Because the training document is always shorter than the test item, so its count is the natural denominator
The question is how much of the test item shows up in train, so it normalizes by the test item's n-grams
questions.explanation: A training document is typically much larger than a benchmark item, so symmetric Jaccard would be tiny even if the whole test item were present. Dividing by the test item's n-gram count makes 'test item fully inside train' read as 1.0.

questions.question: What is the formula for directional n-gram overlap used for contamination detection?
options: $|\text{ngrams}(test) \cap \text{ngrams}(train)| \,/\, |\text{ngrams}(test) \cup \text{ngrams}(train)|$
$|\text{ngrams}(test) \cap \text{ngrams}(train)| \,/\, |\text{ngrams}(train)|$
$|\text{ngrams}(test) \cap \text{ngrams}(train)| \,/\, |\text{ngrams}(test)|$
$|\text{ngrams}(train)| \,/\, |\text{ngrams}(test)|$
questions.explanation: The numerator is the shared n-grams and the denominator is the test item's n-gram count, so the measure asks how much of the test item appears in train. Dividing by the union gives Jaccard; dividing by train's count would make large training docs look clean.

questions.question: What does an n-gram overlap of 1.0 between a training document and a benchmark item mean?
options: The training document and the test item are identical in length and in word order
Every test n-gram appears in the training document (e.g. the test item is a substring of it)
The training document contains none of the test item's n-grams, so it is certainly clean
Half of the test n-grams appear in train, which is the usual flagging threshold for leaks
questions.explanation: An overlap of 1.0 means all of the test item's n-grams appear in the training text, as happens when the test item is contained verbatim. An overlap near 0 means the two share almost no length-n word runs.

questions.question: Why does the course's `ngram_overlap` implementation normalize text to lower-cased `\w+` word tokens before building n-grams?
options: So trailing punctuation and capitalization (e.g. 'Paris,' vs 'paris') do not block a real match
So the resulting word n-grams can be fed straight into the BPE tokenizer for hashing
So the n-gram sets stay smaller than the vocabulary and fit into memory even for large corpora
So that common stop-words such as 'the' and 'of' are removed from both texts before comparing
questions.explanation: Without normalization, 'Paris,' and 'paris' would be different tokens and break an otherwise verbatim match. Lower-casing and keeping only word characters is the same normalization GPT-3 and later reports use for overlap checks.

questions.question: What does the course's `ngram_overlap(train_text, test_text, n=8)` return when the test text has no n-grams (e.g. it is shorter than n words)?
options: It raises a ZeroDivisionError
None
questions.explanation: If ngrams(test_text, n) is empty, the function returns 0.0 before dividing. Otherwise it returns the size of the shared set divided by the number of test n-grams.

questions.question: An 8-word benchmark item is split into word 4-grams by sliding a 4-word window. How many 4-grams does it produce?
options: 8 (one per word)
questions.explanation: A window of n words over L words gives L − n + 1 n-grams. For 8 words and n = 4 that is 5. Non-overlapping chunks would give 2, which is not how n-grams are formed.

questions.question: A training document reads 'Study notes. The mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell, a fact every student memorizes.' Why is its 4-gram overlap with the benchmark item 'the mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell' exactly 1.0?
options: Because the training document has more words than the benchmark item, and the overlap score counts total shared words
After normalization it contains the run 'the mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell', so all 5 test 4-grams appear
Because it shares the word 'the' with the benchmark item, and 'the' starts most of the test item's 4-grams
Because overlap is always 1.0 when both texts are English sentences about the same scientific topic
questions.explanation: Lower-casing and stripping punctuation turn 'The … cell,' into the exact benchmark run, so every one of the 5 test 4-grams is present. 5/5 = 1.0. Sharing a single common word would not make whole 4-grams match.

questions.question: In a decontamination pass, what is removed when a training document is flagged as overlapping a benchmark item?
options: The offending training document — never the benchmark
The benchmark item, so the training data stays fully intact
Both the training document and the benchmark item
Only the overlapping n-grams inside the benchmark
questions.explanation: Decontamination deletes the training documents that overlap. The benchmark stays intact so the evaluation remains meaningful.

questions.question: What kinds of flagging rules does a decontamination pass typically use?
options: Flag a training document only if it is byte-identical to a benchmark item, after Unicode normalization
Flag a training document if it has the same word count as a benchmark item and shares its first sentence exactly
Flag a training document if its perplexity under a small reference model falls below a fixed threshold
Flag a training document with ≥ 0.5 overlap against any benchmark item, or even a single shared long n-gram
questions.explanation: Typical rules use a fractional threshold (e.g. overlap ≥ 0.5) or flag on any single shared long n-gram. Byte-identical matching would miss most real leaks.

questions.question: What two poles does the course's contamination unit test assert for `ngram_overlap`?
options: Overlap = 0.5 for any two English texts, and exactly 1.0 for identical texts of the same length
Overlap is symmetric when train and test are swapped, and it is 0 only when both texts are empty
Overlap = 1.0 when the test text is a substring of the train text, and ≈ 0 for disjoint text
Overlap is always above 0.9 for documents from the same domain, and 0 for documents across domains
questions.explanation: The test checks the extremes: full containment gives 1.0, and unrelated text gives approximately 0. These capture the behavior a decontamination threshold relies on.

questions.question: In a contamination check, what is the effect of choosing a small n (say 4) for the n-gram size?
options: It fires only on long verbatim runs, giving high precision but missing paraphrased leaks entirely
It catches paraphrases and partial leakage but fires on common phrases that are not really contamination
It makes the check unable to detect any leakage, because 4-grams are too short to ever match one another exactly
It makes the overlap measure symmetric, so train and test can be swapped without changing the score
questions.explanation: Short n-grams match partial and lightly-paraphrased leaks (higher recall), but common phrases like 'as a result of' also match by chance, producing false positives.

questions.question: What n-gram size is a common production value for contamination detection, and what is its trade-off?
options: 13 — fires only on long verbatim runs (high precision) but misses lightly-edited leaks
2 — catches every paraphrase with no false positives on common phrases or boilerplate
4 — gives perfect precision and recall on every benchmark at once, with no tuning
50 — required so that punctuation and casing differences never block a real match
questions.explanation: Large n like 13 matches only long verbatim runs, which are rarely coincidental, so precision is high. The cost is recall: light edits break long exact runs, so some leaks slip through.

questions.question: Why do real decontamination pipelines often flag on 'shares any n-gram for large n' rather than on an overlap fraction?
options: Because overlap fractions cannot be computed for long training documents with many millions of distinct n-grams
Because large n-grams cannot be hashed into a Bloom filter without far too many collisions
Because overlap fractions are always exactly 1.0 for large n, so they carry no information at all
A single shared 13-word run is already very unlikely by chance, so one match is strong evidence of leakage
questions.explanation: Long verbatim runs essentially never occur by coincidence, so even one shared 13-gram is strong evidence. That makes 'any shared long n-gram' a natural, high-precision rule.

questions.question: Which major source types make up a typical pretraining corpus, and what is each valued for?
options: Web (always high quality), code (only for code models), books (mostly short), math (abundant, low value)
Only web data, split by domain name into news, forums and encyclopedias, each weighted by its raw size
Web (huge, variable quality), code (structure, maybe reasoning), books (long-form), math (dense, scarce)
Web (small and clean), code (huge and noisy), books (low quality and short), math (abundant and very cheap)
questions.explanation: A corpus mixes sources of very different character: web is the bulk with variable quality; code teaches syntax and (evidence suggests) reasoning; books give long-form coherence; math is scarce but disproportionately valuable. Wikipedia, papers and curated Q&A are also common.

questions.question: In dataset mixing, how many tokens does source s contribute given weight $p_s$ (with $\sum_s p_s = 1$) and total budget $T_{\text{total}}$?
options: $T_{\text{total}} / p_s$
$p_s \cdot T_{\text{total}}$
$p_s$ times the tokens available in source s
$T_{\text{total}}$ divided equally among sources
questions.explanation: Mixture weights partition the total token budget: source s gets p_s · T_total tokens. Because the weights sum to 1, the allocations sum to the budget.

questions.question: Why are mixture weights a first-class design decision in pretraining?
options: They directly shape which capabilities the model gets: math near zero means bad math at any scale
They determine the model's parameter count, since each source gets its own embedding rows
They only affect the throughput of the data loader, not what the model learns from the tokens
They control the tokenizer's vocabulary size, because BPE merges are learned in proportion to each weight
questions.explanation: The proportions of code, math, books and web determine what the model is good at. Over-weighting code often yields a better coder and reasoner, while starving math leaves the model weak at math regardless of size.

questions.question: According to common reports, what is the typical effect of over-weighting code in a pretraining mixture?
options: A worse coder but a better mathematician
No measurable effect on any capability at all
A model that can only ever output source code
A better coder and (often) a better reasoner
questions.explanation: Increasing the code share tends to improve coding and often reasoning more generally. Mixture weights are therefore tuned deliberately rather than set by raw availability.

questions.question: What is the tension that motivates upsampling high-quality sources in pretraining mixtures?
options: High-quality sources are usually too large to fit in the budget, so most of their tokens are dropped
High-quality sources cannot be tokenized with the same BPE, so they need separate vocabularies
High-quality sources are small; weighting by raw size makes them a rounding error the model barely learns
High-quality sources contain more duplicates than web text, so they must be downweighted heavily in the mix
questions.explanation: You may have 900B tokens of filtered web but only 3B of good math. Proportional weighting would make math a tiny fraction of training, so the model would barely learn it.

questions.question: What does it mean to upsample a scarce high-quality source in a pretraining mixture?
options: Generate synthetic copies of it by translating it into other languages until it matches the web source's size
Give it a weight above its raw-token share, so its tokens are seen several times and web less than once
Remove all of the other sources entirely, so that the scarce source is the only data that remains
Increase the learning rate whenever its tokens appear in a batch, so each token has a larger effect
questions.explanation: Upsampling assigns the source a larger weight than its natural share. Because its data is small, filling that allocation means repeating it for multiple epochs, while the abundant web is only partly sampled.

questions.section: Numerical example — a token budget split
questions.question: In a mixture, how is 'epochs over source' computed for a source?
options: Tokens used from the source divided by tokens available in the source
Tokens available in the source divided by tokens used from it
The source's weight times the total token budget of the run
The total token budget divided by the number of sources in the overall mix
questions.explanation: Epochs over a source = tokens used / tokens available. Above 1 means the source is repeated; below 1 means only a fraction of it is sampled.

questions.section: Numerical example — a token budget split
questions.question: With a 300B-token budget, a web source of 900B tokens at weight 0.67 is seen about 0.22 times. What does an epoch value below 1 mean?
options: The source is repeated multiple times during training, once per extra epoch
The source is excluded from training entirely, since it is too big to sample
The source's tokens are each seen exactly once over the course of training
There is far more of that source than needed, so only a fraction of it is sampled
questions.explanation: 0.67 × 300B = 201B used out of 900B available gives 0.22 epochs. Below 1 means much of the source is never seen; the budget only samples a fraction of the abundant web.

questions.section: Numerical example — a token budget split
questions.question: In a 300B-token mixture where math (3B tokens available) has weight 0.07, what is the 'upsampling lever' made concrete?
options: Math is seen only 0.07 times because its weight is small, so it is effectively dropped from the mix
Math is dropped entirely because its raw size is smaller than 7% of the total 300B-token budget
Math's 3B tokens repeat about 7 times to fill its 21B allocation, so a scarce source punches above its size
Math is split into 7 separate datasets for curriculum, each one shown during a different phase of the training run
questions.explanation: 0.07 × 300B = 21B tokens needed from a 3B source, i.e. 7 epochs. Repetition lets a small high-value source count for much more of training than its raw size.

questions.section: Numerical example — a token budget split
questions.question: What is the risk of upsampling a small source too heavily?
options: Upsampling carries no risk at all, because high-quality data cannot be over-learned no matter how often it repeats
Repeating the same tokens many times is duplication and drives memorization; a few epochs is fine, many hurt
Upsampling makes the source's tokens unreadable to the tokenizer once they repeat past the vocabulary limit
Upsampling always causes training divergence after one epoch, because the loss on repeated tokens collapses
questions.explanation: Heavy repetition is duplication in disguise: the model memorizes those exact tokens. Empirically a few epochs over a high-quality source is fine, but many epochs hurts. You are choosing what the model over-learns.

questions.question: Which claim about mixture weights is PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED?
options: Open and frontier models use deliberate, non-proportional weights, e.g. GPT-3 undersampled Common Crawl
That GPT-4 was trained on exactly 30% code, as stated in the data section of its technical report
That Claude's pretraining mixture is 50% books, as stated in Anthropic's published model card for it
That Gemini uses no web data at all, relying only on licensed books, code and curated datasets instead
questions.explanation: GPT-3's paper reports down-weighting Common Crawl relative to its size and up-weighting WebText2, Books and Wikipedia, and The Pile and Dolma publish per-source weights. Exact closed-model mixtures are not public.

questions.question: Which open datasets publish their per-source mixture weights explicitly?
options: GPT-4's training set and Claude's training set
Only C4, in its original T5 release
Only MMLU and GSM8K, as eval sets
The Pile and Dolma
questions.explanation: The Pile and Dolma publish their per-source weights explicitly, giving documented examples of deliberate, non-proportional mixtures. MMLU and GSM8K are benchmarks, not training corpora.

questions.question: What is the REASONABLE INDUSTRY PRACTICE for choosing mixture weights?
options: Set every source's weight proportional to its raw size, then train once on the resulting mix
Choose weights at random and keep the first mixture whose training run converges without any loss spikes
Train many small proxy models on candidate mixtures and pick the one with the best validation loss
Copy GPT-4's published mixture weights, since they are the strongest documented recipe available
questions.explanation: Mixtures are searched, not guessed: labs train small proxy models on candidate mixtures and select by validation loss or downstream evals. Increasing code and math share to improve reasoning is also widely reported.
