questions.question: Why are claims like 'GPT-4 was N% code' classified as INFERENCE / SPECULATION?
options: Because GPT-4 was trained only on web data, so any code share must be guessed from crawl statistics
The exact mixture weights of closed frontier models are not public unless the lab documents them
Because code percentages cannot be measured at all once source documents have been tokenized
Because mixture weights change during inference, so no single training percentage is meaningful
questions.explanation: Closed labs do not publish their exact mixtures, so any specific percentage is a guess. Distinguishing documented facts from speculation avoids overclaiming.

questions.question: What does the Chinchilla rule of thumb (Hoffmann et al., 2022) say about tokens per parameter for compute-optimal training?
options: Tokens should scale roughly with parameters, about 20 tokens per parameter
About 1 token per parameter, so data scales one-to-one with the model's size
About 200 tokens per parameter, ten times the commonly quoted figure
Tokens should be fixed regardless of parameter count once data is clean
questions.explanation: For a fixed compute budget Chinchilla found tokens should scale with parameters, with a rule of thumb near 20 tokens per parameter. A 7B model therefore wants on the order of 140B tokens.

questions.question: Under the Chinchilla rule of thumb, roughly how many training tokens does a 7B-parameter model want?
options: About 7B tokens (1x)
About 1.4T tokens
About 14B tokens
About 140B tokens
questions.explanation: 7B parameters × 20 tokens per parameter ≈ 140B tokens. Modern models often train far past this for better inference economics, as LLaMA did.

questions.question: Why do many modern models train on far more tokens than the Chinchilla-optimal ~20 tokens per parameter?
options: Because Chinchilla's rule was shown to be wrong by a factor of 100 in later scaling work
Because more training tokens shrink the parameter count needed automatically
For better inference economics — a smaller model trained longer is cheaper to serve
Because tokenizers produce many more tokens than expected from the raw text
questions.explanation: Chinchilla optimizes training compute only. Training a smaller model past the optimal token count makes it better per parameter, which pays off when the model is served many times, as LLaMA did.

questions.question: How do the Chinchilla token budget and dataset mixture weights compose?
options: Mixing sets how many tokens to train on, while Chinchilla sets which sources those tokens come from
Chinchilla sets how many tokens; mixing sets which tokens, by partitioning that budget across sources
They are alternatives: you use one or the other, since both of them set the total token budget
Chinchilla sets the peak learning rate, while mixing sets the batch size used for each source
questions.explanation: The total token budget comes from compute and the Chinchilla ratio; mixture weights then divide it among web, code, books, math, etc. Both are set before training starts.

questions.question: Which two data knobs are set before a single training step runs and move final loss more than most architecture choices?
options: Token budget (how many tokens total) and mixture weights (what fraction from each source)
Dropout rate and weight decay, which regularize the final weights after training
Number of attention heads and MLP width, which set the model's capacity per layer
Warmup steps and gradient clipping, which stabilize the early phase of training
questions.explanation: Token budget and mixture weights are both fixed up front. Together they determine how much and which data the model learns from, which matters more than most architecture tweaks.

questions.question: In Module 4's `get_batch`, why does data order not matter?
options: Because the model is trained for only one step in Module 4, so order never has a chance to matter
Because the loss is invariant to example order by definition, for any optimizer and learning rate
Because get_batch sorts windows by quality first, so the order is already fixed and the same on every run
It samples windows uniformly from one packed stream, so every part of the corpus is seen throughout
questions.explanation: Uniform random window sampling washes out order: any region of the corpus is equally likely at any point in training. A curriculum deliberately changes this.

questions.question: What is a data curriculum in LLM pretraining?
options: Removing benchmark text from the training data before it starts
Choosing the tokenizer's vocabulary size in phases as training runs
Deliberately changing what the model sees when during training
Training several models in sequence and averaging their weights
questions.explanation: A data curriculum changes the composition or order of data over the course of training. Its most important instance in modern pretraining is annealing toward high-quality data at the end.

questions.question: What is data annealing in pretraining?
options: At the start of training, using only high-quality data, then switching to web data once loss has dropped
Near the end of training, shifting the mix toward higher-quality data while decaying the learning rate
Gradually increasing the learning rate at the end of training so the model escapes its final local minimum
Removing all code and math data in the final phase so the model finishes on clean natural-language text
questions.explanation: Annealing changes the late-training mixture toward the highest-quality data and pairs it with learning-rate decay. The final, small refining updates are then shaped by the best tokens.

questions.question: What is the intuition for saving the highest-quality data for late in training?
options: Early, big coarse updates tolerate rough web data; late, small refining updates should be shaped by the best tokens
Early training ignores data quality entirely, because the gradients stay close to zero until the warmup phase has finished
Late training has the highest learning rate of the run, so whatever data is shown then has the largest effect
High-quality data cannot be tokenized until late in training, once the BPE merges have finished being learned
questions.explanation: This mirrors learning-rate decay: early steps are large and coarse, so noisy web data is acceptable; late steps are small refinements, so you want the most trustworthy data to determine where the weights settle.

questions.question: Which open-model reports PUBLICLY DOCUMENT a multi-phase pretraining with a late high-quality data phase?
options: GPT-4 and Claude, whose technical reports publish the exact multi-phase mixture schedules they used
BERT and RoBERTa, whose reports describe an easy-to-hard ordering followed by a quality phase
Only Chinchilla, whose report introduces data annealing as part of its compute-optimal recipe
OLMo 2 (two-stage pretrain, late high-quality phase) and Llama 3 (annealing on high-quality data)
questions.explanation: OLMo 2 (2024) describes a two-stage pretrain with a late high-quality phase, and Llama 3 (2024) documents adjusting the mix and annealing on high-quality data toward the end. Closed models' schedules are not public.

questions.question: Which curriculum practice is classified as REASONABLE INDUSTRY PRACTICE rather than publicly documented in a single recipe or speculation?
options: Strict easy-to-hard example ordering throughout pretraining, ranked by a small reference model's loss
Training only on synthetic data from the start, then mixing web data in during annealing
Pairing the quality anneal with LR decay, and folding fresh curated or synthetic data into it
Removing all web data after the first epoch so later epochs see only curated sources
questions.explanation: Combining the anneal with LR decay and using the annealing phase to add fresh curated or synthetic high-quality data is common, sensible, and reported in several technical reports. Strict easy-to-hard ordering is not established.

questions.question: What is the status of strict 'easy-to-hard' example ordering (classic curriculum learning) for large-scale LM pretraining?
options: PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED as standard practice in all frontier models, with their orderings published
SPECULATION: not settled; much pretraining is still IID sampling plus a late quality anneal
Proven harmful in every published study, so it is classified as a documented anti-pattern
Required by the Chinchilla scaling law, which assumes examples are seen from easy to hard
questions.explanation: Claims that strict easy-to-hard ordering reliably helps large LM pretraining are not settled. Elaborate ordering is researched but not standard; most pretraining is IID sampling plus a late anneal. Do not present it as known best practice.

questions.question: How does the meaning of 'curriculum' in modern LLM pretraining differ from its classic ML meaning?
options: Classic ML means ordering examples easy to hard; in LLMs it mostly means phased mixtures and a late anneal
Classic ML means data mixing across sources; in LLM pretraining it means deduplication of the whole corpus
Both mean strictly sorting the training examples by length, from short sequences to long ones
Classic ML means learning-rate annealing; LLM pretraining means strict easy-to-hard example ordering
questions.explanation: Classic curriculum learning sorts examples by difficulty. In LLM pretraining the term is used loosely for phase-based mixtures and LR schedules. Keeping the senses distinct avoids overclaiming what labs actually do.

questions.question: In the complete data pipeline, which steps come between deduplication and BPE encoding?
options: Language identification, then HTML text extraction and boilerplate removal
Packing documents into a stream, then sampling with get_batch
Quality filtering with a classifier, then toxicity and PII filtering
Decontamination, mixing sources by weight, and a late quality anneal
questions.explanation: The order is raw crawl → extract → langid → quality → dedup → decontaminate → mix sources by weight → ordered, quality-annealed documents → BPE encode → pack → get_batch → model.

questions.question: What is the overall lesson of the data-engineering module about where model quality comes from?
options: Data only matters for small models; at scale, architecture choices dominate the final loss instead
Only the tokenizer affects final loss; the other data stages are mostly cosmetic
At the frontier, data engineering is modeling: every pipeline stage is a lever on the loss
Data stages can be ignored once the model is large enough to filter noise itself
questions.explanation: Extraction, filtering, dedup, decontamination, mixing and curriculum all move the final loss without appearing in the model code. At the frontier, these choices are as much 'modeling' as the architecture.

questions.question: When decontaminating with n = 4 and a fraction-based threshold of overlap ≥ 0.5, why might the check over-flag legitimate training documents?
options: Because 4-grams are too long to ever match by chance, so every match the check finds is genuine leakage
Short runs like 'the fact that the' or 'as a result of' occur by chance in unrelated text, giving false positives
Because a threshold of 0.5 is too high to catch anything shorter than a full paragraph of copied text
Because 4-grams ignore punctuation, so unrelated sentences collapse into the same normalized n-grams
questions.explanation: Common 4-word phrases appear across unrelated documents, so a low-n, fraction-based check fires on documents that merely share phrasing with a question. Those false positives delete clean training data.

questions.question: What is a safer decontamination choice than n = 4 with a fraction threshold, and what does it trade away?
options: Use a larger n (8–13) and/or flag any shared long n-gram: high precision, but edited leaks slip through
Use n = 1 so every shared word counts: perfect recall, with essentially no false positives on common text
Use a threshold of 0.01 so even tiny overlaps are flagged: this catches everything with no trade-off
Remove the benchmark items instead of training documents: the corpus stays intact, with no trade-off
questions.explanation: Long verbatim runs are almost never coincidental, so precision is high. The cost is recall: paraphrased or lightly edited leaks break long exact runs. Decontamination deliberately errs toward precision because deleting good data is costly and long-run matches are what truly inflate scores.

questions.question: Why is reporting eval numbers without a decontamination pass a mistake?
options: It makes the eval run slower, since leaked items must be re-scored
It biases the score downward, because memorized items confuse the model at test time
It violates the benchmark's license, which forbids training on it
If benchmark text was in training, the score measures memorization, not skill
questions.explanation: Without decontamination you cannot know whether a high score reflects ability or recall of leaked items. The number loses its value for you and for readers.

questions.question: Why is weighting pretraining sources strictly by raw size a mistake?
options: It makes the total token budget too small to reach the Chinchilla-optimal ratio
It causes far too much upsampling of web data relative to every other source in the mix
It buries scarce high-quality data under abundant web; deliberate weights are the norm
It forces every source to be repeated exactly once, which wastes the small ones
questions.explanation: Proportional weighting lets the largest source — filtered web — dominate, so small high-value sources barely register. Practice is to set non-proportional weights and upsample scarce quality data.

questions.question: What is the 'over-upsampling' mistake in data mixing?
options: Giving the web source a weight larger than 0.5, so it dominates every batch
Repeating a small source too many times: disguised duplication that drives memorization
Using more than four sources in the mix, which makes the weights impossible to tune well
Sampling web data less than once, so most of the crawl is never seen in training
questions.explanation: Upsampling is useful in moderation, but repeating a small source dozens of times makes the model memorize it, just like duplicated data. A few epochs is the safe range.

questions.question: What is the 'overclaiming curriculum' mistake?
options: Presenting strict easy-to-hard ordering as established at scale, when only a late anneal is documented
Claiming that a late quality anneal is documented for open models, when no technical report describes one
Claiming that get_batch samples uniformly, when it actually orders windows from easy to hard
Claiming that learning-rate decay exists in pretraining, when real runs keep the LR constant
questions.explanation: A late quality-anneal is documented (e.g. OLMo 2, Llama 3); strict easy→hard ordering is not established for large LM pretraining. Mark the difference between documented practice and speculation.

questions.question: Which papers should be read for documented data mixing and quality annealing details?
options: Attention Is All You Need, BERT, and RoBERTa, for their data and pretraining sections
Only Chinchilla, since it sets both the token budget and the mixture weights
The Adam, AdamW and Lion optimizer papers, for their data-ordering experiments
GPT-3 (source upsampling), OLMo 2 (late high-quality phase) and Llama 3 (annealing)
questions.explanation: GPT-3's data section documents source upsampling, OLMo 2 describes a two-stage pretrain with a late high-quality phase, and Llama 3 documents data-mix and annealing choices. Chinchilla is the reference for token budgets.

questions.question: Why does a directional overlap normalized by the test item's n-gram count make 'test item inside train' read as 1.0, while symmetric Jaccard would not?
options: Because Jaccard is undefined when one set is contained in the other, so the score falls back to zero
Because directional overlap double-counts the shared n-grams, which pushes contained items up to 1.0
A huge train document's many n-grams swamp the Jaccard union; normalizing by the test item avoids that
Because Jaccard is always exactly 1.0 for any contained set, so it cannot separate leaked from clean items
questions.explanation: If the test item is fully contained in a large training document, Jaccard = |test| / |train ∪ test| is small because the union is dominated by train's n-grams. Directional overlap divides by |test| only, giving 1.0 for full containment.

questions.question: Classify these statements: 'Llama 3 annealed on high-quality data at the end of pretraining' and 'GPT-4 was trained on 30% code'.
options: Both are PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED in technical reports
The first is PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED; the second is SPECULATION
The first is SPECULATION; the second is PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED
Both are REASONABLE INDUSTRY PRACTICE, not publicly documented
questions.explanation: Llama 3's report describes late-stage data-mix adjustment and annealing on high-quality data, so the first is documented. GPT-4's exact mixture is not public, so a specific code percentage is speculation.

questions.question: How does annealing change what happens compared with Module 4's uniform `get_batch` sampling?
options: It changes the stream over time so late training draws from a higher-quality mix, usually with LR decay
It shuffles the same packed stream more thoroughly, so every window is sampled with exactly equal frequency
It increases the batch size late in training, so each step averages over more high-quality windows
It removes the end-of-text separator between documents, so the late stream reads as one long text
questions.explanation: Uniform sampling from one fixed stream makes order irrelevant. Annealing makes the data distribution time-dependent, shifting late training toward the best data while the LR decays, so the best data shapes the final weights.

questions.question: After the full data pipeline (extraction through curriculum), what does the next module upgrade?
options: The tokenizer: BPE is replaced by character-level tokenization for robustness
The optimizer: AdamW is replaced by plain SGD with momentum for stability
The evaluation harness: benchmarks are replaced by held-out perplexity only
The model: the GPT-2 block is upgraded to RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, GQA and MoE
questions.explanation: With clean, weighted, ordered data in hand, the course returns to the model and upgrades the GPT-2 block to modern components used by current frontier LLMs: RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, GQA and MoE.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Which family of current open LLMs uses RoPE as its position encoding?
options: LLaMA, Llama 3, Mistral, Qwen and DeepSeek
Only GPT-2 and GPT-3 style decoder-only models
Only encoder models such as BERT and RoBERTa
Only Mixture-of-Experts models such as Switch
questions.explanation: RoPE is the position encoding in nearly every current open LLM: LLaMA, Llama 3, Mistral, Qwen and DeepSeek. GPT-2 used a learned absolute position table (wpe) instead. That is why swapping in RoPE is the first change when turning a GPT-2 into a modern model.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Which practical capability does RoPE enable for a model trained at a 4K context?
options: Training it without any causal attention mask at all
Removing the need for a KV cache during generation
Halving the number of attention heads at inference
Stretching it to 32K+ context with light adaptation
questions.explanation: Because rotation is defined at any position, a RoPE model trained at 4K context can be stretched to 32K+ with light adaptation (e.g. rescaling the frequencies). A learned position table cannot do this, since it has no rows past its trained length. RoPE does nothing about masks, KV caches or head counts.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: why the GPT-2 scheme runs out of room
questions.question: In a GPT-2 style model, how is a token's input vector formed with respect to position?
options: Token embedding multiplied elementwise by a fixed sinusoid of the position index, with no learned table at all
Token embedding rotated by a position-dependent angle in each pair of channels before the first block
Token embedding plus a learned positional embedding looked up from a table wpe of shape (block_size, C)
Token embedding concatenated with a one-hot position index, doubling the residual width to 2C
questions.explanation: GPT-2 sums two learned vectors: the token embedding (which word) and a positional embedding read from the wpe table of shape (block_size, C) (which slot). Row 0 is position 0, row 1 is position 1, and so on. Rotation by position is what RoPE does instead, at attention time.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: why the GPT-2 scheme runs out of room
questions.question: A GPT-2 style model with a learned position table was trained with block_size = 1024. What happens at position 1024?
options: It reuses row 0, wrapping around like a ring buffer so positions repeat
There is no row for it, so the model cannot represent that position at all
It interpolates between rows 1022 and 1023, extrapolating the learned trend
It falls back to a sinusoidal encoding automatically for positions past the table
questions.explanation: The learned table has exactly block_size rows, indexed 0 to 1023. Position 1024 has never been seen and has no vector, so the model simply cannot represent a context longer than it was trained on. There is no built-in wraparound, interpolation or fallback.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: why the GPT-2 scheme runs out of room
questions.question: Why is an absolute learned position embedding said to not encode relative position?
options: Because the table is too small to hold relative offsets, so it can only keep one vector per absolute position index
Nothing makes a gap of 5 look alike at (10, 15) and (300, 305), so each relationship is relearned at every location
Because absolute embeddings are added to the values V rather than to the queries and keys that form scores
Because absolute embeddings are frozen after initialization, so they cannot adapt to relative structure
questions.explanation: The model learns fixed vectors for 'position 5' and 'position 200', but linguistically what matters is usually the gap between tokens. In the absolute scheme nothing makes '5 apart' look identical regardless of where it occurs, so the model must relearn every relationship at every absolute location. The table is learned (not frozen) and is added to the input, not specifically to V.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: why the GPT-2 scheme runs out of room
questions.question: What is the core idea of RoPE (Su et al. 2021) compared with absolute position embeddings?
options: Rotate each query and key at attention time by an angle that grows with its position, instead of adding an input vector
Add a learned relative-position bias, indexed by the offset between two tokens, to every attention score before softmax
Multiply each token embedding by a position-dependent scalar gain at the input, so later tokens carry larger norms
Append the position index as one extra channel of the residual stream, so every layer can read it directly
questions.explanation: RoPE does not add any position vector at the input. At attention time it rotates each query and key by an angle proportional to its position. Since the dot product of two rotated vectors depends only on the difference of their angles, the score becomes a function of relative offset, and rotation exists for any position.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: why the GPT-2 scheme runs out of room
questions.question: Under RoPE, which of the following is rotated by a position-dependent angle?
options: Queries, keys and values
Only the values and the residual stream
The token embeddings at the input layer
Only the queries and keys
questions.explanation: RoPE rotates Q and K only; nothing is added to V or to the residual stream. Position should steer who attends to whom (the scores), not alter the content passed along via V. The input embedding is left untouched.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: why the GPT-2 scheme runs out of room
questions.question: Why does RoPE not 'run out of room' the way a learned position table does?
options: It stores a larger table of 1 million rows by default, which covers any practical context length
It reuses the last learned position for all longer positions, so attention sees them as one token
Rotation by m*omega is defined for any position m, so there is no fixed-size table to exhaust
It compresses positions logarithmically into a fixed table, so far positions share nearby rows
questions.explanation: RoPE computes the rotation angle from the position on the fly (m times a frequency), which is defined for every integer m. A learned table has exactly block_size rows and nothing beyond. RoPE has no learned position table at all.

questions.section: 2. Intuition: rotating a 2-D vector by its position
questions.question: What does rotating a 2-D vector by an angle theta do to its length?
options: Scales the length by cos(theta) and turns it
Scales the length by theta, measured in radians
Leaves the length unchanged and only turns its direction
Doubles the length when theta = pi, and keeps it otherwise
questions.explanation: A rotation turns the arrow by theta counter-clockwise and keeps its length exactly the same. That is why rotating (1, 0) by angles 0, 1, 2 radians gives (1, 0), (0.5403, 0.8415), (-0.4161, 0.9093), all of length 1. Only the direction encodes position.

questions.section: 2. Intuition: rotating a 2-D vector by its position
questions.question: What is the result of applying the 2-D rotation matrix $R(\theta)$ to the vector $(x_0, x_1)$?
options: $(x_0\cos\theta + x_1\sin\theta,\ -x_0\sin\theta + x_1\cos\theta)$
$(x_0\cos\theta - x_1\sin\theta,\ x_0\sin\theta + x_1\cos\theta)$
$(x_0\sin\theta - x_1\cos\theta,\ x_0\cos\theta + x_1\sin\theta)$
$(x_0\cos\theta,\ x_1\sin\theta)$
questions.explanation: $R(\theta)$ has rows $(\cos\theta, -\sin\theta)$ and $(\sin\theta, \cos\theta)$. Multiplying gives $x_0\cos\theta - x_1\sin\theta$ for the first coordinate and $x_0\sin\theta + x_1\cos\theta$ for the second. The minus sign in the first row is what makes it a counter-clockwise rotation rather than a reflection or scaling.

questions.section: 2. Intuition: rotating a 2-D vector by its position
questions.question: Under RoPE, for a 2-D vector at position m with fixed frequency omega, by what angle is the vector rotated?
options: m * omega
omega / (m+1)
omega^m
m + omega
questions.explanation: RoPE's rule is to rotate by theta = m * omega. Position 0 is not rotated, position 1 is turned by omega, position 2 by 2*omega, and so on, so the angle grows linearly with position. The other forms would not give the clean angle-difference cancellation in the dot product.

questions.section: 2. Intuition: rotating a 2-D vector by its position
questions.question: Under RoPE, what happens to the query or key vector at position 0?
options: It is rotated by the maximum angle, a full half turn of pi
It is zeroed out, because sin(0) multiplies it
It is rotated by exactly 90 degrees in every pair
It is left unchanged, because the rotation angle is 0
questions.explanation: The angle is m * omega, so at m = 0 the angle is 0 and R(0) is the identity. Rotating (1, 0) at position 0 returns (1.0, 0.0). Later positions are turned progressively further.

questions.section: 3. Mathematics: why the dot product becomes relative
questions.question: Under RoPE, a 2-D query $\mathbf{q}$ at position $m$ and key $\mathbf{k}$ at position $n$ are rotated and dotted. What does the score simplify to?
options: $\mathbf{q}^\top R\big((n+m)\omega\big)\mathbf{k}$
$\mathbf{q}^\top R(mn\omega)\mathbf{k}$
$\cos(m\omega)\cos(n\omega)\,\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}$
$\mathbf{q}^\top R\big((n-m)\omega\big)\mathbf{k}$
questions.explanation: The score is $\mathbf{q}^\top R(m\omega)^\top R(n\omega)\mathbf{k}$. Using $R(a)^\top = R(-a)$ and that rotations compose by adding angles, this becomes $\mathbf{q}^\top R((n-m)\omega)\mathbf{k}$. Positions appear only through their difference, which is the whole point of RoPE; a sum $n+m$ would not be translation-invariant.

questions.section: 3. Mathematics: why the dot product becomes relative
questions.question: Which two facts about rotation matrices make RoPE's dot product depend only on relative position?
options: R(a) is symmetric, and rotations commute with all matrices
R(a) has determinant 0, and R(a)R(b) = R(ab)
R(a)^T = R(-a), and rotations compose by adding angles
R(a)^T = R(a), and R(a) + R(b) = R(a + b)
questions.explanation: Transposing a rotation is rotating backward: R(a)^T = R(-a). Rotations compose additively: R(-m*omega)R(n*omega) = R((n-m)*omega). Together they turn the product of two absolute rotations into a single rotation by the offset. Rotation matrices have determinant 1, are not symmetric in general, and do not add linearly.

questions.section: 3. Mathematics: why the dot product becomes relative
questions.question: Under RoPE, two token pairs are both 7 positions apart, one at positions (2, 9) and another at (500, 507). How do their position-dependent score contributions compare (same q and k vectors)?
options: The farther pair gets a smaller score, because its rotation angles are much larger overall
They are identical, because the score depends on m and n only through their difference
The farther pair gets a larger score, because rotations accumulate with position
They differ by a factor of cos(500), the rotation of the farther query
questions.explanation: After rotation the score is q^T R((n-m)omega) k, which contains the positions only through n - m. Two pairs with the same offset therefore produce the same score regardless of where they sit. This is relative position obtained from purely absolute rotations, with no relative-position table.

questions.section: 3. Mathematics: why the dot product becomes relative
questions.question: What does RoPE NOT need in order to obtain relative-position behaviour in attention?
options: A relative-position table or cross terms between positions
Rotating both the queries and the keys at every layer
A position-dependent angle for each token in the sequence
The dot-product form of the query-key attention score
questions.explanation: RoPE gets relative position purely by rotating each side by its own absolute angle; no relative-position table and no cross terms are needed. It does need both Q and K rotated by position-dependent angles, and it relies on the score being a dot product so the rotations cancel to their difference.

questions.section: 3.1 More than two dimensions: pairs and per-pair frequencies
questions.question: How does RoPE handle a head vector with d_h = 64 or 128 channels rather than 2?
options: It splits the channels into d_h/2 pairs and rotates each pair independently with its own frequency
It rotates the whole d_h-dimensional vector with one high-dimensional rotation of a single frequency
It rotates only the first two channels with the base frequency and leaves the other channels untouched
It projects the vector down to two dimensions, rotates it there, and projects it back up to d_h
questions.explanation: RoPE splits the d_h channels into d_h/2 pairs, (x0, x1), (x2, x3), ..., and applies an independent 2-D rotation to each pair. Each pair gets its own frequency omega_p. The relative-offset identity holds per pair, so it holds for the full dot product, which is just the sum over pairs.

questions.section: 3.1 More than two dimensions: pairs and per-pair frequencies
questions.question: In RoPE, what is the frequency of coordinate pair $p$ for head dimension $d_h$?
options: $\omega_p = \text{base}^{2p/(d_h-1)}$
$\omega_p = p/\text{base}$
$\omega_p = \text{base}^{-p}$
$\omega_p = \text{base}^{-2p/d_h}$
questions.explanation: Each pair $p = 0, 1, \dots, d_h/2 - 1$ gets $\omega_p = \text{base}^{-2p/d_h}$, with base usually 10000. So pair 0 has $\omega_0 = 1$ and frequencies shrink geometrically toward the last pair. A positive exponent would make later pairs spin faster, the opposite of the design.

questions.section: 3.1 More than two dimensions: pairs and per-pair frequencies
questions.question: What is the original base value used in RoPE's frequencies, and where does it come from?
options: 1024, matching GPT-2's block_size so angles wrap at the context end
2, so that the frequency of each successive pair halves exactly
10000, inherited from the sinusoidal embeddings of the 2017 Transformer
500000, chosen for the original RoFormer paper to support a 4K context length
questions.explanation: RoPE uses base = 10000, the same constant as the sinusoidal position encodings of the 2017 Transformer. The frequency for pair p is base^(-2p/d_h). The other values are not the original choice described here.

questions.section: 3.1 More than two dimensions: pairs and per-pair frequencies
questions.question: In RoPE, which coordinate pair rotates fastest, and at what rate?
options: The last pair, at 1 radian per position
Pair 0, at 1 radian per position
Pair 0, at 1/10000 radians per position
All pairs rotate at the same rate
questions.explanation: With omega_p = base^(-2p/d_h), pair 0 has exponent 0, so omega_0 = 1 radian per position, the fastest. Later pairs turn ever more slowly, with the last barely moving over the whole sequence. Different speeds per pair are the point of the multi-scale design.

questions.section: 3.1 More than two dimensions: pairs and per-pair frequencies
questions.question: In RoPE, what kind of positional information do the fast-rotating and slow-rotating pairs carry?
options: Fast pairs carry coarse, long-range position; slow pairs resolve the fine, nearby offsets
Fast pairs resolve fine, nearby offsets; slow pairs carry coarse, long-range position
Fast pairs carry token identity, while slow pairs carry the absolute position
Both carry the same positional information, only at different numerical precision
questions.explanation: Pairs spin at different speeds like the hands of a clock. A fast pair changes a lot between neighbouring positions, so it distinguishes small offsets; a slow pair changes little locally but distinguishes positions far apart. Together they form a multi-scale position code.

questions.section: 3.1 More than two dimensions: pairs and per-pair frequencies
questions.question: Why does RoPE's relative-offset property hold for a full d_h-dimensional head when it is proven only for one 2-D pair?
options: The full dot product is the sum of per-pair dot products, and the identity holds for each pair
Because all of the coordinate pairs share one frequency, so the head behaves like a single pair
Because the high-dimensional rotation is orthogonal as a whole, which makes every product shift-invariant
Because softmax normalizes away the absolute positions, leaving only the offset between the two tokens
questions.explanation: Each pair is rotated independently, and for each pair the rotated dot product depends only on n - m. The full head dot product is just the sum over pairs, so it too depends only on the offset. Pairs have different frequencies; it is the per-pair argument plus additivity that matters.

questions.section: 4. Tensor shapes: where RoPE sits in attention
questions.question: At what point in the attention computation is RoPE applied?
options: Before the QKV projection, on the (B, T, C) input, so all three projections see rotated features
After the softmax, on the (B, n_h, T, T) attention weights before they multiply V
After multiplying by V, on the (B, n_h, T, d_h) head outputs before the merge
After the QKV projection and head split, on Q and K of shape (B, n_h, T, d_h), before QK^T
questions.explanation: RoPE acts on per-head queries and keys of shape (B, n_h, T, d_h), right after projection and head split and right before the scores QK^T. Applying it before the head split would mix pairs across heads, and applying it after the softmax would not affect the scores.

questions.section: 4. Tensor shapes: where RoPE sits in attention
questions.question: How does RoPE change the shape of the query and key tensors?
options: It halves d_h, because each pair of channels is merged into one
It doubles d_h by appending separate sin and cos channels
It does not; (B, n_h, T, d_h) in and (B, n_h, T, d_h) out
It adds one extra position channel to d_h for each head
questions.explanation: RoPE only rotates within each length-d_h vector, so the shape is unchanged. The complex view temporarily reads d_h real numbers as d_h/2 complex numbers, but the result is flattened back to d_h. Nothing is appended or removed.

questions.section: 4. Tensor shapes: where RoPE sits in attention
questions.question: Why does RoPE leave the value vectors V and the residual stream unrotated?
options: Because V has a different head dimension than Q and K, so its channel pairs would not line up
Because rotating V as well would make the KV cache too large to store during decoding
Position should steer who attends to whom, not corrupt the content that gets passed along
Because V is computed after the softmax, when the position angles are no longer available
questions.explanation: The relative-position effect comes entirely from rotating Q and K, which changes the attention scores. V carries the content each token contributes; rotating it would distort that content without helping position encoding. V has the same head dim and is computed before the softmax.

questions.section: 4. Tensor shapes: where RoPE sits in attention
questions.question: In RoPE, what is the precomputed table freqs_cis, and how is it used each batch?
options: A float32 table of shape (B, T) that is recomputed from scratch for every batch on the CPU
A complex64 table of shape (T_max, d_h/2), sliced to [:T] and broadcast over the (B, n_h) axes
A learned parameter of shape (block_size, C) that is added to the token embeddings at the input
A complex64 table of shape (n_h, d_h), indexed by head and shared across all sequence positions
questions.explanation: freqs_cis holds the unit rotation e^{i m omega_p} for every position m up to T_max and every pair p, so its shape is (T_max, d_h/2), dtype complex64. It is precomputed once, sliced to the current length T, and broadcast across batch and heads. It is not learned and not added to the input.

questions.question: Why can a 2-D rotation by $\theta$ be implemented as a complex multiplication?
options: Packing $(x_0, x_1)$ as $x_0 + i x_1$ and multiplying by $e^{i\theta}$ gives real and imaginary parts equal to the rotated pair
Because adding $i\theta$ to $x_0 + i x_1$ rotates it by $\theta$, since imaginary offsets act as angles in the plane
Because the complex conjugate of $x_0 + i x_1$ is its rotation by $\theta$, so taking conj applies the turn directly
Because multiplying $x_0 + i x_1$ by the real number $\theta$ itself rotates it by that angle about the origin
questions.explanation: $(x_0 + i x_1)(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) = (x_0\cos\theta - x_1\sin\theta) + i(x_0\sin\theta + x_1\cos\theta)$, exactly the rotated pair. So multiplying by the unit complex number $e^{i\theta}$ (written cis theta) rotates by $\theta$. Adding or multiplying by a real number does not rotate.

questions.question: Why is the LLaMA RoPE implementation built on torch.view_as_complex?
options: Complex tensors use half the memory of the equivalent real-valued tensors on GPU
view_as_complex adds learned phase parameters to each head
Real-valued tensors cannot represent the sine and cosine values
Rotating every coordinate pair becomes one elementwise complex multiply
questions.explanation: Each adjacent pair of channels is reinterpreted as one complex number, and multiplying by e^{i m omega_p} rotates it. So 'rotate every pair' collapses to a single elementwise complex multiplication over the tensor. It is a convenience and efficiency trick, not a memory saving or a source of learned parameters.

questions.question: In precompute_freqs_cis, what does torch.polar(torch.ones_like(angles), angles) produce?
options: A real tensor holding cos(angles) only, with the sine part of the rotation discarded
A complex tensor whose magnitude equals the angle m*omega_p and whose phase is always 0
A tensor of shape (dim, max_seq_len) of random unit vectors, one per coordinate pair
A complex tensor of magnitude 1 and phase m*omega_p, i.e. freqs_cis[m, p] = e^{i m omega_p}
questions.explanation: torch.polar(magnitude, angle) builds magnitude * e^{i angle}. With all magnitudes equal to one, every entry is a unit rotation, which is what RoPE needs so it never changes vector length. The angles come from torch.outer(t, freqs), giving shape (max_seq_len, dim/2).

questions.question: In precompute_freqs_cis, what does torch.outer(t, freqs) compute?
options: A (dim/2,) vector of the frequencies omega_p, one entry for each coordinate pair
A (max_seq_len,) vector of positions m, from 0 to max_seq_len - 1
A (max_seq_len, dim/2) table of angles m * omega_p for every position and pair
A (dim, dim) rotation matrix that is shared by every position in the sequence
questions.explanation: t is the positions 0..max_seq_len-1 and freqs is the dim/2 frequencies omega_p. Their outer product gives every combination m * omega_p, the rotation angle for position m in pair p. This angle table is then turned into unit complex numbers with torch.polar.

questions.question: In apply_rope, what does torch.view_as_complex do to a tensor reshaped to (B, nh, T, hd//2, 2)?
options: Copies the tensor into a new complex buffer of shape (B, nh, T, hd), one complex number per real channel
Reinterprets the last axis of size 2 as one complex number without copying, giving (B, nh, T, hd/2)
Converts each real number into a complex number with zero imaginary part, keeping all axes
Computes the magnitude of each pair, giving a real tensor of shape (B, nh, T, hd//2)
questions.explanation: view_as_complex is a view: it treats each trailing pair (real, imag) as a single complex value without copying memory. The shape goes from (..., hd/2, 2) to (..., hd/2). view_as_real reverses the reinterpretation, and flatten(3) merges the pair axis back into hd.

questions.question: In apply_rope, how is freqs_cis[:T] shaped so it can multiply the complex queries of shape (B, nh, T, hd/2)?
options: It is viewed as (1, 1, T, hd/2) so it broadcasts over the batch and head axes
It is repeated to (B, nh, T, hd/2) with an explicit memory copy before multiplying
It is transposed to (hd/2, T) so that it lines up with the last axis of the queries
It is viewed as (B, 1, 1, hd/2), so one rotation is shared per batch element
questions.explanation: The rotation depends only on position and pair, not on batch element or head, so freqs_cis[:T].view(1, 1, T, hd // 2) broadcasts across B and nh. No copy is needed. Using the wrong axes would rotate by the wrong position.

questions.question: In apply_rope, what does .flatten(3) do after torch.view_as_real(q_c * rot)?
options: Merges the trailing pair axis of size 2 back into d_h, restoring shape (B, nh, T, hd)
Flattens the batch and head axes together into one (B*nh) axis for the matmul
Removes the imaginary part, keeping only the real channel of each rotated pair
Sums each pair into one real number, halving the last axis to hd/2 channels
questions.explanation: view_as_real turns the (B, nh, T, hd/2) complex result into (B, nh, T, hd/2, 2) real numbers. flatten(3) merges axes 3 and 4 into one of size hd. Nothing is summed or dropped; the rotated real and imaginary parts become the two channels of each pair.

questions.question: In apply_rope, why are q and k cast with .float() before the complex view, and then .type_as(q) at the end?
options: Because view_as_complex only accepts float64 inputs, so .float() upcasts first
Because the rotation must always be returned in float32 for the downstream attention kernel
Because type_as adds a learned scaling that restores the original activation norm
The rotation runs in float32/complex64 for precision, then is cast back to the input dtype
questions.explanation: q.float() ensures the complex view is complex64 and the multiply is done in float32 precision, which matters when activations are half precision. type_as(q) returns the rotated tensor in the original dtype so the rest of attention is unaffected. type_as is just a cast.

questions.section: 6. Numerical example: the relative property, verified
questions.question: Under RoPE with q = (1, 2), k = (3, 1) and omega = 1, the pairs (m, n) = (3, 1), (5, 3) and (4, 2) all produce the score -6.627221. What does this demonstrate?
options: The score is constant for every possible pair of positions m and n, whatever q and k
RoPE scores are always negative whenever q and k start out non-parallel
The rotated score depends only on the offset m - n, not on the absolute positions
The score depends only on the sum m + n, which is 4, 8 and 6 here
questions.explanation: All three pairs have offset m - n = 2 but different absolute positions, and the scores agree to six decimals. Changing the offset changes the score; keeping it fixed does not. The sums m + n differ (4, 8, 6), so the score cannot depend on the sum.

questions.section: 7. Under the hood: verify it yourself
questions.question: What is the compute cost of applying RoPE compared with computing attention scores?
options: O(B n_h T^2 d_h), the same as the scores, since every pair is rotated once per key
O(B n_h T d_h) elementwise work, negligible next to the O(B n_h T^2 d_h) of the scores
O(B n_h T d_h^2), because each coordinate pair needs its own small 2 x 2 matrix multiply
O(T^3), because of the outer product used to rebuild the angle table at every step
questions.explanation: Applying RoPE is a single elementwise complex multiply over queries and keys of shape (B, n_h, T, d_h), so it is linear in T. The attention scores are quadratic in T. The freqs_cis table is precomputed once, so its cost is amortized.

questions.section: 7. Under the hood: verify it yourself
questions.question: How many learned parameters does RoPE add to a model?
options: block_size x C, like the wpe table
None
d_h/2 per head, one frequency each
One scalar base per layer
questions.explanation: RoPE's frequencies come from a fixed formula and the rotations are precomputed, so it has no learned parameters. The GPT-2 wpe table, by contrast, held block_size x C learned weights. The base and frequencies are hyperparameters, not trained weights.

questions.section: 7. Under the hood: verify it yourself
questions.question: How do long-context extension methods such as position interpolation and YaRN work on a RoPE model?
options: They rescale the frequencies omega_p rather than adding new table rows
They append new learned rows to the position table and fine-tune them
They remove the slowest-rotating pairs so long positions stay distinct
They switch the model to absolute sinusoidal embeddings at long context
questions.explanation: Since RoPE rotation is defined at any position, you can evaluate past the training length. Extension methods like position interpolation and YaRN rescale omega_p so the angles stay in a familiar range. There is no table to grow, unlike a learned absolute scheme.

questions.section: 7. Under the hood: verify it yourself
questions.question: Some RoPE codebases pair adjacent channels (x0, x1), (x2, x3), ..., while others (e.g. GPT-NeoX / HF default) pair halves (x0, x_{d/2}), (x1, x_{d/2+1}), .... What is the practical consequence?
options: The halves convention loses the relative-position property, so only adjacent pairing gives shift-invariant scores
The adjacent convention only works with complex numbers on GPU, so the halves layout is needed on CPU
Checkpoints are interchangeable between the two, because the rotations of different pairs commute
Both are mathematically equivalent, but a checkpoint trained with one is scrambled if loaded with the other
questions.explanation: Both conventions give identical math and the same relative property; they just apply the rotations to different channel pairs. A trained checkpoint has learned weights tied to its convention, so loading it with the other one rotates the wrong channels and scrambles it. When porting weights, match the convention. LLaMA uses the adjacent (view_as_complex) one.

questions.question: Why is rotating V (or the residual stream) with RoPE a mistake?
options: It makes the attention scores depend on absolute position instead of only on the relative offset
It doubles the number of parameters, since V needs its own frequency table
It distorts the content each token contributes instead of only shaping the attention pattern
It prevents softmax from normalizing, because rotated values no longer sum to one
questions.explanation: RoPE is Q/K only. The score's relative-position property comes from rotating Q and K. Rotating V would change the content being mixed, not the pattern of who attends to whom, and adds nothing useful for position.

questions.question: Why must RoPE be applied after the head split rather than on the full (B, T, C) tensor?
options: Because the full C tensor can have an odd dimension even when every head has an even d_h
Because rotation is undefined before the softmax has been applied to the attention scores
The pairing and frequencies are defined per head dimension d_h, not across the full C
Because the KV cache stores only full-C vectors, so rotations must match that layout
questions.explanation: RoPE's frequencies omega_p = base^(-2p/d_h) and pairs are defined over each head's d_h channels. Rotating the full C-dimensional vector would use the wrong pairing and frequencies relative to how each head computes its dot product. So it acts on (B, n_h, T, d_h).

questions.question: Which requirement on freqs_cis must hold when calling apply_rope?
options: It must have exactly T_max rows and never be sliced, so all positions are covered
It must be on the same device as q and have at least T rows, sliced to [:T]
It must be a learned nn.Parameter so the frequencies receive gradients
It must be float16 to match the half-precision activations of q and k
questions.explanation: A common bug is a freqs_cis on the wrong device or too short for the current sequence. It needs at least T rows and is sliced [:T] before broadcasting. It is a precomputed complex64 buffer, not a learned parameter.

questions.question: Why must the head dimension d_h be even for RoPE?
options: RoPE rotates channels in pairs, so every channel needs a partner
Because complex64 requires a power-of-two size along the last axis
Because base^(-2p/d_h) is undefined for an odd value of d_h
Because softmax requires an even number of logits for each query
questions.explanation: RoPE splits d_h into d_h/2 coordinate pairs and rotates each pair. With an odd d_h one channel would be left without a partner. The frequency formula itself is defined for any d_h; the pairing is what requires evenness.

questions.question: Under RoPE, what score does a query attending to a key at the same position (m = n) get, compared with no RoPE?
options: q . k scaled by cos(m omega), which shrinks as position grows
Zero, because the two rotations cancel each other out exactly
q . k rotated by 2 m omega, doubling the angle at each later position
The plain unrotated dot product q . k, the same at every position
questions.explanation: With m = n the offset is 0, so the score is q^T R(0) k and R(0) is the identity. That is just q . k, independent of where the token sits. A token is always distance 0 from itself, so RoPE leaves its self-score untouched.

questions.question: A student's apply_rope rotates queries with freqs_cis but keys with freqs_cis.conj() (rotating keys by -n omega). What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; conjugation is equivalent to transposing the rotation, so every score comes out the same
The score becomes exactly zero for all positions, because the two rotations cancel each other
The keys change length under conjugation, so the softmax logits grow and become unstable
The score now depends on the sum m + n instead of the difference, so it is no longer translation-invariant
questions.explanation: For the m - n cancellation, Q and K must be rotated in the same direction. Rotating keys by -n omega makes the combined rotation depend on m + n, so the same two tokens get different scores depending on where the pair sits. Conjugation still preserves length, so norms are not the issue.

questions.question: Which paper introduced RoPE?
options: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models (Touvron et al. 2023)
Self-Attention with Relative Position Representations (Shaw et al. 2018)
RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding (Su et al. 2021)
GLU Variants Improve Transformer (Shazeer 2020)
questions.explanation: RoFormer (Su et al. 2021) introduced RoPE and derives it in the complex plane for arbitrary dimension. LLaMA and Llama 3 then adopted it as a building block. Shaw et al. 2018 added learned relative-position representations to attention rather than rotations, and Shazeer 2020 introduced gated FFNs like SwiGLU.

questions.question: With base 10000 and d_h = 4 (two pairs), what are RoPE's two frequencies omega_0 and omega_1?
options: 1 and 0.1 radians per position
1 and 0.01 radians per position
0.01 and 1 radians per position
1 and 0.0001 radians per position
questions.explanation: omega_p = 10000^(-2p/d_h). For p = 0 it is 10000^0 = 1. For p = 1 it is 10000^(-2/4) = 10000^(-1/2) = 0.01. So pair 0 is the fast hand and pair 1 the slow hand; 0.0001 would be the exponent -1, which is wrong here.

questions.question: Why does a RoPE rotation preserve the norm of the query vector?
options: A rotation matrix is orthogonal (R^T R = I), so ||Rq||^2 = q^T R^T R q = ||q||^2
Because the angles stay small enough that cos is approximately 1 and sin is near 0
Because freqs_cis is renormalized to unit length after each training batch
Because RoPE divides each rotated pair by its norm explicitly after rotating
questions.explanation: Orthogonality gives q^T R^T R q = q^T q, exactly the squared norm. This holds for any angle, not just small ones, and requires no explicit normalization. It is why unit-magnitude complex numbers are used in freqs_cis.

questions.question: Why is it desirable that RoPE preserves vector norms?
options: It changes only direction, so it does not rescale the attention logits or destabilize softmax
It ensures that the attention weights are always uniform across all of the key positions
It removes the need for the 1/sqrt(d_k) scaling, since the norms then stay exactly at one
It makes the KV cache smaller, because rotated keys can be stored in lower precision
questions.explanation: Because RoPE only rotates, the magnitude of q and k is unchanged and only the relative-angle information is injected. The logits keep their scale, so softmax is not destabilized. The 1/sqrt(d_k) scaling is still used, and the cache size is unaffected.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Which three architectural changes together define the LLaMA-family architecture relative to GPT-2?
options: RoPE, RMSNorm and SwiGLU
RoPE, LayerNorm and GELU
Learned position embeddings, RMSNorm and ReLU
Sinusoidal positions, BatchNorm and SwiGLU
questions.explanation: LLaMA bundles RoPE (rotary positions), RMSNorm (normalization) and SwiGLU (gated FFN). Every serious open model since 2023 uses them. LayerNorm and GELU are the GPT-2 originals they replace.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: How do RMSNorm and SwiGLU compare with the GPT-2 originals (LayerNorm and the GELU MLP) in cost and quality?
options: They cost far more FLOPs per layer but train much better
They are cheaper per layer but train noticeably worse overall
They only help at inference time and change nothing in training
They cost fewer or equal FLOPs and train at least as well
questions.explanation: RMSNorm does less work than LayerNorm, and SwiGLU at width 8/3 C matches the GELU MLP's budget. Together they cost fewer FLOPs than the GPT-2 originals and train at least as well. That combination is why they became standard.

questions.question: Which three steps does LayerNorm apply to each length-C feature vector?
options: Divide by the root mean square, then apply a learned gain only, with no centering step or bias term
Subtract the batch mean, divide by the batch standard deviation, then add a learned per-feature bias
Subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation, then apply a learned gain gamma and bias beta
Divide by the maximum absolute value, then apply a learned gain gamma and bias beta
questions.explanation: LayerNorm re-centers (subtract the mean), re-scales (divide by the standard deviation), and then applies a learned affine transformation with gain gamma and bias beta. It normalizes per position over the C features, not over the batch. RMSNorm keeps only the re-scaling and the gain.

questions.question: What empirical observation motivated RMSNorm (Zhang & Sennrich 2019)?
options: Centering on the mean is what stabilizes training, while the re-scaling step barely matters at all
In transformers, the re-scaling stabilizes training while subtracting the mean barely matters
LayerNorm's learned bias is essential for stability, while its learned gain is redundant
Normalization layers can be removed entirely once warmup ends without hurting the loss
questions.explanation: RMSNorm asked whether centering pulls its weight. Empirically for transformers it does not: the re-scaling is what stabilizes training. So RMSNorm drops the mean-subtraction and the bias and keeps only scaling plus a learned gain.

questions.question: What is the RMSNorm formula for a length-$C$ vector $\mathbf{x}$ with gain $\mathbf{g}$?
options: $\mathbf{y} = \dfrac{\mathbf{x} - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}}\odot\mathbf{g} + \boldsymbol\beta$
$\mathbf{y} = \dfrac{\mathbf{x}}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{C}\sum_i x_i^2 + \epsilon}}\odot\mathbf{g}$
$\mathbf{y} = \dfrac{\mathbf{x} - \mu}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{C}\sum_i x_i^2 + \epsilon}}\odot\mathbf{g}$
$\mathbf{y} = \dfrac{\mathbf{x}}{\max_i |x_i| + \epsilon}\odot\mathbf{g}$
questions.explanation: RMSNorm divides by the root-mean-square $\sqrt{\frac{1}{C}\sum x_i^2 + \epsilon}$ and multiplies by a learned per-channel gain. There is no mean subtraction and no bias. The first distractor is LayerNorm; the second mixes in a mean subtraction RMSNorm does not have.

questions.question: How is the RMSNorm gain g initialized?
options: To ones
To zeros
To random normal values
To 1/sqrt(C)
questions.explanation: The learned per-channel gain g starts at ones, so at initialization RMSNorm is a pure re-scaling by 1/RMS. In code this is nn.Parameter(torch.ones(dim)). Zero init would kill the signal through the norm.

questions.question: How many reductions over the feature axis does RMSNorm need, compared with LayerNorm?
options: Two, the same as LayerNorm, since it still needs a mean and a variance
Zero, because RMSNorm divides by a fixed scale that is set once at initialization
Three, because it also computes the max to guard against overflow
One (the mean of squares), versus two for LayerNorm (mean, then variance)
questions.explanation: RMSNorm needs only the mean of squares. LayerNorm must first compute the mean and then the variance around it. That, plus skipping the subtraction and bias, is where RMSNorm's small compute saving comes from.

questions.question: How are the RMS and standard deviation $\sigma$ of a vector with mean $\mu$ related?
options: $\operatorname{RMS}^2 = \sigma^2 - \mu^2$ for any vector
$\operatorname{RMS} = \sigma + \mu$
$\operatorname{RMS}^2 = \sigma^2 + \mu^2$
$\operatorname{RMS}^2 = \sigma^2\mu^2$
questions.explanation: RMS measures magnitude around zero, $\frac{1}{C}\sum x_i^2$, while variance measures spread around the mean, $\frac{1}{C}\sum (x_i-\mu)^2$. Expanding gives $\operatorname{RMS}^2 = \sigma^2 + \mu^2$. So RMS is always at least $\sigma$, with equality only when $\mu = 0$.

questions.question: When do RMSNorm and LayerNorm's normalizers (RMS and standard deviation) agree?
options: Exactly when the vector has unit variance and norm
Always, for any vector with C components
Exactly when the vector already has zero mean
Only when all of the components are equal and nonzero
questions.explanation: Since RMS^2 = sigma^2 + mu^2, the two coincide precisely when mu = 0. On a nonzero-mean vector they diverge, and that divergence is exactly the centering RMSNorm skips. A vector with all equal components has sigma = 0 but RMS > 0, the opposite extreme.

questions.question: What is the role of epsilon in RMSNorm, and what values are typical?
options: It is a learned bias added after normalization to shift every output, typically initialized to 0.1
It is added under the square root to avoid dividing by zero for a near-zero vector, typically 1e-5 or 1e-6
It is a dropout rate applied to the input before normalization, typically 0.1 throughout LLaMA pretraining runs
It clips the RMS from below so it is never smaller than 1, typically set to 1.0 for training stability
questions.explanation: epsilon is a small constant under the root so a near-zero vector does not cause a division by zero. Typical values are 1e-5 or 1e-6. It is a fixed hyperparameter, not a learned bias, and is far too small to act as a clip.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example: RMSNorm vs LayerNorm on x = (1,2,3,4)
questions.question: Applied to x = (1, 2, 3, 4) with unit gain, RMSNorm gives all-positive outputs while LayerNorm gives outputs symmetric about zero. Why?
options: RMSNorm never subtracts the mean, so all-positive inputs stay positive; LayerNorm centers on the mean first
RMSNorm applies an absolute value before scaling, so negative outputs are impossible, while LayerNorm does not
LayerNorm subtracts the maximum value before scaling, while RMSNorm subtracts the minimum value instead
RMSNorm adds a positive learned bias after scaling, which shifts every output above zero; LayerNorm does not
questions.explanation: RMSNorm only divides by RMS = sqrt(7.5), so signs and order relative to zero are preserved: (0.365, 0.730, 1.095, 1.461). LayerNorm first subtracts mu = 2.5, sending below-average entries negative, giving (-1.342, -0.447, 0.447, 1.342). Both yield the right scale, which is what the downstream layer needs.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example: RMSNorm vs LayerNorm on x = (1,2,3,4)
questions.question: What do the RMSNorm and LayerNorm outputs for x = (1, 2, 3, 4) have in common, despite being very different vectors?
options: Both are symmetric about zero after scaling
Both are identical up to a sign flip on each entry
Both have exactly zero mean and unit variance
Both have the right scale for the downstream layer
questions.explanation: The outputs differ completely in location: RMSNorm's are all positive, LayerNorm's are centered. What both deliver is a properly scaled vector, which is what the next layer needs. Only LayerNorm's output has zero mean.

questions.question: What are the input and output shapes of RMSNorm on activations of shape (B, T, C), and over which axis is the reduction taken?
options: (B, T, C) to (B, T, 1), reducing over the feature axis C
(B, T, C) to (B, T, C), reducing over the batch axis B only
(B, T, C) to (B, C), reducing over the sequence axis T
(B, T, C) to (B, T, C), reducing over the last axis C only
questions.explanation: RMSNorm is shape-preserving, exactly like LayerNorm. The RMS is computed per position and per sequence, over the last (feature) axis only. Reducing over the batch would make it BatchNorm-like, which is not what RMSNorm does.

questions.question: How many learned parameters does RMSNorm have for feature width C, compared with LayerNorm?
options: 2C, the same as LayerNorm, since it keeps both gain and bias
Zero, because RMSNorm has no learned affine transform at all
C (the gain only), half of LayerNorm's 2C (gain and bias)
C^2, because it learns a full C x C mixing matrix per layer
questions.explanation: RMSNorm's only parameter is the gain g of shape (C,). LayerNorm has both gamma and beta of shape (C,), so 2C. RMSNorm does have a learned affine scale, just no bias.

questions.question: In LLaMA, in what precision is the RMS computed when activations are in half precision?
options: float16, to match the activations
float32, for numerical stability
int8, for speed on tensor cores
float64, for exactness of the sum
questions.explanation: LLaMA computes the RMS in float32 even when the activations are half precision, then casts the result back. Summing many squared half-precision values risks overflow and precision loss. The output keeps the input's dtype and device.

questions.question: In the from-scratch RMSNorm, what does torch.rsqrt(z) compute, and why is it used?
options: 1/sqrt(z) in one op, so the code multiplies by it instead of dividing
sqrt(z) rounded to the nearest integer, which keeps the output scale stable
The square root computed with gradient tracking disabled for speed
The running RMS accumulated across batches, as in BatchNorm
questions.explanation: rsqrt is a reciprocal square root in a single operation. Multiplying x by rsqrt(mean(x^2) + eps) normalizes it without a separate division. It is a normal differentiable op, not a running statistic.

questions.question: In the from-scratch RMSNorm, why is mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True) used?
options: It reduces the C axis to size 1 and keeps it so the result broadcasts against x
It averages over the batch while keeping the batch axis so statistics are shared
It removes the last axis entirely so the normalizer output has shape (B, T)
It computes the mean of x itself rather than the mean of x squared, for centering
questions.explanation: keepdim=True leaves a size-1 trailing axis, so the per-position scale of shape (..., 1) broadcasts against x of shape (..., C). Without keepdim the shapes would not line up for the multiply. The mean is of x.pow(2), i.e. the squares.

questions.question: What is the entire difference between the from-scratch RMSNorm and a from-scratch LayerNorm?
options: RMSNorm adds a learned bias but no gain, and divides by the standard deviation
RMSNorm normalizes over the batch axis instead of the feature axis, like BatchNorm
RMSNorm uses a running average of statistics collected during training
No mean subtraction and no bias tensor, plus RMS in place of standard deviation
questions.explanation: RMSNorm never subtracts the mean and has no bias parameter; it divides by the RMS and multiplies by the gain. Otherwise both normalize per position over the feature axis. Neither keeps running statistics.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: verify, and count the cost
questions.question: Why is RMSNorm's FLOP saving per call small, yet its adoption still worthwhile?
options: It saves roughly half of all model FLOPs, because normalization dominates the cost of each transformer block
It allows removing the residual connections entirely, since RMSNorm keeps activations at a fixed scale
Each call saves little, but it saves memory (no beta, fewer activations) and works as well, since centering did little
It makes the model train about twice as fast, because the mean reduction was the bottleneck kernel
questions.explanation: Per call RMSNorm saves one reduction, a subtraction and a bias add, which is small. Normalization runs 2 n_layer + 1 times per forward pass, and the memory saving is real: no beta and half the norm-related activations kept for backward. The main reason it caught on is that it works as well.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: verify, and count the cost
questions.question: In a pre-norm transformer with n_layer blocks, how many times is normalization applied per forward pass?
options: n_layer (one per block)
2 n_layer + 1
2 n_layer (two per block)
n_layer + 1 (blocks plus final)
questions.explanation: Each block has two norms (before attention and before the FFN), giving 2 n_layer, plus one final norm before the LM head. So 2 n_layer + 1 norm calls per forward pass. Small per-call savings are multiplied by this count.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: verify, and count the cost
questions.question: What does a fused RMSNorm kernel (e.g. torch.nn.RMSNorm) compute?
options: A mean, a variance, a subtraction, a division and a bias add over the features
One reduction, one reciprocal square root, and one elementwise multiply by the gain
A full matrix multiply of each feature vector by a learned C x C weight matrix
A softmax over the feature axis, followed by an elementwise multiply with the learned gain
questions.explanation: RMSNorm is mechanically simple: reduce the squares to a mean, take rsqrt(mean + eps), multiply by x and the gain. The fused kernel does exactly that in one pass. Mean, variance, subtraction and bias belong to LayerNorm.

questions.question: What is the structure of the GPT-2 MLP that SwiGLU replaces?
options: Linear(C to 4C), GELU, Linear(4C to C)
Linear(C to C), ReLU, Linear(C to C)
Linear(C to 8/3 C), SiLU, Linear(8/3 C to C)
Two parallel Linear(C to 4C) multiplied together
questions.explanation: GPT-2 expands to a hidden width of 4C, applies the pointwise GELU nonlinearity, and projects back to C. SwiGLU keeps the expand-and-project shape but replaces the single nonlinear path with a gate. The 8/3 C width with SiLU is SwiGLU's design.

questions.question: What is the SwiGLU feed-forward network?
options: $\operatorname{Swish}\big(\mathbf{x}W_{\text{gate}} \odot \mathbf{x}W_{\text{up}}\big)W_{\text{down}}$
$\operatorname{Swish}(\mathbf{x}W_{\text{up}})W_{\text{down}}$
$\big(\sigma(\mathbf{x}W_{\text{gate}}) + \mathbf{x}W_{\text{up}}\big)W_{\text{down}}$
$\big(\operatorname{Swish}(\mathbf{x}W_{\text{gate}}) \odot \mathbf{x}W_{\text{up}}\big)W_{\text{down}}$
questions.explanation: SwiGLU applies Swish to the gate projection only, multiplies it elementwise by the up projection, then projects down. Applying Swish after the product is a different, ungated function. Addition instead of multiplication would not gate anything.

questions.question: How many weight matrices does SwiGLU have, and what do they map between?
options: Two: a fused W_up maps C to 2h, and W_down maps h back to C
Three: W_gate, W_up and W_down all map C to C
Three: W_gate and W_up map C to h, and W_down maps h to C
Four: gate, up, down and an extra output projection back to C
questions.explanation: SwiGLU uses W_gate and W_up, both C to h, and W_down, h to C. The GELU MLP has only two matrices. The extra matrix is why the hidden width must shrink to 8/3 C to keep the parameter count equal.

questions.question: In SwiGLU, what happens to a hidden channel when its gate value Swish(x W_gate) is near zero?
options: That channel is passed through to W_down unchanged
That channel is amplified to compensate for the small gate
That channel is shut off, regardless of the up signal
The whole FFN output for that token becomes zero
questions.explanation: The gate multiplies the up signal channel by channel. A near-zero gate suppresses that hidden channel, while a large gate lets it through amplified. This data-dependent gating is more expressive than a fixed pointwise nonlinearity.

questions.question: Why do gated feed-forward networks like SwiGLU outperform a plain GELU MLP?
options: They have many more parameters at the same hidden width, and that extra capacity explains the gain
Data-dependent gating, where one projection modulates the other, is more expressive at equal size
They remove the need for normalization layers, so the network trains with fewer bottlenecks
They use a cheaper nonlinearity than GELU, so more training steps fit into the same budget
questions.explanation: SwiGLU lets one learned path modulate another channel by channel based on the input. Gated FFNs consistently win on language modeling loss at equal parameter count, which is the comparison that matters. At equal width SwiGLU has more parameters, which is why the width is reduced to make the comparison fair.

questions.question: What is the Swish (SiLU) function?
options: $\operatorname{Swish}(z) = z\,\sigma(z)$, where $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid
$\operatorname{Swish}(z) = \max(0, z)$, the rectified linear unit with a learned slope
$\operatorname{Swish}(z) = \sigma(z)$, the logistic sigmoid applied elementwise
$\operatorname{Swish}(z) = z\tanh(z)$, a smooth even function of its input
questions.explanation: Swish multiplies its input by the sigmoid of the input, $z\sigma(z)$. It is a smooth version of ReLU: near zero for very negative inputs, roughly linear for large positive ones. Plain sigmoid would saturate at 1 rather than track $z$.

questions.question: How does Swish/SiLU behave compared with ReLU?
options: It is identical to ReLU but with a learned slope for negative inputs, as in the PReLU activation
It saturates at 1 for large positive inputs and at 0 for large negative inputs, just like a logistic sigmoid
It is exactly zero for all negative inputs like ReLU, but smooth and gently curved for all of the positive ones
Smooth everywhere: near zero for very negative inputs, linear for large positive ones, slightly negative just below zero
questions.explanation: Swish is a smooth ReLU: approximately zero for very negative z, approximately z for large positive z, and with a small negative dip just below zero. Unlike ReLU it is differentiable everywhere. In PyTorch it is F.silu.

questions.question: At equal hidden width, how many parameters would a SwiGLU FFN have relative to a two-matrix GELU MLP?
options: The same number, since only the activation function changes
2 times as many, because the gate doubles both of its inputs
0.5 times as many, because each of the matrices is half as wide
1.5 times as many, because it has three matrices instead of two
questions.explanation: SwiGLU has three C x h matrices while the GELU MLP has two. At the same hidden width that is 3/2 = 1.5 times the parameters. To compare fairly, LLaMA shrinks the hidden width to 8/3 C.

questions.question: What hidden width does LLaMA use for its SwiGLU FFN, and why?
options: 4C, to match GPT-2 exactly so the checkpoints stay interchangeable
2C, to halve the FFN cost while keeping all three of the matrices
8/3 C, so the three-matrix SwiGLU has the same 8C^2 parameters as the 4C GELU MLP
16/3 C, to double the capacity of the gated FFN relative to GPT-2's 4C MLP budget
questions.explanation: The GELU MLP has 2 x C x 4C = 8C^2 parameters. SwiGLU with three matrices at width h has 3Ch, and setting h = 8/3 C gives 8C^2. Since 3 x 8/3 = 8 = 2 x 4, the budgets match and the comparison is fair.

questions.question: How many parameters (ignoring biases) does a GELU MLP with hidden width 4C have?
questions.explanation: It has W1 of C x 4C and W2 of 4C x C, so 4C^2 + 4C^2 = 8C^2. SwiGLU at width 8/3 C also has 8C^2. 12C^2 is what SwiGLU would have at width 4C.

questions.question: In practice, how is LLaMA's SwiGLU hidden width h chosen beyond the 8/3 C formula?
options: It is rounded to a hardware-friendly multiple, 256 in LLaMA
It is rounded down to the nearest power of two, 2048 in LLaMA
It is set to exactly 8/3 C, allowing fractional hidden channels
It is tuned separately for each layer with a small search
questions.explanation: 8/3 C is rarely an integer multiple of anything convenient, so LLaMA rounds h to a multiple of 256 for efficient hardware kernels. In code this is the multiple_of argument. Channels cannot be fractional.

questions.question: Does LLaMA use biases in its linear layers?
options: No, LLaMA drops the biases
Yes, in every linear layer
Only in the SwiGLU gate projection
Only in the attention output projection
questions.explanation: LLaMA drops biases, which is why the parameter counting ignores them. RMSNorm similarly has no bias. The from-scratch SwiGLU defaults to bias=False.

questions.section: 9. Numerical example: Swish and the width identity
questions.question: What is Swish(-1), and what does it show about Swish versus ReLU?
options: Exactly 0, the same as ReLU, showing Swish is flat for every negative input
About -1, showing Swish is linear for negative inputs, just as for the positives
About 0.2689, showing Swish is always positive, like the logistic sigmoid
About -0.2689, showing Swish dips slightly negative where ReLU is flat zero
questions.explanation: Swish(-1) = -1 x sigmoid(-1) = -0.2689. Swish is slightly negative for small negative inputs, whereas ReLU is exactly zero there. For large positive inputs Swish tracks z, e.g. Swish(2) = 1.7616.

questions.section: 9. Numerical example: Swish and the width identity
questions.question: For C = 768 (GPT-2 small width), how do a GELU MLP with hidden 4C and a SwiGLU with hidden floor(8/3 C) = 2048 compare in parameters?
options: SwiGLU has 1.5 times as many weights
SwiGLU has half as many weights in total
Identical: both have 4,718,592 weights
GELU MLP has 2048 more weights than SwiGLU
questions.explanation: GELU: 2 x 768 x 3072 = 4,718,592. SwiGLU: 3 x 768 x 2048 = 4,718,592. They are exactly the same budget, which illustrates the 8/3 width identity.

questions.question: What are the tensor shapes inside SwiGLU for an input of shape (B, T, C)?
options: Gate and up are (B, T, C), and their product is the (B, T, C^2) outer product
Gate and up are (B, T, h), their product is (B, T, h), and W_down returns (B, T, C)
Gate is (B, T, h), up is (B, T, C), and the output stays at width h with shape (B, T, h)
Gate and up are (B, h) after pooling over T, and the output is (B, C) per sequence
questions.explanation: W_gate and W_up both project (B, T, C) to (B, T, h). The elementwise product keeps (B, T, h), and W_down maps back to (B, T, C). The time axis is preserved throughout.

questions.question: In the from-scratch SwiGLU, what is computed when hidden_dim is None and multiple_of = 256?
options: 4 * dim, rounded down to the nearest multiple of 256
int(8 * dim / 3), rounded up to the next multiple of 256
8 * dim / 3, rounded up to the nearest power of two
dim, unchanged, so the FFN keeps the model width C
questions.explanation: The code sets hidden_dim = int(8 * dim / 3), then multiple_of * ((hidden_dim + multiple_of - 1) // multiple_of), which is ceiling-rounding to a multiple. That gives a hardware-friendly width near 8/3 C. 4 * dim would be the GELU width.

questions.question: What is the forward computation of the from-scratch SwiGLU module?
options: w_down(F.silu(w_gate(x)) * w_up(x))
w_down(F.silu(w_gate(x) * w_up(x)))
w_down(torch.sigmoid(w_gate(x)) * w_up(x))
F.silu(w_down(w_gate(x) * w_up(x)))
questions.explanation: SiLU is applied to the gate projection only, multiplied elementwise by the up projection, and then projected down. Applying SiLU after the product removes the gating. F.silu is Swish with beta = 1.

questions.question: How do SwiGLU's total FLOPs and parameters compare with the GELU MLP at hidden width 8/3 C?
options: SwiGLU is about 1.5 times cheaper in both FLOPs and parameters at that width
SwiGLU costs about 1.5 times more, since it runs three matmuls instead of just two
SwiGLU is cheaper in FLOPs but stores more parameters than the GELU MLP does
They land on the same 8C^2, so the win is quality at equal cost, not a cost reduction
questions.explanation: SwiGLU runs two input projections and one output projection, but at width 8/3 C the totals match the GELU MLP's 8C^2. So SwiGLU does not reduce cost; it improves quality at the same cost. 1.5x would only apply at equal hidden width.
