questions.question: What extra memory does SwiGLU need in the backward pass compared with the GELU MLP?
options: None; it stores exactly the same activations as the GELU MLP, since h is smaller
It stores the full (B, T, T) attention matrix a second time so the gate can be recomputed
It keeps both the gate and up activations, each (B, T, h), a bit more than the GELU MLP
It stores all three weight matrices twice, once in fp32 and once in half precision
questions.explanation: To backpropagate through the elementwise product, both factors (gate and up, each (B, T, h)) must be kept. The GELU MLP stores one hidden activation. So SwiGLU uses a little more activation memory.

questions.question: Why is adding a bias to RMSNorm a mistake?
options: The bias makes RMSNorm exactly identical to LayerNorm, so the whole change is redundant
The bias causes a division by zero whenever the input vector lies near the origin
RMSNorm has only the gain g; adding a bias makes it a different and generally worse normalizer
The bias doubles the FLOPs of the following attention layer, which dominates block cost
questions.explanation: RMSNorm by definition has no bias term, only a learned gain. Adding one changes the normalizer into something different and generally worse. It would still not be LayerNorm, since there is no centering.

questions.question: Why is it wrong to compute RMSNorm using standard-deviation formulas?
options: Standard deviation is undefined for vectors of length C unless C is a power of two
RMS is the root mean of squares around zero, so the mean must not be subtracted
Standard deviation is taken over the batch axis, while RMS is taken over the features
Standard deviation formulas drop the epsilon term, so they divide by zero more often
questions.explanation: RMS measures magnitude around zero; standard deviation measures spread around the mean. Using sigma means subtracting the mean, which is precisely the centering RMSNorm drops. Both are computed over the feature axis.

questions.question: What goes wrong if a SwiGLU FFN keeps the hidden width at 4C?
options: The FFN inflates to 12C^2 parameters, 1.5 times the GELU budget
The FFN shrinks to 4C^2 parameters, half of the GELU MLP's budget
The gating no longer works, since 4C hidden units saturate
The output shape becomes (B, T, 4C) instead of (B, T, C)
questions.explanation: With three matrices at width 4C, SwiGLU has 3 x C x 4C = 12C^2 parameters, 1.5 times the 8C^2 of the GELU MLP. Use 8/3 C (rounded) to match. The output shape is still (B, T, C) because W_down projects back.

questions.question: Why must SwiGLU's gate and up projections be separate learned matrices?
options: Because a single shared matrix cannot be multiplied elementwise with its own output
Because sharing the matrix would change the shape of the SwiGLU output tensor to (B, T, h)
Because a shared matrix cannot be built with bias=False in nn.Linear and still be trained
Sharing one matrix for both collapses the gate, since both paths would see the same projection
questions.explanation: The gate must be a different learned view of the input so it can modulate the up signal. With one shared matrix, the computation becomes Swish(xW) * xW, so the gate is no longer an independent path. Shapes still work, which makes the bug silent.

questions.question: RMSNorm and LayerNorm produce the same normalized output (up to affine parameters) on a vector x. What must be true of x?
options: x has unit variance
x has all positive components
x has unit L2 norm
x has zero mean
questions.explanation: Since RMS^2 = sigma^2 + mu^2, RMS equals the standard deviation exactly when mu = 0. Then LayerNorm's centering does nothing and both divide by the same quantity. Unit variance or unit norm does not make the mean zero.

questions.question: A student writes SwiGLU as w_down(F.silu(w_gate(x) * w_up(x))). Why is this not SwiGLU?
options: It is equivalent to SwiGLU, because elementwise multiplication commutes with SiLU for any inputs
It applies SiLU twice in a row, which shrinks the output so it no longer matches the residual stream
It multiplies two projections first (a bilinear form) and applies Swish once, so there is no gating
It uses the wrong output projection shape, mapping h back to h instead of mapping h back to C
questions.explanation: SwiGLU applies the nonlinearity to the gate path before the elementwise product. The buggy version forms a bilinear product of two linear projections and only then applies Swish, so neither path modulates the other through a nonlinearity. It is a different, weaker function, and SiLU does not commute with multiplication.

questions.question: Which paper bundled RMSNorm, SwiGLU and RoPE into one reference architecture?
options: GLU Variants Improve Transformer (Shazeer 2020)
LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models (Touvron et al. 2023)
Root Mean Square Layer Normalization (Zhang & Sennrich 2019)
RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding (Su et al. 2021)
questions.explanation: LLaMA combined all three into its reference architecture, and its hyperparameter table lists the 8/3-derived FFN widths. SwiGLU traces to Shazeer 2020, RMSNorm to Zhang & Sennrich 2019, and RoPE to RoFormer. Each of those introduced only one component.

questions.question: Which paper introduced the SwiGLU gated feed-forward network?
options: GLU Variants Improve Transformer (Shazeer 2020)
Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need (Shazeer 2019)
LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models (2023)
RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding
questions.explanation: SwiGLU traces to Shazeer's 2020 paper GLU Variants Improve Transformer. Shazeer's 2019 Fast Transformer Decoding introduced MQA. LLaMA adopted SwiGLU rather than inventing it.

questions.question: Which two things does RMSNorm remove from LayerNorm?
options: The mean-subtraction (centering) and the learned bias beta
The learned gain gamma and the epsilon term under the square root
The division by the scale and the learned gain gamma
The epsilon term and the per-feature learned gain gamma
questions.explanation: RMSNorm drops centering and the bias. It keeps re-scaling, now by RMS instead of standard deviation, and the learned gain. It still uses an epsilon for numerical safety.

questions.question: What is Swish(0), and why does Swish's behaviour for small negative inputs help optimization?
options: Swish(0) = 0.5; for negative inputs it saturates toward zero like a sigmoid, so gradients there vanish quickly
Swish(0) = 1; for negative inputs it is linear with slope one, so it behaves like the identity function there
Swish(0) = 0; its gradient is exactly zero for every negative input, so it behaves like ReLU in that region
Swish(0) = 0; for small negative inputs it is smooth and slightly negative with a nonzero gradient
questions.explanation: Swish(0) = 0 x sigmoid(0) = 0. For small negative z, ReLU is exactly zero with zero gradient, but Swish is slightly negative (e.g. -0.2689 at -1) and has a nonzero gradient. That gradient signal helps optimization.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Which current models use grouped-query attention (GQA)?
options: Llama 2-70B, Llama 3, Mistral and most current models
Only GPT-2 and the original 2017 encoder-decoder Transformer
Only encoder-only models such as BERT and RoBERTa variants
Only models trained and served without any KV cache at all
questions.explanation: GQA is the attention variant in Llama 2-70B, Llama 3, Mistral and most current models. GPT-2 and the original Transformer use standard multi-head attention. GQA's benefit specifically concerns the KV cache used in decoder inference.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: What kind of win does GQA deliver?
options: A large training-speed win, paid for with a significant drop in quality on long-context benchmarks
A reduction in attention FLOPs by a factor of n_h, because fewer heads compute scores at every layer
A quality improvement over MHA, bought with a higher KV-cache memory cost at long context lengths
A pure inference win: a smaller KV cache allows longer contexts and larger batches at little quality cost
questions.explanation: GQA shrinks the KV cache, which lets you serve longer contexts and larger batches on the same GPU, with almost no quality loss. Training speed and attention FLOPs are roughly unchanged. It approximates MHA quality rather than exceeding it.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the KV cache is the bottleneck at inference
questions.question: Why does an autoregressive decoder keep a KV cache during generation?
options: To store the query vectors of all past tokens so they can be reused at each step
To store the softmax attention weights of previous steps so they need not be renormalized
To avoid recomputing the keys and values of all previous tokens at every step
To store the gradients of past positions for use in the next training step
questions.explanation: To generate token t+1, attention needs K and V for every previous token. Recomputing them each step would be quadratic and wasteful, so each token's K and V are computed once and cached. Queries are computed fresh for the current token and are not cached.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the KV cache is the bottleneck at inference
questions.question: In standard multi-head attention, why does the KV cache become a major problem for long contexts and big models?
options: It stores the full T x T attention matrix for every layer and every head, which grows quadratically with context
It stores K and V for all n_h heads and grows with sequence length, often exceeding the model weights in memory
It stores the token embeddings for the whole vocabulary at every layer, which soon dwarfs the model weights
It must be recomputed from scratch at every decode step, so its cost grows with each new token
questions.explanation: The cache grows linearly with the sequence and, in MHA, stores keys and values for all n_h heads in every layer. For long sequences it can exceed the memory of the weights themselves and becomes the dominant GPU memory consumer at inference. It stores K and V, not attention matrices.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the KV cache is the bottleneck at inference
questions.question: Besides memory capacity, why does KV-cache size matter at every decode step?
options: It must be written to disk after each step so generation can resume after a crash
It must be read from memory every step, so its size caps context length and batch size
It is re-projected through W_K and W_V at each step, which costs a full matmul per layer
It is sorted by attention score before each softmax, an O(T log T) operation per step
questions.explanation: Every decode step reads the whole cache from memory to compute attention for the new token. So the cache's size affects memory bandwidth per step as well as capacity. Both directly cap how long a context and how large a batch you can serve.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the KV cache is the bottleneck at inference
questions.question: Which asymmetry between query heads and key/value heads do MQA and GQA exploit?
options: Query heads give expressive power while KV heads set the cache size, so keep many query heads and few KV heads
KV heads give the expressive power while query heads set the cache size, so keep many KV heads and few query heads
Query heads are cached across decode steps, while KV heads are recomputed for each new token from scratch
Query heads hold far more parameters than KV heads, so cutting KV heads saves weight memory but no cache
questions.explanation: Each query head asks a different question, which is where attention's expressiveness comes from. The KV cache stores one K and V per KV head, so the number of KV heads sets cache size. MQA and GQA keep n_h query heads but use fewer KV heads.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: the KV cache is the bottleneck at inference
questions.question: By what factor does using g KV heads instead of n_h shrink the KV cache?
options: g / n_h
n_h * g
sqrt(n_h / g)
n_h / g
questions.explanation: The cache size is proportional to the number of KV heads. Going from n_h to g heads shrinks it by n_h / g, e.g. 64 / 8 = 8 times. This comes with little quality loss for reasonable g.

questions.question: In standard multi-head attention (MHA), how many key/value heads are there relative to query heads?
options: g = 1: all query heads share one KV head
g = n_h / 2: adjacent pairs of query heads share a KV head
g = n_h: every query head has its own K and V head
g = 2 n_h: each query head has two KV heads
questions.explanation: MHA ties the counts: n_h query heads and n_h KV heads. That gives maximum quality and maximum cache. MQA uses g = 1, and GQA uses an intermediate g.

questions.question: What is Multi-Query Attention (MQA, Shazeer 2019)?
options: Each query head gets multiple KV heads of its own, which improves quality at a higher cache cost
Queries are shared across all heads while K and V stay per-head, shrinking the query projection n_h times
All query heads share a single K/V head (g = 1), shrinking the cache n_h times
Attention computed over multiple queries at once during training, which is then cached for inference
questions.explanation: MQA sets g = 1, so every query head attends using the same single K and V head. The cache shrinks by a factor of n_h. A small quality drop and some training instability were reported.

questions.question: What downsides were reported for MQA?
options: A much larger KV cache than MHA, since every query head keeps its own copy
A small quality drop and some training instability
A large increase in attention FLOPs from repeating K and V across heads
An inability to use a causal mask, which restricts it to encoder models
questions.explanation: MQA shrinks the cache maximally but was reported to lose a little quality and to show some training instability. GQA was introduced as a middle ground that recovers almost all of MHA's quality. MQA's cache is the smallest, not the largest.

questions.question: What is Grouped-Query Attention (GQA, Ainslie et al. 2023)?
options: Query heads split into g groups of n_h/g, each group sharing one K/V head, with 1 < g < n_h and g dividing n_h
Each query head is split into g smaller sub-heads, and every sub-head gets its own separate K and V projections
Keys are grouped by sequence position into g buckets, and each query head attends only to its own bucket
The model's layers are split into g groups, and all layers in a group share a single set of K/V projections
questions.explanation: GQA uses g KV heads, with g dividing n_h, and assigns each KV head to a contiguous group of n_h/g query heads. It interpolates between MHA (g = n_h) and MQA (g = 1). It recovers almost all of MHA's quality at a fraction of the cache.

questions.question: How many KV heads do Llama 2-70B and Llama 3 use with GQA?
questions.explanation: Llama 2-70B and Llama 3 use g = 8 KV heads. With 64 query heads in Llama-2-70B that means groups of 8 query heads share each KV head, cutting the cache 8 times. g = 1 would be MQA and g = 64 would be MHA.

questions.question: How does GQA keep the per-head attention math unchanged while using fewer KV heads?
options: It averages the n_h query heads down to g heads before attention, so each group has one query
It concatenates the g KV heads along d_h, giving every query head a single wider key and value tensor
It runs g separate softmaxes, one per KV head, and sums their outputs across all query heads
It computes g KV heads and repeats each one across the n_h/g query heads in its group
questions.explanation: GQA projects only g KV heads, then repeats each across its group so K and V again have n_h heads. After that, attention is computed exactly as in MHA. Query heads are not averaged; all n_h queries remain.

questions.question: What is the formula for KV-cache bytes?
options: n_layer * n_h * d_h * T * b * B
2 * n_layer * n_h * g * d_h * T * B
2 * n_layer * g * d_h * T * b * B
2 * n_layer * d_h * T^2 * b * B
questions.explanation: The factor 2 is for keys and values; then per layer, per KV head g, per head dimension d_h, per cached position T, with b bytes per number and batch size B. Only g appears, not n_h. The cache is linear in T, not quadratic.

questions.question: In the KV-cache size formula, what does the leading factor of 2 represent?
options: Two bytes per fp16 number in the cache
One copy for keys and one for values
Two directions of attention, left and right
The forward and the backward passes
questions.explanation: The cache stores both K and V for every position, so the count is doubled. The bytes per number is a separate factor b, which is also 2 for fp16/bf16. There is no backward pass at inference.

questions.question: Why does reducing KV heads cut the KV cache linearly?
options: Only the number of KV heads g appears in the cache-size formula, not the number of query heads n_h
Because the cache stores one query vector per KV head, so fewer KV heads means fewer stored queries
Because the number of transformer layers is reduced proportionally whenever g is made smaller
Because d_h grows as g shrinks, which keeps the total cache constant only when n_h equals g
questions.explanation: The cache size is proportional to g. Fewer KV heads means proportionally fewer cached K and V vectors, so the ratio of MHA to g-head cache is exactly n_h / g. n_layer and d_h are unchanged.

questions.question: For a Llama-2-70B-shaped model (80 layers, 64 query heads, d_h = 128, T = 4096, fp16, batch 1), what are the KV-cache sizes for MHA, GQA with g = 8, and MQA?
options: About 10.74 GB, 1.34 GB and 0.17 GB
About 140.0 GB, 17.5 GB and 2.19 GB
About 1.34 GB, 10.74 GB and 0.17 GB
About 10.74 GB, 5.37 GB and 1.34 GB
questions.explanation: MHA: 2 x 80 x 64 x 128 x 4096 x 2 bytes = 10.737 GB. GQA with g = 8 is 8 times smaller (1.342 GB), and MQA is 64 times smaller (0.168 GB). 140 GB is roughly the fp16 weight size, not the cache.

questions.question: Why are 70B models served with GQA rather than MHA?
options: MHA cannot run on GPUs at all at 70B scale, because its fused attention kernel needs more than 80 GB
GQA has more query heads than MHA at the same model width, which improves quality enough to justify the switch
GQA removes the need to store the 70B weights in fp16, so the whole model fits on one GPU in int4
MHA's ~10.7 GB cache at 4K context is a big slice of an 80 GB GPU before batching, on top of ~140 GB of weights
questions.explanation: At 4K context and batch 1, MHA's cache is already 10.7 GB, before batching or counting the ~140 GB of fp16 weights. Dropping to g = 8 frees about 9.4 GB, which can be spent on larger batches or longer contexts. GQA keeps the same number of query heads.

questions.question: Why does Llama use g = 8 rather than MQA's g = 1, even though MQA shrinks the cache more?
options: MQA does not work together with RoPE, because the shared key head cannot be rotated per query head
MQA's cache is actually larger than GQA's, because its single KV head uses a wider head dimension
g = 8 is the quality/memory sweet spot, recovering nearly MHA quality while still cutting the cache 8 times
g must equal the number of GPUs used for tensor parallelism, and Llama 2-70B is served on 8 GPUs
questions.explanation: MQA squeezes hardest (0.17 GB) but loses some quality and can be unstable. GQA with g = 8 keeps quality near MHA while still saving most of the memory. That trade-off is why Llama chose g = 8.

questions.section: 5. Tensor shapes: project small, repeat, attend
questions.question: In GQA, what are the shapes of Q and of K/V after projection and head split, for input (B, T, C)?
options: Q is (B, g, T, d_h); K and V are (B, n_h, T, d_h)
Q is (B, n_h, T, d_h); K and V are (B, g, T, d_h)
Q, K and V are all (B, n_h, T, d_h)
Q is (B, n_h, T, d_h); K and V are (B, T, g) per position
questions.explanation: Q is projected to n_h d_h and split into n_h heads. K and V are projected only to g d_h and split into g heads. This is the only shape change from MHA before the repeat step.

questions.section: 5. Tensor shapes: project small, repeat, attend
questions.question: In GQA, what does repeat_interleave(n_h/g) on the head axis do to K and V of shape (B, g, T, d_h)?
options: Tiles the whole block of g heads n_h/g times in order [0..g-1, 0..g-1, ...], giving (B, n_h, T, d_h)
Copies KV head j to query heads j*n_h/g through j*n_h/g + n_h/g - 1, giving (B, n_h, T, d_h)
Averages the g KV heads into one shared head and broadcasts it, giving (B, 1, T, d_h) for all queries
Repeats each head along the time axis instead of the head axis, giving (B, g, n_h T, d_h) for the scores
questions.explanation: repeat_interleave places n_h/g consecutive copies of each KV head, so each contiguous group of query heads sees its own shared KV head. The result matches Q's head count. Tiling the whole block instead would interleave the groups incorrectly.

questions.section: 5. Tensor shapes: project small, repeat, attend
questions.question: After K and V are repeated to n_h heads in GQA, how does the rest of attention differ from MHA?
options: It does not: scores QK^T, causal mask, softmax, weighted V, head merge and output projection are identical
The softmax is taken over the KV-head axis instead of the key positions, so the groups compete for attention
The causal mask is removed, because repeated K and V already prevent tokens from attending to the future
The output projection maps g d_h back to C instead of n_h d_h, so the merged heads are smaller than in MHA
questions.explanation: Once K and V have n_h heads, the per-head attention computation is exactly the same as in MHA. The output projection still maps C to C because the merged head output has n_h d_h = C channels. Only the KV projection sizes differ.

questions.section: 5. Tensor shapes: project small, repeat, attend
questions.question: How do GQA's K and V projection weights compare in size with MHA's?
options: They are larger, C x 2 n_h d_h, because each group stores its keys and values twice
They are identical, C x n_h d_h, since GQA only changes how heads are cached
They are removed entirely and K and V are reused from the W_Q projection output
They are C x g d_h instead of C x n_h d_h, so GQA has slightly fewer parameters
questions.explanation: K and V project to only g heads, so W_K and W_V shrink from C x n_h d_h to C x g d_h. This gives GQA slightly fewer parameters than MHA. W_Q and the output projection are unchanged.

questions.question: In the from-scratch GroupedQueryAttention, what is n_rep?
options: n_kv_head // n_head, the number of KV heads that serve each individual query head
n_embd // n_head, the per-head dimension that each query and KV head projects to
n_head // n_kv_head, the number of query heads sharing each KV head
The number of times the whole attention computation is repeated within each layer
questions.explanation: n_rep = n_head // n_kv_head is the group size: how many query heads use each KV head. It is the repeat factor for repeat_interleave. The per-head dimension d_h is n_embd // n_head.

questions.question: What does the assert n_head % n_kv_head == 0 in GroupedQueryAttention guarantee?
options: The head dimension is even, so RoPE can rotate pairs of channels within each head
The embedding dimension divides the vocabulary size, so the output projection is square
The query heads split into equal groups, one per KV head
The causal mask is square, so every query position has a matching set of key positions
questions.explanation: GQA requires g to divide n_h so every KV head serves the same number of query heads. Without that, repeat_interleave could not produce exactly n_h heads. RoPE's evenness requirement concerns d_h, not this assert.

questions.question: In GroupedQueryAttention, what happens when n_kv_head equals n_head?
options: It becomes MQA, because every query head now shares exactly one KV head across the layer
n_rep = 1, the repeat is skipped, and it computes the same function as standard causal attention
It raises an error, because the divisibility assert requires every group to hold more than one head
It doubles the number of KV heads, because each query head then gets one K head and one V head
questions.explanation: With g = n_h each query head has its own KV head, so n_rep = 1 and no repeat is needed. The module then computes exactly what CausalSelfAttention computes. The only difference is that Q/K/V come from three separate Linear layers instead of one fused c_attn.

questions.question: In GroupedQueryAttention, what happens when n_kv_head = 1?
options: All query heads share the single KV head, which is MQA
It reduces to standard MHA, since each query head keeps its own K and V
It fails the divisibility assert, since n_head % 1 is undefined
Each query head gets n_head KV heads, so the cache grows n_head times
questions.explanation: With one KV head, n_rep = n_head and repeat_interleave copies that single head to every query head. That is exactly Multi-Query Attention. 1 divides any n_head, so the assert passes.

questions.question: Where is RoPE applied in the from-scratch GroupedQueryAttention module?
options: Always, on the input x before the Q, K and V projections are applied
On V only, after the repeat step has expanded it to all query heads
On the output of c_proj, after the heads have been merged back to C
Optionally, by passing freqs_cis to rotate Q and K
questions.explanation: The GQA module is RoPE-optional: passing freqs_cis rotates Q and K. RoPE always acts on queries and keys, not on V or the input. Without freqs_cis no rotation is applied.

questions.question: In GroupedQueryAttention, how is the causal mask built?
options: torch.tril of a T x T tensor of ones with diagonal=0, multiplied elementwise into the softmax output
A random dropout mask over the T x T scores, resampled at every forward pass during training
A g x g mask over KV heads, so each group of query heads sees only its own shared KV head
torch.triu of a T x T tensor filled with -inf, with diagonal=1, so future positions are masked
questions.explanation: torch.triu(torch.full((T, T), -inf), diagonal=1) puts -inf strictly above the diagonal. Adding it to the scores blocks attention to future positions after the softmax. The mask is over positions, not heads.

questions.section: 7. Under the hood: verify the cache numbers, and the MHA-equivalence
questions.question: How is it verified that GQA with g = n_h equals standard MHA?
options: By comparing training loss curves of both modules over 1000 steps and checking they overlap within noise
By checking that both modules have the same parameter count and the same fused c_attn weight shapes per layer
A test copies MHA's fused c_attn weights into GQA's q/k/v projections; outputs match to 1e-10 in float64
By comparing their KV-cache sizes during generation and confirming both store n_h heads per layer
questions.explanation: test_gqa_equals_mha_when_kv_heads_full splits the fused c_attn weights into q_proj, k_proj and v_proj and asserts the outputs agree to 1e-10 in float64. This proves exact functional equivalence, not just similar behaviour. Parameter counts alone would not prove the outputs match.

questions.section: 7. Under the hood: verify the cache numbers, and the MHA-equivalence
questions.question: Why does GQA barely help memory or speed during training?
options: Because training automatically switches GQA to MQA, which has the same cost as MHA without a cache
The repeat materializes all n_h KV heads anyway, and training runs all positions in parallel with no cache
Because gradients cannot flow through repeat_interleave, so the K and V projections end up trained exactly like MHA
Because GQA doubles the backward-pass FLOPs to recover the gradient of the repeated K and V heads
questions.explanation: During training there is no KV cache: all positions are computed in parallel and the repeated K and V are full width. So throughput and memory are roughly unchanged. Gradients flow through repeat_interleave normally.

questions.section: 7. Under the hood: verify the cache numbers, and the MHA-equivalence
questions.question: Why is GQA described as an inference optimization even though it is chosen at architecture-design time?
options: Its savings show up only in autoregressive decoding, where the cache holds g heads and the repeat is on the fly
Because it can be switched on and off after training at no cost, like a decoding flag in the model serving stack
Because it only changes the tokenizer and the cache format, leaving the trained weights untouched
Because it is applied only to the final transformer layer, whose KV cache dominates total serving memory
questions.explanation: The architecture must be designed with g KV heads, but the payoff (smaller cache, less memory bandwidth per decode step) occurs only at serving time. Training sees essentially no benefit. Converting after training requires mean-pooling and uptraining, so it is not free.

questions.section: 7. Under the hood: verify the cache numbers, and the MHA-equivalence
questions.question: What is the standard recipe (Ainslie et al.) for converting an MHA checkpoint to GQA?
options: Mean-pool the KV projection weights within each group into g shared heads, then uptrain on a small compute fraction
Delete all but g of the KV heads, keep the remaining projection weights unchanged, and continue serving right away
Retrain the whole model from scratch with g KV heads, because MHA weights cannot be mapped onto shared heads
Average the query heads into g groups and keep all n_h KV heads, then fine-tune briefly on the original data
questions.explanation: You cannot just drop KV heads, which throws away learned information. The recipe mean-pools KV projection weights within each group, then fine-tunes (uptrains) briefly to recover quality. Full retraining is unnecessary, and query heads are kept intact.

questions.question: How does attention compute (scores and softmax) compare across MHA, GQA and MQA?
options: GQA and MQA reduce it by a factor of n_h/g, since fewer heads compute their scores
MQA needs n_h times more compute, since one KV head serves every query head
GQA doubles it, because the repeat step adds a second pass over the scores
It is essentially unchanged, since all three still run n_h query-head attentions
questions.explanation: All three keep n_h query heads, each doing a full attention, so the score and softmax compute is essentially the same. The differences are in memory: KV-cache bytes, KV-projection parameters and memory bandwidth per decode step.

questions.question: How does quality compare across MHA, GQA and MQA?
options: MQA is best, GQA is in the middle, and MHA is worst, because fewer KV heads regularize
All three are identical in quality, since attention compute is the same for each
MHA is best, GQA is approximately equal to MHA, and MQA is slightly below
GQA is best, while MHA and MQA are roughly equal, since g balances the two extremes
questions.explanation: MHA has the most KV capacity and the best quality. GQA recovers almost all of it at a fraction of the cache. MQA, with one shared KV head, is slightly below.

questions.question: Why is forgetting to repeat K and V in GQA a bug?
options: It only causes a slightly larger KV cache, since the unrepeated heads are then stored separately in every layer
Without the repeat, shapes fail to broadcast for QK^T or broadcast wrongly, so heads see the wrong KV head
It makes the causal mask invalid, because the mask was built for n_h heads instead of only g heads
It silently converts the model into MHA, since every query head then gets its own K and V projection
questions.explanation: K and V have g heads while Q has n_h. Without repeating, QK^T either fails on shape mismatch or silently broadcasts incorrectly. Each group's query heads must be paired with their shared KV head.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to expect GQA to speed up training?
options: GQA actually makes training much slower, because the repeat doubles memory traffic
GQA's benefit is the inference KV cache; training throughput is roughly unchanged
GQA cannot be trained from scratch at all, only converted from an MHA checkpoint
GQA requires training in float64 for the repeated heads to stay numerically stable
questions.explanation: The savings come from caching only g KV heads during decoding. Training has no cache and processes all positions in parallel with full-width repeated K and V, so throughput is roughly unchanged. GQA trains normally.

questions.question: A model has n_h = 32 query heads and uses GQA with g = 4. How many query heads share each KV head, and how much smaller is its KV cache than MHA's?
options: 8 query heads per KV head; the cache is 8 times smaller
4 query heads per KV head; the cache is 4 times smaller
8 query heads per KV head; the cache is 4 times smaller
128 query heads per KV head; the cache is 32 times smaller
questions.explanation: Group size is n_h / g = 32 / 4 = 8. The cache scales with g, so it is n_h / g = 8 times smaller than MHA. Making it MQA would require g = 1.

questions.question: A GQA implementation with KV heads [A, B] and n_rep = 2 uses k.repeat(1, 2, 1, 1) instead of k.repeat_interleave(2, dim=1). What goes wrong?
options: It produces a shape error and crashes immediately, because repeat and repeat_interleave need different ranks
It produces [A, A, B, B], which is the correct grouping for n_rep = 2, so there is no bug here at all
It averages A and B into a single head and then copies that head to every one of the four query heads
It produces [A, B, A, B] instead of [A, A, B, B], silently pairing query heads with the wrong KV head
questions.explanation: repeat_interleave gives [A, A, B, B], so heads 0 and 1 share A and heads 2 and 3 share B, the contiguous groups. repeat tiles the block to [A, B, A, B], so heads 0 and 2 share A. Shapes still match, so it runs, but the grouping is scrambled relative to how the weights were trained.

questions.question: Which paper introduced GQA and the mean-pool-and-uptrain conversion recipe?
options: Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need (Shazeer 2019)
Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models (Touvron et al. 2023)
GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints (2023)
DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model (DeepSeek-AI 2024)
questions.explanation: Ainslie et al. 2023 introduced GQA and the conversion recipe. Shazeer's 2019 Fast Transformer Decoding introduced MQA. Llama 2 adopted GQA for its 70B model but did not introduce it, and DeepSeek-V2 introduced a different approach (MLA).

questions.question: What is the next step in the KV-cache-reduction line after GQA, used by DeepSeek-V3?
options: Removing attention entirely in favor of gated MLPs that need no per-token cache
Doubling the number of KV heads while halving the head dimension in every layer
Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), which compresses the KV cache differently
Storing the KV cache in int1, so each cached element takes a single bit of memory
questions.explanation: DeepSeek-V3 uses Multi-head Latent Attention, which compresses the KV cache in a different way than sharing heads. It continues the same goal of reducing cache memory. The other options are not what DeepSeek-V3 does.

questions.question: Why does the number of KV heads, not query heads, determine the KV-cache size?
options: Because query heads are discarded after training, so only KV heads remain at inference time
The cache stores one K and one V per KV head per past position; queries are computed fresh, not cached
Because each query head stores its own private copy of the shared cache, multiplied by the size of its group
Because the cache stores only the queries of past tokens, and their number is set by the KV heads
questions.explanation: Past tokens' keys and values are needed at every future step, so they are cached, one per KV head. The query is only needed for the token being generated, so it is computed and used immediately. That is why cache size is proportional to g and independent of n_h.

questions.question: Which values of g make GQA reduce to MHA and to MQA?
options: g = n_h gives MHA, and g = 1 gives MQA
g = 1 gives MHA, and g = n_h gives MQA
g = n_h / 2 gives MHA, and g = 2 gives MQA
g = 0 gives MQA, and g = n_h gives MHA
questions.explanation: With g = n_h every query head has its own KV head (n_rep = 1, no sharing), which is MHA. With g = 1 all query heads share a single KV head, which is MQA. g = 0 would have no keys or values at all.

questions.question: In a Mixture of Experts (MoE) transformer layer, which component of a dense transformer block does the set of experts replace?
options: The multi-head self-attention sublayer that mixes information across tokens
The token embedding table at the input of the network
The dense feed-forward network (FFN/MLP) of the block
The final LayerNorm and the unembedding projection to the vocabulary
questions.explanation: An MoE layer replaces the single dense feed-forward network of a transformer block with N expert FFNs plus a router. Attention is left unchanged. Each expert is itself a small FFN (for example a SwiGLU), which is why the dense FFN is the natural thing to swap out.

questions.question: DeepSeek-V3 is described as having 671B parameters but activating only about 37B per token. What does this illustrate about Mixture of Experts models?
options: MoE gives a very large total parameter count at the inference cost of a much smaller model
MoE compresses all 671B parameters into a 37B low-rank form when the model is loaded
Only 37B parameters are ever trained; the remaining experts are frozen after initialization
The 37B are the attention weights, while the other 634B are embedding tables looked up per token
questions.explanation: All 671B parameters are stored and trained, but each token is routed through only a small subset of experts totalling about 37B parameters. That is how frontier models get huge capacity at manageable per-token compute. Nothing is compressed or frozen; the experts just sit idle for tokens that are not routed to them.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: more parameters, same compute per token
questions.question: In a dense transformer, why do the parameter count and per-token FLOPs of the feed-forward network rise together?
options: Because the FFN's FLOPs depend only on sequence length, which grows with model size
Because each token uses a different random subset of FFN weights, sized to the layer width
Because larger FFNs require proportionally more attention heads to feed them inputs
Every token flows through the same FFN, so a bigger FFN costs more for every token
questions.explanation: In a dense model each token passes through the one shared FFN, so every extra FFN parameter is used, and paid for in FLOPs, by every token. MoE breaks this coupling by letting each token use only some experts. The distractor about random subsets describes neither dense FFNs nor MoE.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: more parameters, same compute per token
questions.question: In a Mixture of Experts layer, what does the router (gating network) do for each token?
options: Averages the outputs of all N experts with equal weights so every expert sees each token
Scores every expert and selects the top-k experts that will process that token
Assigns tokens to experts in round-robin order so each expert gets an equal share
Picks which attention heads the token should attend with in the following layer
questions.explanation: The router is a small learned network that produces a score for every expert; the top-k scoring experts are the only ones evaluated for that token, and their outputs are blended with gate weights. Running all experts equally would remove the compute saving, and round-robin assignment would not be learned.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: more parameters, same compute per token
questions.question: With a Mixture of Experts layer of N experts and top-k routing, how do total parameters and per-token FLOPs scale?
options: Both total parameters and per-token FLOPs scale linearly with N, as in a wider dense FFN
Total parameters scale with N, while per-token FLOPs stay close to k dense FFN passes
Total parameters stay constant while per-token FLOPs drop by a factor of N/k
Total parameters scale with k and per-token FLOPs scale with N, since every expert is scored and run
questions.explanation: All N experts are stored, so parameters grow with N, but each token only touches k of them, so per-token compute is roughly k FFN passes regardless of N. This is the whole point of MoE: capacity grows without proportional compute. The tempting 'both scale with N' answer describes a dense model made N times wider.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: more parameters, same compute per token
questions.question: What is meant by 'sparse activation' in a Mixture of Experts model?
options: Most weights inside each expert are exactly zero after magnitude pruning during training
Activations are stored in a sparse tensor format such as CSR to save GPU memory
Only a sparse random subset of the tokens in each batch is processed at every layer
For any given token, most of the network's expert parameters are idle and not computed
questions.explanation: Sparse activation means each token activates only its top-k experts, so most experts do no work for that token. It is not weight pruning or a sparse storage format; the experts themselves are ordinary dense FFNs. Every token is still processed, just by a few experts.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: more parameters, same compute per token
questions.question: What is the intuitive reason a Mixture of Experts can outperform a dense FFN of similar per-token compute?
options: Experts can specialize (code, prose, arithmetic) and the router sends each token to the most useful ones
Each expert sees every token in the batch, so each one is effectively trained on k times more data overall
Experts share all their weights through tying, which acts as a strong regularizer during training
The router replaces the attention sublayer, so the saved compute can be spent on a larger FFN
questions.explanation: A dense FFN must be a jack-of-all-trades, while separate experts can specialize on different kinds of tokens, and the learned router directs each token to the specialists most useful for it. Experts do not see every token and do not share weights, which is exactly what makes them specialists.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: more parameters, same compute per token
questions.question: Mixture of Experts is described as trading memory for capacity. What exactly is traded?
options: Less memory is used per expert in exchange for slower inference, since experts are paged in on demand
Activation memory is traded for fewer parameters, because each expert recomputes its inputs
More stored parameters (memory) buy more capacity without proportionally more per-token compute
Optimizer state is discarded for routed experts in exchange for being able to store more of them
questions.explanation: MoE must hold all N experts' parameters in memory, but each token only computes through k of them. So the cost moves from FLOPs to memory: you pay in stored parameters and get more capacity (knowledge the model can hold) at roughly constant compute per token.

questions.question: In MoE routing $\mathbf{p} = \operatorname{softmax}(W_r\mathbf{x})$, what are the shape of the router weight $W_r$ and the meaning of $p_i$, for token vector $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^C$ and N experts?
options: $W_r\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times C}$; $p_i$ is the output activation of expert $i$ at channel $i$
$W_r\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$; $p_i$ is the load on expert $i$ in the batch
$W_r\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C}$; $p_i$ is the router's affinity (probability) for expert $i$
$W_r\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times N}$ applied after the experts; $p_i$ is expert $i$'s training loss
questions.explanation: The router maps a C-dimensional token vector to N scores, so $W_r$ is $N\times C$, and the softmax turns those scores into a probability vector over experts. $p_i$ is how strongly the router favours expert $i$ for this token. The router runs before the experts, not after, and it does not measure batch load.

questions.question: After selecting the top-k experts $\mathcal{T}$ in an MoE layer, how are the gate weights $g_i$ computed?
options: $g_i = p_i / \sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}} p_j$, renormalizing the kept probabilities to sum to 1
$g_i = p_i$, using the raw softmax probabilities unchanged so the kept gates sum to 1
$g_i = 1/k$ for every selected expert, ignoring the router's probabilities entirely
$g_i = \operatorname{softmax}(p)_i$ applied a second time over all N experts, then masked to the top-k
questions.explanation: The top-k probabilities are divided by their own sum so the k gates form a proper weighted average. Raw $p_i$ would sum to less than 1, shrinking the output, and uniform $1/k$ would throw away the router's confidence information.

questions.question: What is the output of an MoE layer for a token with selected expert set $\mathcal{T}$ and gates $g_i$?
options: $\mathbf{y} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} p_i\,E_i(\mathbf{x})$, a probability-weighted sum over all N experts
$\mathbf{y} = \max_{i\in\mathcal{T}} E_i(\mathbf{x})$, the elementwise maximum over the selected experts
$\mathbf{y} = E_{\text{argmax}}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \sum_i g_i$, the top expert scaled by the total kept gate
$\mathbf{y} = \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} g_i\,E_i(\mathbf{x})$, a gate-weighted sum over the selected experts
questions.explanation: Only the experts in $\mathcal{T}$ are evaluated and their outputs are blended with the renormalized gates. Summing over all N experts would require running every expert, which destroys the compute saving that defines MoE.

questions.question: Where does the compute saving of a Mixture of Experts layer come from?
options: The router matmul replaces the FFN matmul, which is the expensive part of each block
Experts not in the token's top-k set are never evaluated for that token
Experts are evaluated at lower precision (FP8) than a dense FFN would be
Each expert is evaluated on only half its input dimensions, chosen by the router
questions.explanation: The saving is simply that unselected experts do no work for a given token. The router is a tiny extra matmul, not a replacement for the FFN, and experts run at normal precision on the full input.

questions.question: How many experts does each token use in Switch Transformers versus Mixtral and DeepSeek?
options: Switch uses top-2 blended by gates; Mixtral and DeepSeek use top-1 to cut communication
Switch uses top-1 (one expert); Mixtral and DeepSeek use top-2, blended by their gates
All three use top-8 routing, with gates renormalized over the eight selected experts
Switch evaluates all experts with soft gates; Mixtral and DeepSeek use hard top-1 selection
questions.explanation: Switch Transformers introduced k = 1 routing, so each token hits exactly one expert. Mixtral and DeepSeek use k = 2 in this description, with the two expert outputs blended by their renormalized gates.

questions.question: What is 'router collapse' in Mixture of Experts training?
options: The router's softmax outputs become exactly uniform, so every token is routed to a random expert
All experts converge to identical weights, so the router's choice no longer matters for the layer output
The router logits overflow in low precision and become NaN, which then spreads to every expert
A rich-get-richer loop where a few experts get most tokens and the rest are never selected or trained
questions.explanation: Experts chosen slightly more often early get more gradient, improve faster, and get chosen even more. The endpoint is a handful of overworked experts and many dead ones. Uniform routing is the opposite of collapse, and identical experts is a different (redundancy) problem.

questions.question: Besides wasting parameters, why is router collapse especially harmful when experts are sharded across devices (expert parallelism)?
options: One GPU holding the popular experts is swamped while the others sit idle
It causes the gradient all-reduce across the data-parallel ranks to deadlock
It forces every GPU to hold a full replica of every expert's weights
It doubles the size of the KV cache on the device that hosts the router
questions.explanation: With expert parallelism each GPU holds a subset of experts, so if tokens pile onto a few experts, the device holding them does most of the work while others idle. That load imbalance wrecks throughput. It does not change the KV cache or force replication.

questions.question: In the Switch Transformers auxiliary load-balance loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = N\sum_i f_i P_i$, what are $f_i$ and $P_i$?
options: $f_i$ is the mean router probability for expert $i$ (soft); $P_i$ is the fraction of tokens routed to it (hard)
$f_i$ is expert $i$'s share of layer FLOPs; $P_i$ is its share of the layer's parameter count
$f_i$ is the fraction of tokens routed to expert $i$ (hard); $P_i$ is its mean router probability (soft)
$f_i$ is expert $i$'s per-token loss; $P_i$ is the norm of its gradient averaged over the batch
questions.explanation: $f_i$ counts how many tokens actually went to expert $i$ (a non-differentiable fraction from the top-k choice), and $P_i$ averages the router's softmax probability for expert $i$ over the batch (differentiable). Swapping them is the tempting mistake; the hard count is $f$ and the soft average is $P$.

questions.question: What are the minimum and maximum values of the aux loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = N\sum_i f_i P_i$ and when do they occur?
options: Minimum 0 when routing is perfectly uniform; maximum 1 when everything goes to one expert
Minimum N when routing is perfectly uniform; maximum N squared when all tokens hit one expert
Minimum 1 when routing is perfectly uniform; maximum N when everything goes to one expert
Minimum 1 when everything goes to one expert; maximum N when routing is perfectly uniform
questions.explanation: With $f_i = P_i = 1/N$, $N\cdot N\cdot(1/N)(1/N) = 1$. With all mass on one expert, $N\cdot 1\cdot 1 = N$. The N prefactor is what normalizes the balanced value to exactly 1 rather than 1/N or 0.

questions.question: In the auxiliary load-balance loss, through which quantity do gradients flow to the router?
options: Through $P_i$, the mean router probability, which is differentiable
Through $f_i$, the hard per-expert token count taken from the top-k indices
Through the top-k index selection, using a straight-through estimator
Through the expert outputs $E_i(\mathbf{x})$ only, never through the router
questions.explanation: $f_i$ comes from a discrete top-k choice and has no useful gradient, so it is treated as a constant. $P_i$ is a mean of softmax probabilities, so its gradient nudges the router to raise probability on under-used experts. The top-k selection itself is not backpropagated through.

questions.question: How is the auxiliary load-balance loss combined with the language-modeling loss during MoE training?
options: The aux loss replaces the LM loss for the first epoch, then training switches back to LM only
Total loss is $\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}} \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}}$, so imbalance scales the LM gradient
The aux loss is computed only at evaluation time and used to pick which experts to keep
Total loss is $\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}} + \alpha\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}}$ with a small $\alpha$
questions.explanation: The aux loss is added to the LM loss with a small weight $\alpha$ so it encourages balance without dominating the main objective. It is a training regularizer, not an evaluation-time tool or a multiplicative factor.

questions.question: Intuitively, what does the aux loss $N\sum_i f_i P_i$ penalize?
options: Experts whose outputs have large norms, since those dominate the gate-weighted sum of experts
Putting many tokens (high f_i) on experts the router is already confident about (high P_i)
Tokens whose router probabilities are close to uniform, pushing the router to be confident
Experts that receive no tokens at all, by adding a large constant penalty for each dead expert
questions.explanation: Each term multiplies how loaded an expert is by how much probability the router gives it, so the sum is large exactly when the favoured experts are also overloaded. Minimizing it lowers probability on overloaded experts and raises it on under-used ones. It does not look at output norms.

questions.question: Why did DeepSeek-V3 look for an alternative to the auxiliary load-balance loss?
options: The aux loss cannot be computed with top-2 routing, only with Switch-style top-1 routing
The aux loss gradient competes with the language-modeling loss and can slightly hurt quality
The aux loss requires a full extra forward pass through all experts at every training step
The aux loss drives every expert toward identical weights, which removes their specialization
questions.explanation: The aux loss adds a gradient term that pulls on the router in a direction other than lowering LM loss, which can cost a little quality. DeepSeek-V3's aux-loss-free method balances load without adding any loss gradient.

questions.question: How does DeepSeek-V3's auxiliary-loss-free load balancing work?
options: A per-expert bias is added to the gate weights that blend expert outputs, and it is learned by gradient descent
Tokens routed to an overloaded expert are randomly reassigned to an underloaded one after top-k selection
The number of experts is increased during training whenever one expert's load exceeds a fixed threshold
A per-expert bias, used only in top-k selection, is lowered for overloaded and raised for underloaded experts
questions.explanation: A bias $b_i$ shifts which experts win top-k selection but is not used in the gate weights, and it is updated by a simple rule after each step rather than by a loss gradient. Because balance comes from the selection bias, it does not pull on the LM objective. Adding the bias to the gates would change the outputs, which the method avoids.

questions.question: In DeepSeek-V3's aux-loss-free balancing, is the per-expert bias used in the gate weights that blend expert outputs?
options: No; it affects only which experts are selected, not the gate weights
Yes; it is added to both the selection scores and the blending gates
Yes; it replaces the softmax gates entirely once training has warmed up
No; it is added to the expert outputs after they have been blended
questions.explanation: The bias only shifts the top-k selection scores. The gates that weight the chosen experts' outputs still come from the unbiased router scores, so the bias changes routing without distorting the output mixture.

questions.question: Which load-balancing method is implemented in the course's llmre.model.moe code, and how is DeepSeek-V3's bias trick classified?
options: The DeepSeek-V3 bias trick is implemented; the Switch aux loss is labelled INFERENCE/SPECULATION
Neither is implemented; both are described only as REASONABLE INDUSTRY PRACTICE without published details
The Switch-style aux loss is implemented; the bias trick is PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED in the DeepSeek-V3 report
Both are implemented and combined in the default config, with the bias trick switched on after warmup
questions.explanation: The course code uses the classic auxiliary loss, while the aux-loss-free bias balancing is documented in the DeepSeek-V3 technical report and labelled PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED. It is described, not implemented, in the codebase.

questions.question: What are 'shared experts' in DeepSeekMoE?
options: Experts whose weights are tied and shared across all layers of the network in order to save memory
Routed experts that two different tokens are allowed to use at the same time in one batch
One or more FFNs that are always active for every token in addition to the routed top-k experts
Experts shared between the encoder and the decoder stacks so both learn the same features
questions.explanation: Shared experts bypass the router and process every token, while the routed experts handle the top-k selection on top. They are not cross-layer weight sharing; the 'shared' refers to being used by all tokens.

questions.question: What is the motivation for adding always-on shared experts in DeepSeekMoE?
options: They capture common knowledge (syntax, frequent patterns) so routed experts need not relearn it and can specialize
They guarantee each token uses exactly one routed expert, which removes the need to renormalize the top-k gate weights
They reduce memory by replacing half of the routed experts with a single larger always-on network
They remove the need for any load balancing, because every token already has a guaranteed expert to use
questions.explanation: Knowledge common to nearly all tokens would otherwise be duplicated in many routed experts, wasting capacity. Dedicating shared experts to that common case frees routed experts to specialize. Load balancing is still needed for the routed experts.

questions.question: With shared experts, what is the MoE output for a token?
options: $\mathbf{y} = \sum_s E^{\text{shared}}_s(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} g_i E_i(\mathbf{x})$
$\mathbf{y} = \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} g_i E_i(\mathbf{x})$, with shared experts used only in the router
$\mathbf{y} = \tfrac12\sum_s E^{\text{shared}}_s(\mathbf{x})$ only, routed experts used for training
$\mathbf{y} = \sum_s E^{\text{shared}}_s(\mathbf{x}) + \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} g_i E_i(\mathbf{x})$
questions.explanation: The always-on shared expert outputs (ungated) are added to the gate-weighted sum of the routed top-k experts. It is a sum, not a product, and the shared experts contribute directly to the output, not to routing.

questions.question: What are 'fine-grained' experts in DeepSeekMoE and what do they buy?
options: Experts that each operate on a separate slice of channels of the hidden vector, like a grouped convolution
Many small experts instead of a few large ones, giving the router more combinations at the same parameter count
Experts trained at higher numerical precision than the rest of the model so they can capture finer detail
A few very large experts that each cover one whole domain, such as source code, mathematics or natural-language prose
questions.explanation: Splitting capacity into many smaller experts lets the router combine them in many more ways for the same total parameters, enabling finer specialization. It is not per-channel processing or a precision change.

questions.question: In an MoE layer with N = 4 and k = 2, a token's softmax router probabilities are (0.6381, 0.2347, 0.0954, 0.0318). What happens to experts 2 and 3 for this token?
options: They run with gates 0.0954 and 0.0318, so their contribution to the output is small but nonzero
They are never evaluated; only experts 0 and 1 run, with gates about 0.73 and 0.27
They run on the token, but their outputs are discarded before the gate-weighted sum is taken
They receive the token on the next step instead, once experts 0 and 1 have been freed up
questions.explanation: Top-2 selects experts 0 and 1; renormalizing 0.6381 and 0.2347 by their sum 0.8728 gives gates 0.7311 and 0.2689. Experts 2 and 3 are skipped entirely, which is where the compute saving comes from; running them and discarding the output would waste that saving.

questions.question: How does the from-scratch MoE forward reshape tensors before routing?
options: It routes each sequence as a whole, producing (B, N) probabilities so all tokens of one sequence share the same experts
It transposes to (C, B, T) so that each channel of the hidden vector independently picks its own expert
It keeps (B, T, C) and computes (B, T, N, C) outputs for all experts, then masks the unselected ones
It flattens (B, T, C) to (BT, C), routes to (BT, N) probabilities, then reshapes the output back to (B, T, C)
questions.explanation: Routing is per token, so the batch and time axes are merged into one list of N_tok tokens; the router produces one N-way probability vector per token. After dispatch and combination the output is viewed back to (B, T, C). Computing all experts' outputs for every token would defeat the sparsity.

questions.question: In the from-scratch MoE, what architecture is each expert?
options: A SwiGLU feed-forward block from lesson 12.2
A single linear layer with no activation function
A single self-attention head with its own projections
A GELU two-layer MLP whose weights are shared with the router
questions.explanation: Each expert in llmre.model.moe is a SwiGLU module, the same gated FFN used in modern dense LLaMA-style blocks. The router is a separate bias-free linear layer mapping dim to n_experts.

questions.question: In the MoE route() method, what does probs.topk(self.top_k, dim=-1) return and what is done next?
options: The k smallest probabilities and their indices per token, which are then masked out of the softmax output entirely
A one-hot mask over all N experts per token, which is then passed through a second softmax to form gates
The k largest probabilities and their expert indices per token; the kept gates are then divided by their sum
The k tokens most strongly assigned to each expert, so that each expert processes exactly k tokens per batch
questions.explanation: topk along the expert dimension returns, for each token, the k highest probabilities (gates) and the indices of those experts, each of shape (N_tok, k). The gates are then renormalized by their row sum. It selects experts per token, not tokens per expert.

questions.question: In the from-scratch MoE forward, how is each expert's work restricted to its own tokens?
options: Every expert runs on all tokens, and its output is multiplied by a zero gate wherever it was not selected
Tokens are sorted by expert index and padded to equal length so all experts run as one batched matmul
A boolean mask of tokens that chose the expert gathers a sub-batch; the expert runs once and gated results are added back
Each token is processed in its own Python loop iteration, calling only the experts it selected, one after another in order
questions.explanation: For each expert e, sel = (topk_idx == e) marks which tokens chose it, token_mask = sel.any(-1) selects them, the expert runs once on x_flat[token_mask], and the gate-weighted result is scattered into out. An expert with no tokens is skipped. Running every expert on all tokens would give the same output but no compute saving.

questions.question: In the from-scratch MoE, how is the gate weight for expert e extracted for each token?
options: (topk_gate * sel).sum(dim=-1), which picks the gate in whichever top-k slot held expert e
probs[:, e], the router probability for expert e before the top-k gates are renormalized
topk_gate[:, 0] for every expert, since the first slot always holds the largest gate value
sel.float().mean(dim=-1), the fraction of top-k slots in which expert e was selected
questions.explanation: sel is a (N_tok, k) boolean telling which of a token's k slots chose expert e; multiplying by the renormalized gates and summing over k yields that expert's gate (zero if not chosen). Using probs[:, e] would skip the renormalization.

questions.question: How are shared experts applied in the from-scratch MoE forward?
options: Shared experts are added to the router's candidate list and compete with routed experts for top-k slots
Shared experts run only on the tokens that no routed expert selected, as a fallback path
Shared experts' outputs are averaged together and then multiplied by the routed experts' gates
Each shared expert is run on all tokens and its output is added to the routed output without a gate
questions.explanation: The code loops over self.shared and does out = out + sh(x_flat): every token goes through every shared expert, ungated. That matches the always-on term of the DeepSeekMoE output formula.

questions.question: In the MoE aux loss code, why is f detached in aux = n_experts * torch.sum(f.detach() * P)?
options: Detaching f only saves activation memory; it leaves the gradient with respect to the router weights unchanged
f is a hard token-count fraction; detaching it makes gradients flow only through the soft mean probability P
Detaching f stops the expert FFN weights from being updated by the load-balancing term at all
f must be detached because it is computed on the CPU, while P lives on the GPU with the router
questions.explanation: f is computed from one-hot top-k assignments, which carry no meaningful gradient; treating it as a constant means the loss's gradient comes from P, matching the derivation where the router is nudged through $P_i$. It is not a memory trick, and the expert weights are trained by the LM loss regardless.

questions.question: In the MoE aux loss code, how is the per-expert token fraction f computed?
options: Take the softmax router probabilities and average them over all tokens in the batch, separately for each expert
One-hot encode topk_idx, sum over the k slots to get a (N_tok, N) assignment matrix, then average over tokens
Count the number of nonzero expert outputs per token and divide that count by the hidden size C
Divide each expert's parameter count by the total parameter count summed across all N experts
questions.explanation: F.one_hot(topk_idx, n_experts) has shape (N_tok, k, N); summing over k gives which experts each token used, and the mean over tokens gives the fraction of routed assignments per expert. The mean of probabilities is P, the other factor.

questions.section: 7. Under the hood: verify the routing and the aux loss
questions.question: In an MoE with N experts and top-k routing, what is the per-token compute cost?
options: About N dense-FFN passes, since the router must evaluate every expert
About N/k dense-FFN passes, split evenly across the selected experts
About one dense-FFN pass regardless of k, because the gates sum to 1
About k dense-FFN passes plus a tiny router matmul, independent of N
questions.explanation: Each token runs through its k chosen experts, so cost is roughly k FFN passes, and adding more experts does not raise it. The router's C-by-N matmul is negligible. Using k = 2 costs about twice a single FFN, not one.

questions.section: 7. Under the hood: verify the routing and the aux loss
questions.question: What are the real engineering costs of Mixture of Experts at scale, beyond FLOPs?
options: Memory for all experts, all-to-all traffic to ship tokens to experts on other devices, and load imbalance
Extra attention computation for every expert, because each expert needs its own attention sublayer and KV cache
A KV cache that grows linearly with the number of experts, since each expert caches keys and values
Recomputing the router once per expert in the backward pass, which doubles the cost of every layer
questions.explanation: All N experts must be stored, typically sharded across GPUs with expert parallelism, so tokens are sent via all-to-all to wherever their chosen experts live. That communication plus imbalance from uneven routing are the real costs, which is why load balancing matters so much. Experts do not add attention or KV cache.

questions.section: 7. Under the hood: verify the routing and the aux loss
questions.question: In expert parallelism for Mixture of Experts, how do tokens reach their chosen experts?
options: Every GPU holds a full copy of all experts, so tokens never move and only gradients are all-reduced
Expert weights are streamed from CPU memory to each GPU on demand whenever a token in the local batch selects them
Each GPU holds a subset of experts, and an all-to-all exchange ships tokens to the devices holding their experts
Tokens are broadcast to every GPU, and each GPU runs all its experts and keeps the selected outputs
questions.explanation: Expert parallelism shards experts across devices, so routing requires an all-to-all where each device sends tokens to the device of each chosen expert and receives results back. Replicating all experts everywhere would remove the memory benefit of sharding.

questions.section: 7. Under the hood: verify the routing and the aux loss
questions.question: What is the 'capacity factor' in production MoE training, and what happens to overflow tokens?
options: A minimum number of tokens each expert must receive per batch; shortfalls are padded with zero vectors
A multiplier on each expert's hidden size that grows during training as more tokens are routed to it
A cap on tokens each expert accepts per batch; overflow tokens are dropped and pass only through the residual
A cap on experts per token; whenever the router picks more experts than the cap allows, the extras are averaged
questions.explanation: Production kernels give each expert a fixed buffer per batch. If the router sends more tokens than that, the excess skip the expert and only the residual connection carries them forward. Good balancing keeps drops rare; a collapsed router drops heavily.

questions.section: 7. Under the hood: verify the routing and the aux loss
questions.question: Does the course's teaching MoE implementation enforce an expert capacity limit?
options: No; it runs every routed token, which is fine on CPU but differs from how production kernels behave
Yes; tokens above a capacity factor of 1.25 are dropped and pass through only the residual connection
Yes; overflow tokens are rerouted to their next-best expert, as production MoE kernels do
No; instead it runs every expert on every token and zeroes out the unselected outputs
questions.explanation: The teaching code has no capacity cap, so no token is dropped. Production kernels use fixed per-expert capacity and drop overflow. It still runs only the routed experts per token, not all experts.

questions.question: Which is a correct statement about gradients in MoE training?
options: Gradients should flow through both f_i and the top-k selection, using a straight-through estimator
Only f_i should carry gradient, since P_i is a probability and must be detached to keep it properly normalized
The router receives no gradient at all and stays fixed at its initialization throughout training
Detach the hard count f_i; gradients flow through P_i, and the top-k selection itself is not backpropagated
questions.explanation: f_i is a discrete count and is detached; P_i is the differentiable route by which the aux loss trains the router. The top-k choice is not differentiated. The router also learns from the LM loss through the gate weights.

questions.question: What goes wrong if an MoE implementation forgets to renormalize the top-k gate weights?
options: The router selects the wrong experts, because the top-k operation is then applied to unnormalized logits
The kept probabilities sum to less than 1, so the output is not a proper weighted average of the experts
Load balancing becomes impossible, since the aux loss needs top-k gates that sum to exactly 1 for every token
The aux loss becomes negative, which pushes the router toward collapse instead of balance
questions.explanation: Selecting k of N experts leaves probabilities that sum to less than 1, which scales the output down. Renormalizing makes the gates sum to 1. Selection itself is unaffected; only the blending is wrong.

questions.question: Why should MoE models report both total parameters and active parameters?
options: Total counts the parameters used in training, while active counts only those tied to the tokenizer vocabulary
Total measures memory to store all experts; active measures per-token compute; in MoE they differ greatly
The two are always equal in MoE, but reporting both is a convention inherited from dense model papers
Active parameters measure the memory to store the model, while total parameters measure per-token compute
questions.explanation: For DeepSeek-V3, 671B total sets the memory footprint, while about 37B active per token sets the compute cost. Confusing them misjudges either cost. The tempting reversed option swaps which number governs memory and which governs compute.

questions.question: A dense FFN with P parameters is replaced by an MoE of 8 experts, each the same size as the dense FFN, with top-2 routing (ignore the router). What are total parameters, active parameters per token, and their ratio?
options: 8P total, about 8P active, a 1x ratio
2P total, about P active, giving a 2x ratio
8P total, about P active, an 8x ratio
8P total, about 2P active, a 4x ratio
questions.explanation: Eight experts of size P store 8P parameters; each token runs its top-2, so about 2P are active; 8P / 2P = 4. You get 8 times the FFN capacity at about twice the per-token FFN compute. The 8x option would only hold for top-1.

questions.question: An MoE model's expert 3 processes about 90% of tokens after a few hundred steps, yet LM loss keeps falling. What was most likely forgotten?
options: The auxiliary load-balance loss (or an equivalent balancing mechanism), causing router collapse
The renormalization of the top-k gates, so the kept gate weights no longer sum to 1
The causal attention mask, which lets expert 3 see future tokens and so win nearly every routing choice
Weight decay on the router matrix, which lets one expert's logit grow without any bound
questions.explanation: Without a balancing term, the rich-get-richer loop concentrates tokens on a few experts: router collapse. The fix is to add the aux loss or DeepSeek-V3's bias update. Unnormalized gates would scale outputs but not cause this concentration.

questions.question: Why can the LM loss still go down for a while in an MoE suffering router collapse?
options: A collapsed router produces a lower aux loss, and that drop is added directly into the reported LM loss
The dead experts keep receiving gradient through their gates, so they still improve slowly
The one or two overworked experts still learn, so the model behaves like a much smaller dense model
Router collapse speeds up the attention layers, which lowers loss through faster convergence
questions.explanation: The few experts that receive tokens keep improving, so the model trains like a small dense model and loss falls. But it never uses the capacity it paid for, and on sharded hardware the load is badly imbalanced. Collapse actually raises the aux loss, toward its maximum N.

questions.question: Which papers introduced top-1 routing with the aux loss, fine-grained plus shared experts, and aux-loss-free bias balancing, respectively?
options: DeepSeekMoE; Switch Transformers; Mixtral 8x7B
DeepSeek-V3; DeepSeekMoE; Switch Transformers
Switch Transformers; DeepSeekMoE; DeepSeek-V3
Mixtral; DeepSeek-V3; DeepSeekMoE
questions.explanation: Switch Transformers (Fedus et al. 2021) introduced top-1 routing with the load-balance aux loss; DeepSeekMoE (Dai et al. 2024) added fine-grained and shared experts; DeepSeek-V3 (2024) added aux-loss-free bias balancing and scaled to 671B total / about 37B active. Read in that order, each refines the last.

questions.question: Why is the aux loss $N\sum_i f_i P_i$ minimal when load is uniform, and how does its gradient fix router collapse?
options: Uniform $f_i = P_i = 1/N$ gives the minimum 1; gradient through $P_i$ moves probability off overloaded experts onto idle ones
Uniform routing gives the maximum value N, so its gradient pushes the router to concentrate tokens on one expert to lower it
It is minimal at uniform load because $f_i$ is then zero; the gradient through $f_i$ directly reassigns tokens to experts
Uniform load sets $P_i = 1$ for all experts; its gradient raises the router softmax temperature until routing is random
questions.explanation: The sum of products $f_iP_i$ is smallest when both are spread evenly, giving 1. Because the hard counts are detached, the gradient acts on the router probabilities $P_i$, shifting mass toward under-used experts and spreading load. It does not reassign tokens directly or change a temperature.

questions.question: In DeepSeek-V3's '~37B active parameters per token', which parameters are counted as active?
options: All 671B parameters divided by the number of layers, since a token passes through one layer at a time
Only the router weights in every layer, because those are the only weights that every single token is guaranteed to use
Only the attention weights in every layer; expert FFN weights are excluded because they are sparse
The shared experts plus the top-k routed experts a single token actually flows through, which set its compute cost
questions.explanation: Active parameters are those a single token actually computes with: its always-on shared experts plus its selected top-k routed experts. That sets the per-token compute, while the 671B total sets memory.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: In a 2026 model card, what do you need to know about a layer labelled 'Gated DeltaNet' or 'KDA' sitting next to 'GQA' and 'MoE'?
options: Which tokenizer and vocabulary it was trained with, since that fixes how many state slots it allocates
Which optimizer and learning-rate schedule trained it, since linear layers only converge under Muon
What state the layer carries, what it costs, and what it gives up compared with softmax attention
How many experts it routes each token to, and how its router balances load across those experts
questions.explanation: Gated DeltaNet and KDA are linear-attention token-mixing layers used in hybrid stacks. Understanding them means knowing their fixed-size state, their compute and memory cost, and the exact recall they give up relative to softmax attention. They are not MoE routing or optimizer choices.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: Which inference engines are noted as supporting hybrid linear/full-attention models such as Qwen3-Next?
options: vLLM and SGLang
Only TensorRT-LLM
No serving engine; they run only in research code
llama.cpp exclusively
questions.explanation: Hybrid linear/full-attention stacks are shipped in open-weight frontier MoE models and supported by vLLM and SGLang, which use flash-linear-attention Triton kernels for the linear layers. They are not limited to research code.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: What hardware is needed for the Gated DeltaNet teaching code and tests, and what do production versions of these layers need?
options: A single A100 is required even for the toy tests, and production needs a multi-node cluster of H100s
CPU-only works for the tests, and production training simply runs the same per-token Python recurrent loop on CPU
Both need TPU pods, because the d_v x d_k state per head is too large to fit in a single GPU's HBM
CPU-only suffices for toy sizes; production training needs flash-linear-attention's chunked Triton kernels on GPU
questions.explanation: The teaching code runs on toy sizes (T at most 512, C at most 64) on CPU in seconds, with zero GPU-hours. Production training uses the chunked Triton kernels of flash-linear-attention on GPUs because a Python loop over time would leave a GPU idle.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 1. Intuition: GQA made the cache smaller, not bounded
questions.question: After GQA, the KV cache is $2\,n_{\text{layer}}\,g\,d_h\,T\,b$ bytes. Which factor does GQA reduce, and which remains a problem at long context?
options: GQA removes the $T$ factor by caching once per group, but $g$ still grows with layer count
