GQA shrinks $g$, but the cache still grows linearly with context length $T$
GQA shrinks $b$ by quantizing cached keys to int8, but $d_h$ still grows with context length
GQA shrinks $n_{\text{layer}}$ by sharing caches across layers, but $g$ still grows with $T$
questions.explanation: GQA reduces the number of KV heads $g$, making the cache smaller by a constant factor. But every new token still appends a key and value to every layer, so memory grows with $T$, and each decode step reads the whole cache. At 256K context, that growing cache decides how many sequences fit and how fast decoding is.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 1. Intuition: GQA made the cache smaller, not bounded
questions.question: At very long contexts such as 256K tokens, what decides how many sequences fit on a GPU and how fast each decode step is?
options: The model weights, which must be re-read and grow with context
The KV cache, not the weights or the FLOPs
The tokenizer's vocabulary size
The optimizer state
questions.explanation: At long context the per-sequence KV cache becomes the dominant memory, limiting batch size, and every decode step must read all of it, limiting speed. Weights do not grow with context, and the optimizer is not used at inference.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 1. Intuition: GQA made the cache smaller, not bounded
questions.question: What is the core trade-off of using an RNN-style fixed-size state instead of a growing KV cache?
options: Memory becomes constant in T and recall stays exact, because the state stores every token
Recall becomes exact for every past token, but memory grows quadratically with context
Decode becomes slower per token, but memory grows only linearly instead of quadratically
Decode cost and memory become constant in T, but the summary of the past is lossy
questions.explanation: An RNN keeps a fixed-size summary updated once per token, so decode memory and compute do not grow with context. The price is that a fixed-size state cannot remember everything a growing cache can, so recall is approximate.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 1. Intuition: GQA made the cache smaller, not bounded
questions.question: What are the steps from softmax attention to a production hybrid model?
options: Drop the softmax (linear attention), add a forget gate, use the delta rule to correct instead of add, keep full attention in one layer of four
Add more query heads, quantize the KV cache to int4, prune every other layer, then keep softmax attention only in the final layer
Replace attention with an MoE, add a decay gate to the router, use the delta rule on expert weights, then keep dense layers in one of four
Use sliding-window attention, then block-sparse attention, then GQA, then keep one full-attention layer in every eight layers of the stack
questions.explanation: Linear attention turns attention into an RNN with a matrix state; a decay gate alpha lets it forget; the delta rule beta corrects the stored value for a key; and a hybrid stack keeps a full softmax attention layer in one of every four for exact long-range lookup.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 1. Intuition: GQA made the cache smaller, not bounded
questions.question: How do softmax attention and a linear-attention layer differ in what they store and how they look up the past?
options: Softmax compresses the past into one fixed matrix per head and reads it approximately; linear attention stores every key and value and looks them up exactly
Both store every past key and value exactly, but linear attention uses fewer heads and replaces the exp in the scores with a cheaper dot product
Softmax stores every past key and value and looks them up exactly; linear attention compresses the past into one fixed matrix per head, read approximately
Linear attention stores only the most recent key and value per head; softmax stores a fixed-size matrix summary of the past that it reads exactly
questions.explanation: Softmax attention keeps the full K and V history (memory growing with T) and reads it exactly. A linear-attention layer folds the history into a fixed-size state per head, constant in T, at the cost of approximate reads. A hybrid uses mostly the cheap layer plus a few exact ones.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: In causal softmax attention, why can you not pre-sum the past into a single summary independent of the query?
options: Because keys and values have different head dimensions, so their sum has no consistent shape
Because the causal mask changes every step, so any stored summary would include future tokens
The softmax denominator depends on $q_t$ and couples all past positions non-linearly
Because the $\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling is applied separately per position and cannot be factored out
questions.explanation: The weights $\exp(q_t\cdot k_s)/\sum_{s'}\exp(q_t\cdot k_{s'})$ depend non-linearly on the query, so the past cannot be combined into one query-independent object; every $k_s, v_s$ must be kept. Different key and value dimensions are no obstacle, as linear attention shows.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: What change does linear attention (Katharopoulos et al. 2020) make to softmax attention, in the modern form?
options: It replaces $\exp(q\cdot k)$ by a plain dot product (generally $\phi(q)\cdot\phi(k)$), with $\phi$ folded into projections and the normalizer dropped
It replaces the $q\cdot k$ dot product with a negative L1 distance $-\lVert q-k\rVert_1$, keeping the softmax normalizer so weights still sum to 1
It applies the softmax over the value dimension $d_v$ instead of over past positions, so each output channel is normalized and the cache can be dropped
It restricts each query to a fixed window of the most recent $w$ tokens and keeps $\exp(q\cdot k)$, so the cache stops growing beyond $w$ entries
questions.explanation: Linear attention swaps the exponential kernel for a dot product of (feature-mapped) queries and keys. Modern variants fold the feature map $\phi$ into the projections and drop the normalizer. This removes the softmax coupling that prevented pre-summing. A sliding window is a different technique.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: In linear attention, how does $o_t = \sum_{s\le t}(q_t\cdot k_s)v_s$ become a recurrence?
options: It equals $q_t^\top(\sum_s k_s v_s^\top)$, but the sum must be rebuilt every step from all past queries, so no recurrence exists
It equals $\sum_s k_s\,(v_s\cdot q_t)$, so the state is a single vector of size $d_k$ updated by $s_t = s_{t-1} + k_t$
It equals $S_t = S_{t-1}\,v_t k_t^\top$, a running product of outer products, with output $o_t = q_t^\top S_t$
It equals $(\sum_{s\le t} v_s k_s^\top)\,q_t$, so the state $S_t = S_{t-1} + v_t k_t^\top$ with $o_t = S_t q_t$
questions.explanation: Since $(q_t\cdot k_s)v_s = v_s(k_s^\top q_t)$, the sum over the past factors as a matrix times $q_t$. That matrix is accumulated additively, one outer product per token. The recurrence is additive, not a product of outer products.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: In linear attention, what are the shape of the state $S_t$ and its initial value?
options: $S_t\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_k}$, with $S_0 = I$
$S_t\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v\times d_k}$, with $S_0 = 0$
$S_t\in\mathbb{R}^{d_k\times d_k}$, with $S_0 = I$
$S_t\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v}$, a vector, with $S_0 = \mathbf{1}$
questions.explanation: Each write $v_t k_t^\top$ is $d_v\times d_k$, so the state is a $d_v\times d_k$ matrix starting at zero. Its size has no $T$ axis, which is the whole point. Reading $S_t q_t$ gives a $d_v$-dimensional output.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: In linear attention, what does each outer product $v_t k_t^\top$ represent?
options: A full-rank $d_v\times d_k$ matrix that stores all past values at once
A rank-1 $d_v\times d_k$ matrix that stores $v_t$ under address $k_t$
A scalar similarity between $v_t$ and $k_t$ that weights the next read
The attention weight of token $t$ on itself, before normalization by the sum
questions.explanation: The outer product is rank 1: reading it with a query $q$ gives $v_t(k_t\cdot q)$, i.e. the value scaled by how well $q$ matches the key. So it acts like storing $v_t$ at address $k_t$. Reading the summed state returns a mix of stored values weighted by key match.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: How many numbers does a linear-attention state hold per head, as a function of sequence length T?
options: $T\,d_k$, growing linearly with $T$
$T^2$, one score per query-key pair
$2\,T\,d_v$, a key and value per token
$d_v d_k$, regardless of $T$
questions.explanation: The state is a $d_v\times d_k$ matrix whose size does not depend on how many tokens have been processed. By contrast, softmax attention stores $T$ keys and $T$ values per head.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: Why does pure (undecayed) linear attention's state degrade after thousands of tokens?
options: Nothing is ever removed, so it sums thousands of rank-1 matrices in a $d_k$-dimensional space and reads become mush
The state overflows float32 after about 1024 tokens because each outer product doubles its largest entry
The keys become mutually orthogonal as $T$ grows, so every read $S_t q_t$ returns a vector close to zero
The state is reset to zero at every chunk boundary by the kernel, so history older than one chunk is lost entirely
questions.explanation: Each token adds an outer product and none is ever subtracted. With far more writes than the $d_k$ dimensions available, stored items interfere and reads return blurred mixtures. A decay gate addresses this by letting old content fade.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: How does the decay gate modify the linear-attention recurrence, and where does the idea come from?
options: $S_t = S_{t-1} + \alpha_t v_t k_t^\top$, scaling only the new write, an idea from the original Transformer
$S_t = \alpha_t(S_{t-1} + v_t k_t^\top)$ with one learned scalar per layer, taken from LSTM forget gates
$S_t = \alpha_t S_{t-1} + v_t k_t^\top$ with per-token scalar $\alpha_t\in(0,1]$, the Mamba2 / GLA idea
$S_t = S_{t-1} - \alpha_t S_{t-1}k_t k_t^\top$ with per-token $\alpha_t$, the Switch Transformer routing idea
questions.explanation: The decay multiplies the past state before the new write is added, so old contributions shrink geometrically. Scaling only the write would not forget anything, and decaying after the write (third option) would also shrink the token just written. This gating comes from Mamba2 and GLA.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: With the decayed recurrence $S_t = \alpha_t S_{t-1} + v_t k_t^\top$, by what factor is token $s$'s contribution multiplied when it reaches step $t$?
options: $D_{t,s} = \prod_{r=1}^{s}\alpha_r$
$D_{t,s} = \alpha_t^{\,t}$
$D_{t,s} = \prod_{r=s+1}^{t}\alpha_r$
$D_{t,s} = \sum_{r=s}^{t}\alpha_r$ (a running sum)
questions.explanation: Token $s$ is written at step $s$ and then multiplied by each later decay $\alpha_{s+1},\dots,\alpha_t$. So its weight is the product of decays strictly after it. Decays before $s$ do not affect it, and the effect is multiplicative, not additive.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: What is the equivalent quadratic (parallel) form of linear attention with a decay gate?
options: $o_t = \sum_{s\le t} D_{t,s}(q_t\cdot k_s)v_s$: causal attention with no softmax and a decay mask
$o_t = \sum_{s\le t}\operatorname{softmax}_s(D_{t,s}\,q_t\cdot k_s)v_s$: softmax attention with a decay bias
$o_t = D_{t,t}\,(q_t\cdot k_t)\,v_t$: each token attends only to itself, scaled by its own gate
$o_t = \sum_{s} (q_t\cdot k_s)v_s$ over all positions including future ones, with no decay mask
questions.explanation: Unrolling the recurrence gives a $(T,T)$ matrix of $q_t\cdot k_s$ scores multiplied elementwise by the causal decay mask $D$, with no softmax. The function causal_linear_attention_parallel computes this, and tests check the recurrence against it. Including future positions would break causality.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: What problem with decay gating does the delta rule address?
options: Decay makes the recurrence non-differentiable, so the delta rule restores usable gradients
Decay cannot be computed in parallel over the sequence, while the delta rule can be chunked
Decay requires a growing KV cache at decode, while the delta rule keeps the state fixed
Decay forgets everything uniformly, while the delta rule edits one slot selectively
questions.explanation: A scalar decay shrinks all stored associations equally. The delta rule instead reads what the memory currently returns for the new key and corrects just that association. This is selective editing rather than blanket forgetting.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: In the delta rule for linear attention, what is done before writing a new key/value pair?
options: Reset the state to zero, then write $v_t k_t^\top$ so the new pair is the only thing stored
Read the memory's current answer $\hat v_t = S_{t-1}k_t$, then move it a fraction $\beta_t$ toward $v_t$
Add $v_t k_t^\top$ twice to reinforce it, then scale the whole state down by a factor $\beta_t$
Normalize the whole state $S_{t-1}$ to unit Frobenius norm, then add $\beta_t v_t k_t^\top$ on top of the result
questions.explanation: The delta rule first predicts what key $k_t$ currently retrieves, computes the error $v_t - S_{t-1}k_t$, and writes only $\beta_t$ times that error along $k_t$. So existing content for that key is corrected rather than accumulated.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: What is the delta-rule state update?
options: $S_t = S_{t-1} + \beta_t(v_t + S_{t-1}k_t)k_t^\top = S_{t-1}(I + \beta_t k_t k_t^\top) + \beta_t v_t k_t^\top$
$S_t = S_{t-1} + \beta_t(v_t - S_{t-1}k_t)k_t^\top = S_{t-1}(I - \beta_t k_t k_t^\top) + \beta_t v_t k_t^\top$
$S_t = (I - \beta_t k_t k_t^\top)S_{t-1} + v_t k_t^\top$, erasing along $k_t$ from the left and writing at full strength
$S_t = \beta_t S_{t-1} + (1-\beta_t) v_t k_t^\top$, an exponential moving average of outer products with rate $\beta_t$
questions.explanation: The prediction error times $\beta_t$ is written along $k_t^\top$; expanding gives the state multiplied on the right by $I - \beta_t k_t k_t^\top$ plus a scaled write. The first distractor is just scaled linear attention with no correction, and the last is an interpolation that does not depend on the key's current content.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: In the delta rule, what do $\beta_t$ and $(v_t - S_{t-1}k_t)$ represent?
options: $\beta_t$ is the decay of old memory; $(v_t - S_{t-1}k_t)$ is the attention score of token $t$
$\beta_t$ is Adam's momentum coefficient; $(v_t - S_{t-1}k_t)$ is the gradient norm of the layer
$\beta_t$ is the norm of the key; $(v_t - S_{t-1}k_t)$ is the new query used for the next read
$\beta_t$ is the write strength; $(v_t - S_{t-1}k_t)$ is the prediction error, the 'delta'
questions.explanation: $\beta_t\in[0,1]$ controls how far the stored answer moves toward the new value, and the difference between the target value and the memory's current answer is the error being corrected. Decay is the separate $\alpha_t$.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: In the delta rule, under what conditions does key $k_t$ return exactly $v_t$ after the update?
options: When $\lVert k_t\rVert = 1$ and $\beta_t = 1$
Whenever $\beta_t > 0$, for any key norm
Only when $S_{t-1} = 0$
When $\lVert k_t\rVert = 2$ and $\beta_t = 0.5$
questions.explanation: $S_t k_t = S_{t-1}k_t + \beta_t(v_t - S_{t-1}k_t)(k_t^\top k_t)$. With unit key and $\beta_t = 1$ this is exactly $v_t$. Smaller $\beta_t$ moves only partway, and an empty prior state is not required.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: What optimization interpretation does the delta rule have?
options: One Newton step on the language-model loss with respect to $S$, with $\beta_t$ approximating the inverse Hessian of the state
A closed-form least-squares solve $S = VK^{+}$ over all past keys and values, recomputed exactly at every time step
One gradient-descent step on $\tfrac12\lVert S k_t - v_t\rVert^2$ with learning rate $\beta_t$: an associative memory trained online
One step of gradient ascent on the attention entropy, with $\beta_t$ as the step size that sharpens reads over the past
questions.explanation: The gradient of $\tfrac12\lVert Sk_t - v_t\rVert^2$ with respect to $S$ is $(Sk_t - v_t)k_t^\top$, so stepping with rate $\beta_t$ gives exactly the delta-rule update. It is a single online step per token, not a full least-squares solve over history.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: Who are credited with the delta rule and its use in linear attention?
options: Vaswani et al. 2017 originally; applied to linear attention by Katharopoulos et al. 2020 and scaled by Dao 2024
Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997 originally; used for linear attention by Fedus et al. 2021 and scaled by Gu 2023
Widrow–Hoff originally; used for linear attention by Schlag et al. 2021 and scaled up by Yang et al. 2024
Kingma and Ba 2015 originally; used for linear attention by Dai et al. 2024 and scaled up by Shazeer et al. 2017
questions.explanation: The delta rule is the classic Widrow–Hoff learning rule. Schlag et al. (2021) applied it to linear attention and Yang et al. (2024) scaled it up with a parallel training algorithm. Katharopoulos et al. introduced linear attention itself.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: What is the Gated DeltaNet state update (Yang, Kautz & Hatamizadeh, ICLR 2025)?
options: $S_t = \alpha_t S_{t-1}(I - \beta_t k_t k_t^\top) + \beta_t v_t k_t^\top$, with $o_t = S_t q_t$
$S_t = \alpha_t S_{t-1} + \beta_t v_t k_t^\top$, with $o_t = q_t^\top S_t$ and no erase term at all
$S_t = S_{t-1}(I - \alpha_t k_t k_t^\top) + \beta_t v_t k_t^\top$, with $o_t = S_t q_t$
$S_t = \beta_t S_{t-1}(I - \alpha_t k_t k_t^\top) + v_t k_t^\top$, with $o_t = S_t q_t$
questions.explanation: Gated DeltaNet combines decay $\alpha_t$ with the delta-rule correction of strength $\beta_t$. The first distractor is gated linear attention without the correction, and the others swap the roles of $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: What is the 'forget first, then correct' form of the gated delta rule?
options: $S_t = \alpha_t S_{t-1} + \beta_t(v_t - S_{t-1}k_t)k_t^\top$
$S_t = \alpha_t\big(S_{t-1} + \beta_t(v_t - S_{t-1}k_t)k_t^\top\big)$
$S_t = S_{t-1} + \beta_t(v_t - \alpha_t k_t)k_t^\top$ with no decay of $S$
$S_t = \alpha_t S_{t-1} + \beta_t(v_t - \alpha_t S_{t-1}k_t)k_t^\top$
questions.explanation: The state is decayed first, and the prediction is made from the decayed state $\alpha_t S_{t-1}$. Using the undecayed state in the error term (first distractor) is exactly the debugging-exercise bug: the correction then targets a value the decayed state no longer holds.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: In Gated DeltaNet, what do $\alpha_t$ and $\beta_t$ each do, and how are they produced?
options: Both are fixed hyperparameters chosen before training, $\alpha$ near 0.99 for slow forgetting and $\beta$ near 0.5 for gentle writes
$\alpha_t$ erases fast (e.g. at a topic change), $\beta_t$ edits precisely; both come per token and per head from small linear layers on $x_t$
$\alpha_t$ is learned once per layer and shared by all tokens, while $\beta_t$ is a constant 1 so every write fully overwrites its slot
$\alpha_t$ controls how strongly each new value is written; $\beta_t$ controls global forgetting, both computed per token from a softmax over heads
questions.explanation: The decay $\alpha_t$ wipes the state broadly, useful when context changes, while $\beta_t$ performs targeted writes. Both are computed per token and head from the input by small projections, so the model learns when to forget and how hard to write. The last distractor swaps their roles.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: What special cases does Gated DeltaNet reduce to when $\alpha_t = 1$ or $\beta_t = 0$?
options: $\alpha_t = 1$ recovers softmax attention; $\beta_t = 0$ resets the state to zero for that token
$\alpha_t = 1$ recovers DeltaNet; $\beta_t = 0$ means don't write (a pure decay step)
$\alpha_t = 1$ recovers plain linear attention; $\beta_t = 0$ recovers the ungated DeltaNet
$\alpha_t = 0$ recovers DeltaNet; $\beta_t = 1$ means don't write anything (a pure decay step)
questions.explanation: With no decay, the update is just the delta rule (DeltaNet). With zero write strength, the correction term vanishes and only decay acts. Neither choice yields softmax attention, and plain linear attention would need the correction removed entirely.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: Why does Gated DeltaNet L2-normalize q and k?
options: So the softmax denominator equals 1 and the normalizer can be dropped from the read
To make each outer product $v_t k_t^\top$ rank 2, so the state can store twice as much
To reduce the state from $d_v\times d_k$ to $d_k$ numbers, since unit keys need no matrix
So $I - \beta k k^\top$ has eigenvalues in $[0,1]$ and the state cannot blow up
questions.explanation: With unit keys and $\beta\in[0,1]$, $I - \beta kk^\top$ has eigenvalue $1-\beta$ along $k$ and 1 elsewhere, all in $[0,1]$, so it is a contraction and the state stays bounded. There is no softmax in this layer and normalization does not change the state's shape.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: Besides L2-normalizing q and k, what other components does the published Gated DeltaNet layer include?
options: A short causal convolution before the projections and an output gate $\mathrm{RMSNorm}(o_t)\odot\mathrm{SiLU}(W_g x_t)$
A softmax over the state's key axis before every read and a learned absolute positional embedding added to $q$ and $k$
A mixture-of-experts router inside each head that selects which of several states $S^{(e)}$ receives each token's write
A sliding-window KV cache of the last 64 tokens alongside the state, and rotary position embeddings applied to the values
questions.explanation: The paper documents a short causal convolution ahead of the projections and an output gating of RMSNorm-ed outputs by a SiLU-activated projection of the input. These are PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED details. None of the distractors are part of the layer.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: How does Kimi Linear's KDA differ from Gated DeltaNet?
options: It removes the delta rule's error term and keeps only the scalar decay $\alpha_t$, like Mamba2
It uses one decay per value channel (a diagonal on rows of $S$) and drops the write strength $\beta_t$
It replaces the scalar decay $\alpha_t$ with one decay per key channel (a diagonal matrix)
It replaces the fixed state with a growing compressed KV cache, keeping the delta rule only for writes
questions.explanation: KDA (Kimi Delta Attention) generalizes the scalar decay to a per-key-channel decay, effectively a diagonal decay matrix, so different key dimensions can forget at different rates. It keeps the delta-rule structure and the fixed-size state.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: With $d_k = 2$, $d_v = 1$, writes $k=(1,0),v=3$ then $k=(1,0),v=5$, why does pure linear attention read 8 at $q=(1,0)$ instead of 5?
options: Linear attention keeps the maximum of the two writes, 5, and adds the initial bias of 3 on top
The dropped softmax normalizer is replaced by a fixed scale, which multiplies the second value by 1.6
Two writes under the same key collide and add, giving 3 + 5 = 8, neither the old nor the new value
The second key is treated as a new address and ignored by the read, and 8 comes from the initial state
questions.explanation: Linear attention adds $v_t k_t^	op$ unconditionally, so writing the same address twice sums the values. There is no mechanism to overwrite an address, which is the collision problem the delta rule fixes.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: In the same example, how does the delta rule ($\alpha=\beta=1$) handle the second write (k=(1,0), v=5) after storing 3?
options: It predicts 3, writes only the error 5 - 3 = 2, so the address now returns 5
It adds 5 on top to get 8, then halves the slot so the address returns the average 4
It zeroes the whole state first and then writes 5, so every address now returns 5
It writes 5 under a new key orthogonal to (1,0), so the old address still returns 3
questions.explanation: The delta rule reads the current answer for the key (3), computes the error (2), and adds that along the key, giving state (5, 0). The address is overwritten. It does not reset the whole state.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: In the delta-rule hand example, after overwriting address e_1 to 5, the third token writes v = 2 under k = (0,1). What does reading q = (1,0) return, and why?
options: 7, because writes accumulate in the state and every read sees their sum
2, because the most recent write wins globally and overrides every address
0, because the third write overwrites the whole state with its own outer product
Still 5, because the orthogonal write does not disturb address e_1
questions.explanation: The prediction for k=(0,1) is 0, so the error 2 is written along (0,1), giving state (5, 2). Reading with (1,0) still returns 5, and reading with (0,1) returns 2. Orthogonal keys occupy separate slots.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: In the gated delta rule hand example, $\alpha_2 = 0.5$ and $\beta_2 = 0.5$ at step 2 with prior state (3, 0) and new value 5 under key (1,0). What is the resulting read and its meaning?
options: 4.0: the average of the old value 3 and the new value 5, since both gates are 0.5
3.25: a half-forgotten old value (1.5) plus a half-strength correction (1.75)
5.0: the new value exactly, because the error term fully corrects the decayed slot
2.5: half of the new value, because the decay wipes the old 3 before the write
questions.explanation: Forgetting gives 1.5; the error is 5 - 1.5 = 3.5; half-strength correction is 1.75; total 3.25. Because the gates are learned, the model chooses per token how much to forget and how hard to write.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: In the Gated DeltaNet layer, how are q and k processed before the recurrence?
options: Softmax over $d_k$, then multiplied by $\sqrt{d_k}$ so the dot products keep unit scale
SiLU, then L2-normalized over $d_k$, with q additionally scaled by $d_k^{-1/2}$
Left raw from the projection with no activation, then q alone is scaled by $d_k^{-1/2}$
Layer-normalized over the sequence axis, then passed through a ReLU before the recurrence
questions.explanation: q and k of shape (B, H, T, d_k) pass through SiLU and are L2-normalized along $d_k$; q is also scaled by $d_k^{-1/2}$. Leaving k raw is a listed common mistake that can make the state explode.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: How are the decay alpha and write strength beta computed in the Gated DeltaNet layer, and what are their ranges?
options: alpha $= \sigma(W_a x)\in(0,1)$; beta $= \mathrm{softplus}(W_b x)\in(0,\infty)$, unbounded above
alpha $= \tanh(W_a x)\in(-1,1)$; beta $= \exp(W_b x)\in(0,\infty)$, both per head
alpha $= \mathrm{ReLU}(W_a x)\in[0,\infty)$; beta $= 1 - \alpha$, tied to the decay
alpha $= \exp(-\mathrm{softplus}(W_a x))\in(0,1)$; beta $= \sigma(W_b x)\in(0,1)$
questions.explanation: softplus is positive, so $\exp(-\mathrm{softplus})$ lies in (0,1), a valid decay. The sigmoid keeps beta in (0,1), a valid write strength. Both have shape (B, H, T): one scalar per token and head. An unbounded beta could break the contraction.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: What is the shape of the Gated DeltaNet state S, and what precision is it kept in in practice?
options: (B, H, d_v, d_k) with no T axis, kept in fp32
(B, H, T, d_k), one row per token, kept in bf16
(B, T, C) like the hidden states, kept in int8
(B, H, T, T) like the attention map, kept in fp16
questions.explanation: The state is one d_v x d_k matrix per batch element and head, with no time axis, so it does not grow during decoding. It is kept in fp32 because it accumulates many updates and bf16 would lose precision.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: At decode time, how does one layer's per-sequence memory differ between softmax attention and Gated DeltaNet?
options: Both store (B, H, T, d) tensors that grow with T, but Gated DeltaNet keeps them in int8 so each one is a quarter the size
Softmax stores a fixed state of shape (B, H, d, d); Gated DeltaNet appends one key and value of shape (B, H, d) per token
Softmax stores K and V of shape (B, g, T, d_h) each, growing with T; Gated DeltaNet stores S of shape (B, H, d_v, d_k), fixed
Gated DeltaNet stores only K of shape (B, g, T, d_h) and recomputes V from it, halving softmax's growing (B, g, T, d_h) cache
questions.explanation: Softmax attention's cache appends a key and value per token per KV head. Gated DeltaNet carries only its fixed state matrix per head; nothing is ever appended.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: In gated_delta_rule_recurrent, what is the order of operations per time step?
options: Read o_t = S q_t first, then decay S by alpha, then add beta v_t k_t^T with no prediction or error term
Write v_t k_t^T, then decay S by alpha, then predict pred = S k_t and subtract it from the next value
Decay S by alpha, predict pred = S k_t, compute err = beta (v_t - pred), add err k_t^T, then read o_t = S q_t
Predict pred = S k_t from the undecayed S, then decay S by alpha, add beta (v_t - pred) k_t^T, and read o_t = S q_t
questions.explanation: The loop forgets first, then measures the prediction error against the decayed state, adds the rank-1 correction, and finally reads with the query. Predicting from the undecayed state is the bug in the debugging exercise; decaying after writing is a listed common mistake.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: How does linear_attention_recurrent differ from gated_delta_rule_recurrent?
options: It uses S = alpha*S + v_t k_t^T with no prediction or error term
It uses a softmax over the state's key axis before each read o_t = S q_t
It stores all past keys and values in a list and sums them at each read
It applies the write strength beta to each write but never decays S by alpha
questions.explanation: Linear attention (with optional decay) simply decays and adds the outer product, without first reading what the key currently returns. The delta rule adds the prediction/correction step.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: In the GatedDeltaNet layer, how are the per-head decay and write strength produced?
options: From a single shared scalar parameter per layer, broadcast to every head and every token
From the router logits of the following MoE block, one value per expert per token
From the attention scores of the previous full-attention layer, averaged over its heads
From a_proj and b_proj, each nn.Linear(C, n_head), giving one value per head per token
questions.explanation: a_proj and b_proj map the C-dimensional input to n_head outputs, giving one decay and one write strength per head for every token. The layer also has q/k/v projections, per-head RMSNorm, a SiLU output gate and o_proj.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: What two entry points does the GatedDeltaNet layer provide?
options: forward() for training on (B, T, C), and generate() that rebuilds a per-layer KV cache of shape (B, H, T, d_h) at decode
layer(x) mapping (B, T, C) to (B, T, C), and forward_with_state(x_t, state) for token-by-token decode carrying a fixed state
A parallel entry and a chunked entry, both mapping (B, T, C) to (B, T, C) and both requiring the full sequence up front
An encoder entry over (B, T, C) inputs, and a decoder cross-attention entry that reads the encoder's final state for each new token
questions.explanation: The full-sequence call behaves like GroupedQueryAttention as a drop-in token mixer. The decode call takes one token and the previous (B, H, d, d) state and returns the output and new state, so nothing grows with T.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: What do hybrid_layer_pattern and hybrid_decode_cache_bytes compute?
options: The optimal ratio of experts to dense layers in a 3:1 stack, and the total expert parameter count per routed token
The layer types of a 3:1 stack, and the decode memory as KV cache of 'full' layers plus states of 'linear' layers
The chunk size for the Triton kernels of 'linear' layers, and the FLOPs per chunk for the 'full' attention layers
The RoPE frequencies for each 'full' layer, and the decode memory needed to cache rotary embeddings per token
questions.explanation: hybrid_layer_pattern(n_layer, 3) lists which layers are linear and which are full in a 3:1 layout. hybrid_decode_cache_bytes sums the growing KV cache of the full layers and the fixed states of the linear layers.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: Which property is checked by the Gated DeltaNet unit tests about carried state?
options: The state is identical for every input sequence once the decay gate has saturated to 1
The state grows by exactly one row per token, matching the softmax KV cache length
Splitting the sequence in two halves the output norm, because the state is reset between the halves
Running on a split sequence while carrying the state equals running on the whole sequence
questions.explanation: Because the state summarizes the entire prefix, processing a sequence in two pieces and passing the state between them must give the same result as one pass. Tests also check the hand example, causality, beta=0 never writing, write-then-read returning v, and decode matching the full forward.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: What does the Gated DeltaNet test 'recurrent linear attention equals the quadratic form' verify, and at what precision?
options: The recurrent loop matches the (T, T) decay-masked quadratic form with and without decay, in float64 to 1e-10
The recurrent loop matches full softmax attention with a causal mask, with and without decay, in bf16 to 1e-3
The recurrent loop runs faster than the (T, T) quadratic form on CPU for every tested sequence length
The (T, T) quadratic form matches the flash-linear-attention Triton kernels on GPU, in fp16 to 1e-4
questions.explanation: The test compares the RNN form to causal_linear_attention_parallel in float64 with tight tolerance, confirming the two formulations are the same function. It does not compare with softmax attention, which is a different function.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: Why is the Python loop over time not how production kernels implement Gated DeltaNet?
options: The loop computes a different function than the kernels, so its outputs cannot be trusted
The loop cannot handle causal masking, so it leaks future tokens into the state
A loop over T with tiny matmuls leaves a GPU idle; production uses a chunkwise form
The loop uses too much memory because it stores every intermediate state for backward
questions.explanation: The loop is the definition, not the implementation. Tiny sequential matmuls cannot saturate a GPU, so kernels like flash-linear-attention compute the same function in chunks using tensor-core-friendly matmuls. Results match up to float rounding.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: How does the chunkwise form used by flash-linear-attention compute linear attention?
options: Within chunks of e.g. 64 tokens it runs full softmax attention, then discards the state entirely at each chunk boundary
It assigns one token per GPU thread and runs the recurrence in parallel with no matmuls and no state passing
Within chunks of e.g. 64 tokens it uses a small masked quadratic matmul; between chunks it passes the state S along
It builds one global T x T decay-masked matrix for the whole sequence and multiplies it by V in a single matmul
questions.explanation: Splitting into chunks gives intra-chunk work as small dense matmuls (the decay-masked quadratic form) and inter-chunk work as a state hand-off. This balances parallelism and the linear-in-T cost.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: For the delta rule's chunkwise kernel, how is the non-diagonal product of $(I - \beta k k^\top)$ factors within a chunk handled?
options: With a compact WY / Householder-product representation so it also becomes a few matmuls (Yang et al. 2024)
By approximating the product with the identity matrix inside each chunk, since $\beta k k^\top$ is small
By running the sequential part of the product on the CPU while the GPU handles the matmuls (Yang et al. 2024)
By ignoring the $\beta_t$ terms inside a chunk and applying them once at the boundary as a scalar correction
questions.explanation: The product of identity-minus-rank-1 factors is not diagonal like a scalar decay, so Yang et al. (2024) represent it compactly in WY / Householder form, turning it into matmuls. This keeps the kernel exact, not approximate.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: What are the training (prefill) FLOPs per head of softmax attention versus Gated DeltaNet, for T tokens and head dim d?
options: Softmax $O(Td^2)$; Gated DeltaNet $O(T^2 d)$ (chunked $O(T^2 c)$ for chunk size $c$)
Both $O(T^2 d)$, because the chunked kernel still materializes the full $T\times T$ decay mask
Softmax $O(T d)$; Gated DeltaNet $O(d^3)$ per token, so $O(Td^3)$ over the sequence
Softmax $O(T^2 d)$; Gated DeltaNet $O(Td^2)$ (chunked $O(Tcd + Td^2)$ for chunk size $c$)
questions.explanation: Softmax compares every pair of positions, giving $T^2$ scaling. Gated DeltaNet does a $d\times d$ state update per token, linear in $T$; the chunked form adds an intra-chunk quadratic term in chunk size $c$.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: What are the per-token decode FLOPs and decode memory per head of softmax attention versus Gated DeltaNet?
options: Softmax $O(d^2)$ FLOPs and $d^2$ memory (constant); Gated DeltaNet $O(Td)$ FLOPs and $2Td$ memory per head (growing)
Softmax $O(Td)$ FLOPs and $2Td$ memory per KV head (growing); Gated DeltaNet $O(d^2)$ FLOPs and $d^2$ memory (constant)
Both $O(Td)$ FLOPs per token, and both constant memory, since GQA and the state each cap the per-head cache at $d^2$ numbers
Softmax $O(T^2)$ FLOPs and constant memory per KV head; Gated DeltaNet $O(T)$ FLOPs and memory growing as $Td$
questions.explanation: Each softmax decode step reads the whole cache of $T$ keys and values. Gated DeltaNet updates and reads a fixed $d\times d$ state, independent of $T$. The price is that its recall is lossy.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: Can Gated DeltaNet exactly recall any past token, as softmax attention can?
options: Yes; the delta rule guarantees exact recall of every token it wrote
No; its memory is lossy, holding only $d^2$ numbers per head
Yes, as long as the keys are L2-normalized and $\beta_t = 1$ always
No, but softmax attention cannot recall exactly either at long context
questions.explanation: A fixed $d\times d$ state cannot store an unbounded number of facts exactly; old associations get overwritten or interfere. Softmax attention keeps every key and value and can retrieve any past token exactly.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: With head dim d = 128, how does one Gated DeltaNet state compare with what a softmax head reads per step at 256K context?
options: 16,384 numbers versus 32,768 numbers (2 x 128 x 128 for K and V)
128 numbers versus about 33 million numbers (262,144 x 128)
About 67 million numbers in both, since the state is also per token
16,384 numbers versus about 67 million numbers (2 x 262,144 x 128)
questions.explanation: One state is $128^2 = 16{,}384$ numbers. A softmax head at 262,144 tokens touches the keys and values: $2 \times 262{,}144 \times 128 \approx 67$M numbers per decode step.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: What is Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B's layer layout, as given on its model card?
options: 48 layers repeating 3 Gated DeltaNet layers then 1 gated softmax attention layer
48 layers, all gated softmax attention with GQA, each followed by a Gated DeltaNet output gate
48 layers alternating strictly between 1 Gated DeltaNet layer and 1 gated softmax attention layer
24 Gated DeltaNet layers stacked first, followed by 24 gated softmax attention layers on top
questions.explanation: Qwen3-Next uses a 3:1 hybrid, giving 36 Gated DeltaNet layers and 12 full-attention layers interleaved. Its attention layers have 2 KV heads of dimension 256; its DeltaNet layers have 32 value heads and 16 query/key heads of dimension 128.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: For Qwen3-Next at 262,144 tokens (bf16 KV, fp32 states), why does the hybrid approach but not quite reach a 4x memory saving over an all-full-attention stack?
options: The DeltaNet states also grow with T, at one quarter the rate of the KV cache of the full layers
The 12 full layers use 4x more KV heads than a dense model would, cancelling part of the saving
Only 12 of 48 layers keep a KV cache (a 4x cut), but the 36 fixed states add a small constant 75.5 MB
The bf16 KV cache of the full layers is upcast to fp32 at long context, doubling its size per token
questions.explanation: Keeping a cache in one layer of four gives up to 4x savings, and the 36 states add a constant 75.5 MB: 6.44 GB + 0.075 GB = 6.52 GB versus 25.8 GB. At long context that constant is negligible, so the ratio approaches 4.0x.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: For Qwen3-Next at 4,096 tokens, the hybrid saves only about 2.3x rather than 4x. Why?
options: The DeltaNet layers fall back to a full KV cache at short contexts, so they briefly cost like attention
Below 8K tokens the model runs full attention in every layer, so the hybrid layout only applies to long inputs
At short context the constant state memory (75.5 MB) is comparable to the small KV cache of the full layers
Prefix caching keeps two snapshots of each DeltaNet state at short contexts, doubling the constant memory
questions.explanation: At 4K the full layers' KV is only 0.101 GB, so the fixed 0.075 GB of states is a large fraction: 0.176 GB total versus 0.403 GB. Only at long context does the KV cache dominate and the ratio approach 4x.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: Why do newer designs such as the Qwen3.8-Next preview (2026) add sparse attention to the full layers?
options: At long context the remaining cost is the 12 full layers' growing KV cache, so they make even those cheaper
Because the Gated DeltaNet states grow too large at long context and need sparse reads to stay cheap
Because sparse attention in the full layers removes the need for any Gated DeltaNet layers in the stack at all
Because the MoE experts require sparse attention patterns to route tokens to the right expert per layer
questions.explanation: In a 3:1 hybrid at long context, nearly all decode memory comes from the full-attention layers' KV cache, since the linear states are constant. Replacing those full layers with sparse attention attacks the remaining cost.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: Why did vLLM need a hybrid cache manager to serve Qwen3-Next?
options: Because Qwen3-Next keeps its KV cache on the CPU and pages only the active blocks into GPU memory at each decode step
Because each MoE expert needs its own set of KV pages, so the manager must track 512 caches per layer
Because Gated DeltaNet states grow faster than KV pages, so they need larger blocks than the attention layers
A paged KV manager assumes every layer grows one slot per token, but hybrids also keep a fixed state per linear layer
questions.explanation: Hybrid models have two kinds of per-sequence memory: growing pages for full-attention layers and one fixed state per linear layer. vLLM added a hybrid cache manager and flash-linear-attention kernels to handle both. This is PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED for vLLM.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production kernels do, and the cost
questions.question: Why is prefix caching harder for hybrid linear/full-attention models?
options: Linear layers have no state at all, so only the full layers' KV pages can be cached and the whole prefix must be re-prefilled
A linear-layer state summarizes the whole prefix, so it can only be reused at exact positions where a snapshot was saved
Prefix caching needs a softmax in every layer to merge cached keys with new keys, and linear layers have no softmax
The linear states are recomputed from scratch at every token, so a cached prefix state is always stale on reuse
questions.explanation: With a KV cache you can reuse any prefix length by keeping the first n entries. A recurrent state folds the whole prefix into one matrix and cannot be truncated, so reuse is only possible at positions where a snapshot was stored.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 7. Side by side: which to use
questions.question: In a side-by-side comparison, how does decode memory differ between MHA/GQA, pure linear attention/GDN, and a 3:1 hybrid?
options: Constant; grows with T; grows with T squared because of the hybrid's mask
Grows with T; constant; about one quarter of full plus a constant
Grows with T in all three, since even linear layers append to a cache
About one quarter of full; constant; grows with T like plain attention
questions.explanation: GQA's cache grows with context; a pure linear stack has only fixed states; a 3:1 hybrid has a cache in a quarter of the layers plus constant states. The hybrid recovers exact retrieval through those full layers.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 7. Side by side: which to use
questions.question: Which models are cited as using 3:1 hybrid layouts (2025–26)?
options: Llama 3.1 and GPT-2 XL
Mixtral and Switch Transformer
BERT-large and T5-11B
Qwen3-Next and Kimi Linear
questions.explanation: Qwen3-Next uses 3 Gated DeltaNet layers to 1 gated attention layer, and Kimi Linear uses 3 KDA layers to 1 MLA layer. Llama 3 and most models use plain MHA/GQA.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 7. Side by side: which to use
questions.question: When would you still choose plain softmax attention (GQA) over a linear or hybrid stack?
options: Short contexts where the cache is small, tasks needing exact recall of arbitrary earlier tokens, or when you want the simplest supported stack
Only when the context exceeds 1M tokens, since only there is a growing KV cache cheaper than the fixed per-head states of the linear layers
Whenever the model also uses MoE layers, because routed experts cannot be combined with linear-attention token mixing in one block
When decode memory must stay constant in T and the batch is large, since GQA caps each head's cache at a fixed size
questions.explanation: With short context the cache is small anyway; exact copying and long-range lookup are where fixed-state models struggle; and GQA has universal tooling. Constant decode memory is the strength of linear layers, not GQA.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 7. Side by side: which to use
questions.question: In the claim labels for hybrid models, which statement is classified as a company claim rather than PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED?
options: The Gated DeltaNet update and its online-learning view, as published in the ICLR 2025 paper by Yang, Kautz and Hatamizadeh
The 3:1 layouts of Qwen3-Next and Kimi Linear, as stated on their official model cards and config files
Kimi Linear 'outperforms full MLA' with up to 75% less KV cache and up to 6x decode throughput at 1M context
vLLM and SGLang support for serving these hybrid models, as listed in their release notes and docs
questions.explanation: The update rule, the 3:1 layouts on the model cards, and vLLM/SGLang support are publicly documented. Kimi Linear's headline performance comparison is reported by Moonshot and not independently reproduced, so it is a company claim.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: 7. Side by side: which to use
questions.question: Which statement about hybrid attention is labelled INFERENCE?
options: That Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B uses a 3:1 Gated DeltaNet to full-attention layout
That Gated DeltaNet L2-normalizes q and k before the recurrence, as its paper describes
That hybrid linear/sparse attention will become the default for long-context open models
That vLLM added a hybrid cache manager to serve Qwen3-Next and similar models
questions.explanation: Several labs are moving toward hybrid layouts, but full-attention models remain common, so predicting it will become the default is an inference. The other statements are documented facts from papers, model cards, or vLLM.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: Experiment: watch linear attention fill up
questions.question: In the experiment writing N random unit-key / scalar-value pairs (d_k = 16), how does linear attention's read-back error behave as N grows?
options: It grows roughly like N/d, so after 256 writes it is far worse than guessing 0 (MSE well above 1)
It stays near zero for any N, because each unit key writes into its own orthogonal slot
It decreases as more pairs are written, because the growing sum of writes averages out the interference noise
It stays bounded at about 0.2 for any N, because unit keys keep the state's norm fixed
questions.explanation: Every stored pair adds cross-talk to every read and nothing is removed, so error scales with the number of writes relative to dimension. At N = 256 its MSE was about 15.6, versus 1 for always predicting 0.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.section: Experiment: watch linear attention fill up
questions.question: In the same experiment, how does the delta rule (alpha = beta = 1) behave over all pairs versus the last 4 written?
options: Error over all pairs stays at zero for any N, because each write is corrected exactly and nothing is ever lost
Old pairs stay readable for any N, but the most recent writes become unreadable once N exceeds d_k = 16
It behaves identically to linear attention, with error over all pairs growing like N/d and recent writes lost too
Error over all pairs stays bounded as old pairs get overwritten, while recent writes stay readable (about 0.2)
questions.explanation: The delta rule overwrites old associations, so total error is limited by the fixed 1 x 16 memory, but recent pairs remain accurate regardless of how many came before. That recency is what the learned gates shape and what the full-attention layers of a hybrid compensate for.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: If the decode 'cache' of your linear-attention layer grows per token, what has gone wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong; linear-attention caches also grow per token, only at half the rate of softmax KV
You have effectively implemented softmax attention with extra steps; the state should have no T axis
You forgot to apply the decay gate, so the state keeps an extra row for each token it has not forgotten
You are storing the state in bf16 instead of fp32, so the kernel appends a correction term per token
questions.explanation: The defining property of a linear-attention layer is a fixed-size state, so a growing cache means you are storing history like softmax attention. Missing decay would degrade reads but not make the state grow in size.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: Why can unnormalized keys make the delta-rule state explode?
options: Unnormalized keys push $\beta_t$ above 1 through the sigmoid gate, so every write overshoots its target value by a factor $\lVert k\rVert$
With $\lVert k\rVert>1$, $I - \beta kk^\top$ has eigenvalue $1 - \beta\lVert k\rVert^2$, below $-1$ once $\beta\lVert k\rVert^2 > 2$
Large keys make the softmax denominator overflow in bf16, so the normalized reads $S q_t$ become infinite
Large keys shrink every eigenvalue of $I - \beta kk^\top$ toward 0, so the state collapses to zero rather than exploding
questions.explanation: Along $k$, the factor scales by $1-\beta\lVert k\rVert^2$. When this magnitude exceeds 1 the update amplifies the state each step instead of contracting it. L2-normalizing $k$ keeps the eigenvalue in $[0,1]$.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: What is wrong with writing the decay as $S_t = \alpha_t(S_{t-1} + v_t k_t^\top)$?
options: Nothing; it is algebraically identical, since $\alpha_t$ distributes over the sum
It decays only the new write $v_t k_t^\top$ and leaves the past state untouched
It makes the state grow without bound, because $\alpha_t$ multiplies after the add
It also decays the token just written; the definition decays only the past
questions.explanation: The correct form is $\alpha_t S_{t-1} + v_t k_t^\top$, so the fresh write enters at full strength. Wrapping both in $\alpha_t$ shrinks the new contribution too, changing the function.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: Why is computing the outer product as k_t v_t^T instead of v_t k_t^T a dangerous bug when d_k = d_v?
options: The shapes still match, so it runs silently but computes the transpose S^T
It raises a shape error immediately, because torch checks outer-product order
It makes the state rank 2 instead of rank 1, so reads mix two addresses
It doubles memory usage, because the transpose is materialized as a copy
questions.explanation: $S$ must be $(d_v, d_k)$ with writes $v_t k_t^\top$. When $d_k = d_v$, the swapped product has the same shape and produces no error, but reads with $q_t$ then use the wrong orientation.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: Is it correct to assume a 3:1 hybrid saves 4x decode memory at every context length?
options: Yes; the saving is always exactly 4x, because 3 of every 4 layers drop their cache
No; the saving is largest at short context, and it shrinks toward 1x as the context grows longer
No; at short context the constant state memory dominates (only about 2.3x at 4K for Qwen3-Next)
Yes, as long as the states are stored in bf16, which makes them negligible at any length
questions.explanation: The 4x factor applies only to the KV-cache part. The fixed state memory is a large share when the KV cache is small, so short-context savings are lower, approaching 4x only at long context.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: A 64-layer 3:1 hybrid has full layers with 8 KV heads of dim 128 (bf16) and linear layers with 16 heads, d_k = d_v = 128 (fp32 states). At batch 1, at what context length does full-layer KV equal total linear-state memory?
options: 4,096 tokens
256 tokens
768 tokens
32,768 tokens
questions.explanation: 16 full and 48 linear layers. KV $= 2\cdot16\cdot8\cdot128\cdot T\cdot2 = 65{,}536\,T$ bytes; states $= 48\cdot16\cdot128\cdot128\cdot4 = 50{,}331{,}648$ bytes. Equal at $T = 768$; beyond a few thousand tokens the full layers dominate.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: How would Kimi Linear's per-channel decay (KDA) be applied to the state in a from-scratch implementation?
options: alpha of shape (B, H, T, d_k), applied as S = S * alpha_t[..., None, :], scaling each key-channel column of S
alpha of shape (B, H, T, d_v), applied as S = S * alpha_t[..., :, None], scaling each value-channel row of S
alpha of shape (B, H), one scalar per head, applied as S = S * alpha once at the start of each new sequence
alpha of shape (B, H, T, T), applied to the outputs as a decay mask after the recurrence has finished
questions.explanation: S is (d_v, d_k); broadcasting alpha_t over the last axis scales its columns, one decay per key channel. When all channels of alpha are equal it must reduce to the scalar-decay version, which is the suggested test.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: A Gated DeltaNet decode drifts in bf16 and its state norm grows. The update is S = alpha_t * S + beta_t * (v_t - S @ k_t)[..., None] * k_t[..., None, :], with k straight from k_proj. What are the two problems?
options: beta_t should multiply S rather than the error, and the outer product should be k_t v_t^T
alpha_t should be applied after the write rather than before, and v_t should be L2-normalized too
The state should be kept in bf16 to match the activations, and q should not be normalized
The prediction uses the undecayed state (should be alpha_t * S @ k_t), and k is not L2-normalized
questions.explanation: Forget first, then predict: the error must be measured against $\alpha_t S$, otherwise $S_tk_t\ne v_t$ even with $\beta_t=1$ when $\alpha_t<1$. And without normalizing k, $I-\beta kk^\top$ stops being a contraction, the state grows, and bf16 loses precision. Fix: normalize k and keep the state in fp32.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: Which paper introduced the chunked (parallel over sequence length) training algorithm for delta-rule linear attention?
options: Transformers are RNNs: Fast Autoregressive Transformers with Linear Attention (Katharopoulos et al. 2020)
Parallelizing Linear Transformers with the Delta Rule over Sequence Length (Yang et al. 2024)
Gated Delta Networks: Improving Mamba2 with Delta Rule (Yang, Kautz & Hatamizadeh, ICLR 2025)
Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models (Fedus et al. 2021)
questions.explanation: Yang et al. 2024 provides the chunkwise WY algorithm. Katharopoulos et al. introduced linear attention, and the ICLR 2025 paper introduced the gated delta rule itself.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: When reading the Gated DeltaNet paper, which sections should you prioritize and which can you skim?
options: Read only the ablation tables and the long-context benchmarks, and skip the method sections since the code shows the update
Read §2 (background) and §3.1 (gated delta rule, online-learning view); skim §3.2–3.3 (chunkwise WY) unless writing kernels
Read §3.2–3.3 (chunkwise WY kernels) first since they define the layer, then skip §2 because it is only background
Read the appendix proofs and hyperparameter tables only, since the main text repeats the DeltaNet paper almost verbatim
questions.explanation: Background and the core update with its online-learning interpretation are the essentials. The chunkwise WY algorithm matters only for kernel work, and ablation tables can wait. For Kimi Linear, read the architecture and 3:1 ablation and treat headline comparisons as company claims.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: Why do Qwen3-Next and Kimi Linear keep one full-attention layer in four instead of going fully linear?
options: Full attention layers are needed to compute the decay gates $\alpha_t$ for the linear layers, which read their attention scores
Linear layers cannot be trained stably without full layers in between, because their gradients otherwise vanish across long chains of fixed states
Full layers are required for MoE routing, since the router needs softmax scores over all past tokens to pick the right experts
A fixed per-head state cannot store unbounded facts exactly, so a few full layers restore exact retrieval while linear layers mix cheaply
questions.explanation: Tasks like copying, needle-in-a-haystack and long-range lookup need precise access to arbitrary past tokens, which lossy fixed states struggle with. The full-attention layers provide that, and both models chose a 3:1 ratio.

questions.chapter_name: Linear attention, Gated DeltaNet & hybrid stacks
questions.question: Where do the remaining ~6.5 GB of Qwen3-Next's decode memory at 256K tokens come from?
options: Almost entirely the KV cache of the 12 full-attention layers; the 36 DeltaNet states add only 75.5 MB
Mostly the 36 DeltaNet states, which grow with context, while the 12 full layers' KV cache is small
The MoE expert weights that are loaded once per sequence and kept resident alongside the KV cache
Activation memory from the SiLU output gates and short convolutions, which scales with the batch size
questions.explanation: $2\cdot12\cdot2\cdot256\cdot262{,}144\cdot2 \approx 6.44$ GB from the full layers' bf16 KV cache, plus a constant 75.5 MB of fp32 states. The states do not grow with context.

questions.question: Why is getting language-model evaluation right described as critical for every later experiment in an ML research workflow?
options: Every architecture, data, and hyperparameter change is judged by the number evaluation produces, so a flawed metric fools you
Evaluation code is what computes the gradients the optimizer applies, so any error there silently corrupts every training step
Benchmark numbers must be reported to a registry before any model can be released, so evaluation gates every single release
Evaluation determines the learning-rate schedule automatically, so a bad metric changes how fast or slowly each training run proceeds
questions.explanation: You cannot improve what you cannot measure: every change you try is accepted or rejected based on the evaluation number. An honest held-out set, the right metric, and a fair scoring rule separate real progress from self-deception. Evaluation does not compute training gradients — it only measures the model.

questions.question: In language-model training, what exactly is the 'training loss'?
options: The mean cross-entropy (in nats) computed on a held-out stream of text that the optimizer never takes a gradient step on
The fraction of next tokens the model predicts incorrectly on the training batches, averaged over every token position in the whole batch
The exponential of the validation cross-entropy, reported once per epoch and smoothed with a moving average over recent steps
The mean cross-entropy (in nats) between the model's next-token distribution and the true next token, on the batches being optimized
questions.explanation: Training loss is the mean cross-entropy over the true next tokens, in nats, measured on the very batches used for gradient updates. Loss on a held-out stream is the validation loss, and the exponential of a loss is perplexity, not loss. It is a cross-entropy, not an error rate.

questions.question: Why can training loss alone not tell you whether a language model is learning the language?
options: Training loss is measured in nats, which cannot be compared across steps because the vocabulary normalizer keeps changing as training goes on
Training loss is always noisier than validation loss, so its downward trend is meaningless until the run has fully converged
A model with enough parameters can drive training loss very low by memorizing the training tokens while getting no better on unseen text
Training loss ignores the first token of every sequence, so it systematically underestimates the true loss on longer documents
questions.explanation: Training loss mixes memorization and genuine learning: a large model can memorize the training tokens and push training loss down without generalizing. Only a held-out stream the optimizer never touches can separate the two. The units (nats) are perfectly comparable across steps, so that is not the problem.

questions.question: What is a validation set in language-model training?
options: A subset of the training batches that is weighted more heavily in the loss so that the optimizer focuses on representative text
A separate stream of text the optimizer never updates on, on which loss is measured periodically to estimate generalization
The set of prompts used to tune the tokenizer's vocabulary and merge rules before pretraining begins on the main corpus
The final batch of each epoch, which is used to check gradient norms and adjust the clipping threshold periodically
questions.explanation: The validation set is held out: it is never used for gradient updates, and loss on it is measured periodically. Because the model never fit those tokens, validation loss reflects only what generalizes. Using training batches, even reweighted, would still mix in memorization.

questions.question: During training, training loss keeps falling while validation loss stops falling and begins to rise. What does this pattern indicate?
options: Underfitting: the model is too small to fit even the training data, so it should be scaled up
Overfitting: the model is fitting quirks of the training tokens that do not transfer to unseen text
A learning rate that is too low, so the model has stopped learning and only training noise remains
Data leakage from the validation set into training, which makes validation loss look better than it is
questions.explanation: Rising validation loss with falling training loss is the classic overfitting signature: gains on the training set are memorization that does not generalize. Underfitting would show both losses high and flat. Leakage would tend to make validation loss look too good, not rise.

questions.question: Which loss should you report and use for decisions when comparing language-model experiments?
options: The validation (held-out) loss, because it measures only what generalizes
The training loss, because it is computed on far more tokens
The minimum of training and validation loss at each step
The training loss at the final step, because it reflects the finished model
questions.explanation: Decisions should be made on validation loss: training loss measures memorization plus learning tangled together, whereas held-out loss isolates generalization, which is what you actually care about. Taking a minimum or the final training loss still lets memorization leak into the decision.

questions.question: In large-scale LM pretraining, why is classic overfitting (validation loss turning upward) rare during the main run?
options: Large models use dropout rates high enough to prevent any memorization of training tokens, even after many repeated epochs over the corpus
The validation set is resampled from the training data every step, which hides any gap between training and validation loss
Weight decay is set to zero during pretraining, so the parameters cannot grow large enough to memorize individual documents
Models see so much data for so few passes, often a single epoch, that they rarely see the same tokens enough to memorize them
questions.explanation: With huge corpora and roughly a single epoch, each token is seen about once, so train and validation curves sit almost on top of each other. That is a property of the data regime, not of dropout or weight decay. Resampling the validation set would be a mistake, not a reason for the curves to agree.

questions.question: If training and validation loss curves nearly coincide during large-scale pretraining, why is a held-out set still essential?
options: It is needed to compute the gradients for the next epoch, since the optimizer averages training and held-out gradients together
It is required to set the learning-rate warmup length, which is chosen from how quickly held-out loss first starts to fall
It is still the only honest measurement, it catches bugs such as a broken data pipeline, and it is what you compare across experiments
It is used to detect overfitting, which still happens every few thousand steps even in single-epoch pretraining runs over web-scale data
questions.explanation: Even without overfitting, the held-out loss is the honest measurement, it exposes bugs (for example a validation loss that will not move because the pipeline is broken), and it is the yardstick across experiments. It plays no role in computing gradients or schedules.

questions.question: Why is LM quality conventionally reported as perplexity rather than raw loss in nats?
options: Perplexity is the quantity actually differentiated during training, so reporting it matches what the optimizer sees directly
Perplexity is comparable across tokenizers and vocabulary sizes while loss in nats is not, so it allows direct cross-model comparison
Loss in nats is the right quantity to optimize but is not intuitive to report; exponentiating it gives a more interpretable number
Loss in nats can be negative for confident models, so it must be exponentiated into a positive number before it is reported
questions.explanation: Loss in nats is what you differentiate and optimize, but exp(loss) — perplexity — reads as an intuitive effective branching factor. Perplexity is not comparable across tokenizers either, and cross-entropy loss is never negative.

questions.question: If the mean cross-entropy over a held-out set is L nats, what is the perplexity?
options: ln(L)
exp(L)
log2(L)
exp(-L)
questions.explanation: Perplexity is exp(L) when L is measured in nats (natural log); 2^L would be correct only if L were in bits. ln(L) and log2(L) have no interpretation as a branching factor, and exp(-L) is the geometric-mean probability of the true tokens, the reciprocal of perplexity.

questions.question: What does the mean cross-entropy L = -(1/N) Σ ln q(x_i) represent in language-model evaluation?
options: The mean negative log-probability the model assigns to the true tokens
The mean probability the model assigns to its most likely token
The entropy of the model's own predictive distribution, ignoring the true tokens
The fraction of positions where the true token is the argmax
questions.explanation: L averages -ln q(x_i) over the true tokens x_i, i.e. how surprised the model is by what actually occurred. The model's own entropy ignores the true tokens, and argmax accuracy is a different metric entirely.

questions.question: What is the 'effective branching factor' interpretation of perplexity?
options: The average number of tokens the model generates on each prompt before it reaches and emits an end-of-sequence token
The number of attention heads that effectively carry information at each position, averaged over all layers of the model
The number of distinct vocabulary tokens that ever receive nonzero probability from the model on the held-out set
On average, at each position the model is as uncertain as if it were choosing uniformly among PPL equally likely tokens
questions.explanation: Because PPL is the exponential of the mean negative log-probability, it equals the size of a uniform choice with the same average uncertainty. A perplexity of 20 means the model is about as uncertain as picking uniformly among 20 tokens. It has nothing to do with generation length or heads.

questions.question: What loss and perplexity does a perfect language model achieve on held-out text?
options: Loss 1 and perplexity e, because the minimum cross-entropy is one nat
Loss 0 and perplexity 0, because there is no uncertainty left in any prediction
Loss -infinity and perplexity 0, because log-probabilities become maximal
Loss 0 and perplexity 1, because it assigns probability 1 to every true token
questions.explanation: A perfect model puts probability 1 on each true token; ln 1 = 0, so L = 0 and PPL = exp(0) = 1, meaning one effective choice. Perplexity can never fall below 1, so PPL 0 is impossible, and cross-entropy is bounded below by 0, not minus infinity.

questions.question: A model is uniform over a vocabulary of size V. What are its loss and perplexity?
options: Loss 1/V and perplexity V
Loss V and perplexity exp(V)
Loss ln V and perplexity V
Loss ln V and perplexity ln V
questions.explanation: A uniform model gives each token probability 1/V, so the negative log-probability of every true token is ln V. Exponentiating gives PPL = V: all V tokens are equally likely, maximal uncertainty.

questions.question: What sanity check should you run on a freshly initialized GPT-2-style model (vocabulary 50257) before training?
options: Its loss should be about 0 nats and its perplexity about 1, because the weights are initialized near zero; anything else is a bug
Its loss should be about ln 50257 ≈ 10.82 nats and its perplexity about 50257; a very different number signals a bug
Its perplexity should be about 1 and its loss near 0, matching a near-deterministic initial model with tiny random weights
Its loss should be about 50257 nats and its perplexity about e, matching the vocabulary size; a smaller loss signals a bug
questions.explanation: An untrained model is roughly uniform over the vocabulary, so loss ≈ ln V and perplexity ≈ V. If the untrained model reports something wildly different, the loss or the data pipeline is wrong, and you catch it before wasting GPU-hours. Loss equals ln V, not V itself.

questions.question: Why can per-token perplexities of two models with different tokenizers not be compared directly?
options: A bigger vocabulary spreads probability over more tokens and needs fewer tokens per word, so per-token perplexity measures another unit
Perplexity is always computed in bits for byte-level tokenizers and in nats for word-piece ones, so the numbers use different log bases
Models with larger vocabularies always have lower per-token perplexity by construction, regardless of how well they actually model the text
Different tokenizers use different end-of-sequence tokens, and those rare tokens dominate the average loss and therefore the perplexity
questions.explanation: Perplexity is per token, and the meaning of a 'token' changes with the tokenizer: a larger vocabulary has more options per position but fewer positions per word. So the numbers are on different scales. Compare within a fixed vocabulary, or switch to bits-per-byte to cross tokenizers.

questions.question: If you must compare language-model quality across models with different tokenizers, what metric is suggested instead of per-token perplexity?
options: Bits-per-byte
Perplexity divided by vocabulary size
Top-1 next-token accuracy
Loss in nats multiplied by vocabulary size
questions.explanation: Bits-per-byte normalizes by the raw byte count of the text, which is the same regardless of tokenizer, so it is comparable across vocabularies. Dividing perplexity by V or using top-1 accuracy does not remove the dependence on how text is cut into tokens.

questions.question: Why must the validation (and test) stream be carved off the corpus before the training run begins and kept fixed for the project?
options: Splitting after training makes the tokenizer unable to encode validation text
The optimizer needs to know the validation set in advance to schedule the learning rate
A fixed validation set is required to compute perplexity in nats, since the log base depends on the split size
A validation set that changes between experiments cannot be used to compare those experiments
questions.explanation: Splitting first guarantees the model never saw the held-out data, and keeping it fixed for the life of the project means every experiment is measured on the same data, so differences reflect the models, not the data. The optimizer and tokenizer do not depend on the split.

questions.question: If the same document or a near-duplicate appears in both training and validation splits, what does the validation loss end up measuring?
options: Generalization more accurately, because more data is shared
Exactly the training loss, because the two splits become identical
Memorization rather than generalization
Calibration rather than accuracy
questions.explanation: Leakage of the same or near-duplicate documents across the split lets the model score well on validation by recalling what it trained on, so the held-out number stops measuring generalization. This is the deduplication problem applied across the split; its evaluation cousin is benchmark contamination.

questions.question: Why keep a separate test set in addition to a validation set?
options: The validation set is usually too small to compute perplexity reliably, so a much larger test set is needed for a stable estimate
