Tuning hyperparameters against the validation set slowly fits to it, so a rarely-viewed test set gives an unbiased final number
The test set is used for early stopping and checkpoint selection, while the validation set is used for final reporting
The test set must cover tokens missing from the validation vocabulary, so every token type is evaluated at least once
questions.explanation: Every hyperparameter choice made against the validation set leaks a little information into model selection, so over many experiments you overfit to it. A test set you look at rarely, ideally once at the end, remains an unbiased estimate. Early stopping uses validation, not test.

questions.section: 4. Zero-shot vs few-shot: evaluating without fine-tuning
questions.question: How do zero-shot and few-shot evaluation elicit task ability from a pretrained language model?
options: By briefly fine-tuning the model on a handful of task examples before testing
Purely through the prompt the model conditions on, with no weight updates at all
By adding a task-specific classification head trained on the benchmark
By changing the tokenizer to include task-specific tokens for each benchmark's labels
questions.explanation: The key discovery of GPT-2 and especially GPT-3 is that task ability emerges from next-token pretraining and can be elicited purely by the prompt. Neither zero- nor few-shot changes weights, adds heads, or modifies the tokenizer.

questions.section: 4. Zero-shot vs few-shot: evaluating without fine-tuning
questions.question: What does a zero-shot prompt contain?
options: Only a description of the task and the input, with no worked examples
A task description, the input, and exactly one worked example of the task
Only the input, with the task inferred from weights fine-tuned on that task
A set of worked examples of the task, but no instruction or description
questions.explanation: Zero-shot gives just the instruction and the input (e.g. 'Translate English to French. English: cheese French:'), and the model must infer what to do from the instruction alone. Adding one example would make it one-shot.

questions.section: 4. Zero-shot vs few-shot: evaluating without fine-tuning
questions.question: In few-shot (in-context) evaluation, what are the 'shots'?
options: Separate forward passes over the same input averaged together to reduce variance
Gradient steps taken on a handful of task examples just before evaluation starts
Samples drawn from the model at high temperature and combined by majority vote
Worked examples of the task prepended to the prompt before the real input
questions.explanation: A shot is a solved demonstration of the task placed in the prompt ahead of the real query; one example is one-shot, k examples is k-shot. The model reads the pattern and continues it. No gradient steps are involved.

questions.section: 4. Zero-shot vs few-shot: evaluating without fine-tuning
questions.question: Why is few-shot learning described as a prompting method rather than training?
options: The examples are discarded before the forward pass and only their labels are kept as a prior over the answer options
Few-shot updates only the embedding layer on the k examples, not the full network, so it is cheaper than fine-tuning
The k examples only live in the context window for one forward pass; no gradient is computed and no weight changes
The model is trained on the examples for one step, but the weight updates are reverted after the answer is produced
questions.explanation: In-context learning happens entirely inside the context: the examples influence the current forward pass and nothing is stored in the parameters. Once the prompt ends, the model has learned nothing permanent. No layer, not even the embeddings, receives an update.

questions.section: 4. Zero-shot vs few-shot: evaluating without fine-tuning
questions.question: Why does placing a few demonstrations in the prompt help a pretrained language model on a task?
options: The demonstrations increase the model's effective parameter count for that prompt, since each one adds attention keys that act like extra weights for the query
The demonstrations reset internal recurrent state left over from pretraining, so the model starts the real input from a clean hidden state
Pretraining taught it to recognize and continue patterns; the demonstrations pin down which task and format you mean, sharpening its predictions
The demonstrations are memorized permanently into the weights during the forward pass, so every later query on that task benefits from them
questions.explanation: A model trained on a huge varied corpus can continue many patterns; the demos disambiguate which one (task and format) you want, sharpening the distribution over next tokens. They do not add parameters or create permanent memories.

questions.section: 4. Zero-shot vs few-shot: evaluating without fine-tuning
questions.question: According to the GPT-3 results, how does the benefit of few-shot examples change with model scale?
options: The benefit shrinks with scale, because large models already solve most tasks zero-shot
The benefit grows with scale: larger models make far better use of the same in-context examples
The benefit is roughly constant across scales, from 125M parameters up to 175B
The benefit only appears in models below one billion parameters and vanishes entirely beyond that size
questions.explanation: A central finding of GPT-3 ('Language Models are Few-Shot Learners', Brown et al., 2020) is that few-shot accuracy rises with parameter count and larger models exploit in-context examples much better. More shots generally help up to a point.

questions.section: 4. Zero-shot vs few-shot: evaluating without fine-tuning
questions.question: How does the scoring machinery for multiple-choice evaluation differ between zero-shot and few-shot settings?
options: It is identical; the number of shots only changes how much text sits in front of the question
Few-shot requires summed log-likelihood, while zero-shot requires length normalization by option tokens
Few-shot also scores the demonstrations' tokens along with the option tokens
Zero-shot uses greedy generation while few-shot uses log-likelihood scoring
questions.explanation: Both settings change only the prompt. The same scorer runs on [context; option], and the in-context examples are simply part of the context. Demonstration tokens are context, so they are not included in the option score.

questions.section: 5. Scoring a multiple-choice question by log-likelihood
questions.question: How is a pretrained language model graded on a multiple-choice benchmark such as ARC, HellaSwag, or MMLU via log-likelihood?
options: Generate a free-form answer from the context with greedy decoding, then check whether it contains the letter or text of the correct option
Fine-tune a small classifier head on the final hidden state that maps the context to one of the option indices, then take its argmax
Score each option by the perplexity of the context alone when that option is appended as a suffix, then pick the option with the lowest value
For each option, compute how likely the model finds that option's tokens given the context, then pick the option with the highest likelihood
questions.explanation: A pretrained model assigns probabilities to token sequences rather than clicking options, so we ask how likely each option's tokens are given the context and take the argmax. Context-only scoring would be identical across options and could not distinguish them.

questions.section: 5.1 Score the continuation, not the context
questions.question: When scoring option o of a multiple-choice question, what sequence is fed to the model and what is summed?
options: Feed only the option tokens with no context in front, and sum their log-probabilities ln q(x_t | x_<t)
Feed [context tokens] + [option tokens] once and sum ln q(x_t | x_<t) over all of the tokens
Feed the context once and sum the probabilities of each option's first token across the options
Feed [context tokens] + [option tokens] once and sum ln q(x_t | x_<t) over the option tokens only
questions.explanation: The option is conditioned on the full context in a single forward pass, and only the option tokens' conditional log-probabilities enter ℓ_o. Dropping the context loses the question, summing the context adds a shared constant, and scoring only the first token ignores the rest of the option.

questions.section: 5.1 Score the continuation, not the context
questions.question: Why are the context tokens excluded from an option's log-likelihood score in multiple-choice grading?
options: The context tokens have zero log-probability under the model once they are conditioned on, so including them in the score contributes nothing at all
Including the context log-probabilities would make the total score positive, which breaks the argmax over options in the scorer
The context is shared by all options, so its log-probability is the same constant for each and cannot change the winner; it only adds noise
The context is scored separately in its own forward pass and then subtracted from each option's perplexity before taking the argmax
questions.explanation: Every option shares the context, so its log-probability adds an identical constant to every score — it cannot change the argmax, but its large magnitude can bury the small differences between options. Context log-probabilities are not zero; they are negative like any others.

questions.section: 5.1 Score the continuation, not the context
questions.question: How does a multiple-choice log-likelihood scorer relate to a sequence_loglikelihood function that scores a whole sequence?
options: The scorer uses a different, unnormalized softmax than sequence_loglikelihood
The scorer is the same computation restricted to the continuation (option) tokens
sequence_loglikelihood scores only the first token while the scorer scores all tokens
They are unrelated; one uses logits and the other uses hidden states
questions.explanation: sequence_loglikelihood sums ln q(x_t | x_<t) over every token after the first; the multiple-choice scorer does the same arithmetic but restricts the sum to the option tokens. Both use the stable log_softmax of the logits.

questions.question: Why does comparing raw summed log-likelihoods bias multiple-choice scoring toward short options?
options: Every per-token log-probability is negative, so a longer option accumulates more negative terms and looks less likely just for being longer
Longer options are truncated by the context window, so they lose their most probable final tokens and their summed score drops sharply
Short options get a bonus from the end-of-sequence token, whose log-probability is positive and is added to the score of every short option
The softmax assigns systematically higher probabilities to short tokens, so options made of short tokens score higher on every one of their tokens
questions.explanation: Each term ln q is ≤ 0 because probabilities are ≤ 1. Adding more terms can only push the sum lower, so longer options are penalized for length alone, even when they are the better answer. Truncation and EOS bonuses are not the mechanism.

questions.question: What does length normalization do in multiple-choice log-likelihood scoring?
options: Divides each option's summed log-likelihood by its token count and picks the option with the highest mean per-token log-probability
Truncates every option to the token length of the shortest option before scoring, then picks the highest summed log-likelihood
Multiplies each option's summed log-likelihood by its token count to reward longer answers, then takes the option with the highest product
Pads all options with filler tokens to the same length before summing, so every option accumulates the same number of terms
questions.explanation: Length normalization compares mean per-token log-probability, (1/|o|) Σ ln q, and picks the argmax. Truncating or padding would change the content being scored, and multiplying by length would amplify rather than remove the bias.

questions.question: Option A is 1 token with log-prob -1.0; option B is 4 tokens with log-probs [-0.4, -0.3, -0.4, -0.3]. What does this illustrate about summed versus length-normalized scoring?
options: Both rules pick A, because its single token has a higher log-prob than B's total, showing normalization rarely matters
Both rules pick B, because its summed log-prob of -1.4 beats A's -1.0, showing that the plain sum already corrects for option length
The sum picks B and normalization picks A, showing that length normalization favors short options over long ones
The rules disagree: the sum picks A only because it is shorter, while normalization picks B, whose tokens are each more probable
questions.explanation: Sums are -1.0 vs -1.4, so the sum crowns A; normalized means are -1.0 vs -0.35, so normalization picks B. A single mildly confident token beats four more confident tokens under the sum just by having fewer negative terms.

questions.question: Which widely used evaluation tool scores tasks like HellaSwag by length-normalized log-likelihood?
options: vLLM benchmark_serving
TensorBoard HParams
lm-eval-harness
DeepSpeed-Chat
questions.explanation: lm-eval-harness, the standard benchmark harness, scores tasks like HellaSwag by length-normalized log-likelihood because options differ in length. vLLM (benchmark_serving is its throughput script) is an inference server, TensorBoard HParams a logging view, and DeepSpeed-Chat an RLHF training framework.

questions.question: Why is length normalization by token count described as a heuristic rather than a law?
options: It only works for options shorter than five tokens, beyond which the mean per-token log-probability stops being well defined at all
It assumes every token carries equal weight, which is not exactly true; some benchmarks normalize by characters or bytes, or keep the raw sum
It makes scores depend on the length of the shared context, so the same options score differently under different prompts and different shot counts
It is mathematically identical to the raw sum for any model, so calling it a separate scoring rule overstates what it actually changes
questions.explanation: Normalizing by token count is an assumption, not a derivation: tokens are not equally informative, and benchmarks variously normalize by characters, bytes, or not at all. It is not identical to the raw sum (summed and normalized rules can pick different winners) and is not restricted to short options.

questions.question: Two papers both report 'HellaSwag accuracy' but used different normalization rules when scoring options. What follows?
options: The numbers are comparable as long as both papers evaluated the same model size on the same split
The numbers are not directly comparable, because the scoring rule is part of the benchmark definition
The higher number is always the one computed with length normalization, so it should be preferred
Normalization only affects calibration, not the argmax, so the two accuracies remain directly comparable
questions.explanation: The scoring rule is part of what the benchmark measures, so different normalizations produce different accuracies for the same model. Comparisons are meaningful only with the same rule. Normalization changes which option wins, i.e. accuracy, not just calibration.

questions.question: What steps does multiple_choice_score in llmre.evaluation.harness perform?
options: Build [context; option], run the model once per option, sum option-token log-probs via log_softmax, optionally divide by length, return the argmax
Generate a greedy completion from the context, tokenize it, and return the index of the option with the smallest token-level edit distance to it
Run the model once on the context, embed each option with the model's embedding table, and return the option closest to the final hidden state
Sum log-probabilities from a stable log_softmax over both the context and option tokens, optionally divide by length, and return the argmin index of the options
questions.explanation: It implements log-likelihood scoring directly: one forward pass per [context; option], option tokens only, numerically stable log_softmax, optional length normalization, argmax. It does not generate text or compare embeddings, and it returns the highest, not lowest, score.

questions.question: With multiple_choice_score, option A (index 0) is one low-confidence token and option B (index 1) is four higher-confidence tokens. What do length_normalize=False and length_normalize=True return?
options: False returns 1 (option B); True returns 0 (option A)
Both return 0, because option A is listed first and ties go to index 0
Both return 1, because B has more tokens
False returns 0 (option A); True returns 1 (option B)
questions.explanation: Without normalization the summed log-likelihood favors the shorter option A (index 0); with normalization the higher per-token log-prob of B wins (index 1). This reproduces the summed-vs-normalized flip.

questions.question: Why is multiple_choice_score called model-agnostic?
options: It reimplements the transformer internally from the config and ignores the weights of the model passed in, so any architecture works
It works only on raw string inputs, so tokenization and the forward pass are delegated to each model's own generate method
It only calls model(seq) -> (logits, loss), so it works with the from-scratch GPT or any object returning logits of shape (B, T, V)
It uses only the returned scalar loss value, never the logits, so any model that reports a loss of shape () can be scored
questions.explanation: The scorer depends only on the interface model(seq) -> (logits, loss) that GPT.forward exposes, reading logits of shape (B, T, V). It needs the logits, not the loss, since it must pick out each option token's log-probability.

questions.question: In a causal LM, the context has length L_c and the option has length L_o. Which logit positions predict the option's tokens?
options: Positions L_c through L_c + L_o - 1
Positions 0 through L_o - 1, counting from the start
Positions L_c - 1 through L_c + L_o - 2
Positions L_c + 1 through L_c + L_o
questions.explanation: The logits at position p predict token p+1. The option tokens sit at absolute positions L_c … L_c + L_o - 1, so they are predicted by positions one earlier: L_c - 1 … L_c + L_o - 2. Using L_c … L_c + L_o - 1 is the classic off-by-one bug.

questions.question: Option X has 2 tokens with log-probs [-0.8, -0.9]; option Y has 5 tokens with log-probs [-0.5, -0.6, -0.5, -0.5, -0.6]. Which option wins under the summed rule and which under length normalization?
options: Summed picks Y (-2.7 vs -1.7); normalized picks X (-0.85 vs -0.54)
Summed picks X (-1.7 vs -2.7); normalized picks Y (-0.54 vs -0.85)
Both rules pick X, since its tokens are fewer and each is likelier
Both rules pick Y, since its mean and its sum are both higher than X's
questions.explanation: Sums: X = -1.7, Y = -2.7, so X wins the sum. Means: X = -0.85, Y = -0.54, so Y wins normalized. Y is longer, so its sum is dragged down by more negative terms even though each of its tokens is more confident on average.

questions.question: A language model's loss curve looks suspiciously good. What is the first thing to check?
options: That you are plotting the held-out loss rather than the loss on the batches being trained on
That the learning rate is high enough for the loss to have dropped that fast, rather than a lucky seed
That perplexity is reported in bits rather than nats, since base-2 logs make the curve look lower
That the vocabulary is large enough, since a small vocabulary makes per-token loss look artificially low
questions.explanation: A common mistake is reporting training loss, which looks great because it includes memorization. Verify the plotted curve is on held-out data. The other checks do not explain an unrealistically good curve.

questions.question: A multiple-choice scorer accidentally adds the shared context's log-probability into each option's score. What is the effect?
options: It makes the scorer pick the longest option every time, since the context adds more to longer sequences
It converts the scorer into a calibration metric that measures confidence rather than which option is right
It has no effect at all, because the context's log-probabilities are exactly zero once they are conditioned on by the model
It adds the same constant to every option, which cannot change the ideal ranking but buries the distinguishing signal
questions.explanation: The context is shared, so its log-probability is an identical additive constant; the ranking is unchanged in principle, but its large magnitude buries the small differences between options. Context log-probs are negative, not zero.

questions.question: Which statement about few-shot evaluation is a common mistake?
options: Saying the in-context examples live in the prompt for only one forward pass
Saying that zero-shot and few-shot share exactly the same scoring machinery
Saying that the benefit of few-shot examples grows with model scale, as GPT-3 reported
Calling it fine-tuning, as if the in-context examples updated the model's weights
questions.explanation: Few-shot is not fine-tuning: no weights change, and the examples only affect the current forward pass. The other three statements are correct descriptions of in-context evaluation.

questions.question: A zero-shot multiple-choice scorer always picks the option with the fewest tokens, using score = sum(log_probs_of_option_tokens) and argmax. What one change fixes it?
options: Take the argmin instead of the argmax of the summed score, so the option with the least likely total is chosen
Add the shared context's log-probability to every option's summed score before the argmax
Divide the sum by the number of option tokens and take the argmax of the mean per-token log-probability
Multiply the summed score by the number of option tokens before taking the argmax over options
questions.explanation: Summed negative log-probs penalize longer options, so the shortest option wins regardless of content. Length normalization — dividing by the option's token count — removes the bias; this is the length_normalize=True path. Argmin or multiplying by length would make things worse, and adding the context changes nothing.

questions.question: A newly initialized model with a 32000-token vocabulary reports a validation loss of about 10.373 nats. What does this indicate?
options: It signals an initialization bug, because an untrained model should have loss near 0 nats and perplexity near 1
It is expected: ln 32000 ≈ 10.373, so the model is roughly uniform and its perplexity is about 32000
It means the model has already learned the data, since 10.373 is far below the vocabulary size
It means the model's perplexity is about 10.373, so it is choosing among roughly ten tokens
questions.explanation: An untrained model is roughly uniform, so loss ≈ ln V = ln 32000 ≈ 10.373 nats and perplexity ≈ exp(10.373) ≈ 32000. That is the standard wiring sanity check. Perplexity is exp(loss), not the loss itself.

questions.question: Training loss keeps dropping, but validation loss bottomed out 2000 steps ago and is now creeping up. Which response fits?
options: Treat it as overfitting: report at the validation minimum and consider early stopping, regularization, more or deduplicated data, or less capacity
Cut the learning rate and keep training: validation rising while training falls means the step size is too large, so report the final checkpoint instead
Increase model capacity and keep training, since a larger model will push validation loss back down past its earlier minimum
Drop the validation set and rely on training loss, since a held-out split that disagrees with training loss must be corrupted
questions.explanation: Rising validation loss with falling training loss is overfitting. Report and checkpoint at the validation minimum; remedies include early stopping, weight decay or dropout, more or deduplicated data, or reducing capacity. Adding capacity would usually worsen overfitting.

questions.question: Is 5-shot evaluation a form of training?
options: No — the five examples affect only the current forward pass; no gradient is taken and no weight is updated
Yes — the model updates its weights on each of the five examples before it answers the question
Yes — but only the final layer and the output embedding are updated, once per shown example
No — because the five examples are removed from the prompt before inference, leaving only the bare question
questions.explanation: 5-shot is in-context (prompt-time) learning: the examples sit in the prompt and influence only that forward pass, with no gradient or weight change. The examples are not removed; they are exactly what conditions the answer.

questions.question: Two options have lengths 1 and 3. The 1-token option has log-prob -2.0; the 3-token option has log-probs [-0.5, -0.5, -0.5]. What do the summed and length-normalized rules choose, and what does this show?
options: Summed picks the 1-token option and normalized picks the 3-token option, showing the two rules always disagree
Both pick the 1-token option, since shorter options always win the summed rule and normalization only breaks ties
Summed picks the 3-token option and normalized picks the 1-token option, showing normalization favors short options
Both pick the 3-token option; normalization matters only when the length bias would otherwise decide the outcome
questions.explanation: Summed: -1.5 beats -2.0; normalized: -0.5 beats -2.0. Both choose the longer option because its per-token confidence is high enough that even its sum wins. Normalization does not always flip the winner — it matters only when length bias would decide the outcome.

questions.question: Why is a single benchmark accuracy number said to 'hide more than it shows'?
options: Contamination can make a mediocre model look brilliant, miscalibration yields confident wrong answers, and the wrong metric rewards the wrong behavior
Accuracy is always computed on the training set, so it overstates generalization, and the harness silently drops every item the model gets wrong from the denominator
Accuracy cannot be computed for multiple-choice tasks, only perplexity can, so a single accuracy number mixes two incompatible metrics together
Accuracy depends on the GPU and kernel versions used, so it is not reproducible across labs, and ties between options are broken at random each run
questions.explanation: A score can be inflated by leaked test items, can say nothing about whether the model's confidence is trustworthy, and depends on the metric chosen. Knowing what each number does and does not measure is the core skill of an evaluation engineer. Accuracy is normally computed on held-out benchmarks, not the training set.

questions.section: 1. Contamination: when the test leaks into training
questions.question: What is benchmark contamination?
options: Noise injected into benchmark labels by annotators who disagree, so a share of the gold answers are wrong before any model is evaluated
Training data that contains toxic or low-quality content, which drags benchmark scores down when it is mixed into the pretraining corpus
Using a different tokenizer for the benchmark than for training, so test questions are split into tokens the model rarely saw in pretraining
Benchmark test questions, and often their answers, ending up in the pretraining data, typically via web scrapes like Common Crawl
questions.explanation: Benchmarks are published on GitHub, in papers, on leaderboards, and in blog posts, and Common Crawl scoops all of it up, so test items leak into training. It is the evaluation-side twin of training-set deduplication. Label noise and toxicity are different problems.

questions.section: 1. Contamination: when the test leaks into training
questions.question: What does a contaminated benchmark actually measure?
options: Calibration of the model's confidence on familiar items
The model's ability to generalize to novel inputs
Memorization of the test set rather than task ability
The tokenizer's compression rate on the benchmark text
questions.explanation: If the model saw the exact items during pretraining it can score high by recalling them rather than reasoning, and that inflated score transfers to nothing. So it measures memorization, not generalization or task ability.

questions.section: 1. Contamination: when the test leaks into training
questions.question: In which direction, and how visibly, does contamination distort benchmark scores?
options: Downward and loudly — contaminated items cause the evaluation harness to crash with a duplicate-item error
Upward and silently — there is no error; you only discover it when the model fails on genuinely novel inputs
Randomly up or down, with a contamination warning printed by the harness whenever overlapping items are found
Downward and silently, because memorized answers are often stale versions that no longer match the gold labels
questions.explanation: Contamination inflates scores, and nothing flags it: the model simply reports a higher number than it deserves. The problem surfaces when the model fails on novel inputs that 'should' have been easy given its benchmark score.

questions.section: 1. Contamination: when the test leaks into training
questions.question: How does the standard n-gram / substring-overlap decontamination pass work?
options: Shuffle the n-grams of each test item before evaluation so the model cannot recognize memorized text, then score the shuffled items as usual
Flag test items whose text appears as a long enough n-gram in the training corpus, then drop those items or remove the matching training documents
Replace every n-gram in the training corpus that also appears in any benchmark with a hashed placeholder token, then retrain the tokenizer on the masked result
Train a classifier on benchmark items to predict whether each test item is too easy, then drop the flagged items from the reported benchmark
questions.explanation: Decontamination by overlap searches the training corpus for long n-grams from each test item; matches are dropped from the benchmark or the matching documents are dropped from training. GPT-3, Llama, and others report doing this.

questions.section: 1. Contamination: when the test leaks into training
questions.question: Why is near-duplicate detection (e.g. MinHash / Jaccard) used in addition to exact n-gram matching for decontamination?
options: Exact matching misses paraphrases and reformattings that are close but not identical
Near-duplicate detection is the only method that works on numbers and code, since n-grams ignore digits
Exact matching produces too many false negatives only on short questions, which MinHash handles by padding
MinHash removes the need for any training-corpus scan, since it compares only the benchmark items to each other
questions.explanation: Exact n-gram overlap only catches verbatim copies. MinHash estimates Jaccard similarity between shingle sets and catches items that are close but reformatted. It still scans the corpus; it just compares sets approximately.

questions.section: 1. Contamination: when the test leaks into training
questions.question: What is a canary string in the context of benchmark contamination?
options: A special token appended to every benchmark prompt that makes a model refuse to answer if it was trained on that benchmark's files
A deliberately wrong answer inserted into a few benchmark items so that annotators who copy answers instead of labeling can be detected
A checksum string shipped with each benchmark release so that users can verify their downloaded copy of the files was not corrupted
A unique random string (canary GUID) embedded in released benchmark files so anyone can grep a corpus and know the benchmark leaked in
questions.explanation: Benchmark authors include a unique GUID in their files; finding it in a training corpus proves the benchmark files were scraped. It is a detection tool, not a refusal trigger or a download checksum.

questions.section: 1. Contamination: when the test leaks into training
questions.question: What is described as the most robust defense against benchmark contamination?
options: Running the n-gram overlap filter twice with different n, so both short and long overlaps are caught
Evaluating with more few-shot examples, which drowns out any memorized answer with in-context evidence
Test sets created after the training cutoff or kept entirely private, so they cannot have been seen
Publishing the benchmark answers separately from the questions, so scraped copies never contain the gold labels
questions.explanation: A post-cutoff or private test set cannot be in the training data, so it is the strongest defense; this is why leaderboards increasingly rotate to new, time-stamped question sets. Filters remain imperfect, and publishing answers separately still leaks them to the web.

questions.section: 1. Contamination: when the test leaks into training
questions.question: Why is decontamination described as best-effort rather than a guarantee?
options: Decontamination can only be run on corpora smaller than about one billion tokens, so web-scale pretraining sets are never fully scanned
Removing contaminated items always lowers scores to chance level, so labs keep some of them in to report meaningful numbers
Paraphrases, translations, reordered multiple-choice options, and reformatted problems slip past n-gram filters
Canary strings are stripped out by every tokenizer during preprocessing, so the grep step never finds them in the training data
questions.explanation: Overlap filters target surface text, so semantically identical but reworded or translated items evade them. Therefore a headline benchmark number from a web-trained model should be treated as an upper bound on true ability.

questions.section: 1. Contamination: when the test leaks into training
questions.question: How should you treat a headline public benchmark number from a web-trained model?
options: As a lower bound, since decontamination usually removes some of the easiest items from the benchmark
As an upper bound on true ability, trusting a private or post-cutoff evaluation far more
As an exact measure of ability, provided the lab reports having run an n-gram decontamination filter
As meaningless, since every public benchmark is fully contaminated in every web-scale pretraining corpus
questions.explanation: Because contamination inflates scores and decontamination is imperfect, public numbers are best read as upper bounds. A private or post-cutoff evaluation is far more trustworthy. That does not make public numbers meaningless — just optimistic.

questions.section: 1. Contamination: when the test leaks into training
questions.question: What do the Llama and GPT-3 papers document regarding contamination?
options: Their decontamination procedures and how much scores move once contaminated items are removed
That contamination stops affecting scores once models pass a certain scale, so large models need no decontamination
That embedding canary strings in benchmark files is sufficient on its own to guarantee a clean evaluation set
That few-shot prompting removes the effect of contamination, since in-context examples override memorized answers
questions.explanation: Both papers describe their decontamination procedures and report the score changes after removing contaminated items, showing how seriously frontier labs treat the issue and how much a clean number can differ from the raw one.

questions.question: What question does calibration ask that accuracy does not?
options: How often is the model's top prediction correct across the whole held-out test set?
How many tokens does the model need to generate before reaching the correct final answer?
Does the model's accuracy keep improving as more few-shot examples are added to the prompt?
When the model says it is, say, 80% sure, is it actually right about 80% of the time?
questions.explanation: Accuracy asks how often the model is right; calibration asks whether its stated confidence matches its empirical accuracy at each confidence level. They are orthogonal questions.

questions.question: In classification-style evaluation, how is a model's confidence in a prediction usually read off?
options: As the entropy of the softmax distribution over classes, where lower entropy means higher confidence in the choice
As the raw logit of the chosen class, before the softmax, since logits are already on a probability scale
As the difference between the two largest logits, the margin by which the chosen class beats the runner-up
As the max softmax probability — the probability mass placed on the chosen (most likely) class
questions.explanation: After choosing the most likely class, confidence is the probability the softmax put on that class. Entropy and logit margins are related uncertainty signals, but ECE as described uses the max softmax probability.

questions.question: Which pair correctly illustrates that accuracy and calibration are independent?
options: A model 70% correct claiming 70% confidence is overconfident and miscalibrated; one 40% correct claiming 99% confidence is honest
A model with high accuracy is always well-calibrated by construction; a model with low accuracy is always overconfident about its picks
A model 70% correct claiming 99% confidence is accurate but overconfident; one 40% correct claiming ~40% is inaccurate but honest
Calibration is just accuracy measured again on a second held-out set, so a 70%-accurate model has ECE 0.70 on any split it is given
questions.explanation: Calibration compares confidence to accuracy, regardless of the accuracy level. A 70%-accurate model claiming 99% is overconfident; a 40%-accurate model claiming 40% is well-calibrated though inaccurate. Neither property implies the other.

questions.question: For which kind of system does calibration matter as much as accuracy?
options: Systems that only ever use the argmax prediction and discard all probabilities, such as plain multiple-choice leaderboard scoring
Any system that acts on the model's probability, such as flagging low-confidence answers for review, abstaining, or routing to a human
Systems that evaluate perplexity on held-out text, since perplexity is just calibration of next-token probabilities at every position
Systems that train with a fixed learning rate, since an uncalibrated model makes the loss scale and therefore the step size unpredictable
questions.explanation: When a human or downstream component uses the model's confidence to decide what to do, miscalibrated confidence leads to bad decisions; a confident wrong answer is worse than an unconfident one. If only the argmax is used, calibration matters much less.

questions.question: In computing Expected Calibration Error, what two quantities are attached to each of the N predictions?
options: A confidence c_i in [0,1] (the max softmax probability) and a correctness y_i in {0,1}
A raw logit z_i for the chosen class and a temperature T_i fitted per prediction on held-out data
A loss in nats for the prediction and the perplexity exp of that loss, both computed on the true label
A bin index b_i in {1,...,M} and the gradient norm of the loss with respect to that prediction's logits
questions.explanation: ECE needs, for each prediction, its confidence (max softmax probability) and whether it was correct (0 or 1). Predictions are then grouped by confidence.

questions.question: How are predictions grouped when computing ECE?
options: Into M equal-width confidence bins across [0,1], e.g. (0.0,0.1], (0.1,0.2], … for M = 10
Into M bins holding equal numbers of predictions, sorted by loss rather than by confidence
Into one bin per class label, so each bin holds every prediction that chose that class
Into bins by input length in tokens, e.g. (0,64], (64,128], … so long prompts are compared fairly
questions.explanation: The standard recipe uses equal-width confidence bins; for M = 10 the bins are (0.0,0.1], (0.1,0.2], and so on. Grouping by class or by loss would not compare confidence to accuracy.

questions.question: What is the ECE formula?
options: ECE = (1/M) Σ_b |acc(b) − conf(b)|, ignoring bin sizes
ECE = max_b |acc(b) − conf(b)|, the single worst bin
ECE = Σ_b (acc(b) − conf(b))², summed over bins
ECE = Σ_b (|B_b| / N) · |acc(b) − conf(b)|
questions.explanation: ECE is the average per-bin gap between accuracy and average confidence, weighted by the fraction of predictions in each bin, |B_b|/N. The unweighted mean ignores bin populations, the max is a different metric (maximum calibration error), and squared gaps are not ECE.

questions.question: In the ECE formula, what is |B_b|, and what ECE does a perfectly calibrated model get?
options: |B_b| is the width of bin b, e.g. 0.1 for M = 10; a perfectly calibrated model has acc(b) = 1 in every bin, so ECE = 1
|B_b| is the number of correct predictions in bin b; a perfectly calibrated model has ECE = 0.5 because half of each bin is right
|B_b| is the number of predictions in bin b; a perfectly calibrated model has acc(b) = conf(b) in every bin, so ECE = 0
|B_b| is the average confidence in bin b; a perfectly calibrated model has ECE equal to its accuracy
questions.explanation: |B_b| counts the predictions that fall in bin b, giving the weight |B_b|/N. Perfect calibration means every bin's accuracy equals its average confidence, so every gap and thus ECE is 0.

questions.question: Ten predictions: five at confidence 0.6 (3 correct), four at 0.8 (2 correct), one at 0.95 (correct). With width-0.1 bins, what is the ECE?
questions.explanation: Bin (0.5,0.6]: gap 0.00, weight 0.5. Bin (0.7,0.8]: accuracy 0.50 vs confidence 0.80, gap 0.30, weight 0.4 → 0.12. Bin (0.9,1.0]: gap 0.05, weight 0.1 → 0.005. Total 0.125, meaning confidence is off by about 12.5 percentage points on average.

questions.question: In that ECE worked example, what does the (0.7, 0.8] bin show about the model?
options: It is under-confident there: it claims 80% confidence but is right more often than that, so the bin lowers the ECE
It is overconfident there: it claims 80% confidence but is right only half the time, and that bin dominates the ECE
It is perfectly calibrated there, with accuracy equal to confidence, so the bin contributes nothing to the total ECE
It is overconfident there, but the bin holds so few predictions that its weighted gap barely changes the total ECE
questions.explanation: Four predictions at 0.8 with only 2 correct give a 0.30 gap with weight 0.4, contributing 0.12 of the 0.125 total. The (0.5,0.6] bin is perfectly calibrated, and the (0.9,1.0] bin is slightly under-confident but rare.

questions.question: In that same example, the (0.9, 1.0] bin holds one prediction at confidence 0.95 that is correct. How does it affect ECE?
options: It is slightly under-confident (accuracy 1.00 vs 0.95) but rare, so it adds only 0.005
It is heavily overconfident, claiming 0.95 when right, and it dominates the total
It is perfectly calibrated because the prediction is correct, so it adds exactly 0
It is excluded from the sum, because bins holding a single prediction are dropped from ECE
questions.explanation: Accuracy 1.00 versus confidence 0.95 gives a 0.05 gap, weighted by 1/10, contributing 0.005. Being right more often than claimed is under-confidence. Single-prediction bins are not dropped; they are just lightly weighted.

questions.question: Why must ECE be reported alongside a reliability diagram rather than alone?
options: ECE is always exactly 0 for models trained with plain cross-entropy, so a reliability diagram is the only way to see any miscalibration in them
ECE can only be computed for binary classification, so multi-class models need a reliability diagram per class instead of a single number
ECE is numerically identical to 1 minus accuracy, so a diagram is needed to show the calibration information that the number leaves out
ECE depends on the bin count, can read 0 even when over- and under-confident bins cancel, and says nothing about which direction the model errs
questions.explanation: Too few bins hide miscalibration, too many leave bins nearly empty and noisy; aggregate gaps can mask problems; and the absolute value hides direction. A reliability diagram (accuracy vs confidence per bin) shows where and how the model is miscalibrated.

questions.question: How does the choice of number of bins affect ECE?
options: More bins always give a more accurate ECE estimate, with no downside at any sample size
The bin count has no effect on ECE, because each bin's gap is weighted by its size
Too few bins hide miscalibration; too many leave bins nearly empty and noisy
Fewer bins always increase ECE, because wider bins mix more confidence levels together
questions.explanation: Coarse bins average away miscalibration within each bin, while very fine bins contain few predictions and give noisy accuracy estimates. ECE is therefore bin-dependent, which is why the bin count should be reported.

questions.question: What known-answer cases does code/tests/test_eval.py use to check expected_calibration_error?
options: 100 predictions at confidence 1.0 all correct give ECE 1.0; 100 predictions at confidence 0.5 all wrong give ECE 0
Any set of 100 predictions with accuracy above 90% gives ECE 0, whatever their confidences, since calibration simply follows accuracy
100 predictions at confidence 0.5 with exactly half correct give ECE 0; 100 predictions at confidence 0.9 all wrong give ECE 0.9
100 random confidences drawn uniformly from [0,1] with random correctness always give ECE 0.5, matching the expected gap
questions.explanation: At confidence 0.5 with half correct, accuracy equals confidence, so ECE = 0. At confidence 0.9 with all wrong, accuracy is 0 and the gap is 0.9 for all predictions, so ECE = 0.9. These are cases computable by hand.

questions.question: How is instruction-following typically evaluated after supervised fine-tuning?
options: By exact match against a single gold answer written for each instruction, with a fuzzy match for minor wording differences
With held-out instruction sets and, increasingly, a strong model as judge (LLM-as-judge), which is fast but inherits the judge's biases
By measuring perplexity on the pretraining validation set, since better instruction-following always lowers held-out loss
By pass@k against unit tests written for each instruction, which counts a response as correct if any of its k samples passes the tests
questions.explanation: Instruction-following is judged on held-out instruction sets and often by LLM-as-judge. It scales well but the judge's preferences and biases become part of the metric. Exact match and pass@k suit verifiable tasks instead.

questions.question: How are math and logic reasoning tasks with a single verifiable answer (GSM8K, MATH) usually graded?
options: Exact match on the extracted final answer against the gold answer
Human pairwise preference between two full reasoning traces
Perplexity of the reference worked solution under the model
LLM-as-judge rating of the reasoning trace's style, clarity, and rigor
questions.explanation: Reasoning benchmarks with a verifiable answer are graded by extracting the final answer and comparing it to the gold. It is objective and cheap but blind to how the model got there.

questions.question: What is the main blind spot of exact-match grading on reasoning tasks?
options: It is too expensive to run on more than a few hundred problems, since every answer needs a human check
It rewards longer answers over shorter ones, because longer outputs contain the gold string more often
It cannot be applied to numerical answers, because floating-point values never match a gold string exactly
It ignores how the answer was reached, so a right answer from wrong reasoning still scores
questions.explanation: Exact match checks only the final answer, so lucky guesses or invalid reasoning that lands on the right number get full credit. It is cheap and objective, and works fine on numbers once formats are normalized.

questions.question: What does tool-use evaluation check when a model calls tools or functions?
options: Only whether the generated text matches a reference transcript of the tool session exactly, token for token, including call formatting
The perplexity of the tool documentation under the model, since a model that predicts the docs well is assumed to call the tools well
How many tools the model can list and describe from memory when asked, scored by recall against the full registry of available tools
Whether it picked the right tool, formed valid arguments, and used the results correctly — often via task success in a sandbox
questions.explanation: Tool-use evaluation measures tool selection, argument validity, and correct use of results, often by whether the task succeeds in a sandbox rather than by a text match.

questions.question: How is open-ended quality (helpfulness, style, safety) evaluated when there is no single correct string?
options: By exact match against the most common human-written answer, collected from several annotators per prompt
By pass@k with a reward model acting as the verifier, counting a prompt as solved if any of k responses scores high
By collecting pairwise human preferences between two responses and aggregating them, e.g. into win rates or Elo
By measuring ECE on the responses, since a helpful and safe model is one whose stated confidence matches its accuracy
questions.explanation: Human/preference evaluation asks which of two responses is better and aggregates the judgments into win rates or Elo ratings. This same preference data trains reward models and drives RLHF.

questions.question: Besides evaluation, what is pairwise human preference data used for?
options: Building the tokenizer's merge vocabulary
Training reward models and driving RLHF
Choosing the number of ECE bins to report
Decontaminating the pretraining corpora
questions.explanation: Pairwise preferences are the data that trains reward models, which in turn drive reinforcement learning from human feedback. They have nothing to do with tokenizers or decontamination.

questions.question: What is meant by 'the metric encodes what you reward'?
options: Choosing a metric is choosing an objective: exact match rewards final answers, LLM-as-judge what the judge prefers, win rate what annotators like
Metrics are added directly to the training loss as a reward term, so whatever is measured is also what gradient descent optimizes
The metric with the highest number is always the right one to report, since a higher score means the model is rewarded for real ability
Every metric measures the same underlying capability on a different scale, so exact match, judge scores and win rates rank models identically
questions.explanation: Each metric has its own notion of good behavior; optimizing or selecting on it pushes the model toward that notion and away from what it ignores. Pick the metric matching the behavior you want and be honest about what it leaves out.

questions.question: What does pass@k measure for code and reasoning tasks?
options: The probability that at least one of k sampled attempts is correct
The fraction of k attempts that are all correct
The probability that the k-th attempt is correct
The average number of attempts needed before the first correct one, capped at k
questions.explanation: pass@k is the chance that at least one of k samples passes the verifier. It reflects that a model allowed several attempts on a checkable task is more useful than one judged on a single try.

questions.question: What is wrong with estimating pass@k by sampling exactly k completions and scoring 1 if any passed?
options: It always returns 0 for problems that have any wrong samples among the k
It can only be computed for k = 1, since larger k needs the closed-form estimator
It requires a reward model as the verifier instead of the problem's unit tests
It is a noisy and biased estimate, especially for small k and rare successes
questions.explanation: One draw of exactly k samples per problem gives a 0/1 per-problem estimate that is high-variance and biased. The Codex fix is to sample n ≥ k once and compute the expected pass@k analytically.

questions.question: With n samples generated and c of them correct, what is the unbiased pass@k estimator from the Codex paper?
options: c / n raised to the power k
1 − C(n−c, k) / C(n, k)
C(c, k) / C(n, k)
questions.explanation: pass@k = 1 − C(n−c, k)/C(n, k). C(c,k)/C(n,k) would be the chance that all k picks are correct, and (c/n)^k is a with-replacement 'all correct' probability, not 'at least one'.

questions.question: In the unbiased pass@k estimator, what does the ratio C(n−c, k) / C(n, k) represent?
options: The probability that every one of the k chosen samples is among the c correct ones, so pass@k counts only perfect subsets
The probability that a random size-k subset of the n samples contains none of the c correct ones
The fraction (n−c)/n of samples that are incorrect, raised to the power k to account for drawing k samples independently
The expected number of correct samples in a random size-k subset, divided by k to turn it into a per-sample success rate
questions.explanation: C(n−c, k) counts subsets drawn entirely from the n−c wrong samples, and C(n, k) counts all size-k subsets, so the ratio is the chance of missing every correct sample; one minus it is the chance of at least one correct.

questions.question: Why does generating n > k samples and applying the analytic pass@k formula help?
options: It lets you use a weaker, faster verifier without affecting the result, since averaging over subsets cancels false passes
It averages over all size-k subsets of the n samples, giving a far lower-variance estimate than repeatedly drawing exactly k
It guarantees that the estimated pass@k equals pass@1 times k, which makes results comparable across different values of k
It removes the need to check every sample with the verifier, since the formula only needs a few checked samples to extrapolate
questions.explanation: Using all n samples and computing the expectation over size-k subsets uses far more information than one draw of k, sharply reducing variance. Every sample still has to be checked to count c.

questions.question: With n = 5 samples of which c = 2 are correct, what is pass@3 by the unbiased estimator, and why?
options: 0.9 — of the C(5,3) = 10 size-3 subsets, only C(3,3) = 1 consists of all wrong samples
0.4 — two correct out of five samples, and the subset size does not change it
0.6 — three draws out of five, each of which could be one of the correct ones
1.0 — any three of the five samples must include at least one of the two correct samples
questions.explanation: pass@3 = 1 − C(3,3)/C(5,3) = 1 − 1/10 = 0.9. Exactly one 3-subset avoids both correct samples, so a random draw of 3 attempts succeeds 90% of the time; it is not certain.

questions.question: Why does pass@k require a reliable verifier?
options: Because the estimator divides by the number of verifier calls, so a verifier that times out on some samples makes the estimate blow up
Because the verifier sets the value of k, choosing how many samples to draw per problem based on how hard it judges the problem to be
Because pass@k is undefined if any sample fails to run, so the verifier must repair broken samples before the estimator is applied
It counts any solution that passes the checker, so weak unit tests let wrong solutions count as passes and overstate capability
questions.explanation: pass@k measures whether the model can produce a passing answer in k tries, not whether the answer is good. A leaky or incomplete checker inflates pass@k, and comparisons are meaningful only with the same n, k, and verifier.

questions.question: When are pass@k comparisons between two evaluations meaningful?
options: Whenever both report pass@k for the same k, regardless of which verifier was used
Only when n equals k in both evaluations, so that no subset averaging is involved
When both use the same n, the same k, and the same verifier
Only when k = 1 in both evaluations, since pass@k for larger k depends on sampling temperature
questions.explanation: pass@k depends on the sampling budget and especially on the verifier; different tests or settings produce numbers on different scales. Matching n, k, and verifier makes them comparable. n = k is in fact the worse estimator.

questions.question: Which paper introduced pass@k and its unbiased estimator?
options: The GPT-3 paper, 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners' (Brown et al., 2020)
The Llama paper, 'LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models' (Touvron et al., 2023)
The Codex paper, 'Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code' (Chen et al., 2021)
The GPT-2 paper, 'Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners' (Radford et al., 2019)
questions.explanation: pass@k and the unbiased estimator 1 − C(n−c,k)/C(n,k) come from the Codex paper by Chen et al., 2021. The same idea of a checkable answer reappears in RL with verifiable rewards.

questions.section: 5. Staying honest about what a metric measures
questions.question: What does perplexity measure — and not measure?
options: Task ability on downstream benchmarks — not raw token prediction on held-out text
Token prediction on held-out text — not task ability, truthfulness, or reasoning
Calibration of the model's stated confidence — not its accuracy on any task
Reasoning quality across multi-step problems — not memorization of the training set
questions.explanation: Perplexity is a token-prediction metric on held-out text. A low perplexity does not certify task ability, truthfulness, or reasoning; those need other evaluations.

questions.section: 5. Staying honest about what a metric measures
questions.question: What is the blind spot of multiple-choice accuracy?
options: It measures ranking among given options — not whether the model could produce the answer unaided — and depends on the scoring rule and option order
It measures free-form generation quality, since the model must write out its full answer, but it ignores which options were offered and in what order
It measures ranking among the given options and is insensitive to how they are scored or ordered, so it fully captures unaided problem solving
It measures calibration rather than ranking — whether the probability placed on each option matches how often that option is the right one
questions.explanation: Choosing among provided options is easier than generating an answer, and the result depends on the scoring rule (summed vs normalized) and option order. It is a ranking metric, not a generation or calibration metric.

questions.section: 5. Staying honest about what a metric measures
questions.question: Which statement about exact-match grading of reasoning answers is correct?
options: It penalizes broken reasoning even when the final answer is correct, and it accepts any phrasing of a correct answer automatically
It accepts any phrasing of a correct answer automatically, so '1/2' and '0.5' match, but it cannot be applied to numeric answers
It measures the quality of each reasoning step against a gold solution, so a correct answer reached by broken reasoning fails
A correct answer from broken reasoning still scores, and a correct answer phrased differently from the gold string wrongly fails
questions.explanation: Exact match looks only at the final string: wrong reasoning with a right answer passes, and right answers in a different format fail unless normalized. It does not inspect steps.

questions.section: 5. Staying honest about what a metric measures
questions.question: What does pass@k measure, according to its blind spot?
options: The quality of the single best solution among the k, judged independently of the verifier that was used
The average quality of all k sampled solutions, weighted by how many of the verifier's tests each one passes
Whether all k sampled solutions pass the verifier, so a single failing sample drives the score for that problem to 0
Reachability of a passing answer within k tries under a specific verifier — not solution quality
questions.explanation: pass@k only says whether some attempt among k passes the given checker. It does not measure how good, efficient, or correct-in-untested-cases the solution is.

questions.section: 5. Staying honest about what a metric measures
questions.question: What reporting practice follows from the fact that every metric is partial?
options: Report only the single metric that gives the highest score, and describe how it was computed so readers trust that one number over the rest
Report only perplexity on a private held-out set, since it is the one metric with no blind spots and needs no choice of bins, normalization or n/k
Report several metrics, state how each was computed (bins, normalization, n/k, decontamination), and keep a private or post-cutoff set you trust
Avoid reporting computation details such as bins, normalization or n/k, so results stay comparable with papers that did not report them
questions.explanation: None of the metrics is wrong, but each is partial. Reporting several with their computation details lets readers judge them, and a private or post-cutoff evaluation guards against contamination.

questions.question: You sample n = 6 completions of a coding problem and c = 2 pass. What is pass@2 by the unbiased estimator?
questions.explanation: pass@2 = 1 − C(4,2)/C(6,2) = 1 − 6/15 = 0.6. Of the 15 pairs, 6 are drawn entirely from the 4 failing samples; the other 9 include a correct one, so 9/15 = 0.6. 0.4 is the miss probability.

questions.question: Why is estimating pass@k by literally sampling k completions and checking 'any pass' a common mistake?
options: It is biased and high-variance; you should sample n > k and use the analytic estimator
It always underestimates pass@1, since one passing sample out of k is counted as only 1/k
It requires a GPU with more memory than the analytic estimator, since all k samples are kept
It cannot handle problems with zero correct samples, where the any-pass indicator is undefined
questions.explanation: The single-draw approach gives noisy 0/1 per-problem estimates and a biased average. Sampling more completions once and computing 1 − C(n−c,k)/C(n,k) is the recommended fix.

questions.question: A reasoning grader compares strings exactly, and answers '0.5', '1/2', and '½' are graded differently. What is the mistake?
options: Not normalizing the answer format before exact match, so equivalent answers fail a naive string compare
Using exact match instead of the perplexity of the gold answer for grading these reasoning tasks
Using too few ECE bins, so near-equal answers fall into the same bin and get merged
Using pass@1 instead of pass@k, so equivalent answers appearing in the other samples are never counted
questions.explanation: Exact-match grading must normalize answer formats; otherwise semantically identical answers like 0.5, 1/2, and ½ are scored as wrong. Perplexity or ECE do not address this.

questions.question: Which practice reflects a common mistake about accuracy and calibration?
options: Reporting ECE together with a reliability diagram and the number of confidence bins used to compute it
Treating public benchmark numbers from web-trained models as an upper bound on true ability
Using the max softmax probability as each prediction's confidence when computing ECE bins
Assuming a highly accurate model is also well-calibrated, instead of measuring calibration separately
questions.explanation: Accuracy and calibration are independent; a very accurate model can be badly calibrated and vice versa, so each needs its own measurement. The other options are recommended practices.

questions.question: A pass@10 evaluation samples exactly 10 completions per problem and scores 1.0 if any pass. What is the first problem?
options: The code computes pass@1, not pass@10, because 'any pass' over 10 samples is the per-sample rate c/n
The code double-counts problems with multiple passing samples, so scores can exceed 1.0 on easy problems where many of the samples pass
This is pass@10 with n = k = 10 — the biased, high-variance estimator; sampling a larger n and computing pass@10 analytically is more stable
The verifier is called on only the first of the 10 completions, so the other nine samples never affect the score reported for that problem
questions.explanation: With n = k each problem contributes a 0 or 1, giving a noisy average. Sampling, e.g., n = 100 and applying the unbiased estimator for k = 10 is far more stable. The 'any pass' indicator over 10 samples is pass@10, not pass@1.

questions.question: A team reports 'pass@1' using the same 'any of 10 samples passed' indicator they computed for pass@10. What is wrong and how should pass@1 be estimated?
options: Nothing is wrong; pass@1 and pass@10 are equal whenever n = 10, since both average over the same ten samples per problem
That indicator is pass@10 and massively overstates pass@1; pass@1 should be c/n, the fraction of individual samples that pass
The indicator is fine for pass@10, but pass@1 should be estimated as 1 − c/n, the fraction of individual samples that fail the tests
The indicator is fine for pass@10, but pass@1 should be estimated as (c/n)^10, the chance that all ten samples pass
questions.explanation: The probability that one of ten attempts works is far higher than the probability a single attempt works. With the estimator at k = 1, 1 − C(n−c,1)/C(n,1) = c/n, the fraction of passing samples.

questions.question: A web-trained model scores 92% on a public multiple-choice benchmark but 61% on a private set of freshly written questions of the same difficulty. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The private set is mislabeled: freshly written questions usually contain annotation errors, so 92% is the true ability and 61% is just label noise
Contamination: the public benchmark likely leaked into pretraining, so 92% partly reflects memorization and 61% is the more honest estimate
Miscalibration: the model is overconfident on the private set, and its overconfidence lowers accuracy on unfamiliar questions
The private set uses a different tokenizer and prompt template, which lowers accuracy, so the 31-point gap is a formatting artifact
questions.explanation: A large gap between public and fresh private questions of equal difficulty is the signature of contamination. The private, post-hoc set could not have been seen, so its score is the honest one; the 31-point gap is the inflation contamination bought.

questions.question: Model A is 85% accurate with ECE 0.20; model B is 80% accurate with ECE 0.02. Which is likely better for a system that abstains when confidence is low?
options: B, because the system acts on confidence and B's confidence is trustworthy, so it routes the right cases to a human
A, because higher accuracy always wins regardless of how the system uses confidence, and 5 points outweighs the ECE gap
A, because a higher ECE means the model is more confident overall, which makes its abstention decisions more decisive
Neither, because ECE measures average calibration and cannot be used to judge abstention decisions for a deployed system
questions.explanation: In an abstention system, decisions depend on confidence, so calibration is critical. A's confidence is off by about 20 points, so it will confidently emit wrong answers and abstain on the wrong cases. If confidence were never used, A's accuracy would win.

questions.question: You sample n = 4 completions and 0 pass. What is pass@k for any k ≤ 4 by the unbiased estimator?
options: 1/4 for every k, since each sample has an equal chance of passing
k/4, since drawing more samples raises the chance linearly in k
Undefined, because the estimator divides by c, which must be positive
0, since every size-k subset consists entirely of failing samples
questions.explanation: With c = 0, pass@k = 1 − C(n,k)/C(n,k) = 0. No selection of failing samples can contain a correct one, matching intuition. The formula is well-defined for c = 0.

questions.question: Why does process-based evaluation exist alongside exact-match grading for reasoning?
options: Exact match is too slow to run on large benchmarks, so process-based grading samples only a few steps per problem to save compute
Exact match requires human annotators to grade every problem, so process-based evaluation was introduced to automate grading
Exact match measures answer correctness under a fixed format, not reasoning quality, so a separate approach is needed to evaluate the steps
Exact match cannot be applied to math problems with numeric answers, so process-based grading checks each intermediate step's arithmetic instead
questions.explanation: Exact match scores only the final answer string, blind to the reasoning path, so invalid steps that reach the right number score fully. Process-based evaluation addresses reasoning quality directly.

questions.question: Why is an evaluation you cannot reproduce described as worse than none?
options: It produces numbers that drift between runs and lead you to false conclusions
It always takes longer to run than the training run it is meant to measure
It prevents the model from being checkpointed until the evaluation finishes cleanly
It forces you to retrain the tokenizer between experiments so the vocabularies match
questions.explanation: Research velocity is bounded by how quickly and reliably you can measure. A non-reproducible evaluation gives drifting numbers, so differences between experiments may be noise and you draw wrong conclusions. That is worse than having no number at all.

questions.question: What is the ML-project equivalent of a software project's test suite, according to the 'evaluation as a first-class discipline' view?
options: The training loop's gradient-clipping logic, which guards every update against bad batches and silent divergence
The data loader's shuffling routine, which guarantees every experiment sees the same examples in the same order
The checkpoint-saving code, which records every model state so that any experiment can be restored and rerun
The evaluation harness: the code that, given a model, produces the metrics decisions are made on
questions.explanation: Just as you would not ship code without tests, you should not make ML decisions without a harness that measures the model. It deserves production-code seriousness: documented interfaces, deterministic behavior, and its own tests.

questions.question: What does the evaluation harness return so its results can be logged, compared, and asserted on?
options: GPU tensors with autograd graphs
Raw logits for every scored token
Plain Python floats and indices
Matplotlib figures of the loss curve
questions.explanation: The harness orchestrates the forward pass and log_softmax over held-out data and returns plain floats (perplexity, log-likelihoods) and integer indices (chosen options). These are easy to log and assert on, unlike tensors carrying graphs.

questions.question: Which three properties make an evaluation harness trustworthy?
options: Fast (one pass per eval set), GPU-only (every metric computed on device), and distributed (sharded across ranks so results match)
Deterministic (same inputs give the same numbers), documented (shapes/dtype/device stated), and tested (metrics checked against known answers)
Stochastic (fresh samples each run to avoid overfitting), cached (results reused across runs), and approximate (subsampled eval sets)
Fine-tuned (the model adapted to each benchmark), calibrated (temperature-scaled logits), and decontaminated (overlaps removed first)
questions.explanation: A harness must be deterministic, documented, and tested; lose any one and its numbers become unreliable. Speed and hardware are conveniences, not trustworthiness properties.

questions.question: What are the inputs to evaluate_perplexity in the llmre harness?
options: A list of raw held-out strings, a tokenizer to encode them, a learning rate, and a number of evaluation epochs
A flat 1-D torch.long tensor of held-out token ids, a block_size, a batch_size, and an optional max_batches
A 2-D float tensor of precomputed logits of shape (N, V), a target tensor of shape (N,), and a temperature
A model checkpoint path, a vocabulary file, a block_size, and the device on which to load the weights to
questions.explanation: evaluate_perplexity takes the model, a flat long tensor data of held-out ids, the context length block_size, batch_size, and an optional max_batches to stop early on huge streams. Tokenization happens before.

questions.question: How does evaluate_perplexity form input and target for window i of length T?
options: x = data[i·T : i·T + T] and y = data[i·T + 1 : i·T + 1 + T], the same window shifted one token right
x = data[i·T : i·T + T] and y = data[i·T : i·T + T], the same window used as both input and target
x = data[i : i + T] and y = data[i + T], a sliding window that predicts one single next token per step
x and y are random overlapping windows of length T sampled fresh for each batch, as in the training loader
questions.explanation: Non-overlapping windows are cut from the stream, and the target is the input shifted by one, the standard next-token setup. Using the same slice for y is a bug that makes the task trivial.

questions.question: Why does evaluate_perplexity cut the stream into non-overlapping windows of length block_size?
options: Because overlapping windows would require gradient computation across windows, which no_grad forbids during evaluation
Because the model cannot accept sequences shorter than its vocabulary size, so every window must be exactly block_size
Because non-overlapping windows always give the lowest possible perplexity, which is the number papers conventionally report
So each held-out target token is scored once with a fixed context length, making the metric well-defined and reproducible
questions.explanation: Non-overlapping windows partition the stream so each target token is counted once under a defined block_size. Overlap would double-count tokens; gradients are irrelevant here. Lower perplexity is not the goal — consistency is.

questions.question: How does evaluate_perplexity aggregate per-batch losses?
options: Average the per-batch mean losses directly, giving each batch equal weight whatever its size, then exponentiate the result
Take the minimum batch loss across all batches as the most reliable estimate, then exponentiate it to get perplexity
Token-weighted: multiply each batch's mean loss by its token count, sum, and divide by total tokens, then exponentiate
Exponentiate each batch's mean loss into a perplexity first, then average the per-batch perplexities weighted by token count
questions.explanation: Accumulating float(loss) * n_tok and dividing by total_tokens gives exactly the mean over all target tokens, independent of how windows divide into batches. Averaging batch means over-weights a small final batch; averaging per-batch perplexities is also not the same as exp of the mean loss.

questions.question: Why does evaluation run under torch.no_grad() with the model in eval() mode?
options: no_grad enables dropout for regularization during scoring; eval() turns on gradient checkpointing to save activation memory
no_grad converts the weights to fp16 so evaluation runs faster; eval() freezes the tokenizer so token ids cannot change
no_grad builds no autograd graph, saving memory and time; eval() disables dropout so the numbers are deterministic
Both are required for the loss to be computed in nats rather than bits, since training mode uses a base-2 cross-entropy
questions.explanation: torch.no_grad() stops recording operations for backprop, so no graph or saved activations are retained. model.eval() switches dropout (and batch-norm, if present) to inference behavior so an input always yields the same logits. Neither changes units or precision.

questions.question: What does model.eval() change for a GPT with dropout?
options: It stops gradients from being computed for every forward pass
It disables dropout so a given input always produces the same logits
It freezes the weights so that the optimizer can no longer change any of them
It switches the model to half precision for faster inference
questions.explanation: eval() flips modules like dropout and batch-norm into inference behavior; for the GPT it disables dropout, giving deterministic outputs. Gradient tracking is controlled by no_grad, not eval(), and eval() does not touch precision or the optimizer.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the separate roles of model.eval() and torch.no_grad() in evaluation?
options: eval() is required for determinism and no_grad() for memory; forgetting either does not change the correctness of a single deterministic pass
eval() is required for memory and no_grad() for determinism; forgetting either changes the value that a single deterministic pass computes
Both are required for correctness, because without them the cross-entropy is computed on dropped-out logits and so the loss value itself is wrong
Only one is needed, because eval() automatically disables gradient tracking, so wrapping evaluation in no_grad() as well is redundant
questions.explanation: eval() removes dropout randomness; no_grad() avoids retaining the graph. Neither changes the mathematical value of one deterministic pass. eval() does not disable gradient tracking, so both are needed.

questions.question: In evaluate_perplexity, how is the number of windows computed from a stream of data.numel() tokens?
options: data.numel() // block_size, using every token as an input, with the very last target wrapping around
data.numel() - block_size, giving one overlapping window per possible starting position
(data.numel() + 1) // block_size, rounding up so the final partial window is included
(data.numel() - 1) // block_size, since each window needs one extra token for the shifted target
questions.explanation: Each window needs block_size inputs plus one more token for the last target, so the last token can only be a target; hence (numel − 1) // block_size non-overlapping windows. One window per start position would mean overlapping windows.

questions.question: In evaluate_perplexity, why would averaging per-batch losses directly give a wrong answer?
options: It under-weights the first batch, whose loss is inflated by warmup, so the mean comes out too low
It double-counts tokens that appear in several overlapping windows, inflating their weight in the overall average
It converts nats to bits incorrectly, because a mean of per-batch means is taken in base 2 instead of base e
It over-weights a small final batch, whereas token weighting reproduces the single mean over all target tokens
questions.explanation: Each batch loss is already a mean over its tokens, so a mean of means gives every batch equal weight regardless of size. Weighting by token count makes the result independent of batching.

questions.question: What does sequence_loglikelihood(model, ids) compute?
options: The perplexity of the sequence averaged over sliding windows of block_size tokens with stride 1
The probability of the sequence's first token only, given a beginning-of-sequence token in front
The total log-probability Σ_t ln q(x_t | x_<t) over the sequence, from a single forward pass
The entropy of the model's next-token distribution at the last position, from a single forward pass
