questions.explanation: It sums the conditional log-probabilities of tokens 1 … L−1 given their prefixes. One forward pass suffices because the logits at position t are the model's prediction for token t+1.

questions.question: In sequence_loglikelihood, why are logits[:-1] paired with ids[1:]?
options: The first logit is always padding from the beginning-of-sequence slot, so it must be dropped before pairing with the targets
The last position would predict a token past the end, and ids[1:] are exactly the tokens predicted by positions 0 … L−2
ids[1:] removes the end-of-sequence token, which the model never has to predict, and logits[:-1] drops its matching row
It reverses the sequence so that the model reads right to left, which is how causal attention lines up logits with targets
questions.explanation: Logits at position p predict token p+1, so dropping the final position and the first target aligns predictions with what they predict. This index arithmetic is the whole trick.

questions.question: Why is the first token of a sequence never scored by sequence_loglikelihood under a plain LM?
options: It has no prefix, so there is no conditional ln q(x_0 | x_<0) to score
The first token is always a special BOS token with probability 1
Scoring it would require a second forward pass with a dummy prefix token
The first logit is discarded for numerical stability inside log_softmax
questions.explanation: The score of each token is its probability given preceding tokens; the first token has none. The code enforces this by predicting tokens 1 … L−1 from positions 0 … L−2.

questions.question: What does the value returned by sequence_loglikelihood mean?
options: A single Python float ≤ 0; less negative means the model finds the sequence more probable
A positive Python float where larger values mean the model finds the sequence less probable
A tensor of shape (L, V) holding the model's log-probabilities at every position
A perplexity value ≥ 1, the exponential of the mean negative log-likelihood per token
questions.explanation: It returns float(chosen.sum()), the sum of log-probabilities, which is at most 0. A value closer to 0 means higher probability. It is not perplexity and is not a tensor.

questions.question: In sequence_loglikelihood with ids of shape (L,), what are the shapes of logits after taking batch element 0, of logp, and of chosen?
options: logits (1, L); logp (L, V); chosen (L,)
logits (V, L); logp (V, L−1); chosen (V, L−1)
logits (L, V); logp (L, V); chosen (1,)
logits (L, V); logp (L−1, V); chosen (L−1,)
questions.explanation: The model returns (1, L, V); indexing [0] gives (L, V). log_softmax(logits[:-1]) is (L−1, V), and gathering the target token per row gives chosen of shape (L−1,), which is then summed.

questions.question: Where do the option tokens sit in [context; option], and which logits predict them, in multiple_choice_score?
options: At positions 0 … L_o − 1, at the front of the sequence, predicted by logits at those same positions 0 … L_o − 1
At positions L_c + 1 … L_c + L_o, after a separator token, predicted by logits at positions L_c … L_c + L_o − 1
At absolute positions L_c … L_c + L_o − 1, predicted by logits at positions L_c − 1 … L_c + L_o − 2
At absolute positions L_c … L_c + L_o − 1, predicted by logits at those same positions L_c … L_c + L_o − 1
questions.explanation: Option tokens follow the L_c context tokens, and since logits at p predict token p+1, they are predicted by positions one earlier. This is the §3 index arithmetic offset by the context length.

questions.question: How does multiple_choice_score handle zero-shot versus few-shot evaluation?
options: It requires a separate few_shot flag that enables a second forward pass over the demonstrations
Identically; the number of in-context examples only changes how many tokens are in context_ids
It scores the demonstrations as additional options in few-shot mode and drops them from the argmax
It only supports zero-shot scoring; few-shot evaluation needs a model fine-tuned on the examples
questions.explanation: Because it accepts any model(seq) -> (logits, loss) and any context, demonstrations are simply more context tokens. The scoring logic does not change.

questions.section: 5. Reproducibility: seeds, fixed eval set, versioned config
questions.question: Why must every source of randomness be seeded before an evaluation that uses any?
options: Perplexity computed in eval() mode changes from run to run unless the global seed is fixed before each run
Anything involving sampling, such as generating completions for pass@k, is only reproducible if seeded
Seeds control the learning rate and warmup schedule used during evaluation, so unseeded runs differ
Seeding is needed to make torch.no_grad() take effect, since the graph is otherwise built at random
questions.explanation: Perplexity and log-likelihood scoring are deterministic in eval() mode, but sampling-based evaluation is not; seeding torch, NumPy, and Python makes it reproducible. Seeds do not affect no_grad or learning rates.

questions.section: 5. Reproducibility: seeds, fixed eval set, versioned config
questions.question: Why must the held-out stream and benchmark question set be frozen and versioned?
options: Comparing run B with run A is only valid if both were measured on the same data; changing the eval set silently turns comparison into noise
Because the model memorizes whatever eval set it is shown, so any change to the set leaks new answers into the weights over successive runs
Because unfrozen eval sets cannot be tokenized consistently, since the BPE merges are refit from scratch whenever the underlying text changes
Because versioned data is stored contiguously on disk and runs faster on GPUs, which keeps evaluation cheap enough to run after every step
questions.explanation: A comparison between experiments is meaningful only on identical evaluation data. Altering the data changes the numbers for reasons unrelated to the models.

questions.section: 5. Reproducibility: seeds, fixed eval set, versioned config
questions.question: Which items belong in a versioned evaluation config stored next to each result?
options: Only the final metric value and the date it was computed, since the code in the repository at that date fully determines everything else
Only the model's parameter count, the GPU type, and the driver version, since the hardware is what makes evaluation numbers drift
Only the random seed used for the run, since with the seed fixed every other part of the evaluation is fully deterministic and needs no record
Checkpoint hash, tokenizer version, block_size, batch_size, eval-set version/hash, scoring rule, few-shot count, and library versions
questions.explanation: Everything that can affect the number must be recorded so it can be regenerated months later: checkpoint, tokenizer, block/batch sizes, eval-set version, scoring rule (summed vs normalized), shot count, and library versions.

questions.section: 5. Reproducibility: seeds, fixed eval set, versioned config
questions.question: What is the most common silent reproducibility bug in evaluation?
options: Running evaluation on CPU instead of GPU, so fused kernels change the low-order bits and every reported metric shifts slightly between machines
Logging metrics as floats instead of strings, so rounding in the experiment tracker silently changes the third decimal place of every logged metric
Comparing two numbers produced under different settings, e.g. another block_size, normalization, decontaminated vs raw eval set, or tokenizer
Evaluating more often than once per epoch, so the held-out set is seen many times and slowly leaks into the model through checkpoint selection
questions.explanation: Numbers computed under different settings look comparable but are not. Logging the full config with every metric makes such mismatches visible. Hardware choice does not change a deterministic metric meaningfully.

questions.section: 6. Regression testing: lock the metrics in
questions.question: What is an evaluation regression test?
options: A linear regression fit of validation loss against training steps, used to predict when the metric will stop improving
A test that reruns a short training job from a fixed seed and checks that the training loss still decreases as it did before the change
A test that pins a metric to a known value or known-answer synthetic case, so a refactor that changes the number fails loudly
A benchmark run comparing the current model against the previous model release, failing if the new score is any lower
questions.explanation: Like regression tests in software, it catches changes that quietly break behavior: if a refactor shifts the metric on a known-answer case, the test fails before the wrong number reaches an experiment.

questions.section: 6. Regression testing: lock the metrics in
questions.question: What does the uniform-model regression test assert about evaluate_perplexity?
options: A model returning all-zero logits over V tokens must give a held-out perplexity of exactly 1
A model returning all-zero logits over V tokens must give held-out perplexity exactly V
A uniform model over V tokens must give held-out perplexity ln V, the uniform cross-entropy
A uniform model must give perplexity 0, because all-zero logits carry no signal about the data
questions.explanation: All-zero logits produce a uniform softmax with probability 1/V per token, so cross-entropy is ln V and perplexity exp(ln V) = V. evaluate_perplexity(UniformModel(V), data, block_size=16) must return V.

questions.section: 6. Regression testing: lock the metrics in
questions.question: How do the constructed-logits tests pin the behavior of multiple_choice_score?
options: A model putting a large logit on one token must make the scorer pick the option built from that token, and swapping options must flip the answer
A model with random logits must make the scorer pick option 0 more than half the time, and adding a third option must not change the winner
A model with all-zero logits must make the scorer pick the longest option, and turning on length normalization must make it pick the shortest one instead
The scorer must return the same answer index regardless of option order, and a model with constant logits must always pick the first option
questions.explanation: By constructing a model whose preference is known, the test asserts the scorer picks the favored option and that reordering the options flips the returned index, pinning the scoring logic.

questions.section: 6. Regression testing: lock the metrics in
questions.question: What does the length-normalization regression test in test_eval.py check?
options: That length normalization never changes the chosen option when the per-token confidences of the two options are known in advance
That the normalized rule always picks the shortest option, while the summed rule picks whichever option contains the most confident single token
That normalization makes every option's score positive, so the argmax over options is well defined even for very long options
With two known per-token confidences, the summed rule picks the short option and the normalized rule picks the longer, higher-confidence one
questions.explanation: The test reproduces the summed-vs-normalized flip: the sum favors the short option, normalization favors the longer option whose tokens are each more probable. This locks in the normalization behavior.

questions.section: 6. Regression testing: lock the metrics in
questions.question: What makes a good known-answer test for an evaluation harness?
options: Inputs drawn from the real benchmark, with the expected answers recorded from the current harness output so that any later change in the number is caught
Inputs chosen randomly on each run to cover more cases over time, with the expected metric recomputed by the harness on every single run
Inputs that produce the largest possible metric values, e.g. a model that is always confidently wrong, so overflow and edge cases get exercised
Inputs whose correct metric you can compute by hand, e.g. uniform model gives perplexity V, or all-wrong predictions at confidence 0.9 give ECE 0.9
questions.explanation: Known-answer tests compare the harness to values derived independently by hand, so any deviation reveals a bug. Snapshotting the current harness output would lock in existing bugs, and random inputs are not reproducible.

questions.section: 7. Running the harness on a tiny trained model
questions.question: In the tiny-GPT harness demonstration, why is the model trained on the repeating stream 0, 1, 2, …, V−1, 0, 1, …?
options: Because it is effectively random noise to the model, so its perplexity should stay at about V however long it trains
Because it exercises the tokenizer's merge rules on a stream whose byte pairs repeat in a known, countable order
Because its next token is fully learnable, so a few dozen steps suffice to drive perplexity well below V
Because it maximizes the number of distinct n-grams in the stream, so the held-out windows never overlap with training
questions.explanation: The pattern is deterministic: every token determines the next. A 2-layer GPT learns it in a few dozen steps, demonstrating the harness on a real model with a predictable outcome.

questions.section: 7. Running the harness on a tiny trained model
questions.question: What does the tiny-GPT demonstration show before and after a few dozen training steps?
options: Before, perplexity is about 1 because the model is untrained; after, it rises toward V = 16 as the scorer learns to prefer option 11
Before, perplexity is about V = 16; after, it drops well below V and the scorer prefers the true continuation 5 over 11 after context [0,1,2,3,4]
Before and after, perplexity stays at about V = 16, because the tiny model is too small to learn the pattern in a few dozen steps
After training, perplexity drops well below V, but the scorer prefers option 11 over 5 after context [0,1,2,3,4] because 11 has the higher token id
questions.explanation: An untrained model is near uniform (perplexity ≈ V). After learning the pattern, perplexity falls well below 16, and multiple_choice_score returns 0, choosing token 5 as the continuation of 0,1,2,3,4.

questions.section: 7. Running the harness on a tiny trained model
questions.question: Why does the tiny-GPT demonstration call torch.manual_seed(0) and set dropout=0.0?
options: To make initialization and training sampling reproducible and to remove dropout randomness, so the test is deterministic
To speed up training by skipping random initialization of the weights and removing the dropout masks from every forward pass
Because GPTConfig requires a seed of 0 and dropout of 0.0 whenever it is used to build a model on a CPU-only machine
Because dropout must be 0 for perplexity to be finite, and seeding is what makes the uniform-model test hit exactly V
questions.explanation: Fixing the seed makes the random initialization and randomly sampled training windows identical every run; dropout 0 removes stochasticity from the forward pass. Together they make the test reproducible.

questions.section: 7. Running the harness on a tiny trained model
questions.question: What does the full tiny-GPT test assert?
options: That perplexity is finite and positive and that the correct option wins
That held-out perplexity equals exactly 1 after a few dozen training steps
That training loss falls below 0.01 nats and the scorer picks option 0
That the model generates the full pattern from an empty prompt
questions.explanation: Exact post-training perplexity is not pinned; the test asserts it is finite and positive and that multiple_choice_score picks the true continuation. It runs in under a second on CPU.

questions.question: What hardware is needed for the evaluation-harness lesson and its tests?
options: At least one 24 GB GPU, since evaluation keeps the optimizer state and saved activations of the full model in memory
A multi-GPU node, because the token-weighted perplexity requires a distributed all-reduce across at least two ranks
A TPU or TPU emulator, because the harness relies on XLA-specific operations for its log_softmax and gather steps
Any CPU is fully sufficient; a GPU only helps when evaluating a full-size model over millions of held-out tokens
questions.explanation: The harness is inference-only and the toy example finishes in well under a second on CPU. On a real corpus with a full-size model it becomes a batched inference job where a GPU helps. No optimizer state is needed.

questions.question: Why does evaluation under torch.no_grad() use far less GPU memory than a training step?
options: The model weights are automatically quantized to 4 bits inside no_grad
Only the first layer of the model is executed when no autograd graph is recorded
There is no optimizer state and no saved activations for a backward pass
The batch size is forced to 1 and the sequence length to the block size
questions.explanation: Training memory includes optimizer state, gradients, and activations saved for backward. Evaluation under no_grad needs only the weights and the transient activations of the forward pass.

questions.question: A teammate changes evaluate_perplexity to average per-batch losses directly. Batch A has mean 2.0 over 800 tokens and batch B mean 4.0 over 8 tokens. What are the token-weighted and mean-of-means losses?
options: Both equal 3.0, since each batch's mean loss is already token-weighted, so the change is harmless
Token-weighted ≈ 2.02; mean-of-means = 3.0, badly off because the tiny batch gets equal weight
Token-weighted = 3.0; mean-of-means ≈ 2.02, because the mean-of-means favors the large batch
Token-weighted = 4.0; mean-of-means = 2.0, because weighting by tokens favors the higher loss
questions.explanation: Token-weighted: (2.0·800 + 4.0·8)/808 = 1632/808 ≈ 2.02. Mean of means: (2.0 + 4.0)/2 = 3.0. The two agree only when all batches have equal token counts, which fails when the last batch is smaller.

questions.question: What happens if an evaluation runs without model.eval()?
options: Gradients are computed and the optimizer then updates the model's weights after every single evaluation batch
Dropout stays active, so the same input gives different logits each run and the metric is non-deterministic
The loss is reported in bits instead of nats, so the perplexity comes out lower by a factor of ln 2
The model cannot accept target tokens in training mode, so the forward call raises an error at once
questions.explanation: Without eval(), dropout randomly zeroes activations during evaluation, making results vary run to run. It does not update weights — that requires an optimizer step.

questions.question: What happens if an evaluation runs without torch.no_grad()?
options: The values are still correct for one pass, but PyTorch retains the computation graph and evaluation can run out of memory on a real model
The metric becomes non-deterministic, because leaving no_grad off keeps dropout enabled and PyTorch samples new masks each pass
The model's weights are updated during evaluation, because autograd applies the stored gradients to the parameters at the end of every forward
The loss becomes negative, because the retained graph adds the gradient of each token's log-probability back into the value
questions.explanation: Without no_grad, autograd records operations and keeps activations for a backward pass that never comes, inflating memory. Dropout is controlled by eval(), not no_grad.

questions.question: Why is the lack of a regression test on the evaluation harness a common mistake?
options: Without tests the harness runs slower, because results are never cached
Regression tests are required to compute perplexity in the first place
Without tests the harness cannot load checkpoints from older versions
A refactor can silently change the number and you keep trusting it
questions.explanation: Without pinned known-answer tests, a code change that alters a metric goes unnoticed, and wrong numbers flow into experiments. Tests do not affect speed or functionality.

questions.question: An evaluate_perplexity variant returns a far-too-low perplexity. Its targets are ys = data[i*block_size : i*block_size + block_size], the same slice as the inputs. What is wrong?
options: The inputs should be shifted left by one instead of the targets, so the model sees future tokens and predicts the past ones
The block_size is too small for the model, so most positions have almost no context and the loss is clipped toward zero
The targets are not shifted by one, so each position is asked to predict its own input token, making the task trivial
The model is in eval() mode, which turns off dropout and makes held-out loss artificially lower than the true training loss
questions.explanation: Targets must be data[i*block_size + 1 : i*block_size + 1 + block_size]. With unshifted targets the model can read the answer directly, so loss goes near zero and perplexity far too low. eval() mode does not lower loss artificially.

questions.question: Besides the unshifted targets, what smaller second bug is in that faulty evaluate_perplexity variant that appends float(loss) to a list and returns exp(sum(losses)/len(losses))?
options: It exponentiates in base 2 instead of base e, so the perplexity is reported in bits per token
It forgets to call model.eval(), so dropout makes every batch's loss slightly too low on average
The mean of per-batch means is not token-weighted, so a smaller final batch is over-weighted
It omits the torch.no_grad() decorator, so the retained graph adds memory and lowers the loss value
questions.explanation: Averaging batch means gives each batch equal weight regardless of its token count, biasing the result whenever batches are unequal. The variant does call model.eval() and is decorated with torch.no_grad().

questions.question: What is the combined effect of omitting torch.no_grad() and model.eval() from an evaluation harness?
options: Omitting either makes every reported number mathematically wrong, since dropout and the retained graph both change the cross-entropy that is computed
Omitting no_grad risks out-of-memory; omitting eval leaves dropout on and the metric non-deterministic; neither changes one deterministic pass
Omitting no_grad makes results non-deterministic because autograd reorders reductions; omitting eval causes out-of-memory from dropout masks
Neither matters for language models, because GPT-style transformers have no dropout or batch-norm layers and never build a graph at eval time
questions.explanation: no_grad is about memory, eval about determinism. Both are needed for a correct, reproducible, memory-efficient harness, though neither changes the value of one deterministic forward pass. GPTs typically do have dropout.

questions.question: Why is the uniform-model perplexity test a good known-answer case?
options: Its correct value is derivable by hand — cross-entropy ln V, perplexity V — independent of the data or the harness's batching
Because uniform models are what production systems deploy as a safe fallback, so the test mirrors real serving conditions closely
Because it produces the lowest possible perplexity, so any harness bug can only show up as a higher, failing number
Because it requires a trained model, so the same test also checks that the training loop converges to the uniform answer on held-out data
questions.explanation: A uniform distribution gives exactly ln V nats per token on any data, so perplexity must be V regardless of batching. Any deviation exposes a bug such as a bad shift or wrong aggregation. No training is needed.

questions.question: The same model gives perplexity 18.4 with block_size 512 and 21.7 with block_size 128. Can you conclude the first setting is better?
options: Yes — lower perplexity on the same held-out stream always means the better setting, whatever block_size each run happened to use
Yes — but only if both runs used the same batch_size, since batch size is what changes the token weighting of the mean perplexity
No — perplexity is undefined for block_size above 256, so the 18.4 figure must have come from a truncated or otherwise broken evaluation run
No — a longer block_size gives most positions more context, generally lowering perplexity whatever the quality; the configs are not comparable
questions.explanation: Perplexity depends on how much preceding context each position has; longer windows lower it mechanically. To compare fairly, fix block_size and every other setting, which is why the config is versioned with the metric.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: In supervised fine-tuning of a language model, what is a chat template?
options: A fixed, deterministic rule that flattens a list of role-tagged messages into one delimited token string
A learned embedding layer that converts each conversation role into a separate vector before the first attention block
A sampling strategy that decides how many tokens the assistant may generate in each turn
A dataset filter that removes low-quality conversations before fine-tuning begins
questions.explanation: A chat template is the exact, deterministic serialization rule that turns a list of role-tagged messages into a single string with delimiter tokens. It is not learned and has no parameters; it is the interface between a conversation and a sequence of token ids. Because it is fixed, the model can learn where the assistant turn begins and when to stop.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Which post-training stages operate on chat-formatted data?
options: Only SFT; reward modeling and DPO operate on raw pretraining documents
Only RLHF, because it is the only stage that samples from the model
None of them; chat formatting is applied only at inference time
SFT, reward modeling, RLHF and DPO all operate on chat-formatted data
questions.explanation: Everything after pretraining — SFT, reward modeling, RLHF, DPO — consumes chat-formatted data. That is why the chat template is the foundational interface of post-training. Formatting applied only at inference would mismatch the training distribution.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: What is the typical symptom when the chat template used at inference is inconsistent with the one used in fine-tuning?
options: The tokenizer raises an exception, because the new delimiters are missing from its vocabulary
The loss becomes NaN on the first inference step, so generation outputs only padding tokens afterwards
The model silently degrades, often never seeing the stop delimiter it learned and rambling on
The model refuses to answer and returns an empty string for every prompt it is given
questions.explanation: Template mismatch does not crash anything; the model is simply off-distribution. A typical outcome is that it never sees or emits the delimiter it was trained to stop on, so it keeps generating. The failure is silent, which makes it dangerous.

questions.question: What was the only training objective of a pretrained GPT-2-style model?
options: Predict a helpful response to a user request given a system prompt
Predict the next token given the tokens so far, via cross-entropy loss
Classify whether each document is high- or low-quality web text
Reconstruct randomly masked tokens anywhere in the sequence
questions.explanation: Pretraining optimizes next-token cross-entropy: given the prefix, predict the next token. Trained on a large text pile, the model becomes very good at continuing text. It never sees an objective about answering requests, and GPT-style models are causal, not masked-token models.

questions.question: Why might a purely pretrained model continue the prompt 'Write a haiku about the sea.' with 'Write a haiku about the mountains.'?
options: Because the model's context window is too short to hold a full haiku, so it restarts the prompt from scratch
Because in web text, a line that looks like a writing prompt is most often followed by another prompt in a list
Because pretraining loss was computed only on the prompt tokens, never on the answers that follow them in web text
Because the model has a bug in its sampling loop that copies the input back to the output with one word changed
questions.explanation: The pretrained model models text continuation. In its corpus, lines like 'Write a haiku about X' usually appear in lists of writing prompts, so the most probable continuation is another prompt. The model is doing its job perfectly; its job just is not following instructions.

questions.question: What does a pretrained language model fundamentally model, as opposed to an instruction-tuned one?
options: What tokens plausibly come next in a document like the given text
What answer best fulfils the user's request
Which of several candidate responses a human would prefer
Which role (system, user, or assistant) is speaking at each position
questions.explanation: A pretrained LM models text continuation — what plausibly comes next in a document like this one. Nothing in pretraining tells it a prompt is a request to fulfil. Preferences are learned later (reward modeling/DPO), and roles only exist once chat templates are introduced in SFT.

questions.question: How does supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teach a pretrained model to follow instructions?
options: By adding a new classification head that detects instructions in the prompt
By training a reward model and then optimizing against it with PPO
By freezing the model and only editing its tokenizer vocabulary
By continuing training on curated (prompt, ideal response) pairs
questions.explanation: SFT continues training on demonstrations: curated pairs of a prompt and the ideal response. After enough of these, the plausible continuation of a request becomes a helpful answer. Reward models and PPO belong to RLHF, a later stage.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: SFT is just more next-token training, on different data
questions.question: Relative to pretraining, what does SFT change about the model architecture and loss function?
options: It adds a response head and switches to a ranking loss
It keeps the architecture but replaces cross-entropy with a mean-squared error
Neither; it uses the same architecture and the same next-token cross-entropy
It changes the architecture to an encoder-decoder but keeps cross-entropy
questions.explanation: SFT is just more next-token training: same architecture, same cross-entropy loss. What changes is the data (demonstrations of desired behavior) and where the loss is applied (response tokens only). That simplicity is why SFT is the cheapest post-training step.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: SFT is just more next-token training, on different data
questions.question: Which two things change when moving from pretraining to SFT?
options: The optimizer (SGD instead of AdamW) and the tokenizer (word-level instead of byte-level BPE)
The model depth (extra layers for the response) and the attention mechanism (bidirectional)
The training data (demonstrations) and which positions the loss is applied to (response only)
The learning-rate schedule (constant instead of cosine) and the vocabulary size (chat tokens only)
questions.explanation: SFT swaps raw documents for demonstrations of the target behavior, and it scores only the response tokens, not the prompt. Architecture, optimizer family, and tokenizer are unchanged. These two changes are what make the continuation of a request become a helpful answer.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: SFT is just more next-token training, on different data
questions.question: In the post-training pipeline, what is SFT shaping, given what pretraining already installed?
options: Knowledge, replacing the behavior pretraining installed
Behavior, on top of the knowledge pretraining already installed
Tokenization, on top of the embeddings pretraining installed
Model capacity, by adding parameters that pretraining did not have
questions.explanation: Post-training (SFT, reward modeling, RLHF/DPO) is about shaping behavior on top of the knowledge that pretraining already put in the weights. SFT is the first and cheapest of these steps. It does not add capacity or replace knowledge.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: SFT is just more next-token training, on different data
questions.question: Which is the order of the standard post-training pipeline?
options: SFT, then reward model, then RLHF/DPO
Reward model, then SFT, then pretraining
RLHF, then SFT, then reward model
DPO, then pretraining, then SFT
questions.explanation: The standard pipeline runs SFT first (cheapest, imitation of demonstrations), then trains a reward model, then optimizes behavior with RLHF or DPO. Pretraining comes before all of them. SFT is described as the first and cheapest step.

questions.question: What are the three fields of the classic FLAN/Alpaca instruction-tuning example?
options: system, user, assistant
question, context, and label
prompt, chosen, rejected
instruction, input, output
questions.explanation: The classic shape is (instruction, [input], output): what to do, optionally what to do it to, and the demonstrated ideal response. 'system/user/assistant' are chat roles, and 'prompt/chosen/rejected' is the preference-data format used later for reward modeling and DPO.

questions.question: In an (instruction, [input], output) triple, which field is optional?
options: instruction
output
none; all three are always required
input
questions.explanation: The input is optional: some instructions are self-contained, such as 'Write a haiku about the sea.' The instruction and output are always needed, since the output is what the model is trained to produce.

questions.question: In an instruction triple, which fields together form the prompt, and which is the training target?
options: Instruction alone is the prompt; input plus output together form the target the model is trained on
Input alone is the prompt; instruction plus output together form the target the model must produce
Instruction plus input form the prompt; output is what the model is trained to produce
All three fields are concatenated, and every token of all three is scored equally as the target
questions.explanation: The instruction and optional input together form the prompt, and the output is the demonstrated response the model learns to produce. Scoring the prompt as a target would teach the model to generate instructions, which SFT avoids by masking.

questions.question: For the triple instruction='Translate the sentence to French.', input='The cat sat on the mat.', what role does 'Le chat s'est assis sur le tapis.' play?
options: The input: the data that the instruction acts on
The output: the demonstrated ideal response
The system message: persistent behavior
The instruction: what to do
questions.explanation: The French sentence is the output field — the demonstrated ideal response. The English sentence is the input (the thing to act on) and 'Translate the sentence to French.' is the instruction. The triple format has no system field.

questions.question: How was the FLAN instruction dataset (Wei et al. 2021) built?
options: By rewriting existing NLP datasets as natural-language instructions using many phrasing templates
By having a strong LM generate new instruction triples from a handful of human-written seed examples
By collecting human preference rankings between pairs of model responses to the same instruction
By scraping question-answer forums and keeping only the accepted or most upvoted answer per thread
questions.explanation: FLAN took existing NLP datasets (translation, summarization, QA, sentiment, ...) and rephrased each as natural-language instructions with many templates. Generating triples from seeds with an LM is Self-Instruct; preference rankings are reward-modeling data.

questions.question: What generalization result motivates FLAN-style instruction tuning?
options: Fine-tuning on a mixture of instruction-phrased tasks lets the model follow unseen instructions zero-shot
Fine-tuning on one task makes the model better only at that exact task, so each task needs its own run
Fine-tuning on instructions removes the need for pretraining, since instructions carry the needed knowledge
Fine-tuning on instructions makes the model's tokenizer more compact, so unseen prompts use fewer tokens
questions.explanation: FLAN showed that training on a mixture of many tasks phrased as instructions makes the model generalize to instructions it has never seen, zero-shot. It builds on pretraining rather than replacing it, and has nothing to do with tokenizer size.

questions.question: How does Self-Instruct (Wang et al. 2022) create instruction data?
options: Rewrite existing labelled NLP datasets into instruction form with many phrasing templates, then train on the whole mixture
Hire annotators to write every instruction-response pair by hand, then have a second annotator verify each one
Sample many responses from the model and keep those a learned reward model scores highest, then train on them
Seed a few human-written examples, have a strong LM generate many more triples, filter for quality, and train on them
questions.explanation: Self-Instruct bootstraps: start from a small set of human seeds, have a strong LM generate many (instruction, input, output) triples, filter for quality, and fine-tune on the result. This avoids hand-writing every example. Template rewriting of existing datasets is FLAN's approach.

questions.question: Which well-known instruction dataset was built with the Self-Instruct recipe?
options: FLAN
The GPT-2 WebText corpus
Alpaca
Common Crawl
questions.explanation: Alpaca used the Self-Instruct recipe: LM-generated instruction triples bootstrapped from seeds. FLAN rewrote existing NLP datasets, and WebText/Common Crawl are pretraining corpora, not instruction data.

questions.question: When reading the FLAN and Self-Instruct papers for SFT, which parts are recommended to read closely versus skip?
options: Read the per-task appendices closely for the templates; skip the data-construction sections on a first pass
Read the data-construction sections closely; skip the long per-task appendices on a first pass
Read only the abstracts and related-work sections, then go straight to the released datasets and code
Skip both papers entirely on a first pass; they are optional background for anyone doing SFT in practice
questions.explanation: Both are core Module 14 readings. The data-construction sections carry the key ideas — instructions as a training distribution and how to generate it cheaply — while the long per-task appendices can be skipped at first.

questions.question: How can a single-turn (instruction, input, output) triple be represented as a chat?
options: As a three-message chat: a system message (instruction), a user message (input), an assistant message (output)
As a two-message chat: a user message (instruction + input) and an assistant message (output)
As a single user message containing all three fields, with the output kept as an unscored suffix
As a single assistant message containing all three fields, so every token is trained as a response
questions.explanation: A single-turn triple is just a user message holding the instruction and input, followed by an assistant message holding the output. A system message is a separate, optional element that sets persistent behavior; it is not where the instruction goes.

questions.question: In multi-turn chat data, what is the purpose of a system message?
options: To set persistent behavior for the conversation, such as 'You are a terse assistant.'
To mark the end of every turn, so the model knows when it should stop generating
To hold the model's demonstrated responses, which are the tokens scored in training
To store the user's previous conversation history once it no longer fits in context
questions.explanation: The system message sets persistent behavior that applies across the conversation, e.g. 'You are a terse assistant.' Ending turns is the job of the end delimiter, and responses live in assistant messages. The general object to format is therefore a list of role-tagged messages.

questions.question: Why is a chat template needed at all before a conversation can be fed to a language model?
options: Because the model needs each role encoded as a separate input tensor alongside the token ids
Because tokenizers cannot handle newline characters, so turns must be joined with special tokens
Because attention requires every turn to be padded to the same length before it can be batched
Because the model consumes a flat sequence of token ids, not a list of role-tagged dicts
questions.explanation: The model eats one flat sequence of token ids. A list of message dicts must therefore be serialized into one string, with delimiters marking turn boundaries and roles. There is no separate role tensor; the role information lives in the delimiter tokens.

questions.question: In a chat template, what is the load-bearing role of the special delimiter tokens?
options: They compress the conversation so that long multi-turn chats fit inside the context window
They tell the tokenizer which language each turn is written in, so it picks the right merges
They are the only signal the model has for a new turn, who is speaking, and when the turn is over
They carry the positional encoding for each turn, so that the model can tell how far back each turn is
questions.explanation: Delimiters are the only signal for 'a new turn started', 'this is the assistant speaking', and crucially 'the turn is over, stop generating'. Without them the model could not distinguish roles or learn to stop. They do not compress text or carry positions.

questions.question: In the course's chat template, which four delimiter tokens are used?
options: <|im_start|>, <|im_end|>, [INST] and [/INST]
<bos>, <eos>, <pad> and <unk>
<|system|>, <|user|>, <|assistant|> and <|end|>
<|system|>, <|user|>, <|assistant|> and <|pad|>, with <|pad|> closing turns
questions.explanation: The template uses three role headers (<|system|>, <|user|>, <|assistant|>) that open a turn and one end-of-turn token <|end|> that closes it. <|im_start|>/<|im_end|> and [INST]/[/INST] are other model families' delimiters.

questions.question: In the course's chat template, how is one message rendered?
options: The content first, then the role header after it, then a newline
Role header, a newline, the content, then <|end|> and a newline
Role header, then the content on the same line, a newline, and no end token
<|end|> first to close the previous turn, then the role header, the content, a newline
questions.explanation: Each message becomes: its role header, a newline, its content, then <|end|> and a newline. Messages are concatenated. For example: '<|user|>\nCapital of France?<|end|>\n'.

questions.question: Why must chat delimiter tokens like <|end|> be treated as atomic by the tokenizer?
options: So each is exactly one id and is never split into pieces like '<', '|', 'end'
So they are always mapped to the padding id and ignored by attention and the loss
So they can be merged with neighbouring words by BPE to save tokens in long chats
So the model can predict them character by character and learn their exact spelling
questions.explanation: Delimiters must be one id each, never split into '<', '|', 'system', etc. Splitting would blur the boundary the model must learn and make it context-dependent. This is the special-token machinery of a production tokenizer.

questions.question: Why must chat delimiter tokens be reserved in the tokenizer?
options: So they are excluded from the model's output vocabulary and can never be sampled
So they do not count toward the context length when long chats are truncated
So they are always placed at the start of the sequence, before any user text
So ordinary user text cannot forge them and fake a turn boundary
questions.explanation: Reserving delimiters means ordinary text cannot produce their ids, so a user typing the literal string '<|end|>' cannot forge a turn boundary — otherwise it is a prompt-injection vector. The model still outputs them (it must emit <|end|> to stop).

questions.question: The course's from-scratch BPETokenizer does not reserve chat delimiters. How does the code keep turn boundaries exact anyway?
options: It replaces each delimiter with a single unused byte before encoding, then maps the byte back after decoding
It trains the BPE tokenizer on a corpus containing many delimiters, so they are learned as single merges
It strips all delimiters out before encoding and inserts them back into the token ids after decoding
It encodes each segment (header, content, closer) separately, so no BPE merge crosses a boundary
questions.explanation: render_with_response_mask encodes segment by segment — role header, content, closer — so merges never span a boundary and the mask stays exact. A production tokenizer instead adds each delimiter to the vocabulary as a single id.

questions.question: After SFT with a consistent chat template, what two behaviors has the model learned?
options: After '<|user|>\n' produce a likely user question, and after <|end|> produce a fresh system message
After '<|system|>\n' produce a helpful response, and never emit <|end|> so the reply is not cut short
After '<|assistant|>\n' produce a helpful response, and when finished emit <|end|> and stop
After any delimiter produce padding tokens until the context fills, and then emit a single <|end|>
questions.explanation: The template is a contract learned during SFT: after the assistant header, generate a helpful response; when done, emit <|end|> and stop. This contract only holds if inference uses the same format.

questions.question: What is the 'generation prompt' in chat-template inference?
options: A special system message appended at the end that tells the model to be helpful and to answer the last user turn
The conversation rendered through a bare '<|assistant|>\n' with no content, so the model generates the reply
The full conversation including the assistant answer, rendered once as a reference that sampling is scored against
A random prefix sampled from earlier assistant turns and prepended to the prompt to diversify the model's responses
questions.explanation: At inference you render the conversation up to and including a bare assistant header, then call generate. The model fills in the response and emits <|end|>, at which point decoding stops. Including the answer would only be done for training data.

questions.question: What is the most common bug when a model trained with <|end|> as the stop signal is deployed?
options: The decode loop does not treat <|end|> as a stop, so the model runs to the token limit
The model refuses to emit any tokens after the assistant header and returns empty
The model emits <|end|> as its very first token every time, so replies are empty
The tokenizer crashes on <|end|> at decode time because the token id is unknown
questions.explanation: If train-time and inference-time formatting disagree, the model is off-distribution; the most common symptom is that it never stops. If you forget to sample until <|end|> and treat it as the end, generation continues to max tokens every time.

questions.question: Which of these train/inference differences would put an SFT model off-distribution?
options: Any of: a missing newline, a different role header, or no end token
Only using a different random seed at inference than in training
Only using a larger batch size at inference than during training
Only running inference on a different GPU model than training
questions.explanation: The model learned the exact template string. A missing newline, a different header, or a missing end token all change the token sequence it conditions on, so the model is off-distribution. Seeds, batch sizes, or hardware do not change the format.

questions.question: In the course's llmre.sft.chat_template module, what does render_chat(messages[:2], add_generation_prompt=True) produce for a system and a user message?
options: The rendered system and user turns followed by a closing '<|end|>' only
Only the user turn with a bare '<|assistant|>\n', the system turn dropped
The full three-turn chat, including the assistant's answer and its <|end|>
The rendered system and user turns followed by a bare '<|assistant|>\n'
questions.explanation: With add_generation_prompt=True, render_chat renders the given messages and appends the assistant header with no content, ready for generation. Without it, it renders exactly the messages given, which for training includes assistant content.

questions.question: What does render_with_response_mask(messages, encode) return?
options: A torch.long tensor of token ids and a causal attention mask of shape (T, T) over all turns
A rendered string and the character index at which the first assistant turn's content starts
A list of token ids and an equal-length mask with 1 exactly on assistant-response tokens
A list of token ids and a list of role names, one per message, used to weight the loss by role
questions.explanation: It returns input_ids and response_mask, two equal-length lists; response_mask[i] == 1 iff token i belongs to an assistant response. That mask is what the next step (loss masking) uses to build labels.

questions.question: In render_with_response_mask, which tokens are marked as response (mask = 1)?
options: The assistant's content only, excluding <|end|>
The assistant's content and its <|end|> closer
The <|assistant|> header and the assistant's content
All tokens of every turn, including system and user
questions.explanation: Assistant content plus its <|end|> closer are marked response; system text, user text, and all role headers (including <|assistant|>) are prompt. Including the closer is deliberate: it is how the model learns to emit the stop token.

questions.question: Why does the chat-template code deliberately mark the assistant's <|end|> closer as a response token?
options: So the closer is excluded from attention at training time and never seen
So the loss trains the model to emit the stop token at the end of its turn
So the closer is not counted toward the sequence length when packing
So the model learns to predict the next user turn after its own reply
questions.explanation: If <|end|> were masked as prompt, the model would never be trained to produce it and would not learn to stop. Marking it as response makes emitting the stop token part of the learned behavior.

questions.question: How does render_with_response_mask build its outputs internally?
options: It walks (text, is_response) segments, encodes each independently, and extends the ids and a repeated 0/1 flag
It renders the full string once, encodes it, then searches for the assistant header to set the mask
It encodes each character separately and marks characters after '<|assistant|>' as response
It runs the model over the rendered string and marks the tokens it predicts with high confidence as the response tokens
questions.explanation: The function iterates over segments (header, content, closer) tagged with is_response, encodes each segment, appends its ids, and appends [1 if is_resp else 0] * len(seg_ids) to the mask. Encoding per segment keeps boundaries exact with a BPE that does not reserve delimiters.

questions.question: What are the types returned by render_with_response_mask in the course's chat-template module?
options: Two torch.long tensors already on the training device
A torch.bool tensor and a torch.float tensor
A rendered string and a numpy int32 array of mask flags
Two equal-length Python list[int]; no tensors yet
questions.explanation: There are no tensors in the chat-template module: messages is list[dict[str, str]], render_chat returns str, and render_with_response_mask returns two equal-length lists of Python ints. They become a torch.long tensor only later, when labels are built and batches are moved to the device.

questions.question: In HuggingFace, what is tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, add_generation_prompt=...) equivalent to?
options: A learned model that rewrites the message list into a better-performing prompt, with a switch for adding few-shot examples
A function that trains the tokenizer's merges on chat data so delimiters become single tokens, run once per model
The same job as render_chat: a deterministic message-list to delimited-string rule, with a generation-prompt switch
A function that computes only the response mask for the SFT loss, returning a 0/1 list aligned with the token ids
questions.explanation: apply_chat_template does exactly what render_chat does; the template itself is a Jinja string shipped with each chat model. Different families use different delimiters (<|im_start|>/<|im_end|>, [INST]/[/INST]), but the job is the same.

questions.question: In HuggingFace chat models, where is the chat template itself stored?
options: As hard-coded Python inside the Transformers library, identical for all models
As learned weights inside the model's first layer
As a Jinja template string shipped with each chat model's tokenizer
As a separate fine-tuned adapter loaded at inference
questions.explanation: Each chat model ships its own Jinja template string. That is why different families have different delimiters, and why you must use the right model's template. It is not learned and not shared across all models.

questions.question: What goes wrong if you format SFT data for model A using model B's chat delimiters?
options: Nothing; delimiters are interchangeable across model families, since any string can mark a turn
The delimiters are not in either vocabulary as intended, so turn boundaries become gibberish
The model trains faster, because seeing more distinct delimiter tokens gives it a richer turn signal
The tokenizer automatically converts B's delimiters into A's, so the rendered data is identical anyway
questions.explanation: Each family's delimiters are specific to its tokenizer. Using another model's delimiters means they do not exist as the intended single ids, so the turn structure the model must learn is garbled. There is no automatic conversion.

questions.question: What can happen if you forget add_generation_prompt at inference?
options: Without the trailing '<|assistant|>\n' the model is not cued that it is its turn and may continue the user's text
The model emits <|end|> as its first token, because the last thing in context is a closed user turn, and returns nothing
The tokenizer throws an error about a missing assistant role, since every rendered chat must end with an assistant turn
The model still answers correctly but twice as slowly, because it first regenerates the missing header token by token
questions.explanation: The trailing assistant header is the cue that the assistant should speak. Without it, the prompt ends after the user's <|end|>, and the model may continue in the wrong role, such as writing more of the user's message.

questions.question: What is the symptom of a decode loop that ignores <|end|>?
options: No answer at all, only an empty string returned
An answer in the wrong language for the prompt
A tokenizer error raised at the end of generation
A correct answer followed by hallucinated extra turns
questions.explanation: The model dutifully emits the stop token, but if the loop ignores it, sampling continues and the model starts inventing new turns. You get a correct answer followed by hallucinated follow-up turns.

questions.question: Why must prompt tokens be masked out of the SFT loss?
options: Otherwise the tokenizer cannot encode the prompt tokens
Otherwise attention cannot see the prompt during training
Otherwise the context window overflows on long prompts
Otherwise you teach the model to generate user turns
questions.explanation: If prompt tokens are scored, the model is trained to predict user and system text, i.e. to generate user turns. Masking only removes them from the loss; the model still attends to them as context.

questions.question: After SFT on data rendered with <|end|> after every turn, a model answers correctly but then invents a follow-up question and answers it until the length limit. Where is the most likely bug?
options: In training: the rendered data never actually contained the <|end|> token
In the tokenizer: <|end|> is split into several ordinary tokens at decode time
In inference: the generation loop does not stop when <|end|> is sampled
In the optimizer: the learning rate was too high, so the model overfit to long replies
questions.explanation: The training data included <|end|>, so the model did learn to emit it. The generation loop is not treating <|end|> as a stop and keeps sampling for max_new_tokens, so a hallucinated new turn begins. Fix: stop as soon as the sampled token is the <|end|> id or truncate at the first <|end|>.

questions.question: When debugging a fine-tuned chat model that rambles, which observation would point to a training-formatting bug rather than an inference bug?
options: The model emits <|end|> and then keeps generating past it
The model never emits <|end|> at all
The model stops correctly when <|end|> is passed as a stop token
The model answers correctly before it starts rambling on
questions.explanation: If the model emits <|end|> and keeps going, the inference loop ignores the stop token. If the model never emits <|end|>, it never learned to, which points to training formatting (e.g. the closer was missing or masked out).

questions.question: What does SFT change so that the continuation of 'Write a haiku about the sea.' becomes a haiku?
options: The training distribution, so that the continuation of a request is a helpful answer
The model architecture, by adding an instruction-detection module before the first block
The sampling temperature, so that continuing with another prompt becomes less likely
The tokenizer, so that lists of writing prompts are split into different token sequences
questions.explanation: The pretrained model continues a writing prompt with another prompt because that is common in its data. SFT changes the training distribution so that what follows a request is a helpful answer. Architecture and tokenizer are unchanged.

questions.question: When should add_generation_prompt=True be used?
options: At inference, to render the conversation so far before generating; not when formatting training data
When formatting training data, so that the model learns to produce the assistant header on its own
Only when the conversation has a system message, to separate it from the first user turn
Always, for both training and inference, so that the rendered format is identical in the two settings
questions.explanation: It appends an empty assistant header to cue the model's turn, which is only needed at inference. Training data already contains the assistant content after the header, so adding an extra empty header would corrupt it.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Why is masking the prompt out of the SFT loss important?
options: It trains the model to answer rather than also learning to parrot the question
It halves activation memory, since prompt positions skip the backward pass
It stops the model attending to the prompt, so responses stay independent of it
It removes the need for a chat template, since role headers are never scored
questions.explanation: Masking the prompt means the model is only trained to produce responses, not to reproduce questions. The prompt still feeds attention as context; masking only affects which positions contribute to the loss.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Why is sequence packing used in SFT?
options: Mixing unrelated examples in one block acts as a regularizer and improves final accuracy
The loss mask only works on full blocks, so short examples must be packed before masking
Packing merges frequent token pairs across examples, shrinking the effective vocabulary size
Instruction examples are short and uneven, so padding each to the block wastes most compute
questions.explanation: Instruction examples vary wildly in length; padding each to a fixed block wastes most positions. Packing concatenates short examples to fill blocks with real tokens, keeping SFT GPU-efficient. Mixing examples is a hazard to manage, not a benefit.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Which production SFT trainers perform response-only loss masking and packing under the hood?
options: Only DeepSpeed ZeRO
Only vLLM
TRL's SFTTrainer and Axolotl
None; production trainers compute loss on all tokens
questions.explanation: Every SFT trainer you will use, such as TRL's SFTTrainer and Axolotl, does both response-only masking and packing. vLLM is an inference engine and DeepSpeed is a distributed-training system, not an SFT recipe.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: only score what you want the model to generate
questions.question: Why is every position a legitimate prediction target in pretraining but not in SFT?
options: Pretraining sequences are shorter, so every position fits in memory, while SFT conversations do not
Pretraining should continue any text; in SFT the prompt is supplied at inference, never generated
In SFT the prompt tokens are not fed to the model at all, so there is nothing to predict there
In SFT the response tokens are already known from the dataset, so only prompt positions need loss
questions.explanation: Pretraining wants the model to continue any text, so all positions are scored. In SFT, the user and template supply the prompt at inference; the model only generates the response. So training it to predict the prompt is wasted, and masking keeps the loss on responses.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: only score what you want the model to generate
questions.question: What harm can come from including prompt tokens in the SFT loss?
options: It drives the gradients on response tokens to exactly zero, so the assistant text is never learned
It spends capacity predicting user and system text and can teach the model to continue prompts
It prevents the model from attending to the prompt, since scored positions are hidden from attention
It makes the loss negative on prompt tokens, which cancels out the response-token loss in the mean
questions.explanation: Scoring prompt tokens optimizes the model to predict user questions and system messages — a distribution we do not care about. Worse, it can teach the model to continue prompts instead of responding, the very failure SFT is supposed to cure.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: only score what you want the model to generate
questions.question: In SFT, which positions contribute to the loss under the standard loss rule?
options: Only assistant-response tokens; system text, user text and role headers are all ignored
Only user tokens, because they carry the instruction the assistant response follows
All tokens except the final <|end|>, which the sampler handles
Only the role headers, because they define the turn structure to emit
questions.explanation: SFT computes cross-entropy on assistant-response tokens only. Every prompt position — system and user text and all role headers — contributes zero loss and zero gradient. Ignoring is implemented with the sentinel label -100.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: only score what you want the model to generate
questions.question: In SFT loss masking, what is the gradient contribution of an ignored prompt position?
options: Half of a response position's contribution
The same as a response position, but with opposite sign
Proportional to the prompt length
Exactly zero
questions.explanation: Ignored positions contribute exactly zero to the loss and zero gradient. They are simply excluded from the average. They still affect gradients indirectly as context the response tokens attend to, but they are not targets.

questions.question: In the full (pretraining) cross-entropy over N positions, how is the loss formed?
options: The sum over response positions of -log softmax(z_i)[y_i], divided by N
The maximum over positions of -log softmax(z_i)[y_i]
The mean over all N positions of -log softmax(z_i)[y_i]
The mean over positions of the squared error between z_i and y_i
questions.explanation: L_full = (1/N) * sum_i of -log softmax(z_i)_{y_i}, where z_i is the logit row at position i and y_i the true token id. Every one of the N positions counts equally.

questions.question: In the masked SFT loss L_SFT = sum_i m_i * (-log softmax(z_i)[y_i]) / sum_i m_i, what is the denominator?
options: The total sequence length N, prompt included
The vocabulary size V
The number of response tokens
The number of prompt tokens
questions.explanation: The denominator is sum_i m_i, the count of response positions. We average over what we actually scored, not over N. Dividing by N would shrink the loss in proportion to the prompt fraction.

questions.question: In the SFT masked loss, what does the mask value m_i mean?
options: m_i = 1 if position i is padding or a role header, else 0
m_i = 1 if position i is an assistant-response token, else 0
m_i is the attention weight that position i receives from the last token
m_i is the probability the model assigns to the true token
questions.explanation: m_i is a binary response mask: 1 for assistant-response positions, 0 for prompt positions. It multiplies the per-position loss, so prompt positions drop out of the numerator, and sum_i m_i forms the denominator.

questions.question: In the SFT masked loss formula, what do z_i, y_i and V denote?
options: z_i is the logit row at position i, y_i the true token id there, V the vocabulary size
z_i is the final hidden state at position i, y_i the predicted id, V the number of layers
z_i is the softmax probability vector, y_i the mask bit, V the sequence length
z_i is the input embedding of token i, y_i its position index, V the model width
questions.explanation: z_i in R^V is the logit vector at position i, y_i is the target token id, and V is the vocabulary size. The per-position loss is -log softmax(z_i)_{y_i}.

questions.question: In code, how is the SFT response mask usually applied to cross-entropy?
options: Passed as a separate float weight tensor that is multiplied into the logits row-wise
Applied by zeroing the logits at prompt positions so their softmax becomes uniform
Applied by deleting prompt tokens from the input before the forward pass
Folded into the labels: y_i where m_i = 1, the sentinel -100 where m_i = 0
questions.explanation: Instead of carrying a separate mask, the labels themselves encode it: keep the true id where the mask is 1 and write ignore_index = -100 elsewhere. Cross-entropy skips -100 labels, which yields exactly L_SFT. Deleting prompt tokens from the input would remove the context the response needs.

questions.question: The course's GPT.forward uses ignore_index = -1 while the SFT modules use -100. What matters about the choice of value?
options: It must be exactly -100, since cross-entropy errors on any other negative value
It must equal the padding token id, so pads and prompts share one code path
It must equal the vocabulary size V, the first id past the embedding table
It must never be a valid token id, and build_labels and the loss must agree on it
questions.explanation: The sentinel is arbitrary as long as it can never be a real token id and both label construction and the loss agree on it. -100 is HuggingFace's convention and the default of torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy.

questions.question: What is the default ignore_index of torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy?
options: None; there is no default
questions.explanation: torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy defaults to ignore_index=-100, which is also HuggingFace's convention. The course's Module 6 GPT.forward used -1, which also works as long as it is used consistently.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example (worked by hand, verified in Python)
questions.question: For a sequence with mask m = [0, 0, 1, 1] and targets y = [0, 1, 2, 0], what labels does build_labels produce?
questions.explanation: build_labels keeps the target id where the mask is 1 and writes -100 elsewhere. Positions 0 and 1 are prompt, so they become -100; positions 2 and 3 keep 2 and 0. Using 0 instead of -100 would wrongly train the model to predict token 0 on the prompt.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example (worked by hand, verified in Python)
questions.question: In a worked masked-loss example, the response-only loss is 0.3876 while the full loss over all positions is 0.3136. Why do they differ?
options: The full loss also averages in the prompt positions, which were easy here
The masked loss double-counts response positions as input and target
The full loss uses log base 2 while the masked loss uses the natural log
The masked loss divides by vocabulary size, not by position count
questions.explanation: The masked loss averages only over response positions; the full loss averages over all four, including the confident prompt positions, which pulls it down. They measure different things; SFT wants the response-only number.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example (worked by hand, verified in Python)
questions.question: What equality serves as the correctness test for the SFT masking mechanism?
options: Masked cross-entropy on the full sequence equals plain cross-entropy on just the response rows
Masked cross-entropy equals full cross-entropy over all rows whenever the prompt is non-empty
Masked cross-entropy equals exactly log V at initialization, matching a uniform predictor
Masked cross-entropy equals the full-sequence loss multiplied by the fraction of response tokens
questions.explanation: masked_cross_entropy(logits, labels) must equal cross_entropy(logits[response], ids[response]). That identity proves the mask selects exactly the right positions and averages over them, and it is what tests/test_sft.py checks.

questions.question: In the SFT masking code, what dtype and shape are the labels returned by build_labels?
options: torch.float32, shape (T, V)
torch.bool, same shape as input_ids, True where kept
torch.long, shape (V,)
torch.long, same shape as input_ids
questions.explanation: build_labels returns labels with the same shape as input_ids ((T,) or (B, T)) and dtype torch.long, with labels[i] = input_ids[i] where the mask is truthy and -100 elsewhere. The response_mask itself can be bool or int.

questions.question: What does masked_cross_entropy(logits, labels) return, given logits of shape (B, T, V)?
options: A (B, T) tensor of per-position losses, zero at ignored spots
A (B,) tensor of per-example mean losses in nats
A scalar () tensor in nats, on the logits' device
A (V,) tensor of per-class losses summed over positions
questions.explanation: masked_cross_entropy accepts logits (..., V) and labels (...), flattens them, and returns the mean over kept positions as a scalar tensor in nats on the logits' device.

questions.question: masked_cross_entropy scores logits[i] against labels[i] one-to-one. How should a real SFT training loop handle the next-token shift?
options: Pass unshifted ids and let masked_cross_entropy shift logits and labels internally by one
Feed ids[:-1] as input and build labels from ids[1:] and response_mask[1:], outside the loss
Shift the logits left by one inside the model's forward pass and again inside the loss
No shift is needed, because the causal attention mask already stops position i from seeing token i
questions.explanation: Positions are aligned one-to-one, so the caller must shift: input x = ids[:-1], labels from ids[1:] with response_mask[1:], then masked_cross_entropy(model(x)[0], labels). Doing the shift once outside the loss avoids double-shifting or forgetting it.

questions.question: How does build_labels construct the label tensor?
options: It copies input_ids and then overwrites the response positions with the sentinel value -100
It fills a tensor with ignore_index, then writes the true ids back only at response positions
It multiplies input_ids by the response mask so that every prompt position becomes ignored
It deletes prompt positions from input_ids and returns a shorter tensor of response ids only
questions.explanation: torch.full_like(input_ids, ignore_index) creates an all-ignored tensor, then labels[mask] = input_ids[mask] restores response ids. This 'ignore everything, then un-ignore responses' framing is the inverse of masking out the prompt and is less error-prone. Multiplying by the mask would produce 0, a valid token id.

questions.question: In the from-scratch masked_cross_entropy, how are ignored positions removed?
options: Flatten to (N, V) and (N,), keep rows with label != ignore_index, then log-softmax only those
Set logits at ignored positions to negative infinity so their softmax mass vanishes before the loss
Compute loss on all rows, multiply ignored ones by zero, and divide the sum by the full row count N
Sort the labels so ignored ones come first, then drop that many leading rows from the batch
questions.explanation: It reshapes logits to (N, V) and labels to (N,), builds keep = labels != ignore_index, selects the kept rows, and computes the stable log-softmax and gather only on them, returning the mean. So the mean is over kept rows only.

questions.question: How does the from-scratch masked_cross_entropy compute log-probabilities in a numerically stable way?
options: Apply softmax to each logit row, then take the elementwise log of the probabilities
Divide each logit row by its maximum, then take the log of the normalised row
Exponentiate the logits and normalise by the vocabulary size before taking the log
Subtract logsumexp of each logit row, then gather the true-token log-prob
questions.explanation: logp = logits - logsumexp(logits, dim=-1, keepdim=True) is a stable log-softmax that avoids overflow and log(0). Then the true-token entries are gathered with an arange row index. Taking log of softmax directly is less stable.

questions.question: What does torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(logits, labels, ignore_index=-100) do compared to the from-scratch masked_cross_entropy?
options: It ignores the ignore_index argument and averages over all positions
It divides by the full sequence length instead of by the count of kept positions
The same masking, but fused: log-softmax, gather and mask run in a single kernel
It needs a separate float mask, since ignore_index only covers padding
questions.explanation: F.cross_entropy with ignore_index=-100 skips those positions and averages over the rest, just like the from-scratch version, but fuses the steps into one kernel. Its default ignore_index is even -100. Writing it by hand only makes the mechanism visible.

questions.question: Why does padding every instruction example to a fixed block size waste compute?
options: Padding tokens are more expensive to process than real tokens because they bypass the fused kernels
Padding forces the model to recompute attention twice, once with and once without the pad mask
Examples are short and uneven, so most positions in a padded row are padding, not real tokens
Padding adds a new pad token to the vocabulary, enlarging the embedding and output layers
questions.explanation: If an example of 20 tokens is padded to 1024, almost all of the row is padding, yet the GPU still processes every position. Packing several examples into one block fills nearly every position with real tokens, raising throughput on the same hardware.

questions.question: What is sequence packing in SFT?
options: Compressing each example's tokens with a smaller vocabulary so more of them fit per block
Concatenating several short examples end-to-end into one full block of length T
Splitting long examples into many short rows so every row has exactly the same length
Sorting examples by length so each batch holds similar lengths and needs little padding
questions.explanation: Packing concatenates multiple short examples into one block of the full length T so almost every position is real. Sorting by length (bucketing) is a different technique that still pads. Splitting long examples is truncation/chunking.

questions.section: Sequence packing: 2. The catch, and the fix
questions.question: When packing several SFT examples into one block, how is each example's loss mask kept correct?
options: Concatenate per-example response masks in token order, then apply build_labels to the block
Recompute a single mask that marks only the last example's response, since earlier ones are context
Mask the whole block except its final token, which is the only position predicted at inference
Copy the first example's mask across the block, since all examples share one chat template
questions.explanation: Each example keeps its own prompt/response split. Concatenating the masks just like the tokens means build_labels still masks each example's prompt independently.

questions.section: Sequence packing: 2. The catch, and the fix
questions.question: Besides the loss mask, what must stay correct per example when packing SFT data?
options: Each example must have the same length
Each example must use a different chat template so roles stay distinct
Each example must be placed at position 0
Attention must not cross example boundaries
questions.explanation: Example B's tokens must not attend to example A's, or the model 'reads' an unrelated earlier conversation. The fix is a block-diagonal attention mask, often implemented via document ids or position resets.

questions.section: Sequence packing: 2. The catch, and the fix
questions.question: What is the clean fix that prevents cross-example attention in a packed block?
options: A plain causal mask over the whole block, which already stops each token from seeing the future
Shuffling token order within the block so no example forms a coherent prefix for the next one
Inserting a padding token between examples, since pad positions are excluded from attention
A block-diagonal attention mask (e.g. via document_ids) so each example attends only to itself
questions.explanation: A block-diagonal mask restricts each token to attend only within its own example. A plain causal mask allows later examples to see earlier ones. Shuffling tokens would destroy the sequences.

questions.section: Sequence packing: 2. The catch, and the fix
questions.question: What cheaper approximation to block-diagonal attention is sometimes used in packed SFT, and what is its cost?
options: Training one example per row with no padding, accepting slower convergence from small batches
Masking every token except the separator, accepting that most positions get zero gradient
Concatenate with a separator token and only a causal mask, accepting some cross-contamination
Using bidirectional attention within the block, accepting some leakage of future tokens
questions.explanation: In practice some pipelines just concatenate with a separator token and rely on the causal mask, accepting a little cross-example contamination. The honest version resets attention at each boundary.

questions.question: Three examples of lengths 20, 50 and 30 are packed into a block of T = 100. How much padding is there?
options: 50 tokens, half the block
None; the block is exactly filled
80 tokens, padding the shortest example
200 tokens, padding each to T = 100
questions.explanation: 20 + 50 + 30 = 100, so the block is exactly full with zero padding. Padding each to 100 separately would waste 80%, 50% and 70% of their rows — over half the compute.

questions.question: Why is a plain causal mask across a packed SFT block a dangerous bug?
