options: Later examples attend back to earlier unrelated ones, yet nothing crashes and the loss looks fine
It makes the loss NaN on the first step, because separator rows have no valid attention targets
It stops each example attending to its own prompt, since the mask only sees the block start
It raises a shape error in attention, since the mask must match each example's length
questions.explanation: A plain causal mask lets example C attend all the way back to A. There is no error and the loss looks normal, but the model quietly learns to condition responses on unrelated preceding examples. Always reset attention at boundaries or verify your trainer does.

questions.question: Two examples are packed: example 1 has prompt [a, b] and response [c]; example 2 has prompt [d] and response [e, f]. What labels does build_labels produce?
questions.explanation: Concatenated tokens are [a, b, c, d, e, f] and concatenated masks [0,0,1] + [0,1,1] = [0,0,1,0,1,1]. build_labels keeps ids where the mask is 1 and writes -100 elsewhere. Each example's prompt is masked independently.

questions.question: When applying build_labels to a packed block, what happens to the input tokens themselves?
options: Prompt tokens are replaced by -100 in the input as well
Prompt tokens are removed from the input before the forward pass
Response tokens are shifted to the start of the block
They are unchanged; only the labels get -100 at masked positions
questions.explanation: Masking only affects labels. The input still contains every token so responses can attend to their prompts. Replacing input ids with -100 would be an invalid token id.

questions.question: What goes wrong if the masked SFT loss numerator is divided by the sequence length N instead of by the response count?
options: The loss becomes NaN whenever the prompt is longer than the response in a given example
The gradient on prompt tokens becomes nonzero, so the model starts learning to parrot questions
The loss shrinks silently and gradients are skewed between short- and long-response examples
Nothing; dividing by N and by the response count are equivalent up to a fixed global constant
questions.explanation: Dividing by N shrinks the loss by the prompt fraction and weights examples by how much prompt they have rather than how much response. That distorts the gradient. The correct denominator is sum_i m_i.

questions.question: What is wrong with setting ignored SFT labels to token id 0 instead of a sentinel?
options: It makes cross-entropy raise an error, since 0 is reserved for the ignore_index default
It trains the model to predict token 0 at every prompt position instead of ignoring it
It has no effect, because token 0 is always the padding token and is skipped automatically
It only affects the first position of each sequence, where the BOS token is predicted
questions.explanation: 0 is a valid token id, so cross-entropy will score those positions with target 0, actively training the model to predict token 0 on the prompt. Use a sentinel like -100 that can never be a real id.

questions.question: What symptom indicates an off-by-one shift bug in an SFT training loop, where logits[i] is scored against token i?
options: The loss explodes to infinity on the first step and stays there
The loss collapses toward zero and the model learns nothing useful
The model only learns to emit <|end|> after every prompt
The loss stays exactly constant at log V from step one
questions.explanation: Without the shift, each position is asked to predict the token it already sees as input, which is trivial. The loss collapses toward zero but the model learns nothing about predicting the next token.

questions.question: Given input_ids = [5, 6, 7] and response_mask = [0, 1, 1], what does build_labels return?
questions.explanation: Position 0 is prompt and becomes -100; positions 1 and 2 are response and keep ids 6 and 7. Writing 0 would train toward token 0.

questions.question: If an SFT model's prompt positions are easy (low loss), how does the full-sequence loss compare to the response-only loss?
options: The full loss is higher, because summing over more positions raises the average
They are always equal, because prompt positions carry zero gradient anyway
The full loss is always exactly half the response-only loss
The full loss is lower, because easy prompt positions pull the average down
questions.explanation: Averaging easy, confident prompt positions into the mean lowers the full loss. The masked loss ignores them and reflects only response difficulty. Neither is wrong; SFT wants the response-only number.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: By roughly how much does LoRA cut trainable parameters and the optimizer memory that dominates fine-tuning?
options: One to two orders of magnitude
About 10%
Roughly half
It does not change trainable parameters, only activations
questions.explanation: LoRA trains only small low-rank adapters, cutting trainable parameters and therefore gradient and optimizer memory by one to two orders of magnitude. That is what moved fine-tuning from clusters to a single GPU.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: What practical deployment benefit does LoRA give when you fine-tune one base model for many tasks?
options: You can merge all task adapters into one combined adapter with no loss in quality on any task
You can drop the base model at inference, since each adapter fully replaces its weights
Adapted tasks can skip the tokenizer, because adapters operate directly on raw text bytes
Many small per-task adapters share one base model instead of many full model copies
questions.explanation: Each task needs only its adapters (a few MB), so many adapters can share one base model. Without LoRA, each task would require storing a full copy of the base weights.

questions.question: Under fp32 full fine-tuning with AdamW, roughly how many numbers are carried per trainable parameter?
options: 1: just the weight, since AdamW updates parameters in place
2: the weight and its gradient, with moments recomputed each step
About 4: the weight, its gradient, and two optimizer moments
8: the weight, its gradient, and six optimizer buffers per step
questions.explanation: AdamW keeps first-moment (mean) and second-moment (variance) estimates for each trainable parameter, plus you need the gradient and the weight — about 4 numbers per parameter, not one.

questions.question: What two extra tensors does AdamW keep per trainable parameter?
options: The previous step's weight and gradient, used to form a finite-difference update
First-moment (mean) and second-moment (variance) estimates of the gradient
A per-parameter learning rate and a per-parameter weight-decay coefficient
A momentum buffer and a cached copy of the layer's input activations
questions.explanation: AdamW stores two moment tensors per trainable parameter: an exponential average of the gradient and of the squared gradient. These are what make optimizer state the memory hog in fine-tuning.

questions.question: Approximately how much memory does AdamW optimizer state alone take for full fp32 fine-tuning of GPT-2 small (124M params)?
options: About 124 MB (124M x 1 byte per moment)
About 1 GB (124M x 2 moments x 4 bytes)
About 4 GB (124M x 8 moments x 4 bytes)
About 16 GB (124M x 32 moments x 4 bytes)
questions.explanation: 124M parameters x 2 moments x 4 bytes is roughly 1 GB just for optimizer state, on top of weights, gradients and activations. For real models this optimizer state is what blows the memory budget.

questions.question: What is LoRA's basic strategy for reducing fine-tuning memory?
options: Freeze the pretrained weights (no gradient or optimizer state) and train a tiny add-on
Quantize the AdamW optimizer state to 1 bit per parameter while still training all weights
Train only the final transformer layer and its head, freezing every earlier layer
Cut the batch size to one and accumulate gradients over many steps to save memory
questions.explanation: LoRA freezes the pretrained weights so they carry no gradient or optimizer state, and trains only small low-rank matrices. Training only the last layer is a different (weaker) technique.

questions.question: In LoRA, how is the weight update for a frozen weight W (out x in) parameterized?
options: Delta W = alpha r A B with A in R^(in x r) and B in R^(r x out)
Delta W = W A with A in R^(in x in), a full-rank right multiplier of W
Delta W = B + A with both B and A of the full shape (out x in) of W
Delta W = (alpha / r) B A with A in R^(r x in) and B in R^(out x r)
questions.explanation: LoRA factorizes the update as (alpha/r) B A: A maps the input down to an r-dimensional bottleneck and B maps it back up to out. The product B A has the shape of W but rank at most r.

questions.question: In LoRA, how small is the rank r typically relative to the layer dimensions?
options: r equals min(in, out), so the update is full rank
r is larger than max(in, out), e.g. r = 4096
r is much smaller than min(in, out), e.g. r = 8
r equals the number of transformer layers, e.g. 12
questions.explanation: The rank is chosen with r << min(in, out); a common value is r = 8. The small bottleneck is what makes LoRA cheap.

questions.question: What is the LoRA forward pass for an input x?
options: y = (W - (alpha / r) B A) x
y = alpha W x + (r / alpha) A (B x)
y = W x + (alpha / r) B (A x)
y = (alpha / r) B (W (A x))
questions.explanation: The frozen path W x is added to the scaled low-rank path (alpha/r) B (A x). Only A and B are trained.

questions.question: In LoRA, why is B A guaranteed to have rank at most r?
options: Because B is initialized to zero, and that zero init caps the product's rank at r forever
Everything passes an r-wide bottleneck: A maps down to r dimensions, B maps back up
Because the alpha / r factor rescales the product until its rank drops to r
Because W is frozen, so the update must lie in an r-dimensional subspace of W
questions.explanation: B A is out x in, but every column passes through A's r-dimensional output, so the product has rank at most r. The zero init and alpha/r scale do not determine the rank.

questions.question: In LoRA, which tensors are trainable?
options: Only A and B
Only W
W, A and B
Only alpha and r
questions.explanation: W is frozen; only A and B are trainable. alpha and r are hyperparameters, not learned.

questions.question: During LoRA training, why is the forward computed as B (A x) rather than (B A) x?
options: Because (B A) x gives a mathematically different result, so only B (A x) is correct LoRA
Because A x must run on the CPU while B runs on the GPU, so the order is forced
Because autograd cannot backpropagate through a product of two trainable matrices
A x first yields a tiny r-vector, so the full out x in matrix B A is never materialized
questions.explanation: Applying A first produces an r-dimensional vector, and B maps it up — cost proportional to r. Materializing B A each step would create a full out x in matrix and defeat the purpose. Both orders give the same result mathematically.

questions.question: What empirical finding explains why a low-rank update is enough for LoRA fine-tuning?
options: Pretrained weight matrices are already low-rank, so any update to them must also be low-rank to stay consistent with the base
Full-rank updates always overfit downstream data, so a low-rank update is strictly better in quality
Low-rank updates tolerate much higher learning rates, so they converge to full fine-tuning's quality faster
The weight change a task needs lies near a small subspace, so ranks 1 to 8 recover most of full fine-tuning's quality
questions.explanation: Hu et al. (2021) found that the direction fine-tuning moves in is close to low-rank; adapting with rank 1 to 8 recovers most of full fine-tuning's quality. The claim is about the update, not the pretrained weights.

questions.section: The alpha scaling and the zero init
questions.question: How are LoRA's A and B initialized?
options: A to zero and B to small random noise
Both A and B to zero, so the adapter starts silent
B to zero and A to small random noise
Both to the same small random noise matrix
questions.explanation: B starts at zero and A at small random values (Kaiming-uniform). Then B A = 0 at step 0. If both were zero, gradients would be zero too and nothing would learn.

questions.section: The alpha scaling and the zero init
questions.question: Why is LoRA's B initialized to zero?
options: So that A receives no gradient at the first step and stays at its random initial value
So B A = 0 at step 0 and the layer outputs exactly W x, starting from the pretrained model
So that the adapter has fewer effective parameters, acting as an implicit rank regularizer
So that the alpha / r scaling factor cancels out and the update size is independent of r
questions.explanation: With B = 0, the adapter's contribution is zero and the layer behaves exactly like the pretrained one. Training starts from the pretrained model and the adapter learns a correction.

questions.section: The alpha scaling and the zero init
questions.question: What is the purpose of LoRA's alpha / r scaling factor?
options: It decouples the update size from the rank, so changing r needs no learning-rate retuning
It ensures the rank of the adapter product never exceeds r, even after many updates
It normalizes the input x to unit length before the down-projection through A
It sets the adapter's dropout probability, so higher ranks are regularized more strongly
questions.explanation: Changing r changes the raw magnitude of B A. Dividing by r and multiplying by a fixed alpha keeps the effective scale roughly constant across ranks, so the learning rate does not need retuning when r changes.

questions.section: The alpha scaling and the zero init
questions.question: What is a common practical setting of LoRA's alpha relative to r?
options: alpha as a small multiple of r, e.g. alpha = 16 with r = 8
alpha = 1 / r, e.g. alpha = 0.125 with r = 8, giving a tiny scale
alpha equal to the hidden size, e.g. alpha = 768 for GPT-2 small
alpha = 0, disabling the scale so the adapter starts inactive
questions.explanation: People set alpha to a small multiple of r, e.g. alpha = 16, r = 8, giving a scale of 2. alpha = 0 would zero out the adapter.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example (worked by hand, verified in Python)
questions.question: In a LoRA layer with W = [[1,0,2],[0,1,1]], A = [1,0,1], B = [1,2]^T, alpha = 2, r = 1 and x = [1,1,1], what is the output y?
questions.explanation: W x = [3, 2]. A x = 2, B(A x) = [2, 4], scaled by alpha/r = 2 gives [4, 8]. y = [3, 2] + [4, 8] = [7, 10]. [3, 2] is only the frozen path; [4, 8] is only the scaled adapter path.

questions.section: 3. Numerical example (worked by hand, verified in Python)
questions.question: What does LoRA's merged weight W' equal, and what property does it satisfy?
options: W' = W - (alpha / r) B A, and W' x equals the base layer output for every x
W' = (alpha / r) B A alone, and W' x equals only the adapter path for every x
W' = W + (alpha / r) B A, and W' x equals the LoRA forward output for every x
W' = (alpha / r) W, and W' x equals a rescaled base output for every input x
questions.explanation: Folding the scaled low-rank update into W gives W' = W + (alpha/r) B A. By linearity, W' x = W x + (alpha/r) B (A x), identical to the LoRA forward. That is what merge() guarantees.

questions.question: For a 768 x 768 layer with LoRA rank r = 8, how many trainable parameters does LoRA add?
questions.explanation: A is 8 x 768 and B is 768 x 8, so 2 x 8 x 768 = 12,288. Full fine-tuning of that layer would train 768 x 768 = 589,824. 6,144 is only one of the two matrices.

questions.question: For a 768 x 768 layer with r = 8, what is LoRA's reduction factor in trainable parameters versus full fine-tuning?
options: About 8x
About 48x
About 96x
About 768x
questions.explanation: 589,824 / 12,288 = 48. In general the factor for a square d x d layer is d / (2r) = 768 / 16 = 48.

questions.question: Why does LoRA shrink AdamW moment memory in proportion to its parameter reduction?
options: Because optimizer state scales with trainable parameters, and only A and B are trainable
Because LoRA switches to a different optimizer that keeps no moment tensors at all
Because the frozen base weights are deleted from GPU memory as soon as adapters are attached
Because LoRA updates the AdamW moments only once every r steps instead of every step
questions.explanation: AdamW allocates moments only for trainable parameters. With only A and B trainable, moment memory drops from about 4.7 MB to about 0.1 MB for a 768 x 768 layer. The frozen weights stay in memory but carry no optimizer state.

questions.question: What do you need to store to save a new LoRA task, compared to full fine-tuning?
options: A full copy of the base model plus the adapters, merged per task
Only the AdamW optimizer state, from which the adapters are rebuilt
Only the tokenizer and chat template, since the weights are shared
Only the adapters (a few MB), not a fresh copy of the base model
questions.explanation: A LoRA task is fully described by its A and B matrices, which are tiny, while the shared base is stored once. Full fine-tuning would need a full copy of the model per task.

questions.question: Roughly what memory does full fp32 fine-tuning of GPT-2 small (124M) need, excluding activations?
options: About 124 MB in total, one byte per parameter for everything
About 0.5 GB in total, since gradients reuse weight memory
About 0.5 GB weights + 0.5 GB gradients + 1 GB AdamW state
About 50 GB, which forces you to shard across multiple GPUs
questions.explanation: Weights about 0.5 GB, gradients about 0.5 GB and AdamW state about 1 GB, plus activations — several GB, feasible on a 12 to 16 GB GPU but tight.

questions.question: With LoRA (r = 8 on attention/MLP projections), what becomes the dominant memory cost?
options: The gradients of the adapter matrices A and B
The AdamW moment tensors of the adapters
The frozen weights and the activations
The tokenizer vocabulary and chat-template strings
questions.explanation: LoRA trains under 1% of the parameters, so gradient and optimizer memory for the trainable set drops to tens of MB. What remains dominant is the frozen base weights and activations — which is what QLoRA attacks.

questions.question: What does QLoRA make possible in terms of single-GPU fine-tuning?
options: Fine-tuning 7B models entirely on a CPU in a few minutes, with no GPU required at all
7B-scale fine-tuning on a single 24 GB consumer GPU (and 65B on a single 48 GB GPU)
Fine-tuning 65B models with no GPU memory at all used for the frozen base weights
Pretraining a 7B model from scratch on a single laptop GPU in a few days
questions.explanation: By storing the frozen base in 4-bit, QLoRA brings 7B fine-tuning onto a 24 GB card and 65B onto a single 48 GB GPU. The base still occupies memory, just about 4x less.

questions.question: In a LoRALinear wrapping nn.Linear(in, out), what are the shapes of self.A and self.B?
options: A is (r, in) and B is (out, r)
A is (in, r) and B is (r, out)
A is (out, r) and B is (r, in)
A and B are both (out, in)
questions.explanation: Matching nn.Linear's (out, in) weight convention, A is (r, in) — it maps in to r — and B is (out, r) — it maps r to out. Their product B @ A is (out, in).

questions.question: What shapes flow through LoRALinear's forward for an input of shape (..., in)?
options: F.linear(x, B) gives (..., r), then F.linear(., A) gives (..., in), added to base(x) of shape (..., in)
x is first expanded to (..., out, in), multiplied elementwise by B @ A, then summed to (..., out)
F.linear(x, A) gives (..., out) directly, B is unused in forward, and the sum has shape (..., out)
F.linear(x, A) gives (..., r), F.linear(., B) gives (..., out), added to base(x) of shape (..., out)
questions.explanation: Down to the rank-r bottleneck through A, then up to out through B, then added to the base output of the same shape (..., out).

questions.question: In a from-scratch LoRALinear, what is the requires_grad status of self.base.weight?
options: True: it is trained alongside A and B
True only for the first epoch
It depends on alpha
False: it is frozen
questions.explanation: The base weight (and bias) is frozen with requires_grad_(False), so it gets no gradient and no optimizer state. A and B are trainable.

questions.question: What does LoRALinear.merge() return?
options: The same LoRALinear with B reset to zero after folding it into base.weight
A tuple of the A and B tensors, scaled by alpha / r, ready for saving to disk
A plain nn.Linear with weight base.weight + (alpha / r) B @ A and the base bias
A new LoRALinear with doubled rank, initialized from the current A and B values
questions.explanation: merge() builds a new nn.Linear on the same device and dtype, copies base.weight + scaling * (B @ A) into its weight and copies the bias. The result is an ordinary layer.

questions.question: In the from-scratch LoRALinear, how are the dtype and device of A and B chosen?
options: They are always float32 on CPU
They match the base weight's dtype and device
They are always float16 on GPU
They are chosen by the optimizer at the first step
questions.explanation: A and B are created with dtype=w.dtype and device=w.device, matching the wrapped base weight. This keeps the forward sum on one device with one dtype.

questions.question: Which initializer does the from-scratch LoRALinear apply to A?
options: nn.init.kaiming_uniform_ with a = sqrt(5)
nn.init.zeros_, the same as B, so B A = 0
nn.init.ones_ scaled by 1 / sqrt(in_features)
nn.init.orthogonal_ with gain = sqrt(2)
questions.explanation: A is created empty and initialized with kaiming_uniform_(a=sqrt(5)), the same default nn.Linear uses. B is created with torch.zeros and stays zero.

questions.question: Why does LoRA add zero inference cost after merge()?
options: By linearity, W x + (alpha / r) B (A x) = (W + (alpha / r) B A) x, so one matmul with W' does both
Because the adapter is discarded after training and only the original base weights are deployed
Because inference runs only through the frozen base path, while A and B are used during training only
Because A and B are quantized to zero bits at export, so their multiplies cost nothing at runtime
questions.explanation: Linearity lets you fold the scaled B A into W once. The deployed model is byte-for-byte a normal GPT with plain nn.Linear layers, so there are no extra A/B multiplies at inference.

questions.question: What does a helper like mark_only_lora_trainable(model) do?
options: Wraps every nn.Linear in a LoRALinear and leaves all parameters with requires_grad True
Merges every adapter into its base weight, then deletes A and B from each LoRALinear
Deletes all non-LoRA parameters from the model, so only A and B remain in memory
Sets requires_grad = False on all parameters, then True on every LoRALinear's A and B
questions.explanation: It first freezes every parameter, then re-enables gradients for A and B of each LoRALinear module. The base weights stay in the model but are frozen.

questions.question: When training a LoRA model with AdamW, which parameters should be passed to the optimizer?
options: All of model.parameters(), since frozen ones get no gradient and so AdamW allocates nothing for them
Only the base model's parameters, since the adapters are updated by a separate rule
Only those with requires_grad = True, e.g. [p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad]
Only the embedding parameters, since they are the ones LoRA's adapters attach to
questions.explanation: Passing only trainable parameters ensures AdamW does not allocate moment tensors for frozen weights. Handing it all parameters wastes optimizer memory even if the frozen ones never update.

questions.question: What key observation underlies QLoRA?
options: Because the adapters are tiny, they can be stored in 1-bit precision while the base stays in full fp16
Because the base is frozen, full precision is needed only for the matmul, never for an optimizer update
Because gradients are sparse, backward can be skipped for most layers of the frozen base model
Because activations are low-rank, they can be compressed to 4-bit without any loss of accuracy at all
questions.explanation: The frozen base never gets an optimizer update, so it does not need to be stored in full precision. QLoRA stores it in 4-bit and dequantizes on the fly for the matmul.

questions.question: How does QLoRA store and use the frozen base weights?
options: In 8-bit integers, used directly in integer matmuls and never dequantized to compute precision
In 4-bit NF4, dequantizing each block to compute precision on the fly during the matmul
In fp32 on the CPU, streaming each layer's weights to the GPU just before its matmul
In fp16 on the GPU, while the trainable LoRA adapters are stored in 4-bit NF4
questions.explanation: QLoRA stores the frozen base in a 4-bit format called NF4 and dequantizes each weight block to compute precision during the matmul. The small LoRA adapters stay in higher precision.

questions.question: Why is QLoRA's 4-bit format called NF4 suited to model weights?
options: It is matched to the roughly normal distribution of weights
It is matched to the uniform distribution of token ids in the vocabulary
It stores only the sign of each weight plus one scale per tensor
It uses a learned codebook trained separately for every layer
questions.explanation: NF4 is a special 4-bit format whose levels are matched to the roughly normal distribution of neural-network weights.

questions.question: In QLoRA, where do the gradients and optimizer state live?
options: In the 4-bit frozen base weights, updated through a straight-through estimator
In a dequantized fp16 copy of the base, kept permanently in memory
Nowhere; QLoRA updates the adapters in closed form without an optimizer
In the small LoRA adapters A and B, kept in higher precision
questions.explanation: The base is frozen and quantized, so it has no gradients or optimizer state. All of that lives in the higher-precision adapters A and B.

questions.question: How much does QLoRA shrink the memory of the frozen base weights relative to fp16?
options: About 2x
About 16x
About 4x
Not at all; only the adapters shrink
questions.explanation: Going from 16-bit to 4-bit storage shrinks the frozen base about 4x. A 7B model is about 14 GB in fp16.

questions.question: Besides NF4, which engineering techniques are part of QLoRA?
options: Mixture-of-experts routing and speculative decoding
Gradient checkpointing and tensor parallelism only
Double quantization and paged optimizers
Rotary embeddings and grouped-query attention
questions.explanation: The QLoRA paper's engineering includes NF4, double quantization, and paged optimizers. The core concept is simply LoRA plus a 4-bit frozen base.

questions.question: Which parts of the LoRA paper are recommended for close reading?
options: Only the related-work section, which surveys adapter and prefix methods
The rank-ablation section and the 'which weights to adapt' section
Only the appendix listing the GPT-3 hyperparameters used for each task
Only the introduction and the conclusion, skipping all experiments
questions.explanation: The rank-ablation section shows how small r can be, and the 'which weights to adapt' section shows that attention q and v projections give the most per parameter.

questions.question: According to the LoRA paper, which weights give the most benefit per parameter when adapted?
options: The attention q and v projections
The token embedding matrix and LM head
The final layer norm gain and bias
The MLP output projection bias terms
questions.explanation: The 'which weights to adapt' section reports that adapting the attention query and value projections gives the most quality per trainable parameter.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: the production library
questions.question: What does PEFT's get_peft_model(model, LoraConfig(r=8, lora_alpha=16, target_modules=['c_attn'])) do?
options: Quantizes the whole model to 4-bit NF4 and then trains all weights with paged AdamW optimizer state
Merges an existing adapter into the c_attn weights, then discards the adapter and unfreezes the model
Replaces the c_attn attention with a rank-8 low-rank approximation of each full pretrained weight matrix
Wraps matching linears with LoRA adapters, marks only adapters trainable, and saves/loads just adapter weights
questions.explanation: PEFT wraps target linears with a frozen base plus rank-r A/B adapters scaled by alpha/r, with B zero-initialized, marks only adapters trainable, saves just adapter weights, and provides a merge step.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: the production library
questions.question: How is QLoRA done with HuggingFace PEFT?
options: A separate QLoRA library that replaces PEFT and its LoraConfig entirely
By setting r = 4 in LoraConfig, which makes PEFT store adapters in 4 bits
By quantizing only the LoRA adapters to 4-bit while keeping the base in fp16
The same LoRA call on a 4-bit-quantized base model, via bitsandbytes
questions.explanation: QLoRA in PEFT is the same get_peft_model call applied to a base model quantized to 4-bit with bitsandbytes. Setting r = 4 just changes the rank.

questions.question: What goes wrong if LoRA's B is initialized to nonzero values?
options: The adapter cannot receive gradients, because a nonzero B blocks backprop into A entirely
The rank of B A grows larger than r, so the update is no longer low-rank and memory grows
Delta W is nonzero at step 0, so training starts from a perturbed model and often loses quality
merge() raises a shape error, because it assumes B is still all zeros when folding into W
questions.explanation: A nonzero B means B A is not zero at init, so the wrapped layer no longer matches the pretrained model. Training starts from a perturbed point and quality often drops.

questions.question: What happens if you forget to freeze the base weight in a LoRA setup?
options: The adapters stop receiving gradients, because the base weight absorbs the entire update
The optimizer trains the base too, so you pay for LoRA while doing a (worse) full fine-tune
The model's outputs collapse to zero, since base and adapter gradients cancel each other
merge() produces a smaller layer, since the trained base and the adapter are folded twice
questions.explanation: If the base keeps requires_grad = True, it gets gradients and optimizer state. You lose LoRA's memory savings while doing a muddled full fine-tune. Verify with sum(p.requires_grad for p in ...).

questions.question: Why is materializing B @ A in every LoRA forward pass a mistake?
options: It builds an out x in matrix each step and throws away the compute savings
It gives a numerically different output from B (A x), breaking the merge identity
It makes the adapter non-differentiable, so A and B stop receiving any gradient
It changes the rank of the update from r to min(in, out) at every step
questions.explanation: The result is mathematically the same, but computing the full product each step costs out x in memory and FLOPs. Always go input to A to B.

questions.question: A fresh LoRALinear's output differs from its base layer. The code inits A with zeros then kaiming_uniform_, and B with empty then kaiming_uniform_. What is the bug?
options: B is initialized with random Kaiming noise instead of zeros, so B A is nonzero at init
A should be initialized to zero and B to random noise, so the two inits are swapped
A should not be initialized at all, since kaiming_uniform_ on A makes B A nonzero
kaiming_uniform_ should use a = 0 instead of sqrt(5), which keeps the output near base
questions.explanation: LoRA requires B = 0 at init so that B A = 0 and the fresh adapter reproduces the base exactly. Random A is fine and intended. Fix: self.B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(out_features, r)) without calling kaiming_uniform_ on it.

questions.question: Why does freezing the base weights save far more memory than the weights themselves occupy?
options: Because PyTorch automatically deletes frozen weights from GPU memory once requires_grad is set to False, freeing them
Because frozen weights are automatically stored in 4-bit, cutting their own footprint by about 4x
Because freezing halves the activation memory, which dominates over gradients and optimizer state
Gradients and optimizer state scale with trainable parameters; freezing drops about 3 extra tensors per base parameter
questions.explanation: AdamW's two moments plus the gradient are about 3 extra tensors per trainable parameter. Freezing the base removes all of that, leaving it only for A and B. The frozen weights still occupy memory but carry no gradient or optimizer state.

questions.question: For a 1024 x 1024 layer with LoRA rank r = 16, how many trainable parameters are there and what is the reduction factor?
options: 16,384 parameters, a 64x reduction
65,536 parameters, a 16x reduction
32,768 parameters, a 32x reduction
1,048,576 parameters, no reduction

questions.question: In an RLHF pipeline, what role does the reward model play?
options: It defines 'good' numerically; the policy is optimized to maximize its score
It generates the high-quality demonstrations that the SFT stage imitates token by token
It replaces the policy's tokenizer so each completion can be scored one token at a time
It is the frozen reference copy used only to compute the KL penalty during PPO updates
questions.explanation: The reward model turns human preferences into a scalar score, and RL (e.g. PPO) then optimizes the policy to maximize that score. If the reward model encodes the wrong notion of quality, the policy will faithfully optimize the wrong thing. It does not produce demonstrations, and the KL reference model is a separate frozen copy of the SFT policy.

questions.question: Why is the Bradley-Terry reward-model loss relevant even to DPO, which trains no explicit reward model?
options: DPO is derived from the Bradley-Terry preference loss, so it inherits that same foundation
DPO first trains a Bradley-Terry reward model, then distills it into the policy and discards it
DPO uses the Bradley-Terry loss only as an evaluation metric after training
DPO replaces Bradley-Terry with an absolute-score regression on human ratings
questions.explanation: DPO substitutes an implicit reward (a log-ratio of policy to reference probabilities) into the Bradley-Terry loss, so its objective is literally the Bradley-Terry negative log-likelihood. No separate reward model is ever trained. That is why understanding Bradley-Terry is the foundation for the whole preference-learning module.

questions.section: The causal story: imitation has a ceiling
questions.question: What is the structural blind spot of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) by imitation?
options: It cannot learn to follow instructions at all, because next-token loss only continues text
It needs a separately trained reward model to label every demonstration with a scalar score
It only updates the final unembedding layer, so it cannot change the model's behavior much
Every demonstration counts as equally correct, so it never learns one answer beats another
questions.explanation: SFT's next-token cross-entropy only says 'make this exact response more likely'. It never compares two responses, so it can teach a way to answer but not a preference for a good answer over a mediocre one. SFT does teach instruction following; the gap is ranking, not instruction following.

questions.section: The causal story: imitation has a ceiling
questions.question: What capability does SFT on (prompt, ideal response) pairs give a pretrained language model?
options: It makes the model rank two candidate answers by human preference
It guarantees the model's answers exceed the quality of the demonstrations
It makes the model answer instructions instead of merely continuing the text
It trains a scalar head that scores whole sequences
questions.explanation: Imitation via next-token cross-entropy on demonstrations turns a text-continuer into an instruction follower, which is a real capability jump. But it cannot rank answers, and it can at best reach the quality of its demonstrations. A scalar scoring head belongs to the reward model, not SFT.

questions.section: The causal story: imitation has a ceiling
questions.question: Why are human labelers better used for comparisons than for writing gold responses?
options: Comparisons need no prompt, so labelers can work much faster without reading any context
Judging which of two answers is better is far easier and more reliable than writing the ideal one
Writing gold responses leaks label information into the reward model's scalar head during training
Comparisons produce absolute scores that stay well calibrated across different labelers and over time
questions.explanation: Writing an ideal explanation of, say, quantum tunneling for a child is hard, while deciding which of two explanations is better is easy. Humans are therefore far more reliable at comparisons. Comparisons still need the prompt for context, and they produce a direction rather than a calibrated absolute score.

questions.section: The causal story: imitation has a ceiling
questions.question: Why can preference optimization in principle surpass SFT in output quality?
options: Preference optimization uses a larger learning rate, so it escapes SFT's local minimum and converges to a better optimum
Imitation is capped by its demonstrations, while ranking signals can push past them toward what humans prefer
Preference optimization trains on many more tokens per example than SFT, so it sees more of each good answer
SFT cannot use the chat template during training, so its outputs are always lower quality than preference-tuned ones
questions.explanation: The best behavior may lie off the SFT data distribution. Imitation is capped by the demonstrations, but optimizing against a ranking signal can move the model past them toward responses humans prefer most. The advantage is about the signal (ranking vs imitation), not learning rates or token counts.

questions.question: Why are preference datasets collected as pairwise comparisons rather than absolute scores like 'rate 7.3/10'?
options: Absolute scores cannot be stored in the standard JSON preference format, so pairs are used instead
Pairwise data lets the reward model skip reading the prompt, which halves the cost of each forward
Absolute scores would make the Bradley-Terry loss non-differentiable, so gradients could not flow
Humans are unreliable at absolute scores (calibration drifts) but reliable at saying A beats B
questions.explanation: Labelers' numeric scales drift between people and over time, so absolute ratings are noisy. Comparisons are much more consistent, and the Bradley-Terry model only needs comparisons. Storage format and differentiability are not the reason.

questions.question: In a preference record (x, y_w, y_l), what do the three elements denote?
options: x is the reward value, y_w the policy output, y_l the reference model output
x is the prompt, y_w the completion with higher length, y_l the shorter completion
x is the prompt, y_w the chosen (winning) completion, y_l the rejected (losing) completion
x is the label, y_w the importance weight of the pair, y_l the per-pair loss value
questions.explanation: Each preference record is a triple: the prompt x (possibly with conversation history), the chosen completion y_w (w for win), and the rejected completion y_l (l for lose). A labeler saw both completions for the same prompt and marked y_w as better. Length plays no role in the definition.

questions.question: What information does a single pairwise preference label carry?
options: An absolute quality score for each of the two completions, on a shared calibrated scale
Only a direction (which completion is better), not a magnitude of how much better
A per-token correctness mask marking which tokens of the chosen completion were right
The exact reward margin r_w - r_l that the reward model should output for that pair
questions.explanation: The label is just 'y_w is better than y_l' — a direction, not a magnitude. The reward model must learn scalar rewards whose differences explain these directions. No absolute scores or target margins are provided.

questions.question: Which well-known datasets have exactly the (prompt, chosen, rejected) shape?
options: Anthropic's HH-RLHF and OpenAI's InstructGPT preference data
ImageNet and CIFAR-10, the standard labeled image-classification sets
The Pile and C4, the large web-text pretraining corpora
SQuAD and Natural Questions, the extractive QA benchmarks
questions.explanation: Anthropic's helpful/harmless HH-RLHF data and OpenAI's InstructGPT comparison data consist of thousands of (prompt, chosen, rejected) rows. The Pile and C4 are raw pretraining text, and SQuAD-style datasets are extractive QA with span labels, not preferences.

questions.question: Why must a reward function be written r(x, y) rather than r(y)?
options: Because the reward model needs the prompt x to build its tokenizer vocabulary for each batch
Because scoring r(y) alone would require two forward passes per completion instead of one
A preference is always relative to a prompt; an answer is only 'good for this question'
Because the prompt x carries the label that tells the model which completion actually won
questions.explanation: The two completions in a pair share the same prompt, and quality only makes sense in context: a great answer to one question is a bad answer to another. So the reward always conditions on both prompt and completion. The prompt does not carry the label; the ordering (chosen vs rejected) does.

questions.question: What does the Bradley-Terry model say about the probability that y_w beats y_l?
options: It is the ratio r(x, y_w) / r(x, y_l) of the two rewards, clipped to lie in [0, 1]
It is a hard step: 1 if r(x, y_w) > r(x, y_l) and 0 otherwise, with no in-between
It is the sigmoid (smooth and increasing) of the difference r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l)
It is the softmax of the two rewards taken over the whole vocabulary at the last token
questions.explanation: Bradley-Terry sets P(y_w > y_l | x) = sigmoid(r_w - r_l). A large positive margin makes the win nearly certain; equal rewards give 0.5, a coin flip. It is smooth, not a hard step, and it uses the difference, not the ratio, of rewards.

questions.question: In the Bradley-Terry model, what is the logistic sigmoid and what is sigma(0)?
options: sigma(z) = e^{z}/(1+e^{z})^2, mapping reals to (0,1), with sigma(0) = 0.25
sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z}), mapping reals to (0,1), with sigma(0) = 0.5
sigma(z) = max(0, z), mapping reals to [0, infinity), with sigma(0) = 0
sigma(z) = tanh(z), mapping reals to (-1,1), with sigma(0) = 0
questions.explanation: The logistic sigmoid is 1/(1+exp(-z)), the same function used in logistic regression. It maps any real margin into a probability in (0,1), and at zero margin it gives exactly 0.5. e^z/(1+e^z)^2 is the sigmoid's derivative, whose value at 0 is 0.25.

questions.question: In P(y_w ≻ y_l | x), how is the symbol ≻ read?
options: 'is preferred to'
'is longer than'
'is generated after'
'is a prefix of'
questions.explanation: The symbol ≻ denotes a preference relation: y_w ≻ y_l reads 'y_w is preferred to y_l'. The whole expression is the probability, given prompt x, that the chosen completion is preferred over the rejected one.

questions.question: What is the 'reward margin' in the Bradley-Terry model, and what role does it play?
options: r(x, y_w) + r(x, y_l); it normalizes the probability to sum to one
The gap between the reward and the KL penalty; it sets the learning rate
The absolute value of r(x, y_w); it decides whether the completion is accepted
r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l); it is the only quantity the preference probability depends on
questions.explanation: The margin is the chosen reward minus the rejected reward, and P(y_w ≻ y_l | x) = sigmoid(margin). Nothing else about the rewards enters the probability. That is why only differences, not absolute reward levels, are learned.

questions.question: If a constant c is added to every reward (r → r + c), what happens to the Bradley-Terry probabilities?
options: All probabilities shift toward 1 by an amount that grows in proportion to c
All probabilities are multiplied by e^c and then renormalized to sum to one
The loss becomes undefined unless c is zero, since sigmoid needs centered inputs
Nothing; every margin is unchanged, so every probability is unchanged
questions.explanation: Adding c to both r_w and r_l cancels in r_w - r_l, and the probability depends only on that difference. Hence r and r + c give identical preferences and identical loss. The reward is therefore defined only up to an additive constant.

questions.question: What does it mean that a Bradley-Terry reward is 'defined only up to an additive constant'?
options: The reward is always shifted during training so that its mean over the dataset is exactly zero
Absolute reward values are meaningless; training only determines differences between rewards
The reward must be added to a fixed constant baseline before it can be used as a PPO signal
The reward head has a bias term that is frozen at its initial value throughout training
questions.explanation: Because the loss depends only on margins, training can never pin down the absolute level of the reward — any shift gives the same loss. A reward of +4.2 alone is uninterpretable; only comparisons are meaningful. Nothing forces zero mean; that would be an additional normalization choice.

questions.question: How is the reward-model training objective derived from the Bradley-Terry model?
options: By maximum likelihood of the observed preferences, i.e. minimizing -E[log sigmoid(r_w - r_l)]
By regression: minimize the squared error between r_w and a human-assigned absolute 1-10 score
By maximizing r_w alone with gradient ascent, ignoring r_l since it carries no signal
By minimizing the KL divergence between the reward model's outputs and the SFT model's
questions.explanation: Training chooses r to maximize the likelihood of the preferences actually observed. Taking the log and negating gives L_RM = -E[log sigmoid(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l))]. There are no human scores to regress on, and maximizing r_w alone would ignore the comparison.

questions.question: The per-pair Bradley-Terry loss -log sigmoid(r_w - r_l) is equivalent to which familiar loss?
options: Mean squared error between the two rewards, pushing r_w and r_l toward each other
Multiclass cross-entropy over the full vocabulary, computed at the last real token of y_w
Hinge loss max(0, 1 - (r_w - r_l)), with a fixed margin of one between the rewards
Binary cross-entropy with the reward margin as logit and the label always 'chosen wins'
questions.explanation: Logistic regression's binary cross-entropy with logit z and positive label is -log sigmoid(z). Here z is the reward margin and the target is always 1 (chosen wins). It is smooth, unlike a hinge loss, and has nothing to do with vocabulary cross-entropy.

questions.question: What is the Bradley-Terry loss when the reward margin is exactly zero?
options: 0, because the two rewards agree so there is nothing to correct
1, because sigmoid(0) = 1 and the loss equals that probability
log 2 ≈ 0.693, the maximum-uncertainty coin-flip value
Infinity, because sigmoid(0) = 0 and log(0) is undefined
questions.explanation: At margin 0, sigmoid(0) = 0.5, so the loss is -log 0.5 = log 2 ≈ 0.693147. That corresponds to the model being completely unsure which completion wins. The loss is zero only in the limit of an infinitely large positive margin.

questions.question: How does the Bradley-Terry loss -log sigmoid(r_w - r_l) behave as the margin grows?
options: It is strictly decreasing and approaches 0 as the margin goes to +infinity
It is minimized at margin 0 and grows in both directions, like a squared error
It drops to exactly 0 once the margin is positive and stays constant after that
It increases with the margin, penalizing overconfident reward models
questions.explanation: As the margin increases, sigmoid(margin) → 1 and -log of it → 0; e.g. margin 1 gives 0.313, margin 4 gives 0.018. So minimizing the loss pushes the chosen reward above the rejected one. It never becomes exactly constant, and it does not penalize large positive margins.

questions.question: Two pairs have rewards (r_w, r_l) = (2.0, 1.0) and (1.5, 0.5). How do their Bradley-Terry losses compare?
options: They are identical, since both have margin 1.0
The first is larger because its rewards are larger
The second is larger because its rejected reward is smaller
They cannot be compared without knowing the prompt
questions.explanation: The Bradley-Terry loss depends only on r_w - r_l. Both pairs have margin 1.0, so both give sigmoid(1.0) = 0.731 and loss 0.313. Absolute reward levels play no role.

questions.question: Why should the Bradley-Terry loss be computed as -F.logsigmoid(margin) rather than -torch.log(torch.sigmoid(margin))?
options: logsigmoid is faster because it skips the backward pass and computes only the forward value
torch.sigmoid has no autograd support, so the loss would train nothing without the fused op
log(sigmoid(x)) gives a different mathematical value than logsigmoid(x), so results would be systematically biased
Large negative margins make sigmoid underflow to 0 so log gives -inf; logsigmoid is one stable kernel
questions.explanation: Mathematically they are equal, but numerically sigmoid of a very negative number underflows to 0.0 and its log becomes -infinity. F.logsigmoid computes the result in one stable kernel using the softplus identity log(1+exp(.)) and never overflows. It still supports backprop normally.

questions.question: Which identity does F.logsigmoid use internally to stay numerically stable?
options: The identity log sigmoid(x) = x - x^2/2 (Taylor expansion)
Clamping sigmoid(x) to at least 1e-8 before taking the log
The softplus identity: log sigmoid(x) = -log(1 + exp(-x))
Computing sigmoid in float64 and casting back
questions.explanation: log sigmoid(x) = -softplus(-x) = -log(1+exp(-x)), and softplus can be evaluated stably with standard tricks. This is the same reasoning as the stable log-softmax: avoid forming a probability that underflows and then taking its log. Clamping or upcasting are hacks, not what the kernel does.

questions.section: What is a reward model, mechanically?
questions.question: Mechanically, how does a reward model differ from a GPT language model?
options: It has no attention layers, only an MLP over the pooled embeddings
Its lm_head of shape (C → V) is replaced by a scalar head of shape (C → 1)
It uses a bidirectional encoder instead of causal self-attention
It adds a second vocabulary head that predicts special reward tokens
questions.explanation: A reward model is the same transformer backbone with its vocabulary head swapped for a linear head that outputs one number. That head reads one position's hidden state and outputs the reward for the whole sequence. The backbone, including causal attention, is unchanged.

questions.section: What is a reward model, mechanically?
questions.question: At which position is the scalar reward read off the transformer's hidden states?
options: At the first token of the prompt
At the last (real, non-pad) token
At the mean of all positions
At the first token of the completion
questions.explanation: The reward summarizes the entire prompt+completion, so it is read at the final real token. This is the convention used by InstructGPT and HH-RLHF. Reading at a pad token or the first token would miss information or read garbage.

questions.section: What is a reward model, mechanically?
questions.question: Why is the last token's hidden state the natural place to read a sequence-level reward in a causal transformer?
options: The last token has the largest hidden-state norm, so the reward read there is numerically more stable
The last token is always the end-of-sequence token, which carries the preference label itself
Earlier tokens' hidden states are discarded after the forward pass, so only the last remains
With causal attention only the final token has attended over the entire prompt+completion
questions.explanation: In causal attention each token attends only to itself and earlier tokens. Therefore only the final token's hidden state depends on every token of the sequence, making it the right place to pool into one score. Norms and EOS labels are not the reason.

questions.section: What is a reward model, mechanically?
questions.question: Given backbone hidden state h_T in R^C at the last position, what is the reward model's output?
options: r(x) = softmax(W h_T) with W in R^{V×C}
r(x) = ||h_T||_2, the norm of the final hidden state
r(x) = w^T h_T + b, with w in R^C and b a scalar
r(x) = sum over t of w^T h_t, summing over all positions
questions.explanation: The scalar head is a single linear map: one dot product with a weight vector w plus a bias b, applied to the last hidden state. That is the entire reward model on top of the backbone. It does not use a vocabulary softmax or sum over positions.

questions.section: What is a reward model, mechanically?
questions.question: For a reward model on a batch of token ids of shape (B, T), what are the shapes of the hidden states, the head output, and the final rewards?
options: Hidden (B, C); head output (B, 1); rewards (B, T), one reward per token position
Hidden (B, T, C); head output (B, T, 1) squeezed to (B, T); rewards (B,)
Hidden (B, T, V); head output (B, T, V); rewards (B, V), one per vocabulary entry
Hidden (T, C); head output (T,); rewards a single scalar for the whole batch
questions.explanation: Token ids are (B, T) int64; the backbone produces (B, T, C) float hidden states; nn.Linear(C, 1) gives (B, T, 1), squeezed to (B, T); then one position per row is picked, giving a (B,) vector of rewards — one float per sequence. V-sized outputs belong to the language-model head, not the reward head.

questions.section: What is a reward model, mechanically?
questions.question: With right-padded batches of mixed lengths, how should the reward be gathered per sequence?
options: Index each row at seq_lengths - 1, the last real token, instead of a blanket -1
Always index position -1, because padding tokens have zero hidden states and do not interfere
Average the scores over all positions including padding, so every token contributes equally
Index position 0 for every row, since padding is only on the right and position 0 is always real
questions.explanation: With right padding, position -1 may be a pad token for shorter sequences, so the reward would be read at garbage. Gathering at seq_lengths - 1 per row reads the last real token. Pad hidden states are not zero, and position 0 sees only the first token.

questions.section: What is a reward model, mechanically?
questions.question: In reward_from_hidden, what does the code scores[rows, idx] with rows = torch.arange(B) and idx = (seq_lengths - 1).clamp(min=0) compute?
options: A (B, B) matrix holding every row's score at every other row's last index
The maximum score over each row's valid tokens, ignoring the padding positions
For each row b, the score at that row's last real token, giving a (B,) tensor
The score at position 0 for every row, with the clamp zeroing out empty sequences
questions.explanation: Advanced indexing with paired index vectors picks one element per row: scores[b, idx[b]]. With idx = seq_lengths - 1, that is the last non-pad position, and the clamp prevents negative indices for empty sequences. Pairing two (B,) index tensors yields (B,), not (B, B).

questions.section: What is a reward model, mechanically?
questions.question: In the from-scratch RewardModel, what does 'backbone-agnostic' mean?
options: It works without any hidden states at all, scoring the raw token ids with a lookup table
It automatically converts any model's vocabulary head into a scalar head at load time
It accepts any backbone returning (B, T, C) hidden states, or takes hidden states directly
It can only be used with the GPT-2 backbone from Module 6, whose hidden size it hard-codes
questions.explanation: RewardModel only needs (B, T, C) hidden states: either from a provided backbone or passed in directly via reward_from_hidden (as in the unit tests with backbone=None). The scalar head and last-token gather are all it adds. It does not operate on raw ids alone.

questions.section: What is a reward model, mechanically?
questions.question: What does one training step of a reward model on a preference pair consist of?
options: Generate a completion from the reward model, score it, and update with a REINFORCE gradient
Forward chosen and rejected, compute -logsigmoid(r_w - r_l), backprop, optimizer step
Forward only the chosen completion and maximize its next-token likelihood, as in SFT
Compute the KL between chosen and rejected token distributions and minimize it with Adam
questions.explanation: Reward-model training is ordinary supervised learning on pairs: two forwards (chosen and rejected), the Bradley-Terry loss on their reward margin, backward, and step. Over iterations the margin grows and the loss falls. No generation or RL is involved at this stage.

questions.question: How is a reward model usually initialized in practice?
options: From the SFT model, so it already understands language and the chat format
From random weights, so the reward model does not inherit the SFT model's biases
From the pretrained base model's vocabulary head only, with a freshly initialized backbone
From a smaller distilled model, to save compute on the many reward forward passes
questions.explanation: Starting from the SFT checkpoint means the backbone already understands language and the chat template; only the scalar head needs to be taught and the backbone lightly adapted to rank. This reuse is why the reward model and policy are usually the same size. Training from scratch would waste the existing capability.

questions.question: Why are the reward model and policy in RLHF usually the same size?
options: PPO requires their parameter counts to match exactly to compute the KL
The reward model's scalar head must have as many weights as the policy's vocabulary head
Smaller reward models cannot represent the sigmoid function
Both are initialized from the same SFT model
questions.explanation: The reward model is typically initialized from the SFT model, which is also the starting point of the policy, so they share the backbone architecture and size. Nothing in PPO's math requires equal sizes; it is a consequence of reuse.

questions.question: What is the compute cost of reward-model training per preference pair?
options: One forward pass plus autoregressive generation of a new completion
One forward pass of the scalar head only, since the backbone is frozen
Four forward passes: policy, reference, reward, and value models
Two full forward passes (chosen and rejected), with no generation involved
questions.explanation: Each reward evaluation is one full backbone forward, the same FLOPs as an SFT forward, and a pair needs two. There is no sampling, which makes reward-model training far cheaper than the PPO loop. Four models are the PPO setup, not reward-model training.

questions.question: How many parameters does the scalar reward head add to GPT-2 small (C = 768)?
options: 768 × 50257 ≈ 38.6M, the same size as the vocabulary head it replaces
769 (768 weights plus one bias), negligible next to the backbone's ~124M
About 124M, because the head duplicates the whole backbone and doubles the model
768 × 768 ≈ 590K, a full square projection followed by mean pooling
questions.explanation: nn.Linear(768, 1) has 768 weights and 1 bias = 769 parameters. That is tiny compared with the 124M-parameter backbone. The vocabulary head (768 × 50257) is what gets thrown away.

questions.question: What hardware is recommended for training a 7B reward model from an SFT checkpoint, and can CPU be used?
options: 1× A100 40GB recommended; CPU only suffices for the tiny unit tests, not a useful model
8× H100 recommended; CPU is fine for a 7B reward model as long as LoRA adapters are used
A single 8GB consumer GPU is enough, and CPU runs reward-model training equally fast
No GPU is needed at all, because the scalar head adds only C + 1 trainable parameters
questions.explanation: The hardware guidance is min 1× 24GB GPU for a ~1B backbone with LoRA and recommended 1× A100 40GB for a 7B backbone, taking a few hours over ~100k pairs. The from-scratch RewardModel tests run in milliseconds on CPU, but training a useful reward model on CPU is impractical. The head is tiny but the backbone forward passes are not.

questions.question: What goes wrong if a right-padded batch reads the reward with scores[:, -1]?
options: The loss becomes negative, because pad tokens produce negative scores that flip the margin
The gradient flows only to the head's bias term, so the backbone never gets updated
Nothing; causal attention makes pad positions identical to the last real token's state
Shorter sequences have their reward read at a pad token instead of their last real token
questions.explanation: With right padding, the final position of shorter rows is padding, so scores[:, -1] reads a meaningless value. Passing seq_lengths lets the code gather at the last real token. Pad positions are not equivalent to real tokens.

questions.question: Why should one never threshold a Bradley-Terry reward model's absolute reward across different prompts?
options: Absolute rewards are always negative after training, so any positive threshold is meaningless
Thresholding makes the reward non-differentiable, so PPO could no longer backprop through it
Only margins are trained; the absolute level is arbitrary and not comparable across prompts
Absolute rewards are only valid at the first token, not at the last real token of the reply
questions.explanation: The reward is defined only up to an additive constant, and nothing in training ties the level for one prompt to another. A reward of +4.2 on its own carries no meaning. Comparisons within a prompt are what the model learned.

questions.question: Why do reward models in RLHF need to be periodically refreshed?
options: The improving policy produces completions unlike any the reward model saw (distribution shift)
Reward-model weights slowly decay numerically over time when they are stored in bfloat16
The Bradley-Terry loss diverges after one epoch, so the model must be retrained from scratch
The policy's tokenizer changes during PPO, so old reward models can no longer read its outputs
questions.explanation: The reward model was trained on completions from earlier policies. As RLHF moves the policy, it generates outputs off that training distribution, where the reward model's scores are unreliable. Refreshing with new preference data on current-policy samples keeps the reward model relevant.

questions.question: What is 'preference accuracy' for a reward model?
options: The fraction of pairs where the model already ranks chosen above rejected (r_w > r_l)
The average of sigmoid(r_w - r_l) over the dataset, i.e. the mean predicted win probability
The fraction of tokens where the reward model predicts the next token correctly
The correlation between the model's rewards and human absolute 1-10 quality ratings
questions.explanation: Preference accuracy counts how often the margin is positive: (margin > 0).float().mean(). It only needs the sign of the margin, not the sigmoid. It is the standard metric reported next to the reward-model loss.

questions.question: What preference accuracy is typical at the start of reward-model training versus for a well-trained model on held-out human data?
options: About 0.0 at the start; about 0.99 when well trained
About 0.5 at the start; about 0.95 when well trained
About 0.25 at the start; about 0.5 when well trained
About 0.5 at the start; about 0.65–0.75 when well trained
questions.explanation: An untrained model ranks pairs at random, giving ~0.5. A good reward model reaches roughly 0.65–0.75 on held-out human preferences. Expecting ~0.95+ is unrealistic because human labelers themselves only agree about 70% of the time.

questions.question: Why is ~70% held-out accuracy close to the ceiling for a reward model trained on human preferences?
options: The sigmoid saturates at 0.7 for typical margins, capping accuracy
The reward head has only C + 1 parameters, too few to fit the data better
Human labelers themselves only agree with each other about 70% of the time
Distribution shift always costs about 30% accuracy on held-out data
questions.explanation: Preference labels are noisy: different humans disagree on roughly 30% of pairs. No model can consistently predict a label that humans themselves cannot agree on, so ~0.65–0.75 accuracy approaches the achievable limit. The sigmoid does not saturate at 0.7.

questions.question: A reward model's loss is stuck exactly at 0.6931 with non-zero gradients. What does this value indicate?
options: The learning rate is too large, so the loss oscillates and its running mean sits at 0.6931
Every margin r_w - r_l is zero, since 0.6931 = log 2 = -log sigmoid(0)
The model perfectly separates every pair, and 0.6931 is the floor of the loss
The loss is being computed with torch.log instead of F.logsigmoid, which adds log 2
questions.explanation: -log sigmoid(0) = log 2 ≈ 0.6931, so a loss pinned there means the chosen and rejected rewards are identical for every pair. The reward model cannot see any difference between the inputs. A perfect model would have loss near 0.

questions.question: What bugs typically cause a reward-model loss pinned at exactly log 2?
options: Using plain SGD instead of Adam, which cannot move the reward margin away from zero
Chosen and rejected inputs end up identical (same tensor twice, or both read at shared padding)
Initializing from the SFT checkpoint, whose language-model features cannot distinguish two completions
Reading the reward at the last real token instead of position 0, where the prompt begins
questions.explanation: A margin of exactly zero for every pair means both rewards come from the same input: the same tensor passed twice, chosen/rejected swapped into the same variable, or the last-token index landing on a shared pad position. The fix is to check that reward_chosen and reward_rejected come from genuinely different inputs. Optimizer choice and SFT initialization would not produce exact zero margins.

questions.question: Which papers are core readings for the reward-modeling part of RLHF?
options: Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al. 2017) and BERT (Devlin et al. 2019)
Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al. 2022) and Kaplan scaling laws (2020)
FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022) and ZeRO (Rajbhandari et al. 2020)
InstructGPT (Ouyang et al. 2022) and Anthropic HH-RLHF (Bai et al. 2022)
questions.explanation: InstructGPT's reward-model section defines the Bradley-Terry loss and the 'reward at the final token' convention, and Anthropic's HH-RLHF describes collecting helpful/harmless preference data at scale. The recommendation is to read the reward-modeling subsections closely and skim the RL details. The other pairs cover architecture, scaling, or systems.

questions.question: Why does the Bradley-Terry model fit pairwise labels naturally?
options: It requires an absolute quality score per completion, which each labeled pair provides for both sides
It models the probability of each token in the chosen completion, conditioned on the prompt
It maps a pair of rewards to sigmoid(r_w - r_l), the exact event a comparison label supervises
It ignores the rejected completion entirely and only pushes up the chosen completion's score
questions.explanation: Bradley-Terry needs only comparisons: P(y_w ≻ y_l) = sigmoid(r_w - r_l). A pairwise label 'y_w won' is exactly the event whose likelihood it models. It never needs absolute scores, and it uses both completions.

questions.question: What does the scalar reward head of a reward model consist of?
options: An nn.Linear(C, V) followed by a softmax over the vocabulary
An nn.Linear(C, 1) applied to the last real token's hidden state
A two-layer MLP applied to every token and summed
A learned embedding table indexed by the last token id
questions.explanation: The head is a single linear map from the hidden dimension C to one output, applied at the last non-pad position. It turns the summary hidden state into a scalar reward. A C → V head with softmax is the language-model head that was removed.

questions.question: Which algorithm is the 'RL' in classic RLHF as used by InstructGPT and the first ChatGPT?
options: PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization)
DPO (Direct Preference Optimization)
GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization)
Q-learning with a replay buffer
questions.explanation: InstructGPT and the first ChatGPT used PPO to turn a reward model into a better policy. DPO and GRPO came later and are best understood by contrast with PPO's clipped objective and KL term. Q-learning is not the standard LLM RLHF algorithm.

questions.section: The causal story: a reward is not a loss
questions.question: Why can't an LLM be improved with RLHF by simply calling reward.backward() on the reward-model score?
options: Sampling a token from the policy is not differentiable, so the reward has no gradient path back to the weights
The reward model is frozen during PPO, so its parameters block any gradient from reaching the policy weights
The reward is one scalar per sequence, and autograd can only backpropagate from per-token losses, not sequence scores
Backpropagating through both the reward model and the policy would double activation memory and exceed GPU capacity
questions.explanation: The policy produces tokens by sampling from its distribution, and there is no derivative of 'which token got drawn' with respect to the weights. So the reward's dependence on the policy parameters cannot be traced by autograd. RL's policy gradient instead uses the reward value times the gradient of the log-probability of the action taken.

questions.section: The causal story: a reward is not a loss
questions.question: What is the key difference between the training signal in SFT and in RLHF?
options: SFT optimizes a scalar reward from a learned critic; RLHF optimizes cross-entropy against a gold token sequence
SFT must sample completions from the model before each update; RLHF trains on a fixed dataset with no sampling
SFT updates only the value head on top of a frozen backbone; RLHF updates every weight of the whole model
SFT has a differentiable target (the gold token); RLHF has only a scalar reward on a sampled output
questions.explanation: SFT minimizes cross-entropy against known gold tokens, which is ordinary backprop. RLHF only receives a number from the reward model after the model has sampled a completion, and the sampling step blocks the gradient. The policy gradient is the trick that recovers a usable gradient from the reward value.

questions.section: The language model as a policy
questions.question: When viewing a language model as an RL policy, what are the state, action, and policy?
options: State: the reward-model score so far; action: one optimizer gradient step; policy: the Adam update rule
State: the full vocabulary embedding table; action: choosing the next prompt; policy: the reward model
State: the context so far; action: the next token; policy: the model's softmax over the next token
State: the final hidden vector; action: which attention head fires next; policy: the KL penalty term
questions.explanation: In RL vocabulary, the state s is the tokens generated so far, the action a is the next emitted token, and the policy pi_theta(a | s) is exactly the softmax over logits the model already computes. Nothing new is added; it is a renaming. The reward model supplies the reward, not the policy.

questions.section: The language model as a policy
questions.question: In LLM RLHF, when is the reward given during a generation?
options: After every token, because the reward model scores each prefix and adds that score to the token's return
Once, at the end of the full generation (a terminal reward); intermediate tokens get no reward of their own
Only for the first generated token, since that token conditions the rest and the reward model scores it alone
At positions chosen by the value head, wherever its predicted value changes by more than the clip epsilon
questions.explanation: The reward model scores the completed sequence, so the reward is terminal. Intermediate tokens receive no separate reward. With a single terminal reward, the return attributed to every action in the sequence is that same R.

questions.section: The language model as a policy
questions.question: With a single terminal reward R per sequence, what is the return for each action (token) in that sequence?
options: R divided by the sequence length, shared equally across tokens
The same value R for every action in the sequence
Zero for every action except the last token, which gets R
R discounted geometrically by distance from the start
questions.explanation: The return is the total reward attributed to the trajectory, and with one terminal reward and no intermediate rewards, every action's return is that one R. This is what makes the simple advantage R - V exact in the single-terminal-reward case.

questions.question: What does the REINFORCE policy gradient intuitively do?
options: Copies the highest-reward sample as a new SFT target
Backpropagates the reward model's gradient through the sampled tokens into the policy weights
Lowers the temperature of sampling whenever reward increases
Nudges each action's log-probability up in proportion to the reward that followed it
questions.explanation: REINFORCE pushes up the log-probabilities of tokens in good outcomes and down in bad outcomes, scaled by how good or bad. It moves the derivative off the non-differentiable sample onto the differentiable log-probability. It never differentiates through the reward model.

questions.question: What is the REINFORCE policy-gradient identity for J(theta) = E_{y~pi_theta}[R(y)]?
options: grad J = E_{y~pi_theta}[ grad R(y) · pi_theta(y) ]
grad J = E_{y~pi_theta}[ log pi_theta(y) · grad R(y) ]
grad J = E_{y~pi_theta}[ grad log pi_theta(y) · R(y) ]
grad J = grad E_{y~pi_theta}[ R(y) ] * log R(y) / pi_theta(y)
questions.explanation: The policy gradient theorem gives grad J = E[grad log pi_theta(y) R(y)]. The gradient acts only on log pi_theta, which is differentiable; R is a constant scale. Options with grad R would require differentiating through the reward, which is exactly what is impossible.

questions.question: How is log pi_theta(y) of a whole generated sequence computed?
options: The log-probability of the final token only, since it is conditioned on every earlier token of the sequence
The sum over tokens of log pi_theta(a_t | s_t), since pi_theta(y) is a product of per-token probabilities
The log of the mean per-token probability, since averaging first keeps long and short sequences comparable
The reward model's log-score divided by sequence length, since the policy has no sequence-level probability
questions.explanation: The sequence probability factorizes autoregressively as the product of per-token conditional probabilities, so its log is the sum of per-token log-probs. These are values the model already computes from its log-softmax. Averaging probabilities before the log is not the same quantity.

questions.question: In the REINFORCE gradient, how is the reward R(y) treated?
options: As a constant that only scales the gradient; it is not differentiated through
As a differentiable function whose gradient flows back through the reward model's weights
As a learnable parameter updated alongside the policy
As a mask that zeroes out gradients for negative-reward tokens
questions.explanation: R(y) multiplies grad log pi_theta but is itself detached. Autograd differentiates only the log-probability factor. Treating R as differentiable is a common and serious bug.

questions.question: What is the 'log-derivative trick' used to derive the policy gradient?
options: grad log pi = log grad pi
grad pi = grad log pi / pi
grad pi = pi · grad log pi
log(pi · R) = log pi + log R
questions.explanation: Since grad log pi = grad pi / pi, multiplying both sides by pi gives grad pi = pi grad log pi. Substituting into grad of the integral of pi R turns the integral back into an expectation under pi of R grad log pi, which can be estimated by sampling. The other identities are false or irrelevant.

questions.question: How is the REINFORCE update implemented in PyTorch code?
options: Call reward.backward() first, then multiply every parameter's .grad by log pi_theta(y) before the step
Minimize -mean(R) directly with the optimizer, since R already depends on the policy's sampled tokens
Form the surrogate loss -mean(R · log pi_theta(y)) and call .backward(); R rides along as a constant
Compute the gradient of R with torch.autograd.grad through the sampler and add it to the weights
questions.explanation: The surrogate loss is negated because optimizers minimize, and its gradient equals minus the policy gradient. Autograd differentiates only the log-prob factor. Minimizing or differentiating R directly is impossible because R does not depend differentiably on the weights.

questions.question: Why is the raw REINFORCE gradient estimate high-variance?
options: The per-token log-probabilities are always close to zero, so tiny rounding errors dominate the gradient
R can be large and differs for every sample, so the gradient magnitude swings wildly between samples
The sigmoid at the end of the reward model saturates, so most rewards collapse to exactly 0 or 1
Autograd introduces random stochastic rounding in the backward pass whenever bf16 weights are used
questions.explanation: Each sample's gradient is scaled by its own reward, which varies a lot, so small-batch estimates are very noisy. This makes training slow and unstable. The fix is subtracting a baseline.

questions.question: If all rewards are positive, what does vanilla REINFORCE do to the sampled actions?
options: Pushes every sampled action up (some more than others), never directly saying an action was below average
Pushes every sampled action down slightly, because positive rewards are treated as an exploration penalty
Leaves the policy unchanged, because with all-positive rewards the per-sample gradients cancel out exactly
Pushes up only the single highest-reward action in the batch and leaves every other sample untouched
questions.explanation: With all-positive R, each sample's log-prob gradient is scaled by a positive number, so all are increased. It never directly signals 'that one was below average', which is a source of slow, unstable learning. A baseline fixes this by centering the signal.

questions.question: What does subtracting a baseline b(s) from the reward accomplish in the policy gradient?
options: It makes the gradient estimate biased toward the baseline, but much cheaper to compute per sampled sequence
It removes the need to compute log-probabilities, since the advantage alone now determines each token's update
It doubles the effective learning rate for good actions while leaving the update for bad actions unchanged
Actions are pushed up only if they beat expectations; variance drops while the expected gradient is unchanged
