questions.explanation: With R - b(s), an action that merely met expectations gets near-zero gradient, better-than-expected is pushed up, worse is pushed down. The baseline term integrates to zero in expectation, so the gradient stays unbiased, but its variance is drastically reduced.

questions.question: Why does subtracting a state-dependent baseline b(s) not change the policy gradient in expectation?
options: Because a learned baseline is trained to be zero on average across all states in the batch
Because the baseline is detached, so autograd never computes any gradient term involving it
Because PPO's clipping step removes the baseline's contribution before the update
The baseline term integrates to zero, since E[grad log pi] = 0 under the policy
questions.explanation: E_{a~pi}[grad log pi(a|s) · b(s)] = b(s) · grad of the sum of pi(a|s) over actions = b(s) · grad 1 = 0. So the baseline adds no bias, only reduces variance. It is not required to be zero; it is typically a learned value estimate.

questions.question: In LLM PPO, what is the baseline b(s) usually?
options: The reward model's score for the SFT model's greedy completion of the same prompt
A learned value function V(s), implemented as a second scalar 'value head' on the model
A running constant equal to the maximum reward seen so far across all earlier PPO batches
The per-token KL divergence between the current policy and the frozen reference model
questions.explanation: The baseline is typically a learned value function V(s) estimating the average return from state s. In LLM PPO it is an extra scalar head on the policy backbone. It is not the KL term or a fixed constant.

questions.question: What is the advantage A-hat in PPO with a single terminal reward?
options: A-hat = R - V(s): how much the return beat the value baseline's prediction
A-hat = R + V(s): the observed reward plus the reward the value head predicted
A-hat = V(s) / R: the fraction of the observed reward that was predicted in advance
A-hat = log pi_theta - log pi_ref: the per-token log-ratio to the reference
questions.explanation: The advantage is the return minus the baseline value. Positive means above expectation (push up), negative means below (push down). The log-ratio to the reference is the KL estimate, not the advantage.

questions.question: What does Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) do, and when does it reduce to A-hat = R - V?
options: It replaces the reward model with a learned value model; it reduces to R - V exactly when beta_KL is set to 0
It normalizes advantages to zero mean and unit variance per batch; it reduces to R - V when the batch holds one sequence
It clips each advantage into [1 - eps, 1 + eps] before the update; it reduces to R - V when eps is set to 0
It estimates advantages over multi-step trajectories; with one terminal reward per sequence, R - V is the exact case
questions.explanation: The full PPO paper uses GAE to estimate advantages from multi-step trajectories with intermediate rewards. With one terminal reward per sequence, the advantage R - V is the simple exact case implemented from scratch. Normalization (whitening) and clipping are separate mechanisms.

questions.question: Completions with rewards [1.0, 0.0, 2.0] have a value baseline of 0.5 each. What happens to the middle completion's tokens?
options: They get zero advantage and are left unchanged, because a reward of exactly zero yields no gradient
They get a positive advantage (+0.5), because 0.0 is still above the minimum reward the model can give
They get a negative advantage (-0.5) and are pushed down, even though the reward was not negative
They are dropped from the batch entirely, because zero-reward completions carry no learning signal
questions.explanation: A-hat = R - V = 0.0 - 0.5 = -0.5. The completion did worse than expected, so the baseline turns a non-negative reward into a negative signal. That is exactly the baseline doing its job.

questions.question: What does advantage 'whitening' (normalize=True in compute_advantages) do?
options: Standardizes advantages to zero mean and unit variance across the batch, a standard PPO stabilizer
Clips every advantage into the range [-1, 1] so that no single token can dominate the update
Replaces each advantage with its sign, so every token gets +1 or -1 regardless of how good it was
Adds small Gaussian noise to each advantage so the policy keeps exploring alternative tokens
questions.explanation: Whitening subtracts the batch mean and divides by the batch standard deviation. This keeps the scale of the policy-gradient signal stable across batches. It is not clipping or sign-taking.

questions.question: What problem does PPO solve relative to vanilla REINFORCE?
options: REINFORCE can use each expensive sampled batch for only one step; PPO allows several steps safely
REINFORCE cannot handle a terminal reward at the end of the sequence; PPO assigns a reward to every token
REINFORCE needs a separately trained reward model; PPO learns directly from the human preference pairs
REINFORCE cannot compute per-token log-probabilities of a sampled sequence; PPO computes them exactly
questions.explanation: Sampling (generation) is expensive, so reusing a batch for multiple optimizer steps is attractive. But after a step the policy differs from the data-generating pi_old, making the data off-policy, and a big step can wreck the policy. PPO's importance ratio plus clipping makes multiple steps per batch safe.

questions.question: In PPO, what is the probability ratio r_t?
options: r_t = pi_theta(a_t | s_t) / pi_ref(a_t | s_t), current policy vs the frozen SFT model, for the taken action
r_t = R / V(s_t), the observed reward relative to the value baseline's prediction at that token
r_t = the fraction of tokens in the batch whose probability increased since the last update
r_t = pi_theta(a_t | s_t) / pi_old(a_t | s_t), current vs data-generating policy, for the taken action
questions.explanation: r_t compares the current policy to pi_old, the policy that generated the batch, for the action actually taken. r_t = 1 means unchanged. The ratio to pi_ref appears in the KL penalty, not in the clip ratio.

questions.question: How is the PPO ratio r_t computed numerically, and why?
options: As pi_theta / pi_old directly, because computing exponentials of log-probs is slow on GPU
As log pi_theta / log pi_old, because the log-probs are already available from the forward
As exp(log pi_theta - log pi_old), because dividing raw probabilities can underflow
As sigmoid(log pi_theta - log pi_old), to keep the ratio safely bounded inside (0, 1)
questions.explanation: Token probabilities can be tiny, so dividing them directly risks underflow. Subtracting log-probs and exponentiating is stable. A ratio of log-probs is not the probability ratio, and sigmoid would wrongly bound it below 1.

questions.question: What is the PPO clipped surrogate objective?
options: E_t[ max( r_t A_t, clip(r_t, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) A_t ) ]
E_t[ min( r_t A_t, clip(r_t, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) A_t ) ]
E_t[ clip(r_t A_t, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) ]
E_t[ r_t A_t - eps * (r_t - 1)^2 ] with a squared trust penalty
questions.explanation: L_CLIP takes the minimum of the unclipped term r_t A_t and the clipped term clip(r_t, 1-eps, 1+eps) A_t. The min makes it pessimistic. Clipping the product rather than the ratio, or taking a max, would not give PPO's trust-region behavior.

questions.question: What is the typical value of PPO's clipping parameter epsilon, and what band does it define?
options: About 2.0, giving the ratio band [-1, 3]
About 0.2, giving the ratio band [0.8, 1.2]
About 0.01, giving the ratio band [0.99, 1.01]
About 0.5, giving the ratio band [0, 1]
questions.explanation: epsilon is typically 0.2, so the ratio is clipped into [1-0.2, 1+0.2] = [0.8, 1.2]. Moving the ratio outside this trust band gives no further gain in the objective.

questions.question: Why does PPO take the min of the clipped and unclipped terms?
options: It makes the objective optimistic, so that good actions are pushed up as far as the sampled batch data allows
It guarantees the objective is always negative, so the loss passed to backward() stays positive
It averages the clipped and unclipped terms, which halves the variance of the gradient estimate
It makes the objective pessimistic, removing any incentive to push the ratio outside [1 - eps, 1 + eps]
questions.explanation: Taking the smaller value means the objective never rewards moving the ratio beyond the trust band. For good actions the gain is capped once r_t > 1+eps; for bad actions the objective stops improving once r_t < 1-eps. This lets several steps be taken per batch without one update moving the policy too far.

questions.question: In PPO, for a good action (A > 0), what happens once the ratio r_t exceeds 1 + eps?
options: The objective keeps growing linearly with r_t, so the gradient pushes the probability ever higher
The objective drops to zero and the token is masked out of the batch for the remaining epochs
The objective is capped at (1 + eps) A, so pushing the probability higher gives no further gain
The objective flips sign to penalize the action for having moved too far from the old policy
questions.explanation: With A > 0, the clipped branch (1+eps)A becomes smaller than r_t A once r_t > 1+eps, and the min picks it. Because that branch is constant in r_t, its gradient is zero. So there is no incentive to shove the probability arbitrarily high in one update.

questions.question: In PPO, for a bad action (A < 0), what happens once the ratio r_t falls below 1 - eps?
options: The objective keeps improving as r_t approaches zero, so the action's probability is driven toward collapse
The objective is held constant at (1 - eps) A, so nothing drives the probability toward zero in one step
The advantage's sign is flipped to positive, so the action is now pushed back up toward the old policy
The action's log-probability is reset to the old policy's value before the next gradient step is taken
questions.explanation: With A < 0, below r_t < 1-eps the clipped term (1-eps)A is more negative than r_t A, so the min picks the constant clipped value. Its gradient is zero, so further lowering the probability gives no gain. This prevents a bad action's probability from collapsing in one update.

questions.question: In PPO with eps = 0.2, a bad action (A = -2.0) has ratio r_t = 1.5. Which branch does the min select?
options: The unclipped branch (-3.0): a bad action whose probability rose is not helped by clipping
The clipped branch (-2.4), since the ratio 1.5 is outside the band and the penalty must be capped
Neither branch; outside the trust band the objective is defined as zero, so there is no gradient
The clipped branch (-1.6), using the lower band edge 0.8 because the advantage is negative
questions.explanation: Unclipped = 1.5 × (-2) = -3.0; clipped = 1.2 × (-2) = -2.4. The min is -3.0, the unclipped term. So when a bad action's probability went up, PPO keeps the full penalty and its gradient — clipping only removes incentives, it never shields a harmful change.

questions.question: Is the PPO clipped objective L_CLIP maximized or minimized, and what loss is backpropagated?
options: L_CLIP is minimized directly as the training loss
L_CLIP is maximized; the training loss is 1 / L_CLIP
L_CLIP is maximized; the training loss is -L_CLIP
L_CLIP is minimized; the training loss is exp(L_CLIP)
questions.explanation: L_CLIP is an objective to maximize because higher means more advantage-weighted probability on good actions. Optimizers minimize, so the loss passed to backward() is its negation. Confusing the sign is a common mistake.

questions.question: In a from-scratch PPO implementation, which of logprobs, old_logprobs, and advantages carry gradients?
options: All three carry gradients, since each depends on the current policy's forward pass
Only advantages, since they come from the trainable value head and must be updated
Only logprobs; old_logprobs and advantages are detached constants
Only old_logprobs, since they define the trust region the ratio is measured against
questions.explanation: logprobs come from the current policy and must carry grad so the ratio can be differentiated. old_logprobs (from pi_old) and advantages are fixed per batch and .detach()ed. All three have the same elementwise shape, e.g. (N,) over N tokens, and the objective is reduced with .mean().

questions.question: In ppo_clip_objective, which PyTorch operations implement the clip and the pessimistic min?
options: torch.sigmoid(ratio) to bound it and torch.max(unclipped, clipped), followed by .sum()
torch.clamp(ratio, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) and torch.minimum(unclipped, clipped), followed by .mean()
torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(ratio, eps) and torch.min over the batch axis, followed by .mean()
F.logsigmoid(ratio) and torch.where(ratio > 1, unclipped, clipped), followed by .mean()
questions.explanation: The ratio is clamped elementwise into the trust band and multiplied by advantages; torch.minimum picks the smaller of clipped and unclipped per element; .mean() reduces to a scalar objective. Gradient-norm clipping is a different mechanism entirely.

questions.question: What is reward hacking (over-optimization) in RLHF?
options: The policy exploits blind spots of the imperfect reward model, scoring high while actually being bad
The reward model overfits to the SFT data and outputs a near-constant reward for every completion
The value head learns to predict rewards perfectly, so every advantage is zero and learning stops
Labelers deliberately mislabel preference pairs so that their preferred outputs get inflated rewards
questions.explanation: The reward model is only a proxy for human preference. Optimized without limit, the policy finds text that scores high on the proxy but is low quality. The KL penalty to a frozen reference is the guardrail against this.

questions.question: In RLHF-PPO, what is the reference policy pi_ref used in the KL penalty?
options: The policy from the previous PPO iteration (pi_old)
The reward model with its scalar head
A uniform distribution over the vocabulary
The frozen SFT model the policy started from
questions.explanation: pi_ref is the trusted SFT model, kept frozen. The policy may improve but must stay recognizably close to it. pi_old is different — it is the policy that generated the current batch, used for the clip ratio.

questions.question: How is the per-token reward fed to PPO modified by the KL penalty?
options: R_t = r(x, y) + beta_KL · (log pi_theta(a_t | s_t) - log pi_ref(a_t | s_t))
R_t = r(x, y) * exp(-beta_KL * log pi_ref(a_t | s_t)), a multiplicative penalty
R_t = r(x, y) - beta_KL · (log pi_theta(a_t | s_t) - log pi_old(a_t | s_t))
R_t = r(x, y) - beta_KL · (log pi_theta(a_t | s_t) - log pi_ref(a_t | s_t))
questions.explanation: The reward-model score is reduced by beta_KL times the log-ratio of policy to reference for the sampled token. That log-ratio is a single-sample estimate of KL(pi_theta || pi_ref), so drifting from the reference costs reward. The reference, not pi_old, appears here.

questions.question: What does the coefficient beta_KL control in RLHF-PPO?
options: The width of the PPO clipping band around a ratio of 1 for each token
The trade-off between maximizing reward and staying close to the reference
The learning rate of the value head relative to the policy's learning rate
The sampling temperature used during rollouts, trading diversity for reward
questions.explanation: A larger beta_KL penalizes drift from pi_ref more heavily, keeping the policy closer to the SFT model; a smaller one lets the policy chase reward more aggressively. The clip band is controlled by epsilon, a separate hyperparameter.

questions.question: What does (logprobs - ref_logprobs).mean() over sampled tokens estimate?
options: KL(pi_theta || pi_ref), as the mean log-ratio over tokens the policy actually sampled
KL(pi_ref || pi_theta), as the mean log-ratio over tokens the reference would sample
The entropy of the policy, as the mean negative log-probability of the sampled tokens
The PPO clip ratio averaged over the batch, as a log-space measure of policy change
questions.explanation: Since tokens are sampled from pi_theta, the average of log pi_theta - log pi_ref is a Monte Carlo estimate of KL(pi_theta || pi_ref). For two tokens where the policy is 0.5 nats more confident than the reference each, it gives 0.5. Direction matters: sampling is from the policy.

questions.question: What is a known weakness of the plain log-ratio 'k1' KL estimator, and what alternative does production RLHF often use?
options: k1 is biased upward on long sequences; TRL often uses the squared log-ratio (log r)^2 / 2 instead
k1 needs the full vocabulary distribution at every step; TRL approximates it using only the top-k tokens
k1 explodes for long sequences; TRL clips each per-token log-ratio at the PPO epsilon before averaging
k1 is unbiased but can go negative on a finite sample; TRL often uses the nonnegative k3 = exp(d) - 1 - d
questions.explanation: The plain log-ratio is an unbiased estimator of KL, but individual sample averages can be negative even though true KL is not. The k3 estimator exp(d) - 1 - d, with d = log pi_ref - log pi_theta, is always nonnegative. Both estimate the same KL.

questions.section: Under the hood / cost — why PPO-on-LLMs is heavy
questions.question: Which four models are in play during full RLHF-PPO?
options: The tokenizer, the trainable policy, the AdamW optimizer's moment state, and the frozen reward model
The base pretrained model, the SFT model, a DPO-tuned model, and a GRPO-tuned model
The trainable policy, the frozen reference (SFT), the frozen reward model, and the value model
The trainable policy, two separate reward models (helpful and harmless), and a discriminator
questions.explanation: PPO-RLHF keeps the trainable policy, a frozen reference for the KL term, a frozen reward model to score completions, and a value model for the baseline (often a value head on the policy). This is why it is memory-hungry. The other lists are not the PPO setup.

questions.section: Under the hood / cost — why PPO-on-LLMs is heavy
questions.question: What does a single RLHF-PPO iteration involve?
options: Sample rollouts, score them with the RM, compute policy/reference log-probs and advantages, then take several clipped steps
Forward the chosen and rejected completions through the policy and minimize the Bradley-Terry loss on their reward gap
Compute the DPO loss on a fixed offline preference dataset, using the frozen reference only for its log-probabilities
Fine-tune on human-written demonstrations with token-level cross-entropy, then score the result with the reward model
questions.explanation: Each iteration samples rollouts (slow autoregressive generation), scores them, computes log-probs under both policy and reference for the KL term, computes advantages with the value model, and then takes multiple clipped updates. The Bradley-Terry and DPO losses belong to other stages/methods.

questions.section: Under the hood / cost — why PPO-on-LLMs is heavy
questions.question: Why is PPO on LLMs considered heavy and finicky?
options: Several model copies eat memory, generation is slow, and many hyperparameters interact (eps, beta_KL, lr, GAE lambda)
It needs human labelers to rate every single rollout in real time, so each PPO iteration waits on annotation
It cannot run in mixed precision, so every model must be held and trained in full fp32 throughout
It must retrain the tokenizer every iteration, because the policy's token vocabulary drifts as the model is updated
questions.explanation: Four models in memory, slow autoregressive rollouts, and a pile of interacting hyperparameters make PPO engineering-heavy. This engineering weight is exactly what DPO removes. Real-time human rating is not part of the loop; the reward model does the scoring.

questions.section: Under the hood / cost — why PPO-on-LLMs is heavy
questions.question: What does TRL's PPOTrainer provide?
options: A Bradley-Terry trainer that fits reward models on preference pairs, with no generation or policy-update logic of any kind
A tokenizer trainer for chat templates that adds special role tokens and retrains the BPE merges for dialogue data
A distributed data-parallel wrapper that shards the policy across GPUs but leaves the entire RL loop to the user
A loop wiring generation, reward scoring, reference log-probs, GAE, and the clipped update, plus value head and KL control
questions.explanation: TRL (Transformer Reinforcement Learning) packages the full PPO loop. Implementing the clipped objective, advantage, and KL estimate from scratch first means each line of that loop is understandable. It is not merely a reward-model or distributed-training tool.

questions.section: Under the hood / cost — why PPO-on-LLMs is heavy
questions.question: What is the minimum hardware for RLHF-PPO on a ~1B policy, and can it be trained on CPU?
options: Min 1x 8GB consumer GPU with 4-bit LoRA; CPU-only training works but is about 10x slower
Min 64x H100 even at 1B because of the four models; CPU is never used, not even for unit tests
Min 1× A100 40GB with LoRA and a small reward model; CPU-only training is impossible
Any CPU with 32GB RAM is enough for training; GPUs only speed up the rollout generation step
questions.explanation: The hardware track lists min 1× A100 40GB for a ~1B policy with LoRA (slow because of generation), and recommended 8× A100/H100 for 7B+. Runtime is hours to days and tens to hundreds of GPU-hours. CPU training is impossible, though the small llmre.rl.ppo math functions run instantly on CPU for unit tests.

questions.question: In a PPO implementation, what is wrong if the reward or advantage tensor has requires_grad=True during the policy update?
options: Nothing goes wrong; gradients through the reward jointly improve the reward model alongside the policy
Gradients flow through what should be a constant multiplier; only log pi_theta should carry grad
It silently causes the clip ratio to be computed in probability space instead of log space
It disables the KL penalty, because the penalized reward is then treated as a learnable tensor
questions.explanation: R and A-hat are constant scale factors in the policy gradient and must be detached. Letting gradients flow through them computes nonsense rather than the policy gradient. Only the log-probabilities of the current policy should be differentiated.

questions.question: What typically happens in RLHF-PPO if the KL penalty is dropped?
options: Training becomes slower but more stable, since the policy no longer fights a second objective
The policy reward-hacks within a few hundred steps: reward climbs while quality collapses
The value head can no longer be trained, since its regression target depended on the KL term
The clip ratio stays exactly 1 for every token, so PPO degenerates into plain REINFORCE
questions.explanation: Without the KL term nothing anchors the policy to the trusted SFT model, so it quickly finds reward-model blind spots. The reported reward rises but the outputs get worse. The KL term is the main guardrail against this.

questions.question: During PPO, reward-model scores climb, human raters say outputs are getting worse, and KL to the reference rises fast. What is happening and what is the primary fix?
options: The value head is underfitting; raise the value learning rate so advantages become accurate
The clip epsilon is too small to allow progress; increase it from 0.2 to about 0.5
The reward model is too accurate and overconfident; add noise to its output scores
Reward hacking; increase beta_KL (or tighten the KL target) and/or stop earlier
questions.explanation: Rising reward with falling true quality, together with exploding KL, is the classic over-optimization signature: the policy is racing toward inputs the imperfect reward model overrates. Raising beta_KL pulls it back toward the reference; stopping earlier also helps. Increasing epsilon would allow even larger policy moves.

questions.question: In a PPO run, what is the 'tell' that distinguishes reward hacking from genuine improvement?
options: The value loss reaching zero, meaning the critic has fully memorized the rewards
The clip fraction staying exactly at zero, meaning no token ever leaves the band
KL to the reference climbing fast; a healthy run keeps KL bounded
The reward staying flat across steps while the policy loss keeps decreasing
questions.explanation: When the policy drifts far from the trusted SFT model, KL explodes; that drift is what reward hacking looks like. A healthy PPO run improves reward while keeping KL bounded. Longer term, refreshing the reward model on new on-policy samples addresses the underlying distribution shift.

questions.question: In PPO with eps = 0.2, a bad action (A = -2.0) has ratio 0.7. What is its objective value and which branch wins?
options: -1.4, the unclipped branch
-1.6, the clipped branch
-2.4, the clipped branch at the upper edge
0, because the ratio is outside the band
questions.explanation: Unclipped = 0.7 × (-2.0) = -1.4; clipped ratio = 0.8, so clipped = -1.6. The min is -1.6, the clipped branch. A bad action whose probability already dropped below the band is held at the constant clipped value, so there is no gradient pushing it further down.

questions.question: What two things does the policy gradient multiply together to recover a usable gradient from a non-differentiable sampled reward?
options: The reward value and the gradient of the log-probability of the action taken
The gradient of the reward and the probability of the action taken, both from autograd
The reward value and the gradient of the reward model's own training loss on that sample
The KL penalty and the gradient of the value head's prediction for the current state
questions.explanation: The policy gradient is E[R · grad log pi_theta(a)]: the reward value is just a number, and the log-probability of the chosen action is differentiable. This sidesteps the non-differentiable sampling step entirely.

questions.question: What practical change did DPO bring to preference tuning?
options: It replaced a fragile four-model RL loop with a stable supervised loss that runs like SFT
It replaced pairwise preferences with absolute human scores, regressed directly with an MSE loss
It added a second reward model to stabilize PPO, so the policy no longer needs a value head
It made preference tuning require fresh online sampling at every step, like PPO but cheaper
questions.explanation: DPO collapses RLHF into a supervised classification loss on preference pairs, removing the reward model, value model, and generation loop. It is the default alignment method for most open-weight models today. It still uses pairwise preferences and needs no sampling.

questions.question: Why is DPO's derivation considered especially instructive in post-training?
options: It shows the KL-constrained RLHF objective and a simple classification loss are two views of one thing
It proves that SFT on chosen completions and full RLHF always converge to identical final models
It shows the reward model can be replaced by a larger tokenizer that encodes preferences directly
It proves PPO's clipping is unnecessary for any RL problem once a KL penalty is added to the loss
questions.explanation: The derivation turns the RLHF objective, via its closed-form optimum, into a Bradley-Terry classification loss on policy log-ratios. That reveals RLHF and a supervised loss as equivalent formulations. It makes no claims about SFT equivalence or PPO in general.

questions.section: The causal story: keep the goal, drop the machinery
questions.question: What is DPO's core insight about the RLHF objective?
options: It is non-convex in the policy, so it must be approximated by clipping the update ratio as in PPO
It can be solved exactly by greedy decoding from the reference model with the reward as a re-ranker
It is equivalent to maximizing expected reward with no KL term once beta is folded into the reward
It has a closed-form solution; rewriting the loss through it cancels the reward model and sampling
questions.explanation: For a fixed reward the KL-constrained objective has an exact maximizer. Expressing the reward through that optimal policy and substituting into Bradley-Terry removes both the explicit reward model and the need to sample. What is left is a loss computed directly from preference pairs, hence 'Direct'.

questions.question: What objective do both PPO-based RLHF and DPO optimize?
options: min over pi of the cross-entropy against chosen completions only
max over pi of E[r(x, y)] with no constraint
max over pi of E[r(x, y)] - beta · KL(pi(.|x) || pi_ref(.|x))
min over pi of KL(pi_ref || pi) with no reward term
questions.explanation: The KL-constrained RLHF objective maximizes expected reward while penalizing divergence from the reference policy. PPO chases it with RL using a reward term and KL penalty; DPO solves the same objective analytically and fits it with a supervised loss. Dropping the KL term would invite reward hacking.

questions.question: In the KL-constrained RLHF objective, what does a larger beta do?
options: Lets the policy move farther from the reference
Forces the policy to stay closer to the reference
Increases the weight of the reward relative to the prompt
Increases the sampling temperature
questions.explanation: beta weights the KL penalty, so increasing it makes drifting from pi_ref more costly and the policy hugs the reference. A smaller beta lets the policy chase reward further. It plays the same role in DPO's loss.

questions.question: How is KL(pi || pi_ref) defined for a prompt x in the RLHF objective?
options: E_{y~pi_ref}[ log( pi(y|x) / pi_ref(y|x) ) ]
E_{y~pi}[ log( pi(y|x) / pi_ref(y|x) ) ]
E_{y~pi}[ pi(y|x) - pi_ref(y|x) ]
E_{y~pi}[ ( log pi(y|x) - log pi_ref(y|x) )^2 ]
questions.explanation: KL(pi || pi_ref) is the expectation under pi of the log-ratio log(pi/pi_ref). The direction matters: samples come from pi, the policy being optimized. Differences of probabilities or squared log-ratios are different quantities.

questions.question: How is the KL-constrained RLHF objective rewritten to find its maximizer for a fixed reward?
options: As maximizing E_{y~pi}[ r(x,y) · pi_ref(y|x) ], a reward weighted by the reference's own probability
As minimizing the squared error between log pi(y|x) and r(x,y)/beta, summed over all completions
As maximizing log Z(x) with respect to beta, then reading pi off the partition function's gradient
As minimizing a KL from pi to the reweighted reference pi_ref(y|x) exp(r(x,y)/beta)
questions.explanation: Dividing by beta and pulling r into the log turns the objective into a KL between pi and the unnormalized distribution pi_ref exp(r/beta). A KL is minimized (to zero) exactly when the distributions are equal (after normalization), which yields the closed-form optimum.

questions.question: What is the closed-form optimal policy pi* of the KL-constrained RLHF objective?
options: pi*(y|x) = softmax(r(x,y)) with no dependence on pi_ref
pi*(y|x) = pi_ref(y|x) + beta · r(x,y)
pi*(y|x) = (1/Z(x)) · pi_ref(y|x) · exp(r(x,y)/beta)
pi*(y|x) = pi_ref(y|x)^beta · r(x,y)
questions.explanation: The optimum is the reference reweighted by exp(reward/beta) and renormalized by the partition function Z(x). It boosts completions the reward likes in proportion to how much, tempered by beta. It always depends on pi_ref; additive or power forms are wrong.

questions.question: What is the partition function Z(x) in the DPO derivation, and why is it a problem?
options: Z(x) is the number of tokens in the prompt x; it is a problem because prompts vary in length across a batch
Z(x) = sum over y of pi_ref(y|x) exp(r(x,y)/beta); it normalizes pi*, but summing over all completions is intractable
Z(x) is the reward model's scalar bias term; it is a problem because it is never trained and drifts with beta
Z(x) = KL(pi || pi_ref) summed over completions; it is a problem because it can go negative and break the log
questions.explanation: Z(x) sums the reweighted reference over every possible completion to make pi* sum to 1. The space of completions is astronomically large, so computing it is intractable. This is what blocked earlier direct uses of the closed-form solution, and DPO makes it cancel.

questions.question: On which variables does the partition function Z(x) in the DPO derivation depend?
options: On the prompt x but not on the completion y
On the completion y but not on the prompt x
On both the prompt x and the completion y being scored
On neither; it is a global constant
questions.explanation: Z(x) sums over all completions y, so y is marginalized out, leaving dependence only on the prompt (and on beta and the reward). Because it depends only on x, it is identical for the chosen and rejected completions of the same prompt, which is why it cancels.

questions.question: What is the intuitive interpretation of the optimal policy pi* in KL-constrained RLHF?
options: A deterministic policy that always outputs the single highest-reward completion, for any value of beta
The reward model's own distribution over completions, softmaxed with temperature beta, pi_ref ignored
The reference reweighted by exp(reward/beta): completions the reward likes are boosted, tempered by beta
The uniform distribution over completions with positive reward, with negative-reward completions given zero mass
questions.explanation: pi* keeps the reference's shape but multiplies each completion's probability by exp(r/beta). Large beta tempers the reweighting (staying near pi_ref); small beta sharpens it toward high-reward completions. It is not a deterministic argmax unless beta goes to zero.

questions.section: Step 3 — invert it: reward in terms of the policy
questions.question: Inverting the closed-form optimum, how is the reward expressed in terms of the optimal policy?
options: r(x,y) = log pi*(y|x) - log pi_ref(y|x) - log Z(x), with no beta factor
r(x,y) = beta · ( pi*(y|x) - pi_ref(y|x) ) + beta · Z(x)
r(x,y) = beta · log( pi*(y|x) / pi_ref(y|x) ) + beta · log Z(x)
r(x,y) = (1/beta) · log( pi_ref(y|x) / pi*(y|x) ) + log Z(x)
questions.explanation: Taking logs: log pi* = log pi_ref + r/beta - log Z. Solving for r gives beta times the log-ratio of optimal to reference policy, plus beta log Z(x). This shows the optimal policy already encodes the reward up to a prompt-only term.

questions.section: Step 3 — invert it: reward in terms of the policy
questions.question: What is the key conceptual consequence of writing the reward as r = beta log(pi*/pi_ref) + beta log Z(x)?
options: The reward must be recomputed by sampling fresh completions from pi* at every training step
The optimal policy already encodes the reward, so no separate reward network is needed
The reward is independent of the policy, so it must still be learned by a separate network
The partition function becomes tractable, since it is now a sum over the prompt's tokens only
questions.explanation: The reward is expressible through the policy and reference, plus a term depending only on the prompt. So a policy can stand in for the reward model. Z(x) stays intractable; it is eliminated later by taking reward differences.

questions.section: Step 4 — substitute into Bradley-Terry; Z(x) cancels
questions.question: When the reparameterized reward is substituted into the Bradley-Terry margin r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l), why does Z(x) disappear?
options: Both completions share prompt x, so their identical beta log Z(x) terms subtract to zero
Z(x) is approximated as 1 for long completions, so beta log Z(x) is negligible in the margin
Z(x) is absorbed into the learning rate, since it scales every gradient by the same constant
Z(x) is estimated by sampling completions, and the estimates average to zero across a batch
questions.explanation: Bradley-Terry depends only on the reward difference, and the two completions in a pair are for the same prompt. Each reward carries the same + beta log Z(x), which cancels exactly. That cancellation removes the one intractable piece.

questions.section: Step 4 — substitute into Bradley-Terry; Z(x) cancels
questions.question: After Z(x) cancels, what replaces the unknown optimal policy pi* to obtain a trainable loss?
options: The frozen reference policy pi_ref, which pi* is closest to
A separately trained reward model whose scores define pi*
The uniform distribution over the vocabulary at every step
The trainable policy pi_theta, fitted so that it becomes pi*
questions.explanation: We fit theta so that pi_theta becomes pi*, so pi* is replaced by pi_theta in the margin. The margin is then placed inside the Bradley-Terry -log sigmoid and averaged over the dataset. pi_ref stays as the frozen anchor.

questions.section: Step 4 — substitute into Bradley-Terry; Z(x) cancels
questions.question: What is the DPO loss?
options: -E[ log sigmoid( r_phi(x,y_w) - r_phi(x,y_l) ) ], with r_phi a separately trained reward model network
-E[ log pi_theta(y_w|x) ] + beta · KL(pi_theta || pi_ref), i.e. SFT on chosen completions plus a KL penalty
E[ ( log(pi_theta(y_w|x)/pi_ref(y_w|x)) - log(pi_theta(y_l|x)/pi_ref(y_l|x)) - 1/(2 beta) )^2 ]
-E[ log sigmoid( beta log(pi_theta(y_w|x)/pi_ref(y_w|x)) - beta log(pi_theta(y_l|x)/pi_ref(y_l|x)) ) ]
questions.explanation: DPO is the Bradley-Terry loss with the implicit reward beta log(pi_theta/pi_ref) in place of an explicit reward. It needs only the policy and reference log-probs on chosen and rejected completions. The first option is reward-model training, the second is SFT with a KL penalty, and the squared form is IPO-style, not DPO.

questions.section: Step 4 — substitute into Bradley-Terry; Z(x) cancels
questions.question: What does computing the DPO loss require?
options: Sampling new completions from the policy each step and scoring them with a separately trained reward model
Policy and frozen-reference forwards on the given chosen and rejected completions, summing sequence log-probs
Training a value head alongside the policy to estimate per-token advantages for the chosen completion
Collecting absolute human ratings for each completion and regressing the policy's log-probs onto them
questions.explanation: DPO needs no reward model and no sampling. It is a supervised classification loss on fixed preference pairs, as easy to run as SFT, yet it optimizes the same KL-constrained objective PPO does.

questions.question: In DPO, what is the implicit reward of a completion y?
options: beta · ( log pi_theta(y|x) - log pi_ref(y|x) ): how much more likely the policy makes y than the reference
r_phi(x, y): the scalar score a separately trained reward model assigns to y, scaled by beta
beta · log pi_theta(y|x) alone: the policy's own log-probability of y, with no reference term
The sum over y's tokens of PPO advantages, estimated with GAE from a separately learned value head
questions.explanation: DPO's implicit reward is beta times the log-ratio of policy to reference probability for the completion. It measures how much the policy has raised y's likelihood relative to its starting point. No explicit reward model is involved.

questions.question: What does minimizing the DPO loss do to the policy's probabilities?
options: Raises pi_theta(y_w) and pi_theta(y_l) equally, so only the shared prompt likelihood grows
Pulls pi_theta toward pi_ref exactly, so both log-ratios are driven back to zero over training
Lowers pi_theta(y_w) slightly to avoid overconfidence, while leaving pi_theta(y_l) unchanged
Raises pi_theta(y_w) and lowers pi_theta(y_l), each measured relative to the reference
questions.explanation: Minimizing -log sigmoid of the implicit reward margin pushes the margin up: the chosen completion's log-ratio rises and/or the rejected one's falls. Because ratios are relative to the reference, the push is measured against the starting model, not absolute probabilities.

questions.question: Why does DPO not need a separate KL-penalty term the way PPO does?
options: DPO uses PPO-style clipping of the probability ratio instead of an explicit KL penalty term
DPO's loss is defined to be zero once the policy drifts too far, which halts further updates
The reference appears inside the loss itself, so the KL constraint is baked in via beta
DPO freezes all layers except the last, so the policy physically cannot drift from the reference
questions.explanation: The log-ratio to pi_ref in the implicit reward ties the objective to the reference, and beta plays the same role as the RLHF KL weight. Small beta lets the policy move far; large beta keeps it close. No clipping or freezing is involved.

questions.question: In DPO, if the policy already prefers the chosen completion over the rejected one more than the reference does, how does the loss compare with log 2?
options: It is below log 2 ≈ 0.693, because the implicit margin is positive
It is exactly log 2, because the reference is unchanged
It is above log 2, because the policy has drifted from the reference
It is zero, because the preference is already satisfied
questions.explanation: A positive margin (pi_logratios greater than ref_logratios) gives sigmoid(beta · margin) > 0.5 and loss below log 2; for margin 1.0 and beta 0.5 the loss is about 0.474. The loss approaches zero only as the margin grows large. log 2 corresponds to a zero margin.

questions.question: In a DPO loss computation, what are pi_logratios and ref_logratios?
options: pi_logratios = log pi_theta(y_w) - log pi_theta(y_l); ref_logratios = log pi_ref(y_w) - log pi_ref(y_l)
pi_logratios = log pi_theta(y_w) - log pi_ref(y_w); ref_logratios = log pi_theta(y_l) - log pi_ref(y_l)
pi_logratios = pi_theta(y_w) / pi_theta(y_l); ref_logratios = pi_ref(y_w) / pi_ref(y_l)
pi_logratios = log pi_theta(y_w); ref_logratios = log pi_ref(y_l)
questions.explanation: pi_logratios is chosen minus rejected under the policy; ref_logratios is chosen minus rejected under the reference. Their difference is algebraically the same implicit margin as the per-completion log-ratio form. The loss is -logsigmoid(beta · (pi_logratios - ref_logratios)).

questions.question: What quantity does sequence_logprob compute for DPO?
options: The mean per-token log-probability over prompt and completion
The log-probability of only the last completion token
The cross-entropy averaged over the vocabulary
log pi(y|x) = sum over completion tokens of log pi(y_t | y_<t, x)
questions.explanation: DPO needs the log-probability of the whole completion, which is the sum of per-token log-probs of the true tokens. It is the same gather-the-true-token operation as cross-entropy, but summed, not averaged, and restricted to response tokens.

questions.question: In sequence_logprob, which tokens contribute to log pi(y|x)?
options: All tokens including the prompt, since the prompt conditions the completion and shares its loss
Only the prompt tokens, since they are fixed and identical for the chosen and rejected completions
Only completion tokens; prompt and pad labels are set to ignore_index (-100) and masked out
Only tokens whose predicted probability exceeds 0.5, so low-confidence positions are ignored
questions.explanation: log pi(y|x) is about the completion given the prompt, so prompt positions are masked exactly like response-only SFT loss masking. Pad positions are masked too. Including prompt tokens would add a term unrelated to the preference.

questions.question: What are the shapes and dtypes of the inputs and output of sequence_logprob?
options: logits (B, V) float; labels (B,) int64 holding one id per sequence; output (B, T) float
logits (B, T, V) float; labels (B, T) int64 with -100 for prompt/pad; output (B,) float
logits (B, T) float; labels (B, T, V) bool one-hot with -100 for prompt; output scalar
logits (T, V) float16 for one sequence; labels (T,) float; output (V,) float per vocab id
questions.explanation: The policy produces (B, T, V) logits; labels hold the true completion token ids per position with ignored positions at -100; the function returns one summed log-prob per sequence, shape (B,).

questions.question: Why does sequence_logprob call labels.clamp(min=0) before gather?
options: To convert negative log-probs into positive values before they are summed over the completion
gather cannot index with -100, so ignored positions are made valid indices and later zeroed by the mask
To remove padding tokens from the vocabulary so the log-softmax normalizes over real tokens only, not pad
To prevent the log-softmax from overflowing when labels at ignored positions are large negatives
questions.explanation: -100 is not a valid vocabulary index, so gathering with it would error. Clamping replaces it with 0, a harmless index, and the result at those positions is multiplied by the boolean mask, zeroing them before the sum. The clamp has nothing to do with numerical overflow.

questions.question: In sequence_logprob, what does logp.gather(-1, safe.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) produce?
options: A (B, T, V) tensor of all log-probabilities, reordered by the label ids
A (B,) tensor holding the maximum log-probability reached in each sequence
A (B, T) int64 tensor of the argmax token id predicted at every position
A (B, T) tensor of the log-probability of the true token at each position
questions.explanation: gather along the vocab axis picks, for each (b, t), the log-prob at index labels[b, t]. unsqueeze adds the index dimension and squeeze removes it, yielding (B, T). Masking and summing over T then give the (B,) sequence log-prob.

questions.question: In dpo_loss, what is the final returned expression?
options: -torch.log(torch.sigmoid(pi_logratios + ref_logratios)).sum()
F.mse_loss(pi_logratios, ref_logratios) * beta
-F.logsigmoid(beta * (pi_logratios - ref_logratios)).mean()
-(beta * pi_logratios).mean() + ref_logratios.mean()
questions.explanation: dpo_loss forms the implicit margin as policy log-ratio minus reference log-ratio, scales by beta, applies the numerically stable logsigmoid, negates, and averages. Adding the log-ratios or using MSE would not be the DPO objective.

questions.question: In a DPO training step, how are the reference model's sequence log-probs computed?
options: With gradients enabled on both models, so the reference co-adapts slowly with the policy
Under torch.no_grad() on a frozen reference, for both chosen and rejected completions
Only for the chosen completion, since the rejected one's reference term cancels in the loss
By sampling fresh completions from the reference and scoring them under torch.no_grad()
questions.explanation: The reference is a fixed anchor: its log-probs on chosen and rejected completions are computed without gradients (or precomputed and cached). Only the policy's log-probs carry grad. No sampling occurs.

questions.question: What does the unit test for DPO's gradient check after a few SGD steps from zero policy log-ratios?
options: The chosen-minus-rejected margin grows and chosen's implicit reward ends above rejected's
The loss reaches exactly zero, confirming the preference pair has been fully fitted
The policy log-probs become identical to the reference's, so both log-ratios return to zero
The rejected completion's log-prob increases faster than the chosen one's, as the loss expects
questions.explanation: Starting from zero log-ratios, SGD on the DPO loss provably increases the chosen-minus-rejected margin, and the implicit rewards beta log(pi_theta/pi_ref) end with chosen above rejected. This confirms the loss does what the derivation promised. The loss does not reach exactly zero in a few steps.

questions.question: How many forward passes does DPO need per preference pair, and how can this be reduced?
options: Two always: only the policy is forwarded, since the reference's log-probs are taken as uniform
Eight, because both models must also generate fresh completions; batching generation halves that
Four (policy and reference, each on chosen and rejected); caching reference log-probs cuts it to two
One, because chosen and rejected share the prompt; packing both into a single sequence keeps it at one
questions.explanation: DPO forwards the policy on chosen and rejected and the reference on chosen and rejected — four forwards, no generation. Because the reference is frozen, its log-probs can be precomputed once and cached, leaving two forwards per pair in steady state.

questions.question: What must be resident in memory during DPO training, compared with PPO?
options: The policy, reference, reward model, and value model, exactly like PPO, but with no sampling loop
Only the reward model and the frozen reference, since the policy's log-probs are cached up front
The policy and a frozen reference (or its cached log-probs); no reward model, value head, or rollouts
The policy plus a replay buffer of generated rollouts, with the reference dropped after warmup
questions.explanation: DPO keeps just the trainable policy and a frozen reference (or cached reference log-probs). PPO keeps four live models plus a sampling loop. This is a large part of DPO's simplicity.

questions.question: Why is DPO more stable to train than PPO?
options: It uses a much larger batch size by default, which averages away the noise in preference labels
It is a smooth supervised loss with far fewer knobs; beta is the main hyperparameter
It clips gradients and policy ratios at every step, so updates can never exceed a trust region
It updates only the scalar reward head, leaving the transformer body frozen during training
questions.explanation: DPO trains like SFT: a smooth classification loss on fixed data, with beta as the main knob. PPO's many interacting hyperparameters (epsilon, beta_KL, GAE lambda, rollout size) and online sampling make it finicky.

questions.question: What happens if the DPO reference model accidentally trains along with the policy?
options: The log-ratio collapses toward zero, so DPO has no target to push against
DPO converges faster, because both models improve together and share gradient signal
The loss becomes negative and training diverges as the two models chase each other
Nothing changes, because beta automatically compensates for the reference's movement
questions.explanation: The reference must be the frozen starting model (typically SFT), in eval() mode with requires_grad=False and log-probs under no_grad. If it moves with the policy, pi_theta/pi_ref stays near 1, the implicit margin stays near zero, and the objective degenerates.

questions.question: What is the hardware guidance for DPO on a 7B model, and can it run on CPU?
options: Recommended 8× H100 as for PPO; CPU training is practical for 7B with enough RAM
A single 8GB consumer GPU with full fine-tuning and no LoRA; CPU is about as fast
No GPU needed, because without generation a 7B DPO run fits comfortably on CPU
Recommended 1×–2× A100 40GB; unit tests run on CPU but real training needs a GPU
questions.explanation: DPO is roughly SFT cost with a second frozen model: min 1× 24GB GPU for ~1B with LoRA (caching reference log-probs), recommended 1×–2× A100 40GB for 7B, hours of runtime and single-digit to low tens of GPU-hours. dpo_loss and sequence_logprob tests run instantly on CPU, but real training needs a GPU.

questions.question: Why must sequence_logprob sum, not average, per-token log-probs?
options: Averaging would make the loss non-differentiable, because the divisor depends on the integer mask length
Summing is much faster than averaging on GPUs, since it skips a division and a reduction over the mask
Averaging would silently include the prompt tokens, because the mean's denominator ignores the mask
log pi(y|x) is a log of a product of token probabilities, i.e. a sum; a mean rescales the implicit reward vs beta
questions.explanation: The sequence log-probability is the sum of per-token log-probs. The per-token mean is a different quantity that changes the implicit reward's scale and breaks its calibration against beta. Differentiability and speed are not the issue.

questions.question: In DPO, what happens if chosen and rejected are swapped in the margin computation?
options: Nothing, because the sigmoid is symmetric around zero
The model is trained to prefer the worse answer
The loss becomes zero and training stalls immediately
Only beta's sign flips, which Adam's update cancels out
questions.explanation: The margin must be (policy chosen - policy rejected) - (ref chosen - ref rejected). Swapping chosen and rejected flips the sign of the margin, so minimizing the loss pushes the rejected completion up. Sign and ratio-order slips are a classic DPO bug.

questions.question: Which tokens should be excluded when computing log pi(y|x) for DPO, and how?
options: Prompt and pad tokens, by setting their labels to ignore_index
The completion's first token, by slicing it off the shifted logits
High-probability tokens, by thresholding their softmax at 0.9
End-of-sequence tokens, by zeroing their logits before log-softmax
questions.explanation: Only completion tokens should contribute to log pi(y|x). Setting prompt and pad labels to ignore_index masks them out, exactly as in response-only SFT masking. Otherwise prompt likelihood leaks into the implicit reward.

questions.question: A DPO run's loss sits at about 0.6931, and chosen/rejected implicit rewards stay equal, though gradients flow. What is the most likely bug?
options: The learning rate is far too small, so the policy log-probs barely move from their starting values
beta is set too large, so the KL constraint pins the policy exactly to the reference at every step
The prompt tokens were masked out, so only pad positions contribute to each sequence log-prob
The reference is the same object as the policy (or updates with it), so the log-ratios are always zero
questions.explanation: 0.6931 = log 2 = -log sigmoid(0), so the implicit margin is stuck at zero. If the reference is the policy itself, log pi_theta - log pi_ref = 0 for both completions at every step. Fix by making the reference a separate frozen copy (eval, requires_grad=False, no_grad) or by caching its log-probs before training.

questions.question: A loss pinned at log 2 appears both in reward-model training and in DPO. How do the typical causes differ?
options: Reward model: the learning rate is zero; DPO: beta is zero, so both margins are scaled away
Reward model: logsigmoid is used; DPO: log(sigmoid) is used, which underflows to a constant
Reward model: the same input feeds both scores; DPO: the reference is, or trains with, the policy
Both are caused by masking the prompt, which removes every token the two models could compare
questions.explanation: In both cases the margin is identically zero. For a reward model, that usually means the same input reaches both reward computations. For DPO, it usually means the policy and reference log-ratios cancel because the reference is not a separate frozen model.

questions.question: How is DPO's 'reward accuracy' metric computed?
options: The fraction of pairs where chosen's implicit reward beta·log(pi_theta/pi_ref) exceeds rejected's
The fraction of completion tokens where the policy's argmax equals the chosen completion's token
The mean of sigmoid(beta · margin) over pairs, i.e. the model's average preference probability
The fraction of pairs where log pi_theta(y_w) exceeds log pi_ref(y_w), ignoring the rejected one
questions.explanation: Reward accuracy counts how often the implicit reward ranks chosen above rejected. Since beta > 0, beta does not change the sign of the comparison. It is the standard metric logged during DPO training.

questions.question: How does DPO reward accuracy typically evolve in a healthy run?
options: It climbs from about 0.5 toward 0.7 or higher
It starts near 1.0 and decays toward 0.5
It stays at exactly 0.5 for the whole run
It jumps to 1.0 immediately after the first step
questions.explanation: At the start the policy equals the reference, so implicit rewards are equal and accuracy is about chance (0.5). As training proceeds, chosen implicit rewards rise above rejected, and reward accuracy climbs toward 0.7+.

questions.question: Which part of the DPO paper (Rafailov et al. 2023) should be read closely?
options: Only the appendix of hyperparameter sweeps, since the derivation is standard RL and can be skipped
Only the experiments section on image classification, which shows where the loss generalizes
The theoretical equivalence proofs in full, before reading the derivation or any of the experiments
Section 4 (the optimal policy, reward reparameterization, and loss) and the gradient interpretation
questions.explanation: Section 4 contains the derivation — closed-form optimal policy, reward reparameterization, and the loss — and the gradient interpretation explains what the update does. The theoretical equivalence proofs can be skimmed on a first pass. This paper is why most open-weight models are aligned with DPO rather than PPO.

questions.question: What is the DPO loss when the policy exactly matches the reference?
options: 0, because there is nothing left for the policy to learn
Infinity, because the log-ratio log(1) is undefined
log 2 ≈ 0.693, because the implicit margin is zero
beta, because only the scale of the margin remains
questions.explanation: If pi_theta = pi_ref, then pi_logratios equals ref_logratios and the margin is 0. sigmoid(0) = 0.5, so the loss is -log 0.5 = log 2. A policy identical to the reference sits at maximum uncertainty with no preference signal yet.

questions.question: In DPO, how does beta relate to PPO-based RLHF?
options: PPO's clip epsilon under a different name: it bounds how far each update moves the ratio
The same KL weight: large beta keeps pi_theta near the reference, small beta lets it move far
The learning rate of PPO's value head, reused in DPO to scale the step size on the policy
The temperature PPO uses to sample rollouts, reused in DPO to soften the preference labels
questions.explanation: beta is the KL weight from the KL-constrained RLHF objective that PPO also optimizes. In DPO it scales the implicit reward margin, and because the reference sits inside the loss, the KL constraint is built in. It is unrelated to PPO's clipping epsilon.

questions.question: Which two networks does DPO evaluate during training, and what does it not need?
options: A reward model and a value model, as in PPO; no reference model and no policy sampling
The trainable policy and a frozen reference; no reward model and no sampling/generation
The policy and a learned reward model scoring each pair; no reference and no value head
The policy alone, scored against itself; no reference model, no reward model, and no data
questions.explanation: DPO forwards pi_theta and the frozen pi_ref on chosen and rejected completions. It needs no reward model and no generation, which is what makes it as cheap and stable as SFT.

questions.question: Why is choosing the alignment method one of the highest-leverage decisions in a post-training project?
options: It sets the compute budget, the data-collection strategy, and the failure surface
It fixes the tokenizer, vocabulary size, and context length that post-training must use
It retroactively reweights the pretraining data mix toward the chosen preference domain
It decides the attention-head count and hidden width of the policy being aligned
questions.explanation: SFT, RM+PPO, and DPO differ in how much compute and infrastructure they need, what data must be collected (demonstrations vs preference pairs vs on-policy samples), and how they fail. Architecture and tokenizer are fixed before post-training.

questions.question: How are SFT, RM+PPO, and DPO typically related in an aligned model's training?
options: They are stages: SFT first, then preference optimization (PPO or DPO) on top
They are rival recipes; a project picks exactly one of the three and runs only that one
DPO runs first on the base model, then SFT fixes the format, then PPO polishes the output
PPO replaces SFT entirely, and DPO is used only afterward as an offline evaluation metric
questions.explanation: Almost every aligned model does SFT first, then a preference-optimization stage. The real choice is which preference method to use for the second stage. Treating them as competitors is a common mistake.

questions.question: What does SFT teach, and what can it not do?
options: It teaches answer ranking from demonstrations, but it cannot teach the chat format or the turn structure
It teaches a reward model to score answers, but it cannot change the policy's own next-token distribution
It teaches the model to recover from its own sampled mistakes, but it cannot teach basic instruction-following
It teaches instruction format and following, but can't rank answers: each demonstration counts as equally correct
questions.explanation: SFT imitates demonstrations with next-token cross-entropy, so it installs format and instruction-following. Because every demonstration is treated as equally correct, it cannot learn that one answer is better than another. Recovery from its own mistakes is in fact a weakness (exposure bias).

questions.question: How does DPO relate to RM+PPO in terms of objective and machinery?
options: A different objective that drops the reference policy entirely, but is optimized with the same RL machinery
The same reward-model-plus-rollout machinery, but trained on absolute human scores instead of pairwise labels
The same preference objective, rearranged into one supervised loss on pairs with no reward model or sampling
A weaker surrogate objective that only converges once a full PPO run has already initialized the policy
questions.explanation: DPO optimizes the same KL-constrained preference objective as RM+PPO, but as a closed-form supervised loss on preference pairs. It needs no reward model and no rollouts. It still uses a frozen reference policy.

questions.question: What is the SFT objective and its training data?
options: E[r(x,y)] - beta · KL(pi_theta || pi_ref), maximized using on-policy samples drawn each step
-sum_t log pi_theta(y_t | y_<t, x) on response tokens, using (prompt, ideal response) demonstrations
-E log sigmoid(beta · implicit reward margin), using (prompt, chosen, rejected) preference pairs
Mean squared error between a scalar head and human scores, using individually rated completions
questions.explanation: SFT minimizes the negative log-likelihood of a gold response's tokens, matching one demonstration per prompt. The KL-constrained reward objective is RM+PPO's, and the log-sigmoid margin is DPO's.

questions.question: What data pipeline does RM+PPO use?
options: Only (prompt, ideal response) demonstrations, trained with token-level cross-entropy on the response
Preference pairs train a reward model, which then scores on-policy samples generated during RL
A fixed offline set of preference pairs fed directly into a supervised log-sigmoid loss on the policy
Absolute 1-10 human ratings that the policy regresses directly through a mean-squared-error head
questions.explanation: RM+PPO first trains a reward model on preference pairs, then optimizes the policy against that learned reward using samples generated from the current policy. Feeding offline pairs straight into a supervised loss is DPO.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between SFT's target and the target of preference methods?
options: SFT's target is an ordering (chosen beats rejected); preference methods' target is a single gold point
Both targets are points, but preference methods average the two gold answers into one blended target response
SFT's target is a scalar reward value; preference methods' target is the next token of the gold answer
SFT's target is a point (one gold answer); preference methods' target is an ordering (chosen beats rejected)
questions.explanation: SFT pushes the model toward one specific gold response. Preference methods learn that chosen should beat rejected, a relative ordering. That is why SFT hits a quality ceiling at its demonstrations while preference tuning can push past it.

questions.question: Do PPO and DPO optimize different objectives?
options: Yes; PPO maximizes a learned reward model's score, while DPO only maximizes the likelihood of chosen responses
Yes; DPO drops the KL constraint entirely, so it optimizes reward with no anchor to the reference policy
No; both optimize the same KL-constrained objective, via RL on a reward model vs a closed-form supervised loss
No; both reduce exactly to SFT on the chosen responses, so they differ only in how batches are constructed
questions.explanation: DPO's derivation starts from PPO's KL-constrained objective and rearranges it via the closed-form optimal policy. The difference is how they get there: PPO uses RL and a learned reward model, DPO a direct classification loss. DPO's KL constraint is built in through the reference.

questions.question: How many models are resident during training for SFT, RM+PPO, and DPO, respectively?
options: SFT: 2 (policy and reference); RM+PPO: 2 (policy and reward model); DPO: 4 including a critic
SFT: 1; RM+PPO: up to 4; DPO: 2 (effectively 1 if reference log-probs are cached)
SFT: 1; RM+PPO: 1 with the reward folded in; DPO: 1, since the reference is never loaded
SFT: 4 with ensembling; RM+PPO: 3 without a reference; DPO: 2 including a reward model
questions.explanation: SFT trains only the policy. RM+PPO keeps the policy (with value head), a frozen reference, and the reward model — up to four models. DPO needs the policy and a frozen reference, and caching the reference's log-probs makes it effectively one model.

questions.question: Which of SFT, RM+PPO, and DPO requires generation in the training loop?
options: Only RM+PPO, which does autoregressive rollouts every step
Only DPO, which samples fresh chosen and rejected pairs every step
All three, since each scores completions sampled from the policy
Only SFT, which generates its own demonstrations before each epoch
questions.explanation: PPO must sample completions from the current policy each iteration to score them. SFT and DPO train on fixed datasets with no generation. Generation is slow, which is a major part of PPO's cost.

questions.question: What are the main hyperparameters of DPO compared with RM+PPO?
options: DPO: clip epsilon and GAE lambda; RM+PPO: only beta, because the reward model fixes all the other settings
DPO: learning rate and epochs only; RM+PPO: learning rate and epochs only, like any SFT run
DPO: beta and learning rate; RM+PPO: epsilon, beta_KL, learning rate, GAE lambda, rollout/batch sizes
DPO: rollout size, beta_KL and value-loss weight; RM+PPO: beta and learning rate, with nothing else
questions.explanation: DPO has few knobs — mainly beta and the learning rate. PPO has many interacting ones: the clip epsilon, the KL coefficient, the learning rate, GAE lambda, and rollout and batch sizes. SFT mainly needs learning rate and epochs.

questions.question: What two factors dominate PPO's cost relative to DPO?
options: Computing the Bradley-Terry loss over every pair, and re-tokenizing the dataset at each epoch
Saving full optimizer-state checkpoints every step, and logging per-token metrics to disk
Keeping several large models in memory at once, and generating completions every step
Needing a larger vocabulary for the value head, and a much longer context for every prompt
questions.explanation: PPO holds up to four models in memory and runs slow autoregressive rollouts each iteration. DPO removes both — no reward model, no rollouts — which is why it trains like SFT.

questions.question: According to the comparison of post-training methods, why did DPO become the default for open-weight models?
options: Because DPO has been proven to always produce higher-quality models than PPO on every benchmark
Mainly the engineering gap: it trains like SFT without a reward model or rollouts
Because PPO's license terms forbid running it on open-weight checkpoints released by labs
Because DPO needs no preference data at all, only the demonstrations already used for SFT
questions.explanation: DPO optimizes the same objective with far less infrastructure and instability, so it is much easier to run. That engineering advantage, rather than a claim of strictly better quality, explains its dominance in the open-weight ecosystem. It still needs preference pairs.

questions.question: What is DPO's relative training cost?
options: Roughly SFT cost plus a frozen forward pass
Roughly the same as RM+PPO, rollouts included
Lower than SFT, because no labels are needed
Roughly four times RM+PPO, due to paired data
questions.explanation: DPO forwards the trainable policy and a frozen reference (whose log-probs can be cached) on fixed chosen/rejected completions. That is approximately SFT plus one frozen forward. PPO is the most expensive; SFT is the cheapest.

questions.question: What is reward hacking in RM+PPO?
options: The reward model collapses to outputting nearly constant rewards, so PPO's advantage estimates vanish entirely
Labelers coordinate to inflate preference labels for one style, biasing the reward model toward it
The value head overfits the training prompts, so advantage estimates blow up on any new prompt
The policy exploits the proxy reward model's blind spots: high-scoring but bad outputs (verbose, sycophantic)
questions.explanation: The reward model is only a proxy for human preference. Optimizing it hard enough leads the policy to exploit its weaknesses, producing outputs the reward model overrates. Verbosity, sycophancy, and formulaic answers are typical symptoms.

questions.question: Which principle describes reward hacking, and how is it stated?
options: Occam's razor: among reward models that fit the labels, the simplest one generalizes best
The bitter lesson: general methods that exploit more compute eventually beat hand-built ones
Murphy's law: anything that can go wrong in an optimization loop eventually will go wrong
Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure
questions.explanation: Reward hacking is Goodhart's law in action: once the reward model's score is the optimization target, it no longer tracks true quality well. The KL penalty is the main defense against pushing the proxy too far.

questions.question: What is the warning sign of reward hacking in an RM+PPO run?
options: Reward and KL both staying flat for many steps while the value loss slowly creeps upward
Reward climbing while KL to the reference explodes and human ratings drop
Value loss decreasing steadily to zero while the advantage estimates shrink toward zero
The clip fraction falling to zero while the reported reward drops steadily step after step
questions.explanation: Reward hacking shows reported reward rising, KL to the reference rising quickly as the policy drifts, and actual human-judged quality falling. A healthy run keeps KL bounded while reward improves.

questions.question: What is over-optimization in preference tuning?
options: Pushing too hard against a fixed reward or preference signal so measured and real quality diverge
Using so many GPUs that communication dominates and each step's utilization drops sharply
Running the optimizer with too small a learning rate, so the policy barely moves from the reference
Training the reward model for too few steps, so its scores are noisy before PPO even begins
questions.explanation: Even without pathological hacking, optimizing too hard against any fixed signal eventually hurts true quality: past some point the measured metric keeps improving while real quality declines. In PPO this shows up as the KL-vs-reward trade-off.

questions.question: Under which conditions is DPO prone to over-optimization?
options: With a large beta and a single epoch, which lets the policy drift far from the reference
Only when a separate reward model is trained and used alongside it to relabel the pairs
Never, because DPO has no explicit reward model whose blind spots the policy could exploit
With small beta or many epochs, it can over-fit the preference pairs and degrade
questions.explanation: DPO is not immune to over-optimization. A small beta lets the policy drift far from the reference, and many epochs over-fit the fixed pairs. Large beta and fewer epochs are mitigations.

questions.question: What is DPO's known 'margin-only' failure mode?
options: It can drive both chosen and rejected log-probabilities up to exactly zero, making every output certain
It can make the frozen reference model's log-probabilities increase alongside the policy's chosen ones
It can push both chosen and rejected log-probs down, as long as rejected falls faster than chosen
It can make the implicit reward margin turn negative while the reported DPO loss still keeps decreasing
questions.explanation: DPO only optimizes the difference of implicit rewards, so the loss can improve even if the chosen completion's probability falls, as long as the rejected falls faster. This can generally suppress output. Monitoring the absolute chosen log-prob, not just the margin, catches it.

questions.question: When training with DPO, which quantity should be monitored in addition to the margin to catch the margin-only pathology?
options: The absolute log-probability of the chosen completions
The reward model's bias term and its calibration drift
The PPO clip fraction and the approximate KL per step
The tokenizer's out-of-vocabulary rate on the rejected set
questions.explanation: Because the margin can improve while both chosen and rejected probabilities fall, watching the chosen log-prob directly (along with reward accuracy) reveals when the model is being suppressed overall. There is no reward model or clip fraction in DPO.

questions.question: What is distribution shift in RM+PPO?
options: The improving policy produces completions unlike the reward model's training data, so its scores become unreliable
The tokenizer's merge statistics shift during RL, so the same text maps to different token sequences over time
The frozen reference model gradually drifts away from the SFT checkpoint it was copied from during training
The test-set prompt distribution differs from the training prompts, so held-out reward is measured on new topics
questions.explanation: The reward model was trained on completions from some earlier distribution, often the SFT model's. PPO moves the policy into regions the reward model has not been trained on, making its scores unreliable exactly on the outputs being optimized. The reference model stays frozen.

questions.question: How does production RLHF mitigate distribution shift of the reward model?
options: By freezing the policy after the first epoch so its outputs stay inside the reward model's original training range
By increasing the PPO clip epsilon so each update can move further before the reward model goes stale
By removing the KL penalty so the policy explores more widely and the reward model sees more variety
By periodically collecting fresh preferences on the current policy's outputs and retraining the reward model
questions.explanation: Refreshing the reward model on new on-policy samples keeps it accurate where the policy now operates. Freezing the policy or removing the KL term would not address the reward model's coverage, and removing KL would worsen hacking.

questions.question: What analogue of distribution shift does DPO on a fixed offline dataset face, and what addresses it?
options: The reference log-probs drift as training proceeds; recomputing them from the current policy every step fixes it
The tokenizer drifts toward the chosen responses; retraining the tokenizer on rejected ones fixes it
The fixed pairs may not cover the policy's new behavior; online/iterative DPO regenerates them from the policy
There is no analogue, because DPO is fully offline and its loss cannot be affected by the policy's outputs
questions.explanation: As DPO moves the policy, the fixed offline pairs stop reflecting what the policy actually generates. Online or iterative DPO variants sample new pairs from the current policy to keep the data on-policy. The reference stays frozen.

questions.question: What is exposure bias in SFT?
options: The model is exposed to too many distinct prompts per epoch and overfits to their surface wording
Trained only on gold prefixes (teacher forcing), it never learns to recover from its own mistakes
The model memorizes the reward model's preferences and reproduces them instead of the demonstrations
The model is shown the reference policy's sampled outputs during training and copies their errors
questions.explanation: Teacher forcing always conditions on correct previous tokens, so at generation time, when the model conditions on its own possibly flawed outputs, it has no training experience with recovering. Preference methods, which score the model's own style of outputs, partly address this.

questions.question: Besides exposure bias, what are SFT's fundamental limitations?
options: It cannot learn instruction-following or chat format, only the raw style of the demonstration text
It cannot exceed the quality of its demonstrations and cannot express that A is better than B
It requires a trained reward model and online rollouts, so it is as costly to run as full RM+PPO
It cannot be sharded across more than one GPU, because the cross-entropy loss is not decomposable
questions.explanation: SFT is imitation: it is capped by its demonstrations and has no way to encode comparisons between answers. That gap is why preference learning exists. It does successfully teach instruction-following and format.

questions.question: What is the default post-training recipe?
options: PPO first on the base model, then a short SFT pass afterward to repair the chat formatting
DPO directly on the base model, skipping SFT, since preference pairs also teach the format
RLAIF only, with no SFT stage, because AI labels make human demonstrations redundant now
SFT first, then DPO for preference tuning unless a specific need calls for PPO
questions.explanation: SFT always comes first to install instruction-following and provide a sensible reference. DPO then gives most of the benefit of preference tuning at a fraction of PPO's infrastructure and instability. PPO is reserved for cases that need its specific advantages.

questions.question: When is SFT alone the right choice?
options: When you need a reusable reward model for best-of-n sampling and for filtering candidate outputs
When you want tight online control of the reward/KL trade-off while the policy is still moving
When you have good demonstrations, need instruction-following and format, and lack preference data
When the policy must exceed the quality of every demonstration it was trained on, not just match it
questions.explanation: SFT is cheapest and is always the first stage. With good demonstrations and no preference data, it is enough for instruction-following and format. Reward reuse and online control are reasons for RM+PPO; surpassing demonstrations requires preference methods.

questions.question: What advantages justify paying for full RM+PPO over DPO?
options: Lower peak memory than DPO and no generation in the loop, so each step runs noticeably faster
A reusable reward model (best-of-n, filtering, scoring), online reward/KL control, and on-policy data
Fewer hyperparameters than DPO and smoother, more stable training curves on the same preference data
No need for any preference data at all, since the reward model can be bootstrapped from SFT outputs
questions.explanation: RM+PPO is the high-ceiling option: the reward model is a reusable asset, the KL/reward trade-off can be controlled online, and training uses on-policy samples.
