Its costs are higher memory, generation, and more hyperparameters. It still needs preference data to train the reward model.

questions.question: What characterizes a hybrid/iterative post-training recipe?
options: SFT, then a reward model, then iterative DPO or online RL that regenerates preferences from the current policy
Alternating SFT and continued pretraining every epoch so the policy never forgets its base-model knowledge
Training DPO and PPO simultaneously on the same batch, summing both losses into one shared gradient step
Skipping SFT and running RLAIF directly on the base model, with a constitution supplying all the format rules
questions.explanation: Hybrid recipes combine an SFT start with a reward model used to produce fresh preference data from the current policy, followed by iterative DPO or online RL. Llama-3-style post-training uses rejection sampling plus DPO in this spirit.

questions.question: Why should preference optimization not be applied directly to a base (non-SFT) model?
options: Base models expose no token log-probabilities, so neither the DPO loss nor the PPO ratio can be computed
Preference optimization needs the vocabulary retrained with chat tokens, which only SFT is able to do
Both rely on a sensible reference and a policy that already follows the chat format; SFT provides both
Base models are too small to host a reward model head, so the RM must come from a separate SFT model
questions.explanation: Preference tuning refines behavior; it does not install it. Both methods use the starting model as the KL anchor/reference, so it must be a reasonable instruction follower. The SFT model supplies that sensible reference and chat-format policy.

questions.question: What is the bottleneck that Constitutional AI and RLAIF aim to relieve?
options: GPU memory during PPO rollouts, which caps how many models stay resident
The tokenizer's vocabulary size, which limits how well feedback is encoded
Human preference labels, which are slow, expensive, and inconsistent
The shortage of fresh pretraining data once the web has been fully crawled
questions.explanation: All the preference methods depend on human comparison labels, which are costly and noisy. Constitutional AI and RLAIF replace some or all of those labels with AI-generated feedback. They do not directly address compute or pretraining data.

questions.question: What happens in the supervised phase of Constitutional AI?
options: Humans write gold responses for harmful prompts, and the model is then fine-tuned directly on those responses
The model drafts a response, critiques it against written principles, revises it, and is fine-tuned on revisions
A reward model is trained on human harm labels, and the policy is distilled from its top-scoring samples only
The model is fine-tuned on randomly sampled responses with no feedback, relying on scale to remove harm
questions.explanation: Constitutional AI's first phase is self-critique and revision guided by a constitution of principles, followed by fine-tuning on the revised responses. This is self-improvement with minimal human harm labels. Human-written gold responses or human harm labels are what it avoids.

questions.question: What happens in the RL phase of Constitutional AI?
options: A model, not humans, labels which of two responses is better; these labels train a reward model for RL
Humans label every response pair against the constitution, and the policy is then trained with plain DPO
The constitution text is scored directly as the reward signal, so no preference or reward model is trained
The policy is trained only with SFT on the constitution text itself, with no reinforcement learning stage
questions.explanation: The RL phase is RLAIF: AI-generated preference labels train a preference (reward) model, and RL then optimizes the policy against it as in standard RLHF. Human labeling of pairs is replaced by AI feedback.

questions.question: What is a key benefit of the 'constitution' in Constitutional AI?
options: It eliminates the need for any model training, since the principles are enforced at inference time instead
It guarantees the model has no biases, because every principle is reviewed and signed off by a human panel
It removes the need for a reward or preference model, because the principles are scored directly as reward
It makes the values explicit and inspectable, a document you can edit, rather than implicit in human labels
questions.explanation: Writing the principles down makes the target behavior transparent and editable. Values are no longer hidden inside a large set of individual human labels. It still requires training and, in the RL phase, a preference model; it does not guarantee freedom from bias.

questions.question: What is RLAIF, and how does it compare with RLHF on the tasks studied?
options: RLHF with the reward model removed entirely; it performs much worse than RLHF on every task studied
RLHF trained on absolute AI scores instead of pairs; it beats RLHF on all tasks by a wide margin
Supervised fine-tuning on AI-written demonstrations; it is equivalent to SFT and adds no RL stage
RLHF with an AI preference labeler instead of humans; it performs comparably and scales more cheaply
questions.explanation: RLAIF replaces human preference labelers with an AI labeler. The RLAIF paper reports comparable performance to RLHF on the tasks studied, with much cheaper scaling because AI labels are fast and abundant. It is still an RL-with-reward-model pipeline.

questions.question: Which of these claims about post-training is PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED rather than industry practice or speculation?
options: A specific frontier product currently uses DPO rather than PPO for its post-training stage
RLAIF performs comparably to RLHF on the tasks studied in the RLAIF paper
Caching reference log-probs once before training is the standard way teams run DPO today
SFT followed by preference optimization is the standard pipeline used across most labs
questions.explanation: The RLAIF comparability result, the CAI critique-revise recipe, and DPO's equivalence to the RLHF objective are documented in papers. SFT→preference optimization and caching reference log-probs are reasonable industry practice. The exact recipe inside a specific frontier product is generally not public and should not be asserted.

questions.question: Which of these is classified as REASONABLE INDUSTRY PRACTICE rather than a publicly documented finding?
options: Iterating the reward model on fresh on-policy data to combat distribution shift
The Constitutional AI critique-and-revise recipe for the supervised training phase
RLAIF's comparability with RLHF on the summarization and dialogue tasks it studied
DPO optimizing exactly the same KL-constrained objective as the RLHF/PPO derivation
questions.explanation: Refreshing the reward model, SFT→preference optimization, DPO as the open-weight default, and caching reference log-probs are reasonable industry practice. The CAI recipe, RLAIF's result, and DPO's equivalence are publicly documented in papers.

questions.question: What should be avoided when discussing which alignment method a named frontier lab uses for a current model?
options: Mentioning PPO at all, since it is obsolete and no serious lab has run it in recent years
Mentioning DPO, since it is only an academic method that no production lab actually ships
Distinguishing documented facts from speculation, since that confuses readers needlessly
Asserting the lab 'uses X' unless it published that, since exact recipes are rarely public
questions.explanation: The exact post-training recipe, data mix, or RLHF-vs-DPO choice inside a specific frontier product is generally not publicly documented. Such claims are inference or speculation unless published. Separating documented facts from speculation is exactly what is encouraged.

questions.question: When is reaching for PPO by default a mistake?
options: Always, because PPO optimizes a different and strictly weaker objective than DPO does on the same preference data
Never, because PPO always yields better final quality whenever the compute budget allows it
When you need no reusable reward model or online control, since DPO is cheaper for the same objective
Only when the policy has fewer than 1B parameters, since below that size PPO rollouts are unstable
questions.explanation: PPO and DPO optimize the same objective, so PPO's extra infrastructure is only worth it for its specific advantages: a reusable reward model, online reward/KL control, and on-policy data. Otherwise DPO is the pragmatic default.

questions.question: What is the risk of using a stale reward model in a long PPO run?
options: Distribution shift makes it unreliable on the policy's improved outputs, so it should be refreshed
Its scalar head's weights decay toward zero under weight decay, flattening all rewards over time
It stops producing useful gradients for the value head, so advantage estimates freeze in place
It silently changes the frozen reference policy's log-probs, corrupting the KL penalty term
questions.explanation: As the policy improves, it generates outputs unlike those the reward model was trained on, so the stale model scores them unreliably. Periodically retraining on fresh on-policy preferences restores reliability.

questions.question: What is the misconception about AI feedback that RLAIF users should avoid?
options: Assuming AI feedback is free of bias; RLAIF inherits the labeler model's biases and blind spots
Assuming AI feedback costs more than human labels once API calls and filtering are accounted for
Assuming AI feedback cannot train reward models, since AI labels lack the needed pairwise structure
Assuming AI feedback needs a written constitution to work at all, even for simple helpfulness ratings
questions.explanation: AI labels reduce cost, not the need for oversight. The labeler model's biases and blind spots propagate into the preference data and therefore into the trained policy. AI feedback is cheaper, and it is routinely used to train reward models.

questions.question: A DPO run reports 0.95 training reward accuracy and a tiny loss, but answers became shorter and sometimes refuse reasonable requests. What are the two most likely explanations?
options: A data-loading bug that swaps chosen and rejected, plus a tokenizer mismatch between policy and reference
A beta that is far too large, plus a reference model that was accidentally left trainable during the run
Severe under-training from too few steps, plus a learning rate too small for the policy to move at all
Over-optimization (small beta or many epochs), plus the margin-only pathology lowering the chosen log-prob
questions.explanation: High training reward accuracy with worse real quality signals over-optimization: the policy drifted far from the reference and overfit the pairs. Shorter answers and over-refusal also fit the margin-only failure, where lowering the rejected log-prob drags the chosen down too. Both are over-optimization/distribution-shift problems, not a coding bug.

questions.question: What fixes address DPO over-optimization and the margin-only pathology?
options: Lower beta further and train for more epochs so the margin saturates and the loss settles
Remove the reference model so the policy can move freely toward the chosen responses
Raise beta, use fewer epochs, early-stop on held-out data, watch chosen log-prob, add an NLL term
Swap chosen and rejected halfway through training so the two margin effects cancel each other out
questions.explanation: A larger beta keeps the policy near the reference; fewer epochs and early stopping on held-out data limit overfitting. Monitoring the absolute chosen log-prob detects suppression, and adding an NLL term on chosen responses anchors their probability. Lowering beta or removing the reference would make drift worse.

questions.question: Why is DPO usually cheaper than PPO for the same goal?
options: It uses a smaller policy model than PPO by design, so every forward and backward pass costs less
No reward model and no generation loop; it forwards the policy and a frozen reference on fixed pairs
It needs far fewer preference pairs, because it trains on absolute scores rather than comparisons
It skips backpropagation through the rejected completions, halving the backward cost of each pair
questions.explanation: DPO is effectively SFT cost plus one frozen forward, because it only needs the policy and reference log-probs on given chosen/rejected completions. PPO keeps up to four models resident and generates every step, which dominates its cost.

questions.question: In Constitutional AI, what does the constitution replace, and with what?
options: The reward model, replaced by a rule-based keyword filter that blocks responses breaking any principle
Many human harm labels, replaced by written principles used for self-critique and AI preference labels
The SFT stage, replaced by continued pretraining on the constitution text until the model recites it
The reference policy, replaced by an embedding of the constitution that anchors the KL penalty term
questions.explanation: The constitution substitutes for many human harm labels. In the supervised phase it guides self-critique and revision; in the RLAIF phase it guides AI-generated preference labels for a reward model. The values become an explicit, editable document.

questions.question: In GRPO-based reasoning RL, which network that PPO needs is deleted entirely?
options: The frozen reference model used for the KL term
The policy network being optimized
The learned value network (critic)
The tokenizer's embedding network
questions.explanation: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) deletes PPO's learned value network, the critic. Its baseline is replaced by statistics of a group of sampled completions for the same prompt. The policy is still trained, and a frozen reference model is still used for the KL penalty, so those are not removed.

questions.question: Why do SFT and preference tuning alone not reliably teach a model multi-step reasoning?
options: They teach the model to imitate, and imitation never rewards actually reaching a correct answer
They use too small a learning rate to move the deep layers where multi-step reasoning is stored
They only update the final transformer layer, so the earlier layers that plan reasoning stay frozen
They require a learned critic network, which is too unstable to train on long reasoning chains
questions.explanation: SFT and preference tuning make a model helpful in format and tone, but they teach imitation. Imitation does not teach a model to search for a correct multi-step chain of reasoning. To get reliable reasoning, the model is rewarded for getting the answer right and RL is used to find the chains that do.

questions.question: Why is GRPO credited with making RL for reasoning cheap enough to run at scale (DeepSeekMath, DeepSeek-R1)?
options: It removes the need to sample completions from the policy
It replaces gradient descent with a closed-form update
It trains only on human-written demonstrations
It drops the second large network that PPO needs
questions.explanation: GRPO's practical win is that it removes PPO's critic, a second large network roughly the size of the policy. That cuts memory and compute and removes a fragile component. It still samples completions (in fact a whole group per prompt) and still uses gradient-based updates.

questions.question: What is the group-relative advantage used by GRPO for completion i?
options: $\hat A_i = r_i - V(s)$, where $V(s)$ is a learned critic's predicted return
$\hat A_i = (r_i - \mathrm{mean}(r)) / \mathrm{std}(r)$ over the group's rewards
$\hat A_i = r_i / \max(r)$, scaling each reward by the group's best reward
$\hat A_i = \log r_i - \log \mathrm{mean}(r)$, a log-ratio to the group mean
questions.explanation: GRPO standardizes each completion's reward within its group: subtract the group mean and divide by the group standard deviation. The group mean is the baseline, replacing PPO's $V(s)$. The form $r - V(s)$ is PPO's critic-based advantage, which GRPO specifically avoids.

questions.section: 1. The story so far, and where it breaks
questions.question: What did pretraining, SFT and preference tuning each contribute to a model, in order?
options: Following instructions; continuing text by next-token prediction; verifying that final answers are correct
Continuing text; following instructions by imitating good answers; aligning answers with human preferences
Aligning answers with human preferences; continuing text; reasoning correctly through verified multi-step chains
Reasoning correctly through multi-step chains; following instructions by imitation; continuing text fluently
questions.explanation: Pretraining gives a model that continues text. SFT teaches it to follow instructions by imitating good answers. Preference tuning (RLHF with a reward model and PPO, or DPO) makes its answers align with what humans prefer. None of these directly reward reaching a correct answer.

questions.section: 1. The story so far, and where it breaks
questions.question: Why is a reward model trained on human ratings still considered a form of imitation for reasoning purposes?
options: It copies demonstrations token by token with a cross-entropy loss, so it only ever learns the gold wording
It is trained with exactly the same next-token loss as pretraining, so it learns fluency rather than correctness
It can only be used together with SFT, never on its own, so it inherits all of SFT's imitation behaviour
It scores answers by resemblance to what humans rated highly, not by whether the answer is correct
questions.explanation: A reward model scores answers by resemblance to highly rated answers. It does not check that a chain of intermediate steps actually reaches the correct final answer. Copying demonstrations token by token describes SFT, the other imitation method.

questions.section: 1. The story so far, and where it breaks
questions.question: How can a model imitate the surface form of a worked solution yet still get the arithmetic wrong?
options: Nothing in an imitation loss ever checked whether the final answer was correct
Its tokenizer cannot represent multi-digit numbers, so arithmetic is split into noise
Its attention cannot reach tokens far back in long solutions, so earlier steps are lost
Its KL penalty to the reference blocks any change to the arithmetic it learned in pretraining
questions.explanation: Imitation losses reward matching the form of good answers. Since nothing in the loss checks the answer, a model can reproduce the style of a worked solution while making arithmetic mistakes. This is why reasoning RL rewards correctness directly.

questions.section: 1. The story so far, and where it breaks
questions.question: What two ingredients does a model need to learn to reason reliably over multiple steps?
options: Far more demonstration data, and a larger SFT learning rate so the chains are memorized
A bigger human-preference reward model, and a much longer context window for the chain
A reward for reaching a correct answer, and RL to search for the chains that earn it
A learned critic network, and supervised imitation of expert chains with token-level loss
questions.explanation: Ordinary imitation cannot teach reliable multi-step reasoning. The model needs a reward for reaching a correct answer, and reinforcement learning to search for the chains of reasoning that earn that reward. More demonstrations would still be imitation.

questions.section: 2. What PPO needs, and why the critic hurts
questions.question: In PPO, what is the role of the baseline when computing an advantage?
options: It caps the probability ratio between new and old policy so that each update stays small
It is the KL distance to the frozen reference model, subtracted from the reward at each step
It defines the 'expected' reward, so the advantage says how much better than expected an action was
It is the per-step learning rate applied to the policy, scaled by how uncertain the critic is about it
questions.explanation: The advantage answers 'how much better than expected was this?', and 'expected' needs a definition: the baseline. PPO learns this baseline with a value network, and the advantage is roughly $A = R - V(s)$. Capping the ratio is the job of the clip, not the baseline.

questions.section: 2. What PPO needs, and why the critic hurts
questions.question: In PPO's advantage $A = R - V(s)$, what are $R$ and $V(s)$?
options: $R$ is the realized return; $V(s)$ is the critic's prediction of that return
$R$ is the frozen reference model's log-prob; $V(s)$ is the vocabulary size
$R$ is the clipped probability ratio; $V(s)$ is the variance of the rewards
$R$ is the reward model's raw logit; $V(s)$ is the KL penalty to the reference
questions.explanation: $R$ is the return actually received, and $V(s)$ is the value function (critic) output: its prediction of the return from state $s$. Their difference says how much better or worse than predicted the outcome was. GRPO replaces $V(s)$ with the group's mean reward.

questions.section: 2. What PPO needs, and why the critic hurts
questions.question: Why is PPO's critic so costly in memory and compute for an LLM?
options: It must run a separate forward pass for every vocabulary token at every position of the completion
It stores every past completion and its value in GPU memory so that it can replay them every update
It requires full-precision float64 weights and gradients, quadrupling memory compared with bf16
It is a second policy-sized network, so you hold two large models and run two forward/backward passes
questions.explanation: For an LLM the critic is typically the same transformer with a scalar head, so it is about the size of the policy. You hold two large models plus their optimizer states and run two forward/backward passes. On hardware sized for a 7B policy, the critic can nearly double the footprint.

questions.section: 2. What PPO needs, and why the critic hurts
questions.question: What does a PPO critic for an LLM typically look like architecturally?
options: A small two-layer MLP reading the final token's embedding from the policy
The same transformer as the policy with a scalar output head
A lookup table of returns indexed by prompt id and step number
A frozen copy of the SFT model with no head, used only for log-probs
questions.explanation: The critic is usually the same transformer architecture as the policy with a scalar head that predicts the value. That is exactly why it is expensive: it is roughly policy-sized. A frozen copy of the SFT model with no head describes the reference model, which only supplies log-probs for the KL term.

questions.section: 2. What PPO needs, and why the critic hurts
questions.question: Why does a poorly trained critic destabilize PPO's policy updates?
options: It pushes the new-to-old probability ratio outside the clip range on every step
A bad baseline injects bias into every advantage the policy is trained on
It silently changes the tokenizer's vocabulary as value estimates are updated
It forces the KL penalty weight to zero, so the policy drifts from the reference
questions.explanation: The critic is itself learned from noisy returns, and early in training its estimates are poor. Since each advantage is $R - V(s)$, a bad $V$ biases every advantage, which destabilizes the policy update. Much of the folklore of getting PPO to work is really getting the value function to behave.

questions.section: 2. What PPO needs, and why the critic hurts
questions.question: What feature of reasoning RL opens the shortcut that lets GRPO drop the critic?
options: Reasoning rewards are always negative, so a zero baseline already centers the advantages
Reasoning prompts are short enough that every possible answer can simply be enumerated
The frozen reference model already predicts each prompt's expected reward for free
Many completions are sampled per prompt anyway, so the baseline comes from the group
questions.explanation: In reasoning RL you sample many completions per prompt to see which chains land on the right answer. With a whole group of scored completions for the same prompt, the baseline can be computed directly from the group, with no learned critic. The reference model provides log-probs for the KL term, not expected rewards.

questions.section: 3. GRPO: the group is the baseline
questions.question: Which paper introduced GRPO?
options: DeepSeekMath (Shao et al. 2024)
DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI 2025)
Let's Verify Step by Step (2023)
InstructGPT (Ouyang et al. 2022)
questions.explanation: GRPO was introduced in DeepSeekMath by Shao et al. (2024). DeepSeek-R1 later used GRPO with rule-based rewards, but it is not the paper that introduced the algorithm. Let's Verify Step by Step is about process reward models.

questions.section: 3. GRPO: the group is the baseline
questions.question: What are the three steps GRPO performs for each prompt before the update?
options: Sample one completion, train a critic on its return, then subtract the critic's value
Score the prompt's difficulty, sample G completions, and keep only the single best one
Sample G completions, score each, and use the group's reward statistics as the baseline
Sample G completions, rank them pairwise by a judge, and fit a reward model to the ranks
questions.explanation: For each prompt, GRPO samples a group of $G$ completions from the current policy, scores each to get rewards $r_1..r_G$, and computes advantages from the group's own mean and standard deviation. No critic is trained, and nothing is thrown away: every completion gets an advantage.

questions.section: 3. GRPO: the group is the baseline
questions.question: In GRPO, what advantage sign does a completion get if it beat its group's average reward, and what does the update do to its tokens?
options: Negative advantage; its tokens are pushed down
Zero advantage; its tokens are unchanged
Positive advantage; its tokens are pushed up
Positive advantage; its tokens are pushed down
questions.explanation: A completion above the group mean has $r_i - \mu > 0$, so a positive advantage, and the policy-gradient step increases the probability of its tokens. A completion below the mean gets a negative advantage and its tokens are pushed down.

questions.section: 3. GRPO: the group is the baseline
questions.question: Why does GRPO's group-mean baseline cost nothing to learn?
options: It is just an average of rewards already obtained for the sampled completions
It is a fixed constant of 0.5 chosen before training and never recomputed
It is copied from the frozen reference model's output head at every step
It is computed once over the SFT dataset's rewards and then reused all run
questions.explanation: The group mean plays exactly the role of PPO's $V(s)$, but it is simply the average of rewards you already have for the group. There is no network to train and no extra forward/backward pass. It is recomputed per prompt per step, not fixed.

questions.section: 3. GRPO: the group is the baseline
questions.question: Besides removing the critic's memory cost, what other benefit does GRPO's group baseline bring?
options: It eliminates the need for any KL penalty
It makes the policy deterministic
It removes the need to sample from the policy
There is no fragile second model to train
questions.explanation: Dropping the critic halves the large-network memory and also removes a fragile second model whose bad estimates would bias advantages. GRPO still typically uses a KL-to-reference term and still samples groups from the policy.

questions.question: In GRPO's advantage formula, what does the group mean $\mu$ equal when rewards are 1 for correct and 0 for wrong?
options: The number of correct completions
The fraction of the group that was correct
The probability the reference model assigns to the answer
The standard deviation of the rewards
questions.explanation: With 0/1 rewards, $\mu = \frac{1}{G}\sum r_i$ is the count of correct completions divided by $G$, i.e. the fraction correct. It serves as the baseline. The raw count would not be divided by $G$.

questions.question: Which standard deviation does GRPO use for $\sigma$ in its advantage formula?
options: The sample standard deviation, dividing by $G-1$
The population standard deviation, dividing by $G$
The standard deviation across all prompts in the batch
The running standard deviation over all past steps
questions.explanation: $\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{G}\sum (r_i - \mu)^2}$ divides by $G$, the population std, computed per prompt over its group. Using $G-1$ (sample std) breaks the exact unit-std property and blows up for small $G$.

questions.question: What is the purpose of dividing GRPO advantages by the group standard deviation $\sigma$?
options: It removes the baseline from the rewards so each completion is centered on zero
It ensures every advantage is positive so no completion's tokens are pushed down
It converts the raw rewards into probabilities that sum to one across the group
It rescales advantages so groups of different difficulty contribute comparably
questions.explanation: Dividing by $\sigma$ standardizes the spread so that prompts with very different reward spreads contribute on a comparable scale. Removing the baseline is the job of subtracting $\mu$, not dividing by $\sigma$. Standardized advantages are both positive and negative.

questions.question: What is the role of $\varepsilon$ (default 1e-8) in the GRPO advantage $\hat A_i = (r_i - \mu)/(\sigma + \varepsilon)$?
options: It guards the division when $\sigma = 0$
It is the PPO clip half-width
It is the KL penalty weight
It is the exploration temperature for sampling
questions.explanation: $\varepsilon$ is a tiny constant added to $\sigma$ so the division is safe when all rewards in a group are equal. The clip half-width is a different symbol, $\epsilon$, typically 0.2, and the KL weight is $\beta$.

questions.question: What does the group-relative advantage $\hat A_i$ multiply in the policy-gradient step?
options: Completion i's reward
The KL divergence to the reference model
Completion i's log-probability
The group mean reward
questions.explanation: $\hat A_i$ is the weight on completion $i$'s log-prob in the policy-gradient step: positive advantage pushes that completion's log-prob up, negative pushes it down. It does not multiply the reward or the KL term.

questions.question: Within a single GRPO group, what are the mean and population standard deviation of the advantages (ignoring a unanimous group)?
options: Mean approximately 1 and population std approximately 0
Mean equal to the reward mean and std equal to the reward std
Mean approximately 0 and population std approximately 1
Mean approximately 0.5 and population std approximately 0.5
questions.explanation: Subtracting $\mu$ makes the advantages mean zero, and dividing by $\sigma$ makes their population std one. These two invariants are useful debugging checks. They hold only approximately because of $\varepsilon$ in the denominator.

questions.question: In GRPO, if every completion in a group gets the same reward, what advantage does each completion receive?
options: Zero, because the epsilon-guarded division turns 0/0 into 0/epsilon
One, because every completion exactly matched the group baseline
NaN, which the optimizer detects and then skips for that group
The reward value itself, since there is no spread to normalize by
questions.explanation: In a unanimous group $\sigma = 0$ and every $r_i - \mu = 0$. The guard turns $0/0$ into $0/\varepsilon = 0$, so the group contributes zero advantage and zero gradient. Without the guard you would get NaNs.

questions.question: Why is it correct for a GRPO group where every completion is right (or every one is wrong) to contribute no gradient?
options: The KL penalty to the reference already supplies the gradient for those prompts
Such prompts are always filtered out by the verifier before the update is computed
The critic supplies the learning signal for those prompts instead of the group mean
Nothing in the group did better or worse than anything else, so there is no signal
questions.explanation: If all completions earned the same reward, no completion beat its group's baseline, so there is no relative signal. A prompt the policy always gets right, or always gets wrong, teaches that step nothing. GRPO has no critic to supply a gradient.

questions.section: 3.2 Numerical example, worked by hand — a group of four
questions.question: For a GRPO group with rewards [1, 0, 1, 0], what are the advantages?
questions.explanation: The mean is 0.5 and every deviation is ±0.5, so the population std is 0.5. Dividing the deviations [0.5, -0.5, 0.5, -0.5] by 0.5 gives [+1, -1, +1, -1]. The option [±0.5] forgets to divide by sigma.

questions.section: 3.2 Numerical example, worked by hand — a group of four
questions.question: In an evenly split GRPO group with two correct and two wrong completions, how does the update treat winners and losers?
options: It pushes winners up and leaves losers unchanged, like rejection sampling does
It pushes winners up and losers down by equal and opposite amounts
It pushes losers down twice as hard as it pushes the winners up
It leaves all four unchanged, because the balanced group cancels out
questions.explanation: With advantages [+1, -1, +1, -1], the two correct completions' tokens are pushed up and the two wrong completions' tokens pushed down by the same magnitude, because the group was evenly split. Leaving losers unchanged describes rejection sampling, not GRPO.

questions.section: 3.2 Numerical example, worked by hand — a group of four
questions.question: For a GRPO group with shaped rewards [2, 0, 1, 1], which completions receive zero advantage?
options: The completion with reward 0, since a zero reward contributes nothing to the update
None of them, since the rewards are not unanimous and every one has a deviation
The completion with reward 2, since the group's best completion is already the target
The two completions with reward 1, since they sit exactly at the group mean
questions.explanation: The mean is 1, so the two completions with reward 1 have deviation 0 and advantage 0: dead center, no push. The reward-2 and reward-0 completions get symmetric ±1.4142 (deviation ±1 divided by sigma = sqrt(0.5)).

questions.section: 3.3 This is exactly what the code does
questions.question: In `grpo_advantages(rewards)` from llmre/rl/grpo.py, what is the input and output shape?
options: Input (num_prompts, group_size), output (num_prompts, group_size)
Input (group_size,), output (1,), one scalar advantage per group
Input (num_prompts, group_size), output (num_prompts, 1), per prompt
Input (num_prompts, vocab_size), output (num_prompts, group_size)
questions.explanation: Rows are prompts and columns are completions in the group; the function returns advantages of the identical shape. The per-prompt mean and std have shape (num_prompts, 1) internally, but they broadcast back across the group. Dtype and device are preserved.

questions.section: 3.3 This is exactly what the code does
questions.question: In `grpo_advantages`, why are the mean and std computed with `dim=1, keepdim=True`?
options: To reduce across prompts, so every group in the batch shares a single common baseline
To reduce along the vocabulary axis of the logits before the rewards are standardized
To reduce per prompt over the group axis, keeping (num_prompts, 1) so it broadcasts back
To flatten the tensor to one dimension first, so that standardizing ignores prompt rows
questions.explanation: `dim=1` is the group axis, so each prompt gets its own mean and std. `keepdim=True` keeps a column of shape (num_prompts, 1), which broadcasts when subtracting and dividing over the (num_prompts, group_size) rewards. Reducing across prompts would mix baselines from different prompts.

questions.section: 3.3 This is exactly what the code does
questions.question: Why does `grpo_advantages` call `rewards.std(..., unbiased=False)`?
options: To use a faster fused GPU kernel that skips the Bessel correction step
To stop gradients from flowing through the std back into the rewards
To get the population std (divide by G), matching GRPO's $\sigma$
To compute a single std across all prompts in the batch at once
questions.explanation: `unbiased=False` gives the population standard deviation, dividing by $G$, which is the $\sigma$ in the formula. The sample std ($G-1$) would make the unit-std property only approximate and blows up for small $G$. It has nothing to do with gradients or speed.

questions.section: 3.3 This is exactly what the code does
questions.question: Running `grpo_advantages` on rewards [1, 0, 1, 0] prints 0.99999998 instead of exactly 1 for the winners. Why?
options: The $\varepsilon$ added to the std in the denominator makes it slightly below 1
Float16 rounding of the 0/1 rewards before the mean and std are computed
The sample std (divide by G-1) is used instead of the population std
The baseline is averaged across all prompts instead of within each group
questions.explanation: The denominator is $\sigma + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon = 10^{-8}$, so $0.5/(0.5 + 10^{-8})$ is a hair below 1. It is negligible, and exactly why the unit test compares with a tolerance. The function uses population std and per-prompt baselines.

questions.section: 3.3 This is exactly what the code does
questions.question: What does `grpo_advantages(r).mean(dim=1)` return for any non-unanimous batch of groups, and what does it confirm?
options: Ones per prompt, confirming the advantages have unit variance
The fraction of correct completions per prompt, i.e. the baseline
The KL divergence to the reference per prompt, which should be small
Zeros per prompt, confirming the baseline has been removed
questions.explanation: Because each group's mean is subtracted, the advantages in each row average to zero. Seeing tensor([0., 0.]) confirms the baseline was removed. Unit variance is the other invariant, checked with the std, not the mean.

questions.section: 4. The GRPO objective: PPO's clip, fed the group advantage
questions.question: How does GRPO's policy update relate to PPO's clipped surrogate objective?
options: It replaces the clip with an unconstrained log-likelihood loss weighted by the advantage
It uses the same clipped surrogate; only the advantage changes to the group-relative one
It uses a different, one-sided clip that applies only when the advantage is negative
It drops the probability ratio and multiplies raw sequence probabilities by the advantage
questions.explanation: GRPO keeps PPO's clipped surrogate unchanged in form. The only difference is the advantage: group-relative and standardized instead of $R - V$. The ratio and clip work exactly as in PPO.

questions.section: 4. The GRPO objective: PPO's clip, fed the group advantage
questions.question: In GRPO, what is the probability ratio $\rho_i$ for completion $o_i$ on prompt $q$?
options: $\pi_\theta(o_i \mid q) / \pi_{\text{ref}}(o_i \mid q)$, the current policy over the frozen reference
$\pi_\theta(o_i \mid q) / \pi_{\text{old}}(o_i \mid q)$, current policy over the group's sampler
$r_i / \mathrm{mean}(r)$, completion i's reward divided by the group's mean reward
$\pi_{\text{old}}(o_i \mid q) / \pi_\theta(o_i \mid q)$, the old policy over the current one
questions.explanation: The ratio compares the current policy $\pi_\theta$ to $\pi_{\text{old}}$, the policy that sampled the group. The reference model $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ appears only in the KL penalty, not in the ratio. Inverting the ratio would flip the clip's direction.

questions.section: 4. The GRPO objective: PPO's clip, fed the group advantage
questions.question: Why is GRPO's probability ratio computed as exp(log pi_theta - log pi_old) rather than dividing probabilities?
options: Because raw probabilities cannot be differentiated with respect to the policy weights
Because the clip operation is only defined on logarithms, never on raw ratios
Because exponentiating the difference removes the need for any baseline term
Because log-space is numerically stable, which is why the code takes log-probs
questions.explanation: Sequence probabilities are products of many small numbers and underflow easily; differences of log-probs are stable. So the ratio is computed as exp of a log-prob difference, and the code takes log-probs as inputs. Probabilities are differentiable, but dividing them directly is unstable.

questions.section: 4. The GRPO objective: PPO's clip, fed the group advantage
questions.question: Write the per-completion clipped GRPO objective $J_i$ (before the KL term).
options: $\min(\rho_i \hat A_i,\ \mathrm{clip}(\rho_i, 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon)\hat A_i)$
$\max(\rho_i \hat A_i,\ \mathrm{clip}(\rho_i, 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon)\hat A_i)$
$\mathrm{clip}(\rho_i \hat A_i,\ 1-\epsilon,\ 1+\epsilon) \cdot \hat A_i$
$\mathrm{clip}(\rho_i - \hat A_i,\ 1-\epsilon,\ 1+\epsilon)$
questions.explanation: The objective to maximize takes the minimum of the unclipped and clipped terms, a pessimistic bound. Using max would let the clip increase the objective and defeat its purpose. The clip is applied to the ratio, not to the product.

questions.section: 4. The GRPO objective: PPO's clip, fed the group advantage
questions.question: What does the KL-to-reference term subtracted in full GRPO do?
options: It keeps the new policy close to the policy that generated the group
It normalizes advantages to unit variance
It keeps the policy from drifting far from the frozen SFT model
It replaces the clip when the ratio exceeds 1+epsilon
questions.explanation: $-\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_\theta \| \pi_{\text{ref}})$ penalizes divergence from the frozen reference (SFT) model. Staying close to the sampling policy $\pi_{\text{old}}$ within one update is the clip's job. Normalization is done in the advantage.

questions.section: 4. The GRPO objective: PPO's clip, fed the group advantage
questions.question: In GRPO's clipped objective, what is $\epsilon$ and its typical value?
options: The std guard, typically 1e-8
The KL weight, typically 0.2
The clip half-width, typically 0.2
The learning rate, typically 0.2
questions.explanation: $\epsilon$ is the clip half-width: the ratio is clipped to $[1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon]$, typically $[0.8, 1.2]$. The tiny std guard is a different symbol ($\varepsilon$, 1e-8), and the KL weight is $\beta$.

questions.section: 4. The GRPO objective: PPO's clip, fed the group advantage
questions.question: What does the clip in GRPO's objective allow you to do safely with a sampled group?
options: Reuse the group for several gradient steps without the policy running away
Skip computing advantages for that group, since the clip already bounds them
Sample fewer completions per prompt, since clipped groups need less data
Train without a reference model, since the clip replaces the KL penalty
questions.explanation: The min with the clipped term caps how far one update can move the ratio outside $[1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon]$. That makes it safe to take several inner gradient steps on the same group. It does not replace advantages, group size, or the reference model.

questions.section: 4. The GRPO objective: PPO's clip, fed the group advantage
questions.question: In GRPO, what is $\beta$ and where does it come from?
options: The clip half-width for the ratio, typically 0.2
The group size used for sampling, typically 8 to 64
The temperature applied to the logits when sampling
The KL penalty weight, the same kl_penalty from PPO
questions.explanation: $\beta$ weights the KL-to-reference penalty. It is the same `kl_penalty` knob from PPO, reused unchanged. The clip width is $\epsilon$ and the group size is $G$.

questions.section: 4. The GRPO objective: PPO's clip, fed the group advantage
questions.question: On the first on-policy GRPO update, what does the clipped objective reduce to, and why?
options: Zero, because the clip removes all gradient whenever the ratio is exactly 1 at the start
The plain group-baselined policy gradient, since $\pi_\theta = \pi_{\text{old}}$ gives ratio 1
Pure KL minimization, because every advantage is still zero at the very first step
Supervised fine-tuning on the best completion, since only it has a positive advantage
questions.explanation: At the first step the current policy equals the sampling policy, so $\rho_i = 1$, inside the clip range. The objective then behaves as $\hat A_i \cdot \log\pi_\theta(o_i\mid q)$, the plain group-baselined policy gradient. The clip only matters after multiple steps on the same group make the ratio drift.

questions.question: In llmre's `grpo_objective`, where is the KL-to-reference term handled?
options: Inside grpo_objective, using a reference-logprobs argument it subtracts
It is added by the caller, as in PPO; the function computes only the clipped term
Inside grpo_advantages, folded into the rewards before standardization
It is not used anywhere in GRPO, since the clip alone bounds the policy drift
questions.explanation: `grpo_objective` computes the element-wise clipped surrogate: ratio, unclipped, clipped, minimum, then a reduction. The KL penalty is added by the caller, just as in the PPO code. GRPO does use a KL term in full form.

questions.question: Which reduction options does llmre's `grpo_objective` support?
options: "mean" only, with no other options
"max", "min", and "mean"
"batch", "token", and "seq"
"mean", "sum", and "none"
questions.explanation: The function takes `reduction="mean"` by default and also accepts "sum" and "none". "none" returns the per-element objective, which is handy for inspecting individual values such as a hand-worked clip example.

questions.question: How should the training loss be formed from `grpo_objective`?
options: loss = -grpo_objective(...), since it returns an objective to maximize
loss = grpo_objective(...), because the function already returns a loss
loss = 1 / grpo_objective(...), to invert its scale into a minimization
loss = grpo_objective(...) ** 2, to keep it positive for the optimizer
questions.explanation: `grpo_objective` returns a quantity you want to go up. Optimizers minimize, so the loss is its negative. Feeding it directly to backward() would do gradient descent on the objective, making the policy worse.

questions.question: What happens if you call loss.backward() directly on the output of `grpo_objective` without negating it?
options: Nothing changes, since the sign is handled internally
Training diverges with NaNs immediately
You minimize the objective, so the policy gets worse
The clip is disabled but training still improves
questions.explanation: The function returns an objective to maximize. Calling backward on it and stepping an optimizer descends that objective: it pushes down good completions and up bad ones. Always use loss = -grpo_objective(...).

questions.question: A completion's ratio has risen to 1.5 with advantage +2 and clip epsilon 0.2. What is the GRPO objective value?
questions.explanation: Unclipped is 1.5 × 2 = 3.0; clipped is clip(1.5, 0.8, 1.2) × 2 = 1.2 × 2 = 2.4; the min is 2.4. 3.0 would ignore the clip entirely.

questions.question: For a positive advantage, what happens to the GRPO objective once the ratio exceeds 1+epsilon?
options: It flattens, so pushing that completion's probability higher earns nothing more
It keeps growing linearly with the ratio, since only negative advantages get clipped
It flips sign and starts penalizing the completion for having moved too far
It resets the ratio back to 1 by reloading the old policy's log-probabilities
questions.explanation: Beyond $1+\epsilon$ the min picks the clipped term, which is constant in the ratio, so the gradient is as if the ratio were pinned at $1+\epsilon$. This removes the incentive to make a big, destabilizing jump on a single group. It does not flip the sign or reset anything.

questions.question: In the hand-worked GRPO clip example, which arguments to `grpo_objective` produce a ratio of 1.5?
options: logprob = 1.5 and old logprob = 1.0
logprob = 0.0 and old logprob = log(1.5)
logprob = 1.5 and old logprob = 0.0
logprob = log(1.5) and old logprob = 0.0
questions.explanation: The ratio is exp(logprob - old_logprob), so log(1.5) - 0 gives exp(log 1.5) = 1.5. Passing 1.5 directly as a log-prob would give a ratio of exp(1.5) ≈ 4.48. Swapping the two would give a ratio of 1/1.5.

questions.section: 5. Under the hood: what you actually save
questions.question: Per optimization step, what does plain PPO for an LLM run that GRPO does not?
options: A forward pass on the frozen reference model for the KL penalty term, plus caching its outputs
A forward and backward pass on the critic, plus holding its weights and optimizer state
Sampling a fresh set of completions from the current policy for each prompt in the batch
A backward pass through the policy to compute the clipped-surrogate gradient for each token
questions.explanation: PPO runs forward+backward on both policy and critic and holds both sets of parameters and optimizer states. GRPO keeps only the policy plus a frozen reference for the KL term. Both methods sample from and backprop through the policy.

questions.section: 5. Under the hood: what you actually save
questions.question: In GRPO, what does the frozen reference model cost per step?
options: A forward and backward pass with its own separate optimizer
A forward pass, but no gradients and no optimizer state
Nothing at all, since it is never evaluated during training
A full retraining on the latest groups at the end of every epoch
questions.explanation: The reference model supplies log-probs for the KL term, which needs a forward pass. It is frozen, so it has no gradients and no optimizer state. That is much cheaper than a trainable critic.

questions.section: 5. Under the hood: what you actually save
questions.question: What cost does GRPO add back compared with PPO, and why is it acceptable?
options: Training a second, smaller reward model each step; it is still far cheaper than training a full critic
Storing every past group in a replay buffer on disk; storage is cheap compared with GPU memory
Running the policy in float64 for exact advantages; accuracy matters more than speed in RL
Sampling G completions per prompt; generation is cheap next to a critic, and RL samples a group anyway
questions.explanation: GRPO needs $G$ completions per prompt to form the group baseline. Generation is cheap relative to a full critic you must also train, and for verifiable reasoning you would sample a group anyway to find correct chains. GRPO does not add a second reward model or replay buffer.

questions.section: 5. Under the hood: what you actually save
questions.question: Which claim about GRPO is publicly documented in DeepSeekMath, rather than industry practice or speculation?
options: GRPO removes the value network and uses a group-relative advantage plus a KL-to-reference term
Group sizes between 8 and 64 completions per prompt give the best results across all tasks
Each sampled group should be reused for a small number of inner update steps before resampling
Dividing advantages by the group std is always necessary for GRPO to train stably at all
questions.explanation: The DeepSeekMath paper describes GRPO as removing the value network and using a group-relative standardized advantage with a KL-to-reference term. Group sizes of 8–64 and a few inner steps are reasonable industry practice. Whether to normalize by sigma at all is a tuning choice, and some later work drops or modifies it.

questions.section: 5. Under the hood: what you actually save
questions.question: What is reasonable industry practice for GRPO's group size G?
options: Exactly 1, to match PPO
Exactly 2, for pairwise comparison
Somewhere in the range of 8 to 64
At least 1024, to estimate the mean precisely
questions.explanation: Group sizes of roughly 8 to 64 are a reasonable industry practice, not a law. G = 1 would give no group baseline at all (every group unanimous). Very large groups make generation expensive.

questions.section: 5. Under the hood: what you actually save
questions.question: How should GRPO hyperparameters such as G, epsilon, beta, and whether to normalize by sigma be treated?
options: As fixed constants published in DeepSeekMath that must not be changed for any task
As irrelevant details, since GRPO's results are insensitive to all of these settings
As tuning choices to sweep; some later work drops or modifies the std-normalization
As values set automatically by the critic network during the first training steps
questions.explanation: Exact $G$, $\epsilon$, $\beta$, and the choice to divide by $\sigma$ are tuning decisions, and some later work drops or modifies the std-normalization. Treat them as things to sweep. GRPO has no critic to set them.

questions.question: For a GRPO group with rewards [1, 1, 0, 0], what are the advantages?
questions.explanation: The mean is 0.5, deviations are [+0.5, +0.5, -0.5, -0.5], the population std is 0.5, so advantages are [+1, +1, -1, -1]. The two correct completions are pushed up and the two wrong ones pushed down. [+1, -1, +1, -1] is the answer for the order [1, 0, 1, 0].

questions.question: Do GRPO advantages depend on the order in which the completions in a group were sampled?
options: Yes; earlier samples get larger advantages because they are closer to the old policy
Yes; the last sample in each group is treated as the baseline for all the others
No; every completion gets an identical advantage regardless of the reward it earned
No; each advantage depends only on its reward relative to the group's mean and std
questions.explanation: Mean and std are order-invariant, so [1,1,0,0] and [1,0,1,0] yield the same advantage vector up to order. Each completion's advantage depends only on its reward relative to the group. Completions with different rewards still get different advantages.

questions.question: What goes wrong if a GRPO implementation omits the epsilon guard in the advantage denominator?
options: Advantages in every group lose their zero mean and drift positive
All-correct or all-wrong groups have sigma = 0 and produce NaNs
The clip range becomes infinite, so the ratio is no longer bounded
The KL term turns negative and rewards drifting from the reference
questions.explanation: A unanimous group has $\sigma = 0$ and zero deviations, so the advantage is $0/0$ = NaN without the guard. Conceptually those groups should contribute nothing, which the guard achieves by returning 0. The mean-zero property is unaffected for non-unanimous groups.

questions.question: What error occurs if you pass raw probabilities to `grpo_objective` where log-probabilities are expected?
options: The function detects probabilities and converts them to logs, so nothing goes wrong
The ratio exp(logp - old_logp) is computed from the wrong quantities, so it is wrong
Every advantage becomes zero, because probabilities cancel out in the standardization
The clip range is effectively doubled, because probabilities lie between 0 and 1
questions.explanation: The ratio is computed as exp(logp - old_logp), which only equals the probability ratio when given log-probs. Feed probabilities and the exponent of their difference is not the ratio you want. The function does no conversion.

questions.question: What is the main saving from GRPO's use of a group mean in place of a learned value baseline?
options: It removes the need for any reward signal, since the group mean supplies the learning signal
It removes the reference model's forward pass, since the group mean replaces the KL anchor
It removes the need to compute log-probabilities, since advantages come straight from rewards
It removes PPO's second large network, saving memory and the instability of a learned value
questions.explanation: Because GRPO samples a group per prompt, the group mean reward is a free baseline. This eliminates the critic, saving memory and compute, and avoiding the bias of a badly trained value estimate. A reward, a reference forward pass for KL, and log-probs are all still needed.

questions.question: What does RLVR stand for?
options: Reinforcement Learning with Value Regression
Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
Reward-Learned Value Refinement for reasoning
Rejection Learning via Verified Rollouts (RLVR)
questions.explanation: RLVR is RL with Verifiable Rewards: the learned reward model is replaced by an automatic checker that knows the right answer. It is typically paired with GRPO. 'Value regression' would describe training a critic, which RLVR does not need.

questions.question: What single change is credited with making RL for reasoning take off?
options: Adding a larger critic network to PPO so value estimates on long chains stop drifting
Training the reward model on far more human preference pairs collected on math problems
Removing the KL penalty from the objective so the policy can explore new reasoning freely
Swapping the learned reward model for a cheap, exact rule that knows the right answer
questions.explanation: The key change was replacing the fragile, gameable learned reward model with a cheap, exact, rule-based check of correctness. That is why math and code, where correctness is checkable by a program, are where reasoning RL first worked.

questions.question: Why were math and code the first domains where reasoning RL worked?
options: Correctness in those domains is checkable by a program
Their texts are shorter, so rollouts are cheap to sample
They have the most human preference data of any domain
Their tokenizers have the smallest vocabularies to search
questions.explanation: In math and code, a program can check whether an answer is right (compare to the true value, run unit tests). That gives an exact, cheap reward with no proxy to hack. It has nothing to do with text length or preference data volume.

questions.section: 1. The problem with a learned reward
questions.question: In RLHF, what does the reward model output for a completion?
options: A binary correct/incorrect label computed by a hand-written rule that knows the answer
A probability distribution over the next token, used to re-rank the policy's samples
A scalar 'how good is this completion' score learned from human preference pairs
The KL divergence of the completion from the reference model, used as a quality proxy
questions.explanation: An RLHF reward model is a network trained on human preference pairs to output a scalar quality score. It is learned, not a rule. A binary correctness label computed by a rule is what an RLVR verifier produces.

questions.section: 1. The problem with a learned reward
questions.question: For which kind of task does an RLHF learned reward model make sense despite its weaknesses?
options: Single-digit arithmetic, where the true answer can be computed exactly
Code generation, where each completion is run against hidden unit tests
Open-ended helpfulness, where there is no ground truth to check against
Formal proofs, which a proof assistant can type-check line by line
questions.explanation: A learned reward model is useful where no ground truth exists, such as open-ended helpfulness. Arithmetic, tested code and type-checkable proofs all have checkable correctness, so a verifier is preferable there.

questions.section: 1. The problem with a learned reward
questions.question: What structural weakness of a learned reward model does a policy exploit?
options: It is a proxy that only approximates what a human would prefer
It is too slow to evaluate on every sample during RL training
It can only score completions shorter than its own context window
It assigns nearly the same score to every completion it is shown
questions.explanation: The reward model only approximates human preference, so it is a proxy. Optimized hard against it, the policy learns to maximize the proxy's score in ways that diverge from what it was meant to measure. Speed and length limits are not the structural issue.

questions.section: 1. The problem with a learned reward
questions.question: What is reward hacking when optimizing against a learned reward model?
options: The reward model overfits its preference data and its loss stops decreasing during training
The critic's value predictions diverge from the observed returns, so the advantages explode
The KL penalty grows so large that the policy stops changing from the reference altogether
The policy produces text that scores high with the reward model but is actually worse
questions.explanation: Reward hacking is when the policy maximizes the proxy's score through behaviours the proxy wrongly likes, producing outputs that are actually worse. It is the central failure mode of optimizing a learned reward. Critic divergence is a PPO training problem, not reward hacking.

questions.section: 1. The problem with a learned reward
questions.question: Which behaviours are typical symptoms of reward hacking against a learned reward model?
options: Shorter answers, heavily hedged language, and refusals that the reward model happened to like
Over-long answers, confident-sounding nonsense, and formatting tricks the reward model liked
Exact copies of the SFT demonstrations with no variation, because those scored highest
Random token outputs with near-uniform probabilities, as the policy collapses to maximum entropy
questions.explanation: A policy optimizing a learned proxy tends to find whatever the proxy over-rewards, such as length, confident tone, or particular formatting. These score high but are worse in reality. Exact copying of SFT data or random outputs are not the characteristic pattern.

questions.section: 1. The problem with a learned reward
questions.question: What do reasoning tasks have that open-ended RLHF tasks lack, making a verifier possible?
options: Many more human preference labels per prompt
Many problems have a checkable ground-truth answer
Shorter prompts that fit easily in the context window
A pretrained critic network that can grade each step
questions.explanation: For reasoning, many problems have a checkable answer: 3 + 4 is 7, a function passes its tests or not, a proof type-checks or not. When the truth is checkable, there is no need to guess the reward with a network.

questions.section: 1. The problem with a learned reward
questions.question: Why can a verifiable reward not be hacked the way a learned reward can?
options: It is regularized with a much stronger KL penalty to the reference
It is retrained every step on fresh samples to stay ahead of the policy
It gives partial credit for near answers, which removes any incentive to exploit it
It is not a proxy: it measures the actual correctness of the answer
questions.explanation: A learned reward model is a proxy that can be gamed. An exact verifier checks the ground truth itself, so there is no proxy gap: the only way to score is to be correct. This holds as long as the verifier is exact and its parsing is sound.

questions.section: 2. A verifier is a tiny function
questions.question: What is the type signature of a verifier in the llmre codebase?
options: (problem, answer) -> {0.0, 1.0}
(prompt, logits) -> scalar reward tensor
(answer_a, answer_b) -> preference probability
(problem) -> correct answer string
questions.explanation: A verifier takes a problem and an answer and returns 1.0 if correct, 0.0 if wrong. No network, no parameters, no training. A pairwise preference probability is what a preference/reward model handles.

questions.section: 2. A verifier is a tiny function
questions.question: What type does an llmre verifier return, and how are these values used in the training loop?
options: A torch scalar tensor with requires_grad=True, so gradients reach the verifier
A Python bool that the loop casts to an integer per prompt before the update
A Python float; the loop assembles many of them into a tensor
A numpy array of per-token rewards, one entry for each token of the answer
questions.explanation: Verifiers return a plain Python float in {0.0, 1.0}. The training loop stacks many of these into a rewards tensor. They have no gradient: the reward is just a number that weights log-probs.

questions.section: 2. A verifier is a tiny function
questions.question: How many trainable parameters does an llmre verifier have?
options: As many as the policy, since it shares the policy's weights
Only a small scalar head trained on top of the frozen policy
None; it is a plain function with no network or training
One temperature parameter tuned jointly during RL training
questions.explanation: A verifier is just a function that checks the answer. No network, no parameters, no training. That is the contrast with a learned reward model.

questions.question: What do most math RLVR rewards amount to, at bottom?
options: Extract the final answer and compare it to the gold answer
Score each intermediate step with a learned model
Measure the perplexity of the solution under the reference model
Count the reasoning steps in the solution
questions.explanation: Most math RLVR rewards extract the final answer and compare it to a gold answer, which is what exact_match does. Scoring each step is a process reward, a different approach. Perplexity and step counts are not correctness checks.

questions.question: In llmre's `exact_match(pred, gold)`, when is the numeric comparison path used?
options: Always, with non-numeric strings first converted to their character codes
Only when gold contains a decimal point, so that integers stay strings
Only when pred is longer than gold, to tolerate extra trailing zeros
When both pred and gold parse as numbers; their float values are compared
questions.explanation: exact_match first tries to parse both sides as numbers; if both succeed it compares their values, so "3", "3.0" and "+3" all match 3. Otherwise it falls back to comparing normalized strings.

questions.question: Why does `exact_match` compare numeric values rather than raw strings when both sides are numbers?
options: Float comparison is much faster than string comparison for long answers
A model emits strings, and you do not want "7.0" marked wrong against gold "7"
Python strings cannot be compared with == at all unless they are normalized
It lets the verifier award partial credit for answers that are numerically close
questions.explanation: Model outputs are strings, and equivalent numbers can be written many ways. Comparing values means "7.0" matches gold "7". There is no partial credit: values must be exactly equal.

questions.question: What does `exact_match`'s string path do via `_normalize`?
options: Removes all punctuation and digits, then compares what is left
Trims whitespace, lowercases, and drops a leading plus sign
Converts the string to a float and rounds it to six decimal places
Sorts the characters so that anagrams of the gold answer also match
questions.explanation: _normalize trims whitespace, lowercases, and drops a leading +, so " Cat " matches "cat". It does not strip all punctuation or sort characters, and converting to float is the numeric path.

questions.question: What do exact_match("+7", "7") and exact_match(" Cat ", "cat") return?
questions.explanation: "+7" parses as the number 7, so the numeric path matches. " Cat " is not numeric, so the string path normalizes it to "cat", which matches. Both return 1.0.

questions.question: Why does `exact_match` return a Python float rather than a tensor?
options: Rewards are cheap scalars that the caller stacks into a tensor
Torch tensors cannot hold the exact values 0 and 1 in float32
Python floats carry gradients back so the verifier can be trained
The optimizer requires plain Python floats as losses, not tensors
questions.explanation: Each verifier call grades one answer and returns a cheap scalar; the loop collects these into a reward tensor. Floats carry no gradient, and the verifier has nothing to train.

questions.question: What makes `arithmetic_verifier` a self-contained verifiable reward?
options: It looks up the correct answer in a stored dataset of labels keyed by the exact problem string
It asks a small learned reward model to grade the answer against the problem
It recomputes the true result from the problem string itself, so no labels are needed
It compares the answer to the frozen reference model's greedy output on the problem
questions.explanation: arithmetic_verifier parses the two-operand expression, computes the truth, and defers to exact_match. Given only the problem and the model's answer, it regenerates the correct answer: no labels and no learned reward model. That is the essence of a verifiable reward.

questions.question: Which operators does llmre's `arithmetic_verifier` accept?
options: +, -, *, and /, with / meaning integer division
+ and - only
+, -, *, and x, with x meaning multiply
Any Python expression evaluated with eval
questions.explanation: The regex accepts + - * x, with x treated as multiplication. It also allows optional whitespace and an optional trailing =. Division is not supported, and it does not use eval.

questions.question: Which of these problem strings does `arithmetic_verifier` parse successfully?
options: "what is 3 + 4?"
questions.explanation: The parser accepts a two-operand integer expression with + - * x, optional whitespace, and an optional trailing =, so "5 - 2 =" parses. Division, three operands, and surrounding words do not match the pattern.

questions.question: What does `arithmetic_verifier` do when given a problem it cannot parse?
options: It returns 0.0 silently
It returns 1.0 by default
It returns None to the loop
It raises ValueError
questions.explanation: It raises ValueError on unparseable input, and a unit test checks this. A verifier that silently returned 0 for malformed input would hide bugs: you could not tell a wrong answer from a broken problem.

questions.question: Why is it better for a verifier to raise on malformed input than to silently return 0?
options: Raising is faster than computing and returning a reward value
Silently returning 0 would hide bugs in the problem strings or parser
Returning 0 for malformed input would give the policy a positive advantage
The optimizer cannot handle zero rewards and would produce NaN gradients
questions.explanation: If malformed problems silently scored 0, a broken parser or bad dataset would look like the model getting answers wrong, hiding the bug. Raising fails loudly so it gets fixed. Zero rewards are normal and handled fine.

questions.question: What does arithmetic_verifier("6 x 7", "42") return?
options: 0.0, since the answer is a string and must be an int to match
1.0, since x means multiply and the answer "42" matches
ValueError, since x is not one of the accepted operators
0.0, since only the * symbol is treated as multiplication
questions.explanation: x is accepted as multiplication, so the truth is 42. The answer is converted with str() and compared via exact_match, so the string "42" matches. String answers are fine.

questions.question: How does a real math verifier differ from the toy `arithmetic_verifier`?
options: It returns a continuous similarity score between 0 and 1 instead of a hard 0/1 correctness label
It is a learned neural network fine-tuned on graded solutions rather than a plain function
It needs no answer extraction at all, because models are trained to output bare numbers
Its parsing is far hairier (LaTeX, fractions, units, often a CAS), but the signal is still 0/1
questions.explanation: Real verifiers normalize LaTeX, parse fractions and surds, handle plus-minus, units and equivalent forms, and often call a computer-algebra system for symbolic equality. The signal shape is still (problem, answer) -> 0/1. The parsing is where the engineering and the false-positive bugs live.

questions.section: 3. The RLVR loop, end to end
questions.question: What two components does the RLVR training loop combine?
options: A verifier for the reward and GRPO for the update
A learned reward model and PPO with a value critic
A verifier and supervised fine-tuning on all samples
A critic network and rejection sampling of the best
questions.explanation: The RLVR loop in llmre/reasoning/rlvr.py assembles the verifier (reward) and GRPO (group-relative advantages plus clipped objective). Verifier plus SFT on accepted samples is rejection sampling, a different method.

questions.section: 3.1 A toy policy so the algorithm is unobscured
questions.question: In llmre's toy RLVR loop, what is the 'policy'?
options: A small GPT that emits answer tokens one at a time
A lookup table holding the correct answer for each prompt
A table of logits: one row per prompt over a small answer space
A learned critic that predicts each answer's expected reward
questions.explanation: To keep the algorithm visible, the toy policy is a (num_prompts, num_answers) logits tensor: a categorical distribution over answers per prompt. Wiring GRPO to a GPT emitting tokens is engineering, not new algorithm. It is not an answer table; it has to learn.

questions.section: 3.1 A toy policy so the algorithm is unobscured
questions.question: What are the shape, dtype, and device of the toy RLVR policy's logits?
options: (num_answers,), int64, CPU
(num_prompts, group_size), float16, GPU
(num_prompts, num_answers), float32, CPU
(batch, seq_len, vocab), float32, GPU
questions.explanation: logits = torch.zeros(num_prompts, num_answers, requires_grad=True) gives a float32 CPU tensor; row p is the answer distribution for problem p. group_size appears in the sampled tensor, not the logits.

questions.section: 3.1 A toy policy so the algorithm is unobscured
questions.question: Why does the toy RLVR policy start at chance accuracy?
options: Its logits start at zero, so softmax is uniform over the answers
Its logits start random, so it guesses an arbitrary answer per prompt
Its verifier rejects every answer for the first few warm-up steps
Its learning rate starts at zero and warms up over the first steps
questions.explanation: All-zero logits give a uniform softmax, so each answer has probability 1/num_answers. With the default 10-answer space, chance is about 0.1. Logits are zeros, not random.

questions.section: 3.1 A toy policy so the algorithm is unobscured
questions.question: If the toy categorical policy is swapped for a GPT that emits answer tokens, what changes in the RLVR loop?
options: The whole loop must be redesigned around a learned critic that values each token
The verifier must become a learned model, since a GPT's outputs are free-form text
GRPO must be replaced with DPO, since token-level groups cannot be standardized
Only sampling and log-prob scoring change: generate tokens and sum their log-probs
questions.explanation: The outer loop is unchanged. Sampling becomes generation, and the log-prob of an answer becomes the sum of its token log-probs. The verifier and GRPO stay the same.

questions.section: 3.2 The four steps, each mapped to 16.1
questions.question: How does the toy RLVR loop sample a group of answers for one prompt?
options: It takes the top-G answers by logit value, so the group always holds the most likely ones
It softmaxes that prompt's logits and draws G answers with torch.multinomial, with replacement
It samples G distinct answers without replacement, so no answer appears twice in a group
It enumerates every answer in the space and weights each by its softmax probability
questions.explanation: _sample_group softmaxes one prompt's logits and draws G indices with replacement. The stacked result is a (num_prompts, group_size) long tensor of indices. Top-G or without-replacement sampling would not be a Monte-Carlo estimate of the policy.

questions.section: 3.2 The four steps, each mapped to 16.1
questions.question: In the toy RLVR loop, what is the dtype and meaning of the `sampled` tensor?
options: float log-probabilities of every answer, shape (num_prompts, num_answers)
long indices into the answer space, shape (num_prompts, group_size)
float 0/1 rewards from the verifier, shape (num_prompts, group_size)
bool masks marking the correct answers, shape (num_answers,) per prompt
questions.explanation: `sampled` holds long indices into the answers list, one row per prompt and one column per group member. The verifier is called on answers[idx], the value, not the index. Rewards are a separate float tensor of the same shape.

questions.section: 3.2 The four steps, each mapped to 16.1
questions.question: In the toy RLVR loop, what is the verifier called on for each sampled entry?
options: The problem and the sampled index idx, which it treats as the answer
The full logits row for that prompt, so it can grade the distribution
The log-probability of the sampled answer, thresholded at a cutoff
The problem and the sampled answer's value, answers[idx]
questions.explanation: The loop calls verifier(problems[p], answers[sampled[p, g].item()]): the actual answer value, not its index. With answer space range(10) index and value coincide, but in general they differ.

questions.section: 3.2 The four steps, each mapped to 16.1
questions.question: What does the toy RLVR loop log to `history` at each step?
options: The mean of the rewards tensor, i.e. the fraction correct this step
The scalar loss value, i.e. the negated GRPO objective for the step
The KL divergence of the policy to the frozen reference this step
The largest group-relative advantage in the batch for that step
questions.explanation: history.append(rewards.mean().item()) records the fraction of all sampled answers that were correct this step. That is the correct-rate you watch climb. The loss is not logged there.

questions.section: 3.2 The four steps, each mapped to 16.1
questions.question: In the toy RLVR loop's update, why is `torch.gather(logp_all, 1, sampled)` used?
options: To select the log-prob of the correct answer for each prompt, which the loss then pushes up
To sum the log-probs over every answer in the space, giving one total per prompt for the loss
To pick each sampled answer's log-prob, a (num_prompts, group_size) tensor matching the advantages
To pick the answer with the highest log-prob per prompt, which then becomes the group's baseline
questions.explanation: logp_all is (num_prompts, num_answers). gather along dim 1 with the sampled indices picks the log-prob of each answer actually taken, aligned with the advantages. The policy gradient needs log-probs of the taken actions, not of the correct answer or all answers.

questions.section: 3.2 The four steps, each mapped to 16.1
questions.question: What is the large-LLM analogue of `torch.gather(logp_all, 1, sampled)` in the toy RLVR loop?
options: Computing the attention scores between the prompt tokens and the generated answer tokens
Applying the KL penalty against the frozen reference model's token distribution
Reading off each generated token's log-prob, where the 'answers' are vocabulary tokens
Selecting the top-k vocabulary tokens to keep before sampling the next position
questions.explanation: In a real LLM policy-gradient step you read the log-prob of the token actually generated at each position from the log-softmax over the vocabulary. That is the same gather idea, with tokens instead of answers.

questions.section: 3.2 The four steps, each mapped to 16.1
questions.question: Why does the toy RLVR loop pass `logp.detach()` as old_logprobs to `grpo_objective`?
options: It makes the ratio exactly 1 (on-policy), so the step is the plain group-baselined gradient
It stops the verifier's reward from receiving any gradients through the clipped objective
It freezes a detached copy of the policy to act as the reference model for the KL penalty
It prevents the advantages from changing between the forward and backward passes
