options: It gives a dense full-distribution signal at every token, so each position carries the teacher's dark knowledge
It fixes exposure bias, since the student is trained on the same prefixes it will see at inference time
It needs only the teacher's text, so you can distill from a model you can sample from but cannot inspect
It needs no student training run at all, since the teacher's sampled text is simply used as a retrieval cache
questions.explanation: Sequence-level KD only needs the teacher's text, so it works with a model behind an API whose logits you cannot see. Logit distillation needs the teacher's log-probs.

questions.question: Why does SFT on one sampled teacher token throw away information?
options: Because the sampled token is usually wrong at high temperature, so SFT mostly trains the student on noise
Because SFT ignores the prompt tokens, so the student never sees the context the teacher conditioned on
Because the teacher's logits are quantised to 8 bits before sampling, which rounds away the low-probability tokens
Because the teacher has a full distribution over ~150K tokens at each position, and sampling keeps one token
questions.explanation: At each position the teacher has a full next-token distribution. Sampling one token keeps just that token and tells the student everything else is wrong, discarding the teacher's relative preferences among other tokens.

questions.question: After 'The answer is', a teacher puts 0.55 on '12', 0.40 on 'twelve' and 0.05 elsewhere. What does SFT on a single sample of '12' fail to convey?
options: That 'twelve' is almost as good: so-called dark knowledge
That '12' is the correct answer the teacher prefers the most
That the prompt was a math question rather than free text
That the sequence should end right after the number token
questions.explanation: SFT on '12' tells the student '12 is right, everything else is wrong'. The teacher knew 'twelve' is almost as good. This extra information in the soft distribution is called dark knowledge; matching full distributions passes it on.

questions.question: Which paper originated the idea of matching soft teacher distributions ('dark knowledge')?
options: Kim & Rush 2016, Sequence-Level Knowledge Distillation for neural machine translation
Hinton, Vinyals & Dean 2015, Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network
Agarwal et al. 2023, GKD: On-Policy Distillation of Language Models from Self-Generated Mistakes
Gu et al. 2023, MiniLLM: Knowledge Distillation of Large Language Models with reverse KL
questions.explanation: Matching soft teacher distributions is the original knowledge-distillation idea of Hinton et al. (2015). Kim & Rush introduced sequence-level KD; GKD and MiniLLM are on-policy distillation methods.

questions.question: Besides carrying dark knowledge, what training-signal benefit does matching the teacher's full distribution give?
options: It removes the need for a teacher at training time, since the targets are cached
It eliminates the need for prompt masking, since every position gets a target
A dense training signal at every position
It makes the loss exactly zero for every token the student already predicts correctly
questions.explanation: Matching the full distribution provides a full target at every position, a dense signal, rather than a single sampled token per position (or a single scalar per sequence in RL).

questions.question: What is exposure bias in distillation?
options: The teacher has seen far more training data than the student, so its distribution over prefixes is biased toward text the student cannot generate
The student overfits to the prompt tokens, because the loss is computed on every position instead of only the completion, biasing it toward copying the prompt
The student trains on teacher-written prefixes but at inference continues its own, so after a mistake it is in states it never learned to recover from
The teacher is biased toward frequent tokens after temperature scaling, so the student learns to under-predict rare tokens it is later exposed to at inference
questions.explanation: Training only on teacher-written prefixes (teacher forcing) means the student never sees its own mistakes. At inference a small student makes errors the teacher never makes, lands in unseen prefixes, cannot recover, and errors compound.

questions.question: What is logit distillation?
options: At every position, minimising a divergence between the teacher's and the student's next-token distributions
Training the student with cross-entropy on the teacher's argmax token at every position of the teacher's text
Clipping the student's logits to the teacher's per-position range so that neither model is ever overconfident
Averaging the teacher's and student's weights layer by layer, with the teacher's logits used to choose the mix
questions.explanation: Logit distillation minimizes a divergence (forward KL, reverse KL or a JSD) between full next-token distributions at every position, rather than training on one sampled token.

questions.question: What is on-policy distillation (GKD, 'learning from self-generated mistakes')?
options: The teacher generates the text and the student copies its sampled tokens with ordinary cross-entropy
The student generates the prefixes and the teacher scores every token the student produced
The student and teacher take turns generating tokens, and each is scored by the other's log-probs
The teacher is fine-tuned on the student's outputs so that it learns to correct the student's mistakes
questions.explanation: In on-policy distillation the student writes the prefixes, so it sees its own mistakes, and the teacher grades every token of them, telling the student token by token what to do there. Agarwal et al. (2023) call this GKD.

questions.question: How does on-policy distillation sit between SFT and RL?
options: Its data is off-policy like SFT (prefixes written by the teacher) and its signal is sparse like RL (one scalar reward per sequence)
Like RL its data is on-policy; like SFT its signal is dense, a full target distribution at every token, not one scalar per sequence
It uses a learned reward model like RLHF, trained on teacher-versus-student comparisons, but optimises it with SFT on the winning samples
It is identical to RL with a KL penalty to the teacher: the teacher acts as the reference policy and the reward is the sequence's correctness
questions.explanation: On-policy distillation takes RL's on-policy data (the student's own rollouts) and SFT's dense supervision (a full target distribution per token). RL gets only one scalar reward per sequence.

questions.question: In the unified view of distillation, what does SFT on teacher samples correspond to?
options: Reverse KL, estimated exactly over the vocabulary, on the student's own prefixes
JSD with beta = 0.5, estimated on a mixture of teacher and student prefixes
An RL objective with a binary reward on whether the token matches the teacher
Forward KL, estimated with one sample per position, on the teacher's prefixes
questions.explanation: SFT on teacher samples is forward KL with one sample per position on the teacher's prefixes. Logit distillation removes the 'one sample'; on-policy distillation removes 'the teacher's prefixes'. The divergence direction decides what an imperfect student gives up.

questions.section: 2.1 Forward KL: the student must cover the teacher
questions.question: What is the forward KL between teacher p_T and student p_S over vocabulary V?
options: KL(p_T || p_S) = sum_v p_T(v) (log p_T(v) - log p_S(v))
KL(p_T || p_S) = sum_v p_S(v) (log p_S(v) - log p_T(v))
KL(p_T || p_S) = sum_v p_T(v) (log p_S(v) - log p_T(v))^2
KL(p_T || p_S) = max_v p_T(v) |log p_T(v) - log p_S(v)|
questions.explanation: Forward KL sums over the vocabulary weighted by the teacher: sum_v p_T(v)(log p_T(v) - log p_S(v)). The second option is reverse KL, weighted by the student.

questions.section: 2.1 Forward KL: the student must cover the teacher
questions.question: Under forward KL(p_T || p_S), what happens to a token the teacher likes but the student assigns near-zero probability?
options: It costs nothing, because the student's near-zero mass makes its term p_S(v) log p_S(v) vanish
Its cost p_T(v)(-log p_S(v)) goes to infinity, so the student must put mass everywhere the teacher does
Its cost is clipped at log V, since forward KL is bounded by the entropy of a uniform distribution
It is ignored, since forward KL weights each token's log-ratio by the student's own small probability
questions.explanation: Forward KL is teacher-weighted. If p_T(v) is large and p_S(v) -> 0, the term p_T(v)(-log p_S(v)) blows up. Tokens the student likes but the teacher ignores cost nothing directly. This forces mode covering.

questions.section: 2.1 Forward KL: the student must cover the teacher
questions.question: What behaviour does forward KL induce in a student that cannot fit the teacher exactly?
options: Mode seeking: commit to the single teacher mode it can fit well and drop the others
Mode collapse: put almost all of its mass onto the single most frequent token
Mode covering (mean seeking): put mass everywhere the teacher does, even between modes
Zero-forcing: put zero mass wherever the teacher is uncertain, to avoid any penalty
questions.explanation: Because missing any teacher-supported token is infinitely costly under forward KL, the student spreads to cover all teacher modes. This is mode covering, also called mean seeking.

questions.section: 2.1 Forward KL: the student must cover the teacher
questions.question: If the teacher is one-hot on the observed token y, what does forward KL(one-hot_y || p_S) reduce to?
options: log p_S(y), the student's log-likelihood
1 - p_S(y), the student's error rate
Zero, since a one-hot target has no entropy
-log p_S(y), exactly the SFT cross-entropy
questions.explanation: With p_T(y) = 1 the sum has one term and log p_T(y) = 0, leaving -log p_S(y): the cross-entropy loss. So SFT is the special case of forward KL with a one-hot teacher.

questions.section: 2.1 Forward KL: the student must cover the teacher
questions.question: Averaging -log p_S(y) over samples y ~ p_T gives what quantity, and how does it compare with exact forward KL?
options: KL(p_T || p_S) + H(p_T); H(p_T) is independent of the student, so the expected gradient matches, with much higher variance
KL(p_S || p_T) + H(p_S); sampling from the teacher turns the forward KL into the reverse KL, so the gradient points the other way
Exactly KL(p_T || p_S), with lower variance than the full sum because each sample concentrates on the teacher's top tokens
H(p_S), the student's own entropy, which is unrelated to either KL and only rewards the student for becoming more confident
questions.explanation: E_{y~p_T}[-log p_S(y)] = KL(p_T||p_S) + H(p_T). Since H(p_T) is a constant with respect to the student, sequence-level distillation has the same expected gradient as forward KL, but as a one-sample Monte-Carlo estimate it is much noisier.

questions.section: 2.1 Forward KL: the student must cover the teacher
questions.question: What is the gradient of forward KL(p_T || p_S) with respect to the student logit z_v?
options: p_T(v) - p_S(v)
p_S(v) - p_T(v)
p_S(v)(log p_S(v) - log p_T(v))
-p_T(v) log p_S(v)
questions.explanation: d KL(p_T||p_S)/d z_v = p_S(v) - p_T(v): the same 'prediction minus target' as cross-entropy, but with the teacher's soft distribution as target.

questions.section: 2.2 Reverse KL: the student must not invent
questions.question: What is the reverse KL between student and teacher, and whose probabilities weight the sum?
options: sum_v p_T(v)(log p_T(v) - log p_S(v)); weighted by the teacher
sum_v p_T(v)(log p_S(v) - log p_T(v)); weighted by the teacher
sum_v p_S(v)(log p_S(v) - log p_T(v)); weighted by the student
sum_v p_S(v)(log p_T(v) - log p_S(v)); weighted by the student
questions.explanation: Reverse KL(p_S || p_T) = sum_v p_S(v)(log p_S(v) - log p_T(v)) is weighted by the student. The teacher-weighted version is forward KL.

questions.section: 2.2 Reverse KL: the student must not invent
questions.question: Under reverse KL(p_S || p_T), which kind of student error is infinitely costly?
options: Ignoring a mode the teacher puts substantial probability on
Matching the teacher exactly on its highest-probability token
Having much lower entropy than the teacher at that position
Putting mass on a token the teacher assigns near-zero probability
questions.explanation: If p_S(v) > 0 and p_T(v) -> 0, the term p_S(v)(-log p_T(v)) blows up. A teacher mode the student ignores costs nothing directly. So the student must not invent tokens the teacher would not produce.

questions.section: 2.2 Reverse KL: the student must not invent
questions.question: What behaviour does reverse KL induce in a student that cannot fit everything?
options: Mode seeking: pick the modes it can fit well and drop the rest
Mode covering: spread its mass over all of the teacher's modes
Uniform spreading of probability across the whole vocabulary
Copying the teacher's entropy exactly while shifting its modes
questions.explanation: Because reverse KL only penalises student mass where the teacher has little, a limited student commits to the modes it can fit and ignores others. This is mode seeking.

questions.section: 2.2 Reverse KL: the student must not invent
questions.question: Why does MiniLLM (Gu et al. 2023) argue reverse KL is the better default for generative language models?
options: Because it is cheaper to compute than forward KL, needing only the student's top-k tokens per position
Because a student that puts mass where the teacher has none produces text the teacher would never write
Because it needs no teacher logits at all, only the teacher's sampled text, so closed models can be used
Because it is symmetric in teacher and student, so the student cannot be biased toward covering or seeking
questions.explanation: MiniLLM argues that for generation, avoiding invented text matters most: forward KL's mode covering can make the student generate outputs the teacher would never produce, while reverse KL punishes exactly that.

questions.section: 2.2 Reverse KL: the student must not invent
questions.question: With l_v = log p_S(v) - log p_T(v) and K = KL(p_S || p_T), what is the gradient of reverse KL with respect to student logit z_v?
options: p_S(v) - p_T(v)
p_T(v)(l_v - K)
p_S(v)(l_v - K)
p_S(v) l_v + K
questions.explanation: d KL(p_S||p_T)/d z_v = p_S(v)(l_v - K). It reads as a policy gradient where -l_v is the per-token reward and K the baseline.

questions.section: 2.2 Reverse KL: the student must not invent
questions.question: How can the reverse-KL gradient p_S(v)(l_v - K) be read as a policy gradient?
options: As a value-function regression target: l_v is the predicted return of token v and K is the observed return it is regressed onto
As a Bradley-Terry preference loss: each token v is compared with the average token, and K is the log-odds that v is preferred
As a cross-entropy against the teacher's argmax: l_v is the log-loss on that token and K normalises it by the vocabulary size
The per-token reward is -l_v (how much more the teacher likes v) and K is the baseline; worse tokens go down, better ones up
questions.explanation: With reward -l_v and baseline K = E_{p_S}[l_v], tokens whose log-ratio is worse than average get pushed down and better ones up, exactly like REINFORCE with a baseline.

questions.section: 2.2 Reverse KL: the student must not invent
questions.question: When reverse KL is estimated by sampling one token v ~ p_S rather than summing over the vocabulary, what is l_v?
options: Exactly the one-sample 'k1' KL estimator from PPO's KL penalty, now used as a per-token negative reward
A one-sample estimate of the forward KL, since the token was drawn from the student and scored by the teacher
A one-sample estimate of the teacher's entropy at that position, which the student is trained to match
The importance ratio p_T(v)/p_S(v), used to reweight the student's sample toward the teacher's distribution
questions.explanation: l_v = log p_S(v) - log p_T(v) for a sampled v is the k1 KL estimator. Using -l_v as a per-token reward is how some on-policy distillation recipes plug into an RL trainer.

questions.section: 2.3 Generalized JSD: a dial between the two
questions.question: How does GKD's generalized JSD_beta between p_T and p_S work?
options: It averages forward and reverse KL directly: beta KL(p_T||p_S) + (1-beta) KL(p_S||p_T), with no mixture involved
With M = (1-beta) p_S + beta p_T, JSD_beta = beta KL(p_T||M) + (1-beta) KL(p_S||M), for beta in [0, 1]
It computes beta times the squared difference of log-probabilities, sum_v (log p_T(v) - log p_S(v))^2, over the vocabulary
It is the KL from the teacher to a uniform distribution, scaled by beta and added to the student's cross-entropy loss
questions.explanation: GKD forms a mixture M = (1-beta)p_S + beta p_T and computes beta KL(p_T||M) + (1-beta) KL(p_S||M). Each term compares a distribution to a mixture containing it.

questions.section: 2.3 Generalized JSD: a dial between the two
questions.question: Why is JSD_beta bounded, and what is its maximum at beta = 0.5?
options: It is not bounded: like KL, it goes to infinity when one distribution puts mass where the other has none
It is bounded by 1, because each probability is at most 1 and so every log-ratio inside it is at most 1
Each term compares a distribution to a mixture containing it; at beta = 0.5 it is at most ln 2
It is bounded by log V, the vocabulary size, because that is the maximum entropy of any distribution
questions.explanation: Because M contains both p_T and p_S, neither KL term can blow up, so JSD_beta is bounded by a constant. At beta = 0.5 the bound is ln 2.

questions.section: 2.3 Generalized JSD: a dial between the two
questions.question: Taken literally, JSD_beta equals 0 at beta = 0 and beta = 1. How does it relate to forward and reverse KL?
options: They are unrelated at every beta, since a mixture divergence can never recover either KL as a limit
JSD_beta equals the forward KL exactly at beta = 0.5, and the reverse KL exactly at beta = 0 and 1
JSD_beta / beta -> reverse KL as beta -> 0, and JSD_beta / (1-beta) -> forward KL as beta -> 1
JSD_beta / beta -> KL(p_T||p_S) as beta -> 0; JSD_beta / (1-beta) -> KL(p_S||p_T) as beta -> 1
questions.explanation: After rescaling, the endpoints recover the two KLs: forward KL in the beta -> 0 limit and reverse KL in the beta -> 1 limit. That is why TRL special-cases the ends.

questions.section: 2.3 Generalized JSD: a dial between the two
questions.question: In TRL's convention for the generalized JSD, what do beta = 0 and beta = 1 mean, and what is DistillationTrainer's default?
options: beta = 0 is forward KL, beta = 1 is reverse KL; DistillationTrainer defaults to beta = 1.0 (reverse KL)
beta = 0 is reverse KL, beta = 1 is forward KL; DistillationTrainer defaults to beta = 0.5 (symmetric JSD)
beta = 0 is the symmetric JSD, beta = 1 is plain cross-entropy; DistillationTrainer defaults to beta = 0
beta only sets the softmax temperature, not the divergence; DistillationTrainer defaults to beta = 1.0
questions.explanation: TRL's docs document beta = 0 as forward KL and beta = 1 as reverse KL, special-casing the endpoints. DistillationTrainer defaults to beta = 1.0, i.e. reverse KL.

questions.section: 2.4 On-policy vs off-policy: which prefixes the loss is averaged over
questions.question: What is the only difference between the off-policy and on-policy distillation losses L_off and L_on?
options: The divergence D: forward KL for off-policy, reverse KL for on-policy, with prefixes from the same source
Where the prefixes come from: completions y ~ p_T for off-policy, y ~ sg[p_S] for on-policy
Whether the teacher is frozen: off-policy keeps it fixed, on-policy updates it alongside the student
How the loss is reduced: off-policy averages over tokens, on-policy sums over each whole sequence
questions.explanation: Both average a per-token divergence D over prefixes of completion y. Off-policy samples y from the teacher; on-policy samples y from the (stop-gradient) student. D can be forward KL, reverse KL or JSD_beta in either regime.

questions.section: 2.4 On-policy vs off-policy: which prefixes the loss is averaged over
questions.question: In GKD's on-policy loss, what does the stop-gradient sg[p_S] on the sampling distribution mean?
options: The student receives no gradient at all from the on-policy batches, which only update the teacher
The teacher's parameters are frozen, so only the sampling temperature of the student is learned
The student's samples are treated as fixed data; gradients flow only through p_S inside D
Samples are drawn greedily at temperature 0, so the sampling step contributes no randomness
questions.explanation: sg[.] means GKD does not differentiate through which completions the student sampled. Those rollouts are treated as data, and gradients flow only through p_S inside D.

questions.section: 2.4 On-policy vs off-policy: which prefixes the loss is averaged over
questions.question: What does GKD's lambda (TRL GKDTrainer's lmbda) control?
options: The coefficient on a KL penalty to a frozen reference copy of the student
The learning-rate multiplier applied to the on-policy part of each batch
The interpolation weight between forward and reverse KL inside the loss
The fraction of on-policy batches mixed with off-policy ones
questions.explanation: GKD mixes the two regimes with a fraction lambda of on-policy batches. TRL's experimental GKDTrainer exposes it as lmbda. The forward/reverse interpolation is beta, not lambda.

questions.question: For teacher p_T = (0.6, 0.3, 0.1) and student p_S = (0.3, 0.3, 0.4), forward KL is 0.2773 nats and reverse KL is 0.3466 nats. What does this show?
options: KL is asymmetric; reverse KL is larger because the student's biggest error (0.4 on token 3) is weighted by its own mass
Forward and reverse KL are always within about 10% of each other, so the choice between them rarely changes training
Reverse KL is always larger than forward KL for any pair of distributions, because the student is always less peaked than its teacher
The student is closer to the teacher under reverse KL, since a larger divergence means the student is a better fit
questions.explanation: The two directions differ because KL is not symmetric. Reverse KL weights mistakes by student mass, and the student puts 0.4 on token 3 where the teacher has 0.1, giving the large 0.4 ln 4 term.

questions.question: For p_T = (0.6, 0.3, 0.1) and p_S = (0.3, 0.3, 0.4), the forward-KL gradient on the student logits is (-0.3, 0, +0.3). What does gradient descent do?
options: Lowers token 1, raises token 3, and leaves token 2 unchanged
Raises token 1, lowers token 3, and leaves token 2 unchanged
Raises all three tokens equally, so the softmax output is unchanged
Leaves token 1 unchanged, lowers token 2, and raises token 3
questions.explanation: The forward gradient p_S - p_T = (-0.3, 0, +0.3). Descent moves opposite the gradient: token 1's logit rises, token 3's falls, token 2 (where p_S = p_T) is unchanged.

questions.question: Under reverse KL with p_T = (0.6, 0.3, 0.1) and p_S = (0.3, 0.3, 0.4), why does token 2's logit move even though p_S(2) = p_T(2)?
options: Because of floating-point rounding in log_softmax, which leaves a small nonzero log-ratio for token 2
Because the teacher distribution is not normalised, so token 2's equal probability gives a nonzero log-ratio
Its log-ratio 0 beats the average K = 0.3466, so p_S(2)(0 - K) = -0.1040 < 0 and descent raises it
Because reverse KL ignores tokens where the two distributions agree, so token 2 drifts with the softmax
questions.explanation: The reverse gradient is p_S(v)(l_v - K). Token 2 has l_2 = 0 but K > 0, so the gradient is negative and descent raises its logit: relative to the student's average mistake, token 2 is a good token, so mass moves toward it and away from token 3.

questions.question: What property do both the forward and reverse KL gradient vectors with respect to student logits share?
options: They are both all-positive, since KL is non-negative everywhere
They are identical vectors whenever the two distributions differ
They both equal the teacher distribution minus a uniform vector
They both sum to zero, as any gradient through a softmax must
questions.explanation: Adding a constant to all logits does not change a softmax, so any loss through a softmax has a logit gradient that sums to zero. (-0.3, 0, 0.3) and (-0.3119, -0.1040, 0.4159) both sum to zero.

questions.question: What are the shapes of teacher_logits and student_logits in a logit-distillation loss, and which has gradient?
options: Both (B, T, V); only student_logits has gradient; teacher_logits come from no_grad and are detached
Both (B, V), one row per sequence; both have gradient, so the teacher is fine-tuned along with the student
teacher (B, T) holding sampled token ids, student (B, T, V); the teacher has gradient through the ids
Both (T, V), with the batch flattened into time; neither has gradient, since the loss is only logged
questions.explanation: Both are (B, T, V): batch, time, vocabulary. The teacher logits are computed under no_grad and detached inside the loss; the student logits are the only thing with gradient.

questions.question: In logit distillation, what is the shape and meaning of the mask?
options: (B, T, V), float; 1 on the teacher's top-k tokens at each position, 0 on the rest
(B, T), bool/int; 1 on completion tokens, 0 on prompt and padding
(V,), bool; 1 on vocabulary tokens shared by teacher and student tokenizers
(B,), bool; 1 for sequences whose final answer the verifier accepts
questions.explanation: The mask is the response mask from loss masking: shape (B, T), 1 on completion tokens and 0 on prompt and padding. The per-token divergence is (B, T) and the loss is its masked mean, a scalar.

questions.question: What dtypes are used for logits and for the per-token divergence in distillation?
options: Logits always float64 for exactness; the per-token divergence is stored as int64
Logits int8 to save memory; the per-token divergence in float16 for speed
Logits bf16 in production (float64 in tests); per-token divergence at least float32
Everything in bf16, including the per-token divergence and the reduced loss
questions.explanation: Production logits are typically bf16, while the tests use float64 for exactness. The per-token divergence (B, T) and the scalar loss are kept in at least float32.

questions.question: Why must teacher and student share a tokenizer for logit distillation?
options: So they can share embedding weights, which logit distillation copies from teacher to student
So that generation is faster, since the teacher can reuse the student's KV cache directly
So the teacher can be served over HTTP, which requires both sides to agree on token ids
The KL sums over the same V token ids; mismatched vocabularies need extra alignment machinery
questions.explanation: The divergence compares probabilities token id by token id. If id 1234 means different strings in the two models, the KL is meaningless even though it runs. Cross-tokenizer distillation needs alignment machinery.

questions.question: In larger distillation setups, how is the teacher often deployed?
options: Served separately, returning log-probs (TRL has an async variant that queries a teacher over HTTP)
Merged into the student's weights at initialisation, so no separate teacher forward pass is needed
Run only once before training to dump every full distribution to disk, which the student then reads
Replaced by a learned reward model trained to predict the teacher's log-probs from the student's text
questions.explanation: In a simple setup both models live on the training GPUs. In larger setups the teacher is served separately and returns log-probs; TRL has an async variant that queries the teacher over HTTP.

questions.question: In llmre.reasoning.distill, how does forward_kl compute the divergence?
options: kl = (log_ps.exp() * (log_ps - log_pt)).sum(-1), with teacher logits detached and both through log_softmax
kl = (log_pt.exp() * (log_pt - log_ps)).sum(-1), with teacher logits detached and both via log_softmax
kl = ((log_pt - log_ps) ** 2).mean(-1), a squared log-ratio averaged over the vocabulary dimension
kl = F.cross_entropy(student_logits, teacher_logits.argmax(-1)), using the teacher's top token as label
questions.explanation: forward_kl computes log_softmax of the detached teacher logits and of the student logits, then sums p_T (log p_T - log p_S) over the vocabulary. The first option, weighted by the student's probabilities, is reverse_kl.

questions.question: Why do the distillation divergences use log_softmax rather than log(softmax(...))?
options: Because log_softmax runs faster on CPU, though on GPU the two are identical
Because log(softmax) is not differentiable at the largest logit of each row
So tiny probabilities do not underflow to log(0) = -inf
Because softmax needs an explicit temperature argument that log_softmax omits
questions.explanation: Working in log space keeps tiny probabilities representable. log(softmax(z)) can underflow to 0 and give -inf, and then 0 * -inf = nan. generalized_jsd likewise computes log M with logsumexp.

questions.question: How does generalized_jsd compute log M for the mixture M = (1-beta) p_S + beta p_T stably?
options: Compute M in probability space, then take log(M), which is safe because M is a mixture
Clamp M to a minimum of 1e-8 before taking the log, which keeps every term finite
Average log p_S and log p_T with weights (1-beta) and beta, which equals log M exactly
With a logsumexp of log(1-beta) + log p_S and log(beta) + log p_T
questions.explanation: log M = logsumexp(log(1-beta) + log p_S, log beta + log p_T) stays in log space and avoids underflow. Averaging log-probs would compute a geometric, not arithmetic, mixture.

questions.section: 5.1 Experiment A: mode covering vs mode seeking
questions.question: In Experiment A, a 20-bin bimodal teacher (bumps at bins 4 and 15) is fit by a discretized-Gaussian student with two parameters. What problem does this model?
options: The small-student problem: the student can make only one bump, so the divergence decides what it gives up
Exposure bias: the student is trained on teacher bins but sampled from its own, so it drifts into the empty gap
Tokenizer mismatch: the student's 20 bins do not line up with the teacher's, so the KL needs an alignment map
Reward hacking: the student finds a cheap bin the divergence under-penalises and piles all of its mass there
questions.explanation: The student has only mu and log sigma, so it can make one bump and cannot copy the two-bump teacher. Which divergence you use decides what it sacrifices.

questions.section: 5.1 Experiment A: mode covering vs mode seeking
questions.question: In Experiment A, what does the forward-KL-fit student look like?
options: It matches the bin-4 mode exactly (mu = 4, sigma = 1) and puts almost no mass on the bin-15 mode, since forward KL lets a student drop a mode
A wide flat bump between the modes (mu ~9, sigma ~14.6), with 26.8% of its mass on bins 7-11, where the teacher has 0.24%
It collapses onto the bin-15 mode with a very small sigma, because forward KL rewards the student for concentrating its mass
A uniform distribution over all 20 bins with zero loss, since a uniform student covers every bin the teacher uses
questions.explanation: Forward KL makes missing a mode very costly, so the one-bump student spreads wide between them, putting 26.8% of its mass in the gap where the teacher has 0.24%. For an LM, that is generating text the teacher would essentially never produce.

questions.section: 5.1 Experiment A: mode covering vs mode seeking
questions.question: In Experiment A, what does the reverse-KL-fit student do, and what is its loss?
options: Spreads its mass evenly across the gap between the two modes, reaching a loss of 0 once the bins are covered
Covers both modes with two separate bumps, since a reverse-KL fit always splits; loss ln 4 = 1.386
Moves onto the nearer mode and matches it exactly (mu = 4, sigma = 1); loss ln 2 = 0.693, with no mass in the gap
Diverges, with sigma growing without bound, because the student-weighted loss is infinite wherever the teacher is zero
questions.explanation: Reverse KL locks onto one mode and matches it exactly. Its loss ln 2 reflects ignoring the other half of the teacher's mass. JSD_0.5 behaves like reverse KL in this experiment.

questions.section: 5.1 Experiment A: mode covering vs mode seeking
questions.question: When is forward KL the safer choice for distillation, and when is reverse KL?
options: Forward when each sample must be good (precision, pass@1); reverse when the student must keep every teacher behaviour (diversity, coverage, pass@k)
Forward in every case, since it is the only divergence that matches SFT; reverse KL is only useful for analysis, never for training
Reverse for classification heads, where there is a single label; forward for generation, where the student must sample long sequences
Forward when the student must keep every teacher behaviour (diversity, coverage, pass@k); reverse when each sample must be good (pass@1)
questions.explanation: Neither is correct in general. Forward KL keeps coverage, useful for diversity and pass@k. Reverse KL keeps each sample on a real teacher mode, useful for pass@1. Generation has mostly moved toward reverse KL or JSD.

questions.question: Why is Experiment B's 'language model' a bigram chain?
options: So on/off-policy is exact: visitation d_{t+1} = d_t P gives the expected loss over all rollouts as an exact weighted sum
Because a bigram model conditions on only one previous token, so it cannot suffer exposure bias and isolates the divergence choice
Because transformers cannot be distilled on a CPU in reasonable time, and a bigram table is the smallest model that still generates text
So the teacher and student can use different vocabularies, since each row of a bigram table can be aligned to the other model separately
questions.explanation: A (V, V) table where row s is the next-token distribution after token s lets you compute the probability of being at each token exactly via d_{t+1} = d_t P (state_visitation). The expected loss is then an exact weighted sum; real systems sample but the expectation is the same.

questions.question: In Experiment B, how do the teacher chain and the slipping student behave?
options: The teacher wanders uniformly over all 8 tokens with no preferred route, while the student is deterministic and always follows the 0->1->2->3 cycle exactly
The teacher cycles 0->1->2->3->0 w.p. 0.9999, rarely going off-road (tokens 4-7) and returning to 0 from there w.p. 0.9; the student always slips 0.05 uniformly
Both start as exact copies of each other over the 8 tokens, and the student only begins to slip once training moves its rows away from the teacher's own
The student never leaves the road tokens 0-3 because its slip mass is masked out, while the teacher spends most of its time among the off-road tokens 4-7
questions.explanation: The teacher knows how to recover from off-road tokens but its own text almost never shows it. The student can never be perfect: 5% of its mass is always uniform, standing in for limited capacity or temperature, so it sometimes steps off-road.

questions.question: In Experiment B, how do off-policy and on-policy training of the bigram student differ?
options: Off-policy uses reverse KL on each row and on-policy uses forward KL, with the rows weighted equally in both regimes
On-policy is given more steps and a higher learning rate, since its student-visited rows change between every update
Same steps and learning rate; off-policy weights each row by the teacher's visitation, on-policy by the student's, recomputed each step
Off-policy freezes the off-road rows the teacher never visits, while on-policy updates all eight rows of the table every step
questions.explanation: distill_markov trains the same student twice with identical settings. The only difference is which visitation weights each row's divergence: the teacher's (off-policy) or the student's own, recomputed every step (on-policy).

questions.question: In Experiment B, why does off-policy distillation leave the student's recovery probability at chance (0.125)?
options: Because the learning rate is too low for the off-road rows to move in the step budget given
Because reverse KL ignores rare tokens, so the off-road rows are never compared to the teacher
Because the teacher's own recovery probability is also 0.125, so off-policy copies it faithfully
Off-policy training never puts weight on the off-road rows, which the teacher almost never visits
questions.explanation: Off-policy weighting follows the teacher's visitation, which essentially never reaches tokens 4-7, so those rows get almost no gradient and recovery stays at 1/8. On-policy weighting follows the slipping student, so those rows are trained and recovery reaches 0.75-0.77.

questions.question: What were the headline results of on-policy versus off-policy training in Experiment B?
options: On-policy learned to recover (0.75-0.77 vs 0.13), spent ~40% less time off-road, and had ~20% lower on-policy KL
Off-policy was better on every metric, since the teacher's rollouts gave cleaner targets than the student's own slipping rollouts
Both regimes ended identical on every metric, because the bigram chain is exact and the two losses share the same minimum
On-policy recovered perfectly (1.0 vs 0.13) but had about 20% higher on-policy KL, since it spent its capacity on off-road rows
questions.explanation: On-policy training visits the rows the student actually visits, so it learns to recover. It spends about 40% less time lost and its reverse KL measured on its own rollouts is about 20% lower. Both fit the rows they train on; the difference is which rows.

questions.question: In Experiment B, which metric reflects what a user of the student experiences?
options: Reverse KL to the teacher measured on the teacher's own rollouts
Reverse KL to the teacher measured on the student's own rollouts
The training loss measured on the teacher-written prefixes it saw
The teacher's recovery probability from the off-road tokens 4-7
questions.explanation: eval_on_policy_rkl measures reverse KL on the student's own rollouts, i.e. the states a user would actually see the student in. Loss on teacher prefixes misses exactly the states exposure bias creates.

questions.question: When does on-policy distillation's advantage in the bigram toy close?
options: When the teacher is noisier and visits off-road tokens often, so off-policy data already covers recovery
When forward KL is used instead of reverse KL, since forward KL is teacher-weighted in both regimes
When the student can copy the teacher exactly (slip = 0, trained long enough): both converge
Never: on-policy wins by the same fixed margin at every slip value, step count and learning rate
questions.explanation: The toy is built to show the mechanism: a near-perfect teacher and an always-slipping student. With slip = 0 the student stops leaving the road, rarely needs to recover, and both regimes converge. On-policy helps when the student cannot be perfect, the usual case, but it is not a law.

questions.question: Which of these does test_distill.py NOT check?
options: That forward KL with a one-hot teacher equals F.cross_entropy
That the teacher gets no gradient
Agreement with torch.nn.functional.kl_div
That on-policy distillation beats RL on AIME
questions.explanation: The 12 tests check the hand-example values, agreement with F.kl_div, forward KL with one-hot teacher equals cross-entropy, both closed-form gradients vs autograd, no teacher gradient, JSD_beta endpoints and limits, prompt masking, and both experiments' qualitative results. AIME comparisons are from the Qwen3 report, not the tests.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production trainers do, and the cost
questions.question: What three things does TRL's DistillationTrainer do?
options: Generate completions from the student (optionally with vLLM), score them with one teacher prefill pass, and compute a chunked generalized JSD on completions
Generate completions from the teacher with vLLM, SFT the student on them with cross-entropy, then run PPO with the teacher's log-probs as the reward model
Train a reward model from teacher-versus-student comparisons, run GRPO on the student against it, then merge the student and teacher weights
Store the teacher's top-k logits for the whole dataset once, train the student offline on those stored targets, then evaluate on held-out prompts
questions.explanation: DistillationTrainer generates student completions like an online RL trainer, scores them with one teacher forward pass (prefill only, much cheaper than generating), and computes the generalized JSD (beta default 1.0 = reverse KL) over completion tokens in chunks.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production trainers do, and the cost
questions.question: Why is the teacher's scoring step in on-policy distillation relatively cheap?
options: Because the teacher is a smaller model than the student in most on-policy setups
Because it is a prefill-only forward pass with no generation
Because teacher scores are cached and reused from previous training epochs
Because only the last token of each completion is scored by the teacher
questions.explanation: The teacher does not generate; it runs a single forward pass over the student's completion (prefill) to get log-probs at every position. That is much cheaper than autoregressive generation.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production trainers do, and the cost
questions.question: With vocabulary V = 151,936 and a batch of 8 x 4096 tokens, roughly how large is one fp32 logits tensor, and why does that matter for distillation?
options: About 2 GB in fp32, so teacher and student logits fit easily next to the model weights on a single GPU
About 200 MB per tensor, which is negligible next to the optimizer state, so no special handling is needed
About 19.9 GB; distillation needs teacher and student logits plus the student's gradient, so the loss is chunked
About 199 GB per tensor, which no GPU can hold, so logit distillation is impossible at this vocabulary size
questions.explanation: 32,768 tokens x 151,936 x 4 bytes is about 19.9 GB. Logit distillation needs both models' logits plus the gradient, so chunking the vocabulary projection and divergence over positions keeps peak memory to one chunk, the same trick as chunked cross-entropy.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production trainers do, and the cost
questions.question: How do offline logit-distillation pipelines usually store teacher distributions?
options: The full V-dimensional teacher distribution for every token, stored in fp32
Only the teacher's argmax token at each position, as a sparse one-hot target
As a compressed teacher checkpoint that is re-run whenever a target is needed
Only the top-k log-probs per position, renormalised (reasonable industry practice)
questions.explanation: Storing full distributions at V = 150K for a dataset is impossible, so offline pipelines usually keep the top-k log-probs per position and renormalise. The exact k and tail handling vary; this is reasonable industry practice, not a documented standard.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production trainers do, and the cost
questions.question: Why can on-policy distillation not be precomputed offline?
options: The prefixes do not exist until the current student writes them, so the teacher must be live
Because the teacher's weights are updated every step, so its scores go stale after one update
Because top-k storage is too small to hold the teacher's scores for every possible student prefix
Because forward KL requires live teacher gradients, which cannot be stored to disk ahead of time
questions.explanation: Off-policy forward KL works with stored logits since prefixes come from the teacher or a fixed dataset. On-policy prefixes are written by the student, which changes each step, so the teacher must score them live.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production trainers do, and the cost
questions.question: Per step, how does on-policy distillation's compute compare with an RLVR step, and how does the signal differ?
options: Distillation is about 10x cheaper per step because it skips generation; its signal is the same single scalar reward per sequence as RL
About the same cost, dominated by student generation; RL gets one scalar per sequence, distillation a full distribution per token
Distillation is about 10x more expensive per step, since the teacher must also generate, and its signal is sparser than RL's
RL needs no generation because it scores a fixed dataset, while distillation must generate, so it costs far more per step
questions.explanation: Both are dominated by generating student rollouts, so per-step cost is similar. The difference is signal density: one scalar per sequence for RL vs a full distribution per token for distillation.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production trainers do, and the cost
questions.question: What does the Qwen3 Technical Report claim about on-policy distillation of Qwen3-8B versus RL?
options: RL beat on-policy distillation on AIME and coding at about a tenth of the GPU-hours, so the report used RL for every small model
They tied on all benchmarks at equal cost, so the report chose distillation only because it did not require a reward function
On-policy distillation beat RL on AIME and coding from the same start, using ~1,800 vs 17,920 GPU-hours (a company claim)
Distillation needed no teacher at inference or training time, since the 8B model distilled from its own earlier checkpoints
questions.explanation: Qwen3's Table 21 reports on-policy distillation beating RL on AIME and coding from the same starting point at roughly 1,800 vs 17,920 GPU-hours. It is a company claim, not an independent reproduction.

questions.section: 6. Under the hood: what production trainers do, and the cost
questions.question: Why do frontier labs still need RL for their largest models even if distillation is cheaper?
options: Because distillation cannot run on GPUs at frontier scale, since the teacher's logits do not fit in memory alongside the student
Because RL gives a denser per-token training signal than distillation, so it is the only way to improve the very largest models
Because distillation only works for math and code, where answers are checkable, while frontier models must also learn open tasks
Distillation needs a stronger teacher to exist; RL does not, so RL trains the frontier model and distillation passes it down
questions.explanation: Distillation requires a stronger teacher. For the largest model there is none, so labs use RL there and distill the result into smaller models.

questions.section: 7. Side by side: when to use which
questions.question: What does each distillation regime need from the teacher?
options: Sequence-level KD: text only; off-policy logit KD: log-probs on its own text; on-policy: live log-probs on the student's text
All three need only the teacher's sampled text, since log-probs can always be re-estimated from enough samples of each prefix
Sequence-level KD: live log-probs on the student's text; off-policy logit KD: text only; on-policy: the teacher's full weights
All three need direct access to the teacher's weights, since any form of distillation backpropagates through the teacher
questions.explanation: Sequence-level KD works with an API. Off-policy logit KD needs log-probs on the teacher's own text (can be stored). On-policy needs the teacher live to score the student's text.

questions.section: 7. Side by side: when to use which
questions.question: Which distillation regime fixes exposure bias?
options: Sequence-level KD
On-policy distillation
Off-policy logit KD
All three regimes equally
questions.explanation: Only on-policy distillation trains on the student's own prefixes, so it sees and corrects the student's mistakes. Both sequence-level and off-policy logit KD train on the teacher's prefixes.

questions.section: 7. Side by side: when to use which
questions.question: What is the typical role of each distillation regime?
options: On-policy distillation as the first stage from a random student, then off-policy logit KD, with sequence-level KD as the final stage
Off-policy logit KD only when the teacher and student tokenizers differ, since matching logits otherwise adds nothing over sampled text
Sequence-level KD first, or with an API teacher or other tokenizer; off-policy logit KD as a cheap early stage; on-policy last
All three are interchangeable and can be used at any stage, since each gives the same dense per-token signal from the teacher
questions.explanation: Sequence-level KD suits a first stage, a closed-API teacher or mismatched tokenizers. Off-policy logit KD is a cheap first stage when logits are available. On-policy distillation is the final stage for a small student.

questions.section: 7. Side by side: when to use which
questions.question: Why is running on-policy distillation from a random student wasteful?
options: Because the KL between a random student and the teacher is undefined, since the student puts mass everywhere
Because the teacher refuses to score random text, so most of each batch is dropped before the loss is computed
Because random students have no gradient through the softmax, so the first thousands of steps make no progress
The teacher spends compute grading gibberish; an earlier off-policy stage makes the student's samples worth grading
questions.explanation: A common pipeline first does sequence-level or off-policy KD so the student's samples are sensible, then on-policy distillation. Starting on-policy from a random student wastes teacher compute scoring meaningless rollouts. DeepSeek's R1 distillation and Qwen3's first stage both start off-policy.

questions.question: In Experiment A, what happens if reverse KL is initialised in the empty gap (init_mu = 9.5)?
options: It gets stuck at a wide, flat solution (loss ~2.87, far above ln 2): from the gap no small move reaches a mode
It finds the bin-4 mode exactly, since reverse KL is convex and any initialisation reaches the global optimum
It finds both modes by splitting into two bumps, because starting exactly in the gap is symmetric with respect to them
It produces the same wide solution as forward KL, with the forward-KL loss of 0.881 and mu about 9
questions.explanation: From the gap no small move reaches a mode, so reverse KL sticks at a poor wide solution. Starting at init_mu = 13.0 it finds the other mode (mu = 15). Forward KL reaches essentially the same wide solution (loss 0.881) from any start. Reverse KL is non-convex in the student's parameters.

questions.question: In the bigram experiment, what happens with slip = 0.1 instead of 0.05?
options: The gap between on- and off-policy closes, because a sloppier student visits off-road rows under both regimes
The recovery gap stays wide and both on-policy KLs rise, because a sloppier student is more often lost
Off-policy becomes better than on-policy, since the student's noisier rollouts give it worse training targets
Both on-policy KLs drop to about 0.001, since more slipping gives the student more recovery practice
questions.explanation: A sloppier student leaves the road more, so recovery matters more and the gap stays wide; both KLs rise. With slip = 0 and 2000 steps instead, both on-policy KLs drop to about 0.001 and the gap almost disappears.

questions.question: What does F.kl_div(input, target) compute, and what is the classic mistake?
options: KL(input || target) with both in probability space; the classic mistake is passing the teacher as input, which flips the direction
The generalized JSD between input and target; the classic mistake is forgetting to pass beta, which then defaults to reverse KL
KL(target || input) with input in log space; passing the student as target silently turns forward KL into reverse KL
The cross-entropy of target under input; the classic mistake is forgetting the mask, which makes the loss include padding
questions.explanation: F.kl_div(input, target) computes KL(target || input) with input as log-probabilities. Swapping arguments silently changes the direction. Test against a hand example.

questions.question: Why must teacher logits be computed under torch.no_grad() and detached?
options: Only to save time and memory; the gradient into the teacher is harmless because the optimizer never steps it
Because bf16 tensors cannot be backpropagated through, so a teacher in bf16 would raise an autograd error
Because the teacher has no trainable parameters once loaded for inference, so its graph would be empty anyway
Otherwise gradient flows into the teacher and you are fine-tuning it toward the student
questions.explanation: If the teacher's logits carry gradient, the optimizer will update the teacher to match the student, the opposite of distillation. Compute them under no_grad and detach.

questions.question: Why must prompt tokens be masked out of the distillation loss?
options: Prompt tokens are given, not generated; including them trains the student to mimic the teacher's view of user text
Prompt tokens have no logits in the teacher's forward pass, so their divergence is undefined and produces NaNs in the loss
The teacher cannot score prompt tokens, since it was only trained on assistant turns, so its targets there are random noise
Masking prompt tokens is what makes the KL non-negative; without it, the per-token divergences can cancel and go below zero
questions.explanation: Only completion tokens are generated by the model. Including prompt positions would train the student to match the teacher's predictions on the user's text, the same mistake as unmasked SFT.

questions.question: What is the temperature-mismatch mistake in distillation?
options: Using any sampling temperature other than 1, which always biases the student's rollouts relative to the teacher's
Sampling at tau but computing the loss at temperature 1 (or softening one side only), so target and trained distributions differ
Using a different sampling temperature for each batch, which makes the loss scale drift and destabilises the learning rate
Applying the temperature to the completion mask as well as the logits, which down-weights the last tokens of each sequence
questions.explanation: Pick one temperature and apply it to both teacher and student logits. TRL uses its temperature setting for both sampling and the loss.

questions.question: Why is 'on-policy distillation always wins' a mistake?
options: Because on-policy distillation is in fact always worse than off-policy once the student has been pre-trained on teacher text
Because on-policy distillation cannot use reverse KL, so it loses the mode-seeking behaviour that makes students precise
It fixes exposure bias but does not guarantee a better student; measure on your task
Because on-policy distillation needs no teacher at all, so it is really self-training and cannot exceed the student's start
questions.explanation: On-policy distillation addresses exposure bias, which matters when the student cannot be perfect, but its benefit is not guaranteed. A 2026 study found it smaller than expected in some settings.

questions.question: In the sampled on-policy reverse-KL update for one bigram row, what reward is used for each sampled token v_i ~ p_S?
options: r_i = log p_T(v_i)
r_i = p_T(v_i) - p_S(v_i)
r_i = 1 if v_i is the teacher's argmax else 0
r_i = -(log p_S(v_i) - log p_T(v_i))
questions.explanation: The reward is the negative log-ratio, r_i = -(log p_S(v_i) - log p_T(v_i)). The REINFORCE loss is -(1/N) sum_i (r_i - r_bar) log p_S(v_i) with the rewards detached; its expected gradient equals the exact reverse-KL gradient p_S(l - K).

questions.question: Why does the sampled REINFORCE estimator with reward -l_v match the exact reverse-KL gradient in expectation?
options: grad KL(p_S||p_T) = E_{v~p_S}[l_v grad log p_S(v)], since E_{v~p_S}[grad log p_S(v)] = 0; a baseline leaves it unchanged
Because the teacher's gradient exactly cancels the student's score-function term, leaving the pathwise derivative of the KL
Because reverse KL is linear in p_S, so the expectation of any single-sample estimate equals the full sum over the vocabulary
Because sampling from p_S is unbiased only for forward KL, and the reward -l_v converts the reverse KL into a forward KL first
questions.explanation: The extra term E_{p_S}[grad log p_S] vanishes, leaving E[l_v grad log p_S(v)]. Minimizing KL means following -l_v as a reward, and a baseline leaves the expectation unchanged while reducing variance. Cosine similarity with the exact gradient rises toward 1 as N grows.

questions.question: When is the sampled per-token reverse-KL form preferred, and when is the full-vocabulary form preferred?
options: Sampled always, because the one-sample estimator is both unbiased and lower variance than the full sum over the vocabulary
Full-vocabulary when the teacher's whole distribution is available, as a few samples over 150K tokens are noisy; else sampled
Full-vocabulary only for tiny vocabularies below about 1K tokens, since beyond that the sum over V cannot fit in GPU memory
Sampled only for forward KL, since the reverse-KL form needs the teacher's full distribution to compute the baseline K exactly
questions.explanation: On a 3-token vocabulary 10 samples are already close, but with a 150K-token vocabulary a handful of samples per position is very noisy. The sampled form needs only the teacher's log-prob of the sampled token, so it suits teachers that do not return full distributions.

questions.question: A distillation loss F.kl_div(F.softmax(student_logits, -1), F.log_softmax(teacher_logits, -1), log_target=True, reduction='batchmean') is negative and falling. What is wrong?
options: log_target should be False, since the teacher's log-softmax must be exponentiated before F.kl_div can compare it
The teacher must be passed as softmax probabilities rather than log-probabilities, which is what makes the loss go negative
The first argument must be log-probabilities; passing probabilities computes sum p_T(log p_T - p_S), not a KL, and can go negative
reduction='batchmean' should be 'sum', since batchmean divides by B and lets per-token negative values dominate the mean
questions.explanation: F.kl_div expects input in log space. With probabilities passed, the formula is not a KL and can go negative. A true KL is never negative, so a negative value always means a bug. Fix: use F.log_softmax(student_logits, -1) as the first argument, giving forward KL(p_T||p_S).

questions.question: With (B, T, V) inputs, what does reduction='batchmean' in F.kl_div divide by, and what should you do?
options: B * T, the batch times sequence length, so the result is already a per-token mean and nothing needs changing
V, the vocabulary size, so the result is a per-class mean and you must divide by T manually to get per-token
T, the sequence length, so you must reshape to (B, V) by summing over time before calling it
Only the first dimension, B, not B*T; reshape to (B*T, V) and mask first
questions.explanation: batchmean divides the summed KL by the size of the first dimension only. For (B, T, V) that is B, not the number of tokens. Reshape to (B*T, V) and apply the mask so the loss is a mean over completion tokens.

questions.question: What is GKD (Agarwal et al., ICLR 2024) and what does it define?
options: 'On-Policy Distillation of Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes'; defines the generalized JSD and on-policy fraction lambda
'Generalized Knowledge Distillation via Beam Search'; a sequence-level KD method that trains the student on the teacher's top-scoring beam outputs
'Grounded Knowledge Distillation for Reasoning'; a process reward model trained from teacher step scores to guide student distillation
'Generalized Kernel Distillation'; a tokenizer-alignment method that maps teacher and student vocabularies before computing the KL
questions.explanation: GKD defines on-policy distillation using the generalized JSD_beta and a fraction lambda of on-policy data. MiniLLM (Gu et al., ICLR 2024) argues for reverse KL and optimizes it with a policy-gradient method.

questions.question: What did the 2026 study 'On-Policy or Off-Policy Learning? A Systematic Study of Distillation Dynamics' report?
options: On-policy rollouts dominated every other factor, including KL direction and learning rate, across all student and teacher sizes tested
KL direction mattered more than rollout policy: forward KL was robust to rollout source, reverse KL needed on-policy; LR set forgetting
Distillation was never better than RL at matched compute, so the study recommended RLVR for every student size and every task family
Reverse KL was robust to rollout policy while forward KL needed on-policy rollouts; the learning rate had little effect on forgetting
questions.explanation: Varying rollout policy, KL direction and learning rate separately on Llama 3 and Qwen 2.5 students, it found KL direction mattered more than rollout policy, forward KL was robust to rollout policy, reverse KL needed on-policy rollouts, and learning rate governed forgetting. It is a single, unreproduced paper: a reason to ablate, not a settled rule.

questions.question: According to the 2026 distillation-dynamics study, did on-policy data's generalization advantage survive later RLVR?
options: Yes; RLVR amplified the on-policy advantage, widening the generalization gap on harder variants
Yes, unchanged: the generalization gap from on-policy data stayed the same through later RLVR
It helped generalization on harder variants, but the advantage did not reliably survive later RLVR
No; on-policy data hurt generalization from the start, and RLVR later only partly closed the gap
questions.explanation: The study reports that on-policy data helped generalization on harder variants, but this advantage did not reliably survive later RLVR training.

questions.question: Which of these is classified as reasonable industry practice rather than publicly documented in the distillation literature?
options: The GKD and MiniLLM methods, which define on-policy distillation and the reverse-KL objective
Qwen3's two-stage strong-to-weak distillation, off-policy first and then on-policy logit matching
TRL's DistillationTrainer loss defaults and its chunked computation of the generalized JSD
Storing top-k logits for offline KD and staging sequence-level or off-policy KD before on-policy
questions.explanation: GKD, MiniLLM, Qwen3's two-stage distillation (with a company-claimed GPU-hour comparison) and TRL's loss/defaults are publicly documented. Top-k stored logits and staging are reasonable industry practice. Claiming a given lab's small models are distilled this way without a report saying so is inference.

questions.question: In the GKD paper, which parts should be read on a first pass?
options: The KD-divergence background, the GKD algorithm, and the ablations on on-policy fraction and divergence; skim tasks, skip RLHF part
Only the RLHF-combination part, since it shows how GKD plugs into a reward-model pipeline; the KD background and ablations can be skipped
Only the task-by-task result tables for summarisation, translation and arithmetic; the algorithm itself can be read later
Only the appendix proofs that JSD_beta interpolates between the KLs; the method and experiments follow directly from them
questions.explanation: Read the forward/reverse KL and generalized JSD background and the GKD algorithm, and the ablations on the on-policy fraction and divergence. Skim task results and skip the RLHF combination initially.

questions.question: Why is SFT on teacher samples a special case of forward-KL distillation, and what does it lose?
options: It is reverse KL with a one-hot student on the sampled token, so it loses nothing: its expected gradient equals the full reverse KL, and its variance is the same as summing over the vocabulary
One-hot teacher on sampled y gives -log p_S(y); over y ~ p_T that is forward KL plus constant teacher entropy, so gradients match in expectation, but it loses non-sampled preferences and is noisier

It is JSD with beta = 0.5 on the teacher's prefixes, so it is bounded by ln 2; what it loses is exposure bias, which only the full forward-KL form corrects when evaluated on the student's own prefixes
It is not related to KL at all: SFT maximises the likelihood of the sampled tokens, which is a different objective whose minimiser need not match the teacher's distribution even with infinite samples
questions.explanation: SFT cross-entropy is forward KL against a one-hot teacher. In expectation over teacher samples it differs from forward KL only by H(p_T), which does not depend on the student, but the single sample discards the rest of the teacher's distribution and makes the gradient much noisier.

questions.question: Fitting a one-bump student to a two-bump teacher, which divergence yields a student that sometimes produces outputs the teacher would almost never produce?
options: Reverse KL, because it is student-weighted, so the student is free to place mass wherever the teacher is low
JSD_0.5, because it is bounded by ln 2, so placing mass between the modes costs the student at most a constant
Forward KL: it is teacher-weighted, so missing a mode is very costly and the student spreads mass between modes
Neither: forward and reverse KL give the same one-bump student, so it never places mass the teacher would not
questions.explanation: Forward KL forces the student to cover both modes, which a one-bump student can only do by spreading into the gap (26.8% vs the teacher's 0.24%). Reverse KL is student-weighted, punishes that gap mass, and commits to one mode.

questions.question: What does on-policy distillation need in terms of infrastructure, compared with off-policy?
options: Nothing extra; it reads the same stored top-k teacher logits as off-policy KD and simply samples its prefixes from those stored distributions
Only a larger disk, since the teacher's scores for every student rollout are written out before each training epoch
Only a reward model trained to imitate the teacher, which replaces the teacher's log-probs during student training
The teacher running live alongside training (like a reward model in RLHF) plus a fast generation engine for the student
questions.explanation: Off-policy teacher log-probs can be computed once and stored. On-policy prefixes come from the changing student, so the teacher must score them live, and the student needs a fast generation engine for rollouts.

questions.question: When would you still choose plain sequence-level distillation?
options: Only the teacher's text is available (closed API), the tokenizers differ, or as a cheap first stage before on-policy
When you need to fix exposure bias, since training on the teacher's text shows the student the states it will reach
When you want a dense per-token signal, since each sampled token carries the teacher's full distribution with it
When the teacher is weaker than the student, since sequence-level KD lets the student filter out the teacher's mistakes
questions.explanation: Sequence-level KD needs only text and does not require a shared tokenizer, and it is a standard cheap first stage so the student's samples are worth grading later. DeepSeek's R1 distillation used it.

questions.section: Advanced extension: TRL's fused LM head (added 2026-10-11)
questions.question: What changed in TRL v1.15.0 regarding how distillation and other trainers compute token log-probs?
options: They switched to storing the full logits in fp64 so the generalized JSD is computed exactly, which is now the default for distillation
Tokens are scored by a fused Triton LM head that tiles the projection and reduces straight to log-probs and entropy; on by default
They removed reverse KL from DistillationTrainer, since the fused kernel only supports teacher-weighted divergences
They now require the teacher to run on CPU in a separate process, so the student's GPU never holds the teacher's logits
questions.explanation: In TRL v1.15.0 the SFT, DPO, KTO, GRPO, RLOO and Distillation trainers use a fused Triton LM head instead of chunking. It never materialises the logits tensor and is on by default (publicly documented). A separate Triton kernel for the distillation divergence is listed but its internals are not described.

questions.section: Advanced extension: TRL's fused LM head (added 2026-10-11)
questions.question: What mechanism does TRL's fused LM head use to avoid building the logits tensor?
options: Top-k sparsification of the vocabulary, keeping only the 128 largest logits per position
Quantising the logits to int8 per tile, so the full tensor fits in a tenth of the memory
An online logsumexp over vocabulary tiles, as in FlashAttention's online softmax
Caching logits on disk in tiles and streaming them back for the backward pass
questions.explanation: The fused head computes log-probs with an online logsumexp across vocabulary tiles, the same recurrence used in FlashAttention's online softmax. The divergences themselves are unchanged; only how logits are produced changes.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: In LLM tool use, what three parts make up a tool schema shown to the model?
options: A name, a Python source listing of the function, and its return type annotation
A name, a natural-language description, and a JSON-Schema parameters object
A tool id number, an embedding vector of the tool, and a list of example outputs
A URL endpoint, an authentication token, and an HTTP method
questions.explanation: A tool schema has a unique name the model emits to select the tool, a description saying when to use it, and a JSON-Schema object describing the arguments. The model never sees the Python source or an embedding; it only reads this text contract in its context to know which tools exist and what arguments they take.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: What does 'function calling' mean for a language model?
options: The model emits a structured call (tool name plus arguments) instead of prose, which an external runtime parses and runs
The model executes Python functions directly inside its forward pass, using an interpreter built into its decoder layers
The model's weights are updated by calling a training function each time a tool is used, so it learns every tool online
The model's attention layers are replaced by function lookups for arithmetic tokens, so numbers are computed, not predicted
questions.explanation: Function calling is a convention on top of text generation: the model generates a structured message naming a tool and its arguments, and code outside the model runs it. The model itself has no interpreter and never executes anything; it only asks.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Why do abilities like exact arithmetic, lookup, and code execution come from tools rather than from adding more parameters to an aligned model?
options: They require exact computation, fresh information, or effects outside the text stream, which weights cannot provide
Larger aligned models are discouraged from learning exact arithmetic by the alignment objective, which rewards plausible text
More parameters would make the model too slow to emit structured JSON, so labs cap model size once tools are available
Tools are only needed because current models have too few attention heads to track digits; more heads would remove the need
questions.explanation: A model generates text from learned patterns, so it cannot guarantee exact arithmetic, cannot know facts that changed after or were never in its training data, and cannot touch the outside world. Tools supply exactly those capabilities, which is why function calling makes a frozen model useful as the brain of an acting system.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Which later topic is function calling described as the foundation for?
options: Pretraining tokenizers, which need tools to split text
Scaling laws, which use tools to fit compute curves
Agents, which repeatedly call tools to act toward a goal
Mixed-precision training, which calls tools for loss scaling
questions.explanation: Function calling is the interface that lets a model act through external functions; agents (Module 19) are built by putting such calls in a loop with observations. It has nothing to do with tokenization, scaling-law fitting, or precision.

questions.section: 1. The causal story: a smart model that can't multiply
questions.question: Why does a language model asked for 4831 * 7772 usually produce a wrong but plausible-looking number?
options: It generates digits token by token from patterns rather than actually performing the multiplication
It truncates every number to four significant digits during tokenization, so the product loses its precision
It deliberately rounds large products, because alignment training discourages revealing exact numerical answers
Its softmax spreads probability across digit tokens, so it cannot commit to any single digit at each position
questions.explanation: The model has no calculator inside: it predicts likely next tokens, and for long multiplications the pattern-based guess is often wrong. The fix is a calculator tool that performs the exact computation; the model's job is only to ask for it.

questions.section: 1. The causal story: a smart model that can't multiply
questions.question: Why does a model confidently hallucinate when asked for today's exchange rate or the contents of a private file?
options: Exchange rates and file contents are filtered out of all pretraining corpora by policy, so the model fills the gap
The model refuses numerical questions unless the prompt is in JSON, so it guesses rather than refusing in plain text
Private files are always tokenized into unknown tokens, so the model sees no content and invents something plausible
The answer was never in its training data or changed after the cutoff, so it is not in the weights
questions.explanation: Fresh or private facts cannot be stored in weights trained on a fixed corpus before a cutoff. Without a lookup tool, the model still produces fluent text, which is why it hallucinates confidently instead of saying it does not know.

questions.section: 1. The causal story: a smart model that can't multiply
questions.question: A model can write a correct sorting function but still cannot sort a user's list on its own. Why?
options: Its context window is too short to hold both the list and the function it wrote
Sorting requires gradients through the comparisons, which are disabled at inference
It can only produce text and cannot execute code or act outside its text stream
Code it generates is never valid Python unless a tool checks the syntax first
questions.explanation: Writing code and running code are different: the model emits text but has no interpreter and no access to anything outside its own output. A code-execution tool run by the runtime is what turns the written code into an actual result.

questions.section: 1. The causal story: a smart model that can't multiply
questions.question: In a tool-augmented system, how is work divided between the model and the tools?
options: Tools do all the reasoning and planning; the model only formats their results into the final answer
The model and tools alternate generating tokens of the same answer, each writing every other token
Tools replace the model entirely once registered, and the model only routes the user's request to them
The model stays the reasoning engine; tools do the exact, up-to-date, or side-effecting work
questions.explanation: The model decides what to do and interprets results, while tools provide exact computations, lookups, and effects on the world. Neither replaces the other: the tool cannot decide when it is needed and the model cannot compute exactly.

questions.section: 1. The causal story: a smart model that can't multiply
questions.question: What is a 'tool' in the sense used for LLM function calling?
options: A transformer layer specialised for arithmetic tokens that the model routes numbers through
A fine-tuned adapter that is merged into the weights at load time to add a new skill
A special token in the vocabulary that triggers a hardware instruction when it is sampled
Any external function the model can invoke to get something its weights cannot provide
questions.explanation: A tool is external: an exact computation, a lookup, or an effect on the world, implemented outside the model. Function calling is the protocol by which the model asks for it to run and receives the result back as text.

questions.section: 2. Intuition: how a model "calls" a function
questions.question: Since a model only emits text, what is function calling at the mechanical level?
options: A modification of the decoder that adds a jump-to-function instruction the GPU executes mid-sequence
A second neural network that translates the model's text into machine code and runs it on the host
A convention on top of text generation, involving schema, model, runtime, and returned result
A special CUDA kernel that executes Python inside the GPU whenever a call token is sampled
questions.explanation: The model has no interpreter, no memory beyond its context, and no hands, so function calling is a convention: tools are described in the context, the model emits a structured call, the runtime executes it, and the result is pasted back as a new message.

questions.section: 2. Intuition: how a model "calls" a function
questions.question: In the four-actor picture of function calling, what is the runtime's job?
options: Parse the model's JSON, find the real function, run it with those arguments, and capture the result
Write the tool descriptions that appear in the schema, and retrain the model whenever any of them change
Sample tokens from the model's logits under a JSON grammar, so the call is always well-formed
Fine-tune the model on every failed tool call, so it stops making the same argument mistake
questions.explanation: The runtime is code outside the model: it parses the structured call, dispatches to the matching callable, executes it, and captures the output. That output then goes back into the context so the model can continue with the true answer in front of it.

questions.section: 2. Intuition: how a model "calls" a function
questions.question: In function calling, what happens to a tool's result after the runtime executes it?
options: It is pasted into the model's context as a new message and the model continues generating
It is written directly into the model's weights as a new memory through a single gradient step
It is shown to the user only, never to the model, which then waits for the user's next message
It replaces the system prompt for the rest of the session, so later turns are grounded in it
questions.explanation: The result is returned as text in a new context message, so the model's next generation step can condition on it. Nothing changes in the weights; the model simply sees the true answer it could not compute itself.

questions.section: 2. Intuition: how a model "calls" a function
questions.question: In the programmer's analogy for function calling, what role does the runtime play?
