questions.question: Why should a real policy ideally use constrained decoding in the observation/action loop?
options: So that it never produces a prose final answer
So that it can run fully on CPU without a GPU
So that tool observations come back shorter
So any tool call it emits is valid JSON
questions.explanation: Constrained decoding guarantees syntactically valid calls, while the loop still handles correctness through feedback.

questions.question: In the two-turn calculator run of the observation/action loop, why does len(trace) equal 1?
options: Because the second call was deduplicated against the first one
Because the trace stores only successful calls, not failed ones
Because the first turn is not recorded, only the most recent call
trace counts tool calls, not model turns; turn 1 was prose
questions.explanation: Two model turns, one tool call, so the trace has one entry.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Beyond doing real work, what increasingly important roles do LLM agents play for the models being trained?
options: Generating their own training data, running their own experiments, and fixing their own code
Replacing the optimizer during pretraining by proposing per-step learning rates and momentum values
Compressing the trained model's weights for deployment by choosing which layers to quantize
Choosing tokenizer merges during BPE training so the vocabulary fits the target domain
questions.explanation: Agents are how trained models get used, and increasingly how they produce training data, run experiments, and repair code. Research engineers both build agent scaffolds and act as the human debugging them.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: According to the view of agent engineering as a craft, what is the hard part of building an agent?
options: Writing the loop's control flow, which needs complex scheduling, threading, and state machines
Implementing tensor representations of the action space so the model can sample actions
Choosing the GPU type and batch size so the control loop runs at interactive latency
Getting the interface and the feedback right; the loop itself is simple
questions.explanation: The loop is a few lines of control flow. Whether an agent works depends on the tool interface and on the feedback the observations provide.

questions.section: 1. The causal story: one tool call is not enough
questions.question: Why can't a task like 'fix the failing test in this repo' be planned entirely up front?
options: Each step depends on what the previous step revealed, such as a new failure after an edit
Repositories cannot be read by tools, so the agent has to guess file contents from the test name alone
Tests can only be run once per episode, so the plan must be finalized before the first test run
The model's context window forbids writing a multi-step plan before the first tool call is made
questions.explanation: The task is a chain: inspect failure, find file, read code, edit, rerun, see a new failure, revise. You cannot write later actions before seeing earlier observations.

questions.section: 1. The causal story: one tool call is not enough
questions.question: What makes a tool-calling loop an agent?
options: A single tool call with a well-written JSON schema, so that the model's one request is always valid and parseable
A model larger than a fixed parameter threshold, above which multi-tool use becomes reliable enough to deploy
Running on a GPU cluster rather than one device, so that several tools can execute in parallel at every step
Many iterative actions with feedback (inspect, act, observe, correct), driven by a model reasoning about what to do next
questions.explanation: A single call answers one question. Repeating inspect-act-observe-correct under a model's control is what defines an agent.

questions.section: 1. The causal story: one tool call is not enough
questions.question: On the ladder from plain LLM to agent, what distinguishes a tool-calling LLM from a ReAct agent?
options: A tool-calling LLM reasons in natural language but cannot act; ReAct acts on tools but never writes out its reasoning
A tool-calling LLM is trained with RL on tool rewards, while ReAct is trained only with SFT on human traces
A tool-calling LLM emits one structured call and reads one result; ReAct interleaves reasoning and acting in a loop
There is no real difference; the two terms are synonyms used by different labs for the same single-call setup
questions.explanation: Module 18's tool-calling model handles a single call/result. ReAct adds the loop: think, act, observe, repeat.

questions.section: 1. The causal story: one tool call is not enough
questions.question: On the ladder from plain LLM to agent, what does the 'planning + iterative action' rung add beyond ReAct?
options: The agent stops calling tools and switches to reasoning only, having already gathered enough context
The agent's weights are updated by a gradient step after each observation so it learns within the task
The agent maintains a goal, breaks it into sub-steps, and adapts the plan as observations arrive
The agent runs several models in parallel and takes a majority vote over their proposed next actions
questions.explanation: Planning adds explicit goal decomposition and plan revision on top of the think-act-observe loop. The full agent then wraps this with a task, tool interface, and stopping condition.

questions.section: 1. The causal story: one tool call is not enough
questions.question: What three things wrap the loop to make a complete agent on the ladder from plain LLM to agent?
options: A reward model, a value head, and a replay buffer
A tokenizer, an optimizer, and a learning-rate scheduler
A dataset, a validation split, and a held-out test split
A task, a tool interface, and a stopping condition
questions.explanation: The agent rung is the whole loop wrapped with a task to solve, an interface of tools, and a condition for stopping.

questions.question: In ReAct, what is a Thought?
options: A structured tool call with a tool name and JSON arguments that the loop executes immediately
The tool's return value, appended to the history so the model can condition on it at the next step
A hidden activation vector passed between steps that stores the model's plan outside the visible text
A short natural-language reasoning step the model generates about what it knows and what to do next
questions.explanation: A Thought is just generated text, but it forces the model to plan in the open so the plan can condition the next action.

questions.question: In ReAct, what is an Action?
options: A free-form sentence describing what the model intends to do next, written before any tool runs
A gradient update to the policy, applied after each step based on whether the tool call succeeded
A structured tool call (a tool name plus arguments) in the function-calling format
The final answer returned to the user once the loop decides that no further tool calls are needed
questions.explanation: The Action follows the Module 18 function-calling format. The tool's result then becomes the Observation.

questions.question: In ReAct, what is the Observation and what happens to it?
options: The model's own prediction of what the tool will return, used in place of actually running the tool
A human rating of the preceding action, stored as a scalar reward for later RL fine-tuning
A log entry recorded for debugging that is kept out of the model's context to save tokens
The tool's return value, fed back into the context so the next Thought can use it
questions.explanation: Observations ground reasoning in real feedback. They are appended to the running history for the next step.

questions.question: Why did Yao et al. find ReAct outperforms reasoning-only and acting-only approaches?
options: ReAct used a substantially larger model than all the baselines, so most of its gains simply reflect model scale
Reasoning picks good actions and actions ground reasoning in feedback; reasoning-only hallucinates, acting-only flails
ReAct never actually calls tools during evaluation, so it avoids all of the errors that real tool calls introduce
ReAct was fine-tuned on far more demonstration data than the acting-only methods it was compared against
questions.explanation: Each component covers the other's weakness: reasoning without feedback makes things up, while acting without reasoning lacks direction.

questions.question: When does a ReAct loop stop?
options: After exactly three Thought-Action-Observation cycles, regardless of progress
When the model emits a final answer instead of another action
As soon as any tool call returns an error string as its observation
When the newest Observation is identical to the previous Observation
questions.explanation: ReAct repeats Thought, Action, Observation until a final answer appears. A step budget is a separate safety stop.

questions.section: 2.1 Why a *deterministic* loop for a course
questions.question: Why is an LLM policy unsuitable for teaching and unit-testing the ReAct mechanism?
options: It is non-deterministic and needs a GPU or API key, so runs aren't reproducible or testable
It cannot emit structured actions in the function-calling format, so the loop has nothing to parse
It is too accurate on toy tasks, so it routes around loop bugs and hides them from the tests
It requires tensors inside the loop, which forces the whole control flow to run on the GPU
questions.explanation: Non-determinism and external dependencies make tests flaky and costly. A scripted policy makes every run reproducible.

questions.section: 2.1 Why a *deterministic* loop for a course
questions.question: How does the course's ReAct implementation separate concerns between loop and policy?
options: The loop contains the model and generates every thought; the policy is just the list of tools it may call
The loop is deterministic control flow; the policy is any callable policy(history) -> action, scripted in tests
The policy runs the tools and records their outputs, while the loop generates thoughts between tool calls
Both are merged into a single LLM call that returns the full trace and the final answer in one generation
questions.explanation: The loop calls the policy, runs the named tool, appends the observation, and repeats. The policy decides actions. This is how real agent frameworks are structured.

questions.section: 2.1 Why a *deterministic* loop for a course
questions.question: Why is the course's deterministic ReAct agent honestly called a scaffold?
options: Because it cannot run any tools and only prints the actions it would have taken
Without a capable policy it only does what the script says
Because it has no step budget, so any policy that never finishes runs forever
Because it only works on GPUs, so it cannot be run in the course's CPU tests
questions.explanation: The scripted policy lets you understand and test the plumbing, but it contains no intelligence. A real agent needs an LLM policy.

questions.question: In the ReAct trace for computing (3 + 4) × 2 with add and mul tools, where did step 2's argument a=7 come from?
options: From step 1's observation, the result of add(3, 4)
From the task string, which the loop parses before step 1
From the policy computing the sum in advance, without a tool
From the mul tool's default argument, which is preset to 7
questions.explanation: The dependency chain is the point: the second action could not be written before the first observation existed.

questions.question: In the ReAct trace for (3 + 4) × 2, how does the policy signal completion?
options: By emitting the action {"final": 14} on step 3
By calling mul a second time with b=1 to signal no change
By returning an empty dict, which the loop reads as done
By raising StopIteration from inside the policy callable
questions.explanation: The third step's action is {"final": 14}, and the loop stops, reporting finished after 3 steps with answer 14.

questions.question: What does run_react do if max_steps is less than 1?
options: It raises ValueError
It runs exactly one step
It runs until the policy finalizes
It returns answer=None immediately
questions.explanation: The guard raises ValueError(f"max_steps must be >= 1, got {max_steps}") before any loop iterations.

questions.question: How does run_react give the policy access to the task?
options: It passes the task as a separate keyword argument on every single policy call
It stores the task in a module-level global variable the policy reads
It appends the task string to every tool's arguments before each call
It seeds history with a synthetic step 0 whose observation is the task
questions.explanation: history[0] = Step(thought="task", action={"task": task}, observation=task), so the policy reads its goal from history like any other step. No special task channel is needed.

questions.question: In run_react, how does the loop detect that the policy is done?
options: The action's tool name is the reserved string "stop"
The observation returned for the step is None
The thought text contains the keyword 'done' or 'finished'
The action dict contains a "final" key
questions.explanation: If "final" in action, the loop appends the step with observation None and returns ReActResult with answer=action["final"] and finished=True.

questions.question: In run_react, what observation results when the policy names a tool not in the tools dict?
options: A KeyError that ends the episode
The string "error: unknown tool '<name>'"
None, and the step is skipped
The loop calls the first available tool instead
questions.explanation: Unknown tools produce an error string as the observation, which the policy can read and recover from next step.

questions.question: In run_react, what happens when a tool raises an exception?
options: The exception propagates out of run_react and ends the episode with a traceback
The exception is caught and the observation becomes "error: <ExceptionType>: <message>"
The loop retries the same tool call up to three times before giving up on the step
The failing step is removed from history so the policy never sees the failed call
questions.explanation: Errors become observations, not crashes, exactly like a real agent handling a failed command. A crash would end the episode; an observation allows retry.

questions.question: What is the `steps` value in a ReActResult?
options: len(history) - 1, i.e. steps excluding the synthetic task step
len(history), counting the seeded task step as the first step
The number of steps whose observation was an error string
max_steps, always, because the loop records its full step budget
questions.explanation: Because history[0] is the seeded task, the step count subtracts one.

questions.question: Why does run_react take tools as a plain dict[str, callable] instead of importing a tool module?
options: Dependency injection decouples the loop from any one tool set, so it is reusable and testable with tiny tools
Python cannot import a module from inside a function body, so the tools have to be passed in as arguments
A plain dict lookup is much faster than a registry import, which matters because tools run every single step
Tools must be redefined on every step with fresh state, so a statically imported module would go stale
questions.explanation: run_react never imports llmre.tools, so you can drive it with a calculator, filesystem, search API, or test tools. The loop does not care.

questions.question: When run_react exhausts max_steps without a final action, what does it return?
options: It raises RuntimeError with the last observation attached to the error message
The last observation as the answer, with finished=True so callers treat it as done
It restarts the loop from step 0 with max_steps doubled, up to a fixed retry limit
A ReActResult with answer=None and finished=False, a clean, testable halt
questions.explanation: Hitting the budget is a distinct outcome. Real LLM policies sometimes loop forever, so this halt is essential.

questions.question: Where would PyTorch's work happen in a ReAct agent built like run_react?
options: Inside the tools dict, whose entries hold the model's weight tensors between calls
Inside policy(history), where a transformer forward pass yields each Thought and Action
In the history list, which stores the hidden activations of every previous step
In the max_steps check, which runs a small classifier to decide when the loop stops
questions.explanation: The loop has no tensors: an agent is control flow around a policy. Swapping the scripted policy for a model changes nothing about the loop.

questions.section: 5. From a loop to a mini SWE-agent
questions.question: What is the central idea of SWE-agent (Yang et al. 2024)?
options: Coding agents only need a raw shell plus a strong model; any extra interface design is unnecessary overhead
Agents should be trained only on GitHub commit histories so they learn how real developers edit code
The Agent-Computer Interface (commands to view, edit, and run code) matters as much as the model
Test suites should be hidden from coding agents so they cannot overfit their patches to the visible tests
questions.explanation: SWE-agent shows the ACI determines coding-agent performance on real GitHub issues (SWE-bench). A narrow, well-designed interface helps the model reason.

questions.section: 5. From a loop to a mini SWE-agent
questions.question: Why does a narrow, well-designed agent-computer interface beat handing a coding agent a raw shell?
options: Raw shells are too slow for agents, since every command spawns a new process that takes seconds to start
Narrow interfaces let the model skip reading files entirely, because the edit commands infer the context
Raw shells cannot run tests, so the agent never gets pass or fail feedback on its edits without a wrapper
Every command returns a tidy observation, like a clean pass/fail from run_tests, that the model can reason about
questions.explanation: Scoped edits and clean results keep observations interpretable. Raw shell output is noisy and harder to act on.

questions.section: 5. From a loop to a mini SWE-agent
questions.question: What is the course's mini SWE-agent Workspace?
options: An in-memory dict of path -> contents, making the scaffold hermetic and testable
A Docker container with a real filesystem, reset to a clean snapshot after each task
A git repository cloned from GitHub at the commit where the target issue was filed
A tensor of file embeddings that the policy searches to decide which file to open next
questions.explanation: Keeping files in memory means tests never touch disk or network and are fully reproducible.

questions.section: 5. From a loop to a mini SWE-agent
questions.question: Which four tools does the course's mini SWE-agent give the ReAct loop?
options: read_file, write_file, run_tests, and list_files
shell, python, git, and browser, each wrapped as a tool
search, calculator, python_eval, and mock_search
open_file, edit_lines, submit_patch, and find_symbol
questions.explanation: These form the agent-computer interface over the Workspace: inspect, edit, check, and list.

questions.section: 5. From a loop to a mini SWE-agent
questions.question: In the mini SWE-agent, what does run_tests return?
options: The full pytest stdout, including tracebacks for every failure
A bare boolean, True if all tests passed, False otherwise
"PASS: ..." or "FAIL: ..." derived from an injected checker
The number of lines changed since the previous test run
questions.explanation: run_tests formats the injected test_runner's result as a clean PASS/FAIL observation the policy can act on.

questions.section: 5. From a loop to a mini SWE-agent
questions.question: What is solve(policy, workspace, task, test_runner) in the mini SWE-agent?
options: A separate agent loop with its own error handling and step budget
A fine-tuning routine that trains the policy on its successful fixes
Just run_react with file-oriented tools built by make_tools
A planner that writes all of its edits before running any tests
questions.explanation: solve builds the ACI with make_tools(workspace, test_runner) and calls run_react. The same loop becomes a coding agent once its tools are file-oriented.

questions.section: 5. From a loop to a mini SWE-agent
questions.question: What cycle makes the mini SWE-agent an agent rather than a one-shot code generator?
options: read_file (inspect) → write_file (edit) → run_tests (observe) → decide → retry if it failed
Generate the complete patch once from the task description, write it, then stop without testing
Run the tests first, then delete any failing tests from the workspace so the suite reports PASS
List the files repeatedly until one of them changes, then read that file and return its contents
questions.explanation: Inspect-act-observe-correct with retry on failure is the agentic part. A one-shot generator never sees test feedback.

questions.section: 5. From a loop to a mini SWE-agent
questions.question: Why does the course's mini SWE-agent only fix the specific bug its script targets?
options: Because write_file can modify only one file per episode, so multi-file fixes are impossible
Because run_tests checks only one test, so the agent cannot see failures in other parts of the code
Because the Workspace forbids creating new files, so only edits to existing files are possible
Its policy is scripted; a real SWE-agent's LLM policy decides which file to open and what to edit
questions.explanation: The scaffold teaches the interface and loop, not the model. Everything hard about SWE-agent lives in the missing LLM policy.

questions.question: What hardware does the course's ReAct and mini SWE-agent scaffold require?
options: None special: it runs on CPU in well under a second, with no tensors or GPU
A single A100 to run the policy model's forward pass at each loop step
At least 16 GB of GPU memory to hold the history of every step's activations
A multi-node cluster so the four workspace tools can execute in parallel
questions.explanation: The only compute is Python control flow. A real agent's cost is in LLM policy calls, which the scaffold factors out.

questions.question: Where does nearly all the cost of a real LLM agent come from?
options: The Python loop's control flow, which dominates once there are many steps
Appending steps to the history list, which copies the full trace each time
Formatting error strings and observations so the policy can parse them
The LLM policy calls: API latency or GPU inference
questions.explanation: Control flow is negligible. Each policy call is a full model generation.

questions.question: Why do the agent tests in code/tests/test_agents.py define their own add, mul, and noop tools instead of importing llmre.tools?
options: Because llmre.tools has no arithmetic tools, only file and search tools for the SWE scaffold
It shows the decoupling that lets the agents module be built and tested apart from the tools module
Because pytest disallows importing project modules inside a test file that also defines fixtures
Because locally defined tools are compiled and run on the GPU, which makes the test suite faster
questions.explanation: Because run_react takes tools by injection, the tests can use tiny local tools and need nothing from Module 18.

questions.question: Which behaviors do the course's agent tests check?
options: Model accuracy on SWE-bench Verified, per-step latency, and peak GPU memory use during a full agent run on real repositories
Only that every module in llmre.agents imports cleanly without error and exposes each of the documented public functions
The scripted policy solves the arithmetic task in ≤ 3 steps, the loop halts at max_steps, and the SWE scaffold fixes a toy file
That the LLM policy produces identical thoughts across random seeds, so that every agent trace is fully reproducible in CI
questions.explanation: The tests verify the loop mechanics: solving, halting on the budget, and the coding scaffold's fix.

questions.question: With injected sub, add, and mul tools, what is the minimum number of ReAct steps to compute (10 − 3) × (2 + 5)?
options: One step, since the policy can write the whole expression in one call
Two tool-call steps plus a final step, since mul can nest the add call
Three tool-call steps plus a final step
Five steps, one per number, then the operations
questions.explanation: There are three binary operations, each tool returns one value, and mul needs both earlier results. So sub, add, mul, then {"final": 49}.

questions.question: In a scripted ReAct policy computing (10 − 3) × (2 + 5), how does the mul step get the subtraction result?
options: It recomputes 10 − 3 inside the policy without calling a tool
It reads a global variable that the sub tool sets as a side effect
It reaches back into history, e.g. history[1].observation
The mul tool caches previous tool calls and looks up the result
questions.explanation: The running trace is the agent's memory, so earlier observations can be retrieved from history.

questions.question: Why must a ReAct loop treat 'hit the step budget' as a distinct reported outcome rather than success?
options: Because hitting the budget always means a tool crashed and the loop could not recover from the error
It means the policy failed to finish, e.g. looping on the same call, not that the task was solved
Because the last observation at the budget is always the correct answer and must be reported specially
Because the budget is only ever reached on success, when the policy has run every step it planned
questions.explanation: LLM policies sometimes loop forever. Reporting the budget halt separately avoids mistaking non-termination for a result.

questions.question: What is the problem with importing the tool registry into run_react?
options: It makes the loop slower, because the tool module gets loaded twice: once at import and again per call
It causes a circular import in every case, since the tools module itself imports run_react to register
It couples the loop to one tool set, so it can't be tested in isolation or reused with another interface
It prevents the loop from catching tool exceptions, because imported functions raise outside its try block
questions.explanation: Injection keeps the loop generic. Importing tools hard-wires one interface.

questions.question: What is the mistake in 'confusing the scaffold with an agent'?
options: Scaffolds are much slower than agents because they replay every scripted step from the beginning
A deterministic policy is a test harness, not intelligence; the hard part is the LLM that decides
Scaffolds cannot use tools at all, so they only simulate what a real agent's tool calls would return
Agents do not need loops, so any code with a loop is a scaffold rather than a real agent by definition
questions.explanation: The scripted scaffold proves the plumbing works. It doesn't solve unseen tasks.

questions.question: A ReAct policy calls tool 'add' but then checks last.action.get("tool") == "sum" before finalizing. What happens?
options: The loop raises a KeyError on 'sum', since no tool by that name is in the tools dict, and the episode crashes
The check is never true, so the policy keeps calling add(0, 0) and the loop halts at max_steps with answer=None
The policy finalizes after the first add, because get returns None and the comparison falls through to final
The loop finalizes on step 2 with answer 0, because the unknown-tool error string is converted to a zero
questions.explanation: The name mismatch means the final branch is unreachable. Fix by comparing against "add".

questions.question: When a ReAct agent never finalizes, what is the general cause?
options: A tool that returns the wrong type, such as a string where the policy expects an integer result
A max_steps value that is too large, which keeps the loop running long after the answer is known
Almost always a policy that never recognizes the history state in which it should stop
A history list that is truncated too aggressively, so the policy forgets the task before finishing
questions.explanation: The policy branches on history; if no branch matches the stopping state, it never emits final.

questions.question: In the course's run_react, what is appended to history each iteration?
options: Only the observation, since that is the part fed back for the next step
Only the action, so the history is a replayable list of tool calls
The whole Step (thought, action, observation); the policy gets the full history
Nothing; history holds just the task, and the policy reads only the latest step
questions.explanation: The Observation is the part fed back for the next Thought and Action, but the implementation appends the entire Step.

questions.question: Besides testability and reuse, what other benefit does injecting tools into run_react give?
options: It lets tools share one GPU, since injected callables run in the policy's process
It avoids a build-order dependency between modules written in parallel
It encrypts tool arguments in transit, since injected tools never touch disk
It speeds up the policy, because tool lookups are cached between loop steps
questions.explanation: Since the loop doesn't import the tools module, the agents and tools modules can be developed independently.

questions.question: In the mini SWE-agent, what is the signature and role of the injected test_runner?
options: test_runner() -> int, counting the files in the workspace that changed since the episode began
test_runner(policy) -> str, grading the quality of the policy's thoughts with a short written verdict
test_runner(path) -> str, reading one file from the workspace and returning its contents for the policy
test_runner(workspace) -> (passed: bool, message: str), deciding what passing means for the task
questions.explanation: It is injected so the scaffold never hard-codes correctness; each task supplies its checker, like different repos have different test suites. run_tests formats its result as PASS/FAIL.

questions.question: After building agents, what does the course name as the final piece of the research-engineer toolkit?
options: Designing experiments, measuring honestly across seeds, and writing up findings reproducibly
Writing custom CUDA and Triton kernels for every agent tool so that policy calls run faster
Training a larger tokenizer on agent traces so that tool calls compress into fewer tokens
Deploying agents to production clusters with autoscaling, monitoring, and on-call rotations
questions.explanation: The last piece isn't code: it is experiment design, multi-seed measurement, and trustworthy write-ups.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: What is described as a research engineer's real output?
options: Trustworthy knowledge: whether change X helps, by how much, and how sure we are
The largest model checkpoint the compute budget allows, released with its weights
The fastest training code, measured as tokens per second per GPU on the cluster
The highest single benchmark score, reported against the previous state of the art
questions.explanation: Code and checkpoints are means; the output is reliable answers about what works. That requires experimental rigor.

questions.section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
questions.question: Where do most wrong conclusions in ML experiments come from?
options: Bad experimental hygiene (one seed, a moving baseline, a drifting metric) rather than bad models
Insufficient GPU memory, which forces smaller batches and silently changes the optimization dynamics
Using too many seeds, which averages away real effects until every comparison looks like a tie
Choosing the wrong framework or programming language, which introduces numerical differences
questions.explanation: Poor experimental practice produces false beliefs even with good models. Fixing hygiene separates real progress from fooling yourself.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: an experiment is a question with a fair test
questions.question: What turns an idea like 'RMSNorm will train better than LayerNorm' into an experiment?
options: Running the idea once at full scale and observing whether the loss goes down
Finding a published paper whose results agree with the idea at a similar scale
A specific falsifiable question plus a fair test that could return 'no'
Training the largest feasible model with RMSNorm and reporting its final loss
questions.explanation: An experiment must be able to fail. The discipline is making the test fair so any difference is caused by the change and exceeds noise.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: an experiment is a question with a fair test
questions.question: In ML experiments, what is confounding?
options: Running too few training steps, so the two variants have not yet separated in loss
Using a validation set that is so large that it hides real differences between the variants
Reporting the two variants' results in different units, such as nats for one and bits for the other
Changing two things at once (e.g. norm and LR) so the effect can't be attributed to either
questions.explanation: With two simultaneous changes, any improvement has two possible causes. You can't conclude anything about either alone.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: an experiment is a question with a fair test
questions.question: In ML experiments, what is the 'noise' failure mode?
options: The observed difference is smaller than seed-to-seed variation, so it means nothing
The training data contains mislabeled examples that add noise to every gradient step
The evaluation set is so small that per-batch metrics fluctuate from step to step
The loss curve has visible spikes, which are averaged out before reporting the result
questions.explanation: If seed-to-seed variation is larger than the gap, the gap can't be distinguished from chance.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: an experiment is a question with a fair test
questions.question: What is the 'moving target' failure mode in ML experiments?
options: The model's learning rate decays during training, so late steps chase a different optimum
The target labels are reshuffled every epoch, so the model never sees one stable training objective
The model's predictions change with sampling temperature, so the metric depends on decoding
The baseline, data split, or metric changed between runs, so the comparison isn't like-for-like
questions.explanation: Comparing a new variant against a baseline run under different conditions measures the conditions, not the change.

questions.section: 1. Intuition: an experiment is a question with a fair test
questions.question: What does a clean experiment change and report?
options: Several variables at once to save compute, reported as one combined improvement
One variable, reported from a single seed so that the comparison stays cheap
Every hyperparameter in turn, reporting only those changes that improve the main metric
One variable against a fixed baseline, with enough replication to tell signal from noise
questions.explanation: One falsifiable question, one changed variable, a fixed baseline, and replication. Changing two things gives a story, not an experiment.

questions.section: 2. The vocabulary of a clean experiment
questions.question: What makes a hypothesis useful in an ML experiment?
options: It states what you expect and the mechanism why, before you look at results
It is written after the results come in, so that it explains what was observed
It predicts only that the model will improve, leaving the size of the effect open
It names the paper the idea came from, so the claim inherits that paper's evidence
questions.explanation: A hypothesis with a mechanism, stated in advance, is falsifiable in a useful way. For RMSNorm: removing mean-centering is cheap and likely harmless, so expect equal or slightly better loss at lower cost.

questions.section: 2. The vocabulary of a clean experiment
questions.question: Why is 'validation loss 3.1' meaningless without a baseline?
options: Because loss must always be converted to perplexity before it can be interpreted at all
Because 3.1 nats is above the theoretical maximum loss for a typical BPE vocabulary
A number is neither good nor bad until you know what the unmodified system scores
Because validation loss is never comparable across runs that use different random seeds
questions.explanation: The baseline is the reference run under identical conditions. Only the comparison gives a number meaning.

questions.section: 2. The vocabulary of a clean experiment
questions.question: In an experiment comparing RMSNorm and LayerNorm, what is the independent variable?
options: The norm layer, the one thing deliberately changed
The validation loss measured at the end of training
The set of random seeds used for both configurations
The learning-rate schedule shared by the two runs
questions.explanation: The independent variable is what you change. Loss is the outcome; seeds and schedule are controls.

questions.section: 2. The vocabulary of a clean experiment
questions.question: What are controls in an ML experiment?
options: Extra variables changed alongside the main one to test whether the result is robust
Everything deliberately held fixed: data, tokens, steps, batch size, LR schedule, seeds, hardware
Secondary metrics measured in addition to the main metric, such as throughput, memory, and latency
Runs that are discarded before analysis if they underperform the baseline by a set margin
questions.explanation: Controls make the comparison fair by ensuring only the independent variable differs.

questions.section: 2. The vocabulary of a clean experiment
questions.question: What is an ablation study?
options: Training a model with every component enabled at once to establish the best achievable score
Pruning low-magnitude weights from a trained model to reduce its size before deployment
Removing or swapping one component at a time to measure that component's contribution
Evaluating a single model on many benchmarks at once to see where it is strongest
questions.explanation: An ablation is a series of one-change experiments, e.g. 'removing C costs 0.4 loss, removing D costs nothing'. 'The model works' alone is not science.

questions.section: 2. The vocabulary of a clean experiment
questions.question: What is the cardinal sin of experiment design?
options: Running more than three seeds per config
Changing more than one variable per run
Using a fixed learning-rate schedule for all runs
Reporting negative or null results
questions.explanation: If you swap the norm and bump the LR and loss improves, you've learned nothing about the norm. Every confound is a conclusion you can't draw.

questions.question: Which sources of randomness make re-running the same training config with a different seed give a different final loss?
options: Only the tokenizer's merge order, which changes with the seed and shifts token boundaries
Only the learning-rate warmup length, which the trainer re-samples from the seed each run
Weight initialization, data shuffling, and some nondeterministic GPU kernels
Only the evaluation batch size, which changes padding and therefore the reported loss
questions.explanation: Training is stochastic, so one run is a sample of size one from a distribution whose width you don't know.

questions.question: Why is a single-seed result untrustworthy?
options: It is one sample from a distribution of outcomes, with no information about its width
Seed 0 is known to give systematically worse results than other seeds in most frameworks
A single run cannot be evaluated on validation data without leaking into its training set
GPUs need at least two runs to warm their caches, so the first run's loss is always inflated
questions.explanation: Without replication you can't tell whether a difference exceeds run-to-run variance.

questions.question: In the sample standard deviation formula for seed results, why divide by n − 1 instead of n?
options: Because one seed is always discarded as an outlier before the spread is computed
Because n − 1 makes the standard deviation smaller, so the results look more consistent
Because the first run is treated as warmup and excluded from the sum of squared deviations
Bessel's correction: deviations from the sample mean run too small; n − 1 removes the bias
questions.explanation: The sample mean is computed from the same data, so deviations from it underestimate spread. Dividing by n − 1 corrects this, which matters most at tiny n — the seed-count regime.

questions.question: What does the sample standard deviation s of seed results measure?
options: How much a single run bounces around
How well the true mean is known
The difference between two configs
The model's training loss
questions.explanation: s describes run-to-run variation. Uncertainty about the mean is captured by the standard error s/√n and the confidence interval.

questions.question: What is the formula for a confidence interval for the mean of n seed results?
options: $\bar{x} \pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1} \cdot s$
$\bar{x} \pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1} \cdot s/\sqrt{n}$
$\bar{x} \pm 1.96 \cdot s/\sqrt{n-1}$
$\bar{x} \pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n} \cdot s \cdot \sqrt{n}$
questions.explanation: The interval uses the Student-t critical value at n − 1 degrees of freedom times the standard error s/√n. It is the range that plausibly contains the true mean at the stated confidence.

questions.question: Why use the Student-t critical value rather than the normal for a seed-result confidence interval?
options: n is tiny and s is estimated from the same sample, so the distribution has fatter tails
Because the t-distribution is narrower than the normal and so gives tighter intervals
Because the normal distribution assigns probability to negative values of the loss
Because the t-distribution ignores the sample standard deviation and uses n alone
questions.explanation: With few seeds, uncertainty in s widens the distribution of the mean. The t-distribution accounts for this and converges to the normal as n grows.

questions.question: What is the standard error of the mean, and why do more seeds tighten the confidence interval?
options: s·n; it grows with more seeds, since total variance accumulates
s/n²; it shrinks quadratically as seeds are added to the run set
s alone; adding seeds refines the mean but does not change the interval
s/√n; it shrinks like √n as seeds are added
questions.explanation: The standard error measures uncertainty in the mean, not single runs. Doubling precision needs four times as many seeds.

questions.question: What does it mean if the confidence intervals of two configs overlap?
options: The config with the higher mean is definitely better, just by a small margin
The two are not distinguishable at that confidence; the difference is within noise
The experiment contains a bug, since well-run configs always have separated intervals
Both configs are equally good with certainty, so the true effect is exactly zero
questions.explanation: Overlap means the data are consistent with no true difference. You can't claim one is better.

questions.question: In the 3-seed example, baseline A scored 72.6 and variant B 71.4 on seed 0, but means were 71.13 vs 72.00. What does this show?
options: Seed 0 should always be the one used for reporting results
Means over seeds are less reliable than any single seed alone
A single-seed conclusion can point to the wrong winner
Variant B is definitely better, since its mean is higher
questions.explanation: Seed 0 said A wins by 1.2, but the 3-seed mean says B wins by 0.87. One seed pointed the wrong way.

questions.question: Configs A and B have 95% CIs (67.89, 74.38) and (70.03, 73.97), with means 71.13 and 72.00. What is the honest conclusion?
options: B is better by 0.87 points, since its mean is higher and its interval narrower
No detectable difference at 3 seeds; run more seeds if 0.87 points matters
A is better, because its wider interval reaches higher values than B's does
The experiment proves the variant has no effect, since the intervals overlap
questions.explanation: The intervals overlap almost entirely, so the gap is within noise. Saying 'B is better (72.0 vs 71.1)' without the spread would be false. Overlap also doesn't prove zero effect — only that none was detected.

questions.question: What is the reporting rule for training results across seeds?
options: Report the best seed's number as the result, since it shows what the config is capable of
Report mean ± std over ≥ 3 seeds plus a CI; claim a difference only when intervals separate
Report the median of two seeds, which is robust to one outlier run and halves the compute needed
Report a single seed but trained for more steps, so the final loss has converged
questions.explanation: Never report a single-seed number as a result. A result you can't reproduce across seeds isn't a result.

questions.question: For a 95% CI with 3 seeds (2 degrees of freedom), what Student-t critical value is used?
questions.explanation: t_{0.975, 2} = 4.303, much larger than the normal 1.96. (3.182 is the value for 3 degrees of freedom.)

questions.question: What does mean_std in llmre.agents.stats return for a single value?
options: The value and a standard deviation of 0.0
The value and NaN for the standard deviation
It raises ValueError, since ddof=1 needs two values
The value and the value itself as the std
questions.explanation: mean_std uses ddof=1 and returns 0.0 std for a single value rather than failing.

questions.question: What does confidence_interval in llmre.agents.stats return for a single value, and why?
options: (-inf, inf), since a single run implies infinite uncertainty about the mean
(0, 1), the default range used when no spread can be estimated
It returns the normal-approximation interval using z = 1.96
(mean, mean): a signal that one seed carries no uncertainty estimate
questions.explanation: Collapsing to a point makes clear that a single run provides no estimate of spread.

questions.question: How does llmre.agents.stats compute t critical values without SciPy?
options: By downloading critical values from a statistics site on first use
By Monte Carlo simulation of the t-distribution at each call
With a small built-in t-table plus a normal fallback
By always using the normal critical value 1.96 regardless of n
questions.explanation: The module embeds a t-table for common degrees of freedom and falls back to the normal for large n.

questions.question: With 3 seeds, what goes wrong if you use the normal z = 1.96 instead of t = 4.303 for a 95% CI?
options: The interval is less than half as wide as it should be, making you overconfident
The interval becomes too wide, hiding real differences between the two configs
The interval is identical, because the critical value doesn't depend on n
The mean itself shifts by 1.96 units, so the interval is centered on the wrong value
questions.explanation: The t-distribution's fatter tails at 2 degrees of freedom require a much larger multiplier. Using z understates uncertainty.

questions.question: Which checkpoint should be reported from a training run?
options: Always the last checkpoint, since it saw the most training tokens
The one that scores best on the test set, since that is the reported metric
The first checkpoint after warmup, before any overfitting can begin
The best on validation, ideally confirmed once on a held-out test set
questions.explanation: Select on validation, confirm on a test set touched once. Choosing by test score overfits to the test set.

questions.question: Why is picking the checkpoint that looks best on the test set a problem?
options: Test sets are always smaller than validation sets, so their scores are too noisy
Test-set metrics are computed in lower precision, which biases the selection
It is a subtle form of overfitting to the test set, which is then contaminated
It makes training slower, since every checkpoint must be scored on the test set
questions.explanation: Using the test set for selection biases the reported number upward. The test set must be used only once for reporting.

questions.question: Why is the best result from a hyperparameter sweep optimistically biased?
options: Sweeps always favor larger learning rates, which inflate early loss improvements
Taking the max over several noisy runs means the winner is partly luck
Sweeps are run on the test set by convention, so the best run is contaminated
The best run always trains for more steps than the others in a standard sweep
questions.explanation: Selecting the best of many noisy outcomes overstates true performance. Re-run the chosen setting with fresh seeds before believing it.

questions.question: On which data split should a hyperparameter sweep be evaluated?
options: The test set
The validation set
The training set
Whichever split gives the best number
questions.explanation: Sweeping on validation keeps the test set clean for a one-time final report.

questions.question: For an ML training run to be reproducible from its experiment-tracking record, what must be recorded?
options: Only the final metric and the model name, since the rest can be inferred from the code
Only the config file, because the config fully determines everything about the run
The exact config, code commit hash, data version, seed, and resulting metrics
The GPU temperature, driver version, and wall-clock runtime of each training job
questions.explanation: A run you can't reproduce is one you can't cite. The report template therefore demands commit and config.

questions.section: 5. Failure analysis, reproduction, and negative results
questions.question: When a training run underperforms, what does failure analysis do instead of tweaking and rerunning?
options: Immediately launch a larger hyperparameter sweep centered on the current best settings
Discard the run and change the seed until a run reaches the expected metric
Increase the model size step by step until the target metric improves enough
Look at the failures: which examples are wrong, and whether loss spikes or plateaus
questions.explanation: A histogram of per-example losses or reading some wrong outputs teaches more than another sweep. Most learning happens here.

questions.section: 5. Failure analysis, reproduction, and negative results
questions.question: In failure analysis, what does a spiking loss curve typically suggest versus a plateauing one?
options: Spiking suggests too much capacity; plateauing suggests too high a learning rate
Both always indicate a bug in the evaluation code rather than a problem in training itself
Spiking suggests overfitting; plateauing suggests the model has fully converged
Spiking suggests a data or LR problem; plateauing suggests a capacity or data problem
questions.explanation: Spikes point to instability from bad data or too-high LR; plateaus point to limited capacity or data.

questions.section: 5. Failure analysis, reproduction, and negative results
questions.question: Why does paper reproduction usually fail the first time, and why is that useful?
options: Published numbers are usually inflated or fabricated, so a gap is expected and uninformative
It surfaces undocumented details (preprocessing, tokenizer, exact schedule) that matter
Reproductions must use different data for licensing reasons, so numbers rarely match
Papers deliberately hide their model sizes, so the reproduction trains the wrong model
questions.explanation: Matching a published number under stated conditions exposes hidden choices. Treat reproduction like any experiment, with baseline, controls, seeds, and a report.

questions.section: 5. Failure analysis, reproduction, and negative results
questions.question: Why are negative results valuable in ML research?
options: They are not valuable and should be discarded, since only improvements advance a field
They are real knowledge that saves others effort; reporting only wins breeds false beliefs
They are valuable only when the confidence intervals are wide enough to include zero
They are useful only as baselines for future runs and are not worth writing up as findings
questions.explanation: 'RMSNorm did not help at this scale' is publishable knowledge. A clean null with tight intervals is far more valuable than a noisy win.

questions.question: Why does a fixed experiment-report template enforce scientific discipline?
options: It makes reports shorter, so reviewers can skim many experiments quickly
It automates the training runs, so every experiment uses identical scripts
It forces you to state the question before the answer and the limitations with the conclusion
It hides negative results from reviewers, so that only the promising directions get attention
questions.explanation: The structure is the discipline: question first, limitations next to conclusions.

questions.question: In the experiment-report template, what goes in the VARIABLES section?
options: Every hyperparameter tried in the sweep and its range
The one independent variable and the controls held fixed
The numerical results for each seed and each config
The follow-up experiments planned after this report
questions.explanation: VARIABLES names what changed and what was held fixed. Results go in RESULTS.

questions.question: In the experiment-report template, how must RESULTS be reported?
options: As the best seed's value, with the other seeds noted
As a qualitative description of how the runs behaved
As mean ± std over N seeds, with a confidence interval
As the last checkpoint's training loss for each config
questions.explanation: Replicated statistics with intervals are required so readers can judge signal versus noise.

questions.question: In the experiment-report template, what belongs in the LIMITATIONS section?
options: The hardware cost and total GPU-hours the experiment consumed
A list of related papers that tested similar ideas at other scales
The hypothesis restated in other words, together with its mechanism
What it does not show: confounds, untested scales, unmeasured metrics
questions.explanation: Stating limitations alongside conclusions prevents overclaiming.

questions.question: In the experiment-report template, what is the CONCLUSION section?
options: A summary of all prior work on the question, with citations and dates
The next experiment to run, with its expected outcome and cost
The one-line answer to the QUESTION, qualified by analysis and limitations
The raw metrics table for every seed and every configuration that was run
questions.explanation: The conclusion answers the question directly while respecting what the analysis and limitations allow. NEXT EXPERIMENT is a separate section.

questions.question: In the experiment-report template, what does the ANALYSIS section address?
options: How the model was implemented, including any custom kernels
What the numbers mean, especially whether the gap exceeds seed noise
Which GPUs were used and how long each training run took
The original motivation for the project and its research context
questions.explanation: ANALYSIS interprets RESULTS, checking whether the observed gap exceeds run-to-run variation.

questions.question: In the experiment-report template, what does the METHOD section require?
options: A one-sentence summary of the idea being tested and its motivation
Exactly what was done (model, data, tokens, steps, hardware), enough to reproduce
Only the final metric for each config, since the code captures everything else
The hypothesis and its mechanism, stated before any results were seen
questions.explanation: METHOD must allow reproduction. The hypothesis has its own section.

questions.question: Why must QUESTION and HYPOTHESIS be written before running an experiment?
options: Because the template file locks itself after the first training run is logged
Because the results sections are written automatically by the tracking tool
Because reviewers read only the first two sections, so those must be finished before anything else
To prevent HARKing: back-fitting a question to results turns noise into a fake discovery
questions.explanation: Looking at data first always reveals some pattern, which can be dressed up as a prediction. Committing in advance keeps the test honest and gives negative results meaning.

questions.question: Why does a fair 3-seed comparison of two configs multiply compute cost?
options: Because computing the statistics requires a dedicated GPU for each seed
Because each seed must train three times longer to reach the same final loss
It means running training six times; replication multiplies compute by the seed count
Because confidence intervals need a separate held-out evaluation model for every config
questions.explanation: The statistics are CPU-only and instant; the training runs are not. Fix the seed count and sweep grid up front rather than re-running ad hoc.

questions.question: Config A over 5 seeds has 95% CI ≈ (3.088, 3.136) and variant B has ≈ (3.040, 3.080) for validation loss. Can you claim B is better?
options: Yes; B's entire interval sits below A's, so they do not overlap
No; intervals estimated from only 5 seeds are never trustworthy
No; a difference of 0.05 nats is too small to ever be significant
Yes, but only because B's mean validation loss is lower than A's
questions.explanation: The intervals don't overlap, so the ~0.05-nat improvement exceeds seed noise at 95% confidence. A lower mean alone would not be sufficient.

questions.question: Why can a 0.05-nat gap be significant while a 0.87-point gap is not?
options: Significance depends on both the gap and the spread; consistent seeds give tight intervals
Loss gaps are always more significant than accuracy gaps, because loss is a continuous metric
Smaller gaps are always more significant, because they are less likely to be produced by chance
More decimal places make a result more significant, since precision reduces the standard error
questions.explanation: With std ≈ 0.017, intervals are narrow and separate; with std ≈ 1.0, they overlap. You must compute both gap and spread.

questions.question: What is a 'moving baseline' in ML experiments?
options: A baseline whose learning rate changes during training, so its loss target keeps moving over time
A baseline trained on a different random seed from the variant it is compared against
Comparing a variant to a baseline run on an older data split or code, not identical conditions
A baseline that keeps improving over time because it is fine-tuned between comparisons
questions.explanation: Baseline and variant must run under identical conditions. Otherwise the comparison measures the drift.

questions.question: What is the mistake of 'writing the conclusion first'?
options: Writing the conclusion section at the top of the report instead of at the end
Stating the hypothesis and expected effect before running the experiment
Deciding the answer, then choosing the metric, seeds, or checkpoint that supports it
Summarizing the results in one line instead of a full table of every seed
questions.explanation: Fix the protocol before looking at results. Otherwise choices get tuned to confirm a preconceived answer.

questions.question: A colleague claims variant B improves accuracy from 71.1% to 72.0% based on run_training(config, seed=0) for each config. What is wrong?
options: The accuracy values are too close to 100% for a 0.9-point gap to be measurable
Seed 0 is reserved for testing and cannot be used for final comparisons
The two configs should have used different seeds so the runs are independent
Each number is a single seed, so the 0.9-point gap could be entirely seed noise
questions.explanation: One seed per config gives no variance estimate. Run several seeds per config and compare confidence intervals; claim B is better only if its interval sits clearly above A's.

questions.question: Why report a confidence interval for the mean rather than just mean ± std when comparing configs?
options: Because std cannot be computed reliably with fewer than ten seeds per config, so it must be replaced
± std is single-run spread; the CI says how well the true mean is known, i.e. if the gap could be zero
Because CIs are always narrower than ± std, so the comparison between configs looks much cleaner
Because std depends on the learning rate and batch size, while the CI is independent of both
questions.explanation: The CI uses the standard error s/√n and the t critical value. It addresses the comparison question directly.

questions.question: A learning-rate sweep's best run scored 3.05. How should the config's performance be reported?
options: Report 3.05 directly, since it is the best value observed for the config
Report the average over all sweep runs, including the poor learning rates
Re-run the chosen learning rate with fresh seeds and report that mean ± CI
Report the worst sweep run, so that the reported number is conservative
questions.explanation: The sweep chooses the setting; an independent replication estimates its performance. The best-of-sweep number is optimistically biased.

questions.question: What does the capstone after the experiment-design lesson require for every claim?
options: That it be backed by an experiment report
That it be backed by a single benchmark score
That it match a published paper exactly
That it be verified by a ReAct agent
questions.explanation: The capstone designs, trains, evaluates, and writes up a mini frontier LLM, with experiment reports supporting each claim.

questions.question: In the 'Mini Frontier LLM' capstone of an LLM research engineer course, what is a research engineer said to be judged on?
options: The size of the largest model they have personally pretrained end to end
Mastery of a single component, such as attention kernels or tokenizers
How many production frameworks they can configure without reading the code
Making the whole pipeline run, produce a number, and be reproduced
questions.explanation: The capstone frames the job as end-to-end: make the whole pipeline run, get a reproducible number out of it, and let others reproduce it. Knowing one component in depth is not enough if the pieces can't be wired together. Model size and framework familiarity are not the criteria.

questions.question: What sequence of artifacts does the 'Mini Frontier LLM' capstone pipeline produce, starting from raw text?
options: GPT, tokenizer, pretrained model, preference-aligned model, evaluation number, instruction-tuned model, reasoning policy
Tokenizer, GPT, pretrained model, eval number, instruction-tuned model, preference-aligned model, RLVR reasoning policy
Tokenizer, reward model, pretrained model, reasoning policy, instruction-tuned model, evaluation number, aligned model
Pretrained model, tokenizer, instruction-tuned model, evaluation number, GPT, preference-aligned model, reasoning policy
questions.explanation: The order follows the data dependencies: you need a tokenizer before a GPT can see ids, a pretrained model before you can evaluate or fine-tune it, SFT before preference alignment, and the RLVR reasoning stage on top. Each module solves a problem created by the one before it. The scrambled orders break those dependencies (e.g. a GPT cannot be built before its vocabulary is fixed).

questions.question: On what hardware is the tiny end-to-end version of the 'Mini Frontier LLM' capstone designed to run?
options: A free cloud TPU, in about ten minutes
An 8-GPU node, in roughly a day
A single A100 GPU, in about an hour
A laptop CPU, in roughly 20 seconds
questions.explanation: The driver code/scripts/capstone.py runs a tiny version of the pipeline on CPU in under about 20 seconds with less than 1 GB of RAM and 0 GPU-hours. The point is to see every stage work on hardware you already own; the GPU-scale numbers are for scaling each stage up later.

questions.question: In the capstone pipeline diagram, which stage feeds the held-out perplexity measurement?
options: The evaluation harness, applied to the pretrained model
The DPO stage, applied to the chosen/rejected preference pairs
The GRPO stage, applied to the verifiable arithmetic rewards
The BPE tokenizer, applied to the raw held-out corpus
questions.explanation: Held-out perplexity comes from the evaluation harness run on the model coming out of the pretraining loop. It is the pretraining metric. DPO and GRPO are later post-training stages, and the tokenizer only produces ids; none of them yields perplexity.

questions.question: Which optimizer setup does the capstone's pretraining loop use?
options: SGD with Nesterov momentum and a step-decay learning-rate schedule
AdamW with a cosine learning-rate schedule and gradient clipping
Lion with linear warmup, EMA weight averaging, and no clipping
Adafactor with a constant learning rate and no gradient clipping
questions.explanation: The pipeline diagram labels the pretraining loop 'AdamW + cosine LR + clip': a cosine-warmup learning rate, AdamW steps, and global gradient-norm clipping. These are the components built in the optimization modules (llmre.optim.adamw, schedule, clip). The other optimizers are not part of the llmre pretraining loop.

questions.question: In the capstone pipeline, what comes after SFT on the path to alignment?
options: LoRA, then preference data, then DPO or reward-model-plus-PPO
Perplexity evaluation, then MinHash deduplication of the SFT data
Tokenizer retraining on chat data, then pretraining from scratch
Tool use, then new BPE merges, then ablations on the merged vocab
questions.explanation: After response-masked SFT, the pipeline adds LoRA for cheap fine-tuning, then preference data, then either DPO or the classic reward-model + PPO route. Only after that comes GRPO + RLVR, reasoning, tool use and agents. Retraining the tokenizer or re-pretraining are not post-SFT steps.

questions.question: What is the final deliverable at the bottom of the capstone pipeline diagram?
options: A deployed chat endpoint serving the model
A leaderboard submission on a public benchmark
A merged LoRA checkpoint uploaded to a model hub
Ablations leading to a written experiment report
questions.explanation: The diagram ends with 'ablations -> a written experiment report'. The course stresses that the deliverable is not the model itself but a report a colleague can reproduce. Deployment, leaderboards and checkpoint uploads are not part of the capstone pipeline.

questions.question: Where does the code for the 'Mini Frontier LLM' capstone live?
options: In a set of independent notebooks, one per module, with no shared package between them
In one coherent package under code/src/llmre/, built up across earlier modules
Inside Hugging Face Transformers, configured entirely through YAML files
In a fresh standalone repository written from scratch only for the capstone
questions.explanation: The whole codebase is one package, llmre, under code/src/llmre/. The capstone is a guided tour of that package as a project, not new code written from scratch. It does not rely on HF Transformers or disconnected notebooks.

questions.question: Which script runs the tiny end-to-end capstone pipeline and writes a filled-in experiment report?
options: code/scripts/bench_attention.py
code/experiments/scaling_sweep.py
code/tests/test_capstone.py
code/scripts/capstone.py
questions.explanation: code/scripts/capstone.py is the driver: it runs a tiny version of the stages on CPU and writes code/reports/capstone_report.md. scaling_sweep.py is the scaling/ablation experiment, bench_attention.py benchmarks attention, and test_capstone.py is the smoke test that asserts the learning signals.

questions.question: What is the main point of the capstone, given that it is built from code written in Modules 0-19?
options: To see the existing code work end to end and know how each stage scales
To replace the earlier from-scratch modules with optimized kernels
To rewrite every component from scratch with production frameworks
To introduce a new architecture not covered in earlier modules
questions.explanation: The capstone is explicitly not new code you must write from scratch; it assembles what you already wrote and runs it as one pipeline. The goal is to watch it work end to end and understand how each stage scales up. It does not replace or rewrite the earlier modules.

questions.question: In byte-level BPE training, what is the starting vocabulary before any merges?
options: The 26 lowercase letters plus punctuation
The 50,257 tokens of the GPT-2 vocabulary
All Unicode code points that appear in the corpus
The 256 raw byte values
questions.explanation: Byte-level BPE starts from the 256 possible byte values and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new id. Because any string is a sequence of bytes, nothing is ever out-of-vocabulary. Starting from Unicode code points or letters would leave unseen characters unrepresentable.

questions.question: Why is nothing ever out-of-vocabulary for a byte-level BPE tokenizer?
options: Unknown words are mapped to a special <unk> token that is added during BPE training
Every string is a sequence of bytes, and all 256 byte values are in the base vocab
Rare characters are dropped before encoding, so only symbols seen in training remain
The tokenizer retrains its merges on any new text it sees at encode time
questions.explanation: Since the base vocabulary contains all 256 bytes, any input can always fall back to single-byte tokens. That is also why decode(encode(s)) == s holds exactly. An <unk> token or dropping characters would break that round-trip, and BPE does not retrain at encode time.

questions.question: Which round-trip property should a byte-level BPE tokenizer satisfy for any string s?
options: encode(s) == sorted(encode(s))
decode(encode(s)) == s
encode(decode(s)) == s
len(encode(s)) == len(s)
questions.explanation: Byte-level BPE is lossless: encoding a string and decoding the ids gives back exactly the same string. Token count is generally smaller than character count after merges, so the length equality is false. encode(decode(s)) mixes up types (s is a string, decode takes ids).

questions.question: In llmre's BPETokenizer, what is described as 'the whole subtlety' of encoding?
options: Applying merges in random order to regularize the tokenizer
Applying the learned merges in the order they were learned
Applying the longest available merge first, regardless of order
Applying merges in alphabetical order of the byte pairs
questions.explanation: The merges are stored as an ordered dict of (a, b) -> new_id, and encode must apply them in learned order. Later merges may depend on tokens created by earlier ones, so reordering produces different (wrong) tokenizations. Alphabetical, longest-first or random orders do not reproduce training.

questions.question: How does llmre's BPETokenizer store its learned merges?
options: As an ordered dict mapping a pair (a, b) to a new id
As a set of strings with no ordering
As a trie of whole words learned from the corpus
As a matrix of pair frequencies recomputed on each encode
questions.explanation: merges is an ordered dict of (a, b) -> new_id. The ordering matters because encode applies merges in the order they were learned. A set would lose that order, and recomputing frequencies at encode time is not how BPE encoding works.

questions.question: What are the main components of the decoder-only GPT in llmre.model.gpt.GPT?
options: Token + positional embeddings, pre-norm blocks (causal attention + MLP), a final norm, a tied lm_head
An encoder stack, a decoder stack with cross-attention to the encoder output, and an untied output layer
Only token embeddings, a single shared attention layer, and a separate classifier per position
Convolutional embeddings, post-norm blocks with bidirectional attention, and a softmax output head
questions.explanation: The capstone GPT is decoder-only: token and positional embeddings, a stack of pre-norm blocks each containing causal multi-head attention and an MLP, a final norm, and an lm_head tied to the token embedding. There is no encoder or cross-attention, and attention is causal, not bidirectional.

questions.question: In llmre's GPT, what does forward(idx, targets) return?
options: Only the loss as a scalar
Only the sampled next token ids
A tuple (hidden_states, attention_weights)
A tuple (logits, loss)
questions.explanation: forward(idx, targets) returns both the logits and the cross-entropy loss. Sampling is done separately by generate(...). Returning hidden states or attention weights is not the interface described.

questions.question: What does weight tying mean in llmre's GPT?
options: The token embedding matrix and the lm_head weight are the same tensor
Every transformer block shares one set of attention and MLP weights
The query and key projections share a single weight matrix in each head
The positional and token embeddings are summed into one shared table
questions.explanation: Weight tying means transformer.wte.weight is lm_head.weight: the same parameter maps ids to vectors at the input and vectors to logits at the output. It saves vocab_size x n_embd parameters. Sharing weights across blocks or between Q and K is a different (and not used) idea.

questions.question: What scaled residual initialization standard deviation does llmre's GPT use for residual projections?
options: 0.02 * sqrt(2 * n_layer)
1 / sqrt(n_embd * n_layer)
0.02 / sqrt(2 * n_layer)
questions.explanation: Residual projections are initialized with std 0.02 / sqrt(2 * n_layer). Each block adds two residual contributions (attention and MLP), so there are 2 * n_layer additions; scaling by 1/sqrt of that keeps the residual stream's variance from growing with depth. Multiplying by sqrt(n_layer) would do the opposite.

questions.question: In llmre's GPT, which object fixes every tensor shape of the model?
options: The training loop's TrainConfig
The tokenizer's merges dictionary
The GPTConfig dataclass
The capstone report template
questions.explanation: GPTConfig (llmre.model.config) holds n_layer, n_head, n_embd, block_size, vocab_size and so on, which determine every tensor shape. TrainConfig controls the optimization loop, not model shapes. The tokenizer influences vocab_size only indirectly by being passed into the config.

questions.question: What objective does the capstone's pretraining stage minimize?
options: Binary cross-entropy of a real-vs-fake classifier
Mean squared error between embeddings of adjacent tokens
Negative reward from a learned reward model
Cross-entropy of the true next token at each position
questions.explanation: Pretraining is next-token prediction: for each position, minimize the cross-entropy of the actual next token under the model's predicted distribution. MSE on embeddings or discriminator losses are not language-model pretraining objectives, and reward models belong to post-training.

questions.question: In what order does the llmre pretraining loop's inner step act?
options: Forward/backward, AdamW step, then clip the gradients after the update has already been applied to the weights
Set the LR from the cosine-warmup schedule, forward/backward, clip the global grad norm, AdamW step
AdamW step, then forward/backward, then clip the grad norm, then set the LR for the next step
Clip the grad norm, set the LR from the schedule, AdamW step, then forward/backward last
questions.explanation: The loop writes the learning rate for the current step, runs forward and backward to get gradients, clips the global gradient norm, then takes the AdamW step. Clipping must happen after backward and before the optimizer step; clipping after the step has no effect on that update.

questions.question: What does gradient accumulation let the llmre pretraining loop do?
options: Reach a large effective batch size while fitting in small memory
Store the AdamW moment buffers in lower precision to save memory
Skip the backward pass on most micro-batches to save compute
Use a much higher learning rate safely without any warmup phase
questions.explanation: Gradient accumulation sums gradients over several micro-batches before one optimizer step, so the effective batch is large while each forward/backward only holds one micro-batch in memory. It still requires a backward pass on every micro-batch, and it is unrelated to warmup or optimizer precision.

questions.question: Which llmre modules does the training loop llmre.training.loop.train build on?
options: llmre.tools.registry.ToolRegistry, llmre.agents.react.run_react and llmre.reasoning.cot.cot_prompt
llmre.data.minhash, llmre.data.contamination and llmre.data.quality, applied per training batch
llmre.optim.adamw.AdamW, llmre.optim.schedule.cosine_warmup_lr and llmre.optim.clip.clip_grad_norm_
llmre.sft.lora.LoRALinear, llmre.preference.dpo.dpo_loss and llmre.rl.grpo.grpo_advantages
questions.explanation: The pretraining loop is assembled from the from-scratch optimizer (AdamW), learning-rate schedule (cosine warmup) and gradient-norm clipping. LoRA/DPO/GRPO are post-training, tools/agents are later modules, and the data-quality modules feed the corpus rather than the loop.

questions.question: How does the llmre data pipeline turn documents into training data?
options: Re-tokenize a random document at every step, truncate it to block_size, and pad shorter ones
Encode each document once, concatenate into one id stream with end-of-text ids, cut random (x, y) windows
Pad every document to the longest one in the corpus and train on each padded document separately
Shuffle all tokens globally across documents and sample them independently for each batch
questions.explanation: pack_documents encodes everything once into a single id stream with end-of-text separators, and get_batch cuts random fixed-length windows. Packing avoids padding waste. Re-tokenizing every step wastes compute, and globally shuffling tokens destroys the sequences the model must learn.

questions.question: In llmre's get_batch, how is the target window y related to the input window x?
options: y is x with 15% of tokens masked
y is x shifted left by one position
y is x reversed along the time axis
y is the same as x, position by position
questions.explanation: Each target is the next token of the input at the same position, so y is x shifted by one. That single shift is the whole supervision signal for next-token prediction. Masking is BERT-style pretraining, and y == x would teach the model to copy its input.

questions.question: Besides packing and batching, what must a data pipeline do at real scale?
options: Remove every repeated token within each document
Filter, deduplicate and decontaminate the corpus
Translate all documents into a single language
Sort the documents alphabetically before packing
questions.explanation: At real scale the data pipeline is also where you filter low-quality text, deduplicate (e.g. with MinHash) and decontaminate against evaluation sets (llmre.data.quality, minhash, contamination). Translation, alphabetical sorting or removing repeated tokens are not standard pipeline steps.

questions.question: What does the llmre.data.contamination module address in the data pipeline?
options: Balancing the mix of code, prose, and math in the training corpus by domain weights
Fixing invalid UTF-8 byte sequences so the byte-level tokenizer does not fail on them
Removing eval-set content from the training corpus so benchmark scores are not inflated
Detecting malware and phishing pages embedded in web-crawled documents before training starts
questions.explanation: Decontamination removes overlap between the training corpus and evaluation benchmarks; otherwise the model may have seen test items and score artificially high.
