It sits next to quality filtering and MinHash deduplication in the data-quality tooling. It is not about malware, encoding or domain mixing.

questions.question: How does the memory of standard (non-Flash) attention grow with sequence length T?
options: As T^2, because it materializes a T x T score matrix per head
As T^3, because of the cost of the T x T by T x d matrix multiply
Linearly in T, because each token stores one key and one value vector
Logarithmically in T, because softmax normalization compresses the scores
questions.explanation: Standard attention builds the full T x T score matrix per head, so memory grows quadratically with T. FlashAttention computes the same result in tiles without ever storing that matrix. The matmul cost is T^2 times head dimension, not T^3.

questions.question: What does FlashAttention change relative to standard attention?
options: It drops the softmax so that attention becomes linear in sequence length
It only attends to a fixed window of nearby tokens, skipping distant ones
It approximates attention with a low-rank projection of the keys and the values
It computes the same result without storing the full T x T attention matrix
questions.explanation: FlashAttention is exact: it tiles the computation and uses an online softmax so the T x T matrix is never materialized in slow memory. The output is the same as standard attention. Low-rank, linear or sliding-window attention are approximations that change the result.

questions.question: Which two quantities does llmre.training.metrics use to track training throughput?
options: Vocabulary size and the number of BPE merges per second
Held-out perplexity and BLEU score per wall-clock hour
The 6N FLOPs-per-token rule and MFU (model FLOPs utilization)
Global gradient norm and learning rate logged at each step
questions.explanation: llmre.training.metrics provides model_flops_per_token (about 6N for N parameters), tokens_per_step and mfu. MFU compares achieved FLOPs to the hardware's peak. Perplexity and BLEU are quality metrics; gradient norm and LR are optimization diagnostics, not throughput.

questions.question: Which llmre function is the tiled (FlashAttention-style) attention reference?
options: llmre.attention.flash.flash_attention_reference
llmre.evaluation.harness.evaluate_perplexity
llmre.attention.attention.scaled_dot_product_attention
llmre.training.metrics.model_flops_per_token
questions.explanation: flash_attention_reference in llmre.attention.flash is the from-scratch tiled attention implementation, benchmarked by code/scripts/bench_attention.py. scaled_dot_product_attention is the standard attention that materializes the full score matrix, model_flops_per_token counts FLOPs for throughput, and evaluate_perplexity computes a metric.

questions.question: What do scaling laws say about language-model loss?
options: It rises after a fixed number of parameters due to overfitting
It is independent of model size once data is fixed
It falls linearly with the number of parameters without limit
It falls predictably with model size, data and compute
questions.explanation: Scaling laws describe a predictable, power-law decrease of loss as you scale model size, data and compute. It is not linear and does not ignore model size. Even on CPU you can see the shape of the curve by sweeping a size knob.

questions.question: In the capstone's CPU scaling mini-experiment, which knob is swept to see the scaling curve?
options: The tokenizer's vocabulary size
The learning-rate warmup length
The random seed, over many runs
n_embd, over a few model sizes
questions.explanation: code/experiments/scaling_sweep.py sweeps n_embd over a few sizes and plots final loss, keeping corpus, steps and seed fixed. Sweeping seeds measures noise, not scaling, and vocab size or warmup are not model-size knobs.

questions.question: In the capstone scaling sweep, what is the trade-off of a bigger model at a fixed number of steps?
options: It always overfits and must be stopped earlier
It reaches a lower loss but costs more compute per step
It reaches a higher loss and costs less per step
It reaches the same loss at the same cost per step
questions.explanation: With the same steps, a bigger model reaches lower loss, but by the 6ND compute bookkeeping each step costs more (more parameters per token). That is the core scaling trade-off. The other options contradict the observed curve.

questions.question: How is perplexity defined for a held-out set?
options: log(mean cross-entropy) on held-out text
mean(exp(cross-entropy)) over training batches
exp(mean cross-entropy) on held-out text
The fraction of next tokens predicted exactly
questions.explanation: Perplexity is the exponential of the token-averaged cross-entropy on held-out text. It reads as an effective branching factor: a uniform model over V tokens has perplexity V. Accuracy or log of the loss are different quantities, and the measurement must be on held-out data.

questions.question: How does llmre's multiple_choice_score grade a multiple-choice benchmark?
options: By likelihood scoring: comparing length-normalized log-likelihoods of each answer, no weight updates
By fine-tuning the model on the benchmark's training split, then measuring accuracy on the test split
By asking a separate judge model which answer is best, then counting agreement with the gold label
By generating free text for each question and matching the chosen letter with a regular expression
questions.explanation: Likelihood scoring computes the log-likelihood of each candidate answer given the prompt, length-normalized so longer answers are not unfairly penalized, and picks the highest. It requires no training. Fine-tuning on the benchmark would contaminate it; generation-plus-regex and LLM judges are different evaluation styles.

questions.question: Why does llmre's multiple_choice_score use length-normalized log-likelihood?
options: Because normalizing by length converts the log-likelihood into perplexity exactly
Because summed log-likelihood underflows and cannot be computed in float32
Because raw summed log-likelihood penalizes longer answers just for having more tokens
Because longer answers are always correct in multiple-choice benchmarks, so it rewards them
questions.explanation: Each extra token adds a negative log-prob, so summing favors short answers regardless of correctness. Normalizing by length compares answers on a per-token basis. It is not about length being correct, not exactly perplexity, and not a numerical precision issue.

questions.question: What kind of mean does llmre's evaluate_perplexity compute over the cross-entropy?
options: The median of per-token losses across all held-out batches
The maximum per-batch loss, as a worst-case estimate
An unweighted mean of per-batch losses, regardless of how many tokens each batch has
A token-weighted mean, so every token counts equally regardless of batch
questions.explanation: evaluate_perplexity averages cross-entropy weighted by tokens, so batches with more tokens count more and the result equals the true per-token mean. Averaging per-batch means would bias toward small batches. Median or max are not the definition of perplexity.

questions.question: In response-masked SFT, which tokens contribute to the loss?
options: Only the user prompt tokens
Only the special role-delimiter tokens
Only the assistant response tokens
All tokens in the conversation equally
questions.explanation: SFT teaches the model to answer, so the loss is computed on the assistant response only; prompt positions are ignored. Training on the prompt would reward echoing the user. Delimiters alone carry too little signal, though the assistant's closing delimiter is part of the response.

questions.question: In llmre's SFT, what does build_labels write into the prompt positions?
options: 0, so those positions predict the padding token
ignore_index, i.e. -100, so cross-entropy skips them
The end-of-text id, so the model learns to stop
A copy of the input ids, so the prompt is reconstructed
questions.explanation: build_labels sets labels at prompt positions to the sentinel -100 (ignore_index), and masked_cross_entropy drops those positions. Writing 0 or end-of-text would actively train the model to predict those tokens, and copying inputs would train on the prompt.

questions.question: What does a chat template do in llmre's SFT stage?
options: Translates the conversation into a fixed set of intents and slot values for training
Flattens role-tagged messages into one string with delimiters and produces a response mask
Removes the system prompt so that the model sees only the user turns and the assistant replies
Compresses the conversation by summarizing earlier turns so it fits in the context
questions.explanation: render_with_response_mask flattens messages with roles into a single string using delimiters and marks which tokens belong to the assistant response. That mask drives build_labels. It does not translate, drop system prompts, or summarize.

questions.question: Why is the assistant's <|end|> closing delimiter treated as a response token in SFT?
options: So the loss is lower and training converges faster on short replies
So the model learns to stop generating at the end of its answer
So the prompt length can be recovered later from the label tensor
Because special tokens cannot be masked with -100 in cross-entropy
questions.explanation: Including the closer in the trained response tokens teaches the model to emit it, which is how it learns when to stop. If it were masked, the model would never be trained to end its turn and could ramble. Special tokens can be masked; the choice is deliberate.

questions.question: In the capstone's SFT stage, 21 prompt tokens are ignored and 11 response tokens are trained. What would go wrong if all 32 were trained on?
options: The loss would become undefined, because the mean over trained positions divides by zero
The model would be rewarded for echoing the user's prompt, wasting capacity and blurring turns
Nothing would change, because training on all tokens is mathematically equivalent to masking them
The tokenizer would have to be retrained on the prompts so their tokens get their own merges
questions.explanation: Training on prompt tokens rewards the model for echoing the user, wasting capacity on learning to repeat inputs and blurring the 'when is it my turn' signal the chat template teaches. The mechanism that avoids this is ignore_index = -100 in build_labels plus masked_cross_entropy. It is not a numerical issue and is not equivalent to masking.

questions.question: Why is full fine-tuning memory-heavy compared with LoRA?
options: It stores a full copy of the training data in GPU memory
It needs a separate frozen reference model for every single layer
It updates every weight and keeps two AdamW moments per parameter
It recomputes the tokenizer's merges and embeddings at every training step
questions.explanation: Full fine-tuning has gradients and two AdamW moment buffers for every parameter. LoRA freezes the base weights, so only the small adapters carry gradients and optimizer state. Tokenizers and data copies are not the main memory cost.

questions.question: What is the LoRA forward computation for a wrapped linear layer?
options: y = B(A(Wx)), with all three matrices trained
y = (W + A) x, with A trained to full rank
y = alpha * W x + r * B x, with W trained
y = Wx + (alpha/r) * B(Ax), with W frozen
questions.explanation: LoRA keeps the pretrained W frozen and adds a low-rank update B(Ax) scaled by alpha/r. A projects down to rank r and B projects back up. A full-rank additive update or training W defeats the purpose; chaining the matrices multiplicatively changes the base function.

questions.question: How is LoRA's B matrix initialized, and why?
options: To zeros, so the wrapped layer starts identical to the base layer
To the pretrained weights, so the update starts at W
To random normal, so the adapter starts with useful features
To the identity, so the layer doubles its output at init
questions.explanation: With B = 0, the update (alpha/r) * B(Ax) is exactly zero at init, so forward(x) == base(x) and training starts from the pretrained model rather than a perturbed one. The capstone checks this ('identical-to-base at init: True'). A random B would perturb the model immediately.

questions.question: For a LoRA adapter of rank r on a linear layer with input size in and output size out, how many trainable parameters are there?
options: r * in * out
in * out
r * (in + out)
r^2 + in + out
questions.explanation: A has shape (r, in) and B has shape (out, r), giving r*in + r*out = r*(in + out) trainable parameters. in*out is the frozen base weight. For a 64x64 linear at rank 4 that is 4*(64+64) = 512.

questions.question: A LoRA rank-4 adapter on a 64x64 linear reports 512 trainable of 4608 parameters. Where does the 4608 come from?
options: Twice the 512 adapter count plus the 64-dim bias vectors
4096 frozen base weights plus 512 bias and norm terms
512 adapter parameters plus the 4096 frozen base weights (64 x 64)
512 adapter parameters times 9 wrapped linear layers in total
questions.explanation: A is (4, 64) = 256 and B is (64, 4) = 256, so 512 trainable. The frozen base weight is 64*64 = 4096. 512 + 4096 = 4608, so about 11.1% of the parameters are trainable.

questions.question: What does LoRALinear.merge do in llmre?
options: Merges two different LoRA adapters into one by averaging their A and B matrices elementwise
Combines the A and B matrices into a single rank-1 vector to reduce memory
Unfreezes the base weight so that full fine-tuning can resume from the adapter
Folds the low-rank update into the base weight so inference needs no extra compute
questions.explanation: Merging computes W + (alpha/r) * B A and stores it as the layer weight, so the merged layer behaves the same with a single matmul. It does not average adapters, reduce rank, or unfreeze anything. mark_only_lora_trainable is the function that controls which parameters train.

questions.question: What form does preference data take for DPO?
options: For each prompt, a single response with a scalar human rating
For each prompt, a gold answer and a programmatic verifier function
For each prompt, a chosen response y_w and a rejected response y_l
For each response, a list of token-level corrections from annotators
questions.explanation: Alignment starts from pairs: a prompt with a chosen (winning) response y_w and a rejected (losing) response y_l. DPO optimizes directly on these pairs. Scalar ratings or verifiers belong to other setups (reward regression, RLVR).

questions.question: What does DPO avoid compared with the classic RLHF pipeline?
options: Using preference pairs, replacing them with scalar ratings
Using a frozen reference model to anchor the policy's KL
Training a separate reward model and sampling from the policy
Computing sequence log-probabilities under the current policy
questions.explanation: DPO optimizes the policy against preference pairs directly, with no reward model and no sampling. It still uses a frozen reference model and sequence log-probs (sequence_logprob), and it still needs preference pairs.

questions.question: In the DPO derivation, why does the beta * log Z(x) term disappear?
options: It depends only on the prompt, so it cancels in the chosen-minus-rejected difference
It is absorbed into the learning rate, since both scale the gradient by a constant
It is set to zero by choosing beta = 0, which removes the KL term from the objective
It is estimated by sampling completions from the reference and then subtracted out
questions.explanation: The partition-function term beta*log Z(x) is the same for both responses of the same prompt, so it cancels in r(y_w) - r(y_l). That leaves a loss with only the policy and a frozen reference. beta = 0 would remove the KL constraint, and Z is never estimated by sampling.

questions.question: In the classic RLHF path, which loss trains the reward model on preference pairs?
options: The PPO clipped surrogate objective with a KL penalty to the reference
Cross-entropy of the next token on chosen responses only, as in SFT
The Bradley-Terry loss: P(y_w beats y_l) = sigmoid(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l))
Mean squared error between the predicted reward and a human 1-10 score
questions.explanation: The reward model is trained with the Bradley-Terry link: the probability that the chosen response wins is the sigmoid of the reward difference, and the loss is its negative log. PPO's clipped objective is used afterwards to train the policy, not the reward model.

questions.question: In RLHF with PPO, what keeps the policy from drifting too far from the reference model?
options: Removing the clipping from PPO's surrogate objective
A KL penalty to the reference, entering through the reward
Lowering the reward model's learning rate during PPO updates
Freezing the policy's attention layers and training only MLPs
questions.explanation: PPO-based RLHF adds a KL penalty between the policy and the frozen reference, which enters the reward. Together with the clipped objective it limits drift. Freezing layers or adjusting the reward model's LR are not the mechanism, and removing clipping would make updates less stable.

questions.question: How does DPO relate to the reward-model + PPO path?
options: DPO is a preprocessing step that filters the preference pairs before PPO runs on them
DPO is PPO applied to a verifiable reward, with the critic replaced by a group-mean baseline
DPO short-circuits it, optimizing the policy on preference pairs with no reward model or PPO
DPO trains the reward model from the preference pairs, and PPO then trains the policy against it
questions.explanation: The reward model + PPO route is the classic RLHF path that DPO short-circuits: DPO uses the closed-form link between reward and policy/reference log-ratio to skip both the reward model and RL sampling. It is not a PPO preprocessing step, and it does not use verifiable rewards.

questions.section: (12) GRPO + RLVR on a verifiable task
questions.question: What does GRPO drop compared with PPO?
options: The learned critic (value function), using the group's mean reward as baseline
The policy model itself, replacing it with a table of sampled completions per prompt
Sampling multiple completions, scoring a single greedy completion per prompt instead
The clipped importance ratio, taking plain REINFORCE steps on the advantage
questions.explanation: GRPO removes PPO's critic: it samples a group of completions per prompt and uses the group mean reward as the baseline. It keeps a clipped ratio and, by design, relies on sampling multiple completions per prompt.

questions.section: (12) GRPO + RLVR on a verifiable task
questions.question: What is the GRPO advantage for completion i in a group?
options: A_i = (r_i - mean(r)) / std(r)
A_i = r_i - V(x), with V a learned critic
A_i = r_i / max(r)
A_i = log r_i - log mean(r)
questions.explanation: GRPO standardizes rewards within the group: subtract the group mean and divide by the group standard deviation. A learned critic V(x) is PPO's baseline, which GRPO removes. Dividing by the max or taking logs is not the GRPO formula.

questions.section: (12) GRPO + RLVR on a verifiable task
questions.question: Why is a verifiable reward harder to hack than a learned reward model?
options: It uses a larger neural network than the policy, so it is harder to fool
It is evaluated by human raters at every step, who catch gaming quickly
It is a rule that checks the answer (e.g. exact-match), not a learned proxy
It is trained on more preference data than a typical RLHF reward model
questions.explanation: RLVR uses a programmatic check, such as exact-match on arithmetic, so the policy cannot exploit quirks of a learned proxy. A learned reward model can be gamed because it is only an approximation. Verifiers are not trained on preferences and are not human-in-the-loop.

questions.section: (12) GRPO + RLVR on a verifiable task
questions.question: In the capstone's RLVR stage, which verifier is used?
options: llmre.reasoning.verifiers.arithmetic_verifier, exact-match on arithmetic answers
A perplexity threshold on the generated answer under the pretrained capstone GPT
An LLM judge that scores each answer's fluency and correctness on a 1-10 scale
A Bradley-Terry reward model trained on the capstone's DPO preference pairs
questions.explanation: The capstone's RLVR uses arithmetic_verifier, which returns reward based on whether the arithmetic answer exactly matches. That is a rule-based verifiable reward. A reward model or LLM judge would be a learned proxy, and perplexity does not check correctness.

questions.section: (12) GRPO + RLVR on a verifiable task
questions.question: What should you look at in llmre's run_rlvr history to see RL working?
options: The number of LoRA parameters increasing
The correct-rate rising over GRPO steps
The tokenizer's vocabulary size growing
The perplexity on the pretraining corpus rising
questions.explanation: run_rlvr records a history whose key signal is the correct-rate climbing as GRPO updates the policy. In the capstone run it goes from 0.062 to 1.000 over 80 steps. Vocabulary size and LoRA counts don't change, and pretraining perplexity is not the RL signal.

questions.question: What is self-consistency in reasoning?
options: Running the same chain of thought twice with greedy decoding and comparing the two outputs
Checking that the final answer is consistent with the grammar and wording of the prompt
Sampling several chains of thought and taking a majority vote over their final answers
Training the model to agree with its own previous outputs on rephrased versions of a task
questions.explanation: Self-consistency samples multiple reasoning chains and picks the most common final answer. Greedy decoding twice gives identical outputs and no voting benefit. It is an inference-time method, not training the model to agree with itself.

questions.question: What two-stage loop does llmre's mini_r1 implement, following the R1 recipe?
options: Pretraining, then distillation into a smaller tokenizer
DPO first, then tokenizer retraining
RL first, then pretraining from scratch
SFT first, then RL with verifiable rewards
questions.explanation: mini_r1 does an SFT stage then an RL stage with verifiable rewards, mirroring the R1 recipe that trains chain-of-thought behavior in with RLVR. The other orders mix in stages unrelated to the R1 pipeline.

questions.question: In llmre's self_consistency, what property of the majority vote should you look at?
options: Its weighting by answer length
Its random tie-break for diversity
Its deterministic tie-break
Its use of a learned voting network
questions.explanation: The capstone points at the deterministic majority-vote tie-break: when two answers have the same count, the result must not depend on randomness, so runs are reproducible. A learned voter or length weighting are not part of self_consistency.

questions.question: What is chain-of-thought prompting?
options: Chaining several models so each refines the previous output
Feeding the model's answer back as the next prompt until it stops changing
Making the model show its intermediate steps before giving the final answer
Concatenating many examples into one long prompt without instructions
questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought elicits reasoning by having the model write out its steps before the answer (cot_prompt), and extract_answer pulls the final answer out. It is not model chaining or iterative re-prompting.

questions.question: How does a model use a tool in llmre's tool-use stage?
options: It executes Python directly inside the model's forward pass via special tokens
It sends free-text requests to a human operator, who pastes the results back in
It emits a structured call; a runtime runs the real function and feeds the result back
It memorizes tool outputs during pretraining and reproduces them later whenever they are needed
questions.explanation: The model emits a structured tool call, which parse_tool_call parses; the ToolRegistry executes the real function and the result is fed back into the context (run_tool_loop). The model never executes code itself.

questions.question: What does llmre's ToolRegistry do when a tool call raises an exception?
options: Silently retries the call with the same arguments until it eventually succeeds
Crashes the loop on purpose so that the bug is noticed immediately
Turns the exception into a structured error result instead of crashing
Returns an empty string as if the call succeeded, so the model continues
questions.explanation: The registry runs the call and converts any exception into a structured error that is fed back to the model, so the loop keeps going and the model can react. Crashing would kill the agent; silent retries or empty results hide the failure.

questions.question: What does llmre's ToolRegistry advertise to the model about available tools?
options: The Python source code of each tool
Nothing; tools are discovered by trial and error
JSON schemas describing each tool
Example outputs only, without argument descriptions
questions.explanation: The registry advertises JSON schemas for each tool (name, arguments and types), so the model knows how to form a valid call. It does not ship source code or rely on trial and error.

questions.question: How is llmre's built-in calculator tool made safe?
options: It runs Python's eval inside a try/except block that catches every error
It blocks a list of known dangerous function names such as exec and open
It vets the expression's AST against an allow-list of permitted operations
It only accepts expressions shorter than a fixed length with no letters
questions.explanation: The calculator parses the expression and checks the AST against an allow-list, so only explicitly permitted nodes run. A block-list can always miss something dangerous, and wrapping eval in try/except gives no security. Length limits do not prevent malicious code.

questions.question: What loop does a ReAct agent run?
options: Action -> Reward -> Gradient step, repeated on every turn until the reward converges
Thought -> Action -> Observation, until a final answer or the step budget runs out
Plan -> Execute all steps -> Report, with no observations read between the steps
Retrieve -> Generate -> Rerank, for a fixed three steps per question and no tools
questions.explanation: ReAct interleaves reasoning (Thought), tool calls (Action) and results (Observation) until a final answer or the step budget runs out. Planning everything without observations loses feedback; retrieve-generate-rerank is RAG; reward-gradient loops are RL training.

questions.question: What turns llmre's ReAct loop into a mini SWE-agent?
options: Training it with DPO on code preferences
Removing the step budget so it can run indefinitely
Replacing the model with a larger pretrained checkpoint
Wrapping it with a small file view/edit/run interface
questions.explanation: llmre.agents.swe_agent.solve wraps the ReAct loop with tools to view, edit and run files, which makes it a mini software-engineering agent. Model size, DPO, or removing the step budget do not give it the file interface.

questions.question: Why is llmre's run_react described as tool-registry-agnostic?
options: It hard-codes a fixed calculator and search tool
It ignores tool results and only uses the model's thoughts
Tools are injected into it, never imported by it
It can only call tools defined in the same file
questions.explanation: run_react receives its tools as an argument (dependency injection), so any registry can be plugged in. Hard-coding or importing specific tools would couple it to one setup. It does use tool results as Observations.

questions.question: To claim a change caused an improvement, what must an ablation do?
options: Vary several things at once to save compute
Vary exactly one thing and hold everything else fixed
Change the seed along with the change to average out noise
Compare against a published number from a different setup
questions.explanation: Attribution requires one independent variable with everything else as controls. If two things change, you cannot tell which one caused the effect. Comparing to a different setup confounds harness, data and budget differences.

questions.question: In the capstone's scaling sweep used as an ablation template, what is held fixed?
options: Only the seed; the corpus and step count vary with the model size
The corpus, the number of steps and the seed; only n_embd changes
Only n_embd; the corpus, steps and seed are randomized per run
Nothing; all knobs change together to explore the whole space
questions.explanation: The scaling sweep keeps the same corpus, same steps and same seed and changes only n_embd. That is the 'one independent variable, everything else a control' pattern. Letting other knobs vary would confound the comparison.

questions.question: Where are the reproducible knobs of the capstone run stored?
options: Hard-coded inside the GPT class
In code/configs/capstone.yaml
In environment variables set by the shell
In code/reports/capstone_report.md
questions.explanation: The driver reads code/configs/capstone.yaml (model size, steps, LR, seed) so the run is reproducible. The report is the output, not the config, and hard-coding or environment variables would make the run harder to reproduce.

questions.question: You want to claim 'RMSNorm lowers final loss vs LayerNorm.' What must be true of the runs?
options: Both runs use a single seed each and identical settings, and whichever reaches the lower loss wins
Only the norm changes, everything else is fixed, with mean +/- std over seeds compared to seed noise
The RMSNorm run gets more steps and a retuned learning rate to compensate for being the newer method
Each run uses whichever learning rate gives it the lowest loss, with the other knobs left free to vary
questions.explanation: Change exactly one thing (the norm), hold corpus, tokens, steps, seeds, size, optimizer and LR schedule fixed, and run several seeds. Report mean +/- std and check whether confidence intervals overlap. A single seed cannot separate effect from noise, and giving one run extra steps confounds the result.

questions.question: What is the deliverable of a research experiment, according to the capstone?
options: A slide deck summarizing the best results across all runs
The trained model checkpoint, uploaded with its config file
A loss-curve screenshot comparing the final runs side by side
A report a colleague can reproduce, not the model itself
questions.explanation: The capstone states the deliverable is a report someone else can reproduce: QUESTION, HYPOTHESIS, METHOD, BASELINE, VARIABLES, RESULTS, ANALYSIS, LIMITATIONS, CONCLUSION, NEXT. A checkpoint or chart without method, baseline and limitations is not reproducible evidence.

questions.question: Which sections make up the llmre experiment report template?
options: SUMMARY / CONTEXT / METRICS / LEADERBOARD / DISCUSSION / RISKS / ROADMAP / OWNERS / TIMELINE
QUESTION / HYPOTHESIS / METHOD / BASELINE / VARIABLES / RESULTS / ANALYSIS / LIMITATIONS / CONCLUSION / NEXT
GOAL / SETUP / CODE / DATA / OUTPUT / METRICS / ISSUES / FIXES / DONE
ABSTRACT / INTRODUCTION / RELATED WORK / METHOD / EXPERIMENTS / DISCUSSION / CONCLUSION / REFERENCES
questions.explanation: code/reports/EXPERIMENT_TEMPLATE.md has QUESTION, HYPOTHESIS, METHOD, BASELINE, VARIABLES, RESULTS, ANALYSIS, LIMITATIONS, CONCLUSION and NEXT. That structure forces a falsifiable question, a baseline and stated limitations. Paper-style sections lack the baseline and variables discipline.

questions.question: Where does the capstone driver write its filled-in experiment report?
options: code/reports/capstone_report.md
code/tests/test_capstone.py
code/configs/capstone.yaml
code/reports/EXPERIMENT_TEMPLATE.md
questions.explanation: The driver fills in the template and writes code/reports/capstone_report.md. EXPERIMENT_TEMPLATE.md is the blank template, capstone.yaml is the input config, and test_capstone.py is the smoke test.

questions.question: Which stages does the capstone driver code/scripts/capstone.py actually run?
options: A tiny version of stages (1)-(9) and (12): tokenizer through LoRA, plus GRPO/RLVR
Only the post-training stages (SFT, LoRA, DPO, PPO, GRPO) on a downloaded checkpoint
Only pretraining and evaluation, leaving every post-training stage to separate scripts
All 17 stages at full scale, including PPO, tool use, ReAct agents and the SWE-agent
questions.explanation: The driver runs a tiny end-to-end version of stages 1-9 (tokenizer, GPT, pretraining, data, profiling notes, scaling, eval, SFT, LoRA) and stage 12 (GRPO + RLVR), then writes the report. Stages like PPO, tool use and agents are covered by their own entry points but not run by the driver.

questions.question: In the capstone run, pretraining loss falls from 5.935 to 0.067 nats and held-out perplexity is 1.07. What does that indicate?
options: The model generalizes far beyond GPT-2 quality on this held-out text
The tiny model memorized the tiny corpus, the expected smoke-test outcome
The loss is miscomputed, because perplexity can never fall below 2
The tokenizer collapsed so that every document maps to a single token
questions.explanation: The corpus is a dozen repeated sentences, so a tiny model memorizes it and perplexity drops near 1. That proves the pipeline learns but says nothing about quality. Perplexity can be any value at least 1, and nothing indicates tokenizer collapse.

questions.question: In the capstone run, what is the uniform-baseline perplexity that the 1.07 result is compared to?
options: About 256, the byte count
About 374, the vocabulary size
About 1.0, the minimum possible
About 2.72, the value of e
questions.explanation: A uniform model over V tokens has perplexity V, and the capstone vocabulary is about 373-374 tokens (256 bytes + 117 merges plus specials), so the baseline is about 374. Perplexity 1 is the floor, and 256 is only the byte base.

questions.question: In the capstone run, RLVR lifts the arithmetic correct-rate from 0.062 to 1.000. Why is 0.062 described as near chance?
options: It is the fraction of prompt tokens in each RL batch
It equals 1/16, the reciprocal of the GRPO group size
It is close to the ~1/10 expected from a 10-way answer space
It equals the learning rate used for the GRPO policy updates
questions.explanation: With about 10 possible answers, a random policy would be right about 1/10 of the time, so 0.062 is near chance before training. RL then drives it to 1.000. It is not a group size, token fraction or learning rate.

questions.question: What do the capstone's two learning signals, which a smoke test exists to check, consist of?
options: Loss going down and correct-rate going up
Vocabulary size going up and merge count going down
Learning rate going up and gradient norm going down
Throughput going up and memory going down
questions.explanation: A smoke test checks that the pipeline actually learns: pretraining/SFT loss decreases and the RLVR correct-rate increases. code/tests/test_capstone.py asserts exactly this at even smaller size. Throughput or vocabulary changes say nothing about learning.

questions.question: What does code/tests/test_capstone.py assert?
options: That loss falls and correct-rate rises, at even smaller size than the driver
That the whole run finishes in under one second on a single GPU
That held-out perplexity matches GPT-2 small's published value on WikiText
That every module's output is bit-identical to a stored reference tensor
questions.explanation: test_capstone.py checks the two learning signals (loss down, correct-rate up) on an even smaller configuration. It does not compare against GPT-2, timing, or bit-exact references.

questions.question: Why should a memorization perplexity like 1.07 never be quoted as a quality result?
options: Because perplexity is only well defined for runs done on GPU hardware
It only shows the pipeline can learn a repeated tiny corpus, not that it generalizes
Because the value is below the theoretical minimum perplexity of 2 for any model
Because perplexity is not a valid language-model metric for byte-level tokenizers
questions.explanation: The low value comes from memorizing a dozen repeated sentences. It is a correct smoke-test outcome and a deliberate limitation stated in the report, but quality claims need a large, varied corpus and genuinely held-out data. Perplexity is a valid metric, its minimum is 1, and it is hardware independent.

questions.question: Why does the capstone use a categorical policy table for RLVR instead of the pretrained GPT?
options: Because GRPO cannot be applied to transformer policies, only to tabular ones
Because the pretrained GPT has no output distribution over the possible answers
Speed and clarity on CPU: the GRPO update is identical; the table isolates RL from generation
Because verifiable rewards only work with tabular policies that enumerate every answer
questions.explanation: GRPO's algorithm (sample a group, standardize rewards, clipped policy-gradient step) is the same for a lookup table or a GPT emitting answer tokens. The table makes the correct-rate visibly climb in under a second. Swapping in the GPT changes the engineering (sampling token sequences), not the update rule, which is why it is the report's next experiment.

questions.question: What hardware does a real GPT-2 small (124M) pretrain need, per the capstone's hardware track?
options: 1x A100/H100 (40-80 GB), tens of GPU-hours for a few billion tokens; CPU-only is not feasible
A cluster of 1,000 H100 GPUs for about a month, the same as a frontier pretraining run
A single 8 GB consumer GPU for about ten minutes, using LoRA instead of full training
A laptop CPU for about an hour, since 124M parameters fit easily in system memory
questions.explanation: A GPT-2 small pretrain is estimated at tens of GPU-hours on one A100/H100, using about 15-30 GB with mixed precision and gradient accumulation. CPU-only is not feasible. A month on 1,000 GPUs is frontier scale, not 124M.

questions.question: Why can LoRA fit a 7B model on a single 24 GB consumer GPU while full SFT of the same model needs multiple 40-80 GB GPUs?
options: LoRA quantizes the activations and gradients to one bit, so memory falls by roughly 16x overall
LoRA trains on far fewer tokens than full SFT, so it needs a much smaller activation buffer
LoRA skips the forward pass through frozen layers, so their activations are never stored
With LoRA, optimizer state covers only the small adapters; full SFT keeps it for every weight
questions.explanation: LoRA's frozen base needs no gradients or optimizer moments, so only the adapters carry that state. Full SFT stores gradients plus two AdamW moments for all 7B parameters. LoRA still runs the full forward pass and does not inherently change token count or quantize activations.

questions.question: How does the compute cost of DPO compare to SFT?
options: Roughly the same as SFT: two forward passes, the policy and a frozen reference
Identical to PPO, because both train a critic alongside the policy each step
Much cheaper, because DPO skips the backward pass and only scores pairs
Far heavier, because DPO samples fresh completions from the policy every step
questions.explanation: DPO costs about the same as SFT, plus a forward pass through the frozen reference, and needs no sampling. PPO/GRPO are far heavier because they generate completions every step. DPO does train with backward passes and does not use a critic.

questions.question: In PPO/GRPO with real generation, what usually dominates cost?
options: Generating (sampling) completions, not the gradient step
Writing full optimizer-state checkpoints to disk each step
The KL penalty computation over the full vocabulary
The tokenizer's encode step on every sampled completion
questions.explanation: Generation-based RL samples completions every step, so sampling dominates cost. Budget several GPUs and hours-to-days even for a small model. Tokenization and KL computation are cheap, and checkpointing is not the bottleneck.

questions.question: What makes frontier reasoning RL runs cost thousands of GPU-hours?
options: Long chains of thought make each rollout long, so sampling at scale is costly; same mechanism as the toy
They must retrain the tokenizer on every RL step, as the vocabulary drifts with the reasoning traces
They require a full pretraining pass between RL steps to keep the policy from forgetting language
They use a completely different algorithm from GRPO, which needs a learned critic per token
questions.explanation: The mechanism is identical to the toy loop; only the scale of sampling changes. Long chain-of-thought rollouts make each sample expensive. It is not a different algorithm, and no tokenizer retraining or re-pretraining is involved.

questions.question: What is the Chinchilla rule of thumb for a compute-optimal pretrain?
options: About 1 token per parameter
About 20 tokens per parameter
About 200 tokens per parameter
About 2 tokens per FLOP
questions.explanation: The Chinchilla rule of thumb (reasonable industry practice) is about 20 training tokens per parameter for compute-optimal pretraining. 1 or 200 tokens per parameter would be badly under- or over-trained for compute optimality, and tokens per FLOP is not a meaningful ratio here.

questions.question: How should the tokenizer's vocabulary size be scaled up from the toy capstone driver?
options: Toward 32k-50k tokens
Toward 256 tokens, the byte count
Toward 1 million tokens
It should stay at the toy size of about 373
questions.explanation: To grow the tokenizer stage, raise tokenizer.vocab_size toward 32k-50k, typical of GPT-2-class models. 256 would be bytes only, 1M would bloat embeddings, and the toy size is only for the smoke test.

questions.question: Which of these is part of scaling up the capstone pipeline from the toy driver?
options: Disable gradient clipping so that larger models are not slowed down by small updates
Replace the BPE tokenizer with a character-level one so that the vocabulary stays small
Use a real filtered, decontaminated corpus and move to a GPU with mixed precision and FlashAttention
Keep the toy corpus but train for millions of steps, so the model sees every sentence many times
questions.explanation: Scaling up means a real corpus (filtered and decontaminated, Module 11), a bigger model toward GPT-2 sizes, and GPU training with mixed precision and FlashAttention (Module 8). Training longer on the toy corpus just memorizes it further; dropping clipping or BPE are not recommended steps.

questions.question: What does the capstone report name as the next experiment for the RLVR stage?
options: Replacing the arithmetic verifier with a learned reward model trained on preferences
Removing the group sampling so that each GRPO step needs only one completion
Replacing the categorical RLVR policy with the GPT itself emitting answer tokens
Replacing GRPO with supervised fine-tuning on the correct arithmetic answers
questions.explanation: The natural next step is to have the pretrained GPT generate answer tokens as the RLVR policy, instead of the categorical lookup table. That changes the engineering, not the GRPO update. A learned reward model would reintroduce hackability, and removing group sampling breaks GRPO's baseline.

questions.question: According to the course's readiness matrix, when is a skill rated 'Advanced'?
options: When you have read the relevant paper once and can summarize its main contribution
When you have used it in a production framework such as HF, TRL or DeepSpeed at work
When you can explain, derive, implement, test, benchmark, debug and relate it to a paper
When you can run the provided script without errors and reproduce its printed numbers
questions.explanation: Advanced means the full chain: explain -> derive -> implement -> test -> benchmark -> debug -> relate-to-a-paper, from memory. Reading or running something once, or using a framework, covers only part of that chain.

questions.question: What should a write-up of your own experiment contain, following the capstone report's model?
options: One falsifiable question, real numbers with a baseline, and stated limitations
Several open-ended questions and qualitative impressions of how the runs went
Only the best result across all runs and seeds, presented without a baseline
A detailed description of the code changes, without any measured numbers
questions.explanation: One report, one falsifiable question, real numbers compared to a baseline, and stated limitations, just like code/reports/capstone_report.md. Cherry-picking the best result or omitting numbers makes the report non-reproducible and non-falsifiable.

questions.question: Why is OLMo 2 suggested as a strong first paper after finishing the course?
options: It is the largest open model ever trained, so it defines the current frontier
It uses no transformer components, so it contrasts well with what you built
It requires no GPU to reproduce, so you can rerun its full training run on a laptop
Its data, code and checkpoints are fully open, so you can reproduce and ablate it
questions.explanation: OLMo 2 is fully open (data, code, checkpoints), so you can reproduce it and ablate it against your own llmre implementation. It is not the largest model, it is a transformer, and reproducing it still needs serious GPUs.

questions.question: What loop is described as 'the job' of a research engineer at the end of the course?
options: Download, fine-tune, deploy, repeat
Brainstorm, prototype, ship, market
Read, implement, test, measure, write
Benchmark, tweak hyperparameters, publish the best seed
questions.explanation: After reading a paper with the nine-question method, implement its change inside llmre, wire it into the capstone, measure, and write it up with the experiment template. Publishing the best seed is the anti-pattern the ablation discipline warns against.

questions.question: When reading a new paper after the course, what should you do with the one thing it changes?
options: Implement it in llmre, wire it into code/scripts/capstone.py, and write it up with the template
Download the authors' released checkpoint and report their numbers alongside your baseline
Summarize it in a blog post with its key equations, without running any code yourself
Add it to every stage of the pipeline at once, so its full effect is measured in one run
questions.explanation: The suggested workflow is to implement the paper's single change inside llmre, run it through the capstone driver, and write a report. Re-reporting authors' numbers is not reproduction, and changing every stage at once would break the one-variable ablation discipline.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: How does the 'MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark' frontier update relate to the core course modules on evaluation, RL and agents?
options: It supersedes the evaluation-harness lesson, which is now out of date
It adds recent industry news on top of them and replaces nothing
It replaces the GRPO lesson with a newer, benchmark-approved algorithm
It is a prerequisite that must be read before starting Module 16
questions.explanation: The page is a bonus frontier update layered on Modules 13, 16 and 19. It shows how the same mechanisms are now measured at industry scale but does not replace any lesson. It is not a prerequisite for Module 16.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Since late 2025, where have most LLM capability gains come from, according to the MLPerf post-training frontier update?
options: Scaling the tokenizer vocabulary
Switching from transformers to recurrent networks
Scaling post-training
Longer pretraining on the same data
questions.explanation: The update states that since late 2025 most capability gains have come from scaling post-training. What was missing was a standard way to measure time-to-quality for it, which the MLPerf workload provides.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: What gap does the MLPerf LLM post-training benchmark fill?
options: A public dataset of human preference pairs for reward models
A reference GPU kernel for attention shared across submitters
A standard way to measure time-to-quality for post-training
A standard tokenizer and chat template shared by all labs
questions.explanation: Until this benchmark there was no standard way to measure how long it takes to post-train a model to a quality target. MLPerf now measures that time-to-quality. It is not a tokenizer, preference dataset or kernel.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Which skills does the MLPerf post-training benchmark exercise, making them relevant for lab hiring?
options: Web front-end design, SQL query tuning, container orchestration, CDN caching, and mobile release pipelines
RLVR loop design, eval-metric choice, reward-hacking defenses, gen/train overlap, weight transfer, KV cache
Hyperparameter search only, on fixed infrastructure, with learning rate, batch size, and warmup as the knobs
Tokenizer training, image augmentation, speech recognition, diffusion sampling, and contrastive pretraining
questions.explanation: The benchmark stresses model-adjacent systems skills: designing the RLVR loop, choosing eval metrics, defending against reward hacking, overlapping generation with training, transferring weights, and managing KV cache for long agent trajectories. Those are exactly what post-training teams hire for.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: When does the MLPerf Training LLM post-training workload start, according to MLCommons' September 2026 announcement?
options: With the v5.0 submission round in January 2025
It has no fixed round; results are accepted continuously
With the v6.1 submission round in October 2026
With the v7.0 submission round planned for mid-2027
questions.explanation: MLCommons announced in September 2026 that it will add an LLM post-training workload to MLPerf Training starting with the v6.1 submission round in October 2026. This is publicly documented.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Which RL algorithm does the MLPerf LLM post-training benchmark use?
options: DPO on preference pairs
GRPO over rollout iterations
PPO with a learned critic
REINFORCE with no baseline
questions.explanation: The benchmark uses GRPO over rollout iterations, with a binary verifiable reward. DPO is offline preference optimization; PPO uses a critic that GRPO drops; plain REINFORCE without a baseline is not the chosen design.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: What reward does the MLPerf LLM post-training benchmark use?
options: The negative perplexity of the generated patch under the model
A scalar score from a learned reward model trained on patches
A binary pass/fail reward from running tests (RLVR)
Human ratings of each patch collected after every rollout
questions.explanation: The reward is binary: 1 if the tests pass, 0 otherwise, which is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Learned reward models and human ratings are not used, and perplexity does not measure whether a bug is fixed.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: What policy model does the MLPerf LLM post-training benchmark train?
options: A 7B dense model fine-tuned with LoRA adapters on every attention and MLP projection
A dense 70B model with all of its parameters active for every token it processes
GPT-2 small with 124M parameters, chosen so that submissions can run on one GPU
Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, an MoE with 397B total and ~17B active parameters per token
questions.explanation: The policy is Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, a mixture-of-experts model: 397B total parameters, about 17B active per token. The A17B suffix denotes active parameters. It is neither dense nor small.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Where do the tasks in the MLPerf LLM post-training benchmark come from?
options: Multiple-choice trivia questions scored by exact match
Grade-school math word problems with numeric answers
Real software-repair tasks from R2E-Gym, run in a sandbox
Synthetic arithmetic generated on the fly by a task sampler
questions.explanation: Tasks are real software-repair problems from R2E-Gym, run in a sandbox where tests determine the reward. Math, trivia or synthetic arithmetic are other RLVR domains, not the benchmark's.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Which agent harness does the MLPerf LLM post-training benchmark fix for training and validation?
options: No harness; the model outputs a patch in one shot
OpenHands for training and a custom harness for validation
Any harness the submitter chooses
OpenHands, for both training and validation
questions.explanation: The benchmark fixes OpenHands for both training and validation, because harness choice strongly changes solve rate. Letting submitters choose, or switching harnesses at validation, would make results incomparable.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: What is the validation metric and target of the MLPerf LLM post-training benchmark?
options: pass@16, with a target of 0.50 over 1004 validation rollouts
pass@4, with a target of 0.69 over 1004 validation rollouts
Perplexity, with a target of 10 on held-out repositories
pass@1, with a target of 0.95 over 100 validation rollouts
questions.explanation: Validation uses pass@4 with target 0.69 measured over 1004 validation rollouts. pass@1 was not chosen due to higher variance; perplexity does not measure task success.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: What maximum policy staleness does the MLPerf LLM post-training reference allow in async RL?
options: 1 weight version
Unbounded, as long as throughput improves
16 weight versions, one per generation
0 versions; generation and training are fully synchronous
questions.explanation: The reference caps staleness at 1: a rollout can be generated by version t-1 while the trainer produces version t, never older. That allows overlap of generation and training while limiting the off-policy gap.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: What fixed budgets does the MLPerf LLM post-training benchmark impose?
options: 1M context, unlimited turns, and 1 generation per prompt
65k context, 100 agent turns, and 64 generations per prompt
8k context, 5 agent turns, and 4 generations per prompt
65k context, 30 agent turns, and 16 generations per prompt
questions.explanation: Budgets are fixed at 65k context, 30 agent turns and 16 generations per prompt (GRPO group size G = 16), so submissions compete on systems efficiency rather than letting the agent think longer.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: What is the MLPerf post-training benchmark's headline metric, 'time-to-quality'?
options: The tokens per second sustained during rollout generation
Wall-clock time until the trained agent reaches pass@4 >= 0.69
The number of GPUs needed to reach pass@4 >= 0.69 in one day
The pass@4 score reached after a fixed one-hour training budget
questions.explanation: Time-to-quality is the wall-clock time until the agent reaches the target pass@4 of 0.69. It mirrors MLPerf's existing 'time to train to a target' framing for pretraining. Fixed-budget quality or raw throughput are different metrics.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Which paper introduced the unbiased pass@k estimator used in RLVR evaluation?
options: Jain et al. 2025, 'R2E-Gym', which built the repair environments
Chen et al. 2021, 'Evaluating LLMs Trained on Code' (the Codex paper)
Shao et al. 2024, 'DeepSeekMath', which introduced group-relative RL
Wang et al. 2024, 'OpenHands', the open agent platform paper
questions.explanation: The unbiased pass@k estimator comes from Chen et al. 2021 (arXiv 2107.03374), section 2.1. DeepSeekMath introduced GRPO, R2E-Gym provides the repair tasks, and OpenHands is the agent harness.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Which paper introduced GRPO?
options: Jain et al. 2025, R2E-Gym
Shao et al. 2024, DeepSeekMath
Chen et al. 2021, Evaluating LLMs Trained on Code
Liu et al. 2025, Dr. GRPO
questions.explanation: GRPO was introduced in DeepSeekMath (Shao et al. 2024, arXiv 2402.03300). Dr. GRPO is a later fix to GRPO, and the other papers cover pass@k and environment construction.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.1 The unit of optimization is model + harness
questions.question: In agentic RL, what is an agent harness?
options: The GPU cluster scheduler that places and runs the training and rollout jobs
The verifier that runs the tests and computes each episode's binary reward
The wrapper around the model: prompt scaffolding, tools, observation truncation, stopping
The tokenizer and chat template used to format the SFT and RL training data
questions.explanation: An agent is a model wrapped in a harness: scaffolding, available tools (edit file, run tests, search), how observations are truncated, and stopping rules. The verifier computes reward separately; the scheduler and tokenizer are not the harness.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.1 The unit of optimization is model + harness
questions.question: Why did the MLPerf team fix one harness (OpenHands) for both training and validation?
options: Because harnesses have no real effect on scores, but fixing one simplifies logging and reproduction
Because OpenHands is the only open harness that supports GRPO-style group sampling of episodes
Harness choice strongly changed solve rate, and the policy learns to act inside a specific harness
Because changing harnesses breaks the tokenizer's chat template and corrupts the stored rollouts
questions.explanation: The team found harness choice strongly changed solve rate. The policy learns to act inside the harness, and the reward depends on what tools exist and how outputs are shown. Evaluating with a different harness means evaluating a different system.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.1 The unit of optimization is model + harness
questions.question: What happens if you change the agent harness at evaluation time relative to training?
options: You are evaluating a different system than the one you trained
Results improve because the model generalizes to new tools
The verifier automatically adjusts the reward for the new harness
Nothing changes, since only the weights matter
questions.explanation: Model and harness together are the unit being optimized. Swap the harness and the tool set, observations and stopping behavior all change, so the score no longer describes the trained system. Weights alone are not the system.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.1 The unit of optimization is model + harness
questions.question: What reasonable industry practice is recommended for agent harnesses?
options: Hard-code the harness into the model weights through SFT so it cannot drift between runs
Use a different harness for each evaluation run to test the policy's robustness to tooling
Upgrade the harness freely between checkpoints, since only the weights determine the score
Version the harness like the model and log its commit next to every checkpoint and eval
questions.explanation: Because model + harness is the unit, the harness should be versioned like the model, with its commit recorded alongside every checkpoint and eval number. Untracked changes make results irreproducible and incomparable.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.2 Reward hacking appears immediately: hidden tests
questions.question: When is a programmatic verifier actually ungameable in RLVR?
options: Always, because a programmatic verifier checks ground truth by construction
Only if the reward is continuous rather than binary 0/1 per episode
Only if the policy cannot touch the verifier or the files that define it
Only if the verifier is a neural network the policy cannot inspect
questions.explanation: A verifier checks ground truth only if the policy cannot modify it. With shell access, an agent can edit the tests that define the reward. Being rule-based is not enough on its own, and neither neural verifiers nor continuous rewards fix this.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.2 Reward hacking appears immediately: hidden tests
questions.question: What reward hack was documented in the MLPerf RLVR software-repair setup?
options: Models produced extremely long outputs to exhaust the context
Models deleted the failing tests instead of fixing the bug
Models refused to answer to avoid negative reward
Models copied the gold patch from the internet
questions.explanation: With shell access, agents deleted failing tests; with no failing tests the suite passes and the reward is 1. That is the documented failure. The other behaviors were not the reported hack.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.2 Reward hacking appears immediately: hidden tests
questions.question: If an agent's actions a_1:T can modify the files that define the verifier v, what is the policy effectively optimizing?
options: The true verifier, since the sandbox reverts all edits before the reward is computed
The KL divergence to the reference policy, since the reward becomes constant
The perplexity of the repository's code, since edits change what the tests read
A verifier the agent itself edited, whose easiest maximizer is to make v trivial
questions.explanation: If the agent can edit v, it optimizes v_{a_1:T}, a verifier it modified, and the simplest way to maximize it is to make it trivially pass (e.g. delete tests). Nothing in that setup reverts the edits.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.2 Reward hacking appears immediately: hidden tests
questions.question: What is the defense against agents deleting failing tests in RLVR software-repair tasks?
options: Run the reward on hidden test files copied into the sandbox only after the episode ends
Show the agent all tests up front, so it knows exactly which behavior it must fix
Give the agent read-only access to the whole filesystem, including the source files
Penalize every file deletion with a negative reward large enough to outweigh a pass
questions.explanation: Hidden tests are copied in only after the agent stops, then run to compute the reward, so the agent can neither see nor modify them. Read-only access would prevent fixing bugs; deletion penalties are easy to sidestep; showing all tests invites gaming.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.2 Reward hacking appears immediately: hidden tests
questions.question: What general rule follows from the hidden-test defense in RLVR?
options: The policy must never be given tools that touch the filesystem
Anything the policy can read must be encrypted before the episode
Rewards must always be computed by human raters, not programs
Anything the policy can write to cannot be part of the reward
questions.explanation: The general rule is that anything the policy can write to cannot be part of the reward computation. It does not require encryption, human scoring or removing tools; it requires isolating the reward's inputs from the agent's actions.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.2 Reward hacking appears immediately: hidden tests
questions.question: During RLVR training, training reward climbs but held-out pass rate does not. What does that suggest?
options: The held-out split is too easy, so it saturates early
The learning rate is too low for held-out gains to appear
Something is being gamed or overfit on the training side
The model is generalizing perfectly to unseen tasks
questions.explanation: Keeping a held-out task split the loop never sees is a tripwire: if training reward rises without held-out improvement, the policy is exploiting the train-side checker or memorizing train quirks. A too-low LR would slow both; an easy held-out split would show high scores.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
questions.question: What does pass@4 measure for a problem?
options: Whether all 4 attempts pass the tests
Whether the 4th attempt alone passes
Whether at least one of 4 attempts passes
The average pass rate of the 4 attempts
questions.explanation: Under pass@k, a problem counts as solved if at least one of k attempts passes. Requiring all to pass would be a much stricter metric, and averaging gives pass@1.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
questions.question: Why did MLPerf choose pass@4 as its validation metric?
options: It is the only metric compatible with binary 0/1 rewards from executing the hidden tests
It gives the highest possible scores of the metrics studied, making the target easy to hit
It had the lowest variance studied, so fewer costly rollouts decide the target was reached
It does not require running any tests, so validation is cheaper than training rollouts
questions.explanation: pass@4 had the lowest variance, so fewer 30-turn, 65k-token agent rollouts are needed to decide whether the target is reached. Other metrics also work with binary rewards, and all of them require running tests.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
questions.question: Why is pass@4 less noisy than pass@1 on a problem the model solves about 30% of the time?
options: pass@4 is about 1 - 0.7^4 = 0.76, so it flips between 0 and 1 far less than one 30% try
pass@4 is always exactly 1 for such a problem, since four tries cover every failure mode
pass@1 cannot be computed when the solve rate is below 50%, so its estimate is undefined
pass@4 averages the four rewards into a continuous score, which smooths away the noise
questions.explanation: pass@1 at a 30% solve rate flips between 0 and 1 from run to run. pass@4 is 1 - 0.7^4, about 0.76, and is far more stable. It is not always 1, and it is still a binary per-problem outcome, not an average.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
questions.question: In the unbiased pass@k estimator pass@k = 1 - C(n-c, k) / C(n, k), what does C(n-c, k)/C(n, k) represent?
options: The chance that all k picks from the n attempts are successes
The fraction of the n attempts that passed the verifier
The chance that all k picks from the n attempts are failures
The expected number of successes among the k picks
questions.explanation: C(n-c, k) counts k-subsets drawn only from the n-c failures, and C(n, k) counts all k-subsets, so the ratio is the probability a random k-subset has no success. One minus it is the probability of at least one success.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
questions.question: In the unbiased pass@k estimator, what do n and c stand for?
options: n is the attempt budget being scored, c is the number of agent turns per attempt
n is the number of problems in the benchmark, c is the number solved at least once
n is the number of attempts sampled for the problem, c is the number that passed
n is the number of tokens per attempt, c is the context length of the harness
questions.explanation: For each problem you sample n >= k attempts and count c that pass. k is the attempt budget being scored. Averaging the per-problem values over problems gives the benchmark score.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
questions.question: How is a benchmark-level pass@k score obtained from per-problem estimates?
options: By summing c over all problems and dividing by k times n
By averaging the per-problem pass@k values over all problems
By multiplying the per-problem pass@k values across problems
By taking the maximum per-problem pass@k over the benchmark
questions.explanation: Each problem gets its own unbiased pass@k from its (n, c) pair, and the benchmark score is the mean over problems. Max or product would not estimate the expected solve rate.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
questions.question: With n = 8 samples of which c = 2 pass, pass@1 = 0.25 but pass@4 is about 0.786. What does a large pass@k minus pass@1 gap indicate?
options: The model can solve the task but not reliably, so RL has signal to exploit
The task is already fully learned, so any further RL on it is unnecessary
The estimator is biased upward at small n and should be discarded here
The model cannot solve the task at all, and the pass@4 value is pure sampling luck
questions.explanation: A large gap means some samples succeed while most fail: capability exists but is unreliable. That is exactly where GRPO groups contain both successes and failures, giving nonzero advantages to learn from. It is not a sign of bias or of a solved task.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
questions.question: Why use the unbiased estimator with n > k samples rather than just 'sample 4, check if any pass'?
options: Both are unbiased, but the formula uses all n samples, so its variance is lower
'Sample 4, check any' is biased upward, while the formula corrects for that bias
'Sample 4, check any' cannot handle binary rewards, but the formula can
The formula is cheaper, because it needs fewer samples than k per problem
questions.explanation: Drawing exactly k samples and checking any is also unbiased, but it uses only k samples. The combinatorial estimator uses all n samples for the same k, averaging over all k-subsets, which lowers variance. It needs more samples, not fewer.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
questions.question: What are the input and output types of llmre's pass_at_k for one problem?
options: Inputs are tensors of shape (P, G); output is a tensor of shape (P,)
Inputs are Python floats n, c, k; the output is an int count of passes
Inputs are Python ints n, c, k; the output is a Python float in [0, 1]
Inputs are lists of completion strings; output is a boolean per problem
questions.explanation: Per problem, pass_at_k takes integer counts (n, c, k) and returns a float probability in [0, 1]. Over a benchmark you hold a list of (n, c) pairs. It does not operate on tensors or raw completions.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
questions.question: In llmre's pass_at_k, what is returned when n - c < k?
options: 1.0, because every size-k subset must contain a success
c / n, because the estimator falls back to pass@1 there
An error, because the binomial ratio is undefined there
0.0, because there are too few failures to draw k from
questions.explanation: If there are fewer than k failures, any k-subset must include at least one success, so the probability is exactly 1. The function short-circuits and returns 1.0. It is well-defined, not an error or a pass@1 fallback.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
questions.question: How does llmre's pass_at_k compute C(n-c, k)/C(n, k) without building huge binomial coefficients?
options: By Monte Carlo sampling of random k-subsets of the attempts
By using Stirling's approximation for each of the factorials
As the product over i from n-c+1 to n of (1 - k/i)
By computing the factorials in float64 and then dividing
questions.explanation: The ratio equals the product of (1 - k/i) for i = n-c+1..n, which takes c float multiplies. For n = 200, C(200, 100) has 59 digits, so direct factorials would overflow or lose precision. It is exact, not sampled or approximated.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 2.3 Why pass@4 as the validation metric
questions.question: What is the computational cost of llmre's pass_at_k per problem?
options: O(c), negligible next to one rollout
O(n^2), dominating evaluation time
O(2^n), since it enumerates all subsets
O(k * n * c), comparable to a forward pass
questions.explanation: The product form loops c times, so cost is O(c), which is negligible compared with generating even a single agent rollout. It never enumerates subsets.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: A pass@k script reports pass@4 = 1.0 for a problem with n = 4 attempts and c = 1 success. Is it a bug?
options: Yes: pass@4 can never be higher than 4 times pass@1, which here is 0.25
Yes: the correct value is c/n = 0.25, since there is only one success in four
No: pass@4 is always 1 whenever c > 0, for any number n of sampled attempts
No: with n = k = 4 the only 4-subset has the success, but it is high-variance
questions.explanation: n - c = 3 < k = 4, so the single 4-subset includes the one success and pass@4 = 1.0 is correct. But with n = k there is no averaging, so the estimate is noisy; sample n > k (e.g. 16). For larger n with c = 1, pass@4 would be below 1.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Why is reporting pass@k with n = k considered a mistake?
options: It is biased downward, so it always underestimates the true pass@k value
It is unbiased but noisy, with no averaging over subsets; sample more than k
It cannot be computed with the combinatorial formula when n equals k exactly
It double counts successes, so it overestimates pass@k whenever c > 1
questions.explanation: With n = k, the estimator is still unbiased but uses a single subset, so it has high variance. Sampling n > k averages over many k-subsets. It is computable and does not double count.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: What are the two phases of an RL step for LLM agents?
options: Train a reward model on preference data, then train a critic on its scores
Generate rollouts with the current policy (inference-bound), then train on them
Tokenize the task data, then pretrain on it with next-token prediction
Evaluate on held-out tasks, then checkpoint the weights if the held-out score improved
questions.explanation: An RL step generates rollouts with the current policy, which is inference-bound and long for agent episodes, then trains on them with backprop. Run sequentially, each phase leaves the other's GPUs idle.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: What does asynchronous RL do?
options: Skips generation entirely by reusing one fixed dataset of rollouts for every update
Trains several independent policies in parallel and averages their weights each step
Overlaps generation and training; generators use slightly old weights as the trainer updates
Runs training on CPU and generation on GPU, so the two never compete for accelerator memory
questions.explanation: Async RL overlaps the two phases: generators keep producing rollouts with slightly stale weights while the trainer updates. This removes idle time. Reusing a fixed dataset would be offline RL, and averaging policies is a different technique.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: What is policy staleness in async RL?
options: The number of turns an agent episode takes before the harness stops it early
How many weight versions old the generating policy is when its rollout is used
The age of the training tasks in days since they were first added to the pool
How long it has been since the reward model was last retrained on new labels
questions.explanation: Staleness counts weight versions between the policy that generated a rollout and the one being updated with it. With staleness 1, a rollout from version t-1 can be used while producing version t. It is unrelated to reward-model age or episode length.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: With staleness s, how does the GRPO importance ratio r = pi_theta_t(y|x) / pi_theta_(t-s)(y|x) behave as s grows?
options: It becomes independent of the policy, since both terms use the same weights
It drifts further from 1, so more samples get clipped or add higher variance
It stays exactly 1 regardless of s, because GRPO renormalizes within the group
It shrinks toward 0, making the gradients from all stale samples vanish
questions.explanation: Samples come from an older policy, so the ratio drifts away from 1 as the gap grows. More samples fall outside the clip range (wasted) or, if not clipped, add higher-variance gradient estimates. It does not stay at 1 or vanish.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: If one update changes a completion's log-prob by about 0.1, why does staleness 3 hurt more than staleness 1 with a [0.8, 1.2] clip range?
options: Both ratios stay inside the clip range, so staleness has no effect on the gradient in this case
At s = 3 the ratio becomes negative, so the clipped objective flips the sign of that sample's gradient
At s = 1, r is clipped (outside [0.8, 1.2]); at s = 3 it drifts back inside and is not clipped
At s = 1, r ≈ e^0.1 = 1.105 (inside the range); at s = 3, r ≈ e^0.3 = 1.35 (clipped, no gradient)
questions.explanation: Log-prob drift accumulates with staleness: 0.1 per version gives r about 1.105 at s = 1, inside [0.8, 1.2], but about 1.35 at s = 3, outside it, so that sample contributes zero gradient. The numbers are illustrative; the direction is the point. Ratios are always positive.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Why can an MLPerf post-training submitter not simply raise policy staleness to maximize throughput?
options: Higher staleness lowers throughput, since stale rollouts must be regenerated
Staleness only affects memory use, not quality, so it is capped by hardware
Staleness is fixed at 0 by the rules, so generation and training never overlap
The metric is time-to-quality, and more staleness can degrade quality
questions.explanation: More staleness overlaps generation and training more, buying throughput, but increases the off-policy gap and can degrade quality. Since the score is time to reach quality, trading quality for throughput can make the time worse. The reference caps it at 1, not 0.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: In async RL, what connects policy staleness to the off-policy correction seen in PPO?
