options: Both remove the need for a reference model, since the old policy plays that role in the KL term
Both are only relevant when rewards are continuous, because binary rewards need no correction
Both train on older-policy samples via an importance ratio; async RL forces it through system design
Both require a learned critic to estimate how far the old policy has drifted from the current one
questions.explanation: PPO's ratio corrects for reusing a batch sampled from an older policy. In async RL the older policy comes from the system overlapping generation with training. Same correction, different cause. Neither requires a critic or continuous rewards.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Roughly how much data must be transferred per weight sync for a 397B-parameter model in bf16?
options: About 397 MB
About 3.2 TB
About 794 GB
About 34 GB
questions.explanation: bf16 uses 2 bytes per parameter, so 397B x 2 is about 794 GB per sync. How fast you broadcast this from trainer to inference fleet bounds how low staleness can be. 34 GB would be the ~17B active params, but all weights must be transferred.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: What bounds how low policy staleness can be in large-scale async RL?
options: How fast weights can be transferred from the trainer to the inference fleet
The length of the learning-rate warmup before generation can start
The number of hidden tests per task that must run before each update
The tokenizer's vocabulary size, which sets the size of each logit tensor
questions.explanation: Every new weight version must be broadcast to generators before they can use it. For huge models this transfer is large, so its speed limits how fresh the generating policy can be. The other factors don't affect staleness.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Why is generation, rather than training, usually the bottleneck in long-trajectory agent RL?
options: Training uses no GPU memory for activations, so it always finishes before generation does
Each live episode holds a large, growing KV cache over up to 30 turns and 65k context
The verifier must run on the same GPU as the model, blocking generation while tests execute
Tokenization of the agent's outputs is extremely slow for code with long identifiers
questions.explanation: Long multi-turn episodes accumulate big KV caches, consuming memory and limiting how many episodes run in parallel. That makes generation the bottleneck. KV size per token (reduced by GQA) is why it matters. Training still uses activation memory.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: In the MLPerf post-training benchmark, what does '16 generations per prompt' correspond to in GRPO?
options: The GRPO group size G = 16
The number of hidden tests per task
The number of weight versions kept in memory
The number of agent turns per episode
questions.explanation: 16 generations per prompt is the GRPO group: 16 completions sampled for the same prompt whose rewards are standardized into advantages. Turns are capped at 30 separately.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Why are context, turn and group-size budgets fixed in the MLPerf post-training benchmark?
options: Because budgets have little effect on results, so fixing them costs submitters nothing
So submissions compete on systems efficiency, not on letting the agent think longer
Because OpenHands cannot support larger context or turn budgets than these
To keep the benchmark small enough to run on CPU-only submission hardware
questions.explanation: Fixing budgets removes 'we let the agent think longer' as a lever, so the competition is about systems efficiency. Budgets do affect results strongly, which is exactly why they must be fixed and logged.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Why is a pass@1 number reported without its turn and context budget not comparable to anything?
options: Because budgets only affect training speed, not quality, so they are reported separately
Because pass@1 is mathematically undefined unless the turn budget is stated with it
Because pass@1 must always be reported together with pass@16 under the MLPerf rules
Budgets move results as much as learning rate does, so they are part of what was measured
questions.explanation: Turn, context and group budgets are hyperparameters that move results as much as LR. A score without them hides a major variable. Log them per run so numbers can be compared.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Why is comparing agent scores across different harnesses or budgets a mistake?
options: Model + harness + budget is the unit measured, so changing any part changes the system
Because harnesses only affect latency, so their scores differ only in wall-clock time to finish
Because budgets are always identical across papers, so only the harness differs
Because only the model weights determine the score, and those are rarely released
questions.explanation: The measured unit is model + harness + budget. A different harness or budget measures a different system, so scores are not comparable. Weights alone do not determine agent performance.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 3. GRPO with binary rewards, by hand
questions.question: In a GRPO group of 4 attempts with rewards [1, 0, 0, 0], how are the advantages distributed?
options: The one success gets a large positive advantage (≈1.73); each failure a small negative one (≈-0.58)
The success gets 0, since it equals the group maximum, and each failure gets -0.25 below the mean
All four attempts get the same advantage of 0.25, the group's mean reward, before clipping
The success gets +1 and each failure gets -1, since binary rewards are mapped to signs
questions.explanation: Mean is 0.25 and population std is about 0.433, so A = (r - 0.25)/0.433 = [1.732, -0.577, -0.577, -0.577]. The rare success is pushed up strongly; each failure is pushed down a little. The advantages sum to zero.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 3. GRPO with binary rewards, by hand
questions.question: Why does a GRPO group in which every attempt fails give no gradient?
options: The KL penalty cancels the policy-gradient term exactly when every reward is zero
All rewards are equal, so std = 0 and every advantage is 0 (the eps guard returns zeros)
The loss becomes infinite from dividing by a zero std, so the step is skipped
The verifier refuses to score failed attempts, so the group has no rewards at all
questions.explanation: With identical rewards the group mean equals each reward and std is 0, so all advantages are 0 and an eps guard prevents division by zero. There is no better-than-average completion to reinforce. The same holds if all succeed.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 3. GRPO with binary rewards, by hand
questions.question: Why do tasks with pass@G near 0 contribute nothing to GRPO training?
options: If no attempt in the group of G succeeds, all rewards and advantages are 0
Because the verifier skips hard tasks once their failure rate passes a threshold
Because hard tasks are filtered out by the harness before any rollouts are made
Because the importance ratio is always clipped on them, so they give no gradient
questions.explanation: pass@G near 0 means groups almost always contain no success, so rewards are uniformly 0 and advantages vanish. That is why the pass@k - pass@1 gap matters: training signal needs mixed groups.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 3. GRPO with binary rewards, by hand
questions.question: Which llmre function computes GRPO's group-standardized advantages?
options: llmre.rl.ppo.compute_advantages
llmre.rl.grpo.grpo_advantages
llmre.evaluation.pass_at_k.pass_at_k
llmre.rl.gvpo.gvpo_loss
questions.explanation: grpo_advantages in llmre/rl/grpo.py standardizes rewards per group, e.g. [[1, 0, 0, 0]] -> [[1.7321, -0.5774, -0.5774, -0.5774]]. pass_at_k is the evaluation estimator, compute_advantages is PPO's, and gvpo_loss is a different objective.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Which of these is listed as part of eval design for agents in the MLPerf frontier update?
options: Checking right tool selection versus following instructions inside it, with per-step evidence
Using a different harness for each eval run, so that the score reflects robustness to tooling
Reporting a single aggregate score only, so that releases are compared on one number
Gating releases on training loss reaching a threshold rather than on held-out evals
questions.explanation: Eval design for agents separates tool selection from instruction-following within the tool, uses deterministic routing checks, prefers per-step evidence over one aggregate number, and gates releases on evals passing. A single aggregate or training loss hides failures.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Before claiming a gain, what reproducibility step is recommended in the MLPerf frontier update?
options: Run a single seed and report the best checkpoint by its held-out score
Increase the eval set size until the observed gain becomes significant
Compare the training loss curves between runs to confirm the gain is real
Measure the noise floor, e.g. the score shift from a dtype conversion alone
questions.explanation: Measure the noise floor first: the score change from mere checkpoint-format or dtype conversion tells you how big a real gain must be. Also prefer held-out metrics over loss curves and check results across seeds. A single best-seed number is the anti-pattern.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Which RLVR mechanics are listed as the first learning priority from the MLPerf update?
options: Group-relative advantage, binary verifiable rewards, hidden-test defenses, pass@k choice, async staleness
LoRA rank selection, post-training quantization, structured pruning, and adapter merging for model deployment
Tokenizer training, data deduplication, positional encodings, and long-context pretraining schedules
Image augmentation, contrastive losses, diffusion noise schedules, and classifier-free guidance
questions.explanation: The first priority is RLVR mechanics: GRPO's group-relative advantage, binary verifiable rewards, reward-hacking defenses like hidden tests, choosing pass@k, and policy staleness. The other topics are from other parts of ML.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 5. Lab: turn a function-calling task set into a minimal RLVR loop
questions.question: What minimum hardware does the function-calling RLVR lab require?
options: 1x 24 GB GPU (e.g. RTX 4090 / A10G), a ≤3B model with LoRA; CPU-only does not work
A single 8 GB GPU running full fine-tuning of a 7B model in bf16 with gradient checkpointing
8x H100 GPUs for a 70B model, since RLVR needs the full policy plus a reference copy
A laptop CPU with 8 GB RAM, since the lab uses only small models and tiny tasks
questions.explanation: The minimum is one 24 GB GPU with a <=3B model and LoRA; recommended is one 80 GB GPU for a 7B model with LoRA. CPU-only fails for the real lab, though pass@k and GVPO code runs on CPU. Expected cost is roughly 4-20 GPU-hours (an estimate).

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 5. Lab: turn a function-calling task set into a minimal RLVR loop
questions.question: In the function-calling RLVR lab, how should each task's programmatic check be wrapped?
options: As a perplexity score of the completion under the reference model
As a learned reward model trained on human labels of completions
As a continuous similarity between completion and gold-answer embeddings
As reward(task, completion) -> 0.0 or 1.0, like arithmetic_verifier
questions.explanation: Each task's pass/fail check becomes a binary verifiable reward, exactly like arithmetic_verifier in the RLVR lesson. Learned reward models and similarity scores are hackable proxies; perplexity does not measure correctness.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 5. Lab: turn a function-calling task set into a minimal RLVR loop
questions.question: What reward-hacking tripwire does the function-calling RLVR lab require?
options: A hidden held-out task split the loop never sees, with check files out of the policy's reach
Training only on the held-out split, so that any gaming shows up in the reported metric
A penalty for every tool call the agent makes, so it cannot probe the checker repeatedly
Showing the agent the gold answers up front, so that it has no incentive to guess or game
questions.explanation: Split tasks into train and a hidden held-out set never seen in training, and keep code/test files used by checks inaccessible to the policy. Showing gold answers creates a hack target, and tool-call penalties don't detect gaming.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 5. Lab: turn a function-calling task set into a minimal RLVR loop
questions.question: In the function-calling RLVR lab, which metrics are reported on the held-out split before and after RL?
options: Only the training reward, averaged over the last 100 steps
Only pass@16, estimated from a single rollout per prompt
pass@1 and pass@4, via pass_at_k from 4-8 rollouts per prompt
Perplexity and BLEU against the reference tool-call strings
questions.explanation: Sample 4-8 rollouts per prompt and report pass@1 and pass@4 on the held-out split, watching the gap. Training reward alone can be gamed; perplexity/BLEU do not measure task success; pass@16 cannot be estimated from one rollout.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 5. Lab: turn a function-calling task set into a minimal RLVR loop
questions.question: Which budgets must be fixed and logged per run in the function-calling RLVR lab?
options: Only the number of GPUs and the wall-clock time per run
The tokenizer vocabulary size and the embedding dimension
Max context, max turns, group size and sampling temperature
Only the learning rate and the warmup schedule of the run
questions.explanation: Context, turns, group size and temperature all move results and must be fixed and logged, one line per run. Logging only LR or GPU count misses budget variables that change scores.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 5. Lab: turn a function-calling task set into a minimal RLVR loop
questions.question: What GRPO implementation does the function-calling RLVR lab suggest for running at scale, and what does it do?
options: TRL's GRPOTrainer: the same group sampling, standardized advantages and clipped ratio as from scratch
PEFT's DPOTrainer, which turns GRPO into offline preference learning on chosen/rejected pairs
DeepSpeed's PPOTrainer, which adds a learned critic and GAE on top of the group baseline
vLLM's GRPOTrainer, which replaces stochastic group sampling with greedy decoding for speed
questions.explanation: The lab suggests TRL's GRPOTrainer; it implements the same mechanism you built from scratch (group sampling, standardized advantages, clipped ratio) at scale. The other options misname tools or change the algorithm.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: 5. Lab: turn a function-calling task set into a minimal RLVR loop
questions.question: What should the one-page decision note at the end of the function-calling RLVR lab answer?
options: How much the training reward increased and how quickly it plateaued over the run
Which hyperparameters gave the lowest training loss across the sweep of RL runs
Whether RL beat the SFT/LoRA baseline on held-out, at what cost, and where reward was gamed
How many tokens the tokenizer produced per task and how that changed the available context budget
questions.explanation: The note should report held-out improvement over the SFT/LoRA baseline, compute cost, and any reward gaming. Training reward and loss are not evidence that RL helped.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: An RLVR run shows train pass@1 rising from 0.40 to 0.85 but held-out pass@1 only from 0.38 to 0.41. What is the first thing to check?
options: Train longer, since held-out metrics always lag training metrics by several hundred steps
Read ~20 successful train rollouts for gaming: edited checks, hard-coded outputs, special-cased IDs
Switch the held-out split to the training tasks so both metrics measure the same distribution
Increase the learning rate so the held-out gains catch up with the training gains faster
questions.explanation: A large train-only gain means overfitting to train tasks or exploiting the train-side checker. The first action is to inspect successful train rollouts for gaming. Training longer or with a higher LR will likely deepen the problem.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: In an RLVR run, held-out pass@4 drops from 0.62 to 0.60 while held-out pass@1 rises slightly. What does this indicate?
options: Mode collapse: sampling diversity dropped, so extra attempts help less
That the verifier became stricter during training as checks were updated
A bug in the pass@k estimator, since pass@4 can never fall while pass@1 rises
Better exploration, since pass@4 should fall as pass@1 rises in healthy runs
questions.explanation: pass@4 falling while pass@1 barely rises means the policy is concentrating on one strategy, so multiple attempts are less diverse. Fixes: raise the KL coefficient or temperature, stop earlier, add more diverse train tasks.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Which fixes are suggested for RL mode collapse, where held-out pass@4 falls while pass@1 rises?
options: Lower the temperature to zero and train longer, so the policy settles on its best strategy
Reduce the group size to 1, so each update follows a single trajectory with less noise
Remove the KL penalty entirely, so the policy is free to explore away from the reference
Raise the KL coefficient or temperature, stop earlier, or add more diverse train tasks
questions.explanation: Collapse is loss of diversity; a stronger KL to the reference, higher temperature, earlier stopping and more diverse tasks counteract it. Zero temperature, no KL, or group size 1 all reduce diversity or signal further.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Why is trusting training reward curves a common mistake in RLVR?
options: Training reward is not logged by standard GRPO implementations, so the curves are reconstructed
Only held-out metrics show whether RL helped; training reward can rise via gaming or overfitting
Training reward cannot be computed for binary rewards, so the curve is a smoothed proxy metric
Training reward is always lower than held-out reward, so the curves understate real progress
questions.explanation: Rising training reward can reflect reward hacking or memorization. Only held-out metrics, on tasks the loop never sees, show real improvement.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.question: Why is letting the policy see or edit the reward's inputs a mistake in RLVR?
options: It prevents the policy from using tools, since the reward files lock the sandbox
Visible tests, writable config or accessible gold answers all become hacking targets
It slows training because of the extra file I/O every time the reward is computed
It makes the reward continuous instead of binary, which breaks GRPO's advantages
questions.explanation: Anything the policy can read or write that feeds the reward can be exploited, as when agents deleted failing tests. Keep the reward's inputs hidden from the policy.

questions.chapter_name: MLPerf post-training: RLVR as a benchmark
questions.section: What to read / what to skip
questions.question: Which section of the Codex paper should be read for the pass@k estimator?
options: Section 7 on broader impacts
The UI and deployment sections
The appendix on tokenization
Section 2.1
questions.explanation: The Codex paper (Chen et al. 2021) section 2.1 introduces the unbiased pass@k estimator. The reading guide also recommends R2E-Gym's environment-construction and hybrid-verifier sections, and skimming OpenHands architecture while skipping its UI sections.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What is the status of GVPO as a replacement for GRPO, as of September 2026?
options: Validated at scale and adopted as the default RL objective in several frontier labs
Directional, not validated: one paper line and no known frontier-lab adoption
Required by the MLPerf post-training benchmark as the reference RL objective
Deprecated after follow-up work showed it diverges on long reasoning traces
questions.explanation: GVPO is described as directional, not validated: a single paper line with no known frontier-lab adoption. It is worth studying to understand the design space, not to swap into a production pipeline. MLPerf uses GRPO.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: Which earlier ideas do the GRPO fixes (Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO) reuse, combined differently?
options: Byte-level BPE merges and rotary positional encodings
LoRA adapters and input-output embedding weight tying
MinHash deduplication and benchmark decontamination
PPO clipping and DPO's closed-form optimum
questions.explanation: The fixes reuse ideas already covered: PPO-style clipping (DAPO's decoupled clip) and DPO's closed form for KL-constrained reward maximization (GVPO). Tokenizer, LoRA and data tooling are unrelated.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What is the minimum of llmre's gvpo_loss, as a policy?
options: pi* equal to pi_ref, regardless of reward
pi* proportional to pi_ref * exp(R/beta)
pi* putting all mass on the highest-reward sample
pi* proportional to exp(-R * beta)
questions.explanation: gvpo_loss is minimized exactly at pi* proportional to pi_ref(y|x) exp(R(x,y)/beta), the closed-form solution of KL-constrained reward maximization. It neither ignores reward nor collapses to argmax unless beta goes to 0.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What is the GRPO per-sample objective?
options: min(r_i A_i, clip(r_i, 1-eps, 1+eps) A_i), r_i the policy/old-policy ratio, A_i the standardized group reward
max(r_i A_i, clip(r_i, 1-eps, 1+eps) A_i), with r_i the policy/old-policy ratio and A_i the raw reward R_i itself
log r_i - beta * A_i, with r_i the policy/reference ratio and A_i the token count of the completion
r_i * A_i with no clipping at all, where A_i comes from a learned critic's value estimate per sample
questions.explanation: GRPO takes the PPO clipped surrogate min(r_i A_i, clip(r_i, 1-eps, 1+eps) A_i), with r_i = pi_theta(y_i|x)/pi_old(y_i|x) and A_i = (R_i - mean R)/std(R). Taking the max would remove the pessimistic bound, and there is no critic.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: Why is GRPO's importance ratio r_i a source of instability on long completions?
options: r_i is always exactly 1 for long completions, so the update degenerates to plain REINFORCE on reward
r_i ignores the current policy and depends only on the reward, so it swings whenever rewards change
r_i is bounded between 0 and 1 by construction, so long completions get vanishing gradient weight
log r_i is a sum over hundreds of tokens, so small per-token drift compounds and r_i is unbounded
questions.explanation: The sequence ratio is a product of per-token ratios, so its log is a sum; small drifts add up over long sequences and r_i can grow without bound. It is not bounded in [0,1] and does depend on the policy.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What does clipping in GRPO not fix about the importance ratio?
options: It forces the ratio to a constant 1 outside the clip range, which biases the gradient toward the old policy
It makes long completions cheaper to generate but does nothing about the ratio's effect on the update
It caps the objective, not the variance, and clipped samples give zero gradient (wasted compute)
It removes all variance from the gradient, but only for samples whose ratio stays inside the range
questions.explanation: Clipping bounds the surrogate objective, not the variance of the ratio, and clipped samples give no gradient, so their generation compute is wasted. It does not change generation cost or force the ratio to 1.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What bias does dividing by std(R) in GRPO's advantage introduce?
options: It up-weights low-variance groups, i.e. nearly-all-right or nearly-all-wrong groups
It removes all differences in difficulty between prompts, so hard prompts count equally
It down-weights groups with low reward variance, so near-unanimous groups barely count
It biases training toward shorter completions, since short answers have lower variance
questions.explanation: Dividing by a small std inflates advantages, so low-variance groups (almost all correct or almost all wrong) get extra weight. That is one of the normalization biases Dr. GRPO removes. Length bias comes from the separate 1/|y_i| normalization.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What does per-sequence length normalization 1/|y_i| in GRPO change?
options: How much long versus short answers are penalized
The effective value of the KL coefficient beta in the loss
The size of the vocabulary seen by the loss
How many samples are drawn in each group
questions.explanation: Normalizing each sequence's loss by its length changes the per-token weight, so long and short answers are penalized differently. Dr. GRPO argues this biases training, e.g. toward long wrong answers.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: Why do zero-signal groups shrink GRPO's effective batch?
options: All-correct or all-wrong groups have A = 0 for every sample, so no gradient
They make the importance ratio infinite, so the loss has to mask those samples
They are counted twice in the loss, so the batch is renormalized to compensate
They are rejected by the verifier before training, so they are never generated
questions.explanation: When all rewards in a group are equal, every advantage is zero, so those samples cost compute but give no gradient, reducing the effective batch. DAPO's dynamic sampling targets exactly this.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What does Dr. GRPO change relative to GRPO?
options: Removes the 1/|y_i| length normalization and the std division
Adds a learned critic to replace the group-mean reward baseline
Replaces the clipped ratio with a closed-form weight per sample
Adds overlong-response reward shaping and a decoupled clip range
questions.explanation: Dr. GRPO (Liu et al. 2025, arXiv 2503.20783) removes length normalization and std normalization, arguing both bias training, e.g. toward long wrong answers. The closed-form weight is GVPO; overlong shaping is DAPO.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: Which of these is one of DAPO's changes to GRPO?
options: Clip-higher: a decoupled, larger upper epsilon for the clip
Dropping the policy gradient in favor of a supervised loss
Replacing the verifier with a learned reward model
Removing the group and using a single sample per prompt instead
questions.explanation: DAPO (Yu et al. 2025, arXiv 2503.14476) uses decoupled clip ('clip-higher'), dynamic sampling, token-level loss averaging and overlong-response reward shaping. It keeps groups and verifiable rewards.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What is DAPO's dynamic sampling?
options: Changing the group size every step based on how many groups had any reward signal
Sampling a random temperature for each completion to diversify the group's outputs
Dropping all-0 and all-1 groups and refilling the batch with groups that carry signal
Resampling the reference model each epoch from a recent checkpoint of the policy
questions.explanation: Dynamic sampling removes unanimous groups (all wrong or all right), which have zero advantage, and refills the batch so every group contributes gradient. It is not about temperature, group size or the reference.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: Which DAPO change addresses how the loss is averaged?
options: Prompt-level reward clipping
Sequence-level std normalization
Token-level loss averaging
Group-level weight tying
questions.explanation: DAPO averages the loss at the token level rather than per sequence, changing how long completions contribute. Its other tricks are clip-higher, dynamic sampling and overlong reward shaping.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What is the status of DAPO according to the GRPO fixes comparison?
options: Withdrawn after publication over evaluation errors
Publicly documented and used in open RL stacks
Directional and unvalidated, with no known adoption
Proprietary to a single frontier lab and undisclosed
questions.explanation: DAPO is publicly documented and used in open RL stacks. Dr. GRPO is publicly documented and widely discussed. GVPO is the directional one with no known frontier adoption.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: How does GVPO differ from GRPO in what it replaces?
options: It replaces the reference policy with the old policy, so the KL term anchors on the last sampling step
It replaces group sampling with chosen/rejected preference pairs, so each prompt needs only two samples
It replaces ratio + clip with a weight from the closed-form KL-constrained optimum; no importance sampling
It replaces the verifier with a learned reward model, so rewards become continuous instead of binary
questions.explanation: GVPO (Zhang et al. 2025, arXiv 2504.19599) drops the importance ratio and clipping and weights each sample with a term derived from the KL-constrained closed form. It keeps groups and verifiable rewards and anchors on the reference, not the old policy.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What is the key distinction between Dr. GRPO/DAPO and GVPO?
options: Dr. GRPO and DAPO patch GRPO, while GVPO changes the objective
Dr. GRPO and DAPO change the objective, while GVPO only patches normalization
All three are identical up to hyperparameters
GVPO is a pretraining method, the others are RL methods
questions.explanation: Dr. GRPO and DAPO keep the GRPO objective and fix specific weaknesses. GVPO replaces the objective itself with a centered regression onto the closed-form optimum, which is why it is worth understanding even before adopting it.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What does the GVPO++ paper extend GVPO to?
options: Multimodal pretraining
Speculative decoding
Tokenizer merge training
On-policy distillation
questions.explanation: GVPO++ (arXiv 2609.21432) presents on-policy distillation as a natural extension: replace the verifier reward with the teacher's log-probability of the student's sample. It is not about tokenizers, multimodal pretraining or decoding.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What is the closed-form solution to 'maximize reward while staying close to a reference policy in KL'?
options: pi*(y|x) = (1/Z(x)) (pi_ref(y|x) + beta R(x,y))
pi*(y|x) = (1/Z(x)) pi_ref(y|x)^beta R(x,y)
pi*(y|x) = (1/Z(x)) pi_ref(y|x) exp(R(x,y)/beta)
pi*(y|x) = softmax(R(x,y)/beta), with no reference
questions.explanation: The KL-constrained optimum reweights the reference by exp(R/beta) and normalizes by the partition function Z(x). DPO is built on it, and GVPO uses it on GRPO groups. Additive or reference-free forms are not the solution.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: How does GVPO's use of the KL-constrained closed form differ from DPO's?
options: DPO uses it on preference pairs; GVPO uses it on a GRPO group of sampled completions
Both use it only on single completions, so Z(x) is estimated separately for each sample
GVPO does not use the closed form at all; it keeps GRPO's ratio and only changes the KL
DPO uses it on groups of completions; GVPO uses it on chosen/rejected preference pairs
questions.explanation: DPO applies the closed form to a chosen/rejected pair, where Z(x) cancels in the difference. GVPO applies it to a whole group of completions for a prompt, where Z(x) cancels after subtracting the group mean.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What is the obstacle to using the KL-constrained closed form directly, and how does GVPO get around it?
options: pi_ref is unknown, so GVPO replaces it with the uniform distribution over the completions in each group
Z(x) is intractable, but it is shared by all completions of a prompt, so subtracting the group mean cancels it
beta cannot be chosen in advance, so GVPO learns it from data jointly with the policy parameters
R is non-differentiable, so GVPO approximates the verifier with a neural network trained alongside the policy
questions.explanation: The partition function Z(x) sums over all possible completions and is intractable. Because it is shared by all completions of the same prompt, comparing within a group by centering removes it. That is the whole trick.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: In GVPO, what is the implicit reward R_theta(x, y) of the current policy?
options: beta * log pi_theta(y|x) alone
beta * log(pi_theta(y|x) / pi_ref(y|x))
R(x, y) - beta * log Z(x), computed directly
beta * log(pi_theta(y|x) / pi_old(y|x))
questions.explanation: The implicit reward is beta times the log-ratio of the policy to the reference, the same DPO quantity. At the optimum it equals R(x,y) - beta log Z(x). The ratio to pi_old is GRPO's importance ratio, which GVPO drops.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: In GVPO notation, what role does beta > 0 play?
options: The clipping epsilon that bounds how far the ratio can move per step
The learning rate of the optimizer applied to the policy parameters
The KL strength controlling how far the policy may move from the reference
The group size G, i.e. the number of completions sampled per prompt
questions.explanation: beta is the KL-constraint strength: small beta lets the policy move far from pi_ref, large beta keeps it close. It is not the LR, group size or clip parameter (GVPO has no clip).

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: At the GVPO optimum, how is the implicit reward related to the actual reward?
options: R_theta(x, y) = R(x, y) exactly, for every y
R_theta(x, y) = beta R(x, y) - log Z(x)
R_theta(x, y) = 0 for all y at the optimum
R_theta(x, y) = R(x, y) - beta log Z(x)
questions.explanation: Plugging pi* into the implicit-reward definition gives R(x,y) - beta log Z(x). The offset is the same for every completion of a prompt, which is why centering over the group removes it.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What does the GVPO loss minimize?
options: Half the summed squared mismatch between group-centered implicit reward and group-centered actual reward
The cross-entropy between the policy's sequence probabilities and the verifier's binary correctness labels
The KL divergence between the current policy and the old sampling policy, with no reward term at all
The negative clipped surrogate of the standardized advantage, summed over every completion in the group
questions.explanation: L_GVPO = 1/2 sum_x sum_i [(R_theta(x,y_i) - mean R_theta) - (R(x,y_i) - mean R)]^2. It is a centered regression of implicit reward onto actual reward. There is no clipped surrogate.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: How should the bracket in GVPO's gradient, (R_i - mean R) - beta(l_i - mean l), be read?
options: As the importance ratio between the new and old policy, clipped to a fixed trust region
As the standardized advantage divided by the group's reward standard deviation, per sample
As a per-token entropy bonus that keeps the policy from collapsing onto one answer too early
As a weight on each sample's log-prob gradient: centered reward minus how far the policy moved
questions.explanation: Each sample's grad log pi is weighted by its centered reward minus beta times its centered log-ratio to the reference. Once the policy has moved enough toward a good sample, the weight reaches zero. It is not a ratio or entropy term.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: In GVPO's gradient, what does l_i denote?
options: log(pi_theta(y_i|x) / pi_ref(y_i|x))
log(pi_theta(y_i|x) / pi_old(y_i|x))
The length |y_i| of completion y_i in tokens
The reward R_i of completion y_i
questions.explanation: l_i is the log-ratio of the current policy to the reference for sample i; beta * l_i is the implicit reward. It is not the old-policy ratio or the completion length.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What property of GVPO's gradient weights makes Z(x) drop out?
options: The weights are all positive within a group
The weights sum to zero within each group
The weights are clipped to [1-eps, 1+eps]
The weights all equal one over the group size
questions.explanation: Because both reward and log-ratio are centered, the weights sum to zero within each group, so any constant shared across the group, like beta log Z(x), contributes nothing. The paper also proves a unique optimum at pi*.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: How do GRPO and GVPO weight each sample's log-prob gradient?
options: Both by r_i A_i with clipping, but GVPO uses a larger upper epsilon and no KL term
GRPO by r_i A_i (ratio times standardized reward); GVPO by centered reward minus beta times centered log-ratio
Both by the raw reward R_i, with GVPO adding a reference KL penalty after the group mean is removed
GRPO by centered reward only, with no ratio; GVPO by the importance ratio only, with no reward centering
questions.explanation: GRPO uses the ratio times standardized advantage, clipped. GVPO uses (R_i - mean R) - beta(l_i - mean l): no ratio and no clip. The second term acts as a built-in brake.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: Why does the second term in GVPO's weight act as a 'built-in brake'?
options: It clips the importance ratio at 1+eps, so a good sample can only be up-weighted a little per step
It reduces the effective learning rate over time, so later updates are smaller regardless of the samples
It stops training after a fixed number of steps, once the policy has drifted a set KL from the reference
Once the policy has moved enough toward a good sample, the centered log-ratio cancels its centered reward
questions.explanation: As the policy raises a good sample's probability relative to the reference, beta times its centered log-ratio grows until it equals the centered reward, at which point the weight is zero. That stops further movement without explicit clipping.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What does the GVPO paper prove about its objective?
options: It is equivalent to the PPO clipped objective with eps set to beta
It has a unique optimum at pi* proportional to pi_ref exp(R/beta)
It has many optima, one per random seed, all with equal expected reward
It converges to the old sampling policy pi_old as training proceeds
questions.explanation: The paper proves the GVPO objective has a unique optimum at the KL-constrained closed-form policy. It is not equivalent to PPO's clipped objective and does not converge to pi_old.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: In GVPO with k = 2, beta = 1, rewards [1, 0] and pi_theta = pi_ref, what are the gradient weights at the start?
options: -0.5 on the rewarded sample and +0.5 on the other
0 on both, since the policy equals the reference
+0.5 on the rewarded sample and -0.5 on the other
+1 on the rewarded sample and 0 on the other
questions.explanation: Centered rewards are [0.5, -0.5] and centered implicit rewards are [0, 0] at the reference, so the weights are 0.5 - 0 and -0.5 - 0. The policy raises log pi of the rewarded sample and lowers the other. The starting loss is 0.25.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: In GVPO with two samples, rewards [1, 0] and beta = 1, where does training stop?
options: When both samples have equal probability under the policy, so neither one is preferred over the other
When the rewarded sample has probability 1, so the policy has become deterministic on this prompt
When the policy exactly equals the reference again, after an initial overshoot toward the reward
When l_1 - l_2 = (R_1 - R_2)/beta = 1, i.e. the probability ratio is e times the reference's
questions.explanation: It stops when the centered implicit reward equals the centered reward, i.e. l_1 - l_2 = 1, so pi(y_1)/pi(y_2) = e * pi_ref(y_1)/pi_ref(y_2), exactly the ratio pi* prescribes. It does not go to a deterministic policy.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: In GVPO, how does a small beta (e.g. 0.1) change the target policy compared with beta = 1, for rewards [1, 0]?
options: The loss becomes undefined for beta < 1, since the target log-ratio diverges
The target ratio becomes e^0.1, about 1.105, so the policy barely moves at all
The target ratio becomes e^10 (about 22026), so the policy moves much further
The target ratio is unchanged, because beta cancels when the group is centered
questions.explanation: The target log-ratio difference is (R_1 - R_2)/beta, so beta = 0.1 gives 10 and a ratio of e^10, about 22026. Small beta weakens the KL constraint. It does not cancel and is defined for any beta > 0.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: With beta = 0.5, three samples with rewards [1, 1, 0] and a uniform reference, what probabilities does GVPO's optimum assign?
questions.explanation: pi* is proportional to pi_ref exp(R/beta) = e^2, e^2, e^0. With e^2 about 7.389, the total is 15.778, giving about [0.468, 0.468, 0.063]. Check: log(0.468/0.063) is about 2 = (1-0)/0.5. It is never exactly 0 for the zero-reward sample.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What is the shape of the logprobs tensor passed to llmre's gvpo_loss?
options: (P, G, T): per-token log-probs for each completion
(P, G): prompts by group size, each a summed log-prob
(G,): one log-prob per group, averaged over prompts
(P, V): log-probs over the vocabulary for each prompt
questions.explanation: logprobs is (P, G) with P prompts and G completions per prompt, each a sum of token log-probs, requiring grad. Per-token tensors would be (P, G, T), which is a common mistake since the derivation is over whole completions.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: Which input to llmre's gvpo_loss comes from a frozen forward pass with no gradient?
options: rewards (P, G)
ref_logprobs (P, G)
beta (a scalar float)
logprobs (P, G)
questions.explanation: ref_logprobs comes from the frozen reference model forward, with no grad. logprobs comes from the policy and requires grad. rewards are 0/1 verifier outputs, and beta is a scalar hyperparameter.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: In llmre's gvpo_loss, what does reduction='none' return?
options: A scalar mean over all prompts
A per-token loss of shape (P, G, T)
A per-prompt loss of shape (P,)
A per-sample loss of shape (P, G)
questions.explanation: With reduction='none', gvpo_loss returns the per-prompt loss of shape (P,), since the squared mismatch is summed over the group dimension. 'mean' reduces to a scalar.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: In llmre's gvpo_loss, what is the first computed quantity?
options: advantages = (rewards - mean) / std, shape (P, G)
implicit = beta * (logprobs - ref_logprobs), shape (P, G)
kl = logprobs.exp() * (logprobs - ref_logprobs), shape (P,)
ratio = exp(logprobs - old_logprobs), shape (P, G)
questions.explanation: gvpo_loss starts from the implicit reward beta * (logprobs - ref_logprobs). It then centers this and the rewards over dim=1 and sums half the squared difference over the group. There is no old-policy ratio or std standardization.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: In llmre's gvpo_loss, over which dimension are the implicit reward and rewards centered?
options: Over all elements of the batch at once, with keepdim=False
dim=0, the prompt dimension, with keepdim=True
Over the token dimension, before summing each sequence
dim=1, the group dimension, with keepdim=True
questions.explanation: Centering is per prompt, over the G completions (dim=1), so that each prompt's Z(x) cancels. Centering over the batch would mix prompts with different Z(x), breaking the cancellation.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: In llmre's gvpo_loss, what is the GVPO loss when logprobs equals ref_logprobs, with two samples, rewards [1, 0] and beta = 1?
questions.explanation: At the reference the centered implicit reward is [0, 0] while centered reward is [0.5, -0.5], so the loss is 0.5 * (0.25 + 0.25) = 0.25. The loss is 0 only at the optimum.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: How can you construct the GVPO optimum in code to verify gvpo_loss gives zero?
options: ref - R * beta, subtracted elementwise without any normalization
torch.log(R + ref.exp()), elementwise, then normalized by the sum
torch.log_softmax(ref + R / beta, dim=1), i.e. pi_ref * exp(R/beta) / Z
torch.softmax(R / beta, dim=0), ignoring the reference entirely
questions.explanation: log_softmax over the group of log pi_ref + R/beta gives the normalized log of pi_ref exp(R/beta), exactly pi*. Passing it as logprobs yields loss 0 up to float error. The other forms are not the optimum.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: Besides convergence to the optimum, what invariance does code/tests/test_frontier_updates.py check for GVPO?
options: Changing beta while keeping the same rewards leaves the loss unchanged
Adding any per-prompt constant to the rewards leaves the loss unchanged
Multiplying all rewards by any positive constant leaves the loss unchanged
Swapping logprobs and ref_logprobs in the call leaves the loss unchanged
questions.explanation: Because rewards are centered within each group, adding a constant per prompt cancels. The test also runs gradient descent from uniform and checks convergence to softmax(log pi_ref + R/beta). Scaling rewards or changing beta does change the loss.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.section: 3.6 Cost and what real frameworks would do
questions.question: How does GVPO's compute cost compare with GRPO with a KL term?
options: Twice as many forward passes, because centering needs a second pass over each group
It requires generating twice as many samples per prompt to estimate the group mean
Same passes: policy log-probs with grad plus a frozen reference forward; loss is O(PG)
It needs a learned critic forward pass in addition to the policy and the reference
questions.explanation: GVPO uses the same passes as GRPO-with-KL: policy log-probs (with grad) and a frozen reference forward. The loss is O(PG) elementwise operations. No critic or extra sampling is needed.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.section: 3.6 Cost and what real frameworks would do
questions.question: What memory does GVPO avoid compared with GRPO?
options: Storing old-policy log-probs for importance ratios
Storing the policy's gradients between optimizer steps
Storing the frozen reference model's weights in memory
Storing the verifier rewards for every sampled group
questions.explanation: GVPO has no ratio, so there are no old-policy log-probs to keep; the reference forward replaces them. The reference model is still in memory, as in GRPO-with-KL.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.section: 3.6 Cost and what real frameworks would do
questions.question: What guarantee does GVPO not provide by itself, because it has no ratio?
options: A unique optimum of the objective at the closed-form KL policy
Compatibility with binary 0/1 verifier rewards on each sample
The 'safe to reuse this batch for several steps' guarantee of clipping
Cancellation of the partition function Z(x) within each prompt's group
questions.explanation: Clipping in PPO/GRPO limits how far reuse of a batch can push the policy. GVPO lacks that, so its behavior with batch reuse or async staleness is an open practical question (marked as inference). It does have a unique optimum, Z cancellation, and works with binary rewards.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.section: 4. On-policy distillation (why the paper mentions it)
questions.question: How does GVPO become on-policy distillation?
options: Replace the reference policy with the teacher and set beta = 0, so the student copies the teacher's distribution
Train the student on teacher-generated samples with cross-entropy, using the GVPO group as the minibatch
Replace the verifier reward with the teacher's log-prob of the student's own sample: R = log pi_teacher(y|x)
Replace each group with a single teacher completion and regress the student's log-prob onto the teacher's
questions.explanation: Using R = log pi_teacher(y|x) on samples the student itself generated, the same centered-MSE loss pushes the student toward the teacher on its own samples. Same code, different reward. Training on teacher samples is off-policy distillation.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: Why is treating GVPO as a drop-in replacement for production GRPO a mistake?
options: It is mathematically equivalent to GRPO, so swapping it in gains nothing in practice
It requires human preference pairs that typical GRPO pipelines do not collect
It is unvalidated at frontier scale; run it only as an ablation against a GRPO baseline
It cannot be implemented efficiently in PyTorch without custom fused CUDA kernels
questions.explanation: GVPO has no validation at frontier scale, so the safe use is an ablation compared to a GRPO baseline on the same seeds. It is not equivalent to GRPO, is implementable (llmre/rl/gvpo.py), and uses group rewards, not pairs.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What goes wrong if you forget to center both terms in the GVPO loss?
options: Nothing; centering only improves numerical stability
The loss becomes identical to DPO
The gradients become exactly zero
Z(x) no longer cancels, so the loss is wrong
questions.explanation: Centering both the implicit reward and the reward is what removes the shared beta log Z(x) offset. Without it, the regression target includes an unknown constant and the loss no longer has pi* as its minimum.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: Why should GVPO's logprobs be per-sequence sums rather than per-token log-probs?
options: Per-token log-probs would require a learned critic to assign credit to each token
The derivation is over whole completions y, so it needs log pi(y|x) of the full sequence
Per-sequence sums are cheaper to store in bf16 and avoid overflow in the exponent
Per-token log-probs are not differentiable once they are gathered from the logits
questions.explanation: The closed-form optimum and implicit reward are defined for whole completions, so logprobs must be the summed token log-probs per completion, shape (P, G). Per-token values are differentiable but do not match the derivation.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: In GVPO, what is the anchor policy, and what is a common confusion?
options: The anchor is the teacher model in all cases, and it is often confused with pi_ref
The anchor is pi_old, the last sampling policy, and it is often confused with pi_ref
There is no anchor; GVPO is unconstrained, though it is often assumed to use a KL term
The anchor is pi_ref from the KL constraint, not pi_old, the last step's sampling policy
questions.explanation: GVPO anchors on the reference policy of the KL constraint. Confusing it with pi_old (used by GRPO's importance ratio) is a listed mistake. The teacher only appears in the on-policy distillation variant.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: A GVPO run's loss goes to about 0 in 50 steps, but held-out pass@1 does not change, and 95% of groups have all-zero rewards. What happened?
options: Unanimous groups have zero centered reward, so the loss is minimized by staying at the reference; little signal
The learning rate was too high, so the policy diverged and the loss collapsed to a degenerate near-zero value early
beta was too small, so the policy moved too far from the reference and overfit the few rewarded groups
The reference model was accidentally updated along with the policy, so the implicit reward stayed at zero
questions.explanation: With equal rewards, centered reward is 0, so the loss only asks the centered implicit reward to be 0 too: stay at the reference. With 95% such groups, barely moving minimizes the loss. Same root cause as GRPO's zero-advantage groups.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: How do you fix a GVPO or GRPO run where most groups have all-equal rewards?
options: Remove the centering so that zero-reward groups still contribute a nonzero gradient
Lower beta to zero so the reference is ignored and every sample is pushed toward reward
Fix task difficulty or use DAPO-style dynamic sampling that drops unanimous groups
Increase the clip epsilon so that more samples in each group fall inside the trust region
questions.explanation: The problem is a lack of mixed groups. Make tasks the right difficulty or drop unanimous groups and refill (dynamic sampling). Removing centering breaks Z cancellation; GVPO has no clip; beta = 0 removes the KL constraint.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: Which section of the GVPO paper should be read first?
options: The hyperparameter tables, to set up an exact replication first
Section 3: the derivation and the 'weights sum to zero, so Z cancels' argument
The related-work section only, to place GVPO among the GRPO variants
The convergence-rate appendices, which prove the unique optimum in detail
questions.explanation: Read GVPO section 3 for the derivation and the zero-sum-weights argument, then skim GVPO++ for the distillation extension. The convergence-rate appendices are recommended to skip on a first pass.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What exercise is suggested after reading about GVPO?
options: Swap gvpo_loss into the toy RLVR loop for the GRPO objective; plot correct-rate vs step for both on the same seeds
Use gvpo_loss to pretrain the course GPT from scratch, comparing its validation loss with standard cross-entropy
Replace the tokenizer's BPE merges with GVPO-trained merges and measure the effect on compression ratio
Train a reward model with gvpo_loss on preference pairs and compare its accuracy with a Bradley-Terry model
questions.explanation: The toy RLVR loop already has (P, G) log-probs of sampled answers, so gvpo_loss can replace the GRPO objective. Comparing correct-rate curves on the same seeds is a proper one-variable ablation.

questions.chapter_name: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GVPO
questions.question: What does GRPO have that GVPO drops, and why does dropping it matter?
options: The verifier reward; it is easy to hack, so GVPO swaps in the reference log-prob as reward
The group baseline; it adds bias, so GVPO weights each sample by its raw uncentered reward
The ratio pi_theta/pi_old and its clip; the ratio is unbounded and its variance compounds
The reference policy; it uses too much memory, so GVPO anchors on the old policy instead
questions.explanation: GVPO removes the ratio and clip, eliminating an instability source whose variance grows with sequence length. It keeps the group, the verifier reward and a reference policy.
